### Series Title Page

**The Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal, Complete, Uniform, Convenient, and Economical Library of all the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and Ecclesiastical Writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reprint of all the monuments of Catholic tradition that have survived through the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, carefully collated with one another and with several manuscript codices, and corrected with the greatest diligence; continually illustrated by dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged with all works discovered after the extensive editions issued during the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each volume or each author of importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating the subject matter below; expanded with works both doubtful and apocryphal, and also with works possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever each Father has written on any topic may be seen at a glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, from which it is readily apparent to the reader which Fathers have commented on the individual texts of the several books of Scripture, and in what places in their works.**

**The most accurate edition, and easily preferable to all others, if one considers the neatness of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the works reprinted, the very convenient format of the volumes, consistently similar throughout the whole work, the low price, and especially this collection—single, methodical, and chronological—which for the first time gathers in our library six hundred fragments and minor works previously scattered here and there, drawn from works relating to every age, place, language, and form.**

**First Series**, in which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and Writers of the Latin Church from Tertullian to Gregory the Great. Edited by J. P. Migne, publisher of the Universal Library of the Clergy, or of the complete courses in each branch of ecclesiastical learning.

# Dedicatorial Letter of the Benedictine Monks

## To the Most Holy Father Clement XI, Supreme Pontiff

Among all the many and outstanding qualities that have commended the beginning of your pontificate, most blessed Father, that which seems to us especially worthy of praise is this: having sent flatterers away, you have wished to listen only to men of ancient and proven virtue, men who would admonish you with complete freedom and speak the truth without disguise. For no other reason did you decide above all to make the most holy Abbot of Clairvaux a participant in your counsels; because of his complete freedom in speaking, advising, and even reproving, he was especially dear to you. For this reason you ordered us to publish again separately, in a freer style, his books *On Consideration* addressed to Pope Eugenius, so that they might serve you as a handbook, circulate easily, and never be removed from your sight.

How welcome this new edition dedicated to you was to Your Holiness, you graciously indicated in your pontifical letter to our superior general of 8 March 1701. That letter gave us courage to undertake greater things, especially when from it and from other letters written to the same superior on 6 June 1702 we understood that Your Beatitude praised and approved—as we most earnestly desired—the undertaking we had begun of revising the works of the holy Fathers of the Church. What could be more effective in lightening our labors, however arduous, in so difficult a field of the republic of letters as the one we have undertaken?

Accordingly, when we had begun to send the complete works of Saint Gregory the Great to the press—works revised, corrected, augmented, and illustrated with notes over a period of six years by comparison with manuscript codices—we immediately judged that this new fruit of our studies should be dedicated to your sacred name. Nor do we doubt, most holy Father, that our Gregory will be received by you as is fitting—indeed, by many rights he is yours. For if you wished Bernard to participate in all your counsels, Gregory is surely worthy to preside over them. Let him sit beside him who holds the helm of Peter’s ship, he who for so many years guided that same ship with such prudence amid the most serious storms and in times most difficult—times, that is, very similar to this wretched age in which we live. Let the prince of pastors always keep before his eyes that truly golden book, the *Pastoral Rule*, which we read was once given and commended to all bishops at their ordination. From the supreme throne of the Church, let the thrice-greatest Doctor in dignity, learning, and holiness once again pour forth purer oracles—he whose mouth the Lord opened in the midst of the Church and whom He filled with the spirit of wisdom and understanding. Finally, may Gregory recognize himself reborn in Clement.

These, most blessed Father, are nearly the reasons that moved us, prostrate at your feet, to dare to offer Your Holiness the recently published Gregory the Great, although many other serious reasons are available. Indeed, it was fitting that a pontiff so great under so many titles should once again see the light beneath pontifical auspices. The Gregorian works printed at the Vatican press were once dedicated to Sixtus V. Antonius Dadinus Alteserra dedicated to Clement IX the notes and observations he composed on the Gregorian letters. What remained, then, except that we should consecrate this latest edition of all the works of Saint Gregory—richer than all that preceded it and, insofar as possible, more complete than any other—to Clement XI? Therefore let these rivers of knowledge and wisdom return to the Holy See from which they flowed, so that they may flow again and spread throughout the entire Christian world.

From that same source, indeed, the idea of undertaking so great a work and the help needed to complete it shone upon us. When we had published the life of this holy Doctor, and the most eminent Cardinal Spada had informed us by letter, dated 8 April 1698, that it was most welcome to Innocent XII of happy memory, and had urged us to attempt greater things by imparting the apostolic blessing in the name of the Supreme Pontiff, we immediately, as though assured of divine assistance, applied ourselves to publishing Gregory the Great’s works also, with renewed care and in new type. May Your Holiness not disdain to receive what was begun under the auspices of your predecessor [Col. 0011], now completed and offered to you with the greatest humility of spirit. Although, out of fear before so great a majesty, we trembled to approach your throne and offer Gregory the Great, he himself, having slipped from our hands, would freely fly into your embrace—the embrace of one who is a most familiar and beloved guest in a seat known and friendly to him.

Yet there is one matter, most blessed Father, that we greatly fear may make Gregory the Great less pleasing to you. You love those who admonish, as we have said, and you hate those who praise. Nevertheless, do not doubt that you will be praised by a most equitable pontiff, who was accustomed to raise excellent bishops to the heavens with his praises. [Note: [Col. 0011] The letters to Eulogius of Alexandria, Anastasius of Antioch, Dominic of Carthage, Leander of Seville, etc., are to be read.]

Ah! With what exultation he congratulates you, as he sees, almost in astonishment, that—according to the laws he himself promulgated in the book of the *Pastoral Rule* (*Pastoral Rule*, at the beginning)—you have been called to the chair of Saint Peter and, in accordance with those same prescriptions, live, teach, and govern in these most depraved times, and daily recognize your own weakness no less! How joyfully he recognizes in you, happily expressed, the image of the outstanding Pastor delineated either in his own writings or deeds!

We know, most holy Father, how unwillingly you hear such things, since you have more than once ordered us to restrain ourselves from praising you. But allow us to commend to posterity and to eternity—something certainly most honorable to the Church and to our age—how great is your likeness and affinity with Gregory, the greatest of nearly all the pontiffs who have occupied the Roman chair after Peter.

For if we consider your births, each of you belonged to the patrician or senatorial class; your parents were distinguished more by religion than by nobility. If we inquire into your studies, our Gregory “was so trained from childhood in the liberal disciplines—grammar, rhetoric, and dialectic—that no one in this city, although literary studies flourished here, was thought his equal” (Paul the Deacon). Rome, meanwhile, saw you, most blessed Father, cultivated from your earliest age in the higher Latin and Greek letters, while you were not yet twelve years old, and drew an augury from you of future learning in every discipline and science, especially the sacred ones. Some homilies of the holy Fathers [Note: [Col. 0011] He is sometimes praised by the Bollandists.] and an ancient *Menologion* were evidence of this. When you had translated them from Greek into Latin, they were judged worthy of the light of publication, even in the opinion of stricter critics. Thereafter celebrated academies [Note: [Col. 0011] The academies of the Umoristi, the Queen of Sweden, etc.] and gatherings of learned men sought to have you as a member.

Gregory “in the years of adolescence began to devote himself to God and to yearn with all his desires for the homeland of the heavenly life” (Paul the Deacon). You too, even in the slippery period of youth, fortified against vices by the greatest innocence of conduct, immediately devoted yourself wholly to divine matters.

We read that Gregory held the praetorship at Rome. In that office he offered other judges outstanding examples of prudence, honesty, integrity, paternal affection toward the people, and other virtues. The ancient City, Reate, and the Sabines likewise deserved to have you as praetor and prefect; surrounded by no other escort, so to speak, than the virtues just praised, they learned to love you more than to fear you.

When Gregory was taken into the sacred ministry, he assisted Pelagius II in writing letters (Paul the Deacon, book III, *On the Deeds of the Lombards*, chapter 20). You, however, after the death of the most eminent Cardinal Slusius, were called by Innocent XI—with the approval of the Sacred College—and by two other Supreme Pontiffs who preceded you, to that office above all other prelates and even cardinals. You discharged it vigorously, although, after Alexander VIII had enrolled you in the college of cardinal fathers and placed you in charge of many ecclesiastical affairs, you scarcely found any leisure for writing.

By these steps, most blessed Father, you ascended to the summit of the Supreme Pontificate, called by the vote of all and resisted by you alone. We are forced to reopen a scar not yet covered and renew a pain—certainly so great that you fell into a fever. Yet we could not pass over in silence those matters in which you represent and display Gregory the Great more perfectly. For who does not know that the holy man, when he realized that he had been elected pontiff, sought safety by flight and, for as long as he lived, lamented his elevation to that supreme dignity with continual tears as though it were the greatest calamity?

Would that, most holy Father, earthquakes and other disasters—which we mourn as having worn down Rome and all Italy—did not contribute to making your pontificate resemble Gregory’s still more. [Col. 0013] When these scourges of divine justice were raging so fiercely, Gregory once approached as a reconciler and moved the people to repentance by a solemn address (*At the end of a homily on the Gospel*, volume I of Gregory of Tours). It was immediately received with extraordinary applause and flew throughout the Christian world. By instituting public supplications, he did what was pleasing to God and disarmed the avenging angel.

You, in a similar event, when Rome was endangered after being shaken by earthquakes, by an exhortation equally elegant and effective, soon disseminated throughout all the provinces of the Christian world, enjoined works of repentance upon those trembling and fleeing before the bow. Standing between God and the people with tears and prayers like another Phinehas, you appeased Him, and the shaking ceased. At that time you composed a collection and other prayers to be said during earthquakes; we rightly judged that these should enrich the *Book of Sacraments of Saint Gregory*, newly edited by us (volume III), so that in this too you might agree with Gregory, since each of you has contributed to the growth of that sacred book.

Since we have begun to speak of sacred matters, may we be permitted to mention those homilies, entirely worthy to be compared with Gregory’s, which you have already delivered to the people during the solemn celebration of Mass. In them there is no trace of affected eloquence: the discourse is living and effective, being woven wholly from the word of God and the sentences of Sacred Scripture. Because of your constant meditation on Scripture, you bring it with extraordinary ease to bear on any subject you undertake, drawing it forth as though it were eager to come. How great is the applause of the Roman people when they eagerly hear you pour forth oracles from the sacred pulpit and remember Leo the Great and Gregory the Great, who among the Roman pontiffs before you were almost the only ones to perform this pastoral office—because they were occupied with countless affairs! Your Holiness bears the weight of cares no fewer, indeed greater. Almost all Italy, and nearly the whole Christian world, burning with wars and hatreds, requires you anxiously to turn your attention in every direction in order to extinguish those fires. Yet you find time to compose elegant homilies, a matter Bernard rightly admired in our Gregory (*On Consideration*, book I, chapter 9). The infirm health of both men increases our admiration, for it usually urges them to take rest from labor.

While you are so diligent in breaking the heavenly bread and setting it before the peoples entrusted to you, most blessed Father, you are no less concerned to provide the food necessary for sustaining their bodies. Thus Clement may rightly be said to imitate Gregory’s exceedingly generous disposition toward the poor: generous and lavish toward the needy, yet most sparing toward himself, his most worthy brother, his brother’s sons—young men of excellent character and promise—and finally all his own people. So that you may provide for the needs of individuals, you order them to assemble on appointed days and open your ears and hands to those who petition you.

Gregory was accustomed above all to cherish those poor whom the love of Christ had stripped of worldly possessions—namely, monks and nuns—as is clear from so many of his letters. He supplied them abundantly with what was necessary, founded very many monasteries, and provided for their tranquillity by granting various privileges. In this matter you diligently follow his footsteps. For although before your pontificate you had been protector of two religious families, the Carthusians and the Minims, once you became pontiff you became the father of all.

As for us, we cannot conceal, most blessed Pope, how fatherly your affection is toward our congregation, and especially toward its members who labor in revising the works of the holy Fathers. This is also evidence of your reverence for those foremost Doctors of the Church and of your likeness to Gregory, who everywhere professes the highest reverence for the holy Fathers, especially Augustine (book X, letter 37). The writings of the most holy pontiff proclaim how eagerly he drank in the teaching of so great a master and preserved it in the depths of his mind. For he did not wish to abandon the well-trodden path of his predecessors.

But which Roman pontiff has been a more vigorous defender of Augustinian teaching than Clement, when not long ago he condemned a pamphlet injurious to the most holy Father, the strongest defender of Christ’s grace? [Note: [Col. 0013] “Wishing firmly to adhere to the praiseworthy footsteps of our predecessors, the Roman pontiffs, who have always held in the highest esteem the lofty teaching of that same holy Doctor Augustine and embraced it with the whole affection of their minds,” etc. (*Condemnation and prohibition of the pamphlet printed under the title: The True Tradition of the Church on Predestination*, etc.).]

To conclude the comparison in a few words: Gregory always found the kings of the Franks most dutiful and beneficent, especially when he needed their help either to preach or to strengthen the faith among the English. Hence, in the letters written to those kings [Note: [Col. 0013] To Theuderic, Theudebert, Chlothar, and Brunhilda.], expressions of thanks occur so often [Col. 0015] that it is not worthwhile to reproduce them here. Yet we cannot conceal the praise bestowed by that most equitable pontiff upon King Childebert for his zeal on behalf of the Catholic faith:

> “As royal dignity surpasses other human dignities, so the kingdoms of other nations are surely surpassed by the eminence of your kingdom. That you are a king, since there are other kings, is not remarkable; but that you are Catholic, which others do not deserve to be, is sufficient.”

Most blessed Father, even if we were silent, who would not understand that this praise is rightly owed to the Most Christian King Louis the Great? Let us pass over his military glory and the almost countless exploits he has splendidly accomplished by land and sea, by which he surpasses other kings, since we are addressing Clement, the common Father of Christians, whose duty is to quiet wars and reconcile peace among his divided children.

Yet we cannot remain silent about Louis the Great’s zeal for the Catholic faith: the holy king, the most pious queen, the royal child, and their subjects—still sound in the faith—were expelled by rebellious Englishmen because of their orthodox faith. As remnants, so to speak, of the religion once established in England through the work of Gregory the Great, they were received as guests and supported with resources in accordance with royal generosity and dignity. Heresy was driven from the kingdom, though only with the greatest danger. For this reason a large part of Europe took up arms against the Most Christian King and his kingdom, while the heralds and standard-bearers of heresy sounded the trumpet and carried the torch of war. Nevertheless, the greatest of kings could never be induced to consent to any condition of peace that appeared even temporarily to favor heresy. What could be more worthy of the firstborn son of the Church?

What, then, would Gregory the Great have said about these things? Into what praises would he have broken forth had he survived? Yet he still lives in Clement; and there is no doubt that, for so many benefits conferred upon the Church, that most equitable pontiff will prove himself grateful toward the Most Christian King.

These, most holy Father, are the principal features by which the likeness of Gregory the Great is expressed more perfectly in you than in any image engraved in bronze or painted in colors. Therefore, according to custom, we judged that it should be affixed as it were at the threshold of his works, so that it might be a memorial more enduring than any bronze—both of our devoted affection toward the most holy Doctor, of our singular reverence for the Apostolic See, and of the humble obedience that we promise.

[Col. 0015]

# General Preface Placed by the Benedictines at the Beginning of Their Edition of the Works of Saint Gregory

## I. New Editions of the Holy Fathers Already Prepared by Us

It is neither fitting nor necessary for us to recall how great a benefit, both to the republic of letters and to the Christian world, has already resulted from the works of the more distinguished holy Fathers being corrected through our labor and study and brought forth into the light with renewed presentation; for the public expression of gratitude bears witness to this. But after Athanasius, Hilary, Jerome, Ambrose, and Augustine, to what other degree should we proceed except to Gregory, thrice greatest in dignity, doctrine, and holiness?

Nor was it fitting that we should leave for longer the writings of so great a Doctor—whom we venerate as the supreme glory of our family—covered, so to speak, with the thorns of errors, lest, while laboring to cultivate the possessions of others, we should appear to have abandoned our own field uncultivated.

## II. Various Editions of the Works of Saint Gregory the Great

All the works of Saint Gregory have indeed already been published several times, not to mention his individual writings, which were published separately in the meantime. The first edition is the Paris edition prepared by Berthold Rembolt in 1518. It contains the books of the *Moralia*, the *Pastoral Rule*, the *Dialogues*, the Commentary on the *Song of Songs*, the Commentary on the seven Penitential Psalms, the Homilies on Ezekiel and on the Gospels, and the Register of Letters.

This was soon followed by the edition produced at Rouen by François Regnaut in 1521. Two years later another Paris edition appeared from the workshop of Claude Chevallon. In the same city all the works of Saint Gregory were printed again by Charles Guillart in 1542. This edition was preceded by the Lyons edition of 1539 and 1540, in two volumes, enlarged by a Commentary on the First Book of Kings.

It would be lengthy and tedious to mention all the editions subsequently prepared at Paris, Lyons, Basel, [Col. 0017] Antwerp, and Douai. We shall therefore touch only on the more important ones. Among these is the Basel edition of 1551 and 1564, printed by the Froben press under the care of Coccius, who labored greatly to restore the works of Saint Gregory to their former purity and integrity. To achieve this, however, he relied more on his own conjectures—as was generally held in that age—than on ancient and excellent manuscripts. In this edition the division of the chapters of the *Moralia* differs from that in the earlier editions.

John Gilotius Campanus, a highly learned man, also labored considerably in publishing all the works of Saint Gregory the Great and purifying their text. His edition was published at Paris in 1571 and again a few years later.

The edition begun at Rome in the Vatican press in 1589 by the authority of Sixtus V, and later completed under the direction of the most learned Bishop of Venosa, was considered more accurate than all the preceding editions, although not by the heterodox writers whose accusations and complaints we shall soon answer.

## III. The Gussanville Edition, Though More Correct, Requires Many Corrections

Finally, in 1675, all the works of Saint Gregory the Great were published at Paris through the labor and study of Peter Gussanville, a priest, corrected from a great many codices, as that distinguished man himself says. Yet how many and how serious errors still abound in this latest edition may be understood from the few examples we shall bring forward, and from them one may also see how necessary a more carefully corrected edition is.

Of all that Gussanville’s edition contains, we have selected the *Life of Gregory the Great* written by John the Deacon and corrected with the help of ancient handwritten codices, to present here as a specimen of the entire work. We chose it both because it occurs at once in this edition and because in it we have restored many passages excerpted from the *Moralia on Job* and from the letters. The manuscript codices from which we revised this Life will be identified in the preface placed before it.

In book I, chapter 28, column 19, the latest edition reads:

> “In that glory of the heavenly kingdom, therefore, the flesh will exist according to nature, but according to corruption, or even according to the desires of suffering, it will not exist; it will reign in eternal incorruption.”

In this passage, transcribed from the *Moralia*, the text must either be supplemented from the manuscripts or corrected as follows:

> “In that heavenly glory, therefore, the flesh will exist according to nature, but it will not exist according to the desires of suffering, because, having conquered the sting of death, it will reign in eternal incorruption.”

Chapter 29, the same column:

> “Then Tiberius, emperor of Constantinople, of pious memory, etc.”

Read instead, from the manuscripts of John the Deacon and the *Moralia*:

> “Then Tiberius Constantine, emperor, of pious memory.”

For Tiberius gloried in the surname Constantine. Who, moreover, does not know that the title “emperor of Constantinople,” unheard of in those times, arose many centuries later, after the empire had been divided and had declined?

Chapter 32, column 20:

> “Unless God inspires the heart of the most pious prince to grant to his servants the mercy implanted in him, and deigns to grant the Church, in addition to that *diacoposis* or one master of soldiers and one duke, we shall be left in every distress, since the greater Roman territories appear to have been deprived of every defense.”

Who, on reading these words—“to grant the Church one master of soldiers,” and so forth—would not immediately understand that they are the prayers of groaning peoples in desperate circumstances, humbly begging the assistance of the Church and of the Supreme Pontiff? Yet they are the groans of the Supreme Pontiff himself, imploring the emperor’s help. The passage should instead be read:

> “Unless God inspires the heart of the most pious prince to grant to his servants the mercy implanted in him, and in addition to that *diacopiosin*—or, in the Uticensis manuscript, ‘in addition to all those things’—deigns to grant one master of soldiers and one duke, we shall be left in every distress, since the Roman territories especially (*maxime partes Romanae*, as opposed to the erroneous *maximae partes Romanae*) appear to have been deprived of every defense.”

In two manuscripts, the Bigotian and the Uticensis, the same hand adds, after the word *diacopiosin*, by way of interpretation: “that is, the public treasury.”

In the same chapter:

> “For he is recognized as altogether necessary both in your ministry and in the work over which we appointed him.”

But the manuscripts read:

> “For he is recognized as altogether necessary both in your monastery—namely, the Roman monastery of Saint Andrew—and in the work to which we appointed him,”

or, as it appears in the Uticensis manuscript:

> “We recognize him as altogether necessary.”

Moreover, *monastery*, not *ministry*, must be read here. This is proved by the immediately following words of John the Deacon:

> “For this monastery, which Pope Pelagius mentions here, etc.”

Chapter 48, column 24:

> “And sent into the exile of occupation because of my sins, from the face of the ruler, I say with the prophet, as though with the words of a forsaken [alternatively, ruined] widow: ‘He who consoled me has gone far from me.’”

Who would not stumble over this obscure passage? In the manuscripts, whether of John the Deacon or of the Letters, the passage is clear:

> “And sent into the exile of occupation because of my sins, from the face of the ruler, as though with the words of a destroyed Judah, I say with the prophet: ‘He who consoled me has gone far from me.’”

The holy Doctor is plainly alluding to Jeremiah’s Lamentations, in which the calamity of Judah and the overthrow of Jerusalem are mourned.

Chapter 52, the same column:

> “Amid all these things I am troubled and forced, now to direct adversity against the very helm (*in ipsum [Al. ipsam] clavum*), now, with the ship bent, to hide from the assault of the waves and evade the threats of the waves obliquely [Al. *ex obliquo latere declinare*, ‘to evade them from an oblique side’].”

This corrupt passage must be healed from the same manuscripts and restored as follows:

> “Amid all these things I am troubled and forced, now to direct adversity against the very helm, now, with the side of the ship bent, to avoid obliquely the threats of the waves.”

Here it is worth observing two things concerning the variant readings noted by Gussanville, the editor of the latest Gregorian edition. First, he does not say where he obtained those different readings. He gives a few throughout the entire edition, but nowhere, or only very rarely, does he indicate from which codices they were extracted. Second, he banishes the best reading from the text while retaining the faulty one, as in the phrase “to direct adversity against the very helm,” in which the sense is entirely lacking. The same negligence in selecting variant readings persists throughout the whole work.

Some of these errors may perhaps be attributed to the carelessness of the typesetters. Indeed, almost innumerable corruptions of this kind occur here, introduced through the fault of the printer and the press. Thus, in column 15, within only a few lines, we find *aliter senior* for *alter senior*, *accessis* for *accessit*, and “he began rashly to utter great cries” for “he began to tremble and utter great cries.” Yet while those responsible for the press were drowsing, the editor’s diligence ought to have remained awake, so that so many errors might be corrected—or at least that the reader might be warned of them, something that was also neglected.

For the moment I pass over the twenty-two verses beginning, “Receive the Romans, etc.,” which are absent from Gussanville’s edition, although they are found in all the manuscripts we consulted and in most of the printed books. Nor is there any doubt whether they are the work of John the Deacon or belong to the life of Gregory the Great, to which they serve as a kind of dedicatory letter to Pope John VIII, written in concise style.

These are the principal matters requiring correction in the first book of Gregory’s Life. At the very threshold of the second book one immediately strikes against a stone from which there is no small danger of falling. For the following passage, reported as written by Gregory in chapter 4, column 27, has a savor of heresy:

> “I likewise venerate the Fifth Council, in which . . . . . . and Theodore, separating the person of the Mediator into two substances, is shown to have fallen into the impiety of perfidy.”

Theodore of Mopsuestia was brought under suspicion of Nestorianism, not because he acknowledged two substances in Christ—for who, unless favoring Eutyches, would dare deny that Christ consists of two substances?—but because he was thought to divide Christ into two subsistences. In the manuscripts of the Life and of the Letters we likewise read:

> “Theodore, separating the person of the Mediator into two subsistences.”

There are also lighter errors, though they should not be left uncorrected: in column 28, *a Vitelliano sit praesule destinatus* (“he was sent by Bishop Vitellianus”) instead of *a Vitaliano* (“by Vitalianus”); in column 29, *ob hoc se nonnulli* (“for this reason some themselves”); in the same place, *Qui in divino amore districtionem subire appetit servitutem* (“he who desires to undergo strict servitude in divine love”) instead of *qui in divino obsequio districtiorem subire appetit servitutem* (“he who desires to undergo stricter servitude in divine service”); in the same place, *in hac sede* (“in this see”) instead of *in hac re* (“in this matter”); in column 34, *sancto crucis signo* (“with the holy sign of the cross”) instead of *facto crucis signaculo* (“when the sign of the cross had been made”); in column 37, *divino intus auxilio* (“by divine assistance within”) instead of *divino jutus*, or *adjutus*, *auxilio* (“helped by divine assistance”); in column 38, *in eis clericis vel hi qui in sacro sunt ordine constituti* (“among those clergy, or those who are constituted in the sacred order”) instead of *in eis clerici, vel hi qui in sacro sunt ordine constituti* (“among them are clergy, or those who are constituted in the sacred order”).

In the same place:

> “But I wish you to offer forty solidi to my lady, Saint Paterichia” [variant: “Patriarchia”]

instead of:

> “I wish you to offer forty solidi to my lady Pateria, my aunt (*thia*),”

as it is read in all the manuscripts, both of the Life of Saint Gregory and of his letters. The word *thia* is Greek and means “aunt.”

We omit the remaining matters that presented themselves for correction from the manuscripts, whether in book II itself or in the two following books. We approached the task of revealing the errors of others reluctantly; yet it was part of our undertaking to demonstrate, at least briefly, the necessity of a new edition. This was also why, in the individual prefaces placed before each of Gregory’s works, we took care to present examples of some of the errors we had corrected.

## IV. Gussanville and the Roman Editors Excused

Let no one think, however, that we wish to detract in any way from the praise owed to Father Gussanville for publishing the works of Saint Gregory. It was difficult—not to say impossible—for that learned priest, with scarcely any assistance and in modest circumstances, to complete a work of such magnitude. Nor do we intend to obscure the glory of the other editors who preceded Gussanville, especially the Roman editors. Indeed, we have judged it worthwhile here to defend them against the abuse and accusations of Thomas James, a heterodox writer (*Vindications of Gregory*, p. 2).

James begins his Gregorian vindication with the words of the letter to Saint Leander, which is read before the books of the *Moralia*:

> “I thought it better to despise secular dress,”

which he corrects from English manuscripts to:

> “I thought it better to be clothed in secular dress.”

We do not criticize James for making this correction; we admit that it should be read so according to the handwritten codices. But who would not be indignant at his shamelessness when, over so small a matter, he cries out:

> “Behold the Roman correctors—or rather, profane corrupters—of books! They deal with us not by Roman faith, that is, the best and most ancient faith, but by Punic faith, changing everything treacherously and wickedly.”

As though the Roman editors were the authors of this reading, which is in fact found in the older editions—Basel, 1514, and Paris, 1518. In book XXVIII of the *Moralia*, chapter 1, we read, through a typographical error:

> “I saw my servant Job” (Job 1:8)

instead of:

> “You saw.”

To this James insolently declares:

> “The text is corrupted, as is the Roman custom.”

Everyone can see that this error slipped in inadvertently, and there is no reason to suppose what motive the Roman editors would have had for reading *I saw* rather than *you saw*.

Nevertheless, we do not deny that many things in the Roman edition are read otherwise than they ought to be, since in those times it was the very common practice, among both orthodox and heretical writers, to neglect manuscript codices and indulge excessively in conjectures.

## V. The plan of the new edition with the help of manuscript codices

Since it is clear that much is still lacking, whether for the completeness or the perfection of the edition prepared by Gussanvillaeus—although it is judged by all to be the finest—we finally undertook to correct Gregory the Great’s works from manuscript codices, to illustrate them with notes wherever this seemed necessary, and to publish them in new types. Having enlisted many collaborators, especially from our own congregation, we compared all the writings of that outstanding Doctor with nearly innumerable manuscripts of the highest reliability.

At this point we shall refrain from discussing the authority and reliability of manuscript books, which our own Joannes Mabillonius recently defended admirably in chapter 13 of his *Supplement to the Book on Diplomatics*. Their usefulness is also warmly praised by the most learned J. Sirmond of the Society of Jesus in his *Antirrhetic against P. Aurelius* (vol. IV of the new edition of P. de la Beaune, no. 9, p. 266). Certainly, without the aid of those ancient codices, there is no hope of correcting the works of the holy Fathers. Erasmus makes clear with the greatest authority how much diligence and labor their correction requires, in his letter to Waramus, archbishop of Canterbury:

> “This one thing, to speak truly and boldly, I judge: it cost Jerome less to compose his books than it costs us to restore them, and they were produced by him with fewer vigils than they are reborn among us.”

He later compares this labor with that of Hercules in these words:

> “For I do not think that as much labor was expended in subduing a few monsters as has been required of me in removing thousands upon thousands of errors.”

## VI. Whom we had as assistants

There is no need here to list the manuscripts we used, since in the preliminary notices to each work of the most holy Doctor we have taken care to state individually the ancient codices with which it was compared. It is not our custom to publish the names of those from our congregation who assisted us in collating printed books with manuscripts. It is enough to affirm that learned and diligent men were chosen for this work, some of whom are already sufficiently well known in the republic of letters through books they have published.

We shall name only one, now deceased, who died while serving at Rome as procurator for our congregation: Dom Claudius Estiennot. He gave us especially energetic assistance in examining the manuscripts of the Vatican Library, above all the *Register of Letters*.

Among our friends who supported us in this laborious undertaking, particular mention must be made of the most religious Dom Joannes Baptista de Noyville, superior of the monastery of Vallis Clara in the district of Laon, of the Cistercian Order of stricter and more rigorous observance. He not only sent us various readings that he had himself excerpted from many codices, but also shared with us almost entire manuscripts transcribed in his own hand. In addition, he compiled very extensive indexes both of passages from Sacred Scripture and of notable matters and sayings, for volume I and for the *Book of Sacraments*. Ill health, however, prevented him from completing others that he had begun.

## VII. The benefactors whose assistance we experienced

Our libraries, together with many others, supplied us with a great store of ancient codices, especially the Parisian libraries—the Royal, Colbertine, Victorine, and Tellerian.

We obtained access to the manuscripts of the Royal Library through the favor of the most illustrious Abbé de Louvois, its keeper. Following the example of his illustrious uncle, the archbishop and duke of Rheims, he shows himself favorably disposed and generous toward all men of letters.

The Colbertine Library was always open to us by order and through the kindness of the most illustrious archbishop of Rouen, to whom we willingly acknowledge that we owe many other favors as well.

In the Royal Library, the distinguished Clementius and Boivinius pointed out and most obligingly supplied codices to us; in the Colbertine Library, Baluzius, and Quercetanus, who succeeded him as keeper of that library, did the same.

## VII. What we have accomplished in this edition

Enriched by so great a supply of ancient books, and aided also by still older editions, we had nothing more at heart, in accordance with Augustine’s judgment, than to present the sense and the very words of Gregory the Great, cleansed of every interpolation or scribal error, as well as of typographical corruptions.[^c0002-3]

[^c0002-3]: [Col. 0023] Augustine, *On Christian Doctrine*, book I, chapter 14: “Those who desire to know the divine Scriptures ought first to apply their diligence to correcting codices.”

Where, however, the nearly unanimous agreement of the manuscripts compelled us to depart from readings previously accepted—as often happened—we placed the rejected readings in brief notes and identified the manuscript codices by which they were rejected. Sometimes, without changing the text, we recorded variant readings beneath the columns.

Thus, with great labor and even greater fidelity, we offer Gregory the Great to you, devout and Christian reader. If Thomas James thought that his *Vindications of Gregory* deserved this distinguished title, although they contain scarcely a hundredth part of the restorations we have made, with how much greater right does that title belong to this newest edition.[^c0002-4]

[^c0002-4]: [Col. 0023] James’s work is entitled: *Vindiciae Gregorianae, seu restitutus innumeris pene locis Gregorius Magnus*, Geneva: Petrus and Jacobus Chouet, 1625.

Besides the notes in which variant readings are presented or an account is given of the restorations made, we have added others to illuminate particular passages. These, however, are brief, lest we seem to burden the text more than adorn it. For the *Dialogues*, the *Letters*, and the *Book of Sacraments*, we have either composed fuller notes or gathered those already composed by others. We have not failed to explain this procedure in the prefaces preceding each of the most holy Doctor’s works. We must now state the order in which we have arranged them.

## VIII. The division of the entire work into four volumes

We have divided the works of Saint Gregory the Great into four volumes.[^c0002-1]

The first volume contains his exegetical works on Sacred Scripture, namely the thirty-five books of the *Moralia on Job*, the two books of *Homilies on the Prophet Ezekiel*, and an equal number of *Homilies on the Gospels*. The commentary on the First Book of Kings, the *Expositions on the Song of Songs*, and the *Exposition of the Seven Penitential Psalms* could also have been counted among these exegetical works. But the first volume could not contain so much; moreover, the works just mentioned are not so genuinely the works of Saint Gregory that they are free from every interpolation, as we shall explain in their proper place (vol. III, second part, in the preface).

The second volume contains the remaining works of Saint Gregory that are certain and genuine, whether they concern history or ecclesiastical discipline: the *Book of the Pastoral Rule*, the four books of the *Dialogues*, and the *Register of Letters*, to which we have appended a brief supplement and multiple indexes. Concerning the many letters added to this *Register*, and its order as restored, one should read the arguments we have supplied in support of that restoration.

The third volume is divided into two parts. The first presents the *Book of Sacraments*, the *Antiphonary*, and the other liturgical works, together with the learned notes and observations of Dom Hugo Menard, whose addition we judged would enrich this new edition of Gregory’s works. The second part of the same volume contains the commentary on the First Book of Kings, the *Exposition of the Song of Songs*, substantially enlarged, another *Exposition of the Seven Psalms*, and a concordance of certain testimonies of Sacred Scripture.

The fourth volume is likewise divided into two parts. The first contains the life of Saint Gregory written both by Paul Warnefrid and by John the Deacon, as well as the life that we have recently prepared, drawn especially from Gregory’s own writings. The second part contains the genuine Paterius, as it is found in a great many manuscripts of the finest quality, and the *Exposition of the New Testament from Gregorian Sayings* by Alulf of Tournai, a monk, which in earlier editions was unjustly given the name of Paterius.

[^c0002-1]: See what we have stated below, column 37. — Editor.

## IX. Various collections of excerpts from the writings of Saint Gregory

We judged that there was no need to print other collections of this kind, especially since the sayings of Saint Gregory, so often repeated and stitched together by various compilers, would become tedious. The very extensive indexes of passages from Sacred Scripture that we have added can in fact serve in place of all such collections.[^c0002-2]

Of the others who labored to collect testimonies from Saint Gregory after Paterius, the most celebrated is Taio, bishop of Zaragoza, who is said to have come to Rome to seek the books of the *Moralia* under Pope Martin I. He excerpted from the books of blessed Gregory five books of *Sentences*, preserving the words of the holy Doctor himself, with a few additions from Saint Augustine where those words were lacking. Manuscript codices of this work are preserved among the manuscripts of the Thuane Library. Our Mabillonius published its preface to Quiricus of Barcelona, together with the latter bishop’s reply, in volume II of the *Analecta*. The distinguished Stephanus Baluzius inserted Taio’s letter to Eugenius, bishop of Toledo, from a codex of the Colbertine Library, in volume IV of his *Miscellanies*.

[^c0002-2]: [Col. 0025] As usual, we omit them, since we are preparing a general index of Scripture for the whole of the *Patrology*. — Editor.

## X. Whether the holy Doctor explained all four Gospels and wrote on Samson

Joannes Trithemius, in his *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*, lists among Gregory’s works a brief *Explanation of the Four Gospels*, beginning with these words: “Matthew, as first in order.” Honorius of Autun appears to refer to it when he says that Saint Gregory explained the entire text of the four Gospels by preaching to the people (*Book on Ecclesiastical Writers*).

We found two manuscript codices of this purported explanation, approximately nine hundred years old: one beautifully written in the Royal Library, the other in the Bigot Library at Rouen, with this title:

> “Here begins the Exposition according to Matthew … by Saint Gregory … of the city of Rome … Matthew, as first in order, etc.”

But its style, which is extremely corrupt, does not have the character of Gregory, and the sequence of its discourse sufficiently proves that this work should not be numbered among Saint Gregory’s writings.

The most holy Doctor appears to promise an allegorical explanation of some events in Samson’s life when he writes to Venantius, patrician of Palermo:

> “You wish, therefore, that certain matters concerning the deeds of Samson be discussed allegorically. But such weakness has afflicted my body that, even if I should be able to undertake any such task, my mind does not rise to carry it out. Nevertheless, I rejoice with you in your good desire, because in wishing for an exposition of the sacred words, you show that you seek the author of those words themselves with strictness. If, therefore, I recover my health and strength, I shall obey your desires, with the omnipotent Lord as my guide” (*Book XII, Letter 40*).

Yet it is almost certain that Gregory never had the leisure to devote himself to this work, because of the continuous illnesses during the last four years of his life.

### What should be thought about the penitential work bearing his name

Concerning the *Penitential* bearing the name of Saint Gregory, pope of the city of Rome, which James says exists in a most ancient book of the public library at Oxford (*Gregorian Vindications*, p. 144), we have found nothing elsewhere. Therefore, it is enough for us to mention it here.

We must now linger somewhat longer over the doctrine of Saint Gregory and demonstrate that nearly all heretics, both ancient and modern, were refuted by him.

## XI. Saint Gregory’s doctrine against the Manichaeans, Arians, Nestorians and Eutychians, and Pelagians

Saint Gregory destroys the perverse doctrine of the Manichaeans, who, falsely asserting that there are two principles, attempt to maintain that the spirit was created by God but the flesh by Satan, in book IX of the *Moralia*, no. 74:

> “The holy man, filled with the grace of the prophetic spirit, considers what is to come long afterward and, foreseeing the offspring of errors, tramples them down, saying: ‘Your hands fashioned me and made me altogether round about’ (Job 10:8). For he who asserts that he was both fashioned and made altogether round about by God leaves nothing either in his spirit or in his flesh to the race of darkness. He referred to being fashioned in relation to the inward image; but he mentioned being made altogether round about in relation to that which consists of the garment of flesh.”

He refutes the impiety of Arius, who taught that the Son was created, in book XXXII of the *Moralia*, no. 51, on the basis of Job’s assertion that Behemoth was the first angel created by God and the beginning of his ways (Job 40:14):

> “It remains, therefore,” says the holy Doctor, “either for Arius to declare that the Son was not created, or foolishly to suppose that he was created after Behemoth.”

The mystery of the Incarnation is explained most fully in *Homily 38 on the Gospels*, no. 3; Nestorius and Eutyches are refuted in book I on Ezekiel, homily 8, nos. 24 and 25.

In the following homily, no. 2, the necessity of divine grace is asserted against Pelagius and Coelestius, so that we may both will and accomplish what is good. We are taught that evil is to be attributed to us, but good to God and to us. Finally, it is explained how grace precedes and the will follows:

> “In these matters, however, we must consider that our good works are God’s gifts in such a way that nothing in them belongs to us. Why, then, do we seek eternal recompense as though it were due to our merits? But if they are ours in such a way that they are not gifts of Almighty God, why do we give thanks for them to Almighty God? It must be understood that our evils are ours alone; but our good works belong both to Almighty God and to us. For he anticipates us by inspiring us to will, and he follows us by helping us, so that we do not will in vain but are able to accomplish what we will.

> “When grace therefore precedes and a good will follows, that which is the gift of Almighty God becomes our merit. Paul explains this well in a brief statement, saying: ‘I labored more than all of them.’ Lest he appear to attribute what he had done to his own strength, he added: ‘Yet not I, but the grace of God with me.’ Because he had been anticipated by a heavenly gift, he recognized himself as alien to his good work, saying: ‘Yet not I.’ But because prevenient grace had made his free will good, and in his work he followed that same grace by his free will, he added: ‘But the grace of God with me.’ It is as though he said: ‘I labored in the good work—not I, but also I.’ Insofar as I was anticipated by the Lord’s gift alone: not I; but insofar as I followed the gift by my will: also I.”

Having said this briefly against Pelagius and Coelestius, let us return to the order of exposition.

Concerning original sin spreading through the whole of human nature, from which Christ nevertheless was free, see book XVIII of the *Moralia*, no. 84, and book I on Ezekiel, homily 8, no. 21. Concerning the punishment due to this sin even in infants, consult the preface to book IV of the *Moralia*, chapter 3, and book IX, no. 32.

The gratuitous character of predestination is taught in book XXV of the same *Moralia*, no. 32.

## XII. What Saint Gregory thought about the blessedness of the saints after death

The blessedness of the saints immediately after death is asserted in the preface to the books of the *Moralia*, no. 20, from Revelation 6:11: “And individual white robes were given to them,” etc., which the holy Doctor explains as follows:

> “Before the resurrection they are said to have received individual robes because they still enjoy only the blessedness of the mind. They will therefore receive two robes when, together with the perfect joy of their souls, they are clothed also in the incorruption of their bodies.”

See also book IX, no. 17; book XXXV, no. 25; and book IV of the *Dialogues*, chapter 25.

Concerning the veneration and invocation of the saints, we read in book XVI of the *Moralia*, no. 64:

> “Those, therefore, who place no confidence in any work of their own run to the protection of the holy martyrs. They devote themselves with tears to their sacred bodies and pray that, through the martyrs’ intercession, they may obtain pardon.”

See also *Homily 32 on the Gospels*, no. 6 and following, as well as book II of the *Dialogues*, at the end.

### On purgatorial fire

Concerning purgatorial fire, to which even the just who have not yet been cleansed from every stain of sin must be assigned, see book IV of the *Dialogues*, chapter 25. This passage also clearly confirms what we stated above concerning the happiness of the saints immediately after death.

Here Peter asks:

> “Are the souls of the just received into heaven before the restoration of the body?”

The most holy Master replies:

> “We can neither affirm this of all the just nor deny it of all. For there are souls of certain just persons that are delayed from the heavenly kingdom by certain still-existing abodes. What else is indicated by the harm of this delay except that they possessed something less than perfect justice? Yet it is clearer than daylight that the souls of the perfect are received into the dwellings of the heavenly kingdom as soon as they have departed from the prison of this flesh.”

In chapter 39, when the disciple asks whether there is purgatorial fire after death, the holy Doctor replies that before the judgment there is a purgatorial fire for cleansing certain lesser faults; he proves this explicitly below.

Finally, in chapter 55, he says:

> “If sins are not incapable of being loosed after death, the sacred offering of the saving victim often helps the souls of many even after death, so that the souls of the departed themselves sometimes appear to seek it.”

### On the duration of the punishments due to the reprobate

We are taught that the punishments of the reprobate will be eternal in book XXXIV of the *Moralia*, no. 34, but especially in book IV of the *Dialogues*, chapter 44.

### How God can be seen by the saints in this life

In book XVIII of the *Moralia*, no. 88, Gregory considers whether the saints can see God while they live as mortals. He decides that they can see him only through certain images, and not in his own nature.

At no. 89, however, he excepts certain persons from this rule in these words:

> “But if by some people still living in this corruptible flesh, yet growing through an incomparable power, the eternal brightness of God can be seen by a certain intensity of contemplation, this too does not conflict with the judgment of blessed Job, who says: ‘It is hidden from the eyes of all living’ (Job 28:21). For whoever sees Wisdom, which is God, dies completely to this life, so that he is no longer held by its love. No one who still lives carnally has seen it, because no one can simultaneously embrace God and the world. Whoever sees God dies by that very act by which he is entirely separated from the pleasures of this life, either in the intention of his heart or in the effect of his works.

> “Hence it is also said to the same Moses: ‘For man shall not see me and live’ (Exodus 33:21). It is as though it were said openly: No one ever sees God spiritually while living carnally in the world. Thus the apostle Paul, who, as he himself testifies, still knew God’s invisible things only in part (1 Corinthians 13:12), nevertheless declared that he was already wholly dead to this world, saying: ‘The world is crucified to me, and I to the world’ (Galatians 6:14).”

We have noted these things so that it may be clear that the doctrine asserted here does not conflict with the opinion widely accepted in the schools: that Moses, Saint Paul, and Saint Benedict enjoyed the vision of the divine essence. As far as Saint Benedict is concerned, this is drawn from book II of the *Dialogues*, chapter 35.

## XIII. The doctrine of the Eucharist asserted from Saint Gregory against the modern heretics, especially concerning the sacrifice of the new law and the real presence of Christ in the Eucharist

All the articles of faith over which we dispute with the Lutherans, Calvinists, and other modern heretics can be read individually proved and asserted from Saint Gregory in the *Gregorian Confession*, by its author Theodorus Petreius of Kampen, a member of the Carthusian house at Cologne.[^c0002-5]

What could be clearer than this testimony from book IV, chapter 58, of the *Dialogues*, proving both the unbloody sacrifice of the new law and the real presence of the body and blood of Jesus Christ in the Eucharist?

> “We ought, therefore, to despise the present age with our whole mind, since we already see it passing away, and to offer to God daily sacrifices of tears, daily victims of his flesh and blood. For this is uniquely the sacrifice that saves the soul from eternal destruction: through its mystery it renews for us the death of the Only-Begotten. Although, rising from the dead, he dies no more and death shall no longer have dominion over him, nevertheless, living immortally and incorruptibly in himself, he is again sacrificed for us in this mystery of the sacred offering.

> “For there his body is received; his flesh is distributed for the salvation of the people; his blood is poured out—not now into the hands of unbelievers, but into the mouths of the faithful. Let us therefore consider what kind of sacrifice this is for us, since for our absolution it continually imitates the passion of the Only-Begotten Son.

> “For what believer could doubt that, at the very hour of the offering, at the priest’s voice the heavens are opened, the choirs of angels are present in the mystery of Jesus Christ, the highest and lowest things are joined, earthly things are united with heavenly things, and one reality is made from visible and invisible things?”

### On the necessity of priestly confession and absolution, and on the authority of the Church

The necessity of priestly confession and absolution can be proved from many passages, especially book XXII of the *Moralia*, no. 31, and *Homily 26 on the Gospels*, nos. 4–6. There, under the figure of Lazarus, called back from the dead by Christ and released by his apostles, the resurrection and release of the sinner emerging from the tomb through confession of sins are explained.

Lazarus is therefore told: “Come out.” It is as though it were said openly to anyone dead in guilt:

> “Why do you hide your guilt within your conscience? Come out now through confession, you who hide inwardly within yourself through denial.”

Let the dead man therefore come out—that is, let the sinner confess his guilt. Let the disciples release the one who comes out, so that the pastors of the Church may remove the punishment deserved by the person who was not ashamed to confess what he had done. I have said this briefly concerning the order of release, so that the pastors of the Church may strive, with great restraint, either to release or to bind.

The holy Doctor also suppressed all errors against the Catholic faith, whether already arisen or destined to arise, by asserting the supreme authority of the Church in ecumenical councils in his synodal letter to the patriarchs (book I, letter 25):

> “Because one believes with the heart unto justice, but confession is made with the mouth unto salvation, I confess that I receive and venerate four councils just as I do the four books of the holy Gospel: namely, the Council of Nicaea, in which the perverse doctrine of Arius was destroyed; the Council of Constantinople, in which the error of Eunomius and Macedonius was condemned; the First Council of Ephesus, in which the impiety of Nestorius was judged; and the Council of Chalcedon, in which the wickedness of Eutyches and Dioscorus was rejected.

> “I embrace them with complete devotion and preserve them with unimpaired approval, because upon them, as upon a squared stone, the structure of holy faith rises. Whatever a person’s life and conduct may be, anyone who does not hold their solidity, even if he is seen to be a stone, nevertheless lies outside the building.

> “I also venerate the Fifth Council, in which the letter called that of Ibas, full of error, was rejected. Theodore, who separated the person of the Mediator between God and human beings into two subsistences, is shown to have fallen into the perfidy of impiety. The writings of Theodoret, through which the faith of blessed Cyril is attacked, are also refuted as uttered with the audacity of madness.

> “All the persons whom the aforesaid venerable councils reject, I reject; those whom they venerate, I embrace. Since they were established by universal agreement, whoever presumes either to release those whom they bind or to bind those whom they release destroys himself, not them. Whoever therefore thinks otherwise, let him be anathema. But whoever holds the faith of the councils mentioned above, let him have peace from God the Father,” and so forth.

Here you see the same authority attributed to the Fifth Council as to the four preceding councils, and a person who thinks otherwise is declared anathema.

Therefore, when Saint Gregory dealt more mildly with Theodelinda, queen of the Lombards, and with certain others who refused to submit to the authority of this synod in the condemnation of the Three Chapters—as we stated in his Life—and did not regard them as schismatics, he employed a prudent form of accommodation. Perhaps he knew that they suffered from ignorance rather than from any evil intention. Since they did not refuse instruction, he hoped that they would come to their senses.

This is how we wish whatever we have said elsewhere about Saint Gregory’s tolerance toward those who had not withdrawn from communion with the Holy See, yet could not be brought to condemn the Three Chapters, to be understood.

## XIV. The error of the Quietists refuted from Gregory

It would be superfluous to discuss the purer moral doctrine transmitted throughout all Gregory’s works. Certainly, almost no one disputes that Gregory left all teachers of Christian ethics far behind him.

In book XXII of the *Moralia*, no. 35, we corrected a serious error that had entered all later editions from the Basel edition of 1514, against the testimony of the manuscript codices. The former reading was:

> “For from all external movements it seeks that same intention of its own as a kind of most secret retreat; and, clinging there immutably, transcending all mutable things, it is already, by the very tranquility of its repose, in the world outside the world.”

Everyone can see how favorable this reading would have been to the Quietists, and even to the Calvinists who defend the impossibility of losing grace. But instead of *immutably*, one must read *in the immutable one*, as we proved in the note to this passage.

From elsewhere it is clear that, according to the mind of the holy Doctor, the grace of contemplation is not lasting but is granted suddenly and briefly. On this subject see book V of the *Moralia*, nos. 52, 57, 58, and 60, and book VIII, nos. 49 and 50.

In book XXIII, no. 43, the efforts of the devout soul striving toward God yet falling back upon itself are wonderfully explained:

> “Hence at times it is admitted to a certain unusual sweetness of inward taste, and, suddenly breathed upon in some way by an ardent spirit, it is renewed. The more it thirsts, the more it tastes what it loves. It desires within itself what it inwardly feels to be sweet, because through love of that sweetness it has become contemptible to itself in its own sight. After it has been able to perceive it to some degree, it discovers what it had been without it.

> “It tries to cling to it, but by its own remaining weakness it is driven back from its strength. Because it cannot contemplate its purity, it finds sweetness in weeping and in spreading before itself, as it falls back upon itself, the tears of its weakness.

> “For it cannot fix the eye of the mind upon that which it has suddenly glimpsed within itself, because the very habit of its old condition compels it to descend. Amid these things it pants, burns, and tries to rise above itself, but, overcome by weariness, it falls back into its familiar darkness.”[^c0002-4]

[^c0002-4]: [Col. 0031] See also book XXIV, no. 12; *Homily 5 on Ezekiel*, no. 12; book II, homily 2, no. 14; and *Homily 35 on the Gospels*, no. 12.

[^c0002-5]: [Col. 0029] Cologne: Arnold Quentel, 1605.

As regards the possibility of losing grace, Saint Gregory explicitly teaches it in book XIV of the *Moralia*, no. 42, where he explains this verse of Job: “He has stripped me of my glory and taken the crown from my head” (Job 19:9).

## XV. Whether the holy Doctor asserted that angels are corporeal

Since some have thought that Saint Gregory departed somewhat from the common doctrine of the Church by asserting that angels are corporeal and by denying that the books of the Maccabees are canonical, these two points must now be investigated at somewhat greater length.

In book II of the *Moralia*, no. 3, we read that angelic spirits are indeed spirits in comparison with our bodies, but bodies in comparison with the supreme and unbounded Spirit. By these words, although a nature subtler than our bodies is attributed to them, corporeality nevertheless seems to be attributed to angels.

But this erroneous opinion is addressed shortly afterward, namely at no. 8, where it is asserted that evil angels are clothed with no fleshly nature. The entire difficulty, however, is resolved especially by book IV of the *Dialogues*, chapter 29.

There the holy Gregory asks his disciple Peter:

> “Tell me, I ask you: Do you suppose that the apostate spirits cast down from heavenly glory are corporeal or incorporeal?”

Peter replies:

> “Who of sound understanding would say that spirits are corporeal?”

The holy Doctor responds:

> “If, then, the devil and his angels, although incorporeal, are to be tormented by corporeal fire, why should it be surprising if souls, even before they receive bodies, can experience corporeal torments?”

Let us now turn to the books of the Maccabees.

## XVI. Whether he denied that the books of the Maccabees are canonical

In book XIX of the *Moralia*, no. 34, Saint Gregory introduces a commendation of these books as follows:

> “We are not acting improperly in this matter if we bring forward testimony from books that are not canonical, but nevertheless were published for the edification of the Church.”

Peter Molinaeus raised this objection against us in a certain booklet containing a concise account, in French, of the Life of Saint Leo I and Saint Gregory the Great (printed at Sedan by Fr. Chayer, 1650). In it he rather playfully attempts to prove the harmony between Gregorian and Calvinist doctrine.

From the words just quoted, however, a certain difficulty concerning the books of the Maccabees does arise, and we must resolve it.

First, it should be observed that these books had been regarded in the Latin Church as canonical long before Saint Gregory’s time. They are received as such by the Third Council of Carthage, canon 47; by Innocent I in his letter to Exuperius of Toulouse; by Augustine in book II of *Christian Doctrine*, chapter 8, in his *Book on Care for the Dead*, chapter 1, and in book XVIII of *The City of God*, chapter 36; by Cassiodorus in book II of the *Institutions*, chapter 6, where he assigns them a place among the hagiographa; and by others.

We say nothing here about the Gelasian Decree, which receives them among the canonical Scriptures, because Pearson, William Cave, and other critics of heterodox views reject that decree. It is not worthwhile to dispute with them here.

Second, it should be observed that there are two canons of sacred books: one belonging to the Jews, the other to the Christian Church. The former admits no books except those written in Hebrew; the latter is far broader and admits, in addition to the New Testament, many books belonging to the Old Testament that survive only in Greek.

Augustine acknowledges this distinction when, speaking of these books, he adds:

> “Among them are the books of the Maccabees, which not the Jews but the Church holds as canonical.”

It can scarcely be doubted, therefore, that Saint Gregory, following the doctrine of Saint Augustine and mindful of the various catalogues of the books of Sacred Scripture established by his predecessors, denied that the books of the Maccabees belonged only to the Jewish canon and not to the Christian canon.

In this matter he followed Origen and Saint Jerome, who, when speaking of these books according to the understanding of the Hebrew teachers, exclude them from the canon. Elsewhere, however, they praise them more than once as sacred books, following the canon of the Church rather than that of the Synagogue (Origen, book II of *On First Principles*, chapter 1, and his commentary on chapter 5 of the Epistle to the Romans; Jerome, book V of his *Commentary on Isaiah*, on chapter 23, and his commentaries on chapter 9 of Ecclesiastes and chapter 8 of Daniel).

Molinaeus foolishly accuses Saint Gregory of ignorance in the same work (chapter XI) when, explaining the meanings of certain Hebrew or Greek names, he says that Lazarus—which is the same as Elzearus or Eleazarus—means “one who has been helped”; Job means “sorrows” or “one who suffers”; Cherub means “fullness” or “abundance of knowledge”; and *eleos* means “mercy” (where Molinaeus, in bad faith, reads *oleos*).

It would be pointless to waste time refuting Molinaeus’s quibbles on these matters.

## XVII. The judgment concerning the nearness of the day of judgment examined

We must now examine Saint Gregory’s opinion concerning the day of judgment, which he foretold as near.

It was certainly a common belief among the Christians of antiquity that the end of the world was imminent. Tertullian thought that when the Roman Empire fell, the world too would perish, as Franciscus Balduinus observed in his annotations on Optatus, book III of *On the Donatist Schism*, chapter 3.

Sulpicius Severus, in his *Life of Blessed Martin*, no. 24, reports these words spoken by Saint Martin to the devil:

> “If you yourself, wretched one, would desist from persecuting human beings, and at this time, when the day of judgment is near, would repent of your deeds,”

and so forth.

Saint Leo expressly says that, although the day of judgment is hidden, there is no doubt that it is near (*Sermon 8 on the Fast of the Tenth Month and Almsgiving*).

Why, indeed, should the holy Fathers speak in this way, when the chief of the apostles says: “The end of all things has drawn near” (1 Peter 4:7)? And John says: “Little children, it is the last hour” (1 John 2:18), a statement repeated afterward.

Perhaps, when speaking in this way, the holy men were attending to the saying of the royal Psalmist:

> “A thousand years in your sight are like yesterday, which has passed away” (Psalm 89:4).

If, as Saint Gregory teaches in book II of the *Dialogues*, chapter 35, “to one who sees the Creator, who rejoices in immensity, all creation is narrow,” and therefore it is not surprising that the whole world was subject to Saint Benedict’s eyes in a single ray of sunlight, why should we not, by the same reasoning, say that to those contemplating God’s eternity all time is brief, even if it encompasses many thousands of years?

## XVIII. Which Versions of Sacred Scripture He Used

Since Saint Gregory is constantly citing Sacred Scripture, it will not be beside the point to show which version he chiefly used. At the end of his letter to Leander he says:

> “I speak of the new translation; but whenever the need for proof demands it, I now take up the new, now the old, through the testimonies,” etc.

By the old version he means the translation made from the Greek of the Seventy Interpreters; by the new he means that made by Jerome from the Hebrew itself. He seems to prefer the latter to the older version in *Moralia*, book XX, no. 62:

> “The old translation differs widely from this judgment, because what is said here about God is mentioned there concerning adversaries and persecutors. Nevertheless, since this new translation is said to have conveyed everything more faithfully from the Hebrew into Latin, whatever is said in it must be believed; and our exposition ought subtly to examine its words.”

Isidore likewise prefers it, *Etymologies*, book VI, chapter 5:

> “The presbyter Jerome, most skilled in the three languages, translated the divine Scriptures from Hebrew into Latin speech . . . . His interpretation is rightly preferred to the others.”

And in *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, book I, chapter 12:

> “From Hebrew . . . . he translated the Sacred Scriptures, and all the Churches everywhere generally use his edition, because it is more truthful in its meanings and clearer in its words.”

## XIX. On His Style and Manner of Writing

Concerning Saint Gregory’s style and manner of writing, it is enough to read what we said in the preface to the commentary on Book I of the *Kings*, from number 5 through number 9. It is indeed characteristic of him to take verbs which grammarians call deponent in a passive sense, such as *metior* [“I measure”], vol. I, col. 1408 c, col. 1409 d, 1410 d; *venerari* [“to be venerated”], col. 561 d and 623 c; *persequi* [“to be pursued”], col. 459 a; *imitari* [“to be imitated”], col. 1338.

Ever conscious of himself with the utmost humility, he says at the end of the letter to Leander prefixed to the books of the *Moralia*:

> “I do not avoid the confusion of barbarism; I disdain to preserve the cases of nouns, verbs, and prepositions, because I consider it utterly unworthy to confine the words of the heavenly oracle beneath the rules of Donatus.”

Indeed, the most illustrious Huet, in *On the Best Method of Interpretation*, no. 42, has shown how greatly the sacred interpreters neglected an exact manner of expression and the laws of grammar.

Sulpicius Severus, rightly called the Christian Sallust on account of his eloquence, speaks thus of himself in the preface to the *Life of Saint Martin*:

> “Because I would have considered it impious for the virtues of so great a man to remain hidden, I learned for myself that I should not blush over solecisms, since I had never attained great knowledge of such matters.”

Nevertheless, not everything in Saint Gregory’s writings that appears contrary to the laws of grammar should immediately be regarded as a solecism or barbarism. Everyone knows that languages depend upon usage. Thus, since in the time of Gregory the Great certain words that are now obsolete and certain forms of speech contrary to our syntax—which has been brought into conformity with the rules of purer Latinity—had become established and accepted through usage, he is by no means to be blamed or despised for employing those words and expressions.

In Terence’s time, *ipsus* was said for *ipse* [“himself”], *scibo* for *sciam* [“I shall know”], and *face* for *fac* [“do”]. No one will condemn these words in that poet, although they would now be entirely unacceptable. In the same author, *Adelphoe*, act V, scene 4, one reads:

> “Now, at the end of my life, for my labor I receive from them this fruit—hatred,”

with *fructi* for *fructus* [“fruit”].

Hilary, whom Saint Jerome praises for his eloquence—as may be understood from the testimonies to Hilary’s life appended to the new edition of his works—Hilary, I say, very frequently employs forms of speech entirely remote from those of our own day. Thus, in *On the Trinity*, book VII, no. 27, he says:

> “For God, who is life, does not subsist from things compounded and lifeless, nor is he who is power contained by things weak.”

Now, before we proceed farther, let us pause briefly and, recognizing from the errors of others which above we have been compelled to note how great a danger of error also threatens us, let us beforehand seek and merit pardon for all those matters in which we may perhaps slip and err, as is characteristic of human weakness. Let us voluntarily submit whatever we have said to the judgment of the Holy See and the Church, so that it may immediately be corrected.

[Col. 0037]

# Notice of the Editor of the Patrology

Before we set our hand to the work, it was our intention to follow the footsteps of the disciples of Saint Maur so closely that in each edition one volume would correspond to its counterpart. But after considering the matter more carefully, we observed that this could not be done unless the customary number of gatherings in each volume were enlarged beyond reasonable measure. Moreover, since the various Lives of Saint Gregory which the Benedictines had relegated to the final volume ought, with better justification, to be placed at the beginning of all the works, we formed five volumes out of the four Benedictine volumes, varying the order of the material to some extent.

The reader should therefore know that the first volume of our edition contains approximately half of the first Benedictine volume—that is, from the beginning through Book XVII of the *Moralia*, with the Lives of Saint Gregory prefixed. The second volume contains the other half of the first Benedictine volume. The second Benedictine volume corresponds to the third volume of our edition. Our fourth volume consists of the first part of the third Benedictine volume, which is liturgical, together with certain liturgical monuments added to our work. Finally, in the fifth volume we shall present in a continuous sequence the commentaries on Scripture with which the third and fourth Benedictine volumes concluded.

# [Life of Saint Gregory the Great]

[Col. 0037]

## Preface to the Threefold Life or History of Saint Gregory the Great Presented Here

### I

Here we present three Lives of Gregory the Great. The first is briefly composed, and we owe it to Paul the Deacon, a monk of Cassino; the second, which embraces the illustrious deeds of the most holy pontiff in a fuller style, was written by John the Deacon, also an alumnus of Cassino. It was as though this sacred mountain, magnificently celebrated by the writings of Saint Gregory (*Dialogues*, Book II), had wished to show its gratitude for so many benefits received and to repay praises with praises. It was not content to provide a single writer to commit his history to posterity, but added another—and a particularly diligent historian.

After presenting many ancient testimonies concerning Saint Gregory, we have appended a third Life to both of these, which we have drawn out and arranged chiefly from his own works. We must first speak of the earlier, shorter Life and of its author, and then consequently of the others.

### II

Bollandus published this shorter Life in the same year, namely 1668, in the second volume for the month of March; our Mabillon likewise published it in the first century of the *Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*. Peter Gussanvillaeus afterward prefixed it to the works of the most holy Doctor in 1675. He took no care to indicate which manuscript he had used.
