Certainly this edition differs very greatly from the two earlier ones, whether this happened through a defect in the handwritten exemplar, or whether the Editor altered many things at will and deliberately avoided the obsolete expressions that occur frequently in this little work.

Concerning the edition prepared by Bollandus and his associates, we must hear their own words in the preliminary commentary on Saint Gregory, § 2:

> “First we give the Life written after his death by a contemporary but anonymous author. For he asserts as follows in no. 26 [no. 28 in our edition]: ‘After his death, we learned his story from a faithful and religious man, and one exceedingly familiar with our Father—namely, Paul the Deacon, who evidently continued to live not long after the death of Saint Gregory . . . .’ These Acts exist in very many manuscripts, and very ancient ones; some of them belong to our library. We also possess them from manuscripts of the cathedral church of Saint-Omer and of the church of Saint Martin at Trier; and we collated them with two manuscripts of Queen Christina, marked nos. 81 and 569. We also collated them with the distinguished manuscript of the monastery of Bonnevaux in Gaul.”

**Note:** The pen slipped in writing *Paul* instead of *Peter*. We also conjecture that the words “previously narrated to us” were carelessly omitted above, since at the assigned place, namely no. 26, the reading is “narrated to us.”

### III

It is truly remarkable that the name of Paul the Deacon, plainly the genuine author of this Life—as we shall shortly prove and demonstrate—is missing or suppressed in so many manuscripts. Mabillon was more fortunate. In publishing these Acts he used three manuscripts: the Saint-Germain manuscript, the Moissac manuscript, and the Conques manuscript, or that of the monastery of Saint Peter at Conques. In the last he observed—and we ourselves saw the same—that this little work was ascribed to our Paul.

Afterward we came upon many other copies bearing the name of the same author: the Cassino manuscript; that of the principal church of Évreux; those of Lyre, Bec, and the Carthusian monastery [the Grande Chartreuse]. We must also add the manuscript read by Garetus, a regular canon, who in his treatise *On the Real Presence of the Body and Blood of Christ in the Eucharist*, published in 1562, cites certain passages from these Acts, under the name of Paul the Deacon, to confirm his argument.

But even if Paul’s name were concealed and suppressed in every manuscript, it would nevertheless be most certainly established from other evidence that no one but Paul the Deacon was the author of this work. He himself expressly recalls, in Book III, chapter 25, of *The Deeds of the Lombards*, the Life of Saint Gregory that he had written, in these words:

> “For this reason we omit saying more about blessed Gregory, because some years ago we already composed his Life, with God’s help.”

Moreover, anyone who compares this work with another which everyone acknowledges to be John the Deacon’s will have no doubt that it is the same Life we have before us. John was an alumnus and monk of the monastery of Cassino, where Paul too had served, and he was only about eighty years younger than Paul. He therefore could not have been unaware of what Paul had composed, and of its character, concerning Saint Gregory.

Yet in Book IV, chapter 99, he praises Paul’s work, first recalling his name in the most honorable terms and then quoting his very words, which are found in no. 30. Here is John’s clear testimony:

> “His venerable merit, indeed, will continue to increase for as long as the orbit of this world revolves. Thus, together with Paul, that most eloquent man, I confess that it will always receive increase, because to his grace must doubtless be attributed either that the Church of the English is continually made fruitful by a new offspring, or that through his teachings many throughout the world who have been led far away by sin return to the mercy of Christ, or that all good people, inflamed by his exhortations, eagerly seek their heavenly homeland.”

If these most learned men had read this more carefully, they would not have prefixed to this Life the words “By an anonymous contemporary author.”

### IV

“But,” you will say, “whoever the author of this Life may be, he reports certain things about Saint Gregory which he asserts were told to him by a man exceedingly familiar with that most holy Father—undoubtedly Peter the Deacon, his Notary. Thus, in no. 28, he says: ‘Finally, we faithfully learned after his death from a faithful and religious man, and one exceedingly familiar with our Father . . . .’ Consequently, this man lived at least at the beginning of the seventh century and surpasses this Paul the Deacon by at least a full century and a half.”

It must not be concealed that some difficulty arises in explaining these words. But since abundant and most decisive arguments are available elsewhere to prove the contrary, it seems that Paul the Deacon here uses a not unusual manner of speaking, such as we employ when bringing forward the testimony of a writer: for example, when one says, “I learned this from Augustine,” or “Chrysostom tells us,” or something similar.

Moreover, in the Beauvais manuscript and in the older Jumièges manuscript, the reading is not “narrated to us,” but simply “narrated.” The removal of the little word *nobis* [“to us”] eliminates the entire difficulty. On this matter, however, consult Mabillon, vol. I of the *Analecta*, p. 319, where he treats the argument at greater length.

Now, since it is established that Paul the Deacon was the author of this Life, it is worthwhile to add a few words here about him.

### V

He was a Lombard by nation and a native of Friuli. He was a Deacon of the Church of Aquileia and the notary or chancellor of Desiderius, the last king of the Lombards. He describes his ancestry himself in Book IV, chapter 39, of *The Deeds of the Lombards*. His father was Warnefrid, from whom Paul was surnamed Warnefrid.

After King Desiderius was defeated, Paul was carried away among the noble captives by Charlemagne, king of the Franks. Since Charles, as a patron of all men of letters, valued him, Paul was for some time held in great honor because of his exceptional prudence and learning. But because he was suspected of a particularly close love and loyalty toward Desiderius, he was deported to the island of Diomede. From there he fled to Arichis, prince of Benevento and son-in-law of King Desiderius. After Arichis’s death, Paul assumed the monastic habit in the monastery of Cassino.

He wrote six books *On the Deeds of the Lombards*, in which he often mentions Saint Gregory; but especially in Book III, chapter 25, he testifies that he had already composed and elaborated his Life. He also published twenty-four books of *Miscellaneous History*. From these, Vossius says in Book II, chapter 30, of *On Latin History*, that the first eleven books are identical with the ten books of Eutropius. Paul added some material of his own from time to time, in order to accommodate Adalperga, the daughter of Desiderius and wife of Duke Arichis.

Paul then continues Eutropius; the five books that follow are his. The remaining eight are believed to have been added by Landulfus Sagax, chiefly from Theophanes—or rather from Anastasius the Librarian, the translator of Theophanes.

William Cave mentions Paul’s other works, whether extant or lost, in the eighth century of his *Literary History of Ecclesiastical Writers*. There, however, the learned man errs in assigning to him four books *On the Life of Saint Gregory the Pope*, which he says were published by John Mabillon in the first century of the Benedictine series.

### VI

Paul flourished toward the end of the eighth century. It can scarcely be determined when, in particular, he undertook to write the Life of Saint Gregory. That he was then living in Rome is clear from the fact that whenever he speaks of Rome he regularly prefixes the demonstrative pronoun *haec* or *hanc* [“this”].

Thus he begins his history:

> “Gregory, born in this Roman city.”

A little later, in no. 2:

> “Although at that time the study of literature flourished especially here, he was considered second to no one in this city.”

In no. 4:

> “He established the seventh [monastery] within the walls of this city.”

And so he continues to speak consistently in this manner almost to the middle of the volume. Gussanvillaeus deleted these little words, but wrongly, since they are found in all the manuscripts—including those read by Bollandus and Mabillon, and those which we ourselves examined after them, of which there are certainly very many.

### VII

What we have chiefly accomplished in this edition must be indicated briefly. Although we were assured of the fidelity of the earlier Editors, nevertheless, lest we fail in any respect either in our duty or in the diligence we promised, we collated this history anew with manuscript codices—especially the Conques, Bec, and Saint Peter of Beauvais manuscripts, and the two Jumièges manuscripts—as well as with the earlier editions. We have also illuminated the text with certain notes written at the foot of the page, without concealing the names of the learned men from whom we borrowed a few of them.

These are the matters concerning the earlier Life of Saint Gregory which we thought ought to be prefixed here in our edition. We now turn to the second Life, whose author is John the Deacon.

### VIII

John, a monk of Cassino who later became a Deacon of the Roman Church, composed four books on the deeds of Saint Gregory after Paul Warnefrid, at the command of Pope John VIII, who began his pontificate in 872. On this subject, one should read the preface of John the Deacon himself, where he also speaks beforehand about the purpose and arrangement of the entire work.

### IX

The authority which this Life of Saint Gregory enjoyed among the ancients is shown by Guitmund of Aversa, bishop, in Book III *On the Eucharist*. He says:

> “That Life was approved by so many most holy and learned Roman pontiffs, with none hitherto dissenting; and, following their authority, so many Churches have received it and continue to receive it, in harmony with the entire Christian people.”

### X

Nevertheless, the most eminent Cardinal Baronius criticizes several things in this work:

1. That in Book I, chapter 1, it calls Pope Felix IV the great-grandfather of Saint Gregory.
2. That in chapter 25 of the same book it says that the most holy man was made a Deacon by Pope Benedict.
3. That in Book II, chapter 44, it relates that the soul of the Emperor Trajan was liberated by Saint Gregory from the punishments of hell.
4. That it narrates that the books of the holy Doctor were handed over to the fire by his rivals.

Moreover, Baronius does not agree with John when he asserts that Saint Gregory became a monk, observed the Rule of Saint Benedict, and established it to be observed in his monastery of Saint Andrew.

We shall discuss each of these matters in the Life of the most holy pontiff which we have prepared.

### XI

William Cave, in his *Literary History of Ecclesiastical Writers*, attributes to our John—on the authority of Sigebert—a Life of Pope Saint Clement, written at the request of Gauderic, bishop of Velletri; Cave says that this work has perished. A brief commentary or exposition on the Heptateuch, preserved in the library of Saint-Germain-des-Prés in Paris, is also said to be by the same author.

### XII

As for the Life of Saint Gregory, which alone must be treated here, we collated it with the Bigot, Eu, Saint Ebrulf, and Angers manuscripts. We also consulted the manuscript of the Paris metropolitan church, another of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, the manuscript of Saint Martin at Tours, and the Vatican manuscripts.

Since this Life was collected chiefly from Gregory’s writings and composed especially from his letters, we took pains to investigate the excerpts from those letters in the more reliable manuscripts. We observed that both sets of codices—the *Register* and the *Life*—agree in every respect.

[Col. 0041]

### XIII

Besides the works of Paul and John the Deacons, we thought it appropriate to add certain selected ancient testimonies concerning Saint Gregory. We could find no other Lives written in full among the ancient monuments.

Among the unpublished works of Venerable Bede, William Cave does list a Life of Saint Gregory, which he says exists in manuscript in the library of Merton College. Eager to see it, we asked our Mabillon to obtain permission from the most learned Thomas Gals—his friend, benevolent toward all men of letters—to consult the celebrated codex and collate it with Paul’s little work on the Life of Saint Gregory.

That most obliging man not only did this, but also sent us certain excerpts: first, from the opening manuscript sections, beginning, “Gregory, born in this Roman city, of Gordianus his father and Silvia his mother,” etc., through “he was considered second to no one in this city”; and then from the end of the entire work, beginning with the words, “These things have been briefly said about the life of blessed Gregory,” etc., through “he was buried in the church of the blessed Apostle Peter before the sacristy, on the fourth day before the Ides of March. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father,” etc.

From these passages we clearly understood what we had previously suspected: that the Merton College manuscript contains nothing other than Paul’s work. We thought it worthwhile to insert here the entire letter of the excellent Thomas Gals, which is a remarkable testimony to his generous disposition toward us.

> **To the most excellent and devout Lord, John Mabillon, Thomas Gals sends greetings.**
>
> I received your most welcome and long-awaited letter by Gannovius. I immediately wrote to the men of Oxford concerning the Life of Saint Gregory. After a long delay, I received the following information about that Life. I point out—although there will be no need to point this out to you—that it appears to be attributable to Paul the Deacon; he is, as I gather from Surius, *πατὴρ τοῦ λόγου* [“the father of the discourse”].
>
> The entire little work occupies ten leaves in the Oxford manuscript of Merton College. If you should wish to have any part of it, I shall see to it that you may enjoy it. It is certainly fitting that I should always remember your many services to me, and I would most gladly serve you and yours according to my strength and resources.
>
> You would therefore do me a very great favor if, whenever one of your friends should be traveling this way, you would send him to me, so that from time to time I might at least hear about your health and prosperous condition; nothing could happen to me more gladly than that. Farewell.
>
> The noble young man Spencer Compton, who is already acting among you with our ambassador, will shortly convey my greetings to you.
>
> Bloomsbury, London, 14 January 1697.

### XIV

It remains for us to say a few words about the Life of the most holy Doctor which we have composed chiefly from his own writings. We first published it in French in 1698. From that point our entire labor concerning Gregory began.

When the eminent Cardinal Spada informed us, in a letter dated 8 April 1698, that this work—whatever its worth—had been most welcome to the late Pope Innocent XII, and when he encouraged us to attempt greater things by imparting to us, in the name of so great a pontiff, his blessing, we immediately set ourselves to preparing a new edition of all the works of Saint Gregory.

Here we present this Life translated into Latin, but in a shorter form and without always preserving the order of the earlier French version.

At the beginning of the chapters, two years are almost always noted—for example, the years 590 and 591—because we reckon the years of Saint Gregory’s pontificate by indictions. An indiction, however, began in September and corresponded to two years.

As for the usefulness of the work we have composed, it would be superfluous to say anything beforehand. In the Life of this greatest Doctor of the Church, nearly everything relating to the sacred or secular history of those times is explained; the principal doctrines of the Gospel are confirmed; the whole of ecclesiastical discipline and the precepts of Christian life are contained; indeed, the most certain rules of higher perfection are handed down, from which not only the sheep of Christ’s flock but also the shepherds may profit.

Read these things, earnest Christian, in leisure—but not idly—and pray that those who have set before you the fruits of their arduous labor may be blessed with the best rewards.

[Col. 0041]

# Life of Saint Gregory the Great

**By Paul the Deacon, Monk of Cassino**

**Note:** It appears to have been taken for the most part from Venerable Bede, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book II, chapter 1, although it is written in a fuller style.

**Note:** In the Bec manuscript: “Here begins the Life of Pope Saint Gregory, published by Paul, monk of Cassino.”

(C, S)*

[Col. 0041A]

### 1

Gregory was born in this Roman city, his father being Gordianus and his mother Silvia. He derived his origin not only from a distinguished senatorial family but also from a religious one. For Felix, bishop of this apostolic see, a man of great virtue and a glory of the Church in Christ, was his great-great-grandfather.

**Note:** That is, the fourth [ancestor].

Yet Gregory raised this line of such nobility still higher by his character and adorned it with honorable deeds. Finally, as later became openly evident, he did not receive such a name without some great foreshadowing. For *Gregorius*, from the Greek expression, means in our language “watchman” or “watchful.” In fact, he truly kept watch over himself, living commendably by adhering to the divine commandments. He also kept watch over the faithful peoples, when by the resourcefulness of his abundant teaching he showed them by what path they might ascend to heavenly things.

### 2

He was instructed from childhood in the liberal disciplines—that is, grammar, rhetoric, and dialectic—to such an extent that, although the study of literature still flourished at Rome in those days, he was nevertheless considered second to no one in the city itself.

Even at a still young age he possessed a mature intellectual interest: namely, to adhere to the sayings of his elders; and, if he could hear anything worthy of attention, not carelessly to consign it to oblivion, but rather to entrust it to his tenacious memory. Even then he drank in with a thirsting heart the streams of learning, which at the fitting time he would later pour forth with honeyed speech.

While still in the years of adolescence—the age when people ordinarily enter upon the paths of the world—he began to devote himself to God and to yearn with all his desires for the homeland of the heavenly life.

### 3

But while he long delayed and postponed his conversion, and after he had been inspired by a heavenly desire thought it better to remain clothed in secular attire, wishing to serve the present world, as it were, only in outward appearance, many things began to grow up against him from the cares of that same world, so that he was held by it no longer merely outwardly but, as he himself says of himself, also in mind.

At last, when the death of his parents—who had already long since died—gave him freedom to arrange his affairs, he disclosed what he had previously carried in his mind; and what was already visible to divine eyes he also displayed to human eyes.

**Note:** Rather, only his father had died; for his mother lived long afterward, according to John the Deacon, Book I, chapter 9.

Immediately, therefore, he distributed everything he could possess for works of piety, so that, himself needy, he might follow Christ, who became poor for our sake.

### 4

Finally, he built six monasteries in Sicily and gathered brothers there to serve Christ. He established a seventh within the walls of this city, where later, following the regular way of life and joined by many brothers, he himself served under the authority of an abbot.

To these monasteries he assigned from the revenues of his estates as much as could suffice for the daily sustenance of those living there. He sold the remainder, together with all the resources of his household, and distributed it to the poor.

**Note:** Gussanvillaeus reads, “with all the estates of the household”; Bollandus, “with the estate of the whole household,” though the manuscripts resist these readings.

He transformed, by the gift of divine grace, that nobility which he appeared to possess in the world entirely toward attaining the glory of heavenly dignity. He who had formerly been accustomed to pass through the city in a robe woven of silk and glittering with gems, afterward covered in a cheap garment, ministered as a poor man to the poor.

**Note:** Gussanvillaeus reads, “through the cities.”

### 5

For, having suddenly changed his worldly clothing, he went to the monastery and escaped naked from the shipwreck of this world. There he began to live with such a grace of perfection that already at the beginning he could be counted among the perfect.

**Note:** After these words Gussanvillaeus adds: “Having been elected abbot by the unanimous agreement of the brothers, he did not refuse to preside over them. He possessed,” etc. These words are absent from the manuscripts and have been inserted incongruously in this place.

He possessed such abstinence in food, such watchfulness in prayer, and such earnestness in fasting that, with his stomach weakened, he could scarcely remain standing. He also endured constant bodily illnesses, and was especially afflicted by the condition which physicians call *syncopē* in Greek.

**Note:** *Συγκοπή* [*synkopē*], which Celsus calls “fainting” (*animae defectio*). — Bollandus.

He was so tormented by pain in his vital organs through this affliction that, overcome by repeated attacks of distress, he approached death almost at every moment of the hours.

[Col. 0043D]

### 6

What sort of man he was in the monastery, and with how praiseworthy a devotion he lived, we can gather from his own words. Although he was already established in the pontificate, he said the following while weeping in conversation with his deacon Peter:

**Note:** Gussanvillaeus reads, “he seemed to be weeping,” an obvious error.

> “For my unhappy soul, struck by the wound of its occupation, remembers what it once was in the monastery, how all passing things lay beneath it; how far it rose above things that roll away; how it was accustomed to think of nothing except heavenly things; how, even while held by the body, it already passed beyond the prison of the flesh through contemplation; how it loved even death, which is almost universally regarded as a punishment, as the entrance to life and the reward of its labor.
>
> “But now, because of the demands of pastoral care, it suffers the affairs of secular people; and after so beautiful a vision of its repose, it is stained by the dust of earthly activity. I consider what I endure; I consider what I have lost. And when I look upon what I have lost, what I carry becomes heavier.
>
> “For behold, I am now shaken by the waves of a great sea, and in the ship of my mind I am dashed about by the storms of a violent tempest. When I recall my former life, I turn my eyes backward, as it were, and, seeing the shore, sigh; and what is still more serious, while I am carried through immense waves in confusion, I can scarcely see the harbor I have left.”

He was accustomed to speak these things about himself, not boasting of his progress in virtue, but rather lamenting his decline, which he always feared he had incurred through pastoral care. Although he spoke thus out of profound humility, we ought nevertheless to believe that he lost nothing of monastic perfection through the demands of pastoral care. Indeed, he then gained greater progress from the labor of converting many than he had formerly gained from the repose of his own way of life.

[Col. 0044C]

### 7

How this holy man rose first to the office of the diaconate and afterward to the summit of the pontificate, the following account will make clear.

The Roman pontiff who then presided over the Church, seeing Gregory ascend to high things by the steps of virtue, removed him from the monastery and elevated him through the office of the ecclesiastical order. He appointed him as the seventh deacon to assist him.

**Note:** Saint Pope Cornelius wrote, in his treatise against Novatian, preserved by Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book VI, chapter 35, that seven deacons were customarily in attendance upon the pontiff.

Not long afterward he sent him to Constantinople as *apocrisiarius* [papal representative] for ecclesiastical affairs.

**Note:** On this word, see the third note to the letter prefixed to the books of the *Moralia*, col. 1. According to John the Deacon, Book I, chapter 25, Pope Benedict ordained Gregory a deacon, while Pelagius sent him as *apocrisiarius*. We shall explain our view of this difficulty in the Life of Saint Gregory.

Yet although he lived in an earthly palace, he did not abandon his commitment to the heavenly life. Many of his brothers from the monastery followed him, bound by fraternal love.

This is seen to have happened by divine providence, so that, through their example, he might be held fast, as by an anchor’s rope, to the calm shore of prayer. While he was tossed about by the incessant waves of secular affairs, he could withdraw to their company, like the refuge of an exceedingly safe harbor, after the twists and waves of earthly activity.

**Note:** Gussanvillaeus reads incorrectly, “as though by an anchor.”

Although that ministry, after he had been taken from the monastery, had cut him off from his former life of repose with the sword of its occupation, the daily breath of compunction nevertheless kept him alive among them through the intercourse of diligent reading.

**Note:** Mabillon reads, “yet inwardly among them”; Gussanvillaeus and Bollandus, whom we follow, have the Bec manuscript’s reading.

Through their company he was not only protected from earthly attacks but also increasingly inflamed for the exercises of the heavenly life.

### 8

Then, earnestly urged by those same brothers—and especially by Leander, a venerable man and bishop of Seville, who at that time had come to Constantinople as an ambassador on behalf of the Visigoths—he was compelled to explain the Book of Blessed Job, which is filled with many mysteries.

**Note:** On Leander, see what we said in the second note to the letter already mentioned, which serves as the prologue to the *Moralia*.

He could not refuse a task which fraternal love, intervening through affection, imposed upon him as destined to be useful to many. He therefore explained the same book, showing with wondrous method, in a series of thirty-five books, how it was to be understood according to the literal sense; how it was to be referred to the mysteries of Christ and the Church; and how it was to be applied, in its meaning, to each of the faithful.

In these books he discussed virtues and vices in such a way that he seems not merely to explain them in words, but also, in some fashion, to display them through visible forms. Hence there is no doubt that he had attained the perfection of those very virtues whose effect he was able to communicate so effectively.

### 9

While he was still residing in that imperial city, he crushed a new heresy that had arisen there concerning the condition of the resurrection, at the very beginning of its emergence, with the help of the grace of Catholic truth.

For Eutychius, the bishop of that city, taught as a doctrine that our body, in the glory of the resurrection, would be intangible and subtler than the winds and the air.

**Note:** Saint Eutychius, who is found in the manuscripts as *Euticius*, became famous for many miracles and also suffered exile for the faith. His feast is celebrated on 6 April.

When Gregory heard this, he proved, both by the reasoning of truth and by the example of the Lord’s resurrection, that this teaching was altogether contrary to orthodox faith.

For the Catholic faith holds that our very body, raised up into the glory of immortality, will indeed be subtle through the effect of spiritual power, but palpable through the reality of its nature, according to the example of the Lord’s body. Concerning that body, raised from the dead, he himself said to his disciples:

> “Touch me and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see that I have” (Luke 24:39).

In defending this faith, the venerable Father Gregory labored with such determination against the emerging heresy—and, with the assistance also of the most devout Emperor Tiberius Constantine, so weakened it—that afterward no one was found who could revive it.

[Col. 0045D] **10.** Accordingly, after the venerable deacon Gregory had returned to Rome, some time having elapsed, the river Tiber, with such a great flood, left its channel and rose so high [Note: [Col. 0045D] Guss. has, “and it grew so powerful.” Bollandus observes that this occurred in the year 509, in the month of November; we agree.] that its waters [Note: [Col. 0045D] Guss., supported by the Beauvais and Bec manuscripts, has “above the walls.” The same source has “occupied the largest districts,” with the other witnesses differing; [Col. 0046D] and “monuments instead of walls.” What Paulus relates here has been taken from Gregory of Tours, book X, chapter 1.] flowed over the walls [Col. 0046A] of the city and occupied a very large part of the district, so that it destroyed the walls of many ancient buildings. By this same violent inundation the Church’s granaries were overturned, in which several thousand modii of wheat perished. Then indeed a multitude of serpents, together with a great dragon as massive as a beam, descended through the channel of this river into the sea; but the suffocated creatures were cast upon the shore amid the briny waves of the turbulent sea.

Immediately afterward there followed the calamity they call the groin-disease; for, arriving in the middle of the eleventh month, it first struck Pope Pelagius, in accordance with what is read in Ezekiel, “Begin from my sanctuary,” and [Note: [Col. 0046D] Anastasius records that Pelagius died in January of the year 590, on 8 February. Bollandus.] without delay killed him. After his death such slaughter of the people occurred that, the inhabitants having been removed everywhere, very many houses in the city [Col. 0046B] remained empty.

But because the Church of God could not be without a ruler, although the blessed Gregory resisted with all his strength, the entire people nevertheless elected him. Attempting more earnestly to flee this dignity, he loudly declared that he was wholly unworthy of such an honor, fearing, clearly, that the glory of the world, which he had previously rejected, might somehow creep back upon him under the appearance of ecclesiastical governance. Thus it came about that he sent a letter to the emperor Maurice, whose son he had received from the sacred font, adjuring him and earnestly begging that he never give his assent to the people’s elevating him with the glory of this honor.

But the prefect of the city, named Germanus, [Note: [Col. 0046D] More probably Germanus was Gregory’s blood relative and brother; we have established in his Life, book I, chapter 1, no. 5, that Gregory had a brother. The passage of Gregory of Tours from which this is taken is ambiguous.] forestalled his messenger. After seizing him and tearing up the letters, he sent the emperor the consent that the people had given. The emperor, giving thanks to God for the deacon’s friendship, since he had found the opportunity to confer the honor upon him as he wished, immediately issued an order and commanded that Gregory be appointed.

**11.** When only his blessing remained to be performed, and the plague was devastating the people, he began his address to the people concerning the performance of penance in these words:

> “Most beloved brothers, we ought to fear at least the scourges of God that we should have feared would come, now that they are present and have been experienced. Let sorrow open for us the way of conversion, and let the punishment we are suffering itself dissolve the hardness of our hearts. For, as the prophet testifies, it was foretold: ‘The sword has reached even to the soul’ (Jeremiah 4:10). Behold, the whole people is struck by the sword-edge of heavenly wrath, and individuals are suddenly destroyed by slaughter. Nor does illness precede death; rather, as you see, death itself outruns the delays of illness. Each person who is struck is carried away before he can turn to the lamentation of penance. Consider, therefore, what sort of person arrives before the sight of the strict Judge when he has no time to weep for what he has done.
>
> “The inhabitants are not taken away only in part; they fall together. Houses are left empty; parents look upon the funerals of their children, and their own heirs precede them to destruction. Let each one of us therefore flee to the lamentations of penance while there is time to weep before the blow. Let us recall before the eyes of our mind whatever we have committed through error, and punish by weeping what we have wickedly done. Let us anticipate his face in confession; and, as the prophet admonishes: ‘Let us lift up our hearts with our hands to the Lord’ (Lamentations 3:41). To lift our hearts with our hands to the Lord means to raise the devotion of our prayer together with the merit of good works.
>
> “He certainly gives confidence to our trembling who cries out through the prophet: ‘I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live’ (Ezekiel 33:11). Let no one despair because of the enormity of his sins. For a three-day penance wiped away the long-standing guilt of the Ninevites; and the converted thief earned the rewards of life even in the very sentence of his death. Let us therefore change our hearts and presume that we have already received what we ask. The Judge is bent more quickly toward prayer if the mind is corrected from its wickedness.
>
> “Since, then, the sword of so great a punishment is hanging over us, let us persist in insistent weeping. For what is usually importunity displeasing to human beings pleases the Judge of truth, because the pious and merciful Lord wishes to be pressed by prayers—he who does not wish to be angry as much as we deserve. Hence he said through the Psalmist: ‘Call upon me in the day of your tribulation, and I will deliver you, and you shall glorify me.’ He is therefore his own witness that he desires to show mercy to those who call upon him, since he admonishes them to call upon him.
>
> “Therefore, dearest brothers, with a contrite heart and corrected works, beginning at dawn on Wednesday itself, let us proceed in a sevenfold litany, devoted to tears, [Note: [Col. 0047D] Another reading has “of the seventh month.” Guss. has here “with a devout mind,” referring it to the mind, as Gregory says concerning the Litany. The same source has “with tears.” Below it reads: “tempering the sentence of condemnation itself, he may spare,” while all the other printed and manuscript witnesses disagree. Moreover, Paulus the Deacon, *History of the Lombards*, book III, chapter 25, says that the litany was called sevenfold because the entire population of the city was divided by the blessed Gregory into seven groups to entreat the Lord. See Gregory of Tours at the cited place, and [Col. 0048D] John the Deacon, book I, chapter 42.] so that, when the strict Judge sees that we are punishing ourselves for our sins, he himself may spare us from the sentence of condemnation he has announced.”

We thought it appropriate to insert this exhortation of the blessed Gregory into this little work, so that we might show from how great a perfection of preaching he took his beginning.

**12.** Accordingly, when a great multitude of priests, monks, and people of various sex and age had come on the appointed day, according to the command of the blessed Gregory, to pray to the Lord, the plague raged with such violence by divine judgment that, within the space of one hour, while the people were uttering supplicatory cries to the Lord, eighty men fell to the ground and breathed out their spirits. [Col. 0047D] Yet so great a priest did not cease preaching to the people that they should not stop praying, until by divine mercy the plague itself subsided.

**13.** While the future bishop was still preparing a hiding place for flight [Note: [Col. 0048D] In the Moissac manuscript, after omitting much, the text reads “he prepared, was dragged, was seized,” and so forth, as below], concern for the city and guards for the gates were assigned, until, in due and glorious fashion, as the sacred order requires, the divine duties might be fulfilled in him.

He obtained from some merchants that he be carried out of the city hidden in a basket, and in this way concealed himself in hiding for three days, until the Roman people found him through fasts and prayers, a pillar of light having been sent down from heaven over him on the third night. This pillar shone for a considerable portion of the night in a straight line from the summit of heaven down to that very man, revealing to those who sought him the desired answer. Moreover, to a certain anchorite living near the city, angels were seen ascending and descending by means of the aforesaid pillar over him.

The anchorite, immediately taking this as a fortunate and sacred omen, declared that the ladder which holy Jacob had seen in a dream, and the house of the Lord, would be there; indeed, he exclaimed that the ruler of the house of God, which is the Church—or rather that the very temple of God—was hidden there.

At last the chosen and beloved man of the Lord was found, seized, dragged away, and led to the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter; there he was consecrated to the office of pontifical grace and became pope of the city.

**14.** At that time, when he had been reproved by John, bishop of the city of Ravenna, for wishing, despite being so capable a man, to withdraw by hiding himself from pastoral office, compelled by this occasion he composed the distinguished volume [Note: [Col. 0048D] Bec and other manuscripts have “which is called the *Pastoral*”; Bollandus has “the *Pastoral*,” which is what the book is called.] entitled *The Pastoral*. In it he made clear, in manifest light, what sort of person should be taken up into the governance of the Church, how the rulers themselves ought to live, with what discernment they should instruct each individual class of hearers, and with how much reflection they should daily consider their own frailty.

He also composed forty homilies on the Gospels, which he divided equally between two books. He likewise published four books of *Dialogues*, in which, at the request of his deacon Peter, he collected for the example of the living and for posterity the virtues of the saints whom he had been able to know or hear about as the most distinguished in Italy. Thus, just as in his books of Expositions he taught toward which virtues one should strive, so too, by recording the miracles of the saints, he showed the splendor of those same virtues.

He also demonstrated, through twenty-two homilies, how much inner light was contained in the first and last parts of the prophet Ezekiel, which appeared more obscure. [Note: [Col. 0048D] Guss. alone adds: “He also wrote on Proverbs, on the Song of Songs, on the Prophets, on the books of Kings, on the Heptateuch, and several other works; letters, and so forth.”]

He wrote many other things as well, including numerous letters, but, for the sake of brevity, I have omitted listing them individually.

**15.** This is all the more remarkable because he was able to compose so many and such great volumes, although, to use his own words, throughout nearly all the time of his youth he was tormented by frequent pains in his entrails, grew weary at every hour and moment because the strength of his stomach was broken, panted under slow but continuous fevers, and was also severely afflicted by frequent pain in his feet. [Col. 0049A]

Yet amid these sufferings he carefully considered that, as Scripture testifies, “Every son whom he receives, he scourges” (Hebrews 12:6). The more harshly he was pressed by present evils, the more confidently he drew breath in hope of eternal things.

He was also constantly wearied by concern for arranging the watches of the city, lest it be captured by enemies. [Note: [Col. 0049D] Guss. alone, in its customary manner, adds: “His spirit was also consumed on account of the dangers announced concerning his sons, here and there,” and so forth. If only it had at least indicated which manuscript it used!] News of dangers threatening his sons from various directions also continually consumed his mind.

Nevertheless, though caught amid so many and such great troubles, he never indulged in idleness: he was always either serving the interests of his sons, writing something worthy of the Church, or, through the grace of contemplation, participating in the mysteries of heaven.

**16.** Finally, when many people from almost all of Italy, fearing the swords of the Lombards, flocked from every direction to the city of Rome, he diligently cared for them all and provided everyone with bodily support as well as the nourishment of the word. For the love of mercy had so conquered his mind that he not only met the needs of those whom he had present with him, but also extended the help of his generosity to people living far away—so much so that he even sent whatever was necessary to the servants of God stationed on Mount Sinai.

Other pontiffs devoted themselves to building and adorning churches with gold or silver. He, however, also attended to these matters, but, as though setting them aside, devoted himself entirely to winning souls; whatever money he could obtain, he carefully distributed and took pains to give to the poor (Psalm 112:9), so that his righteousness might remain forever and ever, and his horn might be exalted in glory.

Thus he could truthfully say the words of blessed Job:

> “The blessing of him who was perishing came upon me, and I comforted the heart of the widow. I put on righteousness, and it clothed me as a garment, and as a diadem my judgment. I was an eye to the blind and a foot to the lame. I was a father to the poor, and the case that I did not know I investigated most diligently” (Job 29:13 ff.).

And shortly afterward:

> “If I ate my morsel alone, and the orphan did not eat from it, because from my childhood compassion grew with me, and from my mother’s womb it came forth with me” (Job 31:17–18).

**17.** To this work of piety and justice belongs the fact that, through the preachers whom he sent there, he snatched the people of the Angles from the teeth of the ancient enemy and made them participants in eternal freedom.

For since whoever faithfully clings to our God always rises higher through his abundant gift, while this holy man was laboring with ardent zeal to gather the souls of the faithful one by one, the merciful Lord granted him the conversion of the entire people of the Angles together.

The following occasion is thought to have divinely brought about this conversion. One day, when recently arrived merchants had brought many goods for sale into the Roman marketplace and many people were gathering from all directions to buy, Gregory happened to pass through the marketplace—before he had received pontifical dignity—and saw, among other things, some boys placed there for sale, with milk-white bodies, handsome faces, and hair of exceptional fairness.

When he saw them, he asked, as they say, from what region or land they had been brought. He was told that they were from the island of Britain, whose inhabitants all shone with such beauty. He asked again [Note: [Col. 0049D] Guss. has, “whether they were on that same island,”] whether those islanders were Christians or entangled in the errors of pagans. [Col. 0050B]

He was told that they were pagans. Then, drawing a long sigh from the depths of his heart, he said: “Alas! What grief, that people with such luminous faces are possessed by the author of darkness, and that such beauty of brow bears a diseased mind, empty of inward joys!” [Note: [Col. 0049D] Guss. has, “and such grace of forehead holds a mind away from inward joys.” Bollandus has, “and such grace of facial beauty.” We follow the Bec, Conches, Beauvais, and other manuscripts. The Beauvais manuscript nevertheless differs little from the others, for it reads: “such a pleasing race in the appearance of the forehead bears a mind away from inward joys,” and so forth.]

He asked again what the name of that people was. He was told that they were called Angles. “Good,” he said, “for they have the face of angels, and such people ought to be fellow-heirs of the angels in heaven.”

“What is the name,” he asked, “of the province from which these people have been brought?” He was told that they were called Deiri [Note: [Col. 0049D] Guss. explains, “that is, provincials.” A remarkable interpretation of the word *Deiri*! Nevertheless, he could have read it in the Beauvais manuscript. Concerning the word *Deiri*, Mabillon has the following: “Now they are the people of York; the English call it Yorkshire.” See Bede, book III of the *History*, chapter 1, and Bollandus. Deira, in English *Deirland*, is a part of the kingdom of Northumbria, the other part of which is called Bernicia . . . . . Deira is also used for the kingdom of Northumbria. Thus, in the monk of Angoulême, in the *Life of Charlemagne*: “Eardwulf, king of the Northumbrians—that is, from the island of Ireland” (rather, from the province of Deirland) “in Britain, expelled, came to the emperor in the year 808.”]—that is, provincials.

“Good,” he said: “Deiri—taken out of anger (*de ira*) and called to the mercy of Christ.”

“What is the king of that province called?” he asked. He was told that he was called Ælle [Note: [Col. 0050D] Another reading has “Hohel.” Bede has “Ælle,” which is also found in the Beauvais manuscript.]

Then, alluding to the name, he said: “The praise of God the Creator ought to be sung in those regions.” [Note: [Col. 0050D] Bollandus and Guss. have: “Praise of God was there; ‘Alleluia’ ought to be sung . . . .” Gregory clearly alluded to the word *alleluia*, which means “Praise God.”]

**18.** He approached the pontiff of this Roman and apostolic see and asked him to send some ministers of the word to the people of the Angles in Britain, so that they might be converted to Christ. He declared that he himself was prepared, with the Lord’s help, to complete this work, if it pleased the apostolic pope that it be done. [Note: [Col. 0050D] In the Moissac manuscript and in another, that of Saint-Omer, used by Bollandus: “Since he could not accomplish this, because, even if the pontiff granted permission, he thought that the Roman citizens would not allow the man who wished to do what he had requested to withdraw so far from the city.” The Moissac manuscript continues: “As soon as he himself had undertaken the office of the pontificate, he completed the work he had long desired,” as below.]

When the pontiff at first refused his request, he was finally overcome by Gregory’s tireless prayers and gave his consent. Concealing the business of his departure from the citizens—for if they had learned of it, they would never have agreed to it—Gregory set out as quickly as he could, with the apostolic blessing.

**19.** Meanwhile these events became known to the people. By unanimous agreement, all the citizens and suburban residents, and everyone who could hurry to meet him, divided themselves into three groups. As he was setting out, they cried with terrifying voices to the apostolic pontiff Pelagius, at the Church of Saint Peter:

“Ho, apostolic one, what have you done? You have offended Saint Peter; you have destroyed Rome; you have not so much dismissed Gregory as driven him out.”

The pontiff was terribly shaken by these cries and greatly feared the people. He sent after Gregory with the utmost haste, ordering him to return to Rome as quickly as possible and imposing an obligation that he do so.

**20.** But before the messengers had reached him, after he had already completed three days’ journey, Gregory, the man of God, was sitting and reading, as is customary for travelers, around the sixth hour in a certain meadow. Some of his companions were resting, while others stood nearby or were occupied with various necessary tasks.

A locust came to him, leapt, and settled upon the page he was reading. The blessed Gregory saw it remaining so gently in the place where it had settled and began, rejoicing, to repeat its name to his companions and interpret it as though he were saying: “Locust (*locusta*), I say, can be understood as *loco sta*, ‘stay in the place.’” [Note: [Col. 0051D] Bollandus has “this.”]

He added: “Know that we are not permitted to extend the journey we have begun any farther. Nevertheless, rise and saddle the beasts, so that, as far as is permitted, we may hurry toward our destination.”

While they were talking together about this and wondering among themselves, the apostolic messengers arrived on sweating and extremely fatigued horses. Immediately, with great haste, they handed him the letter they had brought. After reading it, he said to his companions: “It is as I foretold: we shall return to Rome more quickly.”

[Col. 0051C] **21.** In this way the fulfillment of his devotion was meanwhile postponed. But as soon as he himself had undertaken the office of the pontificate, he completed the work he had long desired, sending other preachers, while supporting their preaching so that it might bear fruit through his exhortations, prayers, and gifts.

Finally, he sent to that same island the servants of God Mellitus, Augustine, and John, [Note: [Col. 0051D] Augustine ought to have been named first. Mellitus was sent second, as a reinforcement for Augustine and his companions. Nothing is read about John either in John the Deacon or in Bede.] together with many other God-fearing monks. Within a short time they converted that king who lived at the head of the island, named [Note: [Col. 0051D] “of the people of Kent,” with the name Æthelberht.] Æthelberht, together with his people.

The Lord bestowed upon them such grace for performing miracles that they confirmed by the efficacy of signs the word of faith that they preached with their mouths. Thus it came about that, after a few years had passed, the other kings of the island also [Note: [Col. 0051D] So the manuscripts read. Mombritius, whom Guss. follows, has: “the other islands also, and their kings.” Among these was first Saint Edwin, king of the Northumbrians, who married Saint Æthelburh, daughter of King Æthelberht.] came to the faith of Christ the Lord, together with those subject to them.

Concerning the conversion of this people and the wonders of the miracles that occurred there, the blessed Gregory thus testifies in his books of the *Moralia* (book XXVII, formerly chapter 6, now no. 21), saying:

[Col. 0052A]

> “Behold, the tongue of Britain, which had known nothing except to growl barbarously, has long since begun to sound Hebrew words in divine praises. Behold, the Ocean, once proud, now laid low, serves at the feet of the saints; and its barbarous movements, which earthly rulers could not subdue with iron, the mouths of priests restrain through divine fear with simple words. The Ocean that, as an unbeliever, had in no way feared the hosts of warriors now, as a believer, fears the tongues of the humble.
>
> “For, having received heavenly words and with miracles also shining forth, the power of divine knowledge is poured into it; it is restrained by fear of that same Divinity, so that it fears to act wickedly and longs with all its desires to come to the grace of eternity.”

To make all this happen, divine grace granted it to the blessed Gregory in such a way that he deserved to be called the apostle by the peoples of the Angles. For although he is not an apostle to others, he is nevertheless an apostle to them; “for they themselves are the seal of his apostleship in the Lord” (1 Corinthians 9:2).

**22.** Whether this man of such great merit also became renowned through certain miracles is now asked to no purpose, since it is clearer than daylight that he who by his own merits was able to perform signs of power, and by Christ’s generosity to acquire them for others, could more easily have earned such signs for himself had occasion required it.

But so that those who, like the Jews, seek visible signs to demonstrate holiness may not lack an answer, and so that those who seek to be kindled and advanced toward better things by the examples of the saints may receive edification, I judge that certain events should be related—events which the Lord determined to be performed and revealed through him in order to stir and strengthen the sluggishness of our mind and, so to speak, our unbelief rather than our ignorance.

[Col. 0052C] **23.** There was a certain noble woman, the mistress of a household, in this Roman city. Out of devotion and zeal for religion, she was accustomed to make offerings, bring them to the church on the Lord’s Day, and present them to the supreme pontiff as a matter of ecclesiastical custom and familiarity. [Note: [Col. 0052D] This note concerns the ancient custom by which laypeople, including women, were accustomed to offer bread—and even wine—for communion. Hence Cyprian, in his book *On Works and Almsgiving*, reproves a rich woman because she came to the Lord’s Supper without a sacrifice and took part of the sacrifice that a poor person had offered. See Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 65.]

One day, when she approached in the customary order to receive communion from the hand of the apostolic pontiff, and the pontiff had offered her a portion of the Lord’s body, saying, “May the body of our Lord Jesus Christ benefit you for the remission of all sins and eternal life,” [Note: [Col. 0052D] John the Deacon, book II, chapter 41, reports different words: “May the body of our Lord Jesus Christ preserve your soul,” which come closer to the present formula for giving communion.] she smiled.

When the man of God saw this, he withdrew the sacred communion from her, placed it separately upon the altar, and entrusted it to a deacon to keep until all the faithful had communicated.

After the sacred mystery had been completed, [Col. 0052D] the blessed Gregory questioned her, saying: “Tell me, I ask, what arose in your heart when you smiled as you were about to receive communion?”

She replied: “I recognized that the little portion was from the same offering that I myself had made with my hands and presented to you; and when I understood that you had called it the body of the Lord, I smiled.”

Then the holy pontiff of the Lord addressed the people about this and urged them to entreat the Lord humbly, asking that, in order to strengthen the faith of many, he might show with bodily eyes what this woman’s unbelief ought to have perceived with the eyes of her mind and the lights of faith. [Col. 0053A]

When prayer had been offered, he rose from prayer together with the people and the same woman, went to the altar, and, while everyone looked on and pressed together to behold the heavenly spectacle, lifted the corporal cloth [Note: [Col. 0053D] Bollandus has “raises.” The corporal cloth, by which Christ’s body was wrapped and covered, is mentioned in the *Sacramentary*, in the ordination of a subdeacon: “The cloths that are on the lower covering are to be washed in another vessel; the corporal cloths in another. When the corporal cloths have been washed,” and so forth.] before everyone’s eyes. There he found, in the sight of the whole people and of the woman herself, a blood-stained part of a little finger, and said to the woman: “Learn, I say, or at least now believe the truth that testifies: ‘The bread that I give is my flesh, and my blood is truly drink’” (John 6:51).

But our Creator, who knew our weakness, by the power through which he made all things from nothing and fashioned for himself a body from the flesh of the ever-Virgin through the working of the Holy Spirit, converted bread and wine mixed with water into his flesh and blood, while their proper appearance remained, through the sanctification of his Spirit, in accordance with the Catholic prayer, for our restoration. [Note: [Col. 0053D] Here the doctrine of transubstantiation is clearly asserted in words, long before Paschasius Radbertus, whom ministers of the Calvinist sect falsely invent as its author.]

He then ordered all to pray to the divine power that it restore the most sacred mystery to its former form, so that it might be possible for the woman to consume it. This was done.

Thus the aforementioned woman, making great progress in sacred religion and faith, was consecrated through participation in the Lord’s sacrament. And all who had witnessed the event grew more fervent in divine love and orthodox belief.

**24.** A certain man, most noble according to his bodily lineage and most powerful according to the royal magnificence appropriate to his station, had obtained familiarity with the apostolic see through intermediaries. Having also been sufficiently instructed in the worship of God and the saints through frequent admonitions and letters sent by the blessed Gregory, he sent worthy gifts [Note: [Col. 0053D] Guss. has “gifts,” perhaps explaining what is meant by *exenia*. *Xenia* seems preferable. A *xenium* is a gift sent to a *xenos* (Greek ξένῳ, “to a guest”). The same reading is found in the letter formerly numbered 62, book V, now 65, book VI, both in the manuscripts and in the printed editions. In an old manuscript of the *Pastoral Care* at Beauvais, written in the tenth century, there is also this verse concerning Bishop Hugh: “You appoint *xenia*, O Christ; it is the work of your own hand.” Nevertheless, J. Sirmond, Mabillon, and other students of antiquity have often retained *exenium*, *exenia*, in the ancient writers they edited.] through energetic and devout messengers to the pontifical see, asking that relics of the blessed apostles and martyrs be sent to him.

The holy apostolic pontiff received his envoys honorably and without charge, kept them with him for some time, and, according to the ancient custom in such a matter, continually visited the memorials of the holy apostles and the cemeteries of the martyrs, celebrating Masses and consecrating relics in their honor. He always kept the aforesaid envoys as his companions. After he had completed the celebrations of the saints whose relics were requested, he divided into separate portions the consecrated cloths upon which he had celebrated the sacred rites and placed each individual piece in separate little boxes of boxwood [Note: [Col. 0054D] *Buxum* or *buxtula* signifies a box made of boxwood, in French *boîte*. Mabillon has *buxtis* in three manuscripts, while Mombritius has *buxetis*. Another manuscript has *buxis*, and two others *bustis*. Soon afterward, however, all the manuscripts call them *buxtulae* . . . . . Saint Odo, abbot, wrote in the published miracles of Saint Maurus, 15 January, chapter 4, that the relics of Saint Maurus had been enclosed in a wooden box. Bollandus. In the Beauvais manuscript the reading is *buxtis*.]

After securing them with the seal of his holy authority, he handed them over to the petitioners according to ecclesiastical usage. They received them with the reverence due, obtained and accepted the requested blessing, and departed joyfully on their way.

But after they had traveled for several days on their return journey, the one who was regarded as first among the others was overcome by a curiosity that was friendly to human weakness. He told his companions that they had foolishly undertaken so great a journey when they did not know what precious object they were carrying back to their lord.

As the conversation gradually increased and the companions’ suggestion grew stronger, they broke the seals of the apostolic dignity, opened the little boxes, and found in each one a small piece of cloth. [Col. 0054B]

They immediately returned to Rome in indignation and approached the archdeacon, complaining:

“Why,” they said, “has the apostolic lord so despised our lord, who had hoped to have acquired such favor with him? Why did he wish to mock him in this way and subject us to his dishonor and offense? We supposed that we were carrying from here the precious bones of apostles or martyrs, as was fitting for so great a man as our lord, requested from so great a see after such a long and sufficiently difficult journey. Yet we have been given small pieces of cloth, as though this kind of little cloth could not have been found among us.

“Unless cautious concern had come to our aid, enabling us to discover what we were carrying, and we had thus foolishly come to our lord, there is no doubt that we would have incurred danger to his honor and favor.”

The archdeacon reproved them with a moderate reprimand for bursting into such presumption that they had broken the apostolic seals. He urged them to return and deliver what they had received to their lord with due honor.

But they in no way accepted his admonitions. They came into the presence of Lord Gregory, and, when the matter had been explained, he bore their foolishness with the greatest patience. He ordered them to take part in the most sacred solemnities of the Mass.

When the appropriate point in his sermon was reached, he urged the people of God to implore the grace of the saints, asking that in this matter the Lord deign to reveal his power most openly, so that those who were less believing and ignorant might more clearly understand what faith could accomplish.

[Col. 0055A] After prayer had been offered, he took from the man who had violated the seals the knife with which he had done it. Taking one portion of cloth from the altar of the body of Saint Peter, he pierced and cut it through the middle. Immediately blood flowed from it and stained the entire portion. [Note: [Col. 0055D] The Beauvais manuscript has “the little portion.”]

When the envoys mentioned above and all the people saw this wondrous and hidden miracle of sacred faith, they fell prostrate upon the ground, worshiping the Lord and saying:

> “God is wondrous in his saints; the God of Israel himself will give strength and power to his people; blessed be God” (Psalm 67:36).

After silence had been made, among the other instructions in the faith, the blessed Gregory said to them—those who had previously thought little of these venerable relics:

“Know, brothers, that in the consecration of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, when offerings were made upon the most sacred altar for the sanctification of the relics, in honor of the apostles or martyrs of Christ to whom they were specially assigned, their blood, which was poured out for the name of Christ our Lord, always entered these cloths.”

After all who had witnessed the event had been built up in faith, he again secured the little boxes with his seal and handed them the incomparable gifts that fulfilled their desire. They returned with joy and reported everything in order to their lord, making him possess what he had desired.

He reverently received the precious protection of the saints and honorably deposited it in a venerable place, where the Lord deigns to perform more frequent miracles than in the Church of Saint Peter, for the praise and glory of his name, even to the present day. [Col. 0055B]

### 25

Nevertheless, this head of a household was exceedingly wealthy in material possessions at Rome, but extremely poor in religion. No less full of vices than of possessions, when his wife had displeased him, he divorced her, contrary to the commandment of our Savior. This matter could not remain hidden from blessed Gregory, since both the magnitude of the evil and the rank and condition (*magnatio*) of the persons readily revealed themselves. [Thus the German, Bec, Conques, and Moissac manuscripts, and Bollandus; Gussanville reads: “since both the magnitude of the evil and that of the persons.” Perhaps they disapproved of the barbarous word *magnatio*. It appears derived from *magnate*, as though meaning the status and condition of a magnate.]

With many most gentle admonitions, or rather with repeated and very earnest warnings of the terror of the divine judgment, indeed incessantly, blessed Gregory strove to persuade him to receive again in peaceful reconciliation his wife, pledged to him by the marriage compact, from whom he could not in any way be separated except by death or with the consent of both parties. [Bollandus reads “in peaceful reconciliation”; Gussanville omits both *pacatam* and *pactam*, the latter of which is read in our manuscripts, with an excellent sense: as one promised by the compacts of marriage.]

But the man, irreparably possessed by diabolical obstinacy, rejected his admonitions. Blessed Gregory, by apostolic authority, separated him from the Church under anathema unless he should repent.

He bore this excommunication with extreme displeasure and, piling sin upon sin, hired two magicians for money, according to an agreed price, so that they might exercise against the holy apostolic man, for the purpose of taking vengeance on him, an *apodixis* [demonstration, proof, specimen] of their art. [The word *apodixis* is Greek, ἀπόδειξις, “demonstration,” “proof,” or “specimen.”]

Since they did not know him by sight, one day, while blessed Gregory was proceeding according to custom to a procession, they stood at a distance beside the route and asked that he be pointed out to them. They were told that he was the one who alone rode with pontifical dignity and had before and behind him a body of ecclesiastical men.

When they looked at him, they suddenly caused his horse to be tormented by demons through their magic. At once blessed Gregory invoked the name of our Lord Jesus Christ and made the sign of the cross; by this he drove the demons away from the disturbed horse. Then, looking to one side, as soon as he caught sight of the magicians, they were struck blind and, seized by the same demons, fell backward. [A punishment more fitting for magicians: thus Paul struck the magician Elymas with blindness, Acts 13:10.]

From this the man of God understood that their wickedness had brought about the deed. When he ordered them to be brought before him, they were questioned and disclosed the whole sequence of events. The most blessed Pontiff replied to them:

“You ought to remain blind forever, lest, once seeing, you should attempt to return to your accustomed perversity. But, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, through the action of blessed Peter, may you be free from the torment of demons.”

Immediately cleansed of the demons and brought to faith, they were washed in the saving font; and although condemned to permanent blindness, by order of blessed Gregory they were thereafter supported by the Church’s alms.

### 26

A certain tyrant also inflicted great oppression, with almost unbearable persistence, upon the peace of the holy Roman Church, and most cruelly ravaged the properties and slaves belonging to it. Corrected in this matter through the admonition of the blessed Pontiff’s intermediaries, he burst into still greater madness, to such an extent that he set out to lay waste to the city.

As he approached, blessed Gregory went out to meet him and speak with him. He discovered that, by divine providence, such power was present in Gregory’s words that the tyrant, with the greatest humility, made satisfaction to the religious apostolic man and promised that thereafter he would be subject to him and a devoted servant of the holy Roman Church.

Later, when he had become ill and remained so until death, he asked for the prayer of the venerable pope. He received the reply that the Lord was still granting him a period for repentance, and that, in order to recover more fully, he should take the foods by which he had been nourished. Obeying these instructions, he recovered and thereafter lived more devoutly.

### 27

This same most perfect and God-pleasing priest, one day while proceeding through Trajan’s Forum, which is known to have been constructed with remarkable workmanship, saw the memorials of Trajan’s mercy. [In sacred authors, “to proceed” commonly means to go to church in solemn rite; this may be the sense here, for in that procession Gregory reached the tomb of blessed Peter, as the following makes clear. See the notes of the most learned Menard on the *Sacramentary*, at 8 September, where “to the procession” is read. Moreover, although what is said here of Trajan’s deliverance is accepted by Bollandus and some others, Baronius, under the year 604, no. 30 and following, and Bellarmine, Book 2, *On Purgatory*, chapter 8, reject it as a tasteless fable. We likewise refute them from the unquestionable testimonies of Saint Gregory in his Life written in French, both Book 2, chapter 7, no. 11, and Book 3, chapter 5, no. 7, and in the commentary on his Life.] Among them he discovered the memorable event that follows.

When that ruler of the world was setting out on campaign, surrounded by ranks of soldiers, he encountered there a very old widow, exhausted by age as well as by grief and poverty. She addressed him with tears and cries:

“Most merciful Prince Trajan, here are the men who have just killed my only son—the staff of my old age and my entire consolation. Although they wished to kill me along with him, they disdain even to render me any account for him.”

Since the matter required haste, he passed by quickly and said to her:

“When I return, tell me, and I will do you complete justice.”

But she replied:

“Lord, and if you do not return, what shall I do?”

At these words he stopped and ordered the accused to be brought before him. Nor, although everyone urged him to hasten the business, did he move from the spot until he had also arranged for the widow to be paid from the treasury what the legal enactments prescribed for the case. [One manuscript reads: “and finally, moved by inward clemency through the prayers and tears of the petitioners, in repentance for his deed—not merely by authority.”]

Finally, moved by inward clemency through the prayers and tears of those who repented of their deeds, he released from the praetorian chains those whom he had bound, not so much by his authority as by entreaty and gentleness.

Struck with compunction by this event, the venerable Pontiff began, amid tearful sighs and words of prayer, to turn over these prophetic and evangelical oracles:

“You, Lord, have said: ‘Judge the fatherless; defend the widow; and come, and let us reason together’” (Isaiah 1:17).

And elsewhere: “‘Forgive, and you shall be forgiven’” (Mark 6:27). “Do not, I beg you, forget that I, a most unworthy sinner, for the sake of the name of your glory and your most faithful promise, humbly beseech your mercy concerning the deed of this most devoted man.”

When he reached the tomb of blessed Peter, he prayed and wept there for a long time. Then, as though overcome by sleep, he was carried into ecstasy, in which he learned through a revelation that his prayer had been heard. Yet he deserved to be chastised, lest he should thereafter presume to ask such things concerning anyone who had died without holy baptism.

In this matter, although those of less perfect faith and the curious may ask certain questions, and those who faithfully believe the Truth, who says that what is impossible or appears impossible among human beings is easy with the Lord, may offer more extensive and salutary explanations, it nevertheless seems safer to venerate the judgment of divine mercy and power in this deed and to have it examined by no one. [This reading has been restored from the Beauvais and Jumièges manuscripts; earlier printed editions read “by perfectly faithful men,” which is also found in the Beauvais manuscripts and elsewhere.]

### 28

From a faithful and religious man, who, on account of his religion and usefulness, was especially familiar with this our most holy Father, we learned that, after his death, he had faithfully narrated the following to us. [This was Peter the Deacon, Gregory’s intimate associate and secretary, with whom he converses in the *Dialogues*. See Mabillon, first Benedictine century, p. 497. Beauvais and Jumièges simply read “was related,” omitting “to us.”]

When that same chosen vessel and dwelling place of the Holy Spirit was interpreting the prophet Ezekiel’s final vision, he had a curtain stretched between himself and this same notary. While Gregory remained silent for increasingly long intervals during his exposition, the minister pierced the curtain with his stylus. Looking through the opening that resulted, he saw a dove whiter than snow sitting upon Gregory’s head and holding its beak against his mouth for a long time.

Whenever the dove withdrew its beak from his mouth, the holy Pontiff began to speak, and the notary impressed the stylus upon the wax. But whenever the organ of the Holy Spirit was silent, his minister again applied his eye to the opening and saw the dove’s beak, as usual, being received by Gregory’s mouth, while Gregory held both his hands and his eyes raised toward heaven as if in prayer.

At last, when the same Spirit revealed the matter, the holy Pontiff learned of it. He became exceedingly sad and, by apostolic authority, commanded the man who had witnessed the divine miracle performed through him never to disclose it to anyone in any way during Gregory’s lifetime.

The witness kept the secret meanwhile. After the death of the most holy priest, however, compelled by the envy of certain men who disparaged the most blessed man, claiming that in the arrogance of presumption he had spoken such and such things about the mysteries of heavenly secrets, he faithfully related that he had seen all these things exactly as described.

[In earlier usage, “priests” did not mean every presbyter, but bishops who presided over cities. Those appointed over sacred affairs in villages and towns were called “presbyters.” The arrangement was almost the same as that observed by the learned J. Sirmond in his notes on Apollinaris Sidonius, Book 5, Letter 7: while the Roman republic still served idols, there were Flamines in the municipalities but priests in the provinces. Sirmond cites Pacatus in his *Panegyric* and Martian’s Novel 4, which says that a provincial priest was not permitted to have a slave woman as a wife.]

### 29

After the often-mentioned most reverend Pontiff had migrated to the Lord, an extremely severe famine raged not only in this Roman city but also throughout all the surrounding regions. His successor in the pontifical see opened the Church’s granaries to those who bought grain, but closed them to those whom blessed Gregory had ordered to be supported from ecclesiastical resources in monasteries, guesthouses, deaconries, and hospitals.

Driven by the poverty caused by famine, everyone began to trouble the apostolic man’s ears, saying:

“Lord apostolic, do not let your holiness allow those whom your predecessor, our father Saint Gregory, continually strove to feed, to perish from hunger.” [This title of honor, now accorded only to the pope, was formerly granted not only to other bishops but also to presbyters and even deacons. Ennodius, Book 5, Letter 13, writes to Hormisdas, who was only a deacon: “Your Holiness knows well.”]

The same man, angered by their cries, replied:

“If Gregory took care to receive all the peoples for the sake of his fame, we cannot feed everyone.”

Thus he allowed them to depart empty-handed.

When he repeatedly returned this answer to those who cried out to him, blessed Gregory appeared to him in a vision three times. Each time he gently reproved him for his detraction and his stinginess, or rather for his neglect of the poor, and admonished and chastised him.

But he neither inclined his heart to mercy, nor guarded his mouth against detraction, nor extended his hand in generosity. Therefore blessed Gregory appeared to him a fourth time, rebuked him horribly, and, threatening him, struck him on the head. Tormented by the pain, he died shortly afterward.

These brief remarks may suffice concerning the life and deeds of blessed Gregory.

As long as the orbit of this world revolves, however, his praiseworthy merit continually increases. Without doubt, the fact is attributed to his glory that this Roman city, together with his holy apostles, appears to endure through his prayers; that the Church of the English is continually made fruitful with a new offspring; that, through his teachings, many throughout the whole world are drawn away from sins and converted to the mercy of Christ; and that all good people, inflamed by his exhortations, eagerly seek the heavenly homeland.

After this most blessed Pontiff had ruled the see of the Roman and apostolic Church with the greatest glory for thirteen years, six months, and ten days, he was taken from this light and transferred to the eternal dwelling of the heavenly kingdom.

He was buried in the church of the blessed apostle Peter, before the sacristy, on the fourth day before the Ides of March, while our Lord Jesus Christ reigned—he who, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, lives and reigns as God forever and ever. Amen.

### From the same Paul the Deacon

During the calamity of the plague, blessed Gregory, who was then a deacon, was unanimously elected pope by all (Book 5, chapter 11, *History of the Lombards*).

When he had arranged the sevenfold litany, within the space of one hour, while the people were praying to God, eighty of them suddenly fell to the ground and breathed out their spirits.

The litany was called “sevenfold” because blessed Gregory divided the entire population of the City into seven groups to pray to God. In the first choir was all the clergy; in the second, all the abbots with their monks; in the third, all the abbesses with their communities; in the fourth, all the children; in the fifth, all the laymen; in the sixth, all the widows; and in the seventh, all the married women.

We omit saying more about blessed Gregory because, several years ago, with God’s help, we composed his Life, in which we described everything that needed to be said, according to the measure of our limited ability.

### From the same author

At this same time, blessed Gregory sent Augustine, Mellitus, and John, together with several other God-fearing monks, to Britain; through their preaching he converted the English to Christ.

### From the same author

In those same days, the wisest and most blessed Pope Gregory, bishop of the city of Rome (Book 4, chapter 1), after writing many other works for the benefit of the holy Church, also composed four books on the Lives of the Saints. He called the work a *Dialogue* because he published it while conversing with his deacon Peter.
