The aforementioned pope sent these books to Queen Theodelinda, for he knew that she was devoted to the faith of Christ and distinguished in good works. Through this queen also the Church of God obtained very great benefit. For the Lombards had seized almost all the dignities of the Churches while they were still held in the error of paganism. But the king, moved by her salutary entreaty, both held the Catholic faith and bestowed many possessions upon the Church; and he restored to dignity and honor the bishops who had been oppressed and cast down.

### In the same work

King Agilulf, after Maurition had been killed, returned to Pavia. Not long afterward, chiefly at the urging of his wife, Queen Theodelinda, as blessed Gregory had often admonished her in his letters, he made a most firm peace with that most holy man Pope Gregory and with the Romans.

### In the same work

Then blessed Pope Gregory migrated to Christ, when Phocas had been reigning for his second year in the eighth indiction. [It should read “the seventh.” Phocas began to reign in the sixth indiction, and his second year therefore corresponded to the seventh indiction. It is also established that Saint Gregory began to govern the Church in the ninth indiction, ruled for thirteen years and six months, and migrated to heaven in March, during the seventh indiction.]

Sabinian was appointed to the apostolic office in his place. The winter was exceedingly cold, and vines died in almost every region. The crops too, struck by blight, everywhere disappeared. The world ought indeed to have suffered hunger and thirst when, upon the death of so great a teacher, the poverty of spiritual nourishment and the aridity of thirst invaded human souls.

# THE LIFE OF SAINT GREGORY THE GREAT, WRITTEN BY JOHN THE DEACON IN FOUR BOOKS

## A Poem by John the Deacon to Pope John VIII

Receive, venerable Shepherd, the Roman triumphs;

receive the deeds of your holy Gregory.

He shone through deeds, words, and blessed writings,

as the golden-haired sun’s radiance shines throughout the world.

May he be your model, your honor, your mirror, your way, and your life forever,

if you desire to bear the eternal priesthood.

For a bishop who does not follow his footsteps

will not be a bishop before God, but rather a beast.

Hence the Psalmist sings of a man likened to horses,

sluggish among fools, who perishes beneath his honor.

We have given the saint both nocturnal and daytime song;

in verse we sing together of the renowned man.

Repay the favor, writer, preserving cola, commas, and points,

lest your page preserve a work full of errors.

[Thus the Bigot and Tours, or Saint-Martin, manuscripts and others; Mabillon’s edition reads “rendering cola, commas, and points.”]

[I have enjoyed playing with the varied order of the poetic field:

after prose has departed, playful poetry returns.

You grant these things to me, precious teacher Gregory,

you who give good things to your servants and no evil things.

Clothed, I began; naked, I spoke your duties.

Clothe me with your deeds and your fleeces.

And because the commerce of mortal flesh is lacking,

grant me the power to lie beneath your feet.]

[These final eight verses are omitted in the manuscripts of Saint Martin at Tours. All the poems are absent from Gussanville’s edition and the others, except Mabillon’s.]

## Preface

[The Bigot manuscript begins: “In the name of the most holy and undivided Trinity begins the prologue,” etc.]

To the most blessed and fortunate Lord John, bishop of the holy Catholic and apostolic Roman Church, John, the least of the deacons.

Recently, at the vigil of blessed Gregory, Roman Pontiff and apostle of the English people, [“Roman” is absent from the Colbert, Bigot, Jumièges, and Saint-Albin of Angers manuscripts,] while a reading concerning Paulinus, bishop of Nola, was being customarily performed, you were seen, moved by some divine inspiration, asking the venerable bishops why so great a Pontiff, who had composed the Lives of many saints, should have lacked an account of his own deeds in his own Church—especially since among both the Saxons and the Lombards, a people utterly hostile to him, his own deeds were everywhere celebrated.

When the venerable bishops replied that accounts were indeed possessed by both peoples, but only in the briefest form, you summoned my smallness also and ordered me to undertake the Life of this man from the archives of the holy apostolic see, striving to draw it out as fully as it was certain.

But while I, conscious of my own ineptitude, hesitated completely to compare myself with my predecessors and therefore with men wiser than I, who had described his life—though briefly—with pious effort and in a most beautiful style, you repeatedly and forcefully urged me to describe the Pontiff of the Roman See by the authority of the prelate of that same see, to whom Almighty God had unquestionably granted special power to approve or reject all writers.

Thus, compelled at last by such commanding authority, I had scarcely completed the first book of Gregory’s Life when, at the annual return of his vigil, your authority both approved and published it.

Therefore, made more eager to undertake the remainder, I gathered a few things from many, with you as my instigator, my teacher, my supporter, and my judge, and, with the Lord’s help, compressed them into four books.

Following the division of the same teacher, by which he had divided the book of the *Pastoral Rule* according to a fourfold arrangement, I likewise related in the first book of this work how Gregory came to the height of government; in the second I discussed how, having rightly attained it, he lived; in the third I set out how, living well, he taught; and in the fourth I concluded by showing with what consideration he recognized his own weakness each day, even while teaching rightly. [The Jumièges manuscript reads: “teaching perfectly.”]

Nor did I carefully compare one period with another. Rather, I fitted together similar matters [Jumièges and Bigot omit “similar”], because I was concerned to extract not so much when he had done something as how much he had done.

Although, in these books, I omitted many varied and memorable matters for the sake of brevity [the Angers manuscript reads: “for the sake of truth”], I do not remember having included anything that cannot be defended by the authority of ancient writers, except for those miracles which, having occurred in our own times, are celebrated by the living voices of many who still survive. [Printed editions read “of many who still survive”; all the manuscripts agree with the reading followed here.]

If, however, as often happens, anyone should think otherwise, let him return to the fullness of your archives and read through as many parchment volumes of this Father’s letters as the years he is proved to have lived. Since some of these letters, sent at different times, preserve differences of meaning, and since the same letters appear intact in some copies but diminished in part in others, according to the circumstances of persons, places, or times, let him observe this by reading them through to the end. Then, having recognized the clear truth, let him defend me with my admirers or accuse me with my detractors. Nevertheless, since I please your judgment, I presume that I shall forever please all who defend the truth.

I therefore ask that, just as I humbly obeyed your commands, so, through the prayers of blessed Gregory, I may mercifully be freed, through Jesus Christ our Lord, both in this age from the snares of rivals and in the future from the bonds of sinners. Amen.

[After the preface, the Bigot manuscript contains:

“Hereafter shall be written Gregory the pope’s life,

whose noble lineage is introduced here.”]

# BOOK ONE

A full account is given of the manner and virtues by which he rose to the pontificate.

## Table of Contents

1. Concerning the lineage of blessed Gregory.  
2. That he was *pheronymos* (φερώνυμος) [having a significant or fitting name]. [All the manuscripts have this heading; in its place most printed editions read: “Concerning the name that he bore, suited to his pursuits.” The index is absent in Bigot and Utica.]  
3. Concerning his education.  
4. The urban praetor is described. [Jumièges reads: “where he was urban praetor.” The word “where” begins all the headings in the five cited manuscripts: Royal, Colbert, Angers, and Tours as well as Jumièges.]  
5. He founded six monasteries in Sicily.  
6. Serving under abbots in the monastery of his own house, he later became abbot.  
7. He is unable to fast on Holy Saturday.  
8. He obtains from the Lord strength to fast.  
9. His mother Silvia regularly sends him legumes.  
10. He is tested twice by an angel of God and, on the third occasion, proves most generous.  
11. A brother who commits theft is tormented by a demon and freed by Gregory.  
12. A brother intending to flee is blinded and freed from the bites of a black dog. [Printed editions read “a fugitive”; the manuscripts more correctly read “about to flee,” for the monk did not flee but intended to do so.]  
13. A brother plotting flight is seized by a demon and freed by Gregory.  
14. The brothers’ hiding place is discovered through the immobility of the horses.  
15. Brother Justus is severely punished at death for a private possession. [Jumièges reads *pro peculari*; Angers and Tours, *pro peculiari*. The word *re* is not read in any of our manuscripts except the Royal manuscript, where it occurs between the lines.]  
16. His soul is freed from the torments of hell.  
17. Anthony, his sins forgiven, is ordered to die.  
18. Gerontius declares that he will die with certain brothers.  
19. Brother Merulus dreams that he is crowned with white flowers.  
20. John, healed by an apostle, is summoned by a dead man.  
21. He inquires about the boys of the English who are offered for sale.  
22. He is released to go to Britain for the conversion of the English.  
23. He is ordered to return by a bishop overwhelmed by three judgments.  
24. Through a locust he learns that he will return immediately.  
25. Dragged from the monastery, he is consecrated deacon.  
26. He is sent as *apocrisiarius* to Constantinople.  
27. He is earnestly asked to expound the Book of blessed Job.  
28. Disputing with Eutychius, he is recognized as victor.  
29. Eutychius’s book is committed to the flames by the Emperor.  
30. Dying, Eutychius holds the skin of his hand, saying that he will truly rise again in it.  
31. The nature of Gregory’s *apocrisiariate* is explained.  
32. A letter of Pope Pelagius is sent to Gregory.  
33. Maximianus and the brothers are saved from shipwreck.  
34. The city of Rome is flooded by the overflowing Tiber.  
35. The river Athesis is miraculously solidified.  
36. After a dragon has been killed with the beasts in the sea, the air is corrupted.  
37. As heavenly arrows bring disaster, Bishop Pelagius dies.  
38. Theodore is freed from a dragon and converted.  
39. Gregory is unwillingly elected to the pontificate.  
40. Wishing to avoid the pontificate, he secretly sends a letter to the emperor.  
41. He preaches repentance before the assembly.  
42. He arranges the sevenfold litany by districts.  
43. Eighty men are struck down by the plague.  
44. Fleeing from the City, he is revealed by a heavenly sign; brought back, he is consecrated Pontiff of the First See.  
45. It is clearly demonstrated that he did not wish for the supreme priesthood.  
46. The perfect quality of his discernment is indicated.  
47. He strove to be outside the world and outside the flesh, and to yearn toward the vision.  
48. He grieved that the groaning of his ruin was renewed.  
49. Receiving from the writings of Patriarch Anastasius, as it were, the rest of blessedness and salvation, he found a spring while thirsting and shade while burning with heat.  
50. He did not withdraw from the charity and spirit of the illustrious Abbot Andrew.  
51. He experienced the excellence of John the former consul’s goodness.  
52. He refused to reply to Leander, bishop of Seville, when letters were sent to him.  
53. He accepted the supreme priesthood with great anguish of heart.  
54. No human being is capable of investigating the judgments above.

## 1

Gregory was Roman by birth and a philosopher by training, the son of Gordian, a man of the highest distinction, and of blessed Silvia. He presided over the Roman see for thirteen years, six months, and ten days, during the reigns of the emperors Tiberius Maurice and Phocas. [Printed editions read “Tiberius Maurice.” Certainly the period of Tiberius Augustus does not belong to Gregory’s pontificate, since he did not begin it until Maurice was emperor; but Maurice too was called Tiberius.] [Tours consistently reads “Gorgian.” The phrase “Roman see” is absent from Tours, Royal, Utica, and Jumièges; Bigot adds it, while Angers and Colbert read “Roman Church.”]

Born from a senatorial family, he possessed a genealogy both most noble and most religious. Thus the fourth Felix, Pontiff of the apostolic see, a man of great reverence in the Church of Christ, who most beautifully built the basilica of the holy martyrs Cosmas and Damian on the Sacred Way beside the Temple of Romulus, as it remains visible to this day, was his great-great-grandfather. Blessed virgin Tharsilla, who, at the time of her death, heard the harmony of the heavenly promise and was granted to see Jesus Christ coming to receive her, was likewise his paternal aunt. (Bede, Book 2, chapter 1, *Ecclesiastical History of the English*; Gregory of Tours, Book 10 of the *Histories*; Book 4 of the *Dialogues*, chapter 16; *Homily* 38 on the Gospels.)

[Rather, the third Felix, as stated above in the Life written by Paul the Deacon and in his Life for 25 February. Bollandus, following Baronius, gives the fourth Felix in the *Martyrology* under 25 February and in volume 7 of the *Annals* under the year 581. We have discussed these matters in the commentary on Saint Gregory’s Life. The Bigot manuscript adds above the passage on Tharsilla: “of the heavenly procession,” doubtless because Christ came forth to meet her.]

## 2

Gregory elevated this line of twofold nobility through pious conduct and adorned it with honorable deeds, so that, by a kind of presage, he was called in Greek Γρηγόριος, which in Latin sounds as *more watchful*.

For by fulfilling through living works the righteous things he was going to teach, he demonstrated that he had kept watch over himself; and by explaining through teaching the righteous things he did, he is recognized to have kept watch not only for the Christians of his own time but also for those of the future.

## 3

Indeed, while still of immature age, he already possessed mature studies. [The printed editions read “in tender age,” against the manuscripts. Here *acerba* means “unripe,” as in Jeremiah 31:29–30 and Ezekiel 18:2, where grapes are called *acerbae*.] When he was about to hear what was unknown, he attached himself, as a most diligent investigator, to religious old men [Tours and Angers read “with religious dispositions”]; and, having gathered the seeds of instruction to be chewed over by his tenacious memory, he amassed what he would later declaim to the people with a honey-sweet tongue.

Finally, as a teachable young man [Utica, Bigot, Angers, Jumièges, and Royal read *docibilis*], when, having passed through the ordinary course of writing in his early childhood, he came to the fork of Pythagoras’s letter, he immediately abandoned the left branch with its worldly pleasure and began with all his strength to hasten toward the right with heavenly desire.

## 4

But while delaying his conversion for a longer time, thinking that he would serve Christ more safely if, under the appearance of an urban praetor, he served the world outwardly in appearance only, many concerns arising from that same world began to grow against him [thus the manuscripts and Bollandus; other printed editions read: “many concerns of that same world, however, grew against him”], so that he was no longer retained in it merely outwardly, as he had intended, but also in mind.

## 5

At last, after his father’s death, when he had obtained the freedom to dispose of his possessions, he built six monasteries in Sicily and filled them with sufficient numbers of brothers. He bestowed upon them as many estates as could provide, without want, for the daily sustenance of those serving God there (Gregory of Tours, Book 10 of the *History*, chapter 1).

## 6

He built a seventh monastery within the walls of the city of Rome, under the patronage of the holy apostle Andrew, beside the basilica of Saints John and Paul on the Clivus Scauri, on his own property.

There, after giving his silken robes radiant with gold and jewels, together with his other furnishings, to the use of the poor, [that is, after distributing them beforehand] he escaped naked from the shipwreck of this world. Taking on at last the monastic clothing he had long desired, he served by the regular path, first under the rule of the venerable Father Hilarion and then under Maximianus, with many brothers associated with him. [Baronius, under the year 581, no. 8, maintains that Saint Gregory had only Valentius or Valentinus as his superior, and that, once Hilarion is deleted, Maximianus, Pretiosus, and Probus succeeded Valentius. We refute this in Gregory’s Life. Bollandus notes that two manuscripts read *Laurionis* here and considers *Valentionis* the correct reading.]

Later, although he would have preferred to remain subordinate, when the brothers’ unanimous choice required it, he did not refuse to preside over them, as will appear in what follows.

## 7

His abstinence from food, his diligence in prayer and fasting, and his devotion to the study of sacred books were so great that, with his stomach weakened and afflicted, he plainly seemed scarcely able to remain alive.

For when he suffered a cutting of the vital faculties, which the Greeks call *syncope* (συγκοπή), and, assailed by frequent distress, was failing at moments through the hours and drawing near death, [the printed editions, with Colbert and against the other manuscripts, read: “was failing at moments and drawing near death,”] so that, unless the brothers frequently restored him with food, his vital spirit seemed likely to be completely extinguished, the day of Easter arrived.

Since he could not fast on the most sacred Saturday, on which everyone, even little children, fasts, he began to waste away more from grief than from illness (Book 3 of the *Dialogues*, chapter 33).

## 8

Immediately he summoned the most holy man Eleutherius, formerly superior over many near Spoleto and then a monk of his own monastery. From him, indeed, Gregory had heard that a dead man had been raised. He asked to go to the oratory and, with tears, devoted himself to prayer, asking that at least on that day strength might be granted him to fast.

A short while later, after completing his prayer and departing, he realized that such strength had entered his stomach that both food and illness were completely removed from his memory. He began to wonder within himself who he was and who he had been; and whenever his illness returned to his mind, he could recognize nothing of what he remembered in himself.

When his mind was occupied with the administration of the monastery, he entirely forgot his illness. If the illness returned to his memory, then, feeling himself so strong, he wondered whether he had not eaten.

Coming toward evening, he recognized that such strength remained with him that he could have extended his fast into the following day. [Printed editions add “if he had wished,” but this is absent from all our manuscripts.]

Yet, although he was wasting away from almost daily illness, he did not wish to grant his body any rest that might prevent him from praying, reading, writing, or dictating.

## 9

In the inner chambers of this holy monastery, the same man, Gregory, servant of almighty God, was fed on raw legumes by his mother Silvia. At that time she was living near the gate of the blessed apostle Paul, in a place called Cella Nova, where an oratory dedicated to her name has remained to this day, and where the renowned monastery of Saint Baba, confessor of Christ, appears to have been established—its praise being recorded in the sixth and seventh councils.

### 10

While he was writing certain things according to his custom, an angel of God found him and, in the guise of a shipwreck victim, tearfully begged him to have pity on him [Col. 0066B]. Gregory, moved by compassion from the depths of his heart, gave him six coins [Note: [Col. 0066D] Most manuscripts, here and below, consistently read *nomismatibus*, *nomismata*.] and ordered him to depart (Book II, chapter 23 below). Not long afterward, on that same day, the same shipwreck victim returned and declared that he had lost many things but had received only a few. Having received six coins from him in the same way, he went away rejoicing.

But on the third day he returned, and the shipwreck victim again demanded assistance in importunate tones. The most generous Father summoned the wardrobe keeper and ordered that six more coins be given him, but learned that nothing remained in the wardrobe from which the shipwreck victim could be comforted. He did not know what to do. The piety of his God-devoted heart was agitated, unable to endure leaving the neighbor’s misery empty-handed.

He questioned his wardrobe keeper again, asking whether perhaps he had any vessel or garment of any kind. He heard that absolutely nothing remained except his mother’s silver dish, which was customarily sent to him filled with legumes [Col. 0066C]. At once becoming more cheerful, he said: “Well then, brother, bring this, lest the poor man who seeks consolation go away sad.”

And so, when the dish had been brought, Gregory giving it quite cheerfully, the man who was thought to be poor gladly accepted it—no longer to return seeking aid, but to bestow it. From the time of this angelic visitation Gregory became known for such great miracles and such great virtues that to all who lived with him he was both an example and a source of fear. For he was thought to have presided over his monastery not alone, but in fellowship with the blessed apostle Andrew, as clear signs demonstrated.

### 11

For, to mention only a few things among many, one day he sent two brothers from there to buy something for the benefit of that monastery: one was younger and seemed more prudent, the other older and appointed as guardian of the younger [Note: [Col. 0066D] Bigot., Reg., Colb., and Gemet. read “guardian of the younger.”]. Both went forth. Of the money they had received, the one who had been sent as guardian secretly committed theft, without the other’s knowledge.

As soon as they had returned to the monastery and reached the threshold of the oratory, the one who had committed the theft was seized by a demon and fell. After the demon had been driven out by the monks who gathered, he was questioned by order of the abbot, to determine whether perhaps he had stolen something of what he had received [Col. 0067A] [Note: [Col. 0067D] The printed editions read “whether perhaps,” against all our manuscripts.]. He denied it and was again tormented. Released and questioned again, he denied it and was again tormented. Thus he denied it eight times and was tormented eight times. After the eighth denial, when Gregory questioned him, he confessed that he had stolen the money, and, prostrating himself before him, acknowledged that he had sinned [Note: [Col. 0067D] Utic. and some manuscripts read “how many coins.”]. Having received penance, he was never again approached by the demon.

### 12

On another occasion, while the brothers were resting at midday on the feast day of that same apostle, one brother suddenly became blind although his eyes were open. He began to tremble and to utter loud cries, by which he testified that he could not endure what he was suffering. The brothers gathered and saw him trembling and crying out with open eyes, estranged from those present and perceiving nothing that was taking place outside [Col. 0067B].

They lifted him in their arms and, by Gregory’s order, cast him down before the altar of the holy apostle Andrew; they themselves prostrated in prayer on his behalf. He immediately returned to himself and confessed that an old man had appeared to him and had sent a black dog to tear him apart, saying: “Why did you wish to flee from this monastery?”

And when he had been utterly unable to escape the dog’s bites, certain monks came and pleaded with that same old man on his behalf. The old man immediately ordered the dog to depart, and I returned to myself. He also often confessed afterward, saying that on the day when he had suffered these things he had been planning to flee from the monastery.

### 13

Another monk also secretly wished to leave the same monastery. When he had considered this in his mind, he wished to enter the oratory, but when the demon seized him he could not. The demon left him alone as long as he stood outside the oratory; but if he tried to enter, he was immediately handed over to the evil spirit and tormented.

When this had happened repeatedly, he finally confessed, upon Gregory’s inquiry, that he had wished to flee from the monastery. Through divine mercy he was cured over three days, together with the prayers of the brothers, so that afterward the evil spirit never again attempted to approach him.

### 14

On another occasion two brothers fled from the monastery of that Father. They had previously given the brothers some indications in conversation that, traveling down the Appian Way, they intended to make for Jerusalem [Note: [Col. 0067D] The manuscripts simply read this way. The editors added “by the road,” a phrase sufficiently implied.].

When they departed, they turned aside from the road and, finding secluded crypts near the Flaminian Gate, hid themselves inside them so that those following them could not find them at all.

When, toward evening, they were sought by Gregory’s order and could not be found among the community, some brothers mounted horses and followed them as they went out through the Metronian Gate, intending to pursue them along the Latin or Appian Way [Note: [Col. 0067D] Utic. and Bigot. read “Metrovi”; Andeg. and Metroni read “Metroni”; Boll. with Reg. and Colb. reads “Metrovii.”]. Suddenly they formed the plan that they ought to search for them outside the city on the Salarian Way.

Accordingly, they proceeded, turned aside from their route, and, finding them nowhere on the old Salarian Way, decided to return through the Flaminian Gate [Col. 0068A]. As they were returning, as soon as the horses came before those crypts in which the monks had hidden, they stopped. Though struck and urged on, they refused to move a step.

The riders realized that such an event could not be without a hidden meaning. They looked toward the crypts and saw that their entrances had been blocked in advance with masonry. Yet since their horses absolutely refused to go anywhere, they dismounted, removed the stones that had been laid at the mouths of the crypts, entered, and found the monks thrown prostrate on the ground in those dark hiding places.

They brought them back to the monastery. There, both the wonder of the miracle and the exhortation of the venerable Father Gregory so improved them that their brief departure from the monastery proved greatly beneficial to them.

### 15

On another occasion a certain monk named Justus, trained in the medical art, was accustomed to serve the blessed Gregory diligently and to keep watch over him during his frequent illnesses. This man, overtaken by bodily sickness, was brought to the point of death; during his illness his own brother, named Copiosus, attended him (Book IV of the Dialogues, chapter 55).

When the aforesaid Justus realized that he had reached the point of death, he informed his brother Copiosus that he had three gold pieces hidden away. This could not be concealed from the brothers. They investigated carefully, searched all his medicines, and found the same three gold pieces hidden in a medicinal preparation.

As soon as this was reported to Gregory, he could not bear calmly such a grave offense in a brother who had lived in common fellowship with him—especially since he had long before established a rule for that monastery that all the brothers should live in common, so that none of them was permitted to possess anything as private property.

Then Gregory, struck by profound grief [Note: [Col. 0068D] Utic., Bigot., Gemet., Andeg., and Colb. read “compelled.”], began to consider both what he should do for the dying man’s purification and what provision he should make as an example to the living.

He therefore summoned to himself Pretiosus, the monastery’s superior, and said:

“See that none of the brothers joins him as he lies dying, nor does he receive words of consolation from the mouth of any of them. But when, at the point of death, he asks for the brothers, let his own brother by blood tell him that, because of the solidi he secretly possessed, he has been abhorred by all the brothers [Note: [Col. 0068D] The printed editions read: “because of the gold pieces he kept hidden.”]. Thus, at least in death, let the bitterness of his guilt pierce his mind and cleanse him of the sin he committed.

When he has died, do not place his body with the bodies of the brothers. Instead, dig a grave for him in some dung heap and throw his body into it. Then throw upon him the three gold pieces he left behind, while all of you cry out together: ‘May your money be with you unto perdition!’ And so cover him with earth.” [Note: [Col. 0068D] Bigot., Utic., Andegav., Reg., Colb., and Gemet. omit “and throw upon him the three gold pieces,” etc., and read “throw the body into it.” Jerome, cited in the note to Letter 24 of Book XII, relates a similar occurrence.]

In both matters the most resourceful Father Gregory wished to benefit one party: the first instruction the dying man, and the second the living. He wished the bitterness of death to loosen that man from his guilt, and the utter condemnation of such avarice to prevent the others from becoming involved in such things and to keep them from sin [Col. 0069A] [Note: [Col. 0069D] Most printed editions read: “to terrify them and keep them from guilt.” Bollandus agrees with the manuscripts we follow. Reg. and Colb. omit “and to keep them from guilt.”].

This was done accordingly. When that monk reached the point of death and anxiously sought to be commended to the brothers, none of the brothers approached him or attempted to speak with him. His blood brother disclosed to him why he was hated by everyone.

As soon as he heard this, he groaned bitterly over his guilt and, in that very sorrow, departed from the body. He was buried as Gregory had ordered.

But all the brothers, disturbed by the same judgment, began individually to bring forward into the common fund every last possession, however insignificant or worthless, which they had always been permitted by the rule to keep. They were deeply afraid that there might be something among their possessions for which they could be reproached.

### 16

When thirty days had passed after the brother’s death, Gregory’s heart began mercifully to feel compassion for him. With deep sorrow he weighed his punishments and sought whether there might be some remedy for his deliverance [Col. 0069B].

Then he summoned to himself the same Pretiosus, the superior of his monastery, and said sadly:

“It is a long time since our deceased brother Justus has been suffering in the fire. We ought to show him some charity and, insofar as we can, offer him assistance so that he may be delivered. Go, therefore, and from this day strive to offer the sacrifice for him for thirty continuous days, so that no day at all may pass on which a saving offering is not sacrificed for his absolution [Note: [Col. 0069D] Bollandus, together with all the manuscripts, reads this way; other printed editions have “so that the saving offering may not be omitted.” The man called here the monastery’s superior is called οἰκονόμος (*oikonomos*, “steward”) in the Dialogues translated into Greek by Zacharias. Observe here the origin of the thirty Masses for the dead.].”

He immediately departed and obeyed the instructions.

While Gregory was arranging this and was not counting the days that had passed, the same brother who had died appeared one night in a vision to his brother Copiosus [Note: [Col. 0070D] In Turon. and Utic. the man called here Copiosus is called Speciosus; earlier, however, the same codices read Copiosus.].

When Copiosus saw him, he asked: “What is it, brother? How are you?”

He replied: “Until now I was suffering badly, but now I am well, because today I received communion.”

Copiosus immediately went to the monastery and reported this to the brothers. The brothers carefully counted the days and discovered that it was the very day on which the thirtieth offering for him had been completed. Copiosus did not know what the brothers, at Gregory’s direction, were doing for him, and the brothers did not know what Copiosus had seen.

Thus, at one and the same time, when he recognized the offering and they heard the dream and learned that it was the thirtieth day, the agreement between the vision and the sacrifice made the matter plainly clear: the brother whom Gregory had allowed to die under the sentence of punishment had been freed from his suffering by the saving offering (Book IV of the Dialogues, chapter 55).

### 17

Since I have already touched briefly on how that venerable Father was a source of fear to the brothers, I think it appropriate to indicate briefly how they advanced through his example.

A certain brother in the same monastery, named Antonius, clung devotedly to the blessed Gregory. Instructed by the words and examples of so great a Father, he yearned for the joys of his heavenly homeland with many daily tears.

As he searched the sacred Scriptures most diligently, with great ardor of desire and under Gregory’s guidance, he sought in them not words of knowledge but tears of compunction, so that through these his mind, set aflame, might grow fervent and, abandoning lowly things, fly through contemplation to his heavenly homeland [Note: [Col. 0070D] Bollandus reads this way with all our manuscripts. Other editions have “to the region of the heavenly homeland, flying through contemplation.”].

One night he was told in a vision: “Be ready, and depart, because the Lord has commanded it” [Note: [Col. 0070D] The printed editions read: “because the Lord has ordered you to depart.”].

When he said that he had no provisions for making the journey, he immediately heard this reply: “If the matter concerns your sins, they have been forgiven.”

When he had heard this once but still trembled with great fear, he was warned in the same words on another night. After five days he was seized by fever and died, while all the brothers prayed and wept (Book IV of the Dialogues, chapter 47).

### 18

In the same monastery there was a brother named Gerontius. When he had been brought low by a serious bodily illness, he saw in a nocturnal vision men dressed in white and of extraordinarily radiant appearance descending from above into that very monastery.

As they stood before the bed of the man lying there, one of them said: “We have come for this purpose: to send certain brothers from Gregory’s monastery into military service.” Then, ordering another, he added: “Write down Marcellus, Valentinianus, Agnellus, and the others, whose names I do not know” [Note: [Col. 0070D] Most printed editions read: “now I do not remember.”].

When this had been completed, he added: “Write down this man himself, who is watching us.”

From this vision Gerontius became certain of what would happen. When morning came, he informed the brothers how many and which men from that monastery were going to die, and that he himself would immediately follow them [Col. 0070C].

On another day, when the aforesaid brothers began to die, they followed one another into death in the same order in which they had been named in the list. Finally Gerontius himself died, he who had foreseen the death of those brothers.

### 19

There was another brother in the same monastery named Merulus, intensely devoted to tears and almsgiving as a result of the teaching of the venerable Gregory. Psalmody scarcely ever ceased from his mouth, except when he was giving food to his body or surrendering his limbs to sleep.

In a nocturnal vision he saw a crown of white flowers descending from heaven onto his head. Soon afterward he was seized by bodily illness and died with great peace of mind and cheerfulness.

Fourteen years later, when Peter—who had presided over that monastery during the pontificate of this Gregory—wished to prepare a burial place for himself at Merulus’s tomb, such a fragrance of sweetness poured forth from the tomb of the brother Merulus that it seemed as though the perfumes of every kind of flower had been gathered there.

From this it was plainly evident that what the disciple of so great a Father had seen in the nocturnal vision was true (Dialogues, Book IV, chapter 47) [Col. 0071A].

### 20

There was also in the same monastery a young man named John, of great natural ability. Through the sweetness of understanding and humility and the gravity of his conduct, he surpassed his years, with Gregory pressing him on [Note: [Col. 0071D] Mabillon, Gussanville, and others read this against the manuscripts: “who, with Gregory teaching, surpassed his age in understanding, humility, and gravity of conduct.” Bollandus agrees with the manuscripts, except that he reads “with Gregory teaching” for “with Gregory impending.”].

When John fell ill and was brought to the point of death, the blessed apostle Andrew appeared to him in a nocturnal vision in the guise of an old man. He touched him with a staff and said: “Rise. You will certainly not die from this illness now; but be ready, because you will not remain here for a long time.”

Although the physicians had already despaired of him, he was suddenly healed and recovered. He reported what he had seen and, as I have said, presented himself in God’s service for two years beyond the years of his age.

After two years had passed, a certain brother died and was buried by Gregory and the brothers in the cemetery of that monastery. When everyone had departed, John found himself alone. As he later reported to Gregory and the brothers, pale and trembling, the brother who had been buried called him from the tomb.

The end that followed soon afterward also demonstrated the truth of this. For ten days later, having been seized by fever, John died and followed the one who had called him [Note: [Col. 0071D] Mabillon and Gussanville read: “having been seized, he was released from the flesh.” Both, however, note in the margin the manuscript reading, as they have also done elsewhere above and below. Gussanville’s edition does not appear to differ from Mabillon’s.].

But because it would be lengthy, and because many things remain that can be proclaimed about the holiness of this man with reliable testimony—things that I have learned from the accounts of our elders or from the writings of earlier authors—I have decided to insert them here.

### 21

One day, when recently arrived merchants had displayed many goods for sale in the marketplace of the city of Rome and many people had flocked together from every direction to buy, Gregory, a man most worthy of God, happened to pass by.

Among the other goods he saw boys for sale, white of body, exceedingly handsome in appearance, attractive in face, and conspicuous for the brightness of their hair [Col. 0071C]. He asked the merchant from what country he had brought them.

The merchant replied: “From the island of Britain, whose inhabitants all shine with a similar whiteness of face.”

Gregory said: “Are those islanders Christians, or are they still entangled in pagan errors?”

The merchant replied: “They are not Christians; they are ensnared in pagan traps.”

Then Gregory groaned bitterly and said: “Alas! What sorrow! How splendid are the faces now possessed by the prince of darkness, while such an appearance of the forehead bears a mind empty of the grace of God” [Note: [Col. 0071D] Andeg. reads “for the sake of the forehead’s appearance”; Gemet. and Big. read “handsome in the appearance of their forehead”; Utic. reads “handsome in the grace of their forehead.”].

Again he asked what the people were called. The merchant replied: “They are called Angles.”

“But well named Angles,” he said, “because they have angelic faces, and such people ought to be fellow citizens of the angels in heaven.”

He then asked what the province itself was called. The merchant replied: “Those provincials are called Deiri.”

And Gregory said: “Well named Deiri, because they are to be rescued from wrath (*de ira*) and summoned to the grace of Christ.”

He said: “What is the king of that province called?”

The merchant replied: “Aelle.”

And Gregory, playing on the name, said: “Well named Aelle, because ‘Alleluia’ ought to be sung in those regions in praise of the Creator” [Note: [Col. 0072D] Andeg. and Utic. read “Alle”; for the praise of God the Creator ought to be sung in those regions.].

(Bede, *History of the English*, Book II, chapter 1.)

### 22

Immediately he approached Benedict, the pontiff of the apostolic see, and began earnestly to request that he send some ministers of the word to Britain. When he learned that no one was willing to go, he did not hesitate to offer himself, provided that the pontiff would grant him permission.

Although Benedict allowed Gregory—who desired of his own accord to depart—to go only after great hesitation on the part of the entire clergy and people, he nevertheless permitted him to leave, praying that divine assistance might grant him success [Col. 0072B].

### 23

The Romans, greatly disturbed by his absence, formed a deliberate plan. They divided themselves into three groups at the places beside the road along which the pontiff was going to proceed to the basilica of blessed Peter. In a crowd they addressed him as follows [Note: [Col. 0072D] Big. reads: “They addressed him: ‘Hey, apostolic one, what have you done? You have offended Saint Peter and destroyed Rome, because you let Gregory go.’”]:

“You have offended Peter; you have destroyed Rome, because you let Gregory go.”

Thoroughly terrified by these words, the pope immediately sent messengers to recall Gregory, the man of God. Gregory himself had already predicted to his companions that this would happen.

### 24

After they had completed a journey of three days [Note: [Col. 0072D] Bigot. writes above the passage: “that is, after the expense had been incurred.”], they happened to turn aside to a certain place to rest. While the others were resting, Gregory was reading.

A locust came upon him and compelled him to cease reading for a little while. From consideration of its name, it taught him that he ought to remain in that place [Col. 0072C]. It is said that he then remarked: “It may be called a locust (*locusta*), as if to say, ‘Stay in this place’ (*loco sta*)” [Note: [Col. 0072D] The words enclosed in parentheses occur in all printed editions, in Paul the Deacon, and in only one of our manuscripts, Colb.].

Immediately he urged his companions on and strove to proceed more quickly. But the apostolic messengers arrived first. Although he was deeply saddened, he was nevertheless compelled to return to the administration of his own monastery.

### 25

Finally, when Benedict, the venerable pontiff, saw Gregory ascending to higher things through the degrees of virtue, he forcibly drew him away from the repose of his monastery and elevated him to the office of the ecclesiastical order. He consecrated him as the seventh levite—deacon—to assist him.

In this office the venerable levite Gregory flourished in such great humility and served with such great diligence that, in the ministry of the ecclesiastical hierarchy, he seemed in some way to equal the divine angels—not only in the splendor of his habit, but also in the brightness of his praiseworthy conduct [Col. 0072D].

### 26

Not long afterward Pelagius, the bishop, sent him to the city of Constantinople on ecclesiastical business. Although he was living in an earthly palace, he did not abandon his commitment to heavenly life.

Many brothers from his monastery followed him, bound to him by fraternal love. This can be seen to have happened through divine providence: by their example he was tied, as though by an anchor rope, to the calm shore of prayer; and while he was tossed amid the continual whirlwinds of secular affairs, he could flee to their fellowship as to the shelter of the safest harbor [Note: [Col. 0073D] All our manuscripts read “to the harbor, shores, and refuges.” Mabillon also found this reading in his manuscripts. Our reading, which is that of all the editors, agrees with Saint Gregory’s letter to Leander, from which this passage was copied.].

Although that office, having drawn him away from the monastery, had also extinguished the former repose of his life through the sword of its occupations, nevertheless, through the daily conversation afforded by their diligent reading, they kindled in him a daily impulse toward compunction (Bede, *History of the English*, Book II, chapter 1).

### 27

Through the fellowship of these men he was not only protected from earthly assaults but also increasingly inflamed for the practices of heavenly life.

For, earnestly entreated by those same brothers—and especially compelled by Leander, bishop of Seville, who had come to Constantinople at that time as an envoy on behalf of the affairs of the Visigoths [Note: [Col. 0073D] On Leander, see what we said in the letter prefixed to the *Moralia*.]—he was persuaded to explain the book of blessed Job, which was wrapped in many mysteries (Letter on the exposition of blessed Job, chapter 1).

He could not refuse a work that fraternal love imposed upon him as something that would be useful to many. Instead, he explained with marvelous skill, through three modes of understanding, how that book should be understood according to the literal sense, how it should be referred to the mysteries of Christ and the Church, and in what sense it should be applied to each of the faithful [Note: [Col. 0073D] Turon. reads “through the sequence of thirty-five books”; in Bigot. these words have been relegated to the margin.].

Yet in these explanations he discussed virtues and vices in such a way that he seemed not merely to expound them in words but also, in a certain manner, to demonstrate them in visible or tangible forms. Hence there is no doubt that he had attained the perfection of those very virtues whose progress he was able to describe so effectively.

### 28

Moreover, while the venerable levite Gregory was established in that imperial city, with the help of the grace of Catholic truth he crushed a new heresy concerning the state of our resurrection at the very beginning of its emergence [Note: [Col. 0073D] The printed editions, together with the manuscript Colb., read “with the help of the grace of our Redeemer.” Mabillon and Gussanville mistakenly have *attribuit* (“attributed”) instead of *attrivit* (“crushed”).] (Book XIV of the *Moralia*, no. 72 and following; Bede, *History of the English*, Book I, chapter 1).

[Note: [Col. 0074D] A certain pseudo-monk named Hierax held almost the same error. He taught that this flesh will not rise, but another in its place, and that this one dissolves into the earth, says the author of the *Life of St. Epiphanius* and his disciple, in no. 27 of that Life. Epiphanius refuted him both by a miracle and by a most learned dissertation from Sacred Scripture.]

Eutychius, bishop of that city, had composed a book on the resurrection of the dead and taught as dogma that our body in the glory of that resurrection would be intangible, subtler than winds and air.

When Gregory heard this, he proved, both by an argument from truth and by the example of the Lord’s resurrection, that this doctrine was wholly contrary to orthodox faith. For Catholic faith holds that our body, raised up into the glory of immortality, will indeed be subtle through the effect of spiritual power, but tangible through the reality of its nature, in accordance with the example of the Lord’s body. Of that body, raised from the dead, he himself says to the disciples:

“Touch and see, because a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see that I have” (Luke 24:39).

When Gregory had produced this testimony of evangelical truth, Eutychius said:

“The Lord did this for that reason: to remove from the hearts of the disciples their doubt concerning the resurrection.”

Gregory said to him:

“What you maintain is exceedingly strange: that our doubt should arise from the very thing by which the hearts of the disciples were healed of doubt. For what could be said more absurdly than that we should doubt the reality of his flesh because of the very thing by which his disciples were restored to faith from every doubt? If it is maintained that he did not possess what he displayed, then by the very means through which the faith of his disciples was confirmed, ours is destroyed.”

Eutychius said:

“He possessed a tangible body, which he displayed; but after he had confirmed the hearts of those who touched him, everything in the Lord that could be touched was transformed into a certain subtlety.”

To this Gregory replied:

“It is written: ‘Christ, rising from the dead, dies no more; death shall no longer rule over him’ (Romans 6:9). If, then, anything in his body could have been changed after the resurrection, contrary to Paul’s truthful statement, the Lord returned to death after the resurrection. Who would presume to say such a thing, unless he denied the true resurrection of his flesh?”

Then Eutychius objected, saying:

“Since it is written: ‘Flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God’ (1 Corinthians 15:50), how can it be believed that flesh will truly rise?”

Gregory replied:

“In sacred Scripture, ‘flesh’ is spoken of in one way according to nature and in another way according to guilt or corruption.

Flesh is spoken of according to nature, as it is written: ‘This now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh’ (Genesis 2:23); and: ‘The Word became flesh and dwelt among us’ (John 1:14).

But flesh is spoken of according to guilt, as it is written: ‘My spirit shall not remain in these human beings, because they are flesh’ (Genesis 6:3) [Col. 0074C]; and as the Psalmist says: ‘He remembered that they are flesh: a spirit that goes and does not return’ (Psalm 77:39).

Hence the disciple Paul also said: ‘But you are not in the flesh, but in the spirit’ (Romans 8:9). He did not mean that those to whom he was sending letters were not in the flesh; rather, because they had overcome the passions of carnal desires, they were already free through the power of the spirit and were not in the flesh.

Therefore, when the apostle Paul says, ‘Flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God’ (1 Corinthians 15:50), he wished ‘flesh’ to be understood according to guilt, not according to nature. He immediately showed that he was speaking of flesh according to guilt when he added: ‘Nor will corruption possess incorruption.’

In that heavenly glory, therefore, flesh will exist according to nature, but it will not exist according to the desires of passion, because, having conquered the sting of death, it will reign in eternal incorruption.”

After hearing this, Eutychius immediately replied that he agreed. Nevertheless, he still denied that a tangible body could rise. In the little book he had written on the resurrection, he had also included Paul’s testimony:

“Whatever you sow will not be made alive unless it first dies; and what you sow is not the body that is to be, but a bare grain” (1 Corinthians 15:36–37).

He hastened to use this to show that the flesh—or even anything tangible—would not be present, since the holy Apostle, speaking of the glory of the resurrection, had not said that the body that was to be is sown, but rather a bare grain.

To this Gregory replied:

“When the apostle Paul says, ‘You sow not the body that is to be, but a bare grain,’ he indicates what we see: namely, that the grain is born with stalk and leaves, but is sown without stalk and leaves.

Thus, in speaking of the increase of resurrection glory, he did not say that something which the seed possessed would be absent, but that something which it did not possess would be present. You, however, while denying that the true body will rise, do not say that what was lacking will be present; rather, you say that what was present will be lacking” [Col. 0075B].

### 29

Gregory the Roman deacon and Eutychius the Constantinopolitan bishop were then drawn into a prolonged dispute over this matter and began to withdraw from one another in bitter hostility [Note: [Col. 0075D] The manuscripts read *simultatione*, whereas the editors read *simultate*. In the *Moralia*, Book XIV, no. 74, where this matter is also reported, the reading is likewise *simultatione*, as also in Book I, letter 2, and elsewhere.].

Then the emperor Tiberius Constantine, of blessed memory, received both men privately [Note: [Col. 0075D] All printed editions corruptly read “Constantinopolitan” for “Constantine,” which is the reading of all the manuscripts of both the *Moralia* and John the Deacon. The sole ruler of the Roman Empire was not then called “emperor of Constantinople”; Tiberius Augustus was surnamed Constantine.] and learned what disagreement existed between them. Carefully weighing the arguments of both sides, he destroyed the same book that Eutychius had written on the resurrection, together with its arguments [Note: [Col. 0075D] Bigot. writes above the passage: “affirmations.”], and decided that it should be burned.

After they had left that most pious emperor, both men, exhausted by the conflict of their very lengthy debate, fell ill at the same time and took to their beds.

### 30

While Gregory was burning with a very severe fever, Eutychius, struggling with death, held the skin of his hand before everyone and said:

“I confess that we shall all rise in this flesh.”

After this confession of the Catholic faith, he died. Once he was dead, since almost no one remained who followed his teaching, Gregory refrained from pursuing the matter he had begun, lest he seem to be casting words into ashes.

### 31

If anyone wishes to know more fully with what authority he fulfilled the ministry of his *apocrisiariate*, how greatly he was revered by the emperors, and with what solicitude he repeatedly arranged for afflicted Italy to be aided, let him read through the letters sent to him by his predecessor, Pope Pelagius, concerning the many needs of the Church of God. These letters have until now been preserved with the greatest care in the archives of the holy apostolic see.

From among their multitude I insert one here, so that both the character of that ministry and the content of the others that follow may be understood. It runs as follows:

[Col. 0076A] **32.** “Bishop Pelagius to his beloved son Gregory, the venerable deacon. We have taken care to communicate to you everything that was necessary through Honoratus the notary. We have sent him to your Beloved together with our brother and fellow bishop Sebastian, so that, since he has been with the illustrious man, Lord Decius the patrician, in those regions as far as Ravenna until now, he himself may strive by his report to inform you about everything; or, if you judge anything necessary, may be able to bring it to the emperor’s attention. For such great calamities and tribulations have been inflicted upon us by the treachery of the Lombards, contrary to their own oath, that no one could adequately report them. You will be able to learn from his own report how we received the aforesaid brother Sebastian, and with what affection he was held among us, at your suggestion. [Col. 0076B] He also promised us that he would bring the needs and dangers of all Italy to the attention of our most pious lord emperor.

“Therefore speak and deliberate together about how you may quickly come to the aid of our dangers, for the commonwealth here has been so hemmed in that, unless God inspires the heart of our most pious ruler to bestow upon his servants the mercy innate in him, [Note: In Andegav., Utic., Bigot., and Gemet., “has commanded.”] and deigns to grant, besides that *diacoposis* [or *diacopiosis*], either one master of soldiers and one commander, we shall be left in utter distress. For the Roman territories appear to have been deprived of every defense, and the exarch writes that he can provide us no remedy, since he declares that he is not even able to suffice for guarding those regions. Therefore may God command him to come swiftly to the aid of our dangers, before the armies of that most wicked people prevail—God forbid—and seize the places that are still held by the commonwealth.

“Meanwhile hasten, with God’s help, to send the priest back to us, since he is plainly altogether necessary both in your monastery and for the work over which we appointed him. Given on the fourth day before the Nones of October, in the third indiction.” (*Council*, vol. V, letter 3.)

[Note: In Gemet. and Bigot., “of November.” Gussanville, in the margin, instead of the third indiction notes the sixth indiction, which is found in none of our manuscripts.]

[Note: The printed editions, together with Reg., against the opposition of the other manuscripts, read “in addition to that *diacoposin*.” Utic. has “in addition to all that *diacop*.” In this codex and in Bigot. it is noted that the word *diacoposin*, or *diacopiosin*, means the public treasury. Peter Damian seems to have understood it in this way, *Book VII, Letter 3*: “He who incurs the crime of embezzlement is compelled to return what he took into the *diacoposin*.” Bollandus teaches that it means the same as “division,” from Greek **διακόπτω**, “I cut apart.” Cange understood *diacoposis* as trouble or distress, from **κοπέω**, “I weary.” Both were misled by the editors’ printed reading, “and in addition to that *diacoposin*,” whereas nearly all manuscripts read “and in addition to that,” as though meaning “and besides that.” We therefore judge that *diacoposin*, or *diacopiosin*, may more suitably be understood as the treasury and money intended to be disbursed for military service, derived perhaps from **διά**, “because of,” and **κόπος**, “labor.”]

**33.** The Sicilian Maximianus, who later became bishop of Syracuse, was at that time in charge of the monastery of his own which Pope Pelagius mentions here. He came with the brethren to the venerable levite Gregory, who was laboring in the palace of that royal city over ecclesiastical affairs, in order to visit him (*Book III of the Dialogues*, chapter 36). As he was returning by sea to Rome and to the monastery entrusted to him, he was caught by an exceedingly violent storm in the Adriatic Sea and, through an immeasurable and extraordinary miracle, experienced toward himself and all who were with him both the anger and the favor of almighty God.

For when the waves, raised by the violence of the winds, raged as though to bring about their death, the rudder having been lost, the mast was cut down, the sails were cast upon the waves, and the entire vessel, shaken by the enormous waves, had been disjointed from all its structure. Thus, with the cracks gaping open, the sea entered and filled it up to the upper planks, so that it seemed that not the ship was among the waves, but that the waves were already inside the ship.

Then those who were in the same ship, now disturbed not merely by the nearness of death but by the sight of death itself, all gave one another the kiss of peace, received the body and blood of the Redeemer, and commended themselves individually to God, asking him kindly to receive their souls, whose bodies he had delivered to such a dreadful death.

But almighty God, who had wonderfully terrified their minds, preserved their lives even more wondrously through the merit of his servant Gregory, for whose special love they had come. For eight days that same ship, full of water up to the upper planks, continued along its course and floated. On the ninth day it was brought into the harbor of the fortress of Chotronensis. [Note: Other manuscripts have “of Cortona.” Cortona is an ancient city of the Bruttians, on the Ausonian Sea, now called Crotona in Further Calabria.]

All who had been sailing with the aforesaid venerable Maximianus came out unharmed. When he too had disembarked after them, the ship immediately sank into the depths of the same harbor, as though, when they had left it, it had been deprived of the weight that kept it afloat. The vessel that, full of people, had carried water in the open sea and had floated, after Maximianus and the brethren had departed, was unable either to carry water or to float in the harbor without people. Thus almighty God showed that, through the merit of Gregory, whom the brethren had visited, he had held this vessel laden with people in his own hand, since, emptied of people, it could not remain upon the waters.

**34.** After the venerable levite Gregory had returned to Rome, some time having passed, the river Tiber overflowed its bed in so great a flood and rose so high that its waters poured over the city walls, occupied vast districts within the city, and destroyed many monuments of ancient buildings. [Note: Bigot., Colb., Reg., and Gemet. read “walls.” Paul the Deacon does so as well.] It also violently overturned ecclesiastical granaries, in which several thousand *modii* of grain perished.

**35.** At that time, as the same Gregory relates (*Book III of the Dialogues*, chapter 19), the river Athesis, having risen near the city of Verona, came to the church of the blessed martyr and bishop Zeno. Although the doors of that church were open, the water did not enter it at all. It continued to rise little by little until it reached the windows of the church, which were near the roof. There the water stood and closed off the church door, as though that liquid element had been changed into the solidity of a wall. [Note: Another reading is “altered.”]

Many people were inside, but the whole church was surrounded by such a mass of water that they had no way to leave, and they feared that they would perish there from hunger and thirst. They came to the church door and drew water to drink from the water that had risen as high as the windows; yet inside the church [Note: In the printed editions, except for Bollandus, *ut* is lacking; it is found in all the manuscripts we have examined.] the water did not flow in at all.

Standing before the door, it served both to display to everyone the merit of the martyr and to provide assistance; yet it was not water for occupying the space within. This miracle may rightly be considered similar to the miracle of the Babylonian fire, which neither touched the clothing of the three young men nor failed to burn their bonds (Dan. 3).

**36.** At that time also an innumerable multitude of serpents, together with a great dragon as large as a beam, descended through the channel of the Tiber into the sea. But the suffocated beasts immediately fell upon the shore amid the salty waves of the greatly turbid sea, and by their rotting corrupted the entire air (Gregory of Tours, *History*, book X, chapter 1).

**37.** Immediately afterward there followed the groin plague, which ravaged the city of Rome with such violent pestilence that, even to the bodily eye, arrows seemed to come from heaven and strike each person individually. Coming in the eleventh month, it first struck Pope Pelagius, in accordance with what is read in the prophet Ezekiel: “Begin from my sanctuary” (Ezek. 9:6), and without delay killed him.

After his death it raged so fiercely among the remaining populace that, when the inhabitants had been removed, it left very many houses in the city completely empty. [Note: Utic. has: “so that many houses in the city remained entirely empty.”]

**38.** At the same time, in the monastery of the venerable levite Gregory, there lived an exceedingly unruly boy named Theodore, together with a religious brother, more from necessity than from choice. He was extremely troublesome whenever anyone said anything to him for the sake of his salvation. He could neither do good deeds nor even hear them mentioned. By swearing, becoming angry, and mocking, he declared that he would never adopt the way of holy conduct. Nevertheless, struck in the groin by the devastation of that same pestilence, he was brought to the point of death.

When he was breathing his last, the brethren gathered with Gregory so that they might protect his departure by prayer. His body was already dead from its extremities; only in his chest did the living warmth of breath still remain. All the brethren [Note: “Brethren” is absent from Utic., Gemet., Reg., Colb., and Bigot.] who were present began to pray for him with the greater earnestness, the more quickly they saw him departing. Suddenly, while those same brethren stood around him, he began to cry out loudly and interrupt their prayers with great shouts, saying:

“Leave me! Behold, I have been given to a dragon to devour, but because of your presence he cannot devour me. He has already swallowed my head in his mouth. Make room, so that he may no longer torture me but do what he is going to do. If I have been given to him to devour, why do I suffer delay because of you?”

Then the brethren and Gregory began to say to him: “Brother, what are you saying? Make the sign of the holy cross upon yourself.”

He replied with great cries: “I want to make the sign, but I cannot, because I am weighed down by the scales of this dragon.”

When the brethren heard this, [Note: Saint Gregory mentions this story both in Homily 38 on the Gospels and in Book IV of the *Dialogues*, chapter 37, though he nevertheless conceals his own presence there, perhaps out of modesty.] they prostrated themselves upon the ground together with God’s levite Gregory and began with tears to entreat the Lord more fervently for his deliverance. Suddenly the sick man began to shout loudly, saying:

“Thanks be to God! Behold, the dragon that had taken me to devour has fled; driven out by your prayers, he was unable to remain. Now intercede for my sins, because I have been converted and am completely prepared to abandon worldly life.”

Thus the man who, as has already been said, had been dead in his extremities was, through Gregory’s prayers, spared bodily death and gained the salvation of his soul (*Book IV of the Dialogues*, chapter 38).

[Col. 0079B] **39.** But while the pestilence raged beyond measure, since the Church of God could not remain without a ruler, the clergy, senate, and Roman people unanimously elected Gregory as their bishop, although he resisted with all his strength. Determined to avoid that dignity with all his might, he loudly declared himself wholly unworthy of such an honor, fearing, of course, that the glory of the world—which he had previously rejected—might somehow creep back upon him under the guise of ecclesiastical governance.

**40.** When he could not escape the decree of the whole community, he finally pretended that he would consent, and secretly sent a letter to the emperor Maurice, whose son he had received from the sacred font. He adjured him and earnestly begged that he never give his assent to the people, allowing them to exalt him with the glory of this honor.

But the prefect of the city, named Germanus, [Note: In the Life of Gregory, book I, chapter 1, no. 5, we investigated whether he was Gregory’s brother.] forestalled his messenger, seized him, tore up the letters, and sent to the emperor the consent that the people had given. The emperor, giving thanks to God for the friendship of the deacon, because he had found the opportunity of conferring upon him the honor he desired to bestow, issued an order that he be ordained.

**41.** Meanwhile, while he awaited the emperor’s assent from the royal city and the plague was devastating the people ever more fiercely, the venerable levite Gregory began to address the people, saying:

“Dearest brothers, we ought to fear the scourges of God, whose coming we should have feared, at least now that they are present and experienced. Let sorrow open for us the way of conversion, and let the punishment we are already suffering dissolve the hardness of our hearts. For, as the prophet testifies, it has been foretold: ‘The sword has reached even to the soul’ (Jer. 4:10).

“For behold, the whole people is struck by the sword of heavenly anger, and individuals are suddenly destroyed by slaughter. Illness does not precede death; rather, as you see, death itself outruns the delay of illness. Each person who is struck is snatched away before he can turn to the lamentation of repentance. Consider, therefore, how one reaches the presence of the stern Judge when he is not permitted to mourn what he has done.

“The inhabitants are not removed only in part; they fall together. Houses are left empty; parents look upon the funerals of their children, and their own heirs precede them to destruction. Therefore let each one of us flee to the lamentation of repentance while there is still time to weep before the blow falls. Let us recall before the eyes of our mind whatever we have committed through error, and let us punish by weeping what we have wickedly done.

“Let us anticipate his face in confession (Ps. 94:2), and, as the prophet admonishes, let us lift our hearts together with our hands to God (Lam. 3:4). To lift the heart together with the hands to God is to raise the devotion of our prayer together with the merit of good action.

“He surely gives confidence to our trembling who cries out through the prophet: ‘I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he turn and live’ (Ezek. 33:11). Let no one despair because of the enormity of his sins. A three-day repentance wiped away the ancient guilt of the Ninevites (Jonah 3:10), and the converted thief earned the rewards of life even while under sentence of death (Luke 23).

“Let us therefore change our hearts and presume that we have already received what we ask. The Judge is more quickly inclined to prayer if the one who asks is corrected from his wickedness. While the sword of so great a punishment hangs over us, let us persist in urgent prayers. For the importunity that is usually displeasing to human beings [Note: Reg., Colb., Turon., Gemet., Utic., and Bigot. read “judgment.”] pleases the Judge of truth, because the merciful and compassionate God wishes pardon to be demanded from him by prayers; he does not wish to be angry to the extent that we deserve.

“Hence he said through the Psalmist: ‘Call upon me in the day of your tribulation; I shall rescue you, and you shall glorify me’ (Ps. 49:15). He is therefore his own witness that he desires to show mercy to those who call upon him, since he commands that he be called upon.

“Therefore, dearest brothers, with contrite hearts and corrected deeds, let us come tomorrow at first light to the sevenfold litany, [Note: The manuscripts read *letaniam*, “litany,” and do so consistently hereafter. Gregory of Tours, *History*, book X, chapter 1, describes the order of these litanies and processions differently. Perhaps those supplications were held more than once, as Baronius judges for the year 590, no. 12. Paul the Deacon, *Deeds of the Lombards*, book III, relates: “In the first choir was all the clergy; in the second, all the abbots with their monks; in the third, all the abbesses with their communities; in the fourth, all the children; in the fifth, all the laity; in the sixth, all the widows; in the seventh, all married women.”] according to the distribution set out below, with devoted and tearful minds. Let none of you go out into the fields for earthly work; let no one presume to conduct any business. Let us gather together at the church of the holy Mother of God, and, since we have all sinned together, let us all together lament the evils we have committed, so that the stern Judge, when he sees that we have punished our sins ourselves, may spare us the sentence of the condemnation he has decreed.” (This prayer occurs after the homily.)

**42.** “Let the litany of the clergy go out from the church of Saint John the Baptist; the litany of the men from the church of Saint Marcellus the martyr; the litany of the monks from the church of the holy martyrs John and Paul; the litany of the handmaids of God from the church of the blessed martyrs Cosmas and Damian; the litany of married women from the church of the blessed first martyr Stephen; the litany of widows from the church of the martyr Vitalis; and the litany of the poor and children from the church of the blessed martyr Cecilia.” (Gregory of Tours, *History*, book X, chapter 1.)

**43.** When, therefore, on the appointed day, a great multitude [Note: Reg. and Norman manuscripts—namely Gemet., Utic., and Bigot.—read “of a common age.”] of every age, sex, and profession had come, in accordance with the command of the levite Gregory, to beseech the Lord, the plague raged with such violence under divine judgment that, within the space of a single hour, while the people were uttering supplicatory cries to the Lord, eighty men fell to the ground and breathed out their spirits.

But the most eloquent preacher did not cease proclaiming to the people that they should not stop praying until, through divine mercy, the plague itself subsided.

[Col. 0081B] **44.** Indeed, while the man who was soon to be bishop still believed that he had entirely turned the emperor away from consenting to his consecration, he finally discovered that his letters had been intercepted by Germanus, the prefect of the city. For this reason, anticipating the imperial response—which, as he thought, was contrary to his wishes—he cunningly obtained permission to be carried out by merchants, since he could not openly leave through the city gates, disguising his clothing, as is reported. He sought the forest thickets and looked for the hiding places of caves.

While he was being sought there with the utmost care by everyone, he was recognized through the sign of a shining column continually hanging over him from heaven. He was seized and dragged away, and at the church of the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, he was consecrated supreme pontiff. [Note: His ordination is assigned in the ecclesiastical records to the third day before the Nones of September.]

**45.** But since there are some treacherous Lombards [Note: Utic. and Colb. have “of treachery,” a reading followed by Gussanville. In the other manuscripts and printed editions, however, the reading is “treacherous.”] who assert that Gregory desired the pontificate more than he fled from it, I think it worthwhile to insert a few passages from many, by which I may make it clearer than daylight that, insofar as he could without the fault of obstinacy, he did not wish to be pontiff, but rather wished entirely to avoid it as an unbearable burden.

For almost at the very beginning of his consecration he says, in a letter to Paul the scholasticus:

“Whatever outsiders find pleasing to me from the honor of priestly office, I do not value greatly. But I grieve deeply over you who find pleasure in me in this matter, for you know my desire most fully and yet believe that I have made progress. My greatest advancement would have been achieved if I could have fulfilled what I wished, if I had been able to accomplish my intention, which you have long known, by attaining the rest I desired.

“But now that I am confined in the Roman city, bound by the chains of this honor, I have something in which I may rejoice even in regard to your glory, because, with the most excellent Lord Leo, former consul, coming here, I do not suppose that you will remain in Sicily. When you too have begun to be kept in Rome, bound by your own honor, you will understand what grief and bitterness I endure.

“When the magnificent Lord Maurentius the chartularius arrives, I beg you to join him in the necessity of the city of Rome, because outside we are continually pierced by hostile swords, but we are pressed even more gravely by the internal danger of the soldiers’ revolt.” (*Book I*, letter 3.)

**46.** Gregory likewise to John, patriarch of Constantinople:

“If the virtue of charity consists in love of one’s neighbor, and if we are commanded to love our neighbors as ourselves, why does your Blessedness not love me as you love yourself? I know with what ardor and zeal you wished to flee the burdens of the episcopate, and yet you did not resist lest those same burdens of the episcopate be imposed upon me.

“It is therefore clear that you do not love me as you love yourselves, because you wanted me to undertake burdens that you did not want imposed upon you. But because I, unworthy and weak, have taken up an old and greatly shattered ship, waves enter from every side, and the rotten planks, battered by daily and violent storms, resound with shipwreck. By almighty God I ask you to extend to me the hand of your prayer in this danger, for you can pray all the more earnestly the farther you stand from the confusion of the tribulations we suffer in this land.” (*Book I*, letter 4.)

**47.** Gregory likewise to Theoctista, the emperor’s sister:

“I cannot express in words with what devotion my mind submits itself to your reverence. Yet I do not strive to conceal myself, because, even while I am silent, you read in your heart what you should think of my devotion.

“I am astonished that you have withdrawn from me the continence you once bestowed upon me because of this present continence of pastoral office. Under the guise of the episcopate I have been brought back to the world; in it I serve so many earthly cares as I remember that I never served them in lay life.

“I have lost the profound joys of my quiet, and, collapsing inwardly, I seem to have climbed outwardly; for this I lament that I have been driven far from the face of my Creator. Every day I strove to become something outside the world and outside the flesh, to drive every bodily phantasm from the eyes of my mind, and to behold the joys above incorporeally. Longing for the sight of God not merely with words but with the whole marrow of my heart, I said: ‘My heart has said to you: I sought your face; your face, Lord, I shall seek’ (Ps. 26:8).

“Desiring nothing in this world and fearing nothing, I seemed to myself to stand upon a kind of summit of things, so that I believed that almost fulfilled in me was what I had learned from the prophet at the Lord’s promise: ‘I shall raise you above the heights of the earth’ (Isa. 58:14). For he is raised above the heights of the earth who tramples, through contempt of mind, even those things that appear high and glorious in the present world.

“But suddenly, driven from the summit of things by the whirlwind of this temptation, I fell into fears and terrors. For although I fear nothing for myself, I am greatly afraid for those entrusted to me.
