I am shaken by waves of causes on every side and brought low by storms, so that I may rightly say: ‘I have come into the depth of the sea, and the storm has overwhelmed me’ (Ps. 68:3).

“I desire to return to my heart after attending to these causes; but, shut out from it by the tumult of empty thoughts, I cannot return. Thus what is within me has also been made far from me, so that I cannot obey the prophetic voice which says: ‘Return, transgressors, to the heart’ (Isa. 46:8). But, oppressed by foolish thoughts, I am compelled only to cry out: ‘My heart has abandoned me’ (Ps. 39:13).

“I loved the beauty of the contemplative life like Rachel—sterile, yet seeing and beautiful. Although she produces less in her repose, she sees the light more subtly. But by some judgment, I do not know what, Leah has been joined to me in the night: namely, the active life, fruitful but bleary-eyed, seeing less although bearing more.

“I hastened to sit with Mary at the feet of the Lord, to receive the words of his mouth; and behold, with Martha I am compelled to serve in external things and to be busy about many matters. After what I believed was a legion of demons had been driven from me, I wanted to forget those whom I had known and rest at the Savior’s feet; and behold, unwilling and compelled, I am told: ‘Return to your house and announce how much the Lord has done for you’ (Mark 5:19).

“But who can proclaim the miracles of God amid so many earthly cares, when it is already difficult for me even to remember them? Oppressed by the tumult of worldly business in this office, [Note: Colb., Bigot., and Gemet. read “in this burden.”] I see myself among those of whom it is written: ‘You cast them down while they were being lifted up’ (Ps. 72:18). For he did not say, ‘You cast them down after they had been lifted up,’ but ‘while they were being lifted up,’ because the wicked, while supported outwardly by temporal honor, seem to rise externally but fall inwardly.

“The very lifting up is therefore ruin, because, while they lean upon false glory, they are emptied of true glory. Hence it is again said: ‘They shall fail like smoke fails’ (Ps. 36:20). Smoke fails as it rises and vanishes as it spreads. So it happens when present prosperity accompanies the life of a sinner: by the very means through which he is shown to be lofty, he is brought to nonexistence.

“Again it is written: ‘My God, make them like a wheel’ (Ps. 82:14). A wheel is raised at its rear and falls at its front. The rear for us is the good of the present world, which we leave behind; the front is eternal and enduring things, to which we are called, as Paul testifies when he says: ‘Forgetting what lies behind and reaching forward to what lies ahead’ (Phil. 3:13).

“When a sinner has prospered in the present life, he is made like a wheel, because he falls at the front while being raised from behind. For when he receives in this life the glory that he leaves behind, he falls from the glory that comes after this life.

“Many indeed know how to govern external advancement in such a way that through it they do not fall inwardly. Hence it is written: ‘God does not cast away the powerful, since he himself is powerful’ (Job 36:5). And through Solomon it is said: ‘The intelligent shall possess the helm’ (Prov. 1:5).

“But these things are difficult for me, and exceedingly burdensome, because what the mind does not willingly receive it cannot properly arrange. Behold, the most serene Lord emperor has commanded a monkey to become a lion. It may indeed be called a lion because of his command, but it cannot become a lion. Therefore he must attribute all my faults and negligences not to me but to his own mercy, since he has entrusted the ministry of power to a weak man.” (*Book I*, letter 5.)

**48.** Gregory likewise to the patrician Narses: [Note: In the manuscripts Norm., both in the letters and in John the Deacon, the reading is *Narsae*, not *Narsi*, as in the printed editions and in the Reg. and Andeg. codices. Concerning him, see Theophylact Simocatta, book V, chapters 3 and 5.] [Note: Bigot., Gemet., Reg., and several manuscripts read: “when you have described the heights of contemplation [lacuna] you have renewed.”]

“When you described at length the sweetness of contemplation, you renewed for me the groaning over my ruin, because I heard what I lost within while I undeservedly ascended outwardly to the summit of governance. Know that I am struck by such grief that I scarcely have strength to speak. The eyes of my mind are besieged by the darkness of sorrow; whatever is seen is sad, and whatever is believed delightful appears lamentable to my heart.

“I consider that, falling from the lofty summit of my quiet, I have climbed to the summit of external advancement, which is cast down; and, sent into the exile of occupation because of my sins, far from the face of the ruler, I say with the prophet in the voice of devastated Judah: ‘He who consoled me has gone far from me’ (Lam. 1:16). [Note: The Vatican edition and Gussanville most corruptly read “as though a desolate widow.”]

“As for the fact that, by creating a similarity of cause and name through Scripture, you construct endings and declamations, surely, dearest brother, you are calling a monkey a lion. We see you doing this in the same way that we often call mangy puppies leopards or tigers.

“For I, good man, have lost children, as it were, because through earthly cares I have lost right actions. Do not call me Naomi (Ruth 1:20), [Note: The same manuscripts explain the name as “beautiful,” although the other printed editions and manuscripts, both John the Deacon and the letters, resist this.] that is, ‘beautiful’; call me rather Mara, because I am full of bitterness.” (*Book I*, letter 6.)

**49.** Gregory likewise to Anastasius, patriarch of Antioch: [Note: Turon. adds “former patriarch.” We have often discussed him in the letters.]

“I received the writings of your Blessedness as a weary man finds rest, a sick man health, a thirsty man a spring, and one burning with heat shade. [Note: The Vatican edition and Gussanville read “I received,” and shortly afterward have “special love” instead of “spiritual love,” a reading found in other printed editions and supported by the manuscripts.] For those words did not seem to have been expressed by the tongue of the flesh, since you disclosed the spiritual love you bore toward me as though the mind itself were speaking through you.

“But what followed was exceedingly hard, because your love ordered me to carry earthly burdens. You who previously loved me spiritually then, as I judge, loving me temporally, pressed me down to the earth by placing a burden upon me, so that, utterly losing all uprightness of mind and the sharpness of contemplation, I may say not through the spirit of prophecy but through experience: ‘I have been bowed down and humbled exceedingly’ (Ps. 118:107).

“For such burdens of occupations weigh me down that my mind cannot in any way be raised to heavenly things. I am shaken by many waves of causes, and after those intervals of quiet I am afflicted by the storms of a tumultuous life, so that I may rightly say: ‘I have come into the depth of the sea, and the storm has overwhelmed me’ (Ps. 68:3).

“Therefore, as I am in peril, extend to me the hand of your prayer, you who stand upon the shore of virtues. But when you call me the mouth of the Lord, when you call me a lamp, and say that by speaking I benefit many and can shine upon many, I confess that you have led my assessment of myself into the greatest uncertainty.

“For I consider who I am, and I detect nothing in myself corresponding to this sign of goodness. But I consider who you are, and I do not think that you can lie. When I wish to believe what you say, my weakness contradicts me; when I wish to dispute what is said in my praise, your holiness contradicts me. Therefore, holy man, I beg you, let us agree on something concerning this struggle of ours: even if it is not as you say, let it be so because you say it is.” [Col. 0085B] (*Book I*, letter 7.)

**50.** Gregory likewise to the distinguished Andreas:

“May almighty God disclose to your most beloved heart that, although absent in body, I have not withdrawn in spirit from your charity. For even if I wished, I could not forget your goodness. But if you love me, mourn the fact that you know I have reached the rank of the episcopate, because the occupations of this world are so numerous here that through the episcopal office I see myself almost separated from the love of God. I lament this without ceasing and ask you to entreat the Lord for me.” (*Book I*, letter 30.)

**51.** Gregory likewise to John, former consul, quaestor, and patrician:

“Having experienced the goodness of your Excellency, I am bound to you by such great love that your memory can in no way be erased from my heart. But I grieve not a little in opposition to that love, because you knew that I was seeking quiet and have led me into unrest. May almighty God, since you did this with good intention, repay you with eternal blessings; but may he release me from the danger of this office in whatever way he wishes.

“For, as my sins deserved, I have become not the bishop of Romans but of Lombards, whose *synthichiae* are treaties and whose favor is punishment. [The term *synthichiae* is retained alongside its translation.] Behold where your patronage has brought me. Every day I groan, pressed by occupations, and cannot breathe.

“But you who still have the ability, flee the occupations of this world, because the more anyone advances in it, the more, as I see, he declines from the love of God.”

**52.** Gregory to Leander, bishop of Seville: [Note: Utic. and Bigot. add “of Hispania.”]

“I would have wished to answer your letters with my full attention, if the burden of pastoral care did not so wear me down that I would rather weep than say anything. Your Reverence also perceptively understands this in the very text of my letters, when I speak carelessly to one whom I love intensely.

“For I am shaken here by such great waves of this world that I am wholly unable to steer to port the old and rotting ship which, by God’s hidden dispensation, I have undertaken to govern. Now waves rush upon it from the front; now foaming heaps of the swollen sea rise from the side; now a storm pursues it from behind. Amid all these things I am confused and forced at one moment to steer adversity itself toward the very helm, and at another to evade the threats of the waves obliquely by turning the side of the ship. [Note: This passage is extremely corrupt in the Vatican edition and in Gussanville, where it reads: “to steer adversity toward the very helm, and at another, with the ship bent, to evade from the side the attack of the waves and the threats of the waves obliquely.”]

“I groan because I see that, through my negligence, the bilgewater of vices is increasing, and, with the storm violently opposing us, the rotten planks already resound with shipwreck. Weeping, I remember that I have lost the tranquil shore of my quiet; sighing, I look upon the land, yet I cannot hold it because the winds of circumstances oppose me.

“Therefore, dearest brother, if you love me, extend to me the hand of your prayer amid these waves, so that, by helping me in my labor, you may through this very exchange become stronger in your own labors.” (*Book I*, letter 31.)

### 53

But since it has been sufficiently established, as I think, that Gregory not only wished to withdraw from the office but also accepted the supreme priesthood with great anguish of heart, it seems necessary to indicate briefly by what discernment he did so, lest so great a man be thought to have succumbed, even slightly, either to the fault of obstinacy or to that of faintheartedness.

### 54

For he says in a letter to Anastasius, bishop of Corinth [Note: Colb. and Norm.: “archbishop of Corinth.”]:

> “The judgments of God, the more inscrutable they are, the more they ought to be feared by human understanding; for, since mortal reason cannot comprehend them, it must necessarily submit itself to them with a humbled neck of heart, so that wherever the will of the Ruler leads it, there the steps of an obedient mind may follow.  
> 
> “For my part, considering my weakness and recognizing that I could not attain the height of the apostolic see, I preferred to avoid this burden, lest I should fail in the pastoral government through an administration unequal to the task. But since it is not for me to oppose the decision of the Lord who orders all things, I obediently followed what the merciful hand of the Ruler wished to accomplish in me. For it was necessary to inform Your Fraternity—even if the present occasion had not arisen—that although unworthy, I have been deemed worthy by the Lord to preside over the apostolic see.”

*(Book I, Letter 27.)*

Likewise, concerning the same matter, to Philip, count of the excubitors [Note: Turon. and Reg.: “to Philippicus, count of the excubitors.”]:

> “To the degree that a human being is unable to examine and investigate heavenly judgments, to that degree he ought to bend the neck of his heart beneath them, so that, since he does not know by what judgment what is assigned to him is ordered, he may be found neither presumptuous in seeking the position nor obstinate in rejecting it. Therefore I, unworthy as I am, submitted myself to the command of almighty God and to your will, since you wished me to preside over it by the generosity of grace rather than by an assessment of merit. For God is able—on whose account you love me though unworthy—to repay you this reward forever, so that the grace you bestow upon his unworthy servants you may be able to find multiplied with him.”

*(Book I, Letter 32.)*

But here I pause for a little while from the work of excerpting, so that, with the Lord’s help, what must be said specifically about the pontificate may be reported in another little book.

# BOOK TWO

## In which it is explained how Saint Gregory lived during his pontificate

[Col. 0087]

## Argument

1. Gregory, writing of himself as “servant of the servants of God,” is clothed in modest garments.  
2. He dictates an unimpeachable confession of his faith.  
3. He sends his synodical letter to the patriarchal thrones.  
4. He declares that he venerates five councils.  
5. Having convened a synod, he condemns wrongful customs.  
6. Compiling an Antiphonary, he establishes a school of singers.  
7. Why Westerners corrupt the sweetness of song.  
8. They are corrected through John the Roman cantor.  
9. King Charles, offended by the discordance of the chant, leaves two of his clerics in Rome to be trained.  
10. The same man, offended by the discordance of the chant, later receives two Roman singers from Adrian.  
11. Gregory, removing laymen, chooses clerics familiar to him.  
12. He presents the Roman Church as it was formerly under the apostles.  
13. How extensive and distinguished the studies then flourishing at Rome were.  
14. That he summoned wise men, not the rich, to counsel.  
15. Why laymen first began to be tonsured.  
16. He does not admit laymen to ecclesiastical office, but only to the monastic habit.  
17. He abridges the Gelasian Book.  
18. Establishing stations [Note: Gemet.: “through the stations he proclaims expositions of the Gospel.”], he proclaims expositions of the Gospels.  
19. He supplies nourishment to the poor with the food of the word.  
20. He introduces new customs.  
21. He humbly gives satisfaction to those murmuring about them.  
22. He receives the Lord in the person of a guest.  
23. After inviting twelve men, he recognizes that a thirteenth angel has been assigned to him by divine providence.  
24. He determines that provisions should be distributed four times a year through the polyptych.  
25. He gives gold coins and foreign garments.  
26. He distributes various kinds of goods according to the calendar.  
27. He provides eighty pounds annually for three thousand handmaids of God.  
28. He sends out daily stipends collected by mounted couriers.  
29. He mourns most vehemently for a poor man who has died.  
30. How many names, and of what sort, of persons to be rewarded are kept in the archive.  
31. He dedicates to the Lord a basilica of the Arians in the Subura.  
32. How many and how remarkable miracles were divinely displayed there.  
33. He sends Augustine with others to convert the Saxon English.  
34. He urges those wishing to return without success to set out again.  
35. The preachers perform miracles and convert many.  
36. Augustine, consecrated bishop, asks for assistants.  
37. Gregory sends him the pallium and various necessities, together with several replies.  
38. Questioned about relationships by blood, he gives a peaceful explanation [Note: In Reg., “he gives an explanation to Pope Felix.” The same reading occurs in the Bollandist and Mabillon editions.].  
39. How greatly and remarkably Gregory praises the conversion of the Saxons and the signs performed by his disciples.  
40. Gregory warns Augustine not to become proud because of miracles.  
41. He transformed a piece of bread into flesh and flesh back into the beginnings of bread.  
42. He pierced a cloth, and blood flowed out.  
43. He punished sorcerers with blindness.  
44. How it should be understood that Gregory freed Trajan’s soul from the torments of hell.  
45. He miraculously absolves a monk who died under excommunication.  
46. He purchases pagan children so that they may become Christians.  
47. He threatens bishops on behalf of pagan peasants.  
48. He relieves converted Jews from their payments [Note: Gussanville and the Vatican manuscript, together with Reg., read “converting them.”].  
49. He gives garments to those being baptized.  
50. He declares that assistance should be given to the children of Arians.  
51. He appoints administrators over each diaconia or hospice.  
52. Establishing a hospice at Jerusalem [Note: The words “and there” are absent from Gemet.], he assigns annual stipends both there and on Mount Sinai to monks.  
53. He appoints a separate administrator for each patrimony.  
54. He determines that two offices must in no way be entrusted to one person.  
55. He organizes almsgiving locally and personally.  
56. What he willingly gives to everyone who asks him.  
57. What he supplied even to those who did not ask.  
58. His innocence in generosity is demonstrated.  
59. He purchases grain for fifty pounds of gold in order to distribute alms.  
60. What dream the Hermit learned concerning him [Note: Reg., Colb., and Norm.: “in the mirror.”].

[Col. 0087A] 45

### 1

Now then, since in the preceding little book the muscular limbs of Christ’s athlete Gregory, laboring manfully in the gymnasium of his holy Church, have been described, let it be brought forth, with the Lord’s favor, how he also fought in the arena. Indeed, as soon as he obtained the supreme pontificate of the most fortunate city of Rome, while Christ was providing for mortals, he rejected, under a sentence of the strictest prohibition, the presumptuous title “Universal,” which John, bishop of Constantinople, was at that time arrogantly claiming for himself, following the custom of his predecessors, the pontiffs. He was also the first of all to decree, with sufficient humility, that at the beginning of his letters he should be styled “servant of the servants of God.” To all his successors he left, as an inheritance, a lesson in his humility both in this matter and in his modest pontifical garments [Col. 0087B], which are preserved to this day in the holy Roman Church.

### 2

Finally [Note: Reg., Colb., and Norm.: “in the mirror.”], standing as a man of complete [Note: Thus it is read in most manuscripts. But in Reg., Colb., and the printed editions: “of complete humility and orthodox authority.” Bolland: “and of orthodox faith.”] humility, authority, and orthodoxy in the watchtower of the holy universal Church, from which the evangelical herald could be seen and heard more clearly, he fortified the true faith with the divine sword of his mouth and scattered all heresies with a single creed.

This creed of sacred confession is as follows:

> I believe in one almighty God, the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit: three persons, one substance. The Father unbegotten, the Son begotten, but the Holy Spirit neither begotten nor unbegotten, coeternal, proceeding from the Father and the Son.  
> 
> “I confess the only-begotten Son, consubstantial with the Father and born timelessly from the Father, Creator of all things visible and invisible, light from light, true God from true God, the radiance of glory, the likeness of substance. Remaining the Word before the ages, he was made perfect man at the end of the ages, conceived and born of the Holy Spirit and of the Virgin Mary; he assumed our nature without sin. He was crucified under Pontius Pilate and buried; on the third day he rose from the dead. On the fortieth day he ascended into heaven and sits at the right hand of the Father. From there he will come to judge the living and the dead, placing all the hidden things of each person before the eyes of all, giving the saints everlasting rewards in the heavenly kingdom, but punishments of eternal fire to the wicked, renewing the age by fire at the resurrection of the flesh.  
> 
> “I confess one faith, one baptism, one apostolic and universal Church, in which alone sins can be loosed in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.”

### 3

Gregory also sent his synodical letter, according to the ancient custom of his predecessors, to John of Constantinople, Eulogius of Alexandria, Gregory of Antioch, [Note: This is not read in Gemet.] John of Jerusalem, and Anastasius, patriarch of Antioch [Note: Bigot. and Reg.: “ex-patriarch of Antioch.”]. It reads as follows:

> “When I consider that, unequal in merit and resisting with my whole heart, I have been compelled to bear the burdens of pastoral care, a cloud of grief comes upon me, and my sorrowful heart sees nothing except those shadows which allow nothing to be seen. For why is a bishop chosen for the Lord [Note: Norm.: “by the Lord.”] except to be an intercessor for the sins of the people? With what confidence, then, do I come to him as an intercessor for the sins of others, when I am not secure concerning my own?  
> 
> “If perhaps someone were to ask me to become his intercessor before a powerful man who was angry with him and unknown to me, I would immediately answer: ‘I cannot come to intercede, because I do not know him through constant familiarity.’ If, then, I would be ashamed to become an intercessor before a man of whom I had presumed nothing, how great an act of presumption is it that I assume the place of intercessor before God for the people, when I do not recognize myself as familiar to him through the merit of my life?  
> 
> “In this matter I have still another, more serious fear: as we have all clearly recognized, when one who is displeasing is sent to intercede, the mind of the angry person is provoked to worse things. I greatly fear that the faithful people entrusted to me may perish through the addition of my guilt, though until now the Lord has tolerated their sins with patience.  
> 
> “But whenever I manage somehow to suppress this fear and apply my consoled mind to the duties of the pontificate, I am terrified when I consider the immensity of the task itself. For I reflect that the ruler must be watchful in every way: pure in thought, outstanding in action, discreet in silence, useful in speech, near to each person through compassion, raised above all others in contemplation, a companion through humility to those who do good, and, against the vices of sinners, raised up through zeal for righteousness [Note: Gussanville and the Vatican edition: ‘through zeal for justice’].”

And so forth, as he later develops in the *Pastoral Book*.

### 4

> “Moreover,” he says, “since one believes with the heart unto righteousness, but confession is made with the mouth unto salvation (Romans 10), I confess that I both accept and venerate four councils, just as I do the four books of the holy Gospel: namely, the Council of Nicaea, in which the perverse doctrine of Arius was destroyed; the Council of Constantinople, in which the error of Eunomius and Macedonius was refuted [Note: Turon. and Andeg.: ‘is joined together’]; the First Council of Ephesus, in which the impiety of Nestorius was judged; and the Council of Chalcedon, in which the wickedness of Eutyches [Note: Another reading: “of Eutyches,” or “of Eutychius.”] and Dioscorus was rejected.  
> 
> “I embrace these councils with complete devotion and preserve them with unimpaired approval, because in them, as in a square stone, the structure of the holy faith rises. Even if someone should be the norm of every life and action [Note: Some printed editions: “the norm of action stands.”], whoever does not hold their firmness, though he be seen to be a stone, nevertheless lies outside the building.  
> 
> “I likewise venerate the Fifth Council, in which the letter called ‘of Ibas,’ full of error, is rejected, and Theodore is shown to have fallen into the impiety of unbelief by separating the person of the Mediator between God and human beings into two subsistences [Note: In the Sangerman, Reg., Colb., and some other manuscripts, erroneously: “into two substances.” All the printed editions follow them, although it has a heretical implication to deny that Christ consists of two substances, namely divine and human. It should therefore be read “in two subsistences,” or “persons,” as other manuscripts of both John the Deacon’s work and the letters have it.].  
> 
> “The writings of Theodoret, by which the faith of blessed Cyril is attacked, are also rejected as produced with the audacity of madness. I reject all the persons whom the aforesaid venerable councils reject, and I embrace those whom they venerate. Since they were established by universal agreement, whoever presumes either to loose what they bind or to bind what they loose destroys himself, not them. Therefore, whoever thinks otherwise, let him be anathema.”

*(Book I, chapter 25.)*

### 5

In this way, after Gregory had clearly set forth the foundation of his faith before the apostolic thrones, according to the ancient custom of his predecessors, the pontiffs, he recognized that he had been appointed by the Lord as supreme pontiff over nations and kingdoms so that, in accordance with the prophetic saying (Jeremiah 1), he might uproot, destroy, and demolish the roots of vices, and finally build and plant virtues.

Accordingly, all the customs that he recognized as having newly sprouted against the ancient apostolic tradition—namely, matters concerning ministers who were singers; laymen who clung familiarly to the pontiff; the prejudicial assignment of titles to various things; the covering of the apostolic bier with dalmatics; the *pastillaticum* [Note: Norm., Reg., and Colb. read “pastillaticum,” in place of “pallium,” or “the consecration of pontiffs,” and omit “and concerning not admitting,” etc.]; and the indiscriminate admission of laymen to the office of ecclesiastical law, for the sake of the pallium or the consecration of pontiffs—he first separated from the Roman Church and afterward, once he had gathered the bishops of the surrounding provinces, from the whole body of the holy universal Church [Col. 0090C]. He condemned them both generally and perpetually, with a terrible anathema imposed upon them.

### 6

Then, in the house of the Lord, following the example of the wisest Solomon, and for the sake of the compunctious sweetness of music [Note: Gemet.: “an Antiphonary of harmonious study.” The earlier reading, as in Colb., is “with harmony.” Utic. has “the singing of the Antiphonary,” corrected to “with harmony.” Reg.: “the Antiphonary of the singers.”], he most diligently and very usefully compiled a cento Antiphonary for the singers. He also established the school of singers, which to this day performs its melodies in the holy Roman Church according to the same rules. Along with some estates, he built for it two residences: one beneath the steps of the basilica of blessed Peter the Apostle, and the other beneath the buildings of the Lateran patriarchate.

There, even to the present day, his bed, on which he reclined while singing, and his whip, with which he threatened the boys, are preserved with fitting veneration together with the authentic Antiphonary [Col. 0090D]. By the provisions of a decree, and under penalty of anathema, he apportioned these places for the daily benefit of the ministry in each establishment.

### 7

The Germans or Gauls among the other peoples of Europe were remarkably able to learn, and frequently relearn, the sweetness of this modulation. Yet they were entirely unable to preserve it uncorrupted, both because of their levity of spirit, by which they mixed certain elements of their own into the Gregorian chants, and because of their natural harshness.

For their Alpine bodies, resounding loudly with the thunder of their voices, do not properly reproduce the sweetness of the melody they have received. When the barbarous harshness of their wine-soaked throats strives, through inflections and repetitions, to produce a gentle song, it casts forth, with a kind of natural crash, rigid sounds like wagons clattering confusedly over steps. Thus it disturbs and irritates the minds of its hearers rather than soothing them, as it ought to have done.

### 8

This is why, in the time of this Gregory, when Augustine was then making his way to Britain, singers trained in the Roman institution were also dispersed throughout the West and taught the barbarians with distinction. After they had died, the Western Churches so corrupted the musical system they had received that a certain John, a Roman cantor, was sent with Theodore—also a Roman citizen but archbishop of York—to Britain through Gaul, when Vitalian was pope [Note: Theodore was ordained by Pope Saint Vitalian on 26 March, a Sunday, in the year 668. Thus Bede, Book IV, chapter 1. Bolland.].

Restoring the sons of the surrounding Churches to the former sweetness of song, he preserved the rule of Roman teaching for many years, both personally and through his disciples.

### 9

Our own Charles, moreover, a patrician and king of the Franks, was offended at Rome by the discordance between the Roman and Gallican chant. When the insolence of the Gauls argued that the chant had been corrupted by certain dirges of our singers, while our own people, on the contrary, plausibly displayed the authentic Antiphonary, he is said to have asked who customarily preserved clearer water, the stream or the spring.

When they answered, he wisely added:

> “Then we too, who until now have drunk corrupted water from the stream, must necessarily return to the original waters of the perennial spring.”

Immediately, therefore, he left two capable clerics of his own with Adrian, who was then bishop. Once they had been sufficiently and elegantly trained, he restored the metropolitan church of Metz to the sweetness of the former modulation, and through it corrected all his Gaul.

But after a long time, when those who had been trained in Rome had died, and the most prudent of kings saw that the chant of the Gallican Churches differed from that of Metz, he noticed that each side was claiming that the other’s chant was corrupted.

“Let us return to the spring again,” he said.

Then, moved by the king’s requests, Pope Adrian sent two singers into Gaul, as some people truthfully attest even today. On their judgment the king recognized that all the others had somewhat corrupted the sweetness of the Roman chant through a certain levity, whereas the people of Metz differed only slightly because of their natural harshness.

Finally, even to this day, those who love the pure truth confirm that to the extent that the Metz chant yields to the Roman chant, the chants of the Gallican and German Churches yield to that of Metz.

I have therefore related these matters in advance, lest I should seem to have passed over the unexamined [Note: Colb., Gemet., and Bigot.: “vanity.” Utic.: “variety.” It is superscribed: “levity.”] levity of the Gauls.

### 11

Moreover, the most prudent ruler Gregory, having removed secular persons from his bedchamber, chose the wisest of the clerics as his counselors and close associates. Among them were Peter the Deacon, his contemporary, with whom he later held discussions and composed the four books of the *Dialogues*; Aemilianus the notary, who, together with his associates, took down forty homilies on the Gospel [Note: Saint Gregory discusses the note-takers of these homilies in their prologue to the second bishop of Turin. Bolland.]; Paterius, likewise a notary, whom Gregory made *secundicerius* and who excerpted from his books certain highly useful passages; and John the *defensor*, who, sent at Gregory’s command as an investigator to Spain, restored to his own see Januarius, bishop of the city of Málaga [Note: He was the fourth bishop of this city; after his expulsion, a certain John was intruded. See Martin de Roa, *History of Málaga*, chapter 12. Norm. and Colb. manuscripts read *Malalitanae* for *Malacitanae*; Reg. reads *Malanitanae*.], after he had been deposed by his fellow-country bishops [Col. 0092B]. He condemned the men who had deposed him, together with the man who had insinuated himself into his place, under the same sentence.

Among the monks, he chose the holiest as his close associates. These included Maximianus, abbot of his monastery, whom he later made bishop of Syracuse and to whom he entrusted his responsibilities throughout Sicily; Augustine, provost of the same monastery; and Mellitus, through whom he summoned the English peoples to the grace of Christianity; Marinianus, a monk of the same monastery, whom he consecrated bishop of the metropolitan church of Ravenna; Probus, whom he suddenly appointed abbot when the Spirit revealed it and sent to Jerusalem to build a hospice; and also Claudius [Note: On him, see Rubeus, Book IV of the *History of Ravenna*], abbot of the city of Classis, who, while the pope was discussing them, composed much—although not with the same meaning—from Proverbs, the Song of Songs, the Prophets, the Books of Kings, and the Heptateuch.

*(Book XII, Letter 24.)*

### 12

Gregory spent long periods with these men, by day and by night, and left nothing undone that belonged to monastic perfection in the palace or to pontifical discipline in the Church. Everywhere the most devout monks seemed to attend upon the pontiff together with the most learned clerics, and communal life was maintained in various forms, so that under Gregory the Church in the city of Rome was then such as Luke records it to have been under the apostles and Philo under the evangelist Mark at Alexandria.

### 13

At that time Wisdom was, in a certain visible manner, building herself a temple at Rome, and supporting the court of the apostolic see with the seven liberal arts as though with seven columns of noble stones. None of those serving the pontiff, from the least to the greatest, displayed anything barbarous in speech or dress. Instead, Latin of the toga-wearing Quirites, or of the *trabea*, held its own Latium uniquely within that very Lateran palace.

Studies of various arts had flourished there again, and anyone who lacked either holiness or prudence did not, by his own judgment, possess the confidence to remain in the pontiff’s presence.

[Col. 0093A]

### 14

Prudent men were summoned to the pontifical counsels, as I have said—men of wisdom rather than power. While poor philosophy, within, rationally investigated through elaborate arguments what ought to be pursued, or pursued above all, in each matter, rich idleness—which now takes revenge upon the wise with equal fortune—remained despicable outside the doors of the bedchamber.

Only bilingual skill in interpretation was lacking, together with the most eloquent Cecropian maiden, who had once transmitted to the Latins the sharp insights of her mind, when Varro had taken away her celibacy; she was now claiming for herself the magic of impostures, as he himself complains in his letters.

### 15

No layman administered any office of the palace or any ecclesiastical patrimony. Instead, men of the Church undertook all the duties belonging to ecclesiastical law, while laymen were assigned solely to military service with arms or to the continual care of the fields.

For this reason, some of the nobles first began to be tonsured under the pretext of religion. Emperor Maurice wisely countered their evasions. Through a law issued by Longinus the *Strator*, he ordered that whoever was involved in public administrations should not be permitted to enter ecclesiastical office.

Gregory strongly praised this law, saying:

> “He who abandons secular dress and hastens to enter ecclesiastical offices does not wish to leave the world, but to change it.”

*(Book III, Letter 65.)*

### 16

Yet, while an almost innumerable multitude was flowing daily, on various pretexts, into the clerical profession from both ecclesiastical and secular service, the pastor, provident in all things, judged that they should not be admitted to the office of ecclesiastical dignity at all, but only received for the purpose of undertaking the monastic way of life. He said:

> “We know that many hasten from ecclesiastical or secular service to the service of almighty God, so that, freed from human servitude, they may be seen to live more familiarly in monasteries in divine service. If we dismiss them indiscriminately, we provide everyone with an opportunity to flee the authority of either ecclesiastical or secular law [Note: Andeg.: *fugiendi ad ecclesiastici, vel saecularis juris dominium occasionem praebemus*—“we furnish an occasion for fleeing to the jurisdiction of ecclesiastical or secular law.”]. But if we imprudently retain those hastening to the service of almighty God, we find ourselves refusing them something that the one who gave everything has granted.  
> 
> “Therefore, whoever desires to be converted from servitude under ecclesiastical or secular law to the service of God must first be tested while remaining in lay dress. If his character and conduct bear witness to the goodness of his desire, he should, without any hesitation, be permitted to serve almighty God in a monastery, so that the one who departs free from human service may undertake, in divine obedience, a stricter servitude.  
> 
> “But if, even in the monastic habit, he has conducted himself irreproachably according to the rules of the Fathers, then, after the periods prescribed by the sacred canons, he may lawfully be advanced to any ecclesiastical office—provided, however, that he has not been stained by those crimes which are punished with death in the Old Testament.”

### 17

He also abridged the Gelasian Book concerning the solemn rites of Mass, removing much, altering a little, and adding some things, and compressed it into the volume of a single book for the exposition of the Gospel readings [Note: This is said on the authority of Gelasius I, its author. Concerning the addition of the words “And order our days,” etc., see Bede, Book II of the *History*, chapter 1. The very learned Hugh Menardus thinks, in note 2 on the *Book of Sacraments of Saint Gregory*, that after the words “he abridged it into the volume of a single book,” the phrase “which volume he entitled the Book of Sacraments” once stood. He relies on the testimony of Abbot Berno, chapter 1 of his book *On Certain Matters Pertaining to the Mass*: “Whence,” he says, “we also read in his Life: ‘He also abridged the Gelasian Book,’ etc. … ‘which volume,’ etc.” But perhaps those final words belong to Berno, not to John the Deacon. Certainly nothing similar is found in the manuscript copies themselves, nor are there any traces of erasure or tearing away.].

He added to the canon:

> “And order our days in your peace, and rescue us from eternal damnation, and command that we be numbered among your chosen flock.”

### 18

He carefully organized stations throughout the basilicas and the cemeteries of the blessed martyrs, according to which the Roman people, as though he were still alive, continue to hurry competitively to this day.

He himself also went about among them. While he was still able to speak, he proclaimed twenty homilies on the Gospel before the Church at different times. He dictated the remaining number of homilies, but because his stomach was growing weak through continual illness, he entrusted their delivery to others.

### 19

The army of the Lord followed Gregory as he went before them, here and there, and innumerable voluntary companies of every sex, age, and condition flocked from all directions to hear the word of instruction. To all of them, as a teacher of the heavenly militia, he supplied spiritual weapons; but to the poor and to foreigners who had flowed into Rome according to the circumstances of the times, he supplied daily provisions.

### 20

He decreed that the solemn rites of Mass should be celebrated over the bodies of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul [Col. 0094C]. He acquired very numerous olive groves and recorded their total on marble tablets before the doors of the same basilica [Col. 0094C]. He added lamps and appointed diligent services.

He prohibited anyone from expecting a benefit from burial beside the Church. He ordered that seven of the *defensores* be honored with regional rank. He caused the Alleluia to be said at Mass outside the season of Pentecost. He established that subdeacons should proceed stripped of their outer garments. He commanded that the *Kyrie eleison* be sung and judged that the Lord’s Prayer should immediately be recited over the Host after the canon.

### 21

When he later heard some people murmuring about these matters, as though he were following the customs of the Church of Constantinople, the most devout Father did not disdain to give an explanation. He said:

> “In none of these matters have we followed another Church. For the Alleluia to be said here, it is handed down from the Church of Jerusalem, through the tradition of blessed Jerome, in the time of Pope Damasus of blessed memory, that it was brought here. Therefore, in this see we have rather removed a custom that had been introduced here by the Greeks.” [Note: Mabillon and Gussanville read “that it should not be said.” The negation must be removed; otherwise Gregory would not be answering complaints about the introduction of the Alleluia chant.]  
> 
> “As for having the subdeacons proceed stripped, that was the ancient custom of the Church; but it pleased one of our pontiffs—I do not know which one—to order them to proceed clothed. For did the Churches of Sicily receive their tradition from the Greeks? From where, then, do they have it today that subdeacons proceed in linen tunics, unless they received it from their mother, the Roman Church?  
> 
> “As for the *Kyrie eleison*, we neither said nor say it as it is said by the Greeks. In Greece everyone says it together, whereas among us it is said together by the clerics and answered by the people. The *Christe eleison* is also said the same number of times, though among the Greeks it is not said at all. At the daily Masses we omit the other things that are customarily said and say only the *Kyrie eleison* and the *Christe eleison*, so that we may spend a little longer in these words of supplication.  
> 
> “We say the Lord’s Prayer immediately after the prayer for this reason: it was the custom of the apostles to consecrate the sacrificial Host with that prayer alone. It seemed highly inappropriate to me that we should say over the offering a prayer composed by a scholar and not say over the body and blood of our Redeemer the very tradition that he himself composed.  
> 
> “Moreover, among the Greeks the Lord’s Prayer is said by the entire people, whereas among us it is sung by the priest alone. In what respect, then, have we followed the customs of the Greeks? We have either restored our ancient practices or established new and useful ones, while in these matters we are not shown to imitate others [Note: The printed editions read “we are shown to approve,” but the manuscripts oppose this reading, which is contrary to Saint Gregory’s meaning].  
> 
> “Therefore, whenever an opportunity arises for Your Charity to go to the city of Catania or to the Church of Syracuse, let him instruct those whom he believes or understands may have murmured about this matter, after discussion with them, and let him not cease to teach them as though on some other occasion.  
> 
> “As for what they say about the Church of Constantinople, who could doubt that it is subject to the apostolic see? Both the most devout lord emperor and our brother, the bishop of that city, constantly profess this. Nevertheless, if that Church, or any other Church, possesses something good, I am ready to imitate it, along with my inferiors whom I prohibit from illicit practices, in what is good. For the man who thinks himself superior because he refuses to learn the good things he sees is a fool.”

*(Book IX, Letter 12.)*

### 22

Gregory’s hospitality continued even in the patriarchate itself to such an extent that, apart from those whom he mercifully nourished with ecclesiastical assistance as they fled the swords of the Lombard treachery through various regions and even within Rome, he invited all sorts of strangers to his table every day.

One day, among these, a man came to him. Gregory himself, wishing in humble service to pour water over the man’s hands, turned to take up the pitcher, but suddenly did not find the man into whose hands he had intended to pour the water.

As he marveled inwardly at what had happened, the Lord said to him in a vision that same night:

> “On other days you received me in my members; yesterday you received me in my very self.”

[Col. 0096A] **23.** At another time, the same Gregory, according to his custom, instructed the sacellarius to invite twelve pilgrims to dinner. The man went and fulfilled the command, arranging them together at table [Note: [Col. 0095D] Bigot. and Utic. read “invited them.” This sacellarius—or rather saccellarius—is so called because he keeps the bags for almsgiving, but he was a treasurer. In the life of Saint Antony he is written *saccellarius*.]. While they were dining together, the pope looked and counted thirteen. Calling the sacellarius, he asked why he had presumed to invite a thirteenth contrary to his command.

The man, astonished, counted the visiting diners more carefully; and finding only twelve, he replied confidently: “Believe me, venerable Father, there are only twelve, just as you ordered.” But when, after being repeatedly challenged, he counted the twelve again and again, and still did not see the thirteenth whom the pope alone could see, the spiritual Father Gregory noticed that the man sitting near the others repeatedly changed his appearance, now seeming a young man, now an old man with venerable gray hair.

When the meal was over, he allowed the twelve to depart; but taking the thirteenth by the hand, he led him into his chamber, earnestly adjuring him to disclose plainly both who he was and what his name was. He replied:

“Why do you ask my name, which is wondrous? Nevertheless, know and remember that I am that shipwrecked man who once came to you when you were writing in the cell of your monastery beside the Clivus Scauri. You gave me twelve coins and a silver dish which your blessed mother Silvia had sent you with cooked pulses. Know this with certainty: from the day on which you bestowed these things upon me with a cheerful heart, the Lord destined you to become the bishop of his holy Church, for which he shed his own blood, and to be the successor and vicar of the chief of the apostles, Peter, whose virtue you also imitated when you distributed the substance of those who offered it, according as each person had need.”

Hearing this, Gregory said: “And how did you know that the Lord then destined me to preside over his holy Church?”

He replied: “Because I am his angel, and at that time he sent me to examine your purpose.”

Then Gregory, since he had not yet openly recognized the angel, was utterly terrified, and heard him say:

“Do not fear or be afraid. For behold, the Lord has sent me to be your guardian for as long as you remain in this mortal world, so that whatever you ask, you may confidently obtain from him through me.”

Immediately Gregory fell upon his face, saying:

“If the almighty Lord has repaid me so greatly for the small gift of my insignificance that he made me bishop of his holy Church and appointed his angel as my guardian, how much, I should think, will he restore to me if, remaining with all my strength in obedience to his commands, I strive to distribute more to more people?”

[Col. 0096D] **24.** Accordingly, he began to be as much more generous with the temporal benefit entrusted to him as he became more certain of receiving an eternal reward. He reckoned the revenues of all the estates and properties from the Gelasian *polyptych* [Note: [Col. 0097D] From the Greek πτυχίς, it signifies the individual folds, leaves, or plates of garments, documents, and other things that are folded. MABILLON.—Here it is a book in which ecclesiastical revenues were recorded, together with what was distributed to each needy person. On this word, see Letter 40 of Book VII, indiction 2.], whose most diligent attendant he appeared to be [Note: [Col. 0097D] Colb. reads “he collected”; Reg. “to adhere.” In Utic., above the word *adaeravit* is written “or distributed.”]. He decreed in the *polyptych* still used for this purpose how many solidi should be distributed to each person four times a year—in gold and silver, the payments of all ecclesiastical and palatine orders, monasteries, churches, cemeteries, deaconries, and urban and suburban guest-houses having been included—namely at Easter, on the feast of the apostles, on the feast of Saint Andrew, and on his own birthday [Note: [Col. 0097D] The word *singulis* (“to each”) is absent from the Norman manuscripts.].

**25.** In addition to these gifts, at dawn on the day of the Lord’s Resurrection, while seated in the basilica once belonging to the most learned Pope Vigilius, beside which he habitually lived, he distributed gold pieces to all the bishops, priests, deacons, and other persons of rank [Note: [Col. 0097D] That is, men holding dignities, from ἀξίωμα, “dignity.” John the Deacon not infrequently uses Greek words.]. On the feast of the apostles and on his own feast, he offered mixed solidi [Col. 0097B] and likewise gave foreign garments.

**26.** On every single Kalends, he distributed generally to the poor the same kinds of provisions that were collected from the revenues. At the appropriate time, the Lord’s steward most carefully apportioned grain, wine, cheese, pulses, bacon, edible animals [Note: [Col. 0098D] Colb., Gemet., and Big. read *manducalia*, which was formerly also read in Utic.], fish, or oil. He honorably offered spices and other more delicate commodities [Note: [Col. 0098D] Colb., Gemet., and Bigot. read “more valuable.” Utic. preserves both readings.] to the leading men, so that the Church was thought to be nothing other than a collection of common storehouses.

**27.** To three thousand maidservants of God, whom the Greeks call *monastriai*, he gave fifteen pounds of gold for bedding, and he contributed eighty pounds annually for their daily support. Concerning these women he wrote to the patrician Theoctista:

“Their life,” he says, “is such, and so strict in tears and abstinence, that we believe that, if they did not exist, none of us could have remained in this place for so many years amid the swords of the Lombards.” (Book VI, Letter 26.)

**28.** Every day, throughout the villages and crossroads of all the regions, he sent cooked provisions to the sick and to those weakened in any part of the body through appointed couriers. For the more modest, before he himself took food, he arranged for a dish from his table bearing the apostolic blessing to be sent door to door, so that the benevolence of the most merciful provider excluded absolutely no one—he whom knowledge of the almighty Creator had drawn to the faith.

[Col. 0097D] **29.** When it happened that one of these poor men was found dead by corpse-bearers in the narrow recesses of the *androna* [Note: [Col. 0098D] Ἀνδρών: a place in which only men live; hence the form *androna*. BOLL.], he judged that the man had died from lack of support [Note: [Col. 0098D] “Had perished.”]. He mourned so deeply that, as is said, for several days he abstained from celebrating Mass, as though he had killed the man with his own hands—which it is impious even to say.

**30.** To this day, in the most sacred archive of the Lateran palace, there remains a very large parchment volume compiled in his time. It contains, in precise detail, the names of persons of every sex, age, and profession living both in Rome and in the suburban towns and neighboring cities, as well as in the distant coastal cities, together with their surnames, the dates, and the payments made to them. I refrain from transferring its total, lest I weary the reader by passing over it; instead, I direct the reader’s eyes to the fullness of that venerable archive, whose authority I myself followed almost everywhere, with the pope’s permission.

**31.** Moreover, since a basilica of the Arians in a district of this city called the Subura had remained closed until the pontificate of Gregory, he decided that it should be dedicated in the Catholic faith after the relics of the blessed martyrs Sebastian and Agatha had been brought there. This was done.

For when Gregory arrived there with a great multitude of people, singing praises, he entered the basilica mentioned above. While the venerable pontiff was already celebrating the solemn Mass, and the crowd of people was pressing together because of the narrowness of the place, some of those standing outside the sanctuary suddenly felt a pig running back and forth between their legs. Each person felt it and pointed it out to those standing beside him. The pig then made for the doors of the church and filled with amazement all those through whose midst it passed. Yet nothing could be seen, although it could be felt.

Divine mercy showed this so that it might be clear to all that, when Gregory came with the relics of the saints, an unclean inhabitant was leaving that very place.

**32.** After the celebration of Mass had been completed, the pope withdrew with the people. But that same night a great disturbance arose in the roof of the church, as though someone were running about inside it. On the following night the noise grew worse, when suddenly such terror sounded forth as though the whole church had been overturned from its foundations. Then it withdrew, and no further disturbance from the ancient enemy appeared there. Through the terrifying noise he had made, however, it became known that he was being compelled to leave the place he had long occupied through Gregory’s invocation.

A few days later, in perfectly clear weather [Col. 0098D], a cloud descended from heaven upon the altar of that church and covered it with its veil. It filled the entire church with such terror and sweetness of fragrance that, although the doors stood open, no one dared enter. Priests and custodians, and those who had come to celebrate the solemn Mass and saw what had happened, could not enter, though they drew in the sweetness of the wondrous fragrance.

On another day lamps were lit there without any flame. A few days later, after the solemn Mass had been completed and the lamps extinguished, the custodian left the church [Note: [Col. 0099D] Bigot. and Utic. read “basilica.”]. Shortly afterward he entered again and found the lamps he had extinguished burning. He thought that he must have put them out carelessly and extinguished them more carefully; then, leaving, he locked the church.

After an interval of three hours he returned and found the lamps he had extinguished burning again. Thus the light itself made it plainly evident that, through blessed Gregory, that place had come from darkness into light.

**33.** But since Gregory was pressed by continual waves of thought concerning the conversion of the Saxon English, as he had resolved during his monastic life [Note: [Col. 0099D] The manuscripts read “was reproached.”], as soon as he had entered the fourth year of his pontificate, after the affairs of the Church had been set in order [Note: [Col. 0099D] More properly “the sixth,” although the manuscript codices have “the fourth.”], he sent Augustine with other monks of his household monastery [Note: [Col. 0099D] Reg. omits “of the monastery.” Colb. and Norm. read “Britains.”] to Britain for the purpose of evangelizing.

After undertaking their pilgrimage, however, and being weighed down a few days later by sluggish weariness, they decided that they would rather return home than approach a barbarous, savage, and unbelieving people whose language they did not even understand. Without delay they sent Augustine, whom Gregory had appointed to be consecrated bishop if the English received them, back to Rome. They begged the supreme pontiff to remove from them the arduous, uncertain, and dangerous journey recently imposed upon them, and to permit them to return to their own people.

He wrote back to them as follows:

[Col. 0099C] **34.** “Gregory, bishop and servant of the servants of God, to the servants of our Lord Jesus Christ.

“Since it would have been better not to begin a good work than to turn back in thought from what has been begun, it is necessary, most beloved sons, that with the greatest zeal you complete, with the Lord’s help, the good work you have undertaken. Therefore, let neither the toil of the journey nor the tongues of malicious men deter you; but with every effort and fervor carry out, with God as your guide, what you have begun, knowing that a greater glory of eternal recompense will follow great labor.

“Obey humbly in all things Augustine, your superior, whom we have also appointed your abbot, knowing that whatever you complete at his instruction will be wholly profitable to your souls. May almighty God protect you by his grace and grant me to see the fruit of your labor in the eternal homeland, so that, although I cannot labor with you, I may be found together with you in the joy of recompense, since I desire to labor.” [Note: [Col. 0099D] The Vatican Edition, Gussanville, Mabillon, and others read “and of our labor,” against the manuscripts and the sequence of the sentence, which clearly shows that Gregory, out of humility, attributes no share of apostolic labor to himself: “so that, although I cannot labor with you…”] (Book VI, Letter 51.)

**35.** Strengthened by these exhortations, Augustine, with his brothers [Col. 0100A], set out for Britain, obtaining lodging through Aetherius, the Arelatean bishop, through other bishops of Gaul, and through the kings to whom the most devout Father had commended them in letters written by his own hand.

When he came to Ethelbert, king of the Cantii [Note: [Col. 0100D] Gemet., together with Bigot. and Colb., reads “Edilbert”; Utic. “Adelbert.”], with God’s grace cooperating, he easily obtained not only permission to preach but also food and lodging in the city of Dorovernum, which was the capital of his kingdom.

As Augustine approached it with his companions, carrying before them a cross or an image of the Savior, he sang:

“We beseech you, Lord, in all your mercy, that your fury and your anger be taken away from this city and from your holy house, for we have sinned.”

As they preached and performed miracles in the name of Jesus, many believed and were baptized. They marveled at the simplicity of an innocent life and embraced the sweetness of heavenly doctrine.

**36.** Therefore Augustine came to Arelate and, according to Gregory’s command, was consecrated bishop by Aetherius [Note: [Col. 0100D] It should read “by Virgilius,” who was then bishop of Arelate. Aetherius was bishop of Lyons. Bede, Book I of the *History*, chapter 27, provided the occasion for the error.]. He returned to Britain, and immediately informed Pope Gregory through the priest Laurence and the monk Peter of the conversion of the English people and of his own consecration. He urged Gregory to send him many ministers of the word, since he had a very great harvest but few workers.

**37.** Rejoicing in Christ at this report, Gregory sent Augustine many ministers of the word, among whom the principal were Mellitus, Justus, Paulinus, and Rufinianus [Note: [Col. 0100D] Andeg. reads “Erufinus”; Utic. “Rufinus”; Reg. “Rufianus.”]. Through them he sent everything necessary for the worship of the Church: sacred vessels, altar vestments, ecclesiastical ornaments, clerical clothing, relics of the apostles and many saints, and many books.

He also sent him the pallium, ordering him to ordain twelve bishops under his metropolitan authority in Kent, and to send individual bishops to London and York. These bishops were likewise to consecrate twelve bishops under themselves, receive the pallium from the apostolic see, and, after Augustine’s death, the one among them who had first deserved consecration was to be regarded as first.

He also instructed him not to destroy the temples of idols among the English, but to sprinkle them with sanctified water and dedicate them as basilicas. Since the Saxons were accustomed to slaughter many oxen in sacrifices to demons, he ordered that, on the day of the dedication or on the feast days of the holy martyrs whose relics were placed there, they should make tents for themselves from tree branches around those same churches converted from temples, and celebrate the appointed solemnities with religious banquets.

When Augustine asked him about certain matters, including how a bishop ought to live with his clergy, the most humble teacher replied among other things:

“Since your Fraternity, trained in the rules of a monastery, ought not to live apart from your clergy in the Church of the English, which has recently been brought to the faith by God’s agency [Note: [Col. 0101D] The vulgate editions read “converted.”], you should establish the way of life that existed among our fathers at the beginning of the newly born Church, when none of them called anything that they possessed his own, but everything was common to them.”

When Augustine asked why, concerning the celebration of Mass, the Gallican Church differed from the Roman Church, Gregory replied:

“Your Fraternity knows the custom of the Roman Church, in which you remember that you were brought up. But it pleases me that, whether in the Roman Church or in any other Church, you have found something that may please almighty God more, you should carefully select it and introduce it as a special institution into the Church of the English, which is still new in the faith, gathering from many Churches whatever you have been able to collect. Things are not to be loved for the sake of places, but places for the sake of good things. Therefore, from each Church select what is devout, religious, and right; and, gathered together as if in a vessel, turn these things into a custom at the table of the English.”

When he was also asked how they should return what thieves had taken from churches, the most gentle Father said:

“Far be it that the Church should receive back with increase what it appears to lose from earthly goods and seek empty profits.”

When the same Augustine asked how many generations apart the faithful ought to marry, Gregory replied in a spirit of concession:

“A certain earthly law in the Roman commonwealth permits the son and daughter of a brother and sister, or the son and daughter of two full brothers or of two sisters, to marry. But experience has taught us that offspring cannot grow from such a union, and the sacred law forbids the exposure of the shame of kinship. Therefore it is necessary that, beginning with the third or fourth generation, the generations of the faithful should be permitted to marry one another. But from the second generation, as we have said, they must abstain altogether [Note: [Col. 0101D] Norm. reads “from the second”; Andeg. “the second.”].” (Book XI, Letter 64.)

**38.** Some time later, when Felix, bishop of Messana in Sicily, asked whether he had written to Augustine that marriages contracted within the fourth generation among the English should by no means be dissolved, the most humble Father Gregory gave, among other things, this explanation:

“What I wrote to Augustine, bishop of the English people, your disciple—as you have recalled [Note: [Col. 0101D] Many editions read “as I remember, our disciple.” Colb. and Reg. support them. We follow the three manuscripts Norm. and the edition of Bollandus.], concerning blood relationship, I wrote specifically, and not generally, to him and to the English people, who had recently come to the faith, so that they would not withdraw, through fear of more severe demands, from the good which they had begun [Note: [Col. 0102D] Turon. reads: “lest [they withdraw] from one which …” (uncertain, as printed).]. The entire city of Rome bears witness to this. I did not prescribe these things to them with the intention that, after they had been firmly rooted and established in the faith, they should not separate if they were found within their proper consanguinity, or should marry within the line of affinity, that is, as far as the seventh generation.

“Rather, while they were still neophytes, it was necessary first to teach them repeatedly to avoid unlawful things [Note: [Col. 0102D] “To avoid” is absent from Norm., Reg., and Colb.], to instruct them by words and examples, and afterward reasonably and faithfully to exclude what they might do in such matters. For, according to the Apostle who says, ‘I gave you milk to drink, not solid food’ (1 Cor. 3:2), we permitted them to observe these things for the present, not for later times, as was prescribed [Note: [Col. 0102D] Utic. reads “we commanded.”], lest the good which had been planted with a still weak root be uprooted, but so that what had been begun might be strengthened somewhat and preserved until perfection.” [Note: [Col. 0102D] Andeg., together with Colb. and Norm., reads “be burned up.”] (Book XIV, final letter.)

I have taken care to touch upon these matters so that those who contract unlawful marriages on the occasion of this new dispensation may understand that the learned Pope Gregory did not judge the union of the fourth generation to be regularly permissible, but allowed it as a concession and for a time.

[Col. 0102B] Through Gregory’s prayers, almighty God granted Augustine and his companions such abundant grace for performing signs that they confirmed by the power of miracles the word of life which they preached with their mouths. Thus it came about that, after a few years had passed, the other kings of Saxony also approached the faith of Christ the Lord through his disciples.

**39.** Concerning the conversion of this people and the miraculous signs that occurred there, Gregory testifies in this way in his books of the *Moralia*:

“Behold, the language of Britain, which had known nothing but to utter barbarous cries, has long since begun to resound with Hebrew words in the praises of God. Behold, the Ocean, once swollen with pride, now lies humbled and serves at the feet of the saints; and its barbarous waves, which earthly rulers could not subdue with the sword, the mouths of priests bind with simple words through fear of God. The people who, while unbelieving, had no fear of hosts of warriors now, having become faithful, fear the tongues of the humble.

“For when heavenly words have been received and miracles have also shone forth, the power of divine knowledge is poured into it, and it is restrained by dread of that same divinity, so that it fears to act wickedly and eagerly desires, with all its longings, to attain the grace of eternity.” (Book XXVII of the *Moralia*, no. 21.)

When Eulogius, patriarch of Alexandria, sent him a favorable report concerning the teaching of his Church, the conversion of heretics, and the concord of the faithful, Gregory replied:

“Since I know that, in the good works you perform, you also rejoice with others, I return a corresponding acknowledgment of your favor. While the English people, situated in a corner of the world, had until now remained faithless in the worship of wood and stones, it pleased God, through the help of your prayer, that I should send a monk of my monastery to preach to them. After I had granted him permission, he was made bishop by the bishops of Germany, and, with their assistance, he was brought to that people at the end of the world.

“Now reports have reached us concerning his salvation and work: he and those who were sent with him shine among that people with so many miracles that they seem to imitate the powers of the apostles in the signs they display. At the solemnity of the Lord’s Nativity, which has passed in the first indiction [Note: [Col. 0103D] Utic. reads “which passed in this first indiction.”], more than ten thousand English, as we have been informed by that brother and fellow bishop of ours, were baptized by him.

“I have told you this so that you may know what you accomplish by speaking among the Alexandrian people and what you accomplish by praying at the ends of the world. Your prayers are present where you are not, and their holy workings are displayed in the place where you are.” (Book VIII, Letter 30.)

**40.** Nevertheless, concerning these same miracles, he wrote to Augustine among other things:

“I know that almighty God displays great miracles through your love among the people whom he chose as he wished [Note: [Col. 0103D] Colb., Gemet., and Bigot. read “whom he wished to choose.”]. Therefore it is necessary that, concerning this heavenly gift, you both rejoice with fear and fear with rejoicing: rejoice, namely, because the souls of the English are drawn through outward miracles to inward grace; but fear lest, amid the signs that are performed, a weak spirit should raise itself up in presumption, so that, by the very means through which it is lifted outwardly by honor, it should inwardly fall through empty glory, and so forth.” (Book XI, Letter 28.)

**41.** I do not think that the miracles of Gregory commonly recounted among those same Churches of the English ought to be omitted, lest the diligent reader suspect that I have obstinately defrauded him of suitable knowledge or negligently passed it over [Note: [Col. 0103D] Andeg. reads “suitable to knowledge”; Gemet. “suitable to knowledge”; Big. and Utic. “with suitable knowledge.”].

A certain matron had offered the blessed Gregory the customary oblations while he was celebrating the solemn Mass at the public stations. When, after the mysteries, he was about to give it to her, saying, “May the Body of our Lord Jesus Christ preserve your soul,” she laughed suggestively.

Immediately he turned his right hand away from her mouth and placed that portion of the Lord’s Body upon the altar. When the solemn Mass had been completed, he asked the matron before the people why she had presumed to laugh when she was about to receive the Lord’s Body.

After remaining silent for some time, she finally burst out: “I knew that the bread which you were calling the Lord’s Body had been made by my own hands.”

Then Gregory prostrated himself in prayer with all the people on account of the woman’s unbelief. After rising a little later, he found that the piece of bread he had placed upon the altar had become flesh. He showed it to the unbelieving matron before everyone, and was able both to bring her back to the grace of belief and to strengthen the whole people. Then he prostrated himself again with them in prayer and changed the piece of flesh back into the original form of bread.

**42.** At another time the man of God Gregory performed a miracle almost like this one. Certain Westerners had sent envoys to request that he enclose in the customary manner, in individual boxes bearing the names of the martyrs requested, a *brandeum* [Note: [Col. 0103D] In Colb. and Norm. *prandeum* is always written. A *brandeum*, according to Isidore, is a kind of band or veil in which the body of the dead or sacred relics are wrapped. MABILLON.]. After sealing the boxes above, he gave them to the envoys.

They carried away the relics with fitting reverence. But after they had traveled several miles, they began foolishly to complain that they had undertaken such a journey without knowing whether they had received bones of saints or merely pieces of flesh from the Roman pontiff.

Accordingly, by common agreement, they removed the pontifical seal, opened the boxes, and found pieces of *brandeum*. They immediately returned to the city walls in great fury and tearfully complained through the archdeacon that Gregory had deceived them, so that they had received cheap cloth in place of relics. They said that their masters possessed an abundance of beautiful cloths and therefore had no need of the cheap *brandea* of the Romans.

At that time Gregory happened to be celebrating the solemn Mass. When it had been completed, he received the *brandeum* from the same envoys before everyone and placed it upon the altar. Then he devoted himself to prayer with all the others, asking almighty God to reveal as quickly as possible whether what had customarily been sent from the thresholds of the apostles should be venerated as the relics of martyrs.

After rising from prayer, he ordered the unbelieving envoys to stand nearby. He asked for a knife and, following the example of the most holy Pope Leo [Note: [Col. 0104D] Saint Gregory, Book IV, Letter 30, relates that when certain Greeks were doubting, Saint Leo cut a *brandeum* with scissors, and blood flowed from the incision itself.], pierced the *brandeum*. Blood immediately flowed from the punctures.

Terrified by this miracle, both the envoys and all who were present prostrated themselves on the ground with Gregory at his command. They did not cease praying until all the holes in the *brandea* had been closed by divine power.

**43.** Furthermore, one of the wealthy Romans had been deprived of communion by the Roman pontiff after abandoning his wife. He took this very badly and, unable to overcome the authority of so great a pontiff, sought the assistance of magicians.

Persuaded by large gifts, they confidently promised that by their incantations they could cause a demon to enter the pope’s horse and torment it until the horse and its rider were endangered. Delighted by this promise, the impious judge allowed the magicians to stand on an elevated place beside the road along which the pontiff was going to the station, so that they could see those passing by without being seen by them.

When the magicians recognized the great pontiff from the procession of *planetarii* and *mappularii*, they sent in the demon and caused his horse to be tormented so violently that it seemed impossible for either the rider or the grooms to restrain it.

Then Gregory, recognizing through the revelation of the Holy Spirit the demonic assault at work, freed the horse from its present madness by the holy sign of the cross; ordering the sorcerers to be brought down from their concealed height, he condemned them to perpetual blindness.

They confessed their guilt at the instigation of the incestuous judge, and after a long time came to the grace of holy baptism. Gregory refused to restore their sight [Note: [Col. 0104D] Colb., Reg., Utic., and Big. read “lest they practice magic”; Gemet. and And. “lest they read magic.”], but ordered that they nevertheless be supported by the Church’s alms.

**44.** It is also read among those same Churches of the English that, as Gregory was passing through Trajan’s Forum, which he himself had once adorned with exceptionally beautiful buildings, he remembered and admired the judgment of Trajan by which he had consoled a widow [Note: [Col. 0105D] Big. reads “had shown mercy to.”]. The story is as follows, according to the ancient tradition.

Once, when Trajan was hurrying urgently to prepare for an impending war, a certain widow came forward in tears and said:

“My innocent son was killed during your reign. I beg you, since you cannot restore him to me, to deign to avenge his blood according to the law.”

When Trajan replied that, if he returned safely from battle, he would certainly avenge it, the widow said: “But if you die in battle, who will provide this for me?”

Trajan said: “The one who will rule after me.”

The widow said: “And what good will it do you if another gives me justice?”

Trajan replied: “None.”

The widow said: “Is it not better for you to give me justice yourself and receive your reward for it yourself, rather than hand it over to another?”

Then Trajan, moved equally by reason and compassion, dismounted from his horse and did not depart until he had personally settled the widow’s case.

They say that Gregory, remembering this judge’s gentleness, reached the basilica of the holy apostle Peter. There he wept for so long over the error of so compassionate a ruler that on the following night he received an answer that he had been heard on Trajan’s behalf, but that he should never again pour out prayers for any pagan.

Yet although there is no one among the Romans who doubts the preceding miracles, the account read among the Saxons—that through Gregory’s prayers Trajan’s soul was freed from the torments of hell [Note: [Col. 0105D] Colb., Andeg., and Norm. appear to read: “Trajan’s soul . . . freed . . .”]—is especially considered doubtful [Col. 0105C], because so great a teacher would surely not have presumed to pray outright for a pagan. In the fourth book of his *Dialogues* he taught that the reason the saints do not pray in the future judgment for sinners condemned to eternal fire is the same reason why holy men now do not pray for unbelieving and impious dead people.

Those who hold this view fail to notice that it is not said that Gregory interceded for Trajan, but only that he wept. Thus, although Gregory did not pray, he could be heard through his lamentation, just as Moses, when he was silently grieving, could be understood to have cried out. The Lord said to him, though his lips were silent: “Why do you cry to me?” (Exodus 14:15).

For almighty God searches hearts and reins, and frequently in his mercy grants what a human being, although desiring it as a person of flesh, nevertheless does not presume to ask. Hence the Psalmist says: “The Lord has heard the desire of the poor, and your ear has heard the desires of their heart” (Psalm 19:17).

It should also be noted that it is not said that Trajan’s soul was freed from hell and placed in paradise through Gregory’s prayers; that seems altogether incredible because of what is written: “Unless one is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (John 3:3).

It is said simply that he was freed from the torments of hell alone.
