This may indeed seem credible, since a soul can exist in hell without feeling the torments of hell through God’s mercy, just as one fire of Gehenna can hold all sinners together while, through God’s justice, it cannot burn them all equally. Each person will experience punishment in proportion to the guilt he has deserved, according to the just judgment of God.

45. Nevertheless, from the book called by the Greeks λειμών (*leimōn*), while the Latins understand it as *campus*, or meadow, my teacher, interpreting among other things miracles already famed throughout the whole world, wrote to me: 61

> The presbyter [Col. 0106B] Peter told us about the holy Gregory, pope of Rome—for this most reverend presbyter was from there. He said (*Spiritual Meadow*, ch. 192): After he had become pope, Gregory built a large monastery for men and gave orders that none of the monks should possess anything of his own, not even a single obol. [Note: [Col. 0105D] Some printed editions and manuscripts read: “an obol.”]

> A brother from the monastery had a brother who lived in the world, and he made this request of him: “I have no tunic; show me charity and buy me one.” His secular brother said to him: “Here are three coins; take them and buy [Note: [Col. 0105D] Gemet. and Bigot. add: “whatever you like.” A *casula* is the garment or tunic of monks, although commonly the word is used for a priest’s chasuble. On this, note the words of the synod held under Carloman in 742: “We have also decreed that presbyters and deacons shall use *casulae*, after the rite of the servants of God—that is, monks—not cloaks in the manner of laymen.” MABILLON. In the *Spiritual Meadow* one reads: “I have no tunic.” In Greek, καμίσιον. Jerome, *Letter to Fabiola*: “Soldiers commonly have linen tunics, which they call *camisiae*.” Isidore, *Etymologies*, XIX.22, calls them *camisiae* because we sleep in them, *in camis*, that is, in our beds. Consult Rosweyde’s *Onomasticon*. Even today *cama* means “bed” or “sleeping place” in Spanish. BOLLAND.] one of the kind you prefer.”

> The monk therefore received the three coins and kept them with him. Another brother, seeing that he possessed three coins, went and reported it to the abbot. When the abbot heard this, he reported it to the most blessed pope. When the most blessed Gregory learned of it from the abbot, he excluded the monk from communion, as one who had violated the monastery’s rule.

> Shortly thereafter the excluded brother died, without the pope’s knowledge. After two or three days the abbot went and announced to him that the brother had died. Gregory was deeply saddened by this, because before the brother departed this life he had not absolved him from the ecclesiastical penalty of excommunication [Note: [Col. 0106D] *Epitimium*, an ecclesiastical penalty; *pyctacium*, a written tablet or letter. MABILLON.]. He therefore wrote a prayer on a written tablet and gave it to one of his deacons, commanding him to go and have it read over the brother. The prayer absolved the deceased from excommunication.

> The deacon went as he had been commanded and read the tablet containing the prayer over the brother’s tomb. That very night the abbot saw the deceased brother and said to him: “Are you not dead, brother?” He replied: “Indeed, I am.” The abbot asked him again: “Where were you until today?” The brother answered: “Truly, lord, in confinement; and until yesterday I had not been absolved.”

> It thus became known to everyone that at the very hour when the deacon recited the prayer over the tomb, at that hour the brother was absolved from excommunication, and his soul was freed [Col. 0106D] from its dominion [Note: [Col. 0106D] From purgatory, not hell; see the notes on the *Life of Saint Benedict*, ch. 23.].

[Col. 0107A] 46. Gregory therefore dedicated to Christ the Lord not only the Saxons who remained in their own settlements, but also their children who had been dispersed throughout foreign regions. Each year he purchased them at his own expense and led them to knowledge of the faith. Thus he admonishes the presbyter Candidus, saying:

> “As you are going, with the help of our Lord God Jesus Christ, to administer the patrimony situated in Gaul, we wish your Affection to purchase, from the solidi that you will receive, clothing for the poor, or English boys who are seventeen or eighteen years old, so that, once given to God in monasteries, they may make progress. In this way the solidi from Gaul, which cannot be spent in our own country, may usefully be spent in their proper place.

> “If you are able to receive anything from the revenues called *ablatae* [Note: [Col. 0107D] Bigot. and Gemet. read *oblatae*.], we also wish you to use these funds to purchase clothing for the poor, or, as we have said, boys who may advance in the service of almighty God.

> “But since those who may be found there are pagans, I want a presbyter to be sent with them, lest any illness befall them on the journey, so that he may baptize those whom he sees about to die.”

(*Book VI, Letter 7.*)

47. [62] The gentle shepherd Gregory grieved that the peasants of Sardinia continued so persistently in the error of antiquity [Note: [Col. 0107D] Mabillon, Gussanville, and other printed editions read *vetustissimo*, “most ancient.”]. Accordingly, while rebuking Januarius, bishop of Cagliari, for his negligence, he writes among other things:

> “Another matter has occurred that is greatly to be lamented: the peasants whom the Church possesses have, through the negligence of your Fraternity, been permitted to remain in unbelief until now. Why do I admonish you to bring outsiders to the Lord when you neglect to correct your own people’s unbelief? It is therefore necessary for you to remain vigilant in every way concerning their conversion.

> “For if I should find a pagan peasant in Sardinia belonging to any bishop, I shall exact a severe punishment from that bishop. But if a peasant is found to be so impious and obstinate that he absolutely refuses to come to the Lord, he must be burdened with so heavy a tax that the punishment of his own exaction may compel him to hasten toward righteousness.”

(*Book IV, Letter 26.*)

48. When Gregory learned that this course had produced fruitful and salutary results among the peasants of Sardinia, he likewise endeavored to extend it to the Jewish peasants on his patrimonial estates. Thus he writes to the deacon Cyprian:

> “I have learned that there are Hebrews on our estates [Note: [Col. 0107D] Bigot. and some manuscripts read “your estates.”] who are utterly unwilling to convert to God. It seems to me, therefore, that you should send letters throughout all the estates where these Hebrews are known to be, specifically promising them on my behalf that whoever among them converts to the true Lord, our God Jesus Christ, will have the burden of his estate reduced in some measure.

> “I want this to be done in such a way that, if any of them converts and owes a rent of one solidus, a third of a solidus should be remitted to him; if he owes three or four solidi, one solidus should be remitted. If he owes more, the remission should be made according to the same proportion, or certainly according to what your Affection judges appropriate, so that the burden of the convert may be lightened without the Church’s interests being seriously harmed.

> “Nor are we acting uselessly if, by relieving the burdens of their rents, we lead them to the grace of Christ. For even if they themselves come with less than perfect faith, those born from them are nevertheless baptized with greater faithfulness. We therefore gain either the parents themselves or their children, and for that reason whatever we relinquish from the rent for Christ is no great loss.”

(*Book V, Letter 8.*)

49. Indeed, through reductions in their payments as well as promises of the kingdom of heaven, Jews in various places began coming to Christ, whom their fathers had denied. Along with the salvation of their souls, Gregory also supplied those being baptized with suitable clothing. Thus he writes to Fantinus, the defensor:

> “The lady, the abbess of the monastery of Saint Stephen, situated in the territory of Agrigento, has informed us that many Jews, inspired by divine grace, wish to convert to the Christian faith, but that it is necessary for someone to go there on our behalf. Therefore, by the tenor of this authority, we command you to set aside every excuse, hasten to the place mentioned, and, with God’s favor, support their desire through your exhortations.

> “Nevertheless, if they consider it burdensome or distressing [63] to await the paschal solemnity [Note: [Col. 0107D] It was once customary in the Church for baptism to be celebrated only during the vigils of Easter or Pentecost. This practice continued in the Gallican Church not only until the time of Charlemagne but even until the eleventh century. For at the Council of Rouen in 1072, in Orderic Vitalis, *Ecclesiastical History*, IV, p. 529, it was decreed that general baptism should take place only on the Saturday of Easter or Pentecost. MABILLON. It is not possible here to transcribe the lengthy account of this observance in full, although it deserves to be read in its entirety. See the note on Book VIII, Letter 23.], and you learn that they are now eager for baptism, speak with the bishop of that place, so that, under the protection of almighty God’s mercy, he may baptize them—after imposing forty days of penance and abstinence—either on a Sunday or, if some especially celebrated feast should occur. The quality of the times, because of the disaster impending over it, also urges this course, so that their desires should not be postponed by any delay, lest, God forbid, a long postponement turn their hearts back.

> “If you find any of them poor and unable to afford clothing for themselves, we want you to purchase and provide them with clothing to wear at baptism; you should know that the price you pay is to be entered in your accounts.

> “But if they choose to wait for holy Easter, speak again with the bishop, so that for the present they may become catechumens, and so that he may visit them frequently, take care for them, and kindle their hearts through the admonition of his exhortation, so that the longer the feast they await is postponed, the more diligently they may prepare for it and endure the delay with fervent desire.” [Note: [Col. 0108D] Bigot. and Gemet. read: “so that the more the feast is awaited and prolonged”; Andeg. reads: “so that the more the feast that has been awaited is prolonged.”]

(*Book VIII, Letter 23.*)

> Likewise, to Peter, bishop of Corsica, he writes among other things: “We have sent your Fraternity fifty solidi for the purchase of clothing for those who are to be baptized.”

(*Book VIII, Letter 1.*)

[Col. 0109A] 50. Gregory extended his pastoral care no less to the purpose of joining the children of Arians to the Catholic faith. Accordingly, writing to all the bishops of Italy, he says:

> “Because the most wicked Autharith prevented the children of the Lombards from being baptized in the Catholic faith during the Paschal festival that has recently been completed [Note: [Col. 0109D] Corb., Bigot., Gemet., and Andeg. read *exempla*, a reading noted in the margin by Mabillon and Gussanville. Reg. reads *Exorta est*.], for which offense the divine Majesty destroyed him, so that he would not see another Easter solemnity [Note: [Col. 0109D] Thus our manuscripts read, although the printed editions have *Paschae ulterius*, “another Easter.”], it is fitting that your Fraternity admonish all the Lombards throughout your districts that, since a serious mortality is impending everywhere, they should reconcile these same children of theirs, baptized in the Arian heresy, to the Catholic faith, so that they may appease almighty God’s anger against them.”

> Likewise, to Praejectus, bishop of Narni:

> “It has come to our attention that, because of the sins hanging over your city, a very severe mortality is raging there [Col. 0109B], and this has afflicted us greatly. Therefore, greeting your Fraternity, we earnestly urge you never to cease admonishing the Lombards or Romans who live in that place, and especially the gentiles and heretics, so that they may be converted to the true and right Catholic faith.

> “For in this way either divine mercy will perhaps assist them in this life because of their conversion, or, if it should happen that they depart this life, they will pass from it absolved from their sins—which is even more to be desired.”

(*Book II, Letter 2.*)

51. Gregory, the most prudent steward of Christ, therefore appointed suitable men to each of the deaconries and hospices. To enable them to labor more securely, indeed more intelligently, in works of piety and mercy, he decided that they should be protected by privileges of the following kind:

> “Although the devotion of those who, with pious intention, [64] devote themselves to caring for the weak and needy is sufficient to defend them before everyone, it is nevertheless better, for their peace of mind, that they be protected concerning what they have done, lest the occasion of anxiety arise for them from the very thing for which they deserve the greatest praise.

> “Since, moved by your zeal and intention, we have chosen you, a religious man, to be placed in charge of the deaconry responsible for supplying the tables of the poor [Note: [Col. 0109D] In Utic. *Joannem religiosum*, “John the religious,” is read instead.], so that no uncertainty might arise for you from this administration, we have provided you with this safeguard. We establish that, concerning what you have received—or may subsequently receive—for distribution to the tables of the poor or for the support of the deaconry, you shall never be compelled by any person, in any manner or by any device, to render an account, nor shall you be required to endure any harassment.

> “But although we wish you to be released from all human accounting in this matter, you should know that you will render an account to our God for what we have entrusted to you. We therefore urge you to preserve sincerity of faith within you; let your mind be more attentive to these matters, your care more earnest, [Note: [Col. 0109D] Utic. adds: “your willingness more prompt.”] your diligence more watchful, your devotion more distinguished, and your service more effective. Thus, while with divine assistance you diligently fulfill this work, those for whom you care may be usefully comforted by the support of your devotion, and you may receive in eternal life the reward of your goodness, compensated by the grace of our Redeemer.”

(*Book XI, Letter 27.*)

52. Gregory exercised these works of piety both within and outside the city. In addition, he sent the religious abbot Probus to Jerusalem with a large sum of money. Through Probus’s efforts he established a venerable hospice there, and both there and on Mount Sinai, in Arabia, he arranged to send each year, for as long as he lived, an ample supply of daily food and clothing to the servants of God living under the direction of Palladius.

53. Moreover, throughout various provinces, for the preservation of sacred religion and the vigorous administration of the affairs of the poor, he recruited capable men for his Church as administrators of its patrimonies. Among them were Cyprian, deacon and administrator of the Sicilian patrimony; Pantaleon, notary of Syracuse; Fantinus, defensor of Palermo; Sergius, defensor of Calabria; Romanus, notary of Apulia; Benenatus, defensor of Samnium; Anthemius, subdeacon of Naples; Peter, subdeacon of Campania; Candidus, defensor of Tuscany; Urbicus, defensor of Sabina; Optatus, defensor of Nursia; Benedict, [Note: [Col. 0110D] The word *notary* is absent from Norm. and Turon.] notary and defensor of Carsoli; Felix, subdeacon of the Appian district; Castorius, chartularius of Ravenna; Castorius, notary of Istria; Antonius, subdeacon of Dalmatia; John, notary of Illyricum [Note: [Col. 0110D] Utic. reads: “John, notary of Corsica … Boniface … of Illyricum …”]; Symmachus, defensor of Sardinia; Boniface, notary of Corsica; Pantaleon, notary of Liguria; Jerome, defensor of the Cottian Alps; Hilary, notary of Germanicia; and Candidus, presbyter of Gaul.

The prudent Father Gregory judged that these arrangements should be observed perpetually not only in the Roman Church but also throughout the various Churches. Thus he writes among other things to Januarius, bishop of Cagliari:

> “It has been reported to us that, after entrusting the administration of your patrimony to certain laymen, they were later found [65] to have engaged in the plundering and consequent exhaustion of your peasants. They postpone restoring the goods that they improperly retain, treating them as though they were under their own control, because they are not subject to your oversight; and they disdain to render you an account of their actions. [Note: [Col. 0110D] In many manuscripts, immediately after *deprehensi*, one reads: “if this is so.”]

> “If this is true, it is fitting that you investigate the matter rigorously and that the case between them and the peasants of your Church be examined with the greatest precision, so that, whatever fraud is found among them, they may be compelled to restore it under the penalty prescribed by law.

> “For the future, your Fraternity must take care that the property of the Church is not entrusted to secular men or to those who do not live under our rule [Note: [Col. 0110D] Norm. reads: “under your rule.”], but to proven clerics from your own office. If any depravity should be discovered among them, you will then be able to correct in your subordinates whatever has been done unlawfully, selecting those whose established conduct among you is more likely to recommend them for the office than to excuse them.”

(*Book X, Letter 65.*)

54. He ordered that each office belonging to ecclesiastical administration should be entrusted separately to a separate person. He maintained that, just as in one body we have many members, though all the members do not perform the same function (*Romans* XII), so in the body of the Church, according to Paul’s truthful teaching, in one and the same Spirit one person should be assigned this office and another entrusted with that one. Nor should the offices of two different responsibilities be entrusted at the same time to a single person, however experienced, because, if the whole body were an eye, where would hearing be?

For just as the variety of the members, through their different functions, both preserves the body’s strength and displays its beauty, so the variety of persons, likewise distributed among different offices, manifests both the strength and the dignity of the holy Church of God. And just as it is unbecoming for one member of the human body to perform the function of another [Col. 0111B], so it is harmful and exceedingly disgraceful if the individual ministries of administration are not distributed among an equal number of persons.

For this reason he frequently imposed the reins of moderation upon certain ambitious men, as may be found in his letters, which I have omitted for the sake of brevity. Thus, concerning Bishop Paschasius, who himself continued to serve as both his own major domus and his own vicedominus, he ordered the subdeacon Anthemius among other things:

> “We wish our brother Paschasius to appoint for himself both a vicedominus and a major domus, so that he may be capable and ready to deal either with visiting guests or with matters that arise. But if you see that he is negligent or slow to carry out what we have said, his entire clergy must be convened, so that, by common counsel, they themselves may choose persons capable of being appointed to the offices mentioned above.”

(*Book XI, Letter 71.*)

Likewise, he opposed the clerics of Ravenna who were importunately seeking control of monasteries, writing to John, bishop of Ravenna:

> “It has come to me that in some of the churches of your Fraternity certain places formerly consecrated as monasteries have now been made into dwellings for clerics or even laymen [Note: [Col. 0111D] Some printed editions read “in the Church.” The manuscripts contradict this.]. While those who are in the churches pretend to live religiously, they seek to be placed over monasteries, and through their way of life the monasteries are destroyed.

> “No one can both serve ecclesiastical duties [66] and remain orderly within the monastic rule, since the man who is compelled to remain daily in ecclesiastical service cannot himself observe the strict discipline of a monastery. Therefore let your Fraternity hasten to correct whatever of this kind has been done anywhere, because I absolutely cannot tolerate sacred places being destroyed through the ambition of clerics.”

(*Book V, Letter 1.*)

Likewise, to Mariniano, bishop of Ravenna:

> “For some time, reports from many people had reached us that the monasteries established in the region of Ravenna were being excessively burdened by the domination of your clerics, so that, under the pretext of administration, they possessed them—as it is grievous to say—as though they were their own property.

> “We were deeply distressed by this and sent letters to your predecessor, so that he should correct the matter in every respect. But since he was quickly overtaken by the end of his life, lest this burden remain upon the monasteries, we remember having written the same things to your Fraternity. And because, as we have learned, correction in this matter has until now been neglected, we have now judged it necessary to send you this letter again.

> “We therefore urge you, setting aside every delay and every excuse, to relieve these monasteries from such a burden, so that henceforth no clerics or persons belonging to the sacred order may have permission to enter them for any other reason than prayer alone, unless perhaps they have been invited to perform the sacred mysteries of the Mass.

> “But lest they perhaps be forced to bear some burden on account of the promotion of any monk or abbot, we must take care that, if any abbot or monk from any monastery should enter the clerical office or sacred order [Note: [Col. 0111D] Yet Gregory himself, in a letter to Urbicus, abbot, Book IX, Letter 42, says: “We wish the presbyter Domitius to be abbot of the monastery of Lucusianus.” Certainly, at this time very few abbots in Gaul were without priestly ordination—indeed, few monks were either. The rule Gregory prescribes here is therefore a special provision for that particular place, intended to restrain the greed of clerics coveting monasteries. MABILLON.], he should no longer have any authority there, as we have said, lest under cover of this opportunity the monasteries be compelled to endure the burdens we prohibit.

> “Let your Holiness, warned now for the second time, not delay correcting all these matters with vigilant care. For if after this we should discover that you are negligent—which we do not believe—we shall be compelled to provide for the peace of the monasteries by other means. You should know that we will no longer tolerate the congregation of God’s servants being subjected to such a necessity.”

(*Book VII, Letter 43.*)

Likewise, to Maximianus, bishop of Syracuse, after some other matters:

> “Do not permit presbyters, deacons, or clerics of any other rank who in any way serve in the churches to become abbots in monasteries. They must either abandon their clerical service and advance within the monastic order, or, if they decide to remain in the position of abbot, they must in no way be permitted to retain the service of the clergy.

> “It is wholly inappropriate that, when a person cannot carefully fulfill one of these duties because of its importance, he should be judged capable of fulfilling both, so that the ecclesiastical order may obstruct the monastic way of life and the monastic rule may obstruct ecclesiastical usefulness.” [Note: [Col. 0112D] Utic. and Gemet. read: “the rule of the monks may hinder.” Bigot. and Andeg. read: “the rule may hinder the monks.”]

(*Book IV, Letter 11.*)

### 55.

How Gregory, through the administrators of the ecclesiastical estates, kept watch over the whole breadth of the world with the eyes of his pastoral concern, like a certain most luminous Argus, I shall perhaps not inappropriately touch upon here. For he says in a letter to the subdeacon Anthemius:

> “We instructed you when you were learning, and afterward I remember having charged you through repeated commands to care for the poor and, if you discovered any needy people there, to report them by returning letters; yet you have scarcely taken care to do this for a few. I wish, however, that as soon as you receive the present command you offer Lady Pateria, my aunt (*thia*, θεία), forty solidi for the footwear of the boys and four hundred modii of wheat; Lady Palatina, widow of Urbicus, twenty solidi and three hundred modii of wheat; and Lady Viviana, widow of Felix, twenty solidi and three hundred modii of wheat.

[Note: The printed editions, with the Regius, Colbert, and Sainte-Marie de Paris manuscripts, read either *Paterichiae meae* or *Patriarchiae*; the Andegavian, Gemet, Bigot, Uticensis, and other manuscripts more correctly read *Pateriae thiae*, that is, “my aunt,” for this is the meaning of the Greek word *thia* (θεία). Bigot reads “fifty” rather than “forty” solidi. The same manuscript reads *Bibianae* rather than *Vivianae*.] These eighty solidi in all are to be charged to your accounts. Bring the full amount of the allowance with all speed, and, with the Lord’s help, arrive by Easter.”

(*Book I, Letter 39.*)

The same to him:

> “It has been brought to our attention that certain handmaids of the Lord in the city of Nola, living in the house of Aboridanus, are suffering extreme lack of food and clothing. Since God’s command requires us to assist them, we ought, with the Lord’s help, to relieve their poverty as far as we can. Therefore, by this present command, we have instructed Your Experience that in the present ninth indiction you must give them forty gold solidi, and thereafter, in succeeding indictions, provide twenty solidi annually, which may be charged to your accounts. Moreover, we command you to give two solidi each to Paulinus, priest of the monastery of Saint Erasmus, situated on the slope of Mount Soracte, and to the two monks

[Note: The Norman, three Parisian, and Turonensis manuscripts read *Serapti* for *Soractis*.] serving in the oratory of the holy Archangel, which is known to be located at the fortress of Lucullanum beside the basilica of Saint Peter; these too are to be charged to your accounts. Act, therefore, so that you also may share in the reward of this expenditure.”

(*Book I, Letter 24.*)

The same to him:

> “If, moved by compassion, we come with kindly intent to the needs of our neighbors, we undoubtedly find the merciful Lord responsive to our petitions. For Palatina, a woman of distinction, has represented that she is subject to many needs because of continual hostile attack. Therefore, by this present authority, we command Your Experience not to delay giving her thirty solidi annually for her support, which may afterward be charged to your accounts. Act, therefore, so that you too may receive the benefit of a well-administered reward and bring our commands to complete fulfillment.”

(*Book I, Letter 67, ninth indiction.*)

The same Gregory to the subdeacon Peter:

> “It has been brought to our attention that Marcellus of the Church of Baruni, assigned to penance there in the city of Palermo, in the monastery of Saint Hadrian, suffers not only want of food but also extreme distress from lack of clothing. For this reason we find it necessary to command Your Diligence by the present order to provide for him, for food and clothing, a bed suited to continence, and an allowance for his boy, in whatever quantity you judge sufficient,

[Note: The Turonensis, Parisian, and Andegavian manuscripts read “an annual allowance, in whatever quantity you judge sufficient.”] so that his poverty and nakedness may be relieved by such provision; and whatever you assign to this man may afterward be charged to your accounts. Act, therefore, so that you fulfill our command and may yourself share in this reward by arranging it well.”

(*Book I, Letter 18, ninth indiction.*)

The same to him:

> “We have learned from the bearer of this letter that the monastery of the holy Archangel, established at Tropaea, is in need of food. Therefore Your Experience must watch diligently, so that, if you discover that the monks of that place are conducting themselves well and it is manifestly clear that they are in need, you hasten by every means, supported by this authority, to assist them. You are to know that whatever you provide at our command is to be charged to your accounts. They also assert that a small plot adjoining our Church is assessed at one solidus and two tremisses; if this is so, allow it to be held by written lease at a total rent of one tremissis. Let it be the concern of your diligence to complete all this in the manner stated, if, as we have said, the monks of that place persist as they ought in their zeal for God’s service.”

(*Book II, Letter 1.*)

The same to him:

> “The divine commandments admonish us to love our neighbors as ourselves; and since we are commanded to love them with this charity, how much more ought we to assist them in the necessities of bodily support, so that, if not by every means, at least by some forms of assistance, we may relieve their distress? Since, therefore, we have seen that the son of a most worthy man suffers poverty not only through loss of sight but also through lack of food,

[Note: Colbert and the Vatican and Gussan editions read “the son of Filimoud”; Gilot reads “the daughter of Filimoua”; the Bollandists read “the son of the most worthy Godistald”; and Uticensis reads “the son of Odiscalchus.” Most manuscripts read *modia* rather than *modios*, here and below. An alternative reading is: “report delays to me.”] we have judged it necessary to provide for him as far as our means permit. Therefore, by the present command, we instruct Your Experience to provide every year, for the support of his life, twenty-four modii of wheat, twelve modii of beans, and twenty tithes (*decimatae*) of wine, which may afterward be charged to your accounts. Act, therefore, so that the bearer of this letter suffers no delay in receiving the Lord’s gifts and that you may be found a participant in the reward of good administration on the Lord’s Day.”

(*Book I, Letter 46.*)

The same Gregory to the deacon Cyprian:

> “Cosmas says that, through various dangers and difficulties, he has become bound by many debts, so that, because of them, he says that his creditors are detaining his sons. This matter, if it is so, has greatly moved us. Therefore we urge Your Affection, since the issue concerns the distribution of the goods of the poor, to investigate his case with the greatest exactness; and if you find that he is truly so entangled in the debts mentioned that he has no property with which he can repay them, see his creditors and, for the recovery of his sons, settle with them for whatever amount you discover to be appropriate. Since he himself, as he says, has nothing with which to repay, pay it from the goods of the poor by our present authority, knowing that whatever is given there through your provision is to be reckoned among the revenues of our estate.”

(*Book III, Letter 58.*)

The same to the same:

> “Our brother and fellow bishop Zeno has informed us that certain people in his city are suffering want of food. Since we desire, as far as possible, to provide them some relief, we therefore assign you by this letter to give our aforesaid brother one thousand modii of wheat—or, if he can carry more, up to two thousand—in writing. We urge you, therefore, to introduce no delay or excuse in providing this, so that, while the time permits, he may, with God’s help, return safely to his own country and be able more quickly to assist those who are suffering need.”

(*Book VI, Letter 4, fourteenth indiction.*)

The same Gregory to Eusebius, a religious abbot:

> “Let Your Charity believe me: I have been greatly saddened by your sadness, and so forth.”

[Note: The Vulgate editions read *propterea*, “therefore.”]

> “Moreover, we have arranged for one hundred solidi to be given to Your Affection through the subdeacon Peter; I ask that you accept them without considering it an injury.”

(*Book II, Letter 36, tenth indiction.*)

The same Gregory to Candidus, defensor:

> “It is proper that episcopal assistance be given to those suffering need. Therefore, by the present authority, we command Your Experience not to cease providing Albinus, deprived of sight, son of the late Martin, the tenant-farmer, two tremisses every year without any delay, being certain that this will unquestionably be charged to your accounts.”

[Note: The Sainte-Marie de Paris, Colbert, Gemet, and Bigot manuscripts read *Marini* rather than *Martini*.]

(*Book IV, Letter 28.*)

The same Gregory to Fantinus, defensor:

> “The bearer of this letter, Cosmas the Syrian, has stated that he incurred a debt in the business he was conducting; we believe this to be true, as many other circumstances and his tears attest. Since he owed one hundred and fifty solidi, I wished his creditors to reach some agreement with him, because the law also provides that a free man may in no way be held for a debt if he lacks property that can be assigned to it. According to his statement, it may be possible for his creditors to agree to eighty solidi. But since it is excessive for them to demand eighty solidi from a man who has nothing, we have sent you sixty solidi through your notary, so that you may discuss the matter carefully with those creditors and give them an account that, according to the laws, they cannot hold his son, whom they are said to be detaining.

[Note: The same manuscripts, together with the Andegavian manuscript, read “and give an account.”] If possible, persuade them to accept less than we have given; and whatever remains of those sixty solidi, give to him, so that he may live from it with his son. If nothing remains, or if possible, arrange matters so that his debt is reduced to that same amount, enabling him afterward to work freely for himself. In any event, act carefully so that, once they have received the solidi, they draw up a complete written release for him.”

[Note: The same manuscripts, together with the Andegavian manuscript, read: “and return an account.”]

(*Book IV, Letter 45.*)

The same Gregory to Castorius, deacon and chartularius at Ravenna, among other matters:

> “We certainly wish the monk Valerian, whom you delivered, once corrected, to the monastery of blessed John situated at Classe, to remain in that monastery. Moreover, so that Your Experience may suffer no want in meeting expenses, we wish you to meet all your expenses from the revenues of the holy Roman Church collected there under your administration; and if anything remains, bring it to us when you come.”

(*Book V, Letter 28.*)

The same Gregory to Romanus, defensor:

> “The words of the divine commandments admonish us to provide ecclesiastical assistance to those suffering need. Since, therefore, our most beloved son, the deacon Cyprian, has reported that Gaudiosus, defensor of our see, who is known to reside at Syracuse, is constrained by poverty and want, we therefore command Your Experience by this authority to give him six solidi every year beginning with the present second indiction, so that he may enjoy the comfort of this remedy and you may certainly know that what you give is to be charged to your accounts.”

(*Book IX, Letter 39, second indiction.*)

The same Gregory to Libertinus, former praetor:

> “We are not unaware of how great an affliction of this world presses upon you. But since, for those placed in the deepest tribulation, the mercy of the Creator alone is consolation, place your hope in him and turn to him with your whole mind. He both justly permits whomever he wishes to be afflicted and mercifully delivers the person who trusts in him. Give thanks to him, therefore, and patiently endure whatever has been inflicted. For it is the mark of a right-minded person to bless God not only in prosperity but also to praise him in adversity. Let no murmuring against the Lord creep into your hearts amid the things you suffer, because it is unknown for what purpose our Creator is doing this. Perhaps, most illustrious son, while placed in prosperity you offended him in some way, and he wishes to purify you through a merciful bitterness. Therefore let neither temporal affliction break you nor the loss of possessions torment you; for if, giving thanks in adversity, you make God favorably disposed toward you through your patience, what has been lost will be restored many times over, and, beyond this, eternal joys will be granted.

> “I ask you not to consider it insulting that we have written through the defensor Romanus that twenty annual clothing allowances be provided for your boys; for, although the offerings from the possessions of blessed Peter the Apostle are small, they must always be received as a great blessing, since he will be able to bestow greater gifts upon you here and grant eternal benefits before almighty God.”

[Note: Bigot and Gembloux read: “for there is only the consolation of the Creator of all things,” with the phrase “of the Almighty,” as it is said, in one word.]

(*Book X, Letter 31.*)

The same Gregory to Philip, priest:

> “I received the letters of Your Affection, in which you took care to inform me that the venerable man Andrew, priest, had departed this life. I rejoiced at his deliverance, because he has attained the eternal joys for which he always prayed. As for the solidi left at Jerusalem by our son Probus, abbot, for the construction of a hospice, I could not alter what had been decided should be done; but I have sent Your Holiness a small blessing of fifty solidi.”

[Note: Turonensis and Gemet read *expedit*; Bigot reads *expediunt*.]

(*Book XIII, Letter 29.*)

### 56.

It would be long and exceedingly difficult to pursue even this sort of activity of his almsgiving. I state briefly that he distributed freely even to those who did not ask and cheerfully provided for all who asked him. Thus, to Elias, priest and abbot of the province of Isauria:

> “The Gospels,” he says, “as you requested, we have sent.”

And a little later:

> “You wished fifty solidi to be sent to you for the needs of your cell; thinking this a large amount, you gave ten of them back to us so that we might send forty. But, lest even this should perhaps be burdensome, you were kind enough to give us another ten from it. Since, however, we found you extremely generous in your ascetic discipline, we have responded in like manner to that generosity and sent fifty. And lest that should perhaps be too little, we have added another ten. But lest even this should still be too little, we have had another twelve joined to it. In this we recognize your affection: you rely upon us in the same way that you ought to rely upon us.”

[Note: The Vatican and Gussan editions, against the manuscripts, read *evangelistam*, “the evangelist.”]

(*Book V, Letter 37.*)

### 57.

Likewise, to Julianus:

> “When I received the writings of Your Glory, I gladly opened them to read them, but after reading them I went over them with sadness. For they said that it had been a matter of shame for you to have remained silent for so long about things that ought to have been said to me. It is certain that the person who is still treated with embarrassment is loved less. I was deeply saddened because I discovered that I was loved by you less than I had thought. Yet you greatly restrain me in this if you diligently seek the causes of reward by continually providing for me. It ought not to be a matter of shame to speak insistently about alms to someone who plainly possesses not his own goods but those of the poor for distribution.

> “You ought therefore to have dealt freely with the bishop concerning the causes of reward, even if you did not know what my disposition toward you was in affection. Since we love Your Glory wholeheartedly and, as you know, hold the office of administering the goods of the poor, I confess that your embarrassment was highly blameworthy. I pursue it with so many words of reproach in order to drive it entirely from your heart and to have the great comfort of your provision in matters of reward.

> “Accordingly, for your monastery, which was built by you in the city of Catania, we have designated ten solidi annually to be given through Adrianus, notary and administrator of the estate, by a written order that has been issued. We ask that you accept them without considering it an injury, because it is not our offering that is presented to you, but the blessing of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles.”

[Note: The manuscripts read as above; the Bollandists, Gilot, and Mabillon agree in part. Gussan and the Vatican edition read: “you despise me greatly if you do not seek …”]

(*Book XIII, Letter 19.*)

### 58.

Since there are some who give away what they possess but do not cease to seize what belongs to others and what they themselves do not possess, and, while eagerly wishing to appear generous, forcibly take from those who have and distribute what they have taken to those who lack it as though out of mercy, I insert here two letters of Gregory by which the innocence of his generosity may be wonderfully demonstrated.

For he says in a letter to Pantaleo, notary:

> “Your Experience remembers what sort of oath you gave before the most sacred body of blessed Peter the Apostle. Therefore we too, secure in his scrutiny, entrusted you with the investigations concerning the estate of the Syracusan district. You ought, therefore, always to keep your fidelity and fear of that same blessed Peter the Apostle before your eyes and act so that you may be found blameworthy neither by human beings in the present life nor by almighty God at the final judgment.

> “For, as our chartularius Valerius has reported, we have learned that you found the measure by which the tenants of the Church were compelled to give grain to be twenty-five sextarii, something we have utterly condemned, and we were grieved that you had conducted this investigation so late. Since, however, you state that you broke that measure and made it just, we rejoiced. But since the aforesaid chartularius also took care to inform us of the amount already collected through the frauds of the tenant-farmers under Your Experience from two territories, just as we rejoice that you acted diligently by breaking the unjust measure, so also in the future we are concerned about past sins: lest, if the things that the tenant-farmers fraudulently took from the peasants reach us, the sins committed by them should be transferred to us.

> “Therefore we wish you, with complete faith and purity, keeping in mind the fear of almighty God and the strict judgment of blessed Peter the Apostle, to record by each estate the poor and needy tenants under your administration; then, from the money found to have been obtained through fraud, purchase cows, sheep, and pigs and distribute them among the individual poor tenants. We wish you to do this with the advice of the most reverend Lord John, bishop, and our chartularius and administrator Adrianus. If advice is necessary, my son Lord Julianus should also be consulted, but no one else is to know of this; it must be entirely secret.

> “Consider among yourselves, therefore, whether the same amount should be given to those poor tenants in gold or in coin. Whatever you jointly decide, first make the record as I have said, and afterward strive to distribute it to each according to the degree of his poverty. For, as the Apostle to the Gentiles testifies, I have all things and abound, and I seek not money but reward (Phil. 4). Act, therefore, so that on the day of judgment you may show me the fruit you have produced from this cause of reward entrusted to Your Experience. If you act purely, faithfully, and energetically, you will receive him here in your children and afterward have a full recompense at the tribunal of the eternal Judge.”

(*Book XI, Letter 3.*)

The same Gregory to the subdeacon Peter:

> “Because we were occupied with the business of the Paschal festival, we were unable to dismiss your responsalis as quickly as we wished. But you will learn below how we have arranged all the cases about which you took care to inquire, after investigating them thoroughly. We have learned that the peasants of the Church are being heavily burdened in the prices of grain, so that the established amount is not maintained for them during the season of plenty. We wish the measure used in purchasing grain to be observed at the public prices at all times, whether less or more grain is produced. Grain lost in a shipwreck is to be fully reckoned, but only on condition that there is no negligence on your part in forwarding it; otherwise, if the time for forwarding is neglected, the loss will arise from your fault.

> “We have perceived that it is extremely wrong and unjust for anything to be taken from the peasants of the Church on account of sextariatic charges and for them to be compelled to provide a larger measure than is delivered into the Church’s granaries. Therefore, by this present admonition, we command that no more than a measure of eighteen sextarii ever be taken from the peasants of the Church, unless perhaps there is something which, according to custom, the sailors take in addition, and which they themselves attest is lost on the ships.

> “We have also learned that in certain places or estates of the Church an exceedingly unjust exaction is made, so that tenant-farmers are said to exact *septuaginta ternis semis* [reading materially uncertain]—an impious amount to name.

[Note: The edition reads “up to seventy and a half urns”; the manuscripts and John the Deacon’s text are followed here.] Nor is even this sufficient, but in addition they are said to exact something customary for many years. We utterly detest this practice and wish it to be cut out entirely from the estate. Let Your Experience assess both this excess beyond the pound and the other minor burdens, as well as whatever is taken from the peasants beyond the fairness of the account, and reduce everything to the total of the rent. Let them pay a full and weight-equivalent rent up to seventy wine-measures, in proportion to what the peasants’ resources can bear.

[Note: The editions read: “let them pay up to seventy wine-flasks”; the Sainte-Marie de Paris and Regius manuscripts support them. After “reduce,” Uticensis adds: “and not burdens greater than the pound.” The manuscripts read “burdens” and, shortly afterward, “minor charges.”] They must not demand either additional small charges beyond the pound or a larger pound; rather, according to your assessment and to the strength available, the amount should increase toward the total rent, so that no disgraceful exaction occurs.

> “Lest, after my death, these same burdens which we have removed from the assessment and caused to be included in the principal of the rent should again be added in some way, so that the total rent might appear to increase and the peasants be compelled to pay additional burdens, we wish you to prepare written guarantees concerning the rents, stating first that each person must pay such-and-such a rent, with the small charges, vegetables, and grain dues removed. Whatever used to come from these minor charges for the administrator’s use, I wish from this command to come into your use.

> “Above all, we wish you to attend carefully to this: no unjust weights are to be imposed in collecting the rents. If you find any such weights, break them and establish new and correct ones. For my son, the deacon Servusdei, has already found such things as displeased him, but he did not have permission to change them. Therefore, beyond the just weights and the excepted items and cheap foodstuffs, we wish nothing else to be exacted from the tenants of the Church.”

[Note: Normannus reads “and cheap food.”]

> “Moreover, we have learned that the first payment of the *burdatio* [the levy or transport charge paid by the peasants] severely distresses our peasants, so that before they can sell the fruits of their labor they are compelled to pay the taxes. Since they borrow the money they must pay from public moneylenders, because they do not possess it themselves, and pay heavy interest on that favor, they are thereby pressed by serious losses. Therefore, by this present admonition, we command that no more than eighteen sextarii ever be exacted, and that whatever they might have been able to borrow from outsiders for this purpose be provided publicly through Your Experience and collected from the peasants of the Church little by little, as they have the means; otherwise, while they are pressed at the appointed time, they will be compelled to sell cheaply what might afterward have sufficed for the payment and it will be of no use to them.”

[Note: In the same manuscripts: “so that everything borrowed for this purpose …,” with the remainder omitted in others.]

> “It has also come to us that excessive profit is being obtained from the marriages of peasants. Concerning this we command that the entire marriage payment in no case exceed one solidus. If any are poor, they ought to give even less. If any are wealthy, they must likewise in no way exceed the aforesaid sum of one solidus. We do not wish this marriage payment to be entered into our account in any way, but it is to benefit the tenant-farmers.”

> “We have also learned that when certain tenant-farmers die, their relatives are not permitted to succeed them, but their property is taken for the use of the Church. Concerning this we decree that the relatives of deceased tenant-farmers who live on Church property must succeed them as heirs, and nothing is to be removed from the substance of the deceased. If someone leaves young children, careful persons are to be selected to whom their parents’ property may be entrusted for safekeeping until they reach an age at which they can manage their own property.”

> “We have also learned that if someone from the household commits a fault, punishment is inflicted not upon him but upon his property. Concerning this we command that whoever commits a fault be punished in his own person, as is fitting, but that his benefit or property be left entirely untouched, except perhaps for some small amount that may serve the needs of the official sent to him.”

> “We have also learned that whenever a tenant-farmer unjustly takes something from his tenant, it is indeed exacted from the tenant-farmer, but is not returned to the person from whom it was taken. Concerning this we command that whatever has been violently taken from anyone belonging to the household be restored to the person from whom it was taken and not be turned to our advantage, lest we ourselves appear to be the authors of violence.”

> “Moreover, we wish that whenever you send persons in your service on some business outside the estate, they may indeed receive small payments from it, but that these should benefit them in such a way that they seek no profit for themselves under the pretext of our advantage. For we do not wish the Church’s purse to be polluted by shameful profits.”

> “We also order Your Experience to guard this most carefully: tenant-farmers must never be established on the Church’s estates through payment or inducement, lest, while profit is sought, the tenant-farmers frequently be changed. What else results from such change except that the Church’s lands are never cultivated? The written leases themselves are also to be moderated according to the total amount of the rent. Through the cells and storehouses we do not wish you to receive from the Church’s estates more than the custom allows.”

[Note: Some manuscripts read “but whatever things …”; others, “but whatever things of yours are to be purchased.”]

> “The things we have ordered you to purchase are to be purchased from outsiders.”

> “It has come to us that three pounds of gold were unjustly taken from Peter, tenant-farmer of Subpatriana. Investigate this matter carefully with the defensor Fantinus; and if they were manifestly taken unjustly and improperly, restore them without any delay.”

> “We have also learned that the peasants again paid the *burdatio* which Theodosius had failed to pay when it had already been exacted from them, so that they were charged twice over. This happened because his property was insufficient to meet the Church’s debt. Since, however, we have learned through our son, the deacon Servusdei, that this loss can be adequately repaired from the substance of his property, we wish five hundred and seven solidi to be restored to those peasants without any reduction, lest they appear to have been charged twice. If, in addition to the peasants’ loss, forty solidi remain from Theodosius’s property, which you are said to possess, we wish them to be returned to his daughter, so that she may recover the property that he had given as security. We also wish his father’s small vessel or utensil (*batiola*) to be restored to her.”

[Note: Consult the notes on the letters concerning the meaning of *batiola*. It would not be burdensome to consult them if any difficulty arises in the other letters cited by John the Deacon; repeating here what we have already noted elsewhere would be tedious.]

> “Campanianus, the illustrious master of soldiers, had left twelve annual solidi to his notary John from the estate of Varronianus. We command you to give these every year, without hesitation, to the niece of Euplus the tenant-farmer, although she received all of Euplus’s movable property, except only the solidi. We also wish you to give her twenty-five solidi from his solidi. A silver support or stand is said to have been assigned for one solidus, and a cup is said to have been assigned for six solidi. Question Dominicus the secretary, or others who may know, recover what is owed, and restore the aforesaid vessels.”

> “We thank your diligence because, when I ordered you to send back my brother’s silver, you forgot it completely, as though something had been said to you by your most wretched slave. Now let your Experience—or rather your negligence—take care to fulfill this; send back with all speed whatever of his property you discover to have been with Antoninus.”

> “A letter has been found concerning the case of Salpingus the Jew, which we have had sent to you. Reread it, investigate carefully his case and that of a certain widow who is said to be involved in the same matter, and concerning the fifty-one solidi known to be repayable, give such response as seems just to you, so that in no way may another person’s property be unjustly defrauded from the creditors.”

[Note: Some read “which are to be returned.”]

> “Half of Antoninus’s bequest has been given to him, and half is to be redeemed. We wish that half to be fulfilled for him from the common property; and not only for him, but also for the defensores, the pilgrims, to whom he left something by way of bequest, and the household, we wish the bequest to be paid, insofar as it pertains to us. Therefore, having calculated the account, pay on our behalf, that is, for the nine ounces.”

> “Concerning the solidi of the Church of Canusium, we wish you to distribute something to the clergy of that Church, so that both those who now suffer want may have some support and, if God should will that a bishop be ordained there, he may have the means of subsistence.”

> “Concerning fallen priests or anyone from the clergy, we wish you to observe this: do not involve yourself in their property in any way, but seek out very poor regular monasteries that know how to live according to God. Deliver the fallen to those monasteries for penance, and let the property of the fallen benefit the place to which they are handed over to perform penance, so that those who care for their correction may have support from their property. If they have parents, let their property be given to their lawful parents, but in such a way that adequate provision is made for the support of those who have been assigned to penance. If any priests, deacons, monks, clerics, or other persons from the ecclesiastical household should fall, we wish them to be assigned to penance, but their property is not to be removed from ecclesiastical right. They may nevertheless take from it what is necessary for their own support while doing penance, lest, if they are stripped bare, they become a burden to the places to which they have been assigned. If they have parents holding property on their behalf, their property is to be delivered to those parents so that it may be preserved by them for the Church’s right.”

> “Three years ago, the subdeacons of all the Churches of Sicily were forbidden, following the custom of the Roman Church, ever to associate with their wives. This seems harsh and improper to me: a man who has not embraced the practice of such continence and has not previously resolved upon chastity is compelled to separate from his wife, and through this—God forbid—may fall into something worse. Therefore it seems to me that from the present day all the bishops should be told not to presume to make anyone a subdeacon unless he has promised that he will live chastely. In this way past obligations, which were not embraced by a deliberate resolve of the mind, will not be forcibly imposed, and future obligations will be carefully guarded against.

> “Those who, after the prohibition made three years ago, have lived continently with their wives are to be praised and rewarded, and encouraged to remain in their good conduct. But we do not wish those who, after the prohibition was made, refused to abstain from their wives to advance to the sacred order, because no one ought to approach the ministry of the altar unless his chastity has been approved before he undertakes the ministry.”

> “We wish you to provide an annual allowance for Liberatus, a merchant who has commended himself to the Church and lives on the Cincian estate. Determine yourself what the amount of this allowance should be, so that, once reported to us, it may be charged to your accounts.

> “As for the present indiction, I have already learned from our son, the deacon Servusdei, that a certain monk named John, at his death, left the defensor Fantinus as heir to six ounces. Give him what has been left, but charge him solemnly never again to presume to do this. Instead, establish what he is to receive for his labor, so that his work will not be without compensation; and let him remember that a person who lives on the Church’s stipends must not yearn for private profits.

> “If anything comes to the Church without sin or covetous desire through those who conduct the Church’s business, it is proper that they too should not be left without compensation for their labor; but it should remain for our judgment to determine how they ought to be rewarded.”

[Additional editorial notes: Gemet and Bigot read “so that you too, administering well …” in the letter concerning Palatina. The Andegavian manuscript reads *Solerio* for *Valerio*. The printed text’s reading concerning the fraudulent tenant-farmers is corrected from the manuscripts: “because we are also concerned in the future about past sins, lest the things fraudulently taken by the tenant-farmers from the peasants should reach us and the sins committed by them be drawn upon us.” The Regius and Sainte-Marie de Paris manuscripts read “estates” (*massis*) where Colbert and the Cussan edition read “places.”

Note: *Pesino*, which the peasants pay; see Cange’s Glossary. The Andegavian, three Parisian, and Norman manuscripts read “from public moneylenders” (*ab actionariis*), a reading found in most manuscripts of the letters; the manuscripts of John the Deacon almost always agree with those of Gregory’s Register. The same manuscripts read: “that everything which they might borrow …,” with the rest omitted in others. Some manuscripts read “but the things which …”; others, “but the things of yours which are to be purchased.” The editorial note on *batiola* is: “For the meaning of *batiola*, consult the notes on the letters. It would not be burdensome to consult those notes if any difficulty occurs in the other letters cited by John the Deacon; to repeat here what has already been observed elsewhere would be tedious.”]

“Concerning Rusticianus’s money, investigate the matter carefully, and carry out what seems just to you. Admonish Alexander, the magnificent man, that he ought to settle his case with the holy Church. But if he should perhaps neglect to do so, pursue that same case, as you can, with fear of God and with honor preserved. In this matter, moreover, we wish you to grant something; and, if it can be done, let what ought to be given to others be remitted to him, provided only that he bring to an end the case he has with us.

Restore, without any further delay, the donation of the maidservant of God who fell and was given to a monastery, so that, as I said above, that place may have the proceeds of her property for the man who bears the burdens of her care. Also recover whatever is held by others from her possessions [Col. 0123C] and hand it over to the aforesaid monastery.

“Send us the rents of the hospices on the New Way, in the amounts you reported to me, since [Alternative reading: “which”] you have them in your possession. But to the *actionarius* whom you appointed in that same patrimony, grant something as seems appropriate to you.

“Concerning the maidservant of God who was with Theodosius, named Extranea, it seems to me that you should impose continence upon her, if you see this as useful; or else restore the donation she made. Restore, without any further delay, the monastery house that Antonius had taken from the monastery after giving thirty solidi, once the solidi have been received. Carefully investigate the truth concerning the onyx vessels, and restore them; I have sent them back through the bearer of this letter.

“Send Saturninus to us, if he is free and not occupied with business on your behalf. Felix, the tenant of Lady Campana, whom she had left free—or whom she had ordered to remain uninvestigated—said that seventy-two solidi had been taken from him by Maximus the subdeacon. He asserted that, in order to provide these, he had either sold or pawned all his property in Sicily. But the legal experts said that he could not remain uninvestigated concerning frauds. Meanwhile, as he was returning to us from Campania, a storm arose and he died. We want you, therefore, to investigate his wife and children, and, whatever he had pawned or sold, release what he had pawned and restore the price of what he had sold; moreover, provide them [Col. 0124A] with some support, because Maximus had sent him to Sicily and there had taken from him what he claimed. Find out, then, what was taken away and restore it without any delay to his wife and children. Read all these matters carefully, and put aside all that familiar negligence of yours. Have my letters, which I sent to the peasants, reread throughout all the estates, so that they may know, on the authority of our office, what they ought to defend against their acts of violence; and let authentic copies or transcripts of them be given to them. See that you preserve everything without diminution, because, concerning what I write to you for the preservation of justice, I am released from responsibility, whereas you, if you neglect it, are bound. Consider the terrible Judge who is coming, and let reflection on his coming now make you tremble, lest then you fear without cause, when heaven and earth will have trembled before him. [Col. 0124B] You have heard what I want; see what you do.” (*Book I, Letter 44.*)

### 59

It is enough that I have so far recounted the innocence of Gregory’s generosity. I shall not, however, omit the fact that, during a famine, he diligently tried to purchase grain, so that he might have supplies with which to assist Christ’s poor. For in another letter to the same subdeacon Peter, among other things, he says:

“Purchase new grain from foreigners for fifty pounds of gold, and store it in Sicily in places where it will not spoil, so that in February we may send as many ships there as we can, to bring that same grain to us. But if we cease sending ships ourselves, provide ships personally and, with the Lord’s help, send this same grain to us in February, except only for the grain that we are now expecting to be sent in September or October according to custom [Col. 0124C]. Thus let your experience arrange matters so that the ecclesiastical peasants’ grain may be gathered without anyone’s harassment, because the harvest here was so [Alternative reading: *to such an extent*] small [Note: [Col. 0123D] Bigot., “a small crop,” as we have already observed at Letter 72, Book I, note g, where we cited chapter 60 of this book. Note that in some manuscripts this chapter, here numbered fifty-ninth, is the sixtieth, and that the fifty-ninth [Col. 0124D] begins with the words above: “Likewise, the same [Gregory] to Peter the subdeacon: Concerning the responsalis,” where Letter 44 of Book I is cited in large part.] that, unless grain is gathered from Sicily with God’s help, severe famine threatens.” [78] (*Book I, Letter 72.*)

### 60

A certain hermit, a man of great virtue who possessed nothing in the world except one cat, which he often caressed and, as though it were a companion of his dwelling, tenderly warmed in his lap, is said to have learned of the extent of this generosity and prayed to the Lord to deign to show him what dwelling of future recompense he ought to hope for, since he had abandoned the world for love of Him and possessed none of its riches. One night, while he was sleeping, he learned that it had been revealed to him [Col. 0124D] that he ought to expect a dwelling with Gregory, the Roman pontiff.

But he groaned bitterly, thinking that his voluntary poverty and the fasts of his great renunciation had profited him little if he were to receive a dwelling with one who abounded in such worldly riches. [Note: Utic., “of his recompense.”] As he compared Gregory’s riches with his own poverty, sighing over them day and night, he was resting another night when he heard the Lord say to him in a dream:

“When it is not possession of riches but desire that makes a person rich, why do you dare [Col. 0125A] compare your poverty with Gregory’s riches? You are shown to love that cat which you have more than he loves those great riches: you stroke it every day and give it to no one, whereas he scatters his riches—not by loving them, but by despising them and generously distributing them to everyone.”

Thus rebuked by God, the solitary gave thanks. [Col. 0126A] He had thought that his merit was diminished if he were compared with Gregory, but now he began to pray more fervently that he might one day deserve to receive a dwelling with him. But let the end of this second book now arrive, so that what follows may, with the Lord’s help, be continued in the third.

# BOOK THREE

In which it is explained how the life of Saint Gregory corresponded to his teaching.

[Col. 0125]

## SUMMARY

1. With what diligence Gregory governed the Church entrusted to him.  
2. With how many authoritative measures he fought against the heresies of simony and of the newly converted.  
3. That he ordered a synod to be held against them.  
4. That he foretold that those who did not fight against them with all their strength would share a portion with Simon Magus.  
5. How wisely he prohibited the giving or receiving of *pastellaticum*, whether for the use of the pallium or for the consecration of a pontiff.  
6. That he identified three kinds of simoniacal giving.  
7. That, in appointing bishops, he spared neither the cardinals of his Church nor the monks.  
8. That he promoted no one by force.  
9. That he restored those forcibly promoted to their former rank.  
10. That he restored to their orders those whom others had calumniously deposed.  
11. That he recalled cardinals promoted in external parishes to the cardinalate.  
12. That he consecrated as bishops the best men he could find anywhere, and with what strictness he examined those to be consecrated.  
13. That he also invited bishops from another diocese to govern the Churches of his own diocese.  
14. How he united episcopal sees.  
15. That he assigned vacant bishops to vacant Churches.  
16. That he joined expelled prelates to enthroned bishops.  
17. That he changed the locations of sees.  
18. That on no pretext did he transfer, or permit the transfer of, a pontiff from one Church to another.  
19. That he consecrated as a cardinal a parishioner belonging to another bishop.  
20. How he permitted clerics of another Church to be incardinated in other Churches.  
21. That he never preferred clerics ordained later to those ordained earlier.  
22. How he entrusted the Churches of deceased bishops to neighboring visitors.  
23. That he decreed that nothing should be accepted for making an inventory.  
24. That he rejected customary payments and gifts.  
25. That he decreed that bishops should come to the city of Rome only once every five years.  
26. That he also refused to accept the prices of goods.  
27. That he provided necessities for his suffragan bishops.  
28. How carefully he sought holiness, wisdom, and generosity from them.  
29. That he censured Bishop Marinianus for greed.  
30. That he rebuked Bishop Serentus for breaking images.  
31. That he deterred Bishop Januarius from avenging his wrongs.  
32. That he angered the same bishop over the plowing of the harvest-field.  
33. That he reproved Bishop Desiderius for reading pagan books.  
34. That he rebuked Bishop Natalis for negligence and feasting alike.  
35. How humorously he bound the same man by his own assertions.  
36. That he prohibited bishops from being absent from their own Churches.  
37. That he judged that bishops should not wander through various places.  
38. That he did not hesitate to commit to record the lapse of his own aunt.  
39. That he rebuked Bishop Vitalianus concerning a woman who had changed her religious habit.  
40. That he reproved the defender Sergius for negligence.  
41. That he restrained Bishop Paschasius concerning the construction of a ship and his own advantage.  
42. That he rebuked the negligence of the bishops of Campania and of Victor of Palermo.  
43. How moderately he judged Bishop Andrew concerning a concubine.  
44. That he held that one must abstain from wicked advisers.  
45. That he excluded the fallen or guilty from the companionship of bishops.  
46. That he decreed that the anger of superiors should be restrained and that one person’s fault should not harm another.  
47. That he prohibited free men from being flogged or imprisoned.  
48. How, in rebuking the vices of judges, he made them public.  
49. That, at the instigation of the devil, judges raged against him.  
50. That he bravely opposed the emperor Maurice when he issued a very bad law.  
51. Concerning the hypocrisy of John, bishop of Constantinople, who claimed to be universal.  
52. That he rebuked the Augustal letters petitioning on John’s behalf.  
53. That he disgraced the times and morals of Maurice.  
54. How wisely he weakened the pride of the hypocrite.  
55. Demonstrating his constancy, he asserts that he would in no way forfeit his loyalty to the emperor.  
56. Why he did not give the empress the relics she requested.  
57. That, until those times, the Roman pontiff supplied *brandeum* for relics.  
58. With how many miracles the garments of Saint John became renowned.  
59. What should be thought concerning those same garments.  
60. That Gregory drove the plague of the universal title away from the universality of the whole Church.

[Col. 0125B] 79 1. By such endeavors the venerable Pope Gregory effectively governed the Church divinely entrusted to him. He had already compelled the Ligurians, Venetians, [Note: [Col. 0125C] He perhaps alludes to Letter 51 of Book II, in the tenth indiction, whose heading once read, “To all the bishops throughout Hibernia” (better, “throughout Iberia”), concerning the affair of the Three Chapters. See note a to the cited letter. Concerning the Barbaricini, Donatists, Agnoetae, and the others mentioned here, the indexes of the Register of Letters should be consulted.] Iberians, and others who had confessed the schism in writing, to venerate the Council of Chalcedon, and had brought them back to the unity of the holy Church. He had already removed the Barbaricini, the Sardinians, and the peasants of Campania from the vanity of paganism, correcting them by both preaching and blows. With the Lord’s help, through the strongest authorities of his writings and through highly persistent embassies, he had already severed the heresy of the Donatists in Africa, that of the Manichaeans in Sicily, that of the Arians in Spain, and that of the Agnoetae in Alexandria from the body of the entire holy mother Church.

[Col. 0125C] 2. Only in Gaul had the heresy of the Neophytes, sprouting as though from as many roots as there were simoniacal gifts, spread and flowed everywhere far and wide [Note: Utic., “and remained”]. Against it the venerable Father fought vigorously before Queen Brunichild and also before the Frankish kings Theuderic and Theudebert, until, after a general synod had been assembled, he secured its complete condemnation under anathema.

Nor did he give the pallium to Syagrius, bishop of Autun, before the queen and the kings, after making many petitions, had fulfilled—Cyriacus his abbot being present—what they had been instructed to do concerning the expulsion of the heresies. For concerning these matters he writes, among other things, to Queen Brunichild:

“The priestly office has, as we have learned, been brought there to such a degree of ambition that priests are suddenly ordained from among the laity—which is exceedingly grave. But what will these men do, and what will they provide for the people, who desire to become bishops not for usefulness, but for the sake of honor? These men, then, who have not yet learned what they ought to teach, what are they doing except making the illicit advancement of a few the destruction of many, and bringing the observance of ecclesiastical order into confusion, since no regular order is maintained? For one who approaches its governance imprudently or precipitately, by what admonition will he build up his subjects, when his example has taught not reason but error? It is truly shameful—shameful—to command others to observe what one does not know how to keep oneself.

“Nor do we pass over that other matter, which ought to be erased by a similar correction [Note: In Utic., “which must be handed over to a similar correction”]; rather, we utterly detest it as abominable and exceedingly grave: namely, that sacred orders are there conferred through the simoniacal heresy, which first arose against the Church and was condemned by a strict curse [Col. 0127B]. Thus it comes about that the dignity of the priest is held in contempt and that holy honor becomes a crime. [Note: Bigot., “Everything perishes everywhere.”] Reverence indeed perishes and discipline is removed, because the person who ought to have corrected faults commits them, and by wicked ambition the authority of honorable priesthood is perverted. For who would again revere what is sold? Or who would not regard as base what is bought?

“Therefore I am deeply saddened, and I grieve for that land, because, while they disdain to possess as a divine gift the Holy Spirit whom almighty God deigns to grant to human beings through the laying on of hands, and instead obtain him by payments, I do not think that priesthood can long endure there. For where the gifts of heavenly grace are judged to be for sale, service to God does not seek a life of holiness; rather, money is worshiped against God.” (*Book IX, second indiction, Letter 100.*)

The same author writes somewhat later concerning the same Frankish kings, Theuderic and Theudebert:

“It is reported that the simoniacal heresy, which first crept against the Church of God through a diabolical planting and was struck and condemned at its very origin by the weapon of apostolic vengeance, holds sway within the borders of your kingdom. Yet among priests faith must be chosen together with life; if life is absent, faith has no merit, as blessed James testifies when he says: ‘Faith without works is dead’ (James 2:26). For what works can belong to a priest who is shown to have obtained the honor of so great a sacrament through payment? Consequently, those who desire sacred orders do not strive to correct their lives or reform their conduct; instead, they labor to gather the riches by which sacred honor is purchased. Hence it also happens that the innocent and the poor, barred from and despised in respect of sacred orders, withdraw; and while the poverty of innocence is displeasing, there is no doubt that payment commends crimes there, because where gold is pleasing, vice is pleasing as well.

“Thus not only is a deadly wound inflicted upon the soul of the ordainer and the ordained, but your Excellencies’ kingdom is also burdened by the fault of your bishops—those by whose intercessions it ought rather to have been helped. For if the one is considered worthy of priesthood whom not the merits of his conduct but the abundance of his payments supports, it follows that dignity and industry defend nothing in ecclesiastical honors, but that profane love of gold obtains everything. And while vices are rewarded with honor, the one who perhaps ought to have been punished is brought into the place of the avenger; hence priests are shown not to advance but rather to perish.

“For when the shepherd has been wounded, who will apply medicine for the healing of the sheep? Or when will he protect the people with the shield of prayer, who exposes himself to be struck by the darts of the enemy? Or what fruit will he produce from himself whose root is infected by a grievous pest? Greater calamity, therefore, must be feared for those regions [Alternative reading: ‘the calamity of those regions would be more greatly to be feared’] where such intercessors are brought to the place of governance—men who provoke God’s anger against themselves more than they ought to appease it on behalf of the peoples.” [82]

“Nor does our concern permit us to pass over negligently this other evil, equally worthy of detestation: namely, that some men, inflated by the desire for honor, are tonsured when bishops have died and suddenly become priests from the laity; and they shamelessly seize the leadership of a religious vocation, though they have not yet learned even to be soldiers. What, we ask, will these men provide for their subjects, who do not fear to occupy the position of rulers before they have reached the threshold of discipleship, or to appear as teachers before they have been taught?
