They impudently assume the guidance of souls, though the whole path of a guide is unknown to them, and they do not know even where they themselves should walk. How perverse and rash this is is shown even by secular order and discipline. For since a general is chosen only after experience gained through labor and care, what sort of guides of souls ought those be who desire, with immature haste, to climb to the summit of the episcopate? Let them consider themselves by at least this comparison, and fear suddenly to undertake untried labors [Note: Bigot., “let them endure inexperienced labors.” Utic., “let them endure inexperienced honors,” where *endure* means not “suffer” but “wait” or “defer”], lest blind ambition for honor be both a punishment to themselves and sow pestilential seeds of error for others, since they have not learned what they are to teach.

“Therefore, greeting you with paternal affection, we ask, most excellent sons, that you strive to prohibit this utterly detestable evil from the borders of your kingdom, and that no excuse among you, no suggestion against your soul, find a place; for the person who neglects to amend what he is able to correct unquestionably shares the guilt of the one who commits it.” (*Book IX, second indiction, Letter 100.*)

Likewise, concerning the same heresies, to Syagrius, bishop of Autun, and other bishops: [Note: In Utic.: “Likewise, to Etherius, Virgilius, and Desiderius, bishops of Gaul: ‘Since a report,’” with Syagrius’s name omitted. But it was formerly read otherwise; traces of an erasure can be discerned. In three Paris manuscripts the words “and other bishops” are omitted. Saint Syagrius is commemorated on 17 August.]

“Since a report was circulating among us long ago, it has become widely known that sacred orders are conferred in the regions of Gaul through the simoniacal heresy. We are afflicted with profound sorrow if money has any place in ecclesiastical offices and what is sacred becomes secular. Whoever strives to obtain this by the payment of a price vainly desires not to be a priest, but merely to be called one. For what else is accomplished by this except that there is no proof from conduct, no concern for character, no examination of life, but only the person able to give the price is judged worthy? If this matter is weighed by the examination of right judgment, while a man improperly hastens to seize, for empty glory, a position intended for usefulness, precisely because he seeks honor he is the more unworthy.

“As the man who declines when invited and withdraws when sought ought to be brought to the sacred altars, so the one who ambitiously seeks the office of his own accord or importunately thrusts himself forward must without doubt be rejected. For what does one who thus strives to climb to higher things do except diminish himself by growing, and, while ascending outwardly, descend inwardly to the depths? Therefore, dearest brother, let integrity prevail in ordaining priests; let consent be simple and without venality; let a pure election be preferred, so that advancement to the summit of priesthood may be believed to be by God’s judgment, not by the support of sellers.

“For evangelical authority testifies that it is altogether a grave crime either to buy or to sell God’s gift for a price. For our Lord and Redeemer entered the Temple and overturned the seats of those selling doves (Matthew 21). What else is it to sell doves but to receive a price for the laying on of hands and to sell [83] the Holy Spirit, whom almighty God bestows on humankind? That their priesthood falls before God’s eyes was plainly signified by the overthrow of the seats; yet the perversity of wickedness still exerts its power. For it compels those whom it deceived into buying to sell. And, while no heed is paid to the divine command, ‘Freely you have received, freely give’ (Matthew 10:8), the contagion of the offense grows and is doubled in one and the same person, namely buyer and seller. Since it is evident that this heresy, pestilential at the root, crept in before all others and was condemned by apostolic detestation at its very origin, why is it not avoided, why is it not considered that blessing is turned into a curse for the man promoted in order to become a heretic?

“Often the adversary of souls, when he cannot secretly introduce evil in matters that are outwardly evident, strives to undermine by inserting a crafty appearance, as though of piety [Note: Bigot., “with a crafty appearance.”]. Perhaps he suggests that one ought to accept from those who have, in order that there may be something to distribute to those who do not have, so that even thus he may pour out deadly poisons hidden under the shadow of almsgiving. No hunter would deceive a beast, no fowler catch a bird, nor a fisherman take a fish, if the one set his snare openly, the other did not conceal his hook with bait. Therefore the enemy’s cunning must altogether be feared and avoided, lest he more fiercely destroy with a hidden weapon those whom he cannot overthrow by open temptation.

“For it is not to be counted almsgiving if what is received from unlawful sources is distributed to the poor, because the person who receives wickedly with this intention, that he may seemingly distribute well, is burdened rather than helped. The almsgiving pleasing in the eyes of our Redeemer is not that gathered from unlawful things and injustice, but that bestowed from permitted and rightly acquired goods. Hence it is certain that even if monasteries, hospices, or anything else are constructed from money given for sacred orders, it does not profit toward reward; for while a perverse purchaser of office is installed and establishes others like himself by the giving of an advantage, he destroys more by bad ordinations than the man who received ordination-money from him can build. Therefore, lest under the pretext of almsgiving we strive to accept anything with sin, sacred Scripture openly forbids us, saying: ‘The sacrifices of the wicked are abominable to the Lord, which are offered from crime’ (Proverbs 21:27). Whatever is offered from crime in sacrifice to God does not appease the wrath of almighty God but provokes it. Again it is written: ‘Honor the Lord from your just labors’ (Proverbs 3:9). Therefore the man who takes wickedly in order seemingly to give well plainly does not honor the Lord. Solomon likewise says: ‘He who offers sacrifice from the substance of the poor is as one who sacrifices a son in the sight of his father’ (Ecclesiasticus 3:4, 24). Let us consider how great a father’s grief is if his son is sacrificed in his sight; and from this we readily recognize how great is the grief stirred up before God when a sacrifice is offered to him from plunder. Therefore, dearest brother, it must be most carefully avoided that, under the pretext of almsgiving, the sins of the simoniacal heresy be committed. For it is one thing to give alms because of sins, another to commit sins because of alms.

“Nor does our concern permit us to pass over negligently another [84] evil equally worthy of detestation: namely, that some men, inflated by the desire for honor, are tonsured when bishops have died and suddenly become priests from the laity, shamelessly seizing the leadership of a religious vocation although they have not yet learned even to be soldiers. What, we ask, will these men provide for their subjects, who do not fear to occupy the position of teachers before they have reached the threshold of discipleship?

“Therefore, even if someone’s merits are blameless, it is necessary that he first be exercised in ecclesiastical offices through the distinct orders. Let him see what he ought to imitate, learn what he ought to teach, and be formed in what he ought to hold, so that afterward he may not err when he has been chosen to show the way to one who is wandering. Let him therefore be polished for a long time by religious meditation, so that he may please God; and let him shine like a lamp placed upon a lampstand, so that the force of adverse winds, when it rushes upon him, may not extinguish the flame of learning that has been kindled, but increase it.

“For since it is written, as above: ‘Let them first be tested, and then let them serve’ (1 Timothy 3:10), one who is assumed as an intercessor for the people must be tested all the more beforehand, lest bad priests become the cause of the people’s ruin. No excuse and no defense against this can exist, because it is plainly known to everyone how diligent the holy and distinguished teacher is in this matter: he forbids a neophyte to approach sacred orders. Just as at that time a neophyte was called one who had only recently been planted in the instruction of the holy faith, so now a neophyte must be regarded as one who, having suddenly been planted in the religious habit, has crept in to seek sacred honors.

“Orders must therefore be ascended in due order. For the person who seeks to climb to the highest summits of office by steep paths, setting aside the steps, seeks a fall. And since the same Apostle teaches, among the other institutions of sacred order, that hands should not be laid too quickly upon anyone, what could be more rapid or precipitate than for the beginning to arise from the summit, so that, before he has begun to be a disciple, he is a teacher?

“Whoever, therefore, desires to attain priesthood not for the pomp of exaltation but for usefulness should first measure his strength against the burden he is about to undertake, so that the one who is unequal to it may refrain, and even the one who thinks himself sufficient may approach it with fear.

“We do not act irrelevantly if, as a rational argument, we gather an example from irrational things. Timber suitable for buildings is cut from the forests, yet the weight of a building is not placed upon wood while it is still green, unless the passage of many days has dried out its greenness and made it suitable for necessary use. If this precaution is neglected, the wood is more quickly broken by the superimposed mass, and the thing provided for assistance produces collapse.

“Thus physicians who care for bodies do not offer to the sick certain remedies while they are still freshly prepared, but leave them to mature over time. For if anyone administers them prematurely, there is no doubt that what was intended for health becomes the cause of danger. Let priests, then—let them learn in their office, since the care of souls has been entrusted to them—to preserve what people in various arts, taught by reason, preserve; and let them restrain themselves from precipitate ambition, if not through fear, at least through shame.

“But lest anyone perhaps still wish to defend himself by appealing to a wicked custom, let your Fraternity restrain them with the bridle of reason [Note: Bigot., “let them endure inexperienced labors.” Utic., “let them endure inexperienced honors,” where *endure* means not “suffer” but “wait” or “defer”] and not permit them to fall into illicit practices. For whatever deserves punishment should be brought forward not for imitation but rather as an example for correction.” And a little later:

### 3

“Concerning the matters stated above, therefore, we wish you, by God’s authority, to assemble a synod. Through our most reverend brother Bishop Aregius [Note: Elsewhere, Aredius. Much is found concerning him in the Letters. The feast of this saint is observed on the Kalends of May, as the Sammarthani observe in *Gallia Christiana*, from the proper liturgy of the Church of Gap], and our beloved son Abbot Cyriacus, let everything contrary to the holy canons, as we have said, be strictly condemned under the imposition of anathema. That is: no one may presume to give any payment in order to obtain ecclesiastical orders, or to receive one for payments made; no one from the lay habit may suddenly dare to reach the position of sacred governance; and no other women may live with priests except those permitted by the sacred canons.”

### 4

Seeing these pestilential heresies—spread ever more widely through the connivance or silence of priests, like a pestilential cancer, capable not only of corroding weak members but also of corrupting strong limbs with the sword of the most beautiful things—the most prudent teacher Gregory, moved by divine zeal, issued a general judgment to Bishop Victor, saying:

“Whoever, in order to correct this crime—namely, the heresy of simony and of the neophytes—does not burn with intense zeal in consideration of his office, should not doubt that he shares a portion with the one from whom this abominable offense first took its beginning.” (*Register, Book XII, Letter 29.*)

### 5

When the most prudent teacher Gregory learned that some people, in order to avoid the crimes of the simoniacal heresy, cunningly called the gifts of this pestilential commerce *pastellaticum*, and by changing the name sought to conceal the avarice of their greed, he repeated the judgment that he had promulgated before the synod at the beginning of his pontificate, saying:

“Following the ancient rule of the Fathers, I decree that nothing whatsoever may ever be accepted from anyone for ordinations: neither in exchange for the giving of the pallium, nor for the delivery of documents, nor under that name of *pastellus* which a new pretense, born of ambition, has invented.

“For when a bishop is ordained, the pontiff lays on hands, the minister reads the Gospel, and the notary writes the letter of confirmation. Just as it is not proper for the pontiff to sell the hand that he lays on, so the minister or notary ought not to sell at his ordination either his voice or his pen.

“Therefore I entirely prohibit the person who is to be ordained, or who is being ordained, from giving anything for ordination, for the use of the pallium, for documents, or for *pastelli*. If, on the basis of any of the matters mentioned above, anyone should presume to demand or seek some payment under another name, he will be subject to guilt at the strict judgment of almighty God.” (*Roman Synod, canon 5, at the end of the Letters.*)

[Note: Concerning this Bollandus writes: “*Pastillus* is, he says, a little mass cooked in the form of a small loaf. It is also called *pastellus*, and from this comes the gift of *pastellaticum* mentioned here. We have supplied another meaning in the notes to this decree at the end of the letter.]

### 6

Likewise, to John, bishop of the Corinthians, after much else:

“Your Fraternity knows,” he says, “that formerly the pallium was not given unless a payment had been made. Since this was improper, we held a council before the body of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and under strict prohibition forbade accepting anything either for this or for ordinations [86]. Therefore you must neither consent nor permit anyone to be brought to sacred orders through payment, favor, or the supplication of certain persons.” (*Register, Book V, Letter 57.*)

But the cunning wickedness of the most shameful greed could not endure being confined in respect of such great advantages—shameful and indeed extremely dangerous though they were—and it devised a sufficiently artful scheme: namely, to elevate to the priesthood those who, after their consecration, ought to have been all the more subject to their promoters, since they would undoubtedly reckon that they had been promoted not by divine judgment but rather by human judgment.

Therefore Gregory, the herald of almighty God, discusses the matter in his treatises on the Gospels, so that it might be read or heard more frequently, saying:

“There are some who do not indeed accept monetary payments for an ordination, and yet grant sacred orders for the sake of human favor; and from that generosity they seek only the return of praise. Such men plainly do not give freely what they received freely, because from the sacred office they have bestowed they seek the coin of approval.

“Thus the prophet rightly says, when describing the just man: ‘He shakes his hands free from every gift’ (Isaiah 33:15). For he did not say, ‘He shakes his hands free from a gift,’ but added, ‘from every gift,’ because one gift comes from service, another from the hand, and another from the tongue.

“A gift from service is an improperly rendered submission; a gift from the hand is money; a gift from the tongue is favor. Therefore the person who confers sacred orders shakes his hands free from every gift when, in divine matters, he seeks not only no money but also no human favor.” (*Homily 4 on the Gospels.*)

These are the opinions of the most learned Pope Gregory concerning simoniacs and illicit ordinations. He is said to have observed them with the greatest reverence, in that, from the beginning of his consecration and throughout his entire diocese, he most diligently ordained as bishops the best men he could find, wherever they might be. And whenever the need to ordain a priest arose, he did not exempt either the cardinal priests of his own Church or the monks of his own monastery at all from having the governance of a Church entrusted to those who could better build it up alike by example and by word.

For, to touch briefly on a few matters from many, from the cardinal priests of his own Church he consecrated as bishops Boniface of Reggio, Habentius of Perugia, and Donus of Messana in Sicily. From the subdeacons, however, he consecrated Gloriosus of Istria, Festus of Capua, [Note: [Col. 0133D] Bollandus reasonably supposes that an error has entered this passage; for it is not recorded that St. Gregory ever consecrated a bishop of Tricassinum, nor that there was at that time any bishop named Peter in that Church. I suspect, however, that Peter, bishop of Trecalitanum in Sicily, is meant—the recipient of Epistle 12 of Book V. In the Gemetic manuscript *Trecasino* is read for *Trecalitano*, as we observed in note a to that epistle.] Peter of Trecas, and Castorius of Ariminum.

From the monks of his own monastery, moreover, he ordained as prelates Marinianus of Ravenna, Maximianus of Syracuse, and Sabinus of Callipolis. He also ordered Augustine to be ordained among the English by the bishops of Gaul. Through him, likewise, monks of that same father were promoted to the episcopate among the same people at different times: Mellitus, Justus, Laurentius, and Paulinus.

He was somewhat sparing only with the deacons of the Apostolic See in this respect. Although their full number was nineteen, he himself consecrated Boniface, Florentius, and Epiphanius. Nor did he remove any of them from office, except the archdeacon Laurentius, on account of his pride and other crimes, in the Lateran basilica called the Golden Basilica, where he immediately appointed the archdeacon Honoratus.

### 8.

Although Gregory, when the opportunity arose, was quite willing to promote the cardinals of his own Church, provided they consented, he nevertheless made every effort not to promote anyone forcibly, however great the necessity under which he was compelled to act, lest, on the pretext of such necessity, he should appear to eliminate and depose someone. Thus, writing to Scholasticus, [Note: [Col. 0134D] Bigot, three Parisian manuscripts, and other codices read “Duke of Campania.”] the judge of Campania, he says:

> “While we were being exceedingly distressed by the care of the city of Naples, which had been deprived of the assistance of its priest, the bearers of the present letter arrived with a decree drawn up in favor of our subdeacon Florentius, and they had found for us some relief amid the great burden of our anxiety. But when our aforesaid subdeacon, fleeing that city, had tearfully avoided his ordination, you should know that, as though from a still greater despair, our sorrow increased. Therefore, greeting you, we exhort Your Greatness to consult the leading men or the people of the city concerning the election of another man who might be found worthy to be promoted to the priesthood by Christ’s consolation. When a solemn decree has been made and sent to this city, let the ordination there at last proceed, with Christ’s help.”

*(Register, Book III, Epistle 15.)*

### 9.

Those who had also been forcibly promoted by others he restored to their former ranks. Thus, writing to the subdeacon Antoninus, he says:

> “Honoratus, archdeacon of the Church of Salona, had asked my predecessor of holy memory, by a petition that he sent, that he should not be compelled against his will, contrary to custom, by his bishop to be promoted to the rank of a higher order. For he declared that this had been done to him not for the sake of promotion, but because of resentment. On this account our predecessor of holy memory had already forbidden Natalis, our brother and fellow bishop, by his letters, to promote the aforementioned archdeacon Honoratus against his will, or to retain longer in his heart the pain of the resentment he had conceived.

> “Although I too had emphatically forbidden these things to him, he, neglecting not only God’s commands but also disregarding our letters, attempted by a cunning stratagem to degrade the aforesaid archdeacon, ostensibly by promoting him to a higher honor. The result was that, after removing him from that archdeaconate, he summoned another man who could conform to his ways. We believe that this archdeacon Honoratus could have displeased his bishop for no other reason than that he prevented him from giving the sacred vessels to his relatives. We wished to investigate this matter carefully—first my predecessor of holy memory, and now I. But he, conscious of his own actions, postponed sending a representative to judgment.

> “Accordingly, we have considered it necessary to support Your Experience by the authority of the present command, so that, going to Salona, you may at least endeavor to exhort Natalis, our brother and fellow bishop, who has been admonished by so many letters, to receive the aforementioned archdeacon immediately into his former position. But if, as is his custom, he should stubbornly delay doing this, forbid him, by the authority of the Apostolic See, the use of the pallium that has been granted to him by this See. If, even after losing the pallium, you observe that he still persists in the same obstinacy, deprive that same bishop of participation in the Lord’s body and blood.

> “We command, moreover, that the man who consented, contrary to the rule of justice, to be promoted to another’s position be deposed from the honor of that archdeaconate; and if he should presume thereafter to minister in that same position, we deprive him of participation in Holy Communion. For it is just that those who disregard justice toward others placed under them should experience harshness from justice themselves.

> “After Honoratus the archdeacon has been restored to his position, let the aforesaid bishop, compelled by you, send a properly instructed representative who can demonstrate to me by his own arguments that his intention was, or had been, just. We also command that the same archdeacon come to us, so that, after learning the assertions of both parties, we may decide whatever is just and whatever is pleasing to Almighty God. For we defend no one out of personal affection; but, with God as our author, we preserve the rule of justice, setting aside favoritism toward any person.”

*(Register, Book II, Epistle 20.)*

### 10.

Likewise, to Honoratus of Salona, who had already been reduced from the priesthood to the diaconate:

> “Some time ago a command of our predecessor and of ourselves was sent to Your Affection. In it you had been acquitted of the charges falsely brought against you, and we had ordered that you be restored to the rank of your order without any dispute. But because, not long afterward, you came to the city of Rome and improperly complained there about certain proceedings, as well as about the alienation of the sacred vessels; and because, while for this matter we were waiting in this city for persons who could respond to your objections, Natalis, your bishop, departed from this life, we have judged it necessary henceforth to confirm by the present letters both the commands of our predecessor and our own, which, as stated, we formerly sent for your acquittal.

> “Therefore, fully acquitting you of all the charges brought against you, we wish you to remain in the rank of your order without any dispute, so that the controversy raised against you by the aforesaid man may in no way, under any pretext, prejudice you.”

*(Register, Book III, Epistle 32.)*

Likewise, in another epistle, after much else: [Note: [Col. 0135D] In Bollandus’s edition what follows is missing up to chapter X, and it is not found in three Parisian manuscripts, nor in those of Utica, Bigot, and others generally. Certainly, most printed editions contain a serious error, reading: “Likewise, to the same man in another epistle,” namely Epistle 53 of Book III; yet that epistle was written not to this Honoratus but to John of Constantinople.]

> “But even now I say: either receive those same men—namely John of Chalcedon and Athanasius, priests of Isauria—in their orders and grant them peace; or, if you should perhaps be unwilling to do this, setting aside every dispute, observe in their case either the decisions of the ancient authorities or the limits of the canons. But if you ask whether we wish to provoke a quarrel, we do not; nevertheless, we do not avoid one coming from you. Your Fraternity well knows what the canons say about bishops who wish to be feared through beatings. We have been made shepherds, not strikers. And the distinguished preacher said: ‘Reprove, entreat, rebuke with all patience and instruction’ (III Timothy 4:2). A preaching that demands faith through beatings is new and unheard of.”

*(Register, Book III, Epistle 53.)*

### 11.

Likewise, Gregory restored to their former cardinal rank those cardinal clerics who had been ordained by force in rural parishes. [Note: [Col. 0135D] In each episcopal Church there were formerly cardinal priests, so called because they were bound to the city as by a hinge (*cardo*), as is clear from canon 3 of the Roman synod under Sylvester I. The custom at that time was that no clerics were ordained except for a particular Church, as established by canon 6 of the Council of Chalcedon. See below, chapter 15. Nevertheless, St. Paulinus of Nola was exempt from this rule. Read his sixth letter to Severus. Mabillon.]

Therefore, writing to John, bishop of Syracuse, he says:

> “A report from certain persons has reached us that Cosmas, who had been made a subdeacon in the Syracusan Church by your predecessor Maximianus, of venerable memory, after having been a monk of the monastery of Saint Lucy, is said to have been ordained by you as a priest at an estate called Juliana. He has been afflicted by such excessive sadness, and so severely oppressed by the circumstances of his position, that he regards life itself as a punishment and seeks in flight a remedy for his distress. Since we ought to behave toward our subjects as we would have wished our superiors to behave toward us had we been subjects, it would be an act of great kindness if Your Holiness would restore him to the Church in which he served as a subdeacon and endeavor to establish him there as a cardinal priest.

> “You ought to do this, as we think, provided there is nothing that may justly inflame your mind against him. But if there is some fault, let Your Fraternity make it known to us by letter, so that we may know.”

[Note: [Col. 0136D] Thus three Parisian manuscripts, together with Bollandus. In several printed editions: “and the escape from his distress.”]

*(Register, Book XIII, Epistle 28.)*

### 12.

I shall briefly indicate with what care Gregory sought suitable men for the governance of abandoned peoples, so that it may reasonably be concluded that so great a man was a true master of the Lord’s flock not only in teaching but also in action. For in a letter to Maximianus, bishop of Syracuse, he says:

> “Felix, the distinguished man who bears the present letter, has informed us that there is in those regions a certain priest who appears worthy of promotion to the episcopal order on account of his proven life. Therefore let Your Fraternity have him brought before you and, as I am certain you will, examine him carefully because of the danger to his soul. If you determine that he is worthy to be promoted to this rank, endeavor to send him to us, so that, with the Lord arranging it, we may ordain him pastor of the place for which we shall have provided.”

*(Register, Book II, Epistle 24, indiction 10.)*

Likewise, to the deacon Cyprian:

> “In the month of November I received the most bitter letter of Your Affection concerning the death of Domnus Maximianus. He indeed has reached the rewards he desired; but the unfortunate people of the city of Syracuse must be mourned, since they did not deserve to have such a pastor for a long time. Therefore let Your Affection take care that a man be chosen for ordination in that same Church who, after Domnus Maximianus, may not appear unworthy or undeserving of receiving the place of the same governance.

> “I indeed believe that the greater part will choose the priest Trajanus, who, as is said, is a man of good character; but, as I suspect, he is not suitable to govern that place. Nevertheless, if no better man can be found and he is not entangled in any crimes, one may yield to him under the pressure of extreme necessity.

> “But if my preference for this election is sought, I secretly tell you what I want: for no one in that same Church, after Domnus Maximianus, seems to me so worthy as John, archdeacon of the Church of Catania. If it can be arranged that he be chosen, I believe that a very suitable man will be found. Yet you must first inquire of him privately concerning any crimes that might prevent this; if he is found free of them, he may rightly be chosen. If this is done, our brother and fellow bishop Leo must also make a cession to him, so that he may be found free to be ordained.”

*(Register, Book IV, Epistle 17.)*

Likewise, to Clementina, a patrician:

> “You should know, illustrious daughter, that Amandus, a priest, has been elected by the people of Surrentum to the episcopate. Since we have written that he must be sent here, you ought not to grieve at his absence, because one who is with you in mind is not believed to be departing. And since the man whom you formerly desired is pleasing to those who seek a pastor, rejoice in this all the more with Christian devotion, blessing Almighty God. Make every effort cheerfully to ensure that he comes to us more quickly, so that he may benefit others; for it is a mark of sincere charity to rejoice when the one who is loved is called to grow.”

*(Book X, Epistle 18.)*

Likewise, to Passivus, bishop:

> “Your Fraternity well knows how long Aprutium has been deprived of pastoral care. [Note: [Col. 0137D] Aprutium is not a city but a region of Italy, whose episcopal see is the city of Interamna, commonly called Teramo, as Bollandus observes.] We have long sought to determine whom ought to be ordained there, and we have been entirely unable to find anyone. But because Opportunus is said to lead a religious life in every respect, being highly praised for his character, his devotion to psalmody, and his love of prayer, we wish Your Fraternity to have him come to you and admonish him concerning his soul, so that he may grow in good pursuits. And if no crimes for which sacred law imposes death stand in his way, he should then be exhorted either to become a monk or to become our subdeacon; and after some time, if it should please God, he ought himself to be promoted to pastoral care.”

*(Book XII, Epistle 12.)*

Likewise, to Venantius, patrician of Palermo, who requested that a certain priest be consecrated bishop for him, he replies, among other things:

> “Your Excellence should know that it is altogether difficult for us to give you this priest, because the necessity of persons presses heavily upon us as we ordain pastors for other places deprived of them.”

*(Book XIII, Epistle 15.)*

But since he admits that he is hard-pressed by the necessity of ordaining suitable persons, lest he be thought to have promoted anyone without investigation, he appears to teach this by a single example. For in a letter to Bishop John he says:

> “To prevent the careless ordination of those who are chosen for the episcopate, their persons must be investigated with vigilant concern. We have been informed that Florentius, archdeacon of the Church of Ancona, who had been elected to the episcopate, possesses knowledge of sacred Scripture, but is already so weakened by old age that he cannot rise to the duty of governance. They also add that he is so miserly that a friend never enters his house for the sake of charity.

> “Rusticus, a deacon of the same Church, who had likewise been elected, is said to be a vigilant man, but, according to what is asserted, he does not know the Psalms. As for Florentius, deacon of the Church of Ravenna, who is said to have been chosen by everyone, we know that he is diligent, but we do not know at all what he is like inwardly.

> “Therefore let Your Fraternity, together with our brother and fellow bishop Armenius, the visitor of the aforementioned Church of Ancona, hasten to go there and inquire carefully into the life and character of each man, and whether any of them is conscious of a crime that would prevent him from undertaking this office. It must likewise be investigated whether the statement made about the aforementioned archdeacon—that no friend has ever entered his house—is true, and whether this results from necessity or from miserliness; whether he is so old that he cannot rise to govern; or whether, after touching the holy Gospels, he took an oath, as was reported to us, never to enter the episcopate.

> “The inquiry must also determine how many Psalms Rusticus the deacon does not know. As for Florentius, the deacon of Ravenna, if, as we have said, there is no crime standing in his way, it is necessary to act with his bishop so that he may grant him a cession; yet this must not be done by our command or express statement, lest he appear to grant it against his will.”

*(Book XIV, Epistle 11.)*

### 13.

Gregory, wisely recognizing that the whole body of the Church flourishes through good bishops but falls disastrously through bad ones, invited not only clerics of various orders from different peoples, but also bishops without sees, to the episcopates of his diocese. Thus, writing to Sebastianus, bishop of Sirmium, he says, among other things:

> “Having discharged the duty of greeting, I inform you that Boniface the defensor has reported to me that our most holy brother, Domnus Anastasius the patriarch, wished to entrust you with the governance of a Church in one of his cities, and that you were unwilling to consent. I gladly embraced and greatly praised this judgment and wisdom of yours; and I considered you happy and myself unhappy, since I consented at such a time to undertake the governance of a Church.

> “Nevertheless, if your mind should perhaps decide at some time to consent to this out of compassion for your brethren and devotion to works of mercy, I ask that you place no one before my affection. There are Churches in the island of Sicily that are without bishops; and, if it pleases you to govern a Church, with God as author, you can do so better there, near the threshold of the blessed Apostle Peter, with his assistance. But if it does not please you, remain happily where you are and pray for us unfortunate men.”

*(Register, Book V, Epistle 42.)*

[Note: [Col. 0137D] Bollandus reads *Rhisiniensi* here and says that Rhisinum or Rhisina is a city of Mesopotamia on the border of Syria, not far from Edessa. Mabillon, together with Surius, has *Smurnensi*. See the notes on Epistle 28 of Book I, indiction 9.]

### 14.

Meanwhile Gregory reunited Churches that had been scattered by establishing bishops in fortified places. Therefore he writes to Bacauda, bishop of Formiae:

> “The necessity of the times presses us, and the diminishing number of persons requires that we come to the aid of abandoned Churches with a sound and prudent arrangement. Since, therefore, we have learned that the Church of Minturnae has been completely deprived of both clergy and people and lies desolate, and since we foresee that your petition concerning it—that it should be joined to the Church of Formiae, over which Your Fraternity presides and in which the body of the blessed martyr Erasmus rests—is pious and entirely just, we have judged it necessary, with regard both to the desolation of that place and to the poverty of your Church, to transfer by the authority of this command to the right and power of your Church the revenues of the aforementioned Church of Minturnae, and whatever has been or can be considered to belong to it by ancient or modern right, privilege, or any other title. From the present time, therefore, you are to think of it as your own Church and arrange what pertains to it by your provision, so that whatever until now could have been lost may henceforth benefit the needs of the poor of your Church and its clergy.”

*(Register, Book I, Epistle 8.)*

Likewise, to Bishop Benenatus:

> “Both the character of the times and the proximity of the places invite us to unite the Churches of Cumae and Misenum, since they are separated from one another by no great distance. Nor, as a result of sins, is there such a multitude that they ought to have individual priests as they once did. Since, therefore, the priest of the fortress of Cumae has completed the course of this life, know that by the document of our present authority we have united both Churches and committed them to you; and know that you are the proper bishop of both Churches.

> “Whatever you deem necessary to arrange and regulate concerning their property or the appointment and promotion of their clergy, in accordance with the provisions of the canons, you shall have free authority to do, as their truly proper priest, with the consent and permission of our authority. Live wherever you foresee that it will be more convenient or useful, provided that, although you are at present physically absent from one Church, you arrange matters in it with careful and provident concern, so that the divine mysteries may there be solemnly celebrated, with the Lord’s assistance.

> “Therefore let Your Fraternity always watch over the exhortation and acquisition of souls with a care all the more diligent, the more you recognize that you have undertaken the burden of governing united Churches.”

*(Book II, Epistle 45.)*

### 15.

Gregory also endeavored to incardinate the bishops of desolated cities in vacant cities. Thus, writing to Martin, bishop of Corsica, he says, among other things:

> “Since the Church of Tamata, in which Your Fraternity formerly held the honor of the priesthood, has, because of the sins of its people, been so occupied and destroyed by the savagery of the enemy that no hope of returning there remains, by this authority we unquestionably establish you as a cardinal priest in the Church of Aleria, which has long been deprived of the assistance of a bishop, in accordance with the terms of your petition.

> “Therefore, with vigilant zeal and in the love of God, arrange and regulate everything according to the commands of the canons, so that Your Fraternity may rejoice that your desires have been fulfilled and that the Church of God may be filled with reciprocal joy at having received you as its cardinal bishop.”

*(Register, Book I, Epistle 79.)*

Likewise, to John, bishop of Squillace:

> “The care of pastoral office admonishes us to establish proper priests over abandoned Churches, who ought to govern the Lord’s flock with pastoral concern. For this reason we have judged it necessary to establish you, John, the bishop of the city of Lisitana who was captured by the enemy, as cardinal priest in Squillace: so that you may fulfill, with a view to future reward, the care of souls once undertaken; and although you have been driven from your own see by the enemy’s presence, you may govern another Church that is without a pastor.

> “This is to be understood with the provision that, if it should happen that that city is made free from the enemy and, with the Lord’s protection, restored to its former condition, you are to return to the Church in which you were previously ordained. But if the aforementioned city continues to be oppressed by the disaster of captivity, you are to remain in the Church in which you have been ordained by us.”

[Note: [Col. 0139D] Bollandus’s edition rejects the material from here through “Likewise, to Gratiosus”; nevertheless, it is found in our manuscripts.]

*(Register, Book II, Epistle 37.)*

Likewise, to John, bishop of Velletri:

> “After the impiety of the enemy, because of the sins of the people, had so desolated the churches of various cities that, as the populations failed, no hope of restoring them remained, we are bound by a much greater concern lest, after their priests have died, the remnants of the people, governed without the direction of a pastor, should be seized—God forbid—by the envy of the crafty enemy along the inaccessible paths of faith.

> “Frequently reminded by our concern for this matter, we have formed the following plan in our heart: to entrust these Churches to neighboring bishops for governance. Therefore we have decided to commit to Your Fraternity the care and governance of the Church of Tres Tabernae, which must be added and united to your Church, so that, with Christ’s help, you may be the priest and ruler of both Churches. Whatever you deem necessary to arrange concerning its property or the appointment or promotion of its clergy, with vigilant and canonical care, you shall have free authority to do by this present permission of ours, as its proper bishop.”

*(Register, Book II, Epistle 50.)*

[Col. 0140C]

Likewise, he joined the Church of Saint Anthemius, situated in the territory of the city of the Sabines at Cures, to Bishop Gratiosus of Nomentum by incardination. [Note: [Col. 0139D] Perhaps “Saint Euthymius” should be read. Consult Bollandus on this passage. In the same place he derives *Curites* and *Quirites* from *Cures*.]

Likewise, to Agnellus, bishop of Fundi, after some other material:

> “Since, because of the devastation caused by the enemy, no one is permitted to live either in your city or in your Church, by this authority of ours we establish you as cardinal priest of the Church of Terracina.”

*(Book III, Epistle 20.)*

And shortly afterward:

> “You must also know, Your Fraternity, that we have established you as cardinal priest of the aforementioned Church of Terracina in such a way that you do not cease to be bishop of the Church of Fundi, nor neglect its care and governance.”

*(Ibid., Epistle 23.)*

[Col. 0140D]

### 16.

Gregory also temporarily joined expelled bishops—whom he could not so quickly incardinate, or whose return to their own sees he hoped might eventually be possible—to other bishops who were then living in their own places, for the support and expenses of their present life. He issued the following general instruction:

> “Strive to receive our brothers and fellow bishops, who are oppressed by the hardships of captivity and various necessities, with goodwill, so that they may be consoled and may live with you from ecclesiastical resources. This is not, indeed, so that their dignity may be divided through a sharing of the episcopal throne, but so that they may receive from the Church, as far as possible, sufficient provisions for their support. For in this way we show that we love both our neighbor in God and God in our neighbor. We grant them no authority whatsoever in your Churches; we earnestly exhort you only to sustain them by your assistance.”

*(Register, Book I, Epistle 45.)*

### 17.

The most prudent pontiff also changed the locations of episcopal sees when a proper occasion arose. Thus he writes to John, bishop of Velletri:

> “The character of the times advises us to transfer episcopal sees, which were established in ancient times in specific cities, to other places in the same diocese that we consider safer, so that their inhabitants may now live there and more easily avoid barbarian danger.

> “Therefore we command you, John, our brother and fellow bishop of the city of Velletri, and your see, to move from now on to the place called Arenata, at Saint Andrew the Apostle, so that you may be freer from attacks by the enemy and may arrange there the festivals of the customary solemn rites.”

*(Register, Book II, Epistle 14.)*

### 18.

It should be noted that although Gregory united monasteries and episcopates and endeavored to incardinate bishops without sees in cities without bishops, he nevertheless never transferred a bishop from the integrity of his own Church to another, nor did he himself do so, nor did he consent to such a move under any pretext.

For after he had deposed Demetrius, bishop of Naples, on account of manifest crimes, the Neapolitans earnestly sought that Paul, bishop of Nepi, be incardinated among them. Yet the very discerning pontiff, having delegated the visitation of the city of Nepi to Bishop John, did indeed give them that same Paul as visitor; but he first postponed establishing him as cardinal as a matter of administrative dispensation, and afterward refused altogether.

Later, when he granted Paul permission to return to his own diocese, he ordered that one hundred solidi from the Neapolitan Church and one orphan boy, of whatever kind he himself wished from the household of that Church, be given to him.

[Note: [Col. 0141D] See Book II, Epistle 6, and consult the many letters to Paul.]

### 19.

The most discerning pontiff also carefully arranged for the incardination of clerics from other parishes, both for himself and for others. Therefore, writing to Elias, a priest and abbot of the province of Isauria, he says, among other things:

> “You asked us to promote your son Epiphanius to the sacred order and send him back to you. In one respect we have heard you; in the other we could not hear you at all. He has indeed been made a deacon, but whoever has once received a sacred order in this Church no longer has permission to depart from it. Therefore, although I have not been able to see you, I have consolation in this matter, because in your son I find rest.”

*(Register, Book V, Epistle 37.)*

### 20.

Likewise, to Maximianus, bishop of Syracuse:

> “Felix, the deacon who bears the present letter, did not fall into the doctrines of the heretics and did not depart from the Catholic faith. Yet, enticed by misguided suspicions against the Constantinopolitan synod, he had withdrawn himself in the separation of the Istrians. When he came to Rome, he corrected his error after receiving from us, with the Lord’s help, a proper understanding and after receiving Communion in the Lord’s body.

> “Since, therefore, as has been said, he did not fall into heresy but erred by withdrawing from the sacred ministries of the universal Church, as though out of zeal for a right intention, we have taken thought for his weakness and needs, and especially, out of concern for his support, we have provided that he be incardinated in your Syracusan Church.”

*(Register, Book IV, Epistle 14.)*

Likewise, to Fortunatus, bishop of Naples:

> “We recall that Your Fraternity asked us to permit Gratianus, a deacon of the Church of Venafrum, to be incardinated in your Church. Since he has neither a bishop whom he can obey nor a Church of his own in which he ought to perform his ministry, because the enemy prevents him from doing so, we have not judged that your petition should be delayed. Therefore, by this letter, we have considered it necessary to grant him to you, with permission for you, by our intervening authority, to establish that deacon as a cardinal of your Church, with God’s favor.”

*(Register, Book VI, Epistle 11.)*

Likewise, to the deacon Cyprian:

> “Just as Your Affection diligently labored on behalf of our brother and fellow bishop John, so that, with God as author, he might be ordained in the Syracusan Church, so now it is necessary that, through the efforts of Your Affection, the assistance of governance also be provided to him.

> “For he claims to have had a priest of his own, who is nevertheless said to have been ordained by our brother and fellow bishop Leo in the Church of Catania. Since he is going to a new Church and needs to have his own people there, so that, when he is oppressed by the tumult of affairs, he may find a place of rest in private, you must gently and sweetly persuade the aforementioned brother and fellow bishop Leo that he ought to cede the aforesaid priest to him, lest it perhaps appear that he has abandoned after ordination the man whom he so kindly ceded for ordination.”

*(Register, Book VI, chapter 20.)*

### 21.

Gregory observed with such devotion the most ancient order of ecclesiastical custom, handed down from the apostles and solemnly preserved down to his own time, that he placed no one—however distinguished by holiness, wisdom, or nobility—before the clergy who were senior to him in assembly, seating, standing, or subscription.

Thus, writing to Januarius, bishop of Cagliari, he says:

> “Liberatus, about whom Your Fraternity informed us, is said to perform the office of a deacon. If he was not made a cardinal by your predecessor, he should in no way be placed before the deacons ordained by you, lest you appear in some way to reject by placing below them those whom you know yourself to have approved by consecrating them.

> “Therefore restrain the aforesaid Liberatus, whom the spirit of ambition inflates and who must be corrected, from the perversity of his intention with every effort, and establish him at the last place among the deacons. Otherwise, while he strives unlawfully to be preferred, he may be judged undeserving of the position in which he now stands.

> “If, however, you are induced by his obedience and afterward wish to make him a cardinal, remember that you must refrain from incardinating him unless he has duly obtained the cession of his bishop according to solemn custom. For you do not doubt that it is consistent with equity that you should not delay observing toward others what you yourself wish them to observe toward you.”

*(Register, Book I, Epistle 83.)*

### 22.

Prompted, then, by this most ancient custom, Gregory entrusted the Churches of deceased bishops to neighboring bishops for the purpose of making an inventory and choosing a bishop of legitimate reputation. He wrote to John, bishop of Squillace, as follows:

> “A direct report has revealed the death of that bishop. Therefore we solemnly entrust to Your Fraternity the visitation of the abandoned Church. You must carry it out in such a way that no one presumes to undertake anything concerning the advancement of the clergy, the revenues, the furnishings, the ministries, or anything else belonging to the patrimony of that Church.

> “Therefore Your Fraternity shall hasten to go to the aforementioned Church and promptly admonish its clergy and people by frequent exhortations, so that, setting aside personal ambition, they may with one accord seek to have placed over them a priest who can be found worthy of so great a ministry and is in no way rejected by the venerable canons.

> “When he has been requested, let him come to us for consecration with a solemn decree confirmed by the subscriptions of all and accompanied by the testimony of Your Affection’s letters. We also admonish Your Fraternity not to permit anyone to be chosen from another Church, unless, among the clergy of those same cities in which you are carrying out the duty of visitation, no one worthy of the episcopate can be found—a circumstance we do not believe will occur.

> “Above all, take care that lay persons do not presume to aspire to such a rank on the merit of their manner of life, and that you do not, God forbid, incur the danger attached to your office.

> “As for any monasteries established in his parish, we permit them to remain under your care and administration until a proper bishop has been ordained there, so that the vigilance of your concern may, with God’s help, respond to their purpose by appropriate action.”

*(Register, Book II, Epistle 38.)

Also to the clergy, the ecclesiastical order, and the people:

“Having learned of the death of your bishop, we took care to entrust solemnly to our brother and fellow bishop John the visitation of the church now left without a shepherd. We instructed him not to allow anyone to usurp anything from the advancement of the clergy, the revenues, furnishings, or ministries; you ought to obey him in his continual exhortations, so that, in ecclesiastical obedience, a priest may be sought who in no respect differs from the venerable canons. [Col. 0143D] When he has been requested, he is to come to us for ordination with the solemnity of a decree strengthened by the subscriptions of all and accompanied by the visitor’s letter. Above all, take care not to presume to elect a layperson of any kind of life or merit. For you must understand that not only is such a person in no way to be advanced to the summit of the episcopate, but that you yourselves can obtain pardon through no intercessions. Rather, you must know without doubt that all among you who are found to have aspired to a layperson are to be excluded from office and communion.” (Register, Book II, Letter 29.)

23. Gregory allowed nothing belonging to the gifts or estates of any churches to be taken away on any pretext. Therefore he writes among other things to Maximian, bishop of Syracuse:

“We have taken care to admonish your Charity that if any bishop should depart from this life—or, God forbid, should be removed for his offenses—the hierarchs [Note: [Col. 0143D] In Utic. and other manuscripts, *hieraticis* (“priestly” or “sacerdotal”)] and all the principal clergy should assemble, and, while an inventory of the church’s property is being made in their presence, everything found should be recorded in detail. Nor, as was reportedly done before, should any particular object or anything else belonging to the church be taken away as though in payment for the labor of making the inventory. For we desire that those things which belong to securing the resources of the poor be preserved in this way, so that no opportunity whatsoever for trafficking in their possessions be left to greedy men.

“Let the visitors of the churches, and also their clerics, who grow weary with them while traveling through parishes outside their own cities, receive, at your arrangement, some assistance for their labor. For it is just that they should obtain a stipend there where they are found to lend their service for a time.” (Register, Book IV, Letter 1.)

24. Gregory rejected with all the effort of his mind, as though it were some pestilential burden, the custom of receiving gifts or hospitality presents from his bishops. Thus he writes to Felix, bishop of Messana:

“We ought by our consideration to remit customs which are known to impose a burden upon churches, lest they be compelled to impose upon others what they ought rather to expect to be imposed upon themselves. You should indeed preserve inviolate the custom owed to your clergy and to those of others, and each year transmit to them what is customary. But as for us, we forbid that anything further be transmitted.

“And because we take no pleasure in hospitality gifts, we received with thanks the *palmatiana* which your Fraternity sent; but, so that you might not suffer any loss from them, we had them sold for a fair price and sent that price, sealed, to your Fraternity [Note: [Col. 0143D] Thus the manuscripts of the Life of Saint Gregory and many manuscripts of the letters read; [Col. 0144D] from other printed editions we have retained the wording individually]. But since we have learned that your Charity wishes to come to us, by this letter we admonish you that you should not undertake the labor of coming. Rather, pray for us, so that, just as the distances of our journeys separate us, so our souls may, with Christ’s help, be joined to one another in charity; and that, helping one another by mutual prayer, we may return the office entrusted to us whole to the Judge who is to come.” (Register, Book I, Letter 66, indiction 9.)

[Col. 0144D] He also writes to John, bishop of First Justiniana, to whom he sends the pallium and entrusts his authority, after much else:

“As for the hospitality gifts of your Holiness, I had been entirely unwilling to accept them, because it would have been wholly unfitting for us to appear to have received gifts from brothers who had been plundered and afflicted. But your representatives overcame me by another argument, carrying them to one from whom the offerings of your Fraternity could not be rejected.” (Book II, Letter 23.)

25. Hence it was that Gregory, who took pleasure in burdening none of the bishops with travel to the city, entrusted his authority throughout Sicily to Maximian, bishop of Syracuse, [Col. 0145A] ordering that all the bishops should come to Rome once every five years. (Register, Book II, Letter 7.) Accordingly, writing to the deacon Cyprian, he says:

“Your Charity knows that the former custom was for our brothers and fellow bishops to assemble from Sicily at Rome once every three years. But, having regard for their labor, know that we have decided that they should present themselves here once every five years,”

and so forth. (Register, Book VII, Letter 22.) Here it should be noted that, if blessed Gregory had longed for hospitality gifts—as it is impious to believe—he would not have extended the bishops’ arrival from three years to five; rather, he would unquestionably have hastened it from three years to two.

26. But how could he gratefully receive hospitality gifts when, although he feared to refuse to distribute another’s alms, [Col. 0145B] he nevertheless accepted them with fear and distributed them with the greatest care? He was accustomed to give his own things and accept nothing belonging to others, to such an extent that he even entirely refused the price of certain goods. Thus he writes to Eulogius, patriarch of Alexandria, among other things:

“Regarding the wood about which you write that it was small: the size of the ship by which it was sent caused this. If a larger ship had come, I could have sent larger pieces of wood as well. But when you say that, if we send larger pieces, you will pay the price, we give thanks for your generosity, but we are forbidden to accept payment, since the Gospel prohibits it. For we do not buy the wood that we send; and how can we accept payment when it is written, ‘You received without payment; give without payment’?

“Therefore, in accordance with the size of the ship, we have now sent small pieces of wood by the shipmaster. But next year, if it pleases almighty God, we shall prepare larger ones.” (Register, Book VIII, Letter 29.)

27. It is no wonder that the most generous pontiff accepted no customary payments and no hospitality gifts from his suffragans, since he himself supplied whatever seemed necessary with considerable cheerfulness. Thus he writes to Venantius, bishop of Perugia:

“We have learned that our brother and fellow bishop Ecclesius is suffering greatly from the cold because he has no winter clothing. Since he requested that something be sent to him from us, we have sent to your Fraternity, through the bearer of this letter, a cloak, a tunic, and a breast garment, so that they may be sent to him by you without delay. Therefore make every effort to send all this to our aforesaid brother with the utmost speed; and do not fail to report to us in your letters that you have sent it. Act in such a way that, since the cold is severe, you cause no delay whatever in sending it.” [Col. 0145D] (Register, Book X, Letter 53, indiction 5.)

He also writes to the same Ecclesius, bishop of Clusium:

“Having received the letter of your Fraternity, we were saddened to learn from it that you had been seriously ill and were still weak. Although we desired to see your Holiness, you nevertheless did well to remain there for the time being, lest, by coming here, you cause us renewed sorrow through the distress of your illness.”

And shortly afterward:

“We have sent you, from the blessing of Saint Peter, one horse, of the kind we were able to find, so that after your illness you may have something on which to ride.” (Register, Book X, Letter 45, indiction 3.)

28. Under such a patron, the pontiffs of that time, encouraged by him, began both to adorn new churches built from their foundations and to renovate the old ones with the greatest splendor. For Gregory sought nothing more attentively in his bishops than holiness, wisdom, and generosity. To make this clearer, I shall cite some of his letters, by whose testimony my reader may learn of the vices censured in certain bishops. For in a letter to Secundus, servant of God, he says among other things:

29. “Rouse our brother Marinianus, the bishop, with whatever words you can, because I suspect that he has fallen asleep. Some people came to me, among them certain elderly beggars. I questioned them about what they had received from me and received a detailed account of what had been given to them on their journey, and by whom. When I carefully asked them what the aforesaid brother had given them, they replied that they had asked him but had received absolutely nothing from him—indeed, they had not even received bread for the journey, although giving to everyone had always been customary for that church.

“They said: ‘He answered us, saying, “I have nothing that I can give you.”’ And I marvel that one who has clothing, silver, and storerooms should not have what he ought to give to the poor. Tell him, then, to change his mind together with his position. He must not suppose that reading and prayer alone are sufficient for him, so that he withdraws, sits idle, and produces no fruit by his hand. Rather, he should have an open hand, come to the aid of those suffering need, and regard another’s poverty as his own. For if he does not have these qualities, he bears the name of bishop in vain.” (Register, Book VI, Letter 30.)

30. He also writes to Serenus, bishop of Marseille, after some other matters:

“It had been reported to us that, inflamed by inconsiderate zeal, you had broken images of the saints under the pretext that they ought not to be worshiped. We entirely praised you for forbidding their worship; but we reproved you for breaking them. Tell me, brother: by what priest was such a thing ever done or even heard of? If nothing else, at least this ought to have restrained you: [Note: [Col. 0145] The printed editions read *ne despectis* (“lest, despising”); but the manuscripts both of the Life of St Gregory and of the letters consistently read *ut*, not *ne*.] that, by despising the other brothers, you should believe yourself alone to be both holy and wise.

“For it is one thing to worship a picture, and another to learn, through the history represented in a picture, what ought to be worshiped. What writing provides for readers, a picture provides for uneducated people who look at it: in it the ignorant see what they ought to follow; in it those who know no letters read. Hence, especially for the peoples, a picture takes the place of reading. You, who live among the peoples, ought to have paid particularly close attention to this, lest, while rashly inflamed by righteous zeal, you generate scandal in fiercer hearts.

“Therefore what had been placed in the churches not for worship but solely for the instruction of the unlearned should not have been broken. And since antiquity has permitted histories of the saints to be painted in venerable places for good reason, if you had tempered zeal with discernment, you could undoubtedly have achieved what you intended beneficially and, instead of scattering the gathered flock, gathered the scattered one—so that the merit and name of a shepherd might prevail in you, rather than the guilt of a disperser.

“While you were carrying this out in the exceedingly careless agitation of your mind, you are said to have scandalized your children so greatly that most of them withdrew from communion with you. When, then, will you lead wandering sheep to the Lord’s fold, when you cannot retain those whom you already have? Therefore we urge you, at least now, to strive to be watchful and restrain yourself from this presumption. Hasten with all effort and diligence to recall to yourself, with paternal gentleness, the minds of those whom you know to have been separated from your unity.” (Register, Book XI, Letter 13.)

31. He also writes to Januarius, bishop of Cagliari, after some other matters:

“Amid many complaints, the distinguished man Isidore has unjustly complained that he was excommunicated and anathematized by your Fraternity. When we wished to learn from your cleric, who was present, why this had been done, it became clear that there was no other reason than that he had insulted you. This greatly distressed us, because, if it is so, you show that you think of nothing heavenly but reveal yourself to have a worldly manner of life, since, in revenge for a personal insult, you have inflicted the curse of anathema, which the sacred rules forbid.

“Therefore, from now on, be entirely circumspect and watchful, and do not again presume to inflict such things upon anyone in defense of your own insult. For if you do anything of this kind, know that afterward it will be avenged upon you.” (Register, Book XI, Letter 49.)

32. He also writes to the same man:

“The apostle Paul, preacher of almighty God, commands, saying: ‘Do not rebuke an elder’ (1 Tim. 5:1). But this rule of his is to be observed when the elder’s fault does not, by his example, draw the hearts of the young to destruction. For where an elder provides the young with an example leading to destruction, there he must be struck with strict rebuke. For it is written: ‘He is a snare for the young, all of you’ (Isa. 42:22). And again the prophet says: ‘The sinner who is a hundred years old shall be accursed’ (Isa. 65:20).

“Such wickedness has reached my ears concerning your old age that, unless we were still considering you humanely, we would already have struck you with a fixed sentence of condemnation. For I was told that, on the Lord’s Day, before you celebrated the solemn rites of Mass, you went to plow the field of the bearer of this letter; and after plowing it, you celebrated the solemn rites of Mass. After the solemn rites of Mass, you did not hesitate to uproot the boundaries of that man’s property. What punishment ought to have followed such an act is known to all who hear of it.

“We had been uncertain about so great a perversity; but our son Cyriacus, the abbot, when questioned by us while he was at Cagliari, declared that he had learned of it in this way. And because we are still sparing your gray hairs, we urge you: come to your senses at last, old man, and restrain yourself from such levity of conduct and perversity of deeds. For the nearer you become to death, the more watchful and fearful you ought to be.

“Indeed, a sentence had almost been hurled against you; but because we know your simplicity together with your old age, for the time being we remain silent.” (Book IX, Letter 1.)

33. Gregory entirely forbade all bishops to read the books of the pagans. Therefore, to Desiderius, bishop of Gaul, who was requesting the pallium, he writes:

“When many good things had been reported to us about your studies, such joy arose in our heart that we would not at all refuse to grant what your Fraternity had asked to have granted. But afterward it came to us—something we cannot mention without shame—that your Fraternity was explaining grammar to certain people. We received this news with displeasure and rejected it most strongly, so that what had previously been said became for us a cause of groaning and sadness, because praises of Christ and praises of Jove cannot be contained in one mouth. [Col. 0148B] Consider for yourself how grave and abominable it is for bishops to utter what would not befit even a religious layman.

“For although our most beloved son Candidus, the presbyter, came later and, after being carefully questioned about this matter, denied it and attempted to excuse you, it nevertheless has not departed from our mind. For just as it is detestable for this to be reported of a priest, so it must be ascertained through strict and truthful satisfaction whether or not it is so.

“Therefore, if it should become clearly evident afterward that what was reported to us is false, and it should be established that you do not devote yourself to trifles and secular literature, we shall both give thanks to our God, who did not permit your heart to be stained by the blasphemous praises of the impious, and we shall then consider granting what you request with confidence and without any hesitation.” (Register, Book XI, Letter 54.)

34. Nevertheless he writes to Natalis, bishop of Salona:

“From the many who have come from your city, dearest brother, I have learned that, having abandoned pastoral care, you are occupied solely with banquets. I would not have believed what I heard if I had not confirmed it by the evidence of your actions. For the fact that you pay no attention to reading, are not watchful in exhortation, and even ignore the practice of ecclesiastical order is demonstrated by this: you do not know how to preserve the reverence owed to those under whose authority you have been placed.” (Register, Book II, Letter 18.)

35. But when Natalis attempted, through his own writings on empty philosophy, to prove himself blameless, the most gentle teacher Gregory replied as follows:

“In defense of banquets, your Fraternity recalls Abraham’s banquet, at which, according to the testimony of sacred speech, he is said to have received three angels. By this example of a banquet, however, we do not reproach your Beatitude if we know that you receive angels in hospitality. Again, your Fraternity tells of Isaac, who, after being satisfied with food, gave a blessing to his son.

“Would that, since both these events of the Old Testament were enacted historically while also signifying something allegorically, we might read through the events in such a way that we could foresee and perceive the events that ought to be enacted. For when that man greeted one person in the three angels, he declared that the three subsistences of the Trinity are of one substance. The other, after being satisfied, blesses his son because the mind of one who is filled with divine banquets is extended into the power of prophecy. [Col. 0149A] The divine banquets are the words of sacred speech.

“If, therefore, you read constantly, and, drawing an example from external things, penetrate to internal realities, you fill the belly of your mind as though satisfied from the hunting of the field, so that, with the son placed before you—that is, the people entrusted to you—you may announce what is to come. But in this world the one who prophesies something about God becomes dim-sighted, because it is certainly fitting that here the one whose inner sense flashes with understanding should see less through desire.

“Apply these things, then, to yourselves; and if you recognize yourselves as such, there is no reason for you to doubt our assessment. I also find that your Beatitude rejoices if you bear the name “glutton” together with the Creator of all things. I shall explain this briefly: if this is falsely said of you, you truly bear this name together with the Creator of all things; but if it is true of you, who would doubt that it was false of him? A shared name cannot absolve you, since the circumstances are different. For the thief who was destined to perish also took up the cross with Christ; but the equal crucifixion did not absolve the one whom his own guilt held fast.” (Register, Book II, Letter 52.)

Nevertheless, with all the strength I possess, I beg through my prayers that your most holy Fraternity may be joined to our author and God not merely by name but also by cause.

Your Holiness rightly praises in your letters banquets held with the intention of showing charity. Yet it must be understood that they truly proceed from charity when no absent person’s life is attacked in them, no one is reproved with mockery, and the empty tales of secular affairs—not the words of sacred reading—are heard; when the body is served no more than necessity requires, but only its weakness is restored, so that it may be available for the practice of virtue.

If you conduct your banquets in this way, I confess that you are teachers of abstinence. Thus the testimony of the apostle Paul that you cited to me—“Let the one who does not eat not judge the one who eats” (Rom. 14:3)—seems to me entirely inappropriate. For neither do I refrain from eating, nor was this said by the apostle Paul so that the members of Christ, joined to one another in his body—that is, in the Church—by the bond of charity should in no way care for one another.

But if neither I were connected with you nor you with me, I would rightly be compelled to remain silent, so as not to rebuke one who could not be corrected. This saying, then, was spoken only concerning those who strive to judge people whose care has not been entrusted to them. But since, by God’s authorship, we are one, [Note: [Col. 0149D] Another reading: “If we keep silent about those things in you which ought to be corrected”] we commit a serious offense if we remain silent about the things in us that ought to be corrected.

36. Gregory did not permit any bishop to leave his own parish even for a short time without absolutely unavoidable necessity; and he very strongly forbade them to become occupied with worldly affairs. Thus he writes to Romanus, the defensor:

“It has been reported to us that our most reverend brother Basil, the bishop, is occupied in secular affairs like one of the laity and is uselessly attending upon the praetorian authorities. Since this both makes him contemptible and destroys priestly reverence, as soon as your Experience receives this command, compel him to return through strict enforcement, so that, while you are present there, he may not be permitted under any pretext to remain more than five days. For if you allow him in any way to remain there longer, know that you will begin to be seriously culpable before us together with him.” (Register, Book X, Letter 10.)

37. He also writes to Anthemius, the subdeacon:

“It has come to us that Pimen, bishop of the city of Amalfi, is not content to remain in his church but wanders outside through various places. Seeing this, the others do not remain in the fortress either; following his example, they choose to live outside. Since by acting in this way they themselves invite enemies to plunder them, we therefore command you by this authority not to cease warning the aforesaid bishop that he must not presume to do this in the future, but must reside in his church according to priestly custom.

“If, after your warning, you discover that he has not corrected himself, you shall assign him to a monastery and take care by every means to inform us, so that, once again by our command, you may learn what you ought to do.” (Register, Book VI, Letter 23.)

38. It is no wonder that Gregory, by the ministry entrusted to him, took care to rebuke the vices of any superiors with salutary words, since he did not hesitate to commend the fall of his own aunt to the memory of posterity for the instruction of the people. Since he wished to distinguish the calling of the many from the election of the few by examples, in accordance with the Gospel saying, “Many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. 22:14), he relates the following:

“My father had three sisters, all of whom were holy virgins. One was called Tharsilla, another Gordiana, and another Aemiliana. United in one love, consecrated at the same time, and living under strict discipline in their own house, they maintained a common life. After they had remained for a long time in the same way of life, Tharsilla and Aemiliana began daily to increase in love for their Creator and, although they were still present here in body alone, to pass daily in spirit to eternal things.

“Gordiana’s spirit, by contrast, began day by day to grow lukewarm through a decline in its inner warmth and gradually to return to love of this world. Tharsilla often used to say to her sister Aemiliana with deep sighing: ‘I see that our sister Gordiana is not of the same portion as we are. For I perceive that she is flowing outward and is not guarding the heart to which she committed herself.’

“Each day they tried to correct her with gentle reproof and reform her from frivolity of conduct to the seriousness of their way of life. During the words of correction she would suddenly recover an expression of gravity; but when the hour of correction had passed, the assumed gravity of propriety immediately passed away as well, and she returned to light conversation. She delighted in the company of young laywomen, and any person who was not devoted to this world was a great burden to her.

“One night my great-grandfather Felix, bishop of this Roman Church, appeared in a vision to my aunt Tharsilla, who, through continual prayer, devoted affliction, exceptional abstinence, and a venerable gravity of life, had grown in honor and attained the height [Col. 0151A] of holiness among her sisters. As she herself related, he showed her a dwelling of perpetual brightness and said: ‘Come, for I am receiving you into this dwelling of light.’

“Immediately afterward she was seized by a fever and reached her final day. As happens when noble women and men are dying, many people gathered to console their relatives. At that very hour, men and women stood around her bed awaiting her departure; among them was my mother.

“Suddenly she looked upward, saw Jesus coming, and began to cry out loudly to those standing around her: ‘Go away, go away! Jesus is coming.’ As she fixed her gaze upon the one she saw, that holy soul was released from the flesh. At once the whole place was suffused with such a fragrance of wonderful odor [Col. 0151B] that the sweetness itself revealed to everyone that the author of sweetness had come there.

“When her body was stripped, according to the custom for the dead, in order to be washed, the skin on her elbows and knees was found to have become hardened and thickened through the practice of long prayer, like the skin of camels. Her dead flesh bore witness to what her spirit had always done while she lived.

“These things happened before the day of the Lord’s Nativity. After that day had passed, she soon appeared in a nocturnal vision to her sister Aemiliana and said: ‘Come, so that, since I celebrated the Lord’s Nativity without you, I may now celebrate the holy Theophany [Note: Bigot and Uticensis manuscripts: ‘the holy Theophany’] with you.’
