“Concerned at once for the salvation of her sister Gordiana, Aemiliana replied: ‘And if I come alone, to whom shall I leave our sister Gordiana?’ With a sorrowful expression she answered again: ‘Come, for our sister Gordiana has been assigned to the laity.’ This vision was immediately followed by bodily illness; and just as it had been said, before the day of the Lord’s manifestation, as the illness grew worse, she died.

“But as soon as Gordiana found herself left alone, her depravity increased. What had previously remained hidden in the desire of her thoughts she afterward carried out through the act of wickedness. For, forgetting fear of the Lord, forgetting modesty and reverence, and forgetting her consecration, she later took the steward of her estates as her husband.

“Behold: all three had previously embraced the same way of life with one ardor, but they did not all persevere in the same devotion, because, according to the Lord’s word: ‘Many are called, but few are chosen’ (Matt. 22:14).” (Homily 38 on the Gospels.)

39. Gregory also carefully investigated the negligence of subordinates and corrected it through the strictest reproofs. Thus, writing to Vitalianus, bishop of Sipontum, he says:

“If you had been, or had known how to be, a guardian of religious discipline, while you were stationed there you would not, while stationed there, have allowed the daughter of Tullianus, of glorious memory, master of the soldiers, either to abandon the religious habit and return to secular dress or to send us a perverse letter. But because you are weighed down by excessive laziness and extreme torpor, an unlawful matter has for the present been committed there with impunity, to your disgrace.

“For if, as we said, you had been watchful, the punishment of that most wicked woman ought to have reached us before her offense. Since you are so dull and so negligent that, unless you have experienced canonical correction yourself, you do not know how to preserve strict discipline in others, we shall show you, at a suitable time, if it pleases the Lord, how watchful you ought to be.” (Register, Book VIII, Letter 8.)

40. He also writes to the defensor Sergius:

“If you were a man, or possessed any discernment [Alternative reading: ‘strictness’], you ought to have been such a guardian of regular discipline that offenses committed there unlawfully would have been corrected by punishment before their report reached us. But since your excessive folly makes you negligent, we are offended not only by those matters but are also provoked to punish your laziness.” (Register, Book VIII, Letter 9.)

41. He also writes to Anthemius, subdeacon of Campania:

“It has come to us that our brother and fellow bishop Paschasius is so lazy and negligent in everything that he is recognized as a bishop in nothing. Indeed, neither his church, nor the monasteries, nor the children of the Church—whether the oppressed or the poor—experience toward themselves any evidence of his loving concern, nor does he provide any assistance of defense to those who petition him in matters where it is just to do so.

“What is still more grievous to say is that he refuses in any way to accept the counsel of the wise and of those who offer sound advice, so that, if he cannot attend to what is required by himself, he might at least learn it from another. Instead, having neglected the matters belonging to a shepherd’s care, he occupies himself uselessly and with all his effort in building a ship. Hence, as is reported, it happened that he has already lost four hundred solidi or more.

“This too is added to his faults: he is said to descend daily to the sea, despised, with one or two clerics, so that he is a subject of ridicule among his own people and appears so base and contemptible to outsiders that he is judged to possess nothing of episcopal intelligence or dignity.

“If this is so, know that you are not without blame, since you delayed rebuking and restraining him as was fitting. Since all this not only discredits him but is also shown to constitute a reproach against priestly office, we wish you to admonish and exhort him in the presence of other priests or of certain noble sons of his church, so that, having shaken off the vice of torpor, he may no longer be lazy but may be watchful in the care of his church and monasteries; may show paternal charity to his children; may be energetic, with discernment, in defending the poor; may stand firm in matters where justice directs; and may willingly accept the counsel of the wise.

“In this way, both that city may be comforted by his care and he himself may cover over the faults of his laziness. But if—which we do not believe—after this exhortation of ours he should attempt to remain negligent in his customary manner, he must by every means be sent to us, so that, being placed here, he may learn what a priest ought to do and how he ought to act according to the fear of God.” (Book XIII, Letter 26.)

42. He also writes to the same man:

“Whenever we hear such things about our brothers and fellow bishops as show them to be blameworthy and are capable of causing us sadness, necessity compels us to think seriously about their correction. Since it has been reported to us that the bishops of Campania are so negligent that, heedless of their dignity, they show no paternal vigilance either toward their churches or toward their children, nor do they exercise care for the monasteries or devote themselves to protecting oppressed poor people, we therefore command you by this authority to summon them to you and, in our name, warn them strictly that they must no longer be negligent but must demonstrate through their actions that they possess priestly zeal and concern.

“Let them be so watchful in those things which they ought rightly to do according to God that no further complaint about them may provoke us. If you find any one of them negligent after this, send him to us without any excuse, so that he may be made to feel through regular strictness how grievous it is to refuse correction in matters that are blameworthy and greatly deserving of censure.” (Register, Book XIII, Letter 27.)

He also writes to Victor, bishop of Palermo, after some other matters:

“Do you understand what guilt is already yours, that I, though stationed so far away, learn what is being done in your city and, occupied with so many cares, arrange what ought to be done?” (Register, Book V, Letter 6.)

43. It must certainly be noted that, just as Gregory, the most discerning prelate, scarcely ever, or never, released manifest crimes without punishment, so in doubtful matters he never pronounced a definite judgment. Therefore he writes to Andrew, bishop of Tarentum:

“Whoever, conscious of his guilt, strives to appease the eternal Judge with appropriate repentance will look upon that Judge’s tribunal without fear. We have learned with manifest certainty that you had a concubine, concerning whom some contrary suspicion also arose. But since judgment ought not to be absolute in ambiguous matters, we have chosen to entrust this to your conscience.

“Therefore, if, being constituted in the sacred order, you recall that you were defiled by intercourse with her, lay aside the honor of the priesthood and do not presume in any way to approach the ministry. You should know that you will minister at the peril of your soul and will undoubtedly render an account to our God if, conscious of this crime, you choose to conceal the truth and remain in the order in which you are.” (Register, Book III, Letter 45.)

44. For this reason Gregory, the most diligent guardian of the Church of God, reproved the counselors of everyone and, as far as lay within him, strove to save everyone. Thus, writing to Venantius, a former monk and patrician, after some other matters, he says:

“I know that, when my letter is received, friends immediately gather, learned clients are summoned, and counsel concerning the cause of your life is sought from supporters of death. Since they love not you but your possessions, they tell you nothing except what pleases you for the moment. Such, as you yourself remember, were the counselors who previously led you into so great a crime of wrongdoing.

“And, to say something to you from a secular author (Seneca, Letter 5): everything should be discussed with friends, but first the friends themselves. If you are seeking a human counselor in your case, I ask you to accept me as your counselor. No one can be more faithful to you in counsel than one who loves not what is yours but you.” (Register, Book I, Letter 34.)

[Column 0154A] Likewise to John, bishop of Constantinople, after some preliminary remarks:

“I had written to the most blessed lord John; but I believe that your familiar young man wrote back to me—the one who has as yet learned nothing of God, who knows nothing of the inward compassion of charity, who is accused by everyone of criminal deeds, who daily plots the deaths of various people through secret wills, and fears neither the Lord nor the shame of men. Believe me, dearest brother: if you possess a perfect zeal for truth, correct him first, so that, through those who are near you, even those who are not near you may be better corrected by example. Do not admit his tongue. He ought to be directed to the counsel of Your Holiness, not Your Holiness bent toward his words. For if he listens to him, I know that he will not be able to have peace with his brothers.” (*Register*, [Column 0154B] book III, letter 53.)

Likewise to Januarius, bishop of Caralis:

“We decree,” he says, “that those whose counsels led you to plow another’s harvest and who did not fear removing boundary markers be excommunicated for two months, yet in such a way that, if anything humanly should happen to them during that two-month period, they are not deprived of the blessing of Viaticum. Henceforth, however, be wary of their counsels and carefully guard yourself, lest, if you have been their disciple in evil when you ought to have been their teacher in good, we spare neither your simplicity nor your old age.” (*Register*, book IX, letter 1.)

Likewise to Callinicus, exarch of Italy, after some preliminary remarks:

“But know this: it grieved me greatly that the steward, who had received the petition of a bishop wishing to return from schism, declared that he had lost it, and afterward it was held by the adversaries of the Church. I think this was done not through his negligence but through his venality. Hence I am surprised that Your Excellency did not at all punish this fault in him; yet, because I was surprised by it, I quickly reproved myself. For where the lord Justinus gives counsel—he who does not have peace with the Catholic Church—there heretics cannot be condemned. Furthermore, you say that you wish to celebrate the feast of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, in the city of Rome; and we pray almighty God to protect you by his mercy and grant you fulfillment of your vows. But I ask that the aforementioned most eloquent man come at the same time; if he does not come, let him withdraw from your service. Or certainly, [Column 0154D] if Your Excellency should perhaps be unable to come because of circumstances that arise, let him nevertheless communicate with the unity of the holy Church. For I hear that he is a good man, if only he did not belong to the worst error.” (*Register*, book IX, letter 9.)

### 45

Likewise to Serenus, bishop of Massilia, after much preliminary material:

“It has reached me that Your Charity willingly receives evil men into your companionship or counsel, to such an extent that you keep as a familiar associate a certain presbyter who, after falling, is said still to remain polluted in the defilement of his iniquity. We certainly do not believe this altogether, because one who receives such a man does not correct crimes but rather seems to grant others permission to commit such deeds. Yet, lest perhaps some deception or concealment should have persuaded you that he ought to be received and still regarded favorably by you, it is fitting not only that you drive this man far from you, but also that, with priestly zeal, you cut off his offenses in every way. As for the others who are remembered to be wicked, restrain them from their wickedness by paternal exhortation and strive to recall them to the way of righteousness. But if—as God forbid—you see that they make no progress at all from salutary admonition, you must also cast these far from you, lest their wickedness seem not at all displeasing because they are received, and lest not only they remain uncorrected, but others also be corrupted by their reception. Consider how execrable to human beings and dangerous before God’s eyes it is if vices appear to be nourished by the very person through whom crimes ought to be punished. Therefore, dearest brother, attend carefully to these matters and strive to act in such a way that you correct the wicked for their salvation and do not introduce into the hearts of your children a scandal arising from the company of evil men.” (*Register*, book XI, letter 13.)

### 46

The most upright judge, Gregory, by no means allowed one person to be punished for another’s fault. Therefore, writing to Gudiscalcus, duke of Campania, he says:

“That concern of superiors is useful, that caution is praiseworthy, in which reason governs everything and fury claims nothing for itself. Power must therefore be restrained by reason, and nothing should be done before the mind, once stirred, returns to tranquility. For in a time of agitation anger considers everything it has done to be just. Thus it has reached us that Your Greatness was driven by the force of fury to such a point that you not only caused the doors of the monastery of the holy Archangel to be broken, but also ordered whatever was found there to be plundered. Moreover, you are said to have burned with such anger against the abbot of that monastery that, unless he had concealed himself and hidden during the time of your anger, he would have incurred no slight danger; indeed, terrified by fear of you, he has not yet dared to leave the house in which he had formerly taken refuge.

“Perhaps, therefore, lest you should seem to have acted in vain, you charge the monk’s flight against him as a crime, insofar as it has been reported to us that the monk went over to the enemy, asserting that he fled with the abbot’s approval. If this is so, we are grieved and greatly astonished at your wisdom. For if you think it permissible for the fault of some to harm others, many may be liable to this crime. The slaves of various nobles, the clerics of many churches, the monks of various monasteries, and the dependents of many judges have often handed themselves over to the enemy. Therefore, if this is believed, the masters of slaves, the bishops of clerics, the abbots of monks, and the judges of various fugitives are all placed under guilt and accusation. Have not, even in the days of Your Greatness, many fled from the city in which you reside to the soldiers of the Lombards? And who could be found to possess such lack of discernment and such folly as to think that their iniquity should be attributed to you?” (*Book X, letter 11.*)

### 47

Gregory likewise defended the freedom of every human being against the insolence of judges with an unconstrained voice. Thus, writing to Leontius, former consul, after some preliminary remarks, he says:

“If Libertinus is found guilty in this matter concerning the security, I do not know what he might allege on his own behalf regarding the other matters. I know this one thing, firmly and certainly: even if he committed some fraud against the public authorities, his property ought to have been reduced—not his liberty. For in the fact that free men are beaten or imprisoned, to say nothing of the offense against almighty God, to say nothing of the severe burden placed upon your reputation, the very age of our most devout emperor is nevertheless utterly darkened. For this is the difference between the kings of the nations and the emperors of the Romans: the kings of the nations are lords of slaves, whereas the emperor of the Romans is lord of free men.

“Therefore, in everything you do, you must first preserve justice and then safeguard liberty in every respect. For it is written: ‘What you do not wish to be done to you, see that you do not do to another’ (Tobit 4:16). And Truth itself says: ‘Whatever you wish people to do to you, do the same to them’ (Matthew 7:12). In particular, therefore, you must attend to the liberty of those who have been entrusted to you for examination; and if you do not wish your own liberty to be violated by your superiors, preserve and honor the liberty of your subjects. For we know who said: ‘Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away’ (Matthew 24:35). Since his words do not pass away but are fulfilled in every respect, let us fear what he says again: ‘In the measure with which you have measured, it will be measured back to you’ (Matthew 7:2).

“What, then, does Your Glory imagine? If we act arrogantly or cruelly, despising God, do we satisfy a human being? By no means. For he who is despised stirs against us the very person whom, while despising God, we wish to please. Let us therefore take every care to please God, who is able to lead even angry people back to gentleness. For, as I have said, even gentle people are provoked to anger when God is displeased.

“If it is said that public frauds cannot be uncovered without beatings and threats, I might have accepted this, had the lord Leontius not come in a matter involving accounts. For it is true that those who are deficient in understanding and speech are accustomed to go beyond the bounds with their hands.” (*Register*, book X, letter 51.)

### 48

Gregory restrained the greed and crimes of all judges as though with the bit and bridle of his pontificate, by means of the strongest authorities; and, when he could not correct some of them gently from their wickedness, he exposed them publicly through the reproofs of his writings. Thus he writes to Romanus, exarch of Italy, residing at Ravenna, saying:

“Before Your Excellency, the audacity of the wicked ought to encounter the goads of correction rather than the comfort of defense. For it is a grave matter if wicked conduct should find refuge there from which the censure of discipline ought to proceed. It has therefore reached us that a certain Speciosus, a presbyter who, when circumstances required it, had been assigned to a monastery by John, our brother and fellow bishop, departed from it against the will of his pastor and, disregarding the force of ecclesiastical ordinance, resisted the aforesaid bishop, relying upon your protection. Since this unquestionably brings reproach upon Your Excellency, you must, with due discernment, withdraw your protection from him, lest, if he should for a time use your name to defend his disobedience or defiance against his pastor and thereby be compelled to offend Your Excellency, we too should grieve over your discord.

“We have also learned something which it is sacrilegious to say: that certain women who until now have remained in religious and monastic dress have put off their religious clothing and their veil and—what we cannot report without deep sorrow—joined themselves to husbands. Yet they are said to be supported by the patronage of your favor, so that they dare to say or attempt such things. The severity of this perversity does not permit us to believe it. We therefore ask that you in no way involve yourself in so great a sin. For by no means, for God’s sake, do we endure that such iniquity remain unpunished. Hence we ask again that Your Excellency not involve yourself in the defense of such cases, lest God defend his own injury and the guilt of others produce discord between us.” (*Register*, book V, letter 24.)

Likewise to Venantius, former monk and patrician:

“Many foolish people thought that, if I were raised to the episcopal order, I would refuse to address you or to correspond with you frequently. But that is not so, because the necessity of my position itself now compels me not to remain silent.”

And shortly afterward:

“Compelled, therefore, by this consideration, whether you wish it or not, I shall speak, because with all my strength I desire either that you be saved or that I be freed from your death. You remember the state in which you were, and, setting aside the severity of heavenly judgment, you recognize to what you have fallen. Weigh your guilt while there is time; while you can, dread the severity of the future Judge, lest you then hear that bitter sentence when you will no longer escape it by any tears.”

And below:

“By the testimony of the Gospel (Matthew 12), you know that divine severity reproves us for an idle word and carefully demands an account of an unprofitable one. Consider, then, what it will do with a perverse deed, if in its judgment it rejects some people for their speech. Ananias had vowed money to God, but afterward, overcome by the devil’s persuasion, withdrew it (Acts 5); yet you know by what death he was punished. If, then, the man who took back from God the money he had given was worthy of the danger of death, consider how great a danger you will deserve in the divine judgment—you who have withdrawn not money but yourself from almighty God, to whom you had vowed yourself under the monastic habit.

“Therefore, if you listen to the words of my correction and intend to follow them, you will learn at the end how gentle and sweet they are. Behold, I confess that I speak in mourning, and, crushed by sadness over your deed, I can scarcely bring forth words; yet your spirit, conscious of its own action, can scarcely endure what it hears: it is ashamed, confused, and resists. If it cannot bear the words of dust, what will it do at the judgment of the Creator? Yet I confess that I believe the mercy of heavenly grace to be very great: he sees you fleeing from life and nevertheless still preserves you for life; he sees you in your pride and endures you.” (*Register*, book I, letter 34.)

When Venantius, however, remained in the same apostasy and, after certain disputes had arisen, learned that his offerings had been rejected by John, bishop of Syracuse, he became hostile toward the bishop and did not fear accusing him before Gregory. Gregory himself replied to him as follows:

“We found the letter you sent, already greatly grieving us, because we learned that a scandal had arisen between you and John, our brother and fellow bishop, in whose harmony we had desired to rejoice. Whatever the cause may have been, anger ought not to have burst forth to such a point that, as we have heard, your armed men attacked the episcopal residence and committed various acts of violence in a hostile manner, and that this affair meanwhile separated you from paternal charity. [Note: At Column 0157D the Bigotian, Uticensis, and other manuscripts read *in episcopium* (“into the episcopal residence”); the printed editions read *in episcopum* (“against the bishop”), a reading rejected by both printed and handwritten manuscripts of the *Letters*.]

“Could not any dispute, whatever it was, have been settled peacefully, so that neither the interests of the parties suffered loss nor goodwill felt injury? We are not unaware of the gravity, holiness, and gentleness of the aforesaid brother. From this we conclude that, unless excessive force of grief had compelled him, his fraternity would in no way have reached the matter over which you claim to be distressed. But as soon as we learned this from his letter, we immediately wrote to him, admonishing him both to receive your offerings as before and to permit Masses to be celebrated in your house—not only permitting them, but, if you wished, celebrating them himself,” and so forth. (*Register*, book VI, letter 43.)

But when Venantius had been reconciled with the bishop and had refused, despite Gregory’s exhortations in numerous letters over eleven years, to return to his monastic vocation, he fell into a very serious illness. When Gregory heard this from John, bishop of Syracuse, he replied:

“I have received the letter of Your Fraternity, which spoke to me about the illness of my most beloved son, the lord Venantius, and recounted everything that had been done concerning him. But when I heard at one and the same time that he was in despair and seriously ill, and that wicked men were pressing upon the property of orphans—namely, his daughters—I could scarcely contain the grief in my heart. [Note: The Bigotian manuscript reads “in despair and seriously ill,” as do the manuscripts of the *Letters*.] Yet there was this consolation: tears burst forth from me through groans. Therefore Your Holiness must not neglect the first care that is required, namely, to think about his soul—exhorting him, entreating him, setting before him the terrible judgment of God, and promising him God’s ineffable mercy—so that, even at the end, he may return to his habit, lest the guilt of so great a fault stand against him in the eternal judgment.” (*Register*, book XI, letter 36.)

If Gregory observed that any judges were incorrigible in their wickedness, he denounced them in his own writings before rulers. Thus he complains to the empress Constantina, saying:

“When I had learned that there were many pagans on the island of Sardinia, still serving idols through the practices of their wicked paganism, while the priests of that same island remained sluggish in preaching our Redeemer, I sent there one of the bishops of Italy, who, with the Lord’s cooperation, led many pagans to the faith. But someone reported to me a sacrilegious matter: that those who sacrifice to idols on the island pay a fee to the judge so that they may be permitted to do this. After some of them had been baptized [Column 0159A] and had already ceased sacrificing to idols, the same fee that they had previously been accustomed to pay for sacrificing to idols was still exacted from them by the judge of the island, even after baptism. When the aforementioned bishop rebuked him, he replied that he had promised only such official assistance as could not be fulfilled unless it extended even to matters of this kind.

“Corsica, however, is oppressed by such an excess of exactors and such a burden of exactions that those who are there can scarcely fulfill the demands, even by selling their children. Hence it happens that, abandoning the pious commonwealth, the landowners of that island are compelled to flee to the most abominable nation of the Lombards. For what could they suffer more gravely or cruelly from barbarians than to be forced, under constraint and pressure, to sell their children?

“In the island of Sicily, moreover, a certain Stephanus, a chartularius of the maritime districts, is said to perpetrate such great injustices and oppressions by seizing individuals’ property and, without judicial proceedings, placing claims upon estates and houses, that, if I wished to recount one by one the records concerning him that have reached me, I could not complete them in a large volume. Let the most serene lady carefully attend to all these matters and restrain the groans of the oppressed.”

And shortly afterward:

“Consider what the minds and what the hearts of parents must be like when they sell their children so that they themselves may not be tortured. But how one ought to pity other people’s children is well known to those who have children of their own. Therefore it is enough for me briefly to have brought these matters to your attention, lest, if Your Piety did not know what is being done in these regions, the guilt of my silence should cause me to be punished before the strict Judge.” [Column 0159C] (*Register*, book V, letter 41.)

### 49

Hence it is established, on the testimony of the *Dialogues*, that in Gregory’s time so many priests and laypeople shone forth through miracles in various regions as could never afterward be found under later pontiffs.

Therefore, since the enemy of the human race envied such great blessings of the Church of God, he inflamed certain pontiffs as well as secular judges against it. Concerning their affliction he complains, among other things, to John, bishop of Ravenna, saying:

“I attribute this to my sins: that the man who is now present—without doubt the Roman exarch—both pretends not to fight against our enemies and forbids us to make peace, although now, even if he wished, we could not make it at all, because Ariulfus, having the army of Authari and Nordulfus, desires that their petition be granted to him, so that he may deign to discuss something concerning peace with you.” (*Register*, book II, letter 46.)

Likewise to Sebastianus, bishop of Sirmium, after some preliminary remarks:

“What we suffer in this land, most holy brother, from the person of your friend, the lord Romanus, we are quite unable to express. I shall say briefly, however, that his malice toward us has surpassed the swords of the Lombards, so that the enemies who kill us seem kinder than the judges of the commonwealth, who by their malice, robberies, and deceits consume us inwardly. At the same time to care for bishops, clerics, monasteries, and the people; to keep anxious watch against the ambushes of enemies; and always to remain suspicious of the deceits and malice of the dukes—how great the labor and grief involved are, your Fraternity measures all the more truly because you love me, who suffer these things, with greater purity.” (*Register*, book V, letter 42.)

Likewise to Anastasius, patriarch, after much preliminary material:

“I shrink from recounting to Your Beatitude the evils we suffer from the swords of barbarians and from the perversity of judges, lest I increase the grief of one whom I ought to lessen through consolation.” (*Register*, book IV, letter 39.)

Likewise to Palladius, presbyter of Mount Sinai, after very extensive preliminary material:

“I ask that you pray for me, so that almighty God may deign to guard me both from evil spirits and from wicked people, because in this pilgrimage of my life evils, both together and numerous, surround me, so that I may rightly say with the Psalmist: ‘Your angers have passed over me, and your terrors have troubled me. They surrounded me like water all day long; they surrounded me altogether’ (Psalm 87:17–18).” (*Register*, book XI, letter 2.)

### 50

To Maurice, then an exceedingly greedy and rapacious ruler, who, at the urging of his enemies, was issuing a disastrous law forbidding any soldier who had been enrolled in military service to convert, Gregory replied, among other things:

“For this purpose power over all human beings was given from heaven to the piety of my lords: so that those who desire good things may be helped, so that the way to heaven may be opened more widely, and so that the earthly kingdom may serve the heavenly kingdom. And now, in an open proclamation, it is said that a man who has once been enrolled in earthly military service may not enter the service of our Lord Jesus Christ unless he has either completed his military service or been discharged because of bodily weakness.

“But behold, through me, his lowest servant and yours, Christ will answer you, saying: ‘I made you, from a notary, count of the Excubitors; from count of the Excubitors, Caesar; from Caesar, emperor—not only this, but also father of emperors. I entrusted my priests to your hand, and you withdraw your soldiers from my service?’ Tell me, I beg you, most devout lord: what will you answer your Lord at the judgment when he comes to you and says this?”

And shortly afterward:

“Let my lord inquire, I beg, which earlier emperor issued such a law, and let him examine more carefully whether it ought to have been issued.” (*Register*, book II, letter 65.)

Likewise to Theodore, the physician, after some preliminary remarks:

“Because of my sins,” he says, “the emperor issued such a law in his commonwealth during the past year, at the suggestion or counsel of—whether whose, I do not know—that no one who had conducted public business, no one marked by office or by hand, or counted among the soldiers, might convert in a monastery unless his military service had perhaps been completed. This law was first issued, as those who know the ancient laws say, by Julian, of whom we all know how far he was turned away from God.” (*Ibid.*, letter 66.)

### 51

John, then a former monk and bishop of the imperial city, encouraged or at least favored the madness of the judges. At the time when Gregory, sent by Bishop Pelagius as apocrisarius, was residing near Constantinople, John had pretended with apparent humility to flee the highest priesthood; but once he had accepted it, he grew so greatly in the pride of a deceitful mind that, seeking an opportunity on another pretext, he convened a synod in which he attempted to have himself called universal. [Note: We infer that this synod was held in 587 from no. 43 of book V, indiction 13, where eight years are said to have elapsed since its celebration. Consult the cited letter.] As soon as Pope Pelagius learned of this, he annulled the acts of that synod by letters issued on the authority of the holy apostle Peter. He also prohibited the deacon who, according to custom, attended the emperors to deliver ecclesiastical responses from celebrating the solemn Masses with John.

Following this judgment, blessed Gregory likewise punished the aforementioned John with the same sentence, after he had often been admonished but delayed obeying. He also commanded all bishops, under threat of the loss of their own honor, never to write or accept in writing the profane title “universal,” or to subscribe to it wherever it had been written. John therefore, by many deceptions purchasing the assent of the exceedingly greedy emperor to his hypocrisy, obtained a letter from the emperor to Gregory directing Gregory to be at peace with him.

For this reason Gregory writes to the empress Constantina, among other things, saying:

“From a letter written by Sabinianus, my deacon and representative, I have learned how much justice Your Serenity is extending in the affairs of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, against certain men who are arrogantly humble and falsely gentle. I therefore ask again that you not allow anyone’s hypocrisy to prevail against the truth. For there are some who, according to the words of the excellent preacher, ‘through smooth speech and blessings deceive the hearts of the innocent’ (Romans 16). They are despised in clothing but puffed up in heart; they seem to despise everything in this world, yet seek to acquire all the things of the world at once. They confess themselves unworthy of all human beings, yet cannot be content with ordinary titles, because they seek that by which they may appear more worthy than everyone else.” (*Register*, book V, letter 21.)

And shortly afterward:

### 52

“Moreover, I report that I have received a letter from my most devout lords, directing me to be at peace with my brother and fellow priest, John. Indeed, it was fitting for a religious ruler to give such an instruction to a priest. But since this same brother of mine, with new presumption and pride, calls himself the universal bishop, and caused himself to be inscribed with this proud title in a synod during the time of my predecessor of blessed memory—although all the acts of that synod were dissolved in opposition to the apostolic see—the most serene lord has intimated something grievous to me: he did not correct the man who is proud, but rather tried to make me withdraw from my purpose, although in this matter I defend the truth of humility and rectitude established by the Gospels and the canons.

“In this matter my aforementioned brother and fellow priest is acting against the judgment of the Gospel, against the blessed apostle Peter, and against all the churches and the ordinances of the canons. But almighty God exists, in whose hand are all things, of whom it is written: ‘There is no wisdom, no prudence, no counsel against the Lord’ (Proverbs 21:30). Indeed, the most holy brother mentioned above often tries to persuade the most serene lord of many things; but I know well that his prayers and tears are of such force that they do not allow anything to be taken from the one whom he addresses contrary to reason or to his own soul.

“Yet it is very grievous that it should be patiently endured that, despising everyone, the aforementioned brother and fellow bishop of mine should attempt to be called the sole bishop. But in this pride of his, what else is indicated except that the times of Antichrist are already near? For he imitates the one who, scorning the legions of angels established with him in shared joy, attempted to burst forth to the summit of singularity, saying: ‘I will exalt my throne above the stars of heaven; I will sit on the mountain of the Covenant, at the sides of the North. I will ascend above the heights of the clouds; I will be like the Most High’ (Isaiah 14:13).

“Therefore, through almighty God, I beg you not to allow the times of Your Piety to be stained by the elation of one man; nor in any way give assent to so perverse a title. In this matter, let Your Piety in no way despise me, because, even if Gregory’s sins are so great that he ought to suffer such things, the apostle Peter has no sins by which he deserves to suffer such things in your time.

“Therefore, again and again, through almighty God I ask that, just as earlier rulers sought the grace of the apostle Peter, you too take care both to seek it for yourselves and to preserve it; and that, because of the sins of us who serve him unworthily, his honor before you in no way diminish. For he is able both now to be your helper in all things and afterward to forgive your sins.

“We have now spent twenty-seven years living in this city amid the swords of the Lombards. It is unnecessary to explain how much the Church distributes every day so that we may live among them. I shall say briefly, however, that just as in the region of Ravenna Your Piety has a treasurer assigned to the first army of Italy to provide daily expenses when circumstances arise, so in this city I am the treasurer for such matters. And yet this Church, which at one and the same time continually expends so much on clerics, monasteries, the poor, the people, and even the Lombards, is still oppressed by the affliction of all the churches, because many groan over the pride of one man, although they dare not say anything.” (*Ibid.*)

[Column 0162D] ### 53

Gregory also freely opposed the exceedingly greedy ruler, writing after some preliminary remarks:

“Behold, there is no doubt that Peter received the keys of the kingdom of heaven; the power of binding and loosing was granted to him; the care and primacy of the whole Church were entrusted to him—and yet he is not called the universal apostle. But my most holy brother and fellow priest, John, attempts to be called the universal bishop. I am compelled to exclaim and say: ‘O times! O customs!’

“Behold, everything in the regions of Europe has been delivered into the power of barbarians: cities have been destroyed, fortresses overturned, provinces depopulated, and no cultivator inhabits the land. Every day idolaters rage and rule to the death of the faithful; yet the priests who ought to lie weeping on pavement and ashes seek titles of vanity for themselves and glory in new and profane names.

“Am I defending my own cause in this matter, most devout lord? Am I avenging a personal injury, rather than the cause of almighty God and the cause of the universal Church? Who is this man who dares to usurp a new title for himself against the ordinances of the Gospel and the decrees of the canons? Would that he who desires to be called universal could be so without diminishing anyone else. Yet we certainly know that many priests of the Church of Constantinople have fallen into the abyss of heresy, and have been found not only heretics but also heresiarchs.

“For from there came Nestorius, who, thinking that Christ Jesus, the mediator between God and human beings, consisted of two persons, and not believing that God could become human, proceeded as far as Jewish unbelief. From there also came Macedonius, who denied that the Holy Spirit, consubstantial with the Father and the Son, is God. If, then, someone has seized that title in the church from which so many founders of heresies are known to have emerged, the whole Church would—God forbid—fall from its established order when the one called universal falls.

“But may that blasphemous title be far from Christian hearts, in which the honor of all priests is taken away when one man foolishly arrogates it to himself. Certainly, for the honor of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, it was offered to the Roman pontiff through the venerable Council of Chalcedon; but none of them ever consented to use this title of singularity, lest, while something was privately given to one, all priests should be deprived of the honor due to them.

“What, then, is the reason that we do not seek the glory of this title, even though it was offered to us, while another presumes to seize it for himself even though it was not offered? The man who refuses obedience to canonical commands must therefore be bent more by the orders of the most devout lords. He must be restrained—the man who inflicts injury upon the holy universal Church, whose heart is puffed up, who desires to rejoice in a title of singularity, and who by a private title places himself above the honor of your empire.

“Behold, we all suffer scandal because of this. Let the author of the scandal return to the right path, and all quarrels among priests will cease. For I am the servant of all priests insofar as they live as priests. But the one who, through the swelling of empty glory and against the ordinances of the Fathers, raises his neck against almighty God—I trust in almighty God that he will not bend me to himself, even with swords.

“I have explained more fully to Sabinianus, my deacon and representative, what recently occurred in this city when this title was heard.” (*Register*, book V, letter 20.)

54. Likewise to John, bishop of Constantinople:

> “At the time when Your Fraternity was advanced to priestly honor, you remember what peace and harmony among the churches you found. Yet by what audacity or arrogance—I do not know—you have attempted to seize for yourself a new name, by which the hearts of all the brethren could have been brought to scandal. In this matter I am greatly astonished, [Col. 0164A] because I remember that you wished to flee lest you should come to the episcopate; yet, having attained it, you desire to exercise it as though you had hastened to it with ambitious longing. You who admitted that you were unworthy to be called bishop have at last been brought to the point where, despising your brethren, you desire to be called bishop alone.”

And a little later:

> “Truly I say this weeping, and in the deepest anguish of my heart I reckon it among my sins that my brother, who has until now been unable to return to humility, was placed in the rank of the episcopate for this purpose: that he might lead the souls of others back to humility. He who teaches the truth to others has not consented to teach it to himself, even when I have pleaded with him.”

Again, after a little:

> “Who, I ask, is set forth for imitation in this most perverse title, unless it is he who, despising the legions of angels established with him in fellowship, attempted to burst forth to the summit of singularity, so that he might appear to be subject to no one and alone to preside over all? He also said: ‘I will ascend into heaven; above the stars of heaven I will set my throne; I will sit upon the mount of the assembly, on the sides of the North; I will ascend above the heights of the clouds; I will be like the Most High’ (Isaiah 14:13).

> “For what are all your brethren, the bishops of the universal Church, except the stars of heaven, whose life and speech alike shine amid the sins and errors of humanity as among the darkness of night? While you desire to place yourself above them by an exalted title, and to trample upon their name in comparison with your own, what else do you say than: ‘I will ascend into heaven; above the stars of heaven I will exalt my throne’? Are not all the bishops [Col. 0164C] clouds, who both rain down the words of preaching and flash with the radiance of good works? While Your Fraternity despises them and tries to press them beneath yourself, what else do you say than what is spoken by the ancient enemy: ‘I will ascend above the heights of the clouds’?

> “When I see all these things with tears and dread God’s hidden judgments, my tears increase and groans can no longer be contained in my heart: that the most holy man, Lord John, of such great abstinence and humility, has broken out into such pride through the seduction of familiar tongues, that in desiring a perverse title he attempts to become like him who, wishing in his pride to be like God, also lost the grace of the likeness that had been granted to him, and therefore lost true blessedness because he sought false glory.

> “Certainly Peter, prince of the apostles, is a member of the holy [Col. 0164D] and universal Church; Paul, Andrew, and John—what are they other than the heads of individual peoples? Yet under one head they are all members of the Church. And, to gather everything into a brief summary of speech, the holy men before the Law, the holy men under the Law, and the holy men under grace—all these, completing the body of the Lord, have been established among the members of the Church, and no one ever wished to be called universal.

> “Let Your Holiness therefore recognize how greatly she swells within herself, since she desires to be called by that name which no one who was truly holy presumed to bear.”

Again, after a little:

> “Certainly it was formerly proclaimed through the Apostle: ‘Little children, it is the last hour’ (1 John 2:18). And, in accordance with what the Truth foretold, pestilence and the sword rage throughout the world; nations rise against nations; the earth is shaken, while the earth, splitting open, swallows its inhabitants; all that was foretold is coming to pass (Luke 21). The king of pride is near, and—what must not be said—a company of priests is being prepared for him, because those who had been appointed to provide leadership in humility are serving the neck of arrogance. But in this matter, even if our tongue does not openly contradict it, the power of him who specially opposed the vice of pride in himself rises against arrogance.”

And below:

> “You ought to consider lest some root of bitterness, springing upward, cause hindrance, and through it many be defiled. Yet if we neglect to consider this, heavenly judgments will keep watch against such a swelling of pride.”

(*Register*, Book V, Letter 19.)

[Col. 0165B] Likewise to the same man in another letter, after much else:

> “But even now I say: either receive those same persons—namely, John of Chalcedon and Athanasius, the presbyters of Isauria—in their orders and grant them peace; or, if you perhaps do not wish to do this, then, setting aside every dispute, observe in their case the limits established by the ancients or by the canons. If you do neither, we do not wish to introduce a quarrel, but neither do we avoid one coming from you. Your Fraternity knows well what the canons say about bishops who wish to be feared through beatings. We have been made shepherds, not strikers. And the excellent preacher says: ‘Reprove, entreat, rebuke with all patience and instruction.’ But that preaching is new and unheard-of which demands faith through beatings.”

[Col. 0165C] (*Book III, Letter 53.*)

55. Likewise to Sabinianus, deacon of Constantinople:

> “Concerning our most reverend brother John, bishop of Constantinople, I did not wish to compose two letters; instead, a single brief one has been written, which seems to contain a mixture of both things—that is, firmness and conciliation. Therefore Your Belovedness should take care to give him the letter I have now sent, because of the emperor’s wish. For another of a different character will be sent afterward, one from which his pride will not be pleased.

> “For he has gone so far as to send here, under pretext of the presbyter John, documents in which he called himself ‘ecumenical patriarch’ almost throughout every line. But I hope in almighty God that the heavenly majesty will dissolve his hypocrisy.

> “I am astonished, however, that he could deceive Your Belovedness so that you allowed Lord the Emperor to be persuaded to send me his own writing concerning this matter, in which he advised that I ought to be at peace with him. If he wishes to uphold justice, he ought instead to have admonished that man to restrain himself from his proud title; then peace would immediately have been established between us.

> “Nevertheless, you gave no consideration to the cunning with which, as I suspect, our aforesaid brother John acted. He did this so that either Lord the Emperor would be heard and he would appear to have been confirmed in his vanity, or, if I did not listen to the emperor, the emperor’s mind would be provoked against me.

> “But we shall hold to the right path, fearing nothing else in this matter except almighty God. Therefore let Your Belovedness be troubled by nothing. Whatever you see in this world to be exalted against the truth, despise for the sake of the truth, and place your confidence in the grace of almighty God and in the assistance of blessed Peter.

> “Recall the voice of the Truth, which says: ‘Greater is he who is in you than he who is in the world’ (1 John 4:4). In this matter, whatever must be done, do it with the greatest authority.

> “Since we can in no way defend ourselves from the swords of our enemies, since for love of the commonwealth we have lost silver, gold, slaves, and clothing, it is exceedingly disgraceful that through them we should also lose the faith. For to consent to this wicked title is nothing other than to lose the faith.

> “Therefore, as I have already written to you in earlier letters, never presume to proceed with him.”

(*Book V, Letter 19.*)

56. But John, the inventor of this new presumption, [Col. 0166B] after making Maurice, the enemy of God, hostile to Gregory and his associates, saw that the empress Constantina was using every effort to urge that the privileges owed to the Roman Church be preserved. By whatever arts he could, he incited her to ask Gregory to send her, for the church she was building in the palace in honor of the holy apostle Paul, the apostle’s head or some other part of his body.

When the most blessed pope recognized this stratagem, he answered the empress’s mind as follows:

> “Although I wished to have you command me things in which, by displaying the readiest obedience, I might more fully arouse your favor toward me, I was overcome by greater sorrow because you command what I neither can nor dare do. For the bodies of the holy apostles Peter and Paul shine with such great miracles and terrors in their churches [Col. 0166C] that no one can approach them even to pray without great fear.

> “Indeed, when my predecessor of blessed memory wished to move the silver that lay above the most sacred body of the blessed apostle Peter, although it was nearly fifteen feet distant from that body, a sign of no small terror appeared to him.

> “I too wished similarly to improve something near the most sacred body of the holy apostle Paul. Since it was necessary to dig more deeply beside his tomb, the official in charge of that place discovered certain bones—not joined to that tomb—which, because he presumed to lift them and transfer them elsewhere, he died a sudden death after certain grievous signs appeared.

> “Moreover, my predecessor of holy memory, wishing to improve something near the body of the holy martyr Lawrence, did not know where the venerable body had been placed. While it was being sought by excavation, his tomb was suddenly opened unknowingly. All those who were present and working—the monks and the *mansionarii*—who saw the body of that martyr, though they did not presume to touch it at all, died within ten days, so that none remained alive who had seen his holy and righteous body.

> “Let the most tranquil lady know that it is not the Roman custom, when relics of the saints are given, for anyone to presume to touch anything of the body. Rather, only a piece of cloth (*brandeum*) is placed in a small reliquary and set beside the most sacred bodies of the saints. [Col. 0167A] When it is taken away, it is deposited with due veneration in the church that is to be dedicated; and through it such great miracles occur there as though their bodies themselves had been specially brought there.

> “Thus it happened in the time of Pope Leo of blessed memory, as it has been handed down by our ancestors. When certain Greeks doubted such relics, the aforesaid pontiff cut this very cloth with scissors that had been brought, and blood flowed from the cut itself.

> “For in the Roman territories and throughout the whole of the West, it is altogether intolerable and sacrilegious if anyone should attempt to touch the bodies of the saints. If anyone presumes to do so, it is certain that this rashness will in no way remain unpunished.

> “For this reason we are greatly astonished at the custom of the Greeks, who claim that they lift the bones of the saints, and we scarcely believe it. For certain Greek monks who came here two years ago were, in the silence of night, excavating beside the church of Saint Paul the bodies of the dead lying in the field, and storing their bones away to keep them when they departed. When they were caught and carefully questioned as to why they did this, they confessed that they intended to carry those bones to Greece as relics of saints.

> “From their example, as was said above, a greater doubt has arisen for us as to whether it is true that the bones of the saints are genuinely lifted.

> “But what shall I say about the bodies of the blessed apostles? It is certain that, at the time when they suffered, faithful men came from the East who sought to reclaim their bodies as those of their fellow citizens. These bodies were carried as far as the second milestone from the city and placed in a location called the Catacombs. [Col. 0167C]

> “But when all their people gathered and attempted to lift them from there, the force of thunder and lightning so terrified and scattered them that they did not dare to attempt anything of the kind again. Then the Romans came out, lifted their bodies—as they were granted the privilege of doing by the Lord’s mercy—and placed them in the places where they are now buried.

> “Who, therefore, most serene lady, could be so rash as, knowing these things, to presume not merely to touch their bodies, but even in any way to inspect them?

> “Since, then, you have commanded me things which I could in no way obey, I understand that this is not your own doing. Rather, certain people have tried to stir up your piety against me, so that—God forbid—they might deprive me of the favor of your will; and for this reason they sought a pretext by which I might appear disobedient to you. But I trust in almighty God that your most gracious will is in no way being stolen from you, and that you will always possess the power of the holy apostles, whom you love with all your heart and mind, not through their bodily presence but through their protection.

> “As for the sudarium, which you likewise ordered to be sent, it is with his body; and it cannot be touched any more than one can approach his body. But since so religious a desire of the most serene lady ought not to remain unfulfilled, I shall hasten to send you a portion of the chains that the holy apostle Paul himself wore on his hands and neck, from which many miracles are displayed among the people—if indeed I can obtain it by filing them away.

> “For when many people frequently come to those same chains and ask for a blessing, so that they may receive a small amount of the filings, a priest stands by with a file. From the chains, something is quickly struck off for some petitioners, so that there is no delay; but for others who ask, the file is drawn over the chains for a long time, and yet no material can be obtained from them.”

(*Book IV, Letter 30.*)

57. From these truthful words of Gregory it is indeed evident that, down to that time, the Roman pontiff supplied a piece of cloth (*brandeum*) as a relic, whereas in a later period pieces of the garments kept beneath the altar of Saint John in the Constantinian basilica began to be given to those who asked for sacred relics.

58.

> “These garments are proved, even to the present, to shine with such great miracles that, when shaken out outdoors in time of drought, they bring rain, while in time of flooding they restore fair weather. Besides the miracles they perform in the individual churches, I shall not conceal what almighty God has done through them in the oratory of my house in the Subura.

> “Recently, in the time of Pope Hadrian, it seemed to me that the altar of Saint Mary, Mother of God, which stood outside the oratory of Saint John in a very open courtyard and could not be honored with suitable lights, ought to be placed inside the oratory. Gaudericus of Velletri, who appears still to be alive, was summoned. He, a bishop, removed two sealed small reliquaries from the old altar with hymns and songs.

> “At my request, he opened one of them, though with great fear, and found within pieces of those tunics, so far as could be discerned by curious eyes from their resemblance. He solemnly placed them beneath the new altar. From that time onward, as many who are still known to survive testify, lamps lit by divine power appeared there more frequently than usual.

> “For in this eighth indiction, during the week before the day of the Lord’s Nativity, when I was somewhat doubtful about such things, after the morning hymns had been completed, the *mansionarius* extinguished a lamp. When he wished to light it again after Vespers, he found it already burning. Realizing that he must have carelessly extinguished it, he extinguished it again much more carefully the following day. Having locked the doors, he returned at evening to relight the lamp.

> “When he nevertheless found it burning, he recognized from the key he knew he had kept and from the miracle of the oil not having diminished that it was he who had lit the lamp—he who, so that the oil might not be reduced by its burning throughout the day, had divinely increased it.”

59. Of these garments, as I believe, the one made with narrower sleeves is truly the tunic of Saint John, which blessed Gregory, during his own time, received from a certain bishop who brought it. Thus he writes to Abbot John, among other things:

> “I received with complete gratitude your report concerning the tunic of Saint John, because you were diligent in informing me. But let Your Belovedness take care to send me the tunic itself—or, better, the same bishop who possesses it, together with his clergy and with the tunic—so that we may both enjoy the blessing of the tunic and be able to earn a reward from that bishop and clergy.”

(*Book III, Letter 3.*)

The other garment, which has wider sleeves and appears plainly to be not a tunic but a dalmatic, belongs, unless I am mistaken, to Paschasius, a deacon of the Apostolic See. As the same blessed Gregory records in the fourth book of the *Dialogues* (chapter 40), when Paschasius had died in the time of Pope Symmachus, a demon-possessed man touched his dalmatic, which had been laid over the bier, and was immediately healed.

But I believe that both garments came to be called those of Saint John because of an ancient custom: they were habitually deposited beneath his altar. No one doubts that one of them belongs to John the Evangelist, not to John the Baptist, especially since every learned person knows that the Baptist used camel hair for clothing (Matthew 3), whereas the Evangelist, who for so many years after the Lord’s Passion held the office of bishop and very frequently celebrated the solemnities of the Mass, could certainly not have been without priestly garments.

If it is said that, because a tunic and a dalmatic are pontifical garments, both ought to be believed to belong to Saint John, one must consider that Gregory called the garment sent to Abbot John a tunic, not a dalmatic. If he had believed that Saint John’s dalmatic was also present, then, when asking for his tunic, he would consequently not have failed to mention that he possessed the man’s dalmatic as well.

60. Let this suffice concerning the garments of Saint John, about which very many people have doubts, and concerning which I have inserted what I could into the deeds of blessed Gregory.

As for John of Constantinople, the hypocrite who refused, through many evasions, to withdraw from his ambition for the universal title, he recognized that the Lord’s judgments were watching over him, in accordance with the prophecy of the same Father, and after no long interval he died a sudden death. His ambitious pride, which the whole world could scarcely contain, was easily enclosed within the narrowness of a single tomb.

After his gradual departure, when the emperor Maurice—who despised the priests of Christ—urged, on behalf of Cyriacus, who had succeeded John, that Gregory should not labor over the cause of so trivial a title, Gregory resisted by the authority of his pontificate until he had entirely removed the plague of the universal title even from the deceitful lips of flatterers.

Therefore, writing to Eulogius, patriarch of Alexandria, after some other matters, he says:

> “Your Blessedness has taken care to indicate that you no longer write certain proud titles, which have sprung from the root of vanity, and you address me by saying, ‘As you commanded.’ I ask you to remove this word of command from my hearing, because I know who I am and who you are. In position you are my brothers; in character, my fathers. Therefore I did not command, but took care to indicate what is useful.

> “Yet I do not find that Your Blessedness wished to retain perfectly what I brought to your memory. For I said that you ought not to write anything of this kind either to me or to anyone else; and behold, in the preface of the letter which you sent to me—the very man who prohibited it—you took care to imprint the word of a proud title, calling me ‘universal pope.’

> “I ask that Your Most Beloved Holiness do this no more, because what you withhold from yourself you offer to another beyond what reason requires. I do not seek to prosper through words, but through conduct; nor do I consider that to be my honor in which I recognize that my brethren lose their honor.

> “For my honor is the honor of the universal Church. My honor is the solid strength of my brethren. I am truly honored when the honor due to each person is denied to none. For if Your Holiness calls me universal pope, you deny that you yourself are what you confess me to be—the universal one. But may this never be! Let words that inflate vanity and wound charity withdraw.

> “Certainly Your Holiness knows that this was once offered to my predecessors in the holy synod of Chalcedon and afterward by the succeeding Fathers; yet none of them ever wished to use this title, so that, while they loved the honor of all priests in this world, they might preserve their own before almighty God.”

(*Book VIII, Letter 30.*)

## BOOK FOUR

In which it is concluded with what great consideration Saint Gregory, teaching rightly, daily recognized his own weakness.

[Col. 0169]

### Outline

1. Gregory’s temperance.  
2. He withdrew from John, bishop of Ravenna, the use of the pallium and the *mappulae*.  
3. To the same man, repeatedly petitioning for the use of the pallium, he granted it four times a year in the streets.  
4. To the same man, rebuked for various faults, he foretold the day of his calling.  
5. After John’s death, he entrusted the church of Ravenna to a visitor; after consecrating Mariniani as bishop, he granted him the use of the pallium in a similar manner.  
6. To Andrew, petitioning for the pallium, he prescribed an oath.  
7. When Mariniani was unable to defend the custom of the pallium as had been agreed, Gregory remained firm in his judgment.  
8. He rebuked the deacons of Catania for usurping the *campagi*.  
9. Maximus, usurper of the church of Salona.  
10. He defended the authority of his pontificate against a tyrannical emperor.  
11. Excommunicating Maximus and his associates contrary to the imperial command, he compelled his bishops to return to the Church.  
12. He ordered the case of Maximus to be heard at Ravenna.  
13. Maximus fell prostrate on the ground and tearfully asked for pardon.  
14. Gregory decided that mercy should be shown to Maximus, who made satisfaction before the body of Saint Apollinaris.  
15. To Maximus, who humbly made satisfaction, he restored the grace of communion and promised to give him the pallium.  
16. He terrified the proud emperor with learned replies.  
17. Death by the sword threatened Maurice, who raged against Gregory.  
18. Maurice, repentant, saw in a dream that by divine judgment he was delivered, together with his wife and children, to the soldier Phocas.  
19. After a revolt had arisen, Maurice was killed, together with his entire family, at the command of Phocas.  
20. After receiving an imperial portrait, he wisely enumerated Maurice’s faults to the emperor Phocas.  
21. He sent him an *apocrisiarius* in the customary manner.  
22. After removing a great burden, he confessed that he had made the imperial yoke lighter.  
23. He sent his synodical letter according to custom, and noted that the Easterners admitted no one’s name into the diptychs until they had learned his synodical profession of faith.  
24. After receiving the decrees of the people of Milan, he consented to have a bishop ordained for them.  
25. After many years, he restored Anastasius of Antioch to his throne.  
26. Restoring Hadrian, bishop of Thebes, to his order, he placed his diocese under the authority of the bishop of Larissa.  
27. Except in cases of manifest crimes, he deposed no one, but deprived him of communion.  
28. How strictly he handled the lawsuits of accusers, and what decrees he issued concerning judicial procedures.  
29. He confirmed the authority of other bishops by his own authority; he did not diminish it.  
30. Preserving the proper rights of all bishops, he wished executors to be appointed and judges chosen by the accused.  
31. He punished false informers by the law of retaliation.  
32. Once crimes had been brought forward, he did not permit them to be passed over without investigation, and he imposed various penalties on the accusers of sinners.  
33. He ordered the customary stipends to be supplied even to infirm clerics.  
34. He confirmed the guarantees made by bishops to their clerics and ordered that their fourths be fully provided.  
35. He released those bound by obligations to others.  
36. He received those who purged themselves of heresy.  
37. He arranged to invite schismatics to Rome to make satisfaction.  
38. He compelled Severus, bishop of Aquileia, to come to Ravenna. After he returned to unity, he reverted again to his schism and afflicted Catholic priests, becoming the cause of the perpetual division of his diocese.  
39. Because of bodily illness he appointed no successor; and when bishops resigned their sees, he did not deny them successors, ordering that they be supplied with allowances from the revenues of those same sees.  
40. He ordered that a woman who had been violated be taken in marriage by her violator.  
41. He ordered a man already tonsured to be restored to his wife.  
42. He decreed that no force was to be used against Jews.  
43. He judged that Christians ought not to be subjected to them on any pretext.  
44. He ordered Christians to be forcibly taken away from them; if any could not be taken away, he decreed that they should be redeemed.  
45. He forbade the return of their slaves who fled to the Church.  
46. He decreed that their pagan slaves who wished to come to the faith should not be returned.  
47. He declared that the slaves of Jews who preceded their masters into the faith were in no way to be restored to their service, even if the masters themselves followed them to the grace of baptism.  
48. He permitted no pagan to be circumcised.  
49. He decreed that gifts were not to be accepted from Jews.  
50. How Jews were treated by the Roman pontiffs.  
51. Gregory ordered that the Sabbath not be observed and permitted bathing on the Lord’s Day.  
52. How compassionate he was toward the illnesses of the bishops Castorius, Eulogius, and Mariniani, and of the patrician Rusticiana.  
53. He wished a litany to be held because of barbarian incursions.  
54. He possessed the spirit of prophecy.  
55. He foretold that worse things would come than those that had preceded.  
56. He permitted no one to be defended unjustly by the Church.  
57. He ordered sworn assurances to be given to those fleeing to the Church for the preservation of their rights.  
58. He called all priests brothers and fellow ministers; other clerics, most beloved sons; and laypeople of either sex, lords.  
59. He satisfied both the faithful queen Theudelinda and his subdeacon.  
60. He declared himself unworthy of a revelation from God.  
61. Comparing himself with a presbyter, he pronounced that man superior and better.  
62. He confessed himself unworthy of another’s favor.  
63. To a monk who fell prostrate before him, he himself prostrated on the ground.  
64. When accused, he explained his innocence.  
65. What he thought concerning the end of the world.  
66. What he wrote concerning the affliction of the City.  
67. He ceased expounding books because of barbarian incursions.  
68. His death, and the silver finials he prepared, as well as the place and inscription of his burial.  
69. How Deacon Peter defended his books by dying when his rivals attempted to burn them.  
70. How much Claudius learned from his words, and that Gregory dictated many things that now cannot be found.  
71. He left twelve books of his letters, from which, in the time of Pope Hadrian, two volumes appear to have been excerpted.  
72. He began the *Moralia* while he was a deacon, and how he arranged them in books during his episcopate and sent them to Leander, bishop of Seville, at his request.  
73. At the beginning of his episcopate, explaining the book of the *Pastoral Rule* to John, bishop of Ravenna, he restrained the unlearned.  
74. Moving through the stations, he dictated forty readings, which he committed to Secundus, a servant of God, at his request.  
75. He composed four books of the *Dialogues*, which afterward Zacharias, bishop of the Apostolic See, translated into Greek.  
76. At the request of his fellow citizens, he treated the first and last parts of the prophecy of Ezekiel in twenty-two homilies.  
77. How humbly he himself regarded his expositions, which later teachers praise as most polished.  
78. Calling his books, in comparison with Augustine’s treatises, “bran,” he forbade them to be read for as long as he lived.  
79. With what great consideration he daily recognized the weakness of his heart.  
80. His body was translated by Pope Gregory IV; and concerning its antiquity, modest scale, and distinctive regular character.  
81. Not knowing Greek, he discovered false treatises bearing his name as their title.  
82. The monks whom he sent to Saxony were bound to the rules of Saint Benedict.  
83. The physical appearance and clothing of his father and mother.  
84. His appearance, dress, and couplet.  
85. Saturninus, a monk, painted images of the apostles beside his likeness.  
86. John, the provost, who contended with the devil before Christ; and his revelation and terrifying passage from life.  
87. The torments of Andrew, a lessee, who confessed that he had sold documents with the same provost of the monastery.  
88. The omen of the death of Athanasius, the steward, who defrauded the poor of their customary dues.  
89. The devil driven from the monastery cloister, who struck a lying-down monk.  
90. The vision of a monk who foresaw twelve men who would die within the same number of days.  
91. The conversion and death of Lucidus, bishop of Ficulensis.  
92. The revelation of a monk who learned, through the shedding of tears, of the healing and return of his brother, a presbyter in confinement.  
93. The demon driven from the estate of Barbilianus, who, killing the lessee and herdsmen, had pursued Caucus.  
94. The vision of Tergaudus [Note: [Col. 0171B] In the Paris manuscripts, Theutgardus. Mabillon: Tegaudus.], formerly bishop of Trier, who was expelled from the monastery by blessed Gregory.  
95. The rebuke of Faraldus, who was suspended by demons throughout the night.  
96. Indulfus, a deserter from the monastery, struck by an old man; and the revelation of the cleric and the departure of Suppo.  
97. Cednicus, the presbyter who had discovered the Gregorian spring, bound and beaten, and his miserable death.  
98. The monastery’s measure and the variety of its overflowing, as well as the miracle of bread divinely multiplied.  
99. How frequently Gregory is shown in various places.  
100. The division of the copyist, who could be terrified by a rival and deserved to be consoled by blessed Gregory.

[Col. 0171A] 123

### 1.

This is Gregory’s fully reasoned and humble judgment concerning the rejection of the universal title. He knew how wisely to use the serpent’s cunning against the proud, while never departing from the dove’s simplicity toward the humble.

Therefore, conscious of his own moderation, he writes to Dominicus, bishop of Carthage, after other matters:

> “Concerning the privileges of the churches, about which Your Fraternity writes, hold this without hesitation: just as we defend our own rights, so we preserve the rights belonging to each individual church. By the favor of grace I do not grant anyone more than he deserves, nor, prompted by ambition, will I deprive anyone of what belongs to his jurisdiction. Rather, I desire to honor my brethren in all things and strive to assist each one in his honor, provided that there is nothing which one person can lawfully oppose to another.”

[Col. 0171B] (*Book II of the Letters, Letter 47.*)

Likewise he writes to Eulogius of Alexandria and Anastasius of Antioch, patriarchs:

> “Since the excellent preacher says, ‘For as long as I am the apostle of the Gentiles, I will honor my ministry’ (Romans 11:13), and elsewhere again, ‘We became little ones in the midst of you’ (1 Thessalonians 2:7), he undoubtedly sets before us who follow his example that we should both maintain humility in our minds and preserve the dignity of our order in honor, so that there may be neither timid humility nor arrogant elevation in us.”

And so forth. (*Book V, Letter 43.*)

As can be gathered most clearly from what precedes and follows, Gregory both did and said this.

### 2.

For John, bishop of Ravenna, who frequently wore the pallium through an attitude of pride [Note: [Col. 0171B] Most printed editions read *typho*, which has the same meaning. This word has been discussed elsewhere.], and who allowed his presbyters and deacons to proceed in *mappulae*, was first familiarly rebuked through Castorius, the *chartularius*. Later, when he stubbornly defended these practices as having been granted to him by custom or privilege, Gregory punished him with the following judgment, after some other remarks:

> “To summarize briefly what I said above, I admonish you that, unless you prove that these things were granted to you by a privilege through the generosity of my predecessors, you must not presume to use them in the streets any longer. Otherwise you may begin not to possess at Mass what you audaciously usurp in the streets.

> “As for the secretariat, where Your Fraternity sat wearing the pallium and received the children of the Church—something you both did and excused yourself for doing—we make no complaint for the present. Following the judgment of the synods, we refuse to punish lesser faults that are denied. We have learned that this was done once and again, but we forbid it to be done any further.

> “Let Your Fraternity be altogether careful lest what is still being yielded to an initial presumption be punished more severely when that presumption has grown.”

And after a little:

> “As for what you wrote concerning the use of *mappulae* by your clergy, our clerics have strongly opposed it, saying that this was never granted to any other church whatsoever, and that the Ravennate clergy have never presumed, either there or in the Roman city, to do anything of the kind with their own knowledge.

> “They assert that, even if it had been attempted, no precedent would thereby be established for them through furtive usurpation; indeed, even if this had been presumed in any church, they say that it ought to be corrected, since it is presumed not by concession of the Roman pontiff but solely by surreptitious seizure.

> “But, preserving the honor of Your Fraternity, although contrary to the will of the aforesaid clergy of ours, we nevertheless permit your first deacons—of whom certain persons have testified to us that they used them even before that time—to use *mappulae* solely in your service. At any other time, or for any other persons, we most emphatically forbid this practice.”

(*Book III, Letter 56.*)

### 3

This decision was extremely displeasing to that man, who was exceedingly eager for empty glory. Through anyone he could, he urgently demanded that the use of the pallium be restored to him. Gregory therefore wrote to him as follows:

> “I find your Fraternity greatly distressed because the rule of reason forbids wearing the pallium in processions, yet through the most excellent Roman patrician, the most eminent prefect, and other noblemen of your city, you persistently demand that this be granted.
>
> [Col. 0173C] We, however, carefully questioned Adeodatus, formerly a deacon of your Fraternity, and learned that it had never been the custom of your predecessors to wear the pallium in processions except on the solemnities of blessed John the Baptist, blessed Peter the apostle, and blessed Apollinaris the martyr. We certainly ought not to have believed him without qualification, since many representatives of your city have often been here, and they admit that they have never seen anything of the kind. On this matter, therefore, it is better to believe many than one person testifying on behalf of his own church.
>
> But because we do not wish your Fraternity to be distressed, nor to frustrate the petition of our sons before us, until we learn something more precisely and more accurately, we grant the use of the pallium in solemn processions—that is, on the feast days of blessed John the Baptist, blessed Peter the apostle, and blessed Apollinaris the martyr—and also at the celebration of your ordination.
