[Col. 0173D] In the sacristy, however, after receiving and dismissing the sons of the Church according to the former custom, your Fraternity should put on the pallium and proceed from there to the solemn celebration of Mass; and you must not arrogate anything more to yourself through rash presumption. Otherwise, while something is seized improperly in outward appearance, even those things that could properly have been permitted may be lost.”

*(Book V, Letter 11.)*

### 4

But when this same John was restrained from his ambition for empty glory by the bridle of apostolic moderation, he turned entirely to disparaging the pontiff. Accordingly, the very prudent pontiff admonished him in these words:

> “[Col. 0174A] First, what grieves me is that your Fraternity writes to me with a double heart: in your letters you offer one kind of flattery, while in your speech you display another attitude in a worldly manner.
>
> Second, it is grievous to me that my brother John still retains in his speech those mockeries which notaries, while still boys, are accustomed to use. He speaks biting words and seems almost to rejoice in such cleverness. He flatters his friends when they are present and speaks ill of those who are absent.
>
> Third, it is grievous and utterly execrable to me that, whenever he is enraged, he brings shameful accusations against his servants, calling them effeminate—and, what is still worse, doing so more openly.
>
> After this came the fact that there is no discipline for maintaining the life of the clergy; he merely presents himself as master to his clergy.

*Note: We have corrected this passage, corrupted in the printed editions, from the manuscripts both of John the Deacon and of the letters, and restored its sense.*

> [Col. 0174B] Finally—and yet, because of the weight of his arrogance, this is first—there is his use of the pallium outside the church. No one ever presumed to do this in the time of my predecessors, nor was it ever presumed by his predecessors, as our representatives testify, except when relics were being deposited. Yet concerning relics only one person could be found who said that, in my time, he did this not merely once, with the utmost audacity and in contempt of me, but even made a regular practice of it.
>
> From all these things I find that the honor of your episcopate exists entirely outwardly, in display, and not inwardly. Indeed, I give thanks to almighty God that, at the time when this reached me—something that had never reached the ears of my predecessors—the Lombards had been placed between me and the city of Ravenna. Perhaps I would then have had to show people how severe I know myself to be.
>
> [Col. 0174C] But do not think that I wish your church to be burdened or diminished in any respect. Recall what happened at the solemn Roman Masses, where the Ravennate deacon used to stand, and inquire where he stands today; you will understand that I desire to honor the church of Ravenna.
>
> But I cannot tolerate anyone arrogantly seizing anything whatsoever. Nevertheless, on this matter I have already written to our deacon at Constantinople, instructing him to inquire through all those who have under them even thirty or forty bishops. If this custom exists anywhere, namely that they walk in processions wearing the pallia, far be it from me that the honor of the church of Ravenna should appear in any way diminished through me.
>
> Consider, therefore, all these things I have mentioned above, dearest brother. Attend to the day of your calling; consider what account you will have to render for the burden of the episcopate. Correct those habits of a notary; observe what befits a bishop in speech and conduct. Be wholly pure toward your brothers. [Col. 0174D] Do not say one thing while holding another in your heart. Do not desire to seem more than you are, so that you may be more than you seem.”

*(Book V, Letter 15.)*

### 5

Because John disdainfully refused to correct these things out of the arrogance of his pride, in that same year, just as Gregory had foretold to him, he encountered the day of his calling while paying no attention to it. He burst before he had deserved to be satisfied with the covering of the pallium.

[Col. 0175A] For this reason Gregory entrusted the visitation of the church of Ravenna to Severus, bishop of Ficulinus, according to the ancient custom, and consecrated Marinianus, a monk and his own associate, as bishop for the Ravennates. 

*Note: This note appears at the foot of columns 175 and 176, but its callout number has not been printed in the text. Why we have removed this letter from the second indiction, we explained in the dissertation on the restored order of the letters.*

To him he also sent the pallium, writing:

> “Moved by the benevolence of the Apostolic See and by the order of ancient custom, we have determined to grant the use of the pallium to your Fraternity, which is known to have undertaken the office of governance in the church of Ravenna. Remember that you may use it only in the church of your own city, proceeding from the reception room, after the sons have been dismissed, to celebrate the sacred solemnities of Mass. After Mass has been completed, you shall again arrange to lay it aside in the reception room.
>
> Outside the church, however, we permit you to use it no more than four times a year, in the processions that we specified for your predecessor John.”

*(Book V, Letter 25; Book V, Letter 56.)*

### 6

[Col. 0175B] But Marinianus, softened by the suggestions of his clergy, demanded through the magnificent man Andreas, as well as through anyone else he could, that the use of the pallium be restored to his church. Therefore Gregory wrote, among other things, to Castorius the chartularius:

> “Let your Experience consider neither anyone’s person nor anyone’s words; let him keep only the fear of God and uprightness before his eyes. Let him question the older men, the archdeacon of that church—whom I do not suspect of perjuring himself for another’s honor—and other elders who had been in sacred orders before the time of Bishop John. Or, if there are more mature men outside the sacred orders, let them come before the body of Saint Apollinaris and, touching his tomb, swear what the custom had been before the time of Bishop John.
>
> [Col. 0175C] For, as you know, that man was extremely presumptuous and attempted arrogantly to claim many things for himself. Whatever is sworn by the more trustworthy and more distinguished men, according to the memorandum attached below, we wish to be preserved in that church.
>
> But take care that you do not act negligently, lest anyone corrupt your faith or devotion in this matter. I know your zeal. Act carefully, yet in such a way that the aforesaid church is not burdened contrary to justice, but that the custom which existed before the time of Bishop John is preserved for it.
>
> Do not seek only two or three persons to satisfy you; seek as many of the oldest and more distinguished men as you can find, so that we neither deny what was the ancient custom of that church nor grant what was sought through novel presumption. Do everything gently and sweetly, so that your action may be firm while your tongue remains mild.”

> “[Col. 0175D] Therefore I, N., swear by the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, the inseparable Trinity of divine power, and by this body of blessed Apollinaris the martyr, that I testify neither out of favor toward anyone nor because of any advantage intervening; rather, I know this and have learned it personally: before the time of John, formerly bishop, the bishop of Ravenna had the custom of using the pallium, in the presence of the representative of the Apostolic See, this man and that man, on these and those days; and I have not learned that he usurped this secretly or without the representative of the Apostolic See.”

*(Book VI, Letter 61.)*

### 7

[Col. 0176A] Gregory had ordered this oath during the fourteenth indiction. But, as the outcome of the matter makes clear, since the testimony failed, it remained unfulfilled for three successive years. Again, Marinianus, compelled by the suggestions of his clergy, trusted that through the persistence of his petitions he could recover the use of the pallium, which he had been unable to claim by custom as had been agreed.

Therefore Gregory, remaining in the same position, wrote during the second indiction to the same chartularius:

> “When Florentius, a deacon of the church of Ravenna, was acting on behalf of our most reverend brother and fellow bishop Marinianus concerning the use of the pallium, we asked him what the ancient custom was. He replied that the bishop of Ravenna used the pallium in all processions.
>
> [Col. 0176B] We learned from others that this was not so, and it became evident from the letters of John, formerly bishop, which we had ordered to be shown to him; but he asserted what he had been instructed to say. For when you prohibited John, formerly bishop, from presuming to use the pallium improperly and rashly, he wrote to us that the ancient custom had been for the bishop of that city to use the pallium in solemn processions. We have sent you copies of these letters for your information.
>
> Adeodatus, the deacon of the aforesaid church, when he was here, likewise made every effort to discuss the use of the pallium. Wishing to learn the truth, we also took care to question him about what the custom was. To make us believe what he wished and to obtain from us what he was seeking, he testified under oath that the ancient custom had been for the bishop of his city to use the pallium in four or five solemn processions.
>
> [Col. 0176C] Let your Experience therefore watch carefully and, with every concern, inquire how many solemn processions there have been from ancient times. Do not inquire by calling them ‘solemn processions,’ but ‘principal processions,’ so that, once it has been established through the testimony of the aforesaid deacon Adeodatus and the admission of the letter of the aforesaid Bishop John how many solemn processions there were, we may learn how often the pallium used to be put on in processions and grant it most willingly.
>
> But do not inquire of those who are produced by the ecclesiastical authorities; inquire instead of those who are put forward by ecclesiastical persons; inquire of others whom you know to be free from partisan favor. Report to us carefully what you discover through diligent investigation, so that, once the truth has been learned, as we have said, we may restore the spirits of our most reverend brother and fellow bishop Marinianus.”

*(Book VII, Letter 77; now Book VI, Letter 34.)*

[Col. 0176D] But since the ancient custom, carefully investigated by our people, could in no way be proved by the Ravennates, the fact that Gregory remained in his position is undoubtedly shown by this: as far as can be discerned from his letters, no one persuaded him on this matter, nor did he himself change his mind and write any further reply.

### 8

Gregory directed the eyes of his vigilance not only toward important matters; he also took the greatest care in small matters, lest greater things should eventually be rashly presumed with impunity. Accordingly, he wrote to John, bishop of Syracuse:

> “[Col. 0177A] The order of ecclesiastical vigor is thrown into confusion if either unlawful things are rashly presumed or things not granted are attempted with impunity.
>
> It has therefore come to our attention that the deacons of the church of Catania have presumed to go about wearing campagi. You remember well that this has hitherto been permitted nowhere throughout Sicily except to the deacons of the church of Messina, to whom our predecessors are not doubted to have granted it long ago.
>
> Since an attempt at such great presumption must not be treated lightly, let your Fraternity investigate the whole matter with meticulous care. If you find that it is as it has reached us, let us know carefully whether they presumed to do this on their own authority or on someone else’s, so that, once the truth is known, we may determine what ought to be done. For if we negligently overlook things that are wrongly usurped, we open the way for others to transgress.”

*Note: “Campagus,” erroneously printed as “compagus,” is footwear used by bishops or prelates at Mass. See the notes to the letters.*

*(Book VIII, Letter 27.)*

### 9

[Col. 0177B] Meanwhile, after Bishop Natalis had died, the whole body of the Dalmatians unanimously chose Honoratus the archdeacon—whom Natalis himself had advanced from the priesthood to the diaconate—to be placed over them, and the pontiff approved their decree. But Maximus, a man entangled in many crimes, through the faction of Bishop Malchus, rector of the Apostolic patrimony, and by military force, invaded the episcopate of the city of Salona.

When Gregory heard this, he strictly forbade the Dalmatian and Jader bishops to lay hands upon him. [Col. 0177C] But Maximus, who had invaded the episcopal see contrary to the canons, was not afraid also to obtain the priesthood contrary to God through the simoniacal heresy, from bishops who were themselves excommunicated and corrupted by money.

The opportunity of the times favored him, as did the greed and arrogance of Augustus, whom he made so much the defender of his crimes—by dispersing the resources of the church he had invaded—that Augustus not only repeatedly asked Gregory to leave Maximus’s promotion unexamined, but also to receive with honor Maximus when he came to Rome to give satisfaction for simony and his other crimes.

### 10

Gregory, respecting no one’s person against the truth, first deprived Maximus of the solemn celebrations of Mass and then of communion in the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, until he should present himself before him. But Maximus, supported by imperial troops, both celebrated Mass after his excommunication and, wholly unworthy, received the sacraments.

[Col. 0177D] Therefore Gregory wrote to Augusta Constantina, among other things:

> “The bishop of the city of Salona was ordained without my knowledge and without the knowledge of my representative; and an event has taken place that occurred under none of the earlier emperors. When I heard this, I immediately sent to that same transgressor, who had been irregularly ordained, instructing him not to presume in any way to celebrate the solemnities of Mass unless I first learned from the most serene lords whether they had ordered this to be done.
>
> I commanded him this under threat of excommunication. [Col. 0178A] Yet, despising and disregarding me, relying on the audacity of certain secular men to whom, after stripping his church, he is said to offer many rewards, he still presumes to celebrate Mass and refused to come to me in accordance with the order of the lords.
>
> Nevertheless, obeying their pious command, I have forgiven this same Maximus—who was ordained without my knowledge—for having presumed to omit me or my representative at his ordination, as wholeheartedly as if he had been ordained with my authorization.
>
> [Col. 0178B] But I cannot, for God’s sake, pass over without investigation his other perverse acts—namely, the bodily evils of which I have learned: that he was elected with money, and that, although excommunicated, he presumed to celebrate Mass. Yet I desire and beseech the Lord that nothing may be found true concerning him in the matters reported, and that his case may be brought to an end without danger to my soul.
>
> Before these things are investigated, however, the most serene lord has ordered, by a circulating command, that I receive him with honor when he comes. It is extremely serious that a man about whom so many grave reports are made should be honored before he has been examined and investigated.
>
> If the cases of bishops entrusted to me are settled before the most pious lords through the advocacy of others, what am I, unhappy man, doing in this church? Yet I give thanks to almighty God and attribute it to my sins that my bishops despise me and seek refuge against me with secular judges.
>
> I mention this briefly because I am waiting for a little while. If he delays coming to me for long, I will certainly not cease to exercise canonical severity against him.
>
> But I trust in almighty God that long life will be granted to the most pious lords, and that under your authority he will govern us not according to our sins but according to the gifts of his grace.”

*(Book V, Letter 21.)*

### 11

[Col. 0178C] Gregory wrote this to the dissembling Augusta. Meanwhile, since Maximus persisted in his presumption, Gregory separated those who had consecrated him, as well as all the Dalmatian and Jader bishops, from his communion under threat of excommunication, to such an extent that they did not even mention the name of Maximus during the solemn celebration of Mass.

As a result, they were all so shaken in spirit that, abandoning Maximus and offering penitential satisfaction, they sought pardon. Accordingly, the most merciful pontiff wrote to Sabinianus, bishop of Jadera:

> “Just as punishment is rightly owed to persistent guilt, so pardon must be granted to those who repent. For just as the former rightly arouses anger against itself, so the latter is accustomed to foster concord in the fullness of its affection.
>
> [Col. 0178D] Therefore, since your Fraternity, after neglect had first driven you into association and communion with Maximus, was afterwards so restrained, when the gravity of the priesthood returned to your mind, that you could not be content merely with separating yourself from him, but entered a monastery and mourned sins long committed, do not doubt that you have been received into our grace and communion. For as much as your guilt had previously offended us against your charity, so much has your repentance appeased us.”

*(Book VIII, Letter 10.)*

### 12

[Col. 0179A] Thus Maximus, finally recognizing that it was difficult to kick against the goad, abandoned his imperial supports and, through the exarch Callinicus, rather humbly asked Gregory for penance and pardon.

Gregory, unwilling to make him weary by coming to Rome, entrusted the examination of his case at Ravenna to Constantius, bishop of Milan, writing:

> “Maximus, the transgressor of the church of Salona, after being unable to obtain anything through the greater powers of this world, turned to lesser ones and attempted to prevail over us both by the excessiveness of his petitions and by the testimony of good works.
>
> I considered it inhuman if one who says that he greatly fears me could not find me in some respect more moderate. Therefore I have decided that our most reverend brother and fellow bishop Marinianus should examine his case in the city of Ravenna.
>
> [Col. 0179B] If his person should perhaps be regarded with suspicion, we wish your Fraternity also, if it is not burdensome, to undertake the journey to the same city and sit with the aforesaid brother in the same judgment.
>
> Whatever may please the holiness of both of you, know that it will please me in every respect; and I regard your judgment as my own.”

*(Book IX, Letter 67.)*

### 13

Meanwhile, in the seventh year of his excommunication, after Gregory’s chastisements and scourges, the transgressor Maximus came to his senses, went to Ravenna, and cast himself down, stretched out upon a stone in the middle of the city, crying aloud:

> “I have sinned against God and the most blessed Pope Gregory.”

After he had done penance for three hours, the exarch Callinicus and Castorius, chartularius of the Roman Church, came with Bishop Marinianus and lifted him from the pavement. He then began to perform still greater penance before them.

[Col. 0179C] When Gregory heard this, he immediately returned to mercy and wrote to Bishop Marinianus, among other things:

> “We have learned from Castorius, our chartularius and the bearer of this letter, what your Fraternity’s attitude toward Maximus is, and especially what your request is. Therefore, if Maximus, before you and our aforesaid chartularius, has cleared himself by oath concerning the simoniacal heresy, and, when questioned only about the other matters before the body of Saint Apollinaris, has replied that he is innocent, we entrust to your judgment the matter of what penance should cleanse him from the fault of having presumed to celebrate the solemnities of Mass while excommunicated.
>
> [Col. 0179D] Therefore arrange confidently whatever seems right to you according to God, and have no doubts about us. Whatever you decide in this matter, we both gratefully accept and willingly approve.
>
> Nevertheless, we exhort you to be careful and to moderate what you see must be mourned in such a way that, if it seems appropriate, you may grant him communion while preserving the force of ecclesiastical rigor through suitable dispensation, as is proper.
>
> We have instructed the bearer mentioned above what should presently be done with him. Learn everything carefully from him, and conduct yourselves in all things so that through your vigilance we may feel that our presence has been with you.”

### 14

Likewise, to Castorius, notary and chartularius at Ravenna:

> “The more you see that trust is placed in you and necessary matters are entrusted to you, the more energetic and vigilant you must show yourself. [Col. 0180A] Therefore, if Maximus of Salona, having sworn an oath, confirms that he is not bound by the simoniacal heresy, and, when questioned only about the other matters before the body of Saint Apollinaris, replies that he is innocent, and performs the penance we have assigned for his disobedience, we wish your Experience to give him the letter we have written to him, in which we have indicated that we have restored to him both our grace and our communion, for just as it is fitting that we be severe toward those who persist in contumacy, so we must not deny a place of pardon to those who have humbled themselves and repented.”

*(Book IX, Letter 80.)*

### 15

When Maximus had humbly given satisfaction concerning everything before the body of blessed Apollinaris, according to Gregory’s command, Castorius the chartularius gave him a consolatory letter containing these words of Gregory:

> “[Col. 0180B] Although, through the fault of disobedience, you added grave evil to the culpable beginnings of your ordination, we have nevertheless moderated the authority of the Apostolic See with the restraint that was appropriate and have not, until now, burned against you as your case demanded.
>
> We were greatly distressed lest the displeasure which you had yourself provoked against you should be prolonged too far, and lest we seem negligently to overlook certain unlawful things we had heard about you. If you consider these matters carefully, you yourself confirmed them against yourself by delaying to give satisfaction and thereby incited our zeal against you all the more sharply.
>
> But when at last you followed sound counsel, humbly submitted yourself to the yoke of obedience, and your Charity, by doing penance, cleansed itself through the worthy satisfaction we had prescribed, understand that the grace of fraternal charity has been restored to you, and rejoice that you have been received into our fellowship. For just as it is fitting that we be severe toward those who persist in guilt, so we ought to be kind in granting pardon to those who repent.
>
> [Col. 0180C] Since, therefore, your Fraternity knows that you have recovered communion with the Apostolic See, let it send someone to us who may receive the pallium to be delivered to you according to custom. For just as we do not permit unlawful acts to be committed, so we do not deny what belongs to custom.
>
> Although the office of our position has called us to grant these things, the petition of our sweetest and most excellent son, Lord Callinicus the exarch, nevertheless demanded that we act toward you with greater moderation. We neither could nor wished to grieve his most cherished desire.”

*(Book IX, Letter 8.)*

### 16

[Col. 0180D] Moreover, the emperor, exceedingly eager and grasping—a man who, as Roman history relates, very frequently cheated customary payments and even the soldiers of the legions—saw that Gregory had no need at all of the imperial defenses whose support he boasted had advanced him to the height of the pontificate, despite all the uproar of the world. Rather, by canonical authority and through the virtues of his holiness and prudence, with Christ’s favor, Gregory prevailed over all who think lofty thoughts.

The emperor therefore turned more and more toward hatred and defamation of Gregory’s reputation. He criticized the pontiff’s generosity through deceptive assertions because Gregory had distributed both ecclesiastical and public grain to the starving soldiers.

[Col. 0181A] But Gregory did not attribute his advancement to passing human favor. He attributed it to divine judgment, in whose hand the hearts of kings rest and are inclined wherever he wills *(Proverbs 21)*. Speaking freely in opposition, Gregory broke down and disfigured the emperor with these replies, and, discussing the future judgment of God, struck fear into him:

> “In their most serene commands, the piety of the lords, while striving to reproach me on certain matters, did not spare me at all. For in them it calls me foolish under the expression ‘urban simplicity.’
>
> [Col. 0181B] In Holy Scripture, when simplicity is used in a good sense, it is often carefully joined with prudence or uprightness. Thus it is written of blessed Job: ‘He was a simple and upright man’ *(Job 1:1)*. The blessed apostle Paul also admonishes us, saying: ‘Be simple in what is evil and wise in what is good’ *(Romans 16:19)*. Truth itself likewise admonishes us in the Gospel: ‘Be wise as serpents and simple as doves’ *(Matthew 10:16)*, judging it highly unprofitable if either prudence is lacking in simplicity or simplicity in prudence.
>
> Thus, wishing to make his servants instructed in all things, he wanted them to be simple as doves and wise as serpents, so that in them the serpent’s cunning might sharpen the dove’s simplicity, while the dove’s simplicity might temper the serpent’s cunning.
>
> [Col. 0181C] I, then, who in the most serene commands of the lords am declared simple, deceived by Ariulf’s cunning because prudence was not added, am plainly called foolish; and I myself admit that this is so. For if your Piety were silent about it, the circumstances themselves cry out. If I had not been foolish, I would never have come here to endure what I suffer amid the swords of the Lombards.
>
> But in the matter I reported concerning Ariulf—namely, that he had been ready with all his heart to come over to the republic—because I was not believed, I was also reproached for having lied.

*Note: The printed codices read “Arnulf” or “Ariulf”; this reading is refuted by the Bigotian, Uticensis, three Paris manuscripts, and others.*

> Even though I am not a priest, I know that this is a grave injury to a priest: that while serving the truth he should be considered deceitful.
>
> Long ago I learned that Nordulf was believed more than I was, and Leo more than I was. Now credence is given more to those who appear to stand in the middle than to my assertions.
>
> [Col. 0181D] If the captivity of my land were not increasing from day to day, I would gladly remain silent about my contempt and ridicule. But this afflicts me greatly: from the very source of the charge of falsehood that I endure, Italy is daily led captive beneath the Lombard yoke. While none of my suggestions is believed, the strength of the enemy grows monstrously.
>
> Yet I make this brief appeal to the most pious lord: let him judge anything he wishes about me as evil, but concerning the welfare of the republic and the cause of Italy’s deliverance, let him not readily lend his gracious ears to just anyone; let him believe facts more than words.
>
> Let our lord not be quick to become indignant with priests on the basis of earthly power; rather, with outstanding consideration, let him rule them for the sake of the one whose servants they are, so that he may also offer them their due reverence.
>
> [Col. 0182A] For in the divine utterances priests are sometimes called gods and sometimes angels. Through Moses it is said concerning one who is to be brought to judgment under oath: ‘Bring him to the gods’ *(Exodus 22:8)*—that is, to the priests. And again it is written: ‘You shall not revile the gods’ *(ibid. 22:28)*—that is, the priests. The prophet says: ‘The lips of the priest guard knowledge, and they seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts’ *(Malachi 2:7)*.
>
> What wonder, then, if your Piety deigns to honor those whom God himself, granting them honor in his utterance, calls either angels or gods?
>
> Ecclesiastical history also bears witness that when written accusations against bishops were presented to the emperor Constantine of pious memory, he accepted the documents of accusation. Then, summoning the bishops who had been accused, he burned the documents he had received in their presence, saying: ‘You are gods, established by the true God. Go and settle your cases among yourselves, for it is not fitting that we should judge gods.’
>
> [Col. 0182B] In this statement, pious lord, he granted something to himself out of humility rather than to them out of the reverence he showed. Before him, pagan emperors had ruled the republic. Though they did not know the true God, they worshiped gods of wood and stone, and yet they paid the greatest honor to their priests.
>
> What wonder, then, if a Christian emperor deigns to honor the priests of the true God, when pagan emperors, as I have said, knew how to honor priests who served gods of wood and stone?
>
> [Col. 0182C] I make these appeals to the piety of the lords not for myself but for all priests. I am a sinful man; and because I offend almighty God every day without ceasing, I suspect that it may be some remedy for me at his fearful tribunal if I am struck by unceasing blows every day.
>
> I believe that you appease the same almighty Lord all the more, the more severely you afflict me, his wicked servant. I had already received many blows, and through the commands of the lords I found consolation where I had not expected it.
>
> If I can, I will quickly enumerate these blows. First, the peace I had made with the Lombards stationed in Tuscany, without any loss to the republic, was taken away from me. Then, when peace had been broken, soldiers were removed from the city of Rome. Some were killed by the enemy, while others were stationed at Narni and Perugia; and, so that Perugia might be held, Rome was abandoned.
>
> [Col. 0182D] After this, the more grievous blow was the arrival of Agilulf, so that I saw with my own eyes Romans, like dogs, with their necks bound by ropes and being led to Francia for sale.
>
> Because we who were inside the city escaped his hands under God’s protection, the question was raised as to how we might appear blameworthy—namely, why grain was lacking, although large quantities cannot be stored for long in this city, as I have explained more fully in another appeal.
>
> I have not been troubled about myself at all, for, with my conscience as witness, I confess that I am ready to suffer any adversity, provided only that I escape all these things with the salvation of my soul.
>
> But I have been considerably distressed on behalf of the distinguished men Gregory the prefect and Castorius the master of soldiers. They did not neglect to do anything that could be done, and during the siege they endured the immense labors of wakefulness and guarding the city; [Col. 0183A] yet after all this they were struck by the severe indignation of the lords.
>
> I clearly understand that it is not their own actions but my person that burdens them: because they had suffered tribulation together with me, they are now suffering tribulation together after their labor.
>
> As for the fact that the piety of the lords threatens me with that fearful and terrible judgment of almighty God, I beg the same almighty Lord that they do not do this any longer. For we still do not know who will be what there; and the eminent preacher Paul says: ‘Do not judge before the appointed time, until the Lord comes, who will both bring to light the things hidden in darkness and disclose the purposes of hearts’ *(1 Corinthians 4:5)*.
>
> I say this briefly: as a sinner and an unworthy man, I place greater confidence in the mercy of the coming Jesus than in the justice of your Piety. [Col. 0183B] There are many things about his judgment that human beings do not know; perhaps he will condemn what you praise, and praise what you condemn.
>
> Amid all uncertainties [Col. 0183D] I return to tears alone, asking that the same almighty God both govern our most pious lord here by his own hand and find him free from every fault in that terrible judgment; and that, if necessary, he make me pleasing to human beings in such a way that I do not offend his eternal grace.”

*Note: The printed editions, together with three Paris manuscripts, read “therefore I omit everything.” We follow the other manuscripts.*

*(Book V, Letter 40.)*

### 17

Finally, the emperor Maurice, amazed at the freedom of speech of so great a pontiff and at the steadfastness of his reproof—since Gregory had terrified him by speaking of the future judgment of God—was preparing to set out to exercise tyranny against him. But immediately, in that same year, [Col. 0183C] a certain man dressed in monastic clothing, moved by a certain divine power, took a sword in his right hand. Carrying it unsheathed from the forum to the bronze statue of the gladiator, he foretold publicly that the emperor would die by the sword.

When Maurice heard this, he restrained himself from inflicting tyranny upon Gregory, and feared all the more that he would soon undergo the divine judgment with which Gregory had threatened him, because he believed that Gregory could not lie.

*Note: In the Regius manuscript, a second hand writes above the word “according to custom.”*
18. Immediately, therefore, he composed written prayers and sent them, together with much money, candles, and incense, both to that man and to all the patriarchs, bishops, and monks of the cities and the deserts, earnestly asking this above all: that they might supplicate the Lord that in this age he might receive the deserts of his evil deeds, provided only that he might merit being redeemed from future torments. And when he himself also asked this more fervently for a long time with tears, one night, while sleeping, he saw himself standing before a bronze statue of the Savior at the bronze gate of the palace, in the presence of a great crowd. Then a terrible voice came from the image of the incarnate Word, saying: “Give up Maurice.” And the ministers of judgment seized him and placed him beside a boy’s navel, which was there. [Note: Thus the manuscripts of Reg. and of the church of St. Mary in Paris. The printed editions, with Colb. and several others, read “purple.”] To him the same voice of the image said: “Where do you wish me to repay you for the evils that you have perpetrated in this world?” He replied: “Lover of mankind, just Judge, repay them to me here rather than in the world to come.” Immediately the divine voice ordered Maurice and his wife Constantina, together with their sons and daughters and all his family, to be handed over to the soldier Phocas.

When he awoke, Maurice sent for the *parakoimomenos* [Note: Thus it should be read from Theophanes, in Greek, παραχειμώμενον, “bedchamberlain.” This word is corrupt also in the manuscript, but especially in the printed editions.] and summoned Philippicus [Note: Rather, he was the husband of Maurice’s sister. Theophanes explains why he was suspected: his name began with the letter P. The emperor had learned that this was the first letter of the name of the man by whom he was to be killed.] his son-in-law, whom he had long suspected of wishing to seize the empire for himself. Believing that he was being summoned to his death because of this suspicion, Philippicus said his final farewell to his wife Gordia, whom he thought he would never see again. After receiving the sacrament of communion, he went to the palace and, entering the emperor’s chamber, fell at his feet. The emperor rose and likewise fell at his feet, saying: “Forgive me, I beg you, because by a divine revelation I have now plainly learned that you have committed nothing against me of what I suspected. But if you know of anyone in our army who is usually called Phocas, tell me.”

Philippicus, after reflecting for a long time, replied: “I know one Phocas, who recently, when appointed procurator by the army, opposed your rule.” When Maurice inquired about his character, Philippicus said: “He is indeed young and rash, yet timid.” And Maurice said: “If he is timid, then surely he is also a murderer.”

While he was hesitating over this matter, the *magistrianus*, returning the next day from the hermits to whom he had carried the emperor’s prayers, brought back their answer, saying: “God, having received your repentance, will save your soul and establish you with the saints together with your entire household; but from the empire you will fall with disgrace and peril.”

19. When Maurice heard this, he glorified God and persevered in repentance. But he did not withdraw from the avarice of greed to such an extent that he did not threaten the prefect Peter with a fatal letter, ordering the army to winter in dangerous places and, after crossing the Danube, to seek provisions for itself at peril in the land of the Slavs, rather than consume the public supplies. [Note: In three Paris manuscripts and in the printed editions: “so that the army might winter” (or “they might winter”) “in dangerous places and, after crossing the Danube, might seek provisions at peril” (or “perilously”), “lest they should eat … What was impending for Peter … he [said] to the *taxiarchs*.” We follow the other manuscript codices.]

He summoned the *taxiarchs* [Note: That is, the commanders of the units.] and said: “The emperor’s orders seem exceedingly severe to me, ordering Romans to winter in foreign territory. For it is cruel not to obey him, and even more cruel to obey him. Greed produces no good, since it is the mother of all evils; and, because the emperor is afflicted by it, he becomes the cause of these greatest evils for the Romans.”

When the army heard this through the *taxiarchs*, it turned to revolt. They raised Phocas, a centurion, upon a shield and acclaimed him as *exarch*, and, having driven away the prefect, they sent to Theodosius, the emperor’s son, and Germanus, his father-in-law, asking that one of them undertake to rule them. They refused in every way and instead reported the matter to Maurice. He wished to destroy Germanus; but because Germanus had fled into a church, Maurice scourged his son as the betrayer of his plan. He sent many men to drag Germanus out of that same church, but was never permitted to do so; indeed, he was assailed by the people with many insults and called a Marcionist heretic.

When a serious tumult arose within Constantinople, Maurice, disguised, boarded a *dromon* at night with his wife and children. [Note: A very swift kind of vessel, frequently mentioned by Cassiodorus, including in Book X, Letter 37.] Fleeing, he reached the church of Saint Antoninus. [Note: Or “Autonomus.” He was a bishop and martyr in Bithynia under Diocletian and is commemorated on 12 September.]

But Phocas, coming with the army on the seventh day, became emperor. [Note: See at the end of the Letters the sections “On Phocas crowned,” and so forth.] By his order Maurice, together with his wife, sons, and daughters, was beheaded at Chalcedon, just as had been announced to him. And because Gregory’s prayer—that he might be found free from all offenses at the terrible judgment of God—could not have been empty, Maurice received what he deserved; and, blessing God in all his misfortunes, he merited being delivered from everlasting punishment.

20. Therefore, on the seventh day before the Kalends of May, in the sixth indiction, the image of Phocas and Leontia, the Augusti, was brought to Rome together with their favorable letters. After the clergy and senate had acclaimed them in the Basilica of Julius, it was placed, by Gregory’s order, in the oratory of Saint Caesarius, established in the Lateran palace.

Gregory also wrote the following in reply to the emperor Phocas:

“Glory to God in the highest, who, as it is written, ‘changes times and transfers kingdoms’ (Dan. 2:21), and who made known to all what he deigned to speak through his prophet, saying: ‘The Most High rules in the kingdom of men, and gives it to whomever he wishes’ (Dan. 4:14). For the governance of mortal life rests in the incomprehensible dispensation of almighty God. Sometimes, when the sins of many just men must be punished, one person is raised up, through whose harshness the necks of those subject to the yoke of tribulation are bowed down. We have experienced this for a long time in our own tribulation.

“Sometimes, however, when merciful God determines to refresh the hearts of many who mourn with his consolation, he raises one person to the summit of government and, through the compassion of his mercy, pours the grace of his joy into the minds of all. We believe that we shall quickly be strengthened by this abundance of joy, since we rejoice that your piety has reached the imperial height.

“Let the heavens rejoice and let the earth exult (Ps. 95); and let the people of the whole commonwealth, hitherto sorely afflicted, now rejoice in your benevolent acts. Let the proud minds of enemies be restrained by the yoke of your rule; let the contrite and depressed spirits of your subjects be lifted up by your mercy. May the power of heavenly grace make you terrible to your enemies and your piety kind to your subjects. May the whole commonwealth rest in your most fortunate times, with the spoils of peace brought forth under the pretext of legal proceedings. Let the snares of wills cease, and the favors of donations extorted by force. Let secure possession of their own property return to all, so that they may rejoice to hold without fear what they have not acquired by fraud. Let each person’s liberty now be restored beneath the yoke of a pious empire.

“For this is the difference between the kings of the nations and the emperors of the commonwealth: the kings of the nations are lords of slaves, whereas the emperors of the commonwealth are lords of free men.” (Book XIII, Letter 31.)

21. When Phocas repeatedly requested that a deacon of the Roman See be sent to him with the greatest reverence and humility, Gregory replied as follows:

“It is pleasant to consider, with joy and great acts of thanksgiving, how many praises we owe to almighty God, because, once the yoke of sorrow has been removed, we have reached a time of liberty beneath the imperial kindness of your piety. The fact that your Serenity did not find a deacon of the apostolic See remaining in the palace according to ancient custom was not due to my negligence but to the gravest necessity. For while all the ministers of this Church of ours were avoiding and fleeing the harsh and crushing times with fear, none of them could be charged to go to the royal city and remain in the palace.

“But after they learned that, by the ordering of almighty God’s grace, your Clemency had reached the summit of empire, they too, prompted by joy, hastened to come to your feet—those who previously had been very afraid to approach that place. Yet because some of them are so weakened by old age that they can scarcely endure the journey, while others are deeply occupied with ecclesiastical duties, and because the bearer of this letter, who was the first defender of all, is well known to me through long familiarity and has been approved in life, faith, and conduct, I judged him suitable to appear before your piety.

“Accordingly, with God as author, I made him a deacon and hastened to send him, so that, when he finds a convenient opportunity, he may be able to report to your Clemency all that is happening in these regions. I beg that your Serenity deign to incline your pious ears to him, so that you may show us mercy all the more quickly the more truly you learn of our affliction from his account.

“For how we have been oppressed by daily swords and by how many incursions of the Lombards—behold, for the length of thirty-five years—we cannot fully express in any words of petition. But we trust in almighty God, because he will complete for us the good things of his consolation that he has begun; and he who has raised up pious lords in the commonwealth will also extinguish its cruel enemies.” (Book XIII, Letter 38.)

22. Likewise, to Augusta Leontia:

“What tongue could express, what mind could conceive, how great is the thanksgiving we owe to almighty God for the serenity of your rule, since the burdens of so long and harsh a time have been removed from our necks and the light yoke of imperial authority has returned, which subjects may willingly bear?

“Let glory, therefore, be rendered to the Creator of all in heaven by the hymn-singing choirs of angels; let thanksgiving be offered on earth by human beings, because the whole commonwealth, which has suffered many wounds of grief, has now found the consolations of your comfort.

“Therefore it is necessary for us to implore the mercy of almighty God with even greater earnestness, that he may always hold the heart of your piety by his right hand and govern its thoughts through the aid of heavenly grace, so that your tranquillity may rule those who serve you all the more rightly the more truly it knows how to serve the Ruler of all.

“May he make defenders of the Catholic faith those whom he has made our emperors through his benevolent work. May he pour zeal and gentleness together into your minds, so that you may always be able, with pious fervor, both not to leave unpunished whatever is done against God and, by showing mercy, to tolerate whatever offense is committed against you.” (Book XIII, Letter 39.)

23. By such praises Gregory either sought to flatter the new rulers so that, hearing what they ought to be, they might become more merciful than Maurice had been, whose reign they knew to have been entangled in so many crimes; or, because he saw that they were deeply devoted to himself and to his church, he thought that they would not rush into tyranny.

Just as he reproved the vices of anyone whatsoever with free speech and permitted no one to act against the canons or ancient customs, so he wholly denied no one what belonged to custom. For as soon as he became bishop of the apostolic See, he sent his synodical letters to the patriarchal sees. Later, among other things, he wrote to Secundinus, a servant of God living in seclusion, saying:

“This is also why, whenever bishops are ordained in the four principal sees, they send synodal letters to one another, in which they profess that they preserve the holy Council of Chalcedon together with the other general councils.” (Book IX, Letter 52.)

Likewise, to Athanasius, a presbyter from Isauria, after much else:

“We wished to send our letter to our brother Cyriacus, bishop of the city of Constantinople, who was recently ordained in the place of John, the most reverend bishop. But because it is not customary for us to write to him before his synodical letter has been brought to us, we have therefore postponed it for now; later we shall make our position known.” (Book VI, Letter 66.)

This custom, as our own people also testify—those who, two years previously, presided at the holy Eighth Council under Hadrian, the most generous pope—the Eastern sees in particular have maintained down to the present. In their diptychs they write the name of no bishop until they have received his synodical letter, and they continue to number a deceased bishop among the living for as long as his successor has not taken care to send his own letter.

24. This is plainly why Gregory, not departing from the ancient custom, wrote to John, subdeacon and rector of the patrimony of Liguria, saying:

“In proportion as the apostolic See, with God as its author, is established as superior to all churches, so, amid its many concerns, it is greatly troubled whenever our decision is awaited for the consecration of a bishop. Therefore, after Laurence, bishop of the Church of Milan, had died, the clergy informed us by their report that they had unanimously agreed in the election of our son Constantius, their deacon.

“But because that report was not signed, lest we omit anything pertaining to precaution, it is necessary for you, supported by the authority of this command, to proceed to Genoa. Since many Milanese are compelled by the barbarous ferocity of the Lombards to remain there, you must summon them together and investigate their wishes. If no disagreement separates them from the unity of the election, and if you discover that the will and agreement of all continue in the aforementioned son of ours, Constantius, then, as the custom of antiquity requires, have him consecrated by his own bishops with the assent of our authority, with the Lord’s support and help.

“Thus, by preserving this custom, both the apostolic See may retain its proper strength and may not diminish the rights it has granted to others.” (Book III, Letter 30.)

But after several years, when Constantius, having served honorably as bishop, had fallen asleep in the Lord, the clergy and people of Milan chose the deacon Deusdedit. They were intimidated by King Agilulf into choosing the man whom the barbarity of the Lombards desired. They sent their decree to Gregory and asked his advice and permission. Among other things, he replied to them as follows:

“Let what you have reported as having been written to you by Agilulf not disturb your affection. For because we wish to advise what is beneficial to you in a salutary manner, we give our consent in no way to a man who is not chosen by Catholics, and especially not by Lombards; for the vicar of Saint Ambrose is plainly shown to be unworthy if he is ordained when chosen by such men.”

And shortly afterward:

“Therefore, so that no delay may occur in ordaining the deacon Deusdedit, who was chosen by you, we have sent our notary Pantaleon. By the authority of our assenting consent, he is to have him consecrated, as is customary.” (Book IX, Letter 4.)

25. Gregory, the bravest soldier of Christ, vigorously defended those oppressed by hostile powers. Those who had been unjustly deposed he not only did not count among the deposed, but also restored to their former ranks by the privilege of his authority.

Thus, when Anastasius, patriarch of Antioch, had freely reproved John, bishop of Constantinople, and had been driven into exile by order of the emperor Justin, he remained there from the time of Pope John until Gregory’s pontificate. As soon as Gregory attained the highest priesthood, he counted him among the patriarchs and encouraged him with a letter of this kind:

“Moreover, just as I have sent a synodical letter to the other patriarchs, your equals, so I have sent one to you, because in my sight you have always been what you received by the gift of almighty God that you should be, not what you are thought, by human will, not to be.”

Likewise, writing to him in another letter after several other matters, he said:

“I inform your Fraternity that I have asked the most serene lords, with as many prayers as I could offer, to permit you, with your honor restored, to come to the threshold of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, and, for as long as it may please God, to live here with me, so that, when I have deserved to see you, we may relieve the weariness of our exile by speaking together of the eternal homeland.”

Finally, the most devoted father Gregory continued to press the emperor Maurice with his petitions until, after the passage of many years, the great Anastasius was restored to his own throne. Gregory wrote to him in joyful congratulation:

“Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to men of good will, because that great river which once left the rocks of Antioch dry has returned to its proper channel and waters the valleys lying beneath and beside it, so that one may bear thirtyfold fruit, another sixtyfold, and another a hundredfold.” (Book V, Letter 39.)

26. Hadrian, bishop of the city of Thebes, had been unjustly deposed by John, bishop of First Justiniana, and by another John, bishop of Larissa. Gregory not only restored him to his own see but also, defending his church under Roman law, removed it from the authority of the bishop of Larissa. Among other things he said:

“We found that Bishop Hadrian had suffered both from your hatred, contrary to priestly custom, and had been condemned by the judgment of your Fraternity in pecuniary cases without any legal basis. Therefore, since he had also been deposed by the aforementioned John, bishop of First Justiniana, contrary to law and the canons, he could not be deprived of the rank of his honor. We have decreed that he be restored to his church and recalled to the order of his proper dignity.

“Although you ought to have been deprived of communion in the Lord’s Body because, disregarding the admonition of my predecessor of holy memory—which removed him and his church from your jurisdictional authority—you presumed once again to retain some right and power over them, nevertheless, deciding more humanely and meanwhile preserving for you the sacrament of communion, we decree that your Fraternity abstain from all the authority of jurisdiction previously held over him and his church.

“According to the letters of our predecessor, if any case concerning faith, crime, or money should arise against the aforesaid Hadrian, our fellow priest, let it be heard either by those who are or shall be our representatives in the royal city, if the matter is minor, or let it be brought here to the apostolic See, if it is difficult, so that it may be decided by the judgment of our hearing.

“If at any time, or on any pretext or by any fraud, you attempt to act against these decrees of ours, know that you are deprived of holy communion. We decree that you may not receive it again, except at the final hour of your life, unless by order granted by the Roman pontiff.

“For we have sanctioned these things in agreement with the definition of the holy Fathers, so that he who does not know how to obey the sacred canons is not worthy either to administer at sacred altars or to receive communion from them.” (Book III, Letter 7.)

Likewise, to John, bishop of First Justiniana:

“After the long tribulations that Hadrian, bishop of the city of Thebes, suffered from his fellow priests as though from enemies, he fled to the Roman city. And although his first complaint had been against John, bishop of Larissa, and the matter had not been judged by him in pecuniary cases while the laws were reserved, nevertheless afterward he complained most bitterly against the person of your Fraternity, from whom he demanded, not without justice, that he had been removed from the rank of the priesthood.”

And further:

“But as to what now concerns the matter, after first annulling and reducing to nothing the decrees of your aforesaid judgment, by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, we decree that for thirty days you be deprived of holy communion and implore from our almighty God, with the greatest repentance and tears, forgiveness for so great an offense.

“If we learn that you have fulfilled this sentence of ours too lightly, know that, with the Lord’s help, the injustice—and also the contumacy—of your Fraternity will now be punished more severely.

“As for the aforesaid Hadrian, our brother and fellow bishop, who, as we have said, was condemned by your judgment, which had no support in the canons or laws, we decree, with Christ accompanying him, that he return to his own place and rank, so that neither may the judgment issued by your Fraternity against the course of justice harm him, nor may your charity remain uncorrected for the purpose of appeasing the indignation of the future Judge.” (Book III, Letter 6.)

27. Hence, except in cases of crime, Gregory deposed none of the priests; rather, according to the character of their offenses, he deprived them of communion with leniency. Thus, writing to John, bishop of Callipolis, after some other matters, he said:

“Suspend for two months from the solemn celebration of Mass our brother and fellow bishop Andrew, bishop of Tarentum, who had a woman on the church register beaten with rods. Although we do not believe that she died from this eight months later, he caused her to be afflicted in this way contrary to the rule of her profession, so that he may, with due shame, teach her how she ought thereafter to conduct herself.” (Book III, Letter 46.)

28. Whenever something concerning the crimes of priests had to be examined, Gregory proceeded with the utmost strictness and great caution. Seeking the details of every point, he promulgated his judgment with greater reluctance than readiness.

Thus, writing to Natalis, bishop of Salona, he said:

“Although all matters require careful investigation of the truth, those that concern the removal of clerical ranks must be weighed with the greatest strictness. In such cases the issue concerns, in a certain sense, not merely human statutes but resistance to a divine blessing.

“We have been informed that Florentius, bishop of the city of Epidaurus, was accused by certain persons in criminal cases and that, without any canonical proofs being sought and without the prior judgment of a priestly council, he was deprived of the office of his dignity, not lawfully but by authority.

“Since no one can be removed from the rank of the episcopate except for just causes and by the concordant judgment of priests, we exhort your Fraternity to have the aforesaid man released from the exile into which he has been cast and to have his case investigated by episcopal debate. If he is convicted by canonical proof in the matters of which he is accused, he must undoubtedly be punished by canonical penalty.

“But if a synodal inquiry should discover that the matter is otherwise than it has been judged, then it is necessary both that the accusers fear the strictness of just law and that the supports of innocence be preserved intact for the accused.

“We have entrusted the execution of the aforesaid matter to our subdeacon Antoninus by our command, so that through his diligence both what is approved by the canonical laws may be decreed and, with the Lord’s help, what has been decreed may be brought into effect.” (Book III, Letter 8.)

Likewise, to Constantius, bishop of Milan:

“After rereading the letters that you sent to us through Marinianus, the bearer of this letter, we wrote in reply that your concern was pleasing to us, because you did not tolerate passing over in silence what had reached us concerning our brother and fellow bishop Pompeius, who must still be called by us in this way. [Note: This name is read variously. In Reg., St. Mary in Paris, and Bigot, it is read as “Marinus”; in the printed editions as “Marianus,” or, with Colb., as “Maurinus.”]

“But if the care shown in making the inquiry had been matched by precision in the investigation, nothing of what was said about him would have remained ambiguous; rather, it would have become clear whether it was true or fabricated. For, as we have learned, a similar case was previously brought against him in Sicily before our brother of revered memory, Maximianus, the bishop. But because his case was investigated with completely careful scrutiny, he who had been accused of the crime was found innocent.

“Now, therefore, since the statements made against him were not investigated with the strictness that was required, and since the proceedings drawn up on the matter before your Fraternity are shown to be sufficient neither for his condemnation nor for his acquittal, this is no slight matter to be decided carelessly or in passing. For it is exceedingly serious and improper that, in a doubtful matter, a definite sentence should be pronounced.

“These proceedings might indeed have been sufficient for a decision if the accused person’s confession had followed them—provided, however, that the precision of the examination had elicited that confession from hidden facts and that it had not been extorted by severe affliction, which often causes even the innocent to be compelled to confess themselves guilty.

“Since the aforesaid bishop, as is said, claims that he was tortured in custody and consumed by hunger, you must ascertain, if this is so, whether a confession extorted in that manner is prejudicial. Whenever such cases are brought to judgment and an appeal is made to the apostolic See, is not the person being judged also present, so that the truth may be sought with the utmost strictness and from every side, and then a decision may be made as to whether he ought to remain or not?

“Moreover, if the aforesaid bishop wishes to appeal to the apostolic See, must not his case be examined thoroughly and with every diligence? Therefore, since the person is absent and the proceedings that you sent to us do not appear, as we have said, to have adequately satisfied us, we neither ought nor can rashly decide anything concerning the bishop’s person, lest, God forbid, we be found blameworthy in matters where it is lawfully incumbent upon us to reconsider the judgments of others.” (Book X, Letter 29.)

Likewise, to John the defensor, after some other matters:

“Since the bishop Stephen asserts that certain things were fabricated out of hatred against him, that he was accused on false charges, that nothing was done according to due procedure, and that he was unjustly condemned, it must first be carefully investigated whether the trial was properly conducted and whether the accusers were different from the witnesses.

“Next, the character of the charges must be examined: whether they were worthy of exile or deposition; whether testimony was given against him under oath while he was present; whether the proceedings were committed to writing; and whether he himself had the opportunity to answer and defend himself.

“The persons of the accusers and witnesses must also be investigated carefully: what kind of life they lead, what their status and reputation are, whether they are poor, or whether perhaps they had some enmity against the aforesaid bishop; and whether they testified from hearsay or explicitly declared that they knew the facts themselves. It must also be determined whether the judgment was committed to writing and whether the sentence was read in the presence of the parties.

“If these matters were not solemnly conducted, and if no case worthy of exile or deposition was proved, he must in every way be recalled to his own church.” (Book XIII, Letter 45.)

29. Gregory in no way diminished the authority of any supreme pontiff by the greatness of his own authority; rather, he strengthened it in many ways. Although he acknowledged the authority of his own primacy among the guilty, among innocent bishops he presented himself as entirely their equal.

Therefore, writing to John, bishop of Syracuse, among other things he said:

“If the Primate of Byzacena, attacked by his own bishops, says that he submits himself to the apostolic See, then, if some fault is found in bishops, I do not know which bishop is not subject to the apostolic See. But when fault does not demand it, we are all equal as bishops, according to the rule of humility.”

And so forth. (Book IX, Letter 12.)

Also in the book *The Pastoral Rule*: “It is clear,” he says, “that nature brought all human beings into the world equal, but, through the varying order of their merits, guilt has placed some below others. The very difference that arose from vice is dispensed by divine judgment, so that, since no human being is able to stand equally firm, one may be governed by another. Therefore all who rule ought to consider not the power of their rank in themselves, but the equality of their condition; nor should they rejoice that they preside over human beings, but that they benefit them. For our ancient Fathers are remembered to have been not kings of human beings but shepherds of sheep. And when the Lord blessed Noah and his sons, saying, ‘Increase and multiply, and fill the earth,’ he immediately added: ‘And let your terror and dread be upon all the animals of the earth’ (Genesis 9:7 and 2). Since their terror and dread are commanded to be over the animals of the earth, they are plainly forbidden to be over human beings. For human beings have been made superior by nature to irrational animals, not to other human beings; and therefore it is said to them that they should be feared by animals, not by human beings. For it is contrary to nature to be proud and to wish to be feared by one’s equal. Yet it is necessary that rulers be feared by their subjects when they discover that their subjects have no fear of God, so that at least through human fear those may dread sin who do not fear divine judgments.

“Yet superiors must not become proud because of this fear they have sought, in which they seek not their own glory but the justice of their subjects. For in requiring fear from those who live perversely, they rule, as it were, not over human beings but over animals, since, in whatever respect their subjects are beastlike, in that respect they ought also to lie subject to fear. But often a ruler, precisely because he surpasses others, swells with the pride of his thoughts. While everything is subject to his use, while commands are swiftly fulfilled at his wish, while all his subjects exalt in praise whatever has been done well but oppose nothing done badly with any authority; while they often praise even what they ought to have condemned, his mind, deceived by the advantages available below him, is lifted above itself. While he is surrounded outwardly by immense favor, inwardly he is emptied of truth; and, forgetful of himself, he pours himself into the voices of others and believes himself to be what he hears outwardly, not what he ought to discern inwardly.

“He despises his subjects and does not recognize them as equal to himself in the order of nature; and those whom he has surpassed by the lot of power, he believes he has also surpassed in the merits of life. He judges himself wiser than all those whom he sees to be less powerful than himself. He sets himself, as it were, upon a certain summit in his own estimation, and, though bound together with others by an equal natural condition, disdains to regard others as his equals. Thus he is led to resemble him of whom it is written: ‘He sees every lofty thing, and he is king over all the sons of pride’ (Job 41:25). Desiring a solitary summit and despising the communal life of the angels, he says: ‘I will set my throne toward the north, and I will be like the Most High’ (Isaiah 14:13). Thus, by a marvelous judgment, he finds within himself a pit of humiliation while outwardly exalting himself upon the summit of power. A human being becomes like the apostate angel when he disdains to be like other human beings.

“Thus Saul, after the merit of humility, grew through the height of power into the swelling of pride. Through humility he was appointed, and through pride rejected, as the Lord testifies when he says: ‘Were you not little in your own eyes when I made you head over the tribes of Israel?’ (1 Samuel 15:17). Previously he had regarded himself as little in his own eyes, but, supported by temporal power, he no longer saw himself as little. Preferring himself to others because he had more power than all, he considered himself greater than everyone. Yet, in a marvelous way, when he was little in his own estimation he was great before God; but when he appeared great in his own estimation, he was little before God.

“Thus often, when the mind is inflated by the abundance of its subjects, it is corrupted into the luxury of pride, with the very pinnacle of power acting as its enticement. He governs this power well who knows both how to hold it and how to oppose it. He governs it well who knows through it to rise above faults, and knows also, with it, to place himself on an equal footing with others. For the human mind is often exalted even when supported by no power; how much more does it raise itself on high when power is also joined to it? Yet he rightly dispenses that power who carefully knows both to take from it what helps him, to conquer what tempts him, to see himself as equal to others together with it, and nevertheless to place himself above sinners through zeal for punishment.

“But we recognize this discernment more fully if we observe the example of the first shepherd. Peter, by God’s authority holding primacy in the holy Church of God, refused to be excessively honored by Cornelius, who was acting well and humbly prostrating himself before him; he acknowledged himself to be like Cornelius, saying: ‘Rise; do not do this; I myself am also a human being’ (Acts 10:26). But when he discovered the guilt of Ananias and Sapphira, he immediately showed how greatly he had grown in power above the others (Acts 5). By his word he struck down their life, which he had detected through the scrutiny of the Spirit; and he recalled himself as supreme within the Church against sins—something he did not acknowledge before his brothers who were acting well, despite the great honor shown to him. There the holiness of their conduct merited the fellowship of equality; here the zeal for punishment exercised the right of authority.”

And shortly afterward: “But when superiors correct delinquent subjects, it remains necessary that they carefully attend to this: through the obligation of discipline they should strike faults with the right of authority, but through the preservation of humility they should recognize themselves as equal to the very brothers being corrected, although it is often also fitting that we should prefer, in silent thought, those whom we correct. Their vices are struck by us with the force of discipline; yet in the things we ourselves commit, we are not wounded by even a word of reproach from anyone. Therefore we are all the more bound before God the more we sin without punishment before human beings.” And the rest. (*Pastoral Rule*, Part II, chapter 6.)

**30.** With this equality preserved, Gregory writes to the Roman defender of Sicily, saying:

“It has come to our attention that, if anyone has a case against any clerics, you cause those same clerics to be brought before your judgment, disregarding their bishops. If this is so, since it is plainly very improper, we command you by this authority not to presume to do it again. Rather, if anyone has a case against any cleric, let him approach that cleric’s bishop, so that either the bishop himself may hear it or judges may certainly be appointed by him. Or, if for this reason it is perhaps necessary to go to arbiters, let the official appointed by him compel the parties to choose a judge. But if anyone, whether cleric or layman, has a case against a bishop, then you ought to intervene, so that either you yourself may hear it between them or, at your urging, they may choose judges for themselves. For if each bishop’s jurisdiction is not preserved, what else is being done except that the ecclesiastical order is thrown into confusion by those through whom it ought to have been guarded?” (*Register*, Book XI, Letter 37.)

**31.** Just as Gregory left no one convicted of a crime without canonical punishment, so likewise he punished a false accuser through the regular procedure. Hence, writing to the subdeacon Anthemius, he says:

“Since crimes committed against the innocent, and especially against the sacred orders, ought to be punished more severely, consider how culpable you all are who sat in judgment in the case of the deacon John, so that Hilary, his accuser, was subjected to no punishment arising from your decision. Nor should you think that this is an adequate excuse for you: that, as though you wished to judge, our brother and fellow bishop Paschasius alone is said to have delayed the matter for you. For if zeal for rectitude had been vigorous in you, it would have been easier for many to persuade one reasonably than for one, without cause, to delay many.

“Since, therefore, the evil of so great a wickedness must not pass without deserved punishment, we wish our aforesaid brother Paschasius to be admonished to deprive that same Hilary first of the office of the subdiaconate, which he undeservedly holds, and then, after having him publicly scourged, to have him deported into exile, so that the punishment of one may serve as a correction for many. But if the opinion that his deacon’s reputation has been damaged does not yet move his leniency, and if—which we do not believe—he has remained sluggish in this matter, let your experience carry out what we have said and report to us his neglect.” (*Register*, Book XI, Letter 71.)

For this reason Gregory orders the subdeacon to be deprived of his office because he did not prove what he had alleged; for, according to the canonical judgments of the Fathers, one who does not prove an accusation brought by him ought to incur the penalty that the accused would certainly have suffered had he proved it. Consequently, because the subdeacon could not prove the crime against the deacon—for he had not received the laying-on of hands, by which he could have lost his rank—he was deprived not of priesthood but of office, and deserved to be punished by scourging as though he were genuinely infamous. For if any crime is established against someone, as against a layman, with three witnesses, it is not surprising that, when he fails to prove what he alleged, he should, by analogy of law, be subjected to bodily infamy like a layman. For what it would have meant for the deacon to lose his rank, that meant for the subdeacon to lose the fullness of his reputation.

**32.** Gregory did not in any way pass over crimes once heard without investigation, even if the accused had become reconciled with his accuser. Therefore, writing to all the bishops of Corinth, he says:

“It is our desire to bring those who are at odds back to harmony, and that those whom a diversity of wills makes divided in mutual affection should be united in friendship. Reading again, therefore, the letter of your Fraternity, we learned that those who had said certain things against our brother and fellow bishop Hadrian had now become friends with that same bishop; and we have presently experienced great joy over their unity. But because we do not tolerate leaving unexamined what has been said, we are sending a deacon of our see to investigate it, since the nature of the crime reported to us strongly compels us not to disregard what we have heard—especially since you have indicated that the accusers and the accused have made peace with one another. We must examine this more carefully, lest their harmony prove to have been contrived. If—which God forbid—it should be established that it was brought about not through charity but through a reward, it must be punished by a greater correction. For we, who hasten, with God’s revelation, to cut away evils that are indeed true through canonical procedure, in no way permit a fault subsequently committed to be dismissed without punishment.” (*Register*, Book III, Letter 39.)

Likewise, afterward, to John, bishop of the Corinthians:

“Although Paul the deacon, bearer of this letter, is severely confused and reproached by his own fault because, deceived by a promise, he recently withdrew from the accusation of his formerly deposed bishop and agreed, out of a desire for gain, to remain silent against his own soul rather than disclose the truth, nevertheless, because it is more fitting for us to be merciful than strict, we forgive him this fault and judge that he should be restored to his rank and place. For we believe that the affliction he endured from the time the sentence was issued can suffice as punishment for this fault.

“But Euphemius and Thomas, who received the sacred orders in exchange for abandoning the accusation, are to be deprived of those same orders, and we wish them to remain as they were deposed. We decree that they are never to be restored to the sacred orders under any pretext of excuse. For it is utterly unworthy and contrary to the rule of ecclesiastical discipline that they should exercise an honor which they received not for their merits but as a reward for their crime.

“Yet because it is more fitting for us to devote ourselves to mercy than to strict justice, we wish those same Euphemius and Thomas to be restored only to the rank and place from which they had been promoted to the sacred orders, and to receive, throughout all the days of their lives, the maintenance of those places as they had previously been accustomed to receive it. I likewise decree that, out of regard for kindness, the lector Clematius is to be restored to his rank and place. Your Fraternity should also diligently provide all of them—that is, the deacon Paul, Euphemius, Thomas, and Clematius—with their customary allowances, according to the place and rank each one holds, without any reduction, beginning with the present indiction.” (*Register*, Book V, Letter 52.)

**33.** The most merciful father Gregory did not withdraw the customary stipends of clerics on account of any illness whatsoever. Hence, writing to Candidus, bishop of the Old City, he says:

“Since God’s judgment in this matter—whether bodily striking occurs for purification or for punishment—is unknown, we ought not to add affliction to those who have been scourged, lest—God forbid—we be affected by the guilt of the offense. And because the bearer of this letter, Calumniosus, asserts that, on account of the scourging he is undergoing, his customary allowances are being denied him by your Church, we therefore exhort your Fraternity by this letter that this illness should in no way prevent him from receiving what is customary. For, as you know, illness of various kinds often occurs among those serving in the Church. If they are deterred by this example, no one who serves the Church will be found thereafter. Therefore, according to his rank in that place, your Fraternity must not cease, in consideration of the divine judgment, to provide the sick man from the limited resources available to the Church whatever could have been supplied to him if he were well.” (*Register*, Book II, Letter 8.)

**34.** Gregory strengthened, by the authority of the Apostolic See, the promises made by venerable bishops to their own clerics. Hence he writes to John, bishop of Palermo, saying:

“The desires of petitioners must always be fulfilled whenever they request what does not depart from reason. Therefore, because your clerics have asked that certain provisions which you promised to observe be confirmed by our authority, we exhort your Fraternity in these words: you must observe without any resistance what the present letter contains.
