“First, you must provide your Church’s clerics, without any delay, with a full fourth part of the Church’s revenues, according to each one’s merit, office, or labor, in whatever way you determine that it should be given to each. As for what has come in from the offerings of the faithful—that is, the fourth part in coin or in provisions—you must not delay giving it to them according to the established custom. You are to retain all other movable property under your control; all immovable property is to be added to the ecclesiastical revenues, so that, with the amount increased, it may, by God’s gift, benefit the needs of your clerics.

“Remember to appoint a tabularius (financial officer), with the agreement of the elders and clergy; each year he must formally present his accounts in order to remove suspicion of fraud. At the time of the grape harvest, let the same clergy obtain the opportunity to buy wine from the possessions of your Church at fair prices, to the extent that wine is being sold. For it is entirely contrary to reason that what can be sold to outsiders should be denied to clerics when they offer the price.

“Therefore hasten, with every effort and while preserving civility, to restore to the jurisdiction of your Church its possessions, and any other things belonging to ecclesiastical right, if they are being wrongfully held by outsiders, so that you may not appear negligent in any respect. But if anything concerning any cleric should reach your ears that could justly offend you, do not readily believe it, nor let an unknown matter stir you to punishment. Rather, in the presence of the elders of your Church, the truth must be carefully investigated; and then, if the nature of the matter requires it, let canonical strictness strike the faults of the offender.

“Take care, therefore, to guard all these matters with such vigilance and gentleness in your administration that you may neither appear to have forgotten your promise nor allow them to find a legitimate occasion for murmuring against you.” (*Register*, Book XIII, Letter 44.)

Likewise, afterward, to Maximian, bishop of Syracuse:

“We have learned that, with respect to newly acquired Church revenues, the canonical distribution of the fourth part is not being made, but that the bishops of the places distribute only a fourth of the old revenues, while retaining for their own uses what is now acquired. Therefore let your Fraternity promptly correct this wickedly introduced custom, so that, whether from former revenues or from those that have newly come or will come, the fourth part may be distributed according to canonical allocation. For it is improper that one and the same substance of the Church should be regarded as subject to a double kind of right—that is, both usurpation and the canons.” (Book III, Letter 11.)

**35.** Gregory restored to their former communion those whom other bishops had deprived of communion. Therefore, writing to Magnus, a priest of the Milanese Church, he says:

“Just as, when guilt demands it, a person is deservedly excluded from the sacrament of communion, so such punishment must in no way be inflicted upon the innocent. For we have learned that Lawrence, formerly our brother and fellow bishop, deprived you of communion although no faults were present in you. Therefore, protected by the authority of this command of ours, perform your office without fear and receive communion without any apprehension.” (Book III, Letter 26.)

**36.** Gregory not only received those who cleared themselves of the crime of any heresy, but also declared them Catholics. Hence he writes to John, bishop of Constantinople, saying:

“Just as the perversity of heretics must be restrained by zeal for the true faith, so the integrity of a true confession must be embraced. For if one who confesses faithfully is despised rather than believed, the faith of all is thrown into doubt, and deadly errors are generated through incautious severity. Thus not only are wandering sheep by no means brought back to the Lord’s folds, but those already inside are also cruelly exposed to be torn by savage teeth.

“Let us therefore weigh this carefully, dearest brother, and not allow anyone who truly professes the Catholic faith to be afflicted under the pretext of heresy, lest—God forbid—we permit heresy to arise under the appearance of correction. We are greatly angered that those whom you appointed as judges in the matter of John, a presbyter of the Church of Chalcedon, neglected the truth, trusted an opinion, and refused to believe him when he strictly professed the faith—especially since, when questioned about the heresy of the Marcionists which they had mentioned, and by which they were attempting to make him guilty, his accusers openly replied that they did not know what it was.

**Note:** In the manuscript of the letters, *Marcianistarum* is read. But *Marcionistarum* is the best reading, as we also indicated in the notes to this letter.

“From this it is clearly recognized that they wished to burden his person, without regard for God, not justly but solely by their own will, at the peril of their souls. We, therefore, having held a council, carefully investigating and discussing everything necessary, as the record of the proceedings conducted before us shows, were unable to find the aforesaid presbyter guilty of anything—especially since the statement of faith which he presented to the judges delegated by you agrees in every respect with the sincerity of the true faith. Accordingly, rejecting the judgment of those same judges, we declared by our decision that he was Catholic and free from every heretical crime, as the mercy and grace of Christ our God and Redeemer revealed.” (Book VI, Letter 15.)

Likewise, shortly afterward, to the emperor Maurice:

“After rereading in council the proceedings conducted against John, the presbyter of the Church of Chalcedon, together with the sequence of the judgment, we recognized that he had suffered a greater injustice. Although he cried out and demonstrated that he was a Catholic, he was crushed not by the guilt of an offense but by a long and uncertain accusation—especially since his accusers openly professed in their answer that they did not know the heresy of the Marcionists which they had mentioned, and those who should immediately have been rejected at the threshold of the tribunal were allowed to persist in their uncertain accusation against him.

“Yet, lest even the opinion expressed against him should wound him, he presented a statement of faith in which he openly endeavored to show himself a professor and follower of the true faith. But the judges appointed by the most holy John, our brother and fellow bishop, unjustly and irrationally neglecting this, while striving to occupy themselves with his burden, showed themselves rather blameworthy. For no one doubts that it is unbelief not to have faith in the faithful.” (Book VI, Letter 16.)

Likewise, afterward, to the count Narses concerning the same matter:

“Concerning the presbyter John, know that his case was decided by a synod. There I learned plainly that his adversaries wanted to make him a heretic, and strove for a long time to do so, but were completely unable.” (Book VI, Letter 16.)

Likewise, to Athanasius, a presbyter of Isauria:

“Just as we are afflicted and grieve over those whom the error of heretical perversity has cut off from the unity of the Church, so we rejoice with those whom the profession of the Catholic faith holds within its embrace. And just as pastoral concern requires us to oppose their impieties, so it is fitting to extend favor to their pious professions and to declare that their beliefs are sincere.

“Therefore, when suspicion contrary to the integrity of the faith arose against you, Athanasius, presbyter of the monastery of Saint Mila, called Tannaco, established in the province of Lycaonia, you chose to have recourse to the Apostolic See over which we preside, so that the integrity of your confession might become evident. You also asserted that, after being physically scourged, you had done certain things unjustly and violently.

“Although what is done under the force of compulsion is not at all accepted by the judgment of the canons and is rightly considered invalid—for the one who compels someone to confess an injustice himself dissolves what was done—nevertheless, that confession is more properly received and embraced which is shown to proceed from spontaneous will, as you are recognized to have done before us.

“Yet, so that nothing ambiguous might remain for us, we took care to write concerning you to the most holy John, formerly our brother and bishop of the city of Constantinople, so that he might inform us by his letters of what had taken place. After being repeatedly admonished by us, he wrote to inform us that a certain book had been found in your possession containing many heretical statements, and that for this reason he had been moved against you. Because he took care to send it to us for the sake of satisfaction, we read through its earlier sections with attentive examination; and because we found in it unmistakable poisons of heretical perversity, we forbade that it be read again.

“But since you testified that you had read it simply, and, to remove the source of ambiguous suspicion, presented us with a written statement in your own hand, in which, setting out your faith, you most openly condemned all heresies in general and everything contrary to the integrity of the Catholic profession; and since you professed that you had always accepted and continued to accept everything received by the four holy universal synods, and had condemned and continued to condemn everything they condemned; and since you promised that you both accepted and would uphold the synod held in the time of the emperor Justinian concerning the Three Chapters; and since, when we forbade you to read that book in which the poisonous substance of deceit was woven, you most willingly agreed, also rejecting and condemning everything said or secretly inserted in it against the integrity of the Catholic faith, and promising that you would not read it again—moved by this consideration, after your Catholic faith had also become completely clear to us, with God protecting it, from the page of the statement rebuked by you, we decree, in accordance with your profession, that you are free from every stain of heretical perversity. We declare you to have shown yourself Catholic and in all things a sincere professor and follower of the faith of Jesus Christ, by the grace of the Savior; and we grant you free permission to return to your monastery, to your place and rank there.” (Book VI, Letter 66.)

**Note:** The printed editions together with three Paris manuscripts read *etiam exprobrata est a te libelli pagina, et fides* (“even from the page of the statement reproached by you, and the faith…”). The reading *exprobrati a te libelli pagina, fides* (“from the page of the statement reproached by you, your faith…”) is better.

**37.** Gregory invited schismatics to come and offer satisfaction; and, if they were unwilling ever to return to the unity of the Church, he promised that he would use no force against them. Hence, writing to Peter and Providentius, bishops of Istria, he says:

“May God, who rejoices in the unity of the faithful and reveals the truth to those who seek it, open to your hearts, dearest brothers, with what longing I desire you to be held within the bosom of the holy universal Church and to remain concordant in its unity. I have no doubt that this will happen if, having cast aside the goad of contention, you attend to receiving genuine satisfaction concerning the matters about which there is doubt.

“I have learned from the report of my notary Castorius that your Fraternity desires to come to me, provided it is promised that you will suffer no inconvenience. Knowing this, I both desire it and, kindled by the ardor of charity, invite you to undertake the labor of coming to me, so that, conferring together, we may speak jointly about what is true and pleasing to our Redeemer, and hold to it in every way. With the support of divine protection, I am prepared to satisfy you concerning the matters about which you doubt, and I trust in the mercy of our almighty God that my satisfaction will so take root within you that nothing ambiguous will thereafter remain for your charity.

“For those things which the four most holy synods have taught and defined, we hold, follow, and observe just as our predecessor, the most holy Pope Leo did; nor do we in any way dissent from their faith. But because a person present gives greater satisfaction than a letter, I exhort you, dearest brothers, to come to me as I have said, provided that, once the matter has been understood, no dissent separates you from the concord of the holy universal Church.

“Let your Charity be certain of this: I will receive you with the affection that is fitting and release you with favor. I will not permit either you or anyone else who wishes to come to me for this reason to suffer affliction or inconvenience. Whether divine mercy should move your hearts to agree with me—or, God forbid, you should happen to persist in that disagreement—we will ensure, according to my promise, that you return to your own places whenever you wish, released without injury or inconvenience.” (*Register*, Book V, Letter 51.)

**38.** He compelled Severus, bishop of Aquileia and the head of the entire schism, to come to Rome, saying:

“Just as the Lord embraces with complete eagerness one who is walking along wrong paths when he again takes up the straight road, so he is finally grieved over one who abandons the known way of truth with greater sorrow than the joy with which he had rejoiced over one who was converted. For it is a lesser transgression not to know the truth than not to remain in the truth once it has been known; and what is committed by one who is in error is one thing, while what is perpetrated knowingly is another.

“We indeed had rejoiced insofar as we had previously been glad that you had been incorporated into the unity of the Church; now we are much more ashamed that you have been separated from the Catholic fellowship. Therefore, with the bearer of this letter approaching, and in accordance with the command of the most Christian and serene lord of the state, we wish you to come with your followers to the threshold of the blessed apostle Peter, so that, by God’s authority, a synod may be assembled and whatever is just may be judged concerning the dispute that exists among you.” (Book I, Letter 16.)

But Severus, compelled by both apostolic and imperial command, was brought to Ravenna by the approaching exarch Smaragdus, together with Antoninus, defender of the Roman Church. There, fearing to undergo a synodal confrontation with Gregory, he returned to the unity of the holy universal Church through the mediation of John, bishop of Ravenna.

But when he had returned to his own place after the lapse of a year, persuaded by other schismatics, he not only returned to his former vomit but also, after secretly obtaining a command from Maurice—ever hostile to God—which ordered that schismatics should by no means be compelled to return to the unity of the Church, fomented the greatest disturbances while the remaining bishops were joining themselves to the Church. Therefore Gregory thereafter took care to receive no one returning without an oath of security. After this had been given, he commended him in the following letter to the same Patricius, the exarch:

“Firminus, our brother and fellow bishop, bishop of the Church of Trieste, recovering from the schism to which he had clung through a salutary decision before the arrival of Your Excellence and returning to the unity of the mother Church, has been confirmed by our letters so that he might remain firm and steadfast in spirit within the bosom of the true mother Church which he had recognized.

“When Severus, bishop of Grado and the head of that schism, heard this, he first attempted by various persuasions, if he could, to recall him from his good purpose. When, by God’s authority, he was completely unable to accomplish this, he did not fear to stir up a sedition against him among his fellow citizens. How much our aforesaid brother and fellow bishop Firminus has suffered from this instigation, you will be able to learn more fully and more accurately there, from nearby.

“Therefore, by sending commands to Your Excellence, order those who, by God’s authority, are known to act in your place in the regions of Istria with strictness, so that they may both defend our aforesaid brother from the troubles inflicted upon him and in every way secure his peace, which will greatly benefit others as an example to imitate. Thus this provision of yours may be both the desired security of those who have converted and an occasion for those who will follow.” (*Register*, Book XIII, Letter 33.)

Finally, because Severus did not merit returning to the unity of the holy universal Church, by his madness he also provoked the Roman pontiff to divide the unity of his own diocese, so that from the time of Severus’s death the diocese of Aquileia has been divided between two metropolitans, namely, the Catholics and the schismatics. Nor afterward, although all in general returned from the schism to unity, could it be restored to the union of its former communion down to the present.

**Note:** While Gregory was alive, that schism did not cease, as we shall prove below in the life of the holy Doctor.

**39.** Just as Gregory diminished the allowances of no cleric on account of bodily illness, so he taught that no bishop ought to be replaced on account of any illness. Hence, replying to Anatolius, a subdeacon of Constantinople, he says:

“Your Charity wrote to me that our most pious lord ordered my most reverend brother, the bishop of First Justiniana, to be replaced because of the illness of the head from which he suffers, lest, while that city has no bishop’s rights, it should—God forbid—perish at the hands of enemies. But the canons nowhere command that a bishop be replaced because of a bishop’s illness; and it is altogether unjust that, when bodily illness strikes, the sick man should be deprived of his honor. Therefore this cannot in any way be done through us, lest sin arising from his deposition come upon my soul.

“Rather, it should be suggested that, if the man who is in charge is ill, an administrator be sought for him who can undertake all his care and fulfill his place in governing the Church, without deposing him, and in guarding the city, so that neither almighty God is offended nor the city found neglected.

“But if that same most reverend John should perhaps ask, on account of his illness, to be relieved of the honor of the episcopate, it may be granted once he has made the request in writing. Otherwise, out of fear of almighty God, we are in no way able to do this. If he does not wish to ask for what pleases the most pious emperor, whatever the emperor orders lies within his power; let him provide as he knows best. Let him not involve us in the deposition of an innocent man.

“Whatever he himself does, if it is canonical, we follow; but if it is not canonical, insofar as we can do so without our own sin, we bear it.” (Book XI, Letter 47.)

Gregory in no way refused successors to pontiffs who voluntarily renounced their sees, and he held that they should thereafter be adequately supported from the revenues of the church they had left. Thus, indicating this to Marinianus, bishop of Ravenna, he says:

> “Your Fraternity learned some time ago how the church of Ariminum has until now been deprived of pastoral governance because of the bodily illness that, as is known, afflicted the priest ordained by us. Moved by the prayers of the inhabitants of that place, we repeatedly urged him that, if he felt himself improved from the illness of the head by which he was afflicted, he should, with the Lord’s help, return to his own church. After an interval had been granted, he was awaited for four years. When we urged him more insistently—[Col. 0202D] **[Note: In three Paris manuscripts and in the printed editions: ‘and those who came from there, reproaching us with their prayers.’]**—at the prayers of the clergy and citizens who came from there and pressed us with their petitions, that, if he were able, he should return with them with the Lord’s help, he petitioned us in a written supplication that, since he could in no way rise again to the governance of that church or to the office he had undertaken because of the illness by which he was afflicted, we ought to ordain a bishop for that church.

> “Therefore, because the charge of concern imposed upon us for all the churches constrains us lest pastoral protection should be absent from the faithful flock any longer, compelled by their prayers and by this man’s renunciation on account of his incapacity, it seemed to us that a bishop ought to be ordained for the church of Ariminum. And after issuing the customary instructions, we did not cease admonishing the clergy and people of that church [Col. 0202D] to come together in harmonious deliberation to choose a bishop for themselves.”  
> *(Book VII, letter 19.)*

Likewise, to Bishop Etherius:

> “Although what we are saying is exceedingly grievous to us, and fraternal compassion urges us rather than permitting us to determine anything concerning what we have heard, nevertheless the concern of the governance we have undertaken strikes our heart with an insistent goad and compels us, with great care for the churches, to determine with God as author what ought to be done before their welfare can perish.

> “It has therefore come to us that a certain bishop has incurred such an affliction of the head that, when his mind is deranged, one can hear him groaning and weeping. [Col. 0203A] Lest, then, while the shepherd languishes, the flock—God forbid—be exposed to be torn by the teeth of an ambusher, or the interests of that church perish, we must handle the matter with prudent foresight.

> “Therefore, since while a bishop is alive, when necessity caused by illness and not crime removes him from his office, no rational principle permits another to be ordained in his place against his will, if he is accustomed to have intervals of illness, let him himself submit a petition and acknowledge that he can no longer rise to this ministry, namely, to its intellectual duties, because his illness has overthrown him, and let him request that another be ordained in his place. When this has been done, let another bishop who is worthy be consecrated by solemn election, yet in such a way that, for as long as the same bishop remains alive in this world, his due expenses shall be supplied from that church.

> “But if at no time he returns to the office of a sound mind, a faithful person of commendable life must be chosen who can be suitable for the governance of the church, who can consider the welfare of souls, restrain the unruly under the punishment of discipline, care for ecclesiastical property, and show himself mature and effective in all things. If he survives the bishop who is now ill, he too ought to be consecrated in his place.”  
> *(Book XIII, letter 5.)*

### 40.

When a virgin had been violated, Gregory ordered her violator to take her as his wife, or, after punishment by blows, to be assigned to a monastery. Thus he writes to Felix, bishop of Sipontum, saying:

> “We expected your Fraternity, through its preaching, to convert some people to God and recall those who were acting wrongly to uprightness. We are therefore exceedingly saddened, because, by contrast, your guilt has been clearly revealed in the wickedness of your nephew Felix, whom you raised in such a manner. It has come to us that the aforesaid Felix deceived Evangelus, your deacon’s daughter, by fornication. If this is true, although he ought to be punished with the severe penalty prescribed by law, we nevertheless soften the harshness of the law to some extent and, making this provision, order that he either take as his wife the woman whom he violated or, if he thinks he must refuse, be strictly and bodily punished, excommunicated, and shut away in a monastery where he may do penance. He shall have no permission to leave it without our command.”  
> *(Book III, letter 43.)*

### 41.

If a man entered religious life without his wife’s consent, even if he had already been tonsured, Gregory ordered that he be returned to his wife. Therefore, writing to Hadrian, notary of Palermo, he says:

> “Agathosa, the bearer of this letter, has complained to us that her husband has entered the monastery of Abbot Urbicius against her will. Since there is no doubt that this pertains to the fault and discredit of the same abbot, we instruct your Experience to investigate the matter carefully, lest perhaps he entered religious life with her consent, or lest she herself promised to change her way of life. If you discover this, see both that he remains in the monastery and that she is compelled to change, as she promised.

> “But if neither of these things is so, and you learn that the aforesaid woman did not formerly commit the crime of fornication, on account of which a man is permitted to leave his wife, we wish you to return her husband to her, even if he has already been tonsured, [Col. 0204A] with every excuse set aside. For although worldly law prescribes that, for the sake of conversion, a marriage may be dissolved with either party unwilling, divine law does not permit this. Except on account of fornication, it grants no reason whatsoever for a man to leave his wife, because after the union of marriage has made the man and woman one body, one party cannot enter religious life while the other remains in the world.”  
> *(Book XI, letter 50.)*

### 42.

Gregory strove to correct the perfidy of the Jews by reasoning rather than by violence. Therefore, writing to Virgilius and Theodorus, bishops of Gaul, after other matters he says:

> “Many men of the Jewish religion living in this province and frequently traveling through the region of Marseille on various business have brought to our attention that many Jews settled in those parts have been brought to the baptismal font by force rather than by preaching. I regard such an intention as praiseworthy and acknowledge that it descends from love of our Lord; but unless an appropriate result accompanied by sacred Scripture follows this same intention, I fear that either no work deserving reward will result from it or that, contrary to what we desire, harm to the souls we wish to rescue may follow.

> “For when someone reaches the baptismal font not through the gentleness of preaching but through compulsion, he returns to his former superstition and dies more grievously from the very place from which he seemed to have been reborn. Your Fraternity should therefore invite such people by frequent preaching, so that they may desire to change their former life through the gentleness of a teacher. In this way your intention is rightly fulfilled, and the mind of the convert is not changed back again to its former vomit.

> “A discourse must therefore be offered to them that will both burn away the thorns of their errors and illuminate, by preaching, what is darkened in them, so that through frequent admonition your Fraternity may receive a reward and may lead as many of them as God grants to the rebirth of a new life.”  
> *(Book I, letter 47.)*

Likewise, to Victor, bishop of Palermo:

> “Just as Jews must not be permitted to presume anything in their synagogues beyond what the law permits, so in those matters that have been granted to them they must suffer no prejudice.”  
> *(Book VIII, letter 25.)*

### 43.

Just as Gregory refused to permit Jews to be baptized by force, so he absolutely did not permit Christians to be subjected to them in any way. Thus, writing to Libertinus, prefect of Sicily, he says:

> “It is reported that a certain most wicked Jew named Nasas constructed an altar with punishable audacity under the name of blessed Elijah and deceived many Christians there by sacrilegious enticement into worshiping it. It is also said that he purchased Christian slaves and assigned them to his service and interests. Although he ought to have been punished with the greatest severity for such crimes, the glorious Justinus, as has been written to us, softened by the drug of avarice, delayed avenging the insult against God.

> “Let Your Glory investigate all these matters with strict examination; and if you discover that this is manifestly true, hasten to punish that wicked Jew with the utmost severity and bodily penalty, so that by this action Your Glory may both gain the favor of our God and show himself, through these examples, as one to be imitated by posterity for his reward. Whatever Christian slaves he is found to have purchased, lead to freedom without any ambiguity, according to the commands of the laws, lest—God forbid—the Christian religion be in any way polluted by subjection to Jews.”  
> *(Book III, letter 38.)*

Likewise, to Venantius, bishop of Luni:

> “It has reached us through the report of many that Christian slaves are being held in servitude by Jews living in the city of Luni. This matter seemed all the more grievous to us because your Fraternity’s patience has been all the more painstaking. Out of regard for your position and in consideration of the Christian religion, you ought not to have left any opportunity for Jewish superstition, lest simple souls should in some manner serve it not so much through persuasion as by the right of power.

> “We therefore exhort your Fraternity that, following the course of the most merciful laws, no Jew be permitted to retain a Christian slave under his ownership. If any are found in their possession, let their freedom be preserved for them, with the assistance of protection, by the sanction of the laws.”  
> *(Book IV, letter 21.)*

### 44.

If, because of the length of the journey through the provinces, Gregory could not legally free certain Christians from the service of Hebrews, he held that they should be redeemed at a price paid for them. Thus, writing to Candidus, a priest in Gaul, he says:

> “Dominicus, the bearer of this letter, has informed us tearfully that his four brothers were redeemed from captivity among the Jews, and that they are now being held at Narbonne in the service of those same Jews. Since it is altogether grievous and detestable for Christians to be in Jewish service, we exhort your Love by this letter to investigate the matter with every care and diligence. If it is truly so, and it is established for you by manifest truth that neither they themselves have the means of redeeming themselves nor the aforesaid bearer has the means, let it be your concern to redeem them, knowing that whatever you give for them will without doubt be charged to your accounts.”  
> *(Book VII, letter 24.)*

### 45.

When Jewish slaves once took refuge in the Church, Gregory ordered that they never be returned by any persuasion. Thus, writing among other matters to Januarius, bishop of Cagliari, he says:

> “It has come to us that male and female slaves of Jews, fleeing to the Church for the sake of the faith, are either being returned to unbelieving masters or that a price is being paid to prevent their return. We therefore exhort you not to permit such a wicked custom to remain in any way. Whenever a Jewish slave takes refuge in venerable places for the sake of the faith, do not allow him to suffer any prejudice; whether he was formerly a Christian or is now to be baptized, defend him in every way into freedom through the devout protection of the Church, without any loss to poor Christians.”  
> *(Book IV, letter 9.)*

### 46.

Gregory not only legally restored Christian slaves to their former freedom; he also did not permit pagans who wished to come to the faith to be sold in any way. Thus, writing among other matters to Fortunatus, bishop of Naples, he says:

> “Your Fraternity must be vigilant that, if not only a Jew but also any pagan wishes to become a Christian while in Jewish service, once his will has become known, no Jew may have the opportunity to sell him by any device or pretext. Rather, let the person who desires to convert to the Christian faith be vindicated into freedom in every way through your protection.

> “You should, however, preserve with careful consideration the interests of those who must lose such slaves, lest they perhaps irrationally judge their own interests to be obstructed. If it should happen that pagans whom they bought from foreign regions for purposes of trade flee to the Church within three months, while a buyer to whom they may be sold is being found, and they say that they wish to become Christians—or even disclose such a desire outside the Church—let the Christian buyer pay them their price.

> “But if, after the appointed three months, any such slave of the Jews declares his desire and wishes to become a Christian, then neither may anyone afterward buy him, nor may his master dare to sell him under any pretext. He must without doubt be led to the rewards of freedom, because it is understood that his master kept him not for selling but for serving him.”  
> *(Book VI, letter 32.)*

### 47.

He did not restore pagan slaves to the service of their Jewish masters when they had preceded those masters in embracing the faith, even if the masters themselves subsequently became Christians. Thus, to John, bishop of Syracuse:

> “Felix, the bearer of this letter, has complained to us that, although he was born of Christian parents, he was given away by a certain Christian Samaritan—which is a crime to say—and that, while reason of law and reverence for religion do not permit people of such a superstition to possess slaves in any way, he nevertheless claims to have remained in his service for eighteen years.

> “When your predecessor, Maximian of holy memory, learned of this, he was moved by priestly zeal, as was fitting, and freed him from the Samaritan’s wicked service. But because the son of that Samaritan is said to have become a Christian five years later, and certain people are attempting, as Felix himself says, to reduce the aforesaid Felix to his service, let Your Holiness carefully investigate what we have learned. If you establish that the matter is so, strive to protect him and permit no one to oppress him under any pretext.

> “For if the laws expressly prohibit the slaves of a superstitious sect who preceded their masters into the faith from being returned to their service, how much more must this man, born of Christian parents and made a Christian from childhood, be spared such a question? Especially since he could not have been his father’s slave, and it is clear that the father, through this wicked presumption, may instead suffer the penalty imposed by the laws.”  
> *(Book VIII, letter 21.)*

### 48.

Gregory did not permit any pagan, at least, to be circumcised. Therefore, to Leo, bishop of Catania:

> “A matter altogether detestable and hostile to the laws has reached us which, if true, strongly accuses your Fraternity, proving you culpable of insufficient vigilance. We have learned that Samaritans living at Catania purchased pagan slaves and presumed, with reckless audacity, to circumcise them.

> “It is therefore necessary for you to exercise priestly zeal in this matter in every way and to investigate it with complete vigor and care. If you find the report to be true, immediately vindicate those slaves into freedom in every way, extend ecclesiastical protection to them, and do not permit their masters to receive anything whatever in payment. They must not only be punished for this loss but also struck with another penalty under the laws.”  
> *(Book VI, letter 33.)*

### 49.

Since the perfidy of the Jews was accustomed to mock the zeal of Christians by offering gifts against them, Gregory not only accepted absolutely nothing from them but also judged their gifts detestable. Thus, writing to Reccared, king of the Visigoths, after other matters he says:

> “Moreover, I declare that the praises of God have increased through your work in this matter, as I learned when my beloved son Probinius, the priest, related that, after Your Excellence had issued a certain decree against Jewish perfidy, those against whom it had been issued attempted to bend the uprightness of your mind by offering a sum of money. Your Excellence rejected it and, seeking to please the judgment of almighty God, preferred innocence to gold.

> “In this connection I recall the deed of King David. When water he desired from the cistern of Bethlehem, which lay among enemy troops, had been brought to him by his attending soldiers, he immediately said: ‘Far be it from me to drink the blood of these men’ (1 Chronicles 11:19). Because he poured it out and refused to drink it, it is written: ‘He poured it out to the Lord’ (ibid., 11:18).

> “If water rejected by an armed king was thus turned into a sacrifice to God, let us consider what kind of sacrifice to almighty God was offered by a king who, for love of Him, refused to accept not water but gold. Therefore, most excellent son, I say confidently that you have poured out gold to the Lord, since you in no way wished to possess it against Him.”

> And so forth.  
> *(Book IX, letter 122.)*

### 50.

For this reason, as is handed down by our ancestors and as we ourselves saw with our own eyes up to our present time, when we were still growing into manhood, an old custom prevailed: however beautiful the merchandise brought by all the people of that superstition might be, they never enjoyed a pontifical greeting and never obtained the apostolic gaze. Instead, outside the veil of the very long portico, they sat—not on benches but on the marble pavement—and counted the payments they had received, lest they appear to have received anything from the hand of the pontiff.

For Pope Nicholas of revered memory was so opposed to Arsenius, formerly bishop of the city of Orte, when Arsenius first attempted to introduce Jewish garments, that he wished to deprive him of the palace procession unless, renouncing the clothing of that superstitious people, he made every effort to proceed according to custom in the sacerdotal vestments.

### 51.

Gregory refuted in the following manner those who preached that the Sabbath must be observed as forerunners of Antichrist:

> “It has come to me that certain men of a perverse spirit have sown among you various things that are wicked and opposed to the holy faith, to the extent of prohibiting any work on the Sabbath. What else should I call them but preachers of Antichrist? When he comes, he will cause both the Sabbath and the Lord’s Day to be kept from all work. Because he pretends both to die and to rise again, he wishes the Lord’s Day to be held in veneration. And because he compels the people to Judaize, so that he may restore the outward observance of the Law and subject them to the perfidy of the Jews, he wishes the Sabbath to be honored.

> “For what is said through the prophet—‘Do not bring burdens through your gates on the Sabbath day’ (Jeremiah 17:22)—could be observed only as long as it was permitted to keep the Law according to the letter. But after the grace of our almighty Lord Jesus Christ appeared, the precepts of the Law that were spoken figuratively cannot be observed according to the letter. For if anyone says that this concerning the Sabbath must be observed, he must also say that carnal sacrifices must be offered and that the command concerning bodily circumcision must still be retained. But let him hear the apostle Paul speaking against him: ‘If you are circumcised, Christ will be of no benefit to you’ (Galatians 5:2).

> “We therefore understand spiritually what has been written concerning the Sabbath, and we retain it spiritually. Sabbath means rest. Our true Sabbath, however, is the Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer. Whoever knows the light of faith, if through his eyes he brings the sins of desire into his mind, introduces burdens through the gates on the Sabbath day. We therefore do not introduce burdens through the gates on the Sabbath day if, established in the grace of our Redeemer, we do not drag the weight of sin into the soul through the bodily senses.

> “The same Lord and Redeemer of ours is read to have done many things on the Sabbath, so that he reproved the Jews, saying: ‘Which of you does not untie his ox or donkey on the Sabbath and lead it to water?’ (Luke 13:15). If the Truth itself did not command the Sabbath to be kept according to the letter, whoever keeps Sabbath rest according to the letter of the Law contradicts whom other than the Truth itself?

> “Another matter has also been reported to me: that perverse men have preached to you that no one ought to wash on the Lord’s Day. If someone wishes to wash for bodily luxury and pleasure, we do not permit this on any other day either. But if it is for the body’s necessity, we do not prohibit it even on the Lord’s Day. For it is written: ‘No one ever hates his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it’ (Ephesians 5:30). And again it is written: ‘Do not provide for the flesh in its desires’ (Romans 13:14). Whoever therefore prohibits care for the flesh in its desires plainly permits it in necessities.

> “For if it is a sin to wash the body on the Lord’s Day, then neither should one wash one’s face on that day. But if this is permitted for one part of the body, why should it be denied to the whole body when necessity demands it?

> “On the Lord’s Day, however, one must cease from earthly labor and devote oneself entirely to prayers, so that if anything negligent is done during the six days, it may be expiated by prayers on the day of the Lord’s resurrection.”  
> *(Book XIII, letter 1.)*

### 52.

Such abundant compassion toward everyone overflowed in Gregory that, if you wish, you may see him bearing another person’s illness in his own body. Thus, writing to John, bishop of Ravenna, he says:

> “The Lord’s commands require us to love our neighbors as ourselves and to grieve over their illnesses as over our own infirmities. Mindful of these commands, your Fraternity first visited our brother and fellow bishop Castorius in a manner suitable to you, out of compassion, and afterward, when his bodily illness increased, received him in the city of Ravenna.

> “You have therefore made not only us, through the love you showed, but certainly also God your debtor, since you have proved that you grieved over your brother’s illness and not only visited him in the affliction of his body but also received him. I myself entirely refused to ordain him there because of his simplicity, but the persistence of those who petitioned made it impossible for me to object.

> “If it can be done, you will greatly benefit both me and him if you send him to me, even by way of Sicily.”  
> *(Book II, letter 35.)*

Likewise, to Leontius, bishop of Urbino:

> “We are keeping Castorius, our brother and fellow bishop, at Rome because of his bodily illness. Since he is now unable to return to his own church, while he is absent we are arranging for Your Fraternity to undertake the visitation of his church.”  
> *(Book III, letter 24.)*

Likewise, to all the inhabitants of Ariminum:

> “If you wish to consider your fault more attentively, beloved sons, you ought to cleanse yourselves before God by constant prayer because you did not receive your bishop with devoted minds, nor as sons ought to have received him. The unrest and tribulation you inflicted upon him brought him to the point of contracting a bodily illness. We have learned nothing of the matters written to us concerning him, but we saw only that weakness was present in him, on account of which we took care to keep him here.”  
> *(Ibid., letter 25.)*

Likewise, to Eulogius, patriarch of Alexandria:

> “Some time ago the letters of Boniface, my chartulary and representative who resides in the royal city, greatly disturbed me. They said that your Holiness, most sweet and pleasing to me, had suffered a loss of bodily sight. I was struck by deep sorrow because of these letters; but then, through the prospering grace of our Creator and Redeemer, I received a letter from Your Blessedness. Learning from it that you had recovered from the bodily illness I had heard about, I rejoiced greatly, because joy of heart as great as the bitterness of the preceding sorrow followed. For we know that the life of Your Holiness is the salvation of many through the help of almighty God.”  
> *(Book XIII, letter 42.)*

Likewise, to the patrician Rusticiana:

> “Whenever someone comes to us from the royal city, we make it our concern to inquire about your bodily health. But because of my sins I always hear what I am wearied of hearing: that, in spite of such emaciation and weakness, the pains of gout continue to increase in you. I pray almighty God that everything taking place in your body may be directed toward the salvation of your soul, that temporal scourges may prepare eternal rest for you, and that through those pains which have an end he may grant you joys without end.”  
> *(Ibid., letter 22.)*

Likewise, to Marinianus, bishop of Ravenna:

> “Certain men from Ravenna came and found me struck by very great sorrow, because they reported that your Fraternity was ill with vomiting of blood. For this reason we carefully and individually had the physicians whom we know here to be learned through study sought out, and we sent Your Holiness in writing what each of them thought and prescribed. Nevertheless, they all prescribe rest and silence above everything else.

> “I am very doubtful whether your Fraternity can have these in your own church. Therefore it seems to me that, once the church there has been properly organized—whether those who can celebrate the solemn rites of Mass, or one who can manage the episcopal household and provide hospitality and reception, or one who can preside over the monasteries to ensure their supervision—you ought to come to me before the summer, so that I may personally care for your illness as far as I can and protect your rest. For physicians say very emphatically that the summer season is dangerous for this illness.

> “I am very much afraid that, if you undertake any duties amid adverse weather, you may be endangered further by the same illness. I myself am very weak, and it is entirely preferable that, by God’s grace, you return healthy to your church; or, if you are to be called away, that you be called away among your own people. And if almighty God should wish to call me first, though I see myself near death, I ought to pass away in your hands.”  
> *(Register, Book XI, letter 33.)*

### 53.

Because of barbarian incursions, Gregory decreed that litanies should be performed twice a week. Therefore, writing to all the bishops of Sicily, he says:

> “In addition to the afflictions and groans that we have endured here from our enemies through the long continuance of these troubles, a greater fear torments us: we know that our enemies are hastening with every effort to invade Sicily. But lest, while they plot this, the multitude of our sins provide them with success, let us turn with our whole heart to the remedies of our Redeemer and meet with tears those whom we cannot resist by strength.

> “You should gather from the desolation of this province what you must beware of and what you must fear more intensely. I therefore exhort you, dearest brothers, to proclaim a litany without fail every week on Wednesday and Friday, and to implore the aid of heavenly protection against these incursions of barbarian cruelty.”  
> *(Book XI, letter 51.)*

### 54.

Finally, Gregory foretold that Sicily, stained with the simoniacal heresy and lust, would perish, as can now be seen. Writing to Maximian, bishop of Syracuse, he says:

> “Such great evils continually taking place in that province are reported to us that, because of its sins, we believe it will soon perish—may almighty God avert this.”  
> *(Ibid.)*

### 55.

He also writes to Maximus, bishop of Salona, with prophetic foreknowledge, saying that worse things than those already experienced would come:

> “When our common son, the priest Veteranus, came to Rome, he found me so weakened by the pains of gout that I was entirely unable to answer your Fraternity’s letters. I am both deeply distressed and troubled concerning the people of the Slavs, who are pressing upon you so heavily. I am distressed by what I am already suffering on your behalf; I am troubled because they have now begun to enter Italy through the approach of Istria.

> “What shall I say about Julian the Scribe? Everywhere I see that our sins are answering us, so that we are troubled both outwardly by foreign peoples and inwardly by corrupt judges. But do not be distressed at such things in every respect, because those who live after us will see worse times, so that, by comparison with their own age, they will consider us fortunate to have had the days we did.

> “As far as your Fraternity is able, you must oppose yourself on behalf of the oppressed. Even if it is entirely unable to help, the very devotion of mind which he has given is sufficient for almighty God. For it is written: ‘Rescue those who are being led away to death, and do not cease to free those who are being dragged to destruction’ (Proverbs 24:11).

> “If you say, ‘Our strength is not enough,’ he who examines the heart understands. In all that you do, therefore, seek to have the examiner of your heart favorable toward you. Do not omit anything by which you may please him. For human threats and favors are like smoke, which vanishes when carried away by a gentle breeze.

> “Know this with complete certainty: no one can please God without displeasing wicked people. Let your Fraternity therefore judge that it has pleased almighty God to the degree that it knows it has displeased wicked men.

> “Nevertheless, the defense of the poor must be measured and serious, lest, if you act too harshly in anything, people think that you are acting arrogantly out of youthful impetuosity. Your defense of the oppressed must be such that the humble feel its protection, while the oppressors do not easily find anything arising from ill will for which they can criticize you.

> “Consider therefore what is said to Ezekiel: ‘Son of man … they are unbelievers and subverters among you, and you dwell among scorpions’ (Ezekiel 2:6). Blessed Job also says: ‘I was a brother to dragons and a companion to ostriches’ (Job 30:29). And Paul says to his disciples: ‘In the midst of a crooked and perverse generation, among whom you shine like lights in the world’ (Philippians 2:15). We must therefore walk with all the greater caution because we know that we live among the enemies of God.”  
> *(Register, Book X, letter 36.)*

### 56.

Conscious of this caution of his, Gregory says to the defender Romanus:

> “It has come to us that certain men possessing no discernment at all desire to involve us in their dangers and wish to be defended by ecclesiastical persons in such a way that the ecclesiastical persons themselves may also be held liable for their fault.

> “I therefore admonish you by this present command, and through you our brother and fellow bishop, the lord John, as well as the others who may be able to take part, that you provide ecclesiastical protection—whether you receive my letters or whether they have not been sent—with such moderation that, if some are involved in public thefts, we do not appear to defend them unjustly. Let us not in any way transfer the reputation of wrongdoers onto ourselves through the audacity of indiscriminate defense. Rather, admonishing the Church as far as is proper and offering the word of intercession, help those whom you can, so that you may both assist them and not stain the reputation of the holy Church.”  
> *(Book IX, letter 27.)*

### 57.

Likewise, to Januarius, bishop, after other matters:

> “If any of those concerning whom some dispute exists should perhaps take refuge in the Church, the case must be arranged in such a way that neither they themselves suffer violence nor those who are said to have been oppressed sustain losses. Let it therefore be your concern that those concerned promise them on oath to observe law and justice, and that they be admonished in every respect to depart and render an account of their actions. You should also appoint a defender of your church for them, through whose diligence whatever has been promised to them may be preserved.”  
> *(Book X, letter 38.)*

### 58.

How great Gregory’s humility was can be most clearly understood from many things, including this: in his letters he called all priests brothers and fellow ministers, clerics of various orders beloved sons, laymen lords, and laywomen ladies. He also calmly permitted no one to call him supreme pontiff, universal bishop, or lord.

To pass over what has been collected above on this subject, writing to the patrician Rusticiana, he says:

> “I received the letters of Your Excellence, which, when I was placed in a most serious illness, greatly relieved me through their news of their well-being, their devotion, and their sweetness. But I was distressed by one thing: in the same letters you repeatedly addressed me—as could have been done once—as ‘Your servant, your servant.’ I, who through the burdens of the episcopate have become the servant of all, on what grounds do you call yourself my handmaid, when before receiving the episcopate I was your own servant? Therefore I beg you by almighty God never to let me find this expression in your letters to me again.”  
> *(Book XI, letter 44.)*

### 59.

By the gentleness of this humility, Gregory did not refuse to satisfy not only Queen Theudelinda of the Lombards concerning the Three Chapters, but also, among others, his own subdeacon Sabinus, saying:

[Col. 0212C] “Wicked men have gone out and troubled your minds, understanding neither what they say nor the matters about which they make assertions. They claim that something was diminished from the holy Council of Chalcedon in the time of Justinian of pious memory, a council which we venerate with complete faith and devotion; and thus we receive the four councils of the holy universal Church just as we receive the four books of the holy Gospel. As for the persons concerning whom something had been done after the council’s conclusion, the matter was debated in the time of Justinian of pious memory; yet in such a way that neither was the faith violated in anything, nor was anything else done concerning those persons than what had been established at that same holy Council of Chalcedon. But we anathematize anyone who has presumed to diminish anything from the definition of faith issued at that council, or, as though correcting it, to alter its meaning; rather, we preserve it in every respect exactly as it was issued there. Therefore, dearest son, it is fitting for you to return to the unity of the faith, [161] so that you may be able to conclude your life in peace, lest the evil spirit, unable to prevail against you by other means, find in this matter a way to obstruct you on the day of your departure at the entrance to the heavenly kingdom.” (*Book III, Letter 10.*)

60. Likewise, to Gregoria, the empress’s chamberlain, after other matters:

“Your Sweetness added in your letters that you would continue to trouble me until it was revealed to me in writing that your sins had been forgiven. You have asked for something both difficult and useless. Difficult, indeed, because I am unworthy to receive such a revelation; useless, because you must not become confident about your sins except when, on the final day of your life, you will no longer be able to lament them. Until that day comes, you must always fear your sins with suspicion and trembling, and wash them away with daily tears.” (*Book VII, Letter 25.*)

61. Likewise, to Anastasius, a presbyter of Isauria, after some other matters:

“I know, therefore, how perfect your fraternity is in charity; and whoever greatly loves almighty God ought to have great confidence concerning his neighbor. For it is not places or ranks that make us close to our Creator, but either good merits unite us to him or evil ones separate us. Since, then, it remains uncertain what each person is like inwardly, why do you not dare to write, when you do not know which of us is superior, you or I? I know that you live well, but I recognize that I am burdened with many sins. Yet even if you are yourself a sinner, you are still far better than I, because you bear only your own sins, whereas I bear both my own and those of the people entrusted to me. In this I regard you as exalted, in this as great: you have not advanced before human eyes to a great and lofty position. For often, while honor is bestowed outwardly by human beings, the soul is plunged into the depths, because it is weighed down by cares that tear it apart. But for you almighty God has arranged, in accordance with what is written, ‘Ascents in the heart in the valley of tears’ (Psalm 31:6). You could have appeared to me far higher and far more exalted if you had not accepted the leadership of the monastery called Neas.” (*Book VII, Letter 32.*)

62. Likewise, to Stephen, bishop, among other things:

“You show me in your letters an esteem far greater than I deserve to hear. And it is written: ‘Do not praise a man while he lives’ (Ecclesiasticus 11:30). Although I was not worthy to hear such things, I ask in your prayers that I may become worthy, so that, if you did not say good things about me because they are true, they may become true because you said them.” (*Book VII, Letter 8.*)

63. But lest the humility of so great a prelate be thought to be attested only by words, it remains to demonstrate that same humility of the Father through living deeds, from accounts recently translated for me from the Greeks. They are reported as follows:

“Abbot John, a Persian, a holy and venerable man, related to us concerning the most blessed Pope Gregory of Rome. He said: ‘Once I went to Rome to venerate the shrines of the holy apostles Peter and Paul. One day, while I was standing in the middle of the city, I saw Pope Gregory passing by, and I thought that I should go out before him. When the pope approached me and saw that I was going to place myself before him, I declare before God, brothers, that he himself first threw himself onto the ground before me, and did not rise until I had risen first. Then he embraced me with great humility, gave me three coins with his own hand, and ordered that a cloak and all my necessities be provided for me. I therefore glorified God, who had bestowed upon him such humility toward everyone, together with almsgiving and charity.’” (*Spiritual Meadow*, chapter 151.)

64. Thus it was that the most patient shepherd Gregory, when accused before the emperor Maurice—who was utterly hostile to him—of having afflicted Bishop Malchus, the administrator of his patrimony, in prison for so long over withheld payments that he finally breathed his last, wrote to his deacon Sabinianus in Constantinople:

“There is one thing that you should briefly report to our most serene lords: if I, their servant, had wished to involve myself today in the death of the Lombards, the Lombard nation would now have neither king, nor dukes, nor counts, and would be divided in utter confusion. But because I fear God, I dread involving myself in the death of anyone. As for that same Bishop Malchus, he was neither in custody nor under any affliction; rather, on the day when he pleaded his case and was condemned, he was taken, without my knowledge, by Boniface the notary to his own house. There he dined and was treated with honor by him, but during the night he was suddenly found dead.” (*Book IV, Letter 47.*)

65. Accordingly, in all his words and deeds Gregory kept in view the approaching final day of future recompense, and weighed all the affairs of everyone with all the greater caution as he observed that the end of the world was drawing nearer, its ruin becoming more frequent. Therefore, in his *Gospel Homilies*, he says:

“‘Nation will rise against nation and kingdom against kingdom, and there will be great earthquakes in various places, pestilences, and famines.’” After inserting some intervening words, he adds:

“‘And there will be signs in the sun, moon, and stars, and on earth distress among the nations because of the confusion caused by the roaring of the sea and the waves.’ Of all these things, some we already see fulfilled, while we fear that others will soon come to pass. For we see nations rising against nations, and their oppression weighing upon the earth, more clearly now in our tribulations than we read of it in books. You know how frequently we have heard that earthquakes have overwhelmed countless cities in other parts of the world. We suffer pestilences without interruption. But we have not yet plainly seen signs in the sun, moon, and stars; nevertheless, because these things are not far off, we infer this already from the very alteration of the air. Even before Italy was handed over to be struck by the sword of the heathen, we saw fiery armies in the sky, and the blood of the human race—which was afterward poured out—flashing there. The confusion of the sea and the waves, however, has not yet arisen anew; but since many things already foretold have been fulfilled, there is no doubt that the few remaining things will follow as well, because the fulfillment of past events establishes the certainty of those to come.”

And shortly afterward:

“Behold, my brothers, we now see what we used to hear. The world is oppressed every day by new and ever-increasing evils. You see how many of that innumerable multitude have remained, and yet every day the scourges continue to press upon us, sudden disasters overwhelm us, and new and unforeseen calamities afflict us. For just as in youth the body flourishes, the chest remains strong and sound, the neck muscular, and the arms full; but in old age the stature bends, the withered neck droops, the chest is oppressed by frequent sighs, strength fails, and the breath interrupts the words of one who speaks—indeed, if illness is absent, old age itself is often a sickness—so too the world in its earlier years flourished as though in youth. It was strong for propagating the human race, green with bodily health, and rich with abundant possessions; but now it is weighed down by its own old age and, as though approaching death, is oppressed by troubles that grow ever more frequent.” (*Homily 1 on the Gospels.*)

And again:

“‘Go and preach, saying that the kingdom of heaven is near’ (Matthew 10:7). Now, dearest brothers, even if the Gospel were silent, the world itself cries out that this is so. Its ruins are its voices. For the world, worn down by so many blows and fallen from its glory, shows us that another kingdom, which will follow, is already near. It is already bitter even to those who love it. Its very ruin proclaims that it should not be loved. If a house threatened to collapse while someone lived in it, anyone dwelling there would flee, and whoever had loved it while it stood would hasten to withdraw from it as quickly as possible when it began to fall. If, therefore, the world is falling and we embrace it by loving it, we wish to be crushed rather than to dwell in it, because no consideration separates from its ruin those whom love binds to its sufferings. It is therefore easy now, when we see everything destroyed, to detach our spirit from love of the world. But this was exceedingly difficult at that time when the apostles were sent to preach the invisible heavenly kingdom, while they saw the kingdoms of the earth flourishing far and wide.” (*Homily 4 on the Gospels.*)

66. I shall report what Gregory wrote concerning the affliction of this city, so that those who now live amid its ruins and do not suppose that it was once more orderly and therefore stronger may tremble. For in the eighteenth homily of his exposition of Ezekiel he says:

“What is there now, I ask, that can delight us in this world? Everywhere we see mourning; everywhere we hear groaning. Cities have been destroyed, fortresses overturned, fields laid waste, and the earth reduced to solitude. No inhabitant remains in the countryside, scarcely any dweller in the cities; yet even these small remnants of the human race are still struck daily and without interruption, and the scourges of heavenly justice do not cease, because the faults of our conduct have not been corrected even amid the scourges. We see some led into captivity, others mutilated, and others killed. What, then, is there to delight in during this life, my brothers? If we still love such a world, we love not joys but wounds.

“We see what Rome, which once seemed to be the mistress of the world, has become: battered by immense sufferings in many ways, through the desolation of its citizens, the pressure of its enemies, and the frequency of its ruins. Thus we see fulfilled in it what was foretold through Ezekiel against the city of Samaria: ‘Set on the pot, set it on, I say, and pour water into it, and heap its pieces into it’; and shortly afterward: ‘Its boiling boiled over, and its bones were cooked in its midst’; and again: ‘Heap up the bones which I shall set on fire; the flesh will be consumed, the whole composition will boil, and the bones will waste away. Set it also upon the coals empty, so that it may become hot and its bronze may melt’ (Ezekiel 24:10ff.).

“Then the pot was set before us, when this city was established. Then water was poured into it and its pieces were heaped up, when peoples flocked to it from every direction, boiling with the activities of the world like heated water and melting like pieces of meat in the midst of their own fervor. Of this it is rightly said: ‘Its boiling boiled over, and its bones were cooked in its midst,’ because at first the activity of secular glory grew intensely hot within it, but afterward that glory, together with its followers, failed. By the bones are signified the powerful of this world, and by the flesh the peoples; for just as flesh is supported by bones, so the weakness of the peoples is governed by the powerful of the world.

“But behold, all the powerful of this world have now been removed from it: its bones, therefore, have been cooked. Behold, its peoples have failed: its flesh has melted. Let it therefore be said: ‘Heap up the bones which I shall set on fire; the flesh will be consumed, the whole composition will boil, and the bones will waste away.’ For where is the senate? Where is the people now? The bones have wasted away, the flesh has been consumed, and every order of secular dignity has perished in it. Its entire composition has been boiled away; yet even we few who remain are still pressed daily by swords and countless tribulations.

“Let it therefore be said: ‘Set it also upon the coals empty.’ For the senate is gone and the people have perished; yet in the few who remain, pains and groans multiply every day. Now empty Rome burns.

“But why speak of these things concerning human beings, when we see even its buildings themselves being destroyed as the ruins increase? Hence what follows is fittingly said of the now-empty city: ‘Let it become hot and let its bronze melt.’ For now the pot itself is also being consumed, in which flesh and bones were formerly consumed, because after the people have failed, even the walls collapse.

“Where are those who once rejoiced in its glory? Where is their pomp? Where their pride? Where their frequent and immoderate joy? What was said by the prophet against destroyed Nineveh has been fulfilled in it: ‘Where is the dwelling place of the lions, and the pasture of the lion cubs?’ (Nahum 2:11). Were its leaders and princes not lions, who ranged through the various provinces of the world, seizing booty by violence and slaughter? From this the lion cubs found pasture, because boys, adolescents, young men of the world, and the sons of worldly men flocked here from every direction when they wished to advance in this world.

“But behold, it is now desolate; behold, it is crushed; behold, it is oppressed by groans. No one now runs to it in order to advance in this world. No powerful and violent man remains who might seize booty by oppression. Let us therefore say: ‘Where is the dwelling place of the lions, and the pasture of the lion cubs?’

“What happened to it is what we know was said through the prophet concerning Judea: ‘Enlarge your baldness like the eagle’ (Micah 1:16). Human baldness ordinarily occurs only on the head, but an eagle’s baldness covers its entire body, because when it grows very old, its feathers and plumage fall from all its limbs. Thus it enlarges its baldness like an eagle, because it lost its feathers when it lost its people. The feathers of its wings fell, with which it had been accustomed to fly after prey, because its powerful men, through whom it seized the possessions of others, have perished.”

Likewise, in the second book of the *Dialogues*:

“Moreover,” he said, “the bishop of the Church of Canusium used to come to Benedict, the servant of the Lord, whom the man of God greatly loved for the merit of his life. While he was conversing with him about the arrival of King Totila and the destruction of the city of Rome, he said: ‘This city will be destroyed by that king, so that it will no longer be inhabited.’

“The man of God replied: ‘Rome will not be exterminated by the nations, but, exhausted by storms, lightning, whirlwinds, and earthquakes, it will wither away within itself.’

“We, who see in this dissolved city its shattered walls, houses overturned, and churches destroyed by the whirlwind, now understand the mysteries of that prophecy more clearly than daylight. We see its buildings worn out by long old age and prostrate through the increasing ruins.” (*Dialogues*, book II, chapter 15.)

Likewise, in a letter to John, bishop of Ravenna, after some other matters:

“If there is any way of obtaining it, let your fraternity act with the exarch so that we may make peace with Ariulf, if we are able, because the soldier has been withdrawn from the city of Rome [Note: This word is discussed in the note on Book II, Letter 46 of the *Register*], as he himself knows. As for the Theodosian soldiers who have remained here, since they receive no pay, they scarcely apply themselves even to guarding the walls; and if the abandoned city has no peace, how will it endure?” (*Register*, book II, Letter 46.)

67. Gregory was so burdened by the tumult of so many cares, for the protection alike of souls and of the city, that, falling into the affliction of colic, he not only failed—as he had intended—to treat the mysteries of Ezekiel in sequence, but, weighed down by hostile incursions and numerous bodily weaknesses, abandoned the work of exposition altogether, lamented that he had reached those days, and begged with all his strength for the dissolution of his body. Therefore, he complains to the same John, bishop, saying:

“That I have not replied to your blessedness on many matters, attribute not to my sluggishness but to my illness. For, because of my sins, at the time when Ariulf came to the city of Rome, killing some and mutilating others, I was afflicted by such grief that I fell into the illness of colic.” (*Ibid.*)

Likewise, in his exposition of the final vision of the prophet Ezekiel:

“Because I have been pressed by many cares, I have not been able to examine the entire book of the prophet Ezekiel in sequence before your charity. Your good desires have nevertheless seen fit to ask that at least its final vision—the vision granted to him concerning the building situated on the mountain, and the obscurest of all his visions—should be expounded. Indeed, I must obey your wish. But two things disturb my mind in this matter.

“First, this very vision is covered by such clouds of obscurity that scarcely anything in it can be seen when the light of understanding shines through. Second, we have learned that Agilulf, king of the Lombards, hastening with the greatest urgency to besiege us, has crossed the Po. Consider, therefore, in obscure and mystical meanings what a wretched mind can accomplish when occupied by the disturbances of its fear. The more it busies itself with earthly things, the less it sees of heavenly matters; because it is led outside itself by its cares, it is greatly diminished within. For it is written: ‘An earthly dwelling weighs down the mind that thinks of many things’ (Wisdom 9:15). Consider what a mind divided can accomplish when even a mind gathered together is unable to penetrate the things above. We all know that a river divided into many channels dries up in its bed.”

Likewise, in his treatises on the same prophet, homily 11:

“Whether,” he says, “the righteous falls into guilt or the sinner falls into death, the watchman must fear lest the backlash of sinners envelop him also because of his silence. But meanwhile, as I speak, I wish to turn my eyes away from myself—and behold, the divine word again makes me stumble against myself, so that I may see my negligence and fear that these words I hear are being spoken to me.

“For, as I said above, whose heart, scattered among innumerable cares, can gather itself back to itself? When can I both carefully attend to all the things around me and contemplate myself with an undivided mind? When can I correct the wicked by pursuing their crimes, preserve the conduct of the good by praising and admonishing them, and show terror to some and gentleness to others? When can I both think about what my brothers need and remain concerned for the city’s defenses against hostile swords, taking precautions lest the citizens perish in a sudden attack, and amid all these things fully and effectively offer the word of exhortation for the protection of souls?

“To speak of God belongs to a mind that is greatly tranquil and free. For the tongue is guided well in speech when the understanding has rested securely in peace. Shaken water does not reflect the image of the one who looks into it; the face of the observer is seen in it only when it is still. What exhortation, then, can your watchman offer you, dearest brothers, when he is disturbed by the confusion of so many things?”

And shortly afterward:

“Even after contrition and tears, a priest is compelled to learn whatever his children need, to hear patiently what his spirit rejects, and, after sighing for heavenly things, to bear the burdens of any carnal people. Often he must transform his heart into a different condition when others arrive. At one moment he rejoices over spiritual gains; but when someone sorrowful arrives, unless he takes that person’s sorrow upon himself and sympathizes with his tribulation, he does not share in it. At another moment he grieves over the losses of souls; but suddenly people arrive who rejoice in their own prosperity. If the priest does not rejoice with their joy, he is thought to love less the children whose happiness he does not share, especially since Paul says: ‘Rejoice with those who rejoice, weep with those who weep’ (Romans 12:15).

“I see nothing so burdensome in the priestly office as bending the firmness of the mind through compassion and changing one’s disposition according to the persons who arrive; yet this is extremely necessary. For when, through his preaching, a sinner is recalled to the grace of good works, if the preacher himself appears ungrateful, what follows?” (*Preface to Book II on Ezekiel.*)

Likewise, at the end of the same volume:

[Note: Thus the Colbertinus and other manuscripts. The printed editions, supported by Reg. and the codex of Sainte-Marie, Paris: “if henceforth I shall cease speaking.”]

“Behold, dearest brothers, with the Lord’s gift we have searched out these matters before you as best we could. Let no one reproach me if I cease speaking after this discourse, because, as you all see, our tribulations have increased. We are surrounded on every side by swords; on every side we fear the danger of imminent death. Some return to us with their hands cut off; others are reported captured, others killed.

“Now I am compelled to restrain my tongue from exposition, because ‘my soul is weary of my life’ (Job 10). Let no one now seek in me a zeal for sacred eloquence, because ‘my harp is turned to mourning, and my organ to the voice of those who weep’ (Job 30). The eye of my heart is no longer watchful in investigating mysteries, because ‘my soul has slumbered from weariness’ (Psalm 118). Reading is now less sweet to my mind, because ‘I have forgotten to eat my bread because of the sound of my groaning’ (Psalm 101). For one who is not permitted to live, how can it be fitting to speak of the mystical meanings of Sacred Scripture? And when I am compelled daily to drink bitter things, when can I offer sweet ones?” (*Final Homily.*)

Likewise, to Italica, a patrician woman, and Venantius, a former monk and patrician:

“I took care to ask certain people coming from Sicily, with the concern I ought to have shown, about your excellencies’ health, but they answered me sadly about the persistence of your illnesses. In saying this, I too find nothing else concerning myself that I ought to report to you except that, because of my sins, it has now been eleven months during which it has been very rare for me to be able to rise from bed at all. I am so oppressed by the pains of gout and by such anguish of suffering that life is a very heavy punishment for me. Every day I waste away in pain and sigh while awaiting the remedy of death.

“In the clergy and people of this city, such great fevers have broken out that scarcely anyone, free or slave, remains capable of performing any office or service. From the neighboring cities, reports of the daily slaughter caused by mortality reach us. As for how Africa is being devastated by death and illness, I believe that, since you are nearer, you have learned this more precisely. Those coming from the East report even greater desolations. Since in all these things we recognize a general affliction approaching the end of the world, we ought not to be excessively distressed by our own sufferings.” (*Register*, book IX, Letter 123.)

Likewise, to Eulogius, patriarch of Alexandria:

“After a year had passed, I received the exceedingly gracious letters of your holiness, to which until now I have been unable to reply because of the severity of my illness. For behold, it is now almost two years since I have been confined to my little bed, and I am afflicted by such pains of gout that scarcely on feast days can I rise for as much as three hours to celebrate the solemnities of Mass. Immediately afterward I am forced by severe pain to lie down again, so that I cannot endure my torment without interrupting it with groans.

“Sometimes the pain is mild, sometimes excessive; yet it is neither so mild that it goes away nor so excessive that it kills me. Thus it happens that, though I am daily in death, I am driven away from death. Nor is this surprising, since as a grievous sinner I am held for so long confined in such a prison of corruption. Hence I am compelled to cry out: ‘Bring my soul out of prison, that I may confess your name, O Lord’ (Psalm 141, final verse).
