“But because I do not yet deserve to obtain this through my own prayers, I ask that the prayer of your holiness offer me the help of your intercession and make me free from the burden of sin and corruption, into that liberty of the glory of the children of God which you know so well.” (*Book X, Letter 35.*)

Likewise, to the same person:

“I ask that your holiness pray for me with greater earnestness, because I am ceaselessly oppressed by the pains of gout, the swords of the barbarians, and the afflictions of cares. But if you extend to me the help of your prayer, I believe that you will strongly assist me against every adversity.” (*Book IX, Letter 78.*)

Likewise, to the same person:

“I therefore ask you to pray more earnestly for me, a sinner, because bodily pain, the bitterness of my heart arising from the afflictions of cares, and the immense devastation caused by mortality, amid so many barbarian swords, afflict me severely. Amid all these things I seek not temporal but eternal consolation, which I cannot obtain by myself; rather, I trust that through the intercession of your blessedness I may obtain it.” (*Book XIII, Letter 41.*)

Likewise, to Marinianus, bishop of Ravenna [Note: In the printed editions, in the Uticensis manuscript, and in three Paris manuscripts: “to the bishop of Arabia.” In the common editions this bishop is now called Maximianus, now Marianus, or Marinianus]:

“It has been a very long time since I have been able to rise from bed. At one moment the pain of gout torments me; at another, I do not know what fire spreads with pain throughout my entire body. It often happens that at one and the same time burning contends with pain in me, and both body and spirit fail me. I cannot enumerate the many other necessities by which I am afflicted beyond the illnesses I have mentioned. I say briefly, however, that the infection of harmful fluid soaks through me that living is a punishment for me, and I eagerly await death, which I believe, with my groans, to be my only remedy.

“Therefore, most holy brother, implore for me the mercy of divine compassion, so that in his kindness he may mitigate the scourges of his chastisement against me and grant me the patience to endure, lest, God forbid, my heart break into impatience through excessive weariness, and a fault that could have been healed through punishment grow through murmuring.” (*Book XI, Letter 32.*)

Likewise, to the patrician Rusticiana:

“I have been both greatly saddened and greatly pleased by the trouble of gout which you indicated had befallen you. I was pleased because the harmful fluid, moving downward, has surely abandoned the upper parts. But I was saddened because I fear that in so frail a body you are enduring excessive pain. For where flesh is lacking, what strength can there be to resist pain?

“As for me, whom you know as I once was, bitterness of spirit and constant irritation, and consequently the trouble of gout, have so afflicted me that my body has become dried up as though in a tomb; hence I can now rarely rise from bed.” (*Book XI, Letter 44.*)

Likewise, to the same person:

“I live amid such groaning and occupations that I regret having reached the days I am living, and my only consolation is the expectation of death. Therefore I ask that you pray for me, so that he may bring me more quickly out of this prison of the flesh and prevent me from being tortured longer by such labors.” (*Book XIII, Letter 22.*)

Likewise, to Anastasius of Antioch:

“I ask you to pray more earnestly for the weakness of my heart, so that almighty God, through your intercession, may protect my mind from every evil, rescue me more quickly from so many storms of this tempest, and lead me to the shore of eternal rest.” (*Book VIII, Letter 2.*)

68. At last, Gregory was divinely heard through such prayers. After illuminating the See of the Catholic and Apostolic Holy Roman Church for thirteen years, six months, and ten days with doctrines and most blessed works alike, [Note: These chronological data agree with A.D. 604, although the Venerable Bede places the holy Doctor’s death in 605; Paul the Deacon, following him in Book IV of his *History of the Lombards*, assigns it to the eighth indiction. Mabillon.] in the second year of the reign of Phocas, in the seventh indiction, on the fourth day before the Ides of March, he was taken away from the corruption of the flesh, destined to be exalted in the glory of perpetual incorruption.

Throughout his life he had built no new basilicas; nevertheless, he annually repaired the old ones that had been built, restoring them with the greatest care. He enriched them with revenues, lights, services, and gifts. In the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter he built a canopy (*fastigium*) of the purest silver, which was later transferred by Pope Leo III to the basilica dedicated to the name of Saint Mary, the Sixtine Basilica; and in the basilica of the blessed apostle Paul he likewise arranged another canopy over the altar.

His venerable body was buried in the outer portico of the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter, before the ancient sacristy, where Leo, Simplicius, Gelasius, and Symmachus, bishops of the apostolic see, together with several others, are proclaimed by their epitaphs to have been buried. It was honored by the following inscription:

> Receive, O earth, this body taken from a body,  
> that you may restore it, God giving life.  
>   
> The spirit seeks the stars; the laws of death will harm nothing  
> for whom the death of this life is rather the way to another life.  
>   
> In this tomb are enclosed the limbs of the supreme pontiff,  
> who may live everywhere forever through innumerable good works.  
>   
> He overcame hunger with food and cold with clothing,  
> and by sacred admonitions shielded souls from the enemy.  
>   
> By his deeds he fulfilled whatever he taught in speech,  
> so that, speaking mystical words, he might be an example.  
>   
> He turned the English to Christ through the guidance of piety,  
> winning for the faith hosts from a new people.  
>   
> This was your labor, this your care, O shepherd:  
> to offer the Lord abundant gains from the flock.  
>   
> Having become God’s steward through these things, rejoice in your triumphs,  
> for now, without end, you possess the reward of your works.

[Note: Bede: “He converted the English to Christ,” and so forth.]

69. After this most generous shepherd had died, an exceedingly severe famine descended in that same year. How great a patron Rome then lost, although the scarcity of resources throughout almost the entire world made it evident, the ferocity of the envious nevertheless failed to acknowledge. For, as the story is handed down by our predecessors [Note: Baronius regards this history as doubtful under the year 604, and not without reason, since it rests on the testimony of no certain author, and Isidore, Ildefonsus, and Paterius are silent about it], when the instigators of ancient slanders were loudly accusing Gregory of being a prodigal squanderer of the treasure of the manifold patriarchate, once their private resources had failed, they began together to thirst for the burning of his books.

After they had already burned some and wished to burn the rest, his closest associate, the deacon Peter, with whom he had discussed the four books of the *Dialogues*, is said to have resisted with the utmost force. He declared that burning the books would accomplish nothing toward erasing Gregory’s memory, since copies of them had traveled throughout the world in response to the requests of various people. He added that it was an enormous sacrilege to burn so many such books of so great a Father, above whose head he himself had very often seen the Holy Spirit in the likeness of a dove while Gregory was dictating.

When the deacon saw that the formerly devoted people, taking advantage of the circumstances, were joining battle with the envious, he is said to have challenged the judgment of them all in this way: if he deserved to die immediately after confirming by oath what he had said, they should desist from burning the books; but if he survived his testimony, he too would hand himself over to the burners.

Accordingly, when the venerable Levite Peter ascended the ambo with the Gospels, as soon as he had borne witness to Gregory’s holiness, he breathed out his spirit amid words of true confession. Free from the agony of death, he deserved to be buried beside the base of the tower, as may still be seen today, as a confessor of the truth.

[Note: *Pyrgobasis* is a towered structure; the base of a tower is its foot or support. MABILLON. This seems to be understood as a small spiral tower containing the staircase by which one ascended into the ambo.]

### 70

Hence it is that the Holy Spirit is customarily depicted in the form of a dove above the head of Gregory as he writes, and that the greater part of his expositions—remembered, to be sure, as having been burned by envious men—is no longer extant. He himself seems to indicate their substance to John, subdeacon of Ravenna and his *responsalis* (representative), describing it as follows among other things [Col. 0222C]:

> “Because my once most dear son Claudius had heard me say certain things about Proverbs, the Song of Songs, the Prophets, the books of Kings, and also the Heptateuch—things which, because of my weakness, I could not commit to writing—he himself dictated them according to his own understanding, so that they might not perish through forgetfulness, intending to bring these same materials to me at a suitable time so that they might be dictated more accurately. When he had read them to me, I found that the sense of my statements had been altered very unprofitably in many respects.”

[Note: Thus the manuscripts. But the printed editions have: “very greatly in many respects.”]

> “Therefore it is necessary that Your Experience, setting aside every excuse and delay, go to his monastery, have the brothers assemble, and bring forward, in complete truth, however many sheets he has brought together from various Scriptures. Receive them yourself and transmit them to me as quickly as possible.”

*(Register, Book XII, Letter 24.)*

Indeed, since Gregory’s diligence could not have failed—he lived for almost three years after this—it is plainly established that he composed more books than are now extant. Briefly commemorating these in his epitaph, someone says [Col. 0223A]:

> “He expounded Job, Ezekiel, the Gospels, and the Pastoral Rule, and many other works.”

One should understand this to mean works that can no longer be found, since they were in fact burned before they were published, just like the rest of his writings that are still kept under guard in the holy Roman Church, lest they become entirely public.

### 71

Accordingly, if the whole period during which Gregory engaged in exposition and composed the books now extant is examined more carefully, it extends from his diaconate to the penultimate year of his pontificate. Although, when the treachery of the Lombards was raging, he ceased expounding books after the Treatises on Ezekiel, he never ceased, as long as he was able to live, expounding letters. Of these he left in his archive as many books as he lived years.

[Note: This is the reading in the Utica manuscript, and an excellent one, although other manuscripts and printed editions read “from which the thirteenth…” See our Preface to the letters, no. 5.]

For this reason he left the fourteenth book of letters incomplete in the seventh indiction, since he did not reach the end of that indiction. From their abundance, in the time of Pope Hadrian I, certain decretal letters were excerpted for each indiction and gathered into two volumes, as they are seen today.

And when Gregory had long since entered the monastery, where an angel of the Lord had found him writing in the guise of a shipwrecked man, he had evidently dictated certain materials so that he might approach the exposition of the profound subject matter into which he was able to penetrate in the Book of Job all the more prepared, and all the more skilled through his habit of dictation.

### 72

Thus, while Gregory was a deacon, when the business of the apostolic see detained him in the city of Constantinople and an embassy entrusted to Leander, bishop of Spain, had brought him there on account of the faith of the Visigoths [Col. 0223C], the same Leander—as I recall having said in the first book—pressed Gregory, together with the brothers then attached to him, with the greatest insistence to begin expounding the Book of blessed Job *(Book I, 27)*.

With these men present, he spoke the earlier portions of the book before their eyes; and, when he found a little more free time, he dictated the later portions as he expounded them. When he had more ample intervals at his disposal, he added much, removed little, and left some passages just as he had found them; then, by revising the books, he arranged what had been excerpted while he was speaking before the eyes of his listeners.

When, already bishop of Rome, he dictated the final portions, he carefully considered the style in which he had spoken the first portions and arranged that, passing over what he had said with diligent revision, he should raise it, as it were, to the form of dictation, so that what he had dictated would not differ greatly from the speech of one conversing. Thus, while one part was extended and the other drawn together, a work not unlike the first would be produced in a different form.

Although he left almost a third part of the work just as he had delivered it in conversation, because, while the brothers were urging him to expound other matters, they did not wish this portion to be revised more closely, he completed the work—extended through thirty-five books—in six codices, while striving to comply with their many requests, now through the ministry of exposition, now through the ascent of contemplation, and now through the instrument of moral instruction.

[Note: The printed editions, together with three Paris manuscripts, read “through the mystery of exposition.”]

He first distributed copies of these books among the monasteries of the City, and finally sent them to the same Bishop Leander.

### 73

At the very beginning of his episcopate, when John, bishop of the city of Ravenna, had humbly reproached him for wishing, though so capable a man, to evade the burdens of pastoral care by hiding himself, he composed the book of the *Pastoral Rule*. Dividing it according to a fourfold scheme, he taught that it deserves very careful consideration: when necessity requires it, how one should come to the summit of governance; once duly arrived there, how one should live; how, living well, one should teach; and how, teaching rightly, one should recognize one’s own weakness each day with as much reflection as possible [Col. 0224B]—lest humility avoid advancement, or life contradict one’s attainment, or doctrine fail life, or presumption exalt doctrine.

[Note: Some printed editions corruptly read: “lest it avoid the approach of humility.”]

First, therefore, let fear moderate one’s desire for office. Afterwards, let a life of integrity commend the teaching office accepted by one who did not seek it. Then it is necessary that the good of the shepherd, which is displayed in living, also be propagated through speech. Finally, every perfect work must be humbled by consideration of one’s own weakness, lest pride of exaltation extinguish it before the eyes of the hidden Judge.

And because he had learned that certain ignorant men had conspired to obtain the priesthood, and foresaw that others would conspire to do so—men who, unable to measure themselves, desired to teach what they had not learned, and who judged the burden of teaching to be lighter precisely because they did not understand its greatness—he rebuked them at the very beginning of his book, so that if ever unlearned and reckless men should desire to occupy the citadel of teaching, they might be driven back from the audacity of their rashness at the very gate of Gregory’s speech.

Anatolius, the deacon and his *apocrisiarius*, had once presented this book to the emperor when the emperor requested and commanded it. The great Anastasius, bishop of Antioch, translated it into Greek and made this venerable work available to the Eastern churches.

### 74

Next, as I have already related in the second book of this work, while Gregory still possessed sufficient voice and bodily strength for speaking, he went about the stations and proclaimed twenty homilies on the Gospel before the people at different times. He did dictate the remaining homilies of the same number, but, as his stomach grew weak through continual illness and fatigue, he allowed others to recite them *(Book IX, Letter 52)*. He sent copies of these to Secundus, a servant of God, at his request.

### 75

When Gregory’s intimate companions repeatedly and earnestly asked him to write something about the miracles of the fathers, he wrote to Maximian, bishop of Syracuse, saying:

> “My brothers, who live familiarly with me, press me in every way to write briefly about some of the miracles of the Fathers which we have heard occurred in Italy. For this task I greatly need the assistance of your charity, so that you may briefly indicate to me whatever comes back to your memory, and whatever you have happened to learn. I remember that you reported certain things about the abbot Nonnosus, who was with the lord Anastasius near Pentomis, but I have committed them to oblivion [Col. 0225A]. I therefore ask that these, and any other such matters, be set down in your letters and sent to me quickly—unless you yourself are coming to me.”

*(Register, Book III, Letter 51.)*

Strengthened by this, Gregory interrupted his deeper study of exposition and, with Peter his deacon, set forth the miracles of the holy Fathers through inquiry and response; he distinguished them merely by headings bearing their names [Note: The Bigot and Utica manuscripts read: “the pursuit of another exposition”]. He arranged them into four books, so that, just as in his books of exposition he had taught what virtues ought to be diligently pursued, so, through the written accounts of the saints’ miracles, he might demonstrate with the clearest light how glorious those same virtues had been.

Zacharias, bishop of the holy Roman Church and highly learned in both Greek and Latin, translated these books into Greek in the time of the emperor Constantine, approximately one hundred and seventy-five years later, and disseminated them among the Eastern churches.

[Note: See Book II of the *Dialogues*, at the final chapter, and consult the notes. The Greek translation is discussed at length in the Preface to the *Dialogues*.]

Nevertheless, the crafty perversity of the Greeks, when commemorating the Holy Spirit proceeding from the Father, erased and removed the name of the Son by its own arbitrary act.

### 76

He also treated the first and last portions of the prophet Ezekiel, which seemed more obscure, at the request of the Romans. Dividing them into twenty-two homilies, he demonstrated how much light they contain within; and, as was made clear above, he brought this work of exposition to an end while treating these passages.

### 77

Although the learned men of later times truthfully teach that these books were composed both with the most upright judgments and in the most brilliant style of rhetorical eloquence, blessed Gregory, out of the sweetness of his humility, calls them uncultivated. Among other things he writes to Bishop Leander:

> “I ask that, as you read through the statements of this work—surely the *Moralia*—you not seek in them the foliage of words, since throughout the sacred writings the lightness of unfruitful loquacity is deliberately restrained by their interpreters, while the planting of a grove in the temple of God is forbidden. And we all undoubtedly know that whenever the stalks of an excessively luxuriant crop grow thick with leaves, the grains swell with less fullness in the ears.
>
> “For this reason I have also disdained to preserve the very art of speaking that the teachings of external disciplines recommend. As the tenor of this letter itself shows, I do not avoid the collision of *metacism* [Note: Or rather, *mutacism*: the Greeks called it μυτακισμός (*mytakismós*), when the letter *m* is repeated excessively or recklessly, producing a faulty collision. See Vossius, *Institutiones Oratoriae*, Book IV, chapter 2, §2.]; I do not avoid the confusion of barbarism; I even disregard hiatuses, changes, and the cases governed by prepositions. For I consider it profoundly unworthy to confine the words of the heavenly oracle within the rules of Donatus. Indeed, these rules were not preserved by any interpreters in the authority of Holy Scripture.”

[Note: Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions have: “by the interpreters of that time” or “by any interpreter,” and so forth.]

> “Since our exposition plainly arises from Scripture, it is entirely fitting that, as an offspring brought forth, it should imitate the appearance of its mother.”

From these words it may be recognized that Gregory did not strive for ornate diction; rather, he was liable to it through the residual habit of his former secular training.

Isidore, bishop of the city of Seville, admired the harmony of his eloquence in his exposition of Genesis:

> “These works,” he says, “were drawn from the authors Origen, Victorinus, Ambrose, Jerome, Cassian, Augustine, Fulgentius, and, in our own times, from the distinguished speaker Gregory.”

Bede the presbyter, too, in his book on rhetorical figures, stating that orators employ *homoeoteleuton*, offered the following example:

> “Blessed Job, known only to God and to himself, had to be brought to our knowledge through temptation. He was struck with a wound so that he might spread the fragrance of his strength more widely, just as, in the manner of spices, he would give forth a better fragrance when subjected to pressure.”

It is recognized that blessed Pope Gregory himself very frequently employed the figure by which he said this; and I believe that such passages are what Jerome calls the polished declamations of rhetoricians.

### 78

But Gregory, warned by the caution of his humility, not only despised the fragrance of his eloquence; he also called his own dictation bran, in comparison with another’s work, and most emphatically forbade his books to be read while he lived. Among other things he wrote to Innocentius, prefect of Africa:

> “We greatly rejoice in your devotion, by which you wished a copy of the book on holy Job to be sent to you, since we see you devoting yourself to a work that neither allows you entirely to go out of yourself nor fails to gather you back again to your heart, dispersed as you are among worldly concerns. But if you wish to be nourished with a delicious food, read the little works of blessed Augustine, your fellow countryman, and do not seek our bran in comparison with his rye bread.”

*(Register, Book X, Letter 37.)*

[Note: The Bigot and Utica manuscripts read: “fine flour.”]

Likewise, to John, bishop of Syracuse:

> “Moreover, I hear that Your Fraternity has some of the things I remember having written read at your table before strangers. I do not think this should be done, because what you do out of charity may be attributed by some, as far as I am concerned, to vainglory. Therefore, before strangers read the sayings of the ancients, by whose authority those who hear them may be reformed.”

*(Book VIII, Letter 9.)*

Likewise, to John, subdeacon of Ravenna, after much else:

> “I have been informed that my most reverend fellow bishop Marinianus has the commentaries on blessed Job read publicly at the vigils. I did not receive this favorably, because that work is not popular and produces an impediment rather than progress for uneducated hearers. But tell him to read the commentaries on the Psalms at the vigils, since these especially form the minds of worldly people toward good morals. For I do not wish that, while I am in this flesh, whatever I may happen to have said should easily become known to men.”

*(Book XII, Letter 24.)*

### 79

How carefully Gregory recognized his own weakness—he who, as I think, has been sufficiently shown to have reached the summit of governance humbly, to have lived well upon reaching this work, and to have taught rightly by living well—he makes clear in the final book of the *Moralia*, when he says:

> “When this work has been completed, I see that I must return to myself. For even when our mind tries to speak rightly, it is scattered outside itself. While words are being considered so that they may be uttered properly, they draw the integrity of the mind outward and diminish it.
>
> “Therefore we must return from public speech to the senate-house of the heart, so that, as though in a council of deliberation, I may summon the thoughts of my mind to examine myself, in order that I may see there whether I have spoken evil carelessly or good things improperly. For good is then spoken well when the speaker seeks, through what he says, to please only the One from whom he received it.
>
> “Although I do not find that I have said certain evil things, nevertheless I do not defend myself by claiming that I have said none at all. If, receiving certain good things from God, I have spoken them, I confess that through my own fault I have spoken them less well than I ought. For when I return inwardly to myself, setting aside the foliage of words and the branches of sentences, and carefully inspect the very root of my intention, I recognize that I wished above all to please God through it. Yet, somehow, an intention of human praise secretly inserts itself into that same intention by which I strive to please God.
>
> “When I discern this later and too slowly, I find that I am doing otherwise from how I know I began. For often, while our intention begins rightly before God’s eyes, an intention of human praise, secretly attached to it and catching up with it as though on the road, follows and overtakes it. Thus food is indeed taken out of necessity, but during the eating, when gluttony secretly steals in, the pleasure of eating becomes mingled with it. Hence it often happens that we complete for the sake of pleasure the bodily refreshment which we began for the sake of health.
>
> “We must therefore acknowledge that our right intention, which seeks to please God alone, is sometimes accompanied by a less right intention that, through God’s gifts, seeks to please men. If we are strictly examined by God concerning these matters, where does any place of salvation remain, since our evil things are wholly evil, while the good things we believe we possess can in no way be wholly good?
>
> “Yet I believe it worthwhile that I should disclose without hesitation to fraternal ears everything that I secretly reproach in myself. For because I did not conceal what I perceived when expounding, I do not conceal in confession what I suffer. Through exposition I have revealed gifts; through confession I uncover wounds.
>
> “And because in this great human race there are neither lowly people lacking who need to be instructed by my words, nor great people lacking who need to pity my recognized weakness, through these two acts I offer care to other brothers as far as I can, and hope to receive it from others. To the former I have said through exposition what they should do; to the latter I disclose through confession what they should spare. I do not withhold medicines of words from the former; from the latter I do not conceal the laceration of my wounds.
>
> “Therefore I ask that whoever reads this offer me the support of his prayer before the strict Judge, and wash away with tears whatever he discovers to be filthy in me. Through the power of prayer and exposition bestowed upon him, my reader surpasses me in return if, while receiving words through me, he offers tears for me.”

### 80

The venerable body of this most blessed Gregory, translated approximately fifty years later by Gregory IV, bishop of the apostolic see [Note: Read “two hundred and twenty-five years,” since Gregory IV began to occupy the see in 827. Or it should be read, “almost fifty years earlier.” In the *Register*: “after many years.”], is placed beneath the altar bearing his name, in front of the new secretarium, with apses constructed as they are now seen.

[Note: Most printed editions have “beneath the names of his altar.” The Bollandists corrected this error; it can certainly be refuted easily from the manuscripts. Besides this translation, see another in the fourth Benedictine century, the ninth of Christ, where it is reported that the sacred relics of the holy Doctor were transferred to the monastery of Saint Medard of Soissons, while his head was given to the Benedictine monastery of Saint Peter of Jouy at Sens.]

There his annual solemnity is celebrated with the greatest reverence, while all vie with one another in keeping vigil through the night. On that occasion his pallium, his reliquary crosses, and also his belt are customarily kissed.

Considered individually, these objects clearly represent both the man’s antiquity, the modesty of his clothing, and the character of his monastic profession. For, since his pallium is seen to have been woven from shining white linen and pierced by no needles, it is understood that it was wrapped around his shoulders but not fastened, as is shown in the oldest mosaics and paintings.

The fact that the reliquary crosses containing relics appear to have been made of thin silver and suspended from his neck on a cheap pallium demonstrates the modesty of his dress.

Moreover, the thinness of his belt—which never exceeds the measurement of one inch—makes it abundantly clear that he preserved the appearance of the monastic discipline once established by Saint Benedict, whose life he himself described and whose rule he praised in the *Dialogues*. This is especially evident since the same venerable doctor Gregory did not know Greek and sent the monks of his monastery, who were certainly bound by Benedict’s Rule, into Saxony.

### 81

That he did not know Greek he himself testifies in a letter to Eusebius, bishop of Thessalonica, writing:

> “The bearer of this letter, Theodore, a reader of the Church, came to the threshold of the holy apostles. Since, as a stranger, he was unknown there, he innocently deposited with the monk Andrew, who had been enclosed near Saint Paul, the property and documents he had brought, trusting that his mind would correspond with his appearance, as we too had previously thought.
>
> “But Andrew was found to be so depraved that, if his folly had been permitted a little longer under the appearance of enclosure, he would have deceived the souls of many through the falsehood of his wickedness and would have produced no small scandals wherever he could.
>
> “Among the other things that Andrew wickedly conceived and did, he also falsified the letter which you sent to us, after it had been deposited with him by the aforementioned reader, so that anyone who read it would clearly judge that you possessed neither Catholic nor sound opinions.
>
> “Thus it happened that, while we were diligently seeking the truth, the iniquity that had lain hidden in him was made public; and so many things were found in him that they would scarcely have been believed even of some criminal layman.
>
> “And because, among his various evils, he also wrote certain discourses and placed them under our name, and because we fear that he may have sent them somewhere, let Your Fraternity be vigilant. If you discover anything of this kind, have it cut out and entirely destroyed, so that what an unlearned man, ignorant of letters and of divine Scripture, labeled with our name, as we have said, may not infect the minds of some.
>
> “For we neither know Greek nor have ever composed any work in Greek.”

*(Register, Book XI, Letter 69.)*

### 82

That the monks whom Gregory sent into Saxony were bound by the Rule of Saint Benedict is also shown, among other things, by the fact that it is scarcely possible to find in those regions any monk descended from his disciples who does not observe the Rule of Benedict both in profession and in dress.

Therefore, just as it is established that the Gregorian monastery was turned from Latin culture toward Greek culture by necessity rather than by choice, so it faithfully awaits, with the Lord’s favor, its return once more to the cultivation of Latin.

[Note: Or was the monastery of Saint Andrew perhaps granted to Greek monks by Pope Stephen III, who likewise assigned to Greek monks the monastery dedicated to Saint Dionysius the Areopagite that he himself had built? In any case, that asceterium of Saint Andrew was eventually restored to the Benedictines, in accordance with the wish of John the Deacon, and finally assigned to the Camaldolese by Gregory XIII. Mabillon.]

### 83

In the atrium of this venerable monastery, by Gregory’s command, two very ancient images are still seen artistically painted beside the *nymphium*.

[Note: “It is a temple of women, or a part of a temple assigned to women,” says Mabillon. Bollandus, however, takes *nymphium* here as a bath or fountain, because the nymphs were goddesses of waters.]

In one of them blessed Peter the apostle is seen seated, receiving with his right hand the right hand of Gordianus, the *regionarius*, namely Gregory’s father, who is standing.

[Note: That image of Gordianus which Baronius presents in the *Annals*, and which those who published Gregory’s works in the Vatican press—Gussanvillaeus and, more recently, our Mabillon in the *Benedictine Annals*—had engraved, does not appear to be the same one that John the Deacon describes here. For where is Peter the apostle receiving Gordianus by the right hand? Certainly, in these images Gregory is seen between Gordianus and Silvia, who turn their faces somewhat toward him. More will be said of these images below.]

Gordianus wears a chestnut-colored *planeta*, beneath the *planeta* a dalmatic, and leggings on his feet. He is tall, with an elongated face, green eyes, a moderate beard, thick hair, and a serious expression.

In the other image Gregory’s mother, Silvia, is depicted seated. She is covered with a white veil, wrapped from the right shoulder across toward the left in such a way that beneath it she draws out her hand as though from a *planeta*. Around the breast below the throat, an under-tunic of a nearly milky color appears; it falls in a broad sweep over her feet and is distinguished by two bands, like those of dalmatics but much wider.

She is of full stature, with a face that is round and fair, though already wrinkled by old age; nevertheless, old age itself indicates that she had been extraordinarily beautiful. Her eyes are gray-blue and large, her eyebrows moderate, her lips handsome, and her expression cheerful.

On her head she wears a matron’s mitre of gleaming white *brandeum*, sparsely marked [reading uncertain].

[Note: Bigot and Utica have *prandei* in this passage instead of the uncertain reading. Utica reads “broad through its sparse patterns.” Mabillon thinks the reading should be *nimbatam*, “surrounded with a nimbus.” For, he says, a *nimbus* is a transverse band sewn in gold onto linen at women’s foreheads.]

She appears to be about to make the sign of the cross with the two fingers of her right hand, while holding an open psalterium in her left, in which this is written:

> “My soul lives, and it shall praise you, and your judgments shall help me.”

*(Psalm 118, final verse but one.)*

[Note: These details too are omitted from the commonly circulated image of Saint Silvia.]

From the right elbow toward the left, rising around the shoulders, an inscription curves upward and reads:

> “Gregory made this for his mother Silvia.”

The note concerning the mitre also cites Virgil and Lucretius:

> “And now that Paris, with his half-manly retinue, his chin and dripping hair bound beneath a Maeonian cap …”

A mitre had fillets, which Lucretius in Book IV calls *anademata* by a Greek word [Col. 0230C]. The same Virgil says in *Aeneid* IX:

> “And mitres have their fillets.”

[Col. 0230B] 84. In a small apse behind the brothers’ cellar, Gregory himself is displayed painted on a plaster disk by the same artist’s skill.

[Note: The printed editions have *in absidicula*. Gussanvillaeus and many printed editions also read *aurificis* (“of a goldsmith”) instead of *artificis* (“of an artist”).]

He is of proper and well-formed stature, with a face so evenly balanced between the length of his father’s face and the roundness of his mother’s that, while somewhat rounded, it appears most becomingly elongated.

His beard is moderately reddish in the manner of his father’s. He is so nearly bald that in the middle of his forehead he has a few sparse twin curls, turned toward the right. He has a round and spacious crown, with darkish hair neatly twisted and hanging below the middle of his ear.

His forehead is handsome, his eyebrows raised and long but thin, his pupils brown [Note: Mabillon, Gussanvillaeus, and others read “with tawny pupils.” Bollandus follows the manuscripts.], not large but open, with full flesh beneath the eyes. His nose descends in a fine straight line from the root of the eyebrows [Note: In the Regius, German, Bigot, and Utica manuscripts: “of the eyelashes.”], is broader around the middle, then slightly curved, and at the end protrudes with open nostrils.

His mouth is red, his lips thick and somewhat divided, his cheeks well formed, and his chin projects markedly from the junction of the jaws [Note: This is the excellent reading of Bollandus, supported by the Vatican manuscripts and others. Some have “and livid.” Certainly John describes the color of Saint Gregory’s face before it was altered by persistent illnesses, as the following words indicate: “not yet … cardiac.” It should therefore rather be read “lively” than “livid,” although I do not know whether the former is found in any manuscript. Some grammarians say that *aquiline* derives from *aqua*, “water”; others derive it from *aquila*, “eagle.” Suetonius says of Augustus: “A nose more prominent at the top … a color between aquiline and fair.” In the *Life of Virgil* by Tiberius Donatus: “In body and stature he was large, with an aquiline complexion.” A cardiac complexion is pallor contracted from cardiac disease, or from weakness of the stomach; for καρδία (*kardía*) in Greek signifies not only the heart but also the stomach, especially the opening of the stomach. On this disease see Horace, *Satires* II.3:

> “He is not suffering from cardiac disease; suppose that Craterus said, ‘This man is ill.’”]

His complexion is aquiline and lively, not yet cardiac, as it later became. His expression is gentle, his hands beautiful, and his fingers rounded and suited to writing.

Moreover, he wears a chestnut-colored *planeta* over a dalmatic, holds the Gospel in his left hand and the form of a cross in his right, and has a medium-sized pallium drawn from the right shoulder beneath the breast and in a circular fashion over the stomach, then carried upward over the left shoulder and laid behind the back. One part of it comes again over that same shoulder and hangs down in its proper straight line, not through the middle of the body but at the side.

Around the top of his head he bears something resembling a tablet, which is the insignia of a living person, rather than a crown. From this it is made entirely clear that, while he was alive, Gregory wished his likeness to be painted in a salutary manner, so that his monks might look upon it more frequently, not for the glory of exaltation but as a safeguard born of awareness of his own strict accountability.

There he himself dictated this distich:

> Christ, powerful Lord, giver of our honor,  
> Govern with your customary mercy the office you have bestowed.

### 85

At that place, during the time of Peter the archdeacon and John the *hegumenus*, the monk Saturninus painted the images of the holy apostles at the right and left of blessed Gregory, as they are seen today.

[Note: Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions have “John the steward.” Perhaps, when the monastery of Saint Andrew had been ceded to Greek monks, its superior was called by the Greek name ἡγούμενος (*hēgoúmenos*), that is, the president or prefect of the monastery. It is clear below, in chapter 88, that this *hegumenus*, or steward—as the printed editions have—was in charge of the monastery.]

At this place, a candle is sometimes kindled by divine power, and blessed Gregory is often manifested in the image of that likeness for the governance of his monastery.

86. For, to touch on a few matters out of many: in the time of Pope Leo IV, when Megistus, bishop of Ostia and librarian of the Apostolic See, was in charge of that monastery,

[Note: The Uticensis manuscript reads: “bishop of Ostia.”] John the priest, its provost, living disgracefully with a certain woman, was seized by an exceedingly violent attack of gout. Cauterized by physicians, he began to discharge a calcareous substance through the wound caused by the burning. Unable to close it by any treatment, he was driven into such despair that he ceased all visits to that woman, and she joined herself to another man in the same crime.

But after a year the priest returned to his former health. Although he had resolved never again to have intercourse with her, he nevertheless sent her a messenger announcing that he would return on the following Sunday. When he received her message and rejoiced that the woman’s desire also agreed with his own, he went to the baths. Returning from there, he so abandoned himself to drinking and singing that, when sleep overtook him, he could never attend the nighttime offices with the brothers.

That same night blessed Gregory appeared in a dream to a certain priest and monk and said: “Rise, and tell the provost that, doing penance, he must distribute his property—the wealth which he was not ashamed to accumulate for the sake of his sin—for on the third day he will be utterly removed from life.”

When the provost heard this, he was greatly terrified. Since he could not doubt Gregory’s command, he began to do penance and, while still in good health, distributed all his possessions. Then he was seized by such a fever that, from dawn on the third day until the third hour, with tremendous rattle and, because of the burning fever, thrusting out his tongue from his mouth, he prolonged his final breath.

Seeing the priest suffering so terribly, the others assigned monks to remain there and commend his departure with psalmody, while they themselves devoted themselves to offering solemn sacrifices to almighty God on his behalf. But the monks abandoned the psalmody and did not fear speaking against their dying brother. Then, behold, the priests returned from the solemn celebration of Mass around the seventh hour and were astonished to find that John the priest, whom they had left struggling incredibly with death, was in a milder condition. When they began to call him by name, he at once shook his eyes with a smile and said:

“May the Lord forgive you, brothers. Why did you wish to trouble me? From the very beginning of this day until now I have stood before Christ, who presides amid many thousands of angels, with the devil for judgment; and, with the holy Andrew and Gregory assisting me, I answered all his accusations satisfactorily.

“But know that I carried before Christ, who was questioning me most carefully, the monastery’s sextary, modius, pound, customary alms and lights, and every measure, right up to the footstool of his feet. Yet concerning one accusation, I confess, I was afraid when convicted of it; I was tormented by it with excessive suffering, as you saw, and I have not yet been able to free myself.”

[Note: The printed editions, supported by the German, Colbertine, and Reginensis manuscripts, read: “I was ashamed when convicted of it.”]

When the brothers asked him about this, he said: “I dare not tell you. When you called me and I was ordered by Saint Gregory to return to you in order to render an account of the monastery’s measures and customs, the devil complained, thinking that the Father had sent me back to do penance. Therefore I gave blessed Gregory as my guarantor that I would not reveal the accusation he had raised against anyone.”

When they pressed him still more and promised that they would entreat the Lord on his behalf if he would disclose the matter to the brothers, he began to mention the houses of certain dead persons and the merits of the living, saying: “This man is worthy; that one is unworthy.”

Questioned again, he turned toward the monks who had earlier remained with him and said: “I heard everything in which you spoke against me, brothers, although I was unable to answer, and you caused me no small impediment. For, being accused at the same time both by you and by the devil, I did not know which accusation I should answer first.

“But whenever you see someone departing this life, have compassion on the common lot, and do not judge the one who is going to the judgment of so strict a judge together with his accuser.”

After saying this, he ordered everyone to withdraw, keeping with him only the priest who had foretold his death. The priest, afraid to remain alone, retained another with him and urged him not to fear revealing at least to him the matter over which he had struggled.

But the dying man groaned bitterly and, turning his head toward the wall, cried out: “O Andrew, Andrew, may you perish this year, for you compelled me to danger by your wicked counsel.”

[Col. 0233A]

Immediately Zacharias the physician appeared—the man who in the previous year had apostatized and returned to his own people, the Saracens. He felt the priest’s temples and began to swear that the priest would certainly not die of that illness. When the sick man heard this, he repelled him with great indignation, saying:

“Brothers, my whole body is already dead. I retain my spirit only in my final throat, and I shall die immediately. Only sing psalms, so that I may see again the angels whom I was seeing and indicate them to you.”

While they prayed, he began entirely to tremble and grow pale, gazing upward with longing. Suddenly, seeing the spirit approach, he rolled his eyes terribly, gave the monks a sign, and departed. He left them so terrified that for many nights they were afraid to lie down alone.

87. On that same day and at that same moment—as was later discovered—when the dying priest had called down danger upon Andrew, that same Andrew, the tenant of the Barbilian estate situated on the Ostian road, took to his bed. Afflicted there for a long time by continual illness, he wasted away so completely that his whole body seemed to dissolve piecemeal.

Although his flesh was consumed as it flowed away, he could not die. His wife, who could no longer endure the stench of his wounds and his sufferings, understood that he had not fallen into such grievous illness without a sentence of divine vengeance. Weeping, she sought to question him, so that, since it was impossible to obtain an answer from the dying provost, he might reveal to the monks what he had done with him, if perhaps the Lord, accepting his confession, might free him from such torments.

Recognizing that the evil he had committed could not remain hidden, he asked that the monastery’s monks be summoned. He confessed to them that he had stolen certain documents belonging to the monastery together with that same provost and, after receiving payment, had handed them over to outsiders. He declared himself certain that he could not die because of this crime until he had revealed it before everyone.

The outcome clearly showed that this was true. For as soon as the great crime had become known to all, the man who had long wished to die but could not breathed out his life amid the words of his confession.

Almighty God therefore wished him to be tormented for a long time, but permitted him not to die until he confessed his guilt, so that by the example of his suffering he might show what the despoilers of Gregory’s possessions ought certainly to expect for themselves.

[Col. 0233D]

88. During the time of that same pontiff, Athanasius presided over the monastery of the same Father, a man distinguished in charity and exceedingly careful in the administration of his monastery. When he recognized a season of ravaging scarcity, fearing that necessity might perhaps weigh upon the monks, he withdrew the meal of forty poor persons whom blessed Gregory had decreed should be fed once each year.

Thinking that he had done this with impunity, he also entirely abolished the meal of twelve poor persons and the same number of denarii, which on the day of blessed Gregory’s deposition were customarily provided in commemoration of the twelve whom he had once invited—the thirteenth having declared himself to be an angel.

[Note: In the common editions, the text is interrupted entirely at this point.]

During Lent, therefore, blessed Gregory appeared in a dream to the same priest and monk mentioned above and said: “Go and tell the hegumen: Because he has diminished the custom which I established, the Lord will also diminish his days.”

When the hegumen heard this, he trembled at first; afterward, however, he believed it all the less because he knew his life to be extending farther and farther. And behold, while he was attending the evening offices with the brothers in the oratory of Saint Severinus during Easter week, he saw a wall burning and ordered the brothers to extinguish it.

When they thought him drunk, he finally threw down the staff he was holding and, running his hands along the wall, tried to extinguish the flames outside, although it was clear that they were consuming his inward parts.

Finally, on returning to his lodging, he was inflamed by such a fever that he could not possibly reach the seventh day. Because, while he thought he had benefited the monks, he did not fear harming the poor, and thus entirely offended Gregory by what he believed would appease him, he tried in vain to extinguish the flames of the wall: he refused to extinguish the flames of his own greed.

89. At the same time, behind the apse of the oratory of Saint Mary Ever-Virgin, adjoining the oratory of Saint Barbara, where Gregory used to celebrate praises to the Lord, a demon appeared. Making himself a dwelling in the cavern that can be seen there, it made such a din during the night that everyone thought it was wrenching apart the monastery’s foundations.

Sometimes it was heard carrying horses away from the stables and racing about all night; it was established that it had hurled two of them down a precipice. When, through fear of such terrifying noise, it had completely driven the monks away from the refectory, where they were accustomed to lie in the open air because of the summer heat, one of them, trusting in the power of almighty God, lay down before the opening. After praying, he began to sleep.

The demon appeared to him in the likeness of a cat and attacked him, tearing him with its claws. Repelling it by prayer, the monk again gave himself to sleep. Suddenly the demon appeared in the likeness of an Ethiopian, threatening him with a spear, and said: “I am indeed going away from here, but I leave you wounded.”

Having said this, it brandished the spear and, as it seemed, struck the monk in his sleep. He wailed with such loud cries as though he had truly been struck. When the monks came running, he fearfully told them what he had seen. From then on the demon no longer approached that place.

[Note: Bigot’s manuscript reads: “He brandished the spear.”]

90. During the time of Pope Benedict, when the bishop Lucidus Ficulinus presided over the same monastery, a very large number of people were dying each day from a disease of the throat. The same monk, whose throat was closed, came near death. In his despair blessed Gregory appeared to him in a dream and said: “Do you wish to become well?”

He replied that he did. Blessed Gregory said:

“If you promise me that you will say what I shall tell you to say, know that you will be healed; but if not, you will die more quickly.”

When the man promised with complete assurance that he would say it, he heard:

“Go, and announce to the monks Saba, John, Benedict, Martin, Palumbus, and Antony; to Laurence the cook, Gemmosus the carpenter, Acceptus the baker; and to the laymen Andrew, Romanus, and Leo, that, beginning tomorrow, they will all follow one another in dying each day.”

[Note: The manuscripts read *diatim* (“day by day”) and continue: “after whose departure …”]

“After their deaths, announce that Lucidus the bishop, who governs that monastery, will die on the seventh day.”

After saying this, he ordered the monk to yawn, inserted two fingers into his throat, and, tearing open the wound, commanded him to cough out what obstructed it. Coughing, the man actually expelled part of the coagulated blood in the shape of a stone. Freed from the very gates of death, he attended the matutinal hymns that same night, contrary to everyone’s expectation.

The brothers marveled, and he disclosed to them the nature of his recovery. He told them when and how he had foreseen that members of the monastery’s household would die, but, meanwhile, he remained silent, uncertain only about the bishop’s death.

Immediately rumor flew into the ears of all those appointed to die. When, from the monk’s report, they learned that they would die on a fixed day, they arranged their affairs and followed death exactly as they had been named in the dream.

91. The priest-monk was afraid to reveal so dreadful a message to Lucidus the bishop, but he did not dare remain entirely silent. At last he slipped away from the monastery and went to the bishop’s house—not far from the Tiber, in the district situated near the basilica of Saints Cyrus and John—to announce the dream.

[Note: According to the Uticensis manuscript, “the royal residence, namely, beside the basilica.”]

When he learned that the bishop was dining with the pontiff in the palace, he waited for his return and then went to greet him. The bishop was dressed in priestly garments, radiant in appearance, and in excellent health. He said to him:

“By now you are regarded throughout the whole city as divine, since of those whose deaths you foretold, only one remains.”

[Note: Bigot, Germanensis, and Reginensis read *habebere*, “you will be regarded.”]

The monk replied: “Would that, just as the one whom you think alive is dead, so the one foretold to follow him might depart!”

When the bishop questioned him with great curiosity, and the monk faltered in speaking, at last, when he learned that he would die on the sixth day, he grew pale and trembled. Recovering his strength, he growled at the monk and detained him when he tried to leave.

He entered the inner part of the bedroom, and gradually began to feel his throat hurting. Then, having felt his pulse, he immediately recognized the signs of fever. He believed the monk, put his household in order, and went to the monastery over which he presided, wearing the same pontifical insignia with which he had returned from the patriarchal residence.

On Monday, while everyone marveled at so sudden a change, he assumed the monastic habit. As his illness gradually worsened, he fell asleep toward dawn on Friday. Awakened again, he reported that the holy apostle Andrew had appeared to him and that he would be summoned around the third hour. He said that he had been commanded that, since the monks, held in suspense by the expectation of his death, could not celebrate the customary offices of Saint Fabian, they should immediately commit his body to burial, take candles and incense from him, and hasten to perform the solemn rites.

At the third hour, therefore, the bishop died joyfully, so that the joy visible on his face showed to everyone that his conversion had been pleasing to God.

92. At the same time, the brother of that monk suffered mental derangement, so that, fleeing human society, he wandered for a long time through solitary crypts and muddy tombs. His brother, deeply grieved by this madness, prayed daily to Saint Gregory with abundant tears, asking that he might deign to restore his brother to health.

Thus, one night, when he had fallen asleep after such weeping, blessed Gregory appeared to him and said:

“Seeing your tears, I have received your prayer; and behold, today I shall return your brother to you in good health. And this shall be a sign for you: as soon as day dawns, at the pontiff’s command the priest who is confined here will be taken out.”

He rose and told the brothers this in the morning.

At that time, by chance, the same priest, Campanus, from the place called Claustrum not far from Terracina, was being held in that monastery, accused by his own people of some crime.

[Note: According to the Uticensis manuscript, “to the south.”]

As many periods of time passed, he had already been abandoned by his accusers and forgotten by all his own people. He had no relative or acquaintance in the City who could have brought him to the pontiff’s attention. The monks were indeed working on his behalf, but had no avenue by which to make progress.

The pontiff, divinely reminded of him, ordered him at dawn to be taken from prison and released. Not long afterward the monk’s brother returned so completely restored that he seemed thereafter to have served more faithfully in the monastery of that Father, in proportion as he remembered having returned to his former health through his assistance.

[Col. 0236C]

93. In the time of Pope Nicholas, of revered memory, while Zacharias, bishop of Anagni, administered the governance of the same monastery—as it remains to this day—the demon attacked the Barbilian estate, which I mentioned above, because of the crimes of its inhabitants.

Returning from the meadows to the house and bellowing in the likeness of a little bull, it was felt to strike a man at night invisibly with its little horns. It also dragged oxen from their stalls and exhausted them by racing at great speed through the adjoining fields and crossroads.

When it had continued this for a long time and frequently threatened the peasants with harm, it afflicted and destroyed a certain Saxulus, the tenant of that estate, with such blows. Then it attacked the herdsmen and subdued them with such slaughter that within three months it left no one there except one man named Ursellus, whom it afflicted in the same way.

[Note: Reginensis, Germanensis, Uticensis, and Bigot read *caucum ursulum*; Colbertine reads *cocum ursulum*, “the cook Ursellus.”]

When Ursellus came to Rome to inform the brothers of such a great disaster, he left the monastery gates in the middle of his speech and did not return until morning, to the astonishment of the monks. When they carefully questioned him about why he had fled with such sudden speed, he confessed, saying:

“While I was revealing to you the demon’s madness, the little bull appeared. Embracing me with its forefeet and beating me with its little horns, it began to drive me before it. All night it forced me to pass beneath walls and trees.

“When at last it tried to plunge me beneath a bridge, I leapt from its embrace and, fleeing it with all my strength, reached the gates of this monastery which the hegumen Euthymius had made. Finding them closed, I seized both their rings with both hands. While it struggled to tear me away from them, a bald pontiff thrust himself sideways through the gaps in the gates, struck the little bull’s head with a staff, and, driving it into flight, freed me from its blows.”

[Note: The manuscripts, except Reginensis, read “from its persecutions.”]

Thus, when the inhabitants had perished, no one came to live there, and the monks were working to remedy the desolation of the place, Gregory appeared in a dream to one of them and ordered that, if they wished to drive the demon from the monastery’s estate, the brothers should proceed from the oratory of Saint Martina to the oratory of Saint Mary, established there in the Lord’s house, sprinkling exorcised water while chanting litanies.

When this had been done, the demon was so completely driven from the monastery’s entire property that afterward it was observed by the swineherd to cast flames from its mouth, nostrils, and eyes along the boundary lines, and to drive the pigs. But it was never again permitted to enter within the monastery’s boundaries.

94. At another time, Theutgaud, formerly bishop of Trier, who together with Guntarius, bishop of Cologne, had been deprived of his priestly office by Nicholas, of revered memory, received lodging in the same monastery through the generosity of Pope Hadrian.

Blessed Gregory appeared to him in a dream and caused him such terror that he hurried out of his monastery. Thinking that the vision had been merely fantastic, he prayed and again began to sleep.

Gregory then appeared to him wearing pontifical vestments and said:

“Did I not tell you to withdraw from my monastery, which I dedicated to the Lord from my own property through the invocation of the holy apostle Andrew, since it could in no way be made into a lodging-house?”

When Theutgaud replied that he had received permission from the pontiff to lodge there, Gregory said:

“Both you, who asked, and he, who granted it, have acted against God; and you will both quickly incur his vengeance.”

Theutgaud awoke trembling. After praying, he wished to return to sleep, but suddenly heard the sound of people approaching and was greatly frightened. He pretended to be asleep.

Gregory therefore approached, holding the holy apostle Andrew by the right hand, and ordered the subdeacon who went before him with a light:

“Correct him.”

When, after being corrected, Theutgaud sat on his bed with his eyes closed, Gregory said: “Look at us.”

Theutgaud looked at them and trembled still more. He heard Gregory threatening him:

“Because, after being warned a second time, you refused to believe the words of my mouth, and by your disobedience provoked me so far that I have now taken the trouble to bring the apostle of God here, know for certain that, unless you leave this monastery of mine today, you and all your companions will be deprived of life in the coming week.

“But if you leave, you will indeed be freed from this immediate sentence; nevertheless, neither you nor any of those dwelling here with you will ever see his homeland again.”

At once Theutgaud sprang from his bed and revealed the dream first to his own people, then to the monks of the monastery, and finally to everyone he could. Since he could not quickly obtain another lodging from the pontiff, he settled among the Sabines and died the same year, together with all his companions.

95. At the same time Suppo, count of Picenum, arrived there. He showed the monks great generosity and prevented his men from appropriating anything belonging to so venerable a monastery.

[Note: *Dapsilitas* and *dapsilis* are words familiar to writers especially of the Middle Ages: *dapsilitas* means generosity, and *dapsilis* means generous or lavish. Du Cange discusses them extensively in his *Glossary*.]

One of his retainers, named Faraldus, whenever Suppo had gone to the palace, did not hesitate—despite the monks’ disgust—to bring prostitutes there and celebrate unlawful feasts and dances with them.

At the beginning of one night, when he withdrew to the privy, unclean spirits suspended him in the air by his hair. Hanging there all night and unable to use his voice, he was shown blessed Gregory during the morning hours. Gregory said:

“Enemy of God, are the other evils which you stubbornly commit in my monastery not enough for you? In addition, you bring theatrical little prostitutes into the monastic cloister as though into a theater. Believe me: you will perish this year.”

Then Faraldus began with great force to beg for penance and promised complete correction in the future. Immediately Gregory ordered him to be released. Falling to the ground, Faraldus proved by dying that same year that Gregory’s sentence had been true, since he refused to be corrected.

[Col. 0238C]

96. At another time a man of the same count, named Indulfus, was there. When the cook asked him for denarii to purchase firewood, he could obtain them in no way. Instead, by an impious authorization, he was allowed to attack and strip the shelters, windows, and boards of the neighboring dormitory and prepare his meal for himself with their fires.

[Note: San Germano, Reginensis, Colbertine, Uticensis, and Bigot read “the royal windows.” *Attegiae* are small buildings or huts. See Du Cange. Juvenal, *Satires* 14: “Destroy the huts of the Moors.”]

On the following night, when Indulfus was going to the privy, a certain old man questioned him about why he had ordered the monastery’s boards to be burned so wantonly. Indulfus, abusing the holy old man in the Gallic manner and calling him a fool—

[Note: The Gallic word is *fol* or *fou*, whose antiquity is demonstrated by this passage.]

—was struck lightly by him with a staff. But the arrogant man fell with such force that he lay half-dead on the ground.

At that same moment, under the same appearance, the old man appeared to a cleric sleeping outside and said:

“Rise and tell the count to leave this monastery of mine safely, before he provokes me to anger; it is wholly impermissible for it to become a lodging-house. Behold, I shall pour out appropriate healing upon his retainer who is subject to me, the man answerable to me, whom I left struck down before the privy.”

When the cleric asked who he was, the old man declared that he was the one who could easily be recognized from the painting above the cleric’s bed.

The cleric immediately rose, seized a light, and recognized from the likeness in the painting that the holy apostle Andrew had appeared to him. He therefore went to the prostrate Indulfus and found him already half-dead.

Beginning to cry out with great wailing, he compelled both the count and all who were sleeping beneath the same buildings to come by his pitiful shouting. Pouring water onto the face of the man lying there, he finally made him speak through the invocation of the holy apostle Andrew. He then revealed to the count together with him everything that had been revealed to him.

When day came, the count summoned the monks and began, complaining, to inquire what he had done against Saint Andrew. They pointed out the demolished dormitory of the cooks. When the count, devoted to God, wished to subject the perpetrators to punishment, they confessed that they had destroyed the building at Indulfus’s command.

When the count wished to give the monks money for its restoration, Sergius, the master of the soldiers, resisted and promised that he would immediately rebuild it better on his behalf.

The count then humbly withdrew from the monastery cloister and went with all his people to the house of Peter, son of the late Charles. He no longer allowed lodging to be provided for him in that monastery.

Indulfus, however, was abandoned in the house of the same Sergius, master of the soldiers, and perished there. To his own detriment he showed that the holy apostle had prevailed against him.

97. Not long ago, under the episcopate of Zacharias, whom I mentioned above, when he was administering the Gregorian monastery, a certain priest named Dominicus became its provost. Corrupted by the weakness of the flesh, he abducted or secretly removed a certain nun named Eupraxia from the monastery of the holy apostle Andrew called the Clivus Scauri and settled her in the district of the Seven Ways, at a place called Viper.

[Note: Some manuscripts omit *Clivus Scauri*. Germanensis reads *Glibbus Scauri*.]

When the corrupted nun frequently seemed troublesome to him because she had neither a privy nor a furnace nearby, the wretched priest, adding sin to sin so that he might please the little prostitute, did not hesitate to offend blessed Gregory. Stealing the wood—

[Note: The Uticensis manuscript reads “the boards.”]

—and roof tiles of his miraculous, indeed most health-giving, fountain, he was not ashamed to construct a privy and furnace for the prostitute.

When this had been done, and on the following night he slept more securely in the same house, now free from the complaints of the lascivious woman, he saw two terrifying chamberlains leading him back to the venerable monastery with his hands bound.

When he asked by whose command they were doing this to him, he heard that the Roman pontiff had ordered it. At that time Pope John happened to be traveling along the coast against the incursions of the Saracens. Remembering that the priest was bound because of his absence, he objected:

“The lord pope departed against the Saracens the day before yesterday. How can you say that he ordered me to be bound, when you have not seen him since?”

They replied:

“If Pope John has gone away, Saint Gregory has remained here. As he was inspecting the cloisters of his monastery in the customary manner, he found his fountain destroyed by you, and we saw that the furnace and privy of your prostitute had been covered with its roofing materials.”

When the priest heard this, he blushed and trembled. Seeing himself being held by force in the monastery’s enclosure—

[Note: *Cortis* means a court, courtyard, or enclosure; the word often occurs in ancient charters, especially. Martial uses it in *Epigrams* 7.30: “The birds and eggs of Rancae’s court.” It can also mean a household and even a royal household. In the capitularies of Charles the Bald, chapter 14: “so that you may have sufficient means to live decently with your household.”]

—he heard a certain subdeacon emerging from within and saying to the chamberlains:

“Stretch him out, and strike the belly of the fornicator and sacrilegious priest with fifty red lashes, and his back with as many.”

[Note: By “red lashes” he perhaps means blows that would bloody the fornicator’s belly and back.]

The priest, already feverish, was awakened by the pain of these blows in reality. Placed on a horse and supported on either side by others, he hurried back to the monastery, announced the sentence of his guilt to the brothers, and, mangled by invisible blows under the appearance of fever, could say nothing except:

“Lord, I am recovering; Lord, I am recovering.”

[Note: Bigot reads: “Lord, I am failing.” This reading is confirmed by the same priest’s reply: that he was groaning under continual blows.]

When he was asked why he repeated this so often, he said that he was groaning under continuous beating. Thus, on the sixth day, he died with this pitiable cry.

For it has been established by many proofs that, in that same venerable monastery, those polluted by the contagion of fornication cannot remain for long at all.

98. To this day the pound and every measure instituted by that same blessed Gregory are preserved together with the modius. If anyone wishes to make loaves for the monastery according to the measure of that modius, thirty-five loaves are produced, each exactly three pounds; but if he makes them for someone else, he never reaches the same number.

[Note: Sangermanensis, Reginensis, and Bigot read “one by one”; Uticensis reads “individually.”]

When the aforementioned Zacharias, bishop, wished to learn this with certainty, he gave the bakers a measure of ten modii of wheat for the celebration of the feast of the holy apostle Andrew. From it he received loaves multiplied as though from eleven modii, to the astonishment of the bakers themselves. They had first counted them carefully; if they had found any surplus, they would certainly have kept it for themselves.

99. Indeed, because I cannot now relate how frequently blessed Gregory appears there, in the very form by which he is recognized, in the basilicas of the apostles, and also in the patriarchal residence—sometimes exhorting the innocent, sometimes terrifying those bound by guilt—

[Note: Here and above, in chapter 96, *obnoxius* is set in opposition to *innoxius* and signifies one who, because of fault and guilt, is liable to punishment.]

—I bring this work to an end here, with the Lord’s assistance, and leave the remaining miracles of that same Father to be remembered by more learned men after me.

His venerable merit will assuredly continue to increase for as long as the orbit of this world revolves, so that, with the most eloquent Paul, I may confess that it will always receive increase: for to his grace, without doubt, must be attributed either that the Church of the English is continually made fruitful by new offspring, or that through his teachings many who have been separated by sin throughout the whole world return to Christ’s mercy, or that all good people, inflamed by his exhortations, seek the heavenly homeland with longing.

## 100.

Behold, zealous admirer of pontiffs, compelled by the force of your command, while I desired to cull certain deeds of blessed Gregory, your predecessor, namely the apostle of the Saxon people, I, an unskilled writer, have portrayed an eloquent man. But I beg you, with that same eagerness with which you earlier ordered me to collect these things, to bring them, as you have begun, to everyone's notice, so that, since I rejoice that they have pleased your most sacred judgment, I may not be assigned to anyone whatever to be judged, but rather may be found ready to judge.

For very recently, when, with the Lord’s help, I was eager to close this fourth book, on the night when the venerable day of the Lord’s Resurrection was dawning, I dreamed that someone, openly presenting himself to be seen in the guise of a certain ancient adversary, [Col. 0241B] soon stood nearby, dressed priest-fashion in an exceedingly white and very thin tunic, through whose remarkable thinness the blackness of the tunic beneath showed through. He could not restrain his laughter, his cheeks puffed out.

While I was thinking of preparing a curule chair for him, and, seeing him laughing beyond measure, I seemed to address him, asking why, in the silence of night, a man of such weighty office was making so insolent a disturbance. But he replied: “Because you write about dead men whom you never saw alive.”

When I answered that I had written all the more truthfully because, though I did not know him by sight, I was not ignorant of him through reading, and had reported him without any fault of envy or flattery [Note: [Col. 0241D] Utic.: “favor.”], he responded: “You, as I see, have done what you wished; but I shall not cease to do what I am able.”

As he said this, he completely extinguished the flames of the lamp whose light I happened then to be enjoying. He could not extinguish the lamp altogether; nevertheless, he so terrified me, standing as I was in darkness, that I thought he would immediately cut my throat with swords.

After a little while, when I was despairing, blessed Gregory appeared to me, accompanied on his right by Pope Nicholas, of revered memory, and on his left, as it seemed to me, by his deacon Peter. He was made radiant by a great light, and said: “You of little faith, why did you doubt?”

I was so shaken by my earlier fear that I could not answer him. But the kindly Father Nicholas, pointing out with his finger the concealed adversary behind the curtain that then surrounded my bed, said to me: “This envious man extinguished the flames of that lamp as far as he was able.”

At once Gregory seized the deacon’s hand, which seemed to be holding a great torch, and, burning the insolent man’s mouth and face with its flames, blackened him after the likeness of an Ethiopian. From that burning, a tiny spark fell from the insolent man’s mouth and immediately set his shining tunic ablaze; thus he appeared entirely black.

When the deacon said that the adversary had been blackened sufficiently, blessed Gregory said: “We have not blackened him; we have shown that he was black.”

Then, having encouraged me in my misfortune with various consolations, he departed. He carried the torch away with him, but left the place where I was sleeping truly shining with so great a light that, when I awoke, I repeatedly called out to the boys sleeping before me. Nor could they in any way answer under their heavy sleep or rise until the abundance of the remaining light, gradually withdrawing, had completely ebbed away.

But God will judge these matters. I, nevertheless, strengthened by confidence in divine hope, shall, since Gaudericus, bishop of Velletri, presses me, turn my pen, with the Lord’s support, toward the merciful bishop of the Roman see, so that I, who, worn down by continual misfortunes, am unable to repay the favor of my friends by whom I am sustained as best I can, may at least be recognized as not having refused them the words that I am able to offer.

[Col. 0241]

# THE LIFE OF SAINT GREGORY, POPE I, RECENTLY COMPOSED PRINCIPALLY FROM HIS OWN WRITINGS

## BOOK ONE

Containing his history from his birth to the supreme pontificate.

# CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0241D]

## SUMMARY

1. Saint Gregory’s lineage. His father Gordianus.  
2. His holy mother Silvia.  
3. His ancestors, among them Pope Saint Felix.  
4. His paternal aunts, among them Saints Tharsilla and Aemiliana.  
5. He had a brother.  
6. In what year he was born.  
7. What his name signifies.  
8. The education of the holy boy.  
9. His studies. (A.D. 549.)

### 1.

Gregory, surnamed the Great, was born at Rome [Col. 0242D] to parents distinguished no less by the splendor of their lineage [Note: [Col. 0241] Namely, of the Anician family, as common opinion holds; nor does our Mabillon reject this in the sixth book of the Benedictine Annals, p. 163.] than by their integrity of character and holiness.

His father Gordianus, a most noble and wealthy man of senatorial rank, was a regionarius—that is, as the eminent father of the Ecclesiastical Annals conjectures from the account of John the Deacon, Book IV, chapter 83, at the year 604, one of the seven cardinal deacons who were called regionarii because they were placed in charge of particular districts of the City.

Yet the regionarii were not constituted from deacons alone, but also from subdeacons and notaries, and later, with Gregory the Great’s approval, from defensores. (Register, Book VIII, letter 14.)

I shall quote the words of John the Deacon, so that the prudent reader may determine what should be understood from them:

“In the atrium of this venerable monastery [of Saint Andrew], by Gregory’s order, beside the nymphaeum, two very ancient images painted with artistic skill are still visible. In one of them, blessed Peter the Apostle is seen seated and receiving with his right hand the standing Gordianus, the regionarius, namely Gregory’s father, by his right hand. Gordianus is dressed in a chestnut-colored planeta, beneath the planeta a dalmatic, and on his feet he wears leggings.”

These garments seem, indeed, to indicate a deacon. But Ferrarius, in Book I of *On the Art of Dressing*, chapter 38, holds that the planeta and dalmatic were then used interchangeably; and this is clearly proved by John the Deacon himself, since he lists a planeta among the garments of Saint Silvia, blessed Gregory’s mother, as we shall say below.
