On this subject the learned John Mabillon should be consulted in the Preface to Volume I of the *Acts of the Saints*, § CVIII.

That Gordianus was a regionarius and was enrolled among the ministers of the basilica of Saint Peter, or of the Roman Church, is demonstrated both by John the Deacon’s words and by the image of blessed Peter receiving Gordianus with his right hand.

From the same ancient painting John the Deacon (cf. Paul the Deacon; John the Deacon, Book I, no. 1; Bede, Book II of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 1; Saint Gregory of Tours, Book X of the *History*, chapter 1) attributes to Gordianus a tall stature, an elongated face, green eyes, a moderate beard, and a grave expression.

### 2.

When Silvia, Gregory’s mother, withdrew from the world—whether after her husband’s death or while he was still alive is uncertain—she chose a retreat for herself beside the gate of the basilica of Saint Paul the Apostle. John the Deacon testifies that, at the place commonly called Cella Nova, an oratory founded and dedicated to her name still stood in his own time.

Silvia has been entered in the catalogue of the saints, and her name is read in the Roman Martyrology on the third day of November.

The praised writer reports that Saint Silvia was depicted in the monastery of Saint Andrew by order of Saint Gregory:

“Silvia is depicted seated, covered with a white veil folded from her right shoulder across toward the left in such a way that beneath it she draws out her hand as though from beneath a planeta.”

For the rest concerning her clothing and adornment, see John the Deacon, Book IV, chapter 83.

As for her appearance:

“Her stature was full; her face, round and indeed fair, but already wrinkled by old age—though that very old age indicated that she had once been exceedingly beautiful; her eyes were gray and large, her eyebrows moderate, her lips attractive, and her expression cheerful. On her head she wore a matronly mitre.” [Note: [Col. 0243D] Concerning the mitre, see the note on the cited passage of John the Deacon. Properly speaking, mitres are crowns made from bands and oraria [ornamental strips]. (The ancient Greek etymological author.) See also note 947 on the Book of the Sacraments.]

(Cf. John the Deacon, Book I, no. 9.)

### 3.

Nothing certain has been handed down to us about Gregory’s ancestors, except that, as Gregory, bishop of Tours, a contemporary writer, teaches (Book X of the *History*, chapter 1), he was descended from leading senators.

These words may bear a twofold interpretation: either Gregory derived his lineage from the ancient nobles of the Roman senate, those who, while the republic flourished, were masters of affairs; or his fathers held a place among the principal senators of their own time.

He himself testifies in Book IV of the *Dialogues*, chapter 16, and in Homily 38 on the Gospels, that Pope Felix was his great-great-grandfather.

But it is disputed which Felix he was, the third or the fourth. John the Deacon asserts that he was the fourth, whom he calls a man of great authority in the Church of Christ, and says that he built with great elegance the basilica of the holy martyrs Cosmas and Damian on the Sacred Way, beside the Temple of Romulus.

Nor can we readily persuade ourselves that John the Deacon rashly declared Felix IV instead of Felix III. This deacon of the Roman Church undertook to write the life of Saint Gregory at the urging of Pope John VIII, and later published it after it had been approved by the authority of that same supreme pontiff.

He had examined all the ancient monuments; he had gone through the catalogues, acts, and journals of the supreme pontiffs. He had carefully inspected the basilica of Saints Cosmas and Damian, still standing as Pope Felix had built it, and had doubtless discovered from certain inscriptions or other reliable evidence that the pontiff who was Gregory’s great-great-grandfather was Felix by name, the fourth, not the third.

Indeed, before Baronius’s correction, the Roman Martyrology read Felix IV, and it is otherwise established that the basilica of the holy martyrs of which our deacon speaks was built not by Felix III but by the fourth pontiff of that name.

[Col. 0244C]

The eminent Cardinal Baronius attacks John’s opinion, both in his notes on the Roman Martyrology for February 25 and in the *Ecclesiastical Annals* at the year 581, chiefly on the ground that Felix IV is known to have been a Samnite, whereas Gregory the Great’s ancestors were Romans.

But what prevents Felix, although Roman by descent, from having been born among the Samnites? Gregory himself seems sufficiently to suggest that some of his relatives were Samnites when he says in Book III of the *Dialogues*, chapter 26:

“Recently, in the province of Samnium, a certain venerable man named Mennas was leading a solitary life. He was known to many of our people and died approximately ten years ago.”

Moreover, it is not always easy to assign the homeland of great men, because their parents, whether on account of the various provinces they govern for the benefit of the state or because they own estates in many different regions, have scarcely any fixed residence in a single city.

Certainly, Gregory’s great-grandfathers possessed many rich estates outside Roman territory. This is clear from the fact that their heir Gordianus left his son an immense patrimony in Sicily, from which Gregory later not only built six monasteries on that island, as will be said below, but also endowed them with the greatest generosity.

The entire force of this argument also collapses if one says that Gregory was Roman on his father’s side, but that one of his ancestors lived in Samnium, where he fathered Felix.

[Col. 0245A]

Only one difficulty remains to be resolved here. The age of Felix IV, who began his pontificate in 526 and migrated to heaven in 529, scarcely permits us to suppose that he was Gregory’s great-great-grandfather. Five generational degrees would have to be counted between them, even though only eleven years elapsed between Felix’s death and Gregory’s birth, and Felix would have had to see Gordianus, his great-great-grandson, at least seven years old.

I freely admit that it rarely happens that a father embraces descendants propagated down to the fourth generation, as would have been granted to Felix. Nevertheless, this is not altogether impossible, unheard-of, or even completely unusual.

Perhaps, too, this word *atavus* should not be understood strictly as the father of an *abavus* and the grandfather of a *proavus*, but may signify one of the ancestors without regard to the degree of generation.

[Col. 0245B]

Felix IV governed the Church with such prudence and such praise for every virtue that he deserved to be added to the lists of the saints on January 30. Felix III likewise received the same honor, and his feast day is celebrated on February 25.

### 4.

Concerning his three paternal aunts, Saint Gregory records the following worthy of notice, both in Book IV of the *Dialogues*, chapter 16, and in Homily 38 on the Gospel:

“My father had three sisters, all three of whom were sacred virgins. One was called Tharsilla, another Gordiana, and the third Aemiliana. All three were converted with one ardor, consecrated at one and the same time, and, living under strict discipline, led a communal life in their own house.”

The holy Doctor continues by describing the constant progress of Tharsilla and Aemiliana and their desired passage to heaven. Saint Felix, Pope, especially invited his niece Tharsilla to share in the fellowship of eternal light, and Christ the Lord came to meet his dearest bride.

“But,” Gregory says, “Gordiana’s soul began, through daily losses, to grow lukewarm from the warmth of its innermost love and gradually to return to love of this world. Her pious sisters took care daily to correct her with gentle admonition and to reform her from frivolity of conduct to the gravity proper to her state. But after her sisters had died, forgetting fear of the Lord, forgetting modesty and reverence, and forgetting her consecration, she later took as her husband the leaseholder of her estates.”

Behold: all three had first been converted with one ardor, but they did not persevere in one and the same devotion, because, according to the Lord’s word, “many are called, but few are chosen.”

Gregory also mentions another paternal or maternal aunt in Book I, letter 39, writing to the subdeacon Anthemius:

“I wish you to offer twenty solidi and three hundred modii of wheat to Lady Pateria, my *thia* …, for the boys’ shoe allowance.”

The word *thia* derives from the Greek θεία (*theia*), which signifies a paternal or maternal aunt. In the Spanish language, *tia* has the same sound and meaning.

There is no need to investigate at length the circumstances by which Pateria, a most noble woman, had been reduced to extreme poverty, since all Italy was then being ravaged by continuous wars.

### 5.

No one who has read Gregory’s letters attentively will doubt that he had a brother, for he frequently mentions his brother in them.

In Book I, letter 44, he writes to the subdeacon Peter:

“We give thanks for your concern, because, regarding the matter of my brother, I ordered you to see that his money should be sent.”

Book IX, letter 98:

“But if that is so, we shall have our glorious brother, or one of the bishops … subscribe.”

In the same book, letter 102:

“Our son, the magnificent man Occilianus … is known to have brought to him one boy … from the property of our own brother.”

Book X, letter 51:

“Those things from my glorious brother, the Patrician Palatinus, etc.”

Finally, in Book XIV, letter 2:

“Concerning the monastery of Saint Hermes, which … was built by our brother.”

Gregory of Tours also seems to speak of this same brother (Book X, chapter 1), when he says:

“But the prefect of the city of Rome, his brother, anticipated his message.”

For *germanus*, even among writers of the finest Latin, signifies a brother, as though born from the same seed. Hence the Spaniards call a brother *hermano*, and the Italians *germano*.

### 6.

The year in which Gregory was born can be reached more by conjecture than established by the force of argument.

To proceed from what is known toward what is obscure: ancient records establish that he ended his final day in March of the year 604. The most holy pontiff died worn out by continuous illnesses rather than by old age.

His nurse was still alive at least ten years before he himself departed this life; at that time he commended her to the patrician Rusticiana in Book IV, letter 46.

Moreover, Gregory often complains of gout, weakness of the stomach, and various other illnesses, but nowhere of the afflictions of old age. This supplies no slight argument that he had not yet reached an advanced age.

Add to this what the holy man wrote to Januarius, bishop of Cagliari, in Book IX, letter 1, in the ninth year of his pontificate, four or five years before his death.

Compelled to rebuke this elderly bishop, he seems immediately to be restrained by modesty, and applies to himself these words of the Apostle concerning Timothy, who was still young: “Do not rebuke an elder” (1 Timothy 5:1). He therefore acknowledged himself to be younger than Januarius, and consequently it can scarcely be believed that he was then more than sixty years old. But let us examine what he himself teaches about his age in his *Dialogues*.

In Book III, chapter 11, Gregory relates a miracle that occurred to Saint Cerbonius, bishop of Populonia, at the time when Totila, king of the Goths, was encamped at a place called Merulis, eight miles from the city of Rome. He observes that this happened in his own lifetime.

Totila, who began to reign in 541, besieged and captured Rome twice, namely in the years 546 [Col. 0246D] and 549. The first siege lasted an entire year, during which Totila was not far from the City.

It therefore seems more likely that what Gregory relates happened then, and that he and the others living in Rome easily learned of it in this way.

At that time Gregory was at least six or seven years old. We are not accustomed to say that events occurred in our own days when we were still infants and crying.

After weighing these matters, I believe that Saint Gregory’s birth should be assigned to the year 540: the third year of Pope Vigilius—if, indeed, the years of his pontificate are to be reckoned from the time when he was substituted for Saint Silverius, who had been unjustly deposed—the thirteenth year of the Emperor Justinian Augustus, and the fifth and final year of Vitigis, king of the Goths, whom Belisarius, after capturing Ravenna, led in chains to Constantinople.

### 7.

Gregory acquired his name, which means “watchful,” not without some great foreshadowing, says Paul the Deacon (no. 1).

In truth, he watched over himself, since he lived commendably by cleaving to the divine commands; he watched over the faithful peoples, since by the richness of his intellect he showed them by what path they might climb to heavenly things.

How highly Gregory valued watchfulness and vigilance, he makes clear in many places, especially in Book XX of the *Morals*, no. 8:

“None of the elect, so long as they are in this life, promises himself confidence in security. At every hour they are wary of temptations and fear the ambushes of the hidden enemy; even when temptation has ceased, they are disturbed by mere grave suspicion.

For often careless security has been a serious danger to many, so that they came to recognize the ambushes of the cunning enemy not while being tempted, but only after they had already been overthrown.

We must always keep watch, so that the mind, continually vigilant, may never relax its heavenly purpose. Otherwise, abandoning laborious effort and lying in loose thoughts as though upon soft bedding, the relaxed mind may surrender itself to the devil, its corrupter, when he comes.”

I omit the rest, although it is most carefully suited to urging Christian watchfulness.

### 8.

We know nothing about Gregory’s upbringing and education in childhood. Nevertheless, neither the great piety of his parents nor the extraordinary holiness of their son—who, even while serving in the world, endeavored to shape his conduct according to the most exact standard of Christian perfection—allows us to doubt that from his earliest years he was nourished on all the precepts of the evangelical law and exercised and instructed, as far as his age allowed, indeed beyond his age, in the arena of every virtue.

Since the education of children is principally the responsibility of mothers, according to Paul (1 Timothy 5:10), we may reasonably conjecture that Saint Silvia diligently fulfilled this duty toward her Gregory and carefully performed all the offices of a Christian mother in his formation.

Gregory beautifully teaches by what skill and industry boys, especially those of noble and royal stock, should be cultivated and formed in piety. He writes to Theoctista in Book VII, letter 26. The Emperor Maurice had entrusted his beloved sister with his sweetest pledges, namely his sons, to be educated.

Among the many outstanding passages in this letter, the following deserves particular consideration and engraving in the memory:

“The words of those who nourish children,” he says, “will be either milk, if they are good, or poison, if they are bad.”

### 9.

Which teachers and instructors the holy boy used in order to reach such a height of knowledge and wisdom is entirely unknown to us.

“As a result of his training in grammar, dialectic, and rhetoric,” says Gregory of Tours in the passage already cited, “he was so accomplished that no one in the City itself was thought to be his equal.”

Yet, with a rare example of humility among learned men, he admits in Book VII, letter 32, that he was very little versed in Greek.

Many of his letters, especially Book XIII, letter 45, prove that he was highly skilled and thoroughly learned in law.

Paul the Deacon conveys the same account as Gregory of Tours and adds that at this time the study of literature flourished especially at Rome, chiefly through the efforts of the great Cassiodorus, who had revived the fallen letters in Italy and established a celebrated academy in his monastery, as we have described through nearly the whole of the third book of his life.

Most noteworthy among Paul the Deacon’s words (no. 1) are these:

“He possessed, even while still of tender age, a mature eagerness to cling to the sayings of his elders; and if he could perceive anything worthy of hearing, he did not carelessly hand it over to forgetfulness, but rather entrusted it to his tenacious memory.”

Even then he drank in, with a thirsting breast, the streams of learning, which later, at the appropriate time, he would pour forth from a honeyed throat.

John the Deacon agrees with Paul and adds that Gregory was a philosopher by training (Book I, no. 1). But he does not disclose which philosophical school he embraced.

No one can fail to know that Gregory cultivated ethics above all, unless he is a stranger to the reading of his works.

Certainly I should gladly call him the Christian Seneca, unless it seemed better to say of him what Ambrose said of Abraham:

“A truly great man, illustrious with the marks of many virtues, whom philosophy could not equal in its aspirations. In the end, what philosophy imagined is less than what this man accomplished.” (Book I, *On Abraham*, chapter 2.)

He never pursued divinatory astrology or other curious and dangerous arts. On the contrary, he attacks those mathematicians who presume to predict the future in Homily 10 on the Gospels, numbers 4 and 5.

As for what John of Salisbury says in Book II of *The Frivolities of Courtiers*, chapter 26, and Book VIII, chapter 19—that Gregory not only ordered mathematics to withdraw from the court but also, out of ill-timed zeal, set fire to the Palatine Library, in whose archives the books of every discipline were stored, so that the authority of Sacred Scripture might be greater and zeal for reading it more ardent—this must plainly be rejected as nonsense and old-wives’ tales.

Adorned with these virtues and cultivated by these studies, Gregory soon opened for himself a path to the highest offices of the City, the senate, and the state.

Since he was involved in a large part of what was conducted in the administration of either the empire or the Church during his lifetime, it is necessary to explain briefly what the condition of both was at that time, especially in Italy.

# CHAPTER II

## SUMMARY

1. The condition of the Church.  
2. The condition of the empire. The Lombards invade Italy.  
3. Gregory becomes praetor of the City. The date of his praetorship.  
4. How he conducted himself as prefect.  
5. Frequent conversations about holy matters kindle in him the desire for the monastic life. He postpones it for a long time.  
6. He builds seven monasteries.  
7. He becomes a monk. Where and when.  
8. Under which teachers. (A.D. 574.)

### 1.

After Pope Saint Silverius had been deposed, Vigilius occupied the Roman see from 537 until 554 or 555, and later suffered much at the hands of the Emperor Justinian, through whose authority he had invaded it.

When he had finally consented, in obedience to the emperor, to the condemnation of the Three Chapters, many in the West, especially the bishops of Illyricum and Africa, withdrew from communion with him, because they were indignant that three bishops—Theodore of Mopsuestia, Ibas of Edessa, and Theodoret of Cyrus—whom the Council of Chalcedon had regarded as orthodox, had been condemned and rejected by the Easterners at the Synod of Constantinople, commonly called the Fifth Ecumenical Council.

When Vigilius died in Sicily, Pelagius I succeeded him. During his pontificate, the bishops of Istria, Liguria, and Venetia held a synod presided over by Paulinus, bishop of Aquileia, and openly broke into schism on behalf of the Three Chapters. They struck Narses, the count who tried to restrain their disturbances, with the feeble thunderbolt of an empty excommunication.

Pelagius, who had been beset by so many and such great calamities in Italy, was called by death to eternal rest in the year 559. Nevertheless, an appendix to the *Chronicle of Marcellinus Comes* assigns him eleven years and ten months of pontificate.

[Col. 0249B]

His successor, John III, governed the Church for fourteen years. While this pontiff was seated on the throne, Gregory wisely exercised the praetorship of the City, as we shall explain below. But it is not clear in what year he began, or whether Justinian, who lived until 565, was still reigning.

### 2.

We have discussed at considerable length in the *Life of Cassiodorus* the victories won over the barbarians, the recovery of several provinces of the empire, and other notable achievements under Justinian.

Justinian would surely have gained immortal praise if, in ecclesiastical and theological matters, he had learned to exercise sound judgment. But, wishing to lead the bishops, he became a guide and teacher of error, whereas by following them he would have become a disciple of truth.

In order to expel the Goths completely from Italy, the emperor summoned the Lombards from Pannonia and, once the war was over, ordered them to return to their former homes, adding certain cities as payment for the service they had rendered.

But, enticed by the delights of Italy, when they were later given an opportunity to return, they immediately flew back. Since we shall speak of them very frequently from this point onward, their history should be traced briefly from its beginning.

They originated in Scandinavia, which Jornandes aptly calls, as a land exceptionally fertile in warlike peoples, “the workshop of nations and the womb of peoples” (*On Gothic Affairs*, chapter 4). From there they first migrated to that part of Germany now called Pomerania, and then into Pannonia, although the Huns had already occupied much of it.

According to Paul the Deacon (*On the Deeds of the Lombards*, Book I, chapters 1 and 2), the Lombards were named from their long beards. For in their language *lang* means “long,” and *baert* means “beard.”

The affinity of these and many other words that occur throughout Paul the Deacon with Gothic and Germanic words clearly demonstrates the Lombards’ origin. [Note: [Col. 0249D] Such words include *Wodan* or *Godan*, meaning “God”; *Feld*, open fields; *Lama*, water; *Scala*, a cup or bowl; *Schilpor*, a shield-bearer; *Marpahis* or *Marhais*, a horseman, whence perhaps the French word *maréchal*; and *Fara*, a family. Nearly all these words are Germanic. They are explained by Hugo Grotius in *History of the Goths, Vandals, and Lombards*, p. 574 and following; consult him, as well as Mabillon, *Analecta*, vol. II, p. 422 and following.]

At first they obeyed dukes, and later kings. From Agelmund, their first ruler, twelve are counted down to Alboin, under whose reign they invaded Italy at Narses’ invitation, namely in the year 568, as may be gathered from two of Gregory’s letters.

In the first, written in the thirteenth indiction of the year 595, namely Book V, letter 21, he says:

“We have now spent twenty-seven years living in this city amid the swords of the Lombards.”

In the second, written in the year 603, the sixth indiction, namely Book XIII, letter 38, he says:

“How we are oppressed by daily swords … behold, now for the length of thirty-five years.”

These statements wonderfully support our chronology.

Gregory himself teaches us how greatly they devastated almost all Italy with plunder, fires, and slaughter, in Book III of the *Dialogues*, chapter 38:

“Soon the savage nation of the Lombards, drawn from the sheath of its dwelling, rushed upon our neck, and the human race, which in this land had risen in such great multitude like a dense grain crop, was cut down and withered.

For cities were depopulated, forts overthrown, churches burned, monasteries of men and women destroyed, estates abandoned by their inhabitants and deprived of every cultivator; the land lies empty in solitude. No possessor inhabits it. Beasts have occupied the places that a multitude of human beings formerly held.”

He laments the same disasters in Homily 17 on the Gospels and elsewhere.

The other Gregory, of Tours, a contemporary witness, relates similar things in Book IV of his *History*, chapter 38. He especially notes that churches were stripped by the barbarians and priests and bishops killed, as was indeed fitting for a people either still devoted to the worship of idols or corrupted by the impieties of the Arians.

All Italy yielded to the conquerors, except Rome, Ravenna, and the neighboring and maritime districts.

Longinus, appointed as Narses’ successor, was then prefect of Ravenna and of all Italy; he was the first to assume the title of exarch.

Fleeing the fury of the Lombards, Paulinus, bishop or patriarch of Aquileia—for Paul the Deacon calls him by both titles (*On the Deeds of the Lombards*, Book II, chapters 10 and 25), as though he had obtained this new title as a reward for the schism he had fomented—took refuge on the island of Grado and in the city of Forum Julii, inaccessible to the enemy because they lacked ships. After completing twelve years of episcopate, he died and was succeeded by Probinus.

Alboin paid the penalty for his crimes and singular brutality—he had forced his wife to use as a drinking cup the skull of her father, whom he himself had killed—being slain through the machinations of that same wife.

After Cleph, whom they had chosen as their king, was also killed after eighteen months, the Lombards preferred to be governed for ten years by many dukes acting simultaneously.

### 3.

Amid so much clamor of arms and calamities of war, Gregory for some time exercised the office of urban praetor. But it is not readily possible to determine when he began or laid down this magistracy.

He himself testifies (Book IV, letter 2) that, while he was holding the urban prefecture, he subscribed, together with other most noble men, to the pledge or undertaking that Laurence, bishop of Milan, had sent to the apostolic see concerning the three famous chapters.

Baronius asserts, from the lists of the bishops of Milan, that this occurred in the year 581, when Laurence was made bishop and testified to his faith.

Since we know from letters 29, 30, and 31 of Book III that Laurence died and Constantius was ordained in his place in the year 593, if we count twelve years of Laurence’s episcopate, its beginning must be referred to the year 581. All those who have treated the affairs of the Church of Milan and constructed the succession of its bishops from the monuments of that Church agree on this, as the most learned annalist testifies.

Therefore Gregory had not yet, at that time, renounced the praetorship and taken refuge in the harbor of the monastery.

But this reasoning of Baronius is overturned by the list of the archbishops of Milan, edited by our Mabillon from the most ancient records of that Church. According to it, after Frontus or Fronton, Laurence occupied the episcopal see for nineteen years and seven months, and died on the twelfth day before the Kalends of September. (Mabillon, *Museum Italicum*, vol. I, p. 111.)

“If,” says Mabillon, “you subtract these years from the ninety-third year, when Constantius succeeded him, you must accept the year 574 as the date of Laurence’s appointment, and therefore as the date of the pledge sent to the Roman pontiff to which Gregory, as praetor, subscribed.”

Mabillon adds that the Bollandist collaborators subscribed to this opinion in the life of Saint Gregory. Yet there, carelessly following Baronius, they say that Gregory held the prefecture, although in all the handwritten manuscripts, both of the Letters and of the Life written by John the Deacon, the reading is *praetor* and *praetura*, not *praefectus* and *praefectura*.

### 4.

The urban praetor was appointed to administer justice in the City. All authority over public and private law belonged to him, so that he could establish new law and abolish old law.

In authority, as in the splendor and insignia of his dignity, he appeared almost equal to the consuls.

The first person recorded as having held the praetorship in the City was Furius Camillus, the most distinguished Roman of his age, who repeatedly restored his country to liberty.

What Gregory did in this most exalted dignity he wished us not to know. Nevertheless, from his upright character, knowledge of the law, mature judgment, energy, unwearied strength in labors and affairs, and, finally, from the many and great gifts of mind by which he shone more brightly than by the splendor of purple, it may be conjectured that he fulfilled every duty of an excellent praetor.

From this came that exceptional love with which the Roman citizens followed him, and which shone forth most especially in his election to the pontificate.

Thus, without doubt, by his own example he then taught what he later wrote to Justinus, praetor of Sicily:

“Let no profits draw you into injustice; let neither threats nor friendship turn you aside from the path of uprightness. Consider how brief life is, and reflect toward what Judge you will one day go, since you exercise judicial power.

Therefore you must carefully observe that here we leave behind all gains, and carry with us to judgment only the causes of ruinous gains.”

(*Register*, Book I, letter 2.)

To conform to custom and dignity, Gregory was accustomed to proceed through the City in a trabea, covered in silk and sparkling with gems, says the other Gregory of Tours, from whom Paul the Deacon borrowed these very words (No. 2). Yet beneath secular pomp, [Col. 0252A] he served not the world but Christ; he must undoubtedly be counted among those kings and consuls of the earth who, as Job says, “build themselves desolate places” (Job 3:14). Explaining this passage, our Gregory, in *Moralia* IV, nos. 58–59, seems to have portrayed himself when he sat as praetor:

> “To build desolate places,” he says, “is to drive from the secret recesses of the heart the tumult of earthly desires, and with a single purpose to yearn for the love of inward quiet, directed toward the eternal homeland. Those who build desolate places for themselves are rightly also called consuls, because they build within themselves the solitude of the mind while nevertheless not ceasing, in what they are able, to provide counsel to others through charity.”

And in Book XXX, no. 52:

> “If someone is pressed by the crowds of the people and nevertheless suffers no tumult of secular cares in his heart, he is not in the City but enjoys the quiet of solitude.”

[Col. 0252B] **5.** Concerning him Paul the Deacon writes as follows:

> “In the years of adolescence, when that age is accustomed to enter upon the ways of the world, he began to devote himself to God and to yearn with all his desires for the homeland of the life above.”

He had scarcely reached his twentieth year when, through frequent conversations with the blessed Constantine, a disciple of Saint Benedict and his successor in governing the monastery of Cassino—who is said to have died around the year 560—he had already learned almost everything that Gregory himself later wrote about Saint Benedict throughout the entire second book of the *Dialogues*, as Gregory himself left on record in the preface to that celebrated book. From this one may understand what occupied the studies of this most noble young man.

On the same subject, namely the life of Saint Benedict, he also often conversed with Valentinian, who governed the Lateran monastery for many years; with Simplicius, who was the third to govern Saint Benedict’s congregation after him; and with Honoratus, who presided over the monastery at Subiaco. Even then [Col. 0252C] he seemed to be kindled toward the purpose of a stricter and more perfect life.

Yet he long delayed fulfilling the desire for the monastic life that he had conceived, believing himself useful to his fellow citizens and thinking it better to remain covered by secular dress, under which he persuaded himself that he served the world only in appearance, than to change his outward manner of life. Later, however, the pious praetor, who was accustomed often to examine and scrutinize the innermost movements of his soul, finally perceived—enlightened by heavenly light—that he was bound by the ingrained habit of secular life and entangled in the world’s blandishments, and that he was creating delays precisely in abandoning them. He realized that he was being held in the world not merely in body, as he had falsely supposed, but also in the inclination of his mind itself.

Therefore, carefully fleeing everything, he sought the harbor of the monastery; and, leaving behind the things of the world, he escaped naked from the shipwreck of this life, as he himself writes to Leander in the letter that we placed before the books of the *Moralia*, at the very beginning.

**6.** Before, however, he renounced the world, he gathered six monasteries in Sicily from his own possessions, as Gregory of Tours, the writer of that period, says (*Book X*, chapter 1), and established a seventh within the walls of the city of Rome. To these he assigned as much land as was sufficient to provide their daily sustenance; he sold the rest and gave the whole proceeds to the poor.

[Col. 0253A] Let the attentive reader observe in passing that the generous and devout founder’s intention was not that the monks should be compelled to seek their livelihood by their own labor.

[Note: [Col. 0253D] Where monasteries had not been assigned estates sufficient to provide the monks with food and clothing, these were supplied at the Church’s expense, as we gather from Severus Sulpicius’s *Dialogue III on Saint Martin*:

> “But before that burden”—one hundred and twenty pounds—“reached the monastery threshold, he immediately designated it for the redemption of captives” (Saint Martin). “And when the brothers suggested to him that he should reserve something from it for the monastery’s expenses . . . ‘Let the Church,’ he said, ‘feed and clothe us, provided that we do not appear to have sought anything for our own uses.’”

]

Indeed, in all the letters in which he discusses founding monasteries, he wishes sufficient revenues to be assigned to them for the necessities of life. Mabillon, following Rochus Pirrus, lists those six Sicilian monasteries in the *Benedictine Annals*, Book VI, p. 164, and frequently discusses them thereafter. Gregory had obtained, through the death of his parents—if Paul the Deacon is to be trusted—the wealth necessary to build these monasteries and endow them with sufficient estates, together with the freedom to use them. John the Deacon, however, writes (*Book I*, no. 9) that his mother Silvia supplied the monk himself with vegetables. Paul’s passage, therefore, seems to be understood as referring only to his father Gordianus.

[Col. 0253B] The seventh monastery, which he built in his own ancestral house, was the famous monastery of Saint Andrew at the Clivus Scauri. There he embraced the monastic life, following the example of Eucherius, Paulinus, Cassiodorus, and many other men of patrician and senatorial nobility.

[Note: [Col. 0254D] It is likely that there was another monastery of Saint Andrew and Saint Lucy in Rome; others, perhaps more plausibly, read “Saint Luke.” There was a particular reason for joining Saints Andrew and Luke together in the same worship: their relics had been translated on the same day, namely 9 May. See Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*, under Luke. The abbot of this monastery was that Probus who obtained permission to make a will; see it at the end of the *Letters*. Consult the *Benedictine Annals*, Book IX, no. 26, and Book X, no. 6.]

After this asceterium had long been occupied by Benedictine monks, it had, in the time of John the Deacon, passed to Greek monks, perhaps through the favor of Stephen III, who also granted the Greeks another monastery that he had built and dedicated to Saint Dionysius the Areopagite. At length this sanctuary of Saint Andrew was restored to those following the Benedictine Rule by Gregory XIII and given to the Camaldolese. We have said enough about Gregory’s consecrating himself to God; let us now see him offering himself wholly to the monastic life by profession. (Cf. John the Deacon, Book VI, no. 82.)

**7.** It may perhaps seem incongruous that a devout man should have sought a retreat and a tranquil dwelling in his own homeland, in the very city that had obeyed his commands. Yet there was no place in all Italy safer from the arms and incursions of the barbarians, and consequently more suitable for quiet, than the city of Rome, defended by the holy apostles, as the most holy Father frequently asserts in his letters, and with the Lombards’ assault driven back.

To assign, insofar as possible, the time and age at which Gregory put on the monastic habit, we suspect that this occurred shortly after the bond of Laurentiius mentioned above in no. 3—that is, in the year 575, when he was five years short of forty. Certainly, the many things that he relates about himself while living in the monastery, or that we know from other sources that he accomplished, and which we shall report below in due order, do not permit us to accept Baronius’s opinion that he remained in the monastery scarcely two full years.

The foundation of this opinion totters, indeed is completely overthrown, after the nineteen years of Laurentiius’s pontificate have been vindicated. For that most skilled historian of the Church could not have compressed the period during which Saint Gregory lived in the monastery for any other reason than that he believed Laurentiius’s episcopate in the Church of Milan lasted only twelve years and began in 581, the year in which he asserts that the bond signed by Gregory, still praetor, was issued.

Even if no account were taken of the ancient document cited by Mabillon concerning the date of Laurentiius’s episcopate, Gregory himself must certainly be believed, since he repeatedly bears witness that he lived for a long time in the monastery. Thus, in Book V, Letter 48:

> “Marinianus, who for a long time lived with me in the monastery.”

And in *Dialogues* III, chapter 33, concerning Eleutherius:

> “He lived for a long time with me in this city, in my monastery.”

The chronology of the most learned annalist is overturned on another ground by John the Deacon, indeed by Gregory himself. We proved in the preface placed before the *Dialogues*, no. 18, that Gregory wrote them in 593 or 594. In those *Dialogues*, however, in Book IV, chapter 47, while relating the blessed death of certain monks who had shared the monastery with him, as John the Deacon expressly states (*Book I*, no. 19), and as may be gathered clearly enough from Gregory’s words, he says that Merulus’s death had occurred fourteen years earlier. Therefore it occurred either in 579 or 580, and consequently Gregory was not praetor in Rome in 581.

Having weighed these arguments, the most eminent Cardinal Norisius abandons Baronius’s chronology in his historical dissertation *On the Fifth Synod*, §3, and confirms our view. To prove that Saint Gregory had remained for a long time in the monastery, he adduces this passage from *Dialogues* III, chapter 33, where he says of the abbot Eleutherius:

> “He lived for a long time with me in the city, in my monastery.”

**8.** The same eminent writer of the *Annals* infers (*under the year 581*, no. 8), from *Dialogues* IV, chapter 21, that Saint Gregory had Valentinus, or Valentio, as his instructor in the monastic life; that Maximian succeeded him, and Pretiosus succeeded Maximian; and that Probus presided over the monastery of Saint Andrew after Pretiosus. Accordingly, he removes Hilarion from the catalogue of the abbots of this monastery, although John the Deacon reports that Hilarion was Gregory’s first spiritual father and teacher in monastic discipline.

Unless, that is, we say that Hilarion was no other than Valentio, who is mentioned in the aforementioned passage of Book IV of the *Dialogues*. Baronius asserts that Gregory did not serve under Abbot Maximian, because he was not permitted to remain in the monastery for long, contrary to the clear testimony of John the Deacon (*Book I*, no. 6), which we shall support below.

Nor should we fail to mention that this most learned writer is still mistaken when he asserts, on the basis of *Dialogues* IV, chapter 55, that Pretiosus was abbot of Saint Andrew; in that passage Pretiosus is called not abbot but prior. Nor do we read in chapter 21 of the same book that Valentio was Gregory’s instructor in the monastic life. Saint Gregory merely says of him:

> “Valentio, who afterward presided in this Roman city over my monastery as well, as you know.”

As for Probus, whom Baronius counts among the abbots of Saint Andrew, it is likely that he presided over another monastery of Saint Andrew, as we have already noted above in the note to no. 6.

The succession of abbots of Saint Andrew should therefore be restored as follows:

[Col. 0255B] Hilarion, Valentio, Maximianus—who was presiding over the monastery of Saint Andrew when Gregory was appointed as legate—Gregory himself, who governed his monastery after returning from his legation, as we shall see below, and finally Peter, during whose abbacy the holy Doctor wrote his *Dialogues*.

But let us now turn to settle the more serious controversy raised by Baronius concerning the monastic institution that Gregory followed.

# CHAPTER III

**SUMMARY.**—1. Saint Gregory’s monastic profession is certain. —2. Monks in former times, as now, were distinguished by a distinctive habit, and by the tonsure. —3. Baronius’s opinion concerning Saint Gregory’s monastic institution is refuted. —4. Our own view is established. Praise given by Saint Gregory to the life and Rule of Saint Benedict. —5. It was observed in his monasteries. —6. He frequently uses its wording. —7. It was also propagated in Valeria. —8. The objections of opponents are refuted. —9. The testimony of the Council of Douzy concerning the Rule of Saint Benedict. —10. Another invincible argument, drawn from the propagation of this Rule by Saint Gregory’s disciples. —11. Several objections are answered. (A.D. 575.)

**1.** No sensible and sound-minded person can deny that Gregory was a monk, since he himself repeatedly proclaims this concerning himself, both in the *Dialogues*—

[Note: [Col. 0255D] Book IV of the *Dialogues*: “whom I myself, already a monk, saw as a monk”; and in the preface to the *Dialogues*, where he describes his life in the monastery.]

—and in Homily 12 on the Gospels—

[Note: [Col. 0255D] “whom I myself, already a monk, saw as a monk.”]

—and in the preface to the books of the *Moralia*, or in the letter to Saint Leander—

[Note: [Col. 0256D] “I sought the harbor of the monastery,” etc.]

—where he sets out the history of his long-delayed conversion. He says that it would have been burdensome for him to change his outward appearance, especially since he did not doubt that he could serve God while wearing secular dress. But, inspired by heavenly light, he broke through the delays, sought the monastery, and escaped naked from the shipwreck of the world.

Gregory of Tours likewise teaches this about him, and marvels that he exchanged garments precious and sparkling with gems for a cheap garment.

[Col. 0255D] **2.** These statements sufficiently suggest that monastic clothing, as now, was formerly distinctive to monks as well. I would not linger over proving this were it not that I see certain critics raising scruples on the matter.

The point can certainly be demonstrated more clearly than daylight from Gregory. In Book VIII, Letter 5, he writes concerning soldiers who were candidates for the monastic life:

> “According to the regular norm, they must be tested in their own habit for three years, and then, with God’s authority, receive the monastic habit.”

In Letter 8 of the same book:

> “Nor, after casting aside religious clothing, should he return to secular dress.”

And in Letter 9:

> “After casting aside the religious garments that he had voluntarily assumed, he disfigured himself with lay clothing.”

In Book IX, Letter 114, he calls the monastic habit a sacred garment. The same is established by Homily 10 on Ezekiel, no. 8. I omit many other testimonies, since I would waste time needlessly in piling them up.

As they were distinguished by a distinctive garment, so too monks were distinguished by the tonsure. Saint Benedict clearly teaches this in chapter 1 of the Rule, concerning false monks, saying:

> “They are known to lie to God through the tonsure.”

This is also plainly established by Saint Gregory, Book XI, Letter 50, where he orders that the husband of Agathosa, who had become a monk against her wishes, be restored to her:

> “Even if he has already been tonsured.”

That is, even if, after his probation, he had already changed his clothing and received the monastic tonsure.

Read also Book X, Letter 24, from which we learn that among the Greeks the tonsure was likewise an insignia of cenobitic monks, not of hermits, as we learn from Theodore the Studite, Book XI, Letter 137.

[Note: [Col. 0256D] “And what is even more astonishing,” he says, “you who had been shorn, which is the mark of the solitary life . . . are once again letting your promised hair grow in the manner of hermits.” See also Book XI, Letter 50.]

**3.** Having briefly noted these matters as the occasion arose, let us examine Baronius’s opinion concerning Saint Gregory’s monastic institution. He maintains that its founder was not Saint Benedict but Saint Equitius. His only apparent basis is the following statement:

> “It appears from two testimonies of Gregory that Valentio, the first abbot of Saint Andrew, was summoned from a monastery in the province of Valeria, where Saint Equitius’s institution flourished.”

Let us therefore hear the holy Doctor speaking about himself:

> “The venerable Valentius [read: *Valentio*], who afterward, in this city of Rome, presided, as you know, over my monastery also [the word *meoque*, ‘also my,’ is lacking], had previously governed his own monastery in the province of Valeria.”

By what force or art can one extract from these words that Valentio was the first abbot and founder of the monastery of Saint Andrew?

What has this to do with the institution of Equitius or of the Equitian community, to which Valentio supposedly belonged? But, says Baronius, Gregory relates certain things about Saint Equitius that he professes to have learned from his own abbot Valentio. Moreover, Valentio knew these things while living in the monastery of Saint Equitius, which is the only monastery reported to have been famous in the province of Valeria at that time.

As though, while living in some nearby monastery, whether in Valeria or in one of a neighboring region, he could not have learned of a miracle disseminated by public report!

Thus the testimonies produced by Baronius in no way prove that Valentio was a disciple of Saint Equitius or a follower of his institution. Indeed, the opposite may be inferred by comparing two passages with each other.

For in Book I of the *Dialogues*, chapter 4, Gregory asserts that after Equitius’s death he protected his disciples against the Lombards and rescued them from death. But in Book IV, chapter 21, he reports that the Lombards hanged two monks from the monastery of Abbot Valentio in the branches of a tree, and that both died on the same day.

It is also sufficiently clear from Gregory’s statement that Valentio had previously governed his own monastery in Valeria that by “his own” he understood a monastery founded not by Equitius or anyone else but by Valentio himself. In this sense he always calls the Roman asceterium of Saint Andrew “his own.”

Let impartial readers judge, therefore, whether these arguments of the most eminent writer prove that Saint Gregory received his institution not from the monks living in the nearby monasteries of Cassino and the Lateran, as was the common opinion before Baronius, but from monks situated far away in Valeria—and whether they ought to outweigh the weightiest reasons by which we claim this holy man for the Benedictine family.

**4. 1.** It is clear from what was said above—

[Note: [Col. 0257D] Chapter 2, no. 5.]

—that long before he thought of the monastery of Saint Andrew, Gregory knew the deeds, miracles, and writings of Saint Benedict, namely, his Rule.

How highly he valued this Rule is shown in *Dialogues* II, chapter 36:

> “He wrote a Rule for monks,” he says, “preeminent for discernment and radiant in expression.”

He nowhere mentions a Rule composed by Equitius.

For the moment I say nothing of the fact that Saint Gregory was more an admirer than an author of the life of Saint Benedict, to whose portrayal he scarcely found the whole of the second book of the *Dialogues* sufficient. Elsewhere, too, he frequently breaks into praises of Saint Benedict; of Equitius, however, he speaks only in the single chapter 4 of Book I.

How, then, could a man so devoted to monastic perfection, possessing so high an estimation of Saint Benedict and his laws and institutions, have sought another Rule for himself and his monastery instead of that Rule which he called preeminent for its discernment?

**5.** When he calls it, *kat’ exochēn*—“preeminently,” or “by excellence”—the Rule of Monks, he sufficiently shows that it was to be preferred to all others, if any others had already been received in the West.

He is undoubtedly speaking of this Rule in Book XI, Letter 48, when he writes to the abbot Urbicus about the monk Catellus:

> “We have recognized that he is not a monk; for from the small blessing-gift that the monk Bonus had received, he did not hesitate, by asking for a portion, to create a dispute on the journey. Your affection will be able to learn from how much bitterness of heart this proceeded, if you had wished to know the Rule of Monks.”

He is referring to Saint Benedict’s Rule, chapter 54, concerning the prohibition against receiving blessings or any small gifts without the abbot’s command, and chapter 34, where the evil of murmuring is ordered above all to be cut off, and where care is taken that such a vice not creep in under the pretext of procuring necessary things.

Urbicus had been prior in the monastery of Saint Andrew, or at least in another Sicilian monastery founded through Saint Gregory’s generosity, as appears from Book V, Letter 6. Later he became abbot of the monastery of Saint Hermes at Palermo, one of the six Gregorian monasteries, in arranging which he exercised, by the authority of the most holy pontiff, an office resembling that of general prior. This is also clear from the aforementioned Letter 48 of Book XI.

For what reason, then, does Gregory apply to Urbicus and the monks subject to him the Rule of Monks, or the Rule of Saint Benedict—a title by which it is subsequently designated in councils and throughout ecclesiastical writers—unless it was because they were devoted to its precepts?

[Note: [Col. 0257D] Saint Benedict is called “teacher of monks” in the Roman Council under Boniface IV in A.D. 610, six years after Saint Gregory’s death, undoubtedly because of the Rule of Monks written by him. The Council of Clovesho in England, in A.D. 747, praises the Rule of Saint Benedict under the name “monastic Rule,” and quotes its very words from chapter 58. I omit the rest.]

But if this Rule was held as law in the Sicilian monasteries founded by Gregory, why not also in the monastery of Saint Andrew at Rome?

[Col. 0258A] **6.** Certainly Gregory appears to have become so accustomed to the Benedictine Rule, and so nourished by it, that he frequently uses its words.

In Saint Benedict, the word “congregation” means an assembly of monks; the same word occurs hundreds of times in Gregory’s letters in the same sense, as in Letter 48 of Book XI. We observed the same concerning the word *utility*, used to mean useful things.

In Book X, Letters 32 and 61, he calls the divine office the “work of God,” an expression known to those who have read Saint Benedict’s Rule to be familiar to him.

Saint Benedict elegantly admonishes the abbot in Rule, chapter 64:

> “He ought to be more useful than authoritative.”

And Saint Gregory says in *Moralia* XXI, no. 22:

> “They do not rejoice in presiding but in being useful.”

Saint Benedict commands the abbot in Rule, chapter 64:

> “He must hate vices and love the brothers.”

And Saint Gregory writes to the abbot Conon in Book XI, Letter 12:

> “Love persons; persecute vices.”

In Letter 29 of Book XII, Saint Gregory says:

> “For whatever is committed by an inferior concerns the person placed in the first position.”

He is plainly imitating Saint Benedict, who says in Rule, chapter 36, that “whatever is committed by the disciples concerns” the abbot himself.

For Saint Benedict, a “response” is the same as a task or piece of business. Thus chapter 51:

> “Brothers who depart on any task.”

So also in the holy Doctor, especially at the beginning of the letter to Leander placed before the books of the *Moralia*:

> “When the responses of the Apostolic See constrained me there.”

Among both writers, *eulogiae* commonly means small gifts, and *solatium* means assistance. The same holy Legislator often calls the superior of the monastery the prior, as in chapter 53. Saint Gregory does likewise in *Moralia* XXV, no. 36, and frequently elsewhere.

Homily 10 on Ezekiel, no. 31, reads:

> “By the very zeal with which he corrected others, he reproached himself and blushed to think impure thoughts, remembering that he had corrected others for them.”

He had read almost the same thing in Saint Benedict’s Rule, chapter 2, “What kind of person the abbot ought to be,” especially near the end:

> “When he administers correction to others through admonitions, he himself is corrected from vices.”

At the Third Roman Council, held in A.D. 601, Gregory prohibited the celebration of public Masses in monasteries, lest the crowding of the people and the approach of women disturb the servants of God’s peace. He added:

> “This is wholly not advantageous to their souls.”

These words are found verbatim in Benedict’s Rule, chapter 66.

[Note: [Col. 0258D] See Book VIII, Letter 15, and note a, where this council is mentioned. Remove that matter concerning public Masses from the acts of this synod; it scarcely differs from Letter 15.]

In his *Exposition of the First Book of Kings*, however, he uses the sentences and very words of the Benedictine Rule even more frequently. This is not surprising, since he was then abbot and was instructing his pupils in the perfection of the monastic life through these homilies.

In the preface to this commentary you will find many expressions drawn from that celebrated Rule, which we have taken care to collect. We shall now produce only the following passage, but it is so clear that it would suffice to prove that Saint Gregory was a disciple of blessed Benedict:

> “Therefore,” he says, “the excellent teacher of that same most rigorous life, the disciple of supreme truth, also commands, saying: ‘Test the spirits to see whether they are from God’; and again: ‘Let the hard and difficult things by which one goes to God be announced to him, so that he may know what he is entering upon.’”

These words occur almost verbatim in chapter 58 of the Rule.

It would be superfluous to vindicate and affirm here that commentary as Gregory’s, since we have done so in the preceding preface. Nevertheless, we do not deny that some material was added by Abbot Claudius. But if one wishes to attribute to Claudius whatever was drawn from the Rule of Saint Benedict, our opponents still have the same argument to resolve: namely, that the Benedictine Rule was received in the monastery of Saint Andrew.

Claudius was a pupil of this asceterium and, under the discipline of Abbot Gregory, had received what the holy Father had discussed and expounded from the Books of Kings, as he himself testifies in Book XII, Letter 24. If, therefore, Claudius, Saint Gregory’s spiritual son, served under the Rule of Saint Benedict in the monastery of Saint Andrew, what must be thought about the father?

[Col. 0259B] **7. 2.** To overthrow the very foundation of Baronius’s opinion, we must now prove that the Rule of Saint Benedict was propagated in Valeria; indeed, that it alone flourished there when Valentio governed a monastery in that province.

This is clearly demonstrated by the letter of Abbot Fundanus to Simplicius, the third abbot of Saint Benedict’s monastery at Cassino. Mabillon presents it in full in the preface to Volume I of the *Acts of the Saints*, and again defends it in the *Benedictine Annals*, Book VI, no. 2.

The substance of the letter is that at that time all the monasteries of Campania, Samnium, Valeria, Tuscany, Liguria, and the other provinces of Italy had decided, after abandoning their particular Rules, to observe the Benedictine Rule.

Lucas Holstenius, the learned prefect of the Vatican Library, examined this letter in a manuscript codex and approved it on his own authority. Mabillon also inspected the same codex and detected no signs of fraud.

Therefore, shortly after Saint Benedict’s death, the monasteries of Valeria too, even if they had previously been established by Equitius, were following the Rule of the most holy Legislator.

Nor is it surprising that those monasteries, to which Saint Equitius had assigned no definite Rule, later adopted that Rule of Monks which was preeminent for its discernment.

Indeed, it would seem almost miraculous if the Rule of Saint Benedict—which, immediately after its composition, was observed in the twelve monasteries nearest to Subiaco; which was subsequently established, within a short interval, in the monasteries of Cassino and Terracina while Saint Benedict was still alive; which was disseminated in Sicily and shortly afterward in Gaul; and which was sought out and practiced by the Spaniards—had remained, until the time of Saint Gregory, completely unknown and neglected in the province of Valeria, situated not far from Subiaco.

Thus one might argue with Baronius:

> “Valentio was a monk and abbot in Valeria; therefore he was entirely free from the laws of Saint Benedict and obeyed a Rule other than the Benedictine Rule.”

**8.** I know that Gallonius, an advocate of Baronius’s opinion, doubted the authenticity of Abbot Fundanus’s letter because, he says, the names Bernard and Hugo are found in it, although unknown in that century.

But the name Bernard is no more expressed in this letter than are Bartholomew, Barnabas, or others, since only the letter B of an abbreviated name is observed.

Although the name *Bernart* does not seem far removed from the language of the Goths, in which many names ending in *-hart* are found, Smaragdus the abbot provides various examples in Book II, chapter 10, of his commentary on Donatus.

Nor is it surprising that, after the Goths had occupied Italy for a long time, some converts from that people should have entered the monasteries of Italy and later become abbots. Indeed, in the seventh century one of the bishops of Cremona is recorded under the name Bernard, in Volume IV of the *Sacred Italy*.

As for the other name, Hugo or Ugo, which Gallonius noted as unusual in that century, it also seems to breathe of Gothic or Theodisc—Germanic—origin. For nothing occurs more frequently among those northern peoples, who share one origin, than names ending in *God* or *Goth*.

Nor should Gallonius, merely because of one little word, have brought the entire letter under suspicion of fraud, since he himself was the first to publish from a Vatican codex certain verses about our Simplicius that plainly show him to have propagated the Rule of Saint Benedict among all peoples.

Concerning these verses, and the entire subject, see Mabillon, Volume II of the *Analecta*, pp. 200 ff.

**9. 3.** Although I have no intention of disputing the commonly circulated privilege of Subiaco, by which it is said that Saint Gregory confirmed the Rule of Saint Benedict in a synod and proposed it for observance to all monks in the Latin Church, we can scarcely doubt that the most holy pope did this at some time, in view of the clear testimony of the Second Council of Douzy (A.D. 874), chapter 7:

> “That same Rule”—the Rule of Saint Benedict—“promulgated by the Holy Spirit and by the authority of the praise of the blessed Pope Gregory, was decreed to be held among the canonical Scriptures and the writings of Catholic doctors.”

This cannot refer to chapter 36 of Book II of the *Dialogues*—for although the Rule of Saint Benedict is praised in that passage, no decree concerning it is found there—so it is almost certain that Saint Gregory issued such a decree in a synod.

The authority of Boniface IV and of the Roman Council of A.D. 610 also supports this. When a dispute arose between clerics and monks concerning ecclesiastical offices, Boniface and the fathers of the council judged that the controversy should be settled by the Rule of Saint Benedict, since it had already been formally included among the canonical writings of the Church. They decreed that monks should not be excluded from sacred ministries.

> “For Benedict,” said the pontiff, “the teacher of monks, was in no way a prohibitor of this matter.”

**10. 4.** One further argument remains, and it is invincible: it is drawn from the promulgation of the Benedictine Rule in England by the monks whom Gregory the Great sent from the Roman monastery of Saint Andrew. We reserve that argument for another place and shall treat it more suitably when we discuss the conversion of the English to the Christian faith through the work of those monks.

For the present, however, let us answer certain objections that have already been raised or may be raised against the position we have asserted here.

**11.** “Gregory,” you will say, “established certain things greatly at variance with the Rule of Saint Benedict. For while, according to chapter 58 of Benedict’s Rule, the probation of novices scarcely extends to a full year, Saint Gregory writes to Fortunatus, bishop of Naples, in Book X, Letter 24:

> ‘Let your fraternity strictly forbid all monasteries to tonsure those whom they have received for conversion in any way before they have completed two years in the monastic life.’

“Therefore Gregory had not embraced the Rule of Saint Benedict, since in this respect he rejected it.”

I answer that although Saint Benedict does not extend the period of probation for novices beyond one year, he by no means forbids extending it further. Accordingly, in most Benedictine congregations of stricter observance, two years are imposed for the probation of lay brothers, and choir monks are sometimes tested for more than a year for legitimate reasons, without injury to the honor of Saint Benedict or his Rule.

Why Saint Gregory assigned two years for training and testing novices in the monasteries of the diocese of Naples, he himself explains in these words:

> “It has come to our attention that a certain Mauricius, who had recently been converted in the monastery of Barbacianus, fled from that monastery, taking other monks with him. In this matter the aforementioned Barbacianus is vehemently accused by this precipitous action, since he rashly tonsured a secular man who had not previously been tested.”

Indeed, the apostasy of so many monks rashly admitted before sufficient probation was a reason not to be disregarded for decreeing that thereafter they should be trained and tested for two years before making their profession.

Some also object, together with Cardinal Baronius, that Saint Gregory prohibited adolescents from being received into monasteries before their eighteenth year, as is clear from Book I, Letter 50. This plainly conflicts with Saint Benedict’s Rule, which in chapter 59 permits even infants, lacking freedom and the use of reason, to be received into monasteries when offered by their parents.

We reply that this decree of Gregory the Great was promulgated not for all monasteries but only for those founded on certain islands of the Tyrrhenian Sea. The holy pontiff sufficiently indicates this when he writes:

> “Since the monastic community on the islands is harsh, we also prohibit boys from being received in those same monasteries”—the islands of Eumorphiana—“before the age of eighteen . . . . We wish you to observe this in every respect also on Palmaria and the other islands.”

We therefore have the reason why he prohibited adolescents not yet mature in age from being received and made monks in those islands. Their way of life in those places was harsh and rugged, either because of the unhealthy air or because of the sterility of the soil; and tender youths did not possess the strength to endure it.

These are the arguments by which the most eminent writer of the *Ecclesiastical Annals*, or the defenders of his opinion, have attempted to overturn a view concerning Saint Gregory’s monastic life according to the laws of Saint Benedict that had been established for so many centuries by the agreement of almost all learned men.

Let the wise reader judge whether the accepted opinion falls beneath the weight of that artillery, or stands unshaken.

Our Mabillon has written about this controversy at length and learnedly, according to his custom: in the preface to Volume I of the *Acts of the Saints*; in the separate dissertation *On the Monastic Life of Gregory the Great* in Volume II of the *Analecta*; and in the *Benedictine Annals*, Book VI and Appendix I. In the second part, §6, he lists the most authoritative writers from the death of Saint Gregory onward who support our case.

We refrain from naming them, both because, after weighing so many arguments, we scarcely need witnesses, and because the multitude and importance of the matters to be discussed in this controversy do not allow us to linger longer.

Let us now examine what Gregory accomplished in the monastery and how greatly he advanced in the pursuit of virtue.

# CHAPTER IV

**SUMMARY.**—1. Gregory’s progress in the monastery. —2. Evidence for his longer stay there. —3. His abstinence and fasts, and the exceedingly troublesome illnesses that resulted. —4. [Col. 0262B] The extent to which other monks advanced through his example. —5. Even then he was thinking about England. —6. He became a deacon. —7. By which pontiff. —8. Whether he was a cardinal deacon. —9. Whether he was archdeacon. (A.D. 575, 576, etc.)

1. What Gregory became during his peaceful sojourn in the monastery, he himself remarkably portrays when he mourns the quiet he had lost in pastoral care—not with feigned tears of the eyes, but with an inward groaning of the heart—in these words:

> My unhappy soul, struck by the wound of its occupation, remembers what it once was in the monastery; how all passing things lay beneath it; how far it rose above all things that are swept along; how it had been accustomed to think of nothing except heavenly things; how, although still held by the body, it already passed beyond the very confines of the flesh through contemplation; how it even loved death, which is punishment to almost everyone, as the entrance into life and the reward of its labor. But now, because of pastoral care, it endures the affairs of worldly people, and, after so beautiful a vision of its former quiet, it is defiled by the dust of earthly activities. And when it has scattered itself outward for the sake of accommodating itself to many, even when it seeks the interior life, it undoubtedly returns to it diminished. I therefore consider what I endure; I consider what I have lost.  
> *(Preface to the Dialogues.)*

Similar complaints about the lost blessings of monastic life are familiar and almost continual in Gregory when he opens his heart to his friends, as in the letters of Book I, epistles 4, 5, 6, 7, 25, and 26, and in the single prefatory letter to the books of the *Moralia*. Even in his public sermons to the people, he can scarcely suppress and restrain his grief over the loss of the life he had previously led in the monastery with the utmost holiness:

> Indeed, when I was living in the monastery, he says in Homily 11 on Ezekiel, I was able both to restrain my tongue from idle talk and to keep my mind almost continually fixed upon the purpose of prayer.

2. Who could easily persuade himself that Gregory, who, by his own testimony, had to struggle against an ingrained habit of secular, indulgent, and ostentatious living *(Letter to Leander, or Preface to Book I of the Moralia)*, reached at once, while still a novice—as Baronius would have it—that summit of perfection, that height of almost continual prayer and contemplation? Would it not be more reasonable to think that he attained it through arduous labor and constant practice, with divine grace nevertheless assisting him?

Let us, however, grant the point. But how did he acquire, during so brief a stay, such extensive knowledge of moral and spiritual matters as is evident in his exposition of the Book of Job, on which he worked shortly after being taken from the monastery and sent as envoy to Constantinople? Could he perhaps, while almost wholly absorbed in the cares of the praetorship, have made such progress in knowledge of the higher theology, and have searched out the more hidden meanings of sacred Scripture with such ease and success?

Let us therefore attribute to Gregory’s many years of residence and ascetic practice in the monastery that knowledge of divine and sacred things which wise and experienced teachers of the spiritual life rightly admire, since they themselves have been nourished by such studies for almost their whole lives. We have, moreover, already established with sufficient arguments that Gregory’s stay in the monastery was a long one.

3. From the moment he entered the monastic arena, Gregory devoted himself not only entirely to prayer and contemplation but also to abstinence, fasting, and other works of penance, seasoning them with the reading and meditation of the sacred books. He was so devoted to these practices that, with his stomach weakened and his health afflicted, he seemed likely to die shortly.

Yet his frequent illnesses could not persuade him to moderate even slightly such extreme austerity of life. His food consisted of vegetables, which his mother Silvia—who perhaps lived on the same food herself—supplied and prepared. From this diet, as he himself testifies, he contracted a most troublesome illness, which physicians call *syncope*, or “failure of the vital powers.” While suffering from it, he was thought to be approaching death amid repeated attacks of distress from moment to moment; and unless he was frequently strengthened by food, he felt that his vital breath was being cut off. Yet he grieved more over interrupting his fast than over his serious illness.

He was especially distressed that, on the very vigil of Holy Saturday of Easter, when even children fasted, he seemed unable to abstain from food. Nevertheless, through the prayers and tears of his own companions and of Eleutherius, a monk of Saint Andrew’s and his table-companion and associate, he finally obtained the favor. In his supreme humility and modesty, however, he attributed this miracle to Eleutherius alone:

> At the sound of his blessing, he says, my stomach received such strength that food and illness were completely removed from my memory. I began to wonder who I was and what had happened . . . . . and when my mind was occupied with the administration of the monastery, I completely forgot my illness.

What the holy Father here says about his occupation in the administration of the monastery should perhaps be understood as referring to some administration of temporal goods entrusted to him, not to the office of abbot, which, as we have already said with Mabillon, Gregory did not exercise until after his embassy.

[Note: See Book III of the *Dialogues*, chapter 33, concerning the holiness of Eleutherius.]

*(Compare John the Deacon, Book I, nos. 7, 9, 10; Gregory of Tours, Book X, chapter 1; Book III of the Dialogues, chapter 38.)*

4. That very many advanced in the monastery through his example and attained the highest holiness is proved by what he himself relates about many of his fellow soldiers, especially in the *Dialogues*. We have already touched briefly on Eleutherius. Concerning the saints Antonius, Merulus, and John, who, through daily tears, constant prayers, and continual meditation on the sacred writings, were called from heaven and attained eternal happiness, to which they had already flown in spirit, one should read Book IV of the *Dialogues*, chapter 47.

Concerning Saint Maximianus, abbot of the monastery of Saint Andrew and later bishop of Syracuse, see the many passages in the *Dialogues* and the *Letters*. It is extremely difficult to assign precise years to the events that Saint Gregory relates about those saints. It is nevertheless certain that Merulus passed to the better life at least in the year 579, since at least fourteen years elapsed between his death and the time when the *Dialogues* were written, namely in 593 or 594.

[Note: “While Peter . . . had wished to have a burial place made for himself after fourteen years.”]

We shall distinguish the remaining events in the following manner, since John the Deacon perhaps confuses them. We shall say that those events occurred before Saint Gregory’s embassy from whose accounts it is not clear that he was then superior of his monastery; and that those other events occurred after his return from the embassy from which it is evident that he already possessed supreme authority in that monastery.

5. The fervent zeal of the holiest man could not be confined within the cloisters of the monastery. After crossing the ocean to procure the conversion of the English, who were not yet Christians, it burned even more intensely. Paul the Deacon and John the Deacon, following Bede, relate the occasion on which he formed that pious plan.

Although everyone agrees that this occurred before Gregory’s pontificate, John alone asserts that it happened before his embassy to Constantinople; the others neither affirm nor deny this. We shall describe the event from Bede, from whom the account was first taken and who professes to have received it from the tradition of his predecessors. He was a man of the highest reliability and no less diligence, who was not separated from Saint Gregory’s time by a full century.

When Gregory saw in the marketplace boys recently brought from Britain, outstanding in appearance, with fair bodies and remarkable hair, he asked from what people they came. He was told that they were Angles. “Good,” he replied, “for they have an angelic face, and such people ought to be fellow-heirs with the angels in heaven.”

Without delay he approached the supreme pontiff and asked him to send to the English people, whom he heard were still devoted to the worship of idols, some ministers of the sacred word who might work for their conversion. He declared himself ready to undertake this task if it seemed agreeable to the supreme bishop. The pope consented, says Paul the Deacon, overcome by Gregory’s tireless prayers.

Once Gregory had received permission to depart, he selected several companions from his own community at Saint Andrew’s, secretly withdrew as quickly as possible, and set out on the journey. He feared what later occurred: that he might be recalled from the journey by the affection and devotion of his fellow citizens.

When the Romans heard of the holy man’s departure, they approached the supreme pontiff and cried out in a terrible voice: “Come, Apostolic One, what have you done? You have offended Saint Peter; you have destroyed Rome!” Such was the esteem and confidence already conceived for the holy man that the salvation of all seemed to depend upon Gregory alone.

Moved by these cries, and greatly fearing that a revolt was almost imminent, the pope immediately sent messengers to recall the unwilling traveler from his journey as quickly as possible and bring him back to the City, so that the citizens might be calmed when they saw him.

Three days’ journey had already been completed. After a brief rest, Gregory was urging his companions to continue cheerfully along the road they had begun when suddenly messengers sent by the supreme pontiff arrived on sweating horses. They presented a letter ordering Gregory to retrace his steps and return to the City without delay.

The holiest man, who knew that obedience was pleasing to God above all sacrifices, was compelled to obey. He was received at Rome with the greatest rejoicing by people of every rank. Returning to the monastery, he applied himself with renewed fervor to the interrupted labors of the monastic discipline, seeking in them consolation and compensation for the loss he had suffered. But his hope deceived him.

[Note: Paul the Deacon names Pelagius; John the Deacon names Benedict.]

*(Compare Bede, Book II, chapter 1; Paul the Deacon, no. 14; John the Deacon, Book I, no. 20 and following.)*

6. Gregory had scarcely withdrawn into the monastery when the supreme bishop drew him away from its quiet and created him the seventh deacon, both to minister at the altar and to share in the pontiff’s solicitude.

When Gregory is said here to have become the seventh deacon, or *levite*, this indicates that the ancient custom still prevailed at Rome, of which Pope Saint Cornelius speaks in his letter preserved by Eusebius, Book VI, chapter 43: namely, that there should be only seven deacons. This may perhaps have followed the example of the earlier and apostolic Church, in which only seven deacons were ordained.

The number seven also corresponded to the seven principal regions and basilicas of the City, over each of which an individual deacon was placed. Hence they were called *regionarii*, or regional deacons.

[Note: See Mabillon, *Commentary on the Roman Order*. That number of seven deacons was also accepted in the East. For canon 15 of the Council of Neocaesarea, held at the beginning of the fourth century, provides that no more than seven deacons should minister, even if the city is large.]

The holy man explains in his oft-mentioned letter to Leander that force had then been used against him, and testifies that the virtue of obedience had been imposed upon him against his will and resistance, so that he was compelled to yield.

Neither Gregory of Tours nor Paul tells us by which pontiff he was consecrated and summoned to share in ecclesiastical administration. Paul, however, seems to attribute this to Pelagius II. For he expressly testifies that Gregory was made deacon by that same pontiff and sent to Constantinople. Since it is certain that Gregory, not as Benedict’s but as Pelagius II’s envoy or *apocrisiarius*, was present before the emperor, it follows, according to Paul’s account, that he was made deacon not by Benedict but by Pope Pelagius II.

7. John the Deacon had read this in Paul. Since, especially in what he relates about Gregory before he attained the pontificate, he ordinarily does not depart from Paul’s judgment but transcribes his very words and entire periods, it is clear that when he is seen to disagree with Paul, he did so not rashly but for the most serious reason.
