Undoubtedly John had read a different account in the archives of the Roman Church from the one found in Paul’s history.

The most eminent Cardinal Baronius attacks John’s opinion for no other reason than the necessity of defending his own chronology. But we have already shown that his chronology cannot stand, and John’s authority does not otherwise seem to us so contemptible. This deacon of the Roman Church wrote Saint Gregory’s life partly from his letters and other works, and partly from ancient documents of the Church preserved in the archive or record office of the supreme pontiffs.

Those documents have for the most part not reached us. But when we see the diligence and fidelity of that writer in reading the works of the holy Doctor that we possess, and when everything he excerpted from them is found in Saint Gregory with scarcely a single word changed, why should we not be confident and secure concerning his excellent fidelity and sincerity in the other matters he reports?

Certainly, by casting suspicion upon John the Deacon, whether of fraud or of negligence, one also strikes at the authority of another John, namely Pope John VIII. He both encouraged John the Deacon to write Gregory’s life and approved what he had written, undoubtedly after a careful examination, as a work of such importance required.

Therefore, with John the Deacon, we think it must be asserted that Gregory was taken from the monastery by Benedict I and appointed to the ministry of the Church. Benedict I governed the Church after the death of John II, from May 573 until the end of July 577. After three months and a few days had elapsed, Pelagius II was elected supreme pontiff. During his pontificate Gregory began to exercise the office of deacon in the Roman Church, having been ordained by Benedict, his predecessor, shortly before Benedict’s death.

We do not doubt that John the Deacon can be reconciled with Paul in this way. For what prevents us from saying with John that Gregory was appointed by Benedict I to the diaconate of the Roman Church, and perhaps also to an embassy to the emperor, while the embassy itself was not completed until after Benedict’s death, during the pontificate of Pelagius II, his successor? Paul the Deacon would therefore not improperly have written that these things were done by Pelagius.

8. Baronius says that Gregory was made a cardinal deacon *(for the year 581, no. 2)*, although he did not find this stated in any of the ancient writers who wrote about him—unless perhaps we judge that “levite” or “seventh deacon” signifies a cardinal deacon.

Those seven deacons of the Roman Church were indeed attached to individual titular churches, as though to hinges or pivots; hence they could be called cardinals. The same term was also used of priests attached to smaller churches and of bishops attached to larger churches as their proper priests; as Gregory himself says, they were *incardinated*. They are mentioned very frequently in his *Register of Letters*, where the notes should be consulted with the index as a guide.

9. Saint Eulogius, patriarch of Alexandria, appears to have thought that Saint Gregory had been archdeacon, an office possessing supreme administration of all ecclesiastical goods. For Eulogius, who was exceptionally close to our Gregory, asserts in his book *On Ecclesiastical Administration against Novatian* that in the Roman Church, after the death of a bishop, the archdeacon always succeeded him according to ancient custom and constitution.

But how could he have asserted this if he had understood that Saint Gregory, although not an archdeacon, had been advanced to the supreme priesthood? He could not have been ignorant, concerning a friend so intimate to him, whether Gregory had risen to the pontificate from the diaconate alone or from the archdiaconate.

It is nevertheless credible that Eulogius was speaking of an ancient custom of the Church that had by then fallen into disuse. He is discussing Pope Saint Cornelius, by whom, he says, Novatian was made a priest from the archdiaconate, lest, if he remained an archdeacon, he should be appointed Cornelius’s successor; for according to the custom of that period the archdeacon was designated to succeed the supreme priest.

## CHAPTER V

### ARGUMENT

1. Gregory is sent to Constantinople by Pelagius II.  
2. His manner of life at the imperial court.  
3. With which companions.  
4. What he did at Constantinople.  
5. Pope Pelagius’s concern to drive out the Lombards.  
6. Gregory suppresses Eutychius’s new heresy.  
7. Whether he had already disputed with John, Eutychius’s successor.  
8. Our chronology established from the date of the conference held with Eutychius.  
9. Rumors of another new heresy, and Gregory’s opinion concerning it.  
10. He composes the *Moralia*.  
11. His principal friends at court. He receives the emperor’s son from the sacred font.  
12. How long he remained in the imperial city.  
13. He returns to Rome enriched with sacred relics.  

*(From the year 578 to 585.)*

1. Not long after his advancement to the ministry and diaconate of the Roman Church, Saint Gregory was ordered by Pelagius II to move to Constantinople, the seat of the entire empire, so that he might devote himself there to ecclesiastical affairs and their administration and perform the office of *apocrisiarius*—which in Latin one might call a *responsalis*, or rather an administrator of affairs.

Although it is difficult to determine in which year this responsibility was entrusted to him, it is more likely that he was appointed to the office in the year 578 or the following year. Tiberius had begun to rule alone after Justin’s death, and Pelagius II had soon thereafter been substituted for Benedict I. Pelagius doubtless thought he would render himself agreeable to the emperor by sending him as envoy such a distinguished man, formerly outstanding in the chief offices of the state and well known to him personally.

2. Although he lived among courtiers in the imperial city and was compelled to stay in the emperor’s palace itself, he did not abandon his purpose of heavenly living, say the often-mentioned writers of his life, following the venerable Bede.

Since he desired to persevere in the monastery until his final breath but had been unable to fulfill his vow, he somehow caused the monastery to migrate with him and remain continually at his side. Let us hear his own account, written to Saint Leander:

> When I was more freely keeping vigil in an earthly palace, he says, many of my brothers from the monastery, bound to me by genuine love, followed me. I perceive that this happened by divine dispensation, so that, always restrained by their example as though by an anchor’s rope, I might hold fast to the calm shore of prayer and not drift upon the unceasing waves of secular affairs. To their company I fled as though to the inlet of a most secure harbor [lacuna]. And although that ministry, having drawn me from the monastery and from the life of my former quiet, had extinguished me with the sword of its occupation, yet among them, through the conversation of diligent reading, the daily inspiration of compunction kept me alive.

Could Gregory have described more vividly how piously he conducted himself in carrying out his embassy to Constantinople?

3. Among those who joined the holy man as companions on his journey, or who, moved by affection, visited him while he was staying in the imperial city, Saint Maximianus stood out. He was a priest and abbot of the monastery of Saint Andrew, later appointed bishop of Syracuse, and is well known from many of Gregory’s letters, whether addressed to him or written about him.

After remaining there for several years, Maximianus was compelled by order of the supreme pontiff to return to Rome to care for and supervise his monastery. John the Deacon presents Pelagius’s letter recalling Maximianus, from which we can infer when he returned to Rome, leaving Gregory at Constantinople.

The letter is dated the fourth day before the Nones of October, in the third indiction; this is how it is read in all the manuscripts we have consulted. This indiction, which began in September, belongs to the year 584. Maximianus returned either at the end of that year or at the beginning of the next. Thus, in the year 585 Gregory was still staying—or rather exiled—in the imperial city. He grieved at being in exile for as long as he was compelled to live amid the noise of the court.

With regard to Maximianus’s return, Saint Gregory relates that he and his companions were delivered from imminent danger of death in the Adriatic Sea by a remarkable miracle. For eight days the ship in which they were sailing, filled with water up to the upper deck, nevertheless floated onward and continued its proper course:

> On the ninth day it was brought into the harbor of the fortress of Croton. All who were sailing with the aforementioned venerable man Maximianus came out unharmed. When he himself too had disembarked after them, the ship was immediately submerged in the depths of the same harbor, as though, when they had left it, it had lacked the lifting power provided by their weight. The vessel that, full of men, had carried water upon the sea and floated upon it, when Maximianus and his brothers departed, was unable to carry water without men in the harbor.  
> *(Book III of the Dialogues, chapter 36.)*

After Maximianus’s departure, many of the brothers continued always to cling to Gregory. Whether as envoy of the Apostolic See or later as bishop, he valued monks so highly that he always wished to have them, so to speak, as companions at his table, helpers in his works, participants in his counsels, and witnesses—indeed, I might almost say, guides and arbiters—of his life.

For this reason Saint Leander, also a practitioner of monastic life, frequently joined the company of the monks who lodged with Gregory in the imperial city. More will be said about him later.

4. The writers do not relate what Gregory did with the emperor Tiberius Constantine. Gregory himself, wholly free from every desire for self-display, buried the matter in profound silence.

At that time two things especially afflicted the Roman Church and all Italy: the schism formed over the Three Chapters and the war with the Lombards. Pelagius’s letters, which we shall briefly mention, testify how concerned he was to settle the schism and recall the schismatics to the bosom of the Church. Our Gregory pursued the same cause with no less zeal, as is also clear from his letters and other documents. It is therefore sufficiently evident that the most wise envoy frequently acted before the emperor to bring a remedy to so great a scandal, so shameful a division, and so grave a wound.

A great hope of extinguishing the schism had certainly arisen when the pious emperor Tiberius, devoted above all to ecclesiastical peace, began to sit alone at the helm of the state after Justin’s death. The Romans especially promised themselves that he would expel the Lombards from all Italy, after the many splendid victories he had won over the Persians.

At that time, having shaken off the yoke of royal authority, the Lombards obeyed thirty-six dukes, who had divided among themselves the cities they had occupied. Paul the Deacon relates that, throughout a whole decade, these tyrants despoiled churches, killed priests, overthrew cities, and exterminated peoples who had multiplied like crops.

*(Paul the Deacon, Book II of the History of the Lombards, chapter 17.)*

During this period of interregnum and quasi-anarchy, around the year 579 or 580, the monastery of Cassino, the most famous throughout Italy, was plundered and destroyed by the barbarians.

5. Since Italy was suffering so many disasters at the hands of the Lombards, and even more serious dangers threatened Rome, Pope Pelagius thought the time opportune for liberating his country, since the power of the barbarian people seemed weakened by being divided among so many factions and dukes.

For this reason he not only wrote to Gregory the letter reported by John the Deacon *(Book I, no. 32)*, urging that aid be sent as quickly as possible to the endangered Roman state in the form of money, an exceptionally skilled commander, and troops; he also warned Aunacharius, bishop of Auxerre, who was one of the counselors of the Frankish kings, so that he might use the authority he possessed among them to arrange for assistance to be brought to the Roman Church and to Italy, from which the light of faith had shone upon Gaul, and to deter the pious princes—whose faith was one with that of the Romans—from entering into any alliance with the Lombards.

Pelagius’s letter is dated to the seventh year of Tiberius’s reign. The period of that reign must necessarily be calculated from before he began to rule alone. Not long afterward King Childebert successfully waged war against the Lombards, who had already often invaded Gaul, evidently moved by Pelagius’s letters, as it is reasonable to believe.

As for the emperor Tiberius, distracted by other wars and cares, he gave little thought to recovering Italy or even preserving Rome. Thus the City seems at that time and afterward to have stood only through the prayers of the devout—especially the female servants of God—and the protection of the holy apostles.

6. Nothing more beneficial to the Christian commonwealth did Gregory accomplish while at Constantinople than suppressing the nascent heresy of Eutychius, patriarch of Constantinople, concerning the impalpability of the bodies of the saints after the resurrection.

Gregory himself gives a complete account of the dispute in Book XIV of the *Moralia*, sections 72–75; a transcript of it is found in John the Deacon, Book I, chapter 29. The victory went to Gregory. But Eutychius received the fruit of the victory, since shortly before his subsequent death he renounced his error.

The emperor Augustus Tiberius confirmed Gregory’s teaching by his own judgment and resolved to destroy Eutychius’s book by fire. Eutychius was succeeded, unwillingly and reluctantly, by John, surnamed the Faster.

7. Whether Gregory had already disputed with John over the title “ecumenical,” which John had usurped, is unknown to us. Gregory testifies in Letter 68 of Book IX that John had used this proud title at a synod, that Pelagius, his predecessor, had annulled the acts of that synod, and that, after first rebuking John with the utmost severity, Pelagius had forbidden his own deacon or *apocrisiarius* to proceed with John—that is, to communicate with him in the celebration of the sacred rites.

But he passes over in silence who that deacon was: Gregory, or Laurence, who succeeded him. If Gregory wished to speak of himself, why did he not say that Pelagius had ordered him not to proceed with John? He therefore seems to designate someone other than himself.

8. Since we read in Gregory that the emperor Tiberius took part in the dispute with Eutychius, and since the better chronographers and historians consistently assert that Tiberius died in August of the year 582, a new argument arises against Baronius’s opinion that Saint Gregory adopted monastic life at a later date—namely, in 582 or 581, when Baronius maintains that he was still serving as praetor.

Our chronology is confirmed by Gregory of Tours, who writes that Maurice began to reign in the eighth year of King Childebert—that is, in the year 582. Childebert succeeded his father Sigebert, who was killed in 575; and his fifteenth regnal year, which the same writer says was completed, corresponds to the year 590.

The authority of the venerable Bede also supports us. In Book I, chapter 23, of his *Ecclesiastical History*, he says:

> In the year from the incarnation of the Lord 582, Maurice, the fifty-fourth emperor from Augustus, undertaking the empire, held it for twenty-one years;

that is, for twenty complete years and one year begun.

With the chronology established upon such unshakable foundations, one may ask the defenders of Baronius’s chronology how it can be understood that Gregory was still a layman and praetor in the year 581, afterward put on the monastic habit, then taken from the monastery in which he repeatedly asserts that he had lived for a long time, made a deacon, immediately sent to Constantinople, and there disputed with Eutychius the patriarch—at least in April of the year 582—when it is certain, as Baronius himself admits, that Eutychius’s death, according to Eustathius, who was present, preceded by four months the death of the emperor Tiberius, who, as we have said, departed this life in August of 582? But enough of this.

*(Compare Gregory of Tours, Book VI of the History, nos. 25 and 30; Book X, no. 1.)*

9. At the same time that Gregory was staying in the imperial city, a rumor arose concerning a new heresy, though Gregory himself suspected that it was imaginary. He discussed it in Letter 45 of Book XI.

Its adherents were said, under the pretext of religion, to dissolve marriages and to teach that baptism does not completely remove sins. They also taught that if someone did penance for his wickedness for three years, he might afterward live perversely with impunity.

> But with my conscience as witness, Gregory says, I confess that I never found in them any error, any depravity, or any of the things alleged against them. Therefore, setting aside the opinion held about them, I made a practice of receiving them familiarly and, rather, defending them against their persecutors.

This example teaches us how to deal with those who are freely slandered on account of a false doctrine.

10. Whatever time was free from business was devoted to reading sacred Scripture and to pious studies. At that time Leander, bishop of Seville, who was himself serving as an envoy to the emperor, encouraged Gregory to explain the Book of Job.

The common profession of monastic life, nearly equal holiness of conduct, and identical studies had established a deep bond between those two outstanding men.

Concerning Saint Leander’s embassy to the emperor on behalf of Hermenegild, king of the Visigoths in Spain, the Spanish writers should be consulted; and Book III of the *Dialogues*, chapter 31, should be read.

Compelled to yield to the prayers of his very dear friend and of his brothers, Gregory applied himself to unlocking the mysteries of such depth hidden in the Book of Job. He was certain, he says, “that what love commanded from the hearts of brothers could not be impossible.”

But concerning this work, which the holy Doctor dedicated to Leander, it is worthwhile to read what he says in its preface and the admonition that we placed before it.

[Note: Concerning Saint Leander, see Mabillon, *Benedictine Annals*, Book VI, no. 64, and Nicolaus Antonius in the *Bibliotheca vetus Hispana*.]

11. Besides Saint Leander, Gregory acquired many other friends in the imperial city, especially Domitianus, a relative of the emperor Maurice and bishop of Melitene, of whom more will be said below; Theoctista, the emperor’s sister; and the patrician Narses, celebrated for his successful wars against the Persians.

Because he had not sufficiently investigated the matter, Baronius thought this Narses was the same man who, after winning many victories over the Goths in Italy, later stained and disgraced such glorious achievements by inviting the Lombards to ravage Italy in revenge for a private injury.

We pass over the others, who will frequently be mentioned in the history of Gregory’s pontificate. In brief, he gained the familiarity and friendship of many, and the love and esteem of all.

We cannot, however, pass over in silence what Gregory of Tours relates *(Book X, chapter 1)*: that, while he was still staying at Constantinople, Gregory acted as baptismal sponsor for the holy deacon, the son of the emperor Maurice—undoubtedly his eldest son. Everyone can understand how greatly this honored Gregory.

12. From this testimony of the historian Gregory we can more easily determine in what year the holiest man returned to Rome.

Maurice did not marry Constantina, daughter of the emperor Tiberius, until he became emperor; at the same time he received both a wife and the empire as her dowry, namely in August of the year 582, as we have already demonstrated above. Therefore, no son could have been born to him before April or May of the following year.

This proves clearly that Gregory did not leave the imperial city earlier. Yet from the letter of Pelagius written to him and produced by John the Deacon *(Book I, chapter 32)*, a considerably longer stay is inferred. For the letter is read as having been written in October of the third indiction, and therefore in the year 584.

Gregory did not leave Constantinople in that year either, because, as we said above, Maximianus—recalled by the celebrated letter—departed from Constantinople in that year or even the following year, and Maximianus’s departure from Constantinople preceded Gregory’s return, as is clear from Book III of the *Dialogues*, chapter 36.

I do not see how these facts can stand together with the opinion of Baronius and Binius.

[Note: In the notes on the letter of Pelagius II, among the Councils.]

They maintain that immediately after Maurice was proclaimed emperor—which, as we have already shown, occurred in August of the year 582—Laurence was sent by Pelagius to succeed Gregory in the office of *apocrisiarius*.

Further proof of Gregory’s longer stay in the imperial city is supplied by the immense volume of the *Moralia*, which he composed there and which several years could scarcely have sufficed to complete, especially amid so many affairs. Neither Saint Leander nor Gregory’s brothers and companions would have urged him to undertake that work if, as Baronius holds, he had intended to remain at Constantinople only a short time.

13. Let us now consider Gregory’s return to Rome, and follow him as he returns, just as we accompanied him when he departed.

He returned with great gifts, enriched with the most sacred relics—namely, the arm of the apostle Saint Andrew and the head of Saint Luke. After obtaining these holy treasures from the emperor, he placed them in his Roman monastery, as Baronius relates *(for the year 586, no. 24)* from the earlier page of the Vatican manuscript numbered 153.

Nothing contrary to this account is found in what Gregory himself says in Book IV, Letter 30, to the empress Constantina: that it is not customary, when relics of the saints are given, to presume to touch anything from the body. For he is speaking of the custom and practice of the Romans and Latins, not of the Greeks.

Gregory also brought back from the emperor Maurice the hope of imminent assistance for Italy; this arrived shortly afterward under Smaragdus, exarch and successor to Longinus.

If, however, anyone maintains that Smaragdus preceded Gregory’s return, I shall not quarrel over a matter so uncertain. It is not easy to assign with certainty the time when Gregory returned to his homeland.

It is nevertheless certain that this assistance was obtained through his prayers and efforts. Moreover, from Letter 1 of Pelagius to Elias, bishop of Aquileia, we learn what Smaragdus’s arrival accomplished for Italy. The supreme pontiff congratulates him that, through the labors and solicitude of his most excellent son Smaragdus, exarch and registrar (*chartularius*) of the sacred palace, God had deigned to grant peace and quiet.

## CHAPTER VI
## Argument

1. Saint Gregory becomes abbot of his monastery.  
2. Pelagius employs him as his assistant in writing letters.  
3. The subject of the first letter written to Elias against the schism.  
4. Concerning the second letter to the same Elias.  
5. Concerning the third.  
6. Certain bishops falsely renounce the schism.  
7. Saint Gregory revises his books of the *Moralia*.  
(From A.D. 585 to 589.)

### 1

After returning to Rome, Gregory withdrew once more into the haven of his monastery, detesting the turmoil of the city and the imperial court. There, at the request—or rather the insistence—of the brothers, he performed the office of abbot.

[Note: Saint Maximian, formerly abbot of Saint Andrew’s, had recently been appointed bishop of Syracuse.]

That he lived and presided in the monastery after his return and before his elevation to the pontificate is made certain by Gregory himself, who, in Book IV of the *Dialogues*, chapter 55, recounts the unhappy death of Justus, a monk of Saint Andrew’s. He says that it occurred three years previously, that is, shortly before he ascended the apostolic see. From this passage it is clear that this monk, trained in medicine, was accustomed to serve Gregory diligently—who was then established in the same monastery of Saint Andrew—and to keep constant watch during his frequent illnesses.

When Justus, near death, was discovered guilty of concealing money, Gregory could not bear the report of so great an evil with equanimity. Immediately, as the avenger of the monastery’s violated rule—for he was its abbot—he began to consider either what should be done for the dying man’s purification or what provision should be made as an example for the living brothers.

He therefore summoned Pretiosus, the monastery’s superior, and ordered him to ensure that all the brothers withdrew from association with the guilty man. He also commanded that, after his death—even though he repented at the point of death—a burial in a dung-pit be prepared for him, and that the three gold pieces he had concealed be thrown upon his corpse, while the brothers cried out: “Your money be with you unto perdition.”

Finally, because Justus had closed his last day repentant of his sin, Gregory arranged for Pretiosus the superior to offer the sacrifice for his absolution during thirty consecutive days.

[Note: We have already spoken of the sacrifice customarily offered for the dead in the note on Book IV of the *Dialogues*, chapter 55.]

Read either in the aforementioned book of the *Dialogues* or in John the Deacon how greatly the severity of this most wise abbot benefited Justus and the other brothers.

The generous almsgiving that Gregory carried out while he lived in the monastery, as reported by the same John, also proves that he then presided over the monastery; otherwise he would not have ordered the keeper of the wardrobe to distribute so many coins.

[Note: John calls the monk in charge of guarding the wardrobe by this name. In the *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, Book I, chapter 25, *vestiarium* denotes the place where money was also kept. Properly speaking, a *vestiarium* was the place where sacred vestments, vessels used in the altar’s service, and other valuables were stored. Since it was more secure, it may sometimes have been chosen for the safekeeping of money. See note 1054 on the *Sacramentary*.]

John the Deacon subsequently reports many events that occurred while Gregory occupied the place of abbot. Among them were miracles and signs by which God terrified certain monks—whether they were fleeing, considering flight, or guilty of some other offense—and recalled them to a sounder mind.

But this writer is mistaken, since Gregory himself, writing to Rustician in Letter 44 of Book XI, relates the same events and says that he learned them from the abbot and the superior of this monastery.

But why should we seek arguments elsewhere, when Gregory himself expressly declared before a synod that he had once governed a monastery, in these words: “Does not the office which we formerly performed in governing a monastery teach us how necessary it is to have regard for the peace of monasteries . . . ?” (*Third Council*, or Lateran Council under Saint Gregory.)

### 2

Although this holy man sought leisure and seclusion in the recesses of the monastery, he was not long permitted to enjoy them fully or to withdraw altogether from ecclesiastical affairs. For just as Jerome assisted Pope Saint Damasus in writing letters, and Prosper assisted Saint Leo the Great, so Gregory assisted Pelagius the Younger in composing letters.

Baronius held this opinion; and Paulus Warnefridus, in Book III of *The History of the Lombards*, expressly attributes to Gregory a highly useful letter sent by Pope Pelagius to Elias, bishop of Aquileia. He says that “the blessed Gregory, while he was still a deacon, wrote it.”

Three letters were published both by Baronius (*Annals*, A.D. 586, no. 26) and by the collectors of the councils: letters of Pelagius II to Elias and to the other bishops and sons of the Church of Istria, who were agitating on behalf of the Three Chapters.

The three letters have one subject and one aim, and their style is plainly similar. Gregory, therefore, is the author of all three, since Paul’s testimony establishes that he wrote at least one of them.

Moreover, in those letters that Gregory, once he had become pope, wrote to the same schismatics—or to others whom he knew to remain attached to the condemnation of the Three Chapters—the same charity burns toward the enemies of peace, and the same indulgence shines forth toward the anxious and scrupulous.

We shall speak of these matters more fully later. For now, it is necessary briefly to explain what is principally contained in the three letters written in the name of Pelagius II.

### 3

In the first letter, the most devout Father begins by speaking of the division of his inmost being—that is, of the schism tearing the Church apart—and says that he has grieved over it with profound lamentation. With tears he exhorts the dissidents to peace.

To those wavering in the faith he sets against them the unfailing faith of Peter; to those who are stumbling, the firmness of Peter’s see, against which the gates of hell cannot prevail.

Furthermore, so as to remove every opportunity for accusing him, he declares that he embraces what has been handed down by the apostles and their successors and explained and confirmed in the four ecumenical councils—especially in the Council of Chalcedon, whose authority the schismatics complained was being attacked and undermined by the condemnation of the Three Chapters at the Fifth Council.

If these assurances should not seem sufficient to suppress the scandal, he asks them to remain in the charity of unity and to choose and send some of their brothers to present and settle all their questions peacefully.

“And we are ready,” says that good shepherd, compassionate toward the wandering sheep, “according to the apostolic command, both to receive them with charity and, with humility, to give an account in satisfaction of their demands; and, without any impediment, with all affection and the sincerest goodwill, whenever they wish to return, to send them back” (1 Peter 3).

### 4

The schismatics replied to this letter by sending writings infected with various corruptions. They inserted unsuitable testimonies of the Fathers, irrelevant to the case, and so confused the order that what had been written under one person’s name was presented under the title of another, as Pelagius observes in his second letter to Elias and his fellow ministers. Hence he applies to them the words of the Apostle: “Understanding neither what they say nor what they affirm” (1 Timothy 1:7).

Therefore, in order to destroy the false and fabricated material with what was true and genuine, Pelagius arranged for the schismatics’ envoys to be shown the authentic acts of the councils, taken from the ancient registers of the archive of the Holy Apostolic See.

In his second letter he also earnestly exhorted them to charity and unity, the rupture of which is so unpardonable a fault that it is not cleansed even by martyrdom.

Finally, he invited them to hold a conference at Rome through their representatives. Or, if distance between the places proved an obstacle, he asked them to meet near Ravenna, a city bordering Istria. He promised that he would send envoys there to take part in the synod in his place.

### 5

The vigilance and concern of that most watchful shepherd for the sheep wandering outside the Church’s enclosures and pastures proved fruitless.

To defend their obstinacy in the schism, they published an apology on behalf of the Three Chapters condemned at the Fifth Council. To refute it, Pelagius once again made use of Gregory’s assistance and wrote a third letter, which Gregory himself calls a book (Book II, Letter 51).

From this letter we understand that the bishops of Istria and the neighboring regions had advanced so far in madness that, by a deliberate judicial decision, they commanded the supreme pontiff—who was offering such splendid examples of humility and charity—to withdraw from the condemnation of the Three Chapters.

Pelagius laments this rebellion. He grieves that the sheep outside the folds are exposed to the bites of the roaring lion; that branches cut from the vine wither and are prepared for burning; that laborers working and sweating outside the vineyard are deprived of their wages; and that, while a new flood overwhelms the world, insane men flee from the ark.

To satisfy all the arguments the schismatics had put forward, he first examines individually the testimonies of Pope Saint Leo that they misused in support of the Council of Chalcedon. He shows that these testimonies favor only the definition of the faith. He argues that the issue is not the definition of the faith but certain persons, as had already been clearly proved in the preceding letter.

Next, he unties the knot that they had tightened by appealing to the resistance of Pope Vigilius and other Latin bishops—who, it is well known, had previously refused most firmly to consent to the condemnation of the Three Chapters.

He says that the Latins, being less skilled in the Greek language, were initially unable to detect the errors concealed in the writings of Theodoret, Theodore, and Ibas. Once these errors had finally become known, they willingly subscribed to their condemnation and reviewed the earlier acts.

Nor, he says, is it surprising that Peter’s successor changed his judgment, since Peter himself, who had initially resisted the admission of the Gentiles into the Holy Church without circumcision, later yielded when rebuked by Paul and opposed the imposition of the yoke of the Mosaic law upon the Gentiles.

Finally, Pelagius adduces many impious statements concerning Christ from the writings of Theodore of Mopsuestia, as well as many passages from the letter of Ibas, which plainly reveal how stubbornly Ibas adhered to Nestorius and how fiercely he raged against Saint Cyril, the impious Nestorius’s adversary. It is therefore evident that their writings were rightly condemned as either heretical or favorable to heresy.

With respect to Theodoret, Pelagius says:

“We do not condemn all of Theodoret’s writings, but only those that he is shown at some time to have written against Cyril’s Twelve Chapters, only those that were written against the true faith; and yet even these he himself is known to have condemned.”

This letter certainly deserves to be read in its entirety. No one who has any familiarity with Saint Gregory’s writings will be able to doubt that it is his work, for it has the character of Gregory’s phrasing and his method of explaining Sacred Scripture.

The same criterion applies to the other two letters. For this reason, we have judged that they should be inserted here, at least in part.

### 6

Since these weapons could not overcome the obstinate schismatics, the patrician Smaragdus came from Ravenna to Grado. He personally dragged Severus, bishop of Aquileia—or Grado—from the basilica and took him dishonorably to Ravenna together with three other bishops.

These are the words of Paulus Warnefridus in his *History of the Lombards*. Smaragdus threatened them with exile and inflicted violence upon them, compelling them to communicate with John of Ravenna [lacuna].

After a year had passed, they returned from Ravenna to Grado. The people refused to communicate with them, and the other bishops would not receive them.

That Severus was incorporated into the unity of the Church, which he later abandoned, is testified by Saint Gregory in Book I, Letter 16, addressed to him.

### 7

At that time, when Gregory enjoyed a somewhat freer leisure, he revised his exposition of Job, adding much and removing little, as he himself says in the preliminary letter to those books. Read there what else he accomplished in this, as it were, second edition of the *Moralia*.

But that pleasant quiet was disturbed by a very severe plague, which devastated Rome and Italy and carried off Pelagius, the supreme pontiff. Gregory was elected in his place.

These matters must now be treated at greater length.

# Chapter VII

## Argument

1. The overflowing of the Tiber.  
2. The evils that followed, including the plague. After Pelagius was carried off by the plague, Gregory was elected in his place. The emperor’s consent is sought.  
3. Whether this was lawful or unlawful.  
4. Whether money was paid to obtain consent.  
5. The plague rages more fiercely. Gregory urges the Romans to repentance.  
6. He orders public supplications.  
7. By what authority.  
8. He flees and seeks hiding places. He is recognized by the sign of a shining column.  
(A.D. 589 and 590.)

### 1

In the eighty-ninth year after the five-hundredth, in the ninth month, that is, November, the river Tiber covered the city of Rome with such a great flood that ancient buildings were destroyed. The storehouses of the Church were also overturned, and several thousand measures of wheat perished in them, as says the first historian of Frankish affairs, Gregory of Tours (Book X, chapter 1).

He observes that this occurred in the fourteenth year of King Childebert. This must be understood as the completed, not the beginning, of that year. For, according to the same historian Gregory, in the middle of the following eleventh month—that is, in January—Pope Pelagius was struck by the plague.

[Note: When you read here that January is the eleventh month of the year, understand that Gregory of Tours began the year not in January but in March.]

Since the Church of God could not remain without a ruler, the entire people elected the deacon Gregory. No one disputes that Gregory was ordained in September of the year 590.

But if Pelagius had been struck by the plague and died when Childebert’s fourteenth year had only begun—that is, in the year 588—the Roman see would have remained vacant for twenty months, from January 588 until Saint Gregory’s ordination in September 590. Yet none of the historians recorded in writing that Rome, or indeed the entire Church, was then without a shepherd for so long.

Therefore, the flood reported by Gregory of Tours occurred in November 589; in the following January the plague took Pope Pelagius away. Gregory was elected supreme pontiff shortly afterward. But because he resisted and the emperor’s consent had to be awaited, his ordination could not take place before the beginning of the following September.

These certain limits had to be established and the chronology fixed before we could proceed to the other events that either preceded Gregory’s election or followed it.

Gregory himself mentions the flooding of the Tiber in Book III of the *Dialogues*, chapter 19, in these words:

“About five years ago, when the Tiber left its channel near this city of Rome, rising so high that its waters flowed over the walls of the city and then occupied its largest districts, the river Athesis, swollen near the city of Verona, reached the church of the blessed martyr and bishop Zeno.”

These details further confirm the chronology we have established. Gregory wrote the *Dialogues* in the year 593, which was approximately the fifth year—that is, the fifth year beginning—from 589.

The swelling of the Tiber had already more than once been fatal to Rome, and Horace had witnessed it in his own time:

“The Tiber, driven back  
by the waves hurled violently  
from the Etruscan shore,  
goes down, having overthrown  
the memorials of the king  
and the temples of Vesta.”  
(Book I, Ode 2.)

The overflowing of this river was regarded as one of the greatest disasters of the city and the world. Hence Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter 40:

“If the Tiber rises against the walls, if the Nile does not rise over the fields; if the sky stands still, if the earth moves; if famine, if plague—immediately, ‘To the lion with the Christians!’ as though they were the provocateurs and authors of all these calamities through their crimes.”

### 2

Gregory of Tours describes the immense evils caused by this near-limitless overflowing of the Tiber in these words:

“A multitude of serpents, together with a great dragon as strong as a beam, descended through the bed of this river into the sea. But the beasts, suffocated amid the salty waves of the turbulent sea, were cast upon the shore.”

Immediately afterward came the disaster called the bubonic plague. According to the same Gregory, Pope Pelagius was the first of all to be struck by this scourge and to die, in accordance with what is written in the prophet Ezekiel: “Begin from my sanctuary.”

Soon afterward came a great slaughter of the people. In such calamity, therefore, the Roman people fled to Gregory and elected him supreme pontiff.

But he attempted more earnestly to flee this height, lest the pride he had earlier rejected should again steal upon him in the world because of the honor he had attained. He immediately begged Maurice Augustus, whose son he had received from the sacred font, in suppliant letters not to consent to the election by which the people had chosen him and demanded him for the episcopate.

It is also conjectured that he wrote to John, patriarch of Constantinople, asking him to persuade and induce the emperor—at whose court he possessed considerable influence—to annul this election. This may be inferred from Book I, Letter 4, in which Gregory reproaches John because he had not in the least opposed his elevation to the episcopate.

But the prefect of the city of Rome, his brother, forestalling the messenger, sent the emperor the formal decree of election.

[Note: Some read Gregory of Tours as saying “the prefect of the city, Germanus, his . . .,” considering it entirely inappropriate to refer *his* to Germanus. We have already shown above, chapter I, no. 5, that Saint Gregory had a brother.]

Maurice gave thanks to God that the deacon, who was closely bound to him by friendship, had been called by popular vote to so great a summit of honor. Then, issuing the customary order, he commanded that Gregory be installed and ordained.

These details are excerpted from Gregory the historian, who had learned them from an eyewitness, a deacon of the Church of Tours, who was then living in Rome.

Among the leading men who contributed greatly to Gregory’s election by their votes and perhaps also by their counsel and influence, special praise belongs to John, formerly consul and quaestor, a man of patrician nobility, and to Philip, count of the excubitors. Gregory complains about them on this account in Book I, Letters 31 and 32.

That Gregory was only a deacon when he was elevated to the pontificate is clear from the testimony of the other Gregory. Nor do we read that he had been made a priest before he was anointed and consecrated pope. We readily acknowledge that this conflicts with modern practice, but perhaps it did not conflict with ancient practice.

[Note: See the notes on Book X, Letter 34, note d.]

### 3

What the cited writer relates about the emperor’s consent being requested and awaited before the elected Gregory was ordained will undoubtedly trouble the minds of some.

But, at least from the time when the Gothic kings held Italy, it had become customary for an elected pope not to take his seat until the ruler’s confirmation had first been received.

This practice—whether lawful or unlawful—was given the following justification: since the election of the supreme pontiff then belonged not only to the clergy but also to the senate and people of Rome, it ought not to stand without the authority of the emperor or ruler, who was the head of the senate and people.

Nor does Gregory, who acknowledges that the sacred ministry was entrusted to him by the emperor (Book I, Letter 5), appear ever to have condemned or disapproved this custom.

For what Baronius adduces in order to show that the most holy pontiff disapproved of the practice was taken from a spurious, or at least doubtful, commentary on the Penitential Psalms.

[Note: “He entrusted the ministry of virtue to the weak.”]

[Note: See the critique of this commentary in Volume III, Part II, column 463.]

After the restoration of the empire in the West, Charlemagne and his successors possessed this right of confirming the supreme pontiff without opposition, as is clear from Anastasius, librarian of the Roman Church, and from other writers who were generally not hostile to the apostolic see.

### 4

The same eminent cardinal believes that Maurice’s consent to Gregory’s election was obtained by the payment of money.

[Note: *Annals*, A.D. 590, no. 5.]

I do not know whether this is found in any writing of this period or a later one. The complaint about the bride of Christ being made captive and subjected to tribute, which he quotes from the commentary on the Penitential Psalms, neither signifies this nor lies beyond suspicion of interpolation and forgery.

I am not unaware that the Arian Athalaric once demanded three thousand solidi for confirmation of the apostolic pontiff and two thousand for confirmation of the election of other patriarchs—that is, metropolitans. But no one who has read Gregory’s many letters against the simoniacal heresy will be able to persuade himself that Catholic rulers, after Italy had been liberated from the Goths, demanded the same payment, or that Gregory would not have recoiled from such a simoniacal payment of money.

Moreover, the Arian king ordered money to be paid only when, concerning the election or ordination of bishops, a dispute among the people had been brought before the palace.

[Note: Justinian’s order, about which Baronius writes under A.D. 554, nos. 1 and 2, must be understood in the same sense, as must the passage in Anastasius the Librarian under Agatho: “He received an imperial decree by which the amount customarily given for the ordination of a pontiff was reduced; nevertheless, if an election happened after his death, the one elected was not to be ordained unless a general decree had first been brought into the imperial city according to ancient custom.” Volume VI of the Councils, under Agatho, p. 574. In any case, this payment of money seems to have been imposed rather upon the electing people, so that they might retain the right of election, than upon the elected pontiffs.]

But in Gregory’s election the agreement of the people was extraordinary.

I add that this passage from the imperial rescript to Pope John is obscure, since in it the king promulgates highly salutary decrees against simoniacs, whether those who give or those who receive.

(Compare Cassiodorus, Book IX, Letter 15.)

### 5

Meanwhile, while the emperor’s reply and consent were awaited, the plague increased day by day, and Rome was devastated by continual funerals.

The monastery of Saint Andrew’s was not spared this scourge. At that time, the concern and charity of all the brothers toward the young Theodore, who had been stricken by the disease and brought to the point of death, shone forth especially. Gregory reports that through their prayers Theodore was freed from a double death, of soul and body, both in Homilies 19 and 38 on the Gospels and in Book IV of the *Dialogues*, chapter 38.

The holy Father was then absent from the monastery, devoting himself entirely to providing consolation for the afflicted city.

To raise the Romans, who were almost losing heart, through hope in God, and to summon them to repentance despite themselves amid so many scourges, he preached a sermon to the people—one certainly worthy of being committed to writing by Gregory of Tours.

Paul and John the deacons, as well as many others, also mention it.

The earlier editions read that it was delivered in the sixth indiction, but in place of this one should probably read “the eighth indiction.” For it is certain that Gregory was ordained at the beginning of the ninth indiction.

The error arose because this speech was formerly prefixed to Book XI of the *Letters*, now Book XIII, whose indiction is the sixth.

[Note: See the note in which we corrected this error of the earlier editors, Volume I, column 1663.]

The date is assigned no less incorrectly as the fourth day before the Kalends of September.

### 6

After the sermon, Saint Gregory ordered public supplications, or litanies. He commanded that all the clergy, monks, consecrated virgins, children, laymen, widows, and married women should gather at seven designated basilicas in the seven districts of the city and then proceed from there, together with the priests of the respective districts, to the basilica of the Holy Mother of God, in an organized procession accompanied by prayers and tears.

He further commanded the assembled ranks of clergy to sing psalms for three days.

At the third hour—that is, according to our custom, the ninth hour—all the choirs of those singing came to the church, crying through the streets, “Kyrie eleison”—“Lord, have mercy.”

During the supplication itself, eighty people breathed their last within the space of one hour.

Gregory, bishop of Tours, recorded these events on the unquestionably reliable report of his deacon, who was then in Rome; Paul the Deacon also confirms them (Book III of *The Deeds of the Lombards*, chapter 25).

John the Deacon and other writers, however, differ considerably from the others, either in listing the order of the participants or in assigning the basilicas.

John the Deacon assigns the church of Saint John for the litany of the clergy, and the charter concerning the litanies now read in the appendix to the *Letters* agrees with him. Gregory of Tours, however, assigns the basilica of Saints Cosmas and Damian.

This disagreement can be reconciled if we say that these supplications were ordered more than once: in one procession the order reported by Gregory of Tours was observed, and in another the order assigned by John.

This may be confirmed from the ritual books, if we may trust the distinguished author of the *Annals of the Church*.

“According to the ritual books,” says Baronius (*Annals*, A.D. 590, no. 18), “the final litanies proceeded to the basilica of the prince of the apostles, and Gregory carried there with great veneration a holy image of the Mother of God.”

[Note: They say that it was made by Saint Luke.]

At that time, they say, near the Mausoleum of Hadrian beside the Tiber, an angel was seen returning an unsheathed sword to its sheath. This was intended as a sign that the Deity had been reconciled and that the disease had ceased.

We do not wish to argue about supplications held several times, or about the final one held in the basilica of Saint Peter, although all the writers are silent concerning either multiple or even double processions held during the plague.

But what is related about the angel’s appearance and the cessation of the plague seems doubtful.

If it happened, how did Gregory of Tours fail to learn of it from his deacon? If he heard his deacon recounting such great miracles, how could he have refrained from mentioning them, when he sometimes enjoys reporting matters that are extremely slight and not very certain?

Bede, Paul, and John are also profoundly silent about these events.

Paul and John, who treated Gregory’s deeds more carefully, do clearly testify that the plague subsided; but we shall show that it soon broke out again.

Since all the writers are silent about supplications being held again, or more than once, during the plague, perhaps the conflicting accounts can more successfully be brought into agreement by saying that the order of one and the same litany was variously prescribed and arranged.

At first, these and those basilicas may have been assigned so that the various orders could assemble there. Later, others may have been selected, either because they were larger, because they were nearer, or because the plague was raging less fiercely in the districts where those churches stood.

It was necessary, of course, to avoid places where the disease was raging more severely.

According to this opinion—which I freely admit I have read nowhere—both the church of Saint John and that of the holy martyrs Cosmas and Damian were designated for the litany of the clergy, from which place it would then proceed. The same must be said of the other churches about which there is disagreement. The clergy gathered at only one or the other of the two.

The litanies called the Greater Litanies appear to have originated from these supplications and are celebrated every year on the feast of Saint Mark, whereas those held during the three days before the Ascension of the Lord are called the Lesser Litanies.

[Note: Consult the notes on the *Sacramentary* concerning the litanies.]

### 7

One may ask by what title or authority Gregory, who was still only a deacon—though elected to the pontificate and not yet ordained—assumed, in a certain sense, the government of the Roman Church by issuing all the decrees related above.

Some think that he had already been made a priest, among whom Baronius is prominent, because of Gregory of Tours’s words concerning him: “But such a great priest did not cease preaching to the people,” and so forth.

But the ancients did not ordinarily use the term “priest” to designate a presbyter. Gregory, bishop of Tours, therefore calls our Gregory a priest here for no other reason than that he had been elected to the supreme priesthood. Shortly afterward he implies clearly enough that Gregory was still in the rank of deacon.

Nor would the order of the presbyterate have conferred upon him the right to exercise authority over the Roman Church.

We therefore suspect that Gregory, as the elected pontiff, obtained the administration of the vacant see together with the other vicars of the Roman Church.

We infer this from the letter of the Roman clergy to the Scots, delivered when the apostolic see was vacant after the death of Pope Severinus, around the year 640.

That letter is said to have been written in the names of Hilary, archpresbyter and “serving in place”—that is, as I conjecture, vicar of the Holy Apostolic See; John, deacon and, in the name of God, the elected man, who became John IV; John, primicerius and “serving in place of the apostolic see”; and John, servant of God and counselor of the same apostolic see.

The venerable Bede preserves this document in Book II of his *History*, chapter 29. From it we may learn to whom the administration of the Roman Church was entrusted until the man who had been elected pontiff could be consecrated.

### 8

Concerned for the salvation of his fellow citizens, Gregory had almost forgotten himself and had abandoned his plan of fleeing the pontifical dignity.

Perhaps he slept securely because he hoped that the emperor Maurice, moved by his suppliant letters, would not consent to the election that had been held.

But when he learned that his letter to Augustus had been intercepted and that another had been delivered, in which the prefect of the city informed the emperor of the unanimous election and of the extraordinary devotion of the entire people toward the elected man, Gregory judged that he had greatest reason for fear and immediately began to think about flight.

He feared a lofty yet arduous position. To use the words of Gregory himself, “He feared losing the security of his poverty, just as wealthy misers customarily guard riches destined to perish” (Book III of the *Dialogues*, chapter 14).

But while he was preparing hiding places for his flight, he was seized, dragged away, and taken to the basilica of the blessed Apostle Peter. There he was consecrated to the office of pontifical grace and given as pope to the city.

These are the words of Gregory of Tours, whose final words Paul the Deacon copied.

Paul adds that, when watchmen were carefully stationed at the city gates to prevent Gregory’s escape, he obtained from some merchants that he be carried outside the city concealed in a large vessel. He hid there for three days, but on the third night he was discovered and captured through the sign of a shining column.

I pass over the other events that occurred at that time, marvelous and astonishing though they were, since they can be read in Paul.

John the Deacon followed Paul in almost everything, but he mentions no other sign than the shining column.

Gregory himself, although he greatly wished to suppress in silence the miracles then performed, out of modesty and humility—both virtues that shone especially brightly in him—could not altogether conceal them when writing to Natalis, bishop of Salona:

“We make known our conscience: that I accepted the burdens of this honor with a troubled spirit. But because I could not resist the divine judgments, etc.” (Book I, Letter 21).

And to Cyriacus, patriarch of Constantinople:

“I too, who came unworthy to the place of government, conscious of my weakness, had at one time resolved to seek more secluded places. But when I saw that the judgments from above opposed me, I bowed the neck of my heart beneath the yoke of the Creator” (Book VII, Letter 4).

He also mentions his flight and hiding places at the beginning of the *Pastoral Rule*.

Thus Gregory obeyed the signs of God—who was calling, or rather compelling, him—rather than the wishes of men. With the emperor’s consent and approval, he was ordained on September 3, A.D. 590, at the very beginning of the ninth indiction. This day was recorded in the ecclesiastical calendars and was once celebrated with great solemnity.

Since the feast of the most holy pontiff’s birth falls on March 12, a time when in antiquity no solemn festivals of the saints were held because of Lent, the anniversary of his ordination was consecrated to the celebration of his memory.

Let us now pause for a little while. Let us marvel at Gregory’s almost unconquerable persistence in fleeing the pontificate, and let us grieve for the condition of the Church, whose dignities and highest priesthoods are invaded by many ambitious men. They regard such offices as owed either to the splendor of their birth, to the military prowess of their relatives, or to their own continual services, prayers, and vigils at court.

The Most Christian King Louis XIV has already driven this evil largely out of Gaul. Would that all whose interests are involved might follow his example.

And yet the name of Christ retains the power of its own glory even through those who pursue profit.

In such matters, mercenary ministers are produced, like cargo ships [lacuna] “whose captains gape more eagerly after the money of those whom they carry than after their safety.” Nevertheless, the sea of this age needs such ferrymen.

(See Arnaldus of Bonneval, *On the Cardinal Works of Christ*, chapter on the Baptism of Christ.)

# Book Two

Containing the first four years of Saint Gregory’s pontificate

# Chapter One

## Argument

1. Saint Gregory is ordained and issues a statement of faith.  
2. His synodical letter to the patriarchs.  
3. Concerning its inscription.  
4. Why it is called synodical.  
5. How humbly he replied to those congratulating him on receiving the pontificate.  
6. Other reasons, besides humility of spirit, for declining the episcopate: the Church’s gravest evils.  
7. He removed a large part of them.  
8. His assistants in this work: John of Constantinople.  
9. Eulogius of Alexandria.  
10. Anastasius of Antioch.  
11. John of Jerusalem.  
12. Domitian, metropolitan of Arabia.  
13. Dominicus of Carthage.  
14. Saint Leander in Spain.  
15. Virgilius of Arles, Syagrius, and others in Gaul.  
(A.D. 590 and 591.)

[Col. 0283B] **1.** [Note: [Col. 0283D] The day of this ordination is recorded in the ecclesiastical calendars; it is the third of September.] According to custom, Gregory, who was to be consecrated, was led to the Confession of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles—by this name the place of his burial was understood among the ancients—where he set forth the orthodox faith, summing it up in a few articles. Nearly all the handwritten codices of the *Register of Letters* contain this creed, either at the beginning or at the end; it is also found in John the Deacon, Book II, chapter 2. We have therefore decided to append it to the letters as a genuine offspring of Saint Gregory.

**2.** To conform also to a long-established custom [Note: [Col. 0283D] Gregory mentions this custom in Book IX, Letter 52: “Hence it is that whenever bishops are ordained in the four principal sees, they send one another synodal letters, in which they profess that they preserve the holy Council of Chalcedon together with the other general councils.”], he wrote a synodal letter to all the patriarchs, in which he professes that he accepts and venerates four councils: Nicaea, the First Council of Constantinople, Ephesus, and Chalcedon, just as he accepts the four books of the holy Gospel (Book I, Letter 4). In the same synodal letter Gregory embraces, with the reverence that was its due, the Fifth Council, in which the letter called “of Ibas,” full of error, is condemned; Theodore is proved to have fallen into the impious unbelief of separating the person of the Mediator between God and human beings into two substances; and the writings of Theodoret, through which the faith of blessed Cyril is attacked, are rejected as having been produced with mad audacity. He adds: “But all the persons whom the aforesaid venerable councils reject, I reject” (same book, Letter 25). Finally, he strikes with anathema all who think otherwise. In another letter as well (Book III, Letter 10), he assigns the four synods of the universal Church the highest and supreme authority, comparing them with the four books of the Gospels.

[Col. 0283D] **3.** In the superscription of this synodal letter to the patriarchs, the name of John of Constantinople appears first. Baronius rightly judges that this was done by the collectors of Gregory’s letters, not by Gregory himself (*Annals*, under the year 591). For he sent a separate copy of that letter to each patriarch, and in each copy [Col. 0284A] only the name of the patriarch to whom it was being sent was written. The copy delivered to John, therefore, bore no name other than John’s own. [Note: [Col. 0284D] See note *u* on this letter.] Hence we read, “Dearest brother,” not “Dearest brothers.” Our view is confirmed by the fact that *a paribus*—“from his peers”—was added after the names of the patriarchs, as we have noted in the annotations. Nevertheless, once the other patriarchs had agreed, the patriarch of Constantinople held the first place after the Roman pontiff.

[Col. 0284B] At that time there were two patriarchs of Antioch. For [Note: [Col. 0284D] Consult the notes on Book I, Letter 7, concerning him.] after Anastasius had been expelled from that see, Gregory had been substituted in his place. Since this had been done more by injustice than by right, and since Anastasius otherwise shone among the prelates of the Eastern Church with outstanding praise for piety and learning, the holy pontiff did not wish to regard him as deposed, but sent him a synodal letter as he did to the other patriarchs. He had already replied to Anastasius’s letter of congratulations on his own assumption of the supreme pontificate. But since Gregory, having been appointed Anastasius’s successor, was acknowledged throughout the whole Eastern Church, without opposition from anyone, as the legitimate shepherd—and since Anastasius, a man otherwise worthy of the episcopate on account of his most holy conduct, ought not to have been passed over without greeting by the new pope, lest peace be disturbed—Gregory sent the letter to him.

[Col. 0284C] **4.** The aforementioned letter was called “synodal” or “synodical.” As soon as someone had been elected Roman pontiff, he assembled the neighboring bishops and held a synod, in which he professed himself an assertor of the Catholic faith. From that synod a synodal letter was customarily sent to bishops absent throughout the world, and especially to the patriarchs of the principal churches. Examples of this custom are everywhere found in the ancient records of the Church. The person newly elevated to the pontificate sent his confession of faith not only to prove himself orthodox, but also to instruct those subject to him under what faith they ought to live, according to the decrees of the fathers. In this letter as well, Gregory, the chief shepherd, wished to provide the principal bishops of the Eastern Church with a fully developed model for rightly governing and [Col. 0284D] feeding Christ’s flock. He writes to them at great length and with great learning concerning the pastoral office, so that in this letter he seems plainly to have offered a prelude to his golden book on the *Pastoral Rule*. Yet nothing shines forth in it more brightly than the astonishing humility of this most holy man, who sincerely declares himself unequal to the episcopal charge. (Compare Gelasius I, Letter 2, in our volume LIX.)

[Col. 0285A] **5.** He left the same humility attested in many letters that he wrote shortly after assuming the pontificate. As soon as the report of his elevation to the supreme pontificate had spread, many illustrious men—especially those in the imperial city who had witnessed and known his modesty, wisdom, piety, and other virtues—addressed him with friendly and congratulatory letters. In reply, he returned and repaid them with tears and groans rather than words. Above all, one should read Letter 3 together with the four that follow it, as well as Letters 21 and 43 of Book I. In them he grieves most bitterly over the burdens of the episcopate, imposed upon him undeservedly and beyond his strength. “Recognize,” he says in addressing the patrician Narses, “that I am so struck down by grief that I can scarcely speak; for the darkness of sorrow besets the eyes [Col. 0285B] of my mind. Everything that is seen is sad,” and so forth. Since he considered his tears, though unceasing, entirely insufficient to lament his changed condition, he demanded of his friends, as a token of their friendship, tears and sighs on this account.

John, the former consul, had contributed considerably both to Gregory’s election, as we have already noted, and to the confirmation of that election; for this reason Gregory seems to flare up against him in a friendly manner. But nowhere does he reveal more clearly his grief at having lost the tranquility of monastic life and undertaken pastoral care than in Homily 11 on Ezekiel. Hence John the Deacon is not unjustified in attacking the madness of certain Lombards who were not ashamed to claim that Gregory had desired the pontificate more than he had fled from it. (See Book I, Letter 31.)

[Col. 0285C] **6.** It seems worthwhile to investigate what reasons, apart from his singular humility and love of the solitary life, caused this holy man to shrink so greatly from the pontificate. At that time Rome, and all Italy, was being crushed by the most bloody war of the Lombards, accompanied, as if by faithful companions, by famine and pestilence. Yet the Church was suffering from still graver evils. Mourning these, he wrote as follows to his friend Leander:

> I should have wished to answer your letters with undivided attention, had not the labor of pastoral care so worn me down that I prefer to weep rather than say anything. Your Reverence also perceives this attentively in the very text of my letters, when I speak carelessly to one whom I love intensely. For I am being shaken by such great waves in this place of the world that I am utterly unable to steer into harbor the old and rotting ship which, by the hidden dispensation of God, I have undertaken to govern. Now waves rush against it from the front; now foaming heaps of sea swell from the side; now the storm pursues it from behind. Amid all this confusion I am forced at one moment to direct the helm itself against the adversity, and at another, by tilting the side of the ship, to avoid the threats of the waves obliquely. I groan because I perceive that, through my negligence, the bilge of vices is rising; and, while the storm beats violently against it, the planks of the rotten vessel already sound as if shipwreck were imminent. (Book I, Letter 43.)

Certainly, if Peter’s ship could have been overwhelmed by the waves, it would never have emerged from the storms then raging. [Col. 0286A] For the Lombards—either devoted to idolatry [Note: [Col. 0285] On their foolish idolatry, in the worship of a goat’s head, see Book III of the *Dialogues*, chapter 28.] or adherents of Arian impiety—were threatening Rome, the citadel of the entire Christian religion, and came very close to conquering it. Not long before, Authari, their Arian king, had forbidden their children to be baptized in the Catholic faith and had shown himself exceedingly hostile to the orthodox (Book I, Letter 17). The schism stirred up over the Three Chapters was boiling and raging in Istria and the neighboring provinces. In Spain and Narbonese Gaul, the Visigoths had disseminated and extended the Arian heresy down to these times. The Angles who had invaded Britain, still enslaved to the worship of idols, knew nothing of Christ’s name. The Donatists continued to divide and harass the African Church, now for nearly three centuries. The Eastern Church presented a foul appearance because of the errors of Nestorius and Eutyches, which were spreading everywhere and had produced numerous offshoots. To these were added the Agnoites, who had arisen not long before in Alexandria. In Gaul, which had clung more tenaciously to the Catholic faith once received, various corruptions of conduct had crept in and weakened ecclesiastical discipline, especially the simoniacal heresy—as Saint Gregory calls it—and the promotion of Neophytes, that is, according to his meaning, of laymen who were immature and rashly advanced to the priesthood.

**7.** It fell to Gregory to remedy so many evils, since the care of all the Churches had been entrusted to him together with the supreme pontificate. Yet, judging himself unequal to so great a task because of his humility, and suffering especially from a constitution that had always been weak and worn down, he labored under great anxiety of mind. But he found God to be his helper, since he had obeyed God’s call. By God’s aid, he who regarded and repeatedly called himself an unprofitable servant restrained the schismatics troubling Italy, brought the Lombards to the Catholic faith, reconciled the Goths to the Church, instructed the Angles in Christian teachings and baptized them with the sacred washing, checked the Donatists who were causing tumult in Africa, defeated the Agnoites and other heretics in the East, and everywhere uprooted the various errors springing up against the faith or pious conduct. Finally, within the space of a few years, he accomplished so many and such great things that, by the rightful consensus of all nations, he earned the name “the Great.” Let us now enumerate his principal companions and assistants in this labor, namely, those who at that time presided over the greater Churches.

[Col. 0286D] **8.** John, called “the Faster” because of his remarkable abstinence, had been elevated to the see of Constantinople—which already claimed for itself the second place after Rome—after Eutychius’s death, on account of his outstanding virtues, as we have said above. But by usurping at the synod of Constantinople the title of “ecumenical patriarch,” which he never agreed to surrender, he provoked Pope Pelagius and later Saint Gregory against him. We shall often speak of him hereafter. Greek writers praise him highly for his learning, piety, and extraordinary generosity and liberality toward the poor, although he was exceedingly sparing toward himself. He died in 596 and was enrolled by the Greeks in the catalogue of the saints. Cyriacus succeeded him in the same see of Constantinople.

**9.** Eulogius, who became patriarch from being a monk—if credit may be given to the author of the *Spiritual Meadow*—governed the Church of Alexandria from 581 to 608 and always showed himself a most fierce enemy of heretics and a vigorous defender of the orthodox faith. He wrote five books against the Novatians, or against Novatus, and attacked various heretics of his time who rebelled against the Council of Chalcedon and Saint Pope Leo. Photius discusses him and his writings in many places. Because of his exceptional virtues and gifts of mind, Saint Gregory always held him in the highest esteem, as will be clear from the letters mentioned below. After his death he was added to the roll of the saints. (Compare Photius, *Bibliotheca*, codices 182, 208, 225, 226, [Col. 0287B] 227.)

**10.** Anastasius, whom many have considered to be the famous Anastasius the Sinaite on the basis of numerous writings, had been elevated to the see of Antioch and had yielded it to Gregory, who was, as they say, superior of the monastery at Mount Sinai, in 572, after being driven out and deposed by the emperor Justin. Saint Gregory, nevertheless, always regarded him as the legitimate patriarch of that see. Thus he wrote to him (Book I, Letter 26): “You are always, in my eyes, what you received from the gift of almighty God that you are, not what you are thought not to be by human will.” After Gregory of Antioch died—whose praises Evagrius pursues at length in Book IV, on account of his many outstanding virtues and his proper administration of the Church—Anastasius was restored [Col. 0287C] to his see in 594, or, as others prefer, in 592, and governed it most holily until 599, when he died. What he wrote, or is commonly believed to have written, may be found in the catalogues of the sacred libraries. He acquired very many admirers and panegyrists of his renowned sanctity, among whom Gregory the Great unquestionably holds the first place.

Saint Gregory offered no ordinary testimony to the esteem he had formed for Anastasius and to his singular love for him when, immediately after assuming the pontificate, he made a petition full of earnest entreaty to the most pious lords—as he himself testifies (Book I, Letter 28)—that they should send “the most blessed lord Anastasius the patriarch,” with permission to use the pallium, to celebrate the solemn Masses with him at the threshold of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, so that, if he could not return to his own see, he might at least live with Gregory in his honor. Whether he actually sent this petition or supplicatory document, however, leaves us uncertain because of what is added in the same passage. The tender affection with which he embraced this friend is plainly shown by the letters he wrote to him. Thus he begins Letter 26 of Book I: [Note: [Col. 0287D] The beginning of Letter 7 of the same book is almost identical.]

> I found the writings of Your Blessedness as a weary man finds rest, as a sick man finds health, as a thirsty man finds a spring, as a man burning with heat finds shade. For those words did not seem to have been expressed by the tongue of flesh; rather, you revealed the spiritual love that you carried, as though the mind itself were speaking through itself.

We have wished to set these words down here [Note: [Col. 0287] The same may be gathered from many other Gregorian letters. See especially Book III, Letter 54.] so that everyone may understand what kind of man Gregory showed himself to be toward his friends.

**11.** Passing from the see of Antioch to that of Jerusalem, John IV held the latter from 561, when he was appointed in place of the deceased Eustochius, until 595. He was succeeded by Amos, to whom Nicephorus assigns eight years of episcopate. Yet there survives a letter of Saint Gregory to Isaac (Book XI, Letter 46), who succeeded him, written in the fourth indiction—that is, in the year 601 or 600. Nicephorus is therefore shown to be in error, and it is proved that Isaac had already been made patriarch of Jerusalem from the year 600 and had sent a synodal letter to Saint Gregory, who replied to him with this letter of the fourth indiction. (Compare Evagrius, Book V, chapter 16; Nicephorus, Book XVII, chapter 36.)

[Col. 0288B] **12.** Domitian, a relative of Maurice Augustus, was bishop of Melitene and metropolitan of Armenia when the most holy man began his pontificate. The emperor, having found him highly suitable for conducting major affairs and exceptionally prudent in counsel, habitually employed him as an assistant in many matters and appointed him guardian of his children. He was also very dear to Gregory the Great because of his outstanding holiness of life, as is clear from the letters written to him. According to Theophanes’s chronicle, he died in the fifth indiction, which corresponds in part to the year 601 and to 602. Having traversed the East, let us now survey the western world. (Compare Evagrius, Book VI, chapter 18.)

**13.** Dominicus presided over the Church of Carthage and all Africa, recently liberated from the yoke of the Arian Vandals. Saint Gregory praised him in many letters for his pastoral diligence and his energetic labor in restraining heretics. The last letter written to him, at the beginning of the fifth indiction—that is, in September of the year 601—proves that he was still alive at least until that time.

**14.** Although the bishop of Toledo, now called the primate of all Spain, already at that time presided, under the title of primacy, over many Churches of Spain, in the whole Visigothic monarchy—which comprised Spain and Narbonese Gaul—Saint Leander, bishop of Seville, was the most renowned of all the prelates, because he had brought Reccared, the king, and the entire Visigothic people, previously enslaved to Arian errors and impieties, to the Catholic faith. Nicholas Antonius states that the Arian heresy was proscribed by Reccared, with Saint Leander’s support, at the Council of Toledo in 589 or 590.

**15.** Under Gregory’s pontificate, Virgilius, archbishop of Arles, stood out among the other Gallic prelates not only through the dignity of his see but also through his integrity of conduct and all the virtues befitting a shepherd. Having first been made abbot of the monastery of Augustodunum after being a monk of Lérins, he was then, after Licerius, bishop of Arles, died in 588, appointed to the vacant Church through the efforts of Syagrius, a bishop of great authority and influence among the leaders of Gaul, who had thoroughly recognized the holy man’s exceptional gifts. He governed that Church most holily for forty-nine years. At that time the Gallic Church also flourished through Etherius of Lyon, Desiderius of Vienne, Gregory of Tours, Aregius of Gap, and above all the aforementioned Syagrius, as well as others sufficiently known from Gregory’s letters.

There is no need here to say anything about the British islands, in which the kingdoms of England, Scotland, and Ireland are now counted; about Germany toward the north; or about Poland, that is, Sarmatia, and the other northern regions. For down to these times they had rejected Christ’s gentle yoke, not yet having shaken off the slavery of idols.

**CHAPTER II**
