**ARGUMENT.**—1. The political condition of the Christian world under the emperor Maurice.—2. The condition of Italy.—3. Gaul under the three Frankish kings.—4. Spain under Reccared.—5. Greater Britain.—6. What gifts Gregory brought to the government of the Church.—7. His profound humility.—8. And his charity.—9. His steadfastness of mind. (Years 590 and 591.)

**1.** Having briefly sketched, so far as ecclesiastical affairs are concerned, something of the condition of the Christian world, it is worthwhile now to do the same, with equal brevity, regarding its political condition. Maurice, proclaimed emperor in 582, governed the state by the same virtues—especially prudence, courage, and religion—by which he had paved his way to the empire. After winning many victories over the Persians, the Romans’ persistent enemies, he kindly received their king Chosroes when he was a fugitive and, supplying him with an army, restored him to his kingdom and former dignity. Since he burned with zeal for the Catholic faith, during his reign, as Saint Gregory also testifies (Book XI, Letter 46), the mouths of heretics fell silent, and they did not dare to express the perverse opinions they held.

**2.** Concerned for the safety of Italy, and especially of Rome, he had appointed Smaragdus, an outstanding commander, as exarch and had placed him in charge of the war against the Lombards. He had also urged the Franks, who had already been provoked by the Lombards, to seek revenge by sending envoys and offering money. When the Lombard leaders heard this, they seriously considered choosing a king for themselves and elected Authari [or Autharith], the son of Cleph, who had last held the royal title among them, a man second to none in reputation for courage. [Note: [Col. 0289D] The most learned Tillemont observes, in his *History of the Emperors*, under Constantius, article 36, p. 408, that this praenomen, Flavius, was adopted from Silvanus, who had usurped imperial power in Gaul; foreigners especially were accustomed to adorn themselves with it.] He assumed the distinguished Roman praenomen “Flavius” in order to win greater dignity and favor among the Italians. He soon attacked and recovered Brixellum, recently lost through the defection of Droctulf.

When he learned that Childebert, king of the Franks, had crossed the Alps with an army to wage war against the Lombards, but did not trust that he could meet them in battle on equal terms, he ordered his commanders to remain within the walls of fortified cities and strongholds. Meanwhile he sent envoys to Childebert to seek peace, which he obtained through humble entreaties and lavish gifts. Gregory of Tours writes in Book VI, chapter 42, that from this expedition Childebert, who was still almost a minor, brought back a great deal of glory. The Franks later repeatedly renewed the war against the same enemies, usually with uncertain, or even unfavorable, results. Authari was accustomed to break their attack and military strength by stratagems and hesitant prudence. Finally, in the year 590, when Saint Gregory began his pontificate, the king of the Lombards begged for peace and obtained it from the Franks, at great cost to Italy.

The preceding year he had entered into a treaty with the Bavarians and had married Theodelinda, the daughter of their king Garibald. Since she burned with zeal for the Catholic faith, she later drew almost the entire Lombard people to it. Freed meanwhile from fear of the Franks, the Lombards freely possessed almost the whole of Italy, from the furthest boundaries of Istria all the way to Rhegium at the extreme end of Calabria; scarcely did Rome, the head of the world, escape the fury of the barbarians. (Compare Paul the Deacon, Book III of *The History of the Lombards*, chapters 32 and [Col. 0290B] 33.)

**3.** The remarks we have made about the wars Childebert brought into Italy are insufficient to explain the condition of Frankish affairs at that time. The whole of Francia was then divided into three kingdoms and obeyed as many kings. Clotair II, the son of Chilperic—who had been killed in 584—and Fredegund, still a minor, ruled Neustria, or Western Francia. Childebert, the son of Sigebert and Brunhild, descended on his mother’s side from the royal line of the Visigoths, held Austrasia, or Eastern Francia, to which a large part of Germany was then attached. Guntram, the paternal uncle of both kings, ruled Burgundy, which at that time was a province, and, having no children, made Childebert his heir. This division of Francia, and especially the hatred of the two queens, Fredegund and Brunhild, became the seedbed of many wars.

**4.** Spain was much more peaceful after the Visigoths had abandoned the Arian heresy and passed to the orthodox faith. Previously it had been necessary to fight against the Franks. For Guntram, indignant that Ingund, his brother’s daughter and the wife of King Hermenegild, had been tormented to the point of death by Leovigild and Goswintha, Hermenegild’s stepmother, out of hatred for the Catholic faith, had sent two armies and begun war against the Visigoths. But after Leovigild’s death, when his son and successor Reccared embraced the Catholic faith and was reconciled to the Church, he obtained peace from the Franks and, as a pledge of peace and alliance, took Clotsinda as his wife. She was Childebert’s sister, whom Authari had refused to give him in marriage when the Lombard king eagerly sought her.

Saint Gregory extensively pursues Reccared’s praises in Book IX, Letter 122, and in Book III of the *Dialogues*, chapter 31. There he says that Reccared burned with such zeal for the Catholic faith that he would allow no soldier in his kingdom who, through heretical perversity, did not fear being an enemy of the kingdom of God. This contributed greatly to the conversion of that most warlike people.

**5.** Britain, commonly called Greater Britain, occupied by the idolatrous Angles, was divided into several kingdoms. The Britons who survived from the earlier inhabitants withdrew to the inaccessible regions of Wales, fleeing the yoke of their new lords, or to Armorica, a province of Gaul. Ireland obeyed its own kings.

**6.** Behold, we have opened the arena in which Gregory, now about to run and fight, will become a spectacle to the world, indeed to angels and human beings, although, if we believe him, he was a worthless little man, sluggish with cowardice. In truth, however, he was a most powerful giant, and, more than all other shepherds, impatient of the softness of leisure. What gifts and virtues he brought to the pontificate in order to discharge it properly can easily be understood from what has already been said and will shine more clearly from what follows. Let it suffice to observe here that in this most holy pontiff humility and charity shone forth to the point of wonder and amazement. Through humility, he was everywhere and always watchful over the dangers surrounding him, taking care that he should not flatter or congratulate himself on the great honor conferred upon him. Through charity, once he had become contemptible in his own eyes, he was always lifted toward God and, from that supreme height, watched with the greatest vigilance over the needs and welfare of the flock subject to him. (See the Preface to the *Dialogues* and Book IX, Letter 121.)

**7.** The abyss of his humility is revealed by the many passages already quoted from his letters, to which many more could have been added. What, we may ask, was Gregory’s attitude toward the supreme dignity of the Church, to which he had not voluntarily been bound, when, eight years after his inauguration, he wrote to his friend Leander:

> I had resolved above all to become the reproach of human beings and the outcast of the people, and to run in the lot of the one of whom the Psalmist again says: “He has arranged ascents in his heart, in the valley of tears,” so that I might ascend inwardly all the more truly as I lay outwardly more humbly in the valley of tears (Psalm 83:7).

> But now burdensome honor presses me down greatly; innumerable cares resound around me; and whenever my spirit gathers itself toward God, these cares cut it apart by their assaults as if by swords. There is no rest for the heart. It lies prostrate in the lowest places, weighed down by the burden of its own thoughts. The wing of contemplation scarcely ever, or never, lifts it to higher things. The sluggish mind grows numb and, surrounded by barking temporal cares, is almost reduced to stupor; it is forced at one moment to deal with earthly matters and at another even to administer things that belong to the flesh (Book IX, Letter 121).

When Natalis, bishop of Salona, was displeased that Gregory had rebuked him, Gregory replied to him:

> I am ready to be rebuked by all and corrected by all; and I regard as my only friend the one through whose tongue, before the appearance of the strict Judge, I wipe away the stains of my mind (Book II, Letter 52).

He also proved this by his actions. When Anastasius, patriarch of Antioch, treating lightly the controversy that had arisen over the usurped title “ecumenical,” wrote to Saint Gregory with complete freedom that he ought not to give scandals any occasion for any reason and that he should not allow the malicious spirit, which sought souls in order to sift them, to do so—thereby making it fairly clear to his friend that he considered the question over which Gregory’s zeal had grown so heated a trivial one—the most holy father, paying no attention to the primacy of his own chair, received with the greatest modesty and patience the sting of the bee, as he calls Anastasius, and returned honey for the sting. I mean a letter full of the honey of charity, in which he replied, among other things, that “the wounds of one who loves are better than the kisses of an enemy who flatters” (Book VII, Letter 27). And, in order to comply with Anastasius’s advice, he immediately accepted the synodal letter of Cyriacus, recently elevated to the see of Constantinople, in which Cyriacus claimed for himself the title of ecumenical patriarch, lest the unity of the Church be disturbed.

Finally, he left the singular humility of his spirit attested and, in a sense, engraved in all his letters when, first among all the Roman pontiffs, he wished to describe himself at their very beginning as “the servant of the servants of God.” [Note: [Col. 0291] Read our Preface to the *Register of Letters*, section 11.] He opposed this token of modesty to the vain and proud title of “ecumenical,” with which the bishop of Constantinople gloried, while also indicating clearly enough that the pontificate seemed to him a harsh servitude, to which, solely at the command of charity and God, he had bent his neck. (Compare John the Deacon, Book II, no. 1.)

**8.** As for charity, the continuous complaints that he sprinkles through almost every letter about the divine fire lost or diminished through pastoral anxiety sufficiently prove how ardently he burned with love for God. For one who is so anxious over the loss of this sacred fire, who grieves and weeps over it, thereby demonstrates precisely how ardently he loves God. It is unnecessary to say anything here about his charity toward his neighbor, after the many proofs of the generosity he poured out upon the poor supplied by his letters and recorded by John the Deacon, especially in Book II, chapters 22 through 30.

**9.** From those two supreme virtues there arose a certain unbroken steadfastness of spirit, which shone most brightly in difficult circumstances and greater dangers. For the more Gregory distrusted himself through humility, the greater was the confidence in God with which he said, together with the Apostle: “I can do all things in him who strengthens me” (Philippians 4:13). Thus he speaks of himself in Book IV, Letter 47, to Sabinianus:

> You know my character well, because I have borne it for a long time. But if I should once decide not to bear it, I shall go joyfully against every danger.

But if we wish to know what kind of man Saint Gregory was when he approached the supreme pontificate, and how he lived in it, let us read the book of the *Pastoral Rule*, about which we must now speak briefly. For just as he says of Saint Benedict (Book II of the *Dialogues*, chapter 36) that Benedict could not have taught anything other than what he had lived in the *Rule of Monks* promulgated by him, so we may confidently affirm the same of the most holy pope, the author of the *Rule for Pastors*.

**CHAPTER III**

[Col. 0292D]

**ARGUMENT.**—1. Saint Gregory composes the book of the *Pastoral Rule*.—2. He also restores the *Book of Sacraments* and the *Antiphonary* to a better form.—3. He immediately considers establishing and ordering his household.—4. Having dismissed laymen, he takes as his table-companions clerics and monks distinguished for piety and learning.—5. How great was his care for the poor and pilgrims.—6. He appoints no laymen to administer the Church’s patrimonies.—7. He feeds his flock with the word of God.—8. His method of preaching.—9. He sends preachers to barbarians not yet Christian.—10. He is a strict censor of bishops, but most of all of himself. (Years 590 and 591.)

**1.** Shortly after assuming the pontificate, Saint Gregory composed the book of the *Pastoral Rule*, both so that he might always have before his eyes everything pertaining to the pastor’s office in the government of the Church, and so that he might answer the complaints of his friends, especially John, bishop of Ravenna, who continually pressed him on account of his long refusal of the episcopate. In this thoroughly golden work he proves that the burdens of the episcopate are so many and so great that even the strongest shoulders ought to fear them greatly; so that no one who gives the matter proper consideration could aspire to episcopal dignity, or even accept it when freely offered, unless he were out of his mind. But since what we have said in the preface about this book can easily be consulted, we shall now pass over the remaining matters concerning it. It would be best, however, to read and reread the work frequently, in order to absorb inwardly the precepts of Christian life, for which it is an abundantly stocked storehouse. Let us now see how Saint Gregory both lived and governed the Church according to the prescriptions of this most perfect rule.

**2.** Every high priest taken from among human beings is appointed on behalf of human beings in matters pertaining to God, to offer gifts and sacrifices (Hebrews 5:1). Understanding this, Saint Gregory, as soon as he entered the pontificate, began to consider the proper arrangement of the liturgy and sacred matters. He therefore gave the Roman Order, established by Gelasius I, a better form by removing some things, adding others, and altering others. To the canon of the Mass he appended: “And order our days in your peace, and command that we be rescued from eternal damnation and numbered among your chosen flock.”

Concerning the stations and processions to the basilicas and cemeteries of the holy martyrs instituted by him; the solemn Masses that he ordered to be celebrated over the bodies of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul; the many olive groves granted for the lighting of the basilicas; and the increased number of sacred ministers who were to serve in those basilicas, one should consult John the Deacon. He also brought psalmody and ecclesiastical chant—which contribute greatly to the enlargement of divine worship and the cultivation of piety among Christian people—back from the rules of the more serious musical art to a more exact harmony and modulation, establishing a school of singers and arranging an antiphonary. But these matters will be treated more fully in the prefaces to the *Book of Sacraments*, the *Antiphonary*, and so forth. (Compare John the Deacon, Book II, nos. 6 and 17; Bede, Book II of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 1; the same work, chapters 9 and 20.)

### 3.

Since the Apostle censures with grave severity bishops who do not know how to govern their own household, and judges him worse than an unbeliever who does not care for his own, especially those of his household (1 Tim. 3), Gregory immediately devoted particular care to governing his household and family, and so ordered his life that he might offer himself to all as an example of good works and every virtue. His furnishings were plain; his clothing, in accordance with the monastic rule, was simple and unadorned.[^c0029-1] Even the pontifical garments which he used when performing sacred rites were suited more to modesty than to magnificence. For he knew, in accordance with the Apostle’s command (1 Tim. 3:2), that a bishop ought indeed to be adorned—but with chastity, purity of conduct, charity, and learning; pomp, luxury, and costly or soft clothing were rather the insignia of a proud courtier, or even of a wanton woman, than of a bishop and successor of the apostles. At the very beginning of his pontificate he took care that corrupt practices should be eliminated, especially those that even faintly savored of simony. (Cf. John the Deacon, bk. II, no. 11 and following; bk. IV, ch. 80.)

[^c0029-1]: See Mabillon, Preface to the fourth Benedictine century, part II, p. 93, where he proves that bishops, and even the supreme pontiffs themselves when they had come from the monks, formerly never abandoned monastic clothing.

### 4.

A custom had become established among the pontiffs of the preceding age whereby they employed lay boys in the service of their bedchamber.[^c0029-2] Gregory first condemned this by his own example and later condemned it by public decree in a Roman synod. He ordered that selected clerics and monks should serve the supreme pontiff in the duties of the bedchamber:

> “That is, he says, so that he who occupies the place of governance may have such witnesses as see his life in private association and, from their attentive observation, derive an example of improvement.”

John the Deacon mentions this synodal decree in book II, chapters 5, 11, and 15. He says that the most holy pope, having removed secular persons from his bedchamber, chose for himself the wisest counselors and companions: from the clergy, Peter the Deacon, Aemilianus the Notary, Paterius, and John the Defender; from the monks, Maximian, Augustine, Mellitus, Marinian, Probus, and Claudius. What kind of companions of the pope these men were, and by what virtues, studies, writings, or deeds they became distinguished, you will learn both from John the Deacon, book II, chapter 11, and from what will be said below. Thus Gregory confirmed everything he established more by example than by authority.

[^c0029-2]: Bernard beautifully opposes this custom in book IV of *On Consideration*, chapter 6, addressing Eugenius: “Let your fellow bishops learn from you not to keep with them long-haired boys and well-dressed youths. Certainly, among the mitred, it is not fitting for curled-haired young men to run about.”

With these companions and fellow soldiers Gregory always retained the common life, relaxing nothing of monastic perfection, yet omitting nothing that belonged to the office and care of a pontiff. A considerable part of his solicitude was devoted to advancing the study of literature and the liberal arts, which seemed especially to flourish at Rome, and most of all in the papal palace, since he admitted no one into his household or fellowship unless that person was recommended either by exceptional holiness of life or by no ordinary proficiency in some liberal art. (Cf. John the Deacon, bk. II, no. 12.)

### 5.

He nevertheless received pilgrims and the poor as guests[^c0029-3]—and took great care that the other bishops should do likewise—and he not only invited them to his table but compelled them to come. He seasoned his open-handed generosity toward the needy with a remarkable affability, addressing them, especially the elderly, as “fathers” in their honor.[^c0029-4] And in order to free those suffering from want from all embarrassment, whether in asking or receiving, he used to say that what he poured out with so generous a hand was given not by him but by Saint Peter. This will become clear from many of his letters cited below.[^c0029-5]

[^c0029-3]: See book XI, letter 33.

[^c0029-4]: “Please, Father, do you know Bishop Fortunatus?” (*Book I of the Dialogues*, chapter 10).

[^c0029-5]: See especially book X, letters 31 and 45; book XI, letter 2; book XIII, letter 19. John the Deacon, book II, chapters 22 and following, should also be read.

He showed this courtesy particularly toward noblemen and matrons whom he knew to have been reduced to poverty, so that, while relieving their need, he would not overwhelm them with shame. He saw to it above all that everything necessary for their expenses was distributed to those following the monastic life, so that they might devote themselves to God and divine matters with a freer mind. Constant in seeking out, and in a manner hunting down, the poor, he searched every hiding place; he examined the most obscure dwellings, where they lay as though buried. If he encountered people whose mouths had been sealed by fear and shame, he seriously rebuked them for having deprived him of the opportunity to show kindness. He kept with him extensive lists of the needy, formerly called *matriculae*, to whom he abundantly supplied everything necessary.[^c0029-6]

[^c0029-6]: Hence the poor maintained at the Church’s expense were formerly called *matricularii*. Gregory of Tours, book VII, chapter 29: “Some also of the *matricularii* and of the other poor,” and so forth.

### 6.

So that he might provide with still greater solicitude for the needs and welfare of the poor, he entrusted all the Church’s estates—which were very numerous throughout the Christian world—to the clergy alone for their care and administration. Since they had no children, he hoped that they would adopt and receive the poor as sons. If any of them distributed alms too sparingly, he was accustomed to punish them with sharper censure and vengeance than if they had been plunderers of ecclesiastical property. (Cf. John the Deacon, bk. II, ch. 15.)

When laymen therefore found it burdensome that Gregory’s most wise decrees closed every avenue to ecclesiastical estates and offices, they tried by stealth to creep into Christ’s inheritance. Some even of the nobility arranged to be enrolled in the clerical militia by receiving the tonsure. But against their counterfeit conversion the prudent pontiff set new decrees, providing that those who wished to turn to the service of God should first be tested in lay dress, and then permitted to serve God in a monastery. After they had been trained in monastic dress and the periods prescribed by the sacred canons had elapsed, they could lawfully be advanced to any ecclesiastical office. He further declared that anyone who abandoned secular dress and hastened to ecclesiastical offices did not leave the world but merely change it. (Cf. John the Deacon, bk. II, ch. 16.)

### 7.

The excellent shepherd was always as solicitous to provide his children with spiritual food as with bodily food. Indeed, he rightly counts the duty of preaching and teaching among the principal offices of a bishop, and discusses it at great length in the entire third part of the *Pastoral Rule*, by far its longest section. To ensure that he did not fail in this duty, for as long as his bodily strength allowed, he expounded the Gospels and certain selected books of sacred Scripture before the public assembly. He followed the example of his predecessors,[^c0029-7] for whom nothing was more important than to benefit their flock by word as well as by example.

[^c0029-7]: From this it is clear that Sozomen must be accused of falsehood or error when, in book VII, chapter 19, he asserts that in the Roman Church neither the bishop nor anyone else preached or taught. Leo the Great certainly used to preach, as is immediately evident from an examination of his works. Nor do we read that he was the first among the Roman pontiffs to undertake the role of preaching. Indeed, Ambrose, in book III *On Virgins*, reports much from a sermon which Pope Liberius had delivered to the people in the basilica of Saint Peter when he had bestowed the sacred veil upon Marcellina and other virgins. Cassiodorus, whom Valesius cites to confirm Sozomen’s opinion, does not present his own judgment in the *Tripartite History*, but that of the writers whom he abridged—namely, Sozomen, Socrates, and Theodoret. Otherwise, who could imagine that the word of God had not been preached in the Roman Church for so many centuries? That so many most holy shepherds had been dumb dogs and had neglected the greatest part of their office? For, as Saint Gregory says in book I, letter 25: “Whoever comes to the priesthood undertakes the office of a herald.” See Dissertation I on the life and deeds of Saint Leo the Great, under the year 440, sections 8, 9, 10, 11, and 12.

Of his homilies there still survive those which he delivered on readings assigned to various Sundays and solemnities of the year, as well as those preached on the prophet Ezekiel.

### 8.

[^c0029-8]: The prefaces which we placed before those homilies in volume I should be read (see the following volume).

In these homilies nothing gentler or more polished is to be found; rather, an eloquence that is pure and chaste, without affectation or allure, flows throughout. The words are weighty, the judgments grave, suited both to the majesty of sacred Scripture and to the dignity of so great a priest. Testimonies inserted from the divine books are chosen with great care, not forced into place but brought forward as though spontaneously. These are the features that chiefly commend the celebrated homilies.

From the earlier homilies on the Gospels we have selected only a few sentences, which we present here as a sample of the rest. Explaining the words of Luke 21, “When these things begin to happen, look up and raise your heads,” and exhorting us to love and desire Christ’s coming and not to fear death, the holy teacher encourages us as follows:

> Those who love God are commanded to rejoice and be glad at the end of the world, because they will soon find him whom they love, while that which they have not loved is passing away. Let it be far from us that any faithful person who desires to see God should mourn over the blows inflicted upon the world, since he knows that the world will be brought to an end by those very blows. For it is written: “Whoever wishes to be a friend of this world makes himself an enemy of God” (James 4:4). Therefore, whoever does not rejoice as the end of the world approaches testifies that he is its friend, and thereby is proved to be an enemy of God. But let this be far from the hearts of the faithful; let it be far from those who both believe by faith that another life exists and love it through their conduct. To mourn at the destruction of the world belongs to those who have planted the roots of their hearts in love of it, who do not seek the life to come, who do not even suspect that it exists.  
>
> But we, who have come to know the eternal joys of our heavenly homeland, ought to hasten toward them as quickly as possible. We should desire to depart sooner and reach it by the shorter road. For what evils do not oppress the world? What sadness, what adversity does not distress us? What is mortal life except a road? And consider, my brothers, what it means to grow weary from the labor of the journey and yet not wish that the same journey should end.

And after some further remarks, describing the world in its old age, he says:

> Just as in the years of old age the body’s stature bends, the withered neck droops, the chest is oppressed by frequent sighs, strength fails, and breath interrupts the words of one who is speaking—for even if illness is absent, old age itself is often a sickness to the elderly—so the world in its earlier years flourished as though in youth. It was vigorous for propagating the human race, green with bodily health, and rich with an abundance of possessions; but now it is weighed down by its own old age and, as though approaching death, is oppressed by troubles that continually increase. Therefore, my brothers, do not love what you see cannot long remain.

The rest may more conveniently be drawn from the source itself. But a more attentive reader of these homilies will perceive how wisely the Church inserted all of them—except one or two—into its cycle or office.

When he preached on the feast days of the saints, he did not usually indulge in barren praise of them. Rather, he took care to press those points that could contribute to the proper ordering of conduct, as will be evident to anyone reading the homilies on the solemnities of Saint Andrew the Apostle, the holy martyrs Nereus and Achilleus, Saint Felicity, and others. (See Homilies 5 and 28.)

### 9.

When he could not do so personally, Gregory disseminated and extended the Gospel among barbarian peoples not yet subjected to Christ’s yoke through his disciples, especially through the members of his monastery. The pontiffs of the preceding age had indeed accomplished the same task energetically, since they understood that they had been placed in charge of the entire Christian commonwealth. Hence faith spread from the Roman see throughout the world. Yet never with such success and such ease as when Gregory sat at the helm of the ecclesiastical ship.

I dare say that Peter, when the Lord commanded him to put out into the deep and let down the nets for a catch, scarcely ever enclosed a greater multitude of fish within the net than Gregory did at that time. For, having cast his nets once or twice, he captured almost the whole of Britain—the largest of all the islands then known—and drew it to shore, that is, to the secure station of the true faith.

### 10.

If Saint Gregory devoted such diligent labor to gathering new churches for Christ, he was much more solicitous in rightly ordering the ancient ones; and he took particular care that worthy shepherds should be placed over them. If any of them happened at some time to fail in his duty, he admonished him with fatherly charity; but he pursued the obstinate with greater severity. Yet toward no bishop did he exercise a stricter judgment than toward himself.

Who would not admire this outstanding man, whom the whole world revered, publicly confessing—even from the pulpit—the lesser sins which he believed he had committed, in these words?

> O how hard for me are the things I say, because in speaking I strike myself, whose tongue neither holds preaching as it ought, nor does my life follow my tongue insofar as it holds preaching as it ought. I am often entangled in idle words, and, sluggish and negligent, I cease from exhorting and building up my neighbors. In God’s sight I have become both mute and talkative: mute in what is necessary, talkative in what is idle.  
>
> But behold, the word of God compels me to speak about the life of the watchman. I cannot be silent, and yet I fear to wound myself by speaking. I will speak, I will speak, so that the sword of God’s word may pass even through me to pierce the heart of my neighbor. I will speak, I will speak, so that the word of God may resound through me even against me. I do not deny that I am guilty; I see my sluggishness and negligence. Perhaps, before the merciful Judge, the very recognition of guilt will obtain pardon.

(*Homily 11 on Ezekiel*, no. 5 and following.)

I refrain from adding more; these few words sufficiently show that Gregory applied to himself a severity more than censorial in reproving himself.

These preliminary outlines, as it were, of Gregory’s pontificate may suffice for the present. Let us now unfold, preserving as far as possible the order of years and times, the individual matters which he accomplished.

## CHAPTER IV

### Summary

1. Saint Gregory orders a synod to be held annually in Sicily.  
2. From there he arranges for grain to be brought to Rome.  
3. Rome’s grievous condition. On this occasion Saint Gregory exhorts the Romans to repentance.  
4. How he provided for churches that had been destroyed and for the needs of impoverished bishops. Transfers of bishops.  
5. Gregory’s solicitude and generosity toward monasteries.  
6. He restrains wandering and scandalous monks.  
7. He orders new monasteries to be built.  
8. He undertakes the care of widows. (A.D. 590 and 591.)

### 1.

It would have been little for Gregory to govern himself and his household rightly, or even to watch over the Roman Church in particular, unless he had also provided with fatherly charity and solicitude for the entire flock of Christ over which he presided by authority.

His first letter is addressed to the bishops of Sicily, instructing them to assemble every year in synod. He orders Peter the subdeacon, the administrator of Saint Peter’s patrimony on the island, to preside over it; and he thereby indicates that he had entrusted his own authority within that province to Peter. Sicily was one of the suburban provinces, which were immediately subject to the Roman bishop. On these provinces the sixth Nicene canon, according to Rufinus’s translation, should be consulted. The old code of canons edited by Justellus should also be consulted; there the sixth canon from Nicaea mentions the suburban churches.[^c0029-9]

[^c0029-9]: Many controversies have arisen in our own age concerning the suburban provinces, from which we abstain. Read what we observed in the geographical index to Saint Gregory’s letters, at the very beginning.

It is debated whether there were metropolitan bishops in Sicily at that time. We incline toward the negative view, which is followed and defended by Rocco Pirro in the second *Notitia* of the Church of Messina; we confirmed this opinion with many weighty arguments in the notes to the aforementioned letter.

Since the Sicilian bishops might perhaps have found it burdensome to obey a subdeacon acting as the representative of the Apostolic See, Saint Gregory entrusted these responsibilities the following year to Saint Maximian, bishop of Syracuse (book II, letter 7), as we shall say below. Later he granted them permission to assemble at Rome for a synod only once every five years, whereas previously they had been required to appear once within three years.

### 2.

Sicily was the granary of Rome and of all Italy, and it was the duty of the island’s governor to send grain from there to Rome. This office was held by Justin, a friend of Gregory. As soon as Gregory began his pontificate, he asked Justin to arrange for the required and assessed quantity of grain to be transported to the City, lest he become responsible for the destruction of the entire Roman people by carrying out the task too negligently. At the same time he reminded him of his duty:

> Let no profits drag you into injustice. Let neither threats nor friendship turn you aside from the path of righteousness. Consider how short life is. Think upon the Judge before whom you will one day stand, you who exercise judicial power.

(*Book II*, letter 2.)

For Gregory was not accustomed to flatter his friends with words of adulation. He also urged Justin to abstain from every hostility toward ecclesiastical men, desiring especially to foster harmony between priesthood and empire, and between the ministers of both.

### 3.

Saint Gregory describes what the condition of Rome was at that time in Homily 1 on the Gospels, delivered around three months after he became bishop, during Advent, and in book II of the *Dialogues*, chapter 15. Pestilence was raging and overwhelming many by sudden death; ancient trees had recently been uprooted by a violent whirlwind; houses had been destroyed and churches overturned from their foundations. Thus the prophecy of Saint Benedict was being fulfilled, as Gregory himself observes:

> Rome will not be exterminated by foreign peoples, but, worn down by storms, flashes of lightning, whirlwinds, and earthquakes, it will wither within itself.

(*Book II*, letter 2.)

The most devout father of his country rightly feared that famine—perhaps the gravest of all these scourges—might be added to them. This was the principal reason for his writing to Justin the governor.

Gregory tried to bend to repentance and shake with salutary fear those sons who had been chastised by so many scourges and battered by so many calamities:

> If God moved the earth by the breath of a very light wind and demolished the foundations of buildings, if he strikes with so slight a cloud, what will he do when the Judge and Avenger himself comes, and his anger blazes forth in vengeance for sins?

(*Homily 1 on the Gospels.*)

### 4.

His zeal for preaching in no way prevented Gregory from devoting himself constantly to the public needs of the Church. Very many churches in Italy lay destroyed because of the continuous wars of the Goths and afterward of the Lombards; their clergy had been killed or driven away, while almost all the rest had been carried into slavery.

The churches of Minturnae and Populonia had suffered especially grievous disasters. No priest remained in either, so that repentance could be administered to the dying or baptism to infants. Accordingly, he either united these widowed and deserted churches, and the others that had suffered a similar calamity, to neighboring churches that were still intact, or entrusted them to nearby bishops for visitation and governance.

The emperor Maurice had ordered that bishops whom the fury of war had expelled from their own sees should go to bishops who had not been torn away from their churches and should receive from them stipends and the necessities of life. Gregory approved this decree and urged those bishops to associate their brothers and fellow bishops with themselves as companions at table and to relieve their poverty.

He also transferred some bishops who had been expelled from their churches to other episcopal sees, as is evident from several of his letters.

A noteworthy case is that of Paul, bishop of Nepi, whom the most wise pope had appointed visitor and administrator of the Church of Naples while its see was vacant, entrusting the visitation and care of the Church of Nepi to Bishop John, especially so that he might perform the sacred rites during the solemn days of Easter.[^c0029-10]

[^c0029-10]: See book III, letters 1, 2, and 35.

While Paul was carrying out the charge entrusted to him, he suffered a very serious injury at Castrum Lucullanum near Naples. Gregory consoled him by letter; and, so that so great a crime should not remain unpunished, he sent the subdeacon Epiphanius to investigate the offense jointly with the judge of Campania and to pronounce judgment.[^c0029-11]

[^c0029-11]: Here I understand that an ecclesiastical judge and a lay judge were to investigate the same matter jointly and deliver sentence. The note to book III, letter 1, shows that this was not unprecedented.

The foregoing proves that at that time the bishops of Italy were subject immediately to the Roman pontiff as their metropolitan and that, at his command, they sometimes migrated from their own churches to others, while their churches were entrusted to other bishops by the same authority. (See *Register*, book I, letters 8, 15, 45, and 79; book II, letters 37 and 45.)

### 5.

After devoting his first attention to those churches, he reserved a second portion of his care for the monasteries dear to him. Thus he most generously assisted those suffering from want. He took under his protection monks who complained that they were burdened and harassed by bishops, considering it inhumane to forbid them the celebration of Mass and the burial of the dead in their own monasteries.

He offered all prelates a splendid example of humility and justice in his treatment of the monks of Saint Theodore in the territory of Palermo. Gregory, a servant of God, priest, and abbot of that monastery, had complained in a petition that the boundaries of his possessions had been invaded by agents of the Roman Church.

Therefore Saint Gregory ordered Peter the subdeacon, who at that time administered the business and patrimonies of the Apostolic See in those regions, to hasten to restore the properties claimed by the abbot, if it could be proved that the monastery had possessed them peacefully for forty continuous years. In this matter he refused to make use of a privilege of the Roman Church granted by Justinian, by which he could have compelled the abbot to prove possession for a hundred years.[^c0029-12] (See book I, letters 9 and 12; cf. the *Code*, “On the Holy Churches,” law *Ut inter.*)

[^c0029-12]: See note c to book I, letter 9.

### 6.

There was another monastery of Saint Theodore at Messina. Gregory wished the monks of the city of Tauriana in Bruttium, who had been driven out by the barbarians and were wandering throughout Sicily without a superior, to be confined there. On this matter he wrote both to Felix, bishop of Messina, and to the aforementioned Peter the subdeacon (book I, letters 40 and 41).

In another letter of the most holy pope, certain monks of the diocese of Sorrento, who had been carried away by the same license of wandering and were also devoting themselves to acquiring property, are recalled to their duty. Some of these wanderers had even proceeded to such a degree of wickedness that they had publicly taken wives. Gregory wrote to the subdeacon Anthemius concerning them (ibid., letter 42), ordering that they be diligently sought out and compelled to pay the penalty for so great a crime through appropriate discipline in monasteries.

He was so firm an advocate of monastic stability that he judged no permission should be left to clerics who had entered a monastery to return to the churches in which they had previously served, and still less to transfer to other churches, unless the bishop judged that they should be appointed to priestly offices.

How great was the most holy pontiff’s solicitude and vigilance for the monastic order is proved by another letter to the same Anthemius, which contains two commands that should not be passed over lightly.

First, women who had fled to the island of Eumorphiana out of fear of the enemy were to be removed from it, lest they provide an occasion of falling for the monks who lived there. Second, no adolescents were to be received into the monastic habit on that island, on Palmaria, or on the other islands before their eighteenth year. For, says the provident pontiff, “the gathering of monks on the islands is difficult”—that is, because the monks led an exceedingly harsh life there, owing to the severity of the climate and the scarcity of the necessities of life.

Some wrongly argue from this passage that Saint Gregory absolutely established the age for monastic profession, since in the same place he orders that boys found in these monasteries who were under eighteen years of age should be sent to Rome, doubtless so that they could be trained in monasteries where the discipline was milder. We have already discussed these matters in book I, chapter 3, section 11, and in the note to this letter.[^c0029-13]

[^c0029-13]: Letter 50.

Gregory also employed the services of Horosius, the abbot, to restore and build new monasteries, both on these islands and on those nearby, as we learn from various letters written that year (book I, letters 51 and 52).

The monks living on the island of Monte Cristo had completely departed from the precepts of the monastic rule; nor were those living on the island of Gorgona reputed to observe their laws with greater religious seriousness. Such was the condition of those troubled and wicked times, with weapons clashing everywhere; amid them even the holier laws either fell silent or could scarcely be heard.

Nevertheless, Gregory did not despair of correcting those brothers. He instructed the aforementioned abbot Horosius to visit these monasteries as a legate of the Apostolic See and to endeavor to eradicate whatever he found deserving correction, and to recall the monks to better conduct.[^c0029-14]

[^c0029-14]: Saint Gregory wrote to those monks: “Whatever Horosius establishes, guard it with due reverence as though it had been established by me.” This proves that he had been granted the authority of an apostolic legate or vicar.

### 7.

That fair-minded evaluator of circumstances did not judge that the corrupt morals of certain monks should prevent the founding of new monasteries. On the contrary, he ordered Horosius and the Defender Symmachus, in addition to the monastery recently built in Corsica by the religious woman Labina—for which Symmachus had requested monks from Gregory—to arrange for another monastery to be built in a fortified place on the same island:

> So that the island itself, which until now has had no monastery, may also be improved through this way of life.

(*Book I*, letter 52.)

But we must not linger longer over monastic matters.

### 8.

The Apostle orders bishops to honor widows (1 Tim. 5:3), which must also be understood as providing them with food and the other necessities of life. Accordingly, Gregory not only commended them to bishops[^c0029-15] but also always took care himself to protect them and assist them in poverty.

[^c0029-15]: Book I, letters 13 and 62.

The chief evidence of his fatherly charity toward them is letter 39 of book I, in which he commands Anthemius, the subdeacon and administrator of ecclesiastical property in Campania, to distribute a thousand *modii* of wheat and eighty solidi among three widows suffering want. We infer from letter 59 of the same book that this gift was annual.

The opening of the former letter shows that nothing was more deeply at heart to the holy and devout shepherd than the care of the poor, and that the principal duty of his agents and administrators in that province was to bring assistance to the needy. He urged them to this both in person and in writing. But if they attended to their duty too negligently and failed to be present for the poor, they immediately paid the penalty for their indolence when stimulated by Gregory’s sharper rebukes.

Among the three widows just mentioned was Pateria, Saint Gregory’s *thia*—that is, his paternal aunt or maternal aunt. Although he does not expressly call her a widow, he implies it by counting her among the other widows; and when speaking of her children, he says nothing about a husband.

From the example of so great a pontiff, bishops can learn not to close the bowels of mercy toward their relatives and close associates—even though such persons ought not to be enriched with the Church’s goods—but to give them a place among the other poor. If anyone drives away poor relatives because of their relationship to him, let him beware lest this be attributed to proud shame.

Since the most generous man desired to confer benefits, not to lend at interest, and judged it more blessed to give than to receive, he refused gifts, as we learn especially from his letter written that year to Felix of Messina (book I, letter 66). He understood, of course, that he had been placed at the highest summit of the Church so that gifts might flow abundantly and freely from him to his subjects—not, with the order reversed, flow back from his subjects to him.

## CHAPTER V

### Summary

1. Saint Gregory’s mercy toward heretics, tempered by prudence.  
2. How he behaved toward the schismatics who caused tumult over the Three Chapters. Whether the condemnation of the Three Chapters was accepted in Spain and in Gaul.  
3. Examples of Gregory’s charity and justice toward the Jews.  
4. Authari, king of the Lombards, dies. His successor Agilulf favors the Catholics.  
5. What Gregory decreed for the restoration of the faith and discipline.  
6. What he established concerning the celibacy of subdeacons. A foul tale of the heterodox is refuted.  
7. Concerning Venantius, a deserter from the monastic state.  
8. Saint Gregory exhorts him to repentance. What should be thought about the marriages of monks. (A.D. 590 and 591.)

### 1.

What we have already drawn from Gregory’s letters written during the first year of his pontificate demonstrates more than sufficiently the charity with which he embraced his own sons and those of the Church. We must now extract from the same records certain examples of his mercy toward outsiders—namely, heretics and schismatics, and even Jews—and show how he behaved toward all those enemies of Christ and his bride.

That gentleness should be preferred to severity, so that those who have fallen into heresy may be recalled to the true faith, he teaches in his letter to Demetrius, bishop of Naples (book I, letter 14). He says that such persons should readily be received into communion, even at the risk of his own soul.

Yet lest this exceptional indulgence incline toward excessive laxity, prudent moderation was present; it shone forth especially in his response to the question proposed by Saint Leander of Seville concerning whether baptism should be administered by a single immersion or by three immersions.

Among the Arians it was customary to immerse the person three times when conferring baptism, whereas among the orthodox a single immersion was sufficient. The Visigoths, recently converted to the Catholic faith, especially through the agency of King Reccared and Saint Leander as their teacher, wished to retain their former custom of three immersions. The old Catholics, deeply attached to their own rite, resisted.

Leander, consulted on this controversy, judged that the Apostolic See should be approached, and, without consulting it, dared to decide nothing, following the ancient custom of his fathers. Accordingly, he wrote to Gregory and argued on both sides, setting forth various reasons both for a single immersion and for three immersions.

The most holy teacher replied that, without danger to the faith, either rite could be followed indiscriminately, because where there is one faith, diversity of ecclesiastical custom does no harm. He nevertheless added:

> But because until now the infant was immersed three times by heretics in baptism, I do not think this should be done among you, lest, while they count the immersions, they divide the Godhead; and, while doing what they used to do, they boast that they have overcome our custom.

(*Book I*, letter 43.)

A truly prudent response. The same reasoning explains why we do not indulge our brothers who have recently returned to us from Calvin’s erroneous doctrine in many practices which otherwise might be considered *adiaphora*—things indifferent.[^c0029-16]

[^c0029-16]: *ἀδιάφορα*.

### 2.

Gregory employed the same leniency, tempered by prudence, toward schismatics, especially those who were separated from the Church in defense of the Three Chapters. At that time only the bishops of Istria and Venetia stood for this schism. Although it had previously raged more fiercely in Africa and Illyricum, we may safely infer that it had already been quieted in those provinces from the many letters sent by Saint Gregory both to the Illyrian and to the African bishops, in which no mention is made of this schism.

We do not, however, count among the schismatics those who, although they did not accept the Fifth Council and had not at all subscribed to the condemnation of the Three Chapters, nevertheless in no way abstained from communion with those who had accepted this synod and its loudly proclaimed condemnation of the Three Chapters. Certainly Saint Gregory never regarded them as schismatics, but only those who separated themselves on the occasion of the Fifth Council and rejected communion with others, as we shall demonstrate below by clear evidence.

Indeed, it must be observed that in Spain, Gaul, and [Col. 0304A] nearly all the other provinces that were not subject to the Roman emperor (under whose compulsion, although Pope Vigilius resisted, these chapters were condemned), the decree concerning their condemnation was accepted only later. With regard to Spain, the most eminent Cardinal Henricus Norisius proves this by the clearest arguments in his *Historical Dissertation on the Fifth Synod*, chap. 9, § 2, especially from the silence of the councils of Spain, which nowhere decreed that this synod should be received, and from St. Isidore, who both in his *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*, when speaking of Theodore of Mopsuestia, and in his *Chronicle*, more freely reproves the emperor Justinian for compelling bishops within the imperial borders to condemn the Three Chapters.

The same is proved concerning Gaul in Volume II, or in the appendix [Col. 0304B] to the works of Pope St. Leo the Great, in the note on the judgment of Chrodobert, bishop of Tours; letters of the pontiffs Vigilius and Pelagius are also brought forward, clearly indicating this. Indeed, St. Columbanus, who had lived for a long time in Gaul, made his view sufficiently clear in his letter to Boniface V, where among other things he hurls this accusation against Pope Vigilius: “Watch, then, I beg you, pope, because perhaps Vigilius did not watch well—the man whom those who accuse you of guilt proclaim to be the source of the scandal.” Although controversy was at times raised in Gallic synods concerning Columbanus’s doctrine and rites, he was never suspected of error or schism on account of his rejection of the condemnation of the Three Chapters.

Had the bishops of Istria confined themselves within these limits, and been content merely not to subscribe to the oft-proclaimed condemnation, without breaking the bond of communion and charity, they would certainly not have been called schismatics. But they never ceased to foment disturbances and to rage against the Roman See. Nevertheless, St. Gregory, with paternal affection, invited them—and their leader, Severus, bishop of Aquileia or Grado, who had fallen back and returned to the schism he had formerly abjured—to peace and to the synod to be held at the emperor’s command. John the Deacon reports (*Book I, Letter 16*) that Severus, then compelled by both apostolic and imperial authority, came to Ravenna when Smaragdus was threatening him; but, fearing to engage in a synodal dispute with Gregory, he returned to the unity of the Church through the mediation of John, bishop of Ravenna. John testifies that shortly afterward Severus again withdrew from it, after the command of the Emperor Maurice had also been secretly obtained, ordering that the schismatics should not be compelled to return to the unity of the Church. Yet what John relates here had happened earlier, as is clear from Paul the Deacon (*History of the Lombards*, Book III, chap. 27). For it is established that the exarch Smaragdus had already yielded his position to Romanus when Gregory compelled Severus to peace by his letters. In those letters St. Gregory also mentions both Severus’s return to the Church and his subsequent relapse into schism: “As we had rejoiced that you had long ago been incorporated into the unity of the Church, so now we are more deeply ashamed that you have been separated from Catholic fellowship.” The bishop who had incited the schism [Col. 0305A], together with his associates, closed his ears; but the most holy man diminished nothing of his paternal affection toward the rebellious, as we shall show below from other letters of his.

### 3.

Let us now show that the Jews themselves had already experienced Gregory’s justice and charity. Peter, bishop of Terracina, had expelled the Jews from the place [Note: [Col. 0305D] The tenth letter of this book explains why this was done. The synagogue was so close to the church that the voices of the Jews singing psalms could easily be heard from there.] where they had customarily assembled to celebrate their festivals, though he had assigned them another place where they could freely gather for religious purposes. Shortly afterward, however, he forced them to leave that place as well. The Jews complained to the pope of the injury done to them, and he replied to Peter:

“If this is so, we wish your Fraternity to refrain from such a complaint and to allow them to assemble, as had been customary there, in the place which, with your approval, they have obtained for their gathering. [Col. 0305B] For those who disagree with the Christian religion must be gathered into the unity of faith by gentleness, kindness, admonition, and persuasion, lest those whom the sweetness of preaching and fear of the coming Judge could have invited to believe be driven away by threats and terrors.” (*Book I, Letter 35.*)

Entirely consonant with this judgment are the instructions he shortly afterward gave to Virgilius of Arles and to Theodore, bishop of Marseilles: namely, that Jews must not be compelled to receive baptism [Note: [Col. 0305D] See also Book IX, Letter 6.], lest, having become Christians by necessity rather than by choice, they should relapse into their former superstition and consequently die worse than they had appeared to be when reborn. (*Ibid.*, Letter 47.)

Nevertheless, he hastened to restrain delinquent Jews, especially when there was a danger that the Christian religion might be held in contempt. Thus, when he learned that a certain Jew had purchased the furnishings or sacred vessels of the Church of Venafrum—which was forbidden by law—and especially two chalices, he ordered the subdeacon Anthemius to summon the buyer before the provincial judge and compel him to restore those sacred treasures, while relegating the deacon and the other clerics who had impiously sold the sacred vessels to penance.

### 4.

Let us now briefly touch upon the affairs of the Lombards during the first year of Gregory’s pontificate. We learn from *Book I, Letter 17* that Authari, their king, died in this year, the Lombard dominion having extended as far as Regium, at the extreme borders of Bruttium (Paul, *Book III*, chap. 34). Shortly before this, the Arian prince, carried away by zeal for propagating his sect, had solemnly prohibited the children of his own people from being baptized in the Catholic faith. But not long afterward he experienced God as his avenger and was taken from the living for this crime. The historian of Lombard affairs says that he died by poison (*Paul the Deacon, Book III*, chap. 36), after reigning six years.

When his death became known, the Lombard leaders and nobles assembled at Pavia to deliberate about choosing a successor. At this assembly it was unanimously decreed that Theodelinda, a queen of distinguished prudence and virtue, should always occupy the government of the kingdom and should choose from among the dukes whichever man she preferred as her husband and as king of the entire nation. After consulting with the elders, she took as partner of her kingdom and marriage the duke of Turin, named Agone or Agilulf. At Milan, in a crowded assembly of the whole nation, a golden crown was placed upon him; Milanese writers say that it was called the “iron crown” because of the iron ring enclosed within it. It later became famous throughout the world.

Theodelinda, inflamed with zeal for the Catholic faith, moved Agilulf, whom this great favor had bound to her, to embrace the same faith, if we believe Paul the Deacon (*Book IV*, chap. 6). Following the king’s example, a large part of the Lombards renounced Arianism. Yet we understand that Paul’s statement concerning Agilulf’s acceptance of the Catholic faith must be assigned to a later time, from St. Columbanus’s letter to Pope Boniface, written no earlier than the year 607. At that time the king of the Lombards was still an Arian, for Columbanus speaks of him as follows: “For he is said to have declared that, if he knew it to be certain, he too would believe.” For this reason Columbanus composed a book against the Arians, as Jonas testifies.

Nevertheless, it is certain that Agilulf, although he did not yet follow the orthodox faith, was highly favorable toward Catholics from the very beginning of his reign. St. Columbanus himself experienced this, having been kindly received by him.

### 5.

When Gregory heard of the death of King Authari, he wrote to all the bishops of Italy (*Book I, Letter 44*) so that they might endeavor to reconcile to the Catholic faith the Lombard children who had been baptized into Arianism, especially since a severe mortality was imminent. He then turned his attention to restoring ecclesiastical discipline in Italy, which had been ruined amid the swords of barbarian heretics. Concerned for the penance of priests and others from the clergy who had fallen, he ordered them to be confined in the poorest monasteries, where regular observance was vigorous, and sufficient allowances to be provided for them, so that the monks responsible for their correction might also receive support for their livelihood.

He strove to suppress ambition among the clergy. Thus he ordered the deacon Liberatus, who was swollen and distended with the spirit of ambition, to stand last among the other deacons, so that he might become accustomed to humility and submission (*Book I, Letters 83 and 84*). He decreed that bishops accused of a crime should be judged according to custom in a council and deposed by no sentence other than a synodal one (*Book III, Letter 8*). He established that foreign clerics were not to be received or incardinated without the release or letters of dismissal of their own bishop. What he decreed concerning the celibacy of subdeacons must now be examined at greater length (*Book I, Letter 83*).

### 6.

Three years earlier, Pope Pelagius II had imposed the law of celibacy upon the subdeacons of Sicily, following the custom of the Roman Church [Note: [Col. 0306D] St. Leo mentions this practice in Letter 12, chap. 4: “Marriage according to the flesh is not permitted even to subdeacons, so that those who have wives may be as though they had none, and those who do not have wives may remain unmarried.”]; and he had ordered that those who were already married should be separated from their wives. Gregory considered this harsh and unsuitable, and exposed to many greater dangers of falling. Accordingly, the wisest pontiff moderated this decree by allowing married subdeacons to retain their wives, on the condition that they should never advance to sacred orders: “For no one ought to ascend to the ministry of the altar unless his chastity has been approved before he undertakes the ministry” (*Book I, Letter 44, and Book IV, Letter 34*).

For the future, he prohibited bishops from ordaining any subdeacon who did not promise to live chastely. This demolishes the fable that the Magdeburg Centuriators drew from a fabricated letter in the name of St. Ulrich, bishop of Augsburg, to Pope Nicholas—namely, that our Gregory had first taken wives away from priests by a solemn decree, but, when he learned that fishermen had drawn from his fishpond the heads of six thousand infants [Col. 0307B], and attributed this infanticide to himself—for he did not doubt that so many infants had been born from the secret fornications or adulteries of priests—he revoked his decree and repented of so great a crime.

There are as many foul and foolish lies in this story as there are words. Why were these infant heads thrown into the pond of the papal residence rather than into the Tiber or the public sewers? The heads are found and counted; what happened to the rest of the corpses? Is there even the slightest plausibility in the notion that the murderers of those infants, whose great interest it was to conceal so enormous a crime, would have wished to publicize it voluntarily, as though in play, by deliberately throwing the heads of the slain into the papal pond?

How brazen, moreover, are those who claim that Gregory repented because he had bound priests and sacred ministers to the law of celibacy [Col. 0307C], when he was never the author of such a law—for it had always been observed, at least in the Latin Church wherever the canons were in force—nor did he allow almost any year of his pontificate to pass without writing something concerning the celibacy of the higher clergy. Read especially the following letters: *Book I*, Letters 44 and 52; *Book IV*, Letters 26 and 36; *Book IX*, Letter 60; *Book X*, Letter 62; and *Book XI*, Letter 64, to Secunda, where, answering a question, he speaks of clerics who are free to take wives but excludes those who have been established in sacred orders. Finally, see *Book XIII*, Letters 35 and 36.

In any case, it is not worth refuting this fable with many arguments, for it immediately vanishes [Col. 0307D] once the period in which St. Ulrich lived is considered. He could not have been a contemporary of either Nicholas I or Nicholas II. On this matter see Cardinal Baronius, under the year 591, no. 21.

### 7.

With no less zeal than he showed toward the clergy, Gregory guarded the chastity and reputation of monks, as we indicated in the preceding chapter, no. 6. Indeed, he considered them most strictly bound by the vow or commitment of perpetual chastity, as is placed beyond doubt by his letter to Venantius written in this year.

Venantius, apparently born of a patrician family in Sicily, had embraced the monastic life. Later, however, he left the monastery and married a woman named Italica [Note: [Col. 0307D] See Letter 125, Book IX, and Book XI, Letters 35 and 78.], or returned to a wife whom he had previously married [Col. 0308A]. By her he had two daughters, Barbara and Antonina. At that time St. Gregory lamented that certain monks had publicly taken wives (*Book I, Letter 42*) and ordered that, after being torn away from them, they be confined in a monastery, as we have already observed.

Our Mabillon suspects that Italica was Venantius’s mother, not his wife (*Benedictine Annals*, year 601, p. 266); but, with all due respect to so great a man, this conjecture collapses when the heading of Letter 123 of Book IX is read. The title “Chancellor of Italy,” which is gratuitously bestowed upon this patrician, rests on no firmer foundation, since it derives from corrupt headings of the letters found in printed codices, not from manuscripts written by hand. Nothing compels us to say that Barbara and Antonina were born before Venantius’s fall. Venantius had left the monastery several years before Gregory assumed the pontificate. His daughters addressed Gregory in writing in the eleventh year of his pontificate, one perhaps twelve and the other ten years old (*Book XI*, Letters 35 and 78). What objection is there in such an age? It was no more contrary to the piety of the most holy pontiff to greet and protect noble virgins honorably, even though they had been born from an illicit marriage, than it was to write to their parents Venantius and Italica in words filled with reverence and friendship, and to rebuke John, bishop of Syracuse, for rejecting Venantius’s offerings (*Book VI, Letter 44*).

We have strayed somewhat beyond our bounds in examining the conjectures of a most learned man; we must now return to the subject from which we digressed.

### 8.

Gregory wrote a stern letter to Venantius, the deserter of his monastic commitment, to exhort him to penance; it may easily be read. These words are especially worthy of notice:

“Ananias had vowed money to God, which afterward, overcome by the devil’s persuasion, he withheld (*Acts* 5). But with what death he was punished, you know. If, then, he was worthy of death who took from God the money he had given, consider how great a danger you will deserve at the divine judgment, since you have withheld not money but yourself from almighty God, to whom you had devoted yourself under the monastic habit. Consider the judgment of God that awaits one who has vowed himself to God and immediately afterward, entangled in the desires of the world, has falsified the vow he made” (*Book I, Letter 34*).

What could be expressed more clearly to establish the binding force of monastic vows? Long before this, Pope Siricius had condemned the incestuous marriages of monks and nuns as contrary to public laws and ecclesiastical right, writing to Himerius, bishop of Tarragona (*Letter I, chap. 6, Volume I of the Councils*, p. 1019). Support is also supplied by the Council of Chalcedon, canon 16, and the Fourth Council of Carthage, to which Augustine subscribed, chap. 104.

Augustine nevertheless seems to teach that the marriages of those who have vowed continence are not adulteries, although he considers their fall worse than any adultery (*On the Good of Widowhood*, chaps. 10–12). He maintains, however, that the fault belongs to those who marry, not to the marriages themselves, which are holy and must never be condemned. The holy doctor speaks in this way so that he may not appear to agree with the Manichaeans, who condemn marriage. St. Bernard touches upon this question when it is put to him in *On Precept and Dispensation*, chap. 17, but makes no determination.

Venantius did not repent. Gregory nevertheless did not withdraw from his friendship, hoping that a more suitable opportunity would someday arise to exhort his friend again to penance. Indeed, when he later heard of the serious illness with which Venantius was confined, he wrote to John, bishop of Syracuse, concerned for his salvation [231]. He urged, entreated, and set before him God’s terrifying judgment, while promising the ineffable divine mercy, so that Venantius might return to his former habit even at the point of death, lest the guilt of so great a fault stand against him at the eternal judgment (*Book XI, Letter 36*). What followed from this, however, we do not know. Venantius will be discussed again later. For now, let us pass from Sicily to Africa [Col. 0309B], where the authority of St. Gregory’s pontificate and his pastoral concern became known in the first year after he ascended the Roman See.

# CHAPTER VI

**SUMMARY.**—1. What St. Gregory decreed concerning primates among the African bishops. —2. Whether Columbus was then primate of Numidia. —3. St. Gregory’s efforts against the Donatists, and their outcome. —4. Matters worthy of note concerning the judgment of accused bishops; ecclesiastical immunities; lawsuits; those from whom he exempted monks. —5. He abolishes improper customs. —6. The wills of monks. —7. The property of priests who had fallen and been deposed. —8. The dedication of oratories, then especially celebrated. *(Years 590 and 591.)*

### 1.

It was customary among the African bishops for each province to have among them one who, by virtue of the antiquity of his ordination, held the place of primate or metropolitan; hence he was called not “primate” but an elder, or a bishop of the first see. Only the Church of Carthage, among the nearly innumerable churches of the various provinces of Africa, enjoyed a perpetual primacy.

Since episcopal sees had been established even in small and obscure villages (hence the knowledge of the African Church is for the most part obscure and poorly documented), it often happened that the bishop of an undistinguished town presided over the other bishops of his province as primate. Since this appeared incongruous to St. Gregory, as indeed it was, he judged it best, first, that the primate should be elected not according to the rank of the place (*Book I, Letter 74*)—that is, neither because of the antiquity of his ordination nor because of the dignity assigned to his see—but rather with consideration given to his character and merits.

Second, he decreed that the primate should not, as was customary, reside here and there in villages, but in one of the cities, so that he might more easily resist the attacks and efforts of the Donatists then ravaging Africa. Third, he prohibited those who had advanced to the episcopate from among the Donatists from attaining the dignity of primate. He is speaking of Donatists who had returned to the faith and unity of the Church:

“Let it be enough for them,” he says, “to care only for the people entrusted to them, and not also to take precedence in attaining the summit of the primacy over those bishops whom the Catholic faith has both instructed and brought forth within the bosom of the Church” (*Ibid.*, Letter 77).

Gregory wrote this to the bishops of Numidia [Note: [Col. 0309D] Observe the authority of the holy apostolic See, to which it belongs to confirm the customs of the most remote churches. This authority had shone forth much earlier in St. Leo, who, when asked, confirmed the privileges of the Church of Alexandria, second after Rome: “I have carefully opposed the improper ambition of certain persons, while preserving the right of true privileges . . . . Let your Fraternity maintain the custom of your predecessors and, with appropriate authority, arrange the bishops of your province . . . .” St. Leo, Letter 103.], approving the rest of their customs, whose preservation they had humbly requested from Pelagius II.

### 2.

Those who, with Baronius (*under the year 592, no. 4*), assert that Bishop Columbus was then primate of Numidia [Note: [Col. 0310D] Numidia was the second of Africa’s seven provinces. After the proconsular province, whose chief city was Carthage, it is listed in the description of Africa; consult this in the new edition of the *History of the Vandal Persecution*.], are entirely mistaken and are refuted by Gregory himself in his letter to Columbus:

“Therefore, be solicitous toward the primate of your synod.”

Letter 49 of Book III was written to him, and its heading reads: “To Adeodatus, bishop and primate of the province of Numidia.” St. Gregory exhorts him to strive with complete attention and prudence to perform the duty of primate which, by God’s authority, he holds. A little later he advises him to use Columbus above all others as an assistant in everything.

Adeodatus was succeeded in the primacy by Victor. Concerning him Gregory writes in Letter 28 of Book XII, addressed to Columbus: “We have taken care to write to Victor, our brother and fellow bishop, who holds the place of primate among you.”

Nevertheless, in the principal affairs of the province of Numidia, the holy pope regularly wrote to Columbus as though he had appointed him vicar of the holy See; yet nowhere is this said to have been done.

### 3.

Through Gregory’s singular diligence toward the African Churches, the Donatists, who had previously been causing disturbances, finally became quiet. It was not enough for the most vigilant shepherd, faced with those wolves raging against the flock of Christ, to urge other shepherds under his authority to vigilance and steadfastness by writing them many letters and imposing punishment upon the negligent and hirelings (*Book I, Letter 77; Book II, Letter 48; Book IV, Letter 35; Book V, Letter 5*). He also asked Gennadius, the patrician and exarch of Africa, who was distinguished by many brilliant military achievements, to suppress the efforts of the heretics who raised their heads against the Catholic Church, bend their proud necks, and remove every opportunity for them to cause harm (*Book I, Letter 74*).

Later, when he learned that the excessive leniency of Pantaleon, prefect of Africa, had caused the heretics’ boldness to grow daily, so that they became insolent toward the priests of the Catholic Church and baptized again those whom the Catholic clergy had baptized, he rebuked the prefect for his sluggishness and very freely warned him how grave a sin he was committing by giving heresy an opportunity to revive (*Book IV, Letter 34*).

Finally, after St. Gregory’s repeated admonitions to the bishops, the prefects and magistrates, and the emperor himself, a council was held. With the particular support of Dominicus, bishop of Carthage and primate of all Africa, it was decreed that the bishops should investigate the heretics and restrain them (*Book V, Letter 5*), and that those who neglected to carry out this decree should be punished by deprivation of property and rank.

The pope praised Dominicus’s zeal, yet he did not approve in every respect the decree concerning the despoiling of bishops who had undertaken this duty less diligently. We infer that the Donatists finally repented or became quiet [Note: [Col. 0311D] Read the history of the Donatists added to and prefixed to the latest edition of Optatus’s works, at the end.] from the fact that, after the fourteenth indiction, the holy pontiff wrote more frequently to Dominicus and to the other bishops and imperial officials in Africa, yet nowhere again speaks of restraining them.

### 4.

Since the other matters that commend the first year of Gregory’s pontificate cannot be treated at greater length, we shall select from his letters only a few points more worthy of notice that have not yet been touched upon. He wished bishops to be judged only by a synod, even if they were guilty of grave offenses, as he clearly indicated in the case of Blandus, bishop of Hortae (*Book I, Letter 33*).

Letter 37 proves that ecclesiastical enclosures were then regarded as places of asylum. The notes on that letter explain which places are to be understood by “ecclesiastical enclosures.”

Since the most holy man strongly disliked the noise of the courts, whenever an occasion for litigation arose among bishops, clerics, monks, or even noble laymen, he advised that arbitrators be chosen to settle the dispute—men who would assign each litigant his due at no or minimal expense and without useless delays. If a dispute arose concerning boundaries and lands between agents of the Roman Church, who administered its estates, and the owners of neighboring fields, he himself wanted judges of this kind to be chosen. He could not have revealed his attitude toward lawsuits better than in these words:

“We wish not only that lawsuits never initiated should not be stirred up, but also that those improper disputes which are brought before the courts should be hastened toward resolution by every means” (*Book I, Letter 9*).

His letter 69 testifies to the zeal with which he sought to remove monks from forensic disputes and the noise of litigation. When John, the abbot, had informed him that he had many affairs to conduct on behalf of his monastery, which he could scarcely attend to without detriment to regular observance, the prudent father thought it best to entrust the care of defending the monastery against litigants [Note: [Col. 0311D] He seems to refer to a procurator of this kind when St. Gregory writes to John the abbot in *Book III, Letter 3*: “Appoint a procurator in these cases, and devote yourself to reading [Col. 0312D] and prayer.”] to a certain Faustus, former chancellor of the Roman praetor, and to assign him a salary for his work.

“For it is advantageous,” he says, “that by a small inconvenience the servants of God should remain free from the noise of lawsuits, so that the interests of the cell may not perish through negligence and the minds of God’s servants may be freer for the work of the Lord.”

This seems to be the origin of commendatory abbots. If only they were such as to free God’s servants from every business, rather than plunge them into lawsuits.

### 5.

In Letter 44 to the subdeacon Peter, who administered many of the Church’s estates in Sicily, Gregory orders him to correct numerous customs by which he knew the Church’s tenants were being harassed [Col. 0312A], and to restore generously to the peasants whatever had been exacted from them unjustly.
