Indeed, fearing that Peter might carry out his instructions less energetically, he threatens him with the final judgment and concludes the letter with these words:

“See that you preserve everything without diminution, because concerning the matters about which I write to you for the preservation of justice, I am absolved, while you, if you neglect them, are bound. Consider the terrible Judge who is coming, and let your conscience tremble now at his coming, lest it then fear without remedy, when heaven and earth will have trembled before him. You have heard what I want; see what you do.”

### 6.

In the same letter it is stated that the monk John, when close to death, appointed Fantinus the defender as heir to six *uncia*, that is, half of his property. St. Gregory did not disapprove this. Nevertheless, do not infer from it that monks were then permitted to make wills; read the note with which we have explained this passage. Consult also our Mabillon, *Benedictine Annals*, under the year 599, no. 31, and under the year 601, no. 6.

### 7.

From the letter just cited we learn how carefully St. Gregory guarded against the possibility that those whom he employed in the affairs of the Church might seize the property of priests and other clerics who had fallen and been deposed from their rank. Such a seizure could plainly have caused grave scandal: those who had been deposed would undoubtedly have complained that they had been removed from office and thrust into monasteries for penance so that their property and possessions might be exposed as booty for the papal officials.

St. Gregory therefore decrees that their property should either pass to the monasteries in which they perform penance [Col. 0312C] or be given to their relatives. This was to be done, however, on the condition that the support of those assigned to penance should be adequately provided; or, if the fallen men had belonged to the ecclesiastical household, their property was not to be withdrawn from ecclesiastical ownership, while a maintenance allowance was preserved for those doing penance. Consult the notes on this passage of the cited letter.

### 8.

Letter 56 shows how celebrated the dedication of churches and oratories then was, and how generously the poor were treated at such festivals. Churches and oratories were scarcely ever dedicated without sacred relics being placed within them. It also had to be established that no body had previously been buried at the place where they were deposited [Note: [Col. 0312D] St. Gregory repeats this a hundred times—in other words, in every letter in which he discusses the consecration of temples and the placement of relics.], for excellent reasons, as explained in the note on Letter 54 of Book I.

Mabillon does not dare to assert that no churches were then consecrated in the provinces of Italy more closely subject to the Roman See as their metropolitan authority [Col. 0312D]. Nevertheless, he strongly inclines to this opinion, and not without reason. But there may perhaps be a more suitable place to discuss this subject elsewhere. For the present, read Letter 37 of Book V.

# CHAPTER VII

**SUMMARY.**—1. The case of Natalis, bishop of Salona. —2. The archdeacon deposed by him appeals to the apostolic See. —3. What Natalis replied. He repents. —4. After his death, St. Gregory takes care concerning the election of a successor. Honoratus the archdeacon is elected. —5. The Emperor Maurice deals more mildly with the schismatics. —6. The Lombards press upon Rome. —7. St. Gregory expounds the prophet Ezekiel. Rome’s grievous condition. *(Years 591 and 592.)*

### 1.

The order of events and the chronology now require us to speak of Natalis, bishop of Salona and metropolitan of Dalmatia. After rebelling for a long time against the supreme pontiff, he was overcome in the second year of Gregory’s pontificate by Gregory’s unconquerable greatness of spirit and patience, and at last returned happily to a sounder mind.

It was reported that this bishop, having abandoned pastoral care, devoted himself solely to banquets and, more seriously, had sold the sacred vessels and valuable furnishings of the Church in order to enrich his own people. Honoratus the archdeacon opposed this sacrilege, since it was his responsibility to safeguard the sacred property. Natalis therefore wished to remove him from this office by ordaining him a priest, under the pretext of conferring honor, although Honoratus resisted. At that time a priest could not perform the office of archdeacon, as we have shown especially from St. Leo and Apollinaris Sidonius in the notes on the letters indicated.

Natalis arranged for his judgment concerning Honoratus’s removal from the archdeaconate to be ratified in a council of his province and confirmed by synodal acts. Nothing could have been more unjust or absurd: by the same judgment Honoratus was rejected from the ministry of archdeacon as unworthy and admitted to the priesthood as worthy. (*See Book I, Letters 19 and 20; Book II, Letters 18, 19, and 20; Book III, Letter 32.*)

### 2.

Honoratus had already protested against the violence done to him and had appealed to Pope Pelagius, who had ordered both men—the archbishop and the archdeacon [Col. 0313C]—to appear at least through representatives so that he could judge the dispute. In the first year of his pontificate, St. Gregory summoned Natalis again to answer the charge, since he was delaying and creating postponements, and ordered him above all to restore Honoratus to his former rank.

In the following year he threatened him with deprivation of the pallium if he refused to obey, and finally with excommunication, so that he would be excluded from the body and blood of the Lord unless he corrected his wrongdoing. He reserved for another judgment the question of whether Natalis ought to remain in the episcopate itself.

Moreover, he judged that the archdeacon appointed in Honoratus’s place should be punished by deposition, and declared that if he thereafter presumed to continue ministering in the office, he would be excluded from sacred communion.

Gregory informed all the bishops of Dalmatia and the subdeacon Antonius, administrator of the ecclesiastical patrimony in that province, of these matters [Col. 0313D]. He ordered Antonius to announce the sentence pronounced against Natalis and against the archdeacon intruded by him, after first giving both men the foregoing exhortations.

To prevent Jobinus, prefect of Illyricum, from giving Natalis his protection—for Gregory knew that Natalis was highly regarded by the nobles whom he entertained at banquets—he wrote and asked him not to support the accused against justice. (*See Book I, Letters 19 and 20.*)

### 3.

Natalis was distressed that the pope had threatened him with the penalty of excommunication and wrote to him in his own defense. He claimed that banquets did not disgrace a bishop, since they are commended and praised in Sacred Scripture and among the ancient Christians; that, being weighed down by tribulations, he was not free to devote himself to sacred reading, but that this did not mean he had abandoned the work of preaching.

What he replied concerning the sacred vessels he had sold and concerning Honoratus’s removal from the archdeaconate is not stated in the letter that Gregory judged should be written to him. Gregory wished to calm the irritated man, who nevertheless promised sincere obedience, through devout humility and to instruct him in the spirit of gentleness, as the Apostle teaches.

Let us admire Gregory as, in words at once flattering and effective, he pours both oil and wine into Natalis’s wounds:

“Behold, your Fraternity was distressed at being reproved for banquets, whereas I, who, although not in life, nevertheless transgress in rank, am ready to be corrected and amended by everyone” (*Book II, Letter 52*).

After much else he adds [Col. 0314B]:

“If any one of the four patriarchs had done this—that is, had despised the judgments of the apostolic See—such obstinacy could in no way have passed without the gravest scandal. Nevertheless, after your Fraternity returned to its proper order, I remember neither the injury done to me nor that done to my predecessor” (*Ibid.*).

Natalis’s repentance brought Gregory great joy. In that same year he informed John, bishop of Ravenna, of it in these words:

“Concerning our brother and fellow bishop Natalis, I had been deeply saddened because I had learned certain proud things about him. But because he corrected his ways, he consoled me by overcoming both my sadness and myself” (*Book II, Letter 52*).

4. Shortly afterward Natalis was taken from the living, and Gregory wrote to the subdeacon Antoninus, urging him to attend to the election of a successor. Since his letter allows us to understand what form elections then took, we shall here append several excerpts from it. “Let your Experience,” he says, “hasten with every diligence and every concern to admonish the clergy and people of that city that, by common consent, they must choose for themselves the priest to be ordained; and once the decree has been made concerning the person elected, you shall endeavor to transmit it to us, so that he may be ordained with our consent, as was done in former times. Above all, take care that in this election no payment of rewards, in any form whatsoever, should intervene, nor should the influence of any persons prevail” (Book III, Letter 22).

What care the ministers or legates of the Holy See—such as the subdeacon Antoninus—to preserve the Church’s property intact after the bishop’s death is clear from these words: “Have a faithful inventory of the goods and furnishings of that same church drawn up in your presence. And, lest anything should be lost from those goods, admonish the deacon Respectus and Stephanus, chief of the notaries, to take complete charge of their custody, threatening them that they will have to make good from their own resources whatever may have been diminished through their negligence.” Finally, concerning the provision of everything necessary for the election, he gives this instruction: “Let the expenses that may be necessary be disbursed through the steward who was found there at the time of the aforementioned bishop’s death, so that he himself may explain his accounts to the future bishop as he knows how.”

These matters must not be passed over lightly, for they reveal such authority of the Roman See even over metropolitan churches outside Italy. At times Gregory entrusted responsibility for these elections to bishops (Book I, Letter 57; Book II, Letter 38), and at times even to judges and magistrates, as is shown by Letter 15 of Book III, written to the Judge of Campania on this subject. But he entrusted no authority over the Church’s property to laymen, granting them only the opportunity to summon the Christian people for the election of a bishop.

Honoratus the archdeacon, of whom we have already spoken often, was elected by the clergy as archbishop of Salona; this was very pleasing to Gregory, for he had observed the man’s probity, steadfastness, and prudence in conducting affairs. But Maximus seized his see, relying on the authority of the nobles, as will be said below in its proper place. What we have touched upon here concerning Natalis’s death and the election of his successor has been stated in advance, so that everything pertaining to the dispute that arose between Maximus and Honoratus might be brought together before the reader in one continuous account. Let us now return to the order of events, to which chronology calls us back.

5. While imperial affairs in Italy were tottering, the Emperor Maurice warned Gregory for the time being to refrain from force and coercion, lest the schismatics of Venetia and Istria, driven to desperation if compelled to renounce their schism, surrender themselves to the Lombards. Recently Grado, the seat of Severus, the schismatic patriarch, had been devastated by fire. This moved John of Ravenna to ask the holy pontiff to arrange for alms to be sent there (Book II, Letter 46). Gregory replied that Severus had abundant resources from which to shower gifts upon courtiers and draw them over to his side against the Apostolic See. The Church’s mercy, indeed, ought not to be denied to its enemies, but it should first be shown to the faithful. There was, moreover, a nearby city whose many citizens had been carried into captivity; Claudius the abbot was to be sent there with money for their ransom.

We believe that this conflagration at Grado occurred when Agilulf marched against the three dukes who had rebelled. Of these, Minulf, duke of the Island of Saint Julian [or Saint Julius], who had defected to the Franks and openly supported their side, was defeated and killed. Gaidulf [another reading: Gandulfus], of Pergamum or Bergomum, after surrendering, was received back into favor; but Ulfaris, duke of Treviso, was thrown into chains after the city was captured. (Compare Paul the Deacon, Book IV, chapter 3.)

6. In this year Ariulf, the second duke of Benevento after Faroald, invaded the Roman territory and either killed or mutilated very many of the Roman populace, says Gregory (Book II, Letter 46), who, from grief, fell into a cholic disorder. By “choler,” perhaps, he means bile, which troubled the intestines and stomach. His sorrow was increased by the Roman exarch, who, although unequal to war, nevertheless resisted peace with all his might, seeking profit from public calamities. Rome was almost entirely without defenders, and those who had been left to guard the walls—the Theodosians [Note: So called because they belonged to the legion bearing the name of Theodosius, one of the emperor’s sons]—could scarcely be compelled to stand watch or perform other military duties, since they were not receiving their pay. The exarch had led out the remaining forces and, having increased his army, suddenly recovered, as if by assault, Sutrium, Polimartium, Horta, Tuder, Ameria, and Perugia.

Writing to Maurice, Gregory complains of this (Book V, Letter 40), saying that Rome had been abandoned so that Perugia might be held. Above all, that pious angel of peace bitterly laments that the peace he himself had obtained from the Lombards, who held Etruria, had been recklessly violated. Thus, when such great hope had shone forth for the pacification of all Italy, when Ariulf himself was already inclining toward the Roman side and King Agilulf was not averse to peace, having been softened by Theodelinda, who was exceptionally devoted to Gregory, a more savage war broke out again because of the Roman exarch’s treachery. For the king, seeking to avenge the bad-faith injury inflicted upon his people, besieged and captured Perugia, taking prisoner Maurisio, a Lombard duke who had defected to the Romans. (Compare Paul the Deacon, Book IV, chapter 8.)

The letter already mentioned in full (Book II, Letter 46) should be read in order to discover how great was the pope’s concern in those disastrous times that aid should be brought to cities in danger, that those captured in war should be ransomed with money from the Church’s treasury, and above all that peace—entirely necessary in such desperate circumstances—should be secured on equitable terms. Other letters written that year make clear how anxious and how experienced he was in military affairs (ibid., Letters 3, 29, 30, and 31).

7. In the expedition of Agilulf about which we have spoken, the Lombards not only ravaged the Roman territory near Perugia with plundering, fires, and massacres, but also pitched camp beside the walls of Rome itself. At that time the holy Doctor was explaining the prophet Ezekiel to the Christian people with the same calmness of spirit as if there were nothing to fear from the enemy. Even after he learned that the king had already crossed the Po and was hastening to besiege the City, he did not interrupt the work he had begun—a fact that Bernard rightly admires. But I refrain from reproducing his words, which may be read in the preface to the Homilies on Ezekiel, along with the other matters relating to those homilies. Nevertheless, when the enemy was already threatening the City, he was forced to bring his preaching to an end, as he himself says. I append part of the final homily, because in it Rome’s wretched condition is displayed almost before our eyes:

“Behold, then, most beloved brothers, we have examined these matters before you as far as God’s generosity has enabled us. Let no one blame me if I cease speaking after this discourse, because, as you all see, our tribulations have increased. We are surrounded on every side by swords; on every side we fear the danger of impending death. Some return to us with their hands severed; others are reported captured, others killed. I am now compelled to restrain my tongue from exposition, because my soul is weary of my life.”

Elsewhere he testifies that he saw Romans bound like dogs by ropes around their necks and being led to Gaul to be sold (Book V, Letter 40). O harsh fate of those who were once masters of the world!

This expedition of Agilulf is usually assigned among the events of the year 595, but the following considerations persuade me that it belongs rather to the year 592. Agilulf attempted Rome when he set out to conquer Perugia, as may be gathered from Paul the Deacon: “The king immediately left Ticinum and proceeded toward Perugia . . . At the arrival of this king, the blessed Pope Gregory was so terrified that he abandoned his exposition of the temple about which Ezekiel had written” (Book IV, chapter 8). The same writer clearly shows that this happened immediately after the king learned that Perugia, together with the other cities already listed, had been occupied by the exarch. Gregory himself writes that the Roman exarch had gained possession of Perugia at least in the second year of his pontificate, in a letter written during this same year, which should be compared with the other letter so often cited (Book II, Letter 46; Book V, Letter 40).

235 **CHAPTER VIII**

**SUMMARY.—** 1. Rome suffers from famine. — 2. What Gregory endured from his adversaries. — 3. He secures peace from the Lombards. — 4. How far he was removed from sordid profit. — 5. He complains of the judges’ extortions. — 6. He deposes an archdeacon for pride. — 7. He entrusts the functions of the Holy See to Maximian. — 8. Various measures established by him. — 9. He was exceptionally observant of the laws of friendship. — 10. He reconciles Maximian, bishop, and Eusebius, abbot. He gives both of them very prudent admonitions. — 11. A privilege granted to the monastery of Rimini. (Years 591 and 592.)

1. In the same year in which the Roman territory was consumed by the fires of war, the scourge of famine was added to it. Because of this, the enemies and rivals of Gregory our pope dared to accuse before the Emperor Gregory the prefect of the City, Castorius the master of soldiers, and the supreme pontiff of negligence, although our Gregory had taken every care [Note: Immediately after his ordination he had warned Justin, the praetor of Sicily, about this matter. See Book I, Letter 2] to remove the scarcity. Since the previous year’s harvest in Italy had been small because of sterility, he had taken timely measures to have a large supply of grain procured in Sicily by Peter the subdeacon (Book I, Letter 72), or supplied by the tenants of ecclesiastical estates, though without harassment. He had also arranged for many cargo ships to be available to transport it. But he assigns as the cause of the scarcity suffered by the City the fact that grain cannot be stored in Rome for a long time without spoiling. With the enemy threatening and the roads blockaded, it was impossible to supply the City continually with fresh provisions.

2. Gregory’s steadfastness then shone forth extraordinarily, both in enduring calumnies with equanimity and in defending the innocence of distinguished men united to him in friendship against their detractors. It was no secret that the Roman exarch, in order to divert the blame for his unsuccessful conduct of affairs from himself, had shifted it onto the prefect of the City and the supreme pontiff. Saint Gregory speaks of this in a letter to Sebastian, bishop of Sirmium:

“What we are suffering in this land, most holy brother, because of your friend Lord Romanus, we are scarcely able to express. I shall say briefly, however, that his malice toward us has surpassed the swords of the Lombards, so that the enemies who kill us appear more merciful than the judges of the state, who wear us down by their malice, plundering, and deceit. At one and the same time I must care for bishops, clergy, monasteries, and people; I must watch anxiously against the enemy’s ambushes and remain perpetually suspicious of the commanders’ deceptions and malice. Your Fraternity will judge more truly how great this labor and grief are, the more purely you love me, who endure these things” (Book V, Letter 42).

3. Shortly afterward Agilulf withdrew the camp he had brought up to the walls of the City. Paul the Deacon relates that peace was then made at Theodelinda’s urging. Gregory’s prayers and gifts were added to her counsels; through such means he was accustomed to ransom the Roman people’s freedom and life, as he himself describes when explaining the situation to the Empress Constantina:

“For twenty-seven years now we have been living in this city amid the swords of the Lombards. It is unnecessary to tell you how much the Church distributes among them every day so that we may be able to live among them. I shall indicate it briefly. Just as in the territory of Ravenna the piety of our lords has a treasurer attached to the first army of Italy, who pays the daily expenses as circumstances arise, so in this City I am their treasurer in such matters. And yet this Church, which at one and the same time continually spends so much on clergy, monasteries, the poor, the people, and even the Lombards, behold, is still oppressed by the affliction of all the churches” (Book V, Letter 21).

4. It seems little short of a miracle that the resources of the Roman Church—while its patrimonies and estates everywhere lay exposed to plunder—were sufficient for so many needs under Gregory’s administration, especially since he regarded nothing as more important than repairing the damage inflicted upon tenants and peasants by the administrators and stewards of the Church’s estates, as we observed above, and preventing such harm in the future. How greatly he abhorred unjust exactions is shown by these words in Letter 44 of Book I: “We do not wish the Church’s purse to be polluted by sordid profits.” Indeed, in the Roman Council (formerly Letter 44 of Book IV, now printed at the end of the Letters), he decreed that not only administrators of the Church’s estates, if they sought to enlarge them beyond what was proper or invaded others’ boundaries under titles affixed for that purpose, should be punished by the sentence of anathema, but also the pontiffs themselves if they either ordered such things to be done or failed to prohibit them.

5. Yet nowhere do his fairness, integrity, and greatness of spirit shine more clearly than in the letter written to the Empress Constantina on this occasion (Book V, Letter 41). Having learned that many pagans still survived in Sardinia and that the priests of the island, through sluggishness, were insufficiently concerned with their conversion, he arranged to send there a certain bishop from Italy. Through that bishop’s preaching many came to the faith, received baptism, and ceased sacrificing to idols. But since they had formerly been accustomed to pay the praetor or judge a certain fee in order to obtain permission to sacrifice, the judge, unwilling to lose this sordid profit, demanded the same tribute even from those who had been baptized and were now serving no one but the true God.

When rebuked by the bishop concerning this, he replied that such a large sum was imposed upon him personally that he could not pay it unless he exacted this unjust levy. The inhabitants of Corsica, too, were oppressed by such enormous exactions that they could scarcely satisfy them even after selling their children; and Sicily was harassed by no less devastating depredations. Gregory informed the Empress of these crimes and acts of brigandage so that, after finding a suitable opportunity, she might notify Maurice.

In this letter he anticipates what the emperor might have answered: namely, that whatever was collected from the aforementioned islands was being sent to meet expenses in Italy. To this the holy pope replies:

“But I make this representation so that, even if less is contributed to the expenses in Italy, he may nevertheless restrain the tears of those oppressed by his authority. Perhaps, indeed, this is why such great expenditures in this land produce less benefit: because they are gathered with some admixture of sin. Let our most serene lords therefore command that nothing be collected with sin. And I know that, even if little is assigned to the state’s needs, the state is greatly assisted by that little. Even if it should happen that it is assisted less by smaller expenditures, it is nevertheless better that we should not live temporally than that you should encounter some obstacle to eternal life. Consider what the minds and hearts of parents must be when they sell their children so that they may not be tortured.”

Let us now turn to ecclesiastical affairs.

6. At the beginning of this, the second year of Gregory’s pontificate, Laurentius, archdeacon of the Roman Church—perhaps the same man who had been appointed in Gregory’s place at Rome by Pope Pelagius when Gregory returned from Constantinople—was deposed for pride and other offenses. Honoratus took his place in a synod of all the priests and deacons and the entire clergy (at the end of the Letters, formerly at the beginning of Book II). The supreme pontiff thereby made clear how deeply he cared to remove the unworthy from the sacred ministry, wisely understanding that the ecclesiastical commonwealth, like the civil one, is maintained both by reward and by punishment (Cicero, *To Brutus*).

7. In the same year he entrusted the functions of the Apostolic See throughout all the churches of Sicily to Saint Maximian, bishop of Syracuse, whom we have already discussed. He granted this dignity not to the office but to the person, having learned from Maximian’s past life what might reasonably be expected of his subsequent conduct (Book II, Letter 7). Nevertheless, he wished more important and more difficult cases to be referred to him. A letter written to Maximian shortly afterward (ibid., Letter 24) makes clear how carefully Gregory investigated which men, wherever they might be found, appeared worthy to exercise the episcopate, so that he might endeavor to advance them to pastoral care.

8. Among the other noteworthy measures he established this year, the following decree against repeated ordinations must not be passed over casually:

“Just as one who has been baptized once ought not to be baptized again, so one who has been consecrated once cannot validly be consecrated again in the same order. But if someone has come to the priesthood with some slight fault, penance should be imposed for the fault, while the order itself should nevertheless be preserved” (Book II, Letter 46).

These words of the holy pontiff should also be read attentively:

“Far be it from me to violate in any church the statutes of my predecessors concerning my fellow bishops, for I do myself an injury if I disturb the rights of my brothers” (Book II, Letter 52).

By these words he showed how reverently he honored the episcopal power established by Christ, even in bishops subject to him. The same is attested by his reply to Bishop Dominicus:

“Concerning the ecclesiastical privileges about which your Fraternity writes, let it hold this without hesitation: just as we defend our own rights, so we preserve the rights belonging to each individual church. I grant no one, by favor of grace, more than he deserves; nor, moved by ambition, do I take from anyone what belongs to his own right; rather, I wish to honor my brothers in every respect” (ibid., Letter 47).

9. Two bishops had brought Gregory, as a gesture of honor, a congratulatory letter from Dominicus on his assumption of the pontificate; two attendants accompanied them, one a deacon and the other a notary. Since he could not return the honor in kind—for that would have been beneath his supreme dignity—he certainly repaid love with love, and even with interest, being no less concerned to preserve the laws of friendship than the rights of the episcopate. Anyone who reads this letter to Dominicus will recognize the fact.

What fragrance of charity there is in these words:

“Let us hold fast, most holy brother, with unshaken steadfastness, this love, the mother and guardian of the virtues. Let no deceitful tongues diminish it within us; let no ambushes of the ancient enemy corrupt it. For love joins what is divided and guards what is joined. It raises the lowly without swelling them with pride. It brings down the exalted without casting them into degradation. Through it the unity of the universal Church, which is the structure of Christ’s body, rejoices in the equality of minds among its individual members, although there is diversity in the different members. Through it those same members leap for joy at another’s happiness even when afflicted in their own affairs, and waste away at another’s grief even when rejoicing in their own.

“For, as the teacher of the nations testifies, when one member suffers, the other members suffer with it, and when one member is honored, all the members rejoice with it. I cannot doubt that you groan over our disturbance, since it is entirely certain that we rejoice in your peace.”

And after much else:

“Through the bond of charity, what I say about myself is also yours, and what I desire you to do is also mine.”

10. To touch briefly upon matters relating to monasteries in the second year of Gregory’s pontificate, nothing more worthy of notice presents itself than the pope’s concern to settle the dispute between Maximian, bishop of Syracuse, and Eusebius the abbot. We have already stated more than once how holy Maximian was. At the beginning of this year we mentioned that Gregory had entrusted the functions of the Holy See to him. Yet the holy pontiff judged that this holy man, almost foremost among those closest to him, should be rebuked for imposing excommunication upon Eusebius the abbot for too slight a reason and in a fit of anger.

Gregory thought that Peter the subdeacon, acting in Sicily on the business of the Roman See, should admonish him about this. He writes to Peter as follows:

“I was distressed that [Maximian] excommunicated Lord Eusebius, a man of such advanced age and such serious illness. Therefore you must say privately to that lord bishop that he should not be hasty in pronouncing judgments, because cases that must be decided by a sentence need first to be measured by careful and repeated consideration” (Book II, Letter 32).

Notice the title “Lord,” which the pope himself bestowed upon the aged abbot as a mark of honor.

Nor was it enough for Gregory to address Maximian through Peter; he also admonished him in a letter to try to soothe and console Eusebius, who had been so greatly inflamed by anger. In this letter to Maximian he recalls how often he had warned him not to be hasty in pronouncing judgment (Book II, Letter 34). He wonders that Maximian had burned with such fury against an abbot whose long-standing conduct, advanced age, and prolonged illness ought to have turned the bishop’s mind away from anger.

“Whatever his excess may have been,” he says, “the affliction of his illness itself ought to have been sufficient punishment for him . . . But perhaps you were permitted to go too far against such a person so that you might become more cautious in dealing with those of lesser standing.”

Would that bishops and rulers always kept these admonitions of the most holy Doctor before their eyes when judging those subject to them!

Maximian obeyed and wished to restore communion and favor to Eusebius, but the abbot was reluctant to accept them. Therefore Saint Gregory endeavored to recall him to his duty in this letter:

“Let your Charity believe me: I was deeply saddened by your sadness, as if I myself had suffered an injury in your person. But when I afterward learned that, although our most reverend brother and fellow bishop Maximian had restored favor and communion to you, your Affection did not wish to receive communion from him, I understood that what had previously been done was also just.

“The humility of God’s servants ought to appear in a time of affliction. Those who raise themselves against their superiors plainly show that they scorn to be servants of God. Certainly, what was done by him ought not to have been done; but you ought to have accepted it with complete humility. And again, when he was restoring favor to you, you ought to have hastened to him with thanksgiving.

“Since this did not happen on your part, I recognize that we have need of many tears. For it is no great thing for us to be humble toward those by whom we are honored, since any worldly person does this. But we ought to be especially humble toward those from whom we suffer anything. For the Psalmist says: ‘See my humility before my enemies.’

“What kind of life are we leading, if we are unwilling even to be humble toward our fathers? Therefore, dearest son, I ask that all bitterness pass from your heart, lest perhaps the end be near and the ancient enemy, through the wickedness of discord, block the way to the heavenly kingdom.”

We judged that almost this entire letter, wholly golden, should be reprinted here, so that all might learn humility and reverence toward their superiors, even when those superiors act unjustly. Yet, lest Eusebius should perhaps be embittered by this free rebuke, Gregory arranged for Peter the subdeacon to distribute one hundred solidi to him for the needs of his monastery, thereby proving at once the man’s generosity and prudence.

11. In another way he settled disputes between the bishop of Rimini and the monks of the monastery of Saints Andrew and Thomas near Rimini. He granted them an extensive privilege, which he conveyed to Castorius, bishop of Rimini, in these words:

“We urge your Fraternity that, when the abbot of that monastery dies, your Church should not under any pretext interfere in recording, preserving, or administering the property acquired or to be acquired by that monastery. We wish you to ordain as abbot of that monastery not someone else, but the man whom the entire congregation, by common consent, shall request as worthy in character and suited to monastic discipline” (Book II, Letter 41).

We shall speak below of other privileges granted in favor of monks (Book III, chapter 2, section 9).

**CHAPTER IX**

**SUMMARY.—** 1. Saint Gregory chastises two metropolitans in the case of the bishop of Thebes. — 2. He excommunicates a bishop who had beaten someone. — 3. Concerning the ill-treatment of the monks of Isauria by John of Constantinople. The letters of Saint Gregory to John written on that matter. — 4. He absolves the monks after they have offered a confession of faith. He also absolves John the priest from heresy. — 5. John of Constantinople, accusing others of heresy, falls incautiously into error. — 6. Saint Gregory restrains the arrogance of John of Ravenna. — 7. Concerning Domitian, bishop of Melitene. He preaches to the Persians without success. The holy pontiff consoles him. (Years 592 and 593.)

1. As greatly as Gregory embraced the best bishops with charity, so severely did he restrain those who used their authority not for edification but for destruction, disregarding ecclesiastical regulations. He demonstrated this at the very beginning of the third year of his pontificate against John, bishop of First Justiniana, and another John, archbishop of Larissa.

Hadrian, bishop of Thebes, had deposed two deacons: one because he was guilty of violating chastity, the other because he had committed fraud in the administration of ecclesiastical property. Both had appealed to the Emperor Maurice, concerning both financial and criminal matters. The emperor, observing the canonical procedure, decreed that the financial dispute should be settled by John, archbishop of Larissa and metropolitan of Thebes; but concerning the alleged crimes, whatever should be learned and established after investigation was to be referred to him.

We read that the following charges were brought against Hadrian: that he had not removed Stephen, a deacon of the most disgraceful life, from office, and that he had forbidden infants to be baptized, with the result that they later died without baptism. (See Book III, Letters 6 and 7.)

The archbishop of Larissa, disregarding the imperial order, issued judgment on both aspects of the dispute, condemned Hadrian, and nevertheless cast him, though he had appealed to the Emperor, into the strictest confinement. After his appeal had been received, Maurice wished the proceedings to be examined by Honoratus the deacon, the apocrisiarius of the Holy See, and by Sebastian the *antigraphus* [Note: Consult the notes on Letter 28 of Book I concerning this word]. After hearing them, he acquitted Hadrian.

But by I know not what machinations it was later obtained that John, bishop of First Justiniana and vicar of the Apostolic See, should hear and judge the case. He, disregarding both divine and human law, issued a rash sentence condemning Hadrian.

When these matters were reported to Gregory, he restored Hadrian, who had been unjustly deposed, to his former dignity, and wished him and his Church to be removed from the jurisdiction of the bishop of Larissa, which had already been established by Pelagius II. To John, however, the bishop of that city, he remitted the punishment of excommunication due for his misconduct and presumption, on condition that, unless he henceforth refrained from exercising any jurisdiction over the Church of Thebes, he would immediately be deprived of sacred communion and would never receive it again—except at the point of death—unless he were first absolved by the judgment of the Roman pontiff.

John of First Justiniana was treated more severely. His decrees and sentences having been annulled, he himself was deprived of sacred communion for thirty days and ordered to perform penance.

That Hadrian’s accusers were reconciled with him is shown by Letter 39 of Book III, addressed to the bishops of Corinth. There can scarcely be any doubt that the bishop Hadrian mentioned in that letter is the same man. Thus Saint Gregory avenged the injury inflicted upon the bishop and upon the entire episcopal order. Although he regarded all bishops—including the Roman pontiff himself—as equal according to the principle of humility (Book IX, Letter 59), whenever no fault compelled him to take action against them, he was nevertheless careful to exercise the supreme authority he possessed against offenders, regardless of how high their episcopal rank or where in the Christian world they might sit.

2. His magnanimity also blazed forth this year against Andrew, bishop of Tarentum. It had been discovered that he had a concubine, and some suspicion had arisen that he had retained her even after receiving sacred orders. Moreover, forgetful of pastoral gentleness, he had ordered a certain woman to be cruelly beaten with rods; she died eight months later. Because of this cruelty Gregory decreed that Andrew should be suspended from the celebration of Mass and placed in penance for two months (Book III, Letter 45).

Since it was not equally certain that he himself had stained himself with carnal sin, and since in doubtful matters no definitive judgment may be issued, Gregory judged that Andrew should be left to his own conscience, so that it might judge him. At the same time he warned him that, if he were conscious of so grave a crime, he should renounce the honor of the priesthood and never presume to approach sacred service again.

To remove the opportunity for such suspicions, by which even the reputation of the best bishops can suffer, it had formerly been prescribed, as Ennodius testifies (*Opusculum* 7), that all bishops should have cellarers. This may perhaps have been occasioned by the calumnies with which Pope Symmachus had recently been harassed, as we have already said in the notes to Saint Gregory’s decrees, column 1289, note g.

3. At nearly the same time Gregory’s paternal piety was also engaged in restraining the harshness and brutality of John, patriarch of Constantinople. This sufficiently proves that, as he teaches elsewhere, no bishop exists who, should guilt require it, is not subject to the authority and correction of the Apostolic See (Book IX, Letter 59).

One of the monks of Isauria, distinguished by priestly rank, had been beaten with rods in the church at Constantinople. The principal suspect in so great a crime was said to be a certain young man, a familiar of John, well known for the disgrace of many crimes. As Gregory says, this man “had as yet learned nothing of God” and “did not know the heart of charity” (Book III, Letter 53). He was said to lie in wait daily for the deaths of various people through secret wills; he feared neither God nor human beings.

When Gregory learned of this violence and disgrace inflicted upon Athanasius—this is believed to have been the name of the priest and monk—he wrote to John once and again, asking him to investigate the truth of the crime. John, pretending ignorance, replied that he knew absolutely nothing about what he was being questioned. In this way, wishing to avert the odium of the violation of religion in a monk and priest, he increased his guilt: for either he compounded the offense by lying, or he accused himself of senility and sluggishness.

“For,” Gregory objects, “what could be worse than for such things to be done against God’s servants while the man who is responsible is unaware? What excuse can a shepherd have if the wolf devours the sheep and the shepherd does not know?”

After this introduction, the pope calls John back to sounder counsels and urges him to observe the canons, which require bishops to be shepherds, not beaters. “This is a new and unheard-of kind of preaching,” he says, “which demands faith through beatings. But if you do not observe the canons and wish to tear down the statutes of your predecessors, I do not recognize who you are.”

Finally, he advises him to correct the young man, the author of all the evil, reject his counsels, receive into their proper orders the monks whom he had mistreated, and grant them peace. He also instructed Sabinianus, his legate before Maurice, to admonish the patriarch concerning the same matter.

That John did not immediately comply is sufficiently indicated by another letter to the patrician Narses:

“Concerning the case of the priests, which is being conducted with my brother and fellow bishop, the most reverend John the patriarch, I think that we are suffering as an adversary the very man whom you assert wishes to observe the canons. I briefly confess to your Charity that, with the help of almighty God, I am prepared to pursue this case with every strength and every weight of authority. If I see that the canons are not observed toward the Apostolic See in this matter, almighty God will show me what I should do against those who despise them” (Book IV, Letter 32).

Letter 14 of Book VI teaches that Athanasius and his companions had been branded with the infamy of Manichaean heresy.

4. What happened afterward, learn from the same letter and from Letter 66 of the same book, which we reproduce here in full, so that Gregory’s prudence in handling such matters may be shown:

Gregory to Athanasius, a presbyter from Isauria.

Just as we are afflicted and grieve over those whom the error of heretical depravity has cut off from the unity of the Church, so we rejoice with those whom the profession of the Catholic faith embraces within its bosom. And just as pastoral concern requires us to oppose the impieties of the former, so it is fitting that we show favor toward the pious professions of the latter, and declare that those things which they understand are sincere. Therefore, when suspicion contrary to sound faith arose concerning you, Athanasius, presbyter of the monastery of Saint Mile, called Tamnaco, which is situated in the province of Lycaonia, you chose to have recourse to the apostolic see over which we preside, so that the integrity of your profession might become evident. You also asserted that, after being physically beaten, you had done certain things unjustly and violently.

Although things done under the compulsion of force are in no way accepted by the judgment of the canons, and are rightly considered invalid—for the one who compels a person to acknowledge and do what is unjust himself nullifies those acts—nevertheless, that confession must rather be accepted and embraced which is shown to proceed from spontaneous willingness, as you are recognized to have done before us. Yet, so that nothing ambiguous might remain for us, we arranged for a letter to be written about you to our most holy brother and fellow bishop John, formerly our colleague, bishop of the city of Constantinople, so that he might inform us through his letters of what had happened (Indiction 11, Letter 52).

When he had often been admonished by us, he replied and reported (Indiction 13, Letter 18) that a book had been found in your possession containing very much heretical material, and that for this reason he had been provoked against your affection. Since he took care to send the book to us for examination, we went through its earlier sections with attentive reading. Because we found in it manifest poisons of heretical depravity, we forbade it to be read again.

But because you openly testified that you had read it in simplicity, and, to remove the grounds of the ambiguous suspicion, handed us a written statement in your own hand, in which, setting out your faith, you most explicitly condemned all heresies in general, and whatever is opposed to the integrity of the Catholic faith or profession; and because you professed that you had always accepted and continued to accept everything received by the four holy universal councils, and had condemned and continued to condemn whatever they condemn; and because you promised both to accept and to observe the council held concerning the Three Chapters in the time of the emperor Justinian; and because, when we forbade you to read that book in which the poison of a pestilential fraud is interwoven, you most willingly consented; and because you also rejected and condemned everything said or secretly inserted in it against the integrity of the Catholic faith, and promised that you would not read it again:

Moved by these considerations, and after the page of the statement approved by you had also made your Catholic faith plainly evident to us, with God preserving it, we decree that, in accordance with your profession, you are free from every stain of heretical perversity and are Catholic; and we declare that you have shown yourself in all things a professor and follower of sincere faith, through the grace of Christ Jesus our Savior. We also grant you free permission to return to your monastery, to your own place and order as before.

Concerning this matter we also wish to send a letter to our most beloved brother, the bishop of the city of Constantinople, who was ordained in the place of the aforesaid holy John. But because it is not customary for us to write to him before his synodical letter 239 has been delivered to us, we therefore postponed doing so. After it has been brought to us, we shall inform him of these matters when the opportunity is appropriate.

This case is related to that of John, a presbyter of Chalcedon, whom at the same time judges appointed by that same John of Constantinople unjustly condemned, after uninformed accusers had charged him with the heresy of the Marcianists—or rather, of the Marcionites. But when the pope held a council, he absolved him, chiefly because the statement submitted by John agreed in every respect with the sincerity of the faith. Gregory wrote to the emperor Maurice and to Theoctista concerning this judgment, by which he declared the presbyter John free from the charge of heresy (Book VI, Letters 16 and 17). He also informed John himself, the patriarch of Constantinople, of this synodal judgment (same book, Letter 15).

In the letter which Saint Gregory wrote to him, the holy Doctor openly condemns those who, carried away by a falsely directed zeal, impose heresies even upon unwilling people who profess the orthodox faith. Above all, these words deserve attention:

“Just as the depravity of heretics must be restrained by zeal for right faith, so the integrity of true confession must be embraced. For if one who confesses faithfully is despised and not believed, the faith of all is thrown into doubt, and deadly errors are generated by ill-considered severity. Thus not only are wandering sheep by no means brought back to the Lord’s folds, but they are also cruelly exposed, once placed among the teeth of wild beasts, to be torn apart. Therefore, dearest brother, let us weigh this carefully, and not allow anyone who truthfully professes the Catholic faith to be afflicted under the pretext of heresy, lest—God forbid—we permit heresy to arise under the appearance of correction.”

5. That what commonly happens to those detractors who, while accusing others of heresy, are driven into the opposite error also happened to John of Constantinople, Saint Gregory testifies in these words:

“Three years ago, compelled by the case of the monks of Isauria, who were being accused of heresy, my late brother and fellow priest, the lord John, sent me a letter in which he attempted to show that they had contradicted the definitions of the Council of Ephesus. As though from that same council, he sent me certain chapters indicating the points to which they were opposed. Among other things, the document stated that Adam’s soul had not died in sin, because the devil does not enter into the heart of man; and that anyone who said this would be anathema. When this had been read back to me, I was greatly saddened” (Book VII, Letter 34).

The learned Pope refutes this error of John as a shoot of the Pelagian heresy, and that pseudo-Ephesian council as a product of the Pelagians, both in the aforementioned letter and in Book IX, Letter 49. There he asserts that the chapters sent to him from the imperial city under the name of the Council of Ephesus were themselves the corrupt doctrines of Pelagius and Coelestius.

For the monks of Isauria, consult *The Monastic History of the East*, Book IV, chapter 17, p. 753, where they are said to have lived rather in Lycaonia than in Isauria. Certainly, in Book IV of the *Dialogues*, chapter 38, Gregory mentions a certain Athanasius, a presbyter and, as may be conjectured, a monk of Lycaonia, if the reading is reliable in the numerous manuscripts designated in the note at this place. But Isauria and Lycaonia were neighboring provinces; hence it is not surprising that one may have been used for the other.

There is also, in Book V, Letter 37, a letter to Elias, a presbyter and abbot in Isauria, whose disciple Epiphanius, by name, Saint Gregory ordained deacon of the Roman Church. Elias had requested fifty solidi for the needs of his monastery, but the most generous father sent seventy-two. It is entirely uncertain whether those monks accused of heresy lived in that monastery.

From the matters mentioned, it may be understood that John of Constantinople was not sufficiently on guard against the Pelagian heresy—a fact likewise established concerning very many Greeks—and that he was little trained in ecclesiastical history and scholarship, since he ineptly praised spurious and heretical writings as genuine acts of the Council of Ephesus. Gregory had to struggle with this patriarch of the imperial city more than once, as will be related in its proper place.

6. Since we have begun to speak of bishops corrected and reformed by Gregory because they had forgotten their duty, it is worthwhile to add a few words about John, bishop of Ravenna, who was also reprimanded this year for his arrogance and insolent use of the pallium (Book III, Letter 56).

Relying on the authority of the exarchs residing at Ravenna, he thought that he might arrogate to himself certain privileges beyond the common custom of metropolitans. Whereas the other metropolitans did not use the pallium outside the time of Mass, he himself walked about wearing it during solemn litanies and public supplications, which had been instituted as a discipline of penitence. He thus displayed a novel form of dress, although at that time he ought rather to have professed humility in ashes and sackcloth. Gregory, the foremost defender of priestly modesty, disapproved of this. His saying is plainly golden: nothing shines more splendidly on a bishop’s neck than humility.

[Note: In the Greek Church as well, bishops who have been granted the use of the pallium do not wear it throughout the whole Mass, but only until the reading of the Gospel, according to Isidore of Pelusium, Book I, Letter 136. Simeon of Thessalonica gives the same testimony in his book on the Temple and the Mass.]

Following the example of their archbishop, the clergy of the Church of Ravenna, growing proud, presumed to use *mappulae*, a privilege claimed exclusively by the Roman clergy.

[Note: On these matters, read Cardinal Bona, Book I of *Liturgical Matters*, chapter 24, no. 5.]

Gregory immediately took care to write to John about them through Castorius, notary of the Holy Roman Church. John replied that these privileges had been granted to him and to his Church by the supreme pontiffs, and asked Gregory to confirm them. The Roman exarch, the prefect, and other distinguished men of Ravenna also pressed the request.

Accordingly, accommodating them, the pontiff agreed that the archbishop of Ravenna, until something more certain became known concerning the privileges granted to him, might use the pallium during the litanies on only four solemn days: Saint John the Baptist’s day, Saint Peter the Apostle’s day, Saint Apollinaris’s day—the patronal feast of that Church—and the anniversary of his own ordination (Book V, Letter 11).

This judgment did not please John, as may be inferred from the letter later written to him, in which Saint Gregory complained of John’s mocking and biting remarks (same book, Letter 15). To remove every occasion for complaint, he wrote to the archbishop that, through his representative acting at Constantinople, he would investigate whether some of the greater metropolitans, who had thirty or forty bishops under them, customarily walked with the pallium during the litanies. If any such bishops were found, he would gladly grant the bishop of Ravenna the privilege of wearing the pallium during the litanies.

Thus the humble pontiff attempted to pacify the man whom he had provoked. Nevertheless, he did not think John’s faults should be concealed, but diligently admonished him concerning them—especially that he flattered his friends when they were present, spoke against them when absent, raged against slaves and uttered obscene language, and maintained no discipline for regulating the lives of the clergy, but merely presented himself as lord over his own clerics.

[Col. 0327D] 7. As hostile as Gregory showed himself toward such bishops, so kind and attentive did he show himself toward the best pastors. This was especially demonstrated in his treatment of Domitian, bishop and metropolitan of Melitene in Armenia.

Domitian was a kinsman of the emperor Maurice, a prudent and industrious man, extraordinarily powerful in word and deed, and highly effective in undertaking the greatest affairs, as Evagrius says. For this reason the emperor regularly employed him as an assistant in many very important matters. Indeed, when he was dangerously ill in the fifteenth year of his reign, Maurice entrusted his still immature children to Domitian’s protection, as Simocatta relates; Simocatta speaks at great length in Domitian’s praise.

When Chosroes, king of the Persians, had recovered his kingdom with Maurice’s help, and shortly afterward sent to Gregory, patriarch of Antioch, a gold cross sparkling with jewels to be offered in the church of Saint Sergius, and had adorned the basilica of that martyr with numerous gifts—believing that through the martyr’s aid he had been restored to his kingdom, had obtained his beloved wife and offspring, and had recovered his health—great hope had arisen that the Christian faith might be spread and advanced among the Persians.

For this purpose Domitian had gone to the king, whom he had already bound to himself by many benefits. Maurice had sent this bishop to meet the fugitive and exiled king as an honor, so that he might escort him wherever he wished to go.

John of Biclaro in his chronicle and Paul the Deacon, Book IV, chapter 17, relate that Chosroes had then become a Christian.

[Note: Fredegar’s Chronicle, chapter 9, also relates the conversion of this king. It says that he was baptized with sixty thousand Persians and was received from the baptismal font by Gregory of Antioch.]

But it is clear that these writers were deceived by an appearance of religion arising from the king’s generosity toward Christian churches, and that he did not abandon the worship of the pagans. This is evident both from the Greek writers who continued the history of Maurice’s deeds and, above all, from Gregory’s letter of consolation to Domitian written that year:

“Although I grieve that the emperor of the Persians was not converted, I rejoice exceedingly that you preached the Christian faith to him in every way. For although he did not deserve to come to the light, your holiness will nevertheless receive the reward of your preaching. For the Ethiopian enters the bath black and emerges black, yet the bath attendant still receives his money” (Book III, Letter 67).

In this way Gregory gently and ingeniously consoled the most holy bishop, who was closely bound to him by friendship, for his labors having proved fruitless. Domitian had written to him grieving that his journey to the Persians for the sake of preaching had borne no fruit.

(Compare Evagrius, *Life of Maurice*, Book IV, chapter 14; Book VI, chapter 13 and following; Book VIII, chapter 11.)

## CHAPTER X

**SUMMARY.—** 1. Concerning the law of Maurice forbidding soldiers to be received into monasteries. Saint Gregory disapproves of it. — 2. Whether he amended it before it was published. — 3. The occasion on which that law was enacted, and the arguments on which it rested. — 4. Gregory’s concern for monastic discipline. — 5. Whether abbots and monks were forbidden to go outside. — 6. A Jew deceives Christians under the false worship of Elijah. Gregory writes concerning his punishment. — 7. Gregory composes the *Dialogues*. [Col. 0328D] (A.D. 592 and 593.)

### 1.

Before we leave the East, we must deal with a certain law promulgated by the emperor at approximately this time, which caused the most holy pontiff, already suffering from illness, the deepest grief.

Maurice had decreed not only that no one who had been involved in public administration could attain ecclesiastical office, but also that such a person might not enter a monastery and convert there. He had made the same provision concerning those enrolled in military service: thereafter they were not free to seek monasteries for the sake of doing penance.

[Note: The same matter had already been established by many canons and by decrees of the supreme pontiffs. See Letter 2 of Innocent I to Victricius of Rouen.]

Saint Gregory strongly praised the exclusion of curials and those bound to secular business from ecclesiastical dignities. He knew perfectly well, he said, that one who hastens to ecclesiastical offices after abandoning secular dress wishes to alter his secular condition, not to leave the world.

But he by no means approved of forbidding such persons to convert in monasteries. Even if they were debtors or entangled in public accounts, their debts could be settled through the monastery, the holy pontiff said. By this single argument he simultaneously demonstrates that monasteries at that time were endowed with substantial revenues and that the greatest charity prevailed within them.

Above all, the holy father condemned the law by which soldiers were prohibited from entering monasteries unless they had either completed their military service or received discharge because of bodily incapacity. Let us hear him remonstrating with Maurice concerning this law:

“To this, behold, Christ will answer through me, his least servant and yours, saying: ‘I made you from notary a commander of the bodyguard, from commander of the bodyguard a Caesar, from Caesar an emperor; and not only this, but I also made you the father of emperors. I entrusted my priests to your hand, and you withdraw your soldiers from my service? Answer, I beg you, most pious Lord, what will you reply in judgment to your Lord when he comes and says these things to you?’”

The rest may be read as spoken with the freedom befitting the supreme pontiff. Yet he moderated it afterward with these words, breathing humility:

“I, indeed, being subject to the command, caused this same law to be sent throughout the various regions of the earth; and because the law itself is in no way in harmony with almighty God, behold, through the page of my petition I have informed the most serene lords. Thus in both respects I have discharged what I owed: I have shown obedience to the emperor, and I have not kept silent concerning what I thought on God’s behalf.” (See Book III, Letters 65 and 66.)

[Note: From Cassiodorus, Book I of the *Variae*, Letter 4, it may be inferred that notaries held great dignity and authority among the emperors.]

### 2.

Gregory sent this letter to Theodore, the emperor’s chief physician—or head of the physicians—asking him to present it to Maurice at a suitable time. Theodore possessed considerable influence with the emperor, and Gregory asked him, by means of both advice and entreaties, to urge the emperor to reshape or soften this law. We do not know whether Theodore carried this out.

Nevertheless, the holy pontiff seems to indicate that Maurice later withdrew from the law he had enacted. Writing to several metropolitans about soldiers who were to be admitted to the monastic habit after a three-year probation, he adds:

“Concerning this matter also, believe me, the most serene and most Christian emperor is in every way appeased, and gladly accepts the conversion of those whom he knows not to be entangled in public accounts.”

E. C. Baronius likewise holds that Gregory amended and moderated this imperial law before the emperor ordered it promulgated and sent it to the metropolitans. The opinion of the most illustrious D. de Marca is nearly the same (*On Concord*, Book II, chapter 11). He adds that Saint Gregory softened the law by the same authority possessed by the praetorian prefects, who had the power, when civil laws were sent to them by the emperors for publication, either to alter them temporarily or to refrain from publishing them until they had written to the emperor or approached him concerning their amendment.

Others, however, believe that Saint Gregory sent the law without any alteration, exactly as he had received it from the emperor. They contend that this is signified by Gregory’s words: “I caused the same law to be sent throughout the various regions of the earth; and because the law itself is in no way in harmony with almighty God, behold … I have informed [the most serene lords].” Therefore, they say, the law as transmitted by the pope had not yet been corrected or amended, since after amendment it would have agreed with the will and law of God.

Let the reader choose either opinion.

### 3.

In any event, the occasion for enacting this law had been provided to the emperor by the frequent rush to the monasteries of those who were then seeking penance. Many people bound to secular life and to the court by various offices and services, terrified by the threat of so many scourges of divine anger, abandoned both public and private affairs; tax collectors deserted the customs stations; military men—whether common soldiers and rankers, centurions, tribunes, or other commanders—threw aside the insignia of military service and hastened to conversion.

There were, moreover, arguments that persuaded people that soldiers ought to be received into monasteries only after completing their service and receiving discharge. For Canon 4 of the Council of Chalcedon provides that no slave may be received into a monastery under pretext of monastic profession without the knowledge of his master; those who transgress this definition are excommunicated.

And in Canon 3 of the Council of Gangra we read: “If anyone teaches a slave, under pretext of divine worship, to despise his own master and to depart from his service … let him be anathema.”

But throughout the entire period of military service, soldiers were bound to serve the state no less than slaves. They were therefore also marked on the hand at that time like slaves, upon whom certain marks were branded. On this subject Vegetius, Book II, chapter 25, should be consulted. Gregory himself, in the aforementioned letter to Maurice, calls the soldiers “marked on the hand.”

According to modern custom, although no brands are burned into soldiers, nevertheless, as soon as they have professed military service by taking the oath, they cannot abandon it with impunity, even for the purpose of embracing a more sacred service.

These observations may suffice to show that the law was neither impiously enacted by the emperor nor rashly promulgated by Gregory. For although it might seem to oppose piety that soldiers were forbidden to serve in the sacred army of the monks—and for this reason Gregory rebuked Maurice with greater freedom—yet, when the matter is examined more closely and the public good is taken into account, prudence may perhaps have persuaded the wisest advisers that such a regulation was necessary.

### 4.

Since this most holy man was so concerned to enlist soldiers for Christ, he worked ever more earnestly to ensure that discipline should flourish among them. Above all, he diligently urged abbots to watch over the safety and protection of their brothers.

Thus, as soon as he heard that John the abbot, through his own negligence, had stained and weakened the reputation of his monastery, he wrote to him in these words:

“Be entirely concerned for the souls of the brothers. It is already enough that the reputation of the monastery has been stained through your negligence. Do not go outside frequently. Appoint an agent for these matters, and devote yourself to reading and prayer … But among the very brothers of your monastery whom I see, I do not find them devoting themselves to reading. Consider, therefore, how great a sin it is that God has sent you sustenance from another person’s offering, while you neglect to learn the commandments of God” (Book III, Letter 3).

[Note: This is perhaps the John to whom Book V, Letter 50, is addressed.]

The most experienced guide of souls commanded sacred reading not only to clergy and monks, but also to laymen and those devoted to military service, as is clear from the letter written to Maurentius, master of the soldiers (Book VIII, Letter 17). Gregory praises him because, avoiding human gatherings, he devoted himself to reading the sacred books; but he grieves that he had no companion in this pious devotion to reading.

### 5.

From these words of Gregory to John—“Do not go outside frequently”—the author of the newly written French *Ecclesiastical Library* wrongly asserts that both abbots and monks were forbidden to go outside, whereas Gregory censures only frequent excursions into public life.

Saint Benedict, who wished his pupils to be devoted to the solitary life, clearly indicates in two chapters of his Rule—namely, chapters 51 and 67—that they were not forbidden to leave the monastery and attend to business.

Gregory himself not only employed abbots and monks in many ecclesiastical and even political affairs, as we shall often relate below, but also placed them in charge of such matters. In the previous year he had written to John of Ravenna (Book II, Letter 46) that Claudius, abbot of the monastery of Classis, should be sent to the city of Fano with a certain amount of money to redeem captives.

Later, when Queen Theodelinda had suspended herself from communion with Constantius, bishop of Milan, because he had condemned the Three Chapters, Gregory sent her John the abbot and Hippolytus the notary. They were to persuade the queen that the authority of the Council of Chalcedon had not been shaken by this condemnation, contrary to the claims of the schismatics, and to bring her back into communion with Constantius (Book IV, Letters 3 and 4).

He also made use of the monk Secundinus and the abbot Probus to establish peace with Agilulf, king of the Lombards; this succeeded happily (Book VI, Letter 30, and Book IX, Letters 4 and 43).

We do not think it necessary to mention here all the monks whom Saint Gregory sent to preach the Gospel; they will be discussed later.

Nevertheless, monks ought to embrace and pursue withdrawal and freedom from every business, by which the solitary life is chiefly commended, for as long as they are permitted to enjoy them. The example of Saint Gregory especially recommends this. Torn away from the quiet of the monastery and raised to the summit of the supreme pontificate, he issued almost as many cries as a child weaned from its mother’s breast as he produced writings.

### 6.

To speak briefly also of those who are outside and do not belong to the Church: the Jews, who had more than once experienced Gregory’s clemency, were restrained this year by his tireless concern and indefatigable zeal.

A certain man among them, the exceedingly wicked Nasas,

[Note: By this name one perhaps should understand the president or leader of the synagogue, whom the Jews call a *nasi*.]

had built an altar under the honor of blessed Elijah and had drawn many Christians there for the sake of prayer, deceiving them. The vigilant pontiff wrote to Libertinus, prefect of Sicily (Book III, Letter 38), where the crime had been committed and the superstition was flourishing, ordering him to punish this Jew most severely and physically, if the charge were established. He also warned him not to imitate the negligence—and the avarice, which was worse than negligence—of Justin, the praetor of that same island.

For Justin, won over by Jewish gifts, had not taken care to avenge insults against God, as Gregory had learned from letters written to him.

The same Jew was also said to have purchased Christian slaves for himself, which was contrary to the law enacted by Constantine the Great forbidding Christians to serve Jews. Since that same law had provided that if Jews possessed Christians in service or slavery, those Christians were immediately to be set free (Eusebius, Book IV of the *Life of Constantine*, chapter 27), the pope demanded that this provision be vigorously and promptly enforced.

The subject of another letter is nearly the same. It was written to Venantius, bishop of Luna, in the following year (Book IV, Letter 1).

### 7.

That Saint Gregory thought about composing the *Dialogues* in this third year of his pontificate is testified by the letter to Maximian, bishop of Syracuse. From that letter we may also sense that he devoted himself to writing them shortly afterward (Book III, Letter 51).

For the time at which they were written, however, read our preface in volume II, especially no. 17 and the following sections. Everything concerning these books should be taken from that preface.

I shall observe only this here: this excellent work was a fruit of the solitude for which Gregory often longed, so that he might be relieved from the troubles and anxieties of pastoral life and, by mourning the loss of his former quiet with pious tears, somehow repair what he had lost.

What he was like in retreat, and on what matters he then fixed his mind in meditation, learn from the very beginning of the *Dialogues*.

## CHAPTER XI

[Col. 0332D] **SUMMARY.—** 1. Disturbances in the Church of Salona because Maximus was ordained bishop against the pope’s wishes. — 2. Gregory’s steadfastness and patience in this matter. — 3. Maximus’s audacity toward the holy pontiff. — 4. The emperor supports Maximus’s ordination. — 5. Maximus’s repentance and satisfaction. — 6. What was decided concerning the archdeacon Honoratus. — 7. The empress Constantina requests the relics of Saint Paul and is refused. The ancient custom of not moving the bodies of saints from their places. — 8. Nevertheless, several translations were made in ancient times. (A.D. 593 and 594.)

### 1.

Gregory had scarcely tasted leisure and quiet for a short time in the peaceful retreat of the monastery when he had to return to the customary burdens of the pontificate and come to the aid of, and provide for, the Church of Salona and all Dalmatia (Book IV, Letter 10).

The bishops of this province, corrupted by the evil examples of their former metropolitan Natalis, whom we mentioned above, had departed from the path of priestly honor. Immersed in secular affairs, they had cast aside all fear of God; for a long time they had been accustomed to seek and fulfill not what pleased God but what pleased themselves.

Therefore, when Natalis died and Honoratus, the archdeacon—a man of blameless life and remarkable steadfastness, which he had shown more than once in opposing Natalis when he squandered the goods of the Church—had been elected bishop of Salona, those who greatly feared such a severe censor and teacher of morals were said to favor Maximus, who, relying on secular power, had invaded the see.

When Gregory learned this, he decided to write to all the bishops of Dalmatia, instructing them not to presume to ordain anyone bishop of Salona without first consulting and receiving the consent of the apostolic see. He declared that those who acted otherwise were excommunicated and excluded from participation in the body and blood of the Lord, and he pronounced that any future ordination would be invalid. Above all, he forbade them to lay hands on Maximus (same book, Letter 20).

Nevertheless, either because the papal order had not yet been received—which seems more likely—or because it had been disregarded, Maximus, as was reported to the pope, was led into the Church by military force after priests, deacons, and the entire clergy had been beaten. He was perhaps then consecrated bishop, if that can be called a consecration which was performed by excommunicated persons and conferred upon one who was himself excommunicated and devoted to curses.

At that time Antoninus was rector of the ecclesiastical patrimony in Dalmatia, serving as subdeacon (Book III, Letter 22). Since he had worked, at the command of the supreme pontiff, to ensure that the bishop of Salona would be elected according to the canons, he became hated by Maximus the transgressor and was hunted to the death by his followers; he was forced to save himself by flight (same book, Letter 47).

The chief author of the evil was Marcellus, proconsul of Dalmatia, as we learn from Book IX, Letter 5.

### 2.

To remove so great an offense from the Church of Salona, Gregory judged that prudence no less than steadfastness was necessary. He warned Maximus in a letter (Book IV, Letter 20) that neither he nor those who had ordained him should presume to exercise any priestly function until Gregory could investigate whether he had been ordained by a genuine or spurious imperial command, and could write back what he judged appropriate.

If Maximus did not fear doing anything contrary to the prohibition, Gregory threatened him with an anathema from God and from blessed Peter, prince of the apostles.

That Maximus had invaded the see of Salona already in the previous year—namely, toward the end of the eleventh indiction—is shown by what we read concerning his repentance in a fragment now relegated to the end of the letters but formerly placed before the letters of the first indiction.

Accordingly, it is clear that Letters 10 and 20 had not yet reached him or the bishops of Dalmatia. These letters were dated this year, the fourth year of Gregory’s pontificate, in the twelfth indiction, 243 as may also be inferred from Letter 20 itself. This may perhaps have been the reason why Gregory later dealt more mildly with Maximus and finally confirmed his ordination.

I am not unaware that Gregory was informed that, after the prohibition he had issued, Maximus had been brought forward by military force (same book), which must have occurred at the time of his ordination. Yet that bringing forward could also have taken place some time after the ordination.

Moreover, the pope had received many reports concerning this bishop and his corrupt morals that rested on no legitimate testimony. These reports were later disproved: for example, the claims that Maximus had used a surreptitious imperial document, that he had attained the episcopate through simony, and that he was guilty of violating chastity.

Why, then, should we not say that an uncertain or even false rumor reached the supreme pontiff—that Maximus had been ordained in contempt of his letters? Certainly, when Gregory later wrote to the empress Constantina, in the following year, as though he had learned the whole truth, he complained only that Maximus had been ordained without the knowledge of himself and his representative (Book V, Letter 21).

### 3.

What followed afterward Saint Gregory explains in his letter to Sabinian, the apocrisarius, or representative, of the apostolic see at the court of the emperor Maurice (Book IV, Letter 47).

Relying on secular and court authority, Maximus became so audacious that he had the pope’s letters publicly torn apart—those letters threatening him with excommunication unless he submitted and repented—and accused him before the emperor of having killed in custody the bishop Malchus, who owed him a considerable sum of money.

[Note: He had administered some property of the Roman Church in Dalmatia, as is clear from Book II, Letter 46.]

The most holy man dispelled this accusation in the following manner:

“Concerning this matter,” he said to Sabinian, “there is one thing you should briefly suggest to our most serene lords: if I, their servant, had wished to involve myself in the death of the Lombards, today the Lombard nation would have neither king, nor dukes, nor counts, but would be divided in the greatest confusion. But because I fear God, I dread involving myself in the death of any person.

“As for the bishop Malchus, he was neither in custody nor under any affliction. On the day when he pleaded his case and was condemned, he was taken, without my knowledge, by the notary Boniface to Boniface’s house.
