A meal was prepared for him there, and he ate; he was honored by Boniface, and during the night he suddenly died.”

Thus Maximus’s false accusation immediately vanished.

4. Nevertheless, Maurice upheld his ordination, probably at the instigation of the prefects and military commanders who were in charge of public affairs in Dalmatia; for Maximus was said, after stripping his own Church bare, to have offered them many rewards. Concerning this matter, Saint Gregory wrote vehemently to the empress Constantina:

“And if,” he says, “the cases of the bishops entrusted to me are settled before our most pious lords through the advocacy of others, what am I, unhappy man, doing in this Church? But that my bishops should despise me and have recourse against me to secular judges, I give thanks to almighty God and attribute it to my sins. Yet I briefly submit this: I am waiting for a little while; and if he delays coming to me for long, I shall by no means cease to exercise canonical discipline against him.”

[Note: He calls them those whom he governed by patriarchal right, and whose ordinations therefore belonged to him to some extent; for although he presided over all bishops and patriarchs, this was because of the unique primacy of the Roman Church.]

Maurice had ordered Maximus to present himself to the pope and Gregory to receive him with honor. This seemed burdensome to Gregory: what honor, after all, was due to a man about whom such grave and numerous reports were circulating, before he had been examined and proved himself innocent? Nor was there any longer a question about his ordination having been carried out without the knowledge of the Roman pontiff. To comply with the emperor, Gregory agreed to recognize it as valid, as though Maximus had been ordained bishop there with his authorization, even though under the preceding rulers no bishop of Salona had ever, down to that time, been appointed without the authority of the Roman bishop. Yet many charges still remained to be cleared away: that he had lived disgracefully and immorally; that he had been elected after paying money; and that, although excommunicated, he had presumed to celebrate Mass.

Maximus had acted craftily so that Gregory’s letter ordering him to cease celebrating Mass would not reach him. Therefore Gregory, repeating his command, forbade him to perform the sacred ministry. On this matter he wrote to the clergy and leading men both at Salona and at Jadera (Book VI, Letters 27 and 29), instructing them to withdraw from Maximus’s communion. Until then no one had rejected communion with him except Bishop Paulinus and the archdeacon Honoratus. The holy pontiff no longer defended Honoratus’s election, which we discussed above, since he calls him only an archdeacon, not a bishop.

[Col. 0335C] 5. At last, through paternal exhortations and unbroken perseverance, Gregory succeeded in bringing Maximus back to a sounder mind. Most people had already withdrawn from his communion; and Sabinianus, bishop of Jadera, moved by repentance because he had supported an usurper and rebel, had retired to a monastery after surrendering his episcopate, in order to wash away so great a fault with tears. Saint Gregory, however, received him back into his communion and friendship, urged him to resume his pastoral care, and hoped that he would provide the others with an example of returning to the Church (Book VII, Letter 17; Book VIII, Letter 10). Nor was his hope disappointed. Maximus himself eventually came to his senses and submitted to the yoke of the obedience he owed.

When the pope pressed him to come to Rome for judgment, Maximus could plead that the roads were occupied by enemies, as well as the emperor’s order that the matter should be settled at Salona or in Dalmatia—a provision that was also consistent with the sacred canons. Moreover, he could readily reply that the people and the prefects had obstructed his departure and journey by military force. After wisely weighing these considerations, and with the added entreaties of the exarch Callinicus, Gregory agreed that Maximus should purge himself at Ravenna before Marinianus, archbishop, and Castorius, chartulary of the holy Church, both of the simoniacal heresy and of the other charges brought against him, after taking an oath at the body of Saint Apollinaris the martyr (Book IX, Letters 79, 80, 81).

Since Maximus was manifestly guilty of disobedience and rebellion against the Apostolic See—for it was established that after the supreme pontiff had threatened him with excommunication, he had approached the sacred altar—Gregory left it to Marinianus’s judgment to determine by what satisfaction such a fault ought to be expiated. Perhaps on the advice and judgment of that bishop, Maximus lay prostrate for three hours, crying out in profound grief and repentance: “I have sinned against God and the most blessed Pope Gregory” (Appendix to the letters). Raised up by Marinianus, with the assistance of the exarch Callinicus and the chartulary Castorius, he began to mourn still more intensely. Then, as a sign of reconciliation and absolution, Castorius presented him with a letter written by Saint Gregory, in which Gregory announced that the grace of fraternal charity had been restored to him and promised to send him the pallium as soon as possible.

[Col. 0336B] 6. Since Sabinianus, bishop of Jadera, Honoratus, archdeacon of Salona, and many others had asserted the rights of the Apostolic See against Maximus, the most wise pontiff ordered that Maximus should receive them with the charity that was due to them (Book IX, Letter 125). Gregory wished Honoratus not to be removed from the office and dignity of archdeacon, concerning which there had already been controversy since the time of Archbishop Natalis. But the custom of that Church stood in the way: it required archdeacons, after completing five years, to withdraw from their ministry. Maximus asserted that this was held as law in the Church of Salona, and the chartulary Castorius confirmed it. He added that the three preceding archdeacons had been compelled by Honoratus himself to withdraw after they had served for five years. Gregory’s judgment, therefore, was that no judgment should be demanded from Honoratus concerning a matter that Gregory himself had already judged.

This was the outcome of the long dispute over Maximus’s ordination: in the end, the unbroken patience and perseverance of the holy pontiff prevailed, virtues that adversity habitually strengthens. He describes these qualities of mind most aptly in a letter to the deacon Sabinianus:

“I am more ready to die,” he says, “than to see the Church of blessed Peter degenerate during my lifetime. You know my character well, for I have borne things for a long time; but if I once decide not to bear them, I go gladly to meet every danger” (Book IV, Letter 47).

7. Throughout this entire affair Gregory found an opponent at the imperial court in John of Constantinople, as is reasonable to believe; for by rebuking and reproving him concerning his usurpation of the title “ecumenical patriarch,” he had made John hostile to him. Before treating this dispute more fully and explicitly, as will be done shortly, the order of events requires us to explain by what strategy John tried to alienate the mind of the empress Constantina from Gregory. The holy pontiff seems to point directly to him in these words:

“But certain men have wished to stir up your piety against me, so that—God forbid—they might deprive me of the favor of your will” (Book IV, Letter 30).

The most pious empress had arranged for a basilica to be built in honor of the Apostle Saint Paul within the palace of the imperial city. In order to enrich it with his sacred relics, she asked Gregory to hasten to send her either the head of the most blessed apostle or some other part of his body.

[Col. 0337A] Gregory replied to her command that he could neither comply nor dare to do so, since the bodies of the holy apostles could not be moved from their place, or even touched, with impunity; he confirms this by recalling many miracles that had occurred there. Constantina had also requested the apostle’s sudarium, by which name one should perhaps understand some linen cloth stained with his sacred blood and enclosed in the tomb. But since it could not be removed without uncovering and moving the apostle’s body—which was forbidden—he could not grant the pious empress’s request.

In the letter Gregory sent to her, he says:

“For it is not the custom of the Romans, when they give relics of the saints, to presume to touch anything from the body; rather, only a *brandeum* [that is, a covering] is placed in a small box and set beside the most holy bodies of the saints. When it is taken up, it is deposited with devout veneration in the church that is to be dedicated.”

He adds many things in those passages about the miracles customarily performed as though people had gained possession of the bodies of the saints. He further teaches that throughout all the regions of the West it would be wholly intolerable and sacrilegious if anyone should attempt to touch the bodies of the saints. Would that we had preserved forever this pious custom, so consonant with the veneration of the relics of the saints.

The contrary custom of the Greeks might be brought forward: among them there was evidently no religious scruple against raising sacred bodies and transferring them elsewhere. Saint Gregory replied that the relics they transferred and distributed appeared to him of doubtful authenticity, and he confirms his suspicion with this example. Some Greek monks had been caught in Rome two years earlier, silently digging up during the night the bodies of the dead that lay in a field beside the Church of Saint Paul and concealing their bones. When they were asked why they did this, they confessed that they intended to carry those bones to Greece as relics of saints.

In Gregory of Tours and other writers one frequently encounters such frauds—not pious ones, as they are commonly called, but sacrilegious—which have rendered doubtful many relics that were otherwise genuine.

[Note: See Guibert of Nogent, Book on the Relics of the Saints.]

It is therefore clear that no greater or more certain honor can be secured for the saints than by leaving their sacred remains intact and untouched in their original tombs—which nevertheless ought to be adorned. This is also provided for by civil laws.

[Note: Read the final law on the violation of tombs; it is a law of Theodosius the Great from the year 386.]

8. Nevertheless, let us not condemn all translations of the saints’ relics that were carried out for pious reasons.

[Note: Consult Tillemont, under Constantius, article 4, p. 415. Jerome says that this translation took place in the twentieth year of Constantine the Great.]

In the time of the Emperor Constantius, we read that the body of Saint Timothy, previously buried at Ephesus, was brought to Constantinople and placed in the basilica of the holy apostles. Shortly afterward the relics of the Apostle Saint Andrew and of the Evangelist Luke were also brought from Achaea and deposited in the same place. Jerome reports and praises this practice (Jerome, *Against Vigilantius*).

Read in Mabillon (Preface to volume II of the *Acts of the Saints*, Observation 8) about the many translations of saints’ relics carried out in the West during the fourth and fifth centuries, including in Italy itself—translations of which Gregory could certainly not have been ignorant. On these matters also consult the notes to Letter 30 of Book IV. Yet in these translations the sacred remains were taken from their tombs so that they might rest in some more suitable place; they were not carried far away.

Saint Gregory did not disapprove of the bishop and clergy of the city of Euria taking the body of Saint Donatus with them when they migrated and depositing it at the Castle of Cassiopus on the island of Corcyra (Book XIV, Letters 7 and 13). In that case, however, the migration had been made necessary by the barbarian sword and hostile incursions. The priests and clergy of that city therefore feared that the sacred relics of Saint Donatus might suffer some injury from the barbarians in an abandoned and exposed church, and preferred to carry them away with them.

[Col. 0338B] What we have said concerning Saint Gregory’s view that the bodies of the saints should not be moved from their places must not be understood of their clothing or of other objects belonging to the saints. For when he had received from Abbot John a tunic discovered to be that of Saint John, he asked him to arrange for it to be sent to him. John the Deacon teaches that this tunic was that of Saint John the Apostle and Evangelist and had been placed in Rome in the Constantinian basilica (Book III, nos. 57, 58, 59); he says that it shone with many miracles.

We do not know whether this reply from the pope satisfied the Empress Constantina. Many letters of the holy pontiff written to her afterward nevertheless survive, and from them it is clear that she did not take offense at being denied the relics of Saint Paul, but always burned with pious devotion toward the Apostolic See.

CAPUT XII.

ARGUMENT.—1. Theodelinda hostile to Constantius, bishop of Milan, because of the Three Chapters.—2. Gregory sends legates and letters to her.—3. The outcome.—4. He devotes himself to converting idolaters.—5. The negligence of Januarius and the other bishops of Sardinia.—6. Permission granted to Sardinian priests to administer chrism.—7. Matters undertaken by Saint Gregory this year for the benefit of monks.—8. He bars women from entering monasteries.—9. He provides for the honor and peace of nuns.—10. He rules concerning the age of abbesses.—11. His decree concerning clerics as abbots explained. (Years 593 and 594.)

1. At approximately the same time Saint Gregory was compelled to write to Theodelinda, queen of the Lombards, in order to restore her hostility toward Constantius, bishop of Milan, to peace and harmony (Book III, Letters 29, 30, 31).

After Laurentius, bishop of Milan, had died in the preceding year, Constantius, a deacon of that same Church, had been appointed as his successor by the unanimous consent of the entire clergy. Gregory had long known him well, and Constantius had also remained with him for a long period while Gregory was living in Constantinople.

Although Gregory had found nothing in Constantius’s character that could be criticized, he had nevertheless long since resolved that he would not become involved on anyone’s behalf in promoting a person to undertake the burdens of pastoral care. He had therefore completely abstained from advancing Constantius’s election, content to commend him to God only in his prayers. He prayed continually that the supreme Shepherd would provide the people of Milan with such a pastor that they might find the pastures of divine exhortation in his speech and conduct; that humility and uprightness might shine together in his mind, as might severity and compassion; and that he might show them the way of life not only by speaking but also by living, so that by his example they might learn to sigh with longing for their eternal homeland.

Thus, whenever the most wise pontiff claimed for himself the right to make certain episcopal appointments, he withdrew from his earlier policy only when compelled by the gravest reasons. Ordinarily he was satisfied to preserve the ancient custom of sending someone from the Roman Church—the term refers to clerics serving and laboring in the Church—to attend the election and arrange for the candidate to be consecrated by the provincial bishops, though with the consent of the supreme pontiff.

At the very beginning of his episcopate, Constantius submitted his confession of faith to the pope, as was customary. Three bishops publicly circulated the claim that this confession condemned the Three Chapters and injured and assailed the authority of the Council of Chalcedon. Deceived by their evil arts, Theodelinda, queen of the Lombards, immediately turned against Constantius as a deserter of the orthodox faith. Letter 39 of the same book indicates without ambiguity that the bishop of Brescia was one of those three schismatic prelates. From it we learn that he and the citizens of Brescia insistently demanded that Constantius affirm under oath that he had not condemned the Three Chapters. (See Book IV, Letters 2 and 4.)

2. When Gregory heard this, he sent to Theodelinda Hippolytus the notary and John the abbot, so that he might assist both parties: the archbishop who had suffered the calumny and the queen, who was endangering her salvation by rejecting his communion. He also tried to accomplish this through his letters (Book IV, Letter 4).

Constantius did not think that Gregory’s first letter should be presented to the queen, because it mentioned events that had taken place under the Emperor Justinian and referred to the Fifth Synod, matters that might have offended her. Gregory therefore sent a second letter in which, accommodating Constantius’s advice, he said nothing about that synod and praised only the first four, especially the Council of Chalcedon, whose authority the schismatics claimed would be diminished by the condemnation of the Three Chapters.

With this scruple removed, the most holy pontiff exhorts the most pious queen not to believe ignorant and foolish men, and to beware of separating herself from communion with the Catholic Church, lest all her tears and so many good works perish if she were found to be alienated from the true faith.

“It is fitting, therefore,” he says, “that Your Glory should with all speed send word to my most reverend brother and fellow bishop Constantius, whose faith and life were long ago well approved by me, and should inform him by letters sent to him that you have kindly received his ordination and that you are in no respect separated from communion with his Church.”

3. The most prudent and Christian queen returned to unity with the Church, although she could not be induced to condemn the Three Chapters—or, if this was eventually obtained from her, it happened only later. The schism that arose on the occasion of the condemnation of those chapters, however, did not consist in abstaining from condemning them, but in withdrawing from communion with those who condemned them.

Gregory always regarded as true sons of the Church those who, although they feared to reject the Three Chapters, nevertheless remained within the unity of the Church and he always dealt with them more gently. Among these, besides Theodelinda, was Secundinus, a monk of outstanding holiness who was especially dear to the queen.

When the queen returned to communion with Constantius, the three bishops of whom we have spoken apparently became quiet. It may also be inferred that the citizens of Brescia no longer harassed Constantius by demanding that he swear he had never condemned the Three Chapters, since in the many letters subsequently written to him the holy pontiff says nothing at all about the matter.

4. He labored with no less effort and zeal to call unbelievers to the Church than to bring back schismatics. A people called the Barbaricini inhabited part of Sardinia, and until that time they had retained the worship of idols. It is inferred, rather than established by certain arguments, that they had migrated to Sardinia after being driven from Africa by the Vandals.

Gregory describes the customs of those barbarians in these words:

“They live like senseless animals; they do not know the true God, but worship wood and stones” (Book IV, Letters 23 and 24).

It was therefore difficult to draw them to the true faith. Nevertheless, the most holy pope undertook the task, for nothing was difficult to his charity. For this work he chose a certain Bishop Felix and Cyriacus, a servant of God and abbot of Saint Andrew’s.

From them he later learned that almost all the peasants in Sardinia, not only the Barbaricini, were devoted to idolatry (ibid., Letter 25). He therefore immediately wrote to the nobles and to the other landowners in Sardinia, urging them to watch over the peasants in order to turn them away and withdraw them from the worship of idols. He indicated that nothing could be reported to him that would be more welcome or pleasing than how many idolaters each person had led to Christ.

The duke of Sardinia, Zabarda, worked vigorously at this task. Felix and Cyriacus had written to Gregory that he was arranging peace with the Barbaricini on the condition that they embrace the faith and service of Christ (ibid., Letter 24). The most holy pontiff therefore thanked the most pious duke for this and commended the preachers whom he had sent.

That Hospiton, duke of the Barbaricini, had by then become a Christian is clear from the letter written to him (ibid., Letter 23). Gregory praised him for having embraced the true faith, but admonished him that the true faith must be demonstrated by good works. He further reminded him that it was his duty to bring to Christ as many of his subjects as he could and to support with the necessary assistance the preachers laboring for their conversion.

It is not sufficiently clear how much success these efforts achieved at that time. From another letter written much later (Book XI, Letter 22), it is evident that many barbarians in Sardinia had still not abandoned idolatry. Nevertheless, Gregory writes to the governor of the island that they were hastening to embrace the Christian faith.

At the same time he ordered Vitalis, the defender in Sardinia, to purchase Barbaricini slaves (Book IX, Letter 23). Was this so that he might educate them in the faith and afterward employ them to instruct their fellow countrymen in Christianity? We certainly read that, with the same purpose, English boys between seventeen and eighteen years of age were purchased through Gregory’s care and generosity and placed in monasteries so that they might be instructed in the Christian religion (Book VI, Letter 7). He later used their ministry for the conversion of the entire English people, as will be related below.

5. Gregory therefore assigned Felix and Cyriacus the task of announcing the Gospel to the barbarians and peasants in Sardinia because the bishops of that island appeared to be little concerned for their salvation. In these words he rebukes the negligence and sluggishness of Januarius, bishop of Cagliari and metropolitan of the entire island:

“Another matter has occurred that is greatly to be lamented: the peasants belonging to your Church have until now been permitted, through the negligence of your fraternity, to remain in unbelief. Why should I urge you to bring outsiders to God when you neglect to correct your own people from unbelief? Therefore you must keep watch in every way over their conversion. For if I should find a pagan peasant belonging to any bishop in the island of Sardinia, I shall punish that bishop severely” (Book IV, Letter 26).

6. Januarius’s ministers and clerics looked down on him because he was excessively simple-minded; hence neglect and laxity in ecclesiastical discipline arose. This perhaps gave the priests an opportunity to presume to mark children on the forehead with sacred chrism, a practice that Gregory prohibited from continuing (Book IV, Letter 9).

Later, however, he learned that certain people had been deeply offended by this prohibition, and he issued another decree in these words:

“It has also come to our attention that some have been scandalized because we prohibited priests from touching with chrism those who are to be baptized. We acted according to the ancient custom of our Church. But if some are altogether distressed by this matter, we grant that, where bishops are absent, priests too may touch those being baptized on the forehead with chrism” (ibid., Letter 26).

Theologians dispute the meaning of this decree. Some maintain that priests were thereby permitted to administer the sacrament of confirmation; others deny it. We have sufficiently explained our view of this question and controversy in the notes to the letters mentioned above. Let the diligent reader consult them without reluctance.

7. Turning now to monastic matters, which were always close to Gregory’s heart, what is read concerning his generosity toward the monastery at Subiaco, formerly founded by Saint Benedict, and toward Abbot Honoratus appears to belong to the fourth year of his pontificate: namely, that he and his mother Silvia bestowed on that monastery the Castle of Apollonius and many other properties (Mabillon, *Benedictine Annals*, Book VIII, no. 44, p. 231).

Nor should we pass over what happened this year: the admission of monks into the Church of Saint Pancratius, which still exists in Rome on the Via Aurelia. Secular clerics and priests had previously served there and cared for the sacred rites, but so negligently that not even on Sunday was there a priest present to celebrate the solemn Mass.

When the people who gathered there for devotion began to complain about this, Gregory, after mature deliberation, judged that those negligent clerics should be removed and that a community of monks should be established in the monastery adjoining the church. He appointed Maurus as its abbot (Book IV, Letter 18).

The letter to Maurus concerning this matter should be read. In it Gregory entrusts him with the entire administration of the lands, revenues, and offerings of that church, both for the support of the monks and for repairs and maintenance. Mabillon observes here that it can sometimes contribute to the edification of the faithful for monks to be established in heavily frequented places. (Compare Mabillon, cited work, under the year 594.)

[Col. 0342B] 8. Elsewhere, however, the most vigilant father carefully guarded against the regular discipline of the monks being weakened through association with women.

[Note: See Book XI, Letter 25, formerly Letter 20 of Book IX.]

He therefore rebukes Abbot Valentinus for allowing women to enter his monastery and to become the monks’ “co-mothers” (*commatres*), and forbids this from happening again under threat of the severest punishment (Book IV, Letter 42).

Whether Gregory judged that women should be barred from entering the churches of monasteries where the monks observed their rule and celebrated the sacred praises, and whether he established this by his command to Valentinus, is not known with certainty. In Letter 41 of Book II, he seems merely to forbid women more frequent access to the churches of monasteries.

Moreover, people of both sexes frequented the basilica of Saint Pancratius the martyr. For their benefit Gregory decreed that the solemn Mass should be celebrated there every Sunday; nevertheless, he preferred that monks, rather than clerics, should serve there.

9. Since he believed that, because of their more fragile sex, nuns required greater care and stricter protection, he wrote the following to Januarius of Cagliari at approximately the beginning of this year:

“It has come to our attention that you are providing too little protection for the monasteries of the servants of God situated in Sardinia. Although your prudent predecessors had arranged that certain tested men from the clergy should take care of their needs, matters have now been so completely neglected that consecrated women are themselves compelled to travel about through public officials for the sake of taxes and other obligations, and must go through villages and estates to meet fiscal demands, improperly involving themselves in affairs belonging to men.

“Let your fraternity remove this evil by an easy correction. Carefully appoint one tested man, whose life and conduct, age and position give no occasion for evil suspicion, who can assist those monasteries with the fear of God. Thus they will no longer be permitted, for any private or public business, to wander outside their venerable places contrary to the rule; rather, whatever must be done on their behalf shall reasonably be carried out through the man whom you appoint.

“Let the women themselves, offering praises to God and exercising self-restraint in their monasteries, no longer give the minds of the faithful any occasion for evil suspicion” (Book IV, Letter 9).

10. The same concern of the most holy pope for nuns is also reflected in what he established in a letter to Maximianus, bishop of Syracuse:

“We most earnestly prohibit young women from becoming abbesses” (Book IV, Letter 11).

He adds that no virgins are to be veiled and blessed by bishops as abbesses unless they are sixty years old and their age and conduct make this appropriate.

[Note: Consult note l on this passage of the cited letter.]

It may perhaps seem surprising that Gregory required such maturity of age in abbesses. Elsewhere, however, he teaches that those who are still enduring the struggles against assaulting vices—a condition that often occurs in youth and adulthood—ought not to take charge of others. Once the vices have been subdued, even young people may, in the judgment of bishops and prelates, be appointed blameless teachers of conduct and placed over others.

Thus Saint Gregory did not at all disapprove of the blessed Benedict’s having, while still young, after overcoming the temptation of the flesh and extinguishing every sense of pleasure through the thorns, presided over many disciples as a teacher of virtue. (See *Moralia*, Book XXIII, no. 21, and *Dialogues*, Book II, chapter 2.)

11. In the same letter in which Gregory issued these provisions concerning abbesses, he prescribed something concerning abbots that deserves attention:

“Do not permit priests, deacons, or clerics of any other order who serve in churches to be abbots in monasteries. Either, having laid aside their clerical service, let them advance into the monastic orders, or, if they decide to remain in the position of abbot, let them in no way be permitted to retain the service of the clergy. For it is most incongruous that someone who cannot diligently fulfill one of these offices because of its importance should be judged capable of fulfilling both. In this way the ecclesiastical order of life would hinder monastic life, and the monastic rule would likewise hinder ecclesiastical interests.”

From this passage some have attempted to prove that Saint Gregory wished to deter and prohibit clerics from embracing the monastic profession. But this is contrary to his intention, since elsewhere he urges Bishop Desiderius not to impede Pancratius, a deacon of his Church who desired the grace of the monastic life, but rather to inflame him by pastoral exhortation so that the fervor of this desire would not grow cold in him (Book XII, Letter 39).

Moreover, the most holy doctor greatly praises and commends the rule of the blessed Benedict. In chapter 60 of that rule, priests who ask to be received into a monastery are to be admitted on the condition that they promise to observe the entire discipline of the rule. Hence the fathers of the Fourth Council of Toledo

[Note: According to Loaisa, or canon 49.]

establish in canon 50 that bishops should grant free entry into monasteries to clerics who desire the monastic way of life because they wish to follow a better life.

The most wise pope therefore guards in the cited letter against priests, deacons, or other clerics becoming and being ordained abbots in monasteries unless this occurs after legitimate probation and prolonged exercise in monastic life, with their clerical service first laid aside (Book I, Letter 42)—that is, after abandoning the ecclesiastical title to which they had been bound by their ordination and, as Gregory sometimes puts it, into which they had been incardinated.

For the same reason he elsewhere forbids those who have exchanged clerical service for the monastic life to return again at will to their former Church. It should be noted in passing that the holy pope grants clerics permission to embrace the monastic life in these words:

“If, however, some should on any occasion happen to pass from the clergy into the monastic life, etc.”

Some also wrongly suppose that, in the words of Gregory cited above (from Letter 11 of Book IV), monks and abbots were forbidden to be ordained priests or enrolled in the clerical service, on the grounds that the ecclesiastical order obstructs monastic life and, conversely, the monastic rule obstructs ecclesiastical interests.

But Gregory himself prevents us from interpreting him in this way, since he repeatedly judged and ordered that monks should be honored with the priesthood. See Letter 42 of Book VI, in which he urges Victor, bishop of Palermo, to ordain without delay one of the monks of Saint Hermes as a priest, at the request of Abbot Urbicus, whom we also read was honored with the priesthood.

No scruple about this matter will remain for anyone who reads note e to the letter, from which the opportunity for such caviling was taken. (Compare Mabillon under the year 594, p. 233.)

The purpose, therefore, of this most vigilant shepherd in that passage is to exclude from monastic leadership clerics who are now called secular, already attached to the titles of other churches, in keeping with the custom of those times. He intended this both because clerical and monastic service could not be joined in different churches, and especially because he foresaw that the ambition and lax way of life of those clerics who coveted monastic dignities would destroy the monasteries—as indeed later happened:

“While these men,” says the holy man, almost prophetically, “pretend to live religiously, they seek to be placed over monasteries, and through their way of life the monasteries are destroyed” (Book V, Letter 1).

By these words he also indicates that he had already learned this through experience.

BOOK THREE, Containing the history of the pontificate of Saint Gregory from the years 594 and 595 to the years 598 and 599, or from Indiction 13 to Indiction 2.

[Col. 0343]

248 CHAPTER ONE.

[Col. 0343D]

ARGUMENT.—1. The title “ecumenical” assumed by the Patriarch of Constantinople.—2. Which councils were called ecumenical.—3. The pope rejects this title when it is offered.—4. The meaning of this expression.—5. Saint Gregory’s zeal in suppressing this title defended.—6. By what stages the ambition of the Patriarch of Constantinople rose.—7. How great it was in John.—8. Whether he became patriarch from being a monk.—9. Saint Gregory’s letters concerning that controversy examined: the first written to Maurice, and the letter to the empress.—10. He writes to the patriarchs.—11. What answer came from Eulogius of Alexandria.—12. And from Anastasius of Antioch.—13. On the interpolated letters of Saint Ignatius.—14. Summary of the letter written to John of Constantinople.—15. The holy pope’s efforts against John and his successor prove fruitless.—16. The end of the controversy.—17. Heretics who object Saint Gregory’s modesty to his successors are refuted. (Years 594 and 595.)

1. We begin this book with the controversy that broke out between Gregory and John, patriarch of Constantinople, on account of the proud title “ecumenical patriarch,” assumed by John and, through Maurice’s support of this unjust usurpation, asserted and maintained, while the other patriarchs pretended not to notice the insult inflicted upon them by this offensive designation.

Although the insolence of this expression had aroused disturbances and the gravest offense long before Gregory’s pontificate, the most prudent pontiff did not seriously consider eliminating it until this year, for he customarily undertook nothing without mature deliberation.

2. As regards the title “ecumenical” itself, it is clear that general councils had attributed it to themselves long before this. Father Gussanville nevertheless reports that, before the Council of Chalcedon, no other council had been honored with this title (in his notes on Book IV, Letter 32), and that the legates of Pope St. Leo were responsible for introducing it. But anyone who reads the Council of Ephesus attentively will admit that this escaped him while he was heedlessly occupied with something else. For in Part II, Action 3, we find: “Copy of the Letter, etc., the holy, great, and ecumenical council.” In Action 4, in the letter of Cyril and Memnon to the council: “Against the presidents of this ecumenical council.” In the council’s report: “To the most devout and most Christian Theodosius, etc., the sacred ecumenical council.” In the report concerning the subscriptions: “To the most devout, etc., the holy and ecumenical council.” Nevertheless, Louis Maimbourg followed Gussanville, despite his grave error, in Book II of his *History of Pope St. Gregory the Great*.

3. St. Gregory testifies that the title “ecumenical” was offered to the Roman pontiff—namely, St. Leo the Great—as an honor belonging to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, by the venerable Council of Chalcedon. “Yet,” he says, “none of them ever assumed or consented to use this singular title” (Book V, Letter 20). Certainly, at the Council of Chalcedon several supplicatory petitions addressed to the pope were read, in which he was distinguished by this honorific title. In the sixth Action, moreover, Bishop Paschasinus, one of St. Leo’s legates, addressing the holy council, called the supreme pontiff “ecumenical.” Since the Fathers of the council did not object to these expressions, they appeared to approve and ratify them—especially since the proceedings were entered into the council’s records.

4. As regards the meaning of this word, “ecumenical” is the same as “universal.” An ecumenical council is one summoned and assembled from all the inhabited regions of the world to which we believe the Christian religion has reached. Although bishops, or their legates, may perhaps not have come to such councils from every part of the Christian world, a synod that was not universal when it was summoned and assembled has sometimes become general and ecumenical afterward, namely, when the subsequent consent of all the orthodox was added.

If, from this meaning, we determine what an ecumenical bishop or patriarch would be, it will immediately become clear what a monstrosity such a bishop would be within the Christian religion. For no bishop can properly become universal unless all the other bishops are excluded. Indeed, if one person were bishop of the entire Christian world, what place would remain for another? This plainly contradicts Sacred Scripture, which teaches us clearly that the Holy Spirit appointed not one but several bishops to govern the Church of God (Acts 20). Christ’s flock is indeed one, but it has several shepherds, each of whom has undertaken to feed and govern one portion of that flock.

[Col. 0346B] 5. I do not deny that, in a certain sense not departing from the rule of faith, Roman pontiffs could have been called ecumenical, on account of the singular jurisdiction they possess throughout the whole Church, to which individual bishops are also subject. But when they themselves wished modestly to abstain from that title, with what face did the bishops of Constantinople dare to claim it for themselves? As though they could exercise any episcopal authority beyond the boundaries of their own patriarchate, or as though the patriarchate of Constantinople could sensibly be understood and taken as comprising the whole Christian world! I therefore cannot sufficiently wonder at certain writers who, although professing the orthodox faith, have disparaged, or even openly condemned, Gregory the Great’s efforts to oppose this proud title—as though he had fought with excessive vehemence over a mere name and not over a matter of grave importance. I readily concede to them that some innocent senses could have been attached and accommodated to this word and title. But when it is subject to many more harmful meanings alien to the faith, and these are the obvious ones, whereas the sound meanings appear to have been imported from elsewhere, who would dare rashly to condemn so great a pontiff for taking care to suppress a new and insolent expression utterly foreign to episcopal modesty?

Our critics say that “ecumenical” has the same meaning as “general,” a title granted to so many prefects—military, civil and political, and even ecclesiastical and monastic. But “ecumenical” has a much broader meaning. The ministers or prefects cited as examples are called “generals” in order to distinguish them from particular officials, whose authority is lesser. Yet in this sense the patriarchs of Constantinople could by no means be called general. I ask: who were those particular patriarchs from whom they were to be distinguished by this title?

Moreover, since it was uncertain in what sense they boasted of being ecumenical, there was reason to fear that their well-known ambition would adopt the broader meaning—that is, the worst and heretical one. Who, then, in his right mind would fault the holy man for attempting, while himself cultivating humility in the Church’s most eminent and highest dignity, to urge and recall proud bishops to that virtue which Christ chiefly wished us to learn from him?

6. Here it is worthwhile to observe by what stages the bishop of Constantinople rose to such a pinnacle of dignity that he was regarded as inferior to no one except the Roman pontiff. At first, therefore, he was subject to the bishop of Heraclea; afterward he exercised metropolitan and exarchal rights over Heraclea and many other bishops. He was then numbered among the ancient patriarchs. Not long afterward, supported by the emperors’ power, and with bishops—and even patriarchs—being compelled to consent, since they depended upon his influence and favor with the emperors in various affairs of their churches, he obtained at the second general Council of Constantinople and at Chalcedon the privilege of sitting second after the Roman pontiff. St. Leo opposed this, however, and rejected the canon promulgated at Chalcedon on this matter as spurious and fraudulently added after the council had already concluded.

Nor could the ambition of this prelate, established in his see in the royal city called New Rome and excessively flattering and exalting itself, stop and rest at this rank. John III, Epiphanius, Mennas—who was often called “ecumenical patriarch” by the Constantinopolitan synod held under him—and other bishops of that city thereafter either assumed the title “ecumenical” spontaneously or accepted and retained it with both hands when flatterers offered it to them. They would perhaps have claimed universal authority over the entire Christian world and even over the Roman Church itself, had the Roman pontiffs not resisted their ever-growing pride.

7. Of all the bishops of Constantinople, none appears to have sought the designation “ecumenical” with such eagerness as John, surnamed the Faster. For this reason, although another purpose was pretended, he held a synod of the entire East at Constantinople, as several writers, especially St. Gregory, inform us. “As soon as my predecessor Pelagius recognized this,” Gregory says, “he annulled the acts of that synod by letters sent under the authority of the Apostle St. Peter.”

[Note: [Col. 0347D] Except, however, for what had been done at this synod concerning Gregory of Antioch, who had been acquitted and restored, as is clear from Book IX, Letter 68.]

“I have taken care to send copies of those letters to Your Holiness. But he forbade the deacon who, according to custom, remained at the feet of the most devout lords in order to deliver the Church’s replies, to celebrate the solemn Mass with our aforementioned fellow priest” (Book V, Letter 43).

This is Gregory’s account. After he had been appointed Pelagius’s successor, he asked John through his legate Sabinianus to abstain from this title. But having gained nothing by these requests, he tried other remedies.

8. Before discussing the letters written by the holy pontiff on this matter, we must investigate who John the Faster was. It is commonly held that he was a monk. This opinion rests both on the testimony of John the Deacon (Book III, chapter 51) and on the inscription of a certain sermon on penance attributed to him, whose title gives the name “John the Monk, Patriarch of Constantinople, surnamed the Faster.” It is also added that he arranged the Liturgy attributed to Chrysostom in a better order and that in it he designated himself by the name *hieromonazontos* (ἱερομονάζοντος), “sacred monk” or “priest-monk.” But the prayer in which this word occurs is absent from the Liturgy of St. Chrysostom as presented by the most learned James Goar. Nor is it established that this Liturgy was arranged through the efforts of John the Faster.

There were, however, many bishops of Constantinople who, having previously embraced the monastic life, could have been called *hieromonazontes* (ἱερομονάζοντες), or sacred monks. According to the Greek *Menaia*, John the Faster was born at Constantinople,

[Note: [Col. 0348D] St. Isidore nevertheless teaches in *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 26, that he was a Cappadocian.]

where he first practiced the art of statuary—more correctly, *charaktēs* (χαράκτης), the sculptor’s art. But because of his outstanding virtues, he was enrolled in the clergy by the patriarch of that city and made a deacon. Finally, after Eutychius died, he was compelled, against his will, to assume the patriarchal dignity, which he adorned with remarkable abstinence, generous almsgiving, and other pious works. Whether the sanctity of his life was genuine, as the Greeks maintain, or affected, as most Latins prefer to believe, since he appears to have lacked humility, the foundation of all the virtues—this sanctity, or appearance of sanctity, contributed considerably to winning him the favor of the emperor Maurice, whom St. Gregory found most hostile throughout the entire controversy over the title “ecumenical.”

9. In the first letter he wrote on this subject, Gregory complained to the emperor Maurice about John’s pride, by which peace among the bishops had been disturbed and shaken, and by which, he said, the swords of the barbarians were being sharpened against the empire. He depicts him remarkably in these words:

“Our bones are worn down by fasts, yet our minds swell with pride. Our bodies are covered with neglected garments, yet in the exaltation of our hearts we surpass the purple. We lie in ashes, yet we despise lofty things. Teachers of the humble, leaders of the proud, we conceal wolfish teeth beneath a sheep’s face.”

And speaking of the same man still more plainly below:

“He, therefore, must be bent more firmly by the commands of the most devout lords who scorns to render obedience to canonical precepts. He must be restrained who inflicts injury upon the holy universal Church, who swells in his heart, who desires to rejoice in the name of singularity, who by a private title sets himself above even the honor of your empire” (Book V, Letter 20).

He contrasts John’s arrogance with the modesty of the prince of the apostles, who, although he had received from Christ the care of the whole Church, never wished to be called “universal apostle.” The Roman pontiffs, heirs to his dignity, followed his example. Then Gregory cries out:

“O times! O morals! Behold, everything in the regions of Europe has been handed over to barbarian rule; cities have been destroyed, fortresses overthrown, provinces devastated, and no cultivator inhabits the land. Idolaters rage daily and rule over the death of the faithful. Yet the priests, who ought to lie weeping on the pavement and in ashes, seek for themselves names of vanity and glory in new and profane titles.”

Finally, he attacks this title with many arguments, especially those drawn from the perverse meaning underlying it. The principal arguments with which he presses John, both in this letter and in others, are these: the new title “ecumenical” is contrary to Christian humility, which ought to shine more brightly in bishops; it disturbs charity, divides unity, and strips the other bishops of their dignity, making only one bishop—so that when he falls, the whole Church falls. And since we read that many bishops of Constantinople fell into heresy, it would follow that the Church had more often departed from the true faith. Finally, the Roman pontiffs rejected this title when it was voluntarily offered to them.

The emperor had urged the pope to deal peacefully with John. Gregory replied:

“Let the author of the scandal return to a right way of life, and all quarrels among the priests will cease. For I am the servant of all priests insofar as they live priestly lives. But when anyone raises his neck against Almighty God through the swelling of empty glory and against the decrees of the Fathers, I trust in Almighty God that he will not bend mine to himself, even with swords.”

The letter written to the empress Constantina contains nearly the same argument (ibid., Letter 21). Gregory nevertheless attacks John more vehemently, saying that his immeasurable pride foretold the approaching times of Antichrist. For John imitated him who, scorning the legions of angels in their shared joy, attempted to burst forth to the summit of singularity, saying: “Above the stars of heaven I will exalt my throne” (Isaiah 14:13).

10. Since the honor of all bishops, and especially of the patriarchs, was being assaulted by this usurpation, St. Gregory wrote a joint letter to Eulogius, patriarch of Alexandria, and Anastasius, patriarch of Antioch (ibid., Letter 43). He attached to it all the documents of the dispute, together with copies of the letters written to John both by Pelagius II and by himself, so that they might understand that the highest dignity of the episcopate, and therefore of the entire Church, was at stake in this controversy.

He then urged them never to call anyone “universal bishop” in their letters, lest they detract from what is owed to themselves while offering another an honor that is not owed. But since love of peace and unity might prevent them from resisting John, he explained how peace ought to be preserved, citing the Apostle: “If it be possible, as much as depends on you, live at peace with all men” (Romans 12:18).

“For he saw,” Gregory says, “that the good cannot have peace with the wicked; and therefore, as you know, he prefaced the words, ‘if it be possible’ . . . . We truly maintain peace when, with charity and justice together, we pursue the faults of the proud; when we love them but hate their vices.”

With this disposition, he said, war must be declared against John’s pride, and they must contend to defend the honor of their Churches, which that pride had destroyed:

“Stand firm; stand secure. With the falsehood of the universal title, never dare either to give or to receive written communications . . . . If any adversity follows, by persevering unanimously, even in death, we must show that, in condemning the title of generality, we do not love anything of our own in particular.”

[Col. 0350A] 11. Gregory waited a long time for Eulogius’s reply and complained to him as a friend about the delay in another letter, in which he recalled that the blessed evangelist Mark had been sent to Alexandria by the Apostle St. Peter, his teacher (Book VI, Letter 60). From this he inferred that the Alexandrian Church was more closely bound to the Roman Church.

Eulogius eventually replied to the pope that, as he had been ordered, he had refrained, in writing to John, from proud titles, which had sprung from the root of vanity, and that he would no longer use them. But these words wounded Gregory’s profound modesty: “As you commanded.” “I ask,” he says, “that the word ‘command’ be removed from my hearing, because I know who I am and who you are. In place, you are my brothers; in conduct, my fathers” (Book VIII, Letter 30).

He was even more distressed that Eulogius had called him “universal pope” in the address of the letter.

“Let words that inflate vanity and wound charity depart,” he says (ibid.).

12. As for Anastasius, the devout man did not approve of the great controversy that had been stirred up over the title “ecumenical,” as is evident from another letter written to him. Gregory’s remarkable modesty and humility nevertheless shone forth in his reception of this frank admonition from a friend—almost, I might say, a rebuke. He begins the letter, replying to Anastasius’s warning, in these charity-filled words:

“I received the desired letter of Your Most Sweet Holiness, brought by our common son, the deacon Sabinianus. In it, the words were those not of the tongue but of the soul. Nor is it surprising that one who lives perfectly speaks well” (Book VII, Letter 27).

[Col. 0350C] Although he never ceased attacking the word “ecumenical,” since he considered it profane and injurious to all bishops, he nevertheless did not withdraw from communion with the patriarch of Constantinople. After John died, he received the synodical letter of his successor Cyriacus, in which Cyriacus had introduced himself as “ecumenical patriarch,” so that he would not sever the unity of the Church.

It is not difficult to discern why Anastasius thought this title should be tolerated patiently. For shortly before, when Gregory of Antioch, the patriarch, had died, Anastasius had been recalled from exile and restored to his former see. Our Gregory had congratulated him on this event (Book V, Letter 39). Since, therefore, after long struggles he was at last enjoying peace, and had recovered his see through the emperor’s favor, perhaps also with the support of John, patriarch of Constantinople,

[Col. 0350D] whom the emperor commonly consulted on ecclesiastical affairs, he feared encountering dangers again and judged it more advantageous to interpret the title “ecumenical” benevolently than to cause an uproar and contend over its usurpation.

251 13. In this letter the following observation seems worthy of notice: the words “Amen. Grace.” are praised as belonging to the holy martyr Ignatius, bishop of Antioch, and are said to have been used earlier by Anastasius, as though Ignatius had inserted them into his own letters. Yet they are not found at all in the genuine and authentic letters of that martyr, but only in corrupt versions. Hence it is clear that those letters had already been corrupted at that time.

14. We shall not dwell on Gregory’s other letters written for this reason. But we must not pass over in silence the letter in which he attempted to recall John himself to a sounder mind. He immediately complains in it about the peace of the Church, which John had disturbed, and wonders that, although John had approached the episcopate unwillingly, once he had attained it he nevertheless appeared to conduct himself as though he had prepared his way to that sacred dignity through ambition.

Gregory recalls everything that had been done against John in the time of Pelagius II, as well as the gentle remedies he himself had first tried to apply through his legates as the evil grew worse, before he was forced to resort to harsher and canonical measures.

“And because wounds that must be cut away should first be touched with a gentle hand,” he says, “I ask, entreat, and with all the sweetness I can command beg Your Fraternity to oppose all those who flatter you and bestow upon you the name of error, and not to consent to be called by a foolish and proud title” (Book V, Letter 18).

I shall pass over the arguments with which he attacks this title, since they are the same as those already mentioned.

15. All these efforts were fruitless. John retained the title he had assumed until his death, which occurred shortly after he received this letter. The letter was given on the Kalends of January in the thirteenth indiction, that is, in the year 595, the year in which those who wrote about him report that John died.

The wisest pope did receive the synodical letter of his successor Cyriacus, but he warned him (Book VII, Letter 4) to lay aside the profane name, the seedbed of so many scandals. In a letter written to Maurice (ibid., Letter 6), in which he gave thanks for Cyriacus’s election, he called John “the bishop of holy memory.” This sufficiently proves that he had never been rejected from communion with the Apostolic See.

[Note: [Col. 0351D] St. Isidore greatly praises John; he would not have done so if John had died in schism.]

The emperor had deliberated for a long time over John’s successor. It is therefore not surprising that Cyriacus was ordained only later, after an entire year had passed.

16. Shortly after the death of St. Gregory, Boniface III, who had been sent by Gregory as apocrisarius to the emperor Phocas and had won his favor, obtained from him a decree providing that in the future Cyriacus, toward whom Phocas was hostile, or any subsequent patriarchs of Constantinople, should no longer call themselves “ecumenical.” This law, however, did not remain in force for long. For at the Sixth and Seventh General Councils they are distinguished by this title no less than the Roman pontiffs, and the bishop of Constantinople still takes pride in it.

The history of this word resembles that of many others which, because of their novelty, initially appeared dangerous and therefore to be rejected, but which gradually became familiar once it had been established that they were free of poison and could be directed toward a legitimate meaning. Gregory’s opposition to a doubtful, new, foreign expression redolent of pride and liable to many perverse senses and meanings should nevertheless not be condemned. Certainly, those irritable critics who accuse him of having fought so long over a little word would praise to the skies any bishop who resisted with all his strength a Roman pontiff aspiring to and pursuing this or a similarly insolent title, and who willingly exposed himself to every danger in order to defend episcopal dignity.

17. Heterodox writers, the most bitter enemies of the Apostolic See, unjustly appropriate to themselves St. Gregory’s teaching that even the Roman pontiff cannot be granted the name “ecumenical.” They claim that by this statement the primacy and the most extensive jurisdiction of the Roman pontiff over the whole Church are attacked. Thus, from those flowers fragrant with the holy man’s modesty and humility, they make not honey, like bees, but poison, like spiders.

They fail to observe that “ecumenical,” in the sense in which St. Gregory interprets the word, signifies one single bishop in the entire Church—a meaning which, we freely admit, does not suit the pope

[Col. 0352B] and is wholly inappropriate to his supreme dignity and power. They are blind, however, if they do not see that Gregory himself, while thinking so modestly of himself and his authority, nevertheless exercised jurisdiction throughout the whole Church: in Africa, Egypt, and Asia, and even within the boundaries of the patriarchate of Constantinople, as is clear from the case of the monks of Isauria.

In Book III, Letter 30, he says: “By God’s authority, it is established that the Apostolic See is set above all Churches.”

In Book V, Letter 13: “We have taken care,” he says, “of what is entrusted by us to all the Churches.”

In Book VII, Letter 19: “Because the care of concern for all the Churches, entrusted to us, binds us,” and so forth.

In Book IX, Letter 59, on the occasion of the primate of Byzacena in Africa, who professed himself subject to the Apostolic See, he writes to John of Syracuse:

“If any fault is found in bishops, I do not know what bishop is not subject to the Apostolic See.”

He exercised this right over bishops when he entrusted the case of Peter, an African bishop, to Columbus, a bishop in Numidia, for judgment (Book VI, Letter 37); that of Ursicinus, bishop of the city of Taurina, to Syagrius of Autun (Book IX, Letter 115); and that of Januarius, bishop of Malaca, and another bishop named Stephen, to John the Defender (Book XIII, Letter 45).

When Paul, a bishop in Africa, was accused by the patrician Gennadius and came to Rome to submit himself to the pope’s judgment, but no suitable accusers appeared, Gregory sent him back (Book VII, Letter 2).

At the request of the bishops of the province, he confirmed by his authority the ordination of John, bishop and primate of First Justiniana in Illyricum, and bestowed the pallium upon him (Book II, Letters 22 and 23).

We have already presented many other examples of this jurisdiction, and more will appear below.

252 **CHAPTER II**

**CONTENTS.**—1. Gregory’s concern to establish peace.—2. He is not heeded by the emperor. False accusations against him.—3. He mourns the death of St. Maximian. He appoints John, a most holy man, as his successor.—4. John of Ravenna dies.—5. St. Gregory’s concern for the monasteries.—6. Marinianus becomes bishop of Ravenna.—7. Decrees of the Roman synod.—8. Complaints concerning Marinianus.—9. Especially because he allowed the monasteries to be harassed.—10. A privilege granted to the monks. (A.D. 594 and 595.)

1. In this year Gregory labored to establish and consolidate peace between the Romans and the Lombards. King Agilulf was not opposed to peace, but he demanded the restoration of whatever had been taken from him by deceit during peacetime; in turn, he promised to make every satisfaction if anything were shown to have been committed by his own side (Book V, Letter 36).

The holy pontiff judged this equitable. To prevent the exarch from rejecting it, he wrote to Severus, the exarch’s legal adviser, asking him to persuade the exarch not to reject the proposed conditions of peace. It was readily possible to secure peace privately at Rome and in the Roman territory, for Agilulf was inclined to grant it. But Gregory, as the common father, was concerned to establish a general peace, because unless the war with the Lombards were settled, various islands and other places would unquestionably perish.

2. The exarch, however, had no thought of peace. He saw that a war disastrous to the entire state would be highly profitable to himself, for he did not hesitate to extract gain from the losses of others. Deceived, therefore, by the exhortations and counsels of that man and other administrators of the commonwealth like him, Maurice not only refused to bring the war to an end but even accused Gregory, who urged him to lay aside his hatred and enter into a treaty, of excessive simplicity—especially because Gregory had written concerning Ariulf, duke of Spoleto, that he was ready with all his heart to come over to the empire (ibid., Letter 40), that is, inclined to make peace and alliance with the Romans.

Thus, while the pope’s wiser counsels were not believed, the strength of the enemy grew monstrously, and Italy was daily led captive beneath the Lombard yoke. The devout shepherd laments this and enumerates the disasters inflicted both on Italy and especially on Rome.

Since he nevertheless did not cease urging and seeking peace, he employed Castorius the notary, whom he maintained at Ravenna as his representative before the exarch. “Filled with the counsel of a certain evil spirit, someone secretly posted a public accusation against him by night in a place in the city, speaking against him as a criminal and craftily contradicting Gregory even in the matter of making peace” (Book VI, Letter 31).

Against the author of this notorious libel, the pope pronounced a sentence of excommunication unless he came forward and proved the accusations made in the document, or, repenting of his deed, acknowledged his guilt by public confession and begged the prescribed punishment. He imposed the same excommunication upon those who had consented to the counsel of such great iniquity.

[Col. 0353D] 3. Gregory’s grief over the public calamities was increased by mourning for the death of his friend, namely St. Maximian, who had been made bishop of Syracuse after having been a monk and abbot of St. Andrew’s. The most holy father paid his respects and performed the funeral rites for this man, who had deserved so well of him, writing to the deacon Cyprian:

“I received in the month of November the most bitter letters concerning the death of our lord Maximian. He has indeed reached the rewards he desired, but the unhappy people of the city of Syracuse must be mourned, for they were not worthy to possess such a shepherd for long. Therefore let Your Affection take care that one be chosen for ordination in that Church who, after our lord Maximian, will not seem unworthy to assume the place of the same government” (Book V, Letter 17).

From this letter we understand that Maximian died around November of the year 594. The nobles of Syracuse, wisely declining the burdens of the election (ibid., Letter 22), entrusted the matter to Gregory’s judgment. In thanking them, he wrote that he had no pastor like Maximian to give them.

Nevertheless, he informed the deacon Cyprian that John, archdeacon of the Church of Catania, seemed more suitable. If John were elected, Gregory wished a release—or, as we now say, letters of dismissal—to be given to him by Leo, bishop of Catania, before his ordination. Then, after John had been elected and ordained, Gregory sent him the pallium.

John shone in the episcopate with every virtue, especially with his lavish generosity toward the poor. “Even though he had countless poor people with him,” St. Gregory says, thanking him for the alms sent to Gregory, “to satisfy the generosity of his mercy he sought out even other places far away” (Book VI, Letter 18).

Perhaps he showed such kindness to the needy because he shaped himself according to the precepts of the most holy Doctor and took care to absorb them through constant reading of his writings. He even used this reading at his table, including before strangers, seasoning his food, so to speak, with it. The man of supreme humility and modesty was altogether displeased by this. He advised John to abstain from such reading at least in the presence of visitors and to have the sayings of the ancient Fathers read instead, so that those present might be instructed by their authority (Book VII, Letter 9).

4. In the same year in which Maximian died, John, archbishop of Ravenna, also departed this life, while the controversy concerning the use of the pallium had not yet been settled, as is clear from several letters Gregory had written to him shortly before (Book V, Letters 25, 48, and 56).

The most holy Father seems to have foretold his approaching death in these words:

“Consider, therefore, most beloved brother, all the things I have said above. Attend to the day of your calling; consider what account you will have to render for the burden of the episcopate. Correct the conduct of that notary. See what is becoming to a bishop in speech and conduct. Be wholly pure toward your brothers. Do not say one thing while holding another in your heart. Do not seek to appear greater than you are, so that you may be able to become greater than you appear” (ibid., Letters 11 and 15).

He had previously rebuked John for using mocking language, for bringing disgraceful accusations against his servants when he was angry, and for presenting himself as master only to the clergy, whom he subjected to no discipline.

5. His same negligence may perhaps be blamed for the fact that clerics had taken possession of many monasteries. Pretending that they wished to live religiously, they sought to be placed over monasteries. But through their way of life the monasteries were being destroyed, St. Gregory says. For one who serves in the clerical state cannot himself observe the strict discipline of a monastery. How, then, can someone who does not fulfill the monastic rule compel others to observe it more strictly?

The provident Father therefore rightly took care to remedy so great an evil as quickly as possible, refusing to allow sacred places to be destroyed through clerical ambition (Book V, Letter 1).

Some have used this letter to prove that the monastic state is wholly alien to the clerical state. Yet how far this is from the mind of the holy Doctor he himself clearly shows, since he promoted very many monks, both from his own monastery and from others, to sacred orders and even to the episcopate, and placed them in apostolic duties. What is more, he sometimes presents monasticism as both a rank and a preliminary preparation for the episcopate:

“Opportunus should be urged either to become a monk or to be made a subdeacon by you, so that after some time, if it pleases God, he may himself be promoted to pastoral care” (Book XII, Letter 12).

The learned Mabillon should also be consulted, both in the first volume of the Benedictine century, in the Preface, and in the *Annals*.

The mind of the holy Doctor, therefore, so far as we can ascertain from the first letter of Book V and from other passages, was that the governance of monasteries should by no means be entrusted to clerics.

[Note: [Col. 0355D] See above, Book II, final chapter.]

For, since they were accustomed to a looser discipline and had not been trained in the stricter ways of monks, they were less concerned with observing the monastic rule. Moreover, since ambition, greed, or some other evil desire had paved the way to abbatial dignity for the clerics whom Gregory attacks, they followed the manner of life of secular people—in their banquets, furnishings, and clothing—and plundered the monasteries to provide themselves with the means to live in a style equal to their position.

6. After John’s death, the holy pontiff took care over the choice of his successor. The exarch was seeking Donatus the archdeacon. We believe this is indicated by the words: “We wished the will of the most excellent lord patricius to be fulfilled in the person of Donatus the archdeacon” (Book V, Letter 48).

It was certainly dangerous not to comply with the request of so powerful a prefect, who, since he had his seat at Ravenna, claimed considerable influence for himself in the election of the bishop of that city. But when several facts concerning Donatus’s life and character became known that advised excluding him from the episcopate, Gregory decided that consent should not be given to his ordination.

He also refused to promote the presbyter John to episcopal dignity because John was ignorant of the Psalms and insufficiently diligent in priestly office. Finally, Marinianus was elected by unanimous consent, against his will and despite his resistance. He had lived for a long time in the monastery with Gregory, who commended him to his close associate Andrew the scholastic.

To show his gratitude toward his archbishop, Andrew later pleaded before St. Gregory that the use of the pallium in the Church of Ravenna be restored according to ancient custom (Book VI, Letter 61). Before granting Marinianus permission to use the pallium at certain litanies and on solemn days, however, the wise pontiff ordered that the testimony of the archdeacon and the elders of the city concerning the matter be investigated, after each of them had first taken an oath.

### 7.

Marinianus began to govern the Church of Ravenna before 5 July of this year, in which he took part in the synod celebrated by Gregory at Rome. The acts and decrees of this synod, which were formerly included in the sequence of the Letters, may now be read in the appendix to the [Letters, Col. 0356A]. The principal matters concern the office of deacons; the removal of lay boys from service in the pontifical chamber; the restraint of the plundering of ecclesiastical patrimonies by administrators; and the conferral of sacred orders and the pallium freely and without any payment, etc. The enactments of this synod were confirmed by unanimous consent and secured by the subscriptions of twenty-three bishops and of many presbyters who presided over the principal titles or churches of the City, but not by the deacons and other clergy. In the subscriptions Marinianus’s name is read second, immediately after Gregory’s. It is believed that the holy pope was referring to this gathering when, in several letters (Book VI, Letters 14, 15, 16, 17), he testifies that John, a presbyter of the Church of Chalcedon, already mentioned above (Book II, chapter 9, no. 5), was freed from the charge of heresy in the synod, by the judgment of the bishops [Col. 0356B].

### 8.

Not long afterward, Marinianus regretted both the episcopate he had undertaken and the monastic tranquillity he had lost, when the schismatics accused him of venerating the Council of Chalcedon less than was fitting. On this matter St. Gregory wrote to the clergy and people of Ravenna, asserting that Marinianus, nourished from his cradle in the bosom of the holy universal Church, had maintained the right proclamation of the faith (Book VI, Letter 2), and that he held no opinion of the Council of Chalcedon other than was proper. “Therefore,” he says, “receiving his fullest satisfaction, love your shepherd with undivided affection and a pure heart, so that his shepherd’s intercession, poured out more purely for you before God, may be able to benefit you” (ibid.). This was Gregory’s defense of Marinianus.

[Col. 0356C] Later, when Gregory learned that Marinianus was excessively sparing toward the poor, he reproved his stinginess in a letter and arranged for these private admonitions to be conveyed to him through Secundus [or Secundinus], a most holy monk. He should not suppose that reading and prayer alone are sufficient, so that he may sit apart in study and produce no fruit through his hands; rather, he should have a generous hand, hasten to those suffering need, and regard another’s poverty as his own. For if he does not possess these qualities, he bears the name of bishop in vain.

### 9.

There were afterward other occasions for complaint against Marinianus, especially because, though himself a monk, he showed himself more unjust toward monks. Accordingly, St. Gregory wrote to him:

“We marvel why the discernment of your fraternity has so quickly changed, so that it does not perceive what the circumstances demand. For this reason we grieve, because you plainly give evidence that the words of evil counselors have had more influence with you than the study of divine reading has profited you. Although it is your duty to defend monasteries and to gather religious men there with the greatest care, so that you may gain profit from the gathering of souls, you instead desire to impose burdens upon them, as your letters attest; and, what is worse, you strive to make us participants in your fault—namely, by wishing, with our consent, to burden the monastery founded by your predecessor under the pretext of administering its affairs and lawsuits. You ought to remember that, when you were present, and various presbyters, deacons, and your clergy were also present, we granted, as they requested, a decree contrary to his testament. [Col. 0357A] Yet the disposition which your predecessor had made concerning that monastery was thereby confirmed; now you conceal this fact and demand that we issue contrary commands” (Book VI, Letter 29).

It is not clearly established which monastery Gregory undertook to defend in this letter. We conjecture, however, that the excellent father of monks was speaking on behalf of the monastery of St. Apollinaris at Classe, built by Marinianus’s predecessor. Nor did the other monasteries situated in the diocese of Ravenna experience a more benevolent archbishop, as is clear from the conclusion of the letter just mentioned:

“Moreover, it has come to our attention that the monasteries established under your fraternity are being burdened by the importunity of clergy and by their various annoyances. Restrain this by a strict prohibition, so that the monks dwelling there may freely rejoice in the praises of our God” [Col. 0357B].

When the merciful Father heard that, despite his admonition, the monks were still being harassed by the clergy of Ravenna, while the archbishop looked on, no differently than before, he thought it necessary to write again and to press the matter more forcefully. He concludes his letter with these words:

“Therefore let your holiness, already admonished for the second time, not delay correcting all these matters with vigilant care. Otherwise, if after this we should find that you are negligent—which we do not believe—we shall be compelled to provide for the tranquillity of the monasteries by other means. For let it be known to you that we will no longer permit the congregation of God’s servants to remain subject to such necessity” (Book VII, Letter 43).

### 10.

When St. Gregory wrote this, he was perhaps already considering how to protect the tranquillity of monasteries through that famous privilege [Note: [Col. 0357D] See it in the Appendix] which he promulgated in the third Roman council. He had already granted a similar privilege to the monastery of Saints John and Stephen in the city of Classe, whose abbot was Claudius, a disciple of St. Gregory. The most holy pontiff wished the lawsuit that had arisen at Rome between the archbishops of Ravenna and this abbot to be judged there. When certain members of the clergy and people had loudly objected that this was contrary to the laws and canons, the pope replied:

“This could perhaps be objected, if the matter did not appeal to a higher authority and seek from him the proper settlement of its case. Do you not yourself know that the case which arose between the presbyter John and John of Constantinople, our brother and fellow bishop, appealed according to the canons to the apostolic see and was decided by our judgment? If, then, a case from that city where the prince resides was brought to our judgment, how much more must a matter arising among you be settled here, once the truth has been ascertained?” (Book VI, Letter 24).

Thus, in order to cut off this controversy at its roots and remove every occasion for litigation, the wise pontiff fortified this monastery with a broad privilege [Note: [Col. 0357D] It is read in Book VIII, Letter 15], which begins as follows: “How necessary it is to provide for the tranquillity of monasteries,” etc. He likewise fortified convents of nuns with similar privileges [Note: [Col. 0357D] Book VII, Letter 12, and Book XIII, Letter 9] [Col. 0358A]. What St. Gregory’s purpose was in granting these immunities he makes sufficiently clear when writing to Abbot Luminosus:

“When these matters have been completed, be diligent in the work of God and devote yourselves constantly to prayer, lest it appear that you have sought not security of mind in prayer, but—God forbid—that you have improperly avoided the episcopal discipline imposed upon those who live badly” (Book II, Letter 42).

## CHAPTER III

**Summary.—** 1. St. Gregory attacks simony and the ordination of neophytes in Gaul. — 2. He entrusts his authority to the bishop of Arles. The Gallican Church is the daughter of the Roman Church. — 3. On the primacy of Arles. — 4. St. Gregory’s oracle concerning the kings of France. — 5. The praises bestowed by St. Gregory on Brunichild. — 6. How far he was from flattery. — 7. Gregory of Tours visits the pope. At what time. — 8. How he was received by him. — 9. Certain provisions made for monks. — 10. And for nuns. — 11. How St. Gregory conducted himself toward the heterodox. (A.D. 594 and 595.)

[Col. 0358B] 1.
