Shortly after the synod held at Rome this year had suppressed simony, the most vigilant shepherd learned that, in many parts of Gaul or [Note: [Col. 0357D] Gaul is the same as Francia, which he calls Germany, perhaps because the Franks originated in Germany. John the Deacon often speaks in the same way in the Life of St. Gregory, edited above. Apollinaris Sidonius calls the province of Lyons “Lyons Germany” in Book V, Letter 7. Even today the archbishops of Sens boast the title “primate of Gaul and Germany.”] Germany, most of the bishops were guilty of it, and that no one in those provinces could attain sacred orders without giving payment. Wishing to remedy so serious a disease of the Gallican Church, he wrote to Virgilius, bishop of Arles, and to all the bishops in the kingdom of Childebert, as well as to Childebert himself (Book V, Letters 53, 54, 55), asking them to take immediate care to eliminate this corruption. In these letters he also condemns the hasty and premature ordinations of laymen and neophytes [Note: [Col. 0358D] See the Code of Canons of the Roman Church, canon 36: “That neophytes should not become presbyters or bishops.” And canon 39: “That laymen should not become bishops”], as wholly inconsistent with the proper order. “What does this mean?” says St. Gregory. “One who has not been a disciple becomes a teacher through thoughtless ambition; and because he has not learned what he could teach, he bears the priesthood only in name. How, moreover, will one intercede for the sins of others who has not first mourned his own?”

What we have heard above concerning Gregory’s complaint about simony flourishing in Gaul is confirmed by another Gregory, namely Gregory of Tours, who speaks of a matter known to him in the *Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 6:

“Even then,” he says, “that wicked growth had begun to bear fruit, so that the priesthood was either sold by kings or purchased by clerics.”

Nor was it enough for the holy pontiff to write once or twice in order to ward off so great an evil. Indeed, in many letters subsequently sent either to Queen Brunichild or to kings and bishops, he scarcely achieved enough to cleanse the Gallican Church even partially of so great a stain. For corruptions of this kind, arising from greed, require continual remedies if they are to be treated, though they are never healed [Col. 0358D].

### 2.

To Virgilius, a man richly adorned with upright morals and virtues, Gregory granted his own authority, according to ancient custom, within the boundaries of Childebert’s kingdom, together with the use of the pallium, at the request of the king himself and of the archbishop. The authority with which he possessed jurisdiction over the bishops subject to him as vicar of the holy see is explained in the already cited Letter 54. All cases were referred to him for judgment and settlement, except perhaps the more important matters or those concerning the faith, which by their gravity required the judgment of the apostolic see. He convened councils and presided over those he convened; no bishop could travel to distant places without his authority.

We must not omit Gregory’s teaching in his letter to Virgilius (Book V, Letter 53): that the Gallican Church is the offspring of the Roman Church. This agrees with the position of Innocent I, who wrote to Decentius of Gubbio that throughout Italy, Gaul, Spain, Africa, Sicily, and the intervening islands, no one had founded Churches except those whom the venerable apostle Peter or his successors had established as priests (ibid., Letter 54). The Church of Arles, in particular, boasts of this illustrious origin [Col. 0359B]. St. Gregory certainly recalls its ancient nobility when he says that he followed ancient custom in entrusting his authority to Virgilius.

### 3.

Those who have written about Arles report that Valentinian and Honorius called the city “the mother of Gaul,” and that the seat of the praetorian prefect was established there, where the assembly of the seven provinces of Gaul was held each year. Ecclesiastical primacy and exarchate seem to have originated from this political dignity. For Zosimus and the Roman pontiffs who followed him decided to distinguish the bishops of this most noble city with the vicariate authority of the holy see. Their authority was so great that they presided over the synod of the seven provinces, granted letters of form to traveling clerics, and gave bishops themselves permission to depart. If controversies concerning faith or morals arose in Gaul or Spain, they were referred to these bishops, as primates and vicars of the Roman pontiff, for settlement. But when St. Leo learned that Hilary, bishop of Arles, had invaded the rights of the metropolitans and usurped ordinations that belonged to them, he divided the extensive primacy between that bishop and the bishop of Vienne [Note: [Col. 0359D] Before St. Leo, Boniface I and Celestine I had already withdrawn certain privileges from the bishops of Arles] [Col. 0360D].

Later Gregory the Great diminished the vicariate authority of the apostolic see that had been conferred or confirmed upon Virgilius, when, as will be said below, he entrusted his own authority within Childebert’s kingdom to Syagrius, bishop of Autun. Thus the Roman pontiffs, as evidence of the supreme, non-delegated authority they possessed, either granted or withdrew such honors at will, according as it seemed more advantageous to the Christian cause.

[Col. 0359D] 4. We cannot proceed farther without first observing this celebrated encomium of the kings of France, which Gregory delivered in an almost oracular manner in his letter to King Childebert:

“As far as royal dignity surpasses other men, so far does the eminence of your kingdom undoubtedly exceed the kingdoms of all other peoples. That you are a king, since there are others also, is not remarkable; but that you are Catholic, which others do not deserve to be, is of great importance. Whatever the other kings boast of possessing, you possess, etc.” (Book VI, Letter 6).

The wise Father added many other praises, which I pass over, followed by an outstanding exhortation to pursue justice and cultivate the other virtues [Col. 0360A]:

“Therefore, so that they may be surpassed in action as well as in faith, let your Excellency always show yourself kind toward your subjects. And if there are matters capable of offending your mind, do not punish them without investigation. For then you will truly please the King of kings, that is, the almighty Lord, more greatly, if, restraining your power, you believe yourself less permitted to do what you are able to do” (ibid.).

### 5.

Some people judge somewhat harshly the praises poured out by the same devout pontiff upon Queen Brunichild. He considers her worthy of praise not merely because, through vigilant care, she preserved the glory of temporal affairs intact for her son Childebert, but also because, through her pious instruction, she provided for him the rewards of eternal life. Everywhere he honorably commemorates her piety and her supreme devotion to divine matters [Note: [Col. 0360D] See Book XI, Letters 62 and 63, and also Book XIII, Letter 6] [Col. 0360B].

“Among her other good qualities,” he writes to her, “this holds the first place with you above all others: that amid the waves of this world, which commonly confuse the minds of rulers with turbulent agitation, you so turn your heart toward the love of divine worship and the peaceful ordering of venerable places, as though no other concern troubled you. Since the conduct of such rulers is usually a great protection for their subjects, we declare the nation of the Franks happier than other peoples, because it has deserved to have a queen so richly endowed with every good quality” (Book IV, Letter 5).

“Could these things,” ask Brunichild’s accusers, “could such words have been spoken without flattery about a most infamous queen, the bellows of so many wars and disorders, the murderess of so many kings, and the author of so many crimes?”

[Col. 0360C] If we examine Gregory’s letters to Brunichild and weigh the praises bestowed upon her, we shall be compelled to acknowledge that he commended her—properly and not without reason—for governing the kingdom with the greatest prudence and preserving it for her sons; for maintaining the Christian and Catholic faith among the Franks and propagating it among foreign peoples; and for certain notable works of piety in the construction of hospices, monasteries, and other sacred places. It will be clear that Gregory’s praise was justified.

Brunichild had her five-year-old son Childebert, after his father Sigibert’s death, snatched from Fredegund’s hands and proclaimed king at Metz by the nobles of Austrasia. This was a proof of great prudence and ability. She later arranged for him to be designated heir by his uncle Gunthram, king of the Burgundians, rejecting Clothar, the son of Chilperic. After Childebert’s death, she undertook the administration of both kingdoms, Austrasia and Burgundy, and the guardianship of her grandsons Theudebert and Theuderic, who were still children; she discharged these responsibilities extremely well. When she held supreme power, she supported the monks sent by St. Gregory for the conversion of the English and, supplying everything necessary, greatly advanced this holy work. In the construction, adornment, and endowment of sacred places she displayed a generosity plainly worthy of a queen. Who would begrudge her the praises due for so many and such great works of prudence, religion, and liberality?

[Col. 0361A] As for the crimes charged against this queen, they were either committed after Gregory’s letters to her had been written, or they were entirely fictitious, fabricated by her enemies—as, not without reason, some more recent writers believe: Charles Cointius in the *Frankish Annals*, and Cordemoy in the *History of the Kings of France*, which he wrote in French. When Brunichild was finally handed over by the nobles of Austrasia and Burgundy to Clothar, son of Chilperic, than whom she had no more hostile enemy, so that she might be thought justly to have deserved the most cruel death to which she was consigned, accusations were gathered against her from every side. Even murders were charged to her which either Clothar himself had ordered or had been committed by those who supported his cause.

### 6.

To show how far St. Gregory was from flattery in the letters he wrote to Brunichild, it is enough to point to those in which he admonishes her concerning matters requiring correction in her kingdom [Note: [Col. 0361D] See especially Book IX, Letter 109, and Book XI, Letter 69]: namely, the stain of simony, the premature ordinations of laymen, the idolatry that still survived in Gaul, and priests living scandalously. Especially worth reading are these reproachful words, in which he plainly threatens Brunichild and her grandsons with God’s judgments:

“Since it is written, ‘Justice exalts a nation, but sin makes peoples miserable,’ a kingdom is then believed to be stable when the fault that is recognized is corrected without delay” (Proverbs 14:34). “Many reports have therefore reached us—something we cannot say without extreme distress of heart—that certain priests in those regions live so immodestly and wickedly that it is disgraceful for us to hear it and lamentable to report it.”

He adds in a free and almost prophetic voice:

“For what we say must not be concealed, because anyone who can correct a fault and neglects to do so undoubtedly makes himself a participant in the crime. Therefore take thought for your souls; take thought for the grandsons whom you desire to reign happily; take thought for the provinces. Before our Creator stretches out his hand to strike, give the most earnest consideration to correcting this crime, lest he strike more severely later, the longer and more mercifully he now waits” (Book XI, Letter 69).

These words plainly and more than sufficiently demonstrate that Gregory could have said with the Apostle: “We speak, not as pleasing men, but God, who tests our hearts; for we were never guilty of flattering speech” (1 Thessalonians 2:5).

[Col. 0361D] 7. Leaving Gaul and returning to Italy, let us accompany Gregory of Tours as he went to Rome to visit the thresholds of the holy apostles and to see our own Gregory. This sacred pilgrimage, mentioned by St. Odo in his Life, could scarcely be reported either earlier or later than it occurred.

Gregory of Tours could not have gone to Rome later, for according to St. Odo he died in the twenty-first year of his episcopal ordination, which Odo himself says coincided with the fifth year of St. Gregory’s pontificate at the end of the tenth book of his *History*. Many considerations, however, persuade us that the Gallic Gregory did not arrive at Rome earlier. He was certainly not at Rome in the year 590, the first year of the Roman Gregory’s pontificate, since he learned and reported what had happened there at that time from the testimony of his deacon, as is clear from Book X of the *History*, chapter 1. In the following year, the sixteenth of King Childebert, he was in Gaul and at Tours received an Armenian bishop named Simon, as we learn from the same book of the *History*, chapter 24. In that same year he went to the court of King Childebert and crossed through the district of Rheims, according to Book IV of the *Miracles of St. Martin*, chapter 26. In the year 592, his archdeacon Plato, mentioned in the same book, chapter 32, was summoned to the bishopric of Poitiers. Gregory was present when Plato took up that see, as Fortunatus, Plato’s later successor, testifies. In the year 593, in January, he visited St. Leobard, a recluse in the greater monastery near Tours. Shortly afterward—that is, on the eighteenth day of that month, which was a Sunday—Leobard breathed his last [Col. 0362B]. In the year assigned, 18 January was a Sunday. This persuades us that St. Leobard’s death occurred in that year, not five or six years earlier. Since Gregory dealt with St. Leobard for the last time in his *Book on the Life of the Fathers*, we may conjecture that he committed the acts of this most holy monk to writing not many years before his own death.

In the same year, 593, when King Childebert visited the city of Orléans and acquired the kingdom of the deceased Gunthram, Gregory was at his court, according to Book IV of the *Miracles of St. Martin*, chapter 37. He also celebrated the annual feast of St. Martin at Tours in November, according to chapter 38 of the same book. Since St. Gregory of Tours died at Tours, as seems most probable, in November of the year 595, his visit to Rome and his return must be assigned to the year 594 or the beginning of the following year [Col. 0362C].

The historian Gregory says nothing at all about this journey. This is evidence that, once he returned to Tours, death immediately overtook him and he wrote nothing new or added anything to what he had already written. For if he had lived in Gaul afterward for a longer time in good health, he could not have remained silent for long about the many sacred relics of the saints that he had seen at Rome and the miracles he had heard there.

### 8.

Whatever the time may have been when Gregory of Tours visited the thresholds of the holy apostles, St. Odo relates that he was received by the most holy pope with great reverence. “When he introduced him,” Odo says, “to the confession of blessed Peter [or, ‘to the altar’], he stood waiting at his side until Gregory rose. Meanwhile, being a man of profound intelligence, he marveled at the hidden dispensation by which such abundant grace had flowed from heaven upon such a man—for Gregory was short in stature.

“As soon as Gregory perceived this divinely, he rose from prayer and, looking at the pope with the calm expression he habitually wore, said: ‘The Lord made us, and we did not make ourselves; the same in small things as in great.’

“When the holy pope recognized that these words answered his own thought, he rejoiced at having been detected. From then on he began to hold in great veneration the grace that he had previously admired in Gregory, and he so ennobled the see of Tours that he gave it a golden chair, which was to be preserved thereafter at that see [or, ‘in that city’]” [Col. 0363A].

Not long after his return, the holy bishop died on 15 November. There survives a letter of St. Gregory written to his successor Pelagius, dated in the fourteenth indiction, which corresponds to the years 595 and 596 (Book VI, Letter 52). Since it is read among the last letters written during that indiction, however, it must belong to the end of the indiction and therefore to the year 596.

### 9.

Although we have already observed many provisions made by St. Gregory this year for the benefit of monasteries, some still remain worthy of notice, and it will not be burdensome to list them briefly here. Of the monks who were admitted to the priesthood—or rather, to the presbyterate—some were placed in charge of churches, while others were ordained for monasteries, to which they remained devoted and attached. The former could not be removed from the monastery by a bishop without the abbot’s consent, as is plainly established by what is read in the letter written to Candidus, bishop of the Old City (Book VI, Letter 28) [Note: [Col. 0363D] “Therefore, in your presence, we grant you permission by letter to remove monks from monasteries situated in your parish, with the consent of their abbot, and ordain them presbyters”]. This is confirmed by what he wrote two years later to Marinianus, bishop of Ravenna:

“Likewise, care must be taken that, against the will of the abbot of the monastery in question, monks are not removed from it either to be ordained for other monasteries, or for sacred orders, or for the office of the clergy” (Book VIII, Letter 15).

No one was to be ordained for sacred ministry without a serious prior examination of his life and morals (Book VI, Letters 28 and 42). Those who were ordained in this way, as though emancipated, thereafter neither lived in the monastery nor had the power or permission to live there:

“Lest monasteries, under cover of this pretext, be compelled to bear the burdens that we prohibit,” says St. Gregory (Book VII, Letter 43) [Col. 0363C].

Those who were appointed presbyters for monasteries nevertheless remained under the jurisdiction of the abbots and could not cast off the yoke of obedience. This is also provided for in chapter 62 of St. Benedict’s Rule. The bishop ordained only those whom the abbot and his congregation had chosen for this office.

For the supreme priesthood, however, they could be taken without awaiting the consent of the abbots or congregations, solely at the will and request of the clergy and people. At that time, therefore, clergy and monks were taken indiscriminately to exercise episcopal care (Book I, Letter 18) [Note: [Col. 0364D] “From the clergy of those very churches, or from the monasteries, if any worthy men can be found for the priestly office”].

Although it had not yet been established by law that abbots had to be presbyters, those placed in charge of monasteries were nevertheless often distinguished by presbyteral dignity, as is clear from many letters of St. Gregory and from various other records of the Church. Presbyter-abbots who had been ordered to withdraw from sacred ministry because of a lapse were, although they could never return to priestly office, permitted by the indulgence of the most holy pontiff to resume the administration of monasteries (see Book I, Letter 9; Book V, Letters 3, 4, 7, 38).

### 10.

If I wished to list here everything that St. Gregory established this year for the benefit of monasteries, I could scarcely finish counting it all [Col. 0364A]. The devout Father was no less concerned for nuns than for monks. Since they were the weaker sex, he thought that they should be protected by stricter laws. Accordingly, when he learned through the physician Anastasius that many evils had occurred in a convent of virgins, he decided that the doors of this monastery, and of the others inhabited by sacred virgins, should be closed to him, being concerned more for the salvation of the soul than for that of the body (Book V, Letter 6).

He deterred the Roman exarch from giving aid and patronage to nuns who had returned to the world and entered into marriage. He told him freely that he could in no way be his friend if he supported for even a short time so great a crime—one which he would never permit to remain unpunished (ibid., Letter 24).

### 11.

The humble Gregory did not hesitate to alter what he himself had established or to undo what he had fixed whenever experience had shown him that it no longer benefited the Christian commonwealth. Thus, although in many letters (Book I, Letters 35 and 47) he had taught that one should deal more gently with the heterodox and with Jews themselves, and that the Christian religion should be commended not by threats and terrors but by kindness and the sweetness of preaching, he later changed his policy. He frequently wrote that the Manichaeans and Jews who were on the estates of the Roman Church, since they could not be won by gentleness, should be vigorously pursued and burdened with taxes; those converted to the faith, however, were to be strengthened by remitting part of their payments.

“And although,” he says, “they themselves come less faithfully [to the Church], nevertheless those who are born from them are baptized with greater faithfulness. Thus we gain either them or their children” (Book V, Letter 8) [Col. 0364C].

How passionately St. Gregory desired to win souls is shown above all by his sending preachers to the English, who were still devoted to the worship of idols. That holy expedition must now be discussed.

## CHAPTER IV

**Summary.—** 1. St. Gregory sends St. Augustine to England. — 2. The beginnings of the Christian faith in Britain. — 3. The idolatrous English occupy the island. — 4. When Augustine and his fellow monks set out. — 5. They are strengthened by St. Gregory when they consider turning back. — 6. Where they stopped. — 7. Their journey through Gaul is described. — 8. The kingdom of Kent, where they landed; its king and queen. — 9. Augustine approaches the king. — 10. His address to the king. — 11. Ethelbert’s reply. — 12. He enters Canterbury with his companions. With what equipment. (A.D. 595 and 596.)

[Col. 0364D] 1. Gregory had long thirsted for the salvation of the English, as is clear from what was said earlier, and he was thinking about Britain. So that the heralds of the word of God, who were soon to depart for that region, might have some assistants there, the most wise pontiff ordered Candidus, administrator of the Gallican patrimony, to acquire youths from the English people, seventeen or eighteen years of age (Book VI, Letter 7), and to have them taught and trained in monasteries in the faith and rites of Christianity, so that he might later use their ministry for the conversion of the entire nation.

Although these boys did not yet seem mature enough for so great a labor and undertaking—for St. Gregory wrote to Candidus the presbyter about purchasing them at the beginning of the sixth year of his pontificate, and at its end he sent Augustine to Gaul, from which he would afterward transmit him to England—he nevertheless did not think that this expedition should be postponed any longer. This was either because he feared that death, which he suspected was near on account of his persistent illnesses, might overtake him first, or, rather, because, as he himself suggests in writing to the Gallican bishops, he had heard that the English people desired to become Christian. Bertha, the Christian wife of Ethelbert, king of Kent, was undoubtedly drawing her husband and his subjects toward embracing the faith of Christ (ibid., Letters 52, 53, etc., 58, 59).

### 2.

That island, the largest of all those bordering Europe, then called Britain and later called England for the most part after its English inhabitants, had received the Christian faith long before it was occupied by this people [Col. 0365B]. Indeed, according to Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, it had received it from the disciples of Christ the Savior themselves [Note: [Col. 0365D] *Ecclesiastical Demonstration*, Book III, p. 112: “to the islands called British” (*ἐπὶ τὰς καλουμένας Βρετανικὰς νήσους*)]. We do not dare assert who those disciples were. It is commonly believed, however, that Joseph of Arimathea announced Christ to the Britons [Note: [Col. 0365D] See Spelman’s preface to the *Councils of England*, section “On the origin of the Christian religion in Britain,” and Daniel Langhorne’s *British Antiquities* [Col. 0366D], London, 1673].

Some maintain that the holy apostles Peter and Paul crossed into Britain in order to preach the Gospel, as may be read in Spelman; to prove this they cite the testimony of Theodoret. The venerable Bede, who composed the history of the British and English peoples (*History*, Book I, chapter 4), discusses the conversion of King Lucius during the Roman pontificate of Eleutherius. Lucius requested and obtained preachers of the divine word from him, around the year of Christ 177 or 180. Tertullian, a contemporary of Eleutherius, teaches in Book *Against the Jews*, written around the year 208, chapter 7, that places of the Britons inaccessible to the Romans had been opened to Christ and subjected to him. Origen, scarcely inferior in age or authority, supports this in Homily 6 on Luke.

The persecution of Diocletian dyed Britain purple and consecrated it with the blood of many martyrs. Among them St. Alban stands out, celebrated throughout the island by the famous monastery bearing his name. When peace was restored to the Church, many bishops from Britain took part in councils held at various times during the fourth century: the Council of Arles in 314, that of Sardica in 351, and shortly afterward that of Ariminum. From there the Arian heresy proceeded; after corrupting almost the whole world, it infected this island as well, as though it lay outside the world. “For its inhabitants,” says Bede of the peoples known to him and of his own countrymen, “always delight in hearing something new, and firmly hold nothing certain” (ibid., chapter 8).

Later, during the reigns of Arcadius and Honorius, Pelagius the Briton scattered the poisons of his unbelief far and wide against the assistance of heavenly grace. These were introduced and spread among the Britons by Agricola, son of Severianus, an Arian bishop, but were suppressed and extinguished through the efforts of the Gallican bishops. At the petition of the Britons, who felt themselves unequal to overcoming the cunning of the heretics, those bishops sent two bishops distinguished for learning and holiness to assist them: Lupus of Troyes and Germanus, bishop of Auxerre. Those who had remained in the faith were especially strengthened by Germanus’s miracles and preaching, and the heterodox were defeated.

Later, the error of the Scots and their distinctive practice in celebrating Easter almost separated the British Church from the others. The learned Petavius thinks that this practice arose from a passage of Anatolius corrupted by Rufinus’s erroneous translation. St. Columbanus greatly praises Anatolius—who was bishop of Laodicea during the time of Diocletian and Maximian—in a letter to St. Gregory, in which he argues on behalf of this practice of his Scots [Note: [Col. 0366D] See Book IX of St. Gregory’s Letters, Letter 127; compare the observations on Epiphanius, *Heresy* 51].

### 3

The Angles and Saxons, together with other barbarians not yet freed from the service of idols, had almost obliterated the Christian religion on the island [Col. 0366B]. The Britons had summoned them from the farthest parts of Germany, under evil auspices, against the Picts and Scots, their constant enemies. These newcomers occupied the greater part of the island, which was divided, according to the diversity of its peoples, into seven ethnarchies. Meanwhile, the Picts, who had originated in Scythia, and the Scots, who had come from Ireland, held the northern part, while the Britons retained chiefly the southern region.

In such a great upheaval of affairs, the oppressed Britons gave no thought to sowing the evangelical seed among their most hostile enemies; nor, even if they had been concerned to preach the Christian law, would the Angles have embraced it, lest they appear to have surrendered to the vanquished while themselves being the victors. Saint Gregory censures the negligence of the Gallican bishops in carefully undertaking their conversion when he wrote to Theuderic [Col. 0366C] and Theudebert, kings of the Franks:

> News has reached us that the nation of the Angles eagerly desires, by God’s mercy, to be converted to the Christian faith, but that priests nearby are neglecting them and failing to kindle their desires by their exhortation. (Book VI, Letter 58.)

### 4

Moreover, a work of such magnitude and still greater usefulness was owed to Gregory. Bede testifies that he undertook it in the sixth year of his pontificate:

> In the fourteenth year of the Emperor Maurice, that is, according to the same reckoning, in 596, he sent the servant of God Augustine, together with several other monks who feared the Lord, to preach the word of God to the nation of the Angles. (Ecclesiastical History, Book I, chapter 23.)

Augustine’s principal assistants were the priest Laurence and Peter. A stronger indication of the time when this expedition began is drawn from the Letters written on the subject [Col. 0366D], all of which belong to indiction XIV and are contained in Book VI of the Register.

From these same letters it is clear that Augustine was a monk, and specifically a monk of the monastery of Saint Andrew, of which he was provost.

[Note: Saint Gregory, writing to Eulogius in Book VIII, Letter 3, calls Augustine a monk of his monastery.]

That his companions were taken and selected from the same monastery is shown by these words:

> Obey in all humility Augustine, your provost, on his return; we have also appointed him your abbot. (Book VI, Letter 51.)

### 5

When they had set out and completed some part of the journey [Col. 0367A], they were struck by sluggish fear and decided to return home rather than approach a barbarous, savage, unbelieving people whose language they did not even know. Yet they did not dare carry this out without consulting the holy pontiff. They therefore sent Augustine himself to Gregory to beg that he grant permission for him and his companions to return, lest they expose themselves and their nation—or rather the supreme pontiff himself—to the mockery of the Franks and the Angles because they had rashly attempted a hazardous journey, full of uncertainty and labor, without any result.

But Gregory, to strengthen their faltering courage, ordered Augustine to return to his companions and wrote to them as follows:

> Since it would have been better not to begin a good undertaking than to turn back in thought from what has been begun, you must, dearest sons, apply the greatest zeal to completing the good work which, with the Lord’s assistance, you have begun. Therefore let neither the labor of the journey nor the tongues of malicious men deter you; but with every effort and every fervor, carry out, with God as your guide, what you have begun.

The rest may be read both in Bede and in the Register of Letters (Book VI, Letter 51). From the time when this letter was written—for it is recorded as having been given on the tenth day before the Kalends of August—we may infer when Augustine and his companions set out. We understand from Bede, who especially reports it, that Letter 52 was written on the same day and in the same year. I am also readily persuaded that the other Letters in which the pope commended the preachers he had sent, both to the kings and nobles of Gaul and to its bishops, belong to the same period.

For once he had learned that they were wavering, frightened by the danger visible from afar, and ill-prepared for a long journey among unknown peoples [Col. 0367C], he turned his mind to procuring for them assistance by which much of their labor might be relieved. That Letter 52 was written with this purpose, together with the two immediately following it, as well as Letters 57 and the two following it in Book VI, is sufficiently clear from the subject prefixed to each.

### 6

We do not read where these heralds of the sacred word halted. In Bede (Book I, chapter 23) and in the Life of Saint Augustine it is only stated that, after completing part of the journey, or after traveling for several days, they checked their course and waited until Augustine, whom they had sent to Saint Gregory, returned. It is nevertheless conjectured, and not without reason, that they settled in Provence, not far from the island of Lérins.

This is certainly indicated by these words of Letter 56 of Book VI, addressed to Stephen [Col. 0367D], abbot of Lérins:

> The report brought by Augustine, the servant of God and bearer of this letter, has made us glad, because he has told us that your charity is, as it ought to be, vigilant.

For how could Augustine, returning to Rome from the journey he had undertaken, have reported this about the abbot of Lérins if he had returned to his homeland long before entering Provence? Augustine had also visited Protas­ius, bishop of Aix, and the patrician Arigius, about whom he told Gregory many things as an eyewitness when he returned to Rome (Book VI, Letters 55 and 57).

Thus, when Bede says that Augustine and his companions had advanced only some distance, this should not be understood absolutely but comparatively, in relation to the much longer distance that still remained to be covered. The same explanation should be applied to the author of Saint Augustine’s Life when he says that, after several days’ travel, those monks thought about returning. Let us now see them cheerfully taking up the road again.

### 7

From the letters of recommendation which Augustine had received for delivery, we have a description of his journey through Gaul. First they arrived at Massilia, where they paid their respects to Bishop Serenus; a letter was given to him in Gregory’s name (Book VI, Letter 52). They then reached Arles and visited Virgilius, archbishop and vicar of the holy see, to whom the pope had especially commended them (ibid., Letter 53). Next they had to visit Vienne, whose bishop was Desiderius, one of those to whom Gregory wrote (ibid., Letter 54). They then proceeded to Lyons, although no letters written at that time on this matter to Etherius, bishop of that city, survive.

From there they made for Chalon, where King Theuderic customarily resided with his grandmother Brunhild. The pope had commended Augustine and his assistants to both of them in letters (ibid., Letters 58 and 59). They then went to Autun to seek the assistance of Bishop Syagrius and to deliver the pope’s letters (ibid., Letter 54).

After traveling through many places, they either reached Divodurum of the Mediomatrici or Rheims, the residence of Theudebert, king of Austrasia. Saint Gregory earnestly asked him by letter to regard his monks, preachers of the divine word, as commended to him. From that king’s court they came to Caesarodunum-Tours, both to venerate the tomb and sacred relics of Saint Martin and [Col. 0368C] to deliver Gregory’s letter to Bishop Pelagius (ibid., Letter 52).

It is difficult to determine whether, turning aside from their route, they visited Mediolanum Santonum to greet Bishop Palladius, to whom the pope had written. Perhaps, since Palladius possessed great influence with the Frankish kings, they found him at court and delivered to him the letter of the most holy pontiff, who had already bound him to himself by a favor. Gotselinus states in Augustine’s Life that Augustine passed through Angers and recounts a miracle that occurred not far from the Bridge of Sai—or, as others say, the Bridge of Caesar.

### 8

Passing over all these details, Bede writes:

> Strengthened, therefore, by the encouragement of the blessed Father Gregory, Augustine returned with the servants of Christ who were with him to the work of the word, and reached Britain. (Book I, chapter 25.)

He landed on the island called Thanet [Col. 0368D], in the eastern part of the kingdom of Kent. At that time Æthelberht ruled in Kent, a region of Britain facing Gaul and extending as far as the River Humber.

[Note: It should be read “Edilberthus,” not “Adilberthus.” According to Spelmann, *edil* in the Saxon language means glorious or honored.]

His wife was Bertha, daughter of Charibert, king of the Franks, and granddaughter of Clotaire I. She had been given in marriage to the Anglo-Saxon king on the condition that she retain and freely profess the Christian faith. For this reason she brought with her Liudhard, bishop of Senlis, and kept him at court as minister of the sacred rites.

We believe that the king was especially influenced by her to renounce the worship of idols, in accordance with the counsel of Saint Gregory (Book XI, Letter 20). Gregory says that the conversion of the Angles was reserved as her reward and, to bring such a great work to completion, kindles her with the most vehement exhortation—as though daughters of the royal Frankish line had been accustomed to bring the true faith to their husbands as a dowry. Thus Chlodesind, daughter of King Clotaire, made Alboin, king of the Lombards, a Christian; and Ingund, daughter of Sigibert and sister of King Childebert, who had been given in marriage to the Arian Hermenegild, turned him toward the Catholic faith and inspired him to martyrdom.

### 9

From the island of Thanet Augustine sent some of his companions to Æthelberht to tell him that they had come from Rome and were bringing him the best possible message: if he obeyed them, they would promise him, without any doubt, eternal joys in heaven and a kingdom without end with the living and true God (Bede, Book I, chapter 25).

The king received them with great courtesy and ordered them to remain for some time in the place where they had landed, until he determined what ought to be done, while supplying them with everything necessary. After several days the king came to the island and, sitting in the open air, summoned Augustine and his companions to a conference.

> He had taken care that they should not enter any house to meet him, using an ancient superstition, says Bede, lest, if they possessed any magical art, they should deceive him and overcome him by their arrival.

But they came endowed not with demonic power but with divine power, carrying a silver cross as their standard and an image of the Lord and Savior painted on a panel, while singing litanies.

### 10

After obtaining permission to speak, Augustine explained to the king that he and his companions had come for the purpose of teaching him how, after death, he might reign more gloriously and obtain the crown of immortality [Col. 0369C]. He said that Jesus Christ had earned the crown of immortality by his death for those who believed in him and had opened the kingdom of heaven.

God, he continued, had burned with such love for humanity that, in order to secure their salvation, he had handed over his only-begotten Son to the most shameful death, namely the punishment of the cross. Thus the distinguished preacher did not think that the scandal of the cross should be concealed; rather, he wished thereby to commend more strongly its divine power for freeing humanity from the slavery of death and sin. For what is more worthy of God than the salvation of humanity?

He added that this same Christ had risen from the dead, ascended to the kingdom of heaven, and sat at the right hand of the Father [Col. 0369D]; but that he would come at the consummation of the world to judge all mortals. To establish the truth of his teaching, he recounted innumerable and astonishing miracles, sure proofs of Christ’s divinity. Above all, he pointed to the remarkable concord of nearly all nations in accepting the Christian religion and rejecting idols, despite the resistance of the evil inclinations and vices of humanity. Paganism favored these so greatly that it even decreed and paid them divine honors, whereas the evangelical law teaches that eternal death is the payment for moral corruption.

Augustine went on to say that the world, having become Christian, was governed with the greatest wisdom by Gregory, the Roman pontiff. Gregory longed for the salvation of the king and all the Angles and would gladly have hastened to preach these things to them himself, had he not feared abandoning the care of so many sheep entrusted to him; he, Augustine, was acting as Gregory’s ambassador.

### 11

To this the king, wavering and hesitant between the darkness of his accustomed error and the light of truth shining upon him, replied like a sick man who favors his physicians but is not yet ready to undergo treatment. The words and promises seemed beautiful to him, he said; but since they were new and uncertain, he could not give his assent while abandoning the practices that he had preserved for so long together with the entire nation of the Angles.

Nevertheless, because they had come from so great a distance to communicate to him what appeared true and excellent to them, he was very grateful and agreed that anyone who wished to give his name to Christ might be received by them and instructed according to their custom (Bede, Book I, chapter 25).

He also assigned them a place in the city of Dorobernia, the capital of the entire kingdom, where they could live comfortably, and ordered that everything necessary for their livelihood be supplied abundantly.

[Note: Later called Canterbury.]

### 12

They entered the royal city carrying before them, according to their custom, the cross and the image of Christ the Savior, and chanting this litany in harmonious voices:

> We beseech you, Lord, in all your mercy, that your fury and your anger be taken away from this city and from your holy house, for we have sinned, alleluia. (Bede, Book I, chapter 25.)

In the dwelling granted to them, Augustine and his fellow soldiers began to imitate the apostolic life of the nascent Church. They despised everything belonging to this world as though it were foreign and accepted from those whom they taught only what was necessary for their sustenance [Col. 0370C], so that they might commend the holiness of the Christian law by their example rather than by words.

Drawn by these harmless attractions to the nets of truth, not a few embraced faith in Christ. They were permitted to hold their assemblies in the ancient church of Saint Martin near the city, the only one then surviving. But after the king himself believed and was initiated through baptism, the neophytes, unable any longer to resist the irrefutable testimony of the miracles by which God confirmed the teaching and holiness of his servants, began with extraordinary zeal to restore ruined temples and build new ones.

[Note: The acts of Augustine and his companions speak not only of the miracles they performed, but also Bede in the passage cited and Gregory himself, especially in Book VIII, Letter 30, to Eulogius:

> So many miracles shine forth among that people, either through Augustine himself or through those who were sent with him, that in the signs they perform they seem to imitate the powers of the apostles. At the feast of the Lord’s Nativity, which has passed during this first indiction, more than ten thousand Angles are reported to have been baptized by that same brother and fellow bishop of ours.]

The result was that the infant Church received so great an accession, with the Angles eagerly following the king’s example—although he compelled no one to adopt the religion—that the former church could not contain them.

## CHAPTER V

**Summary.—1. Augustine is ordained bishop. 2. He baptizes ten thousand Angles. He sends to Rome and consults the pope. 3. From him he receives a new reinforcement of preachers, together with many other things. 4. Saint Gregory’s letters to the king, to the queen, and to Augustine. 5. The monastery founded near Canterbury, and the monastic life established in the Church of Canterbury. Bede’s clear testimony on the matter. 6. Another decisive argument drawn from Bede.**

### 1

Having made such a successful beginning to the province entrusted to him by Saint Gregory, Augustine crossed into Gaul at Gregory’s command, where he was made bishop by the bishops of the Germanies (Book VIII, Letter 30).

By “the Germanies” Gregory understands the parts of Gaul then occupied by the Franks, who had originated in and come from Germany. Perhaps he also included the province of Arles among the Germanies because its inhabitants, the Burgundians, were Germanic by origin (Book V, Letter 53). For the same reason Apollinaris Sidonius calls the province subject to Lyons “Lyonese Germany.”

Bede reports that Augustine was ordained by the bishop of Arles (Bede, Book I, chapter 27), whom, having suffered a lapse of memory, he calls Etherius.

### 2

After returning to the island, the new apostle baptized more than ten thousand Angles in the waters of purification on Christmas Day itself.

[Note: Pope Siricius, in his second canon in the letter to Himerius of Tarragona, does condemn those who baptize indiscriminately at Christmas and other solemn feasts, assigning only Easter and Pentecost for the celebration of baptism. Yet he exempts cases of necessity from this rule. Clovis, certainly, the first of the Frankish kings to give his name to Christ, was baptized on Christmas Day together with many others, according to the letter of Saint Avitus, bishop of Vienne, to that same Clovis. This is confirmed by Letter 2 of Anastasius II to him:

> We rejoice, glorious son, that your beginning in the Christian faith coincided with the beginning of our pontificate.

Anastasius had begun his pontificate shortly before Christmas.]

Gregory testifies in his letter to Eulogius that this occurred during indiction I (Book VIII, Letter 30), that is, in the eighth year of his pontificate.

Augustine soon sent two of his companions, Laurence and Peter, to Rome to inform the holy pontiff of everything that had taken place and to question and consult him about several matters. We read these questions, together with his responses to each, both in Bede and in the Register of Letters (Book XI, Letter 64).

The principal questions concerned the division into four portions of ecclesiastical revenues and offerings; clerics who had married after receiving clerical status; the degrees of consanguinity and affinity that impeded marriage; and the ordination of bishops. The canons had indeed provided that when one bishop consecrated another, two other bishops should be present, at least as witnesses [Col. 0371C]. But because Augustine was then the only bishop in the Church of the Angles, the pope agreed that bishops might be ordained by him alone.

### 3

Since Gregory had learned from Augustine’s legates that the harvest in England was great but the laborers few—for Augustine had nevertheless arrived on the island with approximately forty companions—he added to Laurence and Peter a new reinforcement: namely, a large number of selected monks for the ministry of the divine word and of the altar. The principal among them were Mellitus, Justus, Paulinus, and Rufinianus.

As they were to pass through Gaul, he gave them letters of recommendation [Col. 0372D] to Queen Brunhild, to the kings, and to the leading bishops of Gaul. In all these letters he calls Mellitus an abbot and the others monks.

[Note: See Book XI, Letters 54, 55, and the seven immediately following.]

These reinforcements of preachers appear to have come from the monastery of Saint Andrew, from which the earlier group had also been taken. This is indicated by the words of the letter to Mellitus the abbot:

> After the departure of our community which is with you, etc. (Book XI, Letter 76.)

This shows how flourishing that Gregorian monastery was.

Through these men the pope sent Augustine everything necessary for divine worship and ecclesiastical ministry: sacred vessels, cloths (*pallia*) for covering and adorning the altars, priestly vestments, relics of martyrs, and many books (Bede, Book I, chapter 29). He added the pallium and a letter in which he congratulated the new apostle on the conversion of the Angles and on the miracles performed by him, while nevertheless urging his disciple to humility and fear concerning the gifts he had received, by setting before him miracles performed by the reprobate (Book XI, Letter 28; Bede, Book I, chapter 31).

### 4

He also wrote to King Æthelberht, giving thanks for the Christian faith which he had received and, like another Constantine, propagated. In that letter he warmly praises Augustine because he had been trained in the monastic rule, was filled with knowledge of sacred Scripture, and, by God’s agency, was endowed with good works. He was therefore worthy for the king to hear when he gave admonition and to obey when he offered counsel (Book XI, Letter 66).

Before that letter to King Æthelberht, Gregory had written to Bertha, his wife, congratulating her because, like another Helena, the mother of the Emperor Constantine, she was inflamed by zeal for the faith and was working for the conversion of the Angles. Yet he subtly reproved her for negligence, since Æthelberht had not yet been turned toward the Christian faith through her care and prudence. Shortly afterward he submitted himself to Christ (ibid., Letter 29).

In addition to the letter sent to Augustine, which we mentioned above (Book I, chapter 29), the venerable Bede presents another in which we read that Augustine was granted the right to wear the pallium and was given authority to ordain twelve bishops who would be subject to his jurisdiction. It was stipulated [Col. 0372C] that thereafter the bishop of London should always be consecrated by his own synod and receive the pallium from the apostolic see (Book XI, Letter 65).

He also decreed that Augustine should ordain the bishop of York, who would thereafter enjoy metropolitan jurisdiction and the honor of the pallium. If the neighboring cities received the word of God, twelve bishops were to be established under him. After Augustine’s death, Gregory—who had wished Augustine to retain the primacy of England for as long as he lived—decreed that among the bishops of London and York the primate should be the one who had been ordained first.

From this letter it may be inferred that the supreme pontiff had initially preferred Augustine to have his see at London rather than at Dorobernia. Later, however, another arrangement seemed preferable, and the first episcopal see of England remained at Dorobernia, or Canterbury.

### 5

Augustine built a monastery near the same city. At his instigation, the king arranged for a church to be built there under the name of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul and endowed it with various gifts. It became the burial place of Augustine himself and thereafter of all the bishops of Dorobernia, as well as of the kings of Kent.

This monastery had as its first abbot Peter, a monk [Col. 0373A] and priest, whom we have already mentioned.

[Note: He was sent to Rome with Laurence. Bede indeed calls him only a priest in the passage indicated; but in chapter 27 of the same book he clearly teaches that he was a monk.]

For an account of his holiness, death, and the miracles performed after his death at his tomb, one should read the venerable writer of the history of the English Church (Bede, Book I, chapter 33).

In the metropolitan Church of Canterbury as well, Saint Augustine observed the coenobitic life with his companions and established it thereafter as an institution, following Gregory’s counsel or command, given in these words:

> Since your fraternity, instructed in the rules of a monastery, ought not to live apart from its clerics in the Church of the Angles, which by God’s agency has recently been brought to the faith, it must establish the way of life that existed among our fathers at the beginning of the nascent Church. None of them claimed as his own anything of what he possessed, but everything was held in common among them. (Book XI, Letter 64.)

I do not deny that these words can equally signify a coenobitic and communal life, such as that of those called regular canons, as well as a monastic life. But the venerable Bede interprets them as referring to a monastic way of life established in the Church of Canterbury, such as was proper for Augustine and his monk-companions; and on this matter he certainly deserves to be heard.

For when that most accurate and learned writer undertook to compose the ecclesiastical history of his people—being nearly contemporary with Saint Augustine or with his disciples, since he began to flourish in the same century in which Augustine laid the foundations of the Christian religion in England and died devoted to that great work—it could not have escaped him what kind of life the most holy man had established in the principal Church of the Angles, whether clerical or monastic.

Let us therefore hear Bede, Book IV of the Ecclesiastical History, chapter 27:

> For indeed Aidan, who was the first bishop of this place, Lindisfarne, came there with monks as a monk himself and established a monastic way of life there, just as the blessed Father Augustine is known previously to have done in Kent. The most blessed pope wrote to him as we have quoted above: “But since your fraternity, instructed in the rules of a monastery, ought not to live apart from its clerics,” etc.

It is therefore evident that those are less trustworthy interpreters of Saint Gregory’s mind who extract from these words the clerical life followed by those commonly called regular canons and claim that it was established by blessed Augustine in the principal Church of the Angles—unless they are willing to admit that monks and those who follow a common life as canons are the same.

### 6

The venerable Bede explains his mind even more clearly in the Life of Saint Cuthbert, chapter 16:

> Nor should anyone be surprised that, although the island of Lindisfarne is very small, we have said that it contains both the bishop’s residence and now the abbot’s and the monks’ place. For this is truly the case. One and the same dwelling of the servants of God contains both together. Indeed, it contains only monks. Aidan, who was the first bishop of that place, was a monk and always accustomed to lead a monastic life with all his companions. For this reason all the bishops of that place, down to the present day, exercise the episcopal office in such a way that, while the monastery is governed by an abbot whom they themselves elect with the advice of the brethren, all the priests, deacons, singers, readers, and other ecclesiastical orders observe in every respect, together with the bishop himself, the monastic rule.

The blessed Pope Gregory showed that he greatly loved this manner of life when, in response to Augustine, whom he had first sent as bishop to the nation of the Angles, asking by letter how bishops ought to conduct themselves with their clerics, he replied among other things:

> But since your fraternity, instructed in the rules of a monastery, ought not to live apart from its clerics in the Church of the Angles, which by God’s agency has recently been brought to the faith, it must establish the way of life that existed among our fathers at the beginning of the nascent Church, etc., as quoted above.

From these words, so clear that they seem almost to come from an eyewitness and an unquestionable witness of faith, it is evident that the Church of Dorobernia, just like Lindisfarne, had only monks as its clergy.

It is therefore astonishing to encounter the invention of a recent writer [Col. 0374B] who, in writing about the order of regular canons (chapter II, articles 1 and following), presents Augustine and his companions as the first example of clerics living communally and according to canonical rule. Unable to find an escape from such explicit testimonies, which prove with the utmost clarity that they were and remained monks, he imagines that they were admitted into the clergy on the condition that they renounce monasticism.

Let us now examine the arguments by which he attempts to support this paradox, although in this discussion we may seem to wander somewhat beyond the limits of Gregory’s history.

## CHAPTER VI

**Summary.—1. Objections drawn from Gregory’s Letters are refuted. 2. A response to another objection. 3. Whether, according to Saint Gregory, a monk promoted to the clerical order is thereafter no longer called a monk. 4. Monks were commonly called clerics in former times. 5. Whether Saint Gregory instituted regular canons. John the Deacon explained. 6. Whether the common life suggests a canon more than a monk. 7. The genuine meaning of the words of John the Deacon adduced in objection is established. Whether all clerics who live according to the canons should be counted among the regular canons. 8. The distinction between secular and regular canons. 9. A new invention concerning the companions of Saint Augustine, allegedly never ordained as monks. 10. Laurence and all the other companions of Saint Augustine were monks. 11. Another fiction concerning the priests of Arles who followed Augustine. 12. Gregory’s response to Augustine explained. 13. The testimony of Urban II examined. 14. The decree of Boniface IV concerning monks performing ecclesiastical duties. 15. His letter concerning the monks serving in the Church of Canterbury, misunderstood by the recent writer.**

### 1

Two letters of Saint Gregory are brought against us. In the first, which is the first letter of Book IV, we read:

> No one can both serve in ecclesiastical offices and remain properly within the monastic rule, etc.

Therefore, says the recent writer, once Augustine’s companions had been admitted into the clergy, they could no longer retain the monastic institutions.

This passage has already been answered many times, both by our Mabillon and by us, in Book II, chapter 12, section 11, and in the notes to this letter, where we explained the genuine meaning of the words. Nevertheless, something further should be added.

We readily admit that monks who serve in certain ecclesiastical offices—such as the continual preaching of the divine word, the administration of the sacraments, the governance of churches, and similar duties—cannot observe with exact strictness every institution of the monastic rule. Gregory signifies this in these words:

> Whoever is compelled to remain daily in the service of the Church cannot observe with exactness all the institutions of the rule with the greatest strictness—in silence, vigils, fasts, and other such matters.

For Gregory, this is what it means to maintain the strictness of the monastery [Col. 0375A]. Thus abbots and other superiors of monasteries, upon whose word and example the vigor of all regular observance depends, cannot at the same time perform ecclesiastical duties and preside over monasteries. Other monks, however, if they take charge of churches and congregations, may be compelled to relax something of the rigor of discipline.

But what prevents the same thing from being said of regular canons—especially those of the more severe and stricter observance, such as still flourishes among the Reformed Premonstratensians—or of their superiors? Will anyone therefore dream that they cannot at the same time perform the office of clerics and devote themselves to ecclesiastical duties unless they first abandon the institution of regular canons?

Perhaps they will answer by making a distinction between two things joined in their institution of regular canons: vows belonging to the essence of their state, and certain pious ascetical practices, such as singing in choir at fixed hours, devoting themselves to reading, prayer, and meditation, taking food in a common refectory, withdrawing from human company and practicing silence, going to bed in the same place and at the same time, and so forth.

They will indeed say that those who devote themselves either to winning souls or to governing them must suffer the loss of these practices, while their vows remain inviolate. But they will provide the same answer for monks who perform the priestly office, thereby offering a solution to the difficulty which they try to derive from Gregory’s earlier testimony.

### 2

Let us now come to the latter passage. The holy Doctor decrees in Book VII, Letter 43:

> If any abbot or monk from any monastery should enter upon the office of the clergy or a sacred order, he shall no longer have there any authority, as we have said.

Therefore, says the recent writer, by the very fact that a monk was ordained to undertake the care of a church, monastic status was removed from him [Col. 0375C].

What an extraordinary inference! As though authority in a monastery and the monastic state were the same thing, when the latter consists rather in obedience and submission than in power and authority. We have already shown the purpose Saint Gregory had in writing this (above, chapter 3, number 9).

But in order to oppose the most certain and incontrovertible arguments to such doubtful—not to say plainly false—claims, let us briefly show, first, that Gregory the Great did not everywhere separate cleric from monk in such a way that anyone whom he once called a cleric should for that reason not be regarded as a monk, which may have been what that writer meant while considering something else; and, second, that monks were commonly called clerics even by the most celebrated writers contemporary with Gregory.

### 3

Saint Augustine was certainly already a cleric and devoted to ecclesiastical—indeed apostolic—duties when the most holy teacher sent him to convert the Angles. It is almost certain that he was then at least a priest or deacon, since Gregory testifies that he was ordained bishop without mentioning the conferral of any other order.

Nevertheless, when writing to Eulogius, Gregory still calls him a monk:

> While the nation of the Angles, situated in a remote corner of the world, remained to that time unbelieving in the worship of wood and stone, it pleased me, with the assistance of your prayers, that by God’s authority I should send to it a monk of my monastery for preaching. After I had granted him permission, he was made a bishop by the bishops of the Germanies. (Book VIII, Letter 30.)

The same must be said of Saint Augustine’s companions and assistants in the conversion of the Angles. Although Saint Gregory sent them to preach and to perform apostolic works, he never ceased to call them monks:

> Since, with the grace of our Redeemer cooperating, so great a multitude from the nation of the Angles is being converted to the grace of the Christian faith that our most reverend common brother and fellow bishop Augustine declares that he and those who are with him cannot suffice to carry out this work in the various places, we have arranged to send him some monks together with our most beloved common sons, Laurence the priest and Mellitus the abbot. (Book XI, Letter 58.)

He repeats the same thing to the point of weariness in the other letters written on this matter (ibid., Letters 54, 55, 56, [Col. 0376B] 57, 59, 60, 61, and 62).

Shortly we shall hear Boniface IV speaking in the same way as his predecessor Gregory, in a letter to King Æthelberht:

> Let the monks, preachers of your salvation, associate with themselves a flock of monks.

Boniface is not ashamed to call those preachers monks—undoubtedly clerics, indeed bishops, priests, and deacons.

### 4

From contemporary writers, Gregory of Tours alone will suffice to show that at that time monks were commonly called clerics. In Book I of *The Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 76, those who were offering praises to God in the monastery of Agaunum are indiscriminately called sometimes clerics and sometimes monks. Gregory says:

> A certain woman, bringing her only son to this monastery, handed him over to the abbot to be educated, namely so that, having become a cleric, he might be dedicated to the holy [Col. 0376C] offices. But when he had already been instructed in spiritual learning and was singing the psalms with the other clerics in the choir, etc.

Here the men of Agaunum are called clerics; but a little farther on they are called monks:

> You will hear his voice among the choirs of the psalm-singing monks.

And shortly afterward:

> When the throng of monks took up the antiphon [lacuna], the mother heard it and recognized the little one’s voice.

Gregory says the same in his *Book of the Miracles of Saint Julian*, chapter 28:

> Now a certain cleric of Aridius, abbot of Limoges, etc.

I pass over much of the narrative, in which he relates that this cleric was miraculously brought into the basilica of Saint Julian. He adds:

> So that no one may doubt this, I call Almighty God to witness that I learned all these things from the mouth of that very abbot, in whose monastery they occurred.

Here you see a monk whom you previously read called a cleric. Conversely, in chapter 35 [Col. 0376D], the man whom he first called a monk he immediately calls a cleric.

Although a monk who had been raised to ecclesiastical responsibilities and dignities might no longer be called a monk, he would nevertheless by no means cease to be one. This is the position maintained by a learned man who was almost a stranger to the reading of Gregory the Great. For since a designation is taken from the more distinguished rank, what wonder is it if someone who has superimposed the episcopate upon monastic status—for example—is no longer called a monk, although he has not laid aside monasticism and continues in monastic practices, vigils, fasts, and prayers?

On the matters we have touched upon only briefly, one should consult our Mabillon, both in the Preface to the Second Century of Benedictine History, no. 27, and in his first reply to the writing of the regular canons concerning their seats in the assemblies of Burgundy [Col. 0377A]; also Hadrian Valesius, in his dissertation on basilicas and in its defense; and Thomassinus, *Ecclesiastical Discipline*, Part I, Book I.

### 5

No one who approaches the arguments of the learned man whose reasoning we are now examining free from every prejudice will deny that he is certainly a great theorist. To set out those arguments is to refute them, as will become clear from what follows. We shall have no difficulty in believing that Gregory the Great instituted regular canons and afterward decreed that clerics from this same institution should occupy the first English Church founded at Canterbury; and finally that the remaining episcopal sees of England likewise passed to canonical clerics.

First, he attempts to prove this from John the Deacon, Book II of the *Life of Saint Gregory*, chapter 12:

> The most religious monks seemed everywhere to cling to the pontiff together with the most learned clerics, and common life was maintained among persons of different professions, so that at that time the Church near the city of Rome under Gregory was such as Luke records it to have been under the apostles, and Philo under Mark the Evangelist near Alexandria.

Here I recognize our Gregory as a devoted adherent of the monastic life and most faithful to his monastic institution. He had monks as his companions, with whom he spent day and night, and, as John says, left nothing of monastic perfection behind in the palace [lacuna]. I also see clerics attached to him who, freely bound by no vows and obligated by no rule, led a common life with the monks.

But concerning an institution of regular canons of which Saint Gregory was the founder, nothing is read here [Col. 0377C], nor anywhere in Gregory’s letters or writings. Are clerics, then, as soon as they share a common life and common sustenance, immediately transformed into regular canons?

“But,” you will say with the learned man, “some poet—I do not know who—mentions canons of the Gregorian order. Therefore Gregory the Great instituted the order of regular canons. And why,” he says, “should we not, as a mark of honor, call them Gregorian canons?”

Far be it from us to call pious and religious men “canons of the Gregorian order” in the sense in which that poet speaks of those whom he reports to have been expelled from the monastery of Saint Walaric in these words:

> Duke Hugh, soon emptying the church of the Gregorian order,  
> Established the standard monastic rule.

For from the historical account of Saint Walaric we learn (Mabillon, Fifth Century) that those canons were secular:

> Then the aforesaid Duke [264], taking great care to provide for the place of Saint Walaric, expelled the secular congregation from it and established there a regular order of monks.

Thus writes a near-contemporary author, who could not have been unaware of who and what sort of men those canons were, cast out like foolish salt. Perhaps they were called of the Gregorian order because in their psalmody they followed the Roman order arranged by Gregory—not the monastic order prescribed by Saint Benedict—and because they were later succeeded in the church of Saint Walaric by Benedictine monks, who observed that order.

### 6

This is where the man inflamed by excessive zeal for his own order goes astray: whenever he encounters mention of common life according to the practice of the earlier and apostolic Church [Col. 0378A], he draws it into his proof of the institution of regular canons. He fails to observe that the coenobitic and common life of monks was also prescribed according to the pattern and norm of that earlier Church instituted by the apostles, and that in nearly all monastic rules the example of that ancient Church of Jerusalem under the apostles is brought forward:

> Let all things be common to all, says Saint Benedict, as it is written (Acts 4), and let no one call or presume anything to be his own.

And in chapter 34:

> If all are to receive necessities equally. As it is written: It was distributed to each according to his need.

In this respect nearly all the founders of monastic rules agree with Saint Benedict, as may be seen in the *Concordance of Rules*, by Saint Benedict, abbot of Aniane, chapters [Col. 0378B] 42 and 43. Monks therefore have a stronger right to claim for themselves the ancient testimonies concerning coenobitic and common life.

As for the Church of Alexandria, which flourished most brilliantly in holiness under Saint Mark, most of the ancient writers who dealt with monastic matters judged that it—and the communities of the *Therapeutae* mentioned by John the Deacon—provided a model of the organization and condition of monks, not of canons.

### 7

Having refuted the false and fabricated meaning attributed to the words of John the Deacon, let us now disclose their sincere and genuine sense. Saint Gregory, who had lived with monks as companions when he served as *apocrisiarius* at Constantinople, so that by their example he might always be drawn back, as though by an anchor-rope, to the calm shore of prayer (*Preface to the Morals*), wished to have those same men as his household companions after he had been unwillingly elevated to the pontificate and had converted his palace, as it were, into a monastery. Certain chosen monks sat familiarly at his side.

John the Deacon lists six monks distinguished for piety and holiness. He also names four clerics conspicuous for prudence and learning, whose assistance and counsel Gregory employed both in the affairs of the Church and in his studies. Moreover, after removing all secular persons from his bedchamber—a measure which the Roman synod later decreed should also be observed by future pontiffs [*Decretals*, 1], on his initiative—he summoned certain clerics and monks indiscriminately to serve him.

John the Deacon admired the unanimity of all these men, though they belonged to different professions, and their shared and common life. He therefore did not hesitate to say that in this fellowship and harmony the Churches founded by the apostles at Jerusalem and by Saint Mark at Alexandria seemed to have returned to life.

As for regular canons instituted by Gregory, he did not even think of them in a dream, since there were none either in Saint Gregory’s time or in John’s. Nor should all clerics who ordered their conduct according to the canons and rules of the Church be counted among them, although it is clear that such clerics existed from the beginning, unless they had been bound by vows.

Indeed, from the eleventh century onward there is frequent mention, in Fulbert, Bernard, Peter of Blois, and other contemporary writers [Col. 0379A], of regular canons who, living in the manner of monks and bound by nearly the same vows, obeyed their abbots or provosts and lived under strict discipline. We know the origins of abbeys and other monasteries then built for such canons, as well as the transformations of already existing establishments that were transferred to them. Several provostships of the Order of Saint Benedict were granted to them, among which the celebrated monastery of Saint Victor at Paris is especially notable. Before that century, however, nothing of the kind is found.

For the canons of Aachen, or those who followed the rule of Chrodegang, and likewise those subject to the rules of Eugenius II and Leo IV, not only lived free from religious and solemn vows, but, according to the prescriptions of their rules, possessed some private property and personal funds [Note: [Col. 0379D] Pages 34, 305, 312, 313, 325.], as the very advocate of regular canons whom we are refuting admits. But even this retention of private property, by the institution of the rule itself, is so contrary to the condition of a regular canon [Col. 0379B] that it overturns it and makes him secular. (Cf. *Gallia Christiana*, Alberic, under the year 1029.)

### 8

I know well that the author of the *Disquisitions* acknowledges very little distinction between a secular and a regular canon. I read with no small astonishment in chapter 1, article 2, page 8:

> Whoever remembers that in the eleventh and twelfth centuries Benedictine monks were distributed into the Cluniac, Tyronian, and Major Monastery orders, as well as many others, will easily understand how at that time the order of regular canons and the order of secular canons could be distinguished and separated from one another, although both ought to have been of one and the same kind.

From this he infers:

> But neither will any learned person, upon seeing regions rich in secular canons that long lacked regular canons, derive anything from this toward charging regular canons with novelty. Otherwise, by a similar argument, he would have to conclude that the beginnings of the Benedictine order must be derived from the Cluniac or similar monks.

Thus, according to the mind of the recent writer, there is no greater distinction between regular and secular canons within the canonical order than there is among the Cluniac, Tyronian, and other monks within the Benedictine order. Since all these monks followed the same rule of Saint Benedict and were bound by the same law of vows, they could differ, he says, only in the minutest rites and only accidentally. It follows that nothing separates a regular canon from a secular canon in essence; vows and institutions of religious life do not belong to that essence, but must be relegated among indifferent matters and constitute only the slightest difference.

At this I confess that I was alarmed. Unless the known piety of the writer and his associates had reassured me, I would have greatly feared that they might be preparing for themselves a defection and transition to the secular canons, whom the author of the *Disquisitions* presents as so close to regular canons and separated from them by scarcely the slightest difference. I would rather believe that these words escaped him carelessly and without consulting the most religious superiors of his congregation than press the matter further.

Setting this aside, after having clearly proved that the writer’s account of regular canons formed by Gregory the Great in the Roman Church is entirely fictitious, let us examine [265] whether he judged more accurately when he asserts that, by order of the most holy pontiff, those same canons were instituted in the Church of Canterbury.

### 9

First, he imagines that among the monks selected to bring about the conversion of the English, Saint Gregory designated or intended to designate no one for ordination except Augustine:

> Gregory had not yet, it seems, been thinking of the ordination of monks; he had arranged only for Augustine to be ordained bishop, if the English accepted them (Book XI, Letter 58 and following).

Therefore, according to him, Gregory sent them not for the preaching of the divine word or for sacred ministry—which he himself everywhere insists upon [Note: [Col. 0379D] See above and below, §§ 14 and 15], with Bede, Boniface IV, the author of the *Life of Saint Augustine*, and others agreeing—but perhaps to plant vegetables or attend to the kitchen. For what sensible person would think of sending laymen, who were never to be ordained, to apostolic work, especially when there was an abundance of sacred ministers?

I do not deny that Gregory selected Augustine alone for episcopal dignity at that time, while the outcome was still uncertain. But concerning the other orders, whether not yet conferred or never to be conferred upon Augustine’s companions, there is everywhere profound silence. Indeed, of the monastic assistants of his whom we know, nearly all were bishops, such as Mellitus of London and Justus of Rochester. On this matter Bede should be consulted.

### 10

Second, the advocate of regular canons is pleased to remove Laurence the priest, one of Augustine’s companions, from the number and class of monks and to claim him for his own order. But by what right, when Saint Gregory, Bede, and others who speak of them all call them monks? Is it because he was a priest? As though at that time there had been no priests in monasteries, contrary to the proof supplied by so many of Saint Gregory’s letters [Note: [Col. 0380D] See especially Book VI, Letter 56].

Gotselinus says in the *Life of Saint Augustine* that Augustine and his fellow ministers had been torn from the maternal womb of the monastic Church. He adds that the number of those soldiers of the Lord’s mission was about forty, precisely the number whom Bede says landed on the Isle of Thanet. Thus no place remains for non-monastic priests taken either from Italy or from Gaul—not even for the priests of Arles, whom the author of the *Disquisitions* most generously assigns to his own order, imagining that the canonical religion was brought by them to the English Church.

The pope had indeed instructed Augustine and his companions to bring priests with them from the neighboring region for the performance of these duties. But perhaps no one was found who was ready for this mission and pilgrimage. For Bede teaches (Book I, chapter 25) that they obtained interpreters from the Frankish nation, yet he says nothing at all about priests being taken along. If this had happened, he would not have concealed it.
