Add to this that Augustine was compelled to summon new preachers of the divine word from the Roman monastery of Saint Andrew, doubtless because he had found little assistance in Gaul.

### 11

Even if some priests from Arles did follow them, why should we not say that they were also monks, perhaps among those priests of the monastery of Lérins whom Saint Gregory praises? To prevent diversity of profession from generating any discord, as often happens, in this holy company, the bishop Virgilius of Arles ought to have joined monks with monks, especially since he himself had been a monk of Lérins, as had many of his predecessors (Book VI, Letter 56).

Let us also grant that some priests who were in no way bound by monastic laws were associated with Augustine. What will the learned man infer from this toward proving the institution of regular canons in the Church of Canterbury? Does he imagine that all clerics and priests of those times belonged to his order?

The single testimony of the venerable Bede quoted above would remove the whole difficulty, if any existed. He alone transmitted to us Saint Gregory’s response to Augustine’s questions concerning the common life to be maintained in the Church of Canterbury, and he is therefore its legitimate interpreter. But he understood Gregory’s words as referring to the coenobitic life of monks.

Nor could that most diligent and learned writer, almost a contemporary of the events, have been unaware of who and what sort of men had served God from the beginning in this Church, the principal Church of the entire English nation: clerics or regular canons, or monks. Even today we know which cathedral churches, although they passed to secular canons three hundred years ago, had formerly been occupied either by regular canons or by monks.

Who, then, except rashly, would believe that a man distinguished for holiness wished to invent the claim that no clergy other than monks had existed in the Church of Canterbury? Anyone born in England could easily have refuted such a falsehood.

### 12

To gather together more fully what has already been said, and to interpret in light of it Saint Gregory’s response to Augustine’s question [Note: [Col. 0381D] See above, chapter 5, § 5]—for the resolution of this controversy depends upon understanding that response—we may proceed as follows.

First, Saint Gregory wishes his disciple to remember the monastic life that he professed at Rome in the monastery of Saint Andrew:

> Since your Fraternity, instructed in the rules of a monastery, etc.

Second, he urges Augustine to lead a coenobitic and common life with his clerics:

> He must not live separately from his clerics.

By “clerics” are meant both the monks assigned to him as assistants in preaching and called to share his labor, and also the younger clerics whom they instructed, as administrators and superintendents of an episcopal seminary.

Third, Gregory provides for the sustenance of those clerics who, since they had not been constituted in sacred orders, were permitted to marry:

> If there are clerics outside the sacred orders who cannot remain continent, they should take wives and receive their stipends externally.

### 13

Against all these arguments—indeed, demonstrations—we are offered only one testimony, that of Urban II. It is certainly weighty, and the Benedictines should be all the less inclined to reject it because Urban himself had been raised to the supreme pontificate from the family of Saint Benedict.

In a certain letter addressed to regular canons, Urban testifies that Gregory had ordered a canonical life to be instituted for Augustine, archbishop of the English. This must undoubtedly refer to the time when Gregory wrote to Augustine instructing him to live in common with his clerics.

Whatever may be said about this letter, to which the compilers of the councils did not grant a place even in the appendix to the letters of Urban II [Col. 0382A], I reply that these words merely signify that Saint Gregory, in his response to Augustine, anticipated the institution of regular canons. In the same way, as we read in that same letter of Urban [266], the apostles are said to have laid the foundations of the discipline of regular canons by establishing that all things should be held in common in the Church of Jerusalem; and Pope Urban, a martyr, is likewise said in his decrees—although all learned men regard those decrees as spurious—to have previously outlined that discipline.

For, plainly, what Saint Luke writes about the Church of Jerusalem cannot properly be understood as referring to the institution of regular canons. Besides the apostles and disciples, and besides clerics, that Church included married laymen, widows, and women of every age and condition.

Indeed, not a few ancient writers, including authors of no mean standing [Col. 0382B], judged that the institution of the monastic life should be traced back to Elijah, John the Baptist, and the apostles. Cassian teaches in Book I of the *Institutes*, chapter 2, that Elijah and Elisha founded the beginnings of this profession. Jerome makes the same assertion in Letter 13 to Paulinus:

> John the Baptist is the prince of monks,

says Chrysostom in Homily 1 on Mark, and Sozomen supports him in Book I of his *History*, chapter 12.

Bernard commends the monastic order in his *Apology to William, Abbot*, because it was the first in the Church, indeed because the Church began from it; no order on earth is more like the angelic orders; its founders were the apostles, and its initiators were those whom Paul so often calls saints.

Bernard confirms this by adducing Luke’s testimony in Acts 4 concerning the common life observed by Christ’s first disciples. We could produce countless passages from the holy Fathers and also from councils that convey the same meaning.

Yet we do not therefore assert that the apostles ever thought of instituting monks, nor do we flatter ourselves with such founders. We say only that monastic and coenobitic life was prefigured in their examples and institutions. This is what the writers cited above intended to signify when, in commending monks, they declared that monks had proceeded from the apostles and derived their origin from them.

The same explanation must be given to what Urban II and others said about canons whom they saw following the coenobitic life and imitating monks. Everything that the learned man derives from this for establishing their antiquity therefore collapses completely.

From what has been said, it is entirely clear that in the Church of Canterbury, from its very beginning, monks alone served, not mere clerics. Hence one may turn the argument against our opponent:

> If I rightly assign this one see to canonical clerics,

he says—where I would say, “to monks”—

> I shall not unjustly conclude that the remaining episcopal sees of England likewise came to canonical clerics,

where I would say, “to monastic clerics.”

### 14

The monks’ outstanding authority in ecclesiastical ministry had aroused the opposition of their rivals. Mellitus, one of Augustine’s companions and bishop of London, therefore went to Rome to discuss the necessary affairs of the English Church with the apostolic pope Boniface.

When the same most reverend pope convened a synod of the bishops of Italy to establish regulations concerning the life and repose of monks, Mellitus himself sat among them [Col. 0383A]. Returning to Britain, he brought with him the commands and observances intended for the Church of the English, together with the letters that the same pontiff sent to Laurence, the beloved archbishop of God, to the entire clergy, and likewise to King Æthelberht and the English people (Bede, Book II of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 4).

Among the commands mentioned, the most celebrated is the Decree that begins:

> There are some who, supported by no doctrine—or, according to another reading, “some foolish men of no doctrine”—are inflamed more by the zeal of bitterness than by love, asserting that monks, because they are dead to the world and live for God, are unworthy of the power of priestly office—or, according to another reading, “of priestly office,” etc.

The supreme pontiff refutes them, especially by the examples of Gregory the Great and his disciple Augustine, who, although monks, shone with pontifical dignity. He adds:

> Nor was Benedict, the teacher of monks, in any way a prohibitor of this matter.

### 15

We possess the letter to King Æthelberht mentioned by Bede in the latest collection of councils. It will be sufficient to transcribe from it what bears upon our subject:

> Therefore, glorious son, what you requested from the Apostolic See through our fellow bishop Mellitus we willingly grant: namely, that your Benevolence may freely establish, in the monastery situated in the city of Canterbury, which your holy teacher Augustine, the disciple of Gregory of blessed memory, consecrated in the name of the holy Savior, and over which our most beloved brother Laurence is at present known to preside, a dwelling for monks living according to a rule in every respect; and we decree by apostolic authority that the monks who preach your salvation should associate with themselves a community of monks [Ibid.].

From this it is clear that the metropolitan Church of the Holy Savior was called a monastery from the beginning because monks inhabited it. The supreme pontiff not only acknowledged that this Church had been entrusted to monks; by apostolic authority he also decreed that the monk-preachers should associate other monks with themselves, through whom the monastic institution might be transmitted to later generations.

We therefore do not contend that monks were admitted to the Church of Christ at Canterbury by the letters of Boniface, as the advocate of regular canons seems to believe, but that they were confirmed and defended in possession of that Church by the authority of the same pope.

I would almost call the advocate of this hopeless cause a dreamer when he imagines that, with Boniface’s consent or decree, monks were added to the regular canons so that they might complete the daily psalmody, while the clerics whom public utility summoned elsewhere freely performed every ecclesiastical function.

This is plainly nonsense, as though the earlier preachers and inhabitants of this Church had not been called monks by Boniface, but clerics; or as though, after all that we have said, any trace appeared of non-monastic clerics received into the Church of Canterbury from the beginning.

## 267 Chapter VII

**Argument.**—1. The monks of England were Benedictines from the beginning. Thus what has already been said concerning Saint Gregory’s adherence to the laws of Saint Benedict is confirmed.—2. The first argument from Aldhelm.—3. The second from the contemporary author of the Life of Saint Wilfrid.—4. The third argument from ancient litanies in which the name of Saint Benedict is inserted.—5. The silence of the Synod of Clovesho is wrongly brought against us.—6. Likewise the silence of the venerable Bede.—7. Another argument from the Rule of Saint Benedict, brought to Germany by English monks.—8. The opinion of the Bollandist associates on this matter.—9. Maresham, holding another view, is refuted.

### 1

The name of Saint Benedict, mentioned by the supreme pontiff Boniface together with the title “teacher of monks,” precisely where the tranquility of the English monks was chiefly at issue, gives us no obscure grounds for conjecturing that the monks of England were then Benedictines—whether they were surviving companions of Augustine or those whom they admitted to their own congregation after legitimate probation.

But what need is there for conjecture where so many demonstrations are available? The arguments gathered by the most learned Mabillon deserve this name: in the Preface to the First Century of Benedictine History, § 8; in the preliminary observations to the Life of Saint Wilfrid, Part I of the Fourth Century of Benedictine History; in Volume II of the *Analecta*, in the dissertation on Saint Gregory’s monastic life, Part II, § 8, page 173 and following; and finally in Book X of the *Benedictine Annals*, § 18, and Appendix I, page 655 and following.

It will be sufficient for our purpose to touch upon the principal points. It will follow from them, as we have already said (Book I, chapter 3, §§ 3–10), that Saint Gregory observed the Benedictine Rule and commended its observance to his own people.

### 2

The first argument is drawn from the indisputable testimony of Saint Aldhelm. Initially educated by Hadrian, abbot of the monastery of Saint Peter at Canterbury, Aldhelm later became a monk and abbot in the monastery of Mailduberi, or Malmesbury, among the West Saxons, of whom he was also bishop. In his poem *On Virginity*, he designates Saint Benedict with this eulogy:

> The first who established the contests of our life,  
> How monasteries might keep the desired rule,  
> And by what straight path the holy worshiper  
> Might hasten upward, climbing the heights of heaven,  
> Whose illustrious life, unfolding from its origin,  
> Gregory the bishop once described in writing.

Here Saint Aldhelm, plainly a monk and abbot who flourished in the same century in which Saint Augustine and his companions brought the English to the Christian faith—he died, according to Bede, only in the year 709—openly testifies that Benedict was the first founder of the monastic life which he himself had professed and which the English monasteries observed.

### 3

The second argument is supplied by the contemporary author of the Life of Saint Wilfrid, Eddius Stephanus. In his account, Saint Wilfrid speaks as follows to the synod assembled on his behalf:

> Did not I—or, according to another reading, “And I”—first, after the death of the first leaders directed by Saint Gregory, take care to uproot the shoots of the poisonous Scottish planting [lacuna], and to establish the life of monks according to the Rule of Saint Benedict the Father, which no predecessor had introduced? (Fourth Century of Benedictine History, Part I, Appendix.)

This refers to the people beyond the Humber. For the following words of Eddius, chapter 14, prove that the Rule of Saint Benedict had already been received in the kingdom of Kent and that Saint Wilfrid brought it from there to establish or restore the monasteries of Northumbria:

> King Ecgberht of Kent, a religious man, also summoned our bishop to him, and there he ordained many priests [lacuna] beloved by all, performing episcopal duties over a long period. Returning to his own region with the singers Ædde and Æona and the builders [lacuna], he greatly improved the institutions of the Churches through the Rule of Benedict.

### 4

The third argument is drawn from the ancient English litanies. The most learned Mabillon proves that they were composed at least a thousand years ago and before the eighth century, both from the characters of a very ancient semi-Saxon manuscript and, above all, because no saint who lived later than the middle of the seventh century is invoked or mentioned in them.

Mellitus, Paulinus, Cuthbert, Wilfrid, Aidan, and many others—far more illustrious in the holiness of their lives and learning than many of those listed in the series of blessed persons in the litanies—are absent. They certainly would not have been omitted if they had already died and their holiness had become established, as it did later in the eighth century.

In these litanies the name of Saint Benedict is invoked twice after Saint Jerome and before Saints Hilary and Martin. This is an extremely strong argument that Benedict occupied the place of a patron among those who used such litanies. Otherwise, why would he alone be mentioned, while Pachomius, Antony, Basil, and Columban were omitted? Why would he be invoked twice, a privilege granted to no other except Saint Stephen and Saint Mary, who is named three times?

Moreover, that these litanies were in use in England, indeed composed for England, is proved by this supplication:

> That you may deign to preserve the clergy and people of the English, we beseech you, hear us.

No other nation is mentioned.

### 5

When these matters are weighed impartially, the silence of the Synod of Clovesho [Col. 0385C] and of the venerable Bede concerning the Rule of Saint Benedict—which was once brought against us by our opponents—could do our cause no harm, even if neither Saint Benedict nor a rule promulgated by him were mentioned in those sources.

But even this objection cannot be made. For the Synod of Clovesho reads:

> It was decreed in the twenty-fourth chapter that if any secular person desires to undertake the service of the holy profession, he should not receive the habit of the tonsure until his conduct and character have been more clearly tested according to the definition of the monastic rule, in accordance with the apostolic precept: “Test the spirits, whether they are from God”; unless some reasonable cause properly persuades that he should be received into the congregation earlier.

I ask: in the middle of the eighth century, when the Council of Clovesho was held [268], what monastic rule was so celebrated that it could be designated simply and without addition by the name “the monastic Rule,” except the Rule of Saint Benedict? In chapter 58 of that Rule we read:

> When a newcomer comes for conversion, he is not to be granted an easy entrance (1 John 4), but, as the Apostle says, “Test the spirits, whether they are from God.”

Then, after all the prescriptions concerning the testing and reception of novices, it adds:

> And from that day onward he shall be counted as a member of the congregation.

Nor should it be passed over in silence that in both contexts Saint John is ordinarily called simply “the Apostle,” a title customarily attributed only to Paul. Hence, even if other arguments were lacking, one might suspect that the Synod of Clovesho, by praising John under the title “the Apostle,” was following the usage of Saint Benedict.

### 6

As for the venerable Bede, in Book I of the *History of the Abbots of Wearmouth and Jarrow*, which he himself published, we read that Saint Benedict Biscop undertook his fourth journey to Rome after arranging the monastery according to a Rule.

[Note: [Col. 0385] This history, mentioned by William of Malmesbury, Book I, chapter 3, was first published by Sir James Ware at Dublin in 1664.]

What rule could he mean other than the Benedictine Rule, since no other rule was widely propagated in the West? Bede later identifies this very rule clearly when, at the end of Book I, he reports these words of his abbot, spoken in his final exhortation to the disciples:

> Take great care, brothers, not to seek a father for yourselves from elsewhere outside; but, according to what the rule of the great abbot Benedict once laid down, and according to what the decrees of your privilege prescribe, seek within the assembly of your congregation, by common counsel, the man who, according to the merit of his life and the teaching of his wisdom, is judged more suitable and more worthy to carry out such a ministry.

These are the qualities that the Rule of Saint Benedict demands in the election of an abbot in chapter 64.

Abbot Ceolfrith, the successor of Biscop, gave the same instruction to his brothers when he was about to cross the sea. Bede, a monk of that same congregation, says in Book II:

> He judged it more useful, after giving the brothers this instruction, that according to the statutes of his privilege and according to the rule of Saint Benedict the Abbot, they should choose from among themselves as father the man who was more suitable.

Since this same venerable writer says in Book I that Biscop handed down to his disciples the rule that he had found in the seventeen monasteries he had visited—including the monastery of Saint Peter at Canterbury—it is perfectly clear that the Rule of Saint Benedict had been received and was flourishing in the monasteries of England long before Biscop himself.

7. An argument no less powerful is drawn from the spread of the Benedictine Rule in Germany and the neighboring northern regions, through the agency of St. Boniface and other monks who came from England to disseminate the Christian faith. These men founded very many monasteries, among them especially the monastery of Fulda, renowned throughout all Europe, not merely Germany; and no one denies that Benedictine observances flourished there from the beginning. For whatever these heralds of the sacred word had received from their forebears Augustine and his companions—the disciples of Gregory the Great and alumni of the Roman monastery—they handed down for observance in the monasteries they established, and they persevered until death in following its prescriptions exactly. To this subject must be referred what we said in Book I, chapter 3, about the Rule of St. Benedict being adopted in the Roman monastery of St. Andrew and observed by St. Gregory himself.

8. Overcome by these arguments, the Bollandist scholars, who had formerly followed the contrary opinion, finally admitted of their own accord that the Benedictines could, with the greatest probability and almost with certainty, count Augustine and his companions among their own members. If they had happened to see the celebrated work of Eddius on the life of St. Wilfrid mentioned above—for our Mabillon had not yet brought it out of darkness when these learned men wrote—they would have assigned St. Augustine, the apostle of the English, and his companions to the Benedictine family without any doubt or hesitation.

9. John Maresham, however, thinks otherwise in the preface to the *Monasticum Anglicanum*. Although he admits that the Rule of St. Benedict was once held in the highest reverence among the English, he nevertheless argues that it was adopted in English monasteries only from the year 965 onward, on account of the silence concerning this Rule in the Council of Clovesho and in the venerable Bede. But we have already sufficiently refuted these negative arguments, producing from both the Council just mentioned and the venerable writer unambiguous testimonies concerning the Benedictine Rule. In another respect Maresham departs wholly from historical truth when he asserts that the Rule of St. Benedict was unknown to English monasteries before the tenth century. How recklessly this is said is shown by John the Deacon alone, in Book IV, chapter 82 of the *Life of St. Gregory*:

> That the monks who were sent by Gregory to Saxony—that is, overseas, or England—were bound to the Rule of St. Benedict is also shown by this among other things: among his disciples it is scarcely possible to find in those regions a monk by whom the Rule of St. Benedict is not observed both in profession and in habit.

John the Deacon wrote in the ninth century, almost a hundred years before the Council of Winchester held in 965, at which, according to Maresham, the question of admitting the Rule of St. Benedict into English monasteries was considered. Already at that time the Rule of St. Benedict had so universally prevailed in the monasteries of England that scarcely a single monk could be found throughout the whole of England who did not observe the laws of St. Benedict. Nor will anyone who reads without negligence the testimonies cited above from Aldhelm, Bede, Eddius, and the Council of Clovesho suspect that John, the writer of the *Life of St. Gregory*, made this assertion lightly. Moreover, it is clear that, in writing about the deeds of St. Gregory and especially about the English Church founded, governed, and propagated by his disciples, John had acquired more than a superficial knowledge of English affairs. He therefore could not have been ignorant of the laws by which the monasteries of England were bound. But enough on this subject, especially since the most learned Mabillon has dealt with it. Let us now return to St. Gregory, rejoicing over the English converted to the Lord and deeply concerned for their salvation.

## CHAPTER VIII

**SUMMARY.**—1. St. Gregory redirects to others the praises due to him for the conversion of the English. —2. How greatly religion was then flourishing in England. —3. Certain concessions granted by the pope to the newly converted. —4. He orders the temples of idols to be consecrated according to Christian worship. —5. What feasts and communal banquets he permitted to the neophytes. —6. Augustine unsuccessfully invites the dissident Britons to peace. They pay the penalty for their obstinacy. The death of Augustine and the sacred cult paid him after death. —7. How much his successors labored to reconcile the Britons and the Scots. —8. Persecution rages against the Christian English. It is finally calmed. —9. The Britons accept the doctrine and rites of the Roman Church. A prayer for the conversion of the English of our own day.

### 1.

When Gregory received reports of the successful daily progress of the English mission carried out by Augustine and his brothers, he urged his friends by letter to give thanks to God for so great a benefit. To St. Eulogius, from whom he had recently received joyful news of the conversion of heretics and the harmony of Catholics, he writes as follows:

> Since I truly know that in the good works which you perform you rejoice with others also, I return thanks to you in turn, and announce something similar: while the race of the English, situated in a remote corner of the world, had until now remained faithless in the worship of wood and stone, it pleased God, with the assistance of your prayer, that I should send to them, for the preaching of the faith, a monk from my monastery. (Book VIII, Letter 30.)

He then relates how Augustine and his companions shone among the English through how many and how great miracles, so that in the signs they displayed they seemed to imitate the powers of the apostles.

> I have related this, he says, so that you may know what you accomplish by speaking among the Alexandrian people and what you accomplish by praying at the ends of the world. For your prayers are present in that place where you are not, and your holy works are displayed in the place where you are.

Thus the humble pontiff tried to divert to others the praises due to him for so great a work, and to assign them to anyone else rather than himself.

### 2.

In the following words he expresses how greatly Christian religion was then flourishing in Britain:

> Behold, the tongue of Britain, which knew nothing except to utter barbarous cries, has for a long time now begun to resound with the Hebrew *Alleluia* in divine praises. Behold, the Ocean, once swollen with pride, now lies prostrate and serves at the feet of the saints; and its barbarous waves, which earthly rulers could not tame with the sword, the mouths of priests restrain with simple words because of divine fear. The one who, while unbelieving, had in no way feared crowds of combatants now, as a believer, fears the tongues of the humble. For, having received heavenly words and with miracles also shining forth, the power of divine knowledge is poured into him; he is restrained by fear of that same divinity, so that he fears to do what is wrong and longs with all his desires to attain the grace of eternity. (*Moralia*, Book XXVII, no. 21.)

### 3.

Nevertheless, he granted certain concessions for the benefit of the neophytes which the laws received in the Church from ancient times prohibited, especially concerning marriage within certain degrees of consanguinity and affinity. He did this so that those newly born into Christ might gradually become accustomed to Christ’s yoke, and so that harsher measures might not force the English people to withdraw from the faith they had embraced (Book XI, Letter 64). He himself gives this reason for the concession in his reply to Felix, bishop of Messana, who had almost reproached him concerning this relaxation of the sacred law (Book XIV, final letter). Thus, having acquired the highest authority in the Church, the most prudent of pontiffs knew how, when it seemed expedient, both to tighten the reins and to loosen them.

### 4.

He had first decreed that the temples of idols should be destroyed, and he had also written to Æthelberht about this (Book XI, Letter 66). But after changing his mind, he thought it better, once the idols had been destroyed and removed, to purify the temples by sprinkling them with blessed water and to consecrate them according to Christian worship, so that the English, newly called to the faith, might more readily gather at their accustomed places (ibid., Letter 76).

### 5.

It was the custom of the pagans, when they offered sacrifices with their idols, to kill oxen and feast upon them. In order to transfer this practice to a pious solemnity, the most holy pope agreed that, on the day of the dedication of a church or on the feast day of the holy martyrs whose relics had been placed in the new churches, the newly Christian English should make shelters for themselves from branches of trees around those same churches, which had been converted from pagan shrines, and celebrate the solemnity with religious banquets.

> For it is undoubtedly impossible, he says, to cut away everything at once from hard minds. Someone who strives to climb to the highest place must necessarily be raised by steps or paces, not by leaps. (Book XI, Letter 76.)

We read that St. Gregory, surnamed Thaumaturgus, once used the same pious prudence toward neophytes, as the other Gregory, called of Nyssa, relates in his life. We have judged this worth noting so that our Gregory may not appear, by granting and readily allowing these things to pagans recently converted to the Christian faith, to have experienced something merely human or to have thought according to the flesh.

Here we have brought together in one continuous account all that was accomplished through the efforts of St. Gregory for the conversion of the English and for the establishment of the nascent English Church, even though the events occurred in different years. It is worthwhile briefly to sketch and place before the reader’s eyes what followed these auspicious beginnings.

### 6.

Although Augustine had nothing more at heart than to lead the English to the Christian faith, he was also concerned to recall the ancient Britons, the inhabitants of the island, to unity with the Roman Church, from which some of them differed in their rites. For this purpose he convened a council once and again. When they resisted, although he had confirmed by a miracle what he had proclaimed in words, the man of God is said to have foretold with a threat that, if they refused to accept peace with their brothers, they would receive war from their enemies (Bede, Book II, chapter 2).

Nor was the prophecy without its fulfillment. For Æthelfrith, the most powerful king of the Northumbrians, after Augustine’s death, defeated the Britons with a great slaughter. He did not spare the priests who had gathered in large numbers, especially from the monastery of Bangor,

> **[Note:]** It was situated in the province of Wales in England and must be distinguished from another monastery of the same name situated in Ulster, a province of Ireland, which St. Bernard seems to mention in the *Life of St. Malachy*, chapter 6.

in which there is said to have been so great a number of monks that, when it was divided into seven sections with their respective superiors, none of the sections contained fewer than three hundred men, all of whom used to live by the work of their hands (ibid.).

Some among the heterodox have tried to burden Augustine with blame for this slaughter, as though he had prompted Æthelfrith to wage war against the Britons (Spelman, vol. I, *Councils of England*, p. 93). But nothing of the kind is found in Bede or in the other ancient writers. Indeed, the venerable Bede explicitly teaches that they were slain only after Augustine had long since been taken up into the heavenly kingdom. Alfred omitted these words in his Saxon translation, but all the Latin copies preserve them.

Augustine passed to heaven in the year 607, on 26 May. That day was made a holiday among the English by this decree of the Council of Clovesho, held in 747:

> The seventeenth decree established that the birthday of the blessed pope Gregory, and also the day of the deposition—which is the seventh day before the Kalends of June—of St. Augustine, archbishop and confessor, who was sent to the English people by the aforementioned pope and first brought them knowledge of the faith, the sacrament of baptism, and knowledge of the heavenly homeland, should all be honored reverently, as is fitting. Thus both days are to be kept as holidays by churches and monasteries, and the name of that blessed Father and our Teacher Augustine is always to be recited in the singing of the Litany after the invocation of St. Gregory.

### 7.

After Augustine had been called to heaven, the bishops whom he had ordained—Mellitus of London, Justus of Rochester [Note: He is called Rochester in Bede, and that name is still retained.], and Laurence, his successor in the see of Canterbury—labored very earnestly to recall both the Britons and the Scots, the inhabitants of the island of Ireland, from schism. They wrote letters to them breathing Christian charity and humility.

The letter sent to the Scots, or Irish, bore the following address, which Bede reports:

> To our most beloved lords, brothers, bishops or abbots throughout all Scotland.

Here bishops and abbots appear to have been one and the same.

### 8.

The most vigilant bishops labored no less for the progress and growth of the new Church. But after the deaths of King Æthelberht and Sabereth, the son of his sister, who had zealously cultivated and upheld the Christian faith, such a serious war broke out against the English Church, with their successors persecuting the faithful, that Mellitus and Justus were forced to cross into Gaul. Laurence was preparing shortly to follow them, had he not been deterred by the most severe rebuke and harsher scourging from the apostle Peter.

He therefore went to King Eadbald, showed him the wounds inflicted upon him, and brought him to renounce idolatry and embrace the Christian faith, which Eadbald afterward sincerely favored in all things. The sons of Sabereth, who had rejected Mellitus and the Gospel he preached, paid the penalty for their rebellion: they were killed with their entire army in battle against the people of the Genissae. Mellitus and Justus were therefore recalled from Gaul by Laurence and returned to the work of preaching that had been interrupted. Bede gives a fuller account of these events. (See Bede, Book II, chapter 6.)

### 9.

After St. Laurence had died, both from his apostolic labors and from life itself, Mellitus was appointed his successor; Justus later succeeded Mellitus; Honorius succeeded Justus. After Honorius came Deusdedit, and after him Theodore, sent by Pope Vitalian. Theodore finally brought the Britons successfully to accept all the rites of the Roman Church.

Here we think we should stop, so that our account may return to the deeds of St. Gregory. Let the descendants of the English recall what we have collected concerning the conversion of the English. Let them question St. Gregory, the father of their faith, and he will declare it to them; let them question Augustine and his fellow-monks, and they will tell them what faith they embraced from the beginning, how great a reverence and obedience they showed toward the apostolic see, what sacraments they once used, and what rites they employed in the worship of God.

Alas! The heterodox have destroyed the altars which those men erected and have rejected their ancestral Catholic religion, admitting every error and impiety. May God grant them repentance for the recognition of the truth, and may they recover from the snares of the devil, by whom they are held captive for his will (2 Timothy 2:25).

## CHAPTER IX

**SUMMARY.**—1. Gregory’s decree concerning episcopal inheritance. —2. His mercy, especially in redeeming captives. —3. He praises the sale of sacred vessels for this redemption. —4. He grants freedom to certain servants of the Church. —5. He provides for the support of those abandoning schism. —6. What wealth and estates the Roman Church then possessed. Many cities subject to its authority. The generous almsgiving of earlier Roman pontiffs, to which St. Gregory added. —7. His judgment concerning episcopal residence. —8. Foreign clerics are not to be received without letters of release from their own bishops. —9. Private Masses and the number of altars in St. Gregory’s time. —10. Where even episcopal cases are to be judged. —11. From whom clerical cases are to be heard. St. Gregory preserves the privileges of the churches inviolate. Concerning the consecration of churches. —12. What method he followed in praising his friends. (Years 596 and 597.)

### 1.

Although Gregory devoted such labor and zeal to gathering and bringing within the Church those who were outside it, he nevertheless relaxed nothing of his pastoral solicitude toward the flock long before entrusted to his care by the supreme Shepherd.

There was a danger that bishops, serving the greed of their relatives and led astray by their wicked counsels, might acquire from the revenues of the Church estates which they would leave to those relatives by hereditary right. The result would be that almsgiving to the needy would become nonexistent or more sparing. This had indeed already been prohibited by the sacred laws, but John, bishop of Ravenna, had disregarded them. He had drawn up a will and written into it various burdens upon his Church (Book VI, Letter 2). On this matter the priests, deacons, and the entire clergy of Ravenna approached the pope in complaint:

> **[Note:]** See the notes on this letter.

He judged that whatever John had established by will, contrary to the statutes of the laws, concerning the property of his Church or concerning things acquired during his episcopate, should be considered void.

> **[Note:]** The same is also decreed in Book IX, Letter 77.

But if he had wished or decreed that anything should be done with his own property, which he had possessed before becoming a bishop and which he had not previously transferred to his Church, then that provision must retain full force in every respect, says the most equitable pontiff.

Later he repeated the same decree and further ordered Scholasticus, the defensor (Book XI, Letter 20), to abstain entirely from the clothing and from anything else found in the house of the recently deceased bishop’s father. For he wished everything that the frugality of bishops and other clerics had perhaps withheld from the poor to pass afterward to those same needy people—the true father of the poor that he was.

### 2.

Because he knew that the revenues of bishops could scarcely suffice to support the poor, he most willingly supplied them with whatever was necessary. One should read his letter to Cyprian, in which he commands him to give Bishop Zeno, for distribution to the needy, from the patrimony of the Church which he administered, as much as two thousand modii, if he had gathered that amount (Book VI, Letter 4).

He showed himself especially generous in redeeming captives, and ordered those whom he had placed in charge of the Church’s affairs to devote themselves energetically to this pious work.

> **[Note:]** See also Book VII, Letters 24 and 28.

Thus he writes to Anthemius, the subdeacon who administered the Campanian patrimony:

> We cannot express how great the grief and distress of heart we feel over what has happened in the regions of Campania, but you yourself can gather it from the magnitude of the calamity. For this reason, for the relief of the captives who are being held, we have sent solidi to your charge through Stephen, a magnificent man and the bearer of this letter. We admonish you that you must be entirely diligent and carry out the work energetically. Free men whom you recognize as unable to provide enough for their own redemption, hasten to redeem. If they are slaves and you find that their masters are so poor that they cannot rise to the task of redeeming them, do not cease to purchase these slaves as well. (Ibid., Letter 35.)

In that same year Croton, lying on the Adriatic Sea, was captured by the Lombards, and many noble men and women were carried away as booty. Children were separated from parents, parents from children, and husbands from wives (Book VII, Letter 26). The most compassionate father spent both his own money and money offered by others to restore them to freedom.

### 3.

For the redemption of captives he not only permitted sacred vessels to be sold but praised such sales, as is clear from many of his letters. Fortunatus, bishop of Fano, had been allowed to sell them in order to repay money that he had borrowed and spent on the redemption of captives, since otherwise he would have been unable to repay it. Gregory wrote back to him:

> Since, as your Fraternity has informed us, we have learned that you borrowed money for the redemption of captives and have no means by which to repay it, and that for this reason you wish, with our authority, to sell consecrated vessels, we have resolved in this matter—since the decrees both of the laws and of the canons agree—to give our consent, and we grant you permission to sell the sacred vessels. (Book VII, Letter 13.)

Here he gave his approval. But in another letter, writing to Donus, bishop of Messana, he ordered:

> Your Fraternity must take care that, if there is indeed ordinary silver belonging to the aforesaid Church, you take the amount stated above from it. Otherwise, it is necessary for you to provide for this matter from the sacred vessels the amount we have specified. For just as it is exceedingly serious to sell ecclesiastical vessels needlessly, so likewise, when such necessity arises, it is a fault to place goods belonging to a deeply afflicted Church before its captives and to delay their redemption. (Ibid., Letter 38.)

### 4.

With the same piety and generosity, he sometimes granted freedom to servants of the Roman Church who had served it well, making them Roman citizens, granting them all their property, and adding gifts besides. You have an example and formula of this type of manumission in the letter written to Montana and Thomas (Book VI, Letter 12).

> **[Col. 0392D]** In another place he teaches us that manumissions were solemnly celebrated by bishops in the Church, writing to Paul, bishop of that city (Book II, Letter 10).

### 5.

Those who had returned to the Church from schism or heresy, while they endured as adversaries their own countrymen, still persisting more stubbornly in rebellion, experienced Gregory’s mercy above all others (ibid., Letters 39 and 47). Imitating this generosity of the most holy and wise pontiff, Louis the Great, most Christian king of the Franks, took care to support by annual pensions those adherents of Calvinist error who had returned to the embrace of the Church, so that in the bosom of their pious mother they might at least obtain the necessities of life which their stepmother, heresy, had previously supplied in abundance.

### 6.

Since we have already spoken many times of the generosity of St. Gregory, poured out upon everyone, it is worthwhile briefly to show what resources the Roman Church then possessed, from which it drew such great and almost immeasurable expenses.

For a long time this foremost of churches had possessed extensive and very large estates throughout the Christian world, which were called the patrimonies of St. Peter. The African patrimony is known from the letters of the holy pontiff; so too the extensive Sicilian patrimony, as is evident from Book I, Letter 44, and from the many letters sent to the defenders and rectors of Sicily, which we have collected under the heading “Sicily” in the geographical index; also the Corsican, Dalmatian, and Gallic patrimonies. It would be superfluous to speak of what the Roman Church possessed within Italy, especially in Campania.

We infer that it possessed very extensive estates granted by Constantine the Great, whose generosity in enriching the churches Eusebius especially praises in his *Life of Constantine*. (See Book I, Letter 75; Book III, Letter 27; Book IX, Letter 18; Book VI, Letter 22; Book III, Letters 22 and 33; Book I, Letters 55 and 65; Book IV, chapter 28.)

We infer from Book II, Letter 11, that the city of Nepi in Etruria was subject to the authority of the Roman pontiff. In that letter Gregory indicates that he had entrusted the care and oversight of the city to Leontius, a most illustrious man, so that he himself might attend to everything he recognized as pertaining to the welfare of the citizens or of the Republic.

In the same letter he admonishes the clergy, the senatorial order, and the people of this city to show obedience in all things to the prefect appointed by him:

> For whoever, he says, improperly resists his appointment will be understood to be resisting our own disposition. Whoever obeys him in the matters mentioned above will obey us. But if anyone—which we do not believe—should think, after this admonition of ours, that he ought to despise him, let him know without doubt that the danger will belong to him.

With what authority and power could Gregory have entrusted Leontius, a most illustrious man, with the custody of the city of Nepi, and commanded the citizens to obey him, adding threats as well, unless the city belonged to the jurisdiction of the Church? That Hydruntum and the fortress of Callipolis likewise belonged to it may be gathered elsewhere (Book IX, Letters 99 and 100).

The same must be said of Naples, since we read that the pope appointed a tribune to guard that city (Book II, Letter 31), and ordered the soldiers who were stationed in its garrison,

> **[Col. 0393D]** 272

with no other evident reason than that it was subject to his authority, although it had not entirely shaken off the yoke of the emperors.

> **[Note:]** See Book IX, Letter 69, where he reproves Maurentius, master of the soldiers, because he did not restrain the bishop of Naples from usurping things that belonged to the patron of that city. We think the only reason was that the temporal lordship of Naples belonged to the Roman see. In Letter 104 of the same book, the *Major Urbis*, who is here called the patron, is referred to; in French, *Maire*.

That the supreme pontiffs had long before been elevated to the highest dignity is attested by Ammianus Marcellinus (Book XXVII, chapter 3). The prefect of the City, although he possessed only secular power, would not have hesitated to regard that dignity as superior even to his own.

Dionysius, bishop of Corinth, who flourished toward the end of the second century, writes as follows to the Romans and to Pope Soter, as reported by Eusebius (Book VI, chapter 23):

> This custom of yours, he says, has existed from the very beginning of the religion: you benefit all the brothers in various ways, and send the necessities of life to very many churches established in the individual cities. In this way you both relieve the distress of the needy and supply what is necessary to the brothers who labor in the mines. … And your blessed bishop Soter not only preserved this custom but even increased it.

The other Dionysius, namely the Alexandrian, in a letter addressed to Pope Stephen around the middle of the third century, testifies that he was accustomed to supply the necessities of life to all the provinces of Syria together with Arabia (ibid., Book VII, chapter 5).

> **[Note:]** See also Letter 220 of St. Basil the Great to Pope Dionysius.

All these things are proofs both of supreme power and of power administered most properly. Gregory did not abolish or diminish this pious custom of his predecessors in relieving the needy; rather, he greatly increased it.

Among the poor to whom he most willingly supplied necessities, he counted three thousand nuns in the city of Rome. He did not think that he himself owed them anything on account of such extensive almsgiving; on the contrary, he professed that he and all the Romans were indebted to them:

> Their life, he says, is such, and they are so strict in tears and abstinence, that we believe that, if they did not exist, none of us would by now, after so many years, have been able to remain in this place amid the swords of the Lombards.

### 7.

So that pastors might always be present to their sheep and supply whatever was necessary for life, whether of soul or body, he did not permit them to be absent from their churches or to wander about. Therefore, when he heard that Pimennius, bishop of Amalfi, was not residing in his church, he wrote concerning him in threatening letters to Anthemius (Book VI, Letter 23), ordering him to compel Pimennius to reside according to priestly custom; if he did not amend his conduct, he was to thrust him into a monastery.

For the sake of episcopal residence, he granted the bishops of Sicily permission to come to Rome only once every five years, whereas previously they had been required to appear every three years. In this matter he also took account of reducing their labor (Book VII, Letter 22).

Felix, bishop of Messana, burned with a great desire to see Gregory. But because, owing perhaps to the prolonged absence of the shepherd, his flock might suffer some harm, he asked his friend not to undertake the burden of so long a journey:

> But pray, he says, for us, so that the greater the distances of travel that separate us, the more, with Christ’s help, we may be joined to one another in charity. (Book I, Letter 66.)

### 8.

He wanted not only bishops but also priests and other clerics to remain fixed in their own churches, not to move from one parish to another or wander about; this was also provided for by the canons of the Church.

If certain bishops requested some clerics from elsewhere, intending to promote them within their own clergy and assign them to specific ministries, the clerics’ own bishop first had to release them, with a formal cession. Without his consent they could not be incardinated (Book VI, Letter 20).

Even those who had been elected bishops required, as they say, such letters of release from their own bishop in order to be ordained (Book V, Letter 17).

For the same reason, bishops were forbidden to take monks, without the consent of their abbot, for the priesthood or for the performance of other ecclesiastical duties (Book VI, Letter 28).

Here observe how great is the agreement in this respect between present-day discipline and the ancient discipline.

> **[Note:]** St. Leo, Letter 12, chapter 9: “Let no one receive another’s cleric against the will of his bishop.” The same letter continues: “Let the metropolitan compel a fugitive cleric to return to his own church.” And Letter 13, chapter 4: “Let no bishop dare claim for himself another bishop’s cleric without the cession of the bishop to whom he belongs, and that cession must be contained in an explicit written document.”

### 9.

It is useful to demonstrate this same agreement concerning private Masses and the number of altars within the same church, so that the heterodox may be refuted when they inconveniently charge us with novelty.

John, bishop of Syracuse, had rejected the offerings of Venantius the patrician. Venantius, taking this badly, sent armed retainers into the bishop’s residence. When the pope heard this, he wrote to Venantius, protesting the injury inflicted upon the bishop, who, on account of his acknowledged gravity, holiness, and gentleness, ought to have been protected from such violence and assault (Book VI, Letter 43).

> Therefore, he says, you must show him priestly reverence, as sons ought, and you must not provoke his spirit to anger. For with whom will you have fellowship of grace if, God forbid, discord should arise between you and a priest?

In another letter (ibid., Letter 44), he urged John to maintain concord and peace with Venantius. For the sake of this reconciliation Gregory not only wished John to accept the patrician’s offerings but also permitted the mysteries of the Mass to be celebrated in Venantius’s house, indeed allowing Venantius himself to celebrate if he wished. This quarrel had arisen chiefly over these two refusals. Who but someone with defective vision could fail to see here the clear evidence of customary and approved private Masses, even in private houses?

As for the plurality of altars within the enclosure of the same church, this is established by a letter also written in the present year to Palladius, bishop of Saintes in Gaul (Book VI, Letter 49). He had built a church in honor of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul and of the holy martyrs Laurence and Pancratius. In it he had placed thirteen altars, and he had sent Leuparicus the priest to Rome to request sacred relics to be placed in four altars that had not yet been dedicated.

The pious pontiff granted his request and sent Palladius relics of the aforementioned apostles and martyrs, asking that they be received and placed with the greatest reverence. Let the diligent reader consult the notes on this letter; from them he will learn that many altars had been erected long before Gregory.

Although the present custom of the Greeks does not admit such a multitude of altars, it is nevertheless shown that they did not reject it in former times, as appears from Letter 219 of Theodore the Studite, who asks:

> There are churches, says Theodore, which have two or three small chambers [Greek: *konchai*]. Of these, one is unoccupied; the question is whether it is lawful to celebrate the sacred rites there or not.

No. 15. If there were a desire to contend with the heterodox, they could easily be pressed by the word “altar,” since in Greek *thysiastērion* means “altar” and compels one to admit sacrifice and an offering under the New Law, which they nevertheless reject entirely.

The word “altar,” moreover, frequently occurs in writers contemporary with the apostles. Let the martyr Ignatius stand for them all:

> Come together, he says in his Letter to the Magnesians, no. 7, as into one temple of God, as to one altar.

And in his Letter to the Trallians, no. 7:

> Whoever is within the altar is pure; whoever is outside the altar is not pure.

This agrees with the apostles Paul and John,

> **[Note:]** Hebrews 13:10; Revelation 6:9.

among whom, even after the old altar had been rejected, mention of another altar often occurs.

But leaving these matters aside, let us hasten to the remaining deeds of St. Gregory belonging to this year.

### 10.

His great modesty in administering the supreme pontificate shines forth in his letter to Columbus, bishop in Numidia. Peter, formerly bishop of that province, had, as he said, approached the apostolic see and requested its judgment. But, says the most wise pope:

> Because, separated by so great a distance, we could not carefully learn the inner details of his case, we were unable, being uncertain, to decide it. (Book VI, Letter 37.)

Therefore he thought it best that Bishop Columbus should sit as judge between Peter and his accusers, since, being present, he could know the case more precisely.

At times he also permitted accused bishops to go to the imperial city to clear themselves and present themselves before the emperor.

### 11.

How vigorously he defended the rights of bishops is proved by his letter to Fortunatus, bishop of Naples, whose words are as follows:

> Since it has come to our attention that clerics and other religious persons of your city and parish are being summoned before other judges, we henceforth prohibit this. We do not wish either your cleric, or your monk, or any other religious person of your city or parish to be summoned by anyone or brought before another’s judgment. But if anyone wishes to raise a legal question against such persons, he must know that he is to approach your Fraternity. Or if, as commonly happens, some suspicion should in any way arise against them and they should perhaps desire the judgment of chosen men, they may have the right, under your supervision, to choose judges, so that in this way neither may you appear to have lost jurisdiction nor may the plaintiff, by litigating before someone he suspects, seem to suffer prejudice. (Book VI, Letter 11.)

It was not tedious to transcribe these words, since they appear to contain the form of ecclesiastical judgments.

He wished the rights and privileges of churches, as of bishops, to remain unimpaired—the most equitable of pontiffs—as he openly declares when sending the pallium to Donus, bishop of Messina, and John, bishop of Syracuse. In the letters sent to each of them, which are entirely similar, I seem to discern the common and customary formula for granting the pallium (Book VI, letters 5 and 18).

[Col. 0397A] It is noteworthy that at that time no churches in the provinces of Sicily and Italy, which were subject to the Roman pontiff as metropolitan, were consecrated without his permission. This is clear not only from letter 45, written in this year [Note: Book VI, letter 45; Book XII, letter 11; Book XIV, letter 9.], but also from many others. The same rule applied to the consecration of baptisteries [Note: Book XIII, letter 20.].

12. An example of the manner to be observed in praising friends is provided by a letter written to Stephen, abbot of Lérins. Augustine, returning to Rome, had informed the pope about the harmony of Stephen’s congregation, in which there were several priests and deacons. Gregory testifies to the joy with which he received this news. Addressing Abbot Stephen as a friend in his letter, he praises his vigilance and gives thanks for the gifts he had received from him for the service of the poor. Nevertheless, after the praises already mentioned, he adds this exhortation:

“Because the enemy of the human race does not cease to lie in wait for our actions, but strives with constant cunning to deceive those who serve God in every possible way, therefore, dearest son, we exhort you to exercise your diligence with watchfulness, and to guard those entrusted to you with prayer and provident care, so that the prowling wolf may find no opportunity to tear anyone apart” (Book VI, letter 56).

# CHAPTER X

**SUMMARY.—** 1. Cyriacus, patriarch of Constantinople, sends an embassy and letter to Saint Gregory, who replies to him. — 2. Praise of Cyriacus. — 3. Those who had misused Sacred Scripture to praise him are rebuked. — 4. Cyriacus’s envoys are accused of error by the pope. — 5. The story of Trajan’s deliverance through Saint Gregory’s prayers is refuted, especially on the basis of the *Dialogues*. — 6. Objections against the eternity of the punishments of hell are resolved. — 7. Why a finite fault is punished without end. — 8. Why the saints do not pray for the damned. By the same reasoning it is proved that Saint Gregory could not have prayed for Trajan. — 9. John the Deacon’s evasion is refuted. — 10. An objection drawn from the Acts of Saint Perpetua is answered. (Years 596 and 597.)

1. Although John of Constantinople had died in January of the year 595, as we noted above (chapter 1, section 15), Saint Gregory did not receive the embassy and synodal letter of his successor Cyriacus—who wrote concerning his election and ordination—until almost twenty months later. The letters of Cyriacus were delivered as a mark of respect by George the priest and Theodore the deacon. In his reply, the pope indeed praises Cyriacus for having fled pastoral responsibility out of his love of quiet, but from this very fact he proves that Cyriacus ought to have been promoted to episcopal dignity:

“For just as a position of governance must be denied to those who desire it, so it must be offered to those who flee it” (Book VII, letter 4).

He therefore reminds him that charity toward one’s neighbor must be preferred to inward tranquility, demonstrating this also by his own example, and teaches how it may be ensured that pastoral cares do not completely overwhelm the mind. As for the confession of faith submitted by Cyriacus, the pope approves it. Nevertheless, he doubts whether a certain Eudoxius should be numbered among the heretics condemned by the four ecumenical councils [Note: See the following letter, no. 31, and the notes on it.]; but Eulogius later removed this doubt and hesitation. He also touches upon the rejection of the title “ecumenical.”

[Col. 0398A] In another, shorter letter to Cyriacus, he testifies that he had long since recognized his good qualities, namely while he was residing in the imperial city. He raises him up when he is disheartened by awareness of his weakness, saying:

“We know that the first virtue is knowledge of one’s weakness; and from this we conclude that you can fulfill the ministry you have rightly undertaken, because we see that through humility you recognize your own weakness and can fulfill well the ministry entrusted to you. For we are all weak, but he is weaker who cannot recognize his own weakness” (Book VII, letter 5).

2. The holy man congratulated the Emperor on Cyriacus’s election, because he had shown such concern to provide the Church of Constantinople with an excellent shepherd (Book VII, letter 6). We shall quote part of his letter to Maurice, from which it will be understood who Cyriacus was and why he was appointed successor to John—who is himself praised not a little—only after some delay:

“It could not have been a small reward that, after John of holy memory had been taken from this light, Your Piety hesitated for a long time to ordain a priest and postponed the matter somewhat, while seeking counsel in fear of the almighty Lord, so that the cause of God might be arranged with great reverence. Hence I consider my brother and fellow priest Cyriacus to be highly suitable for pastoral governance, since the long deliberations of Your Piety brought him to this office. We all know how vigilant and experienced he was formerly in administering ecclesiastical affairs. I therefore do not doubt that this came about through heavenly providence: that he who had managed lesser matters well should fittingly undertake greater ones and pass from the care of possessions [Col. 0398C] to the governance of souls” (Book VIII, letter 34).

3. At Cyriacus’s ordination, certain bishops, rejoicing with excessive enthusiasm, had exclaimed: “This is the day that the Lord has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it” (Psalm 117:24). It was as though this patriarch were the sun whose light had brought daylight into being. Saint Gregory utterly condemned this misuse of the words of Sacred Scripture in a flattering speech, as he informed those bishops in his own letter to them (Book VIII, letter 7). So that he might not be thought to have acted out of jealousy or to have wished to draw to himself the praises bestowed upon Cyriacus, he immediately attempted to lessen the fault of this immoderate praise. How far, however, he was from seeking and courting excessive, immoderate, or indeed any praise at all, he certainly demonstrated a thousand times, and especially in this year, when he rebuked John, bishop of Syracuse, for having had his literary works read aloud before outsiders at his table (ibid., letter 9).

4. Cyriacus’s envoys, according to the testimony of the deacons of the Roman Church, had said that Jesus Christ, descending into hell, saved all who there confessed him to be God and freed them from their deserved punishments. Concerning this matter, Saint Gregory the teacher says:

“I wish your Charity to think very differently. For when he descended into hell, he freed by his grace only those who had believed that he would come and had preserved his commandments by their manner of life. It is certain, however, that after the Lord’s incarnation no one can be saved—not even among those who hold his faith—if they do not possess a life corresponding to that faith” (Book VIII, letter 15).

He proceeds to demonstrate this with many testimonies from Sacred Scripture.

5. This one passage would be sufficient to refute the little tale of Trajan’s deliverance from the punishments of hell through Gregory’s prayers, which Paul and John the Deacon relate in his *Life*, Book II, chapter 44. For what are we to say? Could he really have poured out prayers to God for the deliverance of Trajan, a worshiper of idols and persecutor of Christians to the point of death, when he knew that one who had separated himself from God by evil living could not be drawn to God after death? The distinguished Doctor states precisely this in express words. But this fiction is refuted much more powerfully by the doctrine asserted in the *Dialogues*, Book IV, chapter 44.

The question posed there is: “Do those destined for the fires of Gehenna burn forever?” Saint Gregory replies:

“It is unquestionably established and indubitably true that, just as there is no end to the joy of the good, so there will be no end to the torment of the wicked. For since the Truth says, ‘The wicked will go into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life’ (Matthew 25:46), because what he promised is true, what God threatened will certainly not be false.”

6. Peter objects to this:

“What if someone should say: He threatened sinners with eternal punishment for this reason—that he might restrain them from committing sins?”

Saint Gregory dispels the objection by replying in these words:

“If what he threatened is false, so that he might correct them from injustice, then what he promised is also false, so that he might call them to righteousness. But who, unless insane, would dare say this? And if he threatened something he was not going to fulfill, then, while wishing to assert that he is merciful, we are compelled to proclaim him deceitful—which it is impious to say.”

7. Understanding that this answer had dealt sufficiently with his objection, Peter proposes another problem to be solved:

“I should like to know how it is just that a fault committed within a finite period should be punished without end.”

The most wise teacher replies:

“This would rightly be said if the strict judge weighed not the hearts of human beings but their deeds. The wicked sinned within a finite period because they lived within a finite period. For if they could have lived forever, they would certainly have wished to do so, in order that they might sin forever. They show that they desire always to live in sin, since, while they live, they never cease to sin. It therefore belongs to the great justice of the judge that those who in this life never wished to be without sin should never be without punishment.”

This is indeed an outstanding argument by which the eternity of punishments is proved against those who despise religion and are accustomed to quibble about this doctrine in order to sin more freely. Peter, however, is not yet overcome by the weight of the argument and presses the matter more subtly:

“But no just person feeds upon cruelty, and a delinquent servant is ordered to be beaten by a just master precisely so that he may be corrected from wickedness. He is beaten, therefore, so that he may be reformed. But the wicked who are handed over to the fires of Gehenna, if they do not attain correction, for what purpose will they burn forever?”

The Doctor replies to his disciple:

“Almighty God, because he is merciful, does not feed upon the torment of the wretched; but because he is just, he is not forever satisfied with the vengeance taken upon the wicked. All the wicked, however, who are destined for eternal punishment are indeed punished on account of their own wickedness [Col. 0400A]; nevertheless, they will burn for a purpose: so that all the righteous may see in God the joys they receive, and may behold in those condemned people the punishments they escaped. Thus they may recognize that they are debtors to divine grace forever, all the more clearly because they see forever those evils being punished which, with God’s help, they overcame.”

8. When one weighs these statements, how could it occur to anyone that Gregory—so wise and so instructive—ever poured out prayers for the Emperor Trajan, whom he did not doubt had been condemned to eternal punishments on account of his unbelief and his persecution of Christians, quite apart from other considerations?

The following statements leave not even the slightest difficulty on this matter. Peter asks:

“And where is the holiness of the saints, if they will not pray for their enemies whom they then see burning, when they have certainly been commanded: ‘Pray for your enemies’?” (Matthew 5:44.)

The most wise Doctor replies:

“They pray for their enemies at a time when they can turn their hearts toward fruitful repentance and save them through that conversion. For what else should be prayed for on behalf of enemies than what the Apostle says: ‘That God may grant them repentance for the knowledge of the truth, and that they may recover from the snares of the devil, by whom they are held captive to do his will’?” (2 Timothy 2:25.)

“And how will they then pray for those who can no longer in any way be changed from wickedness to works of righteousness? The reason, therefore, why no prayer is then offered for people condemned to eternal fire is the same as the reason why even now no prayer is offered for the devil and his angels, who have been assigned to eternal punishment. The reason also why holy people now do not pray for unbelieving and impious persons who have died is that, since they already know that those people have been assigned to eternal punishment, they shrink from having the merit of their prayer nullified before the presence of the just Judge.

“And if even now the righteous who are alive have no pity for the dead and unjust who are condemned, while they themselves still know that they are suffering something subject to judgment from their own flesh, how much more strictly will they then look upon the torments of the wicked, when they themselves, stripped of every defect of corruption, will already cling more closely and firmly to righteousness? For their minds are so absorbed by the force of strict judgment, through their adherence to the most just Judge, that they have no pleasure at all in anything that departs from the precision of that eternal rule.”

Can anyone who reads these words doubt or misunderstand Saint Gregory’s position, both concerning the eternity of the punishments of hell and concerning the denial of prayers for all whom we know without hesitation to have been assigned to such punishments?

9. To evade or weaken the force of this argument, John the Deacon devised the following escape. He claimed that Gregory had not prayed to obtain Trajan’s deliverance but had merely wept. As though tears poured out before God for the purpose of obtaining something were not prayers—and indeed highly effective ones.

He adds that Trajan was freed from the torments of hell in such a way that he nevertheless remained in hell and was not raised to the heavenly realms. But the reasoning of the holy Doctor, as well as all the testimonies of Sacred Scripture that he adduces, proves not only the eternal dwelling of the condemned in hell but also their burning.

Nor may one imagine that the holy Doctor held two different opinions on this question at different times. First, he could not have been ignorant of the teaching of Sacred Scripture and of the Church on this matter. Second, he consistently maintains the same position in nearly all his works, though these were composed at different times: in the *Morals*, Book XXXIV, section 34; in the *Dialogues*; and in the letter already mentioned, which provided the occasion for this brief treatise because it refuted the error of Cyriacus’s envoys. Moreover, this opinion, commonly attributed to Origen, had already been attacked by Augustine and Basil the Great. (See Book XXI of *The City of God*, chapter 2; *Shorter Rules*, question 267.)

10. What is read in the Acts of Saint Perpetua (*Patrologia*, volume III)—namely, that she prayed for her brother Dinocrates and thereby freed him from the punishments with which he was being chastised in a dark place—does not at all support the opinion that we are attacking after Gregory. It proves only that the dead who have been assigned to the purgatorial sufferings resulting from slight sins committed after baptism can be freed from them through the prayers of the faithful.

Augustine supplies this answer in Book I of *On the Origin of the Soul*, chapter 10, and Book III, chapter 9, where he says that Dinocrates endured certain punishments because of sins committed after baptism. Since he was seven years old, he could have lied or stained his soul with some other slight offense. That he had been baptized before his death cannot be denied, since Perpetua herself testifies that her entire family, except her father, practiced the religion of Christ.

# CHAPTER XI

[Col. 0401C] **SUMMARY.—** 1. Saint Gregory was an outstanding teacher in forming moral character. What he teaches against excessive security and concerning two kinds of compunction. — 2. The piety of Theoctista, the Emperor’s sister. — 3. Saint Gregory refuses to help friends obtain secular offices. — 4. What consolations he offered to grieving friends. — 5. He praises laypeople who seek the nourishment of the divine word. — 6. A successor is given to the sick bishop of Rimini. — 7. And to the bishop of Cornelium, deposed after his fall. Gregory praises Bishop Stephen. — 8. Certain monastic matters. — 9. The pope provides for the island of Corsica. — 10. Observations concerning the marriage of persons of servile status. (Years 596 and 597.)

1. We have just seen Saint Gregory, an excellent theologian, contending with the utmost strength for the purity and integrity of the faith. Let us now admire him as an outstanding teacher in the formation of character, supplying the most refined counsels of Christian piety and perfection.

Gregoria, a chamber-attendant of the Empress, had written to him that she would never cease from importunate prayers until she learned from him with certainty—namely through divine revelation—that her sins had been forgiven. He replied to her with equal modesty and prudence:

“You have asked for something both difficult and useless. Difficult, because I am unworthy to receive a revelation. Useless, because you must not become secure concerning your sins unless and until you are no longer able to mourn them on the final day of your life. Until that day comes, you must always fear your faults with suspicion and trembling, and wash them away with daily tears.

“Certainly, the Apostle Paul had already ascended to the third heaven, had been taken into paradise, and had heard secret words that it is not lawful for a human being to speak (2 Corinthians 12); yet, still trembling, he said: ‘I chastise my body and bring it into subjection, lest, after preaching to others, I myself should become disqualified’ (1 Corinthians 9:27). Does the one who is already being led to heaven still fear, while the one who still lives on earth no longer wishes to fear?

“Consider, sweetest daughter, that security is usually the mother of negligence. Therefore, in this life you must not possess a security that would make you negligent. For it is written: ‘Blessed is the person who is always fearful’ (Psalm 2:11). And again it is written: ‘Serve the Lord in fear, and rejoice before him with trembling’ (Proverbs 28:14). During the short period of this life, therefore, it is necessary that trembling hold your mind, so that afterward it may rejoice forever through the joy of security” (Book VII, letter 25).

What could be more appropriate here for dispelling the deceptions of a certain masked piety which, under the false name of purer love, removes every fear and every concern for eternal salvation?

In the letter to the patrician Theoctista that follows immediately (Book VII, letter 26), the holy Doctor explains two kinds of compunction: one that fears eternal punishments, and another in which, after the soul has been consumed by prolonged fear and anxiety of sorrow, a certain security arising from confidence in forgiveness begins to arise. This state does not exclude all concern for salvation. It is not complete security but an incipient security—not banishing all fear, but only fear that is too anxious. In this state, I say, the soul sighs for heavenly rewards. The one who previously wept lest he be led to punishment later begins to weep most bitterly because he is delayed from the kingdom.

2. From this letter we understand that Theoctista, the Emperor’s sister, was filled with an abundance of the sacred word and sighed unceasingly for eternal joys. She hastened toward the land of promise with dry feet amid the waves of the world—that is, amid the tumult of human beings and in the very court, by cultivating solitude. Saint Gregory regards this as a miracle and compares it with the passage of the children of Israel through the Red Sea.

The Emperor Maurice had entrusted his most pious sister with the raising of his children. The pope therefore exhorts her to try to form them in the best moral character and to admonish the eunuchs assigned to their custody and service concerning how cautiously they ought to speak in their presence:

“For the words of those who raise children,” he says, “will either be milk, if they are good, or poison, if they are bad.”

In the same letter Gregory shows that he was concerned for the salvation and spiritual progress of the Empress Constantina. He attempted to withdraw those whom he loved from earthly desires and set them ablaze with love of heavenly things; these were the signs and proofs of his friendship.

5. Andreas, a highly distinguished man and Gregory’s friend, had asked him to recommend him to the Emperor so that he might obtain some office in the administration of the state. This struck the holy father with no small grief. He says to his friend:

“I know many who are placed in the service of the state and are greatly afflicted, because they are not permitted to be free for mourning their sins; and why you desire, I do not know, to entangle yourself.”

I omit much concerning contempt for the world, though it is worthy of being read and seriously impressed upon the mind. The letter concludes:

“What a preoccupation of mind it is to be in the service of a most pious ruler; how great is the desire for earthly favor, and how great the fear lest that very favor be lost when it has been obtained!” Consider, therefore, what punishment it is either to be wearied by the desire for prosperity or to tremble from fear of adversity.

“Therefore I advise Your Greatness to persevere in your former purpose: to strive, during the short period of this pilgrimage, to live in a pleasant refuge, to lead a quiet and tranquil life, to devote yourself to sacred reading, to meditate upon heavenly words, to kindle yourself with love of eternity, to perform good works concerning earthly matters according to your strength, and to hope for the everlasting kingdom as their reward. To live in this way is already to possess a share in the life of eternity.

“These things, noble son, I say because I love you greatly. And because you are heading into storms and waves, I draw you back to shore by the ropes of my words.
