If you are willing to follow the one who is pulling you, you will recognize, once placed upon the shore of your tranquility, what dangers you have escaped and what joys you have found” (Book VII, letter 29).

4. When he observed the spirits of his friends growing weary under the weight of hardships, he raised them up through consoling letters, or through the very greatness of soul by which he seemed to rise above all merely human things in them.

We usually grieve when the children or relatives of our friends are taken prematurely by death, and we express this grief to those mourning their loss. But Gregory, who possessed nothing merely human, writes to Andreas, who was especially closely joined to him in friendship:

“I rejoice exceedingly that the illustrious maiden Constantina, before she entered marriage, was taken away from the allurements of this world” (Book VII, letter 29).

And to Narses:

“You have informed me by letter of the passing of the lady Esychia, and I have rejoiced with great exultation, because that good soul has reached her own homeland, though she had been laboring in an alien homeland” (ibid., letter 30).

He perhaps knew that this kind of consolation would not be unwelcome to Narses, a religious man—as he is called in the heading of the letter—who, although he possessed patrician rank, seems, as may be gathered from Book IV, letter 32, to have renounced the world at that time and to have presided over certain monasteries.

His daughter Dominica, a most learned virgin who, although Latin-speaking, nevertheless wrote in Greek, had also fled the court, entered a monastery, and later became its superior. We ought to marvel all the more at what we have said about Dominica’s knowledge of Greek letters because Saint Gregory, writing to her father, states that at that time there were not sufficiently learned interpreters in Constantinople who could properly translate dictated material from Greek into Latin and from Latin into Greek (Book VII, letter 30).

[Col. 0403D] 5. Saint Gregory especially praised friends, even [Note: See above, letter 26, and below, Book XI, letter 78.] laypeople, if they sought comfort and nourishment for their souls in the word of God. This is especially clear from the letter written this year to Dynamus and Aurelia, Gauls (Book VII, letter 36). He congratulates them because they sought the nourishment of sacred reading, and then adds an excellent interpretation of this evangelical saying:

“Everyone who asks receives, and whoever seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it will be opened” (Matthew 7:8).

“Let us ask,” he says, “by praying; let us seek by reading; let us knock by acting” (Luke 11:12).

But enough of this; let us proceed to other matters.

6. After the long stay in the East, let us return to the West, where Gregory’s pastoral concern was especially vigilant in governing the churches.

The Church of Rimini had long been without a bishop because of Castorius’s poor health. Since he had been absent for four years and had not improved, he submitted a written petition to the pope, asking that, since he was entirely unable, because of the illness that afflicted him, to rise either to govern that Church or to undertake the office he had received, the pope should ordain a bishop for the Church. The supreme pontiff granted his request. Since the care of concern for all the churches bound him, he issued the customary instructions, exhorting the clergy and people to choose an overseer for themselves, whom he ordered to be presented to Marinianus of Ravenna for examination (Book VII, letter 19).

[Col. 0404B] 7. Shortly afterward he wrote to the same Marinianus that, since the bishop of the Church of Cornelium had been deposed after falling into a crime, another bishop should be ordained in his place. No hope could remain for the fallen man of returning to his former dignity, and the sacred canons did not permit a church to remain vacant for more than three months [Note: From canon 25 of Chalcedon in the code of the canons of the Roman Church.] (Book VII, letter 41).

When you read above that Gregory attributed to himself the care of concern for all the churches, do not suppose that he was asserting papal authority beyond measure, something entirely contrary to his modesty and humility of spirit. Certainly Leo the Great, who sat about 150 years before him, writing to the bishop of Thessalonica and asking him to undertake his responsibilities (letter XII, chapter 1), says that the bishop had been called to share in concern, not in the fullness of power; he therefore did not hesitate to reserve that fullness of power to himself.

Just as Gregory inflicted suitable punishments upon bishops who failed in their duty, so he endeavored to reward the best shepherds with appropriate praise and honors. Accordingly, he praises Bishop Stephen warmly because, through constant preaching, he recalled the patrician Maria from heresy or schism into the bosom of the Church, along with many others (Book VII, letter 8). Dominica, a distinguished woman and the wife of a certain John, Gregory’s intimate friend, may have been among this number. He wrote to John that he had rejoiced greatly when he learned that she had been joined to the unity of the Church (ibid., letter 37).

8. To touch briefly upon monastic affairs, this year the pope granted privileges to the monastery of Saint Cassian near Marseille, presided over by Respecta. Concerning this monastery, consult the notes on the letter containing these privileges (Book VII, letter 12).

In another letter (Book VII, letter 18), we read that a certain Martin, a deacon and abbot, about whom certain reports had reached the pope—reports that would seriously stain the purpose of his office but could not be proved after careful investigation—had offered binding oaths at the most sacred body of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, by which he asserted his innocence. Saint Gregory therefore absolved him and restored him to his position.

Letter 32 was written to Anastasius the priest, whom Gregory portrays as adorned with many distinguished virtues. Nevertheless, he censures him for having assumed the administration of a monastery called Neas, because many secular activities were being carried on in that cenobium under the appearance of holiness. He urges him to remove and settle the dispute that had arisen between the abbot of that monastery and Amos, patriarch of Jerusalem.

A great quarrel existed between Caesarius, abbot of the monastery of Saint Peter at Baiae, and John, abbot of Saint Lucy’s in the city of Syracuse. Gregory wrote to John, bishop of Syracuse, concerning its settlement (Book VII, letter 39), asking him to go there with Fantinus the defensor, accompanied by John the land-surveyor—for the dispute concerned boundaries—and to deliver a judgment:

“Lest the concern for secular matters separate the hearts of religious men from mutual charity.”

Concerned for the preservation of monastic discipline in Africa, he asked Dominicus, bishop of Carthage, to restrain monks who wandered about with impunity and to ensure that they were again subjected to the yoke of obedience, which they had shaken off. He also commanded him by every means, threatening them, to restrain those bishops whom he had heard were offering protection to these wandering monks from defending them (ibid., letter 35).

9. On another occasion he wrote to Gennadius, prefect of Africa, in order to commend to him the count Ruferius, his fellow citizens, and the island of Corsica itself (Book VII, letter 3). From this we understand that the island belonged to the prefecture, or exarchate, of Africa—perhaps because it lay beside Sardinia, which at that time was counted among the provinces of Africa as the seventh and last.

Corsica was exposed to incursions by enemies, and it was not enough to send an army there unless a highly experienced commander were placed over it. Gregory therefore asks that Anastasius the tribune be appointed, since he had already discharged his duties energetically in that province and, after being removed from it, had left all the inhabitants of the island with a high opinion of him and an even greater longing for his return.

10. We shall close this seventh year of Gregory’s pontificate with an observation concerning the dissolution of a marriage when one of the spouses is of servile status. This was by no means rejected by the most holy pontiff, as is clear from his letter to Fortunatus, bishop of Naples (Book VII, letter 1).

A cleric of that Church had removed his wife from his companionship because she had been denounced as being of servile status. The expelled woman maintained that she was free and approached the supreme pontiff, asking to be restored to her husband. The merciful Father listened kindly to her petition. Since no mark of servile status was found in her, he ordered the cleric to receive back the wife whom he had unjustly repudiated; if he refused, he was to be subjected to strict punishment.

It is therefore clear that the cleric was compelled to receive his wife again for no other reason than that she had falsely been accused of servile status. Thus, if she had married as a free woman and her servile status had later been proved, the marriage would have been invalid on account of the defect of status.

# CHAPTER XII

**SUMMARY.—** 1. The conversion of the Corsican idolaters. — 2. And of the Jews of Agrigentum. — 3. Saint Gregory prohibits the unjust harassment of other Jews. — 4. He consoles Anastasius of Antioch, oppressed by various persecutions. — 5. Anastasius dies. His successor writes to Saint Gregory. The holy Doctor judges that the fraud of heretics who thrust a false synod of Ephesus upon people as genuine should be exposed from ancient manuscripts. — 6. He congratulates Eulogius of Alexandria. — 7. Concerning the antiquity of the Roman Martyrology. The opinion of Henri Valois is examined. — 8. The suspicion of forgery cast upon the Vatican manuscripts is dispelled. — 9. The holy pontiff protects a bishop of Numidia who has suffered an injury. — 10. The African Church derives its origin from the Roman Church. — 11. What Saint Gregory thought about payment made for burial. — 12. What he established concerning the division of ecclesiastical revenues. — 13. And concerning *campagi*. — 14. He appointed seven regional defenders. — 15. The monastic affairs of this year are touched upon. (Years 597 and 598.)

1. Saint Gregory began the eighth year of his pontificate with great joy because of the conversion of the Corsicans, about which Peter, bishop of Aleria, had most recently written to him. After giving thanks to God in the customary manner for the joyful news, he urged Peter to complete the work so happily begun and to continue gathering together and leading to the faith the others who had not yet been baptized, or who, after receiving baptism, had returned to the worship of idols, whether through negligence or necessity.

“For what work,” he says, “will you undertake that is more useful and sublime than to think about bringing souls to life and gathering them together, and to bring an immortal gain to your Lord, who has given you a place in which to preach?” (Book VII, letter 1.)

As usual, he added generosity to his exhortation. He sent this bishop fifty solidi to purchase clothing for those who were to be baptized (Book VI, letter 22). He also assigned and granted an estate as a stipend to the priest who assisted the bishop and governed the Church that had recently been built by order of the pope on a possession of the Roman Church, together with its baptistery.

He further praised Bishop Peter’s plan to ordain another bishop on the same island, not far from a mountain inhabited by many remaining worshipers of idols.

Idolatry was not exiled and hidden away in Corsica alone. From letter 18, written this year to Agnellus, bishop of Terracina, we learn that certain people in that district were still worshiping trees. Two years later he urged Queen Brunhild (Book IX, letter 11) to restrain the peoples subject to her from the worship of idols:

“For it has come to our attention that many Christians both hasten to the churches and—what is impious to say—do not withdraw from the worship of demons.”

He explains the kind of idolatry in these words:

“Let there be no worshipers of trees; let them not offer sacrifices with the heads of animals.”

We have explained these matters in the notes on this passage. In another letter he joins diviners and sorcerers to the worshipers of idols (ibid., letter 65).

2. The joy over the conversion of the idolaters was followed by gladness at the Jews of Agrigentum hastening to come to the Christian faith (Book VIII, letter 22). So that their desire might not grow cold through a longer delay—for from June, when Saint Gregory’s letter on the matter was written, until the following Easter there were at least nine months—the pope allowed them to be washed in the baptismal waters before the solemnity of Easter [Note: See the notes on this letter.], outside which, as well as the feast of Pentecost, baptism was not ordinarily administered in the Latin Church. He first required them to observe forty days of abstinence and penance.

Since many of them were poor, so that they did not appear able, because of the constraints of their household resources, to purchase for themselves the white garment customarily worn by the newly baptized [Note: Consult note 327 on the *Book of Sacraments*.], he ordered Fantinus the defensor to have these garments purchased at the Church’s expense and to ensure that they were distributed to those suffering from poverty.

Meanwhile, he wished the bishop of Agrigentum to be instructed to make these candidates for the Christian religion catechumens, to teach them carefully and in good time the faith they were about to receive, and to form them in the precepts of the evangelical law.

### 3.

So that the most wise pontiff might more easily draw other Jews to the faith by clemency and gentleness, he prohibited their being expelled from the places granted to them by law or their being subjected to other injuries. This is clear from the letter written to Victor, bishop of Palermo, on behalf of the Jews living in that city, [Note: [Col. 0407D] See also Book IX, Letter 6, and Letter 55.] sent shortly afterward to Fantinus concerning the Jews inhabiting Agrigentum (Book VIII, Letter 25). If any Jews nevertheless became insolent toward Christians, he hastened to break and restrain their boldness; and he urged the bishops to resist their wicked counsels (ibid., Letter 21).

### 4.

The joyful news of so many unbelievers converted to the faith was disturbed by the letters of Anastasius, bishop of Antioch, which flowed with tears in place of words (Book VIII, Letter 2). Gregory attempted to lessen his friend’s grief and to raise his spirit, which was almost collapsing beneath the weight of adversity. The consolatory letter of the supreme pontiff does not explain by whom this patriarch was then being harassed. Yet we scarcely doubt that the many heretics then raging in the East, under the various names of Acephalites, Severians, and Theodosians, were the leaders of his opponents. Besides the heterodox groups mentioned, the ever-watchful pope complains that other monsters had recently arisen: namely, new heretics who were attempting to nullify the Prophets, the Gospels, and the sayings of the Fathers.

“But while your Holiness remains alive,” Gregory says to Anastasius, “we hope in the grace of our Protector that their mouths, which have been opened against the solidity of the truth, may soon be silenced; for however sharp the swords that are brought against a rock, when they strike the stone they rebound broken.” A most excellent explanation, certainly, of why so many weapons of the heretics, hurled against the Church’s most solid rock, ultimately fell blunted back upon their authors. Elsewhere hope shone forth that victory over these enemies of the Church would be won—namely, from their division: “For,” says the holy Doctor, “among those who have separated themselves from the teaching of the holy Church, there is no unity.”

Among those hostile to Saint Anastasius, Saint Gregory seems to identify the patriarch of Constantinople, whom he says added burdens when he ought to have relieved them; that beneath the clothing of a sheep he was inwardly a ravenous wolf; and that, unlike the others, he wished to possess alone what he had not been worthy to possess even with his brethren—namely, the usurped title of universal patriarch.

### 5.

Not long after Gregory’s letters had been received, Anastasius passed to a more peaceful and better life. [Note: [Col. 0407D] On Anastasius, see Evagrius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book IV, chapter 4, and Book V, chapter 5.] He was succeeded by another Anastasius, called the younger. When the latter had written to the pope concerning his advancement and had sent, as was customary, a profession of faith, he received from him a most welcome reply, seasoned with the honey of charity.

Just as that patriarch was the successor to the see of the elder Anastasius, so also was he the successor to his troubles and persecutions; for after nine years as bishop, he is said to have died a martyr in a revolt. In Saint Gregory’s letter to Anastasius, recently appointed to the see of Antioch (Book IX, Letter 49), this deserves particular attention: a pseudo-Ephesian synod held by the Nestorians, at which the impious doctrines of Coelestius and Pelagius were approved, had repeatedly been passed off, through the fraud of deceitful heretics, as the very Ecumenical Council of Ephesus. To counter this error, the most learned Father advises that the genuine acts of the Council of Ephesus be sought in the archives of the principal Churches—Roman, Alexandrian, and Antiochene. Here one sees the authenticity and authority of the ancient manuscripts being asserted.

### 6.

We soon saw in the East the heretics rioting against Anastasius. Egypt, however, and the Alexandrian Church were more peaceful under the patriarch Eulogius, who had reconciled most of the heretics to the Church and had strengthened concord among the faithful. When Saint Gregory received this news, he immediately took up his pen to congratulate his friend and, in turn, informed him about the recent conversion of the English. But we have already spoken of these matters. Between the two men there existed a most holy relationship, strengthened by mutual benefits and services.

Eulogius had requested that the supreme pontiff send him the acts of all the martyrs, which had been collected by Eusebius of Caesarea during the reign of Constantine of blessed memory. Gregory replied that, before receiving Eulogius’s letter, he had never heard anything about this Eusebian collection. [Note: [Col. 0408D] See the notes on this letter.] He added:

> “Apart from what is contained in the books of that same Eusebius concerning the acts of the holy martyrs, I know of no such material in the archive of this Church of ours or in the libraries of the city of Rome, except for a few items collected in the volume of a single codex. We, however, possess in one codex the names of almost all the martyrs, collected according to their distinct passions on each individual day, and on each day we celebrate the solemnities of Mass in their honor. Yet in that same volume it is not indicated how each one suffered; only the name, place, and day of the passion are given. Consequently, many who were crowned with martyrdom in different lands and provinces are recognized, as I have said, on their respective days” (Book VIII, Letter 30).

### 7.

Here we have, as it were, the first beginnings of the Roman Martyrology. The Synod of Clovesho, held in the year 747, mentions it; at that synod it was decreed that throughout the entire year the anniversaries of the saints should be venerated on the same day according to the Martyrology of the Roman Church, with the psalmody and chant appropriate to each.

The origin of martyrologies seems to us to be sought in the calendars of the Churches. Each Church had a catalogue of its martyrs and other saints, in whose memory feast days were celebrated. Hence Cyprian writes:

> “Finally, record the days on which they depart, so that we may be able to celebrate commemorations of them among the memorials of the martyrs” (Letter 12, *Patrologia*, volume IV).

On this subject the serious reader should consult Henry Valesius, who published a special dissertation on the Roman Martyrology and appended it to his annotations on Eusebius of Caesarea. He should also weigh the arguments by which that most learned man attempts to establish that there had never been any proper and distinctive Martyrology of the Roman Church before the one published by order of Pope Sixtus V under this title and illuminated by Baronius’s annotations.

His principal argument is drawn from the silence of ancient writers; yet this collapses once the testimony of the Synod of Clovesho cited above is read. Valesius does not deny that the Roman Church, and at least the other more important Churches, possessed their calendars and their own fasti, in which the names of their particular martyrs and holy bishops were recorded. But he maintains that these were not martyrologies, which, he says, were not proper to a single place but common to the whole Church, since they generally contained the martyrs and confessors of the entire world.

Certainly, if we settle the controversy by the definition just cited, Valesius appears destined to lose the case. For Saint Gregory does not mention a calendar containing only the names of martyrs who had suffered in Rome, but a codex in which the names of almost all the martyrs had been collected according to their distinct passions on each day. To show that martyrs who had suffered throughout the world are meant, he adds:

> “In the same volume . . . the name, place, and day of the passion are given. Consequently, many from different lands and provinces are recognized, on their respective days . . . as having been crowned with martyrdom.”

We have judged it worthwhile to state here what we think of Valesius’s opinion, lest anyone perhaps believe that a certain note favoring Valesius, appended to the cited letter from Gussanville, was adopted by us. Far be it from us to approve everything that the learned man observed concerning Gregory’s letters.

### 8.

Certainly, here he raises a suspicion that handwritten codices—even Vatican ones—are spurious; it is our duty to refute it. He says:

> “That there were then in Rome no, or only a few, acts of the martyrs, and no narratives of the martyrs’ passions, is certainly astonishing and inconvenient for the recent authors who everywhere introduce the Vatican codices.”

First, Saint Gregory by no means says that there was no codex in the archive of the Roman Church which Eulogius had requested to have communicated to him; he says only that it had not been found. Hence he adds:

> “In our search we did not find it, but, although we have not yet found it, we continue to search; and if it can be found, we shall send it.”

Second, even if the acts of all the martyrs, which had been collected by Eusebius of Caesarea during the time of Constantine, had not then been preserved in the Roman archives and libraries, it by no means follows rashly that there were then in Rome no, or only a few, acts of the martyrs, or no narratives of the martyrs’ passions.

Perhaps Gregory admits that in his own time the Roman libraries lacked collections in which all, or most, of the martyrs’ acts were found, as though reduced into a single corpus. Nevertheless, they were enriched with individual acts of martyrs, especially of those crowned with martyrdom in Italy and, above all, at Rome. I say nothing of the ancient codices relating to matters other than the histories of the martyrs, of which there might have been a very large supply at Rome; for the holy Doctor is silent about these.

Third, what prevents many codices from elsewhere having been brought to Rome even after the death of the most holy pontiff—codices which we would not now be ashamed to cite even if they were not older than Gregory? For with what reverence are parchments more than eleven hundred years old worthy to be regarded?

Let us now return to the sequence of Gregory’s history.

### 9.

Saint Gregory indicates that war had broken out in Italy in this year while lamenting the evils he was compelled to endure from the swords of the barbarians (Book VIII, Letter 2). It may be inferred from the letter written in the following indiction that the barbarians had made a descent upon Sardinia (Book IX, Letters 1 and following). For this reason Saint Gregory perhaps wished that not even a cleric should be excused from the watches and guard duties necessary for the defense of the cities; the monks were likewise bound by the same law (Book IX, Letter 73).

The holy man grieved no less over the perversity and injustice of judges and magistrates than over the ferocity of the enemy. Amid arms, when the laws were silent, they believed everything was permitted to them.

Gennadius, the Patrician of Africa, had been harassing Paul, bishop in Numidia, for many years. When the bishop had appealed to the Apostolic See, the patrician—who possessed supreme authority in the administration of that province—prevented the prelate, who had been attacked by various accusations, from coming to Rome (Book VI, Letter 63). The pope agreed that the bishop should go to the imperial court and bring his complaints before the emperor (Book VII, Letter 2).

At last Paul was ordered to return to Numidia so that he might be judged by the bishops of that province. Knowing his innocence, Gregory commended his case to the bishops Adeodatus, who at that time held the primacy, [Note: [Col. 0409D] See what we said above in Book II, chapter 6, number 2.] Maurentius, and especially Columbus (Book VIII, Letters 12 and 13). Gregory knew Columbus to be especially devoted to the Church founded by blessed Peter and utterly steadfast in what was right.

Nevertheless, he continued to fortify him against the entreaties and pressures of the nobles, by which his virtue might have been shaken:

> “Therefore, let no circumstance, let no power of persons, suspend you from your zeal for equity. Relying instead upon the Lord’s commands, despise everything opposed to uprightness. Stand firm with constancy in defending the cause of justice. Do not refuse to endure, if there are any, hatred on account of the truth, so that you may find a greater reward of merit at the coming of our Redeemer, insofar as, without neglecting his commandments, you have spent yourself in favor of justice and its defense.”

### 10.

Besides the general concern which the supreme pontiff was bound to exercise for the whole Church, he was obliged to look after the African Church with special zeal and care, since it traced its origin to the Roman Church. Saint Gregory teaches this in writing to Dominicus, bishop of Carthage:

> “Knowing from where the beginning of priestly ordination in the African regions took its origin, you act commendably in loving the Apostolic See and, with prudent remembrance, returning to the origin of your office” (Book VIII, Letter 33).

From this he proves that the bishops of both Churches were bound to foster mutual charity. On this occasion he proceeds to praise charity in these wholly golden words:

> “Great, however, is the power of charity, beloved brother, which by the bond of its sincerity binds hearts together in mutual affection and does not permit them to be dissolved from the structure of grace. It joins what is separated, preserves what is united, and makes those unknown to one another known through love. Therefore, whoever fixes his mind upon this foundation is not torn from the dwelling place of the heavenly homeland by the assault of any adversity; for wherever he turns, he does not depart from the threshold of the commandments” (ibid.).

Thus that most wise teacher of Christian piety sprinkled all his letters with refined teachings concerning charity, contempt for the world, patient endurance of adversity, devotion to sacred literature, and the other virtues belonging to the heavenly life. He took care to season everything he wrote with this salt. [Note: [Col. 0411D] See Letters 17 and 35 of the same Book VIII.]

### 11.

The most holy pontiff especially strove, by word and example, to turn bishops and others devoted to sacred ministries away from sordid gain and avarice. Hence he was displeased that Donus, bishop of Messina, had accepted so large a price merely for a burial that the heirs of the man who had purchased the right of burial appeared to have been reduced to poverty.

He therefore advises the bishop to return what he had received, especially since the testimony of Palumbus, bishop of Consentia, proved that it belonged by right to another (Book VIII, Letter 3). Although he did not prohibit accepting something for burial, and acknowledged that this had been done by ancient custom, he nevertheless said that he had forbidden it in his own Church and would give his consent to no one so that burial places might be obtained for a price.

> “We who are called bishops—what payments ought we to exact for burying the bodies of the faithful?”

Later, writing to Januarius, he allowed only that whatever anyone wished to offer might be accepted for lights:

> “But we absolutely forbid anything to be requested or demanded; for this is exceedingly irreligious, lest the Church—God forbid—should perhaps be called venal, or lest you appear to rejoice at human deaths, if you seek profit in any way from their corpses” (Book IX, Letter 3).

### 12.

Leo, bishop of Catania, was said to divide the fourth part of the ecclesiastical revenues among his clerics not in full but with some reduction, which was an indication of greed. As a result, complaints from the acolytes and others of the clergy reached the pope.

Of the other three portions of the Church’s possessions, one went to the bishop and his household for hospitality and reception of guests, another to the poor, and the third was reserved for the repair of the churches (Book VIII, Letter 7).

To remove every opportunity for complaints and accusations against the bishop, the most wise and equitable judge decreed:

> “We wish that whatever may perhaps accrue to your Church from revenue or under any other title, you must set aside a fourth portion from it without any reduction and, in accordance with the fear of God, divide it discreetly among the priests, deacons, and clergy as you deem appropriate. Thus, in such a way that each receives according to the merit of his labor, you shall have free authority to distribute it as you foresee fitting, so that those who deserve it may feel themselves consoled even by this temporal benefit, and that others, with the Lord’s help, may strive to advance by imitating them for the better” (Book IX, Letter 64).

### 13.

Having been pressed by the just complaints of the Catanian clerics, he issued this judgment against the bishop; shortly afterward he also suppressed their pride and empty vainglory on account of their usurped *campagi*. [Note: [Col. 0411D] See the notes on the cited letter.] The *campagi* were a type of footwear used by prelates when solemnly celebrating Mass.

Although the use of these shoes had formerly been granted by the Roman pontiffs only to the deacons of the Church of Messina throughout all Sicily, the Catanian deacons had nevertheless presumed to appear wearing *campagi*. Hating this rash presumption, the pope wrote to John of Syracuse so that he might investigate the matter and ascertain whether they had presumed to do this with his own authority or that of someone else; afterward he was to decide what ought to be done. “For,” he says, “if we carelessly overlook what has been wrongly usurped, we open the way for excesses by others” (Book VIII, Letter 27).

### 14.

Just as he restrained those who acted proudly and insolently, so he also strove to repay with the proper rewards of honor those who served the Church usefully. The defenders experienced this in the present year: he appointed seven from their college as *regionarii*, because they had diligently performed their duties in the Church’s affairs and in the service of the pontiffs (Book VIII, Letter 14).

Formerly the *regionarii* were chosen only from the deacons; later, by the concession of certain pontiffs, some were appointed from the school of notaries and subdeacons; finally, through the favor of Saint Gregory, this honor reached the defenders.

### 15.

Although in this year especially Saint Gregory made clear through numerous letters how much concern he devoted to monastic affairs, [Note: [Col. 0412D] See Letters 4, 8, 9, 11, 15, 31, and 34.] we shall touch upon only a few of them.

Most notable among them is the privilege granted to the monastery of Saints John and Stephen, situated in the city of Classis, concerning which he wrote to Marinianus, bishop of Ravenna (Book VIII, Letter 15). What this privilege provided for the benefit of the monks must be gathered from that letter.

It is clear from Letters 31 and 34 that the Castellian monastery, once founded by the great Cassiodorus, not only continued to exist at that time but also flourished and had other monasteries united to it. In the first letter, Secundinus, bishop of Taormina in Sicily, is warned not to allow a monastery in his diocese belonging to the Castellian monks to pass into the power of a layperson.

In another letter Saint Gregory appears to rebuke John, bishop of Scillium, in whose city that Castellian monastery was located, because he was attempting to weaken privileges granted to it and confirmed by long usage. From this letter it is established that Scillium itself had been founded on land belonging by right to the monastery, and that its inhabitants were obliged to pay a census to the Castellians.

## BOOK FOUR AND LAST

Presenting whatever remains of the history and life of Saint Gregory.

### CHAPTER ONE

#### Argument

1. Peace is made between the Romans and the Lombards through the efforts of Saint Gregory.  
2. He foretells that it will not last long.  
3. War is renewed by the exarch.  
4. The schismatics return to the Church. What Saint Gregory did to confirm them in the unity of the Church.  
5. The depraved morals of the schismatic bishops.  
6. Saint Gregory’s charity toward the schismatics.  
7. Concerning Secundinus, a most celebrated monk. He writes against the Three Chapters, although he is by no means a schismatic.  
8. Secundinus’s humble confession. Saint Gregory consoles him.  
9. Saint Gregory’s judgment concerning the use and veneration of sacred images is examined. It does not depart from the doctrine now received by the Church.  
10. Objections are answered. In his letters to Serenus, Saint Gregory prohibits only the attribution of the worship of *latria* to images.  
11. He praises the use of images as something accepted from antiquity, but not properly so-called adoration.  
12. His veneration for the relics of the saints. (Years 598 and 599.)

### 1.

For a long time Saint Gregory had been considering how peace might be made and secured between the Romans and the Lombards. To obtain it, he acted both with the emperor and with Agilulf, the king, and his wife Theodelinda, sending not only letters but also envoys.

The Roman exarch had always obstructed this useful and necessary policy for the state, although he was inferior in strength and insufficiently skilled in war and military affairs to free Italy from the Lombards. Not long before, the king of the Huns had obtained peace from Agilulf, who was then residing at Milan. With matters therefore settled with this most warlike people, the Lombards pressed more fiercely upon the cities that remained untouched.

Not long before, they had captured Croton in the farthest part of Italy and carried its inhabitants into captivity. Most recently they had invaded Sardinia to ravage it, as Gregory had foretold; he had warned both Gennadius, prefect of Africa (Book VII, Letter 3), and Januarius, bishop of Cagliari (Book IX, Letters 4 and 43), to provide for the defense of the island.

Who then would have dared promise himself peace? But God, in whose hand are the hearts of kings, moved Agilulf to lay down his arms and accept the conditions of peace offered by the pope.

Gregory had employed the services of Probus, an abbot [Note: [Col. 0413] Mabillon asks who this Abbot Probus was: *Benedictine Annals*, Book IX, no. 26, p. 252.] whom he had sent long before to the king and queen to negotiate peace, though always without success so long as the Roman exarch, the most hostile enemy of peace, remained alive. After the exarch’s death, when Callinicus, better disposed toward the good of the state, had assumed supreme authority in Italy, hope of restoring peace shone forth again.

At last peace was made, especially through the efforts of Theodore, the *curator* of Ravenna. Probus, the envoy for negotiating peace, found him a helper in everything (ibid., Letter 98).

King Agilulf confirmed the agreed terms and conditions of peace by an oath given in complete good faith. Gregory therefore thanked both him and Queen Theodelinda, from Abbot Probus having learned that she had labored especially diligently for concord.

In his letter to Agilulf, Gregory asks him to command his commanders stationed in various places, and especially in the Roman territories, to preserve the peace as it had been promised. He feared that they might seek an opportunity to renew the war.

Nor was his fear groundless. Ariulf, duke of Benevento, refused to swear that he would preserve the peace unless certain conditions were added—conditions by which he secretly and deceitfully sought an opportunity to attack the unsuspecting Romans despite the pledge that had been given. The suspicion was increased by the fact that Warnilfrida, at whose discretion and counsel Ariulf did everything, had utterly scorned to swear the oath. (Compare Paul the Deacon, *History*, Book IV, chapter 13.)

### 2.

On the other hand, Agilulf and the Lombards pressed Gregory to subscribe to an agreement, which he refused because he was the mediator and intermediary between the king and the exarch.

Since matters therefore stood in uncertainty, and war appeared to be threatening more dangerously under the appearance of peace, Gregory advised that, lest a fire deceitfully placed beneath ashes burst forth while the Romans were thinking of nothing of the kind, plans for war should be made even during peace.

He wrote especially to Januarius, bishop of Cagliari, first about reconciling the hearts of the citizens with one another in fear of the enemy:

> “For especially at this time, when there is fear of the enemy, you must not have a divided people.”

He then wrote about fortifying the city of Cagliari and other places on the island:

> “Therefore it is necessary that, while opportunity permits, your Fraternity take care to fortify your city or other places more strongly, and ensure that provisions be abundantly stored in them, so that, when the enemy—God angered against him—approaches there, he may find nothing to harm and may depart in confusion. We too are thinking about you as much as we can, and we are urging those concerned to prepare themselves, with God as their author, to resist; for just as you regard our tribulations as your own, so we likewise consider your afflictions our own” (Book IX, Letter 6).

### 3.

The pope’s fear of a war in the near future did not deceive him; for shortly afterward war broke out again and raged more fiercely.

Recently Agilulf had established a perpetual peace and treaty with Theoderic, king of the Franks. When three dukes rebelled—including the duke of Verona and the duke of Pergamum, whom he had already spared twice—he ordered them to be put to death, so that by this severity he might keep the others in their allegiance. We have spoken above about the peace recently made with the king of the Huns.

Considering these matters, Callinicus—perhaps emboldened by the victories won over the Slavs, and fearing that Agilulf, freed from every other war, might suddenly attack the Romans with united forces—resolved to seize the initiative against him.

Having therefore gathered an army and drawn several Lombard dukes over to the imperial side, he surrounded the strongly fortified city of Parma with a siege and captured it. During this conquest the exarch carried to Ravenna the captured duke Godiscalc and his wife, the king’s daughter.

But Agilulf, desiring to avenge the injury inflicted upon him and to repay it, pretended that he intended to attack Cremona, Mantua, and Mons Silicis in the territory of Padua, while in fact he attacked Padua. Having taken it, he leveled the city to the ground; the garrison, however, withdrew to Ravenna, while most of the population fled to the marshy regions of Venetia.

To prevent the exarch from bringing help to the besieged, the king ordered Ariulf and the Lombards occupying Etruria to harass Rome itself and Ravenna with continual raids. Meanwhile the Avars, joining forces with the Lombards and Slavs, ravaged Istria with sword and fire.

After the capture of Padua, Mons Silicis was conquered, and two Lombard dukes—the duke of Trent and the duke of Friuli—who had defected from the king, asked pardon for their violated faith and were received back into favor.

Thus Callinicus paid the penalty for disturbing the peace that had shortly before been established and consecrated by the sanctity of an oath. (Compare Paul the Deacon, *History of the Lombards*, Book IV, chapters 21, 24, and 25.)

### 4.

It is easier to imagine than to express in words how grievously Saint Gregory, who had labored so greatly for peace, bore this reversal, and how bitterly this angel of peace mourned its loss.

His grief was somewhat eased by the return to the Church of the island of Capritana, [Note: [Col. 0415] In the innermost recess of the Adriatic Sea, not far from the shore of the province of Friuli.] which had long adhered to the schism formed over the Three Chapters. When the pope heard that Callinicus had moved the inhabitants of Capritana to renounce the schism, he thanked him and praised his plan of bringing back to the bosom of the Church both the dissenters and the peoples subject to him who were in turmoil.

The command of the emperor Maurice, sent to Callinicus in defense of the schismatics, seemed to oppose his perseverance in this policy. But Gregory interpreted it as follows:

> “As for your wish that a copy of the command sent to you in defense of the schismatics should be shown to me, your most sweet Excellence ought carefully to have considered this: although the command itself was obtained by subterfuge, it does not order you to repel those who come to the unity of the Church, but only not to compel those who refuse to come at this uncertain time. Therefore you must hasten to report this very matter to our most pious emperors, so that they may learn that in their time the schismatics, with the assistance of Almighty God and through your labor, are hastening of their own accord to return” (Book IX, Letter 9).

In the same letter to the exarch, Saint Gregory complains both about the *major domus* and about Justin, whose counsel Callinicus followed; both of them, evidently, favored the heretics and schismatics openly enough.

The bishop of the island had initially petitioned Callinicus, asking that he and the entire people be permitted to return to the unity of the Church. He later changed his mind and returned again to the schismatics. The pope therefore decided that Marinianus, bishop of Ravenna, should ordain a bishop for the Church of Capritana, so that it might belong to his metropolitan jurisdiction until the bishops of Istria returned to the Catholic faith; the island of Capritana was, of course, assigned to their province (Book IX, Letter 10).

Nevertheless, before the new bishop’s ordination, the most wise pontiff thought it appropriate first to send someone to the schismatic bishop to admonish him about returning to the unity of the Catholic Church and to his own people.

Gregory also wrote to the inhabitants of the island, praising the love of unity with which they were aflame and informing them about what he had written to Marinianus. We have thought it appropriate to excerpt and append a few passages from this letter as little flowers, for they will delight both by their fragrance and by their appearance:

> “Our Redeemer . . . joins the lowest things to the highest in such a way that, while he himself remains in eternity, he orders temporal affairs by a hidden impulse and with pious moderation, so that the ancient enemy may in no way snatch from his hand those whom he foresaw before the ages as destined to be gathered within the bosom of Mother Church. For although one of those among whom he dwells bodily, moved by gusts of wind, may for a time totter like a branch, nevertheless the root of right faith, which emerges from concealment, remains green by divine judgment and is able, when the appointed time arrives, to display the fruit that had lain hidden. We recognize by the illumination of heavenly regard that this has now taken place in you through your desire: rejecting the obstinacy of the schismatics among whom you dwell, you show by the very action of the matter, with the readiest disposition of mind, that you wish to be gathered into the Lord’s fold. For those who dislike division testify that they wish to be sound; and by rejecting error, you show that you love what is right and avoid what is crooked” (ibid., Letter 97).

Other letters of this year deal with the peoples of Istria who had abandoned the schism (ibid., Letters 63, 94, 95, and 99). In bringing them back to the Church, the zeal of Gulfaris, master of the soldiers, shone forth especially. The most pious pastor congratulates him and thanks him for it, and urges him to persevere and to extend protection to those returning from the schism.

### 5.

Those schismatics who had returned to the fold reported many things about the depravity of the bishops of Istria. To bring these matters to the emperor Maurice and seek a remedy, they went to Constantinople and requested that they be commended to Anatolius, the legate of the Apostolic See.

Since the most holy pontiff could not refuse them this, he wrote to Anatolius that he should provide them assistance, consistently with justice. He had no doubt that what was equitable ought to be granted to heretics and schismatics no less than to others (Book IX, Letter 66).

### 6.

He proved this very point by his own example in the case of the clergy of the Church of Como, who had withdrawn from the Roman Church in order to follow the schism of the Istrians.

Constantius, archbishop of Milan, had exhorted them with priestly zeal to return to the unity of the Church. They replied that they had suffered many injuries, especially from the Roman Church, which had usurped a certain estate belonging to their Church. By this wholly unjust manner of acting, they claimed, they were driven away from association with the Romans rather than drawn to it by charity.

When Gregory received this account from Constantius, he replied that he would not continue to retain the estate which the people of Como claimed had been taken from them contrary to the order of justice, if it belonged to them by right, even though they delayed returning to communion. Once the truth had been ascertained, he would order it to be restored.

Moreover, if they should return to the unity of the Church, he would gladly grant them the estate in question, even if it did not belong to them.

### 7.

That the monk Secundinus, who nevertheless had not consented to the condemnation of the Three Chapters, ought not to be counted among those schismatics, as we have already said, is sufficiently clear from the letter written to him this year (Book IX, Letter 52).

Secundinus enjoyed great renown, especially at the court of the Lombard king, and possessed the highest authority with Theodelinda because of his learning and holiness. The queen therefore wished him to receive her son Adaloald from the sacred font, as Paul, the historian of Lombard affairs, bears witness (*History of the Lombards*, Book IV, chapter 26). Paul calls him “Secundus, a servant of Christ from Trent.” [Note: [Col. 0417] The same Paul teaches that he had composed a concise history of the Lombards: Book III of *The Deeds of the Lombards*, chapter 30, and Book IV, chapter 42.]

The heading of the letter calls him an enclosed man; and from the course of the letter, where he is called a *monomachus*—because of the solitary life he practiced—it is clear that he was not a cenobite but a hermit and anchorite.

The strictness of his enclosure was not, however, so great that he was forbidden to leave his cell or even to deal with very serious matters. Mabillon gives the example of Sigobert, an enclosed monk at Saint-Denis in the Parisian territory, who was sent with Grimo, abbot of Corbie, to Pope Gregory IV by Charles, prince of the Franks (*Benedictine Annals*, p. 252).

While the devout queen still remained hesitant, and could not be brought by Gregory’s exhortations or prayers to embrace the condemnation of the Three Chapters, Secundinus, who shared her opinion, wrote a short treatise defending his position. Theodelinda asked Gregory to reply to each of the arguments in the treatise that Secundinus had sent him.

Gregory excused himself from this task because the pains of gout forced him to remain bedridden and prevented all literary work. “But if, by the disposition of Almighty God, I recover,” he says, “I shall answer in detail everything that he [Secundinus] has written to me” (Book XIV, Letter 12).

The most holy Doctor, however, was never able to fulfill this promise because of his continual illnesses.

### 8.

Long before this booklet, in which that devout monk discussed the faith and ecclesiastical matters, he had written to Saint Gregory, asking him for instruction and to be armed by his counsels against the snares of the enemy. In that letter he had humbly confessed that, although more than fifty years old, he was still held and subjugated by youthful desires. The most experienced teacher of the heavenly life raised him up when he was bearing this most painfully and was almost losing heart, replying that it was no wonder if the cunning enemy laid greater snares for one who had prepared greater battles against him:

> “For he seeks the devices of deception with greater ardor,” he says, “the more fervently he recognizes that you yearn for your heavenly homeland . . . We, indeed, who live among human beings, are often tempted by the cunning enemy through human beings. But you, who pursue the way of the present life outside the company of human beings, must necessarily suffer greater conflicts, in proportion as the master of temptations himself approaches you.”

I omit the rest, which is truly outstanding and especially deserving of continual reading by monks, so that from it they may learn to cast off excessive confidence in their own condition, to shake off the sluggishness that commonly arises from it, and to keep watch with greater vigilance against the hidden snares of the enemy.

[Col. 0418A]

### 9.

At the end of the aforesaid letter there is a passage concerning images. On its occasion, we think it necessary to inquire into and assess what Saint Gregory thought about the use and veneration of sacred images. The devout monk had asked the pontiff for holy images; complying with his request, Gregory sent two curtains containing an image of God the Savior, of holy Mary the Mother of God, and of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

He had prefaced this gift by instructing his disciple about the use of images in these words:

> “Your request has greatly pleased us, because with your whole heart and with the whole intensity of your purpose you seek the one whose image you desire to have before your eyes, so that daily bodily vision may make you practiced: so that, while you look upon his picture, you may burn inwardly toward him whose image you desire to see.”

And below:

> “I know, indeed, that you do not ask for an image of our Savior in order to worship it as God, but so that, in remembrance of the Son of God, you may grow warm with love for him whose image you desire to see. We, indeed, do not prostrate ourselves before it as before the divinity; rather, we worship him whom, through the image, we remember either as born, or as having suffered, and also as seated upon the throne. And while the picture itself, like Scripture, brings the Son of God back to our memory, it either gladdens our mind with the resurrection or soothes it with the Passion.”

Here we have the whole doctrine of the Catholic Church concerning the use and veneration of images, including prostration before them. There is no need to discuss this part of the aforesaid letter further, since we have defended it as Gregory’s in our notes.

Moreover, the most holy Father teaches the same thing in other passages whose authenticity is beyond doubt. In a letter to Januarius, written somewhat earlier, he had commanded that the cross and an image of the Mother of God be removed from the synagogue of the Jews, with the veneration appropriate to them (Book IX, Letter 6).

[Col. 0418C]

### 10.

Nor do the things he wrote shortly afterward to Serenus, bishop of Massilia, take away or oppose the veneration due to images. He wrote that images ought not to be broken or thrown out of churches, but rather ought to be kept in temples, so that those who do not know letters might at least read by seeing on the walls what they could not read in books; yet he insisted that they were not to be worshiped. These words, I say, condemn image-worshipers—those, namely, who worship an image as though it were God—as we read above in the letter to Secundinus.

This is clear from Gregory’s own words to Serenus:

> “When your Fraternity saw certain worshipers of images, you broke and threw out those same images in the churches. And indeed we praised your zeal, lest anything made by human hands should be worshiped; but we declare that you ought not to have broken those same images.”

He then adds what we have already partly reported: that images are books for those who do not know letters, in which they may read and learn what they cannot learn from books.

When Serenus had further disregarded the admonition of the supreme shepherd, Gregory wrote another letter in which he rebuked his rash action more severely:

> “It had been reported to us that, inflamed by inconsiderate zeal, you had broken images of the saints under the pretext, as it were, that they ought not to be worshiped. And indeed, because you had forbidden them to be worshiped, we praised you entirely; but we censured you for breaking them. Tell me, brother: from what priest has it ever been heard that he did what you have done? Even if nothing else, should not this alone have restrained you from despising your other brothers and thinking yourself alone holy and wise? For it is one thing to worship a picture, and another to learn from the history represented in a picture what ought to be worshiped.”

Below, he teaches that antiquity admitted images for good reason. Hence he says that Serenus’s deed had produced the gravest scandal in the Church, so that the greater part of its children had withdrawn from communion with him.

> “Therefore,” he says, “we exhort you now at least to take care, to restrain yourself from this presumption, and to hasten to call back to yourself, with fatherly gentleness, every effort, and every diligence, the minds of those whom you recognize as separated from your unity. For the dispersed children of the Church must be summoned, and it must be shown to them by testimonies of Sacred Scripture that nothing made by human hands may be worshiped, since it is written: ‘You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve’ (Luke 4:8). Then it must be added that, because you saw that the painted images which had been made for the instruction of the uneducated people—so that those ignorant of letters might look upon the history itself and learn what had happened—had passed into worship, you were moved to order those images to be broken” (Book XI, Letter 13).

From these words it is clear:

[Col. 0419C]

### 11.

First, that Saint Gregory praised the use of images as something received in the Church from ancient times. Yet we do not think that their use began at the very origins of the Christian religion, since images could have offended Jews recently converted, and might have recalled newly Christianized Gentiles to idolatry. But once they could be admitted without danger, they immediately appeared in churches, especially for decoration and for the instruction of the uneducated, as Saint Paulinus, bishop of Nola, teaches (*On the Nativity 9, concerning Saint Felix*), who flourished in the fourth century.

Second, that by the worship which he forbids to be offered to images, the holy Doctor understood that supreme worship due to God alone. Hence he adduces this testimony of Scripture: “You shall worship the Lord your God,” and so forth. And below, when seeking some excuse for Serenus’s deed, he says that the images had been broken and thrown out for no other reason than that they should not be worshiped—something he had already observed being practiced by certain people.

Certainly Serenus lived among pagans, as Saint Gregory says (Book XI, Letter 13). We have already observed that many remnants of idolatry still survived in Gaul at that time. Therefore, when the bishop of Massilia saw certain people prostrate before images, he rashly judged that they were worshiping the images as God; and with still greater rashness he broke and threw out those same images, an act that compelled most people to abandon communion with him.

[Col. 0420A]

### 12.

Saint Gregory’s attitude toward the veneration of holy images can also be recognized from the exceptional veneration that he teaches should everywhere be shown to sacred relics, even to linens and cloths [Note: [Col. 0419D] See Book IV, Letter 30; Book VII, Letter 26; Book IX, Letter 122.] that had been placed over the tombs of the holy apostles or martyrs, or to similar objects.

Augustine and his companions, who had been formed under Gregory’s discipline, when they entered Dorobernia, resolved—as we related above—to carry before them a cross and an image of the Savior as a sacred standard, so that they might publicly testify how much worship and how much reverence they offered. But the things we read here as having been done by the disciples are evidence of the teaching of their master.

## CHAPTER II

**Summary.—** 1. Abbot Cyriacus is sent as legate to Gaul. — 2. He comes to Massilia, where he is badly received by Serenus. — 3. From there he goes to Arelate. Concerning privileges granted by the Apostolic See at the request of kings. — 4. What Saint Gregory replied to Desiderius of Vienne when he petitioned for privileges for his church. — 5. He grants the use of dalmatics to Aregius of Vapincum. — 6. And the pallium to Syagrius of Augustodunum, with the conditions attached. — 7. Letters to the kings of Gaul concerning the correction of abuses among the Gallican clergy. With what success. — 8. Concerning the bishop of Maurienne. — 9. Cyriacus’s embassy to Spain. — 10. The favorable condition of Spain at that time. Concerning Claudius, praised by the pope as administrator of the kingdom. — 11. The substance of the letter written to Leander. He is given the pallium. — 12. Eulogy of King Rechared. He rejects money offered by the Jews. — 13. Outstanding admonitions given to the king. *(Years 598 and 599.)*

### 1.

The Gallican Church, always especially dear to our Gregory, experienced his fatherly concern particularly in this year. For when he had been informed of various vices and abuses spreading throughout Gaul, he was not satisfied merely to admonish the kings and bishops concerning their correction, but also thought that a legate ought to be sent there:

[Col. 0420C]

> “who might act energetically with the princes and bishops, so that a council might be celebrated as quickly as possible to cut out these abuses” (Book IX, Letters 105 and 120).

This was Cyriacus, abbot of Saint Andrew at the Clivus Scauri, who had previously been sent to Sardinia to assist Bishop Felix in the conversion of the Barbaricini. From this we understand how flourishing that Roman monastery of Saint Gregory then was: from it, at the same time, so many preachers of the sacred word were taken and sent for the conversion of the English, and a legate of the Apostolic See was chosen to conduct the most serious affairs both in Gaul and in Spain. (Compare Mabillon, *Benedictine Annals*, Book IX, p. 256.)

[Note: [Col. 0419D] Especially in the kingdom of Burgundy, beyond which Cyriacus’s embassy did not extend, and Syagrius’s authority to summon synods was conferred.]

[Note: [Col. 0420D] See Book IV, Letters 24, 25, and 26.]

### 2.

Provided with many letters from the pope, Cyriacus first came to Massilia by sea. There, after greeting Bishop Serenus in the name of the pontiff, he delivered the admonitory letters concerning the breaking of images that we mentioned above (Chapter 1, no. 10).

We infer that the legate was not received by the bishop with the charity and reverence that were appropriate from the fact that Serenus, in order to give himself greater liberty to vent his anger, pretended that the papal letters delivered to him by Cyriacus were forged. Saint Gregory later gravely rebuked him for this insulting suspicion against the legate, writing to Serenus as follows:

> “From the fact that you doubted the writings which we sent to you, it became apparent how incautious you are. For if you had carefully attended to the things we advised out of brotherly love, you would not merely have had no doubt, but would rather have understood what it was fitting for you to do with priestly dignity. For Cyriacus, once abbot and bearer of our writings, was not of such discipline or learning that he himself would dare to do something else, as you suppose, nor should you have entertained this suspicion of forgery concerning his person. But while you postponed weighing the salutary admonitions, it happened that you were now culpable not only in deed but also in your accusation” (Book XI, Letter 13).

### 3.

After leaving Massilia, we believe that Cyriacus came to Arelate and delivered to Virgilius the letter of the supreme pontiff by which he confirmed privileges [Note: [Col. 0421D] Concerning this monastery, consult the notes to the aforesaid letter and Mabillon’s *Benedictine Annals*, Book V, p. 128, where he refutes the conjecture of the author of the *Pontifical Book of Arelate* concerning this monastery.] once granted by Pope Vigilius to a certain monastery of men.

We know nothing else about the privileges granted to this monastery [Col. 0421B] except what Saint Gregory teaches us (Book IX, Letter 111): namely, that Childebert, king of the Franks, of glorious memory, had established a monastery of men within the walls of the city of Arelate and had granted certain resources for the support of its inhabitants. So that his will should not be rendered void, and so that the arrangements made for the peace of the monks should not be disturbed, he had asked in his letters that these things be confirmed by apostolic authority.

He had added to his petition a request that certain privileges also be granted to the same monastery both in the administration of its affairs and in the appointment of its abbot, knowing that the faithful showed such reverence to the Apostolic See that whatever had been ordered by its decree would thereafter be troubled by no illicit usurpation.

Pope Vigilius had assented to the royal request and had written about the matter to Aurelius, or Aurelianus, the bishop. But lest what Vigilius had granted be erased by the passage of time and overturned by the bishops of Arelate, Saint Gregory sent Virgilius a copy of the privilege granted by his predecessor and indicated that he approved everything contained in it.

> “For although,” he says, “the things once sanctioned by the authority of the Apostolic See require no further strengthening, nevertheless, out of abundance, we again confirm by our authority in every respect all that our predecessor established for the peace of this matter. Therefore let your Fraternity conduct itself in guarding these things in such a way that it both excludes every opportunity for disturbance and persuades others to carry them out, while showing itself, as is fitting, attentive and devoted to preserving the most devout will of the deceased.”

[Note: [Col. 0421D] From these words we learn not only that Aurelius consented to the privileges granted by the Apostolic See, but also that he wished them to be granted. This seems to suggest that, besides King Childebert, the monastery mentioned above also had Aurelius as its founder—perhaps because he gave the monks the rule according to which they were to live. Read it in Codex Regius, Part II, p. 69.]

The excellent Father was so intent on safeguarding the tranquility of the servants of God.

In any case, these and similar privileges [Note: [Col. 0422D] See especially Book XIII, Letters 6, 8, 9, and 10.] frequently granted by Roman pontiffs to Gallican monasteries at the request even of kings prove that, already at that time, the authority of the Roman pontiffs was regarded as supreme even in Gaul: without it, nothing was considered valid; once it had been given, everything stood firm and unshaken.

[Col. 0422A]

### 4.

On leaving Arelate, Cyriacus perhaps proceeded to Vienne and presented Archbishop Desiderius with Saint Gregory’s letter replying to his petition for privileges. This prelate said that certain privileges had once been granted to his church by the Apostolic See, and that his predecessors had possessed the use of the pallium from ancient times. He earnestly desired that these privileges be restored to himself and to the other bishops of Vienne in the future.

Saint Gregory states, however, that nothing had been found in the archives of the Roman Church by which those privileges could be proven to have been granted at some earlier time. He therefore advises the archbishop to search diligently for the documents of his church and, if any are found by which what he claimed can be proved, to arrange for them to be sent to Rome.

> “For we who grant new things,” he says, “most willingly restore old ones” (Book IX, Letter 112).

From this it is clear that the pallium had not once been granted to all metropolitans. He later wrote almost the same thing to Aetherius of Lyons (Book XI, Letter 56).

### 5.

That Cyriacus sought Vapincum is attested by the letter written to Aregius, bishop of Vapincum (Book XI, Letter 107). In it the most holy pontiff both consoles his friend, who was mourning the death of his relatives, and asks him to attend the synod to be summoned by Syagrius and to inform him of everything done there, since he knew the holiness of so great a man.

Aregius had not long before gone to Rome to visit the thresholds of the holy apostles and to greet Saint Gregory. He had also asked that permission be given to himself and to his archdeacon to use dalmatics. At that time deacons did not all use them indiscriminately, but wore tunics with narrow sleeves, whereas dalmatics had wide sleeves.

We read in the *Life of Saint Caesarius of Arelate* that Pope Symmachus, moved by the great dignity of his merits, “caused his deacons to be distinguished in dress by dalmatics, after the manner of the Roman Church.”

Compelled by the weakness of his men, Aregius had departed hurriedly without yet obtaining the privilege of using dalmatics. Gregory sent it to him through Cyriacus, adding the dalmatics themselves. (Compare John the Deacon, Book III, Chapter 59.)

[Note: [Col. 0422D] Or Aredius: he had succeeded Sagittarius, who, together with Salonius, had been deposed in several councils. At last both were thrust under guard into the basilica of Saint Marcellus at Chalon, as Gregory of Tours records, *History*, Book V, Chapter 28.]

[Note: [Col. 0422D] Edited by Mabillon in Volume I of the *Acts of the Saints*, p. 665.]

### 6.

After traveling through so many cities, the legate finally arrived at Augustodunum, where he had to transact ecclesiastical business especially with Bishop Syagrius. Cyriacus brought him two letters from Saint Gregory.

The first, like an encyclical, was addressed jointly to Syagrius of Augustodunum, Aetherius of Lyons, Virgilius of Arelate, and Desiderius of Vienne. In it Gregory enumerated the evils spreading through the Gallican churches: simony; the premature promotion to the priesthood of neophytes or laymen who had not yet been tested; the cohabitation of women with clerics; and the neglect of synods, which ought to be held every year. He judged that a council should deliberate on removing these abuses.

The second letter, after first giving thanks for Syagrius’s assistance to Augustine, granted him the use of the pallium and decreed that the Church of Augustodunum should hold the first place in the province after Lyons.

[Note: [Col. 0423D] We observed above that the pallium was not formerly given to all metropolitans. The example of Syagrius proves that it was not granted only to them. In Gregory’s letters, it is also read as having been granted to many bishops of Sicily, whether of Syracuse or Palermo.]

He then entrusted Syagrius, as exercising the authority of the Apostolic See, with the task of convening the synod.

This bishop had great authority with Queen Brunichild and her grandsons Theoderic and Theodebert. Nor was this undeserved, for, according to the testimony of John the regionary and many others, he fulfilled the name of priest also in his conduct.

It had already been some time since Brunichild had petitioned the pope that the pallium be granted to him. But learn from the letter soon to be mentioned, addressed to that same queen, what reason there was for the delay in conferring this honor. Indeed, when Gregory granted Syagrius permission to use the pallium only in celebrating the solemnities of Mass, he added this condition:

> “We have decreed that this should be given to you only if you first promise, through the decision of a synod, to correct the things which we have commanded to be corrected.”

And below:

> “Since we know that our most excellent sons, the kings of the Franks, show you great affection, you must act with every zeal and every effort so that, through the vigilance of your Fraternity, what we have commanded concerning the convening of the synod may be fulfilled, and so that everything we have written for the salvation of souls may be considered there. Thus you may demonstrate both your zeal and how displeasing unlawful things are to you there, while we may appear to have made a useful provision in choosing your person above all others for this task” (Book IX, Letter 11).

### 7.

The pope wrote on the same subject both to Brunichild and to Kings Theoderic and Theodebert (Book IX, Letters 109 and 110). The substance of these letters is that many men were ordained through simony and that laymen were suddenly made bishops. They were to arrange for a synod to be held to correct these abuses; moreover, they were to establish that Jews might not be permitted to own Christian slaves.

Two years later he again wrote many letters concerning the celebration of the synod [Note: [Col. 0423D] See Book XI, from Letter 63 onward.]

Yet we do not read that a council was held in Gaul at this time to eradicate and eliminate such abuses from the Gallican clergy, although this was a matter very close to the heart of the most holy pontiff. Perhaps the reason was that the bishops, especially the metropolitans, were unwilling to obey Syagrius, who had been placed over them.

[Col. 0423D]

### 8.

The request he had made of the same kings on behalf of Ursicinus, bishop of Turin, had no happier outcome—namely, that certain parishes taken away from his church should be restored (ibid., Letters 115 and 116).

The dispute concerned especially the districts of Maurienne and Segusium. When King Guntram had occupied them, they no longer wished to be subject to the bishop of Turin, because the city was under Lombard rule. Thus the city of Maurienne began to have its own bishop, who was first assigned to the metropolitan of Tarentaise and afterward to the metropolitan of Vienne, as remains the case today.

[Note: [Col. 0424D] Later called, together with the valley itself, Saint-Jean-de-Maurienne, because of the fame of the miracles of Saint John the Baptist at this place, where his distinguished relics remain. Concerning them, see Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, Book I, Chapter 14 and following.]

### 9.

Cyriacus’s embassy had a more successful outcome among the Spaniards. For, as it is reasonable to believe, through his efforts the Council of Barcelona was held this year on the Kalends of November. Of its four canons, two attack the stain of simony, and a third was enacted against the premature ordination of neophytes.

By this term, as we have said, are understood laymen who, not yet tested by continual practice, dared, encouraged by ambition and led by secular power, to rush into the priesthood and even into the episcopate.

### 10.

Spain was then in a favorable condition under the excellent King Rechared, who had taken upright men as assistants in administering his kingdom. Among them were Claudius and Leander, bishop of Hispalis, of whom we have already often spoken.

Who and what kind of man Claudius was can be recognized no better than from the Gregorian letter carried by Cyriacus:

> “Because the reputation of good men gives off fragrance like ointment, the fame of Your Glory has spread its scent from the western regions all the way here. Sprinkled, so to speak, with the sweetness of this breeze, I confess that I greatly loved one whom I did not know, and with the hand of love I seized you within my heart. I no longer loved him as one who did not know him, since I had come to know his good qualities. For one who is known to me with great attention but remains unknown to me in bodily sight, I can surely say this truthfully: I know his person, but I do not know his dwelling.

> “A great confirmation of your praise is given by the report that Your Glory diligently adheres to the excellent king of the Goths. For since good men are always displeasing to the wicked, it is certain that you are good, because you have pleased a good man” (Book IX, Letter 120).

He afterward exhorts this excellent man to perseverance. At the end of the letter he commends Cyriacus, so that, once he had completed the tasks entrusted to him, no delay in returning should hinder him.

It would not be proper to remain silent about two other letters carried by this legate to Spain, one to Leander and the other to the king himself, both of them truly outstanding.

### 11.

In the first, Gregory wonderfully praises the letter he had recently received from the holy man:

> “When this letter was read, good and wise men were present, whose hearts were immediately moved to compunction. Each began, with the hand of love, to seize you within his own heart, because in that letter it was not possible merely to hear the sweetness of your mind, but to see it. Each person was kindled and amazed, and the very fire of those listening revealed what had been the ardor of the speaker.”

These words naturally arouse a great longing for the lost letter. The pontiff censures one thing in it: its incredible humility, and he grieves that it was written by a friend—namely, the claim that his life was imitable by everyone.

This moves him to tears over the loss of the tranquility of his former life and the acquisition of the pontificate:

> “For I was sailing, as it were, with a favorable wind when I was leading a tranquil life in the monastery. But suddenly a storm arose with violent movements, seized me in its disturbance, and I lost the favorable progress of my journey, because, having lost my tranquility, I suffered shipwreck of mind. Behold, I am now tossed upon the waves, and I seek the plank of your intercession, so that I who did not deserve to reach the shore safely in an intact ship may at least, after my losses, be brought back to land upon a plank” (Book IX, Letter 121).

At the end of the letter he indicates that, through the blessing of Saint Peter, the pallium had been sent to Leander. It was rightly owed to him because of ancient custom, his own dignity and goodness, and the excellent character of King Rechared, who had asked that this honor be granted to his father and teacher in the Catholic faith (Book IX, Letter 122).

### 12.

In the letter in which Saint Gregory replies to the correspondence received from the king, the same supreme humility of spirit shines no less brightly. After exclaiming in astonishment over Rechared’s work in converting all the Goths, formerly Arians, to the Catholic faith—“This is the change of the right hand of the Most High” (Psalm 76:11)—he adds:

> “For whose breast, even if made of stone, would not immediately soften, once this great work had become known, in praise of almighty God and in love for Your Excellence? I confess that I often enjoy telling my assembled sons about what has been done through you, and often admiring it together with them. These things frequently rouse me even against myself, because I, lazy and useless, lie inert in idle repose at the very time when kings are laboring in the gathering of souls for the gain of the heavenly homeland. What, then, shall I say to the Judge who comes at that fearful examination, if I arrive there empty, while Your Excellence leads behind you flocks of the faithful whom you have now drawn to the grace of the true faith through diligent and continual preaching?” (Book IX, Letter 112).

He afterward gives thanks for the royal gifts sent to blessed Peter, among which was a golden chalice. He especially praises the king for rejecting the great sum of money that the Jews had offered so that he would rescind the law enacted against them. By this deed he preferred innocence to gold, and imitated—or rather surpassed—David.

> “For if despised water was turned by an armed king into a sacrifice to God, let us consider what kind of sacrifice the king offered to almighty God who, for love of him, disdained to accept not water but gold. Therefore, most excellent son, I shall say confidently that you have offered gold to the Lord, since you were unwilling to possess it against him. These are great things, and they must be attributed to the praise of almighty God” (Book IX, Letter 61).

### 13.

The more outstanding were the things that Gregory reported about the young king, the greater the danger that threatened him from the spirit of pride. “For,” he says, “robbers on the road do not seek out empty travelers, but those who carry vessels of gold or silver.”

Therefore he thought that the young king must be fortified with exceptional admonitions and instructions against the hidden snares of the deceitful enemy:
