> “For often,” he says, “the malignant spirit, in order to destroy the good things against which it was previously unable to prevail, comes to the mind of the one who has performed the work after the work has been completed, and unsettles it with silent thoughts in which it praises that person in certain ways. Thus the deceived mind admires how great are the things it has done. While it is lifted up within itself by hidden swelling, it is deprived of the grace of the one who bestowed the gift . . . What, then, must be done in these matters except that, whenever the malignant spirit brings back to us the good things we have done in order to lift up our mind, we should always recall our own sins to memory? Thus we may recognize as ours the things we have done by sinning, but recognize as gifts of almighty God alone the things we possess when we turn away from sins.”

In return for the gifts received from the king, Saint Gregory sent sacred relics. Rechared had sent much greater gifts long before through legates who were abbots from monasteries; but, after their ships struck certain reefs near Massilia, they could scarcely save their lives (Book IX, Letter 61).

But enough concerning Gregory’s letter to this king, especially since his excellence is praised in the notes to that letter.

## CHAPTER III

**Summary.—** 1. Gregory, though ill, neglects nothing of his pastoral care. — 2. Crementius, primate of the province of Byzacena, takes refuge in his judgment. — 3. The authority of metropolitans over the bishops of their province. — 4. Saint Gregory orders wandering bishops to be returned to their metropolitans without whose permission they had departed. — 5. The procedure for judging bishops, in the condemnation of the bishop of Melita. — 6. Those who usurp the office of Defenders are punished. — 7. Saint Gregory’s humble reply to unjust complaints. — 8. How much prudence shines forth in his various decrees. — 9. His great concern for monks. — 10. Saint Columbanus consults him. *(Years 598 and 599.)*

### 1.

Although we know that Gregory was particularly weak in health during this year and suffered from gout, he nevertheless never showed himself more energetic in carrying out the duties of his office, as is proved by the letters he wrote on so many different matters to the bishops of nearly the entire Christian world (Book IX, Letter 121; Book X, Letter 35). Indeed, when we weigh what he accomplished for the Church and the commonwealth, we are moved to say that, although Gregory was ill, the pontiff always remained vigorous and strong.

### 2.

From the farthest part of Africa, namely from the province of Byzacena, Crementius, its primate, was finally forced to take refuge in the pope’s judgment. He had been accused of a certain crime, and the emperor had wanted him to be judged by the Roman pontiff in accordance with the canonical statutes. But Theodorus, the master of the soldiers, having received ten pounds of gold, prevented this from happening.

The Augustus nevertheless insisted that the pope send someone and do whatever was canonical. Accordingly, Crementius, attacked by his colleagues and fellow bishops, and with the emperor pressing him from another direction, sent the scholasticus Martin to Sicily, to John of Syracuse. He knew John to be very pleasing and close to Gregory, so that with John’s support he might more easily gain access to the supreme pontiff.

Crementius professed that he was subject to the Apostolic See; but it was uncertain whether he did so sincerely or deceptively. Concerning his claim to submit to the Apostolic See, the holy Doctor says:

> “If any fault is found in bishops, I do not know which bishop is not subject to it.” (See Book IX, Letter 59.)

Crementius and his advocate Martin the scholasticus, in order more easily to deflect the accusations of the bishops of Byzacena and turn them back against those bishops, brought various complaints against them before the supreme pontiff. Their chief complaint was that some of them had gone to the imperial court without letters from their primate and had held unlawful assemblies there.

Gregory indicated that he did not approve this at all, but he refused to give judgment in the matter:

> “Because the origin and nature of the cases are entirely unknown to us, we cannot pronounce anything definitively, lest—and this is highly reprehensible—we appear to give judgment concerning matters that we have not properly investigated” (Book VI, Letter 58).

He wrote to John of Syracuse, leaving it to his discretion to discuss the matter with Martin and to judge what ought to be done.

We learn from Letter 32 of Book XII, written to the same synod, that the case of Crementius was afterward discussed in the synod of the province of Byzacena.

[Note: [Col. 0427D] The same prudence shines forth in Book X, Letter 29, where the case of Bishop Pompeius is discussed. In it Gregory seems entirely to disapprove of extracting a confession of crime by torture. “These proceedings,” he says, “could have been suitable for reaching a decision if the accused’s confession had followed them—provided, however, that the same confession had been drawn out from hidden motives by the subtlety of examination, and not extorted by severe affliction, which often brings it about that even the innocent are compelled to confess themselves guilty.”]

### 3.

From Crementius’s complaint that the bishops of his province had gone to the imperial court without his permission and letters of recommendation, it can be understood how much their suffragan bishops then depended upon their metropolitans or primates.

The same is proved by another letter of Saint Gregory addressed to the bishops of Sardinia. In it he rebukes both those who did not consider it worthwhile to learn from their metropolitan the day of the Easter festival and those who, when necessity required them to travel overseas on account of matters concerning their churches, dared to go without the knowledge or letters of their metropolitan, as the order of the canons requires:

> “Therefore we exhort your Fraternity, as you follow the ancient custom of your churches, that both when receiving the announcement of Easter and whenever necessity compels one of you to travel anywhere on his own affairs, you must seek permission from that same metropolitan according to the rule prescribed for you, and presume in no way to disregard him—except if, as we do not wish, it should happen that you have some case against that same metropolitan, so that for this reason you seek the judgment of the Apostolic See” (Book IX, Letter 8).

### 4.

He ordered wandering bishops who were disobedient to their metropolitans to be returned to those metropolitans, so that they might receive the punishments they deserved.

Thus he writes to Syagrius concerning a certain Theodorus, bishop of the diocese of Milan, who, avoiding the discipline of Archbishop Constantius, was staying in Gaul. Gregory orders that he be sought out with the greatest diligence and brought back to his metropolitan.

In the same letter he also orders that Menas, a bishop from the diocese of the Roman Church whose episcopal title no longer possessed any honor, be driven out of Gaul and sent to Rome, so that, restrained under the discipline appropriate to him, he might strive to convert his worldly habits to priestly dignity (ibid., Letter 113).

### 5.

The procedure for judging guilty bishops is described in a letter to John, bishop of Syracuse. A complaint had been brought against Lucillus, bishop of the city of Melita, and John had instituted an inquiry into his offense, which he later sent in writing to the supreme pontiff. After reading it, Gregory replied to John:

> Since punishment for so great a crime ought not to be postponed by any delay, let your Fraternity associate with you three or four of our brothers and fellow priests, so that, with them also present and the truth having been established and acknowledged, you may strive without hesitation to depose the aforesaid Lucillus from the episcopal order, which the contagion of such a crime has stained.

(*Book IX, Letter 63*).

Certain deacons or presbyters were said to have been aware of and participants in the bishop’s crime. The pontiff wishes these men, after a diligent investigation, to be removed from their rank of honor if they are found guilty and thrust into monasteries for the sake of doing penance. As for the laymen stained by participation in the same offense, he decrees that those whose guilt becomes clear are to be deprived of participation in the Lord’s body and blood, and that litanies and prayers are additionally to be prescribed.

> [Note: [Col. 0428D] No mention is made of the excommunication of the bishop, presbyters, or deacons, because deprivation of their respective ranks constituted a sufficient punishment. When sufficient indications of guilt were present, the holy pontiff ordered presbyters and other clerics to be thrown into strict custody. See Book X, Letter 4.]

He leaves the length of this penance to John’s discretion, admonishing him to ensure that those who were pressed by the danger of death should not be denied the viaticum. When Trajan, abbot of the monastery at Syracuse, had been appointed in place of the deposed bishop, Saint Gregory ordered Lucillus and his son Peter to restore to him the property of the Church of Melita, which that disgraceful bishop—not its ruler or father—had plundered (*Book X, Letter 1*).

The new bishop asked permission to take four or five monks from his monastery, whom he might have as assistants and companions. Although the wisest pontiff judged this reasonable, he nevertheless did not wish to grant them by his own authority; instead, he left the matter to John’s discretion, lest he seem to diminish the bishop’s rights.

### 6.

In this same year the vengeance of the most impartial pontiff blazed against those in Sicily who dared to assume for themselves the name and authority of *defensors*. He wrote to the Roman defensor concerning their investigation and restraint. Since one of them, named Martianus, had delayed to show obedience to John, who administered the Roman patrimony, he ordered the contumacious man to be deported into exile.

> [Note: [Col. 0428D] See Book XI, Letter 71, and Book XIII, Letter 45, where mention is also made of the punishment of exile inflicted or to be inflicted upon clerics, including bishops, in the ecclesiastical court.]

### 7.

In all these judgments he displayed a mind both unbending and upright in its exercise, yet he proved how humble his spirit was, especially in his reply to the often-mentioned John of Syracuse concerning certain complaints against Gregory that John had reported as having been published (*Book IX, Letter 12*).

Some people were displeased that, in arranging certain rites pertaining to the Mass, Gregory had followed the customs of the Church of Constantinople. Carried away by a false zeal for the Roman Church, they alleged that its honor had been diminished by ceremonies borrowed from an inferior church.

To this the pontiff replied with humility superior to his dignity. First, he said that in the matters he had regulated he had imitated the rites of no other church. Second, he said that he was not ashamed to imitate whatever good he found in inferior churches:

> For he is foolish who thinks himself first in such a way that he refuses to learn the good things he has seen.

These words are altogether worthy of so wise a pontiff.

### 8.

The supreme prudence of the holy man shone forth especially in the measures he instituted against Jewish merchants, so that they would not be permitted to retain Christian slaves, something they greatly desired and sought to obtain by various devices. Yet the remarkably perceptive man, with extraordinary simplicity, frustrated them all.

His prudence must also be counted in the decision that, although he allowed no limits to be placed upon his own almsgiving, he nevertheless determined that he could not tolerate property granted as alms for several years being subsequently demanded as though it were a debt (*Book IX, Letter 36*).

Although the law does not permit property belonging to the Church to be alienated, as the holy Doctor himself states at the beginning of his letter to the Roman defensor, he nevertheless judged that the severity of this law should sometimes be tempered out of consideration for mercy (*ibid., Letter 26*). Therefore he ordered that a house donated by Ammonia to the Roman Church be restored to her nephew Calixenus, who was suffering from poverty, although Calixenus strenuously maintained that his grandmother had had no authority to alienate the house—a contention Gregory did not at all approve.

In another letter he admonished the same Roman defensor (*Book IX, Letter 27*) to beware lest, by too readily extending the Church’s patronage, he defend wicked men and thus become an accomplice in their crimes. For this reason Gregory did not wish any consideration to be given to letters of his, should he happen to have carelessly supplied letters of recommendation (*ibid., Letter 69*).

Let us now briefly review what the most impartial father decreed this year for the benefit of the monastic order.

### 9.

First, he declared the testament of a certain abbess invalid and ordered that what she had unlawfully left to others be restored to her monastery:

> Since those who enter a monastery for the purpose of conversion no longer have any license to make a will, even if they have not assumed the monastic habit.

(*Book IX, Letter 7*). On this matter, see the first letter of Book X.

Second, he settled a dispute between his subdeacon Antonius, the superintendent of a hospice, and Domitius, presbyter and abbot of the monastery of Saints Maximus and Agatha, and confirmed the agreements they had made with one another (*Book IX, Letter 20*).

[Col. 0429D] Third, he ordered that the estate called Massa Veneris, unjustly seized by agents of the Roman Church, be returned to the monastery of Saint Mark near Spoleto (*Book IX, Letter 30*).

Fourth, when Valentinus, presbyter and abbot, complained that monks deprived of communion by him for their offenses were nevertheless being admitted to communion in the diocese of Spoleto, Saint Gregory wrote to Chrysanthus, bishop of Spoleto, instructing him not to allow communion to be indiscriminately restored to monks who fled to his Church (*Book IX, Letter 37*).

> [Note: [Col. 0429] On the excommunication of monks for offenses, consult the Rule of Saint Benedict, chapters 23, 24, 25, 26, and 27.]

We have discussed the privileges granted to the monastery at Arles in the preceding chapter.

### 10.

The fame of his exceptional kindness toward monks perhaps prompted the celebrated abbot Columban to seek refuge with him while he was being harassed in Gaul on account of certain distinctive rites of the Scots, especially their observance of Easter, to which he was particularly attached. For this reason he wrote to our Gregory (*Book IX, Letter 127*).

The substance of his letter is that, in the celebration of Easter, the cycle of Victorius should be rejected and the custom of the Scots embraced—a custom favored by Anatolius, whom Jerome praised. He also consulted Saint Gregory concerning bishops ordained either through simony or after falling while in the diaconate, as well as concerning monks who abandoned their monastery. He praised the book of the *Pastoral Rule* and requested expositions of Ezekiel and the Song of Songs.

In the following year a council was held in Gaul at which the Scottish rite observed by Columban was proscribed. After the most holy abbot was expelled from Gaul, he went to Agilulf, king of the Lombards, and in his dominion founded the famous monastery of Bobbio. The reason he preferred to establish his seat in the Lombard kingdom rather than in other parts of Italy may perhaps have been that he knew the condemnation of the Three Chapters had not been accepted among the Lombards. For the pious abbot, otherwise, opposed this condemnation, as is clear from his letter to Boniface IV. (Compare the *Benedictine Annals*, Book IX, p. 256.)

## CHAPTER IV

**SUMMARY.—** 1. Gregory’s patience in illness and his unremitting labor. — 2. With what concern he attempted to suppress the heresy of the Agnoitae. He praises the writings of Saint Eulogius against them. He confronts the emerging error at Thessalonica. — 3. The Slavs invade Italy. A truce is agreed with the Lombards for a year. — 4. A son is born to their king. Lombard clothing and customs. — 5. Augustus punishes those guilty of extortion. Asylums in churches. Gregory’s concern for friends who had been accused. — 6. He attempts to incline a judge toward clemency. — 7. He consoles a friend stripped of his wealth and restores him through generosity. Similar consolatory letter to Dominicus. — 8. He arouses those enjoying prosperity to despise it. — 9. He does not conceal the faults of his friends. — 10. Fortunatus, bishop of Naples, dies. Saint Gregory deliberates at length concerning his successor. — 11. He reproves the duke of Campania for harassing monks. *(Years 599 and 600.)*

### 1.

Gregory’s illnesses grew worse from day to day, yet he could say with the Apostle:

> When I am weak, then I am strong.

(II Corinthians XII, 10).

He vividly sketches the remarkable equanimity of his spirit amid the torments of so many diseases in these words to his friend Eulogius:

> Behold, he says, almost two years have now been completed during which I have been confined to my bed, and I am afflicted with such severe pains of gout that scarcely on feast days can I rise for as long as three hours to celebrate the solemnities of the Mass. Soon afterward I am driven to lie down again by severe pain, so that I can endure my torment by interrupting it with groans. Sometimes this pain is mild for me; sometimes it is excessive. Yet it is neither so mild that it departs nor so excessive that it kills. Thus it happens that, although I am in death every day, every day I am driven back from death. Nor is this surprising, since, as a grievous sinner, I am held enclosed for a long time in the prison of such corruption. Therefore I am compelled to cry out: “Bring my soul out of prison, that I may confess your name” (Psalm CXLI, 8). But since I do not yet deserve to obtain this through my own prayers, I ask that the prayer of Your Holiness provide me with the help of its intercession and set me free from the burden of sin and corruption, restoring me to that freedom of the glory of the children of God which you know so well.

(*Book X, Letter 35*).

The summer heat seemed capable of alleviating the torments of gout, since it was suited to driving away harmful and diseased humors; yet in other respects it was very hostile to his body, as he himself says (*Homily 34 on the Gospels*, no. 1), because he was being consumed by slow and continuous fevers.

Without doubt, another pontiff, thinking of nothing but reducing his discomfort, applying remedies, and summoning physicians, would have dismissed ecclesiastical business at their direction and entrusted all the concerns of the pontificate to deputies. There are not lacking supreme prelates and bishops who seek to take on the pastoral burden, whether out of charity or ambition. But the most holy Shepherd of all Christ’s sheep did not think that the yoke imposed upon him by Christ should be shifted onto foreign or substitute shoulders; for this is how he called the pontifical office.

### 2.

His chief concern, however, was to examine and suppress emerging errors as soon as they became known. Not long before, the heresy of the Agnoitae had arisen at Alexandria. Some trace its beginnings to the deacon Themistius, for which reason they were called Themistians. Saint Eulogius of Alexandria, who fought against heretics of this kind, states that certain monks from Palestine had stirred up this heresy (*John of Damascus, On Heresies*, in Photius, *Bibliotheca*, codex 230).

They attributed ignorance to Christ, misinterpreting certain passages of the Gospel. In particular, when Christ inquired about Lazarus, who had been buried, “Where have you laid him?” (John XI, 34), and elsewhere said, “But concerning that day or hour no one knows, neither the angels in heaven nor the Son” (Mark XIII, 32), they thought that from these passages it had to be asserted that Christ himself had been ignorant of those matters.

Eulogius wrote against this error and took care to send his work to Gregory for approval.

> [Note: [Col. 0431D–0432D] Perhaps this is the very work presented by Photius in the place cited. In it Eulogius excludes all ignorance from Christ, even as man. Athanasius appears to have thought otherwise in *On the Incarnation against the Arians*, Book I, no. 7: “When he says of the last day, ‘No one knows, not even the Son’ . . . he speaks according to his humanity.” On this question see the *Disquisitions* of the Fathers of the Congregation of Saint-Vitton, Part II, p. 168, where they adduce other testimonies of Saint Athanasius from the Letter to Serapion and the Fourth Oration against the Arians.]

The pope praised it highly as wholly consonant with the Church’s doctrine:

> There was much in your doctrine against the heretics called Agnoitae for us to admire; there was nothing to displease us. In the same sense I had long ago written very extensively to our common son Anatolius the deacon. Your doctrine agreed in every respect with that of the Latin Fathers, so that it was no surprise to me that the Spirit should not be different in different languages. For in what you said about the fig tree, blessed Augustine speaks precisely in this sense: when the Evangelist added, “For it was not the season for figs” (Mark XI, 13), it is clearly understood that by the fig tree the Lord had sought fruit in the synagogue, which had leaves—that is, the law—but did not have the fruit of works. The Creator of all could not have been ignorant that the fig tree had no fruit, since, although it was not the season for figs, everyone could know this.

(*Book X, Letter 39*).

The holy Father continues by demonstrating the remarkable agreement between Eulogius’s teaching and Augustine’s teaching, which Gregory himself had drunk in thirstily and, once filled with it, poured forth. Certainly this letter of Gregory is sufficient to refute the dreams of the Agnoitae, for it confronts every point from which any sort of ignorance could be attributed to Christ.

The learned pope had received an opportunity to write on this subject. Two years earlier, certain monks from Jerusalem had come to Constantinople and, as may be inferred, had questioned Anatolius, the representative of the holy see, about this matter. The deacon postponed answering them until he had consulted Gregory. Gregory himself says to Eulogius:

> Long before I received your writings, I answered against this same heresy the very things that I later found in the letter of Your Holiness. I gave great thanks to almighty God, because in all their inquiries the Fathers of the Romans and Greeks, whose followers we are, have spoken with one Spirit.

(*Ibid., Letter 35*).

Gregory teaches that it is clear that the Agnoitae were Nestorians (*ibid., Letter 39*). I therefore do not understand why the most learned theologian Natalis Alexander attributes the contrary error of the Eutychians to them.

> [Note: [Col. 0432D] See Natalis Alexander, sixth century, chapter 4, article 3.]

Certainly neither Gregory nor Eulogius, who had confronted them both personally and in writing, ever counted them among the Eutychians.

At the same time, when the ever-watchful Pastor of the Church learned that a serious scandal had arisen in the Church of Thessalonica because the presbyter Luke and Peter refused to accept the Council of Chalcedon, he immediately wrote to Eusebius, archbishop of Thessalonica, concerning the matter, urging him to work diligently to remove the offense. From this letter we learn especially what must be done by those whose faith has come under suspicion. Saint Gregory issued further instructions concerning Luke in the following year.

### 3.

While heretics were disturbing the Church, affairs of the empire were no more peaceful. The Slavs had already begun to enter Italy through the route of Istria when Saint Gregory replied to Maximus of Salona, who had warned him about the barbarian invasion (*Book X, Letter 36*).

Baronius likewise assigns to this same year the events that Paul the Deacon recounts concerning Chagan, king of the Avars, invading the province of Venetia and seizing the Forum of Julius through the treachery of Ramilda (*Book IV, chapter 12*).

We do not dare assert whether the Lombards favored these barbarians while they were devastating the imperial provinces. For Saint Gregory’s letter to Innocentius, prefect of Africa, testifies that at this very time peace was made with the king of the Lombards—or rather, that a truce was agreed upon until the month of March of the fourth indiction.

In this letter there appears a notable indication of his humility and an outstanding testimony to his profound respect for Augustine, which must not be passed over:

> You wished a volume of the exposition of holy Job to be sent to you, and we rejoice greatly in your zeal, because we see you devoting yourself to a matter whose excellence does not allow you to go wholly outside yourself and which gathers you back again to your heart, where worldly cares had scattered you. But if you desire to be nourished by a delightful food, read the works of blessed Augustine, your fellow countryman, and do not seek our bran in comparison with his wheat.

(*Book X, Letter 37*).

### 4.

From the same letter we understand that the death of the Lombard king had been reported at Rome. Gregory wrote that the report was uncertain, as he later discovered it to be false. Indeed, instead of mourning the death of the prince, the whole nation rejoiced greatly at the birth of a son to him, named Adaloald.

He was born at Modicia, not far from Milan, a place dear to Queen Theodelinda. There she built a basilica of Saint John the Baptist, the patron of the entire nation, adorned it with gold and silver ornaments, and endowed it with extensive estates. Benedictine monks once served in this church, which still stands. In the same place, with royal munificence, she built a celebrated palace, where the chief deeds of the Lombards could be seen depicted. (Compare Paul the Deacon, Book IV, chapters 22, 23, and 26; Mabillon, *Museum Italicum*, pp. 212–213.)

Perhaps it will not be displeasing to the reader to have described here, from Paul the Deacon, what the dress and customs of the Lombards were at that time, as they could be discerned from the painted panels of the palace at Modicia.

They shaved the back of the neck and left it bare as far as the crown. They wore their hair hanging from the face down to the mouth, parted toward either side of the forehead. Their garments were loose, chiefly made of linen, and decorated with bands of various colors. Their shoes were almost open up to the tip of the great toe and were held in place alternately by the laces of their straps. Later they began to wear *hosae*—leg coverings or leggings—over which, when riding, they put on rough *birrei* garments.

> [Note: [Col. 0433D] *Hosa*, *tibiale*, *caliga*. The Gauls once called them *houseux*. The Germanic, Italian, and related words are cognate and have the same meaning.]

But these practices they had adopted from Roman custom. (Compare the place cited above.)

### 5.

Meanwhile the emperor Maurice resolved to use the brief interval of peace to demand accounts from those who had received public funds for distribution and were alleged to have converted them to their own uses.

With this purpose he sent Leontius, a former consul, to Rome. Domitian, metropolitan of Melitene and, as has already been stated, a relative of the emperor, commended Leontius to Saint Gregory, asking in addition that, insofar as reason permitted, Gregory would lend his support in matters entrusted to Leontius by the command of the most serene Lords for the public good.

The pope promised that he would do this most willingly, and he did not delay in fulfilling his promise. When Gregory, the former prefect, and others accused of extortion had taken refuge within the ecclesiastical precincts, which they regarded as an inviolable asylum, Saint Gregory persuaded them to leave and to undertake to present their accounts (*Book X, Letter 50*).

They therefore came out and, after first receiving a pledge that they would suffer no violence, were handed over to Marcus Scribonius, who had come to produce them. The pope commended Gregory, the former prefect, who was very closely bound to him by friendship, both to many bishops in Sicily and to Leontius, the former consul, and to others whom he had as assistants, counselors, or officials in the province he had received.

When, long after the time appointed and fixed by Marcus, or Azimarchus, the *scribo*, the former prefect Gregory came to Sicily to present himself before the former consul for judgment, Saint Gregory informed that *scribo* that the reason for the delay and postponement had been serious illness, not voluntary procrastination. We cannot determine what judgment was rendered concerning him. Nevertheless, it may be inferred from a letter written to him two years later that this former prefect did not fall from his previous status, either with respect to honors or with respect to his property (*Book XII, Letter 22*).

> [Note: [Col. 0434D] See the letters in Book X, Letters 54 through 60 inclusive.]

### 6.

Libertinus, formerly prefect of Sicily and a close associate of Saint Gregory, was treated much more harshly. The devout pontiff had asked the former consul to take his friend under his protection, and he had written to many others for the same purpose.

But Leontius, the former consul, a man of notably excessive severity, sent Gregory a copy of a certain entirely execrable security, which demonstrated with what perverse intent Libertinus had entered upon the prefecture. To the tacit reproach that he had commended a most wicked man, the pope replied that he had never written to anyone concerning him except so that, with justice approving, Leontius might extend his protection.

As for Libertinus, appointed prefect of Sicily, Gregory said that the entire province had given thanks for him, which seemed a sufficient indication of his uprightness. As to who he was, what sort of causes he had, or what answer he gave to the accusations brought against him, Gregory said that he himself was entirely ignorant. Yet he continued:

> I know this one thing clearly and firmly: even if he committed some fraud in public affairs, his property ought to have been punished, not his liberty. For when free men are beaten—not to mention that almighty God is offended, not to mention that your reputation is gravely burdened—the age of our most devout emperor is nevertheless wholly darkened. For this is the difference between the kings of the nations and the Roman emperors: the kings of the nations are lords of slaves, whereas the Roman emperor is lord of free men. Therefore, whatever you do, you must act first with justice preserved and then with liberty safeguarded in every respect.

(*Book X, Letter 51*).

The most holy man continues by reproving the judge’s excessive harshness and offering truly exceptional precepts for softening it. A few of these are worth extracting:

> Whenever anger invades your spirit, tame your mind and conquer yourself. Postpone the time of rage, and when your mind is calm, judge what is right. For anger ought to follow the judgment of the mind in punishing evil, not precede it, so that it may come behind as justice’s maidservant and not burst forth recklessly before its face. Sometimes anger must be displayed but not acted upon; sometimes it must be acted upon, but never followed. For when, in carrying out justice, we become angry with a tranquil mind, we both display our anger and do not follow it.

> [Note: [Col. 0434D] He perhaps knew that Leontius was prone to anger. On the same subject, see Letter 2 of this book.]

Gregory also wrote to Amandinus, a member of the imperial household, in support of Libertinus (*Book X, Letter 52*). Amandinus took this badly, although the letter contained nothing harsh. He was already preparing to write back to Gregory in severe language, but he was prevented from doing so by a dream. He testified that in his sleep he had seen the pope rebuking and reproving him for this very reason.

### 7.

Gregory wrote a consolatory letter to Libertinus, who had been stripped of almost all his property, and urged his friend to endure adversity patiently. He added generosity to his words, seasoning it with his customary courtesy:

> I ask you not to regard it as offensive that we have written to the Roman defensor asking that twenty garments be provided for your servants, since gifts from the property of the blessed Apostle Peter, however small what is offered may be, should always be received as a great blessing.

(*Book X, Letter 31*).

Gregory’s ministry of consolation had to be extended not to one friend alone but to very many, especially to Dominicus, bishop of Carthage, on account of the pestilence raging in Africa. He taught him what fruits should be gathered from this scourge. He asserts that Italy too had not been free from such a blow, for calamities had been added to it in great numbers, as though in heaps (*Book X, Letter 63*).

### 8.

Those whom he knew to be enjoying prosperity, and who had not been instructed by any experience of affliction to despise temporal goods, he stirred more and more toward the love of eternal things. Thus he wrote to a certain illustrious woman:

> The letter of Your Glory has brought us great joy, since it has shown that you possess a desire for eternal life. But because the fleeting glory of the world commonly obstructs this kind of devotion, we exhort you not to allow any transitory matter to recall your mind from its most salutary resolution or turn it aside from the path on which it has begun. Rather, let the love of the heavenly homeland inflame you; let enduring rewards occupy your thoughts; let your hope always rise with certainty toward the promise of the coming Judge; and let your temporal possessions purchase eternal things, so that by this means you may both belong to true glory and be enrolled among the heavenly matrons.

> Bring before your minds the prosperity of the times, the multitude of people, the splendor of dignities, the glory of matrons, and the abundance of riches. Consider where or what all these things have become; and from this weigh how empty they are, and how the person who loves such things sees a dream while awake.

(*Book X, Letter 49*).

### 9.

When writing to his friends, he by no means concealed their faults. Thus he addresses the patrician Clementina:

> It has been reported to me that whenever anyone offends you, you retain the pain of it without forgiveness. If this is true, then, since I love you as much as I grieve over it, I ask you nobly to drive this fault away from you and not allow the enemy’s seed to grow against the harvest of good works. Let the words of the Lord’s Prayer be recalled to mind, and let guilt not have more power with you than forgiveness. Let the goodness of Your Glory overcome the offense, and, by forgiving more beneficially, make devoted the person whom persistent severity could make undevoted. Let him be left with something of which he may be ashamed, and let that which causes grief not be preserved. For very often measured leniency in correction possesses greater force than strictness in exacting punishment.

(*Book X, Letter 58*).

If it happened that friends were offended and embittered by being corrected with frankness, he strove to soothe them with friendly words, so that they might understand that his harsh expressions had flowed not from hatred but from charity.

### 10.

This year Fortunatus, bishop of Naples, died. Shortly before his death Gregory had rebuked him (*Book X, Letters 24 and 25*), both for his scant concern for monasteries and for the occupation of the city gates and aqueduct, whose care and guardianship belonged to Theodore, the *maior populi*, and to Rusticus the elder. Therefore the most impartial pontiff ordered that what had been usurped should be restored.

The *maior populi* was then almost the same magistracy as what we now call the mayor of a city. Naples was already a very extensive city. We learn that its artisans had formed separate corporations according to each craft they practiced from the complaints of the soap-makers against John the Palatine. He was attempting to impose many new measures prejudicial to their corporation and wished to appropriate whatever profit came from admission into it—that is, whatever was paid by those who obtained permission to join this order or corporation (*Book X, Letter 26*).

There was prolonged deliberation concerning Fortunatus’s successor. Part of the people favored John the Deacon, but the pope rejected him because, since he had a young daughter, his continence had not yet been tested and proven for a sufficient period.

The other party had elected another deacon, Peter, who likewise did not please the pontiff because of his excessive simplicity. In addition, he was said once to have lent money at interest. Neither man therefore became bishop; instead, Paschasius was chosen, to whom many of Gregory’s letters are addressed.

### 15.

It would now be appropriate to discuss the monastic affairs belonging to this year, but for the sake of brevity we shall examine only one letter of Saint Gregory written in defense of monks.

A certain monk had left the monastery of Saint Michael near Naples and gone over to the enemy. This drove Godescalc, duke of Campania, into such a fury that he ordered the monastery doors to be broken down and everything found there to be plundered.

Fuscus, the abbot of the monastery, escaped the danger by flight, knowing that the duke was attributing the fugitive monk’s crime to him. Saint Gregory demonstrated how absurd this was, calling him back to a sounder state of mind by an example of his own:

> Surely, even in the days of your greatness, many people did not flee from the city in which you are established and escape to the Lombard soldiers? Who could be found so lacking in judgment and so foolish as to think that their wickedness should be charged to you?

(*Book X, Letter 11*).

The violence inflicted upon this monastery perhaps gave the monk and presbyter Constantius occasion to migrate to Sicily and to take with him the curtains and books of his monastery. When he had died there, Gregory, at the request of the abbot Fuscus, wrote to Fantinus, the defensor, asking him to arrange for the things taken away to be restored (*Book X, Letter 14*).

## CHAPTER V

**SUMMARY.—** 1. Saint Gregory prevents the man whom Agilulf had chosen from becoming bishop of Milan. Deusdedit is ordained. A heterodox person’s dream concerning the equality of the Church of Milan with the Roman Church. — 2. When Amos, patriarch of Jerusalem, dies, Isaac succeeds him. — 3. Saint Gregory’s manifold and most serious illness. — 4. He is more concerned for the safety of his friends than for his own. — 5. He urges sick friends to do penance, especially Venantius. After Venantius’s death, he concerns himself with his daughters. — 6. Enemies threaten Sicily. The faith is propagated in Sardinia. — 7. Saint Gregory consoles Theoctista, who has been accused of heresy. — 8. We ought to remove scandal when we can. — 9. The charges of heresy brought against Theoctista are refuted. — 10. Saint Gregory assigns severe penalties to slanderers. — 11. He punishes a forger. — 12. Ecclesiastical affairs. — 13. Monastic affairs. — 14. The death of King Reccared and his successors. *(Years 600 and 601.)*

### 1.

After Constantius, bishop of Milan, died, the danger of schism threatened the Milanese Church. For the clergy and people had unanimously elected the deacon Deusdedit as his successor. But King Agilulf, in whose dominion Milan lay, demanded that another man be ordained, and had written to the Milanese concerning the matter.

When Gregory learned this, he thought it best to write to them as quickly as possible, to strengthen them in their previous resolve, lest they yield to the king’s threatening letter. He begins his letter with praise of Constantius. Above all, he recalls both his concern in preserving ecclesiastical discipline and his vigilance in defending the city.

He then praises the Milanese for electing Deusdedit by unanimous consent and confirms the election by his own authority. Of the man chosen by the Lombards and by the king himself he speaks as follows:

> But let what you have reported as having been written to you by Agilulf not move Your Affection. For we give our consent in no way to a man who is elected not by Catholics but especially by Lombards. Nor, if the act has been carried out through the usurpation of some presumptuous authority, do we receive that man into the office or rank of a priest; for he is plainly shown to be unworthy to be the vicar of Saint Ambrose if he is ordained after being elected by such men.

(*Book XI, Letter 4*).

He also wrote to Pantaleon, the notary (*ibid., Letter 3*), instructing him to go to the city of Genoa and have Deusdedit solemnly ordained bishop.

This letter itself makes clear that Agilulf had not yet embraced the Catholic faith. Nevertheless, he did not wish to contend with Gregory, perhaps at the urging of Theodelinda, who was devoted both to the Catholic faith and to the most holy pontiff. Deusdedit, elected by the Milanese, was therefore ordained without opposition from anyone.

What we read here, and earlier in the ordination of Constantius, is undoubtedly sufficient to refute the dream of Jacobus Gothofredus in Dissertation 2, *On the Suburban Regions and Churches*, in which he argues that the bishops of Milan and Rome possessed equal and supreme authority.

> [Note: [Col. 0437D] See Book III, Letters 29, 30, and 31.]

### 2.

In this year also the Church of Jerusalem mourned the patriarch Amos, whose chair was assumed by Isaac. Shortly afterward Isaac sent Gregory a synodical letter.

The pope approved the faith that Isaac professed in it and gave thanks to God, who, even when the shepherds of his flock are changed, preserves unchanged after them the faith that he once delivered to the holy Fathers. To his thanksgiving he added prayers for the emperor, in whose time, he said, the mouths of heretics fell silent: although their hearts boiled with the madness of a perverse understanding, they did not dare to express the depraved opinions they held during the reign of an orthodox emperor (*Book XI, Letter 46*).

But because he had heard that in the Churches of the East no one attained the sacred order except through the payment of rewards, he urged the new patriarch to eliminate such abominable simony. He also advised him to restrain quarrels, correcting some matters gently and enduring with equanimity those that could not be corrected.

### 3.

In this year also, the entire Christian world came close to losing its outstanding pontiff. He describes how gravely he was suffering in these words:

> It is now a long time since I have been able to rise from my little bed. For sometimes the pain of gout torments me; sometimes, I do not know what sort of fire spreads through my whole body with pain. It often happens that at one and the same time burning contends with pain within me, and both body and spirit fail me. I cannot enumerate how many other necessities of infirmity afflict me beyond those I have mentioned. But I say briefly that the infection of harmful fluid has so permeated me that life is a punishment for me, and I await death eagerly, believing that it alone can be a remedy for my groans. Therefore, most holy brother, implore for me the mercy of divine compassion, so that in his graciousness he may mitigate the scourges of his chastisement toward me and grant me the endurance to bear it; lest, God forbid, my heart break into impatience through excessive weariness, and what could have been well healed through the wound should grow worse through the fault of murmuring.

(*Book XI, Letter 32*) [Col. 0438B]

### 4.

Nevertheless, though placed amid so many and such great pains, this man of supreme patience—who scarcely thought about what he himself was enduring—remained concerned for the health of his friends. Marinianus, bishop of Ravenna, experienced this personally. When the most devout Father heard that Marinianus was suffering from vomiting blood, he summoned him to himself in order to care for him. Meanwhile, he ordered him to refrain from fasts and vigils. Yet he had another purpose in summoning Marinianus. For, realizing that death was near, he wished to breathe out his soul in the hands of his friend. (*Book X, Letter 33*) [Col. 0438C]

Castorius, bishop of Ariminum, had once experienced the same paternal affection. Gregory had kept him with himself for a long time because of his illness, anxious and concerned to restore his health (*Book III, Letters 24 and 25*). His tender feeling toward sick friends is especially displayed by a letter written this year to the patrician Rusticiana. Although he declares in it that his body is dried up as though in a grave, he appears to forget his own condition in order to sympathize with the grief of this devout woman (*ibid., Letter 44*).

### 5.

Yet Gregory’s principal concern in the illnesses of his friends was to summon them to repentance when they had been worn down by such scourges. Thus he presses Venantius, who was suffering from gout [Col. 0438D] and whose fall we have already discussed:

> What else should we do amid these pains except continually recall our sins to mind and give thanks to almighty God? For we who have sinned greatly through the allurements of the flesh are cleansed through the affliction of the flesh. We must also understand that present punishment, if it turns the mind of the afflicted person, is the end of the preceding fault. But if it does not turn him toward fear of the Lord, it is the beginning of the punishment to come. Therefore we must take care, and keep watch with the utmost diligence and complete conversion of mind amid our tears, lest we pass from torment to torment. We must also consider with what great dispensation of mercy our Creator acts toward us: he continually strikes those worthy of death, and yet does not immediately kill them.

(*Book XI, Letter 30*) [Col. 0439A]

In this letter Saint Gregory says nothing about Venantius’s apostasy, nor does he himself urge him to return to the monastic state that he had abandoned. He preferred that this should be suggested to the sick man by his bishop, namely John of Syracuse. To John he writes that his first duty should be to persuade Venantius—by exhorting him, entreating him, setting before him God’s terrible judgment, and promising him God’s ineffable mercy—to return to his monastic habit, even at the point of death, lest the guilt of so great a sin stand against him at the eternal judgment (*Book XI, Letter 36*).

Gregory commended to the same John Venantius’s daughters, Barbara and Antonina. He also wrote them letters of consolation and promised them his protection against the counsels of wicked men [Col. 0439B], which he in fact provided (*ibid., Letter 78*). Other letters of Saint Gregory sufficiently prove that Venantius did not recover from this illness but died. Whether he had first performed an act of repentance must be left to the divine judgment. His wife Italica had already died. For if she had been alive while her husband lay gravely ill and later died, Gregory would have written to her rather than to his daughters, or at least some mention of their mother would have appeared in those letters. Venantius’s return to the monastic state was therefore easier because the bonds of marriage had been dissolved.

### 6.

Gregory wished noble virgins to migrate from Sicily to Rome, perhaps because he had learned that enemies were hastening to invade that island, though I leave other reasons aside for the moment. The ever-watchful Pontiff warned all the bishops of Sicily of the hostile attack that was now imminent [Col. 0439C] and urged them to prescribe litanies every week on Wednesday and Friday, and thus to implore the aid of heavenly protection against the assaults of barbarian cruelty (*Book XI, Letter 51*).

He ordered them to add good works to their prayers, because, he said, prayer is empty when conduct is wicked. We stated above that the same danger had threatened Sardinia, an island not far away. We suppose, however, that peace and tranquility were restored to it through the successful spread of the Christian religion among the Sardinians—whether they were immigrants and barbarians, or Barbaricini, or native inhabitants. For this reason Saint Gregory asked the governor of the island to assist Bishop Victor, who was laboring to convert the pagans. He was present for all who needed his work and recommendation (*ibid., Letter 22*).

[Col. 0439D]

### 7.

This year Theoctista, a relative of the emperor Maurice, a devout woman whom we have already discussed elsewhere and whom some had rashly accused of heresy, experienced Gregory’s immediate assistance. We have already stated (*Book I, chapter 5, no. 9*) that while Gregory was staying in the imperial city, a rumor had been spread about a new heresy. Sycophants did not hesitate to stamp its mark upon a most noble and holy matron. As a result, a great disturbance arose among the people, who, because of their fickleness, were especially inclined to believe the most atrocious things about rulers.

As soon as the matter was reported to the pope, he wrote to Theoctista (*Book XI, Letter 45*), showing her by several arguments that her mind ought not to be disturbed by slander:

> If we rejoice in praise and are broken by detraction, he says, we have placed our glory not in [Col. 0440A] ourselves but in the mouths of others . . . In everything that is said about us outside ourselves, we must return to the secrets of the heart. Even if everyone condemns us, the person whom conscience does not accuse remains free.

Later he adds another reason:

> There are very many people, he says, who perhaps praise the lives of good men more than they ought. To prevent any pride from stealing in through praise, almighty God allows the wicked to break out into slander and reproach, so that if some fault arises in the heart from the mouths of those who praise, it may be suffocated by the mouths of those who criticize.

He treats a similar subject in a letter to Palladius, a priest of Mount Sinai (*Book XI, Letter 2*), who was also being tormented by the tongues of his detractors [295]. Among other noteworthy statements, Gregory says:

> Amid the words of those who praise or blame, we must always return to the mind [Col. 0440B]; and if the good that is said about us is not found there, great sadness ought to arise. But if the evil that people say about us is not found there, we ought to leap for joy. What does it matter if people praise us while conscience accuses us? Or what sadness ought there to be if everyone accuses us and conscience alone proves us free?

And further:

> What else do detractors do except blow upon dust and stir up earth into their own eyes, so that the more strongly they blow the dust of detraction, the less they see any truth?

### 8.

Nevertheless, in both letters he teaches by what method the scandal may be removed, since we cannot neglect it without sin. He proposes the example of Saint Peter, the chief of the apostles. When believers complained that Peter had entered among Gentiles, eaten with them, and received them into baptism [Col. 0440C], Peter answered them not by appealing to authority but by giving a reason, and explained the matter in order:

> If, when he was being blamed by believers, he had considered the authority that he had received in the holy Church, he could have answered in such a way that the sheep would not have dared to criticize their shepherd . . . But if, in response to the complaint of the believers, he had asserted something about his own authority, he certainly would not have been a teacher of gentleness. He therefore appeased them by a humble explanation . . . If, then, the pastor of the Church, the chief of the apostles, who performed signs and miracles in a singular manner, did not disdain humbly to give an account when he was criticized, how much more ought we sinners, when we are criticized concerning some matter, to appease our critics by a humble explanation?

[Col. 0440D]

### 9.

The most holy Teacher could not have persuaded the distinguished woman to humility by a more effective example. He then reviews and refutes, indeed crushes, all the principal points of the heresy attributed to her.

First, he shows that marriages must not be dissolved for the sake of religion. Second, that all sins are completely washed away and forgiven in baptism. Third, that after repentance has been performed for three years, no permission to sin is granted. Fourth, that even someone who, though compelled by necessity, anathematizes the matter for which he is reproached remains bound by the anathema. Finally, he testifies that many people had been falsely accused, through misguided zeal, concerning those four points; nevertheless, the accusers must be appeased both by reason and by gentleness.

### 10.

Although that supreme teacher of morals taught that slanders must be patiently endured [Col. 0441A], he nevertheless ordered slanderers to be restrained by severe punishments. Thus, when he learned that the subdeacon Hilarus, who had brought a charge against the deacon John, had received no punishment from the judges, he ordered that Hilarus be publicly beaten with rods and deported into exile (*Book IX, Letter 62*). We observed above that this punishment of exile had been decreed by ecclesiastical judgment against a defender who did not obey the bishop.

### 11.

Gregory, the most zealous champion of truth, was no less indignant at falsifiers, who are akin to slanderers. Hence he became gravely enraged against the monk Andrew (*Book XI, Letter 74*), who, as may be inferred, was a Greek. Andrew had not only corrupted the letter of Eusebius, bishop of Thessalonica, which had been entrusted to him so that he might render it into Latin, and infected it with heresies [Col. 0441B]; he had also published certain sermons in Greek, prefacing them with the pope’s name.

Gregory ordered that these works be diligently sought out and destroyed. In addition, he held a council at which deliberation was given to the punishment to be inflicted on this otherwise most disgraceful falsifier; but what was decreed remains unknown to us. The letter from which we learn these things is evidence of Gregory’s humility and modesty. For in it he plainly professes that he did not know Greek literature.

### 12.

To conclude the matters relating to this year, we should briefly note those things that may contribute to illuminating ecclesiastical discipline or history and that we have not yet examined.

When the emperor wished to remove John, bishop of Prima Justiniana, from the episcopate because of a head ailment, the most equitable Father refused to consent unless the sick man himself requested it by submitting a written petition. He did, however, advise that a steward be sought who could perform the episcopal office (*Book XI, Letter 47*) [Col. 0441C].

Quiricus and the other bishops of Iberia had consulted the supreme Pontiff concerning the baptism and ordinations of various heretics. He replied that those baptized in heresy with an invocation of the Trinity were not to be baptized again when they returned to the Church, but were to be reconciled either by the laying on of hands, by anointing with chrism, or by a profession of faith. Those returning from Nestorianism were to be instructed concerning the Incarnation; and if they anathematized Nestorius and professed that they accepted the synods received by the Church, they were to be admitted in their own orders (*Book XI, Letter 67*).

When he heard that Desiderius, bishop of Vienne [Col. 0441D], was teaching grammar and the liberal arts to certain people, he took it very badly, because, he said, “the praises of Christ cannot be contained in one mouth together with the praises of Jove” (*Book XI, Letter 54*). Later, however, the priest Candidus, returning from Gaul, excused Desiderius before the pope and denied that he was wasting his time on such trifles.

Gregory often teaches that clerics’ cases must be referred to the bishops, lest episcopal jurisdiction be destroyed. A Roman defender had expelled from the place where they had been assigned for penance certain clerics whom their bishop, because of their offenses, had sent to perform penance—doing so on his own authority, without consulting or informing the bishop. The pope ordered that the clerics be restored to the bishop without delay; after first rebuking the Roman official, he threatened him with severe punishment if he committed such acts again (*Book XI, Letters 77 and 37*).

[Col. 0442A]

The letter to Vitus (*Book XI, Letter 38*) tells us what qualifications were required for obtaining the office of defender, what their duties were, and by what formula they were appointed.

The great Teacher testifies that he had long searched for the deeds or writings of Saint Irenaeus but had been unable to find anything among them (*Book XI, Letter 56*).

We must now touch briefly on monastic matters.

### 13.

When Agathosa complained that her husband had become a monk against her will—a matter attributed to the fault and jealousy of Urbicius, the abbot in whose monastery her husband had entered the religious life—the pope decreed that he should be returned to her upon her request, even though he had already been tonsured, unless it were established either that she had previously consented to her husband’s conversion and promised her own conversion, or that she herself was guilty of adultery (*Book XI, Letter 50*) [Col. 0442B].

At the same council in which Andrew, the maker of false writings, was condemned, Probus, a monk and abbot, was granted permission to make a will concerning property belonging to him before he had assumed the monastic habit. The granting of this permission was considered so important that the most wise Pontiff judged that the consent of the entire synod was required.

Nor would Probus have been granted permission to make a will unless it had been clearly established [296] that he had been ordered, and almost compelled, by Saint Gregory to enter the monastery suddenly, without being granted time for deliberation or discussion. He therefore had not been free to dispose of his property. There was a danger that, if his goods passed to the monastery, his son would suffer extreme poverty.

[Col. 0442C]

He praised Januarius of Caralis because he had refused to build a monastery for men in a house adjoining the monastery of the handmaids of God. Nevertheless, Gregory wished another place to be sought where the men’s monastery could be established (*Book XI, Letter 25*).

I omit the benefits that the best of fathers conferred this year upon monasteries, even the most remote, especially upon the monastery of Mount Sinai (*Book XI, Letter 1*). Yet the instructions given to Conon, abbot of Lérins, seem to me more valuable than any gifts or benefits. In them Gregory teaches him with what care and skill he ought to govern the monastery entrusted to him, especially because of the careless laxity of his predecessor:

> Let the vigilance of Your Affection always kindle itself with more ardent care; and, with God’s help, let it so fortify everything that the raging wolf, running here and there, may find no opportunity to enter among the Lord’s sheep.

And after some further remarks:

> Therefore let the good find you gentle, and the wicked a corrector. In this correction, know that the following order must be observed: love the persons and pursue the vices. Otherwise, if you should choose to act differently, correction may pass into cruelty, and you may destroy those whom you desire to amend. You must cut away the wound in such a way that you do not ulcerate what is sound; for if you press the knife more deeply than the matter requires, you will harm the person whom you are hastening to help. Your gentleness must itself be cautious, not lax; your correction diligent, not severe. But let one be tempered by the other, so that the good may have, through love, something they ought to fear, and the wicked, through fear, something they ought to love.

(*ibid., Letter 12*) [Col. 0442D]

### 14.

Writers on Spanish affairs report that the devout king Reccared, the restorer of the Catholic faith in Spain, died this year [Col. 0443A]. Because of the zeal with which he burned for orthodox religion, he always found the Arians bitterly hostile to him, especially Goswintha, the widow of King Leovigild. Made bolder by her influence, they conspired against the king more than once. Certain bishops infected with the Arian heresy were their leaders. Two of these were expelled into exile, although they deserved more severe punishments.

Reccared was succeeded by Liuba II, who possessed the kingdom for only two years. He was followed by Witericus.

# CHAPTER VI

**SUMMARY.**—1. Saint Gregory considers restoring the basilicas of the holy apostles. His generosity toward those basilicas.—2. The renewed war turns out disastrously for the emperor.—3. The conversion of heretics and schismatics. What those returning from schism promised.—4. Saint Gregory protects Bishop Firminus, who had returned and was consequently harassed by other schismatics.—5. He provides for the pacification of the Church of Doclea. Judgment concerning Paul, a disgraceful bishop and plunderer.—6. He attends to African affairs. The case of Bishop Paulinus, and that of another man named Victor.—7. Evidence for the authority of the Roman pontiff in Africa.—8. Gregory’s supreme authority accompanied by the greatest humility and modesty.—9. His homilies on various books of sacred Scripture, collected by Claudius. Inquiry concerning Claudius.—10. Saint Gregory’s care in selecting worthy abbots and preserving monastic discipline.—11. Whether he considered monastic life equivalent to the office of subdeacon.—12. He does not permit a deacon who has become a monk to be taken away from his monastery. *(Years 601 and 602.)*

### 1.

Since Saint Gregory foresaw that his death was approaching, he judged that the plan he had already conceived for repairing the basilicas of the holy apostles Peter and Paul should no longer be postponed. Accordingly, he ordered Sabinus, the subdeacon responsible for the Church’s property in Lucania and Bruttium, to procure in those provinces the beams necessary for the work [Col. 0443C] and arrange for them to be transported to the sea, so that they could be loaded onto ships and carried to Rome (*Book XII, Letter 20*).

For this reason he wrote to Arogis—whom the king of the Lombards had appointed duke of Beneventum after the death of Zotto—and asked him to assist the subdeacon Sabinus in transporting this timber, promising the duke an appropriate gift of hospitality (*ibid., Letter 21*).

**Note:** [Col. 0443D] Paul the Deacon, *Book IV, chapter 19*, and elsewhere, gives the name as Arigis or Arechis. *Argis* signifies “strong in honor.”

The same subject is treated in the letters he wrote to Gregory, the former prefect, and to Bishop Stephen (*ibid., Letters 22 and 23*).

Two years later, shortly before his death, he assigned many estates to the basilica of Saint Paul for its lights, so that the herald of the faith who had filled the entire world with the light of his preaching would not be seen to have fewer lights there than Saint Peter.

**Note:** [Col. 0443D] On the lights of the Church, see Athanasius, in his encyclical letter to the bishops, vol. I, p. 114, no. 4. Describing the entry of Gregory of Alexandria’s usurper into the church with a military force, Athanasius says that the soldiers then forcibly took away the oil stored for the church’s lamps. Those accompanying the pseudo-bishop had become so deranged that they immediately put the candelabra back against the wall and lit candles belonging to the church before idols.

Concerning the olive groves and other estates granted by Saint Gregory for supplying and increasing the lights of the basilica of Saint Peter, the deed of donation should be read, which we have decided to append to the *Life of Saint Gregory*. It is recorded elsewhere that he made for the blessed apostle Peter, above the altar, a ciborium with four columns of pure silver. Concerning the roofs made of the purest silver in the basilicas of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, see John the Deacon (*Book IV, chapter 68*).

### 2.

The letter written to Arogis suggests that peace or a truce then existed between the Romans and the Lombards. Nevertheless, this year war again broke out in Italy [Col. 0444A], where affairs went badly for the emperor. They proceeded no more favorably in the East, as though everything were already tending toward the deposition and murder of Maurice.

The Lombards, with assistance from the Slavs sent by the king of the Avars, first besieged and captured Cremona, which Agilulf ordered to be razed to the ground. He then stormed Mantua on the Ides of September; it scarcely experienced a more merciful victor. [Col. 0444D] The Roman garrison burned and abandoned Brixellum.

With the enemy pressing them by force of arms, the exarch obtained peace on the condition that he return the duke Godiscalc, his wife—Agilulf’s daughter—and their children, who had been captured when Parma was taken.

Although Saint Gregory had been accustomed to living among hostile swords for so many years, he nevertheless lamented this war bitterly [297] [Col. 0444B] and remonstrated with his friends. He humbly begged them to provide him with the aid of their prayers, especially those of Saint Eulogius (*Book XII, Letter 50*). (Compare Paul the Deacon, *Book IV, chapters 29 and 21*.)

### 3.

In the letter addressed to this patriarch—the last of all those written in this year—the pope mentions the Monophysites, or heretics who confessed one nature in Christ, who had recently renounced this error. When they came to Sicily, attracted by the fame of the most holy Teacher, they proceeded to Rome. There, having been confirmed in the faith, they asked the supreme Pontiff for letters of recommendation.

The holy Father commends them to his friend Eulogius and asks that the monastery occupied by the heretics be restored to them, unless perhaps the occupiers themselves should prefer to return to the bosom of the Church.

At the same time Firminus, bishop of the city of Tergeste in Istria, who had previously persisted in the schism that had arisen over the three condemned chapters, vomited out his poison and abandoned the schismatic party, returning to the unity of the Church. Gregory rejoiced at his return and judged that a congratulatory letter should be written. In it he urges the restored and repentant bishop to oppose the darts of Satan with the shield of steadfastness and to work to bring others back together with himself. He also promises him material support:

> We shall take every care, he says, to consider the peace of Your Fraternity as is fitting; for since, with God protecting you, you are now one with us, we regard your interests no differently from our own.

(*Book XII, Letter 33*) [Col. 0444C]

[Col. 0444D] There survives a promise made by a certain bishop returning to the unity of the Church, which learned men reasonably believe was given by Firminus (*formerly Book X, Letter 31; now in the appendix*). It should not be passed over without notice that this bishop, in abandoning the schism, says nothing at all about the Fifth Council or the condemnation of the three chapters. Instead, he merely promises and swears that he is returning with ready and spontaneous will to the unity of the apostolic see; that he will never return to the schism; and that he will always remain in the unity of the holy Catholic Church and in communion with the Roman pontiff.

This is clear evidence—as we have already stated more than once—that the [Col. 0445A] Istrian schism did not consist in refusing to condemn the three chapters. Rather, it consisted in excluding from communion those who condemned them, thereby separating oneself from the Catholic Church.

### 4.

[Col. 0445A] What the most holy man had foretold to Firminus—namely, that his steadfastness would be tested by the enemy through threats and enticements so that he might be compelled to turn back—happened shortly afterward. For Severus, bishop of Grado and leader of the schism that Firminus had renounced, hearing of his return, began trying, if possible, to draw him away from his good resolution by various promises of rewards.

When, with God’s help, he was entirely unable to accomplish this, he did not hesitate to stir up a revolt against Firminus among his fellow citizens (*Book XIII, Letter 33*).

Gregory resolved to extend his hand and come to the aid of the bishop in danger. Accordingly, he asked Smaragdus, the exarch [Col. 0445B], to make every effort without delay to protect Bishop Firminus from the troubles inflicted upon him and, by every possible means, to secure his peace, which would benefit many as an example:

> We greet Your Excellency with paternal affection and ask that the zeal you once displayed in this matter now burn with even greater fervor. Let the enemies of God find you as their avenger and defender in proportion as the protection of a soul is more precious before God than that of the body. Let the very rectitude of the faith that flourishes in you arm you against the deviators. In your time, let the body of the Church that has been torn apart in those regions be restored. In this matter you have the one who rewards your work and is the author of uprightness and integrity.

### 5.

Since the concern of the most holy Pope was no less evident than his authority and power, he judged that provision should be made this year for the deeply troubled affairs of the Church of Doclea [Col. 0445C].

Paul, bishop of that city, had fallen, among his other offenses, into a sexual crime. He had been accused by his own clergy and convicted, to the point that he himself had submitted a written statement in which he confessed that the matters of which he had been accused were true (*Book XII, Letter 31*).

Accordingly, he was deposed by episcopal judgment, and Nemesion was ordained in his place with the consent of John, bishop of Prima Justiniana. At that time Doclea belonged to John as primate, although it was subject by metropolitan right to the Church of Scodra.

Later, however, Paul regretted what had happened. Relying on the assistance of secular judges, he entered the episcopal residence like a plunderer, violently seized the property of the Church, and expelled the newly ordained bishop, with the greatest injury and at grave risk to his life.

Nemesion came to Rome and complained to the supreme Pontiff about the violence inflicted upon him. Gregory wrote both to Constantine, bishop of Scodra, whom his words sufficiently indicate to have been the metropolitan, and to John, bishop of Prima Justiniana, who was also primate and vicar of the holy see, ordering them that, if the facts were as reported, they should compel Paul immediately to return everything he had taken.

**Note:** [Col. 0445D] Saint Gregory writes this to John: “Although it was serious and unjust that Paul should not have sought this from you or from his metropolitan.” Therefore John was not Paul’s metropolitan, but Constantine was. Nevertheless, John possessed some jurisdiction over Paul; hence we infer that he was primate or exarch. The notes we made after Gussanville concerning this letter therefore appear to require correction. [Col. 0446D]

If Paul claimed that the property was not the Church’s but his own, Gregory nevertheless ordered that enough of it be retained to repair the losses inflicted upon ecclesiastical goods, since Paul was said to have squandered them. If, however, he attempted to delay, he was to be sent to a monastery until he had restored everything he had squandered or taken from the substance of the Church, so that at least under compulsion he might return what he had not feared to take unjustly, Saint Gregory said [Col. 0446A].

> But if, which we do not believe, after his deposition he should shamelessly and perversely attempt to speak about the episcopate or again aspire to it by any presumption, let the strength of Your Fraternity be wholly aroused against his wickedness. Having deprived him of communion in the Lord’s body and blood, take care that he be confined in a monastery until the day of his death to perform penance, so that he may learn through worthy tears to cleanse the stains of the crime he committed—stains that he wickedly desires rather to increase in the destruction of his soul.

Concerning Nemesion, Gregory decreed that his place and episcopate should be restored to him [Col. 0446B].

### 6.

At the same time Gregory had to consider the affairs of the African Church, where certain bishops and other ecclesiastical men had to be recalled to their offices. There were especially many complaints against Paulinus, bishop of Tegessis in Numidia. His clergy, including those who had been ordained, alleged that he had committed a sexual offense against them (*Book XII, Letter 28*).

Saint Gregory referred the case between the bishop and his clergy for judgment to Victor, primate of Numidia, and to Bishop Columbus. He instructed them to select from among their fellow bishops whichever ones they wished to join them in delivering judgment concerning the accused or the accusers.

Paulinus was also said to confer, or rather sell, ecclesiastical orders by simony. The most holy Pontiff orders that this be investigated with every diligence, so that both the giver and the recipient of the payment might be struck by canonical punishment [298] [Col. 0446C]. But lest the deadly root of simony grow and destroy many, he wished it to be prohibited by a common decision of the entire council, so that no one should ever receive or give payment for any order, and no one should be promoted through favor, but only through merit.

A short time earlier he had sent to the same Columbus a written petition submitted by the deacon Donadeus, who complained that he had been unjustly deposed by his bishop Victor (*Book XII, Letter 8*), so that Columbus might judge the complaint together with the primate and the other fellow bishops.

The bishop maintained that Donadeus had been removed from his order because of a sexual sin. If this could be proved, Gregory wished the deacon to be thrust into penance so that he might be able to dissolve the bond of the disgrace he had committed through his tears [Col. 0446D]. But if it were established that the bishop had savagely persecuted an innocent man, Gregory decreed that canonical severity should be exercised against the bishop himself.

Concerning Crementius, primate of the province of Byzacena, who had been gravely accused and whom the ever-watchful Pontiff judged should be tried by the council of the entire province this year (*ibid., Letter 32*), we have already spoken above. Nothing therefore appears to need to be added here.

### 7.

In these matters the authority of the Roman pontiff shines forth all the more clearly because everyone obeyed his various decisions [Col. 0447A]—the councils, the primates, and even the bishop of Carthage, who possessed supreme authority over the whole African Church.

Certainly Dominicus, who occupied the Carthaginian see while Gregory was seated at Rome, never complained that the Roman bishop had put his sickle into another’s harvest. He never contended with him in defense of his own authority, but always cultivated his friendship.

The African Fathers evidently knew that Gregory was exercising only his own right and following in the footsteps of his predecessors. The memory of Leo the Great had not yet been erased. Leo had sent Potentius to Africa as his representative, with the authority of the apostolic see, to repair ecclesiastical discipline weakened by the Vandal wars and to depose certain bishops ordained contrary to the canons.

In the time of Augustine also, although a dispute concerning appeals to the holy see had arisen with Zosimus, the acts of the councils, the letters written to him, and other records prove how great was the reverence of the Africans toward the Roman pontiff [Col. 0447B].

Cyprian himself consulted the apostolic see concerning the judgment on restoring those who had lapsed; the African Fathers followed him at various times by consulting the supreme pontiffs on various points of ecclesiastical discipline.

**Note:** [Col. 0447] See the letter of Pope Felix, written during the consulship of Dynamius and Sufidius in the year 488; and consult *History of the Vandal Persecution*, part II, chapter 12, no. 9.

Although the great Cyprian held a different opinion from Pope Stephen concerning the baptism of heretics and drew other African bishops over to his side, Stephen’s position nevertheless prevailed, even in Africa, when the decrees of the councils held under Cyprian were rescinded.

We have noted these matters somewhat beyond the limits of our subject against certain people who dare to call the African Church either [Col. 0447C] acephalous or autocephalous, on the ground that it was governed solely by the authority of its own primate, that is, the bishop of Carthage. As though, because of the more powerful primacy of the Roman Church, it were not necessary for the whole Church—that is, all the faithful from every place—to agree with the Roman Church, as Irenaeus says (*Book III, Against Valentinus, chapter 3*).

### 8.

The supreme authority entrusted to Gregory did not in the least detract from his modesty and humility. The clearest evidence of these virtues is certainly the letter written this year to the subdeacon John, who was staying at Ravenna [Col. 0447D].

In it Gregory complains, almost indignantly, about Marinianus, archbishop of Ravenna, because he had the commentary on blessed Job read publicly at vigils. Gregory says that this work was not intended for a popular audience and created an impediment rather than progress for uneducated hearers.

He adds:

> For while I remain in this flesh, I do not wish any things I may happen to have said to become readily known to people. When the deacon Anatolius of blessed memory gave the book of the *Pastoral Rule* to our lord the emperor, who had asked for it and commanded it, I was displeased. My most holy brother and fellow bishop Anastasius of Antioch translated it into Greek. As I have been told, it pleased him greatly, but I was very displeased, since those who possess better things are occupied with trifles.

(*Book XII, Letter 24*)

### 9.

In the same letter Saint Gregory mentions his [Col. 0448A] homilies on Proverbs, the Song of Songs, the Prophets, the books of Kings, and the Heptateuch, which the abbot Claudius had taken down.
