When Claudius died, the pope ordered that all surviving sheets concerning these works should also be sought out and sent to him—perhaps, as his humility suggests, so that they might be destroyed by fire.

On these matters, the prefaces or preliminary notices to the *Commentary on the First Book of Kings*, the *Exposition of the Song of Songs*, and the other *Exposition of the Seven Penitential Psalms* should be consulted.

But since we perhaps said too little there about Claudius the abbot, we must now gather whatever is found scattered concerning him in Gregory’s letters.

That he had been a monk in Gregory’s Roman monastery, and indeed under Gregory’s discipline, is proved by the title of “son” that Gregory gave him. By the second year of the holy man’s pontificate, Claudius had already been appointed to govern the [Col. 0448B] monastery of Saints John and Stephen at Classe. Gregory refers to him as abbot in a letter written at this time to John of Ravenna:

> It seems to me that you ought to send the abbot Claudius there with a certain amount of money.

(*Book II, Letter 46*)

He came to Rome both to defend the rights of his monastery against Marinianus of Ravenna and his clerics, for which purpose he obtained a privilege, and to serve as an assistant and participant in St. Gregory’s studies (Book VII, Letter 45; Book VIII, Letter 15). He remained in the City for a long time, St. Gregory retaining him because he found in him great consolation in the word of God (Book VIII, Letter 16). But since he was eager to return to and revisit his monastery—and since the most vigilant Pastor also understood that the presence of the holy abbot was extremely necessary to the congregation of the brethren [Col. 0448C]—he permitted him to return and commended him to Marinianus, whom he asked to show the monastery and its abbot the paternal affection that was fitting. We suspect that he died shortly before the letter already mentioned, written to the subdeacon John (Book XII, Letter 24), that is, toward the end of the year 601.

### 10

After his death, the monks of his monastery came to Rome and asked that the monk Constantius be appointed abbot for them. But the most holy father did not approve him at all, because he was said to favor private interests and had gone into the province of Picenum without any of his brethren. Having rejected him, Gregory agreed that Maurus, the cellarer, should be ordained, provided that the claims made by those who had chosen him concerning his life and competence proved true. Concerning these matters he wrote to the subdeacon John, and he further ordered him to warn Bishop Marinianus to cut off the practice of private appropriation by four or five monks of the monastery.

### 11

These, certainly, are indications of the singular concern and care that he exercised for the monastic state. How highly he valued it, especially in this year, is demonstrated by two letters. From the first, written to Passivus, bishop of Firmum (Book XII, Letter 12), Thomassinus concludes (Part II, Book I, chapter 34) that at that time the monastic state held the place of the subdiaconate. For when the fortress of Aprutium, in the territory of Firmum, was without a pastor, St. Gregory pointed out a certain Opportunus, praised by many for his innocence of life, his devotion to psalmody, and his love of prayer. He says that Opportunus should be encouraged either to become a monk or to become a subdeacon, and after some time he recommends that he be advanced to pastoral care.

Why would the monastic state be mentioned alongside the subdiaconate, when the matter concerns advancing Opportunus to the priesthood, unless it likewise prepared him for the sacred orders? For this reason perhaps St. Benedict, although he speaks of monks being promoted to the presbyterate and diaconate, is entirely silent about conferring the subdiaconate upon them. On this matter, however, our Mabillon should be consulted, especially *Annales Benedictini*, Book X, year 602, no. 20, col. 277.

### 12

In the other letter, written to Desiderius, bishop of Vienne, on behalf of the deacon Pancratius, who had become a monk, the most holy father urges Desiderius not to hinder the deacon’s great eagerness to maintain his devotion in the holy vocation he had undertaken. “Rather,” he says, “kindle him with whatever exhortations and pastoral admonition you can, so that the fervor of this desire may not grow cold in him: so that he who, withdrawing from the turbulent tumult of secular cares, sought the harbor of the monastery out of a desire for quiet, may not again become entangled in the disturbances of ecclesiastical cares.”

## CHAPTER VII

**Argument.**—1. The deposition and murder of the Emperor Maurice.—2. How he is divinely forewarned.—3. Phocas is chosen emperor by the army. He hastens to Constantinople. He orders Maurice, his sons, and also Constantina Augusta and her three daughters to be killed.—4. St. Gregory writes to Phocas. His letter is examined. Concerning another letter to the same man.—5. Why St. Gregory wrote more harshly about Maurice.—6. He sends an *apocrisiarius* to the new emperor.—7. He sets forth the miserable condition of Italy.—8. The embassy of Theoderic, king of the Franks, and Brunichildis to the pope. They consult him about a mentally incapacitated bishop. The pope’s response. He bars a bigamist from the sacred orders.—9. The queen asks that a legate be sent to Gaul to convene a council.—10. The pope’s concern for ecclesiastical discipline in Italy.—11. He restores what the frauds of the Church’s tenants had unjustly taken away.—12. His zeal in giving alms.—13. Urbicus the abbot is elected bishop of Panormus. Why St. Gregory rejected this election.—14. He writes against errors that had recently arisen at Rome. (Years 602 and 603.)

### 1

This thirteenth year of St. Gregory’s pontificate is remarkable for the downfall of the Emperor Maurice and the slaughter of him and his sons, as well as for the elevation of the centurion Phocas to the imperial power. The emperor had provoked the anger and hatred of the soldiers by refusing to redeem at a modest price those captured by the Avars, whom the barbarians killed—whether this was done, as is commonly believed, out of greed, or whether he wished them to perish by the enemy’s sword because they had revolted.

Unable to bear for long the consciousness and burden of so great a crime, he prayed to the Lord that in this life He would inflict upon him the punishments he deserved and would not reserve him for eternal torments. He also asked all the patriarchs and monks, especially those of Jerusalem, to strive to obtain the same thing from God by their prayers. God heard these heartfelt prayers, as was shown to Theodore of Siceon and to the emperor himself, who had been warned to beware of a man whose name began with the two letters *ph* and to know that he would be killed by him.

### 2

Maurice immediately suspected that Philippicus, his sister’s husband, was plotting against him and preparing his death. But in a dream he saw himself standing before Christ the Judge, with a crowd of captive soldiers accusing him—as the Greek writers relate—and without delay he was ordered to be handed over to the soldier Phocas to be slaughtered together with his wife, children, and entire household.

When the emperor awoke, he immediately sent men to bring Philippicus to him. Seeing that he was being summoned at night, Philippicus had no doubt that death threatened him; for he knew that he had fallen under the emperor’s suspicion. But as soon as Maurice saw him, he threw himself at his feet and said: “Forgive me, brother, for the false accusations and charges I have brought against you, though you are innocent. But I ask you: if you know any soldier in the army named Phocas, tell me.”

“I know,” he replied, “a certain man who, having previously been dismissed from the army, quarrelled with Your Majesty.”

Maurice had no doubt that this was the very man he had seen in his dream.

### 3

About this time Peter, the emperor’s brother, at his command sent a letter to the army ordering the soldiers to cross the Danube and winter there. Since the soldiers resented this, because in their winter quarters they would have to fight continually with the barbarians, they began discussing the creation of a new emperor. Soon they lifted the centurion Phocas, whom they knew to be bold, upon a shield according to custom and acclaimed and saluted him as emperor [Col. 0450C].

When Peter heard this, he came immediately to Constantinople and informed them of it. The emperor shortly afterward boarded a ship with his wife and children; but, driven back by a storm, he was carried to St. Antonomus. That same night he was seized by the pains of gout, which proved a serious impediment to his flight.

Meanwhile the new emperor hastened to Byzantium. When he had already reached the Hebdomon, the patriarch and the senate came out to meet him. He then entered the imperial city and assumed the imperial insignia. Two days later he was carried in the imperial chariot to the palace; on the fifth day he placed a crown upon his wife Leontia and proclaimed her Augusta.

Numerous spectacles were presented to celebrate Phocas’s arrival. While arrangements were being discussed for the procession and ceremonial display to receive Leontia, a dispute arose over the place of the station between the Veneti and the Prasini [Col. 0450D]—there were two factions. The Veneti, badly treated by their rivals, cried out: “Maurice is still alive,” for they knew that he was hostile to the Prasini.

When Phocas learned this, he sent soldiers and ordered Maurice to be brought to the harbor of Eutropius. There, before his eyes, his sons were first killed, while their father meanwhile uttered this saying of David: “You are righteous, O Lord, and your judgment is upright” (Psalm 118:137).

When the nurse of the youngest child, who was still nursing, offered her own son in his place, Maurice nevertheless betrayed the infant. He received death with the same steadfastness. Thus he turned the cup of God’s wrath into a draught of medicine, which profited him for the purification of his sins and the attainment of the soul’s perfect salvation.

The tyrant confined Constantina Augusta and her three daughters in a private house called that of Leo, as Simocatta relates in Book VIII, chapter 15. Other writers, however, report that after a few months he ordered them to be killed. A fragment concerning Phocas’s coronation states that Peter, Maurice’s brother, and several nobles were killed at the same time. From it we also learn the names of five of the emperor’s sons and the time when these events occurred: the sixth indiction, on November 23.

[Note: Some say that there were five, others only three. In the fragment cited by us, Theodosius is counted among those killed; his father had already proclaimed him Caesar. It is nevertheless the common opinion that he was absent when these events occurred, because Maurice had sent him to the king of the Persians to request his assistance. They also say that he was later captured at Nicaea in Bithynia and beheaded. But Theophylact Simocatta, a writer almost contemporary with the events, whom for this reason we have preferred to the others, expressly says that Theodosius was recalled from his embassy by his father Maurice and was present for the slaughter.]

From the same document we learn that images of the Augusti Phocas and Leontia came to Rome on the Kalends of May, and that all the clergy and senate acclaimed them in the Lateran, in the Basilica of Julius. Afterwards St. Gregory ordered those images to be placed in the oratory of St. Caesarius the Martyr within the palace.

### 4

It was not open to the pope to refrain from writing to Phocas a letter congratulating him on having obtained the empire. We have already answered those who accuse Gregory of speaking too unjustly about Maurice but flatteringly about Phocas [Note: In the notes on Book XIII, Letter 31].

Indeed, what are called flatteries and adulations are rather prayers for the emperor, from whom the supreme pontiff desires that the state be governed well, as will be evident to anyone who reads the passage:

“Let the heavens rejoice,” he says, “and let the earth exult; let the entire people of the republic, hitherto grievously afflicted, now grow cheerful because of your kindly actions. Let the proud minds of the enemies be subdued beneath the yoke of your rule. By your mercy let the crushed and oppressed spirits of your subjects be raised up. May the power of heavenly grace make you terrible to your enemies, and piety make you kind to your subjects. In your most blessed times, may the entire republic rest, with the spoils of peace extended under the pretext of legal proceedings. May the snares laid through wills cease, and the gifts of donations forcibly exacted. May secure possession of their own property return to all, so that they may rejoice in holding without fear what they have not acquired by fraud. May each person’s liberty under the yoke of a pious empire now be restored. For this is the difference between the kings of the nations and the emperors of the republic: the kings of the nations are masters of slaves, whereas the emperors of the republic are masters of free men. But we say these things better by praying than by giving advice” (Book XIII, Letter 31).

The words that follow, to the end of the letter [Col. 0451D], are prayers in which the holy man asks God to provide the emperor with the help of grace that he needs.

In another letter to the same Phocas there are no praises that carry the scent of flattery (Book XIII, Letter 38). In the letter in which he greeted Leontia, he likewise offers prayers, not blandishments, as anyone can observe by reading it (ibid., Letter 39).

### 5

As for certain harsher statements written by St. Gregory about the Emperor Maurice in those letters, it is clear that this emperor had almost always shown himself unjust toward the most holy pontiff, Rome, and all Italy, as is evident from so many of Gregory’s letters.

Therefore, when Gregory complains about Maurice’s harsh yoke—though concealing his name—in writing to Phocas or Leontia, he is not seeking through unjust complaints to obscure the reputation of the deceased emperor. It seems rather that the holy man’s purpose was to incline the new emperor’s mind toward mercy and clemency toward his subjects.

He does indeed criticize Maurice’s greed indirectly, as well as the other evils that usually arise from that vice. But Simocatta himself (Book VIII, chapter 6), although more indulgent toward this emperor, does not deny that he suffered from greed. He says that Maurice wanted the army to winter after crossing the Danube so that it could raid the barbarian territory and live on the provisions obtained there, thus avoiding the need to supply the soldiers with rations. This gave the army an opportunity to rebel and choose another emperor.

Although Maurice’s military prowess is praised, he scarcely waged any war after assuming the empire except through his generals. And although he had to wage war almost continually for as long as he ruled, especially against the Avars or Abaros, it is nevertheless clear from the same Theophylact Simocatta that the fighting had varied and often unfortunate outcomes.

Meanwhile the Lombards and other barbarians were laying waste to Italy, Sicily, Sardinia, and Dalmatia, while the emperor scarcely took any care. St. Gregory found this intolerable, and thus he was given occasion to reproach Maurice in his letters to Phocas and Leontia.

### 6

Returning to the new emperor: when Phocas found no *apocrisiarius* of the Roman Church in the palace, he was not at all pleased. Anatolius still held this office in the fourth indiction, in the year 601, as is clear from the letter written to him (Book XI, Letter 47). We cannot determine when or for what reason he left the imperial city.

Gregory, wishing to excuse himself before Phocas, wrote:

“That Your Serenity did not find a deacon of the apostolic see remaining in the palace, according to ancient custom, was not due to my negligence but to the gravest necessity. For while all the ministers of this Church of ours were shrinking back from and avoiding these crushed and harsh times in fear, none of them could be assigned to go to the imperial city and remain in the palace. But after they learned that, by the disposition of almighty God’s grace, Your Clemency had reached the summit of imperial power, they too, urged on by joy, hasten to come to your feet—those who had previously been very much afraid to go there” (Book XIII, Letter 38).

He later indicates that Boniface, the first of the defenders, was chosen for this office. He says that he had known him through long and constant association and had approved him in life, faith, and conduct; for this reason he had made him a deacon, so that he might undertake this embassy and responsibility.

This is the Boniface well known from numerous Gregorian letters, who was later elected supreme pontiff and called Boniface III, although he governed the Church only briefly. We infer how acceptable he was to Phocas from the fact that, after becoming pope, he obtained the result that the patriarch of Constantinople ceased to call himself “ecumenical.”

### 7

In the letter to Phocas, carried by the new *apocrisiarius*, Gregory deplores the miserable condition of Italy:

“How,” he says, “under daily swords and amid how great incursions of the Lombards—behold, for the length of thirty-five years now—we have been oppressed, we cannot express in words sufficient to convey it” (Book XIII, Letter 33).

Certainly, from the letter written this year to Smaragdus the exarch, we learn that war was still being waged with the Lombards, although it was sometimes interrupted by truces lasting a few days. The same letter almost persuades us that the Pisans were already independent at that time and could, at their discretion, enter into peace treaties or declare war. St. Gregory mentions there their *dromones*, already prepared to set out; from this we learn that they were powerful at sea.

The supreme pontiff had urged them to make peace with the Romans by sending a legate, but he could accomplish nothing. He considered this worth reporting to the exarch.

### 8

A little earlier, Theoderic, king of the Franks in Burgundy, had sent distinguished men, Burgoald and Varmaricarius, as legates to the pope, so that with his assistance he might make and secure peace with the emperor and the Roman republic. The most wise father praised his plan and promised to provide his assistance for this purpose (Book XIII, Letter 7).

Perhaps the two brothers, Theodebert, king of the Austrasians, and Theoderic, were already at odds; Theoderic prudently sought the friendship of the Romans. His grandmother Brunichildis favored him and was hostile to her grandson Theodebert, who was eventually defeated and put to flight in two battles and then killed by his own men, who wished to purchase the victor’s favor with his head.

The above-mentioned legates had been instructed by Brunichildis to consult the pope about a certain bishop whom an illness of the mind prevented from administering his office. That this bishop was mentally deranged is shown by the letter written on the matter to Etherius of Lyons, in which Gregory responds to the question as follows:

“Since, while a bishop is alive, no reason permits another to be ordained in his place unless he refuses, when necessity arising from illness rather than guilt removes him from his office, if he is accustomed to experience intervals of illness, he should himself, upon submitting a petition, acknowledge that he can no longer rise to this ministry, since the illness has overthrown his intellectual faculties, and should request that another be ordained in his place.

“Once this has been done, another who is worthy shall be consecrated bishop by the solemn election of all, but in such a way that, for as long as the life of that bishop remains in this world, the expenses due to him shall be supplied from the same Church.

“If, however, he never returns to the exercise of a sound mind, a faithful person of reputable life should be chosen who can be suitable for governing the Church, concern himself with the welfare of souls, restrain the disorderly under the bond of discipline, administer ecclesiastical affairs, and show himself mature and effective in all things. Even if he should outlive the bishop who is now ill, he is to be consecrated in his place.

“As for ordinations of presbyters, deacons, or persons of any other order, if the need arises for them to be carried out in that Church, you should know that the matter is reserved to your fraternity, so that, if it belongs to your diocese, you may investigate the life, conduct, and behavior of the person chosen for this purpose. And if he proves acceptable, with nothing in him deserving canonical censure, he is to enter the order to which he has been assigned only through your ordination” (Book XIII, Letter 5).

The same queen also consulted St. Gregory about whether a bigamist could enter the sacred order. He replied that, according to the canonical rule, this should by no means be permitted.

When she asked him to strengthen with privileges the monastery of St. Martin in the suburb of Augustodunum, another monastery of the servants of God, and a hospice for strangers, which she had arranged to have built in the same city, the pious Pontiff willingly granted her request [Note: These privileges are extant in Letters 8, 9, and 10].

### 9

The queen thought she would gratify the most vigilant shepherd of the whole Church by asking him to send a legate to Gaul who, after convening a synod, could correct everything that was being perpetrated against the most sacred canons.

For this was especially the pope’s desire, as is clear from the many letters that he had written on the matter in previous years to this same queen, to the kings, and to very many bishops of Gaul [Note: Especially in the ninth year of his pontificate].

Accordingly, Gregory thanked the queen and replied that at a suitable time he would send someone to convene a synod, promising to fulfill her pious wishes. No synod was nevertheless convened in Gaul to remedy the clergy’s corrupt practices until almost thirty years later, civil wars having obstructed this good work.

### 10

The most holy father showed still greater concern for restoring ecclesiastical discipline in Italy. He wrote to Chrysanthus, bishop of Spoleto, and to many others about removing foreign women from the households of priests and other clerics (Book XIII, Letters 36 and 35), and he employed the assistance of the defender Optatus for this purpose.

He ordered the subdeacon Anthemius to summon the bishops of Campania and admonish them concerning their duty, of which they seemed forgetful (ibid., Letters 27 and 26). If anyone afterward, once admonished, should prove negligent and idle, Gregory wanted him sent to Rome for stricter punishment.

Bishop Paschasius was said to be especially sluggish through idleness. Gregory therefore ordered Anthemius to rebuke him for his negligence before selected witnesses. If he did not shake off his laziness, he ordered him sent to Rome to be punished more severely.

### 11

He not only punished every fraud committed by the agents and tenants of the Roman Church, but also repaired the losses that their frauds had inflicted upon the tenant farmers. Thus he praised Pantaleon, administrator of the Syracusan patrimony, because he had broken the measuring vessel by which the tenant farmers were compelled to deliver grain, since it exceeded the proper measure. He also ordered that the money obtained through the unjust measure be secretly distributed among the poorer tenants (Book XIII, Letter 34).

### 12

How entirely opposed he was to seizing the property of the poor is certainly proved by his extraordinary zeal in giving alms. Thus he reproached Julian, an illustrious man, because false modesty had concealed his poverty:

“It is certain,” he says, “that one before whom a person is still ashamed is loved less. I have been exceedingly saddened, because I have discovered that I am loved by you less than I had thought. In this respect you greatly keep me back if you earnestly require that opportunities for my reward be continually provided.”

“You ought not to be ashamed to speak insistently to someone about alms when it is clear that he possesses not his own property but the property of the poor, entrusted to him for distribution. You should therefore have spoken freely with the bishop about opportunities for reward, even if you did not know what my disposition toward you was in my affection.”

“For since we love your honor wholeheartedly and, as you know, occupy the position of steward over the property of the poor, I confess that your shame was highly blameworthy. I pursue it by rebuking it with so many words for this reason: that I may drive it completely from your heart” (Book XIII, Letter 19).

From the letter to Pantaleon we learn that the administrators of the patrimonies formerly gave an oath before the sacred body of blessed Peter.

Since he could not, by his own authority, restrain the emperor’s officials who preyed upon private property under the pretext of public utility, he took care to inform the emperor about their evil practices and plundering. This year he warned the patrician Rustician that a certain Beator had come to Rome, claiming to be *comes privatarum*, and was acting unjustly in many ways, especially against her and her nieces, namely Antonina and Barbara, the daughters of Venantius, about whom we shall speak elsewhere [Note: Baronius makes this conjecture].

### 13

This year, after the death of Victor, bishop of Panormus, Venantius, the patrician of Panormus—distinct from the former monk of Syracuse whose death we have already discussed—arranged for Urbicus, abbot of the monastery of St. Hermes, to be elected bishop of that city.

St. Gregory praised this election because he knew Urbicus to be vigilant, diligent, and trained in knowledge of Holy Scripture, which above all should be sought in priests. Nevertheless, the pope did not wish to disturb the abbot’s quiet, lest, by elevating him to higher things, he should force him, sent into the waves, to become less than he had been [Note: See Mabillon, *Annales Benedictini*, Book VIII, nos. 35 and 59].

Urbicus was virtually prefect or general superior of all the monasteries in Sicily, as we have already observed. This may perhaps have been the reason why Gregory did not allow him to be removed from such a prefecture in order to become a bishop.

John obtained the see of Panormus. St. Gregory admonished him to grant his clergy an entire fourth portion of the Church’s revenues and to appoint a record-keeper who would distribute to each cleric what was due to him according to a table or register (*tabula* or *matricula*) (Book XIII, Letter 44). He also gives him outstanding instructions for the best governance of the Church.

The pallium had already been sent to John shortly before. In the letter by which the most holy pontiff granted the recently ordained bishop the right to use the pallium, he says that John had undertaken the office of watchman over the Church of Panormus, correctly interpreting the name “bishop” [Col. 0455D] (ibid., Letter 37).

### 14

Gregory himself certainly proved to be an indefatigable and most vigilant watchman, keeping constant watch, although he lay sick with the gravest illnesses, so that he might ward off from his flock whatever evil threatened it.

When he learned that certain men of perverse spirit in the city of Rome were forbidding people to perform some work on Saturday, he wrote to the Roman citizens, rejecting this Jewish error [Col. 0456A]. He calls its authors preachers of Antichrist, who, he says, when he comes, “will cause both the Sabbath and the Lord’s Day to be observed free from every kind of work.”

The same men, or others of a perverse disposition, were preaching that no one ought to bathe on the Lord’s Day. “Certainly,” he says, “if someone desires to bathe for the sake of bodily luxury and pleasure, we do not permit this on any other day either. But if it is for the necessity of the body, we do not forbid it even on the Lord’s Day.”

## CHAPTER VIII

**Argument.**—1. Gregory sends a defender to Spain to judge episcopal cases. The judgment of John the defender.—2. The pope orders him to inspect the monastery on the island of Capraria. His concern for other monasteries.—3. What he decided concerning a bishop who interrupted the celebration of the sacrifice of the Mass because of illness.—4. How concerned he was to establish peace among the bishops.—5. St. Gregory’s letter and gifts to Queen Theodelinda.—6. St. Gregory’s final labors for the Church. What he replied to the bishop of Messina who consulted him.—7. Advice he gave to his friends. His death. Burial. Sacred cult. Translations. (Years 603 and 604.)

### 1

From the lofty watchtower of the Church, St. Gregory saw the Churches of Spain in disorder because of the unjust deposition of a presbyter and certain bishops. He therefore sent John the defender, who, by the authority delegated to him by the supreme Pontiff, sat as judge between the presbyter and the bishops who had suffered violence, and those who had either unjustly deposed them, invaded their sees, or ordained the invaders. He also judged between them and the illustrious Comitiolus, presumably prefect of Baetica, through whose particular agency it is reasonable to believe that such great evils had been perpetrated in that province.

The occasion for John the defender’s mission was provided by the petition, or humble supplication, presented to the pope by Januarius, bishop of Malaca. In it he complained that one of his presbyters had been removed from office and deported into exile. In the same petition Januarius undoubtedly also complained of a similar punishment inflicted upon himself.

Another bishop of uncertain locality, named Stephen, was deposed and driven into exile together with Januarius and had also appealed to the Holy See.

So that John might give a correct judgment in these cases involving bishops and presbyters, the pope gave him two capitularies, or instructions. One prescribed everything that had to be done in preparing and judging these disputes; the other contained the imperial laws concerning the immunity of clerics.

In the judgment of John the defender, whom all parties acknowledged as their legitimate judge, no mention is made of the bishop Stephen or of the presbyter of Malaca, but only of Januarius, the bishop of that city, who by this solemn judgment was restored to his Church:

“I find no fault in the aforesaid Januarius deserving punishment by exile or deposition; rather, I find that he was violently expelled from his Church. And although the severity of the law most strictly punishes such presumption, I, nevertheless, temper the force of the laws with priestly moderation. With the holy Gospels placed before me, in whose presence I sat from the beginning as judge in this proceeding, I declare that the measures enacted against him, although legally invalid and of no effect, are nevertheless unjust and void.

“I condemn those bishops mentioned by name who, setting aside priestly consideration, acted unjustly and contrary to the fear of God to the prejudice and condemnation of their brother; and I decree and determine that they be received into a monastery to perform penance for a time.

“But I condemn the man who wickedly presumed to invade the place of the aforesaid most holy Januarius contrary to the statutes of the sacred canons, and I decree that he be deprived of the priesthood and removed from every ecclesiastical order, so that he may lose what he wrongly obtained and may not return to the office that he had previously held unworthily.

“As for the aforesaid most holy bishop Januarius, having been absolved, he shall, by God’s authority, return to his place in the episcopal rank” (Book XIII, Letter 45).

### 2

St. Gregory instructed the same defender to visit the monastery of the island of Capricana, or Capraria, near Majorca, and correct the corrupt morals of the monks (Book XIII, Letter 46). They were said to act so perversely that they showed themselves to be serving not God but rather the ancient enemy.

Thus the most holy father demonstrated everywhere his zeal for preserving or restoring monastic discipline.

At the beginning of the fourteenth year of his pontificate, he was concerned to provide for the monastery of Saints Laurence and Zeno in the fortress of Caesena, which Concordius, the bishop of that place, had disturbed by the unjust deposition of the abbot Fortunatus.

Fortunatus had been appointed abbot of this monastery by his predecessor Natalis, bishop of Caesena. Although there was no cause, the new bishop had removed him from office and installed another abbot. Fortunatus brought a complaint about his deposition before the supreme Pontiff.

Although Gregory had learned from Concordius’s own deacon that the abbot had been unjustly deprived, he nevertheless wished Marinianus, archbishop of Ravenna, to investigate the matter, because, he said, “proof can be more certain in the regions where the matter occurred.” If there were no manifest reason for the deposition, he ordered Fortunatus restored to his former rank and the bishop rebuked for attempting to destroy the appointment of his predecessor without being provoked by any misconduct (Book XIV, Letter 6).

At approximately the same time St. Gregory wrote to Vitalis, the defender of the island, concerning certain abbots of the monasteries of Sardinia. He said that those who had fallen while still in the monastic and lower order ought by no means to have assumed the office of abbot unless their lives had been entirely corrected and a worthy period of penance had preceded it.

But since they had already become abbots, the most wise Father wished Vitalis to take care concerning their life, conduct, and diligence. If their actions were found not to conflict with their office, they were to remain in the rank and office they had received. Otherwise, he says, “after they have been removed, let others be appointed who can benefit the souls entrusted to them” (Book XIV, Letter 2).

### 3

In a letter to Vitalis written on this matter, St. Gregory responds to a question concerning Januarius, archbishop of Cagliari, who, when celebrating the sacrifice, frequently suffered such severe distress that he could scarcely return to the place of the Canon after long intervals.

This gave many people occasion for offense, so that they doubted whether they ought to receive communion from his consecration. “But they must be admonished,” says the holy Doctor, “not to fear in any way, but to communicate with complete faith and confidence, because a person’s illness neither changes nor corrupts the blessing of the sacred mystery.”

Nevertheless, he wanted Vitalis to suggest to Januarius that whenever he felt any discomfort, he should not proceed, lest he thereby both make himself contemptible and generate scandal in the minds of the infirm.

Januarius’s poor health in advanced age had caused great losses to the Churches, hospices, and monasteries in Sardinia. The pope ordered the steward and archpresbyter of the Church of Cagliari to take care of the hospices, under penalty of punishment if any neglect should occur thereafter.

4. Gregory’s concern for the whole Church could be diminished neither by advancing age nor by the increasingly severe daily labors, nor by the illnesses that foretold his approaching death—especially when the restoration of peace among bishops was at issue. He himself indicates this in a letter written that year:

“Whenever,” he says, “the discord of those who ought to have been preachers of peace makes us sad, we must strive with great concern so that, once the cause of the dispute has been removed, those who disagree with one another in their differing wills may return to harmony” (Book XIV, Letter 8).

He said this on the occasion of the dispute between Alcyson, bishop of Corcyra, and John, bishop of Eurias in Epirus. John had been forced to flee from that city by the Barbarians, together with his clergy; and, after carrying with him the body of Saint Donatus, he had deposited those sacred relics in the fortress of Cassiopi and established a residence there for himself and his clerics, with the consent of Alcyson, the bishop of Corcyra, in whose diocese the fortress lay.

[Note: [Col. 0457] This city took its name from him and is still called San Donato.]

Against ecclesiastical order, sacerdotal modesty, and the decrees of the sacred canons, John attempted to remove the aforesaid fortress from Alcyson’s jurisdiction and subject it to his own authority, so that those who had previously been received there as strangers might in some way become its masters. Alcyson protested both to the emperor and to Andrew, bishop of Nicopolis and metropolitan of both men, about the bishop’s ingratitude and his unjust usurpation of the fortress. Andrew, acting both by virtue of his office and on the emperor’s command, issued a judgment decreeing that the fortress of Cassiopi ought to remain under the jurisdiction of the Church of Corcyra.

The pope approved the metropolitan’s judgment. And although the fault in this dispute seemed to demand no slight severity against John, because evil had been repaid for good, nevertheless, “we must strive,” says the most merciful Father, “so that benevolence is not overcome by misconduct, and that what is owed to strangers is not denied even to brothers suffering necessity.… Therefore the priests or clergy of the city of Eurias must in no way be driven from their residence in the aforementioned fortress of Cassiopi. They must also be granted permission, with the appropriate reverence, to deposit the holy and venerable body of blessed Donatus, which they brought with them, in whichever of the churches of that place they choose, whether inside or outside the fortress.

“Nevertheless, a security must be obtained and provided for your affection, in whose parish the fortress itself is situated, by which the bishop of Eurias promises that he will claim there no authority, no privilege, no jurisdiction, and no further authority as a cardinal bishop; but that, once peace has been restored by God’s favor, and the venerable body of Saint Donatus has been removed, if they so wish, they will return by every means to their own place” (Book XIV, Letter 7).

The bishop of Eurias did not immediately submit to this judgment. Instead, he obtained from the emperor, by covert means, an order by which he claimed all authority over the fortress of Cassiopi. Saint Gregory took this badly; nevertheless, so that he would not appear to do anything contrary to the emperor’s command or in contempt of the emperor himself, he issued no formal legal judgment to either party. He was content, through the agency of his legate Boniface, to admonish the bishop concerning the injustice of the order he had secretly obtained and to ask him to issue a contrary order confirming the judgment of the metropolitan, which had been ratified by the Holy See (Book XIV, Letter 8).

That the bishop of Eurias repented is shown by the letter written to Alcyson (same book, Letter 13). For he offered a written undertaking in which he humbly requested from the bishop of Corcyra permission to deposit the body of blessed Donatus in the Church of Saint John, situated within the fortress of Cassiopi. He also declared himself ready to provide a guarantee by which he would freely acknowledge that this place belonged to the diocese of Corcyra and promise never to claim any right over it. The pope urged Alcyson, once the requested guarantee had been received, to grant the permission, and to promise both the bishop of Eurias and his clerics that, once peace had been restored and they were permitted to return to their own Church, they would have the right to take the body of Saint Donatus with them.

5. We suspect that the bishop of Eurias was forced to abandon his own Church by the Slavs or Avars, not by the Lombards. For we infer from the letters and gifts sent by Saint Gregory to Queen Theodelinda that at that time there was no war with the Lombards (Book XIV, Letter 21). She had written to the supreme pontiff to make him share in her joy over the birth of her son Adaloald, whom she had arranged to have baptized in the Catholic faith, although Agilulf, his father and king, had not yet renounced Arianism.

The pope sent sacred gifts and other presents to the royal boy and his sister; these are to be read about in the letter written to the queen. He asked her to thank her royal husband, in his name, for the peace that had been made, and, as she was accustomed to do, to incline his mind toward future peace.

In the same letter, since Theodelinda had asked him to reply in writing to Abbot Secundinus, who was contending on behalf of the Three Chapters, he asks that he be excused on account of his illness, of which the queen’s envoys had been witnesses, since, when they departed, they had left him in the greatest peril and danger of his life.

6. Yet he did not cease to concern himself with the Church. At that same time, when the Church of Ancona had become vacant, he deliberated for a long time about appointing a bishop who would be worthy, examining the qualities of mind, virtues, and conduct of the three men who had been selected (Book XIV, Letter 11). He also gave a very full reply to numerous questions from Felix, bishop of Messana (same book, Letter 17), concerning the degrees of kinship within which marriage is permitted, the harassment suffered by bishops from the laypeople subject to them, and Churches whose dedication was uncertain.

To the first question he replied that what he had allowed the newly converted English (Book XI, Letter 64)—namely, that they might contract marriage within prohibited degrees—had not been granted by him to everyone; indeed, not even to the English themselves except temporarily, that is, until the Christian religion had taken root among them.

To the second question he answered:

“If David, the most just of kings, did not dare to lay hands upon Saul, whom it was evident the Lord had already rejected, how much more must care be taken lest certain people lay the hand of detraction or reproach, or of indiscretion or dishonor, upon the Lord’s anointed or upon the preachers of the holy Church? For their harassment or defamation concerns Christ, in whose stead they exercise an embassy in the Church. Therefore all the faithful must take the greatest care not to tear apart their own bishop—that is, the Lord’s anointed—whether secretly or publicly, by detraction or reproach.”

To the third question he said:

“As for the uncertainty concerning the dedication of Churches, about which, among other matters, you wished to consult us, you ought properly to hold to what we have received as handed down by our predecessors: whenever there is doubt either about the baptism or confirmation of certain people, or about the consecration of Churches, and no certain conclusion can be reached from written records or witnesses as to whether the people were baptized or confirmed, or the Churches consecrated, such people should be baptized and confirmed, and the Churches should be dedicated canonically, lest such uncertainty become a ruin to the faithful; for what is not shown by certain indications to have been properly performed is not considered repeated.”

[Col. 0460C] 7. With these answers the most holy Doctor took care to instruct the whole Church, nor did he refrain from privately admonishing friends whenever this appeared beneficial to the Church. He congratulated Paul the Scholastic (Book XIV, Letter 1), both on his zeal in restraining and punishing criminals and on his reconciliation with Leo, bishop of Catania. He urged both men to love peace and foster charity, so that they might always be able to demand from one another a reciprocal affection, as though from one another they were exacting some mutual loan at interest.

When he learned that a soldier had abducted a servant of God, he wrote to Guduinus, duke of Naples, concerning the punishment of so great a crime, in these words:

“Among the many good things that are frequently reported to us about your greatness, it is said that the following is especially praiseworthy in you: that you love chastity and, as is fitting, preserve discipline. We have been sufficiently astonished that, in the case of that soldier who, through the instigation of the devil, destroyed a servant of God, no very strict vengeance has yet been exacted. For it was entirely consistent with your character and goodness that the punishment should reach us before the wickedness of the crime committed did so,” and so forth.

Concerned for the exarch, since he knew that through his lack of restraint in speech he often said things capable of provoking against him all who loved him, Gregory wrote to one of the exarch’s intimates, urging him to admonish his friend about this matter (Book XIV, Letter 15).

8. Worn down by these unremitting labors no less than by his continual illnesses, Gregory finally passed into the desired rest on the fourth day before the Ides of March, in the second year of the emperor Phocas, indiction VII, in the year of Christ 604.

[Note: [Col. 0461B] Bede records his death in indiction VIII, and Paul the Deacon followed him in his History of the Lombards; [Col. 0462B] but both are mistaken, as Baron proves in his note on this year.]

He was buried in the outer portico of the basilica of the blessed Apostle Peter, before the old sacristy. Concerning this and his epitaph, John the Deacon is to be consulted (Book IV, chapter 68). He says that his venerable body was transferred by Pope Gregory IV [305] to a place before the new sacristy, placed beneath an altar bearing his name after apses had been constructed there, where his annual feast was celebrated while everyone vied with one another in keeping vigil through the night (same work, chapter 80).

Sacred honors were decreed for him by the English Church at the Council of Clovesho in the year 747, canon 17:

“Let the birthday of blessed Pope Gregory, and likewise the day of the deposition of Saint Augustine, archbishop, be honorably venerated by all, as is fitting, so that both days may be observed as holidays by the clergy and by the monasteries.”

This most holy man deserved to be honored not only by the Latins but also by the Greeks, whose menologion records his sacred name on 11 March, with an extensive encomium reported by Bollandus.

Concerning the transfer of the sacred relics of Saint Gregory to the celebrated monastery of Saint Medard, see Mabillon and Bollandus (*Saeculum IV Benedictinum*, part I, p. 383; Bollandus, 12 March). Bollandus also discusses the transfer of the same saint’s head to the monastery of Saint Peter the Living at Sens, around the year 876, as a gift from Pope John, with the support of Charles the Bald, king and emperor of the Franks, at the request of Ansegisus, archbishop of Sens.

John the Deacon depicts with sufficient accuracy the stature of the most holy Pontiff, the features of his face, his hair, his beard, and everything pertaining to his appearance (Book IV, chapter 84). But who could describe the state of his extraordinarily distinguished mind, his most ardent love of God, his immense charity toward his neighbor, his profoundest humility, his unbroken courage in adversity, his moderation, self-control, vigilance, prudence, and the other virtues that adorned our Gregory in such abundance? For, to speak with Saint Ildephonsus, “In holiness he surpassed Antony, in eloquence Cyprian, and in wisdom Augustine” (*On Illustrious Men*, chapter 1).

[Col. 0461]

IMAGES OF BLESSED GREGORY THE GREAT AND HIS PARENTS, described by John the Deacon in Book IV of the Life of that Saint, chapters 83 and 84, and illustrated with notes by Angelo Rocca, prefect of the apostolic sacristy.

[Note: [Col. 0463A]

314 This is what John the Deacon says in Book IV, chapters 83 and 84, of the *Life of Blessed Gregory the Great*, who died in the year of the Lord 604 or 605, according to Trithemius; John the Deacon, however, flourished around the year of the Lord 870. Although the images described by John were not in the same place, I have nevertheless arranged them here in the order in which I found them painted in Rome, in the chapel of Saint Andrew. For they appear to have been taken, nearly three hundred years ago, from those which John the Deacon testifies existed in his own time in the monastery’s atrium, although by a painter who was not sufficiently skilled, as the less suitable features, or those less pertinent to the art of painting, persuade us.

For this reason, after being advised by judicious men, I carefully arranged for the said images—represented as though by the brush according to John the Deacon’s most exact description—to be reproduced in every respect from life. To these images also correspond, for the most part, those that can now be seen in the chapel itself, painted in a crude style.

It is not sufficiently clear in which monastery the said images were painted, if John the Deacon’s words in chapter 83 are carefully weighed. I believe, however, that it was the monastery in Rome which was built in the house of the same blessed Gregory on the Clivus Scauri, near the church of Saints John and Paul, in honor of Saint Andrew, as John the Deacon testifies in Book I, chapter 6, and in Book VII of Gregory’s *Register*, Letter 13. Its present Church is now called by the name of Saint Gregory. This may be inferred from what the same John the Deacon writes in chapters 95, 96, and 97.

Moreover, John the Deacon could not have described the said images, nor represented their details—so to speak, with a brush—with such precision if he had not seen them in Rome, where he lived.

There are some who believe that two monasteries were built by blessed Gregory the Great on the Clivus Scauri, prompted by what John the Deacon writes in Book I of the Life of that Saint, chapters 32 and 38; Book II, chapter 45; and Book IV, chapter 97. John the Deacon writes especially in Book II, chapter 45, where he says that he found the following in a book called in Greek *Deimōn* (Δειμών), and in Latin *Campus* or *Pratum*—that is, “Field” or “Meadow”:

“He”—namely, Gregory—“having become pope, built a large monastery for men and gave orders that none of the monks should possess anything of his own, not even a single obol.”

So says John the Deacon. Since it is certain that one monastery was built by blessed Gregory on the Clivus Scauri before his pontificate, after the death of his father Gordianus, one must say that another, and indeed a large one, was built during his pontificate—unless we say that the one mentioned by John the Deacon in Book I, chapter 6, was later enlarged.

Although John the Deacon calls the monastery built by blessed Gregory in Book I, chapter 6, by the name of Saint Andrew, and in chapter 38 by the name of the venerable Levite Gregory, it may nevertheless have been the same monastery, even if there was only one. For it could be called Saint Andrew’s insofar as it was built in his honor, and Gregorian insofar as it was built by Gregory.

Hence Pope Pelagius II, writing, as we read in Book I, chapter 32 of John the Deacon, and in the final letter of Volume I of the *Decretals*, to blessed Gregory, then a Levite and apocrisarius at Constantinople, calls the monastery built by Gregory himself “Gregorian.” The same is written by John the Deacon in Book IV, chapter 88, and in other places; and the same is read in Book III of the *Dialogues*, chapter 36; Book IV of the *Dialogues*, chapters 21 and 26; and elsewhere.

The difficulty, however, is increased by the Deacon himself, who in Book IV, chapter 97, mentions in the same place both the Gregorian monastery and the monastery of the nuns of Saint Andrew, as though one had been for men and the other for women. He expressly says that this place too was called the Clivus Scauri. It may be that the old monastery, called at one time Gregorian and at another Saint Andrew’s for the reason assigned, had become, in John the Deacon’s time, a monastery not of men but of nuns.

In the meantime, some maintain that the chapel called Saint Andrew’s was the oratory of the monastery first built, while the larger Church attached to the monastery was constructed much later by Gregory himself, during his pontificate. They believe that this was the oratory mentioned by John the Deacon in Book I, chapter 12.

These are the things I thought should be said about the monastery and Church of Saint Andrew and blessed Gregory. Let others decide what should be thought, after carefully weighing the arguments on both sides.

In the meantime, four matters concerning the depicted and engraved likeness of blessed Gregory the Great seem worthy of explanation: why the image itself does not represent old age; why it is bearded; why it appears without the likeness of a dove—for he is ordinarily depicted as old, shaven, and with a dove appearing near his head; and finally, why he is shown without a mitre or tiara, which they call the crown.

[Col. 0464C] To resolve the questions proposed, Gregory the Great, while he was still a Levite—as John the Deacon says in Book I, chapters 41, 43, and 44, of the *Life* of that blessed Gregory—or still a cardinal deacon of the Holy Roman Church, was unanimously, though unwillingly, made pope. He was, as may be conjectured, forty-six years old, or at most fifty.

This is because, in the fourth year of blessed Gregory’s pontificate, his nurse was still alive, as may be seen from the final letter of Book III of the blessed Gregory’s *Letters*. For Saint Gregory, writing to the patrician Rusticiana, says:

“As for that lady, my nurse, whom you commend in your letters, I love her wholeheartedly and do not wish her to be burdened in any way.”

This was said by blessed Gregory around the fourth year of his pontificate. Add that blessed Gregory never complained of old age, which itself is often called an illness, since he was neither prematurely aged nor weighed down by advancing age. He frequently stated in many places that he suffered only from gout and stomach troubles. Indeed, in Book VII of the *Register*, indiction 2, Letter 1, written around the year of his ordination, he presents himself as rather young than old, if his words are carefully examined.

In that letter, when he seeks to rebuke Januarius, bishop of Caralis, an old man, he begins his rebuke with the statement of blessed Paul the Apostle in 1 Timothy, chapter 5: “Do not rebuke an older man.” At the beginning of the same letter he interprets this in order not to appear to oppose the apostolic statement by rebuking an older man himself.

Meanwhile, in Book III of the *Dialogues*, chapter 2, he testifies that Totila, king of the Goths, was encamped with his army eight miles from the City “in our time”—that is, as I conjecture, when he was an infant or, at most, a child. Totila, after occupying almost the whole of Italy, captured Rome after besieging it for an entire year in the year of the Lord 546, the ninth year of Pope Vigilius and the nineteenth year of Justinian’s reign—or, as others hold, several years later.

Blessed Gregory, however, was proclaimed Roman pontiff around the year of the Lord 591 and died in the year of the Lord 604 or 605. Hence, as my conjecture suggests, and as may be gathered from Book III of his *Dialogues*, chapters 4, 5, and 11, it seems necessary to affirm that this saint was at most fifty years old when he was raised to the pontificate. For he is indicated to have been born near the beginning of Totila’s reign, approximately two years before the siege of the City, as may be seen from the passages recently cited and carefully examined.

Caesar Baronius, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, seems to agree with this view concerning the age of blessed Gregory the Great, as may be inferred from what he writes with no less accuracy than learning in Volume VII of his *Annals*.

We have represented him as bearded not only in accordance with the painting that exists in the chapel of Saint Andrew and in the oratory attached to the Leonine Palace near the Holy Stair, but also in accordance with the clear testimony of John the Deacon. He flourished approximately 265 years after the death of blessed Gregory and left a written account stating that, in his own time, the said images were visible to the public.

John the Deacon describes the image of blessed Gregory without the likeness of a dove, since it was painted at his command at a time when—as I may put it—the apparition of that dove near his head had not yet been made public by Peter the Deacon, his closest associate. For Peter, writing only after blessed Gregory’s death about the apparition of the dove above Gregory’s head, testified that he had seen it, as John the Deacon reports in Book IV, chapters 69 and 70.

Moreover, according to John the Deacon, the Holy Spirit is ordinarily depicted in the form of a dove above blessed Gregory’s head only when the holy Doctor is represented in the act of writing. It was precisely in this act that Peter the Deacon solemnly affirmed that he had very frequently seen the dove approach blessed Gregory’s head; and he approved and confirmed this by a divine miracle, as John the Deacon writes in Book IV, chapter 69, of the *Life of Pope Gregory*.

Here I have taken care to represent blessed Gregory bareheaded, because I found him painted that way not only in the chapel of Saint Andrew but also described that way by John the Deacon, a most careful writer, even though it is established that, from the time of Pope Sylvester I onward, the episcopal fillet or mitre, as well as the tiara—which they call the *cydaris*, diadem, crown, or *regnum*—existed.

For these objects—the mitre, signifying spiritual authority, and the tiara or crown, signifying temporal power—were given to blessed Sylvester, as Innocent III testifies in Sermon 3, *On the Consecration of the Supreme Pontiff*. This may be seen in Part I of the *Decree*, Distinction 96, chapter 14, and in Theodore Balsamon’s *Nomocanon of Photius*, title 8, chapter 1. Platina therefore makes very clear mention in the *Life of Blessed Sylvester* of the granting and donation of such insignia.

Concerning the mitre used by blessed Sylvester, Platina speaks in the *Life of Eugenius IV* as follows:

“Eugenius himself carried the mitre of Saint Sylvester, brought from Avignon to Rome, from the Vatican to the Lateran.”

So says Platina. Now half of that mitre, or of another mitre belonging to blessed Sylvester, is preserved among the relics at Saint Martin in the Mountains.

Gregory Nazianzen himself speaks of his own mitre in the third sermon of his *Apologetic*. Ennodius, in his *Epigram*, speaks of the mitre of Saint Ambrose in poetic fashion under the name of garlands.

The half of blessed Sylvester’s mitre is of smooth, non-napped silk and green in color. On it the image of blessed Mary, ever Virgin, carrying her Son in her lap, is visible, embroidered with a needle in a crude style and surrounded by winged children and little stars.

There can therefore be no doubt that the use of the mitre was extremely ancient, existing before the pontificate of blessed Gregory the Great.

Although Sigebert assigns the origin of the diadem, crown, or pontifical tiara to the year of the Lord 550, and Aimoinus—or Annonius—the monk, in his *History of the Franks*, Book I, chapter 24, attributes it to Clovis, saying that the emperor Anastasius sent Clovis, king of the Franks, a golden crown with jewels as a gift, and that Clovis then voluntarily offered it to Saint Peter, nevertheless I have read in Anastasius the Librarian, in Platina, and in several others who committed the annals of the Roman pontiffs to writing, that many of the earlier pontiffs, before Clovis, were crowned and adorned with the papal crown or tiara, commonly called the *regnum*.

It seems worth knowing, however, that the tiara decorated with three crowns—royal, imperial, and priestly, representing the complete and universal power of the whole world—did not come into use until Boniface VIII, of the most noble Gaetani family. Before that, I find that the tiara was adorned with only a single crown, which implicitly contained the same meaning, as may be seen in the most ancient mosaics and in the images of all the Roman pontiffs engraved in copperplate.

Therefore, before the pontificate of blessed Gregory the Great, the use of the mitre and tiara already existed, tracing its origin from the Old Testament—to say nothing of the caps and mitres of the pagans. For in Exodus, chapters 20, 29, and 39; Leviticus, chapters 8 and 16; Ezekiel, chapter 21; Zechariah, chapter 3; and other places in Sacred Scripture, we find explicit mention both of the priestly mitre and of the pontifical *cydaris* and tiara.

Nevertheless, I have taken care here to represent blessed Gregory from life with his head bare, not because the use of the mitre and tiara did not exist in his time and before his pontificate, but because, for the reasons assigned at the beginning, this seemed the proper course.

These are the matters concerning the images described by John the Deacon. It remains now to explain certain somewhat obscure expressions and things somewhat difficult to understand contained in the descriptions of the images.]

[Col. 0461C] 312 On the image of blessed Gregory, chapter 84.

In a [Note: The blessed Gregory the Great, after being made pope, was painted in a small apse—which we call the curvature of a vault—within a plaster roundel, constructed, that is, by the art of stucco-work.] little apse, Gregory is shown painted within a plaster roundel, of proper and well-proportioned stature. His face is balanced between the length of his father’s face and the roundness of his mother’s, so harmoniously that it appears most becomingly elongated with a certain roundness. His beard is somewhat reddish-brown, in his father’s manner, and moderate in size. He is so slightly bald that at the middle of his forehead he has two sparse little curls, turned toward the right. His head is round and broad, with darkish hair neatly curled, hanging down to the middle of his ears. His forehead is handsome, with raised and long, though thin, eyebrows. His eyes have yellowish pupils [Al. dark pupils], not large but open, with full under-eye areas [Note: John the Deacon writes that the blessed Gregory had full under-eyes—that is, a full or slightly swollen region beneath the eyes—and slightly parted lips, meaning, so to speak, lips separated from one another by a small space.] His nose runs finely straight from the root of the eyebrows, becomes broader around the middle, then curves slightly, and at its extremity projects prominently with wide nostrils. His mouth is red, with thick and slightly parted lips; his cheeks are well formed; his chin projects gracefully from the junction of the jaws. His complexion is aquiline and livid [Al. vivid], not yet, as happened to him later, cardiac [Note: [Col. 0466C] 317. John the Deacon says that Gregory thereafter had an aquiline and livid complexion, but in old age a cardiac complexion.

I have not found the term “aquiline” among writers who discuss colors, unless it is the color called aquilus by Antonio Thylesius, who says: “The ancients called this color fuscus, from the color of water; it lies between black and white.” Plato also teaches this. Thus Thylesius, chapter 3, On Colors.

Since the explanation of the aquiline color mentions fuscus, which lies between black and white, I think that aquiline—or aquilus, said to derive from the color of water—is almost the same as livid. For the fuscus color appears to differ little or not at all from livid, which is a darkish and leaden color, or at least to approach it closely, since John the Deacon joins the aquiline color with the livid, from which the fuscus color is composed. According to Thylesius, this color is not unpleasant and is very often praised in a human being.

Festus Pompeius describes the aquiline color as follows: “Aquilus is a dark and nearly black color, from which the eagle seems to have been named, although some would have it named from its sharp sight. The aquilus color, however, is named from water. For when the ancients knew only two natural colors, namely black and white, and there was also a color so like neither of them that it nevertheless derived its character from both—especially from water, whose color is uncertain—they named it after water.” Festus is followed by Junianus Sipontinus in his commentaries, as well as by Huguitio, Papias, and others.

If, however, the aquiline color is named from the eagle, a tawny color may be understood. For the eagle is tawny. Hence Ovid, in Book V of the *Fasti*, calls the eagle a tawny bird, and Claudian calls Jupiter’s standard-bearer tawny. I therefore think that by “aquiline and livid” either a dark or a tawny complexion may be understood.

But since many things are said to be tawny—and, as Thylesius says in chapter 11, especially brass, then gold, stars, sand, the lion, and a certain species of eagle, greatly celebrated by Aristotle—I do not think that tawny suits a human being very well. Therefore I think that “aquiline” must here mean only dark. For tawny appears to be a mixture of red and green. Yet they call the jasper, which is known to be purely green, tawny; and an olive is likewise commonly called tawny.

Meanwhile, it should not be passed over in silence that all the Vatican manuscript codices read *colore aquilino et vivido*—“with an aquiline and vivid complexion”—not *livid[o],* “livid.” This reading certainly seems better. A vivid color, that is, one endowed with great vigor, is highly appropriate to an aquiline or dark complexion; for people with dark faces are usually more lively than fair-skinned people.

I think that the cardiac complexion derives its name from cardiac disease. The cardiac disease, named from the Greek word *καρδία* (*kardia*), that is, “heart,” is an affection or palpitation of the heart, or a disorder of the mouth of the stomach; for the ancients sometimes called the mouth of the stomach the “heart.” According to Cornelius Celsus, Book III, chapter 19, a disease of this kind is properly nothing other than excessive weakness of the body, which, when the stomach is languid, is discharged through excessive sweating.

Gregory the Great said more than once that he suffered from this stomach disorder, namely in Homilies 21 and 22 on the Gospels, as well as elsewhere. From this disease he must be thought to have acquired a cardiac complexion—that is, a saffron-like pallor, or one slightly tinged with yellow—since physicians maintain that this sort of complexion can arise from such a stomach affection or weakness, combined with gout, which afflicted the blessed Gregory in a remarkable way.

For this reason I infer that at the beginning of his pontificate the blessed Gregory the Great was painted in the manner described above, namely with an aquiline and livid, or vivid, complexion; and I regard this as established.] His expression is gentle, his hands beautiful, his fingers smooth and well shaped, and suited to writing. In addition, he wears a chestnut-colored *planeta* over his dalmatic; the Gospel-book is in his left hand, and the sign of the cross in his right.

[Note: What John the Deacon says about the pallium seems difficult to understand unless we explain what the pallium is, what form it has, and how it is fitted to the body. The author of the *Book of Ceremonies*, Book I, title 10, chapter 5, citing Maximus the bishop in his homily on priestly vestments and Eusebius of Caesarea in his sermon on the Epiphany, teaches that under the law of grace our ancient ephod—that is, the pallium woven of white wool—was established by Linus, the second Roman pontiff after Peter. It was granted as a distinctive privilege of authority to the supreme pontiff, patriarchs, and archbishops. It has a circle binding the shoulders and two strips hanging down from either side, front and back. Indeed, Rupert of Tuitius, Book I, chapter 27, *On Divine Offices*, says that Maternus, sent by Saint Peter to the Church of Trier, left the pallium as an inheritance to his successors.

The double pallium on the left signifies the hardships of the present life, which are signified by the left side; the single pallium on the right signifies that the wearer should strive with his whole heart to obtain the rest of the future life, which is represented by the right side.

The pallium also formerly had four purple crosses. These represent the four political virtues, which, unless they are purpled by the blood of Christ’s cross, usurp the name of virtue in vain. The first is justice, which ought to be on the front; the second is prudence, which ought to be at the back; the third is fortitude, which belongs on the left; and the fourth is temperance, which corresponds to the right. Nowadays, however, the crosses attached to the pallium are black, not without a mystery.

Finally, three pins, or little needles, are inserted into the pallium. The first signifies compassion for one’s neighbor, the second the administration of office, and the third the strictness of judgment. The first pierces the soul through grief, the second through labor, and the third through fear. Of the three pins or needles, one is fixed at the front, another at the back, and the third on the left shoulder. No pin is fixed on the right, because in the eternal rest represented by the right side there is no sting of affliction.

The circle of the pallium, by which the shoulders—namely, the right and left shoulders—are bound together, signifies fear of punishment, which restrains one from unlawful things, and love of justice, which moderates excess.

These matters are taken from Innocent III, Book I of the *Mysteries of the Mass*, chapter 63, and from others. It should also be added that at the ends of the two strips hanging down before and behind, two lead plates covered with black silk are attached, corresponding to the width of those strips.

Such is the pallium now used by the Latin Church. But the words of John the Deacon concerning the pallium of the blessed Gregory the Great cannot be adapted to this form, but only to the form used by Greek bishops. For these men, in place of a pallium, put around the neck a kind of band or girdle, certainly broader and longer than a stole but worn like a stole. Its right-hand portion is much longer and falls down to the ground; most of it is thrown back over the left shoulder, so that one cross remains at the back, another appears on the right, a third on the left, and the fourth on that part of the pallium hanging from the left shoulder.

Anyone who carefully examines John the Deacon’s words must say that the pallium had this form in the time of the blessed Gregory. Although I found the pallium of the blessed Gregory in the chapel of Saint Andrew made in the Latin fashion—that is, a sufficiently broad and complete circular band binding the shoulders, with two strips or bands of the same width, one descending from the back and the other from the front—I have nevertheless had it engraved here in the Greek fashion, as John the Deacon described it.

I have found the pallium painted in this same form not only in the engraved bronze images of the supreme pontiffs, from Pope Linus to Miltiades, but also in ancient mosaics of churches, especially at Saint Peter’s, in the images of those same supreme pontiffs whom Pope Formosus arranged to have painted at Rome around the year of the Lord 896. The same may be seen at Saint Paul’s and in many other places. There I have also found Honorius I, who died in the year of the Lord 635, John IV, Theodore I, Domnus I, and several others before Gregory the Great, as well as others after his time, adorned with this form of the pallium, the form now used by the Greeks.

This form of the pallium was therefore in use in the time of the blessed Gregory; later, after many centuries, it fell into disuse, when a new form was invented and adopted for greater convenience.

The same is known to have happened with the *casula*, also called the *planeta*. In ancient times, as may be seen in the *planeta* of the blessed Gregory and in ancient paintings of churches, the *casula* or *plancta* had, so to speak, no opening for putting out the arms. Rather, being wholly intact and circular and extending down to the feet on every side, it covered and surrounded the entire body in such a way that the arms could not be put out unless the border or band surrounding the edge of the *casula* were thrown loosely over the shoulders.

Hence it was called a *casula*, as though a “small house,” because it covered the whole person, according to Rabanus, Book I of the *Institutions of the Clergy*; and it was called a *planeta*, as though “wandering,” and is still called so to this day. In our own age and for several centuries previously, as Lindanus says, Book IV, chapter 56, it has been cut away and opened on both sides, right and left; shortened in front and behind; and extended somewhat below the middle of the legs.]

He wears a moderately sized pallium, drawn in a circle from the right shoulder beneath the chest and over the stomach; then carried upward over the left shoulder and laid behind the back. The other portion, coming over that same shoulder, hangs down in its natural straight line, not through the middle of the body but at the side. Around the crown of his head he bears the likeness of a tablet, the distinguishing mark of a living person, not a crown.

[Note: [Col. 0468D] The indication that he is alive is that tablet which the blessed Gregory is seen to have behind his head, that is, at the back of his head. For in ancient times, whenever someone was painted alive, a square tablet was placed beneath his head, as may be seen in certain ancient mosaics of churches.

This was customarily done for the following reason or as the following symbol: a human being established in this mortal life was understood to flourish through the four cardinal virtues represented by the square tablet, as Durandus says, Book I, chapter 3, no. 20, and Stephanus Durantus, Book I, chapter 5, no. 5; or it demonstrated that the condition of the present life is imperfect, bearing many angles—that is, many impediments and obstacles—with it.

But the saints who had attained eternal glory, to indicate that their life was perfect in every respect and entirely without impediment, were accustomed, from the very beginning of the rising Church, to be painted and sculpted with a circle or crown, which they call a diadem, or with solar rays. For by the spherical figure, which is the most perfect of all figures, the perfection of their life is, in a certain manner, represented.

There are also some who maintain that the solar crown was customarily painted and sculpted above the heads of saints, especially the apostles, because, according to Abdias the Babylonian, Book V of the *History of the Apostles*, so great a light appeared over the dying apostle John for almost an hour that no one could endure to look at it.

Whatever the truth may be, it is enough for us here to have explained that painters and sculptors customarily represented a crown for saints who had attained glory in heaven, but a square tablet for those who were still dwelling in this mortal life.] 

From this it is made entirely clear that Gregory, while he was still alive, beneficially wished his likeness to be painted, so that he might be more frequently beheld by his monks, not for the glory of vanity but as a safeguard of the strict life they had come to know [Note: A safeguard of the strictness they had come to know. *Districtio*, or *destrictio*, is a term frequently used by ecclesiastical writers. As is gathered from the *Glosses* preserved by Placidus the Grammarian in the collection of Fulvius Ursinus, a man of great learning and outstanding service to good letters, it signifies severity. Placidus says: “*Destrictus* means attentive or severe, and not lax or gentle.”

In this sense Innocent III calls the strictness of judgment *districtio* in Book I of the *Mysteries of the Mass*, chapter 63; and Gregory calls vengeance and correction *districta*. Here, however, I think that *districtionem* must be understood as a strict life. Hence, as John the Deacon says, the blessed Gregory wisely wished his image to be painted so that the monks, through that image, might recall—not for empty glory but for their own salvation—the strictness of the blessed Gregory that they had come to know, that is, his strict life, and might imitate that life while looking more frequently upon his image in his place. Here *intueri*, “to look upon,” is used passively by John the Deacon.] 

There he himself dictated the following distich:

> Powerful Christ, Lord, giver of our honor,  
> Govern the office granted us with your customary mercy.

### 313. On the image of Gordian, chapter 83.

In the venerable [Note: [Col. 0469B] *Nymphaeum* is commonly taken to mean a bathing-place, fountain, or bath in Pliny, Julius Capitolinus, Josephus, and others, from *nympha*, because the pagans, ignorant of the light of truth, believed the Nymphs to be goddesses of the waters. Add also that the ancient Greeks called a Nymph what we, by changing one letter, call *lympha*, that is, water. I therefore think that *nymphaeum* in this passage may be taken either for a bathing-place or for a fountain. John the Deacon speaks of this fountain in Book IV, chapter 97.] courtyard of the monastery, by Gregory’s order, two very ancient pictures, skilfully executed, can still be seen beside the Nymphaeum. In one of them the blessed apostle Peter is seen seated, receiving with his right hand, by the right hand, the standing Gordianus [Note: [Col. 0469C] Gordianus, the father of the blessed Gregory, is called a *regionarius* by John the Deacon. Although I have nowhere found that he was a member of the clergy, when his garments are examined and John the Deacon’s words are carefully weighed, one must say that he was certainly an ecclesiastical official. The title *regionarius*, derived from the regions, was customarily given to certain notaries, as well as to defenders and deacons.

Regionary notaries were protonotaries, whose duty was especially to record the acts of the martyrs. Regionary defenders, assigned to various provinces, were occupied chiefly with charitable works, as John the Deacon writes in Book II of *The Life of the Blessed Gregory*, chapter 53: namely, they distributed bequests left for pious purposes as alms to the poor, as may be gathered from Book IV of Gregory’s letters, letters 24 and 25; Book VII, letter 66; and Book XI, letter 21.

It was also their office [Col. 0469D] to receive information and investigate accusations concerning the misconduct of bishops, and to correct those in religious orders who acted perversely.
