As Panvinius says, on the basis of a letter of Pelagius, in the chapter on the Primicerius of the Defenders, these defenders handled the investigation of cases, legal summonses, proceedings, public litigation, and whatever ecclesiastical institutions or the needs of petitioners required.

As for regionary deacons—leaving aside the subdeacons whom one may see mentioned in the blessed Gregory’s *Register*, Book VIII, letter 5, and Book XI, letters 20 and 30—there were seven, corresponding to the seven regions of the City, as is read in the *Roman Order*. Alternatively, individual deacons presided over two of the fourteen regions. Later, fourteen were established in accordance with the fourteen regions [320], and they were so called because, as Panvinius testifies, they presided over the deaconries or hospices of the individual regions of the City.

They were ministers of widows suffering from poverty and of orphans, in public houses for the poor, which had oratories and chapels attached to them [Col. 0470A]; in these the deacon supplied the needy with what they required. For this service, serious and devout men chosen by the blessed Gregory were granted privileges, as John the Deacon records in Book II, chapter 51, of his *Life*.

I therefore think that Gordianus belonged either to the college of defenders—which, as Panvinius testifies, was also recruited from the order of the clergy—or, if conjecture may be permitted in this matter, to the college of deacons. This opinion is supported by a careful examination of his ecclesiastical garments, namely the dalmatic and the chasuble. For a deacon customarily wears not only the dalmatic, which properly belongs to him, but also, as Alcuin writes in his book *On Divine Office*, in the chapter on the meanings of the vestments, the *casula*, which Amalarius Fortunatus, Book II of *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 19, says generally belongs to all clerics. At the end of his preface to the work on offices, Alcuin also explains when a deacon is to be clothed in the *casula* and when he is to remove it.] the *regionarius*, namely Gregory’s father. Gordianus’s garment is a chestnut-coloured chasuble [Col. 0462D], beneath the chasuble a dalmatic, and on his feet [Note: [Col. 0470A] John the Deacon additionally says that Gordianus wore *caligae* on his feet. By *caligae* [Col. 0470B] sandals must be understood; it is not at all plausible that the covering of the lower legs could be meant, since a garment extending to the feet makes such a covering impossible to produce or see in a painting.

John the Deacon therefore uses *caligae* for sandals. This is supported by the Vulgate edition of the Bible, which translates *sandalia* as *caligae*, as can be seen in Acts 12, where the blessed Peter is ordered by the angel to fasten his sandals, in these words: “Gird yourself and put on your *caligae*.” The Greek edition has, περίζωσαι καὶ ὑπόδησαι τὰ σανδάλιά σου, that is, “Gird yourself and fasten your sandals.”

More recent Latin writers, however, translate *sandalia* not as *caligae* but as *soleae*, because *caligae* can also be used for coverings of the lower legs. Yet blessed Jerome, explaining Isaiah 20, appears to take shoes, sandals, and *caligae* as the same thing, in these words: “After removing the shoes, which the Septuagint calls sandals, that is, *caligae*,” and so forth.

Blessed Gregory the Great also uses *caligae* for shoes in Book I, chapter [Col. 0470C] 4, and Book III, chapter 20, of the *Dialogues*; indeed, in the second passage he mentions the straps of the *caligae*, which belong to shoes and not to coverings of the legs. Add that the passage in Acts, “Put on your *caligae*,” can refer only to the feet and shoes, since *calceare* means nothing other than “to put on shoes.” Thus in Suetonius’s *Life of Vespasian*, horses or mules are said to be *calceati* when their feet are protected against the damage caused by stones with iron fittings or iron shoes.

By *caligae*, therefore—which Isidore also seems to count among the kinds of footwear in Book XIX, chapter 34, of the *Etymologies*, and from which he thinks *caligarium* is derived—sandals are meant. Isidore believes that *caligarium* is derived not from the callus of the feet but from the Greek word *calo*, meaning “wood,” which the Greeks call τὸ κᾶλον; hence *calopodium*, a wooden shoe or clog.

Thus *caligae* should more properly be understood as sandals than as coverings for the lower legs. That deacons sometimes used sandals is openly acknowledged by Albinus, or Alcuin [Col. 0470D], in his book *On Divine Offices*, in the chapter on the meanings of the vestments, and by Amalarius Fortunatus in Book II, chapter 25, of *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, as well as by others. Indeed, they report that sandals were formerly worn even by priests and subdeacons, but without straps, to distinguish them from bishops and deacons, who had straps on their sandals.

Although the wearing of sandals appears to have been forbidden to deacons in the time of the blessed Gregory the Great, in Book VII of the *Register*, letter 28, and in the canon “Pervenit,” Distinction 93, Gregory nevertheless testifies in that same letter that the use of sandals had formerly been granted to the deacons of the Church of Messana by his predecessors.

Sandals are there called *compagia*; by others they are likewise called *compagia*. Today, however, only the supreme pontiff, bishops, and cardinal priests customarily wear sandals, which differ from the sandals of antiquity. For beneath the foot they had a complete sole, while above they had perforated or windowed leather. This symbolized the fact that the feet of bishops and deacons—or of preachers, whose office was also entrusted to deacons—were to be protected below, so that they might not be defiled by earthly affections, but open above, so that preachers might be disposed to know heavenly things and to reveal [Col. 0471A] and proclaim the mysteries [321].

It may be conjectured that Gordianus’s *caligae*, or sandals, were of this kind. Otherwise there would have been no reason for John the Deacon to mention ordinary footwear so expressly and emphatically. Here I cannot help wondering that John the Deacon, who described these pictures exactly and expressed so many of their details, should have mentioned Gordianus’s sandals but made no mention at all of the blessed Gregory’s sandals. How I might resolve this difficulty I do not know, unless I say that it arose through a lapse of memory.

Accordingly, I was quite uncertain whether the blessed Gregory’s shoes ought to be represented with a perforated or windowed upper part and marked with a cross, as is customary in our own time, because I found the shoes themselves in [Col. 0471B] the chapel of Saint Andrew painted in neither manner.

Although Joseph Stephen Valentinus, formerly bishop of Vesta and now bishop of Oriolo, a truly learned man, conjectures in his book *On the Kissing of the Feet of the Roman Pontiff*, chapter 18, against the cleverness of Papirius Masson, that the custom of wearing pontifical sandals marked with a cross is extremely ancient, I nevertheless wished to be in this matter a witness by sight rather than by hearsay and carefully examined the ancient mosaically decorated apses of the churches of Rome.

In this investigation I found that the shoes of the supreme pontiffs had no perforations or windows at all in their upper part, nor did they cover the foot on every side. Rather, there was a covering only at the toe and heel, with a fastening; from the sole and heel it extended upward toward the ankle and the toe, that is, toward the upper part of the foot. A small cross was impressed or painted above the toes, which were covered by leggings and leather.

Although Innocent III, in *The Mysteries of the Mass*, chapters [Col. 0471C] 34 and 48; Alcuin, in the chapter on the meanings of the vestments; Amalarius Fortunatus, Book II, chapter 25; Rabanus, Book I, chapter 22; Ivo of Chartres, in his sermon on the meaning of the vestments; William Durandus, Book III, chapter 8; Stephen Durandus, Book II, chapter 9; and others who have discussed sandals do not mention a cross customarily placed upon pontifical shoes, I have nevertheless found this custom to be ancient, though sometimes omitted through the negligence of painters and stonecutters, or of those responsible for making statues and paintings.

Beginning with the oldest images of the supreme pontiffs that I could find, I saw in Rome the very ancient apse of the Church of Saint Agnes, decorated in mosaic work around the year of the Lord 624. In it Honorius I, who arranged for the sacred church of blessed Agnes on the Nomentan Way to be built and for the apse to be decorated with mosaics, as Anastasius the Librarian testifies and as the verses in the apse indicate, is seen wearing sandals marked with a clearly visible white cross [Col. 0471D] and holding the church in his hand.

While he was alive, he was painted in that very apse, as what I have said readily persuades us. Although Honorius I wore the sign of the cross on his sandals, Honorius III and Honorius IV, both of the noble family of the Savelli, do not have a cross on their sandals. The former is seen painted near Saint Bibiana, at the church door, around the year of the Lord 1240; the latter, sculpted in marble around the year of the Lord 1287, is seen at the Ara Coeli in Rome.

In the oratory—or rather, church—of Saint Venantius, now called Saint Mary at the Fountain, near the Lateran Baptistery or Fountain, there is an apse decorated in mosaic work. In its vault, besides several sacred images, John IV the Dalmatian is painted; Anastasius the Librarian and Panvinius testify that he built this church around the year of the Lord 639 and adorned the apse with mosaic pictures.

Among the other images painted in mosaic, two Roman pontiffs [Col. 0472A] and two martyrs are seen wearing sandals marked with a small black cross. One of the pontiffs, namely the one painted last on the right, is John IV, holding the church in his hand, since he arranged for it to be built. Several verses found there also plainly inform us of this.

The pontiff painted last on the left, holding a book, is, according to Panvinius, Theodore, John’s successor. As Panvinius says, he perhaps completed the church, or, as I believe, the apse begun by John; for this reason he is seen painted there.

Why Venantius and Domnio, and Maurus outside the apse, the martyrs, are seen wearing a cross on their sandals [322], I do not know, unless I say that this was done at the painter’s discretion or to represent the cross of martyrdom. For only the supreme pontiffs ordinarily observe this custom of wearing a cross on their sandals.

They, thinking humbly and submissively of themselves, preferred that the kiss be given to Christ’s cross rather than that such honour be paid only to themselves, although they recognized that all peoples, by common consent, were inclined to adore their feet, as Joseph Stephen, bishop of Oriolo, writes no less learnedly than accurately and devoutly in chapter 18 of his book *On the Kissing [Col. 0472B] of the Feet of the Roman Pontiff*. They therefore received all Christians graciously for the kissing of their feet.

Thus, in order to reproduce an explicit image of Christ and to bring the Saviour’s Passion to the memory of men, they attached a cross to their sandals, so that Christians, seeing the cross, might more eagerly offer the pontiff those honours which they owed and were required to offer him. Thus Joseph Stephen.

Why, then, martyrs or other saints who were not Roman pontiffs should be represented with shoes marked by a cross, I do not sufficiently understand, unless I relate it to what I have said; or perhaps say that it was done because the martyrs themselves—namely Venantius, Domnio, and Maurus—had been distinguished by episcopal rank. This is suggested by the pallium in which these bishops and martyrs are seen adorned, after the manner of Greek bishops.

Among the Latins, by common right, only the supreme pontiffs, patriarchs, and archbishops [Col. 0472C] may use the pallium; by apostolic concession, however, certain bishops may also use it. Just as the pallium, which properly belongs above all to the Roman pontiff, was given to these men even though they were not pontiffs, so I believe that the cross, which is customarily placed on the sandals of the Roman pontiff alone because of the kissing of his feet, was given to the martyrs in question, without the reason or origin of the custom having been understood.

At Saint Martin in the Mountains, among the relics of Martin I, blessed pope and martyr, a shoe dating from the year of the Lord 647 is preserved. It is windowed in its upper part and covered only at the toe, according to the form that we have just described. The leather covering of the toe is dyed blue and decorated with certain works woven of silk and gold. On it, almost in the form of the Greek letter X, an image of a cross—or, as I might say, a transverse cross—embroidered with thread can be seen. It serves as an ornament and resembles a cross in a certain way, as will be explained below.

Among the same relics there is also a shoe of blessed Silvester I, made wholly of silk, dyed green, not shaggy but already considerably faded through age, though still retaining something of the appearance of green silk [Col. 0472D]. It is likewise decorated with works woven of silk and gold.

This shoe is missing part of the heel because of its extreme age. It does not conform to the older form formerly in use, namely the kind of footwear in which only the soles are covered, with the other parts of the feet left bare and secured only by certain loops joined together above, which are called straps. Nor is it like the shoe that we have just described. Rather, it is a type of footwear with a leather sole and a covering that conceals the whole upper part of the foot, like the shoe that everyone nowadays commonly wears.

For this reason I have come to believe that this shoe differs from the one that blessed Silvester used in ecclesiastical matters and in certain functions appropriate especially for expressing pontifical majesty. [Col. 0473A] Although footwear of this kind does not altogether support our argument concerning the cross, I nevertheless thought that I should not pass it over in silence, since it is a monument of venerable antiquity and worthy of remembrance, and since it secretly represents a certain form of a cross through several intertwined lines, as we shall explain below.

At Saint Martina, in the Forum Boarium at the foot of the Capitoline Hill, there is a very ancient apse, decorated in mosaic work during the time of Domnio, around the year of the Lord 679. In it two Roman pontiffs, one on the right and the other on the left of blessed Mary ever-Virgin, who holds the Son in her lap, are seen adorned with the pallium, fashioned according to the ancient custom.

I conjecture that one of them was either Honorius I or Gregory the Great, who lived before Domnio. I saw him wearing sandals with a small black cross, and near him, on the left, I read these letters: . . . . ORIUS PP. The remaining letters completing the proper name of the supreme pontiff have disappeared. The other pontiff, who lived before Domnio [Col. 0473B], could in no way have that ending of a proper name.

Meanwhile, the pontiff who appears on the right of blessed Mary ever-Virgin, holding the church in his hand, since he arranged for the sacred building to be constructed or at least repaired, [323] must be said to be Domnio. Panvinius also says the following in his annotation on the *Life of Domnio* written by Platina:

“In the ancient mosaic that is in the Church of Saint Martina at Rome, this pontiff is called Domnio, not Donus or Domnus.”

By these words Panvinius clearly states that he read the name Domnio there. But because that pontiff’s name is no longer read in that place, I am convinced that the letters have entirely perished, just as I saw that this has happened in part in the name of the other pontiff.

Therefore, just as the older pontiff is seen wearing sandals marked with a cross, so we must believe that the other, more recent pontiff also did so. For the shoes formerly made in mosaic have now collapsed; in their place are shoes painted in a crude manner, without a cross.

At the Basilica of blessed Peter, prince of the holy apostles, [Col. 0473C] behind the oratory, chapel, or altar of the most holy Shroud of our Saviour above the Holy Door, on the inner side of the basilica, there is an oratory decorated with splendid and elaborate mosaic work. It was built in honour of the immaculate ever-Virgin and Mother of God by John VII around the year of the Lord 706, as Anastasius the Librarian, Platina, and Panvinius testify, and as the inscription itself declares in these words:

“JOHN, UNWORTHY BISHOP, MADE THIS.”

Moreover, John has at the back of his head a square panel which, as was said above, is customarily an indication that the person represented was still living when the painting was made. John is seen near the image of blessed Mary ever-Virgin, wearing sandals marked with a small black cross composed of four mosaic stones.

In the Basilica of Saint Peter there is also a marble statue of Urban VI, made around the year of the Lord 1389. At Saint John Lateran there is the bronze funerary statue of Martin V [Col. 0473D], made around the year of the Lord 1431. In the courtyard of the Monastery of Saint Saviour in Lauro there is a marble statue of Eugene IV, made around the year of the Lord 1447.

In the Basilica of Saint Peter there are also the following funerary statues: Nicholas V, around the year of the Lord 1455; Calixtus III, in the small court near the Sistine Chapel, 1458; Pius II, 1464; Paul II, 1471; Sixtus IV, 1484; Innocent VIII, 1492; and Pius III, 1503.

In the Church of Saint Mary above Minerva there is a funerary image of Leo X, and on the Capitoline Hill there is also a marble statue dating from around the year of the Lord 1521. I saw statues of all these Roman pontiffs and of others more recent than them—namely Paul III, Paul IV, Pius V, Gregory XIII, and Sixtus V—wearing sandals marked with a cross.

I also saw other Roman pontiffs represented in mosaic work, older than Honorius I, but because of the great age of the paintings I found that their shoes had collapsed. By contrast, at Saint Lawrence in Lucina I saw a painting of Sixtus III, and indeed [Col. 0474A] a very ancient one; likewise, I saw Paschal I at Saint Praxedes and Saint Cecilia, around the year of the Lord 807, and Gregory IV at Saint Mark’s, around the year of the Lord 830. They were painted in mosaic work but wore sandals without a cross.

This appears to have happened through the negligence either of the painters or of those who commissioned the paintings, as can be seen in the apse of the Church of Saint Mary across the Tiber, decorated in mosaic work around the year of the Lord 1143. In it, besides other images, the Roman pontiffs—namely, the blessed apostle Peter, Calixtus, Julius, Cornelius, and Innocent II, who commissioned the mosaic work—are represented. But Cornelius alone, who suffered martyrdom in the year of the Lord 253, is seen wearing shoes marked with a cross.

The same is confirmed by the marble statue of Boniface IX preserved in the Basilica of Saint Paul and made around the year of the Lord 1440. It is seen to have shoes without a cross, although we have seen other pontiffs before Innocent II and Boniface IX wearing sandals with a cross [Col. 0474B].

For if it is established that the earlier pontiffs wore shoes marked with a cross, one must admit that the same custom was also observed by the more recent pontiffs. Although I have been unable to find this custom in use before Honorius I—who was elected pontiff around the year of the Lord 622 and died in 635—because the apses of churches decorated in mosaic work have either entirely or largely collapsed through extreme age, I nevertheless conjecture that the custom is older.

This is so even though writers both ancient and recent, when speaking of sandals, have, as I said, made no mention at all of the cross. They spoke only generally [324] of the sandals of bishops, priests, and deacons, and of their form, meaning, and use, passing over the custom devised for the kissing of the feet of the Roman pontiff.

That the blessed Gregory the Great wore sandals of this kind, namely shoes marked with a cross, is readily persuaded by the fact that only about twenty [Col. 0474C] years, more or less, intervened between the pontificate of blessed Gregory the Great and that of Honorius I, whom we have seen to have used shoes adorned with crosses.

It is therefore plausible that the same custom of wearing sandals of this kind, used by Honorius I, who died in the year of the Lord 635, was frequently observed by Gregory the Great and other pontiffs who preceded him. For Honorius I, a Campanian by birth, because of the short interval separating their pontificates, could have seen not only Gregory himself, who departed this life in the year of the Lord 604, or, according to Trithemius, 605, but also Pelagius, Gregory’s predecessor. Indeed, it may and should be believed that he saw them.

Furthermore, something sufficiently worthy of notice in confirming the extreme antiquity of the custom of wearing the sign of the cross on the sandals of the supreme pontiffs is that, when Panvinius was writing the lives of the supreme pontiffs, which had not yet been published, and arranging for their images to be reproduced from life, he found in an ancient apse decorated in mosaic work an image either of blessed Silvester [Col. 0474D] or of another of the earlier Roman pontiffs, represented whole from foot to head and painted with sandals marked by a small cross.

He kept this image among the more distinguished lifelike representations of the supreme pontiffs, considering it worthy of perpetual remembrance, while omitting others that he judged to have been painted at the discretion of the painters. Silvius Antonianus, prefect of the chamber of our most holy Lord Clement VIII, a highly learned man of outstanding integrity and proven reliability, solemnly testifies to this. He says that Panvinius showed him the image and that he himself saw it shod in precisely the manner described, affirming this without any hesitation.

This is what I have to say about the ancient custom of wearing a cross upon the sandals of the Roman pontiff. Since the matter had not yet been explained by others, I thought it appropriate to dwell upon it.]

wearing *caligae*, tall in stature, with an elongated face, green eyes, a moderate beard, thick hair, and a serious expression.

## On the image of Silvia, in the same chapter

In the other picture Silvia, Gregory’s mother, is depicted seated. She is covered with a white veil wrapped from the right shoulder across toward the left in such a way that beneath it she draws out her hand as if from a chasuble, while around the breast, below the throat, an under-tunic of pseudomilk-white colour [Note: [Col. 0474D] John the Deacon says that Silvia’s under-tunic was of a *pseudolactine* colour. *Pseudolactine* is an off-white colour: as it were, a false whiteness; or, as I think, *leucophaeum*, a colour mixed from white and black; or, so to speak, ash-coloured.

For in Greek *pseudo-* means “false” in Latin, and we use it in compounds: *pseudolus*, that is, “false servant”; *pseudographus*, “forger”; *pseudopropheta*, “false prophet”; and very many other such words. Thus *pseudolactine*, named from false milk, by which John the Deacon wished to indicate a certain whiteness, means a false white, that is, an off-white or ash-coloured hue, in some way imitating whiteness.] appears, falling in a broad fold over her feet. It is entirely distinguished by two bands [Note: [Col. 0475A] John the Deacon says that Silvia’s under-tunic, which he writes was of a pseudomilk-white colour, was marked by two bands.

Although a *zona* properly means a belt, in this passage I think that the bands mentioned by the Deacon can only be certain strips of women’s garments running around the hem and worked for ornament. One band placed below the other, at a certain interval, provides both ornament and a kind of division in the garment. In this way the two tunics appear to resemble two dalmatics.

For a dalmatic has at its edge, as an ornament, a certain border, and the strip or band under discussion in John the Deacon is somewhat broader, as he himself states. This seems relevant to what Isidore says in Book XIX, chapter 22, of the *Etymologies*, when writing about the names of garments. Concerning *segmenta* he says: “They are decorated with certain bands and, as it were, with cuttings; for they call the pieces cut from each material *praesegmina*.” Thus Isidore.] like dalmatics, though broader; she is full in stature, with a face indeed round and fair, but already wrinkled by age, although old age itself indicates that she had once been exceedingly beautiful [Col. 0463A]. Her eyes are grey and large, her eyebrows moderate, her lips attractive, and her expression cheerful. On her head she wears a matron’s [Note: [Col. 0475B] John the Deacon records that Silvia wore on her head a matron’s mitre, *niblata* by the fineness of shining *brandeum*.

Matronly women used the mitre, as Varro suggests in Book IV of *On the Latin Language*. Isidore says in Book XIX, chapter 31: “The mitre is a Phrygian cap covering the head, such as is the adornment of consecrated women; but the cap belongs to men, whereas the mitre belongs to women.” That the mitre is a kind of covering used to adorn a woman’s head is clear from Isaiah 3. Indeed, a mitre was shameful for men, as may be gathered from Lucian, Virgil in Books IV and IX of the *Aeneid*, and others.

A matron’s mitre, then—leaving aside the other forms and meanings of the mitre—was a woman’s head ornament. [Col. 0475C] But I think that different kinds of mitres existed among different peoples, both for matrons and for young women or virgins.

Among the Phrygians, *mitra* denoted a woman’s crown used to adorn the heads of young women, from which hung strips called *phylla*, because they hung down like leaves or flowers. Hence Virgil says in Book IX of the *Aeneid*:

“Tunics have sleeves, and mitres have ribbons.”

Optatus, bishop of Milevis, speaks of a virginal mitre in Book VI *Against Parmenianus*. Judith the Hebrew is said in the sacred Scriptures, in Book IX of her history, to have worn a mitre as a head ornament. Lyra calls this mitre a woman’s *cucufa*, which I interpret as a *calantica*, that is, a woman’s head ornament; our people [Col. 0475D] call it a *cuffia*.

A woman’s head ornament, as I have said, was varied. The Turks today, and other Eastern peoples, use turbanned caps made of linen veils or woven silk cloth. In nearly the same manner Turkish women, as is recorded in the *Turkish Chronicles*, Part III, chapters 3 and 4, customarily adorn their heads with turbanned and pointed caps.

The ancient Roman matrons used approximately this sort of ornament, namely a turbanned cap called a mitre, as Varro suggests in Book IV of *On the Latin Language*. This is confirmed by the marble statues of ancient matrons, which can still be seen in many places, especially at Rome.

John the Deacon records that Silvia wore a mitre of this kind, woven from the thinness of shining *brandeum*, that is, made from shining *brandeum*. As may be gathered not only from John the Deacon [Col. 0476A] in this passage and in Book II, chapter 24, but also from Gregory the Great himself, Book III, letter 30, *brandeum* was a white little veil, or linen or silk cloth. It must therefore be said that Silvia’s mitre was woven from this material as a head ornament.

What the word *niblata* properly means I have been unable to discover. I believe it to be a barbarous word used here for *distincta*, “marked or ornamented,” or for *nubilata*, “made in the likeness of a cloud,” or rather woven from the thinness or fineness of a shining or white linen cloth.

Alternatively, *niblata* may be a word corrupted through the negligence of scribes from *nimbata*, derived from *nimbus*. For *nimbus* is not only a sudden and violent rainstorm but also, according to Isidore in Book XIX, chapter 31, a transverse strip sewn with gold onto the linen cloth worn across a woman’s forehead, among women’s head ornaments.

Plautus uses the word *nimbata* in the *Poenulus*, saying:

“The more I look at her, the more *nimbata* she is—and so are my trifles.” [Col. 0476B]

The radiance painted around the heads of angels is also called a *nimbus*, as Isidore says in the same place, although *nimbus* means the density of a cloud.

Thus one may say that the mitre was *nimbata* by the thinness of shining *brandeum*, either because the mitre was adorned with a *nimbus*, or because it was bound with a white, thin, or delicate veil, or fashioned in the form of a white cloud.

This is conjecturally the sense. For what the word *niblata*, which is read in this form in all the Vatican manuscripts, actually means, I confess that I entirely do not know, despite possessing many and varied dictionaries and having carefully searched through and examined both recent and ancient authors.

However the matter may stand, I am persuaded, and regard it as certain, that this mitre, formerly worn by matrons as a head ornament, was woven or bound from some little veil or extremely thin cloth, or was turban-shaped. This can be seen in the ancient marble statues of women that are found everywhere in Rome and elsewhere.

Something similar seems to be found in a very ancient priestly stole, embroidered or ornamented [Col. 0476C] with needlework and, as it were, painted with a brush, which is still preserved in Rome in the Pontifical Sacristy. On this extremely old and truly beautiful stole, among the other sacred images displayed there, is an image of blessed Mary ever-Virgin and Mother of God wearing a mitre of this kind as a head ornament.

Around her image these Greek letters, MP ΘΥ—that is, Μήτηρ Θεοῦ, “Mother of God”—are embroidered. This provides us with strong evidence concerning that mitre, formerly devised as a woman’s head ornament.

This concludes what concerns the images of Saint Gregory, Gordianus, and blessed Silvia. Now, having examined the mitre of Saint Silvester and the ancient sandals of the supreme pontiffs, it remains for us finally to proceed to the scholia on blessed Gregory’s *Book of Sacraments*.

[Col. 0475] These scholia are found in Volume III, column 599, that is, Volume LXXVIII of this *Bibliotheca*.

## 326. On the mitre of Saint Silvester, pope

I thought it appropriate to include here, as an opportunity presented itself to indicate the venerable antiquity of the pontifical mitre, a copper engraving of part of the mitre of Saint Silvester, pope—namely, its front [Col. 0476D] half—even though I arranged for the image of the blessed Gregory to be engraved bareheaded, for the reasons explained at the beginning.

I endeavoured to represent this part of the mitre, preserved among the sacred relics at Saint Martin in the Mountains, exactly, together with its letters and images, although it was painted with considerable ineptitude in needlework, as was characteristic of that age, when the arts both of sculpture and painting had long since deteriorated and become overgrown with defects and absurdities.

Although the half of the mitre preserved at Saint Martin in the Mountains is larger both in width and height, I nevertheless had it engraved at such a size that the mitre, together with the shoes, which were reduced to the same small scale, could fit on the same page.

The mitre is green, wholly of silk and not shaggy, and Phrygian [Col. 0477A], as I explained in its proper place when discussing the mitre of the supreme pontiffs.

## On the sandals or shoes of Saint Silvester I, Saint Martin I, and Honorius I, supreme pontiffs
The shoe that Saint Sylvester wore, also green in color, made of smooth—not shaggy—silk, and adorned with certain designs woven of silk and gold, is preserved among the same relics at Saint Martin in the Mountains. I believe that a shoe of this kind, which the Greeks call σανδάλιον (*sandálion*, “sandal”), differed from the one which blessed Sylvester perhaps used in ecclesiastical functions to signify pontifical majesty; nevertheless, while I carefully observe and consider the knots worked upon the sandal, I do not dare maintain that it was wholly without a cross. For the knots themselves, through the interlacing or wrapping of several lines, provide ornament and form and contain several crosses.

### 327. The shoe likewise worn by Saint Martin

The shoe likewise worn by Saint Martin is preserved in the same place mentioned just above. At its toe there is a leather covering dyed blue and also adorned with certain designs woven of silk and gold. This shoe appears to have been like the sandal of Honorius I, but through age it lacks the covering of the heel and the fastening straps. At the toe of the shoe, that ornament, somewhat resembling the Greek character χ (*chi*) or the Servian letter X, seems to represent a kind of cross, though a transverse one. Hence there are some who write that by means of these letters a cross can be rather elegantly represented.

Although these two sandals do not display an explicitly formed cross, I nevertheless arranged for them to be engraved in copper and placed here, for the reasons explained elsewhere. The shoe of Honorius, represented last, can be seen painted beside the apse of Saint Agnes on the Nomentan Way, which was decorated in mosaic work by that same Honorius, as I showed more fully when I discussed the leggings or shoes of Gordian and the sandals of the supreme pontiffs marked with a cross. For in that very apse, constructed about the year of the Lord 624, Honorius I can be seen wearing sandals of this kind, decorated with a clearly visible white cross.

I therefore judged that this shoe should be represented here both to indicate the ancient custom of wearing a cross upon sandals and to make the ancient form of the sandals readily visible and easily explained. For although the older sandals had only a sole and fastening straps, as I believe was sufficiently stated in the passage cited above, almost all the pontiffs represented in ancient mosaics are seen wearing sandals in the form of those of Honorius I.

As for the sole of Saint Peter, blessed Bonaventure mentions it and testifies that it was preserved at Rome down to his own time, in volume IV, part IV, in the little work on the sandals of the holy apostles. There, with many passages of Sacred Scripture and testimonies of the holy Fathers brought forward and explained, he teaches most learnedly—as he explains everything—and most eruditely how and when our Savior Christ, the apostles, and his disciples walked barefoot.

[The following fragment begins within a preceding sentence:]

…wearing a mitre of shining *brandeum*, made resplendent by its rarity [reading uncertain], and pretending that he wished to bless himself with the sign of the cross using the two fingers of his right hand, while holding open in his left a psalter, in which this is written: “My soul lives, and it shall praise you, and your judgments shall help me.” From the right elbow to the left, around the shoulders, a band rises and bends back, bearing these words: “Gregory made this for his mother Silvia.”

[Col. 0479]

## Marble Tablets of Donations

### Marble tablet affixed to the wall at the portico of Saint Peter

“To the holy and most blessed lords Peter and Paul, princes of the apostles: Gregory, an unworthy servant. Whenever, for the service of your praise, we acquire something—however small—we return it to you; we do not bestow what is ours, so that in doing these things we may not be elated by the gift but secure in the repayment. For what is ever ours without you? We cannot return what we have received unless, through you, we have again received this very thing in order to return it.

“Therefore I, your servant, recalling deeply to mind how greatly I owe you, blessed apostles Peter and Paul, because, by the grace of divine power protecting me, you brought me from my mother’s breasts into the bosom of your Church and deemed me worthy, though unworthy, to advance through each rank up to the highest summit of the priesthood, have resolved to offer meanwhile this small privilege as a humble gift of devotion.

“For I establish and decree that it is to be preserved by me and by my successors without any opposition: that the places or estates described below, which I have recovered for the arrangement of your lights from various persons by whom they were held, and have dedicated to you, shall remain unaltered—that is:

“In the Appian patrimony: Massa Victoriola, an olive grove (*olibetum*); at the estate of Rumellianum, entire, an olive grove; at the estate of Octavianum, entire; Massa Trabatiana, an olive grove; at the estate of Burreianum, as above, an olive grove; at the estate of Appianum, as above, an olive grove; at the estate of Julianum, entire, an olive grove; at the estate of Vivianum, as above, an olive grove; at the estate of Cattia, [lacuna], an olive grove; at the estate of Solificianum, as above, an olive grove; at the estate of Palmes, as above, an olive grove; at the estate of Sagaris, [lacuna], an olive grove; at the estate of Maranum, as above, an olive grove; at the estate of Julianum, as above, an olive grove; at the estate of Saturnianum, as above, an olive grove; at the estates of Canianum and Carbonaria, as above; Massa Caesarianum, an olive grove; at the estate of Floranum, [reading uncertain], an olive grove; at the estates of Priscianum and Grassianum, as above, an olive grove; at the estate of Pascuranum, as above, an olive grove; at the estate of Varinianum, as above, an olive grove; at the estate of Caesarianum, as above; Massa Pontiana, an olive grove; at the estate of Pontianum, as above, an olive grove; at the estate of Casaromanianum, as above, an olive grove; at the estate of Tattianum, as above, an olive grove; at the estate of Casaflorana, as above; Massa Steiana, an olive grove; at the estate of Berranum, as above, an olive grove; at the estate of Caclanum, as above, an olive grove; at the estate of Pontianum, [reading uncertain], an olive grove; at the estate of Aquilianum, as above, an olive grove; at the estate of Steianum, as above, an olive grove; at the estate of Cassis, as above; Massa Tertiana, as above, an olive grove; at the estate of Cammelianum and the estate of Tortillianum, as above, an olive grove; at the estate of Casacuculum, as above; Massa Neviana, an olive grove; at the estate of Arcipianum, as above, an olive grove; at the estate of Corellianum, as above, an olive grove; at the estate of Ursanum, as above.

“In the Labican patrimony: Massa Algisia, an olive grove, which is at Tufum beside Anagnia, entire; an olive grove which is at Sibula; small plots at Catagemmulium [reading uncertain], of the military estate; an olive grove at Aplineae, entire; an olive grove which is at Clavinianum; an olive grove held by Franculus, the tenant, at the estate of Ordinianum, entire.”

### Marble tablet affixed to the wall at the basilica of Saint Paul

“Gregory, bishop and servant of the servants of God, to Felix, subdeacon and administrator of the Appian patrimony.

“Although everything possessed by this apostolic Church of the blessed Peter and Paul, acquired in their honor and through their benefits, ought to be held in common, there must nevertheless be diversity in the administration of affairs and of persons, so that more diligent care may be applied to the things assigned to each.

“Since the duty of concern for the Church of the blessed apostle Paul continually reminds us that the one who filled the whole world with the light of preaching should not be seen to have fewer lights there, and since it would be most incongruous and harsh if that possession in which, taking the palm of martyrdom, he was beheaded should not serve him in a special way, we have judged it useful to assign to the lights, with the grace of Christ, the estate called Aquae Salviae with all its estates, namely: Cella Vinaria, Antoniana, Villa Pertusa, Bifurcum, Primini­anum, Cassianum, Silonis, Corneli Tessellata, and Cornelianum, with every right and instrument belonging to it and with everything generally pertaining to it.

“We further add to this transfer two gardens situated between the Tiber and the portico of that church, going from the city gate on the right-hand side, divided by the river Almo, between the boundaries of the garden of the monastery of Saint Stephen, which is an establishment of women dedicated to God beside Saint Paul, and the boundary of the possession of Pisinius, together with the little plots called Fossa Latronis.

“Likewise, beside the same portico, going from the gate on the left-hand side, where vineyards have now been made, are little plots adjoining on one side the possession of Eugentius the scholasticus and on the other the possession of the monastery of Saint Aristus.

“Since all these things, with God’s help, are to be administered from the present seventh indiction by the provosts of the aforesaid church, whoever they may be in succession, and since whatever is subsequently acquired is to be expended on its lights, with the provosts themselves thereafter rendering accounts, we therefore command Your Experience to remove the aforesaid estate of Aquae Salviae with all the estates named above, as well as the gardens and little plots listed above, from their registers and to take them away, and to transfer everything into the name of the aforesaid Church of the blessed apostle Paul.

“This is so that its serving provosts, thereafter lacking every excuse, may attend to its lights without our supervision in such a way that no neglect may ever be found there.

“After the transfer of all the aforesaid property has been made, we wish Your Experience to restore this decree to the archive of our Church.

“Farewell.

“Given on the eighth day before the Kalends of February, under the emperor our lord N. Phocas, most august emperor, in his second year, and in the first year of his consulship, in the seventh indiction.”

## On the Marble Tablets of Donations in Rome, Dedicated by Blessed Gregory the Great to the Holy Apostles Peter and Paul

[Col. 0483]

I judged that the marble tablets of donations dedicated by blessed Gregory the Great to the holy apostles Peter and Paul for the provision of lights—as he himself says—and affixed in the portico of Saint Peter should be placed here, so that what I said about the ancient manner of writing in the scholia, and especially in scholium 241–242 below—volume IV of the works of Saint Gregory, and volume LXXVIII of Migne’s *Patrologia*—might be corroborated.

Since I also found another donation, carved in stone by the same holy Gregory for the provision of lights to blessed Paul and formerly affixed to the wall of the church in the portico of Saint Paul, but a few days ago transferred to a place near the high altar beside one of the two columns supporting the principal arch on the right, and since I found it recorded in the *Register* of the same blessed Gregory, book XII, letter 19, I decided to print it here as well, in order splendidly to represent and perpetually preserve the Christian and apostolic piety of that saint.

For monuments of deeds, as reason itself suggests and experience teaches, can be rescued from destruction more easily through the typographical than through the sculptural art. The tablets placed first and affixed to the portico of Saint Peter appear to be fragments of two tablets, as their differing stone forms and their mutilated ends of the donations indicate.

Maphaeus Vegius speaks of the marble tablets of donations affixed to the wall of the church in the portico of Saint Peter in his little work on the excellence of the basilica of Saint Peter, in these words:

“Blessed Gregory donated many estates to furnish the lights of the basilica of Saint Peter more abundantly, and especially many olive groves, as is clear from a public document inscribed on marble tablets. Although there were originally seven of them, only two are still affixed to the wall before the entrance of the basilica.”

This is what Maphaeus Vegius says in the said little work, which is preserved in the library of the basilica of Saint Peter.

Meanwhile I warn the reader that every, even trifling, diligence was employed in describing and printing these tablets, so that the ancient writing practice might be represented exactly—or, more accurately, down to its smallest detail—with the exception only of the spaces. Although spaces between individual words are absent from inscriptions carved in stone, I arranged for them to be supplied in these printed texts so that the reading might be easier. In some contracted words, moreover, the points are absent, and small letters are sometimes seen mixed with capitals.

Finally, we left obsolete words that bear the flavor of the ancient age of the early writers exactly as they lie. I wish the reader to be warned that they are free from errors of the stonecutters. For an old letter is sometimes found used in place of another, as:

- *immutilata* for *immutilata*;
- *inmeritum* for *immeritum*;
- *inpendi* for *impendi*;
- *set* for *sed*;
- *adquisita* for *acquisita*;
- *adsignatis* for *assignatis*;
- *intro* for *intra*—that is, an adverb used in place of a preposition;
- *super* for *supra*—that is, a preposition used in place of an adverb;
- *post hoc* for *posthac*—for *post hoc*, “after this,” is used almost as *post hoc tempus*, “after this time,” and has the meaning of the adverb *posthac*;
- *adfines* “neighboring” or “bordering lands” for *affines* and *confines*;
- *adicientes* for *adjicientes*;
- *exsistere* for *existere*;
- *hortus* in the accusative for *hortos*;
- *detenebantur* for *detinebantur*;
- *consolatus* for *consulatus*.

Examples of this kind, for the most part, can be read as ancient usages in Aldine orthography and in other inscriptions, which the younger Aldus used to claim that he possessed—more than sixty thousand of them. For the sake of brevity I judged that these should be passed over in silence. It is enough in this matter to have cited the inscriptions of the ancient Latins described by Aldus. He himself observed all the obscure monuments of antiquity in Latin writing so accurately that he had no equal in this field. There are also writers who say that these words were frequently used among the ancients; I omit them for the sake of brevity.

The age of blessed Gregory also commonly used the letter B for V and V for B, as can be seen above in the first of the two tablets, where one reads:

- *parba* for *parva*;
- *olibetum* for *olivetum*;
- *silbula* for *silvula*;
- *octabiano* for *octaviano*;
- *devitorem* for *debitorem*;
- *uveribus* for *uberibus*.

We explained this ancient writing practice at sufficient length in our scholium 246, cited above, so that the same scholium—which contains several matters perhaps worth knowing—might also serve this tablet. We also explained other matters not wholly unworthy of consideration concerning this kind of writing and pronunciation in our *Commentary on the Vatican Library*, printed in 1591, pages 153 and 297.

I also warn the reader that in the list of olive groves one always reads *olibetum* in the accusative, written in this contracted form as *olibet*, both with and without a point, or as *olibetu*, sometimes with a point and sometimes without it. That the accusative without the letter *m* was in use among those ancient Latins who lived in the age of blessed Gregory is demonstrated for us by many ancient inscriptions carved in stone. For the sake of brevity I omit their examples as well.

Nor does it seem that one should pass over in silence why *olivetum*, which is neuter, is always found masculine in this inscription. I think this happened through the figure called *synthesis*, which disagrees with the word but agrees with its meaning, as in Virgil, *Aeneid* VIII, “Praeneste sub ipsa,” according to the elder Aldus, and “Camerino sub ipsa,” that is, “beneath the city”; for Praeneste and Camerinum are neuter.

Through the same figure, *synthesis*, one says: “The lily is the whitest of flowers,” that is, “the whitest flower of all flowers.” Likewise *olivetum*, which is a place or estate in which olive trees have been planted, disagrees with the word but agrees with the meaning if it refers to the place or estate.

[Col. 0484C]

In the second tablet, which can be seen below, one reads *isdem* in the nominative for *idem*. The word *isdem*, in the singular nominative for *idem*, was used not only twice by Eucherius in book II on Genesis and twice in the book on Kings, but also by Ennius, a very ancient author, in the singular nominative and plural ablative, as Cicero reports in *On the Orator*. Ennius uses the same word, saying: “The same field has … and in the same temples,” and so forth.

Ennius said *in templis isdem* for *in templis iisdem*. Hence Cicero says in the same passage that *isdem* is used both in the singular nominative and in the plural ablative, and that both usages were employed by Ennius. For the word *isdem* is derived from *is, ea, id* and *dem*, according to Priscian, book XII, in the chapter on figures.

Therefore, if the reading were not *isdem* but *idem*, as it is now certainly read, though corruptly, Cicero’s discussion of this word would be pointless. For although Ennius said *isdem*, not *idem campus*, in the singular nominative, he also said in the plural ablative *in templis isdem* for *in templis iisdem*. He preferred to use the same form in the second place, dropping the second *i* to avoid an unpleasant sound, rather than use *eisdem* for *iisdem*. That form, as Cicero says, was richer than the age of Ennius could bear, since his age retained the flavor of antiquity. Thus, by restoring *isdem* in Ennius’s first passage in place of *idem*, Cicero’s text is corrected.

The tablet also has *duo* for *duos*, as in *hortos duo positos*, “two gardens placed.” I would have believed this passage in the second tablet to be erroneous if I had not read the passage of Charisius, who writes that *duo* for *duos* and *ambo* for *ambos* are correctly used according to analogy and Greek declension. For Charisius says in book I:

“Some, following the Greeks—for they say τοὺς δύο (*tous duo*, ‘the two’) and τοὺς ἄμφο (*tous ampho*, ‘both’)—said *hos duo* and *hos ambo*.”

*Ambo* for *ambos* occurs in Virgil, *Eclogue* 6:

> For often the old man, in hope of song,  
> had played with both.

So it should be read according to Charisius and according to a very ancient and especially distinguished manuscript written in capital letters and preserved in the Vatican Library.

The same Virgil, in book IV of the *Georgics*:

> But when you have recalled both leaders from the battle line.

Thus Virgil’s passage should be corrected according to Charisius. The verse is absent from the distinguished Vatican manuscript because several pages are missing from book IV of the *Georgics*.

Afranius, in *Pantaleus*:

> You call us both back to battle.

The same Virgil, in book XII of the *Aeneid*:

> Having joined this man and that man in combat,  
> both from afar, from afar.

Thus it is read in a very ancient and especially distinguished Vatican manuscript.

Terence, *Andria*, act II, scene 2:

> I want you both conveniently.

So it should be read according to Charisius; others read: “Conveniently—I want you both.”

Charisius, book I, says that *duo* for *duos* is correctly written. Attius, in *Epinausimache*:

> You would think that two had met in arms.

So it should be read according to Charisius.

Terence, *Adelphoe*, act V, scene 3:

> You once took up those two for your own advantage.

Here Helenius Acron says *duo* for *duos*. Thus it is read in a very ancient and especially distinguished Vatican manuscript. It is also read this way in Terence by Gabriel Faernus, and this passage of Terence should be corrected according to Charisius.

Cicero, *Against Verres*, book I, act 2:

> His father died twenty-two years ago.

So it was read, and so it ought to be read.

The same author, *Letters to Atticus*, book IV, final letter:

> Two ex-consuls who would speak of you.

So it should be read.

The same author, *Letters to Quintus Frater*, book I, letter 2:

> Two Mysians.

So it should be read, and Paulus Manutius corrected it in this way from Bessarion’s book.

The same author, *Letters to Friends*, book III, letter 4:

> For I value two men of different ages above all: Gnaeus Pompey, the father-in-law of my daughter, and Marcus Brutus, your son-in-law.

The same author, book VII, letter 25:

> Apart from the two of us, no one speaks in this way.

So it is read, and so it ought to be read.

The same author, in the same book, letter 29:

> To whitewash two walls from the same jar.

The same author, *On Friendship*:

> So that all affection might be joined either between two or among a few.

Sallust, *Histories*, book IV, in the letter of Mithridates:

> Between me and Lucullus, nearly want again seized us both.

Virgil, *Eclogue* 5:

> And I shall set up two bowls for you.

Pierius read it this way to avoid the sibilant, and thus it is also read in a very ancient and especially distinguished Vatican manuscript.

The same author, *Aeneid* II:

> If the land of Ida had borne two such men besides.

Thus it is read in a very ancient and especially distinguished Vatican manuscript, and it cannot be read otherwise, because both syllables in *duo* are short, whereas in the first position there is a dactyl, in which the first syllable is long and the following two are short.

Priscian, book VII, says: “One must indeed know the principle of analogy, but one must imitate the usage of authors more closely. They pronounce the accusatives *duo praeterea* and *ambo* according to this declension as *ambos* and *duos*. C. Julius Romanus, in his little book on analogy, gives the correct declension as *hos duo*.”

Therefore it must be acknowledged and affirmed, on the authority of Charisius and other thoroughly trustworthy authors, that *duo* for *duos* and *ambo* for *ambos* are correctly written.

As for orthography, two words in the first tablet are written without a diphthong. The first is *quedam*, the other *Cesariano*. In the second tablet one reads *Fhoca* for *Phoca*. I do not think these words are free from the errors of the stonecutters.

*Massa* in these tablets does not have the meaning of a mass of gold or silver or anything of that kind, but is used for an estate or villa, which people commonly call a possession. Hence the administrator entrusted with the care of an entire villa is called a *massarius*, as Huguittio explains. Thus in some places a rural possession, understood as a villa or estate, is commonly called a *massaria*.

These are the matters concerning the glosses, or obscure words of the ancient Latins, written in both tablets of donations. I wished to warn the reader about them so that no one might suppose that the obsolete words had been printed through the carelessness of printers, nor suspect that all of them were errors of the stonecutters.

The tablet of donations now standing at the basilica of Saint Paul is also read in the *Register* of blessed Gregory, book XII, letter 19. But in the letter inserted in the *Register* several things are missing. In the epistolary salutation, the following words, which appear on the marble tablet, are absent: “Bishop, servant of the servants of God.” At the end of the letter, the following words are also absent:

“Farewell. Given on the eighth day before the Kalends of February, under the emperor our lord N. Phocas, most august emperor, in his second year, and in the first year of his consulship, in the seventh indiction.”

These words appear on the marble tablet.

Some words also differ, for example:

- *in foro* in the *Register*, where the tablet reads *bifurco*;
- *hortos duos* for *hortos duo positos*;
- *ibidem* for *id est*;
- *similiter parte sinistra ad portam* for *similiter a porta, parte sinistra*;
- *Eugentis* for *Eugenitis*;
- *possessionibus monasterii sancti Edistii* for *possessioni monasterii sancti Aristi*;
- *hortos* for *hortus*;
- *deleri facias ac auferri* for *delere debeat ac auferre*.

I wished to warn the reader about these matters as well, so that if anyone compares the marble tablet with the letter inserted in the *Register*, he may know that this comparison was not made when the *Register* was printed. At that time the tablet, not yet transferred into the church, was affixed to the wall in the portico of Saint Paul, situated in a very elevated place and therefore known to very few, indeed almost no one, since scarcely anything could be read from it.

But while I was arranging for the scholia and other works on blessed Gregory that I had prepared to be published, I happened, while engaged on another matter, upon Panvinio, who had left the whole tablet written in his little work on the seven churches of the City, when he was discussing the basilica of Saint Peter.

Therefore, after applying every diligence and effort, I found it by searching for it; once found, I faithfully copied it from the marble; and after copying and printing it, I was pleased to place it here for the reasons assigned at the beginning.

It remains briefly to explain why blessed Gregory the Great dedicated and assigned to the basilicas of the holy apostles Peter and Paul so many estates and possessions, and finally so many olive groves, solely for lights or lamps to be kindled in honor of the holy apostles. For from the revenues of so many and such great estates, and especially of the olive groves, we can infer that an enormous number of lamps was once used in those churches.

This becomes clear to everyone who reads the lives of the supreme pontiffs written by Anastasius the Librarian and by Platina, as well as the sacred history written by Peter Mallius. For after Pope Sylvester, the popes Celestine, Hilary, Simplicius, Symmachus, and, after Gregory the Great, his successor Sabinian, then Honorius, Agatho, Gregory II, Zachary, and others donated to the basilica of Saint Peter at Rome various kinds of silver candelabra, known by various names—namely, crowns, *phara*, *canthara*, *cerostata*, and *rethia*—as well as many pounds of gold and silver for lamps.

The emperor Constantine the Great did the same; then King Theodoric under Hormisdas; and Belisarius under Vigilius. They offered to the church of Saint Peter and likewise to that of blessed Paul various kinds of highly valuable candelabra and many weights of gold and silver, appropriate to imperial and royal wealth and generosity.

Panvinio, in book V of his work *On Ancient Memorials and the Excellence of the Basilica of Saint Peter*, preserved in the library of that church, says:

“Matilda, celebrated for her holiness, made such a gift to the basilica of Saint Peter that, so that it might be more splendidly adorned with lights, she donated her patrimony to it as a dowry owed to it—that is, the principal parts of Liguria and Etruria, with all their towns and their rights.”

This is what Panvinio says.

Platina, in the life of Paschal II himself, speaks as follows:

“At this time Countess Matilda, worn out by extreme old age, died and by her will left to the Roman Church whatever land lies from the river Pissia and the territory of Siena at San Quirico as far as Ceprano, between the Apennines and the sea, adding Ferrara, which is still tributary to the Roman Church.”

This is what Platina says.

But Ferrara had come under the Church’s rule much earlier—nearly a thousand years previously, namely in the time of Vitalian, as can be seen in the chronicles of Peregrinus Priscianus and Gaspare Sardi; and afterward in the time of Pepin, Charlemagne, Louis I, Henry I, and Otto I, before Matilda. This is also established by their privileges and those of the emperors who followed Matilda, which are preserved in the archive of the Castel Sant’Angelo.

Concerning this donation and its confirmation by Countess Matilda in the time of Gregory VII and Paschal II, in the year 1102, there are also authentic written records, preserved in all the archives of the Holy Roman Church.

Since I have happened, not deliberately but because the matter itself supplied it, to fall into a discussion of Ferrara, I shall say briefly and almost in passing what occurred concerning Ferrara while I was sending this work on the lamps of the holy apostles Peter and Paul to the press.

In the preceding year of the Lord 1597, on 27 October, Alfonso d’Este, second of that name and the last duke of Ferrara, died without sons or descendants. When the most holy Lord Clement VIII, our lord, the most vigilant shepherd of the Church and the most steadfast and indefatigable defender of the patrimony of Saint Peter, first learned that the duchy of Ferrara, once granted as a fief by his predecessors the Roman pontiffs, had reverted to the Roman Church because Alfonso’s line had ended, he lost no time in dealing gravely and wisely with its recovery together with the entire college of cardinals of the Holy Roman Church, the same cardinals earnestly pressing for its recovery.

Accordingly, in the decree issued on this matter, the most holy Lord, setting human considerations aside, assigned and consecrated the entire territory of Ferrara with steadfast purpose and remarkable religious fervor to Christ our Lord and Savior, to the glorious and ever-virgin Mary, Mother of God, and to the holy apostles Peter and Paul.

Thus, with the order of law and the canons observed and with both swords finally unsheathed, Cardinal Peter Aldobrandini, deacon of Saint Nicholas in Prison and nephew of Clement himself, born for the swift and successful accomplishment of great and difficult enterprises on behalf of the Roman Church, was sent with military forces to recover the duchy of Ferrara.

Caesar d’Este, without awaiting any military encounter, promised by a written agreement to restore the duchy of Ferrara to its ancient and legitimate lord, the Holy Roman Church, on 12 January of this very year, 1598. In fact, on the twenty-ninth day of the same month—that is, the day before the feast consecrated to Saint Hippolytus, on which the anniversary of the pontificate of Clement, formerly called Hippolytus, is celebrated—he restored it freely and peacefully, with the evident assistance of divine aid, not merely through human means.

Ferrara rejoiced, the whole city of Rome exulted and gave abundant thanks to God, and all Italy marveled.

So much for Ferrara. Let us now return to our subject: the lamps once customarily kindled in honor of the holy apostles Peter and Paul.

Peter Mallius, in his book on the history of the basilica of Saint Peter, as can be seen in the Vatican Library, after listing various kinds of gifts and revenues used to kindle lamps in the basilica of Saint Peter, speaks of the lights perpetually burning in that church. He testifies that in his own time 150 lamps burned day and night in the basilica of Saint Peter, and 250 on station days. He also lists the various kinds and names of lamps and candelabra, as well as all the places in which the candelabra were suspended, after recounting all the stations of the year.

A candelabrum was also lit that had as many lamps as there are days in the year—that is, 365. Indeed, as Anastasius the Librarian says in his life of Hadrian I, Hadrian himself gave the basilica of Saint Peter a candelabrum representing the form of a cross and adorned with 1,360 candles or lamps. It hung before the presbytery and was accustomed to be lit four times each year: on the Nativity of the Lord, at Easter, on the feast of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, and at the election of the Roman pontiff, which was celebrated each year during his lifetime. In addition, 1,370 lamps were accustomed to be lit before the presbytery.

Much the same is read concerning the basilica of Saint Paul. Since so many lamps therefore burned perpetually in the basilicas of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, no one should find it surprising that so many estates and so many olive groves were dedicated and assigned to those basilicas.

[Col. 0487]

## Testimonies and Eulogies of Ancient Writers Concerning Saint Gregory the Pope

[Note: He was a contemporary of Saint Gregory the Great.]

### Gregory of Tours, *History*, book X, chapter 1

[Note: Compare book I, *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 83, where the pilgrimage of this deacon is discussed.]

In the fifteenth year of King Childebert, our deacon, coming from the city of Rome with relics of the saints, reported the following:

[Note: See book III of the *Dialogues*, chapter 19, and Paul the Deacon, *History of the Lombards*, book III, chapter 24. The same account is read in both previously published lives of Saint Gregory.]

“In the preceding year, in the ninth month, the river Tiber flooded the city of Rome with such force that ancient buildings were destroyed, and even the Church’s granaries were overturned, in which several thousand measures of wheat perished. A multitude of serpents, together with a great dragon as strong as a beam, descended through the riverbed into the sea. But the suffocated beasts were cast upon the shore amid the salty waves of the troubled sea.

“Immediately afterward there followed a disaster which they call the inguinal plague. For when the eleventh month arrived, it first struck Pope Pelagius, in accordance with what is written in the prophet Ezekiel: ‘Begin from my sanctuary’ (Ezek. 9:6), and killed him without delay. After his death, a great multitude of the people perished from this disease. But because the Church of God could not be without a ruler, the whole people elected Gregory, a deacon.

“He belonged to one of the foremost senatorial families. From his youth he had been devoted to God. From his own property he established six monasteries in Sicily and a seventh within the walls of the city of Rome.

[Note: On these monasteries, read our commentaries on the life of Saint Gregory.]

“To them he assigned so great a quantity of land as was sufficient to provide daily sustenance; he sold the remainder, together with all the household property, and distributed it to the poor.

[Note: This word is familiar to Gregory of Tours—see *History*, book VI, chapter 4, and book IX, chapter 20—and means money, furnishings, and movable goods. See the notes on the *Sacramentary*, column 472.]

“He who had previously been accustomed to go through the city clothed in silk, glittering with jewels, and wearing the senatorial robe was now consecrated to the ministry of the Lord’s altar, clothed in a humble garment,

[Note: That is, a monastic garment.]

“and, as the seventh Levite, he was appointed as the pope’s assistant.

[Note: At that time only seven deacons, namely the regional deacons, were ordained in the Roman Church. This custom will be discussed more fully below.]

“His abstinence in food, his watchfulness in prayers, and his diligence in fasting were so great that, after his stomach became weak, he could scarcely stand. He was so well trained in grammar, dialectic, and rhetoric that no one in the city itself was thought to be his equal.

“Trying especially to flee this eminence, lest some pride in the honor he had attained in the world should steal back upon him—an honor he had previously rejected—he sent a letter to the emperor Maurice, whose son he had received from the holy font, beseeching him and asking with many prayers that he never give his consent to the people’s desire to raise Gregory to the glory of this dignity.

“But the prefect of the city of Rome, his brother, anticipated the messenger, seized the letters, tore them up, and sent the consent expressed by the people to the emperor. The emperor, giving thanks to God for the friendship of that deacon and because he had found a place for his honor, issued an order that Gregory should be appointed.

“When only his blessing remained to be given, and the plague was devastating the people, he began to address the people concerning the performance of penance in this manner:”

## Prayer of Pope Gregory to the People
«It is fitting, dearest brothers, that the scourges of God, etc. [Col. 0489C]

[Note: [Col. 0489D] As they were published both in the *Life* by John the Deacon and at the end of the homily on the Gospel, vol. I (*Patrologia*, vol. LXXVI). We have judged that what is read concerning the sevenfold Litany in Gregory of Tours should also be printed here, since in these matters it does not agree with John the Deacon, indeed not even with Saint Gregory himself. We have given the reason for this disagreement elsewhere.]

Therefore, dearest brothers, with contrite hearts and our deeds amended, from the first light of Wednesday let us come with minds devoted even to tears to the sevenfold Litany, according to the arrangement set out below, so that, when the strict Judge sees us punishing our own sins, he himself may spare us the sentence of the condemnation that has been decreed.

Let the clergy go out from the church of the holy martyrs Cosmas and Damian, with the priests of the sixth region; all the abbots with their monks from the church of the holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius, with the priests of the fourth region; all the abbesses with their communities from the church of the holy martyrs Marcellinus and Peter, with the priests of the first region; all the children from the church of the holy martyrs John and Paul, with the priests of the second region; all the laity from the church of the protomartyr Stephen, with the priests of the seventh region; all the widowed women from the church of Saint Euphemia, with the priests of the fifth region; [Col. 0489D] and all the married women from [Col. 0490A] the church of the holy martyr Clement, with the priests of the third region. Thus, going out from the individual churches with prayers and tears, let us gather at the basilica of blessed Mary, ever-Virgin, Mother of our Lord God Jesus Christ, so that there, beseeching the Lord for a long while with weeping and groaning, we may be able to merit forgiveness for our sins.»

When he had said this, he gathered the ranks of the clergy and ordered them for three days to sing psalms and entreat the Lord’s mercy. At the third hour all the choirs of those singing also came to the church, crying through the streets of the City: “Kyrie eleison”—“Lord, have mercy.” Our deacon, who was present, asserted that within the space of one hour, while the people were raising voices of supplication to the Lord, eighty people fell to the ground and breathed their last. [Col. 0490B] Yet so great a priest did not cease preaching to the people that they should not stop praying.

It was from this deacon also that our deacon received the relics of the saints, as we have said, while he was still living as a deacon. And while he was preparing hiding places for flight, he was seized, dragged away, and led to the basilica of blessed Peter the Apostle. There he was consecrated to the office of pontifical grace and given to the City as pope. But our deacon did not cease until he had returned from the port [Note: [Col. 0490D] The manuscripts of Beccensis read *de portu* (“from the port”); most printed editions have *de porta* (“from the gate”). We follow the edition of our Dom Thierry Ruinart. *De portu* perhaps means that the deacon of the Church of Tours was led to the port with the sacred relics, as is read in Book I, chapter 83, *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, and from there returned to Rome so that he might witness Gregory’s ordination with his own eyes.] to attend Gregory’s episcopal consecration and witness with his own eyes how he was ordained.

## Prologue of Saint Paterius, his disciple, to the Book of Testimonies

While he undertook to examine the history of one holy man—namely, blessed Job—covered by the obscure shadows of mysteries through a threefold exposition, that is, typological, moral, and historical, and, having dispelled the cloud of ignorance, to display it with a clear revelation, brighter than daylight, openly to all, he was compelled by the necessity of explaining the matters to expound almost the entire sequence of events in the Old and New Testaments.

[Note: [Col. 0490D] He was a contemporary of Saint Gregory.]

## Isidore of Seville, *On Illustrious Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 27

Pope Gregory, bishop of the apostolic see of Rome, full of the compunction of the fear of God and supreme in humility, was endowed with so great a light of knowledge through the grace of the Holy Spirit that not only was there no teacher among his contemporaries equal to him, but in former times as well there had never been his equal.

At the beginning of his episcopate he published the book *The Pastoral Rule*, addressed to John, bishop of the see of Ravenna. In it everyone is taught what sort of person should come to the office of governance, and how, once he has come, he should strive to live and to teach his subjects.

At the urging of Bishop Leander, he also expounded the book of blessed Job in a mystical and moral sense, explaining the whole history of its prophecy in thirty-five volumes, through a rich stream of eloquence. [Col. 0490D] In these works such great mysteries of the sacraments [Col. 0491A] are disclosed, such numerous precepts of conduct leading to love of eternal life are given, and such splendid ornaments of language shine forth, that no wise person would be able to explain them, even if all his limbs were turned into tongues.

He also wrote certain letters to the aforementioned Leander, one of which he attaches to the same books of Job as a preface. Another discusses immersion in baptism; among other things it says:

“By no means,” he says, “can it be reproved to immerse an infant in baptism either once or three times, since in three immersions the Trinity of persons can be signified, and in one the unity of the Godhead.”

It is nevertheless reported that this most excellent man also wrote other moral works and expounded the entire text of the four Gospels to the people by preaching—an otherwise unknown work. Happy, indeed exceedingly happy, is the person who was able to know the sayings of all his studies.

He flourished under the emperor Maurice and died at the very beginning of the reign of the Roman ruler Phocas.

## John the Deacon, Book I, chapter 17, *On the Life of Saint Gregory*

Gregory was earnestly entreated by many people, especially by Leander, bishop of Seville, who at that time had come to Constantinople as an envoy on behalf of the Visigoths. He was compelled to unravel the book of blessed Job, which was wrapped in many mysteries.

Nor could he refuse a work that brotherly love imposed upon him as destined to be useful to many. He therefore taught the meaning of the same book in a remarkable manner according to three modes of understanding: how it should be understood according to the letter, how it should be referred to the mysteries of Christ and the Church, and in what sense it should be applied to each of the faithful. Yet in discussing virtues and vices he did so in such a way that he seems not merely to explain them in words, but somehow to demonstrate them in visible or tangible forms.

[Note: [Col. 0491] He flourished at the end of the seventh century and for approximately thirty-five years of the eighth.]

## The Venerable Bede, *Ecclesiastical History of the English People*, Book II, chapter 1

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 605, blessed Pope Gregory, after ruling the Roman and apostolic Church with the highest glory for thirteen years, six months, and ten days, died and was transferred to the eternal seat of the heavenly kingdom.

Concerning him it is appropriate for us, since through his efforts he converted our people—that is, the English—from the power of Satan to the faith of Christ, to speak more extensively in our ecclesiastical history. We can and ought rightly to call him our apostle, because, although he held the chief pontificate throughout the whole world and had been set over a Church whose members had long since been converted to the faith of truth, he made our people, until then enslaved to idols, into the Church of Christ.

Thus we may apply to him that apostolic statement: “For though he is not an apostle to others, yet he is to us; for you are the seal of his apostleship in the Lord” (1 Cor. 9:2).

He was Roman by nationality, descended through his father Gordian from ancestors who were not only noble but also religious. Moreover, Felix, formerly bishop of that same apostolic see, a man of great glory in Christ and in the Church, was his great-great-grandfather.

Gregory himself practiced a nobility of religion no less than that of his parents and relatives, through the virtue of his devotion. The nobility that he appeared to possess in worldly affairs he entirely turned, by the gift of divine grace, toward attaining the glory of a higher dignity.

For, suddenly changing his secular clothing, he sought a monastery. There he began to live with such grace of perfection that, as he himself later used to testify with tears (Preface to Book I of the *Dialogues*), all passing things seemed beneath his mind, so that he rose above everything that revolves; he was accustomed to think only of heavenly things; while still held in the body, he passed beyond the very confines of the flesh through contemplation; and he loved even death—which is punishment to almost everyone—as the entrance to life and the reward of his labor.

He used to relate these things about himself, not boasting of his progress in virtue, but rather lamenting the decline that he seemed to have suffered through pastoral care. Finally, at a certain time, speaking privately with his deacon Peter, he enumerated the former virtues of his soul and then sorrowfully added:

“But now, because of the opportunity afforded by pastoral care, the affairs of secular people burden me, and after so beautiful a state of quiet, I am stained by the dust of earthly activity. When, out of condescension toward many, I spread myself outward, even when I desire inward things I return to them undoubtedly diminished. I therefore consider what I endure; I consider what I have lost. And while I look upon what I lost, what I bear becomes heavier.” (The same work.)

The holy man said these things with the intention of great humility. Yet we ought to believe that he lost nothing of monastic perfection through the demands of pastoral care; rather, he then acquired a greater gain from the labor of converting many than he had formerly possessed from the quiet conversion of his own life—especially since, after undertaking the episcopal office, he took care to make his own house a monastery.

When he was first taken from the monastery, ordained for service at the altar, and sent by the apostolic see to Constantinople as its representative, he nevertheless did not, while living in an earthly palace, abandon his resolve concerning the heavenly life. For he began to keep certain brothers from his monastery, who had followed him to the imperial city out of fraternal love, as a safeguard of regular observance.
