In this way, as he himself writes, by their constant example he might always be drawn back, as if by an anchor’s rope, to the calm shore of prayer whenever he was tossed by the unceasing force of secular affairs, and might daily strengthen his mind, shaken by worldly business, through earnest conversations about reading. [Col. 0492D]

Through their companionship, therefore, he was not only protected from earthly assaults but also increasingly inflamed for the practices of heavenly life. They encouraged him to examine the book of blessed Job, wrapped in great obscurities, by mystical interpretation. Nor could he refuse a work that brotherly love imposed upon him as destined to be useful to many.

He accordingly taught, through thirty-five books of exposition, how the same book should be understood according to the letter, how it should be referred to the mysteries of Christ and the Church, and in what sense it should be applied to each of the faithful. He began this work while serving as representative in the imperial city, but completed it at Rome after becoming pontiff.

While he was still stationed in the imperial city, he crushed at its very birth, with the help of the grace of Catholic truth, a new heresy that had arisen there concerning the condition of our resurrection. For Eutychius, bishop of that city, taught that our body in the glory of the resurrection would be impalpable, more subtle than winds and air.

When Gregory heard this, he proved by both the argument of truth and the example of the Lord’s resurrection that this doctrine was altogether contrary to orthodox faith. For the Catholic faith holds that our body, raised up in that glory of immortality, is indeed subtle through the effect of spiritual power, but tangible through the truth of its nature, according to the example of the Lord’s body. Of that body, raised from the dead, he himself says to the disciples: “Touch me and see, because a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have” (Luke 24:39).

In defending this faith, the venerable Father Gregory strove so vigorously against the rising heresy and reduced it so thoroughly, with the assistance also of the most devout emperor Tiberius Constantine, that from then on no one was found to revive it.

He also composed another distinguished book called *The Pastoral*, in which he clearly revealed what kind of person should be appointed to govern the Church, how its leaders ought to live, with what discretion they should instruct each of their hearers individually, and with what consideration they should daily weigh their own frailty.

He also composed forty homilies on the Gospel, [Col. 0493C] which he divided equally into two books. He produced four books of *Dialogues*, in which, at the request of his deacon Peter, he collected for the example of later generations the virtues of the saints whom he could learn about or hear of as the most illustrious in Italy. Thus, just as he taught in his books of exposition which virtues should be pursued, so, by recording the miracles of the saints, he showed the splendor of those same virtues.

He explained through twenty-two homilies the first and last parts of the prophecy of Ezekiel, which seemed more obscure, and demonstrated how much light they contain within. In addition to the little book of *Responses* that he wrote to the questions of Saint Augustine, the first bishop of the English, as we have taught above—and in which we have incorporated the whole work into these histories—there was also the synodal booklet that he composed with the bishops of Italy, most useful for necessary ecclesiastical affairs, as well as letters to various friends.

This is all the more remarkable because he was able to produce so many and such great volumes despite being afflicted for nearly the whole time of his youth, to use his own words, by frequent pains in his vital organs. At every hour and moment, he grew weary from the weakened strength of his stomach and labored with slow but continual fevers. Yet amid these sufferings, as he carefully considered that, according to the testimony of Scripture, every son who is received is chastised, the more harshly he was weighed down by present evils, the more confidently he breathed in hope of eternal things.

These things may be said concerning his immortal intellect, which even such great bodily pain could not restrain. Other pontiffs devoted themselves to building and adorning churches with gold and silver; he, however, was wholly occupied with the gain of souls.

Whatever money he possessed, he diligently made a practice of distributing and giving to the poor, so that “his righteousness might endure forever, and his horn be exalted in glory” (Ps. 111:8). Thus he could truthfully say what blessed Job said:

“The ear that heard me blessed me, and the eye that saw me bore witness to me, because I delivered the poor man who cried out, and the orphan who had no helper. The blessing of the perishing came upon me, and I consoled the widow’s heart. I was clothed with righteousness, and clothed myself in my judgment as with a garment and a diadem. I was an eye to the blind and a foot to the lame. I was a father to the poor, and the case that I did not know I investigated with the greatest diligence. I crushed the jaws of the wicked and tore the prey from his teeth” (Job 29:11 ff.).

And shortly afterward:

“If I denied,” he says, “what the poor desired, and made the eyes of the widow wait; if I ate my morsel alone, and the orphan did not eat from it—because from my infancy compassion grew up with me, and it came forth with me from my mother’s womb” (Job 31:16 ff.).

To the work of his piety and righteousness also belongs the fact that, through the preachers whom he sent here, he snatched our people from the teeth of the ancient enemy and made them participants in eternal liberty. Rejoicing in their faith and salvation, and commending everything worthy of praise, he himself says in his exposition of blessed Job:

“Behold, the tongue of Britain, which had known nothing except to growl barbarously, has long since begun to resound with the Hebrew ‘Alleluia’ in divine praises. Behold, the once swollen Ocean, now subdued, serves beneath the feet of the saints; and its fierce barbarians, whom earthly rulers could not tame, are bound by the mouths of priests with simple words, for those who, as unbelievers, had never feared bands of fighting men now fear the faithful tongues of the humble.

Because, having received heavenly words and with miracles also shining forth, the power of divine knowledge is infused into it, it is restrained by the terror of that same divinity, so that it fears to act wickedly and longs with all its desires to come to the grace of eternity.” (Book XXVII, no. 21.)

By these words blessed Gregory also makes clear that Saint Augustine and his companions led the English people to recognition of the truth not only through preaching words but also through the display of heavenly signs.

Among other things, blessed Pope Gregory arranged that Masses should be celebrated in the churches of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul over their bodies. In the celebration of the Mass itself he also added three words full of the highest perfection:

“Order our days in your peace, and command that we be rescued from eternal damnation and numbered among the flock of your elect.”

He ruled the Church during the reigns of the emperors Maurice and Phocas. In the second year of Phocas, passing from this life, he departed into the true life that is in heaven. His body was buried in the church of the blessed apostle Peter, before the secretarium, on the fourth day before the Ides of March, where one day he will rise in glory with the other pastors of the holy Church.

An epitaph of this kind was written on his tomb:

“Receive, O earth, this body taken from your body, etc.” (as in John the Deacon, Book IV of the *Life*, chapter 68).

Nor should we pass over in silence the account concerning blessed Gregory that has been handed down to us through the tradition of our ancestors, explaining why he was moved to take such diligent care for the salvation of our people.

They say that one day, when recently arrived merchants had brought many goods for sale into the marketplace and many people had gathered to buy, Gregory himself came among the others and saw, among the goods, boys put up for sale. They had fair bodies, handsome faces, and particularly beautiful hair.

When he looked at them, he asked, they say, from what region or land they had been brought. He was told that they came from the island of Britain, whose inhabitants had such an appearance.

He asked again whether these islanders were Christians or were still entangled in pagan errors. He was told that they were pagans.

Then, drawing a long sigh from the depths of his heart, he said: “Alas, what sorrow, that people of such radiant countenance should be possessed by the author of darkness, and that such grace of facial beauty should bear a mind empty of inward grace!”

Again he asked what the people were called. He was told that they were called Angles.

“Good,” he said, “for they have an angelic face, and such people ought to be fellow heirs of the angels in heaven.”

“What is the name of the province from which these people have been brought?”

He was told that the inhabitants of that province were called Deiri.

“Good,” he said, “Deiri: rescued from wrath and called to the mercy of Christ.”

“What is the king of that province called?”

He was told that he was called Aelle.

Playing upon the name, he said: “Alleluia, the praise of God the Creator, ought to be sung in those regions.”

Then he approached the pontiff of the Roman and apostolic see—for he had not yet himself become pontiff—and asked him to send to Britain some ministers of the word for the English people, through whom they might be converted to Christ. He declared himself ready, with the Lord’s cooperation, to accomplish this work, provided that the apostolic pope approved it.

Since he could not carry this out—for although the pontiff wished to grant what he had requested, the Roman citizens could not permit him to withdraw so far from the City—as soon as Gregory himself had undertaken the office of pontiff, he completed the work he had long desired: he sent other preachers, while supporting their preaching himself, so that it might bear fruit, through his exhortations and prayers.

We have thought it best to insert this in our ecclesiastical history according to the account that we received from the ancients.

## Ado, archbishop of Vienne

[Note: [Col. 0495D] He flourished after the year 850.]

At Rome, the burial of Saint Gregory the pope, who was born of noble family and educated in the liberal arts. After the death of his parents, he built six monasteries in Sicily and established a seventh within the walls of the City.

In that monastery, after exchanging his secular clothing, he joined many brothers and served energetically under the authority of an abbot. He raised the lineage of his nobility through his conduct and adorned it with upright deeds. For he who had formerly been accustomed to proceed through the City in a robe of state, glittering in silk garments and jewels, afterward, covered with a cheap cloak, served the poor as a poor man himself.

He assigned to these monasteries from the revenues of their estates as much as could suffice for the daily sustenance of those living there. He sold the remainder and distributed it to the poor.

Then, compelled and strongly resisting, he was made supreme pontiff of the City of Rome and converted the English people to the faith by sending monks from his monastery—Mellitus, Augustine, and John, together with many other brothers.

He ruled the Roman Church with the greatest glory for thirteen years, six months, and ten days. He also added to the Preface of the Canon: “Order our days in your peace.”

## The same author, in the *Chronicle*

Gregory, while still serving as representative of the Roman Church at Constantinople, composed thirty-five books of exposition on Job. In the presence of Tiberius he so convicted Eutychius, bishop of that same city, of having erred concerning our belief in the resurrection, that the emperor decided that the book Eutychius had written about the resurrection ought to be burned in the flames.

[Note: [Col. 0495D] He ruled the Church from the year 772 to the year 795.]

## Pope Hadrian I, *To the Bishops of Spain*, vol. VII of the Councils, p. 1017

Now let us see what our predecessor, blessed Gregory, that outstanding teacher, most discerning investigator of the word of God, and venerable Father, thinks about this matter. For in the *Moral Books*, filled with the Holy Spirit, etc. [Col. 0496C]

[Note: [Col. 0496D] He flourished in the middle of the ninth century.]

## Hincmar of Reims, *On Predestination*, chapter 18

What blessed Gregory, distinguished ornament of the first and holy Roman see, saw, saying in Book I of the *Dialogues*:

“The predestination of the everlasting kingdom,” he says, “has been so arranged by almighty God that the elect reach it through labor, so that by asking they may merit to receive what almighty God determined before the ages to grant them.”

Therefore, as is also read in the *Deeds of the Roman Pontiffs*, he took care to increase the hidden mysteries of the heavenly sacraments: “that he may order our days, rescue us from eternal damnation, and command that we be numbered among the flock of his elect.”

## *Life of Saint Gregory the Great* by Symeon Metaphrastes

[Note: [Col. 0496D] He lived at the beginning of the tenth century.]

Blessed Gregory, who was pontiff of the holy Church of God at Rome, was a monk before he became patriarch, in the monastery of the holy apostle Andrew at the Clivus Scauri, near the church of the holy martyrs John and Paul. He himself presided over that monastery.

His mother was blessed Silvia, who at that time lived near the gate of the holy apostle Paul, in her ancestral residence called Cella Nova.

It happened that while Gregory was sitting and writing in his little cell, a beggar approached him in a suppliant voice:

“Have mercy on me,” he said, “servant of the Most High God. When I was a ship’s captain, I suffered shipwreck and lost both the property of others and my own.”

But Gregory, being kind toward the poor and truly a servant of Christ, called the steward and said: “Brother, give this man six gold coins.”

The brother did what the servant of God Gregory had commanded and gave the money to the beggar.

On that same day the poor man came again to blessed Gregory and said: “Have mercy on me, servant of the Most High God. Although I have lost much, I have received little from you.”

Blessed Gregory called his servant again and told him to count out six more coins for the same poor man. The brother obeyed.

But after the poor man had departed with twelve coins, he returned to blessed Gregory a little later that same day:

“Have mercy on me,” he said, “servant of the Most High God, and give me something more, for I have suffered a great loss.”

Calling the steward for the third time, Gregory said: “Brother, give this poor man six more coins.”

But the steward replied: “Believe me, Father, not a single coin remains in the chest.”

Blessed Gregory said to him: “Do you have nothing else in the storeroom, such as a vessel or garment, that you can give to the poor man?”

“We have no vessel,” he replied, “except that silver one which a great lady customarily sent, filled with legumes.”

“Go,” said the servant of God Gregory, “and offer it to the poor man.”

The brother did what blessed Gregory had commanded him. The poor man therefore departed with the twelve coins and the silver vessel.

When Gregory had been chosen patriarch in the most holy and greatest Church of God in ancient Rome, he one day instructed the treasurer, as is customary for patriarchs, to summon twelve poor men to his table to dine with him. The treasurer obeyed and summoned the poor men.

But when they had reclined at table with the patriarch, they were found to number thirteen. Gregory therefore called the treasurer and said:

“Did I not command you to call twelve? Why, contrary to my instruction, have you called thirteen?”

The treasurer was terrified when he heard this:

“Believe me, revered lord,” he said, “there are twelve; no one except the patriarch saw thirteen.”

During the meal, then, the patriarch kept looking at the thirteenth man, who was seated on the highest bench. And behold, his face assumed various forms. At one moment he appeared to be an old man, at another a young man.

When they had risen from the table, blessed Gregory dismissed everyone else, took the thirteenth man—who had appeared so wondrous to him—by the hand, led him into a room, and addressed him as follows:

“I adjure you by the great power of almighty God to reveal to me who you are and by what name you are called.”

He replied:

“Why do you ask my name, which is wondrous? I am the poor man who came to you at the residence of the holy apostle Andrew at the Clivus Scauri, when you were sitting and writing in your little cell. You gave me twelve coins and the vessel that your blessed mother Silvia had sent you with legumes.

“Since it became clear that you had remained constant in simplicity of heart and patience from the day on which you gave me these things, the Lord determined that you should become pontiff of his holy Church, for which he shed his own blood, and successor of Peter, prince of the apostles, so that you might provide everyone with whatever was necessary.”

“From where,” said blessed Gregory, “do you know that the Lord then decided that I should become pontiff?”

“Because I am an angel of almighty God,” he replied, “I know it.”

Then the Lord sent me to test the purpose of your heart, to see whether you gave alms out of human kindness or for display.

When blessed Gregory heard this, he was afraid, for previously he had not known that the man was an angel. Therefore he had dealt and spoken with him as with a human being.

The angel said to blessed Gregory: “Do not be afraid, for God sent me to remain with you in this life.”

When Gregory heard this, he fell face down upon the ground and worshiped the Lord:

“If, because of this small inclination of the mind toward earning merit, the most merciful Lord has shown such an abundance of kindness that he sent his angel to be my perpetual guardian, how great will be the glory of those who obey his commandments and cultivate righteousness?

“For he is truthful who said that mercy is granted in judgment and that the person who has compassion on the poor lends to God.

“Indeed, the Lord of angels himself, who is the author of human salvation, will address those placed at his right hand in this way: ‘Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world. For I was hungry, and you gave me food; I was thirsty, and you gave me drink; I was a stranger, and you welcomed me; I was sick, and you visited me; I was naked, and you clothed me; I was in prison, and you came to me.’

“‘Truly I tell you, insofar as you did it for one of the least of these my brothers, you did it for me’” (Matt. 25:43).

Would that we all who either read or hear these things might hear that blessed voice and attain those everlasting goods that God has prepared for those who love him, through the grace and kindness of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.

## Sigebert of Gembloux, *Book on Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 41

[Note: [Col. 0497D] He is said to have died in the year 1113.]

Gregory, Roman by nationality, formerly urban prefect, then a monk and abbot, the seventh levite of the Roman Church, and representative of the pope of the Roman Church, wrote many works.

At the request of Leander, bishop of Seville, he expounded the book of Job in three ways—historically, allegorically, and morally—and, dividing the book into six books, completed this remarkable work in thirty-five books. He expounded the first and last parts of the prophet Ezekiel, which were more obscure, in homiletic discourse.

He wrote forty-two homilies on the Gospel [Note: [Col. 0497D] Not to Marianus, or Marinianus, but to Secundinus, bishop of Tauromenium. In any event, we recognize only forty homilies.] for Bishop Marianus.

At the beginning of his pontificate he wrote to John, bishop of Ravenna, the book *The Pastoral Rule*. He sent the book of the *Dialogues*, which records a dialogue he held with his deacon Peter about the miracles of the saints of his own time, as a gift to Theudelinda, queen of the Lombards.

He left to posterity as many books of letters as the years he lived in the pontificate, namely thirteen and a half.

He also wrote other works, which the Romans burned after his death. They would have burned all his works as well, had not his deacon Peter intervened and confirmed under oath that he had seen the Holy Spirit, like a dove, seated above Gregory’s head while Gregory was dictating, inserting its beak into his mouth.

Peter made this very oath on the condition that, if he died immediately after taking it, the Romans would cease burning Gregory’s books; but if he did not die, he too would lend his hands to the burners of the books.

Thus Peter breathed his last amid the words of the oath, and the madness of the Romans ceased.

This writing brought Gregory as much distinction as the fact that he arranged the *Antiphonary* into regular musical composition and established singing schools in the Roman Church.

## Honorarius of Autun, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*

[Note: [Col. 0499C] He flourished when the twelfth century was already well advanced.]

[Col. 0499B] Gregory, bishop of the city of Rome, organ of the Holy Spirit, incomparable among all his predecessors, wrote many works brighter than the sun and more precious than refined gold.

For the aforementioned John he wrote *The Pastoral Care*. For Bishop Leander he explained the book of Job in thirty-five volumes through a rich stream of eloquence. He wrote the *Dialogue on the Miracles of the Saints* for Peter the archdeacon.

He is said to have expounded forty Gospel oracles—or rather, the entire text of the four Gospels—to the people through preaching. [Note: [Col. 0499C] Concerning these, read what we have observed below under the testimony of John Trithemius.]

He also wrote twenty homilies on Ezekiel and countless letters, the collection of which is called the *Register*. He flourished under Maurice.

[Col. 0500A]

[Note: [Col. 0499C] He flourished at the beginning of the sixteenth century.]

## John Trithemius, *Book on Ecclesiastical Writers*

Pope Gregory I, a Roman by nationality and formerly a monk of the order of Saint Benedict, succeeded Pope Pelagius and sat in the chair of Peter for thirteen years and six months.

He was exceedingly learned in the divine Scriptures and also highly educated in secular literature: the foremost of theologians, the splendor of philosophers, and the light of rhetoricians. In life and conduct he was upright and most holy.

When he was explaining the divine Scriptures, the Holy Spirit appeared to him several times in visible form and disclosed to him, through invisible instruction, the hidden mysteries of those Scriptures.

At Rome, in a synod held at Saint Peter’s with twenty-four bishops, he established many measures for the benefit of the Church and promulgated a decree of immunity for monasteries.

He also wrote many necessary volumes, of which the following are reported: [Col. 0500B]

To Leander, bishop of Seville: *Morals on the Book of Job*, Book XXXV. “Among many, often …” *On Pastoral Care*, Book II. “Pastoral care, me …” *Dialogues on the Miracles of the Saints*, Book IV. “One day, exceedingly …” *On the Song of Songs*, Book IV. “After … from paradise.” *On the Prophet Ezekiel*, Book II. “Of almighty God …” *Forty Homilies on the Gospels*, Book II. “The Lord and Redeemer …”

> [Note: [Col. 0499C] We found two manuscript codices of this exposition, nine hundred years old: one, and that most elegantly written, in the Royal Library; the other, written less accurately, in the Bigot Library, with this title: “Here begins the exposition according to Matthew . . . . . . . . . . by Saint Gregory . . . of the City of Rome. Matthew, as the first in order,” etc. The dots marked here indicate words so erased that they cannot be read. This exposition [Col. 0500C] does not have the characteristic style of Saint Gregory the Great, although Honorius of Autun seems to attribute it to him when he says of him: “He is said to have expounded to the people in sermons the forty Gospel oracles—indeed, the entire text of the four Gospels.” (*Book of Ecclesiastical Writers*, under “Gregory.”) The Bigot codex is mutilated, for the exposition on Luke is almost entirely absent. It is preceded by an exposition of the Gospel according to John. The format of the codex corresponds to our octavo volumes, and on its spine is written: “Homilies of Saint Gregory. Concordance of the Months. Canons of the Apostles.”]

A Brief Exposition of the Four Gospels, Book IV. “Matthew, as the first in order.”

# [THE MORALS]

[Col. 0499]

## PREFACE TO THE BOOKS OF THE MORALS

### I

We begin the new editing and printing of Gregory’s works with the *Morals on Job*, because of both the antiquity of the work—for it is the first of all that the holy Doctor composed—and the antiquity of the sacred author explained in this commentary, since the book of Job has either Moses, as most believe, or a patriarch older than Moses as its author. Our Gregory undertook this exposition while carrying out the office of apocrisarius, or envoy of the Apostolic See, at Constantinople, as he explains more fully in the letter to Leander that follows immediately. Later, having obtained greater leisure, he brought it back to the anvil and revised it. Thus, after that work had been reviewed a second and third time with greater diligence by the most holy and learned Father—a claim that cannot be made concerning any other of his compositions—it deservedly attained the first place in rank as a work complete in every respect.

In this exposition, equally abundant and elegant, he surpasses all the other writers who have attempted to illuminate the book of Job with commentaries by as much as he was superior to them in knowledge and contemplation of divine mysteries, in knowledge joined to experience of Christian ethics, and in general expertise in all sacred matters. Consequently, in these books we possess at once a most fully equipped arsenal for establishing and confirming ecclesiastical doctrines and an exceptionally rich storehouse for teaching and shaping morals.

### II

How eagerly those books were received as soon as they were published—even to the point that bishops ordered them to be read at the sacred vigils—and how painfully this was borne by a man preeminent in humility, he himself teaches us in his letter to John, subdeacon at Ravenna, in these words:

> “As for what has been brought to my attention through the report of certain persons, namely, that my most reverend brother and fellow bishop Marinianus has the commentaries on blessed Job read publicly at the vigils, I did not receive this with pleasure, because this work is not suited to the common people; and for untrained hearers it would generate an impediment rather than advancement. But tell him to have the commentaries on the Psalms read at the vigils.” (*Book XII, Letter 24.*)

[Col. 0501]

### III

The opinion formed concerning Saint Gregory’s *Morals* and handed down to posterity is also attested and bequeathed to us by our predecessors, especially since they made so many epitomes of them, under various titles, so that they might always be readily available. Here we shall mention the more notable ones that we found in libraries.

In the Corbie Codex, now belonging to the Library of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, which contains a collection of certain letters of Saint Gregory sent by Paul the Deacon to Saint Adalard, abbot of Corbie, there is also a small work bearing this title:

> “In the name of God the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Here begins the Eclogue written by Lateen, son of Haith, from the *Morals on Job* composed by Gregory.”

It appears to be at least eight hundred years old. Some leaves have been lost. After the thirtieth book, nothing can be read from the remaining five.

In the Library of Saint-Ouen at Rouen we possess a handwritten *Mirror of Adalbert the Levite for Hairmannus the Priest*, or an abridgment of the *Morals of Blessed Gregory*. The codex is six hundred years old. A copy from the same collection had already come to the attention of our learned John Mabillon when he was examining the Premonstratensian Library (*Ancient Analecta*, vol. I, p. 317).

In a manuscript codex of the Library of Jumièges are abbreviations of the *Morals* under the title *The Soul’s Reclining Place*.

Simon of Affligem, a monk, is said to have collected the same material in ten small books, and Garnerius, canon and subprior of Saint-Victor in Paris, in sixteen books. Garnerius’s Gregorian work exists in the Navarre Library. Yet more illustrious than all who composed such compendia was Saint Odo, formerly a canon of Saint-Martin of Tours and later a monk and abbot of Cluny. His thirty-five books collected from Gregory’s *Morals* were published in Paris by Dom Martin Marrier, a monk of Saint-Martin-des-Champs, in 1617. They are found in the *Library of the Fathers of Lyon*, volume XVII. Odo devoted himself to this composition while he was still a young member of the community of Saint-Martin. Following Odo’s example, his disciple John, who composed Odo’s life in three books, prepared a small work excerpted from Gregory’s *Morals*. Mabillon himself testifies that he found it in the Library of Monte Cassino (*Italian Museum*, vol. I, p. 123).

In the Library of the distinguished Church of Laon there is a handwritten codex presenting the same books of the *Morals* in abridged form. It was donated to that church by two of its canons, Adalelmus the Treasurer—later, according to Flodoard, made bishop of the same church in the year 921—and Bernard (*Christian Gaul*, under the bishops of Laon). The work begins as follows:

> “In the name of the Lord. The Prologue of Blessed Job. Among the many things often asked is who is regarded as the author of the book of blessed Job. Some indeed say Moses,” etc.

The prologue ends:

> “He narrated the deeds of his victory.”

After the prologue one reads:

> “Here begin the *Morals of Saint Gregory the Pope* on the book of Job. There was a man in the land of Uz whose name was Job.”

For this reason, it is said where the holy man lived, so that the excellence of his virtue might be expressed. For just as a more serious fault is, etc.

The first book ends with these words:

> “because without ceasing he displays to the Father his incarnation on our behalf.”

Thirty-three books follow in order, for the thirty-fifth is missing. We have not yet discovered who the author of this collection was.

### IV

From these facts it is clear how assiduous the ancients were in reading and gathering, as though into bundles, the books of Gregory’s *Morals*; this is the clearest possible evidence of the esteem in which they were held. So that ignorance of the Latin language would not prevent their being read, very many translations of them were made into vernacular languages. Notker is said to have translated them into German, while Grimoald, a monk of the monastery of Saint-Aemilianus, translated them into Spanish toward the end of the eleventh century, to say nothing of others (*Ancient Spanish Library*, vol. II, book VII, chapter 1, no. 13).

The almost innumerable multitude of handwritten codices reproducing those books proves no less clearly the eagerness with which the *Morals* were read. We have thought it worthwhile to list here the principal codices that we read and examined.

The most outstanding in antiquity is the codex of the distinguished Étienne Baluze, believed to reach almost to Gregory’s own age. Would that it contained more than five books—namely, books twenty-three through twenty-seven!

Second place on account of antiquity belongs to the Rheims codex, more than nine hundred years old, which was given to the Church of Rheims by Archbishop Hincmar. We call it *Rhem. vet.*, or *1 Rhem.*, to distinguish it from another codex of the same church, but of more recent date.

The library of the archabbey of Saint-Remi at Rheims supplied us with three codices. We shall call the first, of larger format, *Remig. 1*; the following ones, *2* and *3*.

We had access to a notable codex of the Church of Beauvais through the efforts of the distinguished Dom Foy of Saint-Hilaire, a canon of that church, who throughout his life showed himself exceptionally devoted to letters and to all learned pursuits. The codex is seven hundred years old and contains the first twenty books of the *Morals*. In certain places it was corrected by a more recent hand—or rather corrupted; but we took account of the earlier reading, which can easily be recognized. Book XI is preceded by an index of chapters, whose divisions are taken from the passages of the book of Job that are explained. Certain arguments are added, concerning eternal fire, blessedness, the fear of God, and so forth. *Remigianus Codex 1* also presents certain summaries written in place of titles. The Beauvais codex will be designated in the apparatus by the initial letters *Bellov.*, or *Belvac.*

We excerpted variant readings for the first ten books of the *Morals* from two Corbie codices. Since they almost never differ from one another, both will be designated *Corb.* Another Corbie codex is often mentioned; since it is now preserved in the Library of Saint-Germain-des-Prés in Paris, it will be called *Corb. Germ.* The same Library of Saint-Germain provided us with a codex of excellent quality, whose designation will be given below as *Germanensis*.

There was formerly at the Dionysian Abbey near Paris a codex copied about eight hundred years ago. We call it *Colbertinus*, because it is now preserved in the celebrated Colbert Library.

From the Church of Laon we received for use two codices containing the books of the *Morals* from book XVII through the last book. They will be designated below *Laud. primus* and *Laud. secundus*.

We obtained the first six books and the same number of later books, together with books XX, XXI, and XXII, from the library of the monastery of Clairvaux, of the Cistercian order in the diocese of Laon. This was done with the permission of the most reverend abbot and through the favor of the equally learned and most courteous Dom de Noyville, the monastery’s highly vigilant provost, through whose assistance and labor we obtained many other materials for preparing our edition. We assign this codex the designation *Val. Clar.*

We found the first ten books of the *Morals*, together with the last eleven, in the monastery of Longpont, of the same Cistercian order. They are on parchment of excellent quality and are approximately six hundred years old. They will easily be distinguished from the others by the abbreviated name *Longipont.*

We used two codices of Saint-Corneille at Compiègne, one seven hundred years old and the other more recent. We shall call the older one *Compend. 1*, and the other *Compend. 2*.

We consulted, and examined for the most part, codices of the Royal Library in Paris, recommended more by elegance and beauty than by antiquity. One contains all the books of the *Morals*, another eighteen, a third only five, and a fourth—of much larger format and written in exceptionally elegant characters—only seventeen.

From a codex of the Church of Chartres, written in the tenth century, we sampled a few readings, since it did not differ from others that we had already read.

In the monastery of Saint Peter in the Chartres valley there is a codex of the *Morals* written eight hundred years ago. It is said to have been brought with him by Ardeus, dean of the Church of Chartres, later a monk in the monastery of Fleury, and subsequently sent from there to Chartres to restore the monastery of Saint Peter. We consulted it only in certain more important passages, because it is largely mutilated.

The library of the monastery of Fleury, once abundantly stocked with manuscripts, preserves three handwritten copies of the *Morals*, from which we excerpted a considerable number of variant readings.

From the Library of Saint-Martin of Tours we obtained an old copy of the same *Morals* for examination, through the sponsorship of the distinguished Dom de Galiczon, doctor and fellow of the Sorbonne, canon and precentor of that church, to whom letters owe a great deal.

From the codex of Saint-Albin at Angers we received many variant readings of the *Morals*, and inserted them into the new edition.

In the library of the monastery of Vendôme we found three extremely old handwritten codices of the *Morals*. The oldest contains the last thirteen books; another, the first twelve; the third, twenty-two. In one of them, each book is preceded by certain indexes of arguments or titles, as it were chapters, into which the books are divided. The same codex often presents a double reading; we observed the same in the Utica, Lyranus, and Bigot codices mentioned below.

But Normandy supplied us with a greater abundance of manuscript codices and a richer harvest of variant readings. It is chiefly in that province that this new edition was prepared.

We received the first fifteen books from the library of the Church of Bayeux, especially through the favor of the most illustrious and most reverend Bishop Henri de Nesmond. Since he was exceedingly devoted to the restoration of ecclesiastical discipline according to the teaching of Saint Gregory, he considered it necessary to ensure that the works of that holy Doctor should appear in corrected form.

We read all the books of the *Morals* in codices lent to us by the Church of Évreux, chiefly through the kindness of the distinguished gentlemen Dom Bitaut, dean; Petit, precentor; and Aubery, canon and librarian.

We collated the same books with various manuscripts of Saint Michael in Peril of the Sea, Saint-Martin-de-Sées, Saint-Evroul in the district of Utica, Notre-Dame de Lyre, Saint-Pierre de Conches, the monastery of Bec, Pratelles, and Jumièges. Almost all these codices appear to be seven hundred years old and are of excellent quality, especially those of Pratelles and Jumièges, which are outstanding in antiquity. We shall sometimes call the codices of Saint-Evroul “Uticenses,” after the district of Utica in which that monastery is situated. The Conches codex is now preserved in the celebrated Bigot Library at Rouen, from which we received it together with many others through the generosity of the distinguished Dom Bigot de Monville, an exceptionally upright senator of the supreme court of Normandy. For this reason we shall call it not *Conchense* but *Bigotianum*.

Thomas James supplied us with variant readings from eight English manuscripts in his *Gregorian Vindication*, but only a very few. Nevertheless, from them it is possible to understand that the handwritten codices of England do not differ from ours.

Finally, Dom Claude Estiennot sent us the variant readings of Roman and Vatican codices. We mourn his death in connection with this work and with many others undertaken for the benefit of the republic of letters.

### V

The zeal of Christians for the books of Saint Gregory’s *Morals* is no less proved by their frequent editions, from the time when the art of printing relieved copyists of their labors, than by the abundance of handwritten codices. It will be sufficient here to list only those editions that we used, whether the books were printed separately or together with other works of the holy Doctor. To enumerate them all would be an immense and unnecessary labor.

The oldest edition that we read is the Paris edition of 1495, produced under the care of Master Udalric Gering of Constance and Bercthold Rembolt of Strasbourg, partners residing at the Golden Sun in the Sorbonne quarter.

It was followed by many Paris editions: namely, that of 1518, with all of Saint Gregory’s works, prepared through the efforts of the same Rembolt—or another of the same name—in the house of Jean Petit; those of 1533, 1542, 1551, 1562, 1571, and 1575—the last two of which were produced through the work of the most learned Jean Gilot of Champagne—then those of 1586, 1605, 1619, 1640, and 1675, prepared by Gussanville.

The first Basel edition is that of 1496, followed shortly afterward by the edition printed in the workshop of Nicolaus Kesler in 1503. This was followed by the edition published in the same city at the expense and cost of Ludwig Horneken, bookseller and citizen of Cologne, but through the labor and care of Adam Petri of Langendorf, printer [perhaps *typographus*], on the day before the Kalends of February, 1514, from noble Basel, while our Savior, clothed in flesh, reigned. This edition does not appear to differ from the preceding Basel edition either in its text or in the division of its chapters. A fourth was published in 1551 and again in 1564, from the Froben press, under the care of Ulrich Coccius.

All the editions mentioned above are surpassed in age by the Roman edition of 1475, during the pontificate of Sixtus IV. It is prefaced by a brief preface of the bishop of Brescia, Dominicus. We have already spoken in the general preface of another Roman edition prepared by the bishop of Venosa.

We frequently used the Venetian edition of 1494, designated below by the abbreviated name *Barthol.*, because it was supervised by Bartholomew of Cremona, a canon regular. It was preceded by the earlier Venetian edition of 1480, which we did not encounter. We shall pass over the other editions produced at Lyon, Rouen, Douai, Antwerp, and elsewhere, so that we may explain more fully what we have accomplished in this latest edition.

### VI

First, by collating various manuscripts with great labor and no less fidelity, we restored, insofar as we were able, the pure text of Saint Gregory. Here is a specimen of the passages corrected by us in the first and second books; the limits of a preface do not permit us to examine all the books of the *Morals*.

In Book I, no. 17, the earlier reading concerning Christ was: “he took upon himself a humble death for him”; it should read “he took upon himself a humble mind,” etc.

In no. 18, the reading was: “which [the jubilee year], with a monad added, is fulfilled in the totality of our union,” where *totality* is redundant and changes the sense, as may be seen in the note on this passage.

In no. 20, the reading was: “we receive the weaker minds of the faithful, holding the faith of the Trinity.” We removed the last three words, which had been added against the manuscripts, as entirely superfluous; this is immediately evident to anyone reading what follows.

In no. 21, the earlier reading was: “the sons and daughters having been mentioned,” although in this passage only daughters should be mentioned.

In the same place, the corrupt reading was: “the entire depravity of the Gentiles,” instead of “the twistedness of the Gentiles,” a reading established by the manuscript codices and by what follows: “in the twisted and depraved ways of the former life.” Here earlier editors corruptly read *intortis* as one word.

In no. 22, instead of “in everything that they do”—a manner of speaking familiar to Gregory—the former reading was “that whole thing.”

In the next number, other printed editions read: “For what is it, by sitting, to come to Jerusalem on a donkey?” Here, contrary to the mind of the holy Doctor, Gussanville read “on a female donkey.”

In no. 31, the same editor has: “through them the grace of preaching is conveyed,” instead of “the grace of purification.”

In the same place, a more serious error occurs in the passage concerning Christ: “for although he knows all things, yet in himself he assumes our ignorance,” etc. This is wholly contrary to the doctrine of Saint Gregory, as we observed when correcting the passage. Therefore, following the manuscript codices, we restored: “But in his speech he assumes our ignorance.”

In no. 37, the former reading was: “which is abandoned through fear,” instead of “which is abandoned in the mind”; we restored the latter from the manuscripts.

In Book II, no. 9, the former corrupt reading was: “it is said to those who were present,” whereas it should read—both according to the manuscripts and according to the sequence of the discourse—“it is said to those who cling to it.”

No. 11 had been corrupted by the intrusion of “he utters a much greater voice into the ears of the circumscribed spirit,” instead of “of the uncircumscribed spirit,” that is, God.

In the same place, the reading was: “how are they said to desire vengeance?” instead of “how are they said to seek vengeance?”

In no. 13, where the reading is “we say that God lost in his proposition,” the word “victory” had been gratuitously added by other editors.

In no. 15, the same editors changed *addicat*, meaning “condemns,” into *addiscat*, “learns.”

In no. 19, contrary to the authority of the manuscripts and to the mind of the holy Doctor, the other printed editions add, after the words “he gives other things for testing,” the words “other things for afflicting.”

In no. 28, instead of “the blows of lashes,” the Gussanville edition has “the blows of words.”

In no. 35, the printed editions read: “he speaks of temporal things published,” carelessly adding *de*, “of,” which changes the sense.

In no. 49, the reading is “to think lofty thoughts,” instead of “to grasp.”

In no. 56, after the words “he lost the unity of concord,” the printed editions contain this long addition, rejected by the manuscripts and connected neither with what precedes nor with what follows: “and after his resurrection he concealed himself from certain people who would not believe.”

In no. 59, where the simple reading should be, “Therefore, when he appears conspicuous even to the Synagogue,” the editors changed it to: “Therefore, whenever he appears conspicuous, so that he may appear even to the Synagogue.”

In no. 60, the printed editions read “he receives everything,” instead of “he receives among everything”; and in no. 61, “in persecution,” instead of “in striking.”

In no. 76, the genuine reading, “the house is drawn out,” had been changed to “the house is overwhelmed.”

Finally, in no. 92, shortly before the end of the book, this sentence concerning the Holy Spirit—“Therefore the Spirit dwells in him in a dissimilar manner, from whom by nature he never departs”—had been read with this interpolation: “he dwells in him, to whom he substantially presents himself according to desire, and from whom,” etc.

For these restorations and emendations made by us, we have always appended an explanation in brief notes, often based on the agreement of the manuscripts. When the old copies disagree, it was sufficient for us to indicate certain variant readings that appeared to have some importance.

### VII

Second, we followed the division of this work into six parts instituted by the holy Doctor and observed in our manuscripts, but neglected in the printed editions and perhaps unknown to most editors. Saint Gregory speaks of this division in the letter to Leander that follows immediately:

> “I completed this work, extending through thirty-five volumes, in six codices.”

At the beginning of Book XI he says:

> “In the letter prefixed to the books, I explained why I did not bring the third part of this work to completion through correction in the same manner as the others.”

Finally, at the end of Book XVI:

> “I have passed over these matters briefly, as I remember promising at the beginning of the third part of this work.”

There is no need to confirm this with more numerous testimonies drawn either from Gregory himself or from other writers. Thus the first part, as can easily be understood from inspection of the manuscripts, contains the first five books. The second part contains the next five, through Book X. The third part begins with Book XI. The fourth begins with Book XVII, not Book XVIII, as it is erroneously stated in the Paris edition of 1518. The fifth begins with Book XXIII and ends with Book XXVII. Book XXVIII, together with the remaining books, belongs to the sixth part.

> [Note: [Col. 0505] In the Paris edition of 1518 there are some traces of this division. Before Book XI one reads: “The eleventh book of the entire work; it marks the third part of the moral exposition,” etc. At the beginning of Book XVIII: “The eighteenth moral book of Saint Gregory, and the fourth part of the entire work.” Finally, in the heading of Book XXIII: “The fifth part of the entire work.” No mention, however, is made of the first, second, or sixth parts.]

### VIII

Third, although we had intended to retain the division into chapters established by the editors who preceded us, we were compelled to change it for very serious reasons. It is acknowledged by everyone that Saint Gregory paid no attention to dividing the books of the *Morals* into chapters. Concerning the first author of the division into chapters, the following is read in the Colbert Codex marked 62, after the letter to Leander and the preface to the books of the *Morals*:

> “In the name of God the Father, and of our Lord Jesus Christ, and of the Holy Spirit. Here begins the prologue to the chapters of the *Morals* of the most venerable blessed Gregory, pope. Gregory, servant of Christ Jesus and most venerable pope of the city of Rome, composed and entitled many volumes of books. He also prefixed to the books a series of chapters. He made an exposition of the words of Job, but he did not add an arrangement of chapters corresponding to its several statements. Therefore, in the time of the emperor Henry II, the priest Rainerius, a canon of the Church of Arezzo, by vigilant study and reflection, placed chapter-headings beneath almost every statement of the exposition mentioned above—not for the favor of empty glory, but moved by zeal for divine love and by concern for readers, or even for those hearing readers—so that whatever useful thing anyone might seek for the moment in those statements, he might find quickly and, as it were, without labor.”

> [Note: [Col. 0505] Henry II began to reign in 1002, and this codex was not written later than that.]

In the earlier Paris editions, and in others either older or nearly contemporary, the books of the *Morals* were divided into various very brief sections, with no mention of chapters. The Basel edition of 1503 presents a division into chapters, which succeeding editors retained until Coccius. He, following another method of division, as he himself explains in his preface, established new chapters. This division continued in all the later printed editions.

What persuaded us to depart both from this method and from the one that preceded it was our observation that the same chapter often embraced entirely different subjects, or that one subject, which deserved a single chapter, was distributed among several. Examples in the older editions before Coccius are chapters 3, 4, and 5 of Book I. In the later editions, beginning with Coccius and continuing thereafter, chapters 3, 4, and 5 of the same book conclude the historical and literal explanation of the text of Job, and, with a change of style, begin the allegorical exposition at the words: “There was a man in the land of Uz,” etc., “we believe that these things happened historically,” etc.

Since neither method of assigning chapters pleased us, we adopted the method suggested by the verses of the book of Job, whether complete or partial, that the holy Doctor proposes to explain one by one. Thus, almost invariably, the beginning of the chapter is also the beginning of the paraphrase or explanation. Nevertheless, we took care to divide the text into smaller sections marked by numerals. We also placed the chapter divisions of the earlier editions in brackets, so that passages cited throughout the books according to those editions might easily be found. We call the editions older than the Coccius edition *Vet.*; the Coccius edition and those that followed it, *Rec.*

### IX

Fourth, we changed the chapter summaries almost everywhere, because they did not correspond to the text. An immediate example occurs in the summary of chapter 1 of the preface. The Paris edition of 1518 reads: “From what stock, or at what time, Job came,” and this continued in the later editions, including the Gussanville edition of 1675. Yet it does not represent Saint Gregory’s purpose at all. At this point he discusses the author of the book of Job: he asks whether it was Moses or another of the prophets, and finally teaches that the Holy Spirit alone is the author of this sacred book, although he used Job’s pen. We therefore judged that this should be expressed in the summary.

[Col. 0507]

Since in the earlier printed editions the summaries had until now been placed before the chapter headings in reverse order, we preferred to follow the custom ordinarily observed in publishing other books. We judged that the chapter should be given its title first, and that the subject treated in the assigned chapter should then be disclosed in a brief summary. In addition, whatever in the text seemed worthy of observation, we described briefly in the margin.

> [Note: [Col. 0507] We have expressed these marginal lists in the text in italic type. EDITOR.]

We also relegated brief notes to the foot of the columns, where we illustrated certain obscure passages not at all clear to less experienced readers. How ancient is the practice of writing in the outer margin summaries of matters more fully contained in the text is clear from Jerome’s Letter 101 to Pammachius. When Eusebius of Cremona asked him to translate a certain letter of Epiphanius into Latin, Jerome writes of the work as follows:

> “I did what he wished, and, summoning a notary, dictated rapidly and quickly, writing briefly in the margin of the page what sense each chapter contained within.”

Fifth, we removed as useless the long passages from the book of Job that contained entire chapters, since we found them in none of the manuscript books.

Sixth, we prefixed testimonies and commendations of ancient writers concerning the books of the *Morals*, adding some and removing others.

### X

We did not wish to remove from this edition the account of the discovery of the *Morals* by Tajon, bishop of Zaragoza, although it is not certain in every respect. We read it not only in all the older editions but also in the handwritten codex of the monastery of Longpont. There are many reasons for doubting the truth of this narrative.

First, it is said here that Saint Leander brought to Spain, to the see of Seville, the exposition of Job made by Saint Gregory. Yet it is clear that, at Leander’s request, it was sent by the holy Doctor through the priest Probinus, as is read in Book V, Letter 49. Moreover, how could it be proved that Saint Leander came to Rome while Saint Gregory was pope?

Second, in this account the Roman pontiff is simply called “the pope” and “the lord pope,” as though he already uniquely possessed that title at that time. We do not know sufficiently whether this usage reflects that period and antiquity.

Third, there is a letter from Tajon himself to Eugenius of Toledo, published by the distinguished Étienne Baluze in volume IV of the *Miscellanies* from the Colbert Codex. In it there is no mention of the miracle of the discovery of the *Morals*, although Tajon would have had an opportunity to mention it. Indeed, he denies ever having seen Gregory: “We saw,” he says, “our Gregory established at Rome, not with the eyes of the body, but with the gaze of the mind. We saw him not only in his notaries, but also in his intimates,” etc. Therefore, what the account of the discovery of the *Morals* says about Gregory’s having been seen by Tajon must be rejected.

Fourth, the statement in this account that Augustine occupies a higher place than any of the successors of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, among whom many martyrs are numbered, does not appear worthy of belief. On Tajon and the *Morals* discovered by him, one may read Mariana, *History*, Book VI, chapter 8, and Mabillon, volume II of the *Analecta*, p. 78.

Concerning the style of writing observed by Saint Gregory in the books of the *Morals*, nothing need be added beyond what we said above in the general preface. He is speaking chiefly of these books when he says at the end of his letter to Leander:

> “I do not avoid the collision of metacism; I do not shun the confusion of barbarism,” etc.

Here we conjectured that *metacism* could mean the frequent hyperbata, or transpositions of words, which occur both in the *Morals* and in Saint Gregory’s other works.

> [Note: [Col. 0507] See Book III, nos. 51 and 82; Book IV, nos. 10 and 18; Book V, no. 10; Book VII, no. 13; Book XXX, nos. 6 and 52; Book XXXI, no. 4; Book XXXIII, no. 25; Book XXXIV, no. 44. See what we said in the preface to the commentary on the First Book of Kings.]

Nevertheless, perhaps *metacism* should instead be understood, in the grammarians’ sense, as the frequent repetition of the letter *m*, which produces an unpleasant collision in speech, although we have not detected such repetitions in the *Morals*.

In column 767, a note reads “with the punctuation changed,” and adds: “This word, *punctuatio*, although less customary or even recently coined, will occasionally be required by necessity, lest circumlocutions be needed.” Nevertheless, since we encountered this word in the notes of Angelo Rocca on the *Book of Sacraments* and in similar writers, we afterward abstained from it and preferred *interpunctio*.

[Col. 0507]

## ON THE DISCOVERY OF THE BOOKS OF THE MORALS OF SAINT GREGORY (C, S)*

> [Note: [Col. 0507A] We collated this with the manuscript codex of the monastery of Blessed Mary at Longpont, of excellent quality and approximately six hundred years old, in which the following title is read: “How the books [Col. 0508A] of the *Morals* were discovered.” We also collated it with the old editions Basel 1514 and Paris 1518.]

[Col. 0507A] Blessed Pope Gregory expounded the Book of blessed Job at the request of Saint Leander, bishop of Seville, as can plainly be seen in the Prologue to the *Moralia*, and he handed the exposition over to him; Leander carried the completed work to Spain, to the see of Seville. The city of Seville is called *Sibilia* in the vernacular, and it is the metropolitan city of Spain. When blessed Leander died, Saint Isidore, his brother, an outstanding teacher, was made archbishop in his place. After Isidore’s death, the books of the *Moralia* that blessed Leander had brought were lost through such negligence that they could not be found anywhere in Spain. After some years, Cyndesindus [Ms., *Cyncynder*], king of Spain, summoned a council of thirty bishops in the city of Toledo. There, when a complaint had been made about the loss of the *Moralia*, the king, by unanimous decision of the bishops, sent the aforesaid Tagio, bishop of Zaragoza, to Rome with letters to the pope, to seek the same books [Ms., “sent Trajo … with his letters to request them”]. For Tagio [Ms., *Trajo*] was an exceedingly zealous lover of [Col. 0509A] divine Scripture. He therefore came to Rome, and after presenting the royal letters and gifts, when he saw that from day to day the pope kept postponing his request—as though, because of the multitude of other books, those he sought could not be found in the archive of the apostolic see—he finally asked that at least permission be granted him to spend one entire night watching and praying in the church of Saint Peter.

Having obtained this permission, while he earnestly entreated God that the outcome of his journey might at last prosper, behold, around midnight, as he remained absorbed in the fervor of prayer, he saw the whole church filled with immense light. Then he saw a great multitude of venerable men clothed in snow-white garments entering through the church door and proceeding in an orderly fashion, two by two, toward the altar [Col. 0509B] of Saint Peter. Terrified by extreme fear, and daring not to move from the place where he stood, he then saw two of them leave their company and come toward him. One of these, greeting him kindly, asked who he was, where and why he had come, and why he was keeping vigil there at that hour.

When the bishop had answered each question and related the whole reason for his journey and prayer, the newcomer pointed with his finger and said: “In that chest which you see are contained the books you seek.” Then, taking courage, the bishop said: “I beseech you, my lord, deign to disclose to me, your servant, who that most glorious procession of men is which I behold.” At once the other replied: “Those two whom you see going in front, embracing one another with their hands joined, [XXII] are the blessed apostles Peter and Paul. The others whom you see standing behind them are their successors, the pontiffs of this apostolic see. They follow them now in the same order in which they succeeded them in the episcopate. And just as they loved this Church during their life, so they love it now after death, and they frequently come to visit it.”

Then the bishop said: “I beg you, my lord, tell me who you yourself are.” He replied: “I am Gregory, for whose books you have endured the labor of so long a journey. Therefore I have now come to satisfy your request.” Then the bishop said: “I beseech you, my lord, if he is here, tell me which of these is blessed Father Augustine, whose books I have loved no less than yours.” He replied: “The place of greater height among us contains blessed Augustine, the outstanding man about whom you ask.” Having said this, he immediately returned with his companion, who had come with him, to the company of the others.

Afterward, in the bishop’s presence, all of them together reverently bowed their heads toward the altar of blessed Peter, returned to the church door in the same order in which they had come, and departed with the light he had previously seen. When morning came, the aforesaid bishop reported to the lord pope everything he had seen. Thus, after obtaining and copying the books of the *Moralia*, he carried them back to Spain. From that time onward he instituted that this vision should be noted beforehand and prefixed to them.

[Col. 0509]

# The Books of the *Moralia* of Saint Gregory the Great, Roman Pontiff, or Exposition of the Book of Blessed Job (C, S)

## Epistle

[Note: [Col. 0509D] Saint Isidore of Seville mentions this epistle in *On Illustrious Men of the Church*, chapter 27. “He also wrote,” he says, “some epistles to the aforesaid Leander, one of which is attached to the same books of Job under the title of a preface.” Hence it is called a preface or prologue in the Colbertine, Germanic, Norman, and other manuscripts; this may perhaps have been the reason why it was not entered in the Register of the epistles. Gregory himself testifies that the books of the *Moralia* were dedicated to Leander in these words: “Especially since I have written this very work for your Reverence” (*Book I, Epistle 41*).]

In it he explains the time, occasion, division, purpose, and manner of speaking and interpreting proper to his work.

## Chapter One

When the following work was begun, on what occasion, at whose urging, and what they requested.

[Col. 0509D]

### 1

To his most reverend and most holy brother Leander [Note: [Col. 0510D] The Rheims Church manuscript, written about nine hundred years ago, reads: “To Father Leander.” On Saint Leander, see *Dialogues*, Book III, chapter 31, and Gregory’s many letters to him. Mabillon included his eulogy in the first century of the Benedictines.] his fellow bishop, Gregory, servant of the servants of God.

Long ago, most blessed brother, when I knew you in the city of Constantinople, while the affairs of the apostolic see [Note: [Col. 0510D] That is, its business. *Rule of Saint Benedict*, chapter 51: “Brothers who depart to obtain some response,” that is, for some business. The same usage of the word ἀπόκρισις, “response,” prevailed among the Greeks. In the work of an uncertain author under the name of Athanasius, entitled *Instruction to Antiochus*, volume II of the new edition of Athanasius, p. 259, ἀποκρισιάριος τῆς μονῆς [Col. 0511D] is the person placed in charge of managing the monastery’s affairs. Moreover, the learned Quesnell maintains that Leo the Great was the first of the Roman pontiffs to have an *apocrisiarius* at Constantinople in his retinue, following the example of the bishop of Alexandria, on the basis of Epistle 86 of that same Saint Leo (see Quesnell’s Dissertation 1, on the year 453, no. 4, p. 314).] constrained me to give responses, and a delegation of the Visigoths, entrusted to you on matters of the faith [Col. 0511A] [Note: [Col. 0511D] Or “of the Visigoths,” as it is read in the more ancient manuscripts. These were the western Goths who occupied Spain and Narbonese Gaul. The Goths of the East were called Ostrogoths.], had brought you there, I disclosed to your ears everything about myself that displeased me: how I had long and far delayed the grace of conversion, and how, after I had been inspired by a heavenly longing [Note: [Col. 0511D] The printed editions, except Gussanville’s, read “to despise secular dress,” contrary to the testimony of all the manuscripts. Our reading is confirmed by John the Deacon, *Life of Saint Gregory*, Book I, chapter 4: “While prolonging the grace of his conversion for too long, he thought he would serve Christ more safely if, under the appearance of an urban praetor, he served the world outwardly.”] I thought it better to remain covered by secular dress (John the Deacon, Book I, chapter 27).

For the love of eternity was already opening before me what I should seek, but ingrained habit bound me, preventing me from changing my outward way of life. And while my mind still compelled me to serve the present world, as it were outwardly and in appearance only, many things began to grow against me from the same worldly concern, so that I was now held in it not merely outwardly but, what is more serious, in mind. Finally, fleeing all these things anxiously, I sought the harbor of the monastery and, abandoning what belongs to the world, escaped naked, as I then foolishly believed, from the shipwreck of this life.

For just as a rising storm can tear away a ship carelessly [Note: [Col. 0512D] Corbie and Vendôme manuscripts: “left behind.”] moored even from the bosom of the safest shore, so suddenly I found myself, under the pretext of ecclesiastical office, in the sea of secular affairs; and because I had not held firmly to the monastery’s quiet when I possessed it, I learned through losing it how carefully it ought to have been held. For when the virtue of obedience opposed my receiving the ministry of the sacred altar, I accepted under the guise of the Church what, if it could be done with impunity, might again be avoided by flight [Note: [Col. 0512D] Here most manuscripts have various readings. Two Rheims manuscripts, the second Remigius, and Lyra read: “that it be abandoned again in flight, that it be lamented again in flight.” Corbie and Colbert read: “that it be turned aside again in flight.”].

After this, although I was unwilling and resisted, since the ministry of the altar was burdensome, the weight of pastoral care was also imposed upon me. I now endure this so much more harshly because, recognizing myself unequal to it, I find no relief in any consolation of confidence. For since the times of the world have been thrown into confusion by the increase of evils as the end approaches, we ourselves, who are believed to serve the inner mysteries, are entangled in external cares. Thus, when I approached the ministry of the altar, this was done concerning me without my knowledge: I received the burden of sacred office so that I might keep watch more freely in the earthly palace. Many of my brothers from the monastery, bound by fraternal love, followed me there.

I perceive that this happened by divine dispensation, so that, whenever I was tossed by the unceasing thrust of secular affairs, I might always be fastened by their example to the peaceful shore of prayer, as by an anchor’s rope. To their company, as to the bosom of the safest harbor, I fled from the waves and whirlpools of earthly affairs [Note: [Col. 0512D] Coccius prefixed the particle *post* here; thereafter it prevailed, against the manuscripts and ancient editions.], and although that ministry, having drawn me away from the monastery, had extinguished the life of my former quiet by the sword of its occupation, nevertheless among them, through the conversation of diligent reading, the daily breath of compunction revived me.

Then those same brothers, at your urging as well, decided—as you yourself remember—that they should compel me by their insistent request to expound the Book of blessed Job, and that, insofar as truth supplied me with strength, I should disclose to them the mysteries of such profound depth. They added this also to the burden of their request: that I should not merely examine the words of the historical narrative through allegorical meanings, but immediately direct the allegorical meanings toward the practice of morality; and, adding something still more burdensome, that I should surround each point understood with testimonies, and, if the testimonies brought forward should perhaps seem obscure, clarify them by inserting an additional explanation.

## Chapter II

With what humility of spirit and confidence in God. How the same work was revised, completed, and divided. What meanings he seeks.

As soon as I realized that I was being drawn into this obscure work, hitherto unexamined by anyone before us, and into matters so great and so extraordinary, I confess that, overcome by the sheer burden of listening and wearied, I faltered and collapsed. But suddenly, caught between fear and devotion, when I raised the eyes of my mind toward the giver of gifts, I set hesitation aside and immediately attended with confidence, because it could not be impossible that which charity commanded me through the hearts of my brothers.

I despaired of being capable of such things; but, made stronger by that very despair of myself, I immediately raised my hope toward him through whom the tongue of the mute is opened, who makes the tongues of infants eloquent (Wisdom 10:21), who distinguished the immense and unmeasured braying of an ass into the intelligible forms of human speech [Note: [Col. 0512D] The first Remigius manuscript reads “the senseless and brutish”; Corbie has “mouths,” another Regius manuscript “roarings.” Here “immeasurable,” that is, without measure, is set against speech divided into distinct forms.]. What wonder, then, if he gives understanding to a foolish man, who, whenever he wishes, even speaks his truth through the mouths of beasts (Numbers 22:28)?

Strengthened, therefore, by consideration of this, I roused my dryness to investigate the spring of such profundity. And although the lives of those to whom I was compelled to expound these things far surpassed my own, I nevertheless did not think it improper if a leaden pipe supplied streams for human use. Thus, with those same brothers present before me, I first spoke the opening portions of the book before their eyes; and when I found somewhat more leisure, I dictated the later portions while working through them.

When broader intervals of time became available, adding much, removing little, and leaving some passages just as they had been found, I arranged in books by correction what had been taken down before their eyes while I was speaking. For, when I dictated the final portions, I carefully observed the style in which I had spoken the first. I therefore acted so that, passing over what I had said with careful revision, I might raise it, as it were, to the likeness of dictation; and so that what I had dictated would not differ greatly from the speech of one conversing. Thus, while the one form was extended and the other drawn together, the same subject, published in a different manner, might be fashioned in a corresponding form.

I scarcely revised a third part of this work at all after producing it in conversation, because, when the brothers drew me on to other matters, they did not wish this part to be corrected more carefully. While they were giving me many commands, and I wished to obey them now through the ministry of exposition, now through the ascent of contemplation, now through the instrument of morality, I completed this work, extending over thirty-five books, in six volumes. Hence I am often found in it almost to set aside the order of exposition, and to labor somewhat longer over the breadth [Note: [Col. 0513D] The second Rheims, Floriac, second Remigius, Regius, Michael, Saint-Albans manuscripts read *height*. This agrees with “the ascent of contemplation.” Here, however, since the method of extending the discourse and ranging through moral interpretations follows, *breadth*, found in the better manuscripts, seems preferable.] of contemplation and morality.

Nevertheless, whoever speaks about God must necessarily take care to seek whatever instructs the morals of his hearers, and must regard this as the proper order of speaking: if the opportunity for edification demands it, he should usefully turn aside from what he had begun to say. For the interpreter of sacred discourse ought to imitate the custom of a river. When a river flows through its channel, if it touches hollow valleys at its side, it immediately diverts the course of its current into them; and when it has sufficiently filled them, it suddenly pours itself back into its channel.

So, indeed, the interpreter of the divine word ought to act: when he is discussing any subject, if he should perhaps find, near at hand, an opportunity for suitable edification, he should turn the waves of his speech toward the neighboring valley; and when he has sufficiently flooded the field of instruction [Note: [Col. 0514D] Ebroic, Lyra, and Bigot read “of edification.”], he should return to the channel of the discourse he had begun.

## Chapter III

In what order he explains the several meanings. Allegory must sometimes necessarily be adhered to.

It must be understood that we pass rapidly over some matters by historical exposition; in others we investigate a typological meaning through allegory; some we examine solely through the instruments of allegorical morality; and still others we investigate more carefully through all these approaches together. For first we lay the foundations of history; then, through typological significance, we raise the structure of the mind into the citadel of faith; and finally, through the grace of morality, we clothe the building, as it were, with an added color.

Or surely, what are sayings of truth to be regarded as except nourishment for the restoration of the mind? By explaining them in varied ways, alternating the modes, we offer food to the mouth, so that we may drive away the distaste of the reader invited as our guest, who, while considering the many dishes set before him, may take up whichever he judges more elegant.

Sometimes, however, we neglect to explain the plain words of the history so that we may arrive more quickly at obscure matters. At other times they cannot be understood according to the letter, because, if accepted merely on the surface, they generate not instruction but error in their readers.

For example, it is said: “Under him those who carry the world are bowed down” (Job 9:13). And who, in regard to so great a man, does not know that he in no way follows the empty fables of poets, so as to suppose that the mass of the world is borne aloft by a giant’s labor? Again, oppressed by blows, he says: “My soul chose hanging, and my bones death” (Job 7:15). And what sensible person would believe that a man of such high praise—whom we know to have received rewards from the inward Judge for the virtue of his patience—decided, amid his blows, to end his life by hanging?

Sometimes, moreover, the very words of the text themselves oppose the possibility that they should be understood according to the letter. For he says: “Let the day perish on which I was born, and the night in which it was said: A man has been conceived” (Job 3:2). A little later he adds: “Let darkness seize it, and let it be enveloped in bitterness” (ibid., 5). And in the curse of that same night he continues: “Let that night be solitary” (ibid., 7).

That day of birth, having passed away through the very movement of time, could not stand still. How, then, could he wish it to be enveloped in darkness? Having slipped away, it no longer existed; and yet, if it continued in the nature of things, it could not feel bitterness. It is therefore clear that this is in no way said of an insensible day, when it is desired that it be struck by the sensation of bitterness. And if the night of conception had passed away joined to the other nights, how could he desire it to become solitary? Just as it could not be fixed after the passage of time, so it could not be separated from its conjunction with the other nights [Note: [Col. 0514D] The Norman, Saint-Albans, Floriac, and Colbert manuscripts read “bring forth.”].

Again he says: “How long will you not spare me, nor let me go, that I may swallow my saliva?” (Job 7:19). Yet a little earlier he had said: “What my soul did not wish to touch before, these are now my foods because of anguish” (Job 6:7). Who does not know that saliva can be swallowed more easily than food? Since, therefore, he declares that he takes food, it is exceedingly unbelievable that he denies being able to swallow saliva.

Again he says: “I have sinned; what shall I do to you, O guardian of mankind?” (Job 7:20), or: “You wish to consume me because of the sins of my youth” (Job 13:26). Yet in another reply he adds: “For my heart does not reproach me in all my life” (Job 27:6). How, then, is he not reproached at all by his own heart when he publicly testifies that he has sinned? The guilt of an action and the blamelessness of the heart can never occur together.

The words of the text, therefore, since they cannot agree when set beside one another, reveal that there is something else within them to be sought, as though they were saying in certain words: “While you see us destroyed by our surface meaning, seek in us that which, properly ordered and agreeing with itself, can be found within.”

## Chapter IV

Sometimes the literal sense must be adhered to.

At other times, whoever neglects to understand the historical words according to the letter conceals the light of truth offered to him; and, while laboriously seeking something else within them, loses what he could have attained without difficulty on the outside.
