For the holy man says: “If I denied the poor what they wanted, and made the eyes of the widow wait; if I ate my morsel alone, and the orphan did not eat of it; if I despised the passerby because he had no clothing, and the poor man without covering; if his sides did not bless me, and he was warmed by the fleeces of my sheep” (Job 31:16 and following).

If we violently bend these statements toward an allegorical meaning, we empty all the deeds of his mercy of their force. For the divine discourse, just as it exercises the wise through mysteries, so it often nourishes the simple through its surface meaning. In public it has food with which to nourish little ones; in secret it preserves what can suspend the minds of the lofty in wonder.

It is, so to speak, like a river both shallow and deep, in which a lamb may walk and an elephant swim. Thus, as the suitability of each passage requires, the order of exposition changes itself through careful study, so that it may discover the meaning of divine speech all the more truly as it varies according to whatever the subject requires.

## Chapter V

Gregory completed the following work while suffering from illness. He neglected the art of speaking. Which versions of Scripture he uses.

I have sent this exposition to your blessedness for revision—not because I owed it to you as something worthy, but because, since you requested it, I remember promising it. Whatever your holiness finds lukewarm or uncultivated in it, may you forgive me all the more quickly, since you know that I dictated it while ill.

For while illness wears down the body, the attentions of speech also grow weak in an afflicted mind [Note: [Col. 0515C] The printed editions read *afflicta*, “afflicted.” The manuscripts Regius, Corbie, Saint-Albans, and the first Vendôme more elegantly read *affecta*, “affected.” The second Vendôme has both readings.]. For many years now I have been tormented by frequent pains in my entrails; at every hour and moment I grow weary, broken by the weakened power of my stomach, and I gasp under slow but continuous fevers.

Meanwhile, as I anxiously consider that, according to the testimony of Scripture, “Every son who is received by God is scourged” (Hebrews 12:6), the more harshly I am weighed down by present evils, the more confidently I breathe in the hope of eternity [Note: [Col. 0515C] So the manuscripts read, except that Regius and Colbert have: “more certain of eternal consolation.” The printed editions read: “of eternal things.”]. And perhaps this was the purpose of divine providence: that I should expound Job, who had been struck, as one who was himself struck, and that I should better perceive the mind of one who had been scourged through my own scourges.

Yet it is clear to those who consider the matter rightly that bodily illness greatly obstructs the work of my study, because, while the strength of the flesh scarcely suffices to provide the service of speech, the mind cannot adequately express what it feels. For what is the body’s function except to be the instrument of the heart? And however skilled a singing artist may be, he cannot complete his art unless the external instruments cooperate with him in it. For the song commanded by the trained hand is not properly returned by damaged organs; nor does the breath express the art if a flute split by cracks gives a harsh sound.

How much more severely, then, is the quality of my exposition burdened, in which the brokenness of the instrument so dissipates the grace of speech that no art of skill can restore it? As you read through the sayings of this work, I ask you not to seek here the foliage of words, because throughout the sacred writings the lightness of unproductive talk is carefully restrained by their interpreters, while the planting of a grove in the temple of God is forbidden (Deuteronomy 16:21).

We all certainly know that whenever stalks of a badly flourishing crop grow among its leaves, the grains swell with lesser fullness in the ears. For this reason I have also neglected the very art of speaking that the disciplines of external instruction teach. As the tenor of this epistle itself declares, I do not avoid the collision of metacism, nor do I evade the confusion of barbarism; I do not care to preserve the arrangement and movement of words or the cases governed by prepositions, because I consider it exceedingly unworthy [Distinction 38, chapter “Indignum”] to restrict the words of the heavenly oracle under the rules of Donatus.

Nor were these things preserved by other interpreters in the authority of Holy Scripture. Since our exposition arises from it, it is surely fitting that, like offspring brought forth, it should imitate the appearance of its mother. I expound the new translation; but when the need for proof requires it, I draw upon testimonies sometimes from the new and sometimes from the old, so that, since the apostolic see over which I preside by God’s authority uses both, the labor of my study may likewise be supported by both.

## Preface

[Note: [Col. 0515D] In all the ancient manuscripts, the first part and Book I begin here, with no mention of a preface. That the holy Doctor nevertheless prefaced the work is clear from these words, which are to be read at the end [Col. 0516D]: “We have drawn out the words of the preface at length.”]

In it he briefly touches upon what is to be discussed throughout the whole work.

[Col. 0515]

# Chapter One

[Col. 0515D]

### 7. 1. Who wrote the Book of Job

Among many people it is often asked who should be regarded as the author of the Book of blessed Job. Some suspect that Moses was the author of this work; others, one of the prophets. For, since the Book of Genesis describes Jobab as descended from the stock of Esau and as succeeding Bale son of Beor in the kingdom (Genesis 36:33), they believed that this blessed Job lived long before the time of Moses. They plainly did not know the custom of sacred discourse: in its earlier sections it is accustomed to touch briefly upon events that will occur much later, when it is hastening on to enumerate other matters more carefully.

Thus Jobab is there remembered as having existed before kings arose in Israel. He is therefore by no means shown to have existed before the Law, since he is indicated as belonging to the time of the Israelite judges. When some people consider this less carefully, they suppose that Moses wrote an account of his deeds because Moses lived so much earlier; namely, they believe that the one who was able to publish the precepts of the Law for our instruction also transmitted to us examples of virtue from the history of a gentile man.

Others, as has been said, believe that one of the prophets was the author of this work, asserting that no one could have known such mystical words of God except one whose mind the spirit of prophecy had raised to heavenly things.

### 2. The Holy Spirit is the author

But it is very pointless to ask who wrote these things, when the Holy Spirit is nevertheless faithfully believed to be the author of the book. He, therefore, wrote these things who dictated what was to be written. He wrote them who was both the inspirer in that man’s work and, through the writer’s voice, transmitted his deeds to us for imitation.

If we were reading the words of a great man in letters he had received, but were asking with what pen they had been written, it would surely be ridiculous to know the author and understand the meaning of the letters while investigating with what pen their words had been impressed. Since, then, we know the matter and hold the Holy Spirit to be the author of that matter, when we seek the writer, what else are we doing except, while reading the letters, questioning the pen [Note: [Col. 0517D] Corbie, Rheims, Remigius, and most others read “we inquire.” The standard editions read “we investigate.”]?

### [Vet. II.] 3. Under whose inspiration Job described his struggles

We may nevertheless more truly suppose that blessed Job himself, who endured the struggles of spiritual combat, also narrated the deeds of his completed victory. Nor should it trouble us that the same book says, “Job said,” or, “Job endured this or that.” For it is the custom of sacred Scripture that those who write speak of themselves in it as though of others.

Thus Moses says: “Now Moses was the most gentle man above all the men who dwelt on the earth” (Numbers 12:3). Thus John says: “The disciple whom Jesus loved” (John 19:26). Thus Luke says: “Two of the disciples were walking on the road, Cleopas and another” (Luke 24:13); by deliberately keeping silent about this “other,” as some say, he showed that the other was himself.

The writers of sacred discourse, then, because they are moved by the impulse of the Holy Spirit, give testimony about themselves in it as though about others. Thus the Holy Spirit spoke through Moses about Moses; the Holy Spirit spoke through John about John. Paul likewise indicates that he was not speaking from himself when he says: “Do you seek proof of Christ who speaks in me?” (2 Corinthians 13:3).

For this reason the angel who is described as having appeared to Moses is sometimes called an angel and sometimes the Lord: an angel, because outwardly he served by speaking; the Lord, because, presiding inwardly, he supplied the efficacy of speech. When the speaker is directed from within, he is named an angel by his service and the Lord by his inspiration.

For this reason David says: “Attend, my people, to my law; incline your ear to the words of my mouth” (Psalm 77:1). It was not David’s law or David’s people; but, assuming the person of the one through whom he was speaking, he speaks with the authority of the one whose inspiration filled him.

We see this happening daily in the Church, if we observe attentively. A reader standing in the midst of the people cries out: “I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” (Exodus 3:6). He certainly does not truly say that he himself is God; yet by what he says he does not abandon the rule of truth, because by his voice he presents the dominion of the one for whom he performs the ministry of reading.

Thus the writers of sacred discourse, because they are filled with the Holy Spirit, are carried beyond themselves and become, as it were, outside themselves; and so they speak sentences about themselves as though about others. Hence blessed Job, inspired by the Holy Spirit, could write his own deeds—which were plainly gifts of heavenly inspiration—as though they were not his own. For what he spoke belonged to another insofar as a man was speaking what belongs to God; and he spoke what belonged to another insofar as the Holy Spirit was speaking what belongs to man.

# Chapter II [Vet. III]

### 9. 4. The precepts given to man

But now we must set these matters aside and hasten to consider the deeds of sacred history. Every human being, by the very fact that he is human, ought to understand his creator, and serve his will all the more faithfully the more he reflects that, of himself, he is nothing.

But behold: we neglected to consider God our creator. Precepts were given, and we refused to obey the precepts. Examples were added, and we shrink from imitating those examples, which we see were performed by those placed under the Law [Note: [Col. 0517D] Gilot, Vatican, and Gussanville read “set before us who have been placed under the Law.” We have emended the text on the basis of the manuscripts, supported by this consideration: Saint Gregory is speaking of Christians who, placed under the Gospel, avoid the examples of the saints who were placed under the Law. Nevertheless, this is an ancient reading, for in the Utica manuscript, or that of Saint-Ebrulf, one finds *positis* and *positos*.].

Because God spoke openly to certain people placed under the Law, we regard ourselves as strangers to those same precepts, since he did not speak these things specifically to us. Therefore, to refute our shamelessness, a gentile is brought forward as an example: since a person under the Law disdains to obey the Law, let him at least be roused by comparison with one who lived lawfully without the Law.

The Law was therefore given to a man who had gone astray; and to the man who had gone astray even while under the Law, testimony is brought forward from those who were outside the Law. Thus, because we refused to preserve the order proper to our condition, we might be admonished by precepts; and because we scorned obedience to precepts, we might be put to shame by examples—not, as has been said, by the examples of those whom the Law bound, but of those whom no law restrained from sin.

[Col. 0518D]

### 5. The example of Job, a gentile man, added for one who despises the precepts

Divine providence has hemmed us in; it has surrounded our excuse. Every avenue of human evasion has been closed. A gentile man, a man without the Law, is brought into the midst so that the perversity of those who are under the Law may be put to shame.

This is aptly and briefly shown by the prophet’s words: “Be ashamed, Sidon, says the sea” (Isaiah 23:4). In Sidon is represented the stability of those placed under the Law; in the sea, the life of the gentiles.

“Be ashamed, Sidon, says the sea,” because the life under the Law is reproved by the life of the gentiles, and the conduct of religious people is put to shame by the conduct of secular people: the former do not keep, even when they promise, what they hear in the precepts, while the latter, by their way of life, keep things by which they are in no way bound by legal commandments [Vet. IV].

The very authority with which this book is endowed is attested by the solidity of the sacred pages, when it is said through the prophet Ezekiel (Ezekiel 14:14) that only three men will be saved: Noah, Daniel, and Job.

Nor is it without reason that, among the lives of the Hebrews, the life of a righteous gentile is brought forward for the reverence of authority. For just as our Redeemer came for the redemption of Jews and gentiles, so he wished himself to be foretold by the voices of Jews and gentiles, so that he who would one day suffer for both peoples might be proclaimed through both peoples.

[Col. 0519B] **6. His virtue, the more fragrant because it was crushed by blows.**—This man, therefore, supported by the greatest strength, was known to himself and to God; if he had not been scourged, he would in no way have been known by us. His virtue indeed exercised itself even in repose, but the reputation of his virtue, stirred by blows, gave off its fragrance. While at rest he contained within himself what he was, when shaken he scattered the aroma of his strength for all to know.

For perfumes do not spread their scent widely unless they are stirred, and spices do not release their fragrance unless they are burned. So holy men become known in tribulations for everything with which their virtues give off fragrance. Hence it is rightly said in the Gospel: “If you have faith like a grain of mustard seed, you will say to this mountain, ‘Move from here,’ and it will move” (Matt. XVII, 19). A mustard seed, unless it is crushed, does not reveal the power of its virtue. When uncrushed, it is mild; but when crushed, it grows hot and displays what exceedingly sharp quality lay hidden within it.

So every holy man, when he is not struck, appears contemptible and mild; but if the grinding of persecution presses upon him, he immediately displays everything that has a fiery savor. Whatever in him previously seemed contemptible and weak is turned into the heat of virtue; and what he had willingly concealed during times of tranquility becomes known when, driven by tribulations, he is compelled to reveal it. Hence the prophet rightly says:

> “By day the Lord commanded his mercy, and by night he declared it” (Ps. XLI, 9).

[Note: Thus the Rhemish, Remigius, Corbie, Bayeux, and other manuscripts. The printed editions of Gilot, the Vatican, and Gussanville instead read: “In the day he will command … he will declare.”]

The Lord’s mercy is commanded by day because it is perceived through knowledge in a time of peace; but it is declared by night because the gift received in tranquility is manifested in tribulations.

## CHAPTER III [Vet. V]

**7. Job’s virtues are enumerated.**—But we must examine more subtly why he endured so many scourges, although he preserved such great guardianship of the virtues without reproach. He possessed humility, as he himself testifies: “If I have refused to enter into judgment with my servant and my maidservant when they contended against me” (Job XXXI, 13).

[Note: The manuscripts of Évreux read, “when they contended.” The Hebrew word means “to litigate.”]

He displayed hospitality, as he himself declares: “The stranger did not remain outside; my door was open to the traveler” (Job XXXI, 32). He maintained the vigor of discipline, as he himself indicates: “The princes ceased speaking and placed their finger upon their mouth” (Job XXIX, 9). He guarded gentleness within strength, as he himself admits: “And when I sat like a king, with the army standing around me, I was nevertheless a comforter of the sorrowful” (ibid., 25). He embraced generosity in almsgiving, as he himself suggests: “If I ate my morsel alone, and the orphan did not eat of it” (Job XXXI, 17).

Since, therefore, he fulfilled all the commands of virtue, one thing was lacking: that he should also know how to give thanks when scourged. It was known that he had learned to serve God amid gifts; but it was fitting that the severity of discipline should test whether he would remain devoted to God even amid blows. Punishment asks whether someone truly loves when at peace. The enemy asked that he might fail, but received him so that he might advance. The Lord kindly permitted what the devil wickedly requested. For although the enemy had sought him in order to destroy him, by tempting him he acted so as to increase his merits.

For it is written: “In all this Job did not sin with his lips” (Job I, 22). Some of his words in reply do indeed sound harsh to inexperienced readers, because they do not know how to understand the sayings of the saints piously as they are spoken. Since they cannot take upon themselves the mind of one who is suffering and yet just, they are therefore unable to interpret the words of his grief correctly. Compassion born of suffering knows how to weigh rightly the mind of the one who suffers.

**8. He is acquitted by God’s judgment from the accusations of the inexperienced.**—They therefore believe that blessed Job sinned in his speeches, because they look less carefully into the matter. For if they condemn the replies of blessed Job, they also testify that the Lord’s judgment concerning him was false. The Lord says to the devil:

> “Have you considered my servant Job, that there is none like him on the earth: a simple and upright man, fearing God and turning away from evil?” (v. 8).

The devil immediately answers him:

> “Does Job worship God for nothing? Have you not fenced him around, together with his whole household? But stretch out your hand and touch him, and see whether he will not bless you to your face” (v. 10).

[Note: The printed editions, following the Vulgate, read “and his whole substance”; the manuscripts read “his household.”]

The enemy therefore exercised his strength against blessed Job, but nevertheless undertook battle against God. Blessed Job was placed between God and the devil as the material of the contest. [Vet. VI.] Whoever, then, asserts that the holy man, placed amid scourges, sinned in his words—what else does he do than accuse God, who had proposed to contend on his behalf, of having been defeated? For God himself chose to take upon himself the cause of the one who was being tested: he had preferred him even before the scourges and, in preferring him, permitted him to be tested through scourges.

If Job is said to have gone too far, his praiser is said to have succumbed, although even the gifts bestowed upon him testify that he did not sin at all. For who does not know that rewards, not punishments, are owed to faults? Since, therefore, he deserved to receive double what he had lost, his recompense teaches that everything he said was not vice but virtue.

This assertion is further supported by the fact that he intercedes for his sinful friends. When someone is placed in grave sins, “he who is weighed down by his own sins does not wash away those of another” (Cause 3, q. 7, c. *In gravibus*). Job is therefore shown to be clean in himself, since he was able to obtain cleansing for others.

If it displeases some that he himself recounted his good deeds, they should know that, amid the loss of so many possessions, the wounds of his body, and the deaths of his children, when his friends came to console him but broke out into reproaches, he was driven to despair of his own life; and he whom so many losses had afflicted was also struck by the insulting words of his reprovers.

[Note: The Carnutian manuscript adds: “of the friends who came to him”; this perhaps entered from the margin.]

Those who had come to console him, while reproaching him as though he were guilty of injustice, forced him to despair completely of himself. When, therefore, he recalls his good deeds, he does not exalt himself through boastfulness; rather, as though fallen amid words and wounds, he restores his mind to hope.

For the mind is struck by the grievous weapon of despair when it is pressed by the tribulations of heavenly anger and harried outwardly by the insults of tongues.

[Note: The printed editions read *desperationis stimulo* (“by the goad of despair”), instead of *telo* (“by the weapon”), which is found in almost all the manuscripts.]

[Note: The Colbert manuscript reads, “when he is afflicted from above”; two manuscripts of Vendôme read, “when he is pressed by the retributions of evils for good deeds.”]

Blessed Job, therefore, pierced by so many darts of grief, feared that he might be shaken by reproaches, and recalled himself to a firm state of confidence by strengthening himself through his former life. He did not fall into the vice of arrogance, because he fought against the inward assault of despair with the outward words of his own praises. By saying what good things he had done, he did not despair of the good that he had sought.

[Note: Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions instead read, “into the vice of boastfulness.”]

[Note: Thus Bartholomew’s edition together with the manuscripts. The Vatican and Gussanville read, “of what he had foreknown”; the old Paris and Basel editions, together with Gilot, read, “of both what he had sought.”]

## CHAPTER IV [Vet. VII]

**9. All Satan’s devices are raised against Job.**—But now let us follow the very order of his temptation. The raging enemy, striving to conquer the exceedingly strong breast of the holy man, raised against him every engine of temptation: he took away his possessions, killed his children, struck his body, incited his wife, and brought his friends to console him, but stirred them to the harshness of reproach. He also reserved another friend, more severe in reproving him, for the final and sharper attack, so that by striking his heart more repeatedly he might touch it with a wound that was always renewed.

Because he saw that Job was powerful in the world, he thought that he could move him through the loss of his possessions; but when he saw that the death of his children had not shaken him, he struck him with bereavement. Seeing that even through the wound of bereavement he had grown toward the increase of divine praise, he asked that the health of his body should be struck. And when he perceived that through bodily pain he could not reach the suffering of his mind, he incited his wife.

He saw that the city he desired to conquer was exceedingly well fortified. Therefore, inflicting so many blows from outside, he brought his army, as it were, up to the walls; but by inflaming the mind of Job’s wife with words of evil persuasion, he corrupted the hearts of the citizens within. From external wars we learn what to think about internal ones. When a raging enemy surrounds a city with armies and, seeing its defenses unconquered, turns to other strategies of attack in order to corrupt the hearts of some citizens within, he acts so that, while bringing attackers from outside, he may also have internal accomplices; and, as the battle outside grows, the city may be captured because it has been deprived of the loyalty of those within whom it trusted.

**10. He employed war outside and poisonous counsels within.**—Thus, having set up a battering ram outside, he struck the wall of this city with as many blows as there were reports of calamity. Within, he corrupted the hearts of its citizens, striving to destroy the strong defenses of this city through the persuasion of its wife. He therefore brought the assault of war from outside and the poison of counsel from within, so that he might capture the city more quickly by disturbing it both outwardly and inwardly. [Vet. VIII.]

Since words sometimes disturb more than wounds, he armed himself, as has been said, with the tongues of Job’s friends. Because they were older men, their words could perhaps cause less pain.

[Note: Some editions read *dolere* (“to grieve”), as do Gilot, the Vatican, and Gussanville.]

Elihu, the younger, is brought forward so that he might strike the holy breast with a sharper wound, insofar as he raised against it a blow from a more contemptible arm.

[Note: Thus the English, Norman, and almost all other manuscripts. The Basel edition of 1514 and those following it, except Gussanville, read “a blow from a stronger arm.” Another manuscript of Remigius has “a blow from a younger arm.” The reading may have arisen because Elihu, mentioned shortly before, was younger.]

Behold how many darts of temptation the raging enemy found with which to strike invincible strength; behold how many engines of siege he set around it; behold how many weapons of assault he sent through. Yet amid all these things the mind remained undaunted and the city stood unshaken.

## CHAPTER V

[Col. 0522C] **11. Job’s patience amid adversity.**—Enemies customarily send others from concealment when they approach face-to-face, so that those hidden assailants may strike the flank of the fighter more freely while he watches the advancing enemies more intently before him. [Rec. V.]

Job, therefore, caught in the battle of this conflict, received his losses as enemies before his face; he endured the words of his consolers as enemies attacking from the side. But, having turned everywhere the shield of his dignity, he stood fortified on every side and vigilantly met the swords coming from all directions. He silently despised the loss of his possessions; he grieved with equanimity over the death of his children; he patiently endured the wound inflicted upon himself; and he wisely instructed his wife when she gave evil counsel.

In addition, his friends launched into harsh correction; they had come to calm his grief but added force to it. Thus all the engines of temptation were turned for the holy man into an increase of virtue. His patience was tested through wounds, and his wisdom exercised through words. He met everything courageously, because he overcame the scourges by strength and the words by reason.

His friends, who came indeed to console him but exceeded the bounds into words of reproach, should be regarded as having sinned more through ignorance than malice. For we should not believe that so great a man had wicked friends; rather, because they were unable to discern the cause of his scourges, they slipped into guilt.

[**Vet. IX.**] **12. Different kinds of blows.**—There are different kinds of blows. One is the blow by which a sinner is struck so that he may be punished without reprieve; another, by which a sinner is struck so that he may be corrected; another, by which someone is sometimes struck, not so that he may correct past faults, but so that he may not commit future ones; another, by which someone is often struck, neither to correct a past fault nor to prevent a future one, but so that, when unexpected salvation follows the blow, the power of the one who saves may be recognized and loved more ardently, and so that, when an innocent person is worn down by the scourge, the highest measure of his merits may be increased through patience.

Sometimes a sinner is struck so that he may be punished without reprieve, as is said to doomed Judah: “I have struck you with the wound of an enemy, with cruel correction” (Jer. XXX, 14). And again: “Why do you cry out over your affliction? Your pain is incurable” (ibid., 15).

Sometimes a sinner is struck so that he may be corrected, as is said to someone in the Gospel: “Behold, you have been made well; now do not sin, lest something worse happen to you” (John V, 14). The words of the Savior indicate that the preceding sins demanded the force of the pain he had suffered.

Sometimes someone is struck not to erase a past fault but to prevent a future one. The Apostle Paul openly testifies to this concerning himself:

> “Lest the greatness of the revelations should exalt me, a thorn in my flesh was given to me, an angel of Satan, to buffet me” (II Cor. XII, 7).

By saying not “because it exalted me” but “lest it should exalt me,” he clearly indicates that this blow restrained what might occur, rather than cleansing a fault that had occurred.

Sometimes, however, someone is struck neither for a past nor for a future iniquity, but so that the power of divine virtue alone may be displayed through the removal of the blow. Thus, when the disciples asked the Lord concerning the man born blind, “Did this man sin, or his parents, that he should be born blind?” (John IX, 2), the Lord answered:

> “Neither did this man sin, nor his parents; but that the works of God might be manifested in him” (ibid., 3).

[Note: Thus the old edition together with the Corbie, Rheims, Remigius, Colbert, German, and most other manuscripts. The Évreux manuscript reads: “What sin did this man commit, or his parents?” Coccius’s edition and those following it read: “Who sinned, this man or his parents?”]

[Note: Two manuscripts of Rheims, two of Remigius, and two of Vendôme add “of God.”]

What happens in this manifestation except that the power of merits is increased through the scourge, and that, when no past iniquity is erased, great strength is generated from patience?

Hence blessed Job himself is first preferred by the voice of the Judge and then handed over to the hand of the tempter. After the scourge, when God rewards him and speaks to him more familiarly, it is clearly shown how much he had grown through the blow.

Job’s friends, therefore, because they did not know how to distinguish the kinds of blows, believed that he had been struck on account of guilt. While attempting to assert that God was just in his striking, they were compelled to condemn blessed Job as unjust, not knowing that he had been scourged so that the praise of divine glory might grow through his scourge, not so that sins he had never committed might be corrected through scourges.

Hence they return more quickly to forgiveness, because they sinned through ignorance rather than malice. Divine justice humbles their pride all the more severely by restoring them to his grace only through the one whom they had despised. A mind that has risen very high is thoroughly humbled when it is subjected to the very person over whom it exalted itself.

## CHAPTER VI [Vet. X]

**13. All the saints, like stars, illuminate the night of the present life.**—Amid these wonderful works of divine dispensation, it is pleasing to observe how the several stars appear in turn upon the face of heaven to illuminate the night of the present life, until, at the end of the night, the Redeemer of the human race rises like the true morning star.

The span of night, illuminated by the courses of stars that set and rise, is completed with great beauty in the heavens. Therefore, so that the ray of the stars, appearing in its own time and succeeding one another in turn, might touch the darkness of our night:

- Abel came to display innocence.
- Enoch came to teach purity of action.
- Noah came to suggest perseverance in hope and work.
- Abraham came to manifest obedience.
- Isaac came to demonstrate chastity in married life.
- Jacob came to suggest endurance in labor.
- Joseph came to repay good in return for evil.
- Moses came to display gentleness.
- Joshua came to teach confidence against adversity.
- Job came to display patience amid scourges.

[Note: Gussanville reads “to restore”; the reading is corrected from another edition and the manuscripts.]

Behold how brightly shining stars we see in heaven, so that we may walk with an unimpeded step along the path of our night. For divine providence has presented to human knowledge as many righteous persons as though it had set as many stars in the heaven above the darkness of sinners, until the true morning star should rise.

[Note: In Gussanville the word *verus* (“true”) had dropped out. We have supplied it from the manuscripts and other printed editions.]

He would announce eternal morning to us and shine more brightly in divinity than all the other stars.

**14. All announced Christ beforehand, and Job especially.**—All the elect, by going before him through good living, proclaimed him beforehand both in deeds and in words. For there was no righteous person who did not become, in figure, his herald. It was fitting that all should display in themselves the good from whom all good people derive their goodness and which they knew would benefit everyone.

Therefore it was necessary that the one who was both received without measure and retained without end should be promised without ceasing, so that all the ages together might declare what the end of the ages would reveal in the common redemption.

[Note: The editions, with the Colbert manuscript and some others, read *saecula discerent* (“the ages might learn”). We prefer *dicerent* (“might declare”), with two Rheims manuscripts, Remigius, one Vendôme manuscript, Corbie, and German manuscripts—especially because Job is shortly thereafter said to signify in his conduct the one whom he would proclaim by voice. Gussanville erroneously reads “by conversion” in that latter phrase.]

Thus it was also necessary that blessed Job, who brought forth such great mysteries of Christ’s incarnation, should signify through his life the one whom he proclaimed with his voice; and that, through what he endured, he should show what Christ would suffer. He foretold the mysteries of that passion all the more truly because he prophesied them not only by speaking but also by suffering.

[**Vet. XI.**] Since our Redeemer presented himself as one person with the holy Church whom he assumed—for it is said of him, “who is the head of us all” (Eph. IV, 15), and it is written of his Church, “the body of Christ, which is the Church” (Col. I, 24)—whoever signifies him in himself designates now the head, now the body, so that he preserves not only the voice of the head but also that of the body.

Hence the prophet Isaiah, expressing the words of the same Lord, says:

> “He has placed upon me a mitre like a bridegroom, and adorned me with an ornament like a bride” (Isa. LXI, 10).

Since he himself is the bridegroom in the head and the bride in the body, whenever something is said about the head, it is necessary that the voice should gradually and suddenly pass also to the body; and, again, when something is said about the body, it should suddenly rise to the voice of the head.

[**Vet. XII.**] Blessed Job therefore prefigures the coming Redeemer together with his body. His wife, who urges him to curse, signifies the life of carnal people who, placed within the holy Church with uncorrected morals, are close to the good by faith but oppress them more harshly by their life. Since, as professed believers, they cannot be avoided, they are endured by the faithful all the more painfully because they are also within.

**15. Job’s friends prefigure heretics.**—His friends, who offer advice while attacking him, express the figure of heretics, who under the appearance of giving counsel carry on the business of seduction. Thus they speak to blessed Job as though on behalf of the Lord, yet they are not approved by the Lord, because all heretics, while striving to defend God, offend him.

Hence the holy man himself openly says to them:

> “I desire to dispute with God, first showing you to be fabricators of lies and worshipers of perverse doctrines” (Job XIII, 3–4).

It is therefore clear that those whom the holy man reproves for serving the worship of perverse doctrines bear, through their error, the type of heretics.

[**Rec. VII.**] Every heretic, in appearing to defend God, opposes his truth, as the Psalmist testifies:

> “That you may destroy the enemy and the defender” (Ps. VIII, 3).

[Note: Coccius, followed by all later editions, reads—without support from any manuscript—“who attacks by his conduct the God whom he preaches.” The present passage does not concern corrupt conduct, but the bad faith of those who assume the appearance of giving counsel while carrying on the business of seduction.]

He is both enemy and defender who attacks the God whom he proclaims.

## CHAPTER VII

[Col. 0525D] **16. Job signifies Christ by his name, and his friends signify heretics.**—That blessed Job bears the figure of the coming Redeemer is also demonstrated by his name. *Job* is interpreted as “one who grieves.” By this grief either the passion of the Mediator or the labor of the holy Church is expressed, for she is afflicted by the manifold weariness of the present life.

His friends likewise indicate by the meaning of their names the character of their deeds. *Eliphaz* is said in Latin to mean “contempt of the Lord.” And what else do heretics do except, while holding false opinions about God, despise him in their pride?

[Note: Rheims, Remigius, Colbert, Baldac, and Corbie read *Baldach* rather than *Baldad*.]

*Baldad* is interpreted as “mere antiquity.” All heretics are rightly called “mere antiquity” in what they say about God, because they seek to appear as preachers not through right intention but through the pursuit of temporal glory. They are stirred to speak not by the zeal of the new man but by the perversity of the old life.

*Sophar* is likewise said in Latin to mean “the dispersal of the watchtower,” or “one who disperses the watchtower.”

[Note: One manuscript of Rheims, one of Remigius, and one of Regensburg read “or one who disperses the watch.” Two manuscripts of Vendôme give both readings.]

The minds of the faithful raise themselves to contemplate heavenly things; but when heretics seek to pervert those who contemplate what is right, they attempt to disperse the watchtower.

[**Vet. XIII.**] In the three names of Job’s friends, three falls leading to the destruction of heretical minds are expressed. Unless they despised God, they would not think perversely about him; and unless they drew their hearts toward antiquity, they would not err in understanding the new life; and unless they destroyed the contemplation of good things, heavenly judgments would not reject them with such strict examination for the fault of their words.

[Note: Thus read the manuscripts of Beauvais, Compiègne, Corbie, the first Évreux, the first Remigius, Rheims, and the German manuscript. The Colbert manuscript comes close, but incorrectly reads *vetustatis contraherent*. One Regensburg manuscript reads *vetustatis vitium contraherent*; another, like Bartholomew’s edition, reads *vetustates contraherent*. The Utica manuscript gives both *vetustatis cor traherent* and *vetustates contraherent*. The Basel edition of 1514 and later editions read *nisi vetustatis prava verba elate loquendo contraherent*. Gilot and subsequent editions further have: *Et nisi in se [lacuna] destr[lacuna] superna justitia [lacuna] reprobaret*.]

By despising God, they remain in antiquity; but by remaining in antiquity, they harm the contemplation of the upright through their perverse speeches.

## CHAPTER VIII

**17. The conversion of heretics is represented in the reconciliation of Job’s friends.**—Since heretics are sometimes flooded with the abundance of divine grace and return to the unity of the holy Church, this is well signified by the reconciliation of Job’s friends.

Yet blessed Job is commanded to pray for them, because the sacrifices of heretics cannot be acceptable to God unless they are offered for them by the hands of the universal Church, so that they may find the remedy of salvation through the merits of the Church whom they had attacked with the darts of their words.

Hence seven sacrifices are said to have been offered for them, because, when they confess and receive the sevenfold Spirit of grace, they are cleansed, as it were, by seven offerings. Thus in John’s Apocalypse the universal Church is signified by the number seven churches (Apoc. I, 11). Thus through Solomon it is said of Wisdom:

> “Wisdom has built her house; she has hewn out her seven pillars” (Prov. IX, 1).

By the very number of the sacrifices, therefore, the reconciled heretics reveal what they formerly were: they are joined to the perfection of sevenfold grace only by returning.

**18. Their pride must be slaughtered so that they may be restored to the Church through this sacrifice.**—They are rightly described as offering bulls and rams for themselves. In the bull, the neck of pride is signified; in the ram, the leadership of the flocks that follow.

What, then, is it to slaughter bulls and rams for them except to kill their proud leadership, so that they may think humbly of themselves and no longer seduce the hearts of the innocent after them? With an inflated neck they had recoiled from the unity of the Church and dragged weak peoples behind them like following flocks.

Let them therefore come to blessed Job—that is, return to the Church—and offer bulls and rams to be slaughtered in a sevenfold sacrifice.

[Note: One manuscript of Remigius reads: “For, in order that they may be joined … it is necessary that they should be killed through humility.”]

In order that they may be joined to the universal Church, let them, with humility intervening, kill whatever previously tasted proud in their leadership.

## CHAPTER IX

**19. The proud person, though holding correct opinions, must be reproved. Why he does not require a sacrifice.**—Through Elihu, who speaks with correct understanding but turns toward foolish words of exaltation, the person of every arrogant man is represented.

Many who are placed within the holy Church disdain to express rightly the sound things they know. They are therefore reproved in the words of divine correction, yet no sacrifice is offered for them, because they are faithful but arrogant. Through the truth of their belief they are within; but through the obstacle of their pride they are not acceptable.

Correction therefore reproves them, but sacrifice does not restore them, because they possess the faith in which they ought to be, while heavenly justice, reproving them for their excesses, rejects them.

Hence Elihu is rightly said in Latin to mean “This is my God,” or “God the Lord.”

[Note: Bartholomew, Remb, Coccius, and the Basel edition of 1514 add *meus* (“my”) here.]

Arrogant men within the holy Church, although they reject God through their proud way of life, nevertheless confess him truly through their belief. For what does it mean to say, “This is my God,” by the name itself, except openly to display the one in whom one has believed? Or what does it mean to say “God the Lord” except to believe that he is God through his divinity and to acknowledge him as Lord through his incarnation?

## CHAPTER X [Vet. XIV]

**20. What Job’s receiving double signifies. The saints have one blessedness before the resurrection and a double blessedness afterward.**—After the loss of his possessions, the deaths of his children, the torments of his wounds, and the battles and conflicts of words, he is rightly raised up through a double reward. For the holy Church, still placed in this life, receives double gifts for the labors she endures when, after fully receiving the Gentiles, she converts to herself at the end of the world the hearts of the Jews as well.

[Note: The word *munera* (“gifts”), omitted in the Vatican and Gussanville editions, is restored from the manuscripts and the older printed editions.]

For it is written:

> “Until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter, and so all Israel should be saved” (Rom. XI, 25).

She will also receive double afterward, because, when the labor of the present age is finished, she will rise not only to the joy of souls but also to the blessedness of bodies. Hence the prophet rightly says:

> “In their land they shall possess double” (Isa. LXI, 7).

The saints possess double in the land of the living, because they rejoice in blessedness of mind and body together.

Hence John, in the Apocalypse, because he saw the souls of the saints crying out before the resurrection of their bodies, perceived that they had received single robes, saying:

> “And single white robes were given to each of them, and it was said to them that they should rest for a little while longer, until the number of their fellow servants and brothers should be fulfilled” (Apoc. VI, 11).

[Note: A noteworthy passage for proving the blessedness of the saints before the final day of judgment. Bernard and many others explain this passage of the Apocalypse in the same way.]

Before the resurrection they are said to have received single robes because they still enjoy only the blessedness of the mind. They will therefore receive two when, together with the perfect joy of their souls, they are clothed also in the incorruption of their bodies.

**21. Affliction here is certain; how long it will last is uncertain.**—It is rightly said that blessed Job was afflicted, but the length of time of his affliction is left unstated. For the tribulation of the holy Church is visible in this life, but it is unknown for how long she will be crushed and delayed here.

Hence the Truth says with his own mouth:

> “It is not for you to know the times or moments which the Father has established in his own authority” (Acts I, 7).

Through the fact that blessed Job’s suffering is described, we are taught what we know by experience. Through the fact that the length of time of his suffering is left unstated, we are taught what we ought not to know.

We have prolonged the words of the preface, speaking as though we were briefly touching upon the whole matter. But since, by speaking at length, we have reached the beginning of our discourse, we must first establish the root of the historical account, so that afterward we may be able to satisfy the mind with the fruit of allegories.

[Note: In the manuscripts this title occurs here: “The Moralia of blessed Gregory, gathered through contemplation.” The word “blessed” is omitted in the Corbie manuscript.]

**Part One, comprising five books.**

[Col. 0527]

# BOOK ONE

Explaining the opening verses of the first chapter of the Book of Job first in the historical, then in the allegorical, and finally in the moral sense.

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0527D]

**VERSE 1.**—“There was a man in the land of Uz, whose name was Job.”

### THE HISTORICAL SENSE

**1. Job is called good among the wicked, which is the highest praise.**—The holy man’s place of habitation is mentioned so that the excellence of his virtue may be expressed. Who does not know that Uz is the land of the Gentiles? The Gentiles were bound to vices because they were ignorant of the knowledge of their Creator.

Let it therefore be said where he lived, so that it may contribute to his praise that he was good among the wicked. For it is not greatly praiseworthy to be good among the good, but to be good among the wicked. Just as it is a more serious fault not to be good among the good, so it is an immense commendation to have been good even among the wicked.

Hence blessed Job himself testifies concerning himself:

> “I was a brother to dragons and a companion of ostriches” (Job XXX, 29).

Hence Peter extolled Lot with great praise because he found him good among the reprobate, saying:

> “He rescued righteous Lot, oppressed by the unjust conduct of the wicked” (II Pet. II, 7).

[Note: Most manuscripts read “oppressed by the injury of the wicked’s way of life.” The first manuscript of Remigius reads, “he rescued him from the injury and conduct of the wicked.” The Colbert manuscript reads, “from their shameful conduct.”]

> “For, by sight and hearing, he was righteous while living among those who from day to day tortured the soul of the righteous man by wicked deeds” (ibid., 8).

He could not have been tortured in this way unless he both heard and saw the depraved deeds of those around him. Yet he is said to have been righteous in sight and hearing because the life of the wicked touched the eyes and ears of the righteous not by delighting them but by wounding them.

[Note: The Corbie manuscript reads, “they did not touch”; and earlier, in a second correction, “vices instead of life.”]

Hence Paul says to the disciples:

> “In the midst of a crooked and perverse generation, among whom you shine like lights in the world” (Phil. II, 15).

Hence it is said to the angel of the church of Pergamum:

> “I know where you dwell, where Satan’s throne is; and you hold fast my name and have not denied my faith” (Apoc. II, 13).

[Note: The Vatican and Gussanville, together with almost all the manuscripts, read: “to the angel of the church of Pergamum.”]

Hence the holy Church is praised in the voice of the Bridegroom, when it is said to her in the Song of Love:

> “As a lily among thorns, so is my beloved among the daughters” (Cant. II, 2).

Blessed Job is therefore rightly described as having lived among the wicked after the Gentile land has been mentioned, so that, in accordance with the Bridegroom’s praise, it might be shown that a lily grew among thorns.

Hence it is rightly added immediately:

## CHAPTER II

**THE SAME PLACE.**—“Simple and upright.”

## 2. Job’s Simplicity and Rectitude. Both Are Necessary

For some people are so simple that they do not know what is right. But they abandon the innocence of true simplicity precisely by failing to rise to the virtue of rectitude; for, because they do not know how to be prudent through rectitude, they cannot in any way remain innocent through simplicity. Hence Paul admonishes the disciples, saying: “I want you to be wise in what is good, but simple in what is evil” (Rom. 16:19). Again he says: “Do not become children in understanding, but be infants in malice” (1 Cor. 14:20). Hence Truth itself commands the disciples, saying: “Be wise as serpents and simple as doves” (Matt. 10:16). For he necessarily joined both together in his admonition, so that the serpent’s cleverness might instruct the dove’s simplicity, and again the dove’s simplicity might temper the serpent’s cleverness.

Hence the Holy Spirit revealed his presence to human beings not only in a dove but also in fire (Matt. 3:11, 16). Through the dove, simplicity is signified; through the fire, zeal. He is therefore shown both in the dove and in the fire (Acts 2:3), because all who are filled with him serve the gentleness of simplicity in such a way that they are also kindled by zeal for rectitude against the faults of sinners. It follows:

## CHAPTER III

**IBID.—“Fearing God and turning away from evil.”**

### 3. What It Means to Fear God. Good Deeds Mixed with Evil Are Rejected

To fear God is to omit none of the good things that ought to be done. Hence Solomon says: “Whoever fears God neglects nothing” (Eccl. 7:19). But because some people do certain good things while nevertheless failing to withdraw from certain evils, after Job is called one who feared God, he is rightly also described as turning away from evil. For it is written: “Turn away from evil and do good” (Ps. 36:27). Indeed, good deeds are not acceptable to God when they are stained before his eyes by a mixture of evil. Hence Solomon says: “Whoever offends in one thing will lose many good things” (Eccl. 9:18). [Note: One Remigian manuscript reads: “Hence the apostle James.”] James likewise testifies, saying: “Whoever keeps the whole law but fails in one point has become guilty of all of it” (Jas. 2:10). Paul also says: “A little leaven corrupts the whole lump” (1 Cor. 5:6). [Ancient version III.] Thus blessed Job is carefully shown to have been as free from evils as he was pure in good deeds.

### 4. Why Job’s Virtues Are Described at the Beginning

It is customary for narrators, when they introduce a contest in the arena, first to describe the limbs of the wrestlers: how broad and strong the chest is, how sound it is, how full the muscles swell, and how the belly beneath neither burdens the body with its bulk nor weakens it by excessive thinness. Once they have first shown limbs suited to the contest, they then narrate the blows of great strength.

Because, then, our athlete was destined to contend against the devil, the sacred writer of this history, as though before the spectacle in the arena, enumerates the spiritual virtues of the athlete and describes the limbs of his mind, saying: “That man was simple and upright, fearing God and turning away from evil.” Thus, while the strong arrangement of his limbs is recognized, the victory that follows may already be foreseen from this very strength of disposition. It follows:

## CHAPTER IV

**VERSE 2.—“And seven sons and three daughters were born to him.”**

### 5. The Multitude of His Children Did Not Entice Him to Greed

The fertility of offspring often tempts a parent’s heart toward greed. For he is inflamed with ambition to gather an inheritance precisely in proportion as he becomes the father of many heirs. Therefore, to show how holy blessed Job’s mind was, he is both called righteous and said to have been the father of many children. [Note: All the printed editions read “Who at the beginning of this book”; perhaps the editors considered *libri sui* (“of his book”), as found in the manuscripts, unsuitable Latin, though overly scrupulously.]

He is said at the beginning of his book to have been devoted to offering sacrifices, and afterward he is also remembered as ready to give generously. Let us therefore consider how great was the strength with which he was endowed: not even the affection aroused by so many heirs inclined him toward clinging to his inheritance. It follows:

## CHAPTER V [Ancient version IV]

**VERSE 3.—“And his possession was seven thousand sheep, three thousand camels, five hundred yoke of oxen, and five hundred she-asses, and a very great household.”**

### 6. He Possessed Wealth Without Loving It

We know that greater losses stir the mind to greater grief. Thus, to show how great his virtue was, he is said to have possessed much, which he patiently lost. For nothing is ever lost without grief except what is possessed without love. Therefore, since great wealth is described and yet is shortly afterward said to have been patiently lost, it is clear that he lost it without grief because he possessed it without love.

It should also be noted that the riches of his heart are described first, and afterward the wealth of his body. Abundance of possessions ordinarily loosens the mind from divine fear all the more as it forces the mind to think about many different things. For while the mind is scattered among many matters, it is prevented from standing fixed in its depths. Truth himself indicated this when he explained the parable of the sower, saying: “The one sown among thorns is the one who hears the word, but the anxiety of this age and the deceitfulness of riches choke the word, and it becomes fruitless” (Matt. 13:22; Luke 8:7–8; Mark 4:7). Behold: blessed Job is said both to possess much and shortly afterward to serve divine sacrifices with earnest devotion.

### 7. He Had Already Abandoned Everything in His Heart

Let us consider, then, what holiness this man possessed, who, while so occupied with such assiduous service of God, nevertheless remained free for it. The power of the command had not yet shone forth—a command that would prescribe leaving everything behind—but blessed Job already kept the force of that same command in his heart. For he had indeed abandoned in his mind the substance that he possessed without delight.

## CHAPTER VI

**IBID.—“And that man was great among all the people of the East.”**

### 8. How Great His Wealth Was

Who does not know that Eastern peoples are exceedingly rich? Thus he was great among the Eastern peoples, as though it were openly said: he was richer than the rich.

## CHAPTER VII

**VERSE 4.—“And his sons went and held banquets in their houses, each on his appointed day; and they sent and invited their three sisters to eat and drink with them.”**

[Note: Manuscripts and Berthol. read “they held a banquet in their houses”; other editions read “banquets.”]

### 9. The Substance to Be Divided among the Sons Did Not Divide Their Hearts

Among brothers, greater wealth often becomes the cause of more serious discord. O immeasurable praise of their father’s instruction! The father is said to be rich, and the sons are declared to be united. Although wealth to be divided among them was present, an undivided charity filled all their hearts.

## CHAPTER VIII [Ancient version V, Revised version IV]

**VERSE 5.—“And when the days of the banquet had gone round, Job sent for them and sanctified them; and rising early, he offered holocausts for each one.”**

### 10. Banquets Are Almost Never Without Guilt, Because of Pleasure and Talkativeness

When it says that he “sent for them and sanctified them,” it plainly shows what strict discipline he exercised toward them while present, and with what concern he was not absent from them even when away. But we must carefully observe that, once the days of the banquet had been completed, purification was provided for each one through a holocaust. [Note: Most manuscripts read *pro singulis* (“for each individual”).]

The holy man knew that banquets could scarcely be celebrated without guilt. He knew that the feasts of banquets must be cleansed by a great purification of sacrifices, and that whatever the sons had defiled in themselves while feasting, their father cleansed by offering sacrifice. For there are certain vices that can scarcely be separated from banquets—or certainly cannot be separated from them at all. [Note: “Almost” is absent in the Compendium, the Ebroic manuscript, and others.] Almost always pleasure accompanies feasts. For while the body is relaxed by the enjoyment of refreshment, the heart is released into empty pleasure. Hence it is written: “The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play” (Exod. 32:6).

### 11. Talkativeness Almost Always Follows Feasting

When the belly is being refreshed, the tongue is given free rein. Hence the rich man is rightly described as desiring water in the underworld, saying: “Father Abraham, have mercy on me, and send Lazarus to dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue, for I am tormented in this flame” (Luke 16:24). [Note: The manuscripts read: “that he may dip the tip of his finger in water.”]

First, he is said to have feasted splendidly every day; afterward, he is remembered as asking for water for his tongue. Since, as we have said, talkativeness ordinarily flows very freely amid feasting, he indicates the guilt by his punishment when Truth says that the man who had feasted splendidly every day burned more intensely in his tongue.

Those who tune the harmony of strings distribute it with such skill that often, when one string is struck, another far away and separated by many intervening strings is shaken; and when one gives forth a sound, the other, tuned to the same melody, trembles without being struck. So Scripture often treats virtues and vices: while it indicates one thing by speaking, it makes another known by silence. [Ancient version VI.] Nothing is mentioned against the rich man concerning talkativeness; but when punishment is said to be in his tongue, it shows what a grave fault talkativeness had been among the other faults committed at the banquet.

### 12. By Offering Sacrifice on the Eighth Day, Job Honors the Mystery of the Resurrection

When the seven brothers are described as holding banquets on successive days, and, after the days of the banquet had been completed, Job is said to offer seven sacrifices, the history plainly indicates that blessed Job, offering sacrifice on the eighth day, honors the mystery of the resurrection.

The day now called the Lord’s Day is the third day from the death of the Redeemer, but in the order of creation it is the eighth, which is also the first in creation. Since it follows the seventh after the cycle has been completed, it is rightly counted as the eighth. Therefore, because he is said to offer seven sacrifices on the eighth day, he is understood to have served the Lord for the hope of the resurrection, filled with the Spirit’s sevenfold grace.

Hence a psalm “for the eighth” is prescribed, in which joy concerning the resurrection is announced. [Ancient version VII.] But because the sons of blessed Job had been so thoroughly girded with the discipline of good instruction that they did not sin either in their deeds at the banquets or in their words, this is plainly shown when it is added:

## CHAPTER IX [Revised version V]

**IBID.—“For he said: ‘Perhaps my sons have sinned and blessed God in their hearts.’”**

### 13. One Must Not Rashly Judge Another’s Heart. On Rulers of the Faithful Who Do Not Know Their Works

He had taught them to be perfect in deed and speech, since he feared for them only with regard to their thoughts. Because we must not rashly judge the hearts of others, we recognize this in the words of the holy man, who did not say, “Because they blessed God in their hearts,” but, “Perhaps they have blessed God in their hearts.”

Hence Paul rightly says: “Do not judge before the time, until the Lord comes, who will bring to light the things hidden in darkness and disclose the purposes of hearts” (1 Cor. 4:5). [Ancient version VIII.] For anyone who strays from rectitude in thought sins in darkness. Therefore, the less we are able to illuminate the darkness of another’s thought with our own sight, the less boldly ought we to rebuke another’s heart.

But we must carefully consider with what severity this father could correct his sons’ deeds, since he strove with such concern to cleanse their hearts. [Note: The Remigian, Remense, Ebroic, and other manuscripts read: “But this must be carefully considered.”] What do the rulers of the faithful say to this—those who do not know even the outward actions of their disciples? What do they consider in their own defense, when they do not care to heal the wounds of actions entrusted to them?

To show that this holy work was also marked by perseverance, it is rightly added: [Note: The Corb., Germ., and most manuscripts read “of this holy man’s work”; the printed editions read “of this holy work.”]

## CHAPTER X

**IBID.—“Thus Job did every day.”**

### 14. Job’s Perseverance

For it is written: “The one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. 10:22; 24:13). In the sacrifice, therefore, holy action is shown; in the fact that the sacrifice was offered every day, constancy in holy action is shown.

Following the historical account, we have passed over these matters briefly. Now the order of the exposition requires that, returning to the beginning, we disclose the mysteries of the allegories.

## CHAPTER XI [Ancient version IX]

**VERSE 1.—“There was a man in the land of Uz, whose name was Job.”**

### 15. ALLEGORICAL SENSE: Christ Is Signified by the Name Job

We believe that these things happened historically, but let us now see how they have been fulfilled allegorically. As we have said, Job is interpreted as “suffering” or “one who grieves”; Uz means “counselor.” Whom, then, does blessed Job express by his name except the one of whom the prophet speaks, saying: “He himself bore our sorrows” (Isa. 53:4)? He dwells in the land of Uz because he reigns in the hearts of the people who belong to the Counselor.

Paul says that Christ is “the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Cor. 1:24). This same Wisdom says through Solomon: “I, Wisdom, dwell in counsel, and I am present among learned thoughts” (Prov. 8:12). Therefore Job dwells in the land of Uz because Wisdom, which endured the suffering of the Passion for us, made the hearts devoted to the counsels of life its dwelling place.

## CHAPTER XII [Ancient version X]

**IBID.—“And that man was simple and upright.”**

### 16. He Maintained Simplicity and Rectitude

Rectitude signifies justice, while simplicity signifies gentleness. Often, when we carry out the rectitude of justice, we abandon gentleness; and when we desire to preserve gentleness, we turn aside from the rectitude of justice.

But the incarnate Lord maintained simplicity together with rectitude: neither in the gentleness of his disposition did he lose the strictness of justice, nor again in the strictness of justice did he lose the virtue of gentleness. Thus, when certain people brought an adulterous woman and wished to test him, so that he might fall into either a fault of harshness or a fault of injustice, he answered both purposes, saying: “Let the one among you who is without sin be the first to throw a stone at her” (John 8:7).

“The one among you who is without sin” gives the simplicity of gentleness; “the first to throw a stone at her” gives the zeal of justice. Hence the prophet also says to him: “Set out, prosper, and reign because of truth and gentleness and justice” (Ps. 45:5). In pursuing truth, he preserved gentleness together with justice, so that he would neither lose the zeal of rectitude under the weight of gentleness nor disturb the weight of gentleness through zeal for rectitude. It follows:

## CHAPTER XIII

**IBID.—“Fearing God and turning away from evil.”**

### 17. How He Feared God

It is written of him: “And the spirit of the fear of the Lord filled him” (Isa. 11:3). For the incarnate Lord displayed in himself everything that he inspired in us, so that what he commanded by precept he might commend by example. [Note: All the manuscripts—the Remense, Remigian, Colbert, Corbie, Tours, and others—read “what he inspired in us”; the Basel edition of 1514, the Paris edition of 1518, and others read “what he commanded us.”]

According to the nature of his humanity, therefore, our Redeemer feared God, because, in order to redeem proud humanity, he undertook a humble death for it. [Note: The St-Germain, Royal, Remense, and other manuscripts, as well as the older Paris and Basel editions, read “he undertook a humble death for it.” One Remigian manuscript reads “he took upon himself a humble death for him.” Apparently using this manuscript, Joannes Gilotius Campanus adopted both readings in his edition of 1571; later editions retained only the latter.]

His action is also fittingly indicated by the fact that Job is said to turn away from evil. He himself turned away from evil—not from something he had committed, but from something he rejected when he encountered it. For he abandoned the ancient way of human conduct that he found at his birth and impressed upon the conduct of his followers the new way that he brought with him.

## CHAPTER XIV [Revised version VI]

**VERSE 2.—“And seven sons and three daughters were born to him.”**

### 18. The Number Seven Is Perfect

What is understood by the number seven except the sum of perfection? To say nothing of the explanations offered by human reasoning concerning the number seven—that it is perfect because it consists of the first even number and the first odd number, of the first divisible number and the first indivisible number—we know with complete certainty that sacred Scripture customarily uses the number seven to signify perfection (Gen. 2:3).

Hence it says that the Lord rested from his works on the seventh day. Hence also the seventh day was given to human beings for rest, that is, as the Sabbath. Hence the jubilee year, in which complete rest is expressed, is completed after seven weeks; and, with a monad added, it is fulfilled in our reunion.

[Note: Manuscripts vary here: some add *monadi* (“to the monad”), while several others add *monade* (“with a monad”), which is preferred by the Corb., Germ., and Utic. manuscripts. In the Utic. manuscript and the edition the reading *nostrae adun. summa* (“the sum of our union”) also occurs. *Summa* is redundant and corrupts the sense. Gregory calls the monad that reunion at the end of the world in which the elect will be gathered, as will become clear from what follows.]

### 19. Job’s Sons Signify the Apostles

Seven sons were therefore born to him: the apostles, advancing courageously to preach. Since they fulfilled the precepts of perfection, they maintained in their conduct the strength associated with the superior sex.

This is why twelve were chosen to be filled with the perfection of the Spirit’s sevenfold grace. From the number seven one rises to the number twelve. For when the number seven is multiplied by its constituent parts, it tends toward twelve: whether four is multiplied by three or three by four, seven is turned into twelve. [Note: Rem., Vindoc., and Ebroic. read *vertunt* (“they turn”) rather than *vertuntur* (“are turned”).]

Thus the holy apostles were chosen as twelve because they were sent to preach the Holy Trinity in the four quarters of the world, so that by their number they might also show the perfection that they preached by life and voice.

### 20. The Daughters Are the Multitudes of the Faithful. The Three Orders of the Faithful

Three daughters were also born. What are we to understand by the daughters except the weaker multitudes of the faithful? [Note: Only the printed editions add here, “holding the faith of the Holy Trinity”; this gloss has been rejected.] Although they do not remain in the perfection of works with strong virtue, they nevertheless steadfastly hold the faith of the Trinity once they have come to know it.

Thus the order of preachers is signified by the seven sons, while the multitude of hearers is signified by the three daughters. The three daughters may also designate the three orders of the faithful. The daughters are named after the sons because, after the apostles’ displayed strength, three distinctions of the faithful followed in the life of the Church: pastors, the continent, and the married.

[Ancient version XIII.] Hence the prophet Ezekiel also says that he heard of three men who were delivered: Noah, Daniel, and Job (Ezek. 14). For what is signified by Noah, who guided the ark upon the waters, except the order of superiors? By presiding over peoples according to the pattern of life, they govern the holy Church amid the waves of temptations.

What is signified by Daniel, whose remarkable abstinence is recorded, except the life of those who practice continence? By abandoning everything belonging to the world, they rule Babylon, which they despise, with an elevated mind.

What is signified by Job except the life of good married people? While they perform devout works with the worldly possessions they hold, they advance toward the heavenly homeland as though by a road across the earth.

Since these three distinctions of the faithful followed after the holy apostles, it is rightly recorded that three daughters were born after the sons. It follows:

## CHAPTER XV

**VERSE 3.—“And his possession was seven thousand sheep and three thousand camels.”**

### 21. The Innocent Are Foreshadowed by Sheep; the Vicious Gentiles and the Samaritans by Camels

Because faithful hearers have been gathered from varied ways of life, what is first said universally, after the daughters have been mentioned, is subsequently presented distinctly under the names of animals. [Note: The printed editions read “after the sons and daughters have been mentioned,” contrary to the manuscripts and to Gregory’s meaning, since he has just taught that the three daughters, without mention of sons, signify the three orders of the faithful.] For what is expressed by seven thousand sheep except the perfect innocence of certain people, which comes to the perfection of grace from the pastures of the Law? [Note: The older and later editions read “to the reception of grace”; the Utic. and some other manuscripts read “to the grace of perfection.” The Corbie manuscript is followed here.]

What, on the other hand, is designated by three thousand camels except the twisted depravity of the Gentiles coming to the fullness of faith? [Note: The Vatican and Gussanville editions incorrectly read “the whole depravity of the Gentiles.”] [Ancient version XIV.] In sacred Scripture, the name “camel” sometimes expresses the Lord himself and sometimes the Gentile people.

The Lord is designated by the name “camel,” as he says to the opposing Jews: “Straining out a gnat and swallowing a camel” (Matt. 23:24). A gnat wounds by buzzing, whereas a camel willingly bends itself to receive burdens. Thus the Jews strained out a gnat because they asked for a seditious criminal to be released; but they swallowed a camel because they tried, by shouting, to destroy the one who had willingly descended to receive the burdens of our mortality.

Again, the Gentile people are designated by the name “camel.” Hence Rebecca, when she came to Isaac, was brought riding on a camel’s back (Gen. 24:61), because the Church, hastening to Christ from among the Gentiles, is found in the twisted and vicious practices of its former life. [Note: Gilotius, the Vatican, and Gussanville editions read *intortis* (“in untwisted”), against the manuscripts and older editions.] When it saw Isaac, it descended, because, once the Lord was known, the Gentiles abandoned their vices and sought the lowliness of humility instead of the height of self-exaltation.

It is also truly covered with a veil out of modesty, because it is ashamed before him of its former life. Hence the Apostle says to these same Gentiles: “What fruit did you have then in those things of which you are now ashamed?” (Rom. 6:21).

Since, therefore, by the sheep we understand the Hebrews coming from the pastures of the Law to the faith, nothing prevents us from understanding by the camels the Gentile peoples, twisted in their ways and laden with the worship of idols. For because they found gods for themselves whom they might worship, a burden had grown upon their backs, as it were, from themselves, which they had to carry.

[Ancient version XV.] ### 22. The Life of the Samaritans May Also Be Signified by Camels, Since They Are Common Animals

[Note: The first Remigian manuscript reads “a common animal”; the Corbie and St-Germain manuscripts read “they are common animals.”]

Camels chew the cud but do not divide the hoof. [Note: The Corb. and Germ. manuscripts read *Samarii*; Reg. reads *Samarei*. This is the form used in Book VI, formerly Letter 3, and Book VIII, formerly Letter 21.]

The Samaritans, as it were, chew the cud because they accept words from the Law in part; and, as it were, do not divide the hoof because in part they disregard it. They also carry a heavy burden on the back of their minds because in everything they do they labor without hope of eternity. [Note: The Corbie, St-Germain, Remense, and other manuscripts, with the older editions, read “in everything”; the Vatican and Gussanville editions read “for all that.”] They do not know the faith of the resurrection.

What could be heavier or more burdensome than to endure the affliction of the passing age and never hope for the joys of reward that would relieve the mind?

But because the Lord, appearing in the flesh, both filled the peoples of the Hebrews with the grace of perfection and led some of the Samaritans to knowledge of the faith by displaying wondrous works, it is rightly said of the shadow that expressed the truth that he possessed both seven thousand sheep and three thousand camels. It follows:

## CHAPTER XVI

**IBID.—“Five hundred yoke of oxen and five hundred she-asses.”**

### 23. What Is Signified by the Name “Oxen,” and What by the Name “Asses”

It has already been said above that the number fifty, which is completed by seven weeks with a monad added, signifies rest; while the number ten expresses the sum of perfection. Since perfection of rest is promised to the faithful, multiplying fifty by ten brings us to five hundred.

[Ancient version XVI.] In sacred Scripture the name “oxen” sometimes signifies the dullness of fools and sometimes the life of those who work well. Because the senselessness of fools is represented by the name “ox,” Solomon rightly says: “Immediately she follows him like an ox led to the slaughter” (Prov. 7:22).

Again, because the life of every worker is expressed by the name “ox,” the precepts of the Law testify. Through Moses it commands: “You shall not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain” (Deut. 25:4). This is plainly repeated in the words: “The laborer is worthy of his wages” (Luke 10:7).

The name “asses” sometimes signifies the laziness of fools, sometimes the uncontrolled lust of the wanton, and sometimes the simplicity of the Gentiles.

The laziness of fools is represented by the name “asses,” as Moses says: “You shall not plow with an ox and an ass together” (Deut. 22:10). It is as though he said: Do not join fools with the wise in preaching, lest the one who is unable to complete the task obstruct the one who is able to do so.

The uncontrolled lust of the wanton is likewise expressed by the name “asses,” as the prophet testifies, saying: “Whose flesh is like the flesh of asses” (Ezek. 23:20).

Again, the simplicity of the Gentiles is shown by the name “asses.” Hence, as the Lord traveled toward Jerusalem, he is said to have sat upon a young ass (Matt. 21:5). [Note: The Remense and Remigian manuscripts and the old Basel edition read *sedendo asinum* (“sitting [upon] an ass”); the 1514 edition reads *sedendo asinam* (“sitting [upon] a she-ass”), followed by later editions. The former is preferable and better accords with Gregory’s explanation below, which concerns the ass, not the she-ass. The construction is not unusual for Gregory or foreign to sacred writers: Optatus writes, “Peter first sat in the one chair,” and elsewhere, “whose chair you sit,” and “who would sit the other chair.”] For what does it mean for him to come to Jerusalem while sitting upon an ass except to possess the simple hearts of the Gentiles, guiding and ruling them and bringing them to the vision of peace?

This is shown by a single and readily understood testimony: oxen designate the workers of Judea, and the ass the Gentile peoples, when the prophet says: [Note: Gilotius and subsequent editions read “Jewish workers”; the Corbie and most manuscripts read “workers of Judea,” which accords with what follows: “Judea had oxen.”] “The ox knows its owner, and the ass its master’s manger” (Isa. 1:3).

For who was the ox except the Jewish people, whose neck the yoke of the Law wore down? And who was the ass except the Gentile people, whom any seducer found like a brute animal, resisting with no reason, and drove into whatever error he wished?
