The ox recognized its owner and the ass its master’s manger because the Hebrew people found the God whom they worshiped but did not know, while the Gentiles received the nourishment of the Law, which they had not possessed. What, therefore, is said above through the sheep and camels is repeated below through the oxen and asses.

### 24. The Preachers of the Jews Were Oxen Pressed by the Yoke of the Law

Before the Redeemer’s coming, Judea also had oxen, because it sent out workers to preach. To them Truth says: “Woe to you, hypocrites, who travel around sea and land to make one proselyte; and when he has been made, you make him twice as much a son of Gehenna as yourselves” (Matt. 23:15).

A heavy yoke of the Law pressed upon them because they bore the external commandments of the letter. To them Truth says: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart” (Matt. 11:28–29).

Therefore, what is promised in the Gospel to those who labor well—rest—is what is signified here by the five hundred yoke of oxen. For those who submit their necks to the dominion of the Redeemer, where do they tend except toward rest?

[Ancient version XVII.] Hence five hundred she-asses are also mentioned, because the summoned peoples of the Gentiles, while desiring to reach rest, willingly bear all the burdens of the commandments.

Therefore, when Jacob addressed his sons, he rightly took care to signify prophetically that the Gentile people would seek this rest, saying: “Issachar is a strong ass, lying down between the boundaries; he saw that rest was good and that the land was excellent, and he put his shoulder to bear” (Gen. 49:14–15). [Note: The Remense, Remigian, Corbie, Vendôme, and nearly all manuscripts read “lying down between the boundaries.”]

To lie down between the boundaries is to rest while awaiting the end of the world and to seek nothing of the things now present in the midst of it, but to desire the final things.

The strong ass sees rest and the excellent land when the simple Gentile people raise themselves to the strength of good works precisely because they are journeying toward the homeland of eternal life. [Note: The same manuscripts read: “and it puts its shoulder to bear.”] They put their shoulder to bear because, having seen the rest above, they submit themselves in action even to difficult commandments; and whatever weakness declares intolerable, the hope of reward shows to be light and easy.

Since, therefore, Judea and the Gentile world are gathered for the sake of the elect into eternal rest, it is rightly said that there were five hundred yoke of oxen and five hundred she-asses. It follows:

## CHAPTER XVIII [Ancient version XVIII]

**IBID.—“And a very great household.”**

### 25. The Fools of the World Were Called Before the Wise

Why is the multitude of animals described first, while the household is mentioned at the end, except to show that the foolish things of the world were first gathered for knowledge of the faith, so that afterward its clever things might also be called? Paul bears witness to this, saying: “Not many wise according to the flesh, not many powerful, not many noble; but God chose the foolish things of the world to confound the wise” (1 Cor. 1:27).

The beginnings of the holy Church itself are said to have been ignorant of letters, so that the Redeemer might show through all his preachers that it is not eloquence but the truth of the matter that persuades believing peoples to life. It follows:

## CHAPTER XVIII [Ancient version XIX]

**IBID.—“That man was great among all the people of the East.”**

### 26. Christ Was Like Others in His Humanity but Unique in His Divinity

That our Redeemer is called “the East” is attested by the prophet, who says: “And behold, the man whose name is the East” (Zech. 6:12). All who stand in faith in this East are therefore rightly called Easterners.

But because all human beings are merely human, while the East himself is God and human, it is rightly said: “He was great among all the Easterners.” It is as though it were openly said: He surpasses all who are born to God in faith, because adoption does not exalt him as it does the others; rather, the nature of divinity exalts him. Although in his humanity he appeared like the others, in his divinity he nevertheless remained uniquely above all.

## CHAPTER XIX [Revised version VII, Ancient version XX]

**VERSE 4.—“And his sons went and held banquets in their houses.”**

### 27. The Sons Who Hold Banquets Are to Be Understood as Preachers

The sons went to hold banquets in their houses when the apostolic preachers, in the various regions of the world, served the feasts of virtues to their hearers as though to those who were eating.

Hence it is said to these same sons concerning the hungry multitudes: “You give them something to eat” (Matt. 14:17; 15:32; Mark 6:37; Luke 9:13). Again: “I do not want to send them away hungry, lest they faint on the way”—that is, let them receive the word of consolation in your preaching, lest, remaining hungry for the nourishment of truth, they collapse in the labor of this life.

Again, it is said to these same sons: “Work not for the food that perishes, but for the food that endures unto eternal life” (John 6:27). How these banquets were to be provided is added when it immediately continues:

## CHAPTER XX

**IBID.—“Each on his appointed day.”**

### 28. Hearers Are to Be Nourished According to the Measure of Their Understanding

If the darkness of ignorance is unquestionably the night of the heart, understanding is not improperly called day. Hence Paul says: “One person judges one day to be above another; another judges every day alike” (Rom. 14:5). It is as though he plainly said: One person understands certain matters while leaving others aside; another recognizes all things that are possible for understanding, seeing them as they are. [Note: The Corb., Germ., and many other manuscripts, together with the old Paris and Basil editions, read “all things possible for understanding.”]

Each son therefore provides a banquet on his own day because every holy preacher, according to the measure of his illuminated understanding, feeds the minds of his hearers with the feasts of truth.

Paul prepared a banquet on his day when he said: “They will be happier if they remain as they are, according to my advice” (1 Cor. 7:40). He urged each person to think of his own day when he said: “Let each person abound in his own understanding” (Rom. 14:5). It follows:

## CHAPTER XXI

**IBID.—“And they sent and invited their three sisters to eat and drink with them.”**
29. [Earlier XXI.] These are signified by Job’s daughters. Sacred Scripture is sometimes food, sometimes drink.—The sons invite their sisters to the feast because the holy apostles proclaim to weak hearers the joys of heavenly refreshment; and, seeing their minds hungry for the nourishment of truth, they feed them with the banquets of divine discourse. It is rightly said: “That they might eat and drink with them.” For sacred Scripture is sometimes food for us and sometimes drink.

It is food in its more obscure passages, because it is, as it were, broken by exposition and swallowed by chewing. It is drink in its clearer passages, because it is imbibed just as it is found. The prophet saw sacred Scripture as food—food to be broken by exposition—when he said: “The little ones asked for bread, and there was no one to break it for them” (Lam. IV, 4); that is, the weak asked that the more difficult statements of sacred Scripture be broken down by exposition, but no one capable of explaining them could be found.

The prophet saw sacred Scripture as drink when he said: “All who thirst, come to the waters” (Isa. LV, 1). If drink did not signify open commandments, Truth himself would not have cried out: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink” (John VII, 37). The prophet saw Judea deprived of food and drink, as it were, when he said: “Her nobles have perished from hunger, and her multitude has dried up from thirst” (Isa. V, 12). For it belongs to the few to know what is strong and hidden, but to the many to perceive what is openly presented in history. Therefore he asserts that Judea’s nobles perished not from thirst but from hunger, because those who seemed to preside, while giving themselves wholly to outward understanding, had nothing to chew by probing into inward matters.

But because, when those of higher rank fall away from inward understanding, the understanding of the little ones also dries up even in outward matters, it is rightly added there: “Her multitude has dried up from thirst.” It is as though he said openly: while the common people abandon concern for their life, they no longer even seek the streams of history.

And they testify that they understood both the hidden commandments and the open ones when, complaining to the judge who rejected them, they say: “We ate and drank in your presence” (Luke XIII, 26). They add, explaining this openly: “And you taught in our streets” (ibid.).

Since, then, sacred discourse is broken by exposition in its obscure passages, but in its clearer passages is drunk just as it is found, it is rightly said: “They sent and invited their three sisters, that they might eat and drink with them.” As though it were said openly: they drew the weak to themselves by gentle persuasion, so that they might both feed their minds by expounding great matters through contemplation and nourish them by presenting small matters through history.

It follows:

## CHAPTER XXII [Earlier XXI]

[Col. 0541B] **VERSE 5.**—“When the days of the feast had passed in their cycle, Job sent and sanctified them; and, rising at dawn, he offered holocausts for each one.”

30. Christ cleanses the hearts of his preachers.—The days of the feast pass in their cycle when the ministries of preaching are carried out. When the feasts had been completed, Job offered a holocaust for his sons, because the Redeemer prayed to the Father for the apostles returning from their preaching.

He is rightly said to sanctify them by sending, because, while granting the Holy Spirit who proceeds from him to the hearts of the disciples, he cleansed whatever guilt might have been present.

[Note: Corb., Vindoc., Ebroic., Utic., and others read: “who proceeds from himself.”]

He is also rightly described as rising at dawn to offer holocausts, because, by presenting on our behalf the petition of his intercession, he illuminated the darkness of the human mind after the night of error had been dispelled: so that the mind might not be secretly defiled by any contagion of sin arising from the very grace of preaching; so that it might not attribute its deeds to itself; and so that, by attributing to itself what it had done, it might not lose it.

Hence it is rightly added:

## CHAPTER XXIII [Earlier XXIII; Revised VIII]

**IBID.**—“For he said, ‘Perhaps my sons have sinned and blessed God in their hearts.’”

31. How the stains contracted by preachers are to be washed away.—To bless God—that is, to curse him—is to claim glory for oneself from his gift. Therefore the Lord rightly washed the feet of the holy apostles after their preaching (John XIII, 5), clearly showing that often even in a good work the dust of sin is contracted, and that the footprints of those who speak are stained by the very source from which the hearts of their hearers are cleansed.

For often, while certain people speak words of exhortation, they inwardly exalt themselves, however slightly, because through them the means of purification is conveyed; and while by their words they wash away the deeds of others, they take up, as it were, the dust of evil thought from a good road.

[Note: The English manuscripts and most of our copies, as well as the old editions, read: “because through them the grace of preaching is conveyed.” One manuscript of Vindoc. has this reading also. The following words seem to recommend the former reading: “And while by their words they wash away the deeds of others, they take up, as it were, the dust of evil thought from a good road.”]

What, then, was the washing of the disciples’ feet after preaching except the wiping away of the dust of thoughts after the glory of preaching, and the cleansing of the steps of the heart from inward exaltation?

Nor does the phrase “perhaps” conflict with the Mediator’s complete knowledge. For, knowing all things, yet assuming our ignorance in his speech, and teaching while he assumes it, he sometimes speaks as though from our uncertainty, as when he says: “When the Son of Man comes, do you suppose he will find faith upon the earth?” (Luke XVIII, 3).

[Note: All our manuscripts read: “but, assuming our ignorance in his speech.” The editions of Basel 1514, Paris 1518, and others read: “but, assuming our ignorance in himself”; this is plainly erroneous and contrary to the mind of the holy Doctor, whom it makes favorable to the Agnoite heretics. See what we said in his Life concerning his teaching against the Agnoites. See also the letter to Eulogius, patriarch of Alexandria, formerly book VIII, letter 42, in the third indiction, now letter 10. In that letter he removes every ignorance from Christ even as man.]

When, therefore, the feasts had been completed, Job offered sacrifice for his sons and said: “Perhaps my sons have sinned and blessed God in their hearts,” because, after our Redeemer has cleansed his preachers from the evil assaults directed against them, he also protects them from temptations amid the good works they have done.

It follows:

## CHAPTER XXIV [Earlier XXIV; Revised IX]

[Col. 0542B]

**IBID.**—“Thus Job did throughout all the days.”

32. The holocaust offered continually for us by Christ.—Job does not cease to offer sacrifice throughout all the days, because without interruption the Redeemer offers a holocaust for us, continually displaying to the Father his incarnation undertaken for our sake. His incarnation itself is the offering of our cleansing; and when he shows himself as man, by intervening he removes the sins of humanity. Through the mystery of his humanity he offers an everlasting sacrifice, because the things he cleanses are also eternal.

33. [Earlier XXV.] What has so far been pursued concerning the historical and allegorical sense, and what must henceforth be pursued concerning the moral sense.—Since, then, at the very beginning of this exposition we said that the person of blessed Job was announced in such a way that by him the head and the body—that is, Christ and the Church—could be signified, and since we have shown how our head is believed to be represented, let us now indicate how his body, which is us, is expressed. We have heard from the history what we are to wonder at, and we have learned from the head what we are to believe; let us now consider from the body what we are to hold fast by living accordingly.

For we must transform within ourselves what we read, so that when the mind is roused through hearing, life may proceed to perform what it has heard.

## CHAPTER XXV [Earlier XXVI; Revised X]

**VERSE 1.**—“There was a man in the land of Hus, whose name was Job.”

34. **THE MORAL SENSE.**—Job signifies the elect. Their disposition concerning earthly and eternal things.—If Job is called “sorrowing,” and Hus “counselor,” then surely every elect person is represented by both names, because a sorrowing soul inhabits the counselor: sorrowing over present things, it hastens toward eternal ones.

For there are some who neglect their life; while they pursue transitory things, and either do not understand eternal things or despise them once understood, they feel no sorrow and do not know how to exercise judgment. Since they do not consider the heavenly things they have lost, they think—alas, wretched beings!—that they are happy in their good things.

[Note: The editions read, “they think themselves happy in their good things.” We have removed “happy” as a mere gloss unknown to the manuscripts.]

They do not raise the eyes of their minds toward the light of truth for which they were created; they do not direct the edge of their desire toward contemplation of the eternal homeland. Instead, abandoning themselves in the things to which they have been cast, they love as a homeland the exile they endure, and rejoice as though in the brightness of light amid the blindness they suffer.

But, by contrast, when the minds of the elect perceive that all transitory things are nothing, they seek to know for what they were created.

[Note: Colb. and Corb. read *ad quem* (“to whom”); Reg. reads *ad quod* (“for what”).] Since nothing outside God suffices for their satisfaction, their thought, wearied by the very exercise of seeking, rests in hope and contemplation of its Creator. It desires to be joined to the citizens above; and each one of them, while still placed in a bodily existence in the world, already rises beyond the world in mind, bewails the misery of the exile he endures, and continually stirs himself toward the sublime homeland by the goads of love.

When, therefore, the sorrowing person sees how eternal is what he has lost, he discovers the wholesome counsel of despising this temporal existence through which he passes. And the more his knowledge of counsel increases, so that he abandons perishing things, the more his sorrow grows that he has not yet reached what endures.

Hence Solomon rightly says: “He who increases knowledge increases sorrow” (Eccles. I, 18).

[Note: Two manuscripts, Reg. and Corb., and several others read this way. Ebroic., one manuscript of Remig., Compend., and Longip. read: “For whoever does not yet possess the highest knowledge suffers less concerning…”]

For whoever already knows the highest things that he does not yet possess suffers more over the lowly things in which he is still held.

35. Job dwells in the land of Hus, that is, in counsel.—Job is therefore rightly said to dwell in the land of Hus, because the sorrowing mind of each of the elect is held in the counsel of knowledge.

It should also be observed how no sorrow of mind exists in an action undertaken precipitately. Those who live without counsel, abandoning themselves headlong to events, are not meanwhile wearied by any pain of thought. But whoever carefully fixes his mind upon the counsel of life examines himself cautiously in every action, looking all around; and, lest a sudden and adverse outcome steal upon him from what is being done, he first tests it gently with the foot of thought.

He weighs whether fear might hinder him in what must be done; whether haste might drive him into what ought to be postponed; whether corrupt desires might overcome what is right by open assault; and whether good things might be overthrown by lying in wait through empty glory.

Job therefore dwells in the land of Hus: the more the mind of the elect strives to live by counsel, the more it is wearied by the sorrow of the narrow path.

It follows:

## CHAPTER XXVI [Earlier XXVII; Revised XI]

**IBID.**—“Blameless and upright, fearing God and turning away from evil.”

36. The simplicity and uprightness of the righteous.—Whoever longs for the eternal homeland undoubtedly lives simply and uprightly: simply in deed, uprightly in faith; simply in the good things he performs below, uprightly in the highest things he perceives inwardly.

For there are some who are not simple in the good things they do, since they seek in them not an inward reward but outward approval. Hence a certain wise man rightly says: “Woe to the sinner who enters the earth by two ways” (Ecclus. II, 14). The sinner enters the earth by two ways when what he displays in action belongs to God, but what he seeks in thought belongs to the world.

37. He begins with fear and is brought to completion in love.—It is rightly said: “Fearing God and turning away from evil,” because the holy Church of the elect begins the ways of its simplicity and uprightness with fear, but brings them to completion in love.

[Note: The Vindoc. manuscripts read: “begins the ways with fear.”]

A person turns away completely from evil when, through love of God, he has begun already to be unwilling to sin. But when he still does good through fear, he has not completely departed from evil, because he sins precisely in that he would wish to sin if he could do so with impunity.

Job is therefore rightly said both to fear God and to turn away from evil, because when love follows fear, the fault abandoned in the mind is also trampled underfoot by the purpose of thought.

[Note: The older Rem., Corb., Germ., Vindoc., and other manuscripts read “what is abandoned through fear”; the editions read “what is abandoned.”]

[Earlier XXVIII.] And because every vice is restrained by fear, while virtues arise from love, it is rightly added:

## CHAPTER XXVII [Revised XII]

**VERSE 2.**—“And seven sons and three daughters were born to him.”

38. Job’s seven sons signify the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit; his three daughters, hope, faith, and love.—Seven sons are born to us when, through the conception of a good thought, the seven virtues of the Holy Spirit arise within us.

The prophet counts this inward offspring when the Spirit makes the mind fruitful, saying: “The Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety; and the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him” (Isa. XI, 2).

When, therefore, through the coming of the Holy Spirit, wisdom, understanding, counsel, fortitude, knowledge, piety, and the fear of the Lord are begotten in each of us, offspring destined to remain is propagated in the mind. It preserves the lineage of our heavenly nobility for life all the longer because it joins it to the love of eternity.

But these seven sons certainly have three sisters among us, because whatever these masculine faculties of virtue accomplish, they join to hope, faith, and love. For the seven sons do not attain the perfection of ten unless everything they do is found in faith, hope, and love.

Since the abundance of these virtues that go before is followed by the thought of many good works, it is rightly added:

## CHAPTER XXVIII [Revised XIII]

**VERSE 3.**—“And his possession was seven thousand sheep and three thousand camels.”

39. He possesses sheep who feeds an innocent mind inwardly with truth.—While preserving the truth of the historical account, we can imitate spiritually what we hear carnally.

[Note: Rem. and Remig., Corb., and Germ. read: “For we possess seven thousand sheep.” The old editions of Paris and Basel read likewise.]

We possess seven thousand sheep when, with perfect purity of heart, we feed innocent thoughts within ourselves by seeking the nourishment of truth.

40. He possesses camels who either subjects what is lofty and crooked in himself to faith, or bends it through love.—We shall also have three thousand camels as our possession if everything in us that is lofty and crooked is subjected to the reason of faith and, under the knowledge of the Trinity, willingly bends itself toward the desire for humility.

We possess camels when we humbly lay down whatever lofty thoughts we entertain. We certainly possess camels when we bend our thoughts toward compassion for a brother’s weakness, so that, bearing one another’s burdens, we may know how to sympathize with another’s weakness by condescending to it.

Camels, which do not divide the hoof but nevertheless chew the cud, can also signify the good administration of earthly affairs. Since these have something of the world and something of God, they necessarily have the character of a common animal.

For earthly administration, even when it serves eternal usefulness, cannot be carried out without disturbance of mind. Since through it the mind is troubled in the present and reward is prepared for eternity, it is like a common animal: it possesses something from the Law and something that it does not possess. It does not divide the hoof, because the soul does not completely separate itself from every earthly activity; yet it chews the cud, because, by managing temporal things well, it hopes for heavenly things through the confidence of certainty.

Earthly administrations, therefore, like camels, agree with the Law in their head but differ from it in their feet: the things rightly pursued belong to heaven, while those in which they are occupied by their actions belong to this world.

When, therefore, we subject these same earthly administrations to the knowledge of the Trinity, we possess camels, as it were, by faith.

[Note: The manuscripts have this reading. The printed editions add: “within an indivisible number, that is …”]

It follows:

## CHAPTER XXIX [Earlier XXX]

“And five hundred yoke of oxen, and five hundred she-asses.”

41. The yoke of oxen signifies harmonious virtues; the she-asses, unruly impulses or simple thoughts.—The yokes of oxen become part of our possession when harmonious virtues plow the hardness of the mind.

[Note: Ebroic., S. Ebrulph., Germ., and others read: “when harmonious virtues plow.”]

We possess five hundred she-asses when we restrain unruly impulses and curb by the spiritual rule of the heart whatever in us seeks to rise up carnally.

Or certainly, to possess she-asses is to govern simple thoughts within us. Since these cannot run in subtler understanding but walk, as it were, more slowly, they therefore carry the burdens of our brothers more gently.

There are some who, because they do not understand lofty things, humble themselves more deeply in the outward practices of their way of life.

[Note: The manuscripts read this way: the particle indicates preparation of the mind. Shortly afterward, *premunt* means “press down” or “depress.” The editions read “through outward things.”]

We rightly understand simple thoughts through the she-asses, a sluggish animal yet devoted to carrying burdens, because, while we recognize our own ignorance, we bear the burdens of others more lightly. And when the height of exceptional wisdom does not lift us up, our mind bends itself calmly to endure the dullness of another’s heart.

Whether the yoke of oxen or the five hundred she-asses is mentioned, the reference is rightly made, because whether in what we understand prudently or in what we humbly fail to understand, while seeking the rest of eternal peace, we are held, as it were, within the number of the jubilee.

It follows:

## CHAPTER XXX [Earlier XXXI; Revised XIV]

**IBID.**—“And a very great household.”

42. A great household signifies a multitude of thoughts that must be restrained.—We possess a very great household when we restrain innumerable thoughts under the rule of the mind, lest by their very multitude they overcome the spirit, or trample upon the primacy of our discernment through disorderly arrangement.

The crowd of thoughts is rightly designated by the expression “a great household.” For we know that, when the mistress is absent, the tongues of the maidservants clamour, abandon silence, neglect the duties of their assigned work, and completely confuse their whole manner of life. But if the mistress suddenly arrives, the clamouring tongues immediately fall silent, and each resumes the duties of its work; thus they return to their proper task as though they had never departed.

If, then, reason departs from the house of the mind to the tomb, the clamour of thoughts multiplies itself like a babbling crowd of maidservants in the mistress’s absence. But when reason returns to the mind, the tumultuous confusion is immediately restrained; and, like maidservants quietly limiting themselves to the task assigned, the thoughts at once submit themselves to their proper concerns for the sake of usefulness.

We therefore possess a great household when by the right of reason’s discernment we rule innumerable thoughts. When we diligently do this, we strive through the same discernment to be joined to the angels.

Hence it is rightly added:

## CHAPTER XXXI

**IBID.**—“And that man was greater than all the Orientals.”

43. We are made great by restraining them.—We become great among all the Orientals when, with the cloud of carnal corruption pressed down, we are joined, insofar as our capacity permits, to those spirits who cling to the light of the East, through the rays of our discernment.

Hence Paul also says: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. III, 20). Whoever follows temporal and perishable things seeks the setting sun; whoever desires heavenly things shows that he dwells in the East.

He is therefore made great, not among those of the West, but among those of the East, who strives to advance not amid the low and fleeting things sought in the actions of the wicked, but among the choirs of the citizens above.

[Note: The older Rem. reads: “who strives not amid the low and fleeting things of action.” Corb. omits “of the wicked.”]

It follows:

## CHAPTER XXXII [Earlier XXXII; Revised XV]

**VERSE 4.**—“And his sons went and held a feast in their houses, each one on his day.”

[Note: This note appears at the foot of column 547, but the callout letter (b) has not been printed in the text. First Remig. reads: “and fortitude is greatly weakened.”]

44. Each virtue holds a feast on its own day.—The sons hold a feast in their houses when each virtue feeds the mind according to its proper measure.

[Note: Second Rem., first Remig., Corb., and Germ. read: “according to its measure, they feed their own mind.” The Paris edition of 1640 reads likewise.]

It is rightly said: “Each one on his day.” For the day of each son is the illumination of each virtue. To repeat briefly these gifts of the sevenfold grace: wisdom has one day, understanding another, counsel another, fortitude another, knowledge another, piety another, and fear another.

For it is not the same thing to have wisdom as to have understanding, since many have some wisdom concerning eternal things but are by no means able to understand them.

Wisdom therefore holds a feast on its day, because it refreshes the mind with hope and certainty concerning eternal things. Understanding prepares a feast on its day, because, penetrating what it hears, it illuminates the mind’s darkness while refreshing the heart. Counsel presents a feast on its day, because, preventing precipitous action, it fills the mind with reason. Fortitude holds a feast on its day, because, fearing no adversity, it sets food of confidence before the trembling mind.

Knowledge prepares a feast on its day, because it overcomes the fast of ignorance in the belly of the mind. Piety presents a feast on its day, because it fills the heart’s inward parts with works of mercy. Fear holds a feast on its day, because, restraining the mind from becoming proud over present things, it strengthens it with the food of hope concerning future things.

45. If separated from one another, they fail.—But in this feast of the sons I see something that must be investigated: they feed one another. For every single virtue is greatly weakened if one virtue does not support another.

Wisdom is lesser if it lacks understanding; and understanding is very useless if it is not sustained by wisdom. When it penetrates higher things without the weight of wisdom, its levity raises it only to make its fall more grievous.

Counsel is worthless when it lacks the strength of fortitude, because, having discovered something by deliberation, it cannot bring it to completion in action if it lacks strength. Fortitude, too, is greatly destroyed unless it is supported by counsel, because the more it sees itself capable of doing, the more disastrously a virtue without the moderation of reason rushes headlong.

There is no knowledge if it does not possess the usefulness of piety, because, while neglecting to carry out the good things it has learned, it binds itself more tightly for judgment. Piety is also very useless if it lacks the discernment of knowledge, because, when no knowledge illuminates it, it does not know how to show mercy.

Fear itself, unless it also possesses these virtues, certainly rises to no work of good action, because, trembling at everything, it remains torpid through its own dread and is incapable of every good.

Since, therefore, through alternating service one virtue is refreshed by another, it is rightly said that the sons feast with one another. And when one raises another by supporting it, numerous offspring, as it were, prepare a feast to be nourished on their respective days.

It follows:

## CHAPTER XXXIII [Earlier XXXIII; Revised XVI]

**IBID.**—“And they sent and invited their three sisters, that they might eat and drink with them.”

46. Hope, faith, and love must be invited to the feast of the virtues.—When our virtues summon hope, faith, and love to everything they do, the sons, as workers, invite three sisters to the feast, so that faith, hope, and love may rejoice in the good work administered by each virtue.

[Note: All—Rem., Remig., Longip., Corb., Germ., Ebroic., and others—read: “They know hope, faith, and love, as workers…” Carnot. reads: “They thirst for hope, faith, and love.” The reading should be *ciunt*, “they summon,” from *cio*, “I call.” The word *fulciuntur* (“are supported”) does not properly correspond to *vocabant* (“they invited”).]

They receive strength, as it were, from food, becoming more confident through good works; and, desiring afterward to be infused with the dew of contemplation, they are, as it were, intoxicated from the cup.

[Note: Almost all manuscripts read: “as though they were intoxicated from the cup.”]

[Earlier XXXIV.] 47. By the very good things we do, we sometimes draw near to what is worse.—But what is accomplished in this life without contamination by even the slightest stain? Sometimes we draw near to what is worse through the very good things we do, because, while they produce joy in the mind, they also generate a certain security; and when the mind is made secure, it relaxes into sluggishness.

Sometimes they pollute us with a little pride, and make us all the more abased before God the more they make us swollen in our own eyes.

[Note: At this point the editions add “the virtues,” a word absent from the manuscripts; “good works” is to be understood.]

Hence it is rightly added:

## CHAPTER XXXIV [Revised XVII]

**VERSE 5.**—“When the days of the feast had passed in their cycle, Job sent and sanctified them.”

47. The intention must be purified in good works.—When the cycle of the feast-days has been completed, to send to the sons and sanctify them is, after the perception of the virtues, to direct the intention of the heart and cleanse everything that is done by a strict examination of reconsideration: lest things that are evil be judged good; lest even genuinely good things be thought sufficient when they are not perfect.

The mind is often deceived in this way, being misled either by the quality of evil or by the quantity of good.

[Earlier XXXV.] Yet prayers discover these perceptions of virtue better than examinations do. For what we strive to scrutinize more fully within ourselves, we often penetrate more truly by praying than by investigating. When the mind is raised upward by a kind of machinery of compunction, it contemplates with greater certainty whatever presents itself to it concerning itself, judging it beneath itself.

[Note: Ancient Rem., Corb., Germ., first Remig., Vindoc., Ebroic., and other Norman manuscripts read: “Whatever concerning itself is beneath itself, it judges by discerning…” Second Rem. and second Remig. read: “Whatever concerning itself seemed lofty to it, it judges beneath itself…”]

Hence it is rightly added:

## CHAPTER XXXV [Revised XVIII]

[Col. 0548D] **IBID.**—“And, rising at dawn, he offered holocausts for each one.”

48. A holocaust of prayer must be offered for the purification of each virtue.—We rise at dawn when, filled with the light of compunction, we abandon the night of our humanity and open the eyes of the mind to the rays of the true light.

We offer a holocaust for each son when, for every virtue, we sacrifice to the Lord the offering of our prayer: that wisdom may not exalt us; that understanding, while running subtly, may not go astray; that counsel, while multiplying itself, may not become confused; that fortitude, while providing confidence, may not rush headlong; that knowledge, while knowing but not loving, may not inflate us; that piety, while inclining itself beyond rectitude, may not distort us; and that fear, while trembling more than is right, may not plunge us into the pit of despair.

When, therefore, we pour out prayers to the Lord for each virtue, so that it may be pure, what else do we do but offer a holocaust for each one according to the number of the sons?

A holocaust is so called because it is wholly burned. To give a holocaust, therefore, is to set the whole mind ablaze with the fire of compunction, so that the heart may burn on the altar of love and, as it were, consume the sins of its own offspring—the stains of thought.

49. [Earlier XXXVI.] He does not offer this who fails to restrain inward impulses.—But only those know how to do these things who, before their thoughts emerge into action, carefully examine and restrain their inward impulses.

[Note: Corb., the manuscripts of Rheims, two of Remig., Lyr., Bigot., and several editions, especially the older editions of Paris and Basel, read this way. Gilot., Vatic., and Guss. read: “unless they know how to avoid these things.”]

They do not know how to do these things unless they know how to fortify the mind with manly vigilance.

Hence Isbosheth is rightly said to have been killed by an unexpected death. Sacred Scripture testifies that he had not a male doorkeeper but a female one, saying:

“When the sons of Rimmon the Beerothite, Rechab and Baanah, came, they entered the house of Isbosheth in the heat of the day, while he was sleeping on his bed at noon. They entered the house; and the female doorkeeper of the house, cleaning wheat, fell asleep. Taking wheat-grains, they entered secretly and struck him in the groin” (2 Kings IV, 5).

The female doorkeeper cleans the wheat when the guardianship of the mind separates virtues from vices by discernment. If she falls asleep, she admits assassins against her own lord, because when vigilance in discernment ceases, it opens a path for evil spirits to kill the soul.

Those who enter take away the grains because they immediately remove the shoots of good thoughts. They strike in the groin because they kill the virtue of the heart through carnal pleasure. To strike in the groin is to pierce the life of the mind with carnal pleasure.

Isbosheth would by no means have succumbed to this death if he had not assigned a woman—that is, a soft and weak guard—to the entrance of the house, the access of the mind. A strong and manly sense must be placed at the heart’s doors, one that is overcome neither by the sleep of negligence nor deceived by the error of ignorance.

Hence Isbosheth was aptly named: he is stripped by hostile swords while guarded by a woman. For *Isbosheth* means “man of confusion.” He is a man of confusion who is not protected by a strong guard of mind, because, while he thinks he is practicing virtues, the vices that enter secretly kill him without his knowing.

The entrance of the mind must therefore be fortified with every virtue, lest at any time lurking enemies penetrate it through an opening created by neglected thought.

Solomon says: “Guard your heart with all vigilance, for from it flows life” (Prov. IV, 23).

We ought therefore to examine with the greatest care the virtues that we practice, beginning with the intention, lest they arise from an evil source, even when the things they display are right.

Hence here too it is rightly added:

## CHAPTER XXXVI [Earlier XXXVII; Revised XIX]

**IBID.**—“For he said: ‘Perhaps my sons have sinned and blessed God in their hearts.’”

50. The enemy’s various snares by which he corrupts good works: at the beginning, in the course, and at the end of the work.—The sons curse in their hearts when our upright works proceed from thoughts that are not upright; when they bring forth good things openly but secretly contrive harmful things.

They curse God when our minds think they possess from themselves what they are. They curse God when they understand that they have received strength from him, yet nevertheless seek their own praise from his gifts.

[Earlier XXXVIII.] It must be understood that the ancient enemy pursues our good works in three ways, so that what is done rightly before human beings may be corrupted in the sight of the inward Judge.

Sometimes he pollutes the intention in a good work, so that everything that follows in the action does not emerge pure and clean, because he disturbs it from the beginning.

Sometimes he cannot corrupt the intention of the good work, but opposes it within the action itself, as though on the road, so that when someone proceeds more confidently by the purpose of his mind, he is secretly killed by a vice introduced as if from ambush.

Sometimes he neither corrupts the intention nor trips the person up on the road, but entangles the good work at the end of the action. The farther he pretends to have withdrawn either from the house of the heart or from the road of the work, the more cunningly he waits for the completion of the good action in order to deceive it; and the more he has rendered an unwary person so—as though by withdrawing—the more he sometimes pierces him with a sudden wound harshly and incurably.

[Note: Most editions read: “having made an unwary person secure, as though by withdrawing.” *Secure* is redundant and is absent from the Corb., Germ., and other manuscripts.]

51. He pollutes the intention in a good work because, when he sees human hearts easily deceived, he applies to their desires the breeze of transient approval, so that in the upright things they do they incline, through the force of their intention, to desire lowly things.

Hence, rightly, under the figure of Judea, the prophet says of every soul captured by the snare of a wretched intention: “Her enemies have become her leaders” (Lam. I, 5).

It is as though he said openly: when a good work is undertaken with a bad intention, hostile spirits take control of it from the very beginning of thought; and they possess it all the more completely because they hold dominion over it from its beginning.

### 52. When they cannot prevail in corrupting the intention, they cover the traps set along the way

[Note: The older Remensis manuscript, Turonensis, Saint-Martial, Corbeiensis, and some others read: “he covers the traps placed along the road.”]

They cover the traps set along the way, so that, in what is being done well, a heart exalting itself may be diverted from the side toward vice; so that what it had purposed differently when beginning, it may carry through in action far differently from how it began. Often, while human praise confronts a good work, it changes the mind of the person acting: although praise had not been sought, its arrival nevertheless gives pleasure. When the mind of the person acting well is relaxed by this pleasure, it is scattered away from all the strength of its innermost intention.

Often anger attaches itself from the side to our justice, begun well; and while it disturbs the mind excessively through zeal for uprightness, it wounds the whole health of inward tranquility. Often sadness follows the gravity of the heart, as though attached from the side; and it overshadows with a veil of grief every work that a good mind begins with good intention. Sometimes it is expelled all the more slowly because it serves the oppressed mind as though it had arrived late. Often excessive joy attaches itself to a good work; and when it demands that the mind become happier than is fitting, it drives all the weight of seriousness away from the good action.

Because the Psalmist had seen that traps lie along the way even for those who begin well, he rightly said, filled with the prophetic spirit: “Along this way by which I walked, they hid a trap for me” (Psalm 141:4).

[Note: The Remenses, first Remigius, Corbeiensis, Germanus, and others read “they hid traps for me.”]

Jeremiah indicates this well and subtly. While he endeavored to report outward events, he revealed what was taking place inwardly within ourselves, saying:

“Eighty men came from Shechem, and from Shiloh, and from Samaria, with shaved beard and torn garments, squalid; they had offerings and frankincense in their hands, to offer in the house of the Lord. But Ishmael son of Nethaniah went out from Mizpah to meet them; he went along weeping. And when he had met them, he said to them, ‘Come to Gedaliah son of Ahikam.’ When they had come into the middle of the city, he killed them” (Jeremiah 41:5).

[Note: One Remensis and the second Remigius read “with their beards shaved”; the third Remigius reads “having shaved their beard.”]

[Note: In the same place, instead of “squalid,” all the Remenses and Remigii read “squalid with dust.”]

Those shave their beards who withdraw their confidence from their own strength. Those tear their garments who do not spare themselves in the outward rending of their dignity. Those come intending to offer frankincense and gifts in the house of the Lord who promise to present themselves in God’s sacrifice with prayer and works.

But if they do not know how to watch over themselves carefully on that very road of holy devotion, Ishmael son of Nethaniah comes to meet them; for every evil spirit, begotten in the error of pride after the example of his predecessor, namely Satan, sets himself against them as a trap of deception. Of him it is also rightly said: “He went along weeping.” For, so that he may prevail in striking down devout minds, he conceals himself as though under a veil of virtue; and while he pretends to be in accord with those who are truly mourning, he is admitted more securely into the heart’s depths and kills what virtue lies hidden within.

[Note: The Corbeiensis and Germanus manuscripts read “that he may kill.” Hence earlier one may perhaps read “so that, while,” rather than “and while.”]

He often promises to raise them to higher things. Hence he is also said to have declared: “Come to Gedaliah son of Ahikam.” And while he promises greater things, he also takes away the smallest. Hence it is rightly said: “When they had come into the middle of the city, he killed them.”

[Note: The supplied column reference is printed as “[Col. 0551D]”.]

Thus he kills in the middle of the city men coming to offer gifts to God, because minds devoted to divine works, unless they guard themselves with great vigilance, lose their life in the very course of carrying the sacrifice of their devotion, when the enemy steals it away. No one escapes from the hand of this enemy unless he hastens to take refuge in repentance.

Hence it is appropriately added there:

“But ten men were found among them who said to Ishmael, ‘Do not kill us, for we have treasures in the field: wheat, barley, oil, and honey’; and he did not kill them” (Jeremiah 41:8).

A treasure in the field is the hope found in repentance; because it is not seen, it is held as though buried in the soil of the heart. Those, therefore, who had treasures in the field were preserved, because those who, after the fault of their heedlessness, return to the lamentation of repentance do not die as captives.

### 53. When the ancient enemy strikes neither at the beginning of the intention nor in the course of the action, he stretches out harsher traps at the end

The more wickedly he besieges a person, the more he sees that only the end remains for him to deceive. The Prophet had perceived these traps set at the end when he said: “They will watch my heel” (Psalm 55:7).

Because the heel is the end of the body, what is signified by it except the conclusion of an action? Whether evil spirits or wicked people, their followers in pride, watch the heel when they desire to corrupt the end of a good action.

Hence it is also said to the same serpent: “She will watch your head, and you will watch her heel” (Genesis 3:15, according to the Septuagint).

To watch the serpent’s head is to observe the beginnings of his suggestion and, by the careful attention of the hand, to uproot it completely from the entrance of the heart.

[Note: The words “and, by the careful attention of the hand, to uproot it completely” are absent from many manuscripts and are marked with dots in one manuscript, but they are present in Corbeiensis. They are also read by Paterius in his commentary on Genesis, chapter 25. In the Michaelensis manuscript these words are present, but not the chapter number 25.]

Yet when he is detected at the beginning, he strives to strike the heel; for even if he does not strike the intention by his first suggestion, he seeks to deceive at the end. But if the heart is once corrupted in its intention, the middle and the end of the subsequent action are securely possessed by the cunning enemy, since he sees that the whole tree will bear fruit for him after he has corrupted it at the root with the tooth of his poison.

Since, therefore, the greatest care must be taken lest the mind serving good works be polluted by a blameworthy intention, it is rightly said: “Lest perhaps my sons have sinned and blessed God in their hearts.” It is as though it were said openly: Nothing done outwardly is good unless, for its sake, the sacrifice of innocence is first offered inwardly before God’s eyes upon the altar of the heart. [Old recension XXXIX.]

Accordingly, the whole stream of action must be examined to see whether it flows pure from the spring of thought. With every care the eye of the heart must be guarded from the dust of wickedness, lest what it displays to human beings as upright in action it twist inwardly within itself through the vice of a corrupt intention.

### 54. Therefore we must take care that our good works be neither few nor unexamined

We must therefore take care that our good works be not few; we must take care that they be not unexamined—lest, by doing few things, we be found barren, or, by leaving them unexamined, foolish. For no virtue is truly a virtue if it is not joined with other virtues.

Hence it is rightly said to Moses: “Take for yourself spices: stacte and onycha, galbanum of good fragrance, and the clearest frankincense; all shall be of equal weight, and you shall make a compound incense, the work of a perfumer, carefully mixed and pure” (Exodus 30:34).

[Note: Many manuscripts, namely the Remensis, Remigius, Turonensis, and Corbeiensis, with which the old editions agree, have “galbanum.”]

We make incense composed of spices when, upon the altar of good work, we give off the fragrance of a multiplicity of virtues. It becomes mixed and pure because the more one virtue is joined to another, the more sincerely the incense of good work is offered.

Hence it is also rightly added: “And when you have pounded all of it into the finest powder, you shall place some of it before the tabernacle of the testimony” (ibid., 36).

[Note: The words “They shall all be of equal weight” are absent from many manuscripts.]

We pound all the spices into the finest powder when we beat our good works, as though in the mortar of the heart, through hidden examination; and, if they are truly good, we scrutinize them minutely. To reduce spices to powder, therefore, is to wear down virtues through reflection and to bring them back to the subtlety of hidden examination.

[Note: The English manuscripts and our manuscripts, except Corbeiensis, read “in the mortar of the heart.” Paterius likewise reads this.]

It should also be noted that it is said of this same powder: “You shall place some of it before the tabernacle of the testimony.” For our good works truly please the Judge’s sight when the mind crushes them through more subtle reflection and, as it were, renders powder from spices—lest the good being done be coarse and hard; lest, if the tight hand of reconsideration does not crumble it, it fail to scatter its fragrance more subtly.

For this reason the virtue of the bride is praised in the bridegroom’s voice when it is said: “Who is this that comes up from the wilderness like a column of smoke, perfumed with myrrh and frankincense and every powder of the perfumer?” (Song of Songs 3:6).

Holy Church rises like a column of smoke from spices because, from the virtues of her life, she advances daily toward the uprightness of inward incense; nor does she disperse and flow away through her thoughts, but she constrains herself within the secrets of the heart like a rigid rod. While she never ceases to reconsider and reexamine what she does, she has myrrh and frankincense in her work, but powder in her thought.

For this reason it is again said to Moses concerning those who offer a sacrifice: “Having removed the skin of the sacrifice, let them cut its limbs into pieces” (Leviticus 1:6). [Old recension XL.]

We remove the skin of the sacrifice when we take away from the eyes of our mind the outward surface of virtue. We cut its limbs into pieces when, distinguishing its inner parts with subtle care, we think about them member by member.

We must therefore take care lest, when we overcome evils, we be supplanted by good things running riot; lest perhaps what is fluid emerge, what is heedless be caught, what is erroneous abandon the way, or what is broken by weariness lose the merit of previous labor. In all things the mind must vigilantly watch over itself and persevere in that very prudence of self-watchfulness.

Hence it is rightly added:

## CHAPTER XXXVII [Recent recension XX]

### THERE—“Thus Job did all the days”

[Note: In the printed editions “of his life” is added. Those words are unknown to the Colbertine, Remensis, Remigius, Compendiense, Germanus, and other manuscripts; nor are they found above in the exposition, whether of the historical or allegorical sense.]

### 55. Perseverance is necessary

Good is done in vain if it is abandoned before the end of life; for the person who fails before reaching the goal also runs swiftly in vain. Hence it is said of the reprobate: “Woe to those who have lost endurance” (Ecclesiasticus 2:16). Hence Truth says to his elect: “You are those who have remained with me in my temptations” (Luke 22:28).

Hence Joseph, who is described as having persevered in righteousness among his brothers to the end, is said alone to have had a long robe (Genesis 37:24, according to the Septuagint). For what is a long robe except a completed action? Just as an extended robe covers the body’s ankle, so a good action covers us before God’s eyes all the way to the end of life.

[Note: The older Remensis and the first Remigius, together with Corbeiensis, read “extended.”]

Hence Moses is commanded to offer the tail of the sacrifice upon the altar (Exodus 29:22; Leviticus 3:9), so that we may complete every good thing we begin with a persevering end. Good beginnings must therefore be carried out through all the days, so that when evil is driven back by struggle, the victory of goodness may itself be held in the hand of steadfastness.

### 56. We have said these things under a threefold interpretation

We have said these things under a threefold interpretation so that, by setting varied nourishment before a soul that is becoming weary, we may offer it something to choose and take. Yet we earnestly ask that whoever raises the mind to spiritual understanding not depart from reverence for the historical sense.

[Note: In the first Remigius, “with the second hand” reads “from the true meaning of the history.”]

# BOOK TWO

An exposition of the first chapter, from verse six to the end, according to the threefold sense.

[Col. 0553]

# CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0553C]

### 1. Holy Scripture is a mirror

Sacred Scripture is set before the eyes of the mind like a certain mirror, so that our inward face may be seen in it (see Augustine on Psalm 103, sermon 1, no. 4). In it we recognize what is ugly in us and what is beautiful. In it we perceive how far we have progressed and how far we remain from advancement.

It narrates the deeds of the saints and summons the hearts of the weak to imitation. While it recalls their victorious deeds, it strengthens our weakness for the battles against vices. Through its words the mind becomes less fearful amid the struggles, because it sees before it the triumphs of so many strong men.

Sometimes, however, it not only affirms their virtues to us but also makes known their falls, so that we may see both what to seize by imitation in the victory of the strong and what to fear in their lapses. For behold, Job is described as strengthened by temptation, but David as struck down by temptation, so that the virtue of our elders may nourish our hope and their downfall may gird us with the caution of humility. Thus, while the former joyfully lift us up, the latter press us down in fear; and the spirit of the listener, instructed there by confidence in hope and here by humble fear, neither grows proud through presumption, since it is weighed down by dread, nor despairs under fear, since it is strengthened toward confidence in hope by the example of virtue.

[Note: The Remensis and many others read “the deeds of the strong.” Some add “the deeds of strong heroes.” Some have “the deeds of men.” Corbeiensis, in a second hand, has “of the saints,” while in the first hand it has “of their”; Germanus also has “of the saints.”]

# CHAPTER TWO

### VERSE 6

“Now one day, when the sons of God had come to stand before the Lord, Satan was also present among them.”

### 2. THE HISTORICAL SENSE: How accurately Holy Scripture describes events

It is pleasing to observe how sacred discourse, in the beginnings of its narratives, expresses qualities and the boundaries of causes. Sometimes it indicates what it is about to set forth concerning an action by the location of a place, sometimes by the position of a body, sometimes by the condition of the air, and sometimes by the quality of the time.

By the position of places, divine Scripture expresses the merits of what follows and the ends of causes. Thus, concerning Israel, it says that the people could not hear the words of God on the mountain but received the commandments in the plains: clearly indicating the people’s subsequent weakness, since they were unable to climb to the heights but, by living negligently, let themselves fall into the lowest places.

By the position of the body it announces what is to come, as in the Acts of the Apostles Stephen openly declares that he saw Jesus standing at the right hand of God’s power (Acts 7:55–56). To stand is the posture of one who helps. And rightly he is seen standing who offers assistance in the battle of conflict.

By the condition of the air the subsequent event is demonstrated. Thus, when the evangelist said that no one from Judea would then believe while the Lord was preaching, he prefaced it by saying: “Now it was winter” (John 10:22). For it is written: “Because iniquity will abound, the love of many will grow cold” (Matthew 24:12). He therefore took care to specify the season of winter in order to indicate that the cold of wickedness was present in the hearts of his hearers.

Hence it is said beforehand concerning Peter, who was going to deny: “Because it was cold, and he stood by the fire warming himself” (John 18:18). For inwardly he had already grown numb from the warmth of charity, and, with weakness burning within him, he was warming himself again toward love of the present life as though at the fire of his persecutors.

The quality of time also expresses the end of an action. Thus Judas, who would not return to forgiveness, is said to have gone out into the treachery of betrayal at night; as he went out, the evangelist says: “And it was night” (John 13:30). Hence it is also said to the wicked rich man: “This night they will demand your soul from you” (Luke 12:20).

[Note: The same manuscripts repeat “this night they will demand your soul.” Lyra and Bigotius likewise have the repetition.]

The soul that is led into darkness is said to be demanded not in the day but in the night.

Hence Solomon, who received wisdom without persevering in it, is described as having received it in a dream and at night (1 Kings 3:11). Hence angels come to Abraham at midday, but, when they are about to punish Sodom, they are said to have come to it in the evening (Genesis 18:1–2; 19:1).

Since, therefore, the temptation of blessed Job is led to victory, it is said to have begun in the day, when the text says:

# CHAPTER THREE

### THERE—“Now one day, when the sons of God had come to stand before the Lord, Satan was also present among them.”

### 3. How angels are present to God even when sent on a ministry; how great is the subtlety of angels

Who are called the sons of God except the elect angels? Since it is established that they serve the sight of his majesty, it must be carefully asked from where they come in order to stand before the Lord. For Truth says concerning them: “Their angels in heaven always see the face of my Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 18:10). The prophet says concerning them: “Thousands of thousands ministered to him, and ten thousand times a hundred thousand stood before him” (Daniel 7:10).

If, therefore, they always see and always stand before him, we must inquire with vigilant care from where those who never depart come. But when Paul says concerning them: “Are they not all ministering spirits sent into service for the sake of those who are to receive the inheritance of salvation?” (Hebrews 1:14), by recognizing that they are sent, we discover from where they come. [Old recension III.]

But behold, we join one question to another and, as though trying to loosen a strap, tie a knot. For how can they always stand before him or always see the Father’s face if they are sent outwardly on a ministry for our salvation? We resolve this more quickly if we consider how subtle the angelic nature is.

They do not go forth from the divine vision in such a way as to be deprived of the joys of inward contemplation. For if, when going out, they lost sight of the Creator, they could neither raise up those who lie prostrate nor announce the truth to those who are ignorant; nor could they offer to the blind the fountain of light that they themselves would lose when they went forth.

In this, then, the angelic nature is distinguished from the condition of our nature: we are confined by place and constrained by the blindness of ignorance, whereas the spirits of angels are indeed circumscribed by place, but their knowledge is extended far beyond ours in an incomparable way.

[Note: In the Colbertine manuscript, above these words is written: “or, as regards our mode, they are not circumscribed in knowledge.” Shortly afterward, “or, diffused” is written above “extended”; and a little later “circumscribed” above “narrow.” When copyists adopt such glosses, they provide us with corrupt books.]

They are extended in knowledge inwardly and outwardly because they contemplate the very fountain of knowledge. What do they not know among the things that are to be known, when they know the One who knows all things? Their knowledge, therefore, is greatly extended in comparison with ours, but narrow in comparison with divine knowledge. Likewise, their spirits, compared with our bodies, are spirits; but compared with the supreme and uncircumscribed Spirit, they are body.

[Note: All our manuscripts read “extended in knowledge.” The Roman edition of Sixtus V and Gussanville read “they are extended, knowing.”]

Thus they are both sent and stand before him: by being circumscribed, they go forth; by being present inwardly as well, they never depart. They always see the Father’s face and yet come to us, because they go forth to us by spiritual presence while, through inward contemplation, they preserve themselves there from which they had departed.

Let it therefore be said: “The sons of God came to stand before the Lord,” because by a turning of spirit they return there from which they never depart through any turning away of mind.

# CHAPTER FOUR

### THERE—“Satan was also present among them.”

[Col. 0557B]

### 4. Satan is among the angels because he did not lose his nature

It must be carefully asked how Satan could be present among the elect angels, since, compelled by pride, he long ago departed condemned from their lot. Yet he is rightly described as having been present among them, because although he lost blessedness, he did not lose the nature similar to theirs; and although he is weighed down by his merits, he is raised up by the subtle condition of his nature.

He is therefore said to have been present among the sons of God before the Lord because, by that vision with which almighty God beholds all spiritual beings, he also sees Satan in the order of a more subtle nature, as Scripture attests when it says: “The eyes of the Lord observe the evil and the good” (Proverbs 15:3).

But this statement, that Satan was present before the Lord, confronts us with a serious question. For it is written: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5:8). Satan, however, who cannot be pure in heart—how could he have been present to see the Lord?

[Note: The Remensis, Remigius, and many others read: “How could he have been present before the Lord by seeing him?”]

### 5. He is present to God because God sees him

But we must observe that he is said to have been present before the Lord, not to have seen the Lord. He came to be seen, not to see. He was in the Lord’s sight, but the Lord was not in his sight—just as when a blind man stands in the sun, he is indeed bathed in the sun’s rays but does not see the light by which he is illuminated.

So Satan too was present among the angels in the Lord’s sight, because the divine power, which penetrates all things by looking upon them, saw the unclean spirit, though he did not see. Since even those things that flee from God cannot remain hidden, while all things are naked before the heavenly gaze, Satan was present as one absent to the One who is present.

It follows:

# CHAPTER FIVE [Old recension IV, Recent recension III]

### VERSE 7

“To whom the Lord said, ‘From where have you come?’”

### 6. For God, not to know is to reject

What does it mean that, when the elect angels come, they are by no means asked, “From where have you come?” but Satan is asked from where he comes? We inquire only about things we do not know. For God’s not knowing is rejection. Hence at the end he will say to some: “I do not know where you are from; depart from me, all you workers of iniquity” (Luke 13:27).

Likewise, a truthful man is said not to know how to lie because he disdains to slip into falsehood—not because, if he wished to lie, he would not know how, but because, out of love for truth, he rejects speaking falsely.

What, then, does it mean for God to say to Satan, “From where have you come,” except to reject his ways as though they were unknown? The light of Truth therefore does not know the darkness that it rejects; and because it judges and condemns Satan’s paths, it is fitting that it should inquire as though unaware.

Hence the Creator’s voice says to the sinful Adam: “Adam, where are you?” (Genesis 3:9). The divine power was not unaware into what hiding places the servant had fled after his fault. But because it saw him fallen into guilt, already hidden under sin as though from the eyes of Truth, and because it does not approve the darkness of his error, it asks as though ignorant where the sinner is; and it both calls and questions him, saying: “Adam, where are you?”

By calling him, it gives a sign that it is recalling him to repentance. By questioning him, it openly indicates that it does not acknowledge sinners who are rightly condemned.

[Note: The Vindocinenses read “it does not acknowledge them by rightly condemning them.”]

The Lord therefore does not call Satan, but nevertheless questions him, saying: “From where have you come?” For God does not recall the apostate spirit to repentance; rather, as though not knowing the ways of his pride, he condemns them.

Thus, while Satan is questioned about his path, the elect angels are not asked from where they come, because their ways are known to God in proportion as they are carried out by their very Author; and while they serve his will alone, they cannot be unknown to him, since through the eye of approval they are always made from him and before him.

It follows:

# CHAPTER SIX

### THERE—“Satan answered and said: ‘I have gone around the earth and traversed it.’”

### 7. Satan’s circling is evidence of his anxiety

A circular circuit commonly signifies the anxiety of labor. Satan, therefore, went around the earth in labor because he disdained to stand peacefully at heaven’s summit. And when he indicates that he did not fly but traversed the earth, he shows how heavily the weight of sin presses him down in the lowest places.

Thus he went around the earth by traversing it, because, having fallen from the flight of spiritual power, oppressed by the burden of his wickedness, he came outward into the circuit of labor.

Hence it is also said through the Psalmist concerning his members: “The wicked walk around” (Psalm 11:9), because, while they do not desire inward things, they are wearied by labor among outward things.

It follows:

# CHAPTER SEVEN [Recent recension IV]

### VERSE 8

“Have you considered my servant Job, that there is none like him on earth, a simple and upright man, fearing God and turning away from evil?”

### 8. The various ways in which God and spirits speak

Because we have explained above, carefully and part by part, the statement that blessed Job is called by the divine voice simple and upright, fearing God and turning away from evil, we avoid repeating what we have said, lest, by repeating what has already been examined, we come more slowly to what has not yet been examined.

[Old recension V.]

We must therefore carefully consider what it means that the Lord is said to speak either to Satan or that Satan is reported to answer the Lord. For we must examine what kind of speech this is.

Neither the Lord, who is the supreme and uncircumscribed Spirit, nor Satan, who is clothed in no bodily nature, draws an airy breath through a bodily bellows as human beings do, so that it may be released through the organ of the throat by the utterance of a voice.

But when the incomprehensible nature speaks to an invisible nature, our mind must rise above the condition of bodily speech and be lifted toward the lofty and unknown modes of inward speech.

When we express outwardly what we sense inwardly, we cast it forth through the organ of the throat by the sound of the voice. We stand before other people’s eyes within the secrecy of the mind, as though behind the wall of the body; but when we wish to reveal ourselves, we go forth as though through the door of the tongue, so that we may show outwardly what we are inwardly.

A spiritual nature is not like this, since it is not composed in two ways from mind and body. Yet we must also know that, when that incorporeal nature itself is said to speak, its speech is by no means formed in one single and identical manner.

God speaks one way to angels, angels another way to God; God one way to the souls of the saints, the souls of the saints another way to God; God one way to the devil, and the devil another way to God.

### 9. How God speaks to angels

Since nothing obstructs spiritual nature by bodily opposition, God speaks to the holy angels by displaying his hidden and invisible things to their hearts. Thus whatever they ought to do, they read in the contemplation of truth itself, and the joys of contemplation are, as it were, certain commands of the voice.

For what is inspired to those who see is spoken, as it were, to those who hear. Hence, when God infused into their hearts the judgment of vengeance against human pride, he said: “Come, let us go down and confuse their tongue” (Genesis 2:7).

[Note: Nearly all manuscripts read “their tongues.” The same has been observed in what follows, where this passage is cited.]

He says “Come” to those who cling to him, because never to decrease from divine contemplation and always to increase within divine contemplation is itself to come; and never to depart in heart is, in a certain stable movement, always to come.

He also says to them: “Let us go down and confuse their tongue.” The angels ascend insofar as they behold the Creator. The angels descend insofar as, by the scrutiny of strict judgment, they press down creation when it raises itself unlawfully.

For God to say, therefore, “Let us go down and confuse their tongue,” is to show them in himself what ought rightly to be done and, through the force of inward vision, to inspire their minds by hidden movements with the judgments that are to be displayed.

[Note: The editions available read “those who were present.” This is corrected with the help of the Corbeiensis and Germanus manuscripts.]

### 10. How angels speak to God

Angels speak in another way to God, as they also say through the Apocalypse of John: “Worthy is the Lamb who was slain to receive power, and divinity, and wisdom” (Revelation 5:12).

For the voice of the angels in praise of the Creator is the very inward wonder of contemplation. To be astonished at the miracles of divine power is to have spoken, because an awakened movement of the heart, accompanied by reverence, is a great cry of the voice in the ears of the uncircumscribed Spirit.

This voice unfolds itself as though through distinct words while forming itself through countless modes of wonder. God therefore speaks to the angels when his inward will is made manifest to them for contemplation.

[Note: The Remensis, Remigius, Longipontanus, Valeriacensis, and Corbeiensis read “by seeing the inward will.”]

The angels, however, speak to the Lord when, by looking above themselves, they rise into a movement of wonder.

[Old recension VI.]

### How God speaks to the souls of the saints, and how they speak to God

God speaks one way to the souls of the saints, and the souls of the saints speak another way to God. Hence it is again said in the Apocalypse of John:

“I saw beneath the altar the souls of those who had been slain because of the word of God and because of the testimony that they held; and they cried out with a loud voice, saying: ‘How long, Lord, holy and true, will you not judge and avenge our blood upon those who dwell on the earth?’”

Immediately it is added: “White robes were given to each of them, and it was said to them that they should rest for a little while longer, until the number of their fellow servants and their brothers should be completed.”

For what does it mean for souls to request vengeance except to desire the day of the final judgment and the resurrection of their extinguished bodies? Their great cry is their great desire. Each person cries less the less he desires, and expresses a greater voice in the ears of the uncircumscribed Spirit the more fully he pours himself into desire for him.

[Note: The Corbeiensis, Germanus, all the manuscripts, and the older Paris and Basel editions read “into the ears of the circumscribed spirit.” Gilotius, in 1571, and the editions thereafter have the same reading. This is clearly an error. Saint Gregory understands God by “the uncircumscribed Spirit.”]

The words of souls, therefore, are their desires. For if desire were not speech, the Prophet would not say: “Your ear has heard the desire of their heart” (Psalm 9:17).

But since the mind of one who asks is accustomed to be moved in one way and that of one who is asked in another, and since the souls of the saints cling to God in the bosom of inward secrecy in such a way that they rest by clinging to him, how are they said to ask when they are clearly in no way separated from the inward will? How are they said to ask when it is certain that they neither fail to know God’s will nor are ignorant of the things that are to come?

[Note: The printed editions read “how are they said to desire vengeance?” None of our manuscripts agrees.]

Yet, being placed in him, they are said to ask something from him—not because they desire anything that conflicts with the will of the one whom they see, but because, the more ardently they cling to him in mind, the more they receive from him the knowledge to ask for what they know he wills to do.

From him, therefore, they drink what they thirst for from him; and, in a manner still incomprehensible to us, they are satisfied through foreknowledge in that for which they hunger by asking.

They would be in conflict with the Creator’s will if, seeing what he wills, they did not ask for it; and they would cling to him less if they knocked with a more sluggish desire upon the one whom they see willing to give.

To them, as they desire, the divine answer is given: “Rest for a little while longer, until the number of your fellow servants and your brothers is completed.” To say “Rest for a little while longer” to the souls that desire is to breathe into them, from foreknowledge itself, the consolation that exists amid the ardor of desire, so that the voice of the souls may be what they desire in love, and the speech of the God who answers may be what confirms them amid their desires by the certainty of reward.

His answering, therefore, consists in infusing into their minds the willingness to await the gathering of their brothers, so that they may gladly await the delay; and, when they desire the resurrection of the flesh, may also rejoice in the increase of their brothers who are to be gathered.

[Vet. VII.] 12. God speaks to the devil in one way, and the devil to God in another.—God speaks to the devil in one way, and the devil to God in another. God’s speaking to the devil consists in rebuking his ways and activities through the judgment of hidden strictness, as is said here: “From where have you come?” But the devil’s answering him consists in being unable to conceal anything from his almighty majesty. Hence he says here: “I have gone around the earth and traversed it.” It is as though he were saying what he has done, acknowledging that he cannot hide his actions from God’s eyes.

It should be understood that, as we learn in this passage, God speaks to the devil in four ways, while the devil speaks to God in three. God speaks to the devil in four ways: he rebukes his unjust ways; he sets before him the justice of his elect against him; he permits their innocence to be tested by granting him permission; and at times he forbids him to dare to tempt them.

He rebukes his unjust ways, as has already been said: “From where have you come?” He sets before him the justice of his elect against him, as he says: “Have you considered my servant Job, that there is none like him upon the earth?”  

[Note: In the printed editions: “Have you considered?” In all the manuscripts we consulted, *nunquid* is not found. We have therefore removed it here and below.]

[Col. 0561C] He permits their innocence to be tested by granting permission, as he says: “Behold, all that he has is in your hand.” Again, he forbids him to tempt him when he says: “Only do not extend your hand against him.”
