The devil, however, speaks to God in three ways: when he discloses his ways, when he accuses the innocence of the elect with fabricated charges, or when he requests that the same innocence be tested. He discloses his ways when he says: “I have gone around the earth and traversed it.” He accuses the innocence of the elect when he says:

(Verses 9–10) “Does Job fear God for nothing? Have you not fenced him in, his house, and all his possessions around him?”

[Note: Gilot., Vatican, Gussanville, and others read *substantiam ejus*, “his possessions.” *Ej us* is redundant and is not found in our manuscripts or in the old edition.]

He requests that the same innocence be tested when he says: “Extend your hand and touch all that he possesses, unless he blesses you to your face.”

But God’s saying, “From where have you come?”—as we indicated above—is to rebuke the paths of his malice by the force of his justice. God’s saying, “Have you considered my servant Job, that there is none like him upon the earth?” is to make his elect righteous, such that the apostate angel may envy them.

[Note: Some manuscripts read, “that there is none like him on earth.”]

God’s saying, “Behold, all that he has is in your hand,” is to release that hidden assault of his malice against the faithful for the purpose of testing them. God’s saying, “Only do not extend your hand against him,” is to restrain him, even while permitting him, from an excessive assault of temptation.

The devil’s saying, “I have gone around the earth and traversed it,” is to acknowledge that he cannot conceal the ingenuity of his malice from God’s invisible eyes. The devil’s saying, “Does Job fear God for nothing?” is to complain against the good in the hiding places of his thoughts, to envy their progress, and, in his envy, to search for cracks through which they might be rejected. The devil’s saying, “Extend your hand a little and touch all that he possesses” (verse 11), is to pant with the heat of malice for the affliction of the good. For the more enviously he desires their temptation, the more he asks for it as though pleading for their testing.

Since we have briefly explained the various forms of inner speech, let us return to the order of our exposition, which we interrupted for a little while.

## CHAPTER VIII [Vet. VIII; Rec. V]

[Col. 0562B]

**VERSE 8.**—“Have you considered my servant Job, that there is none like him upon the earth: a simple and upright man, fearing God and turning away from evil?”

13. The battle between God and the devil, whose subject was Job.—It was already treated in the preceding discourse that the devil proposed a contest not against Job but against God; blessed Job, however, was placed in the middle as the subject of the contest. And if, in our discussions, we say that Job sinned amid the blows—which it would be impious to believe—we would be saying that God lost his case in the proposition he had made.

[Note: The printed editions add here *victoriam*, “the victory,” against the manuscripts and against Gregory’s manner of expression. In the preface, no. 8, we read: “he reproves him for having lost what he had proposed.” See Book XXIII, no. 1.]

For behold, it must also be observed in this passage that the devil did not first ask the Lord for blessed Job; rather, the Lord praised him in defiance of the devil. And if he had not known that Job would remain steadfast in his righteousness, he certainly would not have proposed him as an example. Nor would he have permitted him to be destroyed in temptation, when, even before the temptation, the praises of God had kindled the flames of envy in the tempter’s mind.

14. How cunningly the devil seeks grounds on which to accuse us.—But when the ancient adversary finds no evils of which to accuse us, he seeks to bend good things themselves toward evil. When he is defeated by our deeds, he examines our words in order to accuse us. When he finds no accusation in our words, he strives to darken the intention of the heart—as though good deeds were not done with a good purpose, and therefore ought not to be judged good by the Judge.

For when he sees the fruits of a tree remaining green even in the heat, he seeks, as it were, to place a worm at its root. Thus he says:

## CHAPTER IX

**VERSES 9–10.**—“Does Job fear God for nothing? Have you not fenced him in, his house, and all his possessions around him? You have blessed the works of his hands, and his possessions have increased in the land.”

15. He tests us through prosperity and adversity.—As though he were saying plainly: “He who has received so many good things on earth—what wonder is it if he conducts himself innocently in return for them? He would truly be innocent if he remained good amid adversity. Why is he called great when the reward of each of his works accompanies him with such abundance of possessions?”

For when the crafty adversary observes that the holy man has acted well amid prosperity, he hastens to condemn him before the Judge through adversity. Hence it is rightly said in the Apocalypse, in the voice of an angel: “The accuser of our brothers has been cast down, who accused them before the presence of our God day and night” (Rev. 12:10).

[Vet. IX.] Holy Scripture, moreover, often uses “day” for prosperity and “night” for adversity. He therefore does not cease accusing us by day and by night, because he strives to show us as blameworthy now in prosperity, now in adversity. He accuses us by day when he suggests that we misuse prosperity. He accuses us by night when he demonstrates that we lack patience in adversity.

Since blessed Job had not yet been touched by blows, he had, as it were, no occasion by which he could accuse him in the night. But because Job had flourished in great holiness amid prosperity, the devil pretended that he had acted well for the sake of that prosperity, lying through a crafty assertion that Job did not possess wealth for the service of the Lord, but worshiped the Lord for the sake of wealth.

[Note: Corb., Germ., Rhem., Remig., Ebroic., and the other Norman manuscripts read *magna sanitate*, “with great soundness.”]

Some people use this world in a measured way in order to enjoy God. Others wish to use God only temporarily in order to enjoy this world. Therefore, when the devil recounts the good things bestowed by divine generosity, he thinks that he diminishes the deeds of the strong worker, so that, since he cannot criticize his life on the basis of his works, he may, as it were, condemn his mind on the basis of his thoughts; lying that everything he had lived innocently in outward conduct had served not the love of the Lord but the pursuit of temporal prosperity.

[Note: This is how the English manuscripts and others read. The editions of Gilot, Rome, Sixtus V, and many others have *addiscat*, “may learn.” The verb *addicit*, meaning “condemns,” is familiar to Gregory. It is also frequently found in this sense among sacred writers, both earlier and later. Ambrose, Book I, *On Virginity*, concerning the executioner of Saint Agnes: “you might see the executioner tremble, as though he himself had been condemned”; Bernard, Book II, *On Consideration*, chapter 14: “the frequent condemnation of the innocent.”]

Though he did not know the strength of blessed Job, he nevertheless knew truly that each person is tested by adversity. He therefore sought to have him tested, so that he who had walked with unhindered step through the day of prosperity might at least stumble in the night of adversity and lie prostrate before the eyes of his praiser, overthrown by an act of impatience. Hence he continues:

## CHAPTER X [Rec. VI]

**VERSE 11.**—“But extend your hand a little and touch all that he possesses, unless he blesses you to your face.”

16. The devil can do nothing except by God’s permission.—When Satan desires to tempt the holy man, yet says to the Lord that he should extend his hand, it must be carefully observed that he does not even attribute to himself the power to strike, although he displays singular pride against the Author of all things.

For the devil knows that he is not sufficient to do anything of himself, since he does not even exist as a spirit through himself. Hence, in the Gospel, the legion being expelled from the man said: “If you cast us out, send us into the herd of swine” (Matt. 8:31). If he could not go into the swine by himself, is it surprising that, without the hand of the Author, he could not touch the house of the holy man?

[Vet. X.] 17. The devil’s will is evil, but his power is just.—It must be understood that Satan’s will is always wicked, but his power is never unjust, because he has his will from himself but his power from the Lord. What he wickedly desires to do, God permits to be done only justly.

Hence it is rightly said in the Books of Kings: “An evil spirit from the Lord rushed upon Saul” (1 Kings 18:10). Behold, one and the same spirit is called both “from the Lord” and “evil”: from the Lord, namely, through the permission of just power; evil, however, through the desire of an unjust will.

Therefore he who can do nothing except by permission ought not to be feared. The only power to be feared is that which, when it has permitted the enemy to rage, makes even his unjust will serve the use of just judgment.

He asks that the hand be extended only a little, because it is outward things that he desires to have destroyed. For Satan does not think he has accomplished much unless he wounds the soul, so that, by striking it, he may recall it from that homeland from which he himself lies prostrate far away, struck down by the weapon of his pride.

18. The face of God signifies the regard of grace.—But what does he mean by saying, “Unless he blesses you to your face”? We look upon what we love; but from what we wish to shun, we turn our face away. What, then, is the face of God except the regard of his grace?

[Note: The editions read *perhibetur*, “is said”; the manuscripts read *adhaeremus*, “we cling.”]

He therefore says: “Extend your hand a little and touch all that he possesses, unless he blesses you to your face.” As though he were saying plainly: “Take away the things you have given him. For if he loses what he has received, he will not seek the regard of your grace once his temporal possessions have been removed. If he does not possess the things in which he delights, he will despise your favor even by cursing you.”

By this cunning request Truth is not at all provoked into defeat; rather, what will contribute to the increase of the faithful servant’s reward is granted to the enemy for his own deception. Hence it immediately follows:

## CHAPTER XI [Vet. XI; Rec. VII]

**VERSE 12.**—“Behold, all that he has is in your hand; only do not extend your hand against him.”

[Note: Gussanville prefixes here: “Then the Lord said to Satan,” which is absent from both the printed and handwritten codices.]

19. God permits some things to the tempter and denies him others.—The administration of holy mercy in the Lord’s words must be considered: how he permits and restrains our enemy, releases and curbs him. He gives him some things for tempting, but binds him with respect to others.

[Note: In the editions, by interpolation, one reads: “he gives some things for afflicting, but …”; this is plainly contrary to the authority of the manuscripts and to Gregory’s purpose, who here takes up two—not three—points to be demonstrated: that our enemy is both released and restrained. He is released when he is permitted to tempt; he is restrained when this power is bound by definite conditions.]

“Behold, all that he has is in your hand; only do not extend your hand against him.” He exposes Job’s possessions, yet protects his body, which he will afterward hand over to the tempter. Nevertheless, he does not release the enemy all at once to attack everything, lest he strike from every side and shatter the man.

For when many evils befall the elect, they are distributed over time by the wondrous grace of the Creator, so that what would destroy them if heaped together may be endured when divided. Hence Paul says: “God is faithful, who will not permit you to be tempted beyond what you can bear, but with the temptation will also provide a way out, so that you may be able to endure” (1 Cor. 10:13).

[Note: Rhem., Remig., and the Norman manuscripts add: “beyond what you are able to bear.”]

Hence David says: “Test me, Lord, and try me” (Ps. 25:2). As though he were saying plainly: “First examine my strength, and then permit me to be tested insofar as I am able to bear it.”

Yet the statement, “Behold, all that he has is in your hand; only do not extend your hand against him,” can also be understood in another way. The Lord knew his warrior to be strong, but he wished to divide the battles he would fight against the enemy, so that, although victory over all things was available to the robust warrior, the enemy might first return defeated to the Lord from one contest; then, by granting him another contest to conquer, the Lord would make the faithful servant victorious all the more wondrously, since the defeated enemy would recover himself for new battles against him.

It follows:

## CHAPTER XII [Vet. XII; Rec. VIII]

[Col. 0565B] **IBID.**—“And Satan went out from the presence of the Lord.”

20. God is within and outside all things, above and below all things.—What does it mean that Satan is said to have gone out from the presence of the Lord? For where can one go out from him who is everywhere?

Hence he says: “I fill heaven and earth” (Jer. 23:24). Hence his Wisdom says: “Alone I encompassed the circuit of heaven” (Ecclus. 24:8). Of his Spirit it is written: “The Spirit of the Lord has filled the world” (Wis. 1:7). Again, the Lord says: “Heaven is my throne, but the earth is the footstool of my feet” (Isa. 66:1). Again, it is written of him: “He measures heaven with his span and encloses the whole earth in his fist” (Isa. 40:12).

The seat over which he presides remains both within and outside.

[Note: The Corbey and German manuscripts read: “and remains above.”]

He is shown to measure heaven with his span and enclose the earth in his fist, signifying that he is outside on every side of all the things he created. For what is enclosed within is held by the one who encloses it from without.

By the seat over which he presides, therefore, he is understood to be within and above; by the fist with which he contains, he is signified to be outside and below.

[Note: In the Corbey, German, and many other manuscripts, *intelligitur* is absent, and the passage reads: “By the seat, therefore, over which he presides, it is signified that he is within and above; by the fist with which he contains, that he is outside and below.”]

Because he himself remains within all things, outside all things, above all things, and below all things, he is above through power and below through sustaining; outside through greatness and within through subtlety: ruling above, containing below; surrounding outside, penetrating within.

He does not remain superior on one side and inferior on another, or exterior on one side and interior on another. Rather, one and the same whole is everywhere: presiding while sustaining, sustaining while presiding, surrounding while penetrating, penetrating while surrounding; from the place where he presides above, sustaining below; and from the place where he encompasses outside, filling within.

He rules above without disturbance; sustains below without labor; penetrates within without diminution; surrounds outside without extension. Thus he is lower and higher without place; greater without breadth; subtler without diminution.

[Note: Rhem., Remig., Vindocin., Corb., Germ., and others read: “He is vast without breadth; he is subtle,” and so forth.]

[Col. 0566A] 21. Satan goes out from the presence of the Lord when he reaches the fulfillment of his desire.—Where, then, can one go out from him who, although he is nowhere through bodily mass, is absent nowhere through his unbounded substance?

But as long as Satan, pressed down by the power of divine majesty, was unable to exercise the desire of his malice, he stood, as it were, before the presence of the Lord.

[Vet. XIII.] He went out from the presence of the Lord because, divinely released from the confinement of inner restraint, he came to the fulfillment of his desire. He went out from the presence of the Lord because a harmful will, long bound by the chains of discipline, at last proceeded to action.

For when, as has been said, he was unable to accomplish what he wished, he stood, as it were, before the presence of the Lord, because heavenly providence had constrained him away from the effect of his malice. But he went out from his presence because, receiving the power of temptation, he attained the fulfillment of his malicious desires.

It follows:

## CHAPTER XIII [Rec. IX]

**VERSES 13–15.**—“Now, when his sons and daughters were eating and drinking wine in the house of their firstborn brother, a messenger came to Job and said: ‘The oxen were plowing, and the donkeys were grazing beside them; then the Sabeans fell upon them and carried everything away, struck the servants with the sword, and I alone escaped to tell you.’”

22. The devil chooses suitable times for tempting.—We must observe what times are suited to temptations. The devil chose the time for tempting when he found the children of blessed Job at a banquet. For the enemy observes not only what someone is doing, but also when he is doing it.

Although he had received power, he nevertheless sought a suitable time for overthrowing him, so that it might be shown to us, by God’s ordering, that the joy of satiety is a herald of tribulation.

[Note: The older Rhemish and German manuscripts read *ad submersionem*, “for submersion”; so also the old Compendium, Val-Dieu, and Beauvais manuscripts.]

It should also be observed how cunningly the very losses inflicted are announced. It is not said, “The oxen were carried away by the Sabeans,” but, “The oxen that were plowing were carried away,” so that, by recalling the fruit of their labor, the cause of sorrow might increase.

[Note: Vindocin reads: “The oxen were carried away by the Sabeans,” rather than “the oxen that were carried away.” So also Saint-Michel and others.]

Among the Greeks, moreover, not only female donkeys but pregnant female donkeys are reported to have been carried off, so that, while the smallest animals might strike the hearer’s mind less by their size, they might wound it more through their fertility.

And because adversity strikes the mind more severely when, besides being extensive, it is announced suddenly, the measure of the groans was increased even through the successive details of the messengers’ reports.

[Note: This is how we read in the Rhemish, Remigian, Corbey, German, Compendium, and Val-Dieu manuscripts. Gregory uses the same word as a neuter in Book VIII, formerly chapter 7, now chapter 11, no. 27: “No point of death yet breaks in.” The Paris edition of 1495 varies, reading *etiam particula*, “even in a part.” The Basel edition of 1514 has *etiam per auricula*, “even through the ear.” The remaining editions have *per particulam* or *per particulas*, “through a detail” or “through details.”]

For it follows:

## CHAPTER XIV [Vet. XIV]

[Col. 0566D] **VERSE 16.**—“While he was still speaking, another came and said: ‘The fire of God fell from heaven, consumed the sheep and the servants, and I alone escaped to tell you.’”

23. He attempts to overthrow Job’s steadfastness through sudden disasters.—So that the hearer might not experience diminished sorrow at the loss of his possessions, the devil urges Job toward excess even through the very words of the messengers.

For observe how cunningly the report says, “The fire of God,” as though it were saying: “You are enduring the punishment of the one you wished to appease with so many sacrifices; you are suffering the anger of the one whom you served daily with toil.”

By indicating that the God whom Job had served had brought adversity, the devil presents him as injured, so that Job might recall his former services to mind and, judging that he had served in vain, grow proud against the Author.

[Note: The old edition reads *laesionem*, “injury.” Coccius and Gilot read *laeso*, “having been injured”; Gussanville reads *ab eo laesum*, “injured by him.” The manuscripts simply read *laesum*, “injured.”]

For a devout mind, when it sees itself suffering adversity from human beings, rests in the consolation of divine grace; and when it sees the storms of temptation increasing outwardly, it seeks refuge in hope in the Lord and flees within the harbor of conscience.

But the crafty enemy wished at one and the same time to shake the strongest heart of the holy man with human adversities and with despair of God. He first reported that the Sabeans had fallen upon him, and immediately announced that the fire of God had fallen from heaven. Thus, as though he were closing every avenue of consolation, he showed even the one who might have consoled Job’s mind to be acting against him.

He intended that, while the tempted man considered himself abandoned and oppressed on every side, he might break out against God with all the greater boldness because he was also in despair.

It follows:

## CHAPTER XV

**VERSE 17.**—“While he was still speaking, another came and said: ‘The Chaldeans formed three bands, fell upon the camels, and carried them away; they also struck the servants with the sword, and I alone escaped to tell you.’”

24. He heaps wound upon wound.—Behold, again, lest he should have felt too little sorrow over human adversity, the devil announces that bands of Chaldeans have fallen upon him. And lest the adversity coming from above strike him less severely, he displays a repeated anger in the air. For it follows:

## CHAPTER XVI [Vet. XV]

**VERSES 18–19.**—“While he was speaking, behold, another entered and said: ‘While your sons and daughters were eating and drinking wine in the house of their firstborn brother, suddenly a powerful wind rushed in from the region of the desert and shook the four corners of the house. When it collapsed, it crushed your children, and they died; and I alone escaped to tell you.’”

25. He attempts to provoke hatred of God.—He who is not overthrown by one wound is struck a second and a third time, so that at last he may be wounded to the depths.

Adversity from the Sabeans had therefore been announced; divine punishment through fire from heaven had been announced; then the seizure of the camels and the slaughter of the servants by human beings were announced again; and the anger of divine indignation was repeated when the invading wind was said to have shaken the corners of the house and killed the children.

Since it is known that the elements cannot be moved without a heavenly command, it is subtly suggested that the very one who permitted them to move had moved the elements against Job. Yet Satan, once he has received power from the Lord, can also shake the elements for the purposes of his wickedness.

Nor should it seem surprising that a spirit cast down from the heights could disturb the air and stir the winds, since it is plainly established that even water and fire serve the use of those condemned to the mines.

It was therefore intended that the evils be announced; intended that they be many; intended that they be sudden. When he first announced the adversities, he inflicted a wound upon a still tranquil heart, as upon a sound limb. But when he struck the wounded heart again by repeated blows, so as to drive it toward words of impatience, he inflicted wound upon wound.

26. Job’s blows were sudden and manifold.—It should be observed how cunningly the ancient enemy took care not so much to break the holy man’s patience through the loss of his possessions as through the order of the announcements.

He first took care to announce lesser things and afterward greater ones, finally bringing news of the children’s death, lest Job consider the lesser losses of his property insignificant if he heard of them after being bereaved; and lest the loss of his possessions strike him less severely when he already knew of the children’s death, since there would be no inheritance if he first removed the heirs who were being preserved.

[Note: The older Remigian manuscript, together with Corb., Germ., and Colb., reads *quibus servabatur haereditas*, “for whom the inheritance was being preserved,” instead of *qui servabantur haeredes*, “the heirs who were being preserved.”]

Beginning with the smallest matters, therefore, he announced the more grievous ones last, so that, as Job gradually learned of worse and worse events, every wound might find a place for sorrow in his heart.

It should also be noted how cunningly the weight of so many evils was announced both in separate parts and suddenly, so that the sorrow itself, growing abruptly and piece by piece, could not contain itself in the hearer’s heart, and might kindle him to blasphemy all the more ardently as he burned within under the pressure of sudden and multiplied reports.

[Note: The same manuscripts read *angustiis*, “under pressures” or “in anguish.”]

[Vet. XVI; Rec. X.] 27. When those set over others serve pleasure, the restraints of their subordinates are loosened. The devil finds an opening even in moderate banquets.—Nor do I think that the fact that the children were feasting in the house of their eldest brother when they perished should be passed over carelessly.

It was said above that banquets can scarcely be held without fault. To speak, then, not of others but of ourselves, we must understand that what is done indulgently by those of lesser rank is restrained by the discipline of their superiors. But when the superiors themselves serve pleasure, the reins of wantonness are plainly loosened for their subordinates.

For who would hold himself within the constraints of discipline when even those who have received the authority to impose restraint release themselves to pleasures?

[Note: Gussanville reads “not of others.” Other books more appropriately read “not of them,” namely, Job’s children, concerning whom Saint Gregory does not allow an unfavorable judgment.]

Thus they perish while feasting in the house of the eldest brother, because the enemy then gains greater strength against us when he sees that even those who have been placed over others for the guardianship of discipline serve pleasure.

[Note: The manuscripts read this way; the editions have *ventri*, “the belly.” Immediately after the word *occupat*, Coccius added *subditos*, “subordinates,” which no later editor removed, although it is absent from the manuscripts.]

For he seizes them with greater freedom to strike the more freely as those who could intercede for the guilty are occupied with pleasure.

Let it not be supposed, however, that the sons of so great a man devoted themselves to stuffing their bellies through the pursuit of banquets. Yet we know truly that, even when someone does not exceed the bounds of necessity in eating because of the guardianship of discipline, the mind’s attention nevertheless grows dull amid banquets; and he considers less carefully how great a battle of temptations he is engaged in when he relaxes through security.

[Note: The editions read *qui*, “who,” and shortly afterward *in domo ergo*, “therefore in the house.” We restore from the manuscripts *quae*, referring to “the mind,” and *in die ergo suo*, “therefore on his own day.” This alludes to Job 1:4, where it is said that they held banquets “each on his own day.”]

Therefore, the children of the firstborn brother are crushed on their day, because the ancient enemy seeks an opening for overthrow through the negligence of superiors in the death of those beneath them.

But since we have learned by how many spears of messengers he was struck, let us hear what our strong warrior was like as he stood amid his wounds. It follows:

## CHAPTER XVI [Rec. XI]

**VERSE 20.**—“Then Job arose, tore his garment, and, falling to the ground with his head shorn, worshiped.”

28. It is a fault either not to feel God’s blows or to feel them excessively.—Some consider it a philosophy of great steadfastness if, when corrected by the harshness of discipline, they do not feel the blows of the whip or the pains.

[Note: Gussanville has, mistakenly, *verborum*, “of words.”]

Others feel the blows of punishments so excessively that, moved by immoderate pain, they even slip into an outburst of speech. But whoever strives to hold true philosophy must walk between these two extremes.

Insensibility of heart is not the measure of true virtue. For limbs are very diseased through numbness when, even after being cut, they cannot feel pain.

[Note: Coccius and the editions that follow read “to feel pain,” against the manuscripts.]

Again, the one who feels the pain of blows more than necessary abandons the guardianship of virtue. For when the heart is touched by excessive affliction, it is stirred even to insults born of impatience; and the person who ought to correct wrongdoing through punishment instead causes wickedness to increase through the punishment.

Against the insensibility of those who are struck, the prophet says: “You struck them, and they did not grieve; you consumed them, and they refused to receive discipline” (Jer. 5:3). Against the faintheartedness of those who are struck, the Psalmist says: “They will not endure in miseries” (Ps. 139:11). They would indeed endure in miseries if they bore adversity with equanimity. But after they collapse in mind amid the blows, they lose, as it were, the steadfastness required to endure the miseries inflicted upon them.

[Vet. XVII.] 29. Job avoided both extremes. The custom of growing or cutting the hair in times of affliction.—Blessed Job, therefore, because he held to the rule of true philosophy, preserved himself against both extremes by a remarkable art of moderation: he neither despised the blows by failing to feel pain, nor, by feeling pain beyond measure, raged against the judgment of the one who struck him.

[Note: We have removed the particle *quasi*, “as though,” on the authority of the Regius, Corbey, German, and other manuscripts.]

After all his possessions had been lost and all his children taken away, he arose, tore his garments, and, falling to the ground with his head shorn, worshiped. His tearing his garments and falling to the ground with his head shorn plainly show that he felt the pain of the blow. But the statement that he worshiped openly shows that, even while in pain, he did not go beyond the judgment of the one who struck him.

[Note: Two Rhemish manuscripts together with one Remigian read: “because through the blows.”]

He was therefore neither wholly unmoved, lest he despise God through insensibility, nor wholly moved, lest he sin through excessive grief. Since there are two commandments of charity—love of God and love of neighbor—he fulfilled love of neighbor by mourning for his children; and, lest he abandon love of God, he completed prayer amid his groans.

[Note: The Corbey and German manuscripts read *adorationem*, “worship,” as was also formerly read at Utica.]

Some people love God in prosperity, but when placed in adversity love the one who strikes them less. Blessed Job, however, by the outward motion he displayed, showed that he recognized the blows of his Father; by remaining humble in worship, he showed that he did not abandon the Father’s love even in pain.

Thus, lest he be proud through not feeling pain, he fell when struck; but lest he make himself a stranger to the one striking him, he fell in order to worship.

It was the custom of the ancients that whoever preserved the appearance of his body by growing his hair would cut it during a time of affliction; and again, whoever cut his hair in a time of tranquility would grow it out as a display of affliction.

Blessed Job is therefore shown to have preserved his hair during a time of tranquility, since he is said to have shorn his head for the use of sorrow, so that, when the heavenly hand struck him in all things, even the altered appearance voluntarily assumed for repentance might darken him.

But let us hear what this man, stripped of his possessions, bereaved of his children, who tore his garments, shaved his head, and fell to the ground, said.

## CHAPTER XVII [Rec. XII]

**VERSE 21.**—“Naked I came forth from my mother’s womb, and naked I shall return there.”

30. Temporal things should be considered of little account, since once we did not have them and shall not have them.—O how high a seat of inward counsel this man presides over, who lies prostrate on the ground with his garments torn!

Because, by the Lord’s judgment, he had lost everything, he recalled to mind the time when he did not yet possess the things he had lost, in order to preserve his patience. By considering that he once had not possessed them, he moderated the pain of having lost them.

For, in the loss of possessions, it is a great consolation to recall those times when we happened not to possess the things we have lost.

Since the earth gave birth to us all, we rightly call it our mother. Hence it is written: “A heavy yoke is upon the sons of Adam from the day they come forth from their mother’s womb until the day of burial in the mother of all” (Ecclus. 40:1).

Blessed Job, therefore, wishing to mourn patiently what he had lost here, carefully considered what sort of person he had been when he came here. To increase the preservation of his patience, he considers even more diligently what sort of person he will be when he departs, and says: “Naked I came forth from my mother’s womb, and naked I shall return there.”

As though he were saying: “The earth brought me forth naked when I entered here; the earth will receive me naked when I leave.” Therefore, since I have lost things that I received but was bound to leave behind, what have I lost that was truly my own?

[Vet. XVIII.] Since consolation must be drawn not only from consideration of our condition but also from the justice of the Creator, he rightly adds:

[Col. 0571A] **IBID.**—“The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away; as it pleased the Lord, so it has happened.”

31. When God strips us of good things, he takes away not what is ours but what is his.—The holy man had lost everything while the adversary was tempting him. Yet, knowing that Satan had no power to tempt him except by the Lord’s permission, he did not say, “The Lord gave, the devil took away,” but, “The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away.”

Perhaps there would have been cause for grief if the enemy had taken away what the Creator had given. But since the one who gave was himself the one who took it away, he took back what was his; he did not take away what was ours.

For if we receive from him the things we use in this life, why should we grieve when, by his judgment, we are required to surrender what he graciously lent us? A creditor is not unjust when, without being constrained by the fixed time for repayment, he demands when he wishes what he has lent.

Here too the text rightly adds: “As it pleased the Lord, so it has happened.” When in this life we suffer what we do not want, it is necessary that we incline the inclinations of our will toward him who cannot will anything unjust.

For there is great consolation in what displeases us when we know that it is brought about toward us by the ordering of the one who is pleased only by what is just. If, therefore, we know that what pleases the Lord is just, while we can suffer nothing except what pleases the Lord, then everything we suffer is just; and it is extremely unjust if we murmur against a just suffering.

### 32. The devil, attacking us, is pierced by our humility and patience

But since we have heard how the brave speaker brought forward the assertion of his side against his adversary, let us now hear how, at the conclusion of his speech, he praises the Judge by blessing him. It follows:

“Blessed be the name of the Lord.”

Behold, he concluded everything he rightly understood with the blessing of the Lord, so that the adversary might take notice of this and, defeated, blush at his punishment: for he had been rebellious against the Lord even when established in blessedness, whereas a human being, though struck down, sings a hymn of glory to the Lord. [Old edition XIX.]

It should also be observed that our enemy strikes us with as many arrows as he afflicts us with temptations. Every day we stand in battle; every day we receive the weapons of his temptations. But we too hurl arrows against him if, pierced by tribulations, we respond with humility.

Blessed Job, therefore, struck by the loss of his possessions and struck by the death of his children, turned the force of his grief into praise of the Creator, saying:

“The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away; as it pleased the Lord, so it has happened; blessed be the name of the Lord.”

By humility he struck down his proud enemy; by patience he overthrew the cruel one.

Nor should we suppose that our warrior received wounds without inflicting any. For as many words of patience as he returned, though struck down, in praise of God, so many arrows—as it were—he twisted into the breast of his adversary, and he fixed in him weapons far sharper than those he himself endured. [Note: Thus read the Royal, Corbie, German, Colbert, corrected Uticensis, and other Norman manuscripts. The printed editions, however, read “inflicted.”]

The afflicted man lost earthly possessions, but by enduring affliction humbly he multiplied heavenly ones. It follows:

## CHAPTER XIX [Revised edition XIV]

### Verse 22

“In all these things Job did not sin, nor did he speak anything foolish against God.”

[Note: In the editions of Gilot, the Vatican edition, and Gussanville, which followed Coccius, the words “with his lips” are added; they are unknown in the manuscripts.]

### 33. Job refrained from murmuring in mouth and heart

Because, caught amid the tribulations of temptations, we can sin even without speaking, by the silent movement of our thoughts, blessed Job is given testimony both of his mouth and of his heart. First it is said, “He did not sin,” and only then is it added, “Nor did he speak anything foolish against God.”

He who did not speak foolishly restrained guilt from his tongue; but since “he did not sin” is placed first, it is clear that he also restrained the vice of murmuring from his thoughts. Thus he neither sinned nor spoke foolishly, because he neither silently swelled up in his conscience nor loosened his tongue into rebellion.

For he speaks foolishly against God who, placed beneath the scourges of divine judgment, attempts to justify himself. If he should presumptuously dare to assert his innocence, what else does he do but accuse the justice of the one who strikes him?

Let it suffice that up to this point we have passed rapidly over the words of the historical account. Now the discourse of the exposition turns to investigate the mysteries of the allegory. But in the passage where it is written:

## CHAPTER XX [Old edition XX, Revised edition XV]

### Verse 6

“On a certain day, when the sons of God had come before the Lord”—[Note: Vindocinus, Corbie, and German manuscripts read, “On a certain day, when the sons of God were before the Lord.” Another reads, “On a certain day, when they were standing before him.” Rheims, Remigius, and German manuscripts read, “when they had come.”]—“Satan also came among them.”

### 34. God orders times without time

First we must examine why something is said to have happened “on a certain day” before the Lord, since with him the passage of time is in no way varied by the alternation of day and night. For in that light which illuminates what it chooses without approach and abandons what it rejects without withdrawal, no defect of mutability occurs. Remaining immutable in itself, it orders all mutable things. Thus it created things that pass away within themselves in such a way that they cannot pass away in its presence; nor does time flow inwardly before its sight as it runs outwardly among us.

Hence, in his eternity, those things remain fixed which, not being fixed externally, pour forth through the revolutions of the ages. Why, then, is it said of him, “On a certain day,” when his one day is plainly his eternity? The Psalmist saw that this eternity was neither enclosed by an end nor opened by a beginning when he said:

“One day in your courts is better than thousands” (Psalm 83:11).

### 35. He gradually leads those accustomed to temporal things toward eternal realities

But when Sacred Scripture speaks to those born in time, it appropriately uses temporal words, so that by condescending it may lift us up. [Note: The printed editions read, “of temporal things.” This should be corrected from the manuscripts and from Saint Gregory’s purpose; for the discourse concerns eternal things, which those accustomed to temporal things cannot grasp except through temporal things.] When it narrates something about eternity in temporal language, it gradually transports those accustomed to temporal things toward eternal realities; and eternity, unknown to our minds, may enter them gently while it accommodates itself to familiar words.

What wonder is it, then, if in sacred discourse God does not at once disclose his unchangeableness to the human mind, when even after celebrating the solemnity of his resurrection he made known the incorruption of the body he had assumed through certain gradual advances?

For, as Luke testifies (Luke 24:4), we learn that he first sent angels to certain people who were seeking him in the tomb. Again, when the disciples were speaking of him on the road, he himself appeared to them, but in such a way that they did not recognize him (ibid., 15). After delaying to exhort them, he showed himself recognizable in the breaking of the bread; finally, entering suddenly, he presented himself not only as recognizable but also as tangible.

Because the disciples still carried weak hearts, they had to be nourished in their recognition of so great a mystery by this divine arrangement, so that they might seek something for a little while and find it; finding, they might grow; and growing, they might hold more firmly what they had come to know. Since, therefore, we are led not suddenly but by the growth of causes and words, as though by certain steps toward eternity, something is said to have happened “on a certain day” before him who himself also beholds times without time.

[Old edition XXI.]

### 36. He sees darkness in the light

Or did Sacred Scripture, by saying that this happened “on a certain day” while Satan also was present, wish to indicate that God saw darkness in the light?

We cannot behold light and darkness with one and the same glance. When the eye is fixed on darkness, light is driven away; and when it turns toward the brilliance of light, the shadow of darkness departs. But that power which sees all mutable things immutably saw Satan as present to him “in the day,” because it comprehended the darkness of the apostate angel without obscurity.

We, as has been said, cannot contemplate with one and the same gaze both what we choose by approving it and what we condemn by rejecting it. When the mind turns toward one, it is separated from the thought of the other; when it is brought back to the other, it is removed from the one to which it had clung.

### 37. In ordering diverse things, he is not himself diverse

But God, because he beholds all things simultaneously without mutability and comprehends them without division—both the good things that he helps and the evil things that he judges, both those whom he rewards by helping and those whom he condemns by judging—is not himself diverse in the things he orders in different ways.

Satan is therefore described as having been present to him “in the day,” because the light of his eternity is touched by no darkening of mutability. In this respect, too, he is said to have been present among the sons of God, because the unclean spirit is penetrated by the same power of justice by which the hearts of the pure spirits are filled; and he is pierced by that ray of light with which they are suffused so that they may shine.

[Note: Rheims and one Remigius manuscript read, “who does not order by a divided arrangement while himself divided.”]

### 38. Good angels serve God for assistance, evil ones for testing

He was present among the sons of God because, while the good angels serve God for the assistance of the elect, this one serves for their testing. He was present among the sons of God because, while the good angels offer the ministry of compassion to those who labor in this life, he, serving his hidden justice without knowing it, attempts to carry out the ministry of condemnation.

[Revised edition XVI.]

Accordingly, it is rightly said through the prophet in the Books of Kings:

“I saw the Lord sitting upon his throne, and the army of heaven at his right and at his left. And it was said: ‘By what means shall I deceive Ahab, so that he may go up and fall at Ramoth-gilead?’ And one spoke thus, and another otherwise. And one went forth and said: ‘I will deceive Ahab.’ And it was said: ‘By what means will you deceive him?’ He answered, saying: ‘I will go forth and be a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets’” (1 Kings 22:19ff.).

For what should we understand by the throne of the Lord except the angelic powers, over whose minds he presides in a higher way while disposing all things below? And what is meant by the army of heaven except the multitude of ministering angels?

What, then, does it mean that the army of heaven is said to stand at his right hand and at his left? God, who is within all things in such a way that he is also outside all things, is enclosed neither by a right nor by a left. But the right hand of God signifies the chosen part of the angels, while the left hand of God signifies the rejected part of the angels.

For it is not only the good who minister to God, those who assist, but also the evil, those who test—not only those who lift up people returning from guilt, but also those who burden people unwilling to return. [Note: In certain printed editions, especially the Paris editions of 1619 and 1640, the reading is “who reprove.” The Roman edition of Sixtus V likewise has this reading.]

Nor does the designation “army of heaven” prevent us from understanding the rejected part of the angels by it. We call birds that we know to be suspended in the air “birds of heaven.” Paul likewise speaks of these spirits:

“Against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” (Ephesians 6:12).

Naming their ruler, he says:

“According to the prince of the power of the air” (Ephesians 2:2).

The army of angels therefore stands at the right and left hand of God, because the will of the elect spirits agrees with divine mercy, while the understanding of the rejected spirits, serving their own malice, obeys the judgment of his severity.

Thus immediately afterward the lying spirit is described as leaping forth into the midst, by whom King Ahab, as his merits demanded, was to be deceived. For it is not right to believe that a good spirit wished to serve deceit when he said, “I will go forth and be a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets.”

But because King Ahab, through his preceding sins, was worthy to be condemned by such a deception, so that he who had often willingly fallen into guilt might at last be unwillingly seized for punishment, hidden justice grants evil spirits permission to drag those whom they willingly strangle in the snare of sin, even unwillingly into the punishment of sin.

Therefore, what is described there—the army of heaven standing at the right and left of God—is here represented by Satan’s being present among the sons of God. Behold, angels stood at God’s right hand because they are called the sons of God; behold, angels stand at his left because Satan also was present among them.

[Old edition XXII.]

### 39. The mysteries of the allegory

But since we have resolved to investigate the mysteries of the allegory, we may appropriately understand that the Lord saw Satan “in the day” because, in the incarnation of his Wisdom, he rebuked his ways—as though he had not seen him, since he had tolerated his wickedness for so long in the destruction of the human race. [Note: Some manuscripts read, “to investigate the mysteries allegorically,” and so forth. Lyra and Bigot read, “for it was as though he had not seen him, so long …,” etc.]

Therefore the divine voice immediately says to him:

## CHAPTER XXI

### Verse 7

“Where do you come from?”

### 40. God exposed the devil’s ambushes by the light of incarnate Wisdom

Satan is questioned about his ways “in the day” because, in the light of manifested Wisdom, the ambushes of the hidden enemy are exposed.

Since, therefore, the devil is rebuked when the Lord is incarnate and is restrained from his destructive license, it is rightly added:

“To whom the Lord said: ‘Where do you come from?’”

Then he reproved Satan by questioning him about his ways, when, through the coming of the Mediator, he restrained and rebuked the wickedness of Satan’s persuasion.

Nor is it without reason that the sons of God are reported to have stood before the Lord on this day, since all the elect were gathered for the calling of the eternal homeland, as the light of Wisdom illumined them. Although incarnate Wisdom had come to gather them through the effect of his work, they were already inwardly present to his divinity through his foreknowledge. [Note: Two Rheims manuscripts, Corbie, German, and one Remigius manuscript read, “already stood before him through his presence.” Some printed editions likewise have this.]

But because the ancient enemy is questioned about his ways when the Redeemer comes, let us hear what he says.

## CHAPTER XXII [Revised edition XVII]

### Ibid.

“I have gone around the earth and traversed it.”

### 41. The devil went around the earth because he deceived and possessed all human beings

From Adam onward, before the Lord’s coming, he drew all the nations of the peoples after him. He went around the earth and traversed it because he impressed the traces of his wickedness upon the hearts of the nations.

Falling from the heights, he rightly possessed human minds, because he bound them willingly in the chain of their guilt. He wandered more widely through the world to the extent that no one was found entirely free from his guilt. It was as though he had gone around the world by right of possession, because he had found no human being who fully resisted him.

But now let Satan return—that is, let divine power restrain him from the effect of his wickedness—because the one who had nothing of the weakness of the flesh in the contagion of sin has now appeared in the flesh. [Note: Vindocinus and many others read, “who had nothing in the contagion of sin.” The older Rheims, Corbie, German, and one Remigius manuscript read, “who had nothing of the weakness of the flesh in the contagion of sin.” Two Rheims and one Remigius manuscript read, “who had nothing from the contagion of sin.” The Norman manuscripts also read, “had nothing.”]

He came in humility, so that the proud enemy might marvel at him; thus the enemy who had despised the strength of his divinity might also fear the weakness of his humanity.

Therefore, with wondrous significance, that very weakness of his humanity is set before the enemy as something astonishing, and it is said:

## CHAPTER XXIII

### Verse 8

“Have you considered my servant Job, that there is none like him on the earth?”

### 42. Until Christ came, the words concerning Job are explained again. He assumed the humility of flesh without injury to his majesty. By his virtues he restrained the devil’s pride

We said shortly before that Job is interpreted as “suffering.” He is rightly said figuratively to be one who truly suffers, since the Prophet testifies that he bears our sorrows.

There is none like him on earth because every human being is merely human, whereas he is God and human. There is none like him on earth because, although each adopted son may advance toward participation in divinity, he does not thereby receive divinity by nature. [Note: The Norman manuscripts read, “for although each adopted son advances toward the reception of divinity, he receives it so that he may be God by nature.” Corbie and German manuscripts read, “so that he may be God by nature.”]

He is also rightly called a servant, because he did not disdain to assume the form of a servant. The humility of the assumed flesh did not injure his majesty, because, although he assumed what was to be saved, he did not exchange what he possessed; he neither diminished the divine by the human nor consumed the human by the divine.

For although Paul says:

“Though he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Philippians 2:6),

his emptying himself means that he showed himself visible from the greatness of his invisibility, so that the form of a servant might conceal what, by his divinity, penetrated all things without limitation.

For God to say figuratively to Satan, “Have you considered my servant Job?” is for him to show the only-begotten Son, wondrous against Satan, in the form of a servant. By making him known in the flesh as possessing such great virtue, he indicated to the proud adversary that he should consider the one who was suffering.

But since he had introduced something for the enemy to admire, it remains for him to restrain the enemy’s pride by continuing to enumerate Christ’s virtues. It follows:

## CHAPTER XXIV [Old edition XXIII]

### Ibid.

“A simple and upright man, fearing God and turning away from evil.”

### 43. In what sense Christ is simple, upright, and so forth. Because of what he suffered, he made his divinity seem doubtful to the devil

The mediator between God and human beings, the human Christ Jesus, came among human beings: simple, in order to provide an example of life to human beings; upright, in order not to spare evil spirits; fearing God, in order to conquer pride; and turning away from evil, in order to cleanse the impurity of life in his elect.

For of him Isaiah says principally:

“And the spirit of the fear of the Lord will fill him” (Isaiah 11:3). [Note: Some manuscripts read, “and he filled him.” We suspect that this is an interpolation caused by a scribal error, and that Saint Gregory’s text should be restored as follows: “Fearing God. For of him Isaiah says principally: ‘And the spirit of the fear of the Lord will fill him.’ In order to cleanse the impurity of life in his elect, turning away from evil.” But we have not wished to alter the text without manuscript authority.]

He alone turned away from evil in a unique manner, because he did not wish to imitate the deeds he found among human beings; for, as Peter testifies:

“He committed no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth” (1 Peter 2:22).

It follows:

“Satan answered and said: ‘Does Job fear God for nothing? Have you not fenced him in, and his house, and all his possessions around him? You have blessed the works of his hands, and his possessions have increased in the earth.’”

The ancient enemy recognized that the Redeemer of the human race, his conqueror, had come into the world. Hence, through the man possessed by him, he says in the Gospel:

“What have we to do with you, Son of God? Have you come here before the time to torment us?” (Matthew 8:29).

Yet when he first saw him subject to suffering, when he saw that his humanity could endure mortal things, everything he had suspected about his divinity became doubtful to him through the arrogance of his pride. Knowing nothing but pride, he doubted that this man was God when he saw him humble.

Thus he also turned to the devices of temptation, saying:

“If you are the Son of God, command these stones to become bread” (Matthew 4:3).

Because he saw him capable of suffering, he believed that he had been born not God alone but preserved by God’s grace. [Note: The older Rheims reads, “not God alone”; one Vindocinus manuscript reads, incorrectly, “not God alone, but in knowledge.”]

Therefore he is now said to have continued:

## CHAPTER XXV

### Verses 9–10

“Have you not fenced him in, and his house, and all his possessions around him? You have blessed the works of his hands, and his possessions have increased in the earth.”

### 44. Seeing him humble, the proud devil doubted that he was God

He says that he and his house were fenced in by God because, when tempting him, he could not penetrate his conscience. He asserts that his possessions were fenced in because he does not dare to attack Christ’s elect.

He complains that God blessed the works of his hands and that his possessions increased in the earth, because, wasting away with envy, he sees that Christ’s faith is multiplied among human beings through the preaching of the apostles. His possession is said to increase when, as the preachers labor, the number of the faithful grows daily.

Thus, Satan said these things to God by his envy; Satan said these things to God by grieving and wasting away over them. It follows:

## CHAPTER XXVI [Old edition XXIV]

### Verse 11

“But stretch out your hand a little, and touch all that he possesses, unless he blesses you to your face.”

### 45. He tested Christ’s divinity through temptations

He had believed that the one whom he saw in a time of tranquility was protected by God’s grace; he therefore thought that suffering might make him capable of sin. It was as if he said openly:

“A human being questioned by afflictions is recognized as a sinner, although in miracles he is thought to be God.”

Then the Lord said to Satan:

## CHAPTER XXVII

### Verse 12

“Behold, all that he has is in your hand; only do not stretch out your hand against him.”

### 46. Satan’s hand should be understood not as power but as temptation

When we examine the sacred history under its figurative meaning, Satan’s hand should be understood as temptation, not as power.

Thus everything he possesses is given into the hand of the tempter, while the hand of temptation is forbidden to extend against him. This is nevertheless permitted to happen after his substance has been lost, because first Judea, which had been his possession, was taken away in unbelief, and afterward his flesh was fastened to the cross.

He who first endured the opposition of Judea and afterward came even to the cross therefore lost, as it were, what he had possessed first, and later endured in himself the wickedness of the adversary.

## CHAPTER XXVIII

### Ibid.

“And Satan went out from the presence of the Lord.”

### 47. The devil leaves the presence of the Lord after obtaining what he desired

As was said above, Satan went out from the presence of the Lord because he reached the object of his desire. He was, as it were, before him while he was unable, because of him, to fulfill what he wickedly thirsted for.

## CHAPTER XXIX

### Verse 13

“Now, on a certain day, while his sons and daughters were eating and drinking wine in the house of their firstborn brother.”

### 48. The firstborn son of the Lord is the Jewish people

We said that the sons and daughters of blessed Job signify either the order of the apostles or the multitude of all the faithful.

But the incarnate Lord first chose a few from Judea for the faith, and afterward joined to himself the multitude of the Gentile people. Who, then, should be understood as the Lord’s elder son except the Jewish people, generated long ago by the instruction of the law given to them? The younger is the Gentile people, gathered at the end of the world.

Since, therefore, Satan unknowingly served the benefit of human beings and sought permission for the Lord’s passion by corrupting the hearts of persecutors, while the holy apostles did not yet know that the Gentiles were to be gathered to God and preached the mysteries of the faith only to Judea, the sons and daughters are reported to have been feasting in the house of their firstborn brother when Satan is said to have gone out from the Lord.

For they had been told:

“Do not go into the way of the Gentiles” (Matthew 10:5).

After the Lord’s death and resurrection, they turned to preaching among the Gentiles. Hence they say in the Acts of the Apostles:

“It was necessary that the word of God should be spoken to you first; but since you reject it and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts 13:46).

These are the sons of the bridegroom, of whom the same bridegroom says:

“The sons of the bridegroom will not fast as long as the bridegroom is with them” (Matthew 9:15).

They feast in the house of their firstborn brother because, at that time, the apostles were still feeding on the delights of Sacred Scripture within the gathering of the Jewish people alone.

## CHAPTER XXX [Old edition XXV, Revised edition XVIII]

### Verses 14–15

“A messenger came to Job and said: ‘The oxen were plowing, and the donkeys were feeding beside them; then the Sabeans fell upon them and carried everything away, and they struck the servants with the sword; and I alone escaped to tell you.’”

### 49. The simple, clinging to the more perfect, are nourished by their understanding

What else do we understand figuratively by oxen than those who work well? What else by donkeys than certain people who live simply?

They are rightly said to feed beside the oxen, because the minds of the simple, even when they cannot grasp lofty things, are all the closer to them insofar as they regard the goods of their brothers as their own through charity. Since they do not know how to envy the understanding of others, they are not separated from them in their pasture.

Thus the donkeys feed together with the oxen because, joined to the wise, the slower are nourished by their understanding. Sabeans are interpreted as “captors.” And whom else are we to understand by the name of captors except unclean spirits, who lead into captivity all whom they subject to themselves, carrying them captive into unbelief?

They also strike the servants with the sword because they gravely wound with the arrows of their temptation those whom youthful steadfastness does not yet preserve as free or strong. Such people indeed begin good things, but while still tender in the beginning of their progress, they are laid low by the unclean spirits that capture them. The enemy strikes them with the sword because he pierces them with despair of eternity.

[Revised edition XIX.]

### 50. Prophecy remains forever while all else perishes

What does it mean that a messenger came and said, “I alone escaped”? Who is this messenger who alone escapes while others perish, except the prophetic word, which, while all the evils it foretold take place, returns alone to the Lord as though unharmed?

When it is recognized that it spoke truly concerning the destruction of the lost, it is shown, as it were, to have lived among the dead. Hence a servant is sent to bring Rebekah to Isaac in marriage (Genesis 24:9), because prophecy serves as an intermediary in betrothing the Church to the Lord.

When the Sabeans rushed upon them, the servant alone escaped to bring the news, because, while evil spirits carry the minds of the weak into captivity, the prophetic sentence grew strong. Foretelling that same captivity, it says:

“Therefore my people have been led away captive, because they had no knowledge” (Isaiah 5:13).

Prophecy is therefore saved, as it were, when the captivity it foretold is shown to have occurred. It follows:

## CHAPTER XXXI [Old edition XXVI, Revised edition XX]

### Verse 16

“While he was still speaking, another came and said: ‘The fire of God fell from heaven and consumed the sheep and the servants after striking them; and I alone escaped to tell you.’”

### 51. The fire consuming Job’s sheep and servants signifies the envy of the priests against Christ. Fire now torments the wicked through envy, and later through vengeance

All who held the office of preaching in the synagogue were rightly called heaven, because they were believed to understand heavenly things. Hence Moses, when he roused the priests and the people to the words of his admonition, said:

“Give ear, O heaven, and I will speak; and let the earth hear the words from my mouth” (Deuteronomy 32:1, according to the Septuagint).

By “heaven” he signified the order of those set over others; by “earth,” the people subject to them. [Note: The printed editions read, “the multitude of the subjects.” The manuscripts more correctly read, “the subject people.” Likewise below, in section 53, we read, “the apostles preaching, and the subject peoples.”]

In this passage, therefore, we may appropriately understand heaven as the priests, Pharisees, or teachers of the law. Since they served heavenly offices before human eyes, they appeared to shine from above.

But because they were greatly stirred against our Redeemer, fire seemed to fall from heaven when, for the deception of the ignorant people, the flame of envy was kindled even by those who were thought to teach the truth. For we know from the Gospel that, while envying the doctrine of truth, they sought an opportunity to betray the Lord; but, fearing the people, they did not dare to make known what they were plotting.

Hence it is also written that they said, in dissuading the people:

“Has any one of the rulers or of the Pharisees believed in him? But this crowd, which does not know the law, is accursed” (John 7:48–49).

What else are we to understand by the sheep and the servants except innocent people, but still weak? Because they feared enduring the opposition of the Pharisees and rulers, they were consumed by the burning of unbelief.

Let it therefore be said:

“The fire of God fell from heaven and consumed the sheep and the servants after striking them”—

that is, the flame of envy fell from the hearts of the leaders and burned whatever good arose among the people. For when wicked leaders demand honor for themselves against the truth, they overturn the hearts of their followers from every form of righteousness. [Note: The ancient Remigius and Vindocinus manuscripts read, “they are overturned.” Corbie and German manuscripts read, “they overturned.”]

It is rightly added:

“And I alone escaped to tell you,”

because, while the foretold cause of wickedness is being fulfilled, the prophetic word escapes the destruction of deceit. It says:

“And now the fire will consume the adversaries” (Isaiah 26:11).

It is as though it said openly:

“The wicked are not only tormented afterward by fire through vengeance; they are also now burned by envy, because those who will later be punished by the penalty of retribution now afflict themselves with the torment of envy.”

The servant therefore returns alone in flight and announces that the sheep and the servants perished by fire, while prophecy, abandoning the Jewish people, makes clear that it spoke truly when it said:

“Zeal has seized an uneducated people.”

[Note: It is not sufficiently clear what prophecy this is. Nevertheless, the whole of Sacred Scripture may be understood by the name of prophecy. Moreover, in Romans 10:2 the Apostle says of the Jewish people that they have zeal for God—Greek ζῆλον—but not according to knowledge. This amounts almost to saying that an uninstructed people seized zeal, that is, zeal devoid of knowledge.]

It is as though it said openly:

“Because the people would not examine the words of the prophets but gave their faith to the words of the envious, they perished in the fire of zeal, because they burned themselves in the flame of another’s envy.”

It follows:

## CHAPTER XXXII [Old edition XXVII]

### Verse 17

“While he was still speaking, another came and said: ‘The Chaldeans formed three bands, attacked the camels, and carried them away; they also struck the servants with the sword; and I alone escaped to tell you.’”

### 52. The Chaldeans forming three bands signify the Pharisees, Herodians, and Sadducees. The camels signify either the Samaritans or Jews clinging to the mere letter of the law

Since we know that Chaldeans are interpreted as “fierce,” whom else are we to understand by the name of the Chaldeans except the authors of persecution, bursting forth into open cries of wickedness when they say:

“Crucify, crucify!” (Luke 23:21; Mark 3:6)

They form three bands from themselves when the Pharisees, Herodians, and Sadducees divided themselves in order to put questions to the Lord.

They were indeed defeated by the mouth of Wisdom; but because we must believe that they drew certain foolish people after them, they carried away the camels by forming bands. Each of their groups corrupted the hearts of the foolish with the perverse ideas it held; and by persuading them and dragging them to destruction, it led the twisted minds of the weak into captivity, as it were.

When the Lord preached in Samaria, many of the Samaritans were received into the possession of the same Redeemer. But did not those who tested the Lord concerning the resurrection—on the basis of the seven men who had successively married one woman and died—attempt to lead the believing Samaritans away from the faith, when it is clear that the Samaritans were ignorant of the hope of resurrection? Since they receive some things from the law and reject others, they are like camels: as clean animals they chew the cud, but as unclean animals they do not divide the hoof.

The camels chewing the cud but not dividing the hoof may also signify those who, in Judea, had heard the history according to the letter but did not know how to discern its spiritual power.

The Chaldeans seize these people in three bands when the Pharisees, Herodians, and Sadducees pervert them from every sound understanding through their wicked persuasion.

They also strike the servants with the sword, because, although some among the people were already capable of using reason, these leaders opposed them not by the power of reason but by the authority of their position. While they wished their subjects to imitate them as leaders, even if those who followed were capable of understanding something, they nevertheless dragged them to destruction by the authority of the government they had assumed.

From these people the servant who was to bring the news rightly escapes alone, because, while the Pharisees, Herodians, and Sadducees commit wickedness, the prophetic word grows strong after abandoning them. It says:

“They who held the law did not know me” (Jeremiah 2:8).

It follows:

## CHAPTER XXXIII [Old edition XXVIII, Revised edition XXI]

### Verses 18–19

“While he was speaking, behold, another entered and said: ‘While your sons and daughters were eating and drinking wine in the house of their firstborn brother, suddenly a powerful wind rushed in from the region of the desert and shook the four corners of the house. When it collapsed, it crushed your children, and they died.’”

[Note: The printed editions here and below read, “while he was still speaking,” whereas the manuscripts simply read, “he was speaking.”]

### 53. The Jewish people are represented by Job’s firstborn

We said shortly before that by the sons and daughters we understand the apostles preaching and the subject peoples, who are reported to have feasted in the house of their firstborn brother because they were still feeding on the delights of sacred preaching within the dwelling of the Jewish people.

But suddenly a powerful wind rushed in from the region of the desert. The region of the desert is the heart of unbelievers, which, when the Creator abandons it, no inhabitant cultivates.

What else, then, should we understand by a powerful wind except a strong temptation? A powerful wind therefore rushed in from the region of the desert because, in the passion of our Redeemer, a strong temptation came from the hearts of the Jews against his faithful.

The region of the desert may also appropriately be understood as the abandoned multitude of unclean spirits. From it the wind came and shook the house, because from those spirits temptation proceeded and stirred the hearts of the persecutors.

### 54. Its House Overthrown Is the Synagogue, Destroyed When Its Four Corners—That Is, Its Four Orders—Were Shaken. Hence Its Children Were Crushed

But this house in which the sons were feasting stood upon four corners. For we recognize three governing orders in the synagogue: priests, scribes, and elders of the people. If we add the Pharisees to these, we find four corners in this house. Therefore the wind came from the region of the desert and shook the four corners of the house, because temptation burst forth from unclean spirits and stirred the minds of the four orders to the wickedness of persecution.

When this house fell, it crushed the children, because, when Judaea fell into the cruelty of the Lord’s persecution, it overwhelmed the apostles’ faith with the fear of despair. They saw only that their master had been seized, and, already denying him, fled in various directions. Although an inner hand, in foreknowledge, held their spirit for life, carnal fear meanwhile extinguished them from the life of faith. Thus those who abandoned their author while Judaea raged were killed, as though the house had been overthrown when its corners were shaken.

But what do we believe happened at that time to the flock of the faithful, when we know that even the rams themselves fled? Yet amid all this one escapes to announce it, because the prophetic word that had foretold these things shows that it has recovered its strength. It says concerning the persecuting people: “My beloved has committed many crimes in my house” (Jer. 11:15); concerning the good preachers, who nevertheless fled in the Passion: “Those near to me stood at a distance” (Ps. 37:12); and concerning all those who were greatly afraid: “I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered” (Zech. 13:7; Matt. 26:31). It continues:

## CHAPTER XXXIV  
*Formerly XXIX; Revised XXII*

### Verse 20

> Then Job arose and tore his garments.

### 55. Job’s Rising and Tearing His Garment Prefigure Christ

When the house had fallen and the children had been killed, Job arose. This signifies that, when Judaea had been lost through unbelief and the preachers had fallen in the death of fear, the Redeemer of the human race raised himself from the death of his flesh and demonstrated with what judgment he had abandoned his persecutors.

For his rising means that he shows with what strictness he abandons sinners, just as his lying down means patiently enduring evils. He rises, therefore, when he exercises the judgment of justice against the reprobate.

Rightly, then, he is also said to have torn his garments. For what was the Lord’s garment except the Synagogue, which, while the prophets preached, clung to the expectation of his incarnation? Just as he is now clothed in those who love him, as Paul bears witness, saying: “That he might present to himself a glorious Church, not having spot or wrinkle” (Eph. 5:27). That which is said to have neither spot nor wrinkle is plainly shown to be a rational garment, clean through its actions and stretched through its hope. Thus, when Judaea believed that he would become incarnate, it was nevertheless a garment through its adherence to him.

### 56. His Synagogue-Garment Was Torn: Some Believed, Others Did Not

But because the one who had been awaited came, and, coming, taught new things; because, teaching, he performed wonders, and, performing wonders, endured evil—he tore the garment with which he had been clothed when, among the Jews, he raised some from unbelief but left others in unbelief.

What, then, is the torn garment except Judaea, divided among contrary opinions? If his garment had not been torn, the Evangelist would not have said that, while the Lord was preaching, contention arose among the people: “Some said, ‘He is good’; others said, ‘No, but he is deceiving the crowds’” (John 7:12). His garment was, as it were, torn: divided in its opinions, it lost the unity of concord.

It continues:

## CHAPTER XXXV

### The Same Passage

> And, having shaved his head, he fell upon the ground and worshiped.

### 57. He Falls upon the Ground as Though with His Head Shaved, When, Rejecting the Jewish Priesthood, He Descends to the Gentiles

What is signified by the cut hair except the subtle meaning of the mysteries? And what by the head except the summit of the priesthood? Hence it is said to the prophet Ezekiel: “You, son of man, take for yourself a sharp sword, a razor for shaving the hairs; take it and draw it over your head and your beard” (Ezek. 5:1). Thus the prophet’s action expresses the judgment of the Redeemer: appearing in the flesh, he shaved his head because he removed the mysteries of his commandments from the Jewish priesthood; he shaved his beard because, abandoning the Israelite kingdom, he cut away its adornment of virtue.

What, then, is expressed here by the earth except sinful humanity? For it was first said to the human being who sinned: “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Gen. 3:19). Therefore, under the name of earth, the sinful Gentile people are designated. For while Judaea considered itself righteous, it is evident how it regarded the Gentiles, as Paul bears witness: “We are Jews by nature, and not sinners from the Gentiles” (Gal. 2:15).

Our Mediator, therefore, fell upon the earth as though with his head shaven, because, abandoning Judaea and removing his mysteries from its priesthood, he came to the knowledge of the Gentiles. He shaved the hairs from his head because he removed the mysteries of the Law from that first priesthood of his; and he fell upon the earth because he gave himself to sinners who were to be saved. While he abandoned those who seemed righteous to themselves, he took up those who both knew and confessed themselves to be unrighteous.

Hence he himself says in the Gospel: “I have come into this world for judgment, so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” (John 9:39). Hence also the pillar of cloud that went before the people in the wilderness (Exod. 13:21) shone with the brightness of fire not by day but by night. For our Redeemer, offering guidance to those who followed him by the example of his way of life, gave no light to those who trusted in their own righteousness; but to those who acknowledged the darkness of their sins he kindled the fire of his love.

Nor should the mind consider it unworthy of the Redeemer that Job is said to have fallen with this meaning. For it is written: “The Lord sent a word into Jacob, and it fell upon Israel” (Isa. 9:8). Jacob is called “supplanter,” whereas Israel means “seeing God.” What, then, is designated by Jacob except the Jewish people, and by Israel except the Gentile people? The one whom Jacob strove to supplant through the death of the flesh, the Gentiles saw through the eyes of faith as God. The word sent to Jacob therefore fell upon Israel, because the Gentile people, suddenly confessing him, found the one whom the Jews rejected when he came to them. Of the Holy Spirit it is written: “The Spirit of the Lord fell upon them” (Acts 10:44).

### 58. How the Word of God or the Holy Spirit Is Said to Fall
