For this reason the Word of God or the Holy Spirit is said in sacred Scripture to fall: to express the unexpectedness of his coming. Whatever rushes or falls comes suddenly to the lowest place. Thus for the Mediator to have fallen upon the earth means that he came unexpectedly to the Gentiles, without preceding signs.

It is aptly said that, falling, he worshiped, because, while he himself assumed the humility of the flesh, he infused those who believed in him with the vows of humility. He did this because he taught that it should be done, just as it is said of his Spirit: “The Spirit himself pleads for us with unspeakable groanings” (Rom. 8:26). For one who is equal does not ask; but he is said to plead because those whom he fills he makes into petitioners. Yet the Redeemer also showed this in himself: as he drew near to his Passion, he entreated the Father.

What is surprising, then, if, in the form of a servant, he subjected himself to the Father by entreating him, in which form also he endured the hands of sinners to the very end of death?

It continues:

## CHAPTER XXXVI  
*Formerly XXXI; Revised XXIII*

### Verse 21

> Naked I came forth from my mother’s womb; naked I shall return there.

### 59. Christ Will Return at the End of the World to the Jews from Whom He Came Forth

The Synagogue was the Redeemer’s mother according to the flesh, from which he came forth to us visibly through the body. But it kept him covered within itself by the veil of the letter, since it neglected to open the eyes of its mind to his spiritual meaning. Because it refused to see God hidden in the flesh of a human body, it disdained to contemplate him naked in his divinity.

But he came forth naked from his mother’s womb because, proceeding visibly from the flesh of the Synagogue, he came to the Gentiles. This was well signified when Joseph fled, leaving his cloak behind (Gen. 39:12). When the adulterous woman wished to misuse him, he left his cloak and fled outside. Thus, when the Synagogue, believing the Lord to be merely human, wished to bind him in an adulterous embrace, he left the veil of the letter before its eyes and made himself visible to the Gentiles so that they might recognize the power of his divinity.

Hence Paul said: “Until this day, whenever Moses is read, a veil lies over their heart” (2 Cor. 3:15). The adulterous woman retained the cloak with herself and lost naked the one whom she had held improperly. Therefore, coming from the Synagogue and appearing visibly to the faith of the Gentiles, he came forth naked from his mother’s womb.

But does he abandon her entirely? Where, then, is what is said through the prophet: “If the number of the children of Israel be as the sand of the sea, a remnant shall be saved” (Isa. 10:22; Rom. 9:27)? Where is what is written: “Until the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, and thus all Israel shall be saved” (Rom. 11:25)? At some time, then, he will also appear visibly to the Synagogue. Without doubt this will occur at the end of the world, when he makes himself known as God, as he is, to the remnants of his own people.

Hence it is rightly said here: “Naked I shall return there.” He returns naked to his mother’s womb when, at the end of this world, the one who, having become human in the world, is despised is declared God before the ages to the eyes of his Synagogue.

It continues:

## CHAPTER XXXVII  
*Revised XXIV*

### The Same Passage

> The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away; as it has pleased the Lord, so it has happened; blessed be the name of the Lord.

### 60. God Gave Judaea to Christ and Took It Away

Our Redeemer, insofar as he is God, gives all things with the Father; but insofar as he is human, he receives from the Father among all things.

Let him therefore speak concerning Judaea, when it believed that the mystery of his incarnation would come: “The Lord gave.” Let him speak concerning Judaea, when it had despised the presence of his expected incarnation: “The Lord has taken away.” It was given when, through certain people, it believed what was to come; but, because the merit of its blindness demanded it, it was taken away when it refused to venerate through certain people what it had believed.

### 61. Christ Taught by His Example That God Should Be Blessed in Afflictions

Let him teach those who believe in him to know how to bless the Lord while placed under afflictions, when it is added: “As it has pleased the Lord, so it has happened; blessed be the name of the Lord.” Hence, as the Gospel testifies (Matt. 26:26), when he is said to have drawn near to his Passion, he is reported to have given thanks after taking the bread.

He therefore gives thanks who receives the scourges of another’s iniquity. He who displayed nothing deserving punishment blesses humbly in the midst of punishment, so that he may show what each person ought to do in the scourge of his own guilt, if he himself bears with equanimity the scourges of another’s guilt; so that he may show what a subordinate should do under correction, if an equal gives thanks to the Father while placed under the scourge.

It continues:

## CHAPTER XXXVIII

### Verse 22

> In all these things Job did not sin, nor did he speak anything foolish against God.

### 62. What Is Prudence among Human Beings Is Foolishness before God

That he neither sinned nor spoke anything foolish against God is openly attested concerning him by Peter, as we have already said: “He committed no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth” (1 Pet. 2:22). Deceit in the mouth, the more cleverly it excels among human beings, the more foolishly it is senseless before God, as Paul bears witness: “The wisdom of this world is foolishness with God” (1 Cor. 3:19). Since, therefore, there was no deceit in his mouth, he certainly said nothing foolish.

The priests and rulers foolishly believed that he had spoken against God when, questioned at the time of his Passion, he testified that he was the Son of God. Hence they complain, saying: “Why do we still need witnesses? Behold, now you have heard the blasphemy” (Matt. 26:65). But he spoke nothing foolish against God, because, speaking the truth, he brought this testimony about himself even to unbelievers by dying, and shortly afterward showed it to all the redeemed by rising again.

## [Formerly XXXII]  
### 63. Moral Meaning: Satan Stands with the Holy Angels before God, Inserting Evil Thoughts among Good Ones

We have briefly passed through these matters as they signify our Head. Now, for the edification of his body, let us repeat them in a moral sense, so that we may understand how inwardly in the mind what is narrated as outwardly enacted in deed.

When the sons of God stand before God, Satan also stands among them, because the ancient enemy often craftily inserts and joins himself to our good thoughts—thoughts sown in our heart through the working of the Holy Spirit’s coming—in order to disturb what has been well conceived and tear apart what has been wrongly disturbed.

Yet the one who created us by no means abandons us in temptation. He makes our enemy, who conceals himself in ambush against us, detectable by the illumination of his light. Therefore he immediately says to him:

## CHAPTER XXXIX

### Verse 7

> From where have you come?

### 64. To Whom It Must Be Said, “From Where Have You Come?”

To inquire after the cunning enemy is to disclose his ambushes to us, so that, when we see where he enters our heart, we may watch against him with strong vigilance.

## CHAPTER XL

### The Same Passage

> He answered and said: I have gone around the earth and traversed it.

### 65. May God Reveal His Ambushes to Us

For Satan to go around the earth means to search out carnal hearts and inquire where he may find an opportunity for accusation. He goes around the earth because he surrounds human hearts: to take away good things, to implant evil in minds, to increase what has been implanted, to bring to completion what has been increased, and to acquire those perfected in iniquities as companions for punishment.

It should be noted that he says he has not flown over the earth but traversed it. For he by no means quickly abandons the one whom he tempts. Rather, when he finds a soft heart, he fixes there the foot of his miserable persuasion, so that by lingering he may imprint the traces of evil action and, through the likeness of his own iniquity, make reprobates of those whom he can.

But blessed Job is praised against him, and it is said:

## CHAPTER LXI

### Verse 8

> Have you considered my servant Job, that there is none like him on the earth, a simple and upright man, fearing God and turning away from evil?

### 66. God’s Praise Consists in Giving Good Things and Preserving What He Has Given

Divine inspiration strengthens against the enemy the one whom God praises, as it were, in Satan’s hearing. For God’s praise consists in first granting good things and afterward preserving what he has granted.

But the ancient enemy rages more fiercely against the good the more he sees them surrounded by the gift of divine protection. Hence he adds:

## CHAPTER XLII

### Verse 9

> Does Job fear God for nothing? Have you not fenced him around, his house, and all his possessions on every side? You have blessed the works of his hands, and his possessions have increased in the land.

### 67. A Human Being Does Not Stand by His Own Strength

It is as though he openly said: “Why do you praise one whom you strengthen by protecting him? If you disregarded me, a human being would be worthy of your praise if he stood against me by his own strength.”

Therefore he immediately and maliciously asks something of the human being which the protector of the human being nevertheless benignly grants. For it follows:

## CHAPTER XLIII

### Verse 11

> But stretch out your hand a little and touch all that he possesses, unless he blesses you to your face.

### 68. The Elect Advance through Temptation

Often, while we produce the fruit of virtues abundantly and flourish in continual prosperity, the mind is lifted up somewhat, so that it supposes that the good things it possesses arise from itself. The ancient enemy maliciously seeks to touch these goods; but God permits them to be tested only in his goodness, so that, when the mind is shaken by the assault of temptation in the good things over which it rejoiced, it may recognize the weakness of its own frailty and be strengthened more firmly in hope of divine assistance.

By a wonderful dispensation of mercy, what the malignant enemy uses to tempt the heart in order to destroy it is used by the merciful Creator to instruct it so that it may live. Hence it is rightly added:

## CHAPTER XLIV

### Verse 12

> Behold, all that he has is in your hand; only do not stretch out your hand against him.

### 69. God Grants Perseverance

It is as though he openly said: “I grant you permission to test externally the goods of each of the elect, but you must nevertheless know that I preserve him persevering in me at the root of his mind.”

Here it is also rightly added:

## CHAPTER XLV

### The Same Passage

> And Satan went out from the presence of the Lord.

### 70. Under God’s Restraint, the Devil Does Not Wound the Hearts of the Good unto Destruction

Because, since he is by no means permitted to prevail to the point of weakening the heart, he is excluded from the inner depths and wanders outside. Even if he often disturbs the virtues of the mind, he is outside precisely because, with God resisting him, he does not wound the hearts of the good unto destruction.

He is permitted to rage against them only insofar as it is necessary for them to be strengthened by instruction through temptations: lest they attribute the good things they do to their own powers, lest they abandon themselves in the torpor of security, and lest they be loosened from the girding of fear. Rather, they should watch over the preservation of their progress with greater vigilance, seeing that they always stand against the adversary in the battle line of temptations.

## CHAPTER XLVI  
*Formerly XXXIII*

### Verses 13–15

> Now, while his sons and daughters were eating and drinking wine in the house of their firstborn brother, a messenger came to Job and said: The oxen were plowing, and the asses were grazing beside them; and the Sabeans fell upon them and took everything, and struck the servants with the sword; and I alone escaped to tell you.

### 71. Faith Is the First of All the Virtues

In the heart of the elect, the wisdom that follows the other good things is born first, and this wisdom is brought forth as the firstborn offspring through the gift of the Spirit. This wisdom is certainly our faith, as the prophet bears witness: “Unless you believe, you will not understand” (Isa. 7:9, according to the Septuagint).

For we truly become wise for understanding when we offer the faith of our belief to everything the Creator says. The sons therefore feast in the house of their firstborn brother when the remaining virtues feast upon faith. If faith is not born first in our heart, none of the others can be good, even if they appear good.

The sons feast in the house of their firstborn brother when our virtues, in the dwelling of faith, are nourished by the food of sacred speech. For it is written: “Without faith it is impossible to please God” (Heb. 11:6). Our virtues therefore take the true banquets of life when they begin to be nourished by the mysteries of faith.

The sons feast in the house of their firstborn brother because, unless the remaining virtues, filled with the banquets of wisdom, prudently do what they desire, they can in no way be virtues.

### 72. In How Many Ways the Devil Lies in Wait for Our Virtues

But behold: while the good things we do are nourished by the banquets of wisdom and faith, our enemy takes away the oxen that are plowing and the asses that are grazing, and kills the servants with the sword.

What should we understand by the plowing oxen except our more serious thoughts? While these work the heart through diligent exercise, they yield abundant fruits of progress.

What should we understand by the grazing asses except the simple movements of the heart? While we carefully restrain these from the error of duplicity, we nourish them, as it were, in the field of free purity.

But often the cunning enemy, when he sees serious thoughts in the heart, corrupts them through an introduced pleasure of delight. When he sees the simple movements of the heart, he displays subtle refinements of invention, so that, while praise is sought for subtlety, the simplicity of purity may be lost. Even if he cannot drag them as far as an evil deed, he nevertheless harms good thoughts by stealing upon them through temptation, so that, when he is recognized as disturbing the good things of the mind, he may appear to have taken them away completely.

The plowing oxen can also be understood as thoughts of charity, by which we try to benefit others when, through preaching, we wish to break up the hardness of a brother’s heart.

The asses may also signify the gentleness of patience, since they offer no resistance, with any madness of ferocity, to those who load them. Often, when the ancient enemy sees that we wish to benefit others by speaking, he plunges the mind into a certain torpor of idleness, so that we no longer desire to benefit others even when we are free from our own affairs.

He therefore takes away the plowing oxen when, through a subdued torpor of negligence, he breaks the thoughts of the mind devoted to the fruits of usefulness for our brothers. Although the hearts of the elect remain vigilant within the secret places of their thoughts and consider what they endure from the tempter as they overcome him, the malicious enemy nevertheless rejoices that he has snatched away something precisely when he prevails over the thoughts of the good, even for a moment.

## [Formerly XXXIV]  
### 73. With What Vigilance His Attacks Must Be Met; The Gift of Discernment in Temptation

Often, when he sees a mind prepared for endurance, he searches out what it loves most and inserts the snares of scandal there, so that the more something is loved, the more easily patience may be disturbed through it.

The hearts of the elect indeed always return anxiously to themselves and severely afflict themselves even over a slight movement of transgression. As they learn, through having been disturbed, how they ought to have stood, they are sometimes made firmer by being shaken.

But when the ancient enemy disturbs thoughts of endurance even for a moment, he exults as though he had taken the asses from the field of the heart.

In the matters we intend to undertake, we carefully consider with reasonable vigilance what is suitable to each circumstance. But often, when the enemy bursts upon us through the sudden disturbance of temptation, unexpectedly anticipating the watchfulness of the heart, he kills the very servants who were its guardians with the sword.

Yet one escapes to announce that the others have perished, because, in what the mind suffers from the enemy, the discernment of reason always returns to the soul. It indicates that it alone has escaped, since it courageously weighs within itself whatever it has endured.

When the others have perished, one therefore returns to the house, while discernment returns to the conscience amid the movements disturbed by temptation. Thus what the mind, overtaken by sudden assaults, reckons that it has lost, it recovers through the effort of compunction.

## CHAPTER XLVII

### Verse 16

> While he was still speaking, another came and said: The fire of God fell from heaven and consumed the sheep and the servants it touched; and I alone escaped to tell you.

### 74. The Devil Tries to Corrupt Chaste Thoughts, but Discernment Escapes the Danger

What is signified by the sheep except the innocence of thoughts? What by the sheep except the purity of good hearts?

We said shortly before that heaven here means the aerial heaven, from which we also call the birds “birds of heaven.” We know that unclean spirits, who fell from the ethereal heaven, wander through this space between heaven and earth. The more they see themselves cast down from heavenly things through the impurity of their pride, the more they begrudge human hearts their ascent to heavenly things.

Therefore, because a flame of envy bursts forth from the aerial powers against the purity of our thoughts, fire comes from heaven upon the sheep. Often they set the pure thoughts of our mind ablaze with the heat of lust; they burn the sheep, as it were, with fire, when they disturb chaste movements of the spirit through the temptation of luxury.

This fire is called the fire of God because, although it is not generated by God’s action, it is generated with his permission. And because they sometimes overwhelm the very watchfulnesses of the mind through a sudden impulse, they kill the servants who guard them with the sword.

Yet one escapes unharmed when persevering discernment carefully observes everything the mind suffers and alone escapes the danger of death. Even amid disturbed thoughts, discernment does not succumb, so that it may report its losses to the soul and, as it were, summon its master back to lamentation.

## CHAPTER XLVIII  
*Revised XXVI*

### Verse 17

> While he was still speaking, another came and said: The Chaldeans formed three bands and fell upon the camels and took them; they also struck the servants with the sword; and I alone escaped to tell you.

### 75. How Many Dangers Threaten the Administration of Earthly Affairs

Through the camels, which possess something clean because they chew the cud, and something unclean because they do not divide the hoof, we said above that good administrations of temporal affairs are understood. The more widely their care is extended, the more abundantly the enemy lies in wait for us.

For everyone who presides over the administration of earthly affairs lies more broadly exposed to the arrows of the hidden enemy. He attempts to act while providing for many things; and often, while cautiously foreseeing the future with subtlety, he does not see present losses through lack of caution. Often, while watching over present matters, he sleeps with regard to foreseeing what is imminent. Often, while sluggishly doing certain things, he neglects what ought to be done vigilantly. Often, while showing himself more vigilant than is right in action, he harms the matters entrusted to him more seriously through the very restlessness of his activity.

Sometimes he tries to restrain his tongue, but the burden of administration demands that he not remain silent. Sometimes, while restricting himself with excessive severity, he is silent even about what he ought to say. Sometimes, while relaxing himself too broadly in order to say what is necessary, he also says what he ought not to say.

Often he becomes entangled in such great masses of thoughts that he can scarcely bear what, in his prudence, he turns over within himself. Although he does nothing outwardly, he sweats violently under the great weight of his heart. Since what he suffers inwardly within himself is hard, he becomes weary outwardly while quiet and idle.

Often the mind sees what is about to happen and directs its entire attention against it. A great ardor of struggle enters; sleep flees; night is turned into day. Though a bed holds the limbs in outward quiet, inwardly great disputes are waged in the forum of the heart.

Often, however, nothing of what is foreseen actually occurs, and all that thought which had long prepared itself with complete attention suddenly rests empty. The farther the mind withdraws from what is necessary, the more broadly it thinks about empty things.

Because malignant spirits strike the cares of administration sometimes through sluggish or hasty action, sometimes through lazy or excessive speech, and almost always through excessive burdens of thought, the Chaldeans carry off the camels in three bands.

To form three bands against the camels is, as it were, to devastate the concerns of earthly administration in three ways: now through unlawful action, now through superfluous speech, now through disordered thought. Thus, while the mind tries to extend itself effectively to administer external affairs, it is separated from consideration of itself; and it fails to recognize the losses it suffers in itself because it labors on behalf of the affairs of others with greater zeal than is fitting.

A rightly ordered mind, when it takes up administrative cares, attends to what it owes to itself and what it owes to its neighbors. It neither neglects its own concerns through immoderate solicitude for another nor postpones the concerns of others through vigilance for its own advantage.

Yet often, while the mind diligently watches over both, while it devotes itself to great acts of vigilance concerning itself and the matters entrusted to it, it is suddenly disturbed by the crisis of some unforeseen matter and swept headlong, so that all its watchfulness is suddenly overwhelmed.

Hence the Chaldeans strike the servants guarding the camels with the sword. Yet one returns, because amid these events the reasoning of discernment presents itself to the eyes of our mind, and the anxious soul understands what it has suddenly lost inwardly through the impulse of temptation.

It continues:

## CHAPTER XLIX  
*Revised XXVII*

### Verses 18–19

> While he was speaking, behold, another entered and said: While your sons and daughters were eating and drinking wine in the house of their firstborn brother, suddenly a violent wind rushed in from the region of the desert and shook the four corners of the house. When it collapsed, it crushed your children, and they died; and I alone escaped to tell you.

### Editorial and Textual Notes

- [Col. 0581D] The Norman and German manuscripts, one Remigian manuscript, and Val. Cl. read, “is said to have been shaken at the four corners.” “[Tres.]” is uncertain in the supplied text. We retain the received reading, which is that of the better manuscripts.

- [Col. 0581D] Lyr., Bigot., and Utic. read: “and the flocks will be scattered.”

- [Col. 0581D–0582D] The printed editions, except Barthol., read “in the fear of death.” Better is the reading “in the death of fear,” found in Rhem., Remig., Cor., Germ., 1 Vindoc., and Val. Cl., which is followed here. Utic. has “in the fear of death.”

- [Col. 0582D] Two Rhem. manuscripts, 1 Remig., Corb., Germ., Norm., and Val. Cl., omitting the preceding words, read: “the Redeemer of the human race demonstrated with what judgment he had abandoned his persecutors.” In Colb., after “raised,” there is added: “or certainly rose again, when with what judgment,” etc.; these words perhaps ought to be regarded as a gloss.

- [Col. 0583D] The words from “as though,” etc., through “enduring,” are absent from Corb., Germ., Reg., and Utic. manuscripts, and perhaps slipped from the margin into the text.

- [Col. 0583D] The editions read, against the manuscripts, “he left others in unbelief.”

- [Col. 0583D–0584D] In the Paris edition of 1518 and all subsequent editions, the following has been inserted here: “when, after his resurrection also, he appeared to some who would believe and hid himself from some who would not believe.” It is a mere addition, coherent with neither what precedes nor what follows. It is nevertheless written in the margin of the Colbert manuscript, but is absent from the other manuscripts and earlier editions.

- [Col. 0584D] In the editions, except the older ones, “the dignity of the priesthood” is read.

- [Col. 0584D] Some manuscripts read “he shone with fire,” as occurs in several witnesses.

- [Col. 0584D] Rhem., Remig., and Val. Cl. manuscripts read: “For what wonder is it if, in the form of a servant, he entreated the Father? What wonder if, in the form of a servant, by entreating,” etc.

- [Col. 0585D] The editions read “to behold.”

- [Col. 0585D] Some manuscripts read: “because, coming forth from the flesh of the Synagogue”; this reading would seem preferable if supported by the better codices.

- [Col. 0585D] Coccius added *positum* (“placed”), which slipped into subsequent editions.

- [Col. 0585D] The printed editions read “at some time visibly,” so that also. The reading has been corrected from the manuscripts.

- [Col. 0585D–0586D] We have restored from the manuscripts the particle *inter* (“among”), omitted in the printed editions. Thus below, in book IX, chapter formerly 16, now 30, §48: “they acknowledge him as God above all things and human among all things.” See book XV, §20, and book XVI, §36.

- [Col. 0586D] Coccius, Gilot., Vatic., and Gussanv. read “in persecution,” contrary to the authority of the manuscripts.

- [Col. 0586D] Here we have removed “with his lips,” added by Gilot. and later editors.

- [Col. 0586D] Ancient Rem. and Vindoc. manuscripts read “blasphemies.”

- [Col. 0587D] Corb. Germ. reads “unless [he blesses you] to your face.”

- [Col. 0587D–0588D] Where the editions read *profectus* (“advance”), the manuscripts almost always have *provectus* (“progress”). We have restored the latter here, though not in every occurrence, since *profectus* is synonymous.

- [Col. 0588D] This verse is absent from the Corb. Germ. manuscript.

- [Col. 0589D] Wherever the editions have *subrepens, subrepit* (“stealing in, steals in”), as here, our handwritten codices repeatedly read *subripiens, subripit* or *surripiens*, etc.

- [Col. 0589D] The printed editions read “in whatever matters.”

- [Col. 0589D] The printed editions read “who announces that the others”; better manuscripts read “who announces that the other things—namely, the oxen, asses, and servants—have perished.”

- [Col. 0589D–0590D] Norman, Rem., Remig., Turon., and Val. Cl. manuscripts, etc., read “while discernment returns to the conscience amid disturbed movements in temptation”; all printed editions depart from this, reading “while [it returns] amid the movements of disturbed temptation,” or “of disturbance in temptation.”

- [Col. 0590D] The editions and two Reg. manuscripts read “What [is signified] by the servants?” This is not unsuitable in sense; nevertheless, following Rem., Remig., Norm., Turon., Corb., and Germ. manuscripts, the reading should be “What [is signified] by the sheep?”

- [Col. 0591D] Norman manuscripts and some others read “by the very restlessness of his activity.”

- [Col. 0591D] Ancient Rhem., Turon., Corb., Germ., Val. Cl., and others read “under the great weights of his heart.”

- [Col. 0591D] Here, as above in chapter 21, we have removed the particle *adhuc* (“still”) on the authority of the manuscripts.

76. The spiritual building rests on four virtues; how it is shaken.---As we have already said above, the “region of the desert” signifies the abandoned multitude of unclean spirits. When it deserted the blessedness of its Creator, it was like losing the hand of its cultivator; from that region the violent wind comes and overthrows the house, because a powerful temptation arising from unclean spirits assails the conscience and overturns it from its state of tranquility. [Col. 0592B]

This house stands upon four corners because, plainly, the solid structure of our mind is upheld by prudence, temperance, fortitude, and justice. This house rests upon four corners because the entire structure of a good work rises upon these four virtues. Thus, too, four rivers of Paradise water the earth, because when the heart is infused with these four virtues, it is restrained from every burning of carnal desires.

Yet sometimes, when sloth creeps over the mind, prudence grows cold; for when the mind lies torpid with weariness, it does not foresee what is to come. Sometimes, when a certain pleasure steals upon the mind, our temperance withers; for in proportion as we are drawn toward present delights, we restrain ourselves less from what is unlawful. Sometimes fear insinuates itself into the heart and disturbs the strength of our fortitude; and we are weaker against adversity in proportion as we more immoderately fear losing things we have loved. Sometimes, however, self-love inserts itself into the mind and, by a hidden movement, turns it aside from the straight path of justice; and the more it neglects to surrender itself wholly to its Creator, the more it opposes the claims of justice within itself. [Note: Thus the Old Edition, with the manuscripts. Gilot, the Vatican Edition, and Gussanville read “love of himself” (amor sui).]

The violent wind therefore shakes the four corners of the house when a strong temptation shakes the four virtues by secret movements; and, as though the corners had been shaken, the house is overturned when the conscience is disturbed by the virtues being struck. [Note: All our manuscripts read “is overturned” (evertitur), not “is crushed” (obruitur), as was formerly read. And rightly so: the house is not crushed, but crushes when it falls.]

77. The other virtues, like offspring of the heart, nourish one another.---Within these four corners of the house the children feast, because within the secret places of the mind—which is raised principally by these four virtues to the summit of perfect rectitude—the other virtues, like offspring of the heart, nourish one another. The gift of the Spirit, which first forms prudence, temperance, fortitude, and justice in the mind submitted to it, immediately disciplines that same mind with seven virtues, so that it may be instructed to confront each temptation: against folly, wisdom; against dullness, understanding; against rashness, counsel; against fear, fortitude; against ignorance, knowledge; against hardness, piety; against pride, fear. [Note: Two Rheims manuscripts and one Remigius manuscript read “let it give humility.” This is a scribal error, arising from the thought that humility is more opposed to pride than fear is. But here the holy Doctor is enumerating the gifts of the Holy Spirit, among which fear is counted last, not humility.]

78. To those endowed with these virtues, grace sometimes withdraws itself beneficially.---Yet sometimes, when our mind is supported by the fullness and abundance of so great a gift, if it continually enjoys security in these things, it forgets from whom it has received them and thinks that it possesses from itself what it never considers absent from it. Thus it happens that this same grace sometimes beneficially withdraws itself and shows the presumptuous mind how weak it is in itself.

For then we truly recognize where our good things come from, when, as though losing them, we perceive that they cannot be preserved by us. Accordingly, as a lesson intended to impress humility, it often happens that, when the critical moment of temptation arrives, such folly strikes our wisdom that the troubled mind does not know how to confront impending evils or prepare itself against temptation. Yet by this very folly the heart is wisely instructed: precisely because it is foolish for a moment, it afterwards becomes wiser—and more humbly so—and the wisdom that seems to be lost is thereby possessed more securely.

Sometimes, while the mind raises itself in exaltation by understanding sublime things, it grows sluggish through grave dullness in lowly and insignificant matters, so that suddenly it finds even the lowest things closed to it, although previously it penetrated the heights with swift understanding. [Note: The Ancient Remigius manuscript reads, “which had swiftly penetrated the heights.” The Old Paris and Basel Editions, with Bartholomew, read, “which had stubbornly penetrated the heights.” This is the reading found in the Corbie and German manuscripts.]

Yet this very dullness preserves understanding for us when it withdraws it, because, while it humbles the heart for a moment, it afterwards strengthens it to understand sublime things more truly.

Sometimes, while we rejoice that we conduct everything with the gravity of counsel, when the moment of an emerging matter strikes us, we are carried away by sudden rashness; and we who have always believed that we lived in an orderly manner are suddenly overwhelmed by profound confusion. Yet through the instruction of that same confusion we learn not to attribute our counsels to our own strength; and we are brought back to gravity all the more promptly because we return to it as though we had lost it.

Sometimes, while the mind strongly despises adversity, when adverse events arise, violent fear strikes it. But, shaken by this fear, it learns whom to credit for the fact that it stood firmly in certain matters; and afterwards it retains fortitude more powerfully in proportion as, when fear suddenly rushed upon it, it saw that fortitude had almost slipped away.

Sometimes, while we rejoice that we know great things, we grow torpid through the blindness of sudden ignorance. But in proportion as ignorance closes the eye of the mind for a moment, it opens it afterwards more truly to knowledge, so that, instructed by the scourge of its blindness, the mind may also know from whom it has received knowledge itself.

Sometimes, while we arrange everything religiously and rejoice that we possess the full entrails of piety, we are struck by a certain hardness of mind that suddenly falls upon us. But, as though hardened, we recognize to whom we should attribute the good of the piety we possessed; and piety is received more truly, as though extinguished, when it is loved more deeply as though lost.

Sometimes, while the mind rejoices that it is subject to divine fear, it suddenly stiffens when pride tempts it. Yet, soon fearing greatly because it does not fear, it hastily bends itself again toward humility; [Col. 0594A] and it receives humility all the more firmly in proportion as, by almost losing it, it has weighed the value of that virtue.

79. Humility and vigilance are acquired through temptations.---When the house has therefore been overturned, the children die, because the virtues born in the heart are suddenly and momentarily crushed, for the benefit of self-knowledge, when the conscience is disturbed in temptation. [Note: The Ancient Rheims, Corbie, and several other manuscripts read, “for the benefit of knowledge of oneself.”]

These children plainly live inwardly through the spirit while they die outwardly in the flesh, because although our virtues, in the time of temptation, fail for a moment from the security of their proper state when they are disturbed, they nevertheless remain whole at the root of the mind through perseverance of intention.

With them three sisters also fall, because in the heart charity is sometimes disturbed by scourges, hope shaken by fear, and faith assailed by questions. Often we grow sluggish, as though toward the love of our Creator, when we are wearied by a scourge beyond what we believe suitable for us. Often, when the mind fears more than necessary, it weakens its confidence in hope. Often, when the spirit is stretched by immense questions, disturbed faith is wearied as though it were about to fail.

Yet the daughters live, although they die when the house is shaken, because although the disturbance itself declares that hope, faith, and charity within the conscience have almost fallen, perseverance in right intention preserves them alive before the eyes of God.

Thus the boy who reports these things alone escapes, because discernment of mind remains unharmed even amid temptations. The boy enables Job to recover his children by weeping, when the reporting of discernment causes the grieving spirit, through repentance, to preserve the powers it had begun almost to lose.

A marvelous dispensation is at work with us when our mind is sometimes struck by the assault of guilt. For a person would believe himself to possess great strength if he never felt any failure of that strength within the secret places of his mind. But when he is shaken by the onset of temptation and almost exhausted beyond what is sufficient, the protection of humility is shown to him against the snares of his enemy; and from the very point at which he fears falling weakly, he receives the power to stand firmly.

The person who is tempted learns not only from whom he receives strength, but also with what vigilance he must preserve it. For often someone whom the struggle of temptation could not overcome is brought down still more disastrously by his own security. When a person relaxes himself in leisure because he is tired, he exposes his disordered mind to the corrupter. But if, by the dispensation of heavenly mercy, temptation strikes him—not suddenly and violently, but by approaching with measured force and instructing him—he awakens to foresee the snares, so that he may cautiously arm himself for battle against the enemy. Hence it is rightly added:

CHAPTER L.

VERSE 20.---Then Job arose.

80. Discernment is advanced by temptations.---To sit belongs to one who is at rest; to rise belongs to one who is fighting. Therefore, to rise after hearing adversities is for a mind tested by temptations to prepare itself more robustly for battle. Through these temptations discernment also advances, because it learns to distinguish virtues from vices with greater subtlety. Hence it is rightly added:

CHAPTER LI [Old Edition XXXVIII].

THE SAME PLACE.---He tore his garments.

81. Those struck by temptations should flee to the grief of repentance and to humility, so that they may be healed.---We tear our garments when, by discernment, we review our actions. For if our actions did not cover us before God like garments, the angelic voice would never say: “Blessed is the one who keeps watch and guards his garments, lest he walk naked and they see his shame” (Revelation 16:15).

Our shame is seen when a blameworthy life is not covered before the eyes of the righteous at the judgment by the garment of subsequent good works. But when we are tempted by guilt, we are inflamed to lamentation; and, awakened by those very laments, we open the eyes of the mind more subtly to perceive the light of justice. Thus, in sorrow, we tear our garments, because as discernment grows through weeping, we judge everything we do more strictly with an angry hand. [Note: The Norman manuscripts and many others read “we vindicate.”]

Then all our elation collapses; then every excess of thought falls from the mind. Hence it is added:

CHAPTER LII.

THE SAME PLACE.---And, having shorn his head, he fell upon the ground and worshiped.

82. How elation and the vanity of thoughts are cut away.---For what do we understand morally by hair except the thoughts of the mind that flow downward? Thus it is said elsewhere to the Church: “Your lips are like a scarlet thread, O bride, and your speech is sweet” (Song of Songs 4:3). [Note: In some copies: “Your lips are like ribbons” (sicut vittae sunt).] A ribbon binds the hair of the head. The bride’s lips, therefore, are like a ribbon because, through the exhortation of holy Church, all the thoughts diffused in the minds of hearers are bound together, so that they do not flow loosely, do not scatter themselves among unlawful things, and do not, once scattered, depress the eyes of the heart; rather, they gather themselves toward a single intention when the ribbon of holy preaching binds them.

It rightly calls the ribbon scarlet, because the preaching of the saints burns with the heat of charity alone. What, then, is signified by the head except the mind itself, which is the governing principle of each person’s action? Hence it is said elsewhere: “Let oil not fail from your head” (Ecclesiastes 9:8). Oil upon the head is charity in the mind; and oil fails from the head when charity departs from the mind.

To shear the head, therefore, is to cut away superfluous thoughts from the mind. He falls upon the ground with his head shorn who, with the thoughts of his presumption restrained, humbly recognizes how weak he is in himself.

[Old Edition XXXIX.] 83. It is difficult to do great things and not place confidence in what has been done.---It is indeed difficult to do great things and not to place, within oneself, confidence in one’s great deeds. By the very fact that one lives courageously against vices, presumption of thought is generated in the heart; and when the mind vigorously crushes faults outwardly, it often secretly swells within itself. It now considers itself to possess some great merit and does not think that it sins in its own estimation of itself.

Before the eyes of the strict Judge, however, the offense is all the worse in proportion as the fault is committed more secretly and therefore almost incurably. [Note: We have restored this from the manuscripts. Formerly it read: “the more secretly and almost incurably the fault is committed.”] The pit is open for swallowing more widely in proportion as the life more proudly boasts of itself.

Hence, as we have often said, by the merciful dispensation of the Creator it happens that a soul trusting in itself is struck by a providential temptation, so that, when weakened, it may discover what it is and lay aside the arrogance of its presumption. As soon as temptation strikes the mind, all presumption and tumult of our thoughts become quiet.

84. An exalted mind breaks out into tyranny; its attendants are scattered by temptation.---When the mind raises itself in elation, it breaks out as if into tyranny. It has attendants of its tyranny: its own thoughts, which flatter it. But if an enemy attacks the tyrant, the favor of the attendants immediately ceases. When the adversary enters, the attendants flee; terrified, they withdraw from the one whom, while he was at peace, they praised with cunning flattery.

When the attendants have been withdrawn, he remains alone before the enemy, because, as the elated thoughts recede, the troubled mind sees only itself and the temptation. [Note: The printed editions read “sees itself in the temptation.” We follow the manuscripts.] Thus the head is shorn after adversities are heard, when, under the violent assault of temptations, the mind is stripped of the thoughts of its presumption.

For what does it mean that the Nazirites grow their hair (Numbers 6:5), except that, through a life of great self-restraint, thoughts of presumption increase? But what does it mean that, when his devotion has been completed, the Nazirite is commanded to shave his head and place his hair upon the fire of the sacrifice, except that we reach the summit of perfection when we overcome external vices in such a way that we also cut away superfluous thoughts from the mind?

To burn these thoughts in the fire of sacrifice is to set them aflame with the fire of divine love, so that the whole heart burns with love of God and, consuming its superfluous thoughts, uses up the hair of the Nazirite, as it were, in the perfection of devotion.

[Old Edition XL.] It should also be noted that he fell upon the ground and worshiped. He offers true worship to God who humbly sees that he is dust, who attributes no virtue to himself, and who recognizes that the good things he does come from the mercy of the Creator. Hence he appropriately says:

CHAPTER LIII.

VERSE 21.---Naked I came forth from my mother’s womb; naked I shall return there.

85. Whoever considers himself naked of virtues is better clothed by that very humility.---It is as though the tempted mind, caught in the poverty of its weakness, were saying: “Grace first begot me naked in faith; the same grace will save me naked when I am taken up.” [Note: 1 Reg. reads: “and oppressed by the poverty of his weakness.”] There is great consolation for a troubled spirit when, assailed by vices and seeing itself as though stripped of virtues, it turns back to the sole hope of mercy; and it does not allow itself to be stripped precisely because it humbly considers itself naked of virtues.

Even if it is perhaps laid bare of some virtue in temptation, yet, recognizing its own weakness, it is better clothed by humility itself. It lies far more robustly than it had stood when it ceases to attribute to itself, without divine assistance, what it possesses. Hence it immediately humbly acknowledges the hand of the Giver and Judge, saying:

CHAPTER LIV.

THE SAME PLACE.---The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away.

86. Instructed by temptation, we grow.---Behold, instructed by temptations, he grew: in the virtue he possessed he recognized the generosity of the giver, and in the disturbance of his strength he recognized the power of the one who takes away. Yet that strength is not taken away; it is disturbed and wearied, so that the shaken mind, while trembling that it is about to lose it altogether, may remain humble and therefore never lose it.

CHAPTER LV.

THE SAME PLACE.---As it has pleased the Lord, so it has come to pass; blessed be the name of the Lord.

87. What the tempted person should do.---When we are shaken by inward disturbance, it is right to return to the judgment of the Creator, so that our heart may offer greater praise to its helper precisely where, being struck, it more truly weighs its own weakness. It is rightly said:

CHAPTER LVI.

[Col. 0597C]

VERSE 22.---In all these things Job did not sin, nor did he speak anything foolish against God.

88. Let him not murmur because of temptation.---The grieving mind must guard itself with watchful care, lest, when temptation pricks it inwardly, it break out into unlawful speech outwardly; lest it murmur against its testing, and the fire that burns it as gold be changed, through excessive unlawful speech, into the ash of straw.

[Old Edition XLI, Revised Edition XXVIII.] 89. The gifts of God are sometimes beneficially withdrawn; the spirit of prophecy is not always present to the prophets.---There is no obstacle to understanding by the gifts given in the manifestation of virtue by the Holy Spirit what we have said concerning virtues. To some are given prophecy, to others kinds of tongues, and to others gifts of healings.

But because these gifts themselves are not always present in the mind in the same way, it is clearly shown that they are sometimes beneficially withdrawn, lest the mind lift itself up in presumption. For if the spirit of prophecy were always present to the prophets, the prophet Elisha would certainly not have said: “Let her alone, for her soul is in bitterness, and the Lord has hidden the matter from me” (2 Kings 4:27).

If the spirit of prophecy were always present to the prophets, the prophet Amos, when questioned, would not have said: “I am not a prophet,” whereupon he added: “Nor am I a prophet’s son; I am a herdsman, and I gather sycamore fruit” (Amos 7:14). [Note: Earlier editions read “a herdsman’s boy” (armentarius puer).] But how was he not a prophet, when he foretold so many true things about the future? Or how was he a prophet, if he truthfully denied this about himself in the present?

Because at the very hour when he was questioned he perceived that the spirit of prophecy was absent from him, he truthfully gave testimony about himself, saying: “I am not a prophet.” Yet he immediately continued: “And now hear the word of the Lord. Thus says the Lord: Your wife shall commit fornication in the city, and your sons and your daughters shall fall by the sword, and your land shall be measured out by a measuring line; and you shall die in a polluted land” (Amos 7:16–17). These words of the prophet clearly show that, while he was speaking that way about himself, he was filled with the prophetic spirit; and immediately he deserved to possess the spirit of prophecy because he humbly acknowledged that he was not a prophet.

And if the spirit of prophecy were always present to the prophets, the prophet Nathan would never have granted King David’s request concerning the construction of the temple only to deny it shortly afterward (2 Samuel 7:3, 5).

90. Permanently possessing the Spirit is Christ’s privilege; how it is said that he will remain also in the disciples.---Hence it is rightly written in the Gospel: “Upon whom you see the Spirit descending and remaining upon him, he is the one who baptizes” (John 1:33).

The Spirit comes upon all the faithful, but remains uniquely in the Mediator alone, because it never abandoned his humanity, from whose divinity it proceeds. [Note: The word “always,” inserted here in the printed editions, is absent from the Corbie, German, and Regius manuscripts and appears to be an addition.] It remains in him who alone can do all things and can do them always.

For the faithful who receive him, when they cannot always possess the gifts of signs as they wish, testify that they have received him as a passing manifestation. [Col. 0598C] But when, again, the disciples are told concerning the same Spirit by the mouth of the Truth: “He will remain with you and will be in you” (John 14:17), what does it mean that, by the divine voice of the Mediator, this same abiding of the Holy Spirit is declared a sign, when it is said: “Upon whom you see the Spirit descending and remaining upon him”? [Note: The printed editions read “this sign”; all our manuscripts instead read “this [abiding],” which has been restored.]

If, then, according to the Teacher’s word, he remains also in the disciples, how will it already be a unique sign that he remains in the Mediator? We understand this more quickly, however, if we distinguish the gifts of that same Spirit.

[Old Edition XLII, Revised Edition XXIX.] 91. He remains in the gifts by which holiness is conferred, not in those by which it is displayed for the benefit of others.---Some of his gifts are indispensable for attaining life; others reveal the holiness of life for the benefit of others. Gentleness, humility, patience, faith, hope, and charity are his gifts, but they are gifts without which human beings cannot reach life.

Prophecy, the power of healings, kinds of tongues, and interpretation of speech are also his gifts, but they reveal the presence of his power for the correction of those who behold them.

In those gifts without which life cannot be attained, the Holy Spirit always remains, whether in his preachers or in all the elect. But in those gifts by which our life is not preserved through his manifestation, but the benefit of others is sought, he does not always remain in his preachers. He always presides in their hearts so that they may live well, but he does not always display signs of power through them. Sometimes he withdraws himself from them in the manifestation of signs, so that his virtues may be held more humbly in proportion as, once possessed, they cannot be retained.

92. He remains in Christ in a wholly different way.---The man Christ Jesus, Mediator of God and human beings, has him present in all things, always, and continually, because the same Spirit proceeds substantially from him. Therefore, although he remains in holy preachers, he is rightly said to remain uniquely in the Mediator: in them he remains by grace for something; in him he remains by substance for everything.

Just as our body recognizes only the sense of touch, while the head of the body possesses the use of all five senses at once—seeing, hearing, tasting, smelling, and touching—so the members of the heavenly Head shine forth in certain virtues, whereas the Head itself burns with all virtues.

The Spirit therefore remains in him in a different manner, since by nature he never departs from him. [Note: In Gilot, the Vatican Edition, Gussanville, the later Coccius, and others, the following is added: “to whom he substantially presents himself according to his will.” This is absent from the manuscripts and ancient editions and ought to be absent, for it seems to conflict with the following statement.]

His gifts, however, by which one strives toward life, cannot be lost without danger; but the gifts by which the holiness of life is demonstrated are often, as has been said, withdrawn without harm. The former must therefore be retained for our instruction; the latter must be sought for the advancement of others.

In the former, fear should terrify us lest they perish; in the latter, when they are withdrawn for a time, humility should console us, because they may perhaps lift the mind toward elation.

When, therefore, the signs of virtue granted to us are withdrawn, let us rightly say: “The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away; as it has pleased the Lord, so it has come to pass; blessed be the name of the Lord.” For then we truly show that we have rightly retained what we received, when we endure with equanimity what has been taken away for a moment.

BOOK THREE. The whole second chapter of the Book of Job is explained historically, allegorically, and morally, in the manner of the preceding books.

[Col. 0599]

CHAPTER ONE.

[Col. 0599B]

THE HISTORICAL MEANING.---1. Blessed Job, assailed unto death in temptation, grew unto life through the blow; [Note: Some manuscripts read “grew from the wound” (crevit ex vulnere).] and from the very point at which the ancient enemy thought to destroy his goods, he grieved that he had multiplied them. But because he sees that he was defeated in the first contest, he restores himself for other battles of temptation and still shamelessly hopes for evil from the holy man, because the wicked cannot believe good even when it has been experienced.

The things that were stated earlier concerning his first striking are repeated when it is said:

VERSES 1–3.---“It came to pass, when on a certain day the sons of God had come and stood before the Lord, and Satan had come among them and stood in his presence, that the Lord said to Satan: ‘From where have you come?’ He answered and said: ‘I have gone around the earth and traversed it.’ And the Lord said to Satan: ‘Have you considered my servant Job, that there is none like him upon the earth, a simple and upright man, fearing God and turning away from evil?’”

The weakness of the devil’s pride is rebuked.---Because we have discussed these matters more fully above, we shall better pass over them in silence, lest, by repeating what has already been examined so often, we come more slowly to what has not been examined. Yet I do not think that, when the Lord’s voice says to Satan, “From where have you come?”, it is said to him in quite the same way as before.

When he returns defeated from that contest in which he had been given leave to act, and he is asked from where he has come, although it is known from where he comes, what else is rebuked but the weakness of his pride? It is as though the divine voice were openly saying to him: “Behold, you are defeated by one man placed in weak flesh, although you attempt to raise yourself against me, the Creator of all things.”

Hence, when the Lord immediately speaks of the good things of blessed Job as before, he adds them while enumerating the trophies of victory:

CHAPTER II.

THE SAME PLACE.---And still he holds fast to his innocence.

2. Job preserved his innocence more gloriously in affliction.---It is as though he openly said: “You indeed exercised your malice, but he did not lose his innocence; and by the very means through which you thought to diminish his progress, you were compelled to serve his progress, because the innocence of mind that he held gloriously in tranquility he preserved even more gloriously in affliction.”

It follows:

CHAPTER III [Revised Edition II].

THE SAME PLACE.---But you moved me against him, to afflict him without cause.

3. God afflicted Job without cause because he did not punish sin in him; and not without cause because he increased his merit.---Since God is just and truthful, it must be carefully considered how he declares that he afflicted blessed Job without cause. Because he is just, he could not afflict without cause; yet, because he is truthful, he could not have said otherwise than he acted.

Therefore, so that both claims may suit the just and truthful God—that he speak truth and do nothing unjust—we must recognize that blessed Job was struck both without cause in one respect and not without cause in another.

Because the just and truthful God asserts this about himself, let us show both that what he said was true and that what he did was right. It was necessary that the holy man, known to God alone and to himself, should be made known to all in the measure of his virtue, so that all might imitate him.

For he would not openly give others examples of virtue if he himself remained without temptation. It therefore came about that the force of the blow revealed to all his strength for imitation, and that the scourges brought to light what had lain hidden in tranquility.

Through those same scourges, however, the virtue of patience grew, and the glory of reward increased through the pain of affliction. Therefore, so that truth may be preserved in the Lord’s statement and rectitude in his action, blessed Job is struck not without cause, because his merit is increased; yet he is struck without cause, because no offense is punished. He was struck without cause because no guilt was cut away in him; and he was not struck without cause because the merit of his virtue was increased. [Col. 0601A]

[Old Edition II.] 4. How God is understood to have been moved.---But what does it mean when it says: “You moved me against him”? Is Truth inflamed by Satan’s words, so that it is provoked to torment his servants? Who could think such things about God, things that even a righteous human being would rightly judge unworthy?

But because we know how to strike only when moved, the divine striking itself is called “being moved”; and the divine voice descends to the level of our words so that his action may in some fashion be grasped by human beings.

That power which created all things without necessity, presides over all things without despising them, sustains all things without labor, and governs them without being occupied, also corrects without being moved. [Note: This is the reading of all our manuscripts and of the old Paris and Basel editions. Some printed editions read “without defect”; the former reading is preferable, signifying that God governs all things by his providence without disregarding even the lowliest beings.] Thus it forms human minds through scourges according to its will, without passing from the light of its own unchangeableness into the shadow of change.

It follows:

CHAPTER IV.

VERSES 4–5.---Satan answered and said: “Skin for skin, and a person will give everything he has for his life. But otherwise, stretch out your hand, touch his bone and his flesh, and then you will see whether he will not bless you to your face.”

5. God allows the devil to renew battle against the saints so that, defeated again and again, he may fall silent.---The ancient enemy gathers from external events an argument that he turns against the blessed man as an accusation of the mind. He asserts that “skin is given for skin,” because often, when we see a blow coming against the face, we place our hand before our eyelids to protect our eyes from the blow; and we expose one part of the body to a wound so that we may not be wounded in a more delicate part of the body.

Knowing that such things are customarily done, Satan says: “Skin for skin, and a person will give everything he has for his life.” It is as though he were openly saying: “Job endures so many scourges outside himself with equanimity for this reason: he fears being struck himself. He is therefore concerned for his flesh, since he is not moved by the loss of carnal possessions; for, while he fears for himself, he feels the blows against his possessions less.”

Hence he immediately requests that Job’s flesh be struck, saying: “Stretch out your hand, touch his bone and his flesh, and then you will see whether he will not bless you to your face” (Job 2:5). Earlier he had said: “Touch all that he possesses, and then you will see whether he will not bless you to your face” (Job 1:11). Now, as though forgetting his earlier proposition, defeated, he asks for one thing after another. [Note: The Remigius, Compendium, Corbie, and German manuscripts, corrected by a second hand, and the old editions have this reading; Coccius, Gilot, and the subsequent editions read “having become forgetful” (oblitus factus).]

Yet this is rightly permitted by the divine dispensation, so that the shameless disputant, defeated again and again, may fall silent. It follows:

CHAPTER V [Revised Edition III].

VERSE 6.---Then the Lord said to Satan: “Behold, he is in your hand; nevertheless, preserve his life.”

6. Job is delivered into the adversary’s hand in such a way that he is always retained in the hand of his helper.---Behold, permission to strike is again accompanied by the protection of guardianship. The divine dispensation, in guarding its chosen one, abandons him; in abandoning him, it guards him. It exposes some things concerning him and protects others.

For if it abandoned Job entirely into the hand of so great an adversary, what would become of the human being? Thus, within the very justice of the permission, a certain balance of mercy is mixed, so that in one and the same contest the humble servant may advance through oppression and the proud enemy may be defeated through the permission granted him.

The holy man is therefore delivered into the adversary’s hand, yet he is retained inwardly in the hand of his helper. He belonged to those sheep of whom the Truth itself says in the Gospel: “No one shall snatch them from my hand” (John 10:28). Yet to the enemy who asks for him it is said: “Behold, he is in your hand.”

He is therefore at once in God’s hand and in the devil’s hand. For when he says, “He is in your hand,” and immediately adds, “Nevertheless, preserve his life,” the merciful helper is plainly revealed: he held the one whom he permitted to be taken, and in giving him over he did not surrender him, but concealed him by casting him into the darts of his adversary. [Note: Gussanville alone reads, “by exposing him to the darts.”]

[Old Edition III.] Satan is said to preserve that which he is not permitted to invade.---But what does it mean when Satan is told: “Preserve his life”? How does he preserve what he always desires to invade once it has been guarded?

Satan is said to preserve it in the sense that he does not dare to invade it, just as, conversely, in prayer we ask the Father, saying: “Do not lead us into temptation” (Matthew 6:13). For the Lord does not lead us into temptation, since he mercifully protects his servants from temptation; yet to “lead us into temptation” is, as it were, to fail to fortify us against the lure of temptation. He does not lead us into the snare of temptation when he does not permit us to be tempted beyond what we can bear.

Thus, just as God is said to lead us into temptation if he permits us to be led into it by the adversary, so the adversary is said to preserve a person’s life when he is forbidden to overcome it by tempting it.

VERSE 7.---Then Satan went out from the presence of the Lord.

How Satan goes out from the presence of the Lord is already made clear by what was said above. It follows:

CHAPTER VI.

[Col. 0602D] THE SAME PLACE.---He struck Job with a very grievous ulcer, from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head.

8. Nothing in Job’s body is free from pain, so that nothing in his soul may be free from glory.---Scourges must always be weighed in two ways: namely, according to what they are and according to how great they are. For often many are lightened by their quality, and often severe things by their quantity—provided that, when they are many, they are not severe, and when they are severe, they are not many.

To show, therefore, how harshly the adversary raged against the holy man—not only through the wickedness of the scourge’s quality but also through the weight of its quantity—it says, to indicate its quality: “He struck him with a very grievous ulcer.” [Note: The Corbie and German manuscripts, here and above, read “wound” (vulnere).] To indicate its quantity, it adds: “From the sole of his foot to the crown,” so that plainly nothing in his mind might be free from glory, since nothing in his body was free from pain.

It follows:

CHAPTER VII [Revised Edition IV].

VERSE 8.---He scraped the discharge from his body with a potsherd, while sitting on a heap of refuse.

9. Job scraping the bodily discharge with a potsherd teaches us that the clay vessel we bear will soon be broken.---What is a potsherd made from, unless from clay? And what is bodily discharge, except clay? Thus Job is said to scrape away the discharge with a potsherd, as though it were plainly said: “He wiped clay with clay.” For the holy man considered from what material that which he bore had been taken, and with a fragment of an earthen vessel he scraped an earthen vessel that had been broken. By this action it is clearly shown how, while it was sound, he held his body in subjection to himself, and how, when it had been struck, he cared for it while despising it. What softness did he permit to his healthy flesh, who applied to his wounds neither a garment nor his fingers, but even a potsherd? He therefore scraped away the discharge with a potsherd, so that, considering himself even in the fragment, he might also draw from the wiping of his wound care for his mind.

[Vet. IV.] 10. Lying in the dungheap, he considers that his body will soon become dung.---Since the mind is often puffed up by the things that surround the body, and by what is done to us the frailty of our body is removed from the eyes of the heart—as when some worldly people, supported by temporal dignities, preside over higher places, see that the services of many are available to them at will, neglect to contemplate their own frailty, and, forgetting how quickly the earthen vessel they bear will be broken, pay no attention to it at all—blessed Job, so that he might draw a consideration of his frailty even from what surrounded him and increase before his eyes the force of his own contempt, is described as sitting not on just any ground, which is found almost everywhere clean, but in a dungheap [Note: All the printed editions read “not on just any ground,” contrary to the testimony of the manuscripts].

He placed his body in a dungheap, so that a mind making good progress might reflect what the substance of flesh, taken from the earth, was. He placed his body in a dungheap so that, from the stench of the place also, he might understand that the body would swiftly return to stench.

[Rec. V.] 11. From the scourges of the saints we should understand what reward is reserved for them and what punishment for the wicked.---But behold: when blessed Job endures the losses of so many things, grieves, struck by the deaths of so many children [Note: Ebroic., “by the deaths of so many children”], and bears so many wounds; while he scrapes away the running discharge with a potsherd, while he sits in the dungheap amid the decay flowing from him, it is pleasing to consider what it means that almighty God afflicts so vehemently, as though despising them, those whom he foresees will be so dear to him forever.

But as I consider the wounds and sufferings of blessed Job, suddenly I bring the eyes of my mind back to John, and with the greatest astonishment reflect that he who was filled with the spirit of prophecy within his mother’s womb and, so to speak, reborn before he was born; he who was the friend of the bridegroom; he than whom no one greater has arisen among those born of women; he who was a prophet, and even more than a prophet (Matt. XI, 9)—was sent by the wicked into prison, beheaded for the dancing of a girl, and a man of such great strictness died for the amusement of the shameless.

Can we perhaps believe that there was something which that despised death cleansed from his life? But when did he sin even in food, who ate only locusts and wild honey? In what respect did he offend God concerning the quality of his clothing, who covered his body with camel hair? In what respect could he offend by his way of life, who did not withdraw from the wilderness? What guilt of loquacity polluted him, who lived far removed from human beings? When did the fault of silence touch him, who rebuked so vehemently those who came to him, saying: “Brood of vipers, who showed you to flee from the coming wrath?” (Matt. III, 7; Luke III, 7; Mark I, 4.)

What, then, does it mean that Job is preferred by the testimony of God, yet is stretched out under blows as far as the dungheap? What does it mean that John is praised by the voice of God, yet dies, because of the words of a drunken man, as the reward of a dance [Note: This is the reading of almost all manuscripts; some printed editions read “as the reward of the dancing girl”]? What does it mean that almighty God so vehemently despises in this world those whom he chose so sublimely before the ages, except that which is evident to the devotion of the faithful: that he presses them so heavily in lowly places because he sees how he will reward them in the highest; and casts them outwardly down as far as things despised because inwardly he leads them as far as things incomprehensible?

From this, then, let each person gather what those whom he rejects will suffer there, if here he so torments those whom he loves; or how those will be struck who must be accused at the judgment, if here the life of those who are praised by the testimony of the Judge himself is so heavily burdened.

It follows:

CHAPTER VIII [Rec. VI].

VERSE 9.---Then his wife said to him: “Do you still remain in your simplicity? Bless God, and die.”

12. The devil attempts either to break those who stand firm through tribulations or to soften them through persuasion. He seeks a woman as a ladder by which he may climb into Job’s heart—but in vain.---The ancient enemy is accustomed to tempt the human race in two ways: namely, either to break the hearts of those who stand firm through tribulations, or to soften them through persuasions. In both ways, therefore, he exercised himself vehemently against blessed Job [Note: Two Rheims manuscripts read: “for he who first …”].

First, he brought losses upon the head of the household, deprived the father through the death of his children, and struck the man who was still sound with wounds of decay. But when he saw that, although decaying outwardly, he still stood inwardly sound, and that the man whom he had made outwardly naked was becoming richer inwardly through the praise he offered to his Creator, he was jealous. He cunningly weighed the matter, realizing that the athlete of God was lifted up by the very thing by which he was oppressed, and, defeated, turned to subtler devices of temptation.

[Vet. V.] For he renews the ambushes of his ancient art; and because he knows how Adam is accustomed to be deceived, he returns to Eve. He saw blessed Job, amid the loss of so many things and the wounds of so many blows, standing unconquered as though in a fortress of virtues. For he had fixed his mind on high, and therefore the enemy’s ambushes could not break into it.

The adversary therefore sought by what steps one might climb into this most strongly fortified citadel. A woman is close to a man and subordinate to him [Note: All manuscripts read “subordinate,” as opposed to the reading in the printed editions, “subjected.” Shortly afterward, however, we read “the holy man’s wife, subject to him,” and this is found in all the manuscripts]. He therefore seized the woman’s heart and found in it, as it were, a ladder by which he could climb into the man’s heart. He occupied the wife’s mind as the ladder to her husband.

But by this device he achieved nothing, because the holy man regarded the woman as subordinate to him, not placed over him; and, speaking rightly, he taught her [Note: Most manuscripts read “and taught her to speak rightly”] what the serpent had incited her to speak perversely. For it was fitting that masculine judgment should restrain a wavering mind, since from the first fall of the human race he knew [Note: All manuscripts confirm this reading; some printed editions read “harms” or “teaches” for “knew”] that a woman did not know how to teach rightly.

Hence Paul rightly says: “I do not permit a woman to teach” (1 Tim. II, 12), because once, when she taught, she separated man from eternal wisdom.

Thus the ancient enemy, who had overthrown Adam in paradise, lost Adam in the dungheap [Note: The manuscripts vary here. The ancient Remigius manuscript, together with Corb. and Germ., reads: “Thus the ancient enemy lost Adam in the dungheap”; we adopt this reading below. The old Paris edition, the second edition of Rheims, all the Remigius manuscripts, Vindoc., Norman., Val. Cl., and others read: “Thus the ancient enemy lost Adam in the dungheap.” The old Basel edition has the same reading]. He stirred up his helper, the woman, to the words of an evil persuasion, and sent her to the teaching of holy instruction; she who had been aroused in order to destroy was instructed so that she might not perish. Thus, thus is the enemy struck by our strong men, so that even his own weapons are snatched from him.

For from the point where he thinks he will magnify the pain of the wound, from that very point he supplies them with weapons of virtue against himself [Note: The old Paris, Basel, and other editions mistakenly read “from there to him.” The reference is to the strong men discussed above: from that point Satan suggests to them weapons of virtue against himself].

13. The devil tempts us through those who adhere to us.---From the words of the wife who offered evil counsel, we must watch carefully how the ancient adversary strives to weaken the stability of our mind not only through himself, but also through those who adhere to us. When he cannot overthrow our heart by his own persuasion, he creeps toward it through the tongues of those who adhere to us.

Thus it is written: “Beware of your children, and be attentive to your household” (Ecclus. XXXII, 26). Through the prophet it is said: “Let each one guard himself from his neighbor, and let him not trust in any of his brothers” (Jer. IX, 4). Again it is written: “A man’s enemies are his household” (Matt. X, 36).

For the cunning adversary, when he sees himself repelled from the hearts of the good, seeks out those who are greatly loved by them; and through their words he speaks flatteringly, through those who are loved more than the others, so that, while the force of love pierces the heart, the sword of his persuasion may easily break through to the innermost defenses of uprightness.

After the losses of possessions, after the deaths of the children, after the wounds and lacerations of the limbs, the ancient enemy moved the wife’s tongue.

14. The enemy’s devices in the sequence of Job’s temptations.---We should also note at what moment he attempted to corrupt the man’s mind with poisonous speech. He brought words after the wounds, so that, when the force of pain was increasing, the suggestion of a perverse persuasion might easily prevail.

[Vet. VI.] But if we carefully examine the order of his temptation, we discover with what cunning he rages. First he brought about losses of property, which were certainly outside nature and outside the body. He took away the children, which was no longer wholly outside nature, but was still in some measure outside his own body. Finally, he struck the body itself.

But because he could not reach the wound of the mind through the wounds of the flesh, he also sought the tongue of the wife who was joined to him. Since he grieved that he had been overcome in open combat, he hurled a dart from the mouth of his wife as if from an ambush, and she said: “Do you still remain in your simplicity? Bless God, and die.”

Behold: by tempting, he took everything away; behold: by tempting, he left the woman; and he cunningly stripped the holy man of all things, but still more cunningly preserved the woman as his helper, so that she might say: “Do you still remain in your simplicity?”

She repeats the words of Eve. For what does it mean to say, “Abandon your simplicity,” except: “Despise obedience by eating what is forbidden”? [Note: Corb. and Germ. read “what is forbidden”; the printed editions read “the forbidden fruit,” but no manuscript contains “fruit.”] And what does it mean to say, “Bless God, and die,” except: “By transgressing the commandment, live beyond the measure in which you were created”?

But our strong Adam lay in the dungheap, whereas once he had stood weak in paradise. Immediately, therefore, he answered the words of the woman offering evil counsel, saying:

CHAPTER IX [Rec. VII].

VERSE 10.---“You have spoken as one of the foolish women. If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, why should we not endure evil things?”

15. Job, outwardly empty of possessions, inwardly full of God. Why scourges are called “evils.”---Behold, the enemy is everywhere broken, everywhere overcome; he has fallen before every device of temptation, because he lost even his familiar consolation through the woman.

Amid all this, it is pleasing to contemplate the holy man, outwardly empty of possessions, inwardly full of God. When Paul saw within himself the riches of inner wisdom and perceived that outwardly he was a corruptible body, he said: “We have this treasure in earthen vessels” (2 Cor. IV, 7).

Behold: in blessed Job, the earthen vessel outwardly felt the cracks of ulcerous wounds, but the treasure within remained whole. Outwardly, through the wounds, it cracked; but the treasure of wisdom, continually arising within, flowed forth through words [Note: The Norman and Val.
