Cl. manuscripts, and others, read “through the words”] of holy instruction, saying: “If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, why should we not endure evil things?”

He calls good things the gifts of God, whether temporal or eternal; but he calls present scourges “evils.” Of these the Lord says through the prophet: “I am the Lord, and there is no other, forming light and creating darkness, making peace and creating evils” (Isa. XLV, 7).

For the evils that have no existence by their own nature are not created by the Lord. Rather, the Lord indicates that he creates evils when he turns things well created into a scourge for us who act badly, so that the same things are evils for sinners through the pain by which they strike, but good through the nature by which they exist.

Thus poison is death to a human being, but nevertheless life to a serpent.

Through love of present things we withdrew from the love of our Creator; and the perverse mind, while submitting itself to the delight of the creature [Note: The ancient Rheims manuscript, one Remigius manuscript, Compend., Corb., Germ., Colb., and the old Paris and Basel editions read “to the delight of the creature”], separated itself from the fellowship of the Creator. Therefore it was necessary that it be struck by the Creator through those things which, in its error, it had placed before the Creator, so that from the source where the proud person was not afraid to admit guilt, he might find punishment by which he would be corrected; and so that he might return more quickly to what he had lost, the more he perceived that what he had sought was full of pain.

Hence it is rightly said: “Forming light and creating darkness,” because when the darkness of pain is created outwardly through scourges, the light of the mind is kindled inwardly through instruction. “Making peace and creating evils,” because peace with God is restored to us when those things that were well created but not well desired [Note: The printed editions read “but wrongly desired”; the manuscripts read “but not well desired”] are turned into scourges that are evil for us.

Through guilt we became alienated from God; therefore it is fitting that through scourges we return to his peace, so that whenever each well-created thing is turned into pain for us, the corrected mind may be humbly restored to the peace of its Creator.

Blessed Job therefore calls these scourges “evils,” because he weighs with what disturbance they strike the good of salvation and tranquility.

16. The punishment of the scourge should be tempered by remembrance of the gift, and joy by fear of the scourge. It is the mind, not the sex, that is at fault.---But we should observe very carefully how, in opposition to his wife’s persuasion, he gathers himself together through such a considered method, saying: “If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, why should we not endure evil things?”

[Vet. VII.] Great indeed is the consolation of tribulation if, while we suffer adversity, we recall to mind the gifts of our Creator. What comes against us through pain does not break us if what raises us up through grace comes more quickly before the mind.

Hence it is written: “In the day of good things do not be forgetful of evils, and in the day of evils do not be forgetful of good things” (Ecclus. XI, 27).

Whoever receives gifts but, in the time of gifts, does not at all fear scourges, falls through joy into pride. Whoever, however, is worn down by scourges but, in the time of scourges, does not console himself at all with the gifts he has been granted to receive, is destroyed from the stability of his mind by utter despair.

Thus both must be joined, so that one may always be supported by the other: the memory of the gift should temper the punishment of the scourge, and suspicion and fear of the scourge should bite into the joy of the gift.

The holy man, therefore, to soothe his oppressed mind amid the wounds, weighs the consolations of gifts in the pains of the scourges, saying: “If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, why should we not endure evil things?”

Here he rightly prefaces: “You have spoken as one of the foolish women.” For since it is the perverse mind of the woman, not her sex, that is at fault [Note: The manuscripts read “because it is the perverse mind of the woman”; the printed editions read “because it is the mind of the perverse will of women”], he does not say: “You have spoken as one of the women,” but “as one of the foolish women,” so that it may be shown that what thinks perversely belongs to an accidental folly, not to created nature [Note: Gilot., Vatic., and Gussanv. read “of one who is approaching,” contrary to the testimony of the manuscripts].

It follows:

CHAPTER X.

[Col. 0608B] HERE.---“In all these things Job did not sin with his lips.”

17. Job did not sin with his lips because he neither spoke unjustly nor kept silent about what was just.---We sin with our lips in two ways: when we either say what is unjust or keep silent about what is just. For if silence were never at times a fault, the prophet would not say: “Woe is me, because I was silent” (Isa. VI, 5).

Blessed Job, therefore, in all that he did, did not sin at all with his lips, because he neither spoke proudly against the one who struck him nor kept silent about what was right against the one offering counsel. He sinned neither by speaking nor by keeping silent: he gave thanks to the Father who scourged him and supplied the wife who offered evil counsel with the wisdom of instruction.

Because he knew what he owed to God and what he owed to his neighbor—namely, patience to the Creator and wisdom to his wife—he both reproved and instructed her, and praised him by giving thanks.

But which of us, if he received a single wound from such a blow, would not immediately lie prostrate from the depths of his being? Behold, outwardly laid low by wounds of the flesh, he remains inwardly upright through the protection of his mind. He sees every dart fly beneath him, and watchfully detects the missiles which the raging enemy, striking with a severe hand, fixes in him outwardly: now wounds hurled against him from in front, now words launched as if from the side.

Our warrior, caught amid the heat of battles surrounding him, everywhere presents the shield of his patience. He meets the darts coming from every direction and, on every side of his virtues, turns his watchful mind against the wounds rushing upon him [Note: Corb., Germ., and all our manuscripts read “turns his mind,” not “strengthens his mind,” as appears in most printed editions].

[Vet. VIII.] 18. He is tempted through friends.---But the more powerfully the ancient enemy is defeated, the more ardently he is stirred to further ambushes. Since the wife, after being rebuked, kept silent, he immediately aroused others who would rise to insult him in their rebuke [Note: The ancient Rheims manuscript reads “who would suggest insults for rebuking him”; the second Rheims and the second Remigius read “who would suggest insults by rebuking him”; the first Remigius reads “who would rise to rebuke him with insults”; Germ. reads “would rise to insult him in rebuke”; Corb. and Germ., in later corrections apparently by the same hand, read “by rebuking him,” which is not a bad reading].

For just as he had striven to strike him repeatedly by reporting the losses of his possessions, so now he endeavors to penetrate the strong breast by striking it again and again with verbal insults.

It follows:

CHAPTER XI [Rec. IX].

VERSE 11.---“Now when Job’s three friends heard of all the evil that had happened to him, they came each from his own place: Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite. For they had agreed among themselves that they would come together to visit him and console him.”

19. The right intention of Job’s friends is darkened by lack of discretion.---They came by agreement to console the afflicted man, and this shows how great their affection was both among themselves and toward the one who had been struck. Although the fact that Scripture testifies that they were friends of such a great man also shows that they possessed good zeal and right intention, nevertheless this very intention of theirs was darkened before the eyes of the strict Judge by the indiscretion that arose when they burst into speech.

It follows:

CHAPTER XII [Rec. X].

VERSE 12.---“And when they had lifted up their eyes from afar, they did not recognize him; and crying out, they wept, and, tearing their garments, they scattered dust upon their heads toward heaven.”

20. One who will console the afflicted ought to grieve; but he should set a limit to his grief.---Because the blows had changed the appearance of the stricken man, his friends cried out in tears, tore their garments, and sprinkled dust upon their heads, so that when they saw the man whom they had come to visit transformed, spontaneous grief might also transform the very appearance of the consolers.

The order of consolation is that, when we wish to lift someone afflicted from sorrow, we should first strive, by grieving, to agree with his grief. For one who does not agree with the grief of the sorrowful cannot console the sorrowful, because, precisely insofar as he differs from the affliction of the grieving person, he is received less by the one from whom he is separated in the quality of his mind.

The mind must therefore first be softened, so that it may correspond to the afflicted person; corresponding, cling to him; clinging, draw him along. Iron is not joined to iron unless both are melted by the heat of fire; and the hard does not adhere to the soft unless its hardness is first tempered and softened, so that it may become, as it were, the very thing it is being treated to hold.

Likewise, we do not raise up those who lie prostrate unless we bend from the rigidity of our own standing position. For when the uprightness of one who stands differs from the posture of one who lies fallen, it does not lift the one to whom it neglects to condescend.

The friends of blessed Job therefore, so that they might raise the afflicted man from his pain, necessarily took care to grieve together with him. When they saw his wounded body, they themselves took care to tear their garments; and when they saw him transformed, they took care to defile their heads with dust, so that the afflicted man might receive their words more readily, insofar as he recognized in them something of his own affliction.

[Vet. IX.] 21. But in all this we should know that the person who desires to console the afflicted must necessarily set a measure to the grief he assumes, lest he not only fail to soothe the grieving person but, by grieving intemperately, press the mind of the afflicted under the weight of despair.

Our grief must therefore be joined to the grief of those who mourn in such a way that, through moderation, it lifts them up, not that, through increase, it burdens them. Hence perhaps we may gather that the friends of blessed Job grieved in their consolation more than was necessary. While they saw the blow but did not know the mind of the one struck, they turned to immeasurable mourning, as though the man who had been struck, though so strong, had also fallen from his heart because of the wound to his body.

It follows:

CHAPTER XIII.

VERSE 13.---“And they sat with him on the ground seven days and seven nights, and no one spoke a word to him; for they saw that his grief was very great [Note: The word “his” is absent in Corb., Germ., and most manuscripts].”

22. It is uncertain whether the friends sat with Job for seven continuous or interrupted days and nights.---Whether they sat with afflicted Job for seven continuous days and seven nights, or whether for seven days and as many nights they remained with him through frequent and sustained visits, we do not know.

Often we are said to do something for so many days, although we are not continuously occupied with it on those same days. Often, too, Holy Scripture is accustomed to put the whole for the part, just as it puts the part for the whole.

It speaks of the part for the whole when, describing Jacob’s household, it says: “Jacob entered Egypt with seventy souls” (Gen. XLVI, 27). When it mentions souls, it is plainly understood that it also includes the bodies of those who entered.

Again, it signifies the whole by the part when Mary complains at the tomb, saying: “They have taken the Lord from the tomb, and we do not know where they have placed him” (John XX, 2). She had come seeking only the Lord’s body, yet she laments as though the whole Lord had been *tultum* (“taken away”) [Note: Two Rheims manuscripts, two Remigius manuscripts, Val. Cl., Corb., Germ., and others read “and I do not know where,” etc. The ancient Remigius, one Remigius manuscript, Turon., Corb., Germ., and other old manuscripts read *tultum*. Gregory sometimes uses this form in his letters; it was also used by the author of the *Speculum* and by Abbot John of Fécamp. Utic. likewise has *tultum*, but a later hand has written *sublatum* above it, as in the printed editions. From *tultum* later came *toltum*; hence *mala tolta*, “a thing unjustly exacted.” The Germ. manuscripts read *sepultum*, “buried”].

Thus whether “seven days and seven nights” in this passage also signifies the whole by the part is uncertain.

23. Speech should be neither hasty nor indiscreet after the proper period of silence.---Nevertheless, we must not pass over carelessly the fact that they remained silent for a long time and were eventually reproved when they spoke.

There are some who begin to speak precipitately and carry out what they have begun without restraint, with still greater lack of restraint. There are others who begin to speak slowly, but once they have begun do not know how to impose a measure on their speech.

The friends of blessed Job, seeing his grief, remained silent for a long time; but, beginning late, they spoke indiscreetly, because they did not wish to spare the grieving man. They held back their tongue so that it would not begin too soon; but once it had begun, they did not moderate it at all, lest it run without restraint from consolation into insults.

They had come to console him with a good intention; but what a devout mind offered to God was spoiled by precipitate speech.

For it is written: “If you offer rightly, but do not divide rightly, you have sinned” (Gen. IV, 7, according to the Septuagint). Something is offered rightly when it is done with a right intention. But it is not rightly divided if what is done is not also carefully discerned.

To divide rightly what has been offered is to weigh all our good endeavors through careful discernment [Note: Ebroic. and some others read “by carefully discerning”]. Whoever neglects to do this sins even when offering rightly.

[Vet. X.] 24. Care must be taken that what we begin with a right zeal be completed with a right end.---Often, therefore, even what we do with good zeal, when we neglect to discern carefully, we do not know by what end it will be judged; and sometimes what is thought to be the cause of virtue becomes an accusation of guilt.

But whoever considers the actions of blessed Job’s friends cannot fail to recognize with what devout intention they came to him. Let us weigh how great their charity was in coming together in agreement to the afflicted man; how great the virtue of long-suffering in remaining silent with him for seven days and nights; what humility was shown by sitting on the ground for so many days and nights; what compassion was shown by sprinkling dust upon their heads.

Yet when they began to speak, the very thing from which they thought they would acquire the reward of their merit became for them an occasion of reproach, because what is begun only for the sake of reward often turns, through carelessness, toward the end of sin.

Behold: through their precipitate speech they lost the good they had acquired with such great labor. And unless divine grace had commanded them to offer sacrifice for their guilt, they could justly have been punished by the Lord for the very thing by which they remarkably thought they were pleasing him.

They displease the Judge precisely where, as though in defense of the Judge, they please themselves through their lack of restraint.

We say this so that we may recall to the minds of readers how severely the Lord punishes deeds performed with an evil intention, if he chastises with such a forceful rebuke deeds begun with good zeal but mixed with negligent indiscretion.

Who would not believe that he had completed a meritorious work if he said something against his neighbor in defense of God, or if he remained silent for seven days and nights out of grief for his neighbor? Yet the friends of blessed Job, while doing these things, arrived at guilt through their labor, because they knew the good of consolation that they were performing, but did not know with what measure of discretion it ought to be performed.

Therefore it is necessary not only to observe what we are doing, but also with how much discretion we carry it out. First, we must avoid doing evil in any way; afterward, we must avoid doing good carelessly.

The prophet urges us to perform these good works diligently, saying: “Cursed is the person who does the work of the Lord negligently” (Jer. XLVIII, 10).

Let these things serve to make us fear, before the subtle and incomprehensible examination of the terrible Judge, not only the evils we have committed but also whatever good deeds may be in us, because often in his judgment what is thought to be virtue before judgment is found to be guilt; and from the very place where a devout reward for the work is expected, the punishment of just retribution follows.

[Col. 0612A] [Vet. XI. Rec. XI.] 25. ALLEGORICAL MEANING.---The greatness of the union of Christ and the Church.---We have briefly reviewed these matters according to the historical sense; now let us turn the words toward the mystery of allegory.

But because, at the beginning of this work, when treating of the unity of head and body, we carefully prefaced how great is the bond of charity between them—for the Lord still suffers many things through the body that we are, while his body, that is, the Church, already glories in heaven through its head, namely, the Lord—so now the sufferings of that same head must be expressed in such a way as to show how many things he also endures in his body.

For if our torments did not touch our head, he would never cry out from heaven to his persecutor on behalf of his afflicted members: “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?” (Acts IX, 5). If our sufferings were not his sufferings, Paul, converted and afflicted, would not say: “I make up what is lacking in the sufferings of Christ in my flesh” (Col. I, 24).

And yet, exalted already by the resurrection of his head, he says: “He raised us up together and made us sit together in the heavenly places” (Eph. II, 6). Indeed, the torments of persecution had constrained him on earth; but, pressed under the weight of his sufferings, behold, through the glory of his head he was already seated in heaven.

Since, therefore, we know that head and body are united in all things, we begin with the blow against the head so that afterward we may come to the scourges of the body [Note: Most printed editions read “from persecution”; all manuscripts, together with Corb. and Germ., read “from the blow”].

But because we have already often discussed the fact that Satan is said to have stood before the Lord on a certain day, that he is asked where he comes from, and that blessed Job is preferred by the great praises of his Creator, we avoid repeating it. For if the mind is long entangled in matters already examined, it is hindered from reaching those not yet examined.

We therefore begin the allegory at the point where, after words often repeated, we know that something new has been added. Thus he says:

CHAPTER XIV.

“You have moved me against him, to afflict him without cause.”

26. Christ was afflicted without cause for himself, but not without cause for us.---If blessed Job bears the image of our Redeemer placed in his Passion, how is it said by the Lord to Satan: “You have moved me against him”?

The Mediator of God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus, came to endure the scourges of our mortality in order to extinguish the guilt of our transgression. But since he is of one and the same nature with the Father, how does the Father claim that he has been moved against him by Satan, when it is clear that the concord of the Father and the Son is interrupted by no inequality of power and no diversity of will?

Nevertheless, he who is equal to the Father in divinity came, for our sake, to the scourges in the flesh. He would not have received those scourges unless, by redeeming us, he had taken the form of condemned humanity. And if the first human being had not sinned, the second would never have come to the disgrace of the Passion [Note: The Remigius manuscripts, together with Corb. and Germ., read “to the disgrace of the Passion”].

When, therefore, the first human being was moved by Satan away from the Lord, then the Lord was moved in the second human being. Satan therefore moved the Lord to this affliction when, in paradise, he cast the first human being down from the height of justice through the guilt of disobedience.

For unless Satan had drawn the first Adam into the death of the soul through voluntary fault, the second Adam, without fault, would not have come voluntarily to the death of the flesh.

Thus it is rightly said to Satan concerning our Redeemer: “You have moved me against him, to afflict him without cause.” It is as though it were said more openly: “While this one dies not for his own sake but for the sake of that other, you moved me to afflict him when you drew the other away from me by your crafty persuasion.”

And it is rightly added: “without cause.” For he was afflicted without cause: he was weighed down by the punishment of guilt, yet was not stained by the contagion of guilt. He was afflicted without cause: although incarnate, he had committed no sins of his own, and yet without guilt he accepted the punishment of the flesh [Note: All manuscripts—Rheims, Remigius, Corb., Germ., Utic.—read “who was incarnate”; Val. Cl. reads “because he was incarnate.” The printed editions read “who was born in the flesh”].

Hence he speaks through the prophet, saying: “What I did not take, I then repaid” (Ps. LXVIII, 5). For Adam, created for paradise, wished arrogantly to seize the likeness of divine power; but the Mediator, without guilt, paid the penalty for this arrogance [Note: The Norman manuscripts and many of those cited above read “For Adam,” etc.].

Hence a certain wise man says to the Father: “Although you are just, you dispose all things justly, condemning even one who does not deserve to be punished” (Wis. XII, 15).

27. Why God afflicted the innocent Christ with punishments.—But one must consider how he is just and arranges all things justly, if he condemns one who ought not to be punished. For our Mediator ought not to have been punished on his own account, since he committed no contagion of sin. Yet if he had not undertaken what was undeserved, he would never have freed us from the death we deserved. Therefore the Father, being just and punishing the Just One, arranges all things justly, because by this he justifies everything: he condemns the Sinless One on behalf of sinners, so that all the elect might rise to the summit of righteousness through the fact that the One who is above all things bore the penalties of our injustice. Thus, what is there said to be “condemned though he ought not to be,” is here remembered as “afflicted in vain.” Yet he was afflicted in vain with regard to himself, but not in vain with regard to our deeds [Note: Thus all our manuscripts. The printed editions have: “For the rust of sin.”]. 85 For the rust of vice could not be cleansed except by the fire of torment. Therefore he came without vice, to subject himself willingly to torment, so that the punishments owed to our iniquity might justly release their guilty victims precisely to the degree that they had unjustly held him, who was free from them, in their power. He was therefore afflicted both in vain and not in vain: he had no transgressions in himself, but by his own blood he wiped away the stain of our guilt.

## CHAPTER XV [Old XII]

[Col. 0613D]

**Verses 4–5.**—Satan answered and said: “Skin for skin, and all that a man has he will give for his life. Otherwise, stretch out your hand and touch his bone and his flesh, and then you will see that he will bless you to your face.”

28. How Satan knows Christ, and how he doubts about him. How he is deceived in assessing Christ’s charity and patience. Satan’s speech, both directly and through his agents.—When the evil spirit sees our Redeemer shining forth in miracles, he cries: “We know [Note: The ancient Rheims, Norman, Corbie, Germain, and most manuscripts have: “We know who you are, the Holy One of God.” Some have: “We know that you are the Son of God”; others: “We know that you are the Holy One of God”; and finally some: “I know who you are, the Holy One of God.” Germain has: “We know who you are.” For he fears the Son of God, but nevertheless, and so forth. Shortly afterward the particle *nonnunquam* (“sometimes”), which was lacking in the printed editions, is restored from the manuscripts.] who you are, the Holy One of God” (Luke 4:34). In saying this, he fears because he recognizes the Son of God; nevertheless, because he does not understand the power of heavenly mercy, when he sometimes observes him subject to suffering, he supposes him to be merely human.

He had learned that many who occupied pastoral office under the appearance of holiness were very far removed from the inward disposition of charity and regarded the losses of others as of little importance. Thus, as though drawing an inference from the others, because he did not see Christ overcome when many things had been taken away, he burned with such desire to test him even in his flesh, by the touch of suffering, that he said: “Skin for skin, and all that a man has he will give for his life. Otherwise, stretch out your hand and touch his bone and his flesh, and then you will see [Col. 0614B] that he will bless you to your face.”

It is as though he were saying openly: “He does not care to be moved by what is outside himself; but who he truly is will then be recognized, if he experiences pain in himself.” When Satan himself desired these things to happen, he spoke them not with words but with desires. Through his members he brought them forward both in words and in desires. For he himself speaks when, in the words of the prophet, his followers say: “Let us put wood into his bread, and let us eradicate him from the land of the living” (Jeremiah 11:19). To put wood into his bread means to fasten the stake of the cross to his body; and they suppose that they can eradicate from the land of the living one whom, when they see him mortal, they suspect can be brought to an end by death.

## CHAPTER XVI

**Verse 6.**—The Lord said to Satan: “Behold, he is in your hand; nevertheless preserve his life.”

29. Satan’s members are all who live wickedly. Satan’s hand is his power. By handing himself over to him, the Lord compels him to serve his purposes.—Who, even if foolish, would believe that the Creator of all things was handed over to Satan’s hand? Yet, instructed by the truth, who does not know that all who are joined to that same Satan by living perversely are his members? Pilate was his member, for he did not recognize, even to the extremity of death, the Lord who came for our redemption. The chief priests were his body, for they tried to drive the Redeemer of the world out of the world by persecuting him even to the cross.

When, therefore, the Lord handed himself over for our redemption into the hands of Satan’s members, what else did he do but permit Satan’s hand to rage against him, so that by the very means through which he himself died outwardly, he might free us outwardly and inwardly? If, then, Satan’s hand is understood as his power, he endured according to the flesh the hand of the one whose bodily power he tolerated through spitting, blows, scourges, the cross, and the spear. Hence, as he came to his passion, he said to Pilate—who was, so to speak, a member of Satan’s [Note: The printed editions have “a member of his body,” contrary to the manuscripts. It is clear that Gregory here calls those by whom Christ suffered the devil’s body.] body: “You would have no power over me unless it had been given you from above” (John 19:11).

Nevertheless, the power which he had given him externally against himself, he compelled him inwardly to serve his own purposes. For Pilate—or Satan, who had become Pilate’s head—was held under the power of the One over whom he had received power; because the One who is higher had himself ordained that which, when it came about below, he endured from the persecutor. Thus, although the cruelty arose from the evil mind of unbelievers, it nevertheless served the benefit of all the elect.

He therefore arranged inwardly with mercy what he permitted himself to suffer wickedly outwardly. Hence it is said of him at the supper: “Jesus, knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, and that he had come from God and was going to God, rose from supper and laid aside his garments” (John 13:3). Behold: as he was about to go into the hands of his persecutors, he knew that he had received even the persecutors themselves into his own hand. For since he knew that he had received all things, it is evident that he also held those by whom he was held, so that he might turn to the service of mercy whatever their malice, permitted against him, violently inflicted upon him.

Let it therefore be said to him: “Behold, he is in your hand,” because Satan received permission to rage against his flesh, but unknowingly served the power of that One.

[Old XIII.] 30. The devil is shown to be unable to overcome Christ’s soul.—But he is commanded to preserve his life, not because he is forbidden to tempt it, [Note: The ancient Rheims, Remigius, Colbert, Corbie, Germain: “but because he is shown to be unable to tempt it.” The second Rheims, two Remigius manuscripts, and the old Clairvaux: “but because the tempter is shown to be unable to overcome it.” Others: “but because he is shown to be unable to overcome it by tempting it.”] but because he is shown to be unable to overcome it. For the soul of our Redeemer was not shaken by the necessity of temptation as we are, who are merely human beings and are often disturbed when temptation bursts upon us.

For although our enemy was permitted to take him up onto a high mountain, if he declared that he would give him the kingdoms of the world, and if he showed him stones that could supposedly be turned into bread (Matthew 4:8; Luke 4:4), nevertheless he could not shake the mind of the Mediator between God and human beings by temptation [Note: Rheims, Remigius, Corbie, Germain, Vendôme, old Clairvaux, Norman, Fleury, and others read thus; it is also found in the old Paris edition. Others read: “For although our enemy took him, whom he was permitted to assume, onto a high mountain; if he declared that he would give …,” and so forth.]. He graciously accepted all these things externally in such a way that his mind, inwardly clinging to his divinity, nevertheless remained unshaken.

And although he is sometimes said to have groaned in spirit when troubled (John 11:33, 38), he himself, in his divinity, determined how far he would be troubled in his humanity. Remaining unchangeably sovereign over all things, he displayed himself as changeable in the satisfaction of human weakness. Remaining therefore quiet within himself, he ordained whatever he did, even when agitated, to display the humanity he had assumed.

[Col. 0615D] 31. Christ’s soul can signify the elect. They are rescued from the devil’s power.—Since, when we love rightly, we love nothing among created things more dearly than our soul, and since we say that we love as our soul those whose importance in our love we try to express, the life of the elect can be signified by Christ’s soul.

When Satan is permitted to strike the Redeemer’s flesh, he is separated from the soul; for when he receives his body for suffering, he loses the elect from the right of his power. And when his flesh dies through the cross, their minds are strengthened against temptations.

Let it therefore be said: “Behold, he is in your hand; nevertheless preserve his life.” It is as though he heard openly: “Receive permission against his body, but lose the right of wicked domination over his elect, whom, foreknowing them before the ages, he possesses as his own.”

## CHAPTER XVII [Old XIV]

**Verse 7.**—“Satan therefore went out from the presence of the Lord and struck Job with a very grievous ulcer, from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head.”

32. Christ was struck in his members from the beginning of the world.—No one among the elect comes into this life without enduring the assaults of this enemy. Even those who lived piously from the very beginning of the world and suffered cruelly were members of our Redeemer.

Did not Abel show himself to be his member? [Note: Thus the Corbie, Germain, Colbert, and Regensburg manuscripts. Others, followed by the printed editions, read: “because, beginning first with …”; the Utica manuscript reads: “because, beginning with pure men,” and “because [he was] first.”] The one of whom it is written, “As a lamb before its shearer he will be silent, and he will not open his mouth” (Isaiah 53:7), signified Christ’s death not only by pleasing God in sacrifice but also by dying in silence.

From the very beginning of the world, therefore, Satan attempted to attack the body of our Redeemer. From the sole of the foot to the crown of the head he inflicted a wound, because, beginning with pure human beings, he advanced in his rage all the way to the very head of the Church. It is rightly said:

## CHAPTER XVIII

[Col. 0616C]

**Verse 8.**—“He scraped the discharge with a potsherd.”

33. The potsherd—that is, his flesh taken from the earth—scraped away the discharge of sin.—What else is the potsherd in the Lord’s hand except flesh taken from the clay of our substance? A potsherd, after all, is hardened by fire. The Lord’s flesh became stronger through his passion precisely because, dying in weakness, he rose from death without weakness. Hence it is rightly said through the prophet: “My strength has dried up like a potsherd” (Psalm 21:16). His strength dried up like a potsherd because he strengthened the weakness of the flesh he had assumed by the fire of his passion.

What, however, should be understood by the discharge except sin? Through flesh and blood the sins of the flesh are usually signified. Hence the Psalmist says: “Deliver me from blood-guilt” (Psalm 50:16). Discharge is therefore the corruption of blood. [Note: The printed editions read, “What then do we understand by discharge?” The manuscripts followed here read simply, “What then do we understand discharge [to mean]?” This manner of speaking is familiar to Gregory; below, chapter XXV, §48: “Just as we understand the garments of the Church [to be] all the faithful”; and Book II, formerly chapter 16, now 21, §38: “What indeed do we understand the throne of God [to be], except the angelic powers?”]

What, then, do we understand by discharge except sins of the flesh made worse through long continuance? A wound turns into a discharge when a neglected fault is aggravated by habit. Therefore the Mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 2:5), handing his body over to the hands of his persecutors, scraped away the discharge with a potsherd, because he destroyed sin in the flesh.

For he came, as it is written, “in the likeness of sinful flesh, and on account of sin he condemned sin” (Romans 8:3). When he set the innocence of his flesh before the enemy, he wiped away the contagions of our flesh; and through that by which the enemy held us captive, he purified us and made us free. For what we had made an instrument of guilt was turned for us by the Mediator into a weapon of righteousness.

The discharge is therefore scraped away by the potsherd when guilt is overcome by flesh. It is rightly added:

## CHAPTER XIX

**The same passage.**—“Sitting on a dung heap.”

34. He sat on a dung heap because he chose the weak things of the world.—He does not sit in the forum, where the law resounds; nor in a building that raises itself high with its summit; but he remains seated on a dung heap, because the Redeemer of the human race, coming in the flesh, chose, as Paul testifies, “the weak things of the world, to confound the strong” (1 Corinthians 1:27).

Does he not sit, as it were, amid falling buildings on a dung heap, when, having abandoned the proud Jews, he rests among the Gentiles whom he had once rejected? Outside a dwelling he is found in his wound: in the very fact that he endured hostile Judea, he experienced the pain of his passion, despised by his own people, as John testifies when he says: “He came to his own, and his own did not receive him” (John 1:11).

But how he rests while sitting on a dung heap, let Truth herself speak concerning him: “There will be joy in heaven over one sinner doing penance, more than over ninety-nine righteous persons who do not need penance” (Luke 15:10). Behold: he sits grieving on a dung heap, possessing with joy the hearts of penitents after they have committed their sins.

Are not the hearts of penitents like a dung heap? When they consider their own evils with tears, they heap up, as it were, dung before themselves by casting themselves down. Thus Job, though struck, did not seek the mountain but sat again on a dung heap, because, coming to his passion, the Redeemer abandoned the lofty hearts of the proud and rested in the humility of the afflicted [Note: The printed editions read, “in the humility of afflicted hearts”; *hearts* is absent from the manuscripts.]. 88 He had already indicated this concerning himself before he was incarnate, when he said through the prophet: “To whom shall I look, except to the humble and quiet one who trembles at my words?” (Isaiah 66:2, according to the Septuagint).

35. Christ suffers many things in his members, both from unbelievers and from carnal believers.—Who could consider how much he, who brought so many acts of goodness to human beings, has endured from human beings in return? Who could consider how much he continues to endure even now, while he reigns from heaven over the hearts of the faithful?

For he himself suffers daily everything by which his elect are torn apart by the reprobate. And although he is already the head of this body—which, of course, is us—and puts himself forth free above all things [Note: This reading is found in all the Rheims and Remigius manuscripts, Beauvais, Florence, Corbie, Germain, Saint-Martin, and others. The printed editions read *erexerit* (“has raised”) instead of *exerit* (“has thrust out” or “has extended”).], he still feels the wounds of the reprobate through his body, which he keeps below.

But why speak of unbelievers, when even within the Church itself we see many carnal people fighting against the Redeemer’s life by their wicked conduct? There are some who, since they cannot pursue him with swords, pursue him by perverse actions. When they see that what they desire is lacking to them in the Church, they become enemies of the good. They not only insert themselves into wicked activity but also strive to bend the uprightness of the just toward perversity.

They neglect to look toward eternal things and, through the smallness of their minds, yield to the desire for temporal things. The more they imagine temporal goods to be almost the only goods, the more deeply they fall away from eternal ones. They dislike the simplicity of the just, and whenever they find an opportunity for disturbance, they persuade them to seize their own duplicity.

Thus what follows also aptly corresponds:

## CHAPTER XX

**Verse 9.**—“Then his wife said to him: ‘Do you still persist in your simplicity? Bless God and die.’”

36. Job’s wife, giving evil counsel, represents carnal people placed within the bosom of the Church.—Whom did the woman giving evil counsel represent except any carnal people placed within the bosom of the Church? To the degree that they are inwardly present through their professed faith, they oppress the good all the more severely by their uncorrected conduct.

Perhaps they would have done less harm if holy Church had not admitted them within and received them even into the chamber of faith. But when she receives them through their professed faith, she undoubtedly makes them almost impossible for herself to avoid.

Hence, when a crowd was pressing upon our Redeemer, one woman touched him; and immediately our Redeemer said: “Who touched me?” When the disciples replied, “The crowds press upon you and afflict you, and you say, ‘Who touched me?’” he immediately added: “Someone touched me, for I know that power has gone out from me” (Luke 8:44–46).

[The Old XX.] 37. These people press Christ but do not touch him.—Many, therefore, press upon the Lord, but one touches him, because all the carnal in the Church press upon the One from whom they are far away; only those touch him who are truly joined to him in humility.

The crowd presses because the multitude of the carnal, the more it is admitted within, is endured with greater difficulty. It presses but does not touch, because it is intrusive in presence but absent in life. Sometimes they pursue us with wicked words, sometimes merely with perverse conduct. At times they advise what they themselves practice; at times, even if they do not advise it, they nevertheless do not cease to offer examples of iniquity.

Those who entice us to evil either by words or by examples are therefore certainly our persecutors, from whom we receive the contests of temptation, which we must at least conquer in our hearts.

38. Sometimes they persuade through fear, sometimes through audacity.—It must be understood that the carnal within the Church sometimes strive to persuade us to perversity through fear and sometimes through audacity. When they themselves fail either through cowardice or through pride, they attempt, as though out of affection, to pour these dispositions into the hearts of the just.

Peter retained a carnal mind before the Redeemer’s death and resurrection. With a carnal mind, the son of Zeruiah had clung closely to his commander David. Yet one sinned through fear and the other through pride.

When Peter heard of his master’s death, he said: “God forbid it, Lord; this shall never happen to you” (Matthew 16:22–23). The other, unable to endure insults against his commander, said: “Shall Shimei not be put to death for these words, since he cursed the Lord’s anointed?” (2 Samuel 19:21–22). To the former it was immediately said: “Get behind me, Satan”; and the latter, together with his brother, immediately heard: “What have I to do with you, sons of Zeruiah? Why are you becoming Satan to me today?”

Those who give evil counsel are therefore designated by the name of apostate angels: with flattering words, as though out of affection, they draw people toward what is unlawful. Yet those are far worse who succumb to this fault not through fear but through pride. Job’s wife especially represented them. She attempted proudly to advise her husband, saying: “Do you still persist in your simplicity? Bless God and die.”

She reproved the simplicity in her husband: he despised all passing things and desired only eternal realities with a pure heart. It is as though she were saying: “Why do you seek eternal things with simplicity and groan with equanimity under present evils? Depart, despise eternal things, and escape present evils, even by dying.”

[Old XVI.] But when the elect endure evil within from carnal people, let us learn from the words of one who was wounded yet unharmed, seated yet upright, how great a pattern of righteousness they display [Note: Thus Corbie, two Rheims manuscripts, and two Remigius manuscripts. One Remigius manuscript with the old Clairvaux reads: “how great a form of righteousness they derive from themselves.” Tours and one Compendiense manuscript: “how great a form of righteousness they possess in themselves.” The printed editions have: “how great a form they possess,” or “how great a form of righteousness they derive from themselves.”]. He says:

## CHAPTER XXI

**Verse 10.**—“You have spoken as one of the foolish women. If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, why should we not endure evil things?”

39. The holy oppose the shield of patience to those who strike them, and hurl the darts of instruction at those who give evil counsel.—When holy men, caught in the warfare of tribulations, endure at the same time those who strike them and those who give counsel, they oppose the shield of patience to the former and hurl the darts of instruction at the latter. With remarkable strength and skill they rise to meet both kinds of combat, so that they may wisely instruct those who are perverse within and bravely despise adversities outside; correcting the former through teaching and subduing the latter through endurance.

By enduring, they despise enemies who rise up against them; by compassion, they restore weakened fellow citizens to salvation. They resist the former so that they may not carry others away; they fear for the latter, lest they completely lose the life of righteousness [Note: Thus Corbie and all the manuscripts: “they fear for the latter, lest they completely lose the life of righteousness,” not “they heal the latter,” as found in the old Paris, Basel, and other editions.].

[Recension XII.] 40. This is confirmed by the example of Saint Paul.—Let us look at the soldier of God’s army fighting on both fronts. He says: “Battles without, fears within.” He enumerates the wars he endures externally, saying: “In dangers from rivers, in dangers from robbers, in dangers from my own people, in dangers from the Gentiles, in dangers in the city, in dangers in the wilderness, in dangers at sea, in dangers from false brothers” (2 Corinthians 7:5; 11:26).

In this battle he adds the weapons he hurls against the adversary: “In labor and hardship, in many vigils, in hunger and thirst, in many fasts, in cold and nakedness” (ibid.). But, caught amid so many struggles, let him say by what defense of vigilance he also guards the camp. For he immediately adds: “Apart from those things which are external, my daily urgency, the care of all the churches.”

Behold: he bravely accepts battles against himself and mercifully devotes himself to protecting those near him. He recounts the evils he suffers and adds the good things he imparts. Let us therefore consider what sort of labor it is to endure adversities outside and protect the weak within at one and the same time.

He suffers battles outside because he is torn by blows and bound with chains; he endures fear within because he is afraid that his suffering may harm not himself but his disciples. Hence he writes to them: “Let no one be moved by these tribulations. For you yourselves know that we have been appointed to this” (1 Thessalonians 3:3). He feared the downfall of others in his own passion, lest, when the disciples saw him afflicted with blows for the faith, they should refuse to profess themselves believers.

O the inward depths of immense charity! He despises what he himself suffers and takes care that his disciples suffer nothing in their hearts from evil persuasion. In himself he disregards wounds of the body; in others he heals wounds of the heart.

The righteous have this characteristic: when placed in the pain of their own tribulation, they do not abandon concern for another’s welfare. While suffering adversity themselves, they foresee what others need by teaching them; and, like great physicians who have themselves been struck, they fall ill. They endure the tearing of their own wound and offer medicines of healing to others.

It is a much lesser labor either to teach when one tolerates nothing or to tolerate when one teaches nothing. Therefore holy men diligently extend themselves to both tasks. Even when they are struck by tribulations, they undertake external battles while carefully considering that the inward parts of those near them must not be torn apart.

Thus holy men stand bravely in the battle line: on one side they strike hostile breasts with darts; on the other, they protect the weak who stand behind them with a shield. In this way they remain watchful on both sides with swift vigilance, piercing the bold who stand before them and defending the fearful behind them from wounds.

Because holy men know how to endure adversities outside while also correcting perversities within, it is rightly said: “You have spoken as one of the foolish women.” Since the elect are told, “Act manfully, and let your heart be strengthened” (Psalm 30:25), the minds of carnal people, who serve God with unstable devotion, are not improperly called women.

41. One who strives toward eternal goods does not resent temporal evils.—“If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, why should we not endure evil things?” It is as though he were saying: “If we are striving toward eternal goods, what is surprising if we suffer temporal evils?”

Paul had carefully considered these goods when he endured the evils inflicted upon him with equanimity, saying: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory to come, which will be revealed in us” (Romans 8:18).

**The same passage.**—“In all these things Job did not sin with his lips.”

He was insulting neither God nor his adversaries.—When holy men suffer persecution both outside and within, they not only do not go beyond the bounds of propriety in their complaints against God, but they also do not hurl insulting words against their adversaries. Peter, the leader of the good, rightly admonishes this, saying: “Let none of you suffer as a murderer, or a thief, or a reviler” (1 Peter 4:15).

A reviler suffers when, at the time of his suffering, he is carried away into insulting his persecutor under the pretext of seeking his own salvation. But because the body of the Redeemer—namely, holy Church—bears the weight of sorrows without exceeding the measure of humility in its words, it is rightly said of this suffering body:

## CHAPTER XXII [Old XVII]

**The same passage and verse 11.**—“In all these things Job did not sin with his lips, nor did he speak anything foolish against God. Then, when Job’s three friends heard of all the evil that had befallen him, they came, each from his own place: Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite.”

[Col. 0621B] 42. Job’s friends prefigure heretics.—In the preface to this work we said that although the friends of blessed Job came to him with a good intention, they nevertheless represent heretics because through indiscriminate speech they slide into guilt. Hence blessed Job himself says to them: “I desire to dispute with God, first showing you to be fabricators of lies and worshipers of perverse doctrines” [Recension XIII].

Holy Church, therefore, throughout the entire period of her pilgrimage, remains in affliction. While she bears wounds and grieves over the fall of her members, she also endures other enemies of Christ under Christ’s name. To increase her suffering, heretics too gather in contention and pierce her, as though with darts, by irrational words.

43. The place from which they came signifies pride.—It is rightly said: “They came from their own place” [Note: The Corbie and Germain manuscripts have: “They gathered from their own place.”]. For the place of heretics is pride itself; unless they first became swollen in heart, they would never enter contests of perverse assertion. Thus pride is the place of the wicked, just as humility, by contrast, is the place of the good.

Of this Solomon says: “If the spirit of one in authority rises up against you, do not leave your place” (Ecclesiastes 10:4). It is as though he were saying openly: “If you perceive the spirit of the tempter prevailing against you in any respect, do not abandon the humility of repentance” [Note: Colbert, here and shortly afterward: “the humility of patience,” with Corbie and Regensburg agreeing here but not below.].

He shows that our place is the humility of repentance by the words that follow: “For healing will cause the greatest sins to cease” (ibid.). For what else is the humility of lament except the medicine of sin? Heretics therefore come from their own place, because they are moved against holy Church by pride.

44. The names of Job’s friends signify the activity of heretics.—Their perverse activity can also be inferred from the interpretation of their names. They are called Eliphaz, Bildad, and Zophar. As we said above, Eliphaz is interpreted as “contempt of God.” Unless they despised God, they would certainly not think perversely about him.

Bildad is interpreted as “antiquity alone.” Because they refuse to be truly conquered and seek to be victors through perverse zeal, they neglect the conduct of the new life; what they pursue derives from antiquity alone.

Zophar, however, means “destroying the watchtower.” For those who are established in holy Church humbly contemplate the mysteries of their Redeemer with true faith. But when heretics come with false arguments, they destroy the watchtower, because they incline the minds of those whom they draw to themselves away from the purpose of right contemplation.

[Old XVIII; Recension XIV.] 45. The curiosity, loquacity, and hypocrisy of heretics are signified by the places of Job’s friends.—The places from which they come are also aptly described in accordance with the activity of heretics. They are called Temanites, Shuhites, and Naamathites. Tema is interpreted as “south”; Shuh, “speaking”; Naamah, “beauty.”

Who does not know that the south wind is hot? Heretics, therefore, because they desire knowledge more ardently, strive to become hot, as though beyond what is necessary. Sluggishness agrees with the cold of torpor, and restless immoderate curiosity with excessive heat [Note: In some manuscripts: “with the cold of torpor.”].

Because they desire to receive the heat of wisdom more than they ought, they are said to come from the south. Paul took care to temper the minds of the faithful against this heat of immoderate wisdom when he said: “Do not be wiser than you ought to be, but be wise unto sobriety” (Romans 12:3).

Hence David strikes the valleys of salt (2 Samuel 8:13), because our Redeemer, by the examination of his strictness, extinguishes the foolishness of immoderate discernment in those who think perversely about him.

Shuh is said to mean “speaking.” They desire to possess heat not so that they may live well but so that they may speak proudly. They are therefore said to come from Tema and Shuh—that is, from heat and loquacity—because, while they display themselves as devoted students of Scripture, they possess only the words of loquacity and not the inward depths of charity.

Naamah, however, is interpreted as “beauty.” Because they desire not to be learned but to appear learned, they assume the appearance of those who live well through the language of instruction; and through the heat of their loquacity they display in themselves an image of beauty. Thus, by the beauty of their speech, they easily persuade people of what is perverse, precisely because they cunningly conceal the ugliness of their life [Note: Thus the Norman, Corbie, Germain, Colbert, Regensburg, Florence, and almost all manuscripts. The first Remigius manuscript has: “so that they cunningly conceal the ugliness of their life inwardly.” The printed editions read: “so that they conceal it by cunning.”].

Nor are the names of the places distinguished in an unordered narrative. First Tema is placed, then Shuh, and afterward Naamah: first disordered heat kindles them, then the brilliance of loquacity raises them up, and finally hypocrisy displays them as beautiful to human beings.

## CHAPTER XXIII

**The same passage.**—“For they had agreed to come together to visit him and console him.”

46. Heretics agree against the Church. They can be called friends.—Heretics make agreements among themselves when they hold certain perverse opinions against the Church in concord; and in the matters in which they differ from the truth, they agree with one another in falsehood.

But all who instruct us concerning eternity—what else do they do except console us in the affliction of our pilgrimage? Heretics, however, because they desire to teach holy Church their own doctrines, approach her as though to console her.

Nor is it surprising that those who represent the form of adversaries are called friends, since the betrayer himself is also addressed: “Friend, why have you come?” (Matthew 26:50); and the rich man who is consumed in the fire of hell is called “son” by Abraham (Luke 16:25). For although the wicked neglect to be corrected by us, it is nevertheless fitting that they be called friends by us, not because of their wickedness but because of our kindness [Note: “Friends” is lacking in the Corbie, Germain, Norman, Compendiense, and most other manuscripts.].

## CHAPTER XXIV

**Verse 12.**—“When they had lifted up their eyes from afar, they did not recognize him.”

47. They do not recognize the Church. Why.—When heretics consider the deeds of holy Church, they lift up their eyes, because they themselves are situated below and, when they look upon her works, they see things placed on high. Yet they do not recognize her when she is situated in grief.

She desires to receive evils here so that, purified, she may reach the reward of eternal recompense. Often she fears prosperity and rejoices in the discipline of instruction. Heretics, therefore, because they desire present things as something great, do not recognize her when she is situated among wounds.

What they see in her they do not choose in the thought of their own hearts [Note: The Norman manuscript, one Compendiense manuscript, one Remigius manuscript, and the old Clairvaux: “they do not choose in the thought of their own hearts.” Longipont: “they do not choose in the knowledge of their own hearts.”]. When she advances through adversities, they remain attached to their own stupor, because through experience they do not understand what they see.

## CHAPTER XXV [Old XIX]

[Col. 0623C]

**The same passage.**—“And having torn their garments, they scattered dust upon their heads toward heaven.”

48. They are torn into many divisions.—Just as we understand all the faithful as the garments of the Church—hence it is said through the prophet, “You will clothe yourself with all these as with an ornament”—so the garments of heretics are all who adhere to them in agreement and become wrapped in their errors.

Heretics have this characteristic: they cannot remain long at the level from which they leave the Church. Instead, they fall daily into worse things; by thinking worse thoughts, they tear themselves into many divisions; and often, through disputes arising from their confusion, they separate themselves from one another still further.

Because they continue to rend into many divisions those whom they join to their own faithlessness, it is rightly said that the friends who come tear their garments. When the garments are torn, the body is exposed, because, when their followers have often been divided, the malice of their thought is revealed. Discord exposes the deceits that the grave fault of their former concord had concealed.

49. They derive earthly meanings from heavenly words.—They scatter dust toward heaven upon their heads. What is signified by dust except an earthly understanding? What by the head except that which is our principal part, namely the mind? What by heaven except the command expressed through heavenly speech?

To scatter dust upon the head toward heaven is therefore to corrupt the mind with worldly understanding and to derive earthly meanings from heavenly words. They usually examine divine words more deeply than they comprehend them. Thus they scatter dust upon their heads because, through earthly understanding, they strive beyond the capacity of their minds in the commandments of God.

## CHAPTER XXVI [Recension XV]

### Verse 13.—“And they sat with him on the ground seven days and seven nights.”

**50. By feigned humility they try to persuade others of prideful things.**—In the day we recognize the things we see; in the night, either we see nothing because of blindness, or we are clouded by uncertainty. Thus “day” signifies understanding, while “night” signifies ignorance. By the number seven, moreover, the totality of the universe is expressed. Hence this whole transitory period is completed in no more than seven days.

What, then, does it mean that the friends of blessed Job are said to sit with him seven days and seven nights, except that heretics—whether in those matters in which they understand the true light or in those in which they suffer the darkness of ignorance—pretend to condescend to holy Church as though she were infirm, and under the appearance of flatteries prepare for her the snares of deception? Although, whether in the things they understand or in those they cannot understand, they are swollen with the mark of pride—[Note: Corb., Germ., and a second hand in the ancient manuscript read *typho* (“with pride”) instead of *typo* (“with the mark”).]—and consider themselves great in their own eyes, nevertheless they sometimes bend themselves toward holy Church in outward appearance; and while they soften their words, they pour in poison. To sit on the ground, therefore, is to display something of the image of humility, so that, while they present humble things, they may persuade others of the proud doctrines they teach.

**[Old edition XX.] 51. They sit with us on the ground when they agree with us concerning the Incarnation.**—The ground can also signify the Incarnation itself of the Mediator. Hence it is said to Israel: “You shall make an altar of earth for me” (Exod. 20:24). To make an altar of earth for God is to hope in the Incarnation of the Mediator. For our offering is then accepted by God when, upon this altar—that is, upon faith in the Lord’s Incarnation—our humility has placed whatever it accomplishes. We therefore place an offering upon an altar of earth when we establish our deeds upon faith in the Lord’s Incarnation.

There are, however, certain heretics who do not deny that the Mediator’s Incarnation took place, but either judge his divinity to be otherwise than it is, or disagree with us about the very character of his Incarnation. Those, therefore, who confess with us the true Incarnation of the Redeemer sit together with Job, as it were, on the ground. They are described as sitting on the ground seven days and seven nights because, whether in understanding something of the fullness of truth or in being blinded by the darkness of their folly, they cannot deny the mystery of the Incarnation. To sit with blessed Job on the ground is to believe with holy Church in the true flesh of the Redeemer.

**52. They are friends to the silent, but become adversaries to those who contradict them.**—Sometimes heretics rage against us even with punishments; sometimes they pursue us only with words; sometimes they assail us while we are at rest; [Note: The manuscripts read “they provoke us,” and below “provoking,” consistently thereafter.] and sometimes, if they see us silent, they themselves keep quiet. They are friends to the mute but adversaries to those who speak.

Since blessed Job had not yet said anything in discussion with them, it is rightly added: “And no one spoke a word to him.” We have adversaries who remain silent when we neglect to generate sons of the true faith by preaching. But if we begin to speak what is right, we immediately experience grievous insults in their response. At once they leap into opposition [Note: That is, into opposition, as explained above in book II, chapter 31, section 51; see also below, chapter 33, section 65.] and break out against us in a voice of grief, because they fear that the straightforward voice of one who speaks may draw upward hearts weighed down in the depths by the burden of folly.

Since, therefore, as we have said, adversaries love us when we are mute and hate us when we speak, it is rightly said of the silent Job:

### Chapter XXVII

**The same passage: “No one spoke a word to him.”**

**53. Heretics are sometimes compelled to be silent.**—Nevertheless, whenever they observe that the hearts of the faithful are sluggish through torpor—[Note: All manuscripts read “through torpor.” Earlier printed editions read “through the torpor of inactivity of the faithful hearts.”]—they do not cease speaking and scattering the seeds of error. But when they see that the minds of the good are thinking lofty thoughts, seeking a return to their homeland, and earnestly grieving over the misery of this exile, they restrain their tongues with watchful care, because they see that, by speaking vainly against grieving hearts, they would quickly become silent.

Thus, when it was said, “No one spoke a word to him,” the reason for the silence is immediately supplied:

### Chapter XXVIII

**The same passage: “For they saw that his grief was very great.”**

**54. When the heart grieves out of love for God, the adversary fears to speak perversely.**—When the sharp pain of love for God pierces our hearts, the adversary fears to speak perversely in every direction, because he sees that, by assaulting an attentive mind, he can not only fail to draw it toward perversity but may perhaps even lose those whom he had held captive. [Note: The old edition reads “through exercised wisdom”; others read “through awakened wisdom.” The latter expression is redundant and absent from the manuscripts.]

**[Old edition XXI; recension XVI.] 55. In Scripture, things done well sometimes signify things that ought to be done badly, and conversely.**—Perhaps some are disturbed that we have said these things, since what was done well by Job’s friends is presented as signifying what is to be done badly by heretics. But frequently a matter is virtuous in the historical account and blameworthy in its symbolic meaning. Sometimes an event, as an actual deed, is a cause of condemnation, while in the written account it is a prophecy of virtue.

We shall demonstrate this more quickly if we bring forward one testimony from sacred Scripture to establish both points. Who, hearing it, would not utterly detest—not only the faithful but even unbelievers themselves—the fact that David, walking on the roof, desired Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah? [Note: Here Gussanville, rejecting the words *hoc factum juxta historiam* (“this deed according to the historical account”), observes that these four words are absent from certain copies. They occur only in one Colbert manuscript, whose glosses are not always sound; they are absent also from the old edition.] Yet when Uriah returned from battle, David urged him to go home and wash his feet. He immediately replied: “The ark of the Lord is under coverings, and I shall rest in my own house” (2 Sam. 11:11). David then received him at his own table and handed him a letter by which he was to be put to death.

But whose figure does David represent when he walks on the roof, except the one of whom it is written: “He has set his tabernacle in the sun” (Ps. 18:6)? And what does it mean to bring Bathsheba to himself except to join the law of the letter, united to the carnal people, to himself through spiritual understanding? Bathsheba is said to mean “the seventh well,” because through knowledge of the law, with the infusion of spiritual grace, perfect wisdom is supplied to us.

Whom, then, does Uriah signify except the Jewish people? His name is interpreted as “my light is of God.” [Note: Gilot has corruptly “my law.” Gussanville has “my light is God,” rather than “of God,” as all the manuscripts and printed books read.] The Jewish people, because they are lifted up by the knowledge of the law they have received, glory as though in the light of God.

But David took Uriah’s wife away from him and joined her to himself. For the Strong-Handed One—for that is what “David” means—appearing in the flesh as the Redeemer, made known that the law speaks spiritually about him. By this, he showed that he had separated her from the Jewish people inasmuch as she was held according to the letter; and he joined her to himself because he declared that he was preached through her.

David nevertheless urged Uriah to go home and wash his feet, because the incarnate Lord, coming among the Jewish people, commanded them to return to conscience and wipe away the filth of their deeds with tears; to understand the commandments of the law spiritually; and, after such hardness under the commandments, to find the fountain of baptism and return to the water after labor.

But Uriah, remembering that the ark of the Lord was under coverings, replied that he could not enter his house. It was as though the Jewish people were saying: “I see the commandments of God in carnal sacrifices, and I do not seek to return to conscience through spiritual understanding.” For the one who understands the commandments of God only as providing the service of carnal sacrifice is, as it were, saying that the ark is under coverings.

Yet David also calls this man, who refuses to return home, to his table. For although the Jewish people disdain to return to conscience, the coming Redeemer nevertheless preaches spiritual commandments to them, saying: “If you believed Moses, you would perhaps also believe me, for he wrote about me” (John 5:46). The Jewish people therefore possess the law, which speaks of his divinity, while that same people disdain to believe in him.

Hence Uriah is sent to Joab with letters by which he is to be killed, because this same Jewish people carries the law by which it is convicted and must die. For while retaining the commandments of the law, yet resisting their fulfillment, it itself carries the judgment by which it is condemned.

What, then, could be more wicked in the deed than David? What could be said to be purer than Uriah? Yet again, in the mystery, what could be found holier than David and more unbelieving than Uriah? [Note: Two Remigius manuscripts, two Rheims manuscripts, and Corb. Germ. read “what more sacred than David?” Vallicelliana reads more suitably “more holy.”]—when the former, through the guilt of his life, signifies innocence in prophecy, while the latter, through the innocence of his life, expresses guilt in prophecy? [Note: Several manuscripts, Gilot, and Gussanville, omitting the preposition *in*, read “the singular innocence of prophecy.” The manuscripts Corb., Germ., Colb., and Reg. read *prophetiae*, perhaps for *prophetice* (“prophetically”), as several manuscripts have.]

Thus it is not inappropriate that what was done well by Job’s friends signifies what is to be done badly by heretics. The sacred word narrates past events in such a way as to express things to come; it approves a matter in the deed while contradicting it in the mystery; and it condemns what was done while persuading that it be done symbolically.

## MORAL MEANING

**[Old edition XXII.] 56. Why the devil sometimes ceases from temptation.**—Since we have now completed the disentangling of the mysteries of the allegory piece by piece, let us next touch briefly upon the moral meaning. The mind hastens to discuss more obscure matters; and if it is long entangled in what is clear, it is prevented, as is fitting, from knocking upon what is closed.

Often the ancient enemy, after inflicting upon our mind the contest of temptations, withdraws for a time from that very contest—not in order to put an end to his malice, but so that, when he has made hearts secure through repose, he may return suddenly and break in more easily because he is unexpected. Hence he returns again to tempt the blessed man and seeks to increase his sufferings, though heavenly mercy permits this to be done to him, saying:

### Chapter XXIX

**Verse 6.—“Behold, he is in your hand; only preserve his life.”**

**57. Sometimes God abandons us in order to guard us. Temptation occurs while the soul is preserved when consent is denied. Nevertheless, the wound of pleasure must be healed by repentance.**—Thus he abandons us in such a way as to guard us; and he guards us in such a way that, while permitting the moment of temptation, he nevertheless reveals to us the condition of our weakness.

He immediately went out from the presence of the Lord and wounded Job by striking him from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head, because, when he receives permission, he begins with the smallest things and advances to the greater, piercing and lacerating, as it were, the whole body of the mind with the temptations he inflicts. [Note: Gussanville mistakenly reads “the body, the mind.” Read “the body of the mind,” which in Gregory signifies the whole complex of the mind’s faculties and thoughts.]

Yet he did not reach the soul by striking it, because, deeper than all the thoughts, amid the very wounds of pleasure that it receives, the intention of the hidden purpose resists. Thus, although pleasure bites the mind, it does not bend the resolve of holy uprightness as far as the softness of consent.

Nevertheless, we must wipe away these wounds of pleasure through the severity of repentance and cleanse, by the strict judgment of rigorous discipline, whatever fluidity flows out in thought. Hence it is appropriately added at once:

### Chapter XXX [Recension XVII]

**Verse 8.—“For he scraped away the discharge with a potsherd.”**

**58. To scrape away the discharge with a potsherd means to cleanse sin by judging oneself and contemplating one’s frailty.**—What is signified by the potsherd except the vigor of strict discipline? What by the discharge except the flow of unlawful thought? Thus, when struck, we scrape away the discharge with a potsherd when, after the pollution of unlawful thought, we cleanse ourselves by judging ourselves severely.

The potsherd may also be understood as the frailty of mortality. To cleanse the discharge with a potsherd is therefore to weigh the course and frailty of mortality and wipe away the corruption of miserable pleasure. For when someone considers how quickly flesh returns to dust, he quickly overcomes that which inwardly and shamefully attacks him through the flesh.

When an evil thought flows into the mind from temptation, the discharge runs out as though from a wound. But the discharge is wiped away more quickly if, in our consideration, frailty is held as a potsherd in the hand.

**59. Evil thoughts are not to be despised.**—Nor should those things be considered insignificant which, although they do not lead all the way to action, nevertheless move unlawfully within the mind. Hence our Redeemer came, as it were, to scrape away the discharge from wounds when he said: “You have heard that it was said to the ancients, ‘You shall not commit adultery.’ But I say to you that whoever looks upon a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. 5:27–28). The discharge is therefore wiped away when guilt is cut off not only from the deed but also from the thought.

Hence Jerobaal, while threshing wheat from the straw, saw an angel. At the angel’s command he immediately cooked a young goat, placed it upon a rock, and poured out the broth of the meat over it. The angel touched these things with his staff, and fire came out from the rock and consumed them (Judg. 6:11–12, 19). [Note: Vaticanus and Gussanville have “Gideon” instead of “Jerobaal.”]

For what does it mean to strike wheat with a staff except to separate the grains of virtues from the straw of vices by the uprightness of judgment? But an angel appears to those engaged in these acts because the Lord discloses inward things all the more as people cleanse themselves more diligently from outward things.

The angel commands the young goat to be killed—that is, every appetite of our flesh is to be sacrificed—and the flesh is to be placed upon the rock, with its broth poured out over it. Whom else does the rock signify except him of whom Paul says: “The rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10:4)? We place flesh upon the rock when we afflict our body in imitation of Christ.

He also pours out the broth of the meat over it who, in the conduct of Christ, empties from himself even carnal thoughts. [Note: Floriacensis, Germ., and Corb. corruptly read “as though it were indeed a matter.” Vaticanus, Gilot, and Gussanville have *liquidum* (“liquid”) instead of *liquida* (“liquid flesh”).] For the broth flows from liquid flesh onto the rock when the mind is emptied of the flow of carnal thoughts.

The angel then immediately touches these things with his staff, because the power of divine help never abandons our intention. Fire comes out from the rock and consumes the broth and the flesh, because the Spirit breathed forth by the Redeemer burns our heart with so great a flame of compunction that it consumes everything unlawful in it, both in deed and in thought.

What it means there to pour the broth upon the rock is what it means here to cleanse the discharge with a potsherd. The perfect mind watches carefully not only to refuse to perform perverse deeds but also to wipe away everything that shamefully melts within it through thoughts.

**[Old edition XXIII.]** But victory itself often gives rise to battle, so that when an impure thought is overcome, the victor’s spirit is assaulted by pride. The mind must therefore be raised through purity in such a way that it is nevertheless carefully laid low in humility. Hence, when it was said of the holy man, “He scraped away the discharge with a potsherd,” the following is appropriately added:

### Chapter XXXI

**The same passage: “Sitting on a heap of refuse.”**

**60. The victor over temptation must preserve humility. The pride of those who do little but think much of themselves. The pride of the wicked when others sin in ways in which they themselves do not sin.**—To sit on a heap of refuse means to think of oneself as vile and contemptible. [Note: Coc. and subsequent editors read “some vile things,” contrary to the manuscripts and the old edition.] To sit for ourselves on a heap of refuse is to bring the eyes of the mind back in repentance to the things we have done unlawfully, so that, when we see before us the refuse of sins, we may bend down everything that rises in the soul through pride.

He sits on a heap of refuse who carefully regards his own weakness and does not exalt himself over the good things he has received through grace. Did Abraham not sit before himself on a heap of refuse when he said: “I will speak to my Lord, although I am dust and ashes” (Gen. 18:27)? We clearly see the place in which he had positioned himself before himself, since even while speaking with God he considered himself dust and ashes.
