If, then, one who rose as far as the honor of divine conversation so despises himself, we must carefully consider with what punishment those deserve to be struck who neither advance to lofty things nor cease exalting themselves over the smallest things.

For there are some who do little but think great things about themselves. They lift their minds on high and suppose that they surpass others in the merits of virtue. These inwardly abandon the heap of humility before themselves and climb the heights of pride, imitating the one who first exalted himself before himself but overthrew himself by exalting himself; imitating the one who was not content with the dignity of his created condition and said: “I will ascend into heaven; I will exalt my throne above the stars of heaven” (Isa. 14:13).

Hence Babylon—that is, the confused multitude of sinners—says to him in wicked union: “I sit as queen, and I am not a widow” (Isa. 47:8, according to the Septuagint). Whoever swells inwardly has placed himself on high before himself. Yet he sinks all the more heavily into the depths because he refuses truly to think lowly things about himself.

There are others who make no effort to perform any virtue, yet when they see others sin, they suppose themselves righteous in comparison with them. The same or a similar fault does not pierce every heart. Pride ensnares one person; perhaps anger brings down another; avarice torments this one, while lust inflames that one.

It often happens that one whom pride oppresses observes another burning with anger; and because anger does not immediately provoke him, he considers himself better than the angry person and exalts himself before himself as though on account of justice, because he neglects to weigh the vice by which he himself is held more severely.

It often happens that one wounded by avarice sees another sunk in the gulf of lust; and because he regards himself as free from carnal pollution, he does not notice the filth of spiritual vice with which he himself is inwardly polluted. While he weighs the evil that he does not have in another, he neglects to consider in himself what he does have. Thus it happens that, while the mind is led to judge what belongs to another, it is deprived of the light of its own judgment; and it becomes more arrogantly severe against another’s faults the more carelessly it ignores its own.

**[Old edition XXIV.] 61. The perfect person must not lose humility through contemplating another’s fault. Temptation sometimes knocks from outside and within.**—By contrast, those who truly desire to rise to the heights of virtue, when they hear of the faults of others, immediately bring their hearts back to their own faults. They judge the former all the more rightly because they lament the latter more truly.

Since, therefore, each elect person restrains himself by considering his own weakness, it is rightly said that the holy man sits grieving on a heap of refuse. For the one who truly humbles himself weighs, with the eye of continual reflection, the filth of sins by which he is surrounded as he makes progress. [Note: Some manuscripts read “of continual watchfulness.” The first Rheims manuscript reads “by which he is enclosed.”]

We should know, however, that the mind is often touched by intrusive temptation in prosperity. Yet sometimes we also suffer adversities outwardly and are wearied inwardly by the force of temptation, so that lashes afflict the flesh while carnal suggestion nevertheless floods the mind. Hence, after so many wounds of blessed Job, the words of his wife, who offered evil counsel, are also appropriately added:

### Chapter XXXII

**Verse 9.—“Do you still persist in your simplicity? Bless God and die.”**

**62. Job’s wife, offering evil counsel, is carnal thought.**—The wife who offers evil counsel is carnal thought assaulting the mind. Often, as we have said, we are worn down outwardly by blows and wearied inwardly by carnal suggestion. Hence Jeremiah laments, saying: “Outside the sword kills, and inside death is like it” (Lam. 1:20).

Outside, the sword kills when vengeance strikes us from without and pierces us. But inside, death is similar, because although the flesh endures blows, the conscience is nevertheless not clean within from the filth of temptation.

Hence David says: “Let them become like dust before the face of the wind, and let the angel of the Lord afflict them” (Ps. 34:5). Whoever is carried away in his heart by the breeze of temptation is raised like dust before the face of the wind. And when divine severity strikes amid these things, what else afflicts them except the angel of the Lord?

**63. The elect and the reprobate receive temptation differently.**—But these things take place differently in the reprobate and in the elect. The hearts of the reprobate are tempted in such a way that they consent. [Note: Gussanville notes another reading, namely “of the righteous.” It is found in some manuscripts.] The elect, however, receive temptations but resist them.

The mind of the reprobate is captured pleasurably; and if, for a time, what is suggested wickedly displeases it, afterward it becomes pleasing through deliberation. The elect, however, receive the arrows of temptation in such a way that they are always wearied by resisting. If at any time a tempted mind is carried away as far as pleasure, it nevertheless soon feels shame at the very stealth of its pleasure and rebukes with strong discipline whatever carnal movement it detects rising within itself.

Hence it is appropriately added at once:

### Chapter XXXIII [Recension XIX]

**Verse 10.—“You have spoken as one of the foolish women speaks. If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, why should we not endure evil things?”**

**64. How to resist harsh or flattering thoughts.**—It is fitting that a holy mind should restrain through spiritual correction whatever carnal thing insolently murmurs within it, lest the flesh, speaking harshly, draw it into impatience, or, speaking flatteringly, dissolve it into the laxity of lust.

Therefore masculine discipline, rebuking the suggestion of unlawful thought, should restrain the relaxed softness of shameful behavior, saying: “You have spoken as one of the foolish women speaks.” And again, reflection upon the gifts received should restrain the impatience of harsh thought, saying: “If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, why should we not endure evil things?”

Whoever desires to subdue vices and advance by the steps of true purpose toward the heights of eternal inner reward sees himself surrounded on every side by the battle of vices. The more he perceives this, the more strongly he girds himself with the weapons of virtue; and he fears the arrows all the less because he fortifies his breast firmly against their coming.

**65. Vices conceal themselves under the appearance of virtues.**—Yet often, while we strive to support ourselves with great virtues against this battle of temptations, certain vices conceal themselves from us under the appearance of virtues and come to us with an almost flattering face; but when examined, they are recognized as belonging to the opposite side.

Thus Job’s blessed friends come together as though for consolation but break out into insults, because vices lying in ambush take on the appearance of virtues but strike us with hostile attack. Often immoderate anger wishes to appear justice; often uncontrolled leniency wishes to appear mercy. Often heedless fear wishes to appear humility; often unrestrained pride seeks to appear liberty.

The friends therefore come to console, but they slip into words of reproach, because vices cloaked in the appearance of virtues begin with a flattering surface but disturb us with harsh opposition. It is well said:

### Chapter XXXIV

**Verse 11.—“For they had agreed together to come and visit him.”**

**66. They enter into an alliance against us.**—Vices agree among themselves under the pretext of virtues, because certain things join together against us through a kind of mutual arrangement, such as pride and anger, leniency and fear. Anger is close to pride, and leniency to fear. Thus the things that unite against us through a certain kinship of perversity come together by agreement.

**[Old edition XXV.]** But if we recognize the misery of our captivity, if we grieve inwardly out of love for our eternal homeland, the vices that creep upon those who are wrongly joyful cannot prevail against those who are rightly sorrowful. Hence it is appropriately added:

### Chapter XXXV

**Verse 12.—“And when they had lifted up their eyes from a distance, they did not recognize him.”**

**67. Affliction drives away vices.**—Vices do not recognize us when we are afflicted, because as soon as they assail a sorrowful heart, they recoil, rejected. They had known us as joyful because they penetrated us; but they cannot recognize us when we grieve, because they are broken by our very firmness.

The ancient enemy, however, the more he sees himself strongly detected in these things, the more deeply hides them under the appearance of virtues. Hence it is added:

### Chapter XXXVI

**The same passage: “And crying aloud, they wept, tore their garments, and scattered dust upon their heads toward heaven; and they sat with him on the ground seven days and seven nights.”**

**68. Unless they deceive us under the appearance of virtues.**—Piety is signified by weeping, discernment by the tearing of garments, the disposition toward good works by the dust upon the head, and humility by sitting.

Sometimes the enemy, lying in wait, pretends to be pious in order to lead us to the end of cruelty. This happens when he prevents a fault from being punished through discipline, so that what is not restrained here may be struck by the fire of Gehenna.

Sometimes he places before our eyes an image of discernment and leads us into the snares of indiscretion. This happens when, at his urging, we grant ourselves more food, as though discreetly, on account of weakness, but indiscreetly stir up battles of the flesh against ourselves.

Sometimes he feigns zeal for good works, but thereby imposes the restless toil of labors. This happens when someone cannot rest and fears being judged because of idleness. [Note: Some read “the effect” instead of “the affection.”]

Sometimes he displays an image of humility in order to take away the desire to be useful. [Note: The old edition and many manuscripts read “the result of usefulness,” not in a bad sense. Nevertheless, “the desire to be useful” is better supported by the more authoritative manuscripts.] This happens when he declares certain people to be weaker and more useless than they are, so that, while they consider themselves excessively unworthy, they fear to undertake the tasks through which they could benefit their neighbors.

**69. Compunction fortifies against vices.**—But the hand of compunction examines with great subtlety these vices that the ancient enemy hides under the appearance of virtues. Whoever truly grieves inwardly carefully foresees what should be done outwardly and what should not be done.

For if the virtue of compunction afflicts us inwardly, every clamor of evil suggestion falls silent. Hence it follows:

### Chapter XXXVII

**Verse 13.—“And no one spoke a word to him, for they saw that his grief was very great.”**

**70. Vices can sometimes be made to serve the use of virtue.**—If the heart truly grieves, vices have no tongue against us. For when a life of uprightness is sought completely, the useless suggestion of perversity is stopped. [Note: The first manuscript of Remigius, one manuscript of Vendôme, Corb., and Germ. read “is hardened” instead of “is stopped.”]

Often, however, if we restrain ourselves with strong zeal against the incitements of vices, we even transform the vices themselves for the use of virtue. Anger possesses some people; but when they subject it to reason, they turn it into the service of holy zeal. Pride raises others up; but when they incline their spirit before the fear of God, they transform it into a voice of free authority for the defense of justice.

The allurements of the flesh entice still others; but when they subject the body to the performance of pious works, they gain profits of piety from the very source from which they suffered the goad of iniquity.

Hence blessed Job appropriately offers a sacrifice for his friends after many struggles. Those whom he endured for a long time as enemies through dispute, he eventually restores as fellow citizens through sacrifice. For when, by subduing them, we turn every vicious thought into virtues, we change the hostile efforts of temptations, through the sacrifice of our intention, into something like friendly hearts.

Let what we have discussed in three volumes in three different ways suffice. At the very beginning of this work, as though in the mass of a tree about to grow, we fixed the root of the tongue, so that afterward we might extend the branches of exposition wherever individual passages require them.

## BOOK FOUR

In this book Gregory, after briefly prefacing that the literal text of Scripture sometimes conflicts with itself, and that Job’s imprecations, like those of Jeremiah and David, cannot be understood without absurdity according to the sound of the words alone, expounds Job’s words from the beginning of chapter 3 through verse 20 historically, mystically, and morally.

### Chapter One

[Note: That what follows should be marked with the title “Preface,” in accordance with the mind of the holy Doctor, is demonstrated by what we read at the end of chapter 4: “Since, therefore, we have in some fashion distinguished the matters that had to be examined in the preface, let us now proceed by discussing the words of the historical account.”]

## Preface

**101. The letter of Scripture sometimes contradicts itself. The meaning of Scripture is penetrated by humble people through persistent reading.**—Whoever considers the text but does not understand the meaning of sacred speech does not so much instruct himself through learning as confuse himself through ambiguity, because sometimes the words of the letter contradict one another. [Note: Corb. Germ. reads *dissident* (“are at odds”).] But while they disagree among themselves through contradiction, they send the reader toward an understanding of the truth. For what is the meaning of Solomon’s statement: “It is better to eat and drink” (Eccl. 2:24)? [Note: Two manuscripts of Rheims, two of Remigius, Compend., and Vallicelliana read more fully: “It is better to eat and drink than to go to the house of mourning.”] And not long afterward he adds: “It is better to go to the house of mourning than to the house of feasting” (Eccl. 7:3).

Why did he prefer mourning to feasting, when earlier he praised eating and drinking? If eating and drinking are good by choice, then surely it ought to be better to hasten to the house of joy than to the house of lamentation.

Again, he says: “Rejoice, young man, in your youth” (Eccl. 11:9). And shortly afterward he adds: “For youth and pleasure are vanity” (ibid., 10). What does this mean except that he either first commands what ought to be condemned or later condemns what he had commanded, thereby suggesting through the very words of the letter that the person who encounters difficulty outwardly should consider the understanding of truth that he ought to follow?

This understanding of truth is penetrated when it is sought through humility of heart and persistent reading. Just as we see the faces of people we do not know but do not know their hearts, yet if we join ourselves to them in familiar conversation, through the practice of speaking with them we investigate even their thoughts, so, when only the history is observed in sacred speech, nothing other than its face is seen. But if we join ourselves to it through continual practice, we penetrate its mind, as it were, through the familiarity of conversation.

For when we gather one thing from another, we easily recognize in its words that what they communicate is one thing and what they sound like on the surface is another. The more anyone is made a stranger to that knowledge, the more tightly he is confined to its surface alone.

### Chapter Two
## Job’s Imprecations Cannot Be Understood Literally Without Absurdity

Behold, blessed Job is described as having cursed his day, saying: “Let the day perish in which I was born, and the night in which it was said, ‘A man has been conceived.’” If one attends only to the surface, what could be found more objectionable than these words? Who, however, does not know that the day on which he was born could not then have continued to exist?

**[Note: Gilot, Vatican, and Gussanville, departing from the manuscripts, read *motus* (“movement”) here. *Modus* (“measure” or “form”) is better, as the ancient editions also retained it, which will immediately become clear to anyone who considers the matter; for a day is truly a measure or form of time.]**

For it is a measure of time, and therefore has no fixed permanence. Since it moves toward coming into existence, it is always hastening from what has passed toward nonexistence. Why, then, would so great a man curse something that he knew could in no way endure?

Perhaps someone may say that the weight of his virtue is discerned precisely in this: moved by tribulation, he curses something that plainly does not subsist. But reason, once the matter is examined, quickly overturns this. If the thing he cursed subsisted, he uttered a harmful curse; but if it did not subsist, he uttered an idle one. Whoever is filled with the spirit of him who said, “For every idle word that people speak, they will give an account of it on the day of judgment” (Matthew 12:36), fears to admit idle words just as he fears harmful ones.

To this statement the following is also joined: “Let that day be turned into darkness; let God not seek it from above; let it not be remembered, and let it not be illumined by light. Let darkness and the shadow of death obscure it; let gloom seize it, and let it be enveloped in bitterness. Let a dark whirlwind possess that night; let that night be solitary and not worthy of praise. Let it await the light and not see it, nor the rising of the dawn as it appears.”

**[Note: The printed editions read, “let it not be illuminated.” This reading is contradicted by all our manuscripts.]**

**[Note: We judged that the editors’ insertion here—“let it not be counted among the days of the year, nor numbered among the months”—must be removed, following all the manuscripts.]**

Why is the day known to have passed with the course of time said to be turned into darkness? And since it was certain that it would not continue to exist, why is it wished that the shadow of death should obscure it?

**[Note: We have restored this very corrupt passage from the manuscripts. Formerly Coccius and the subsequent editions read: “that day which gloom may seize, which the enfolding of bitterness does not envelop,” or something similar. The particle *non* was added contrary to the evidence of all the manuscripts and overturns the sense, which is otherwise sufficiently clear and obvious: “What gloom can seize, or what bitterness can envelop, a day that has already passed?” The same point is made immediately afterward: “What dark whirlwind possesses the night?”]**

Or what gloom seizes it, what enfolding of bitterness envelops it? Or what dark whirlwind possesses a night that no fixed condition holds? Or how is that night wished to become solitary which, by passing away, had already become nothing? Or how does it await the light, since it is without perception and does not remain in its own condition?

With these words he continues:

## CHAPTER III

### Why did I not die in the womb? Why, when I came forth from the womb, did I not perish immediately? Why was I received upon the knees? Why was I suckled at the breasts? For now I would be lying asleep and resting in my sleep.

### Confirmation of the Proposed Argument: How People Were Freed from Original Sin before the Institution of Baptism

If he had perished immediately upon coming forth from the womb, would he thereby have acquired the merit of retribution from that very destruction? Do miscarried children enjoy eternal rest? Whoever is not released by the waters of regeneration remains bound by the guilt of the first bond.

**[Note: Coccius, Gilot, Vatican, and Gussanville read “held by the bonds of the guilt of the first [sin],” which gives excellent sense. Yet the authority of the manuscripts prevents us from following that reading. Compare Augustine, *Letter to Dardanus*, now Letter 187, chapter 11.]**

What baptismal water accomplishes among us was accomplished among the ancients either, in the case of children, by faith alone; in the case of adults, by the power of sacrifice; or, in the case of those descended from Abraham, by the mystery of circumcision. For since each person is conceived with the guilt of the first parent, the Prophet testifies, saying: “For behold, I was conceived in iniquities” (Psalm 50:7).

**[Note: The editions add, “and in sins my mother conceived me,” but this is absent from the manuscripts.]**

And because the one whom the water of salvation does not cleanse does not escape the punishments of original sin, the Truth itself openly declares: “Unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he will not have eternal life” (John 3:5).

What, then, does he mean by wishing that he had died in the womb and hoping that he could have rested through the benefits of that death, when it is certain that the rest of life would in no way have received him if the sacraments of divine knowledge had not freed him from the guilt of original sin?

He further adds with whom he might have rested, saying: “With kings and consuls of the earth, who build solitary places for themselves.” Who does not know that the kings and consuls of the earth are as far from solitude as they are surrounded by innumerable crowds of subjects? Or how difficult it is for those to advance toward rest who are bound by such hard knots of multiple responsibilities? Scripture bears witness, saying: “The severest judgment will be upon those who rule” (Wisdom 6:6).

**[Note: We have restored the preposition *in*, omitted in the editions: “The severest judgment will be upon those who rule.”]**

Hence the Truth says in the Gospel: “From the one to whom much has been given, much will be required” (Luke 12:48).

He further indicates whom he would have had as companions in that same rest, saying: “Or with princes who possess gold and fill their houses with silver.” It is exceedingly rare for those who possess gold to advance toward rest, since the Truth itself says: “Those who have wealth will enter the kingdom of heaven with difficulty” (Matthew 19:24). For what hope do those who here thirst for the multiplication of riches have in the joys of the next life? Yet, to show that this is exceedingly rare and can occur only through a divine miracle, our Redeemer said: “With human beings this is impossible, but with God all things are possible.”

Since, therefore, these words on the surface disagree with reason, the letter itself now indicates that, in their literal sense, the holy man says nothing of the sort.

## CHAPTER IV [Formerly III]

### The Imprecations of David and Jeremiah Must Not Be Taken Literally

But if we first examine other curses in sacred eloquence, let us investigate more subtly what was uttered by the mouth of blessed Job.

What does it mean that David, who did not repay evil to those who inflicted evil upon him, cursed the mountains of Gilboa when Saul and Jonathan had fallen in battle, saying: “Mountains of Gilboa, let neither dew nor rain come upon you, nor fields of firstfruits; for there the shield of Saul was cast away” (2 Samuel 1:21)?

**[Note: In the editions of Coccius, Gilot, Vatican, and Gussanville, “the shield of the mighty” is inserted. We do not know on what authority.]**

What does it mean that Jeremiah, when he saw his preaching hindered by the difficulty of his hearers, cursed, saying: “Cursed be the man who announced to my father, saying, ‘A male child has been born to you’” (Jeremiah 20:15)?

What, then, had the mountains of Gilboa done wrong when Saul died, so that neither dew nor rain should fall upon them and the word of the sentence should dry them of every green growth? But since *Gilboa* means “descent,” and through Saul, the anointed and dead man, the death of our Mediator is represented, the proud hearts of the Jews are rightly signified by the mountains of Gilboa. As they flowed downward into the desires of this world, they became implicated in the death of Christ—that is, of the Anointed One. And because the anointed king died bodily among them, they themselves are dried up from every dew of grace.

Of them it is also rightly said: “So that they cannot be fields of firstfruits.” For the proud minds of the Hebrews do not bear the first fruits, because, remaining for the most part in unbelief at the coming of the Redeemer, they refused to follow the beginnings of faith. Holy Church, made fruitful at its beginnings by the multitude of the Gentiles, will scarcely receive at the end of the world whatever Jews it finds; gathering the last, it will place them like gleanings of the harvest. Of these remnants Isaiah says: “Though the number of the children of Israel be like the sand of the sea, a remnant will be saved” (Isaiah 10:22, according to the Septuagint; Romans 9:27).

The mountains of Gilboa may also be cursed by the prophet’s mouth for this reason: when no fruit arises because the earth has dried up, the owners of the land may be struck by the harm of its sterility, so that those who, because of their wickedness, deserved to receive the king’s death among themselves might themselves receive the sentence of the curse.

But what does it mean that the prophet’s curse fell upon the man who announced his birth to his father? This is filled inwardly with a mystery all the greater because outwardly it lacks human reason. For if something rational had perhaps sounded on the surface, it would not have kindled us to seek an inward understanding. The more completely, therefore, something inward is suggested to us, the less rationality it displays outwardly.

If the prophet came forth from his mother’s womb to be afflicted in this world, what wrongdoing did the messenger of his birth commit? But what is signified by the person of the wavering prophet except the instability of the human race, which comes under the merit of punishment? And what is signified by his father except this world from which we are born?

Who is the man who announces our birth to his father except the ancient enemy? When he sees us wavering in our thoughts, he stirs up the wicked minds of those who hold positions of prominence by the authority of this world, urging them to persuade us into deception. And when he sees us doing weak things, he exalts them with praise as though they were strong,

**[Note: This is how nearly all the manuscripts read: *et quasi natos masculos loquitur* (“and he speaks as though male children had been born”)—namely, the Corbie German manuscript, the two Rheims manuscripts, the two Remigius manuscripts, all the Norman manuscripts, the two Compiègne manuscripts, Saint-Albans, Longpont, Vallicelliana, and one Vendôme manuscript. One Remigius manuscript and another Vendôme manuscript read *et quasi natus masculus loquitur* (“and he speaks as though a male child had been born”). No manuscript reads, as do the other editions, *et quod sit natus masculus loquitur* (“and he speaks that a male child has been born”). The old Paris edition has *et quasi nato masculo loquitur* (“and he speaks as though a male child had been born”); the old Basel edition, *et quasi natis masculis loquitur* (“and he speaks as though male children had been born”).]**

and speaks as though male children had been born, when he rejoices that, through falsehood, we have become corrupters of the truth. He announces a male child born to the father when he shows this world that the person whom he has persuaded has become a corrupter of innocence. For when it is said to any sinner and proud person, “You have acted like a man,” what else is being declared than that a male child has been born into the world?

Rightly, therefore, the man who announces the birth of a male child is cursed, because his announcement reveals the corruptor’s perverse joy.

From these curses of sacred Scripture, then, we learn what we should seek in Job’s language of cursing, lest anyone presume to condemn his words without understanding them, when God rewards him after his wounds and words.

**[Note: The editions and some manuscripts read “after wounds and blows.” With the Corbie German and German manuscripts one must read “after wounds and words”; the context supports this reading, referring to the words of his wife, who gave evil counsel, and perhaps also to his friends’ words and reproaches.]**

Since, therefore, we have to some extent distinguished the matters that had to be examined in the preface, let us now proceed to explain the words of the narrative itself.

## CHAPTER I [Recension V]

### Chapter 3, Verses 1–3

“After this Job opened his mouth and cursed his day, saying: ‘Let the day perish in which I was born.’”

### 1. The Historical and Mystical Sense

#### Job Did Not Utter His Curse Out of Impatience

We must not pass over carelessly what is said: “He opened his mouth.” For sacred Scripture indicates through what it briefly sets forth beforehand that what follows is to be awaited with reverence. Just as we do not know what closed vessels contain within them, but when the mouths of the vessels are opened we recognize what they hold inside, so the hearts of the saints, whose secrets are hidden when their mouths are closed, are disclosed when their mouths are opened. When they reveal their thoughts, they are said to open their mouths, so that with attentive minds, as though the vessels had been opened, we may hasten to learn what they contain within and refresh ourselves with their innermost fragrance.

Hence, when the Lord was about to utter sublime commandments on the mountain, it is first said: “Opening his mouth, he spoke” (Matthew 5:2).

**[Note: One Rheims manuscript and another Remigius manuscript read *daturo* (“when he was about to give”), the word used by Augustine in Book I of *On the Sermon on the Mount*, which Gregory partly follows here.]**

Yet that passage may also be understood in this way: at that time he opened his mouth in the commandments in which he had earlier opened the mouths of the prophets.

It must be observed with great care that the text says, “After this,” so that the force of what is being done may truly be understood from its temporal sequence. First the devastation of his possessions, the death of his children, the pain of his wounds, the persuasion of his wife, and the arrival of his friends are described. They are said to have torn their garments, wept aloud, sprinkled dust upon their heads, and sat silently on the ground for a long time. Then it is added: “After this Job opened his mouth and cursed his day.” Thus the very order of the narrative makes clear that he did not utter his curse out of impatience, since he burst into the voice of cursing while his friends were still silent.

**[Formerly V.]**

If he had cursed while moved by anger, the pain would surely have driven him to curse upon hearing of the loss of his possessions and learning of the death of his children. But we have heard what he said then: “The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away” (Job 1:21).

Again, if he had cursed when angered, he could at least have done so after being struck in his body or after being badly advised by his wife. But we recognize what he answered then. He said: “You have spoken as one of the foolish women speaks. If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, why should we not endure evil?” (Job 2:10).

After this, however, his friends are described as coming, weeping, sitting, and remaining silent; and immediately it is added that he cursed his day. It is therefore exceedingly unfitting to suppose that he, with no one urging or provoking him, burst out in impatient cursing—he whom we know, amid the loss of his possessions and the death of his children, amid the wounds of his body and the words of his badly advising wife, to have rendered great praises to the Creator with humble spirit.

He therefore revealed with what frame of mind he had spoken these words in tranquillity, since even when struck he poured forth so many praises of God.

**[Note: Thus all the Rheims, Remigius, Corbie German, Colbert, Fleury, Vendôme, Norman, and other manuscripts, as well as the old edition, read *percussus emanavit* (“he poured forth when struck”). The more recent editions read *percussus enarravit* (“he recounted when struck”).]**

For one who did not become proud afterward could not have been proud before; and pain itself showed him humble when he was struck. But since we know with certainty that sacred Scripture forbids cursing, why do we say that something is rightly done at one time which the same sacred eloquence teaches us must be avoided?

### [Recension VI] 2. One Curse Proceeds from Judgment, Another from Vengeance

We should know that sacred Scripture records curses in two ways: one it approves, the other it condemns (24, question 3, chapter 1, canon *Cum sancti*). A curse is uttered either through the judgment of justice or through the resentment of vengeance.

A curse through the judgment of justice was pronounced upon the first sinful man when he heard: “Cursed is the earth in your work” (Genesis 3:17).

**[Note: Some manuscripts read *ipso primo homine peccante* (“when the first man himself was sinning”); others, *in ipso primo homine peccante* (“in the first man himself when he was sinning”).]**

A curse is pronounced by the judgment of justice when God says to Abraham: “I will curse those who curse you” (Genesis 12:3).

Again, we are warned by the voice of the apostle Paul that a curse may be uttered not through the judgment of justice but through the resentment of vengeance. He says: “Bless, and do not curse” (Romans 12:14). And again: “Nor will the cursers possess the kingdom of God” (1 Corinthians 6:10).

God, therefore, is said to curse, while human beings are forbidden to curse, because what a human being does through the malice of vengeance, God does only through the examination and power of justice.

**[Formerly VI.]**

When holy men pronounce a sentence of cursing (24, question 3, canon *Cum sancti*), it does not burst forth from a desire for vengeance but from the judgment of justice.

**[Note: Nearly all our manuscripts, the old edition, and other editions read “from the examination of justice” (*ex justitiae examine*). The second Rheims manuscript reads, “but from the desire for the justice of vengeance,” namely, from the examination of justice.]**

For inwardly they behold God’s subtle judgment and recognize that the evils emerging outwardly deserve to be struck by a curse. They therefore do not sin in cursing precisely because they do not depart from the inward judgment.

Hence Peter hurled a sentence of cursing at Simon, who offered him money, saying: “May your money be with you unto perdition” (Acts 8:20). By saying not “it is,” but “may it be,” he indicated that he spoke in the optative rather than the indicative mood.

Hence Elijah said to the two captains of fifty who came to him: “If I am a man of God, let fire come down from heaven and consume you” (2 Kings 1:10).

The outcome of the matter showed how greatly the sentence of both was confirmed by the reason of truth.

**[Note: The manuscripts and the old Paris and Basel editions read *veritatis* (“of truth”); other editions have *severitatis* (“of severity”).]**

Simon perished in eternal destruction, and fire descending from above consumed the two captains of fifty.

The subsequent effect, therefore, testifies with what disposition a sentence of cursing is uttered. When the innocence of the one who curses remains, yet the curse absorbs the one who is cursed even unto destruction, it is gathered from the end of both parties that the sentence has been hurled against the guilty by one and the same inward Judge.

**[Note: One Rheims manuscript and two Remigius manuscripts read: “When someone is cursed, and the innocence of the one who curses remains.”]**

### 3. Job’s Curse Proceeded from the Rectitude of Judgment

If, therefore, we weigh the words of blessed Job subtly, his curse did not proceed from the malice of a sinner but from the rectitude of a judge; it did not proceed from an enraged man but from a tranquil teacher. For one who brought forward such a righteous curse did not succumb to the fault of disturbance but supplied instruction.

He saw his friends weeping aloud; he saw them tear their garments; he saw them sprinkle dust upon their heads; he saw them become silent as they considered his affliction. The holy man perceived that those who desired temporal prosperity had concluded, by comparison with their own state of mind, that he had been broken by temporal adversity.

He understood that they would not weep despairingly over one struck by a passing affliction unless they themselves withdrew their despairing minds from hope of inward security. And when he broke forth outwardly into a voice of grief, he showed those inwardly wounded the power of the remedy, saying:

> Let the day perish in which I was born.

### [Recension VII] 4. He Curses the Day of Mutability from Contemplation of Eternity

What should be understood by the day of birth except all this time of our mortality? As long as it holds us in the corruption of our mutability, the unchangeableness of eternity does not appear to us. Therefore, whoever already sees the day of eternity bears with difficulty the day of his mortality.

It should also be noted that he does not say, “Let the day in which I was created perish,” but, “Let the day in which I was born perish.” Humanity was created in the day of justice but was born into the time of guilt. Adam was created, but Cain was the first to be born.

What, then, is it to curse the day of birth except openly to say: “Let the day of mutability perish, and let the light of eternity break forth”?

### [Formerly VII.] 5. The Time of Our Mutability Will One Day Perish Completely

#### The Day That Is Here Wished to Perish as Evil Is the Apostate Spirit

We commonly speak of perishing in two ways. We say that something perishes when we wish it not to exist; and we say that something perishes when we wish it to exist in an evil condition.

What is added concerning this day—“Let gloom obscure it, and let it be enveloped in bitterness”—clearly shows that the day is wished to perish not in the sense that it should not exist, but in the sense that it should exist in an evil condition. For what has not been utterly destroyed in every way cannot be enveloped in bitterness.

This time of our mutability, however, will not one day perish—that is, pass away—in an evil condition, but will perish so as not to exist at all, as the angel testifies in sacred eloquence: “By him who lives forever, time shall be no more” (Revelation 10:6).

Although the Prophet says, “Their time shall be forever” (Psalm 80:16), because their time diminishes moment by moment, he called their diminution by the name of their time, showing that those who are separated from the innermost consolation of vision are diminished without any end.

**[Note: In accordance with the older manuscripts, we have removed the word *fine* (“end”), which appears in other editions: “that they are diminished by every diminution without end,” and so forth. The Uticensis manuscript formerly read *sine fine*, but the word *fine* has been deleted. The reading remains in the Colbert manuscript.]**

Since, therefore, this time of our mortality perishes not so as to be evil but so as not to exist, we must ask what is meant by that which is wished to perish not so as not to exist, but so as to be evil.

The human soul, or the angelic spirit, is immortal in such a way that it can die, and mortal in such a way that it cannot die. It loses blessed life, whether through vice or punishment. But it does not lose existence itself through either vice or punishment. It falls away from the quality of living, but even in dying it does not experience the destruction of its existence in any manner whatsoever.

To put it briefly: it is immortally mortal and mortally immortal.

Thus, when the day is wished to perish and shortly afterward is said to be enveloped in bitterness, whom should we think the holy man intended to signify by the name of day, except the apostate spirit, who subsists in the essence of life even while dying? The loss of life does not take him away, because immortal death destroys him while preserving him in eternal pain. Already cast down from the glory of blessedness, he is still wished to perish: that, confined in fitting punishments, he may lose even the license to tempt.

### [Recension VIII; Formerly VIII, Recension IX.] 6. Why It Is Called Day, and Why Night; What Is Wished for It When It Is Wished to Perish

The spirit in question presents itself as day because it entices through prosperity, but it ends in night because it leads to adversity.

It displayed itself as day when it said, “On whatever day you eat from it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like gods” (Genesis 3:5); but it brought on night when it led humanity into the darkness of mortality.

Day, therefore, is the promise of better things that was introduced; night is the actual experience of calamities that was brought about.

The ancient enemy is day by nature, because he was created good; but he is night by merit, because he descended into darkness.

He is day when, by promising good things, he pretends before human eyes to be an angel of light, as Paul testifies: “For Satan himself transforms himself into an angel of light” (2 Corinthians 11:14). But he is night when he darkens the minds of those who consent to him with the darkness of error.

The holy man, therefore, while in his own pain mourning the cause of the whole human race and thinking of nothing whatever in his particular mortal wound, recalls the origin of guilt and tempers the grief of punishment by the consideration of justice. He sees from where and to where the human race has fallen, and says:

> Let the day perish in which I was born, and the night in which it was said, “A man has been conceived.”

As though he were openly saying: “Let the hope introduced by the apostate angel perish—the one who, pretending to be day, shone forth through a promise of divinity, but, presenting himself as night, darkened for us the light of our immortality. Let the ancient enemy perish, who displayed the light of promise and brought the darkness of sin; who, flattering us, made himself known as though he were day, but through the blindness impressed upon our hearts led us all the way into the darkness of night.”

The text continues:

## CHAPTER II

### Verse 4

> Let that day be turned into darkness.

### 7. The Day Is Turned into Darkness When What It Promises as Prosperity Is Understood to Be Adversity

That day seems to shine upon human minds when the persuasion of its wickedness is believed to promise prosperity and its inward nature is not perceived. But when its iniquity is recognized as it truly is, the day of false promise is darkened before the eyes of our judgment, so that it is perceived in its flattering guise according to the merit it actually possesses.

**[Note: The editions, contrary to the manuscripts, read “before the eyes of our judge.” The passage, however, concerns not the judgment of the Lord but the judgment of our minds.]**

The day, therefore, is turned into darkness when we understand as adversities even those things that it promises while persuading us that they are prosperous. The day is turned into darkness when the ancient enemy, raging as he truly is, is perceived by us as hiding beneath his flatteries, lest through fictitious prosperity, as though by the light of day, he deceive us and drag us through genuine miseries into the darkness of sin.

The text continues:

## CHAPTER III [Formerly IX]

### The Same Passage

> Let God not seek it from above, and let him not illumine it with light.

### 8. Why Human Nature Was Restored, but Not the Angelic

The almighty God was able to create good things from nothing; and, when he willed, he also restored through the mystery of his incarnation the good things that had been lost.

He had created two kinds of creatures capable of knowing him: the angelic and the human. Pride struck both and shattered them from the state of their innate uprightness. But one possessed the covering of flesh, whereas the other carried nothing weak from flesh. An angel is spirit alone, while a human being is both spirit and flesh.

Therefore, when the Creator took pity and wished to redeem, he ought to restore to himself the one who, in committing sin, evidently possessed something derived from weakness. He ought to drive the apostate angel back more deeply because, when he fell from the strength of perseverance, he carried nothing weak from flesh.

**[Note: The printed editions have *amplius* (“more deeply” or “more”), but the Corbie German, Rheims, Remigius, and Norman manuscripts consistently read *altius* (“more deeply,” literally “from a higher place”).]**

Hence the Psalmist rightly expressed the very cause of mercy when he said that the Redeemer had taken pity on human beings: “And he remembered that they are flesh” (Psalm 77:39).

### [Recension X.]

As though he were saying: “Because he saw their weakness, he did not wish to punish their sins with strict severity.”

There is also another reason why fallen humanity had to be restored while the proud spirit could not be restored: the angel fell through his own malice, whereas humanity was overthrown by another’s.

Since, therefore, the human race is led back to the light of repentance by the coming of the Redeemer, while the apostate angel is recalled to the light of restoration by no hope of pardon and no correction through conversion, let it rightly be said:

> Let God not seek him from above, and let him not illumine him with light.

**[Note: The Vatican and Gussanville editions, together with the Colbert manuscript, read *conversationis* (“conversion” or “change of life”); the other editions read *conversionis*.]**

As though it were openly said: “Because he himself brought in darkness, let him endure without end what he has done; and let him never receive the light of his former state, because he also lost it without being persuaded by another.”

The text continues:

## CHAPTER IV

### Verse 5

> Let darkness and the shadow of death obscure him.

### 9. The Devil Is So Overwhelmed by the Blindness of Error That He Will Not Rise Again to the Light of Repentance

By the shadow of death, forgetfulness should be understood. For just as death destroys life, so forgetfulness extinguishes memory. Since the apostate angel is handed over to eternal forgetfulness, he is obscured by the shadow of death.

Let it therefore be said:

> Let darkness and the shadow of death obscure him;

that is, let the blindness of his error overwhelm him so completely that he may never again rise to the light of repentance through the remembrance of divine regard.

The text continues:

## CHAPTER V [Formerly X]

### The Same Passage

> Let gloom seize him, and let him be enveloped in bitterness.

### 10. What He Suffers Now and What He Will Suffer after the Judgment

The ancient enemy, bound by the chains of his wickedness, suffers one thing now and will suffer another at the end. Because he fell from the order of the innermost light, he now inwardly confounds himself in the gloom of error. But afterward he is enveloped in bitterness, because, according to the merit of his voluntary darkness, he is tormented by the eternal punishment of Gehenna.

Let it therefore be said:

> He who lost the serenity of the innermost light—what does he endure before the final punishment? Let gloom seize him.

Let the punishment that follows and devastates him without end also be added:

> Let him be enveloped in bitterness.

For whatever is enveloped seems not to reveal its end anywhere. Just as it does not show where it begins, so it does not disclose where it ceases. The ancient enemy is therefore said to be enveloped in bitterness because punishments for his pride are prepared for him not only in their entirety but also without end.

His punishment begins when the stern Judge comes for the final judgment. Hence it is rightly added:

## CHAPTER VI [Recension XI]

### Verse 6

> Let a dark whirlwind possess that night.

### 11. With What Storm He Is Swept Away to Eternal Punishments

It is written: “God will come manifestly, our God, and he will not be silent. Fire will burn before him, and a mighty storm will surround him” (Psalm 49:3).

**[Note: The better manuscripts read this way. In the Uticensis manuscript it is clearly noted in the margin that this is the reading adopted by the Vulgate editions.]**

A dark whirlwind therefore possesses this night, because that terrifying storm sweeps the apostate spirit from the presence of the stern Judge into eternal punishments.

This night is possessed by a whirlwind because its proud blindness is struck by strict retribution.

The text continues:

## CHAPTER VII

### The Same Passage

> Let it not be counted among the days of the year, nor numbered among the months.

### 12. What the Names “Day,” “Month,” and “Year” Signify in Job’s Words

We may appropriately understand the year as the preaching of heavenly grace. Just as time is completed in a year through the gathering together of days, so a manifold life of virtues is completed through heavenly grace.

The year may also be understood as the multitude of the redeemed. Just as a year is formed from a multitude of days, so that innumerable community of the elect is completed from the gathering of all good things.

Isaiah proclaims this year of perfect multitude, saying:

> “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because the Lord has anointed me. He has sent me to announce good news to the meek, to heal the brokenhearted, to proclaim release to captives and opening to those who are shut in, to proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord” (Isaiah 61:1).

**[Note: One Rheims manuscript, two Remigius manuscripts, and the Vallicelliana manuscript read *placabilem Domino* (“acceptable to the Lord”).]**

The acceptable year of the Lord is proclaimed when the future people of believers are foretold as being illumined by the light of truth.

What is signified by days except the individual minds of the elect? What by months except their multiplied churches, which together make one catholic Church?

Let that night, therefore, not be counted among the days of the year, nor numbered among the months, because the ancient enemy, oppressed by the darkness of his pride, indeed sees the coming of the Redeemer but in no way returns with the elect to forgiveness.

For it is written: “He nowhere takes hold of angels, but he takes hold of the seed of Abraham” (Hebrews 2:16).

### [Recension XII.]

For this reason our Redeemer became not an angel but a human being, because undoubtedly he had to become what he redeemed: by not taking hold of the fallen angel, he would leave him abandoned; by taking hold of humanity in himself, he would restore it.

### [Formerly XI.]

These days that remain in inward light may also be understood as angelic spirits, and the months as their orders and dignities. Each spirit individually is a day because it shines. But because they are distinguished by certain dignities—some being thrones, others dominions, principalities, or powers—they are called months according to this distribution of ranks.

Since the ancient enemy, however, is never restored to the merit of light or to the order of the heavenly ranks, he is counted neither among the days of the year nor among the months. The blindness of the pride he committed weighs upon him so heavily that he will never again return to those heavenly ranks of the innermost brightness. He is never again mingled with the dignities of light that remain standing, because, by the merit of his darkness, he is continually thrust down to the depths.

Because he remains forever excluded from the assembly of the heavenly homeland, it is rightly added:

## CHAPTER VIII

### Verse 7

> Let that night be solitary and not worthy of praise.

### 13. The devil, when humanity has been redeemed and idols rejected, becomes solitary and without praise

That night becomes solitary because it is separated by an everlasting distinction from the company of the heavenly homeland. [Note: The Rheims Antiquus has “because of everlasting destruction.” Some, together with Corb. Germ., read “because of everlasting strictness.”] Yet this may also be understood in another way: namely, that it loses the human being whom it had made its companion in destruction, and that the enemy perishes alone with his own body, while the grace of the Redeemer restores many whom he had destroyed. Thus the night becomes solitary when, after those who have been chosen are removed, the ancient enemy alone is handed over to the eternal fires of Gehenna.

It is rightly said: “Nor worthy of praise.” For when the human race, oppressed by the darkness of error, believed stones to be gods, what else did it praise by serving idols than the works of its seducer? Hence Paul rightly says: “We know that an idol is nothing; but the things that the Gentiles sacrifice, they sacrifice to demons” (1 Corinthians 8:4). Those therefore who have been subjected to the worship of idols—what else have they praised than the darkness of night? But now we plainly see that this night is recognized as not worthy of praise, since the worship of idols is rejected by redeemed humanity; and the night is left solitary, because one does not go with the condemned apostate spirit to punishment. It continues:

### CHAPTER IX

**Verse 8.** “Let those who curse the day curse it, who are ready to rouse Leviathan.”

### 14. Christ is already destroying his wickedness; at the end of the world his power will be extinguished

In the Old Translation this is not expressed in that way, but rather: “Let him curse it who cursed the day, who is about to capture the great sea-monster.” These words clearly show that the holy man foresees the destruction of Antichrist, which is to come at the end of the world. For the malignant spirit, which is night by its merit, pretends to be day at the end of the world when it displays itself to human beings as though it were God, falsely attributes divine glory to itself, and exalts itself above everything that is either called or worshiped as God.

He therefore curses the night who curses the day, because the one who now destroys his wickedness will then, by the illumination of his coming, also extinguish the power of his strength. Hence it is rightly added: “Who is about to capture the great sea-monster.” For the strength of this sea-monster is captured in the waters, because the cunning of the ancient enemy is overcome through the sacrament of baptism.

### 15. His chosen angels disclose to us the darkness of his deceit

But what the Old Translation attributes to the author of all things, this translation—which has come down to us from the Hebrew and Arabic language—speaks of his chosen angels. (See what we said in Book 35, formerly Chapter 13, on verse 14 of the final chapter of the Book of Job.) Of these it says: “Let those who curse the day curse it.”

This proud spirit wished to display itself as day even to the angelic powers, when, exalting itself above the others as though possessing divine power, it drew so many legions after itself to destruction. But those who remained humble in their Creator, when they perceived that his error contained night, trampled upon the day of his brightness by thinking humbly of themselves. They now disclose to us the darkness of his deceit and demonstrate how contemptible his feigned brightness is.

Let it therefore be said concerning the dark night that closes the eyes of human weakness: “Let those who curse the day curse it”—that is, let those chosen spirits denounce the darkness of his error by condemning it. [Note: Rheims, Corb. Germ., Remigius, Norman, and Floriac preserve this reading, followed by the older Paris and Basel editions and by Coccius. Others thereafter read *damnandos*, “those who are to be condemned.”] They see that the greatness of his brightness was fabricated from the beginning.

It is rightly added: “Who are ready to rouse Leviathan.” For Leviathan is interpreted to mean “their addition.” Whose, unless that of human beings? It is rightly called “their addition,” because after introducing the first sin through evil suggestion, he does not cease daily to increase it by more serious persuasions.

Or certainly he was called Leviathan by way of reproach, that is, “the addition of human beings.” He found them immortal in paradise; but by promising divinity to the immortals, he professed that he would add something to them beyond what they were. Yet while he deceitfully claimed that he would give them what they did not possess, he cunningly took away even what they did possess. [Note: In the Norman, Vindobonensis, and German manuscripts one reads: “Therefore the Lord also describes him in this way through the prophet.” In the Uticensis, the earlier reading was as in the printed editions.]

Thus the prophet describes this same Leviathan, saying: “Upon Leviathan the bar-serpent, upon Leviathan the crooked serpent” (Isaiah 27:1). This Leviathan, in promising that he would add something to humanity, crept into it through winding coils; for while he falsely promised impossible things, he truly took away even possible ones.

[Note: In the manuscripts the following appears: “And therefore the Lord describes this same one through the prophet.”]

We must ask why, after saying “serpent,” he immediately adds “crooked,” yet inserts “bar”—unless perhaps the serpent’s crookedness signifies pliant softness, while the bar signifies the hardness of rigidity. Therefore, to indicate that he is both hard and soft, he calls him both a bar and a serpent. [Note: The printed editions have “the rigidity of hardness.”] He is hard through malice, soft through flattery.

He is therefore called a bar because he strikes even to death; but a serpent because he insinuates himself softly through ambushes. [Note: The second Compendium has *inflectit*, “bends,” instead of *infundit*, “insinuates.” Longpont has the same reading.]

### 16. The chosen angels press the devil down, shut up in the pit of the abyss

But the spirits of the chosen angels now press this Leviathan, shut up in the pit of the abyss. Hence it is written: “I saw an angel descending from heaven, having the key of the abyss and a great chain in his hand; and he seized the dragon, the ancient serpent, who is the devil and Satan, and bound him for a thousand years, and cast him into the abyss” (Revelation 20:1–2 and following).

At the end of the world, however, they call him back to more open combat and release him with all his strength against us. Hence it is written there again: “When the thousand years have been completed, Satan will be released” (ibid., verse 7).

For that apostate angel, since he had been created to excel the other legions of angels, fell through pride so completely that he was subjected to the dominion of the angels who stood firm. Thus, either he now lies bound and hidden, while they minister for our benefit, or then, when they release him for our testing, he will exercise all his strength against us after being set free.

Since, therefore, these chosen spirits restrain the proud apostate—those who, in their humility, refused to follow him—and since through their ministry it has been arranged that he will eventually be recalled for open combat, in which he is to be utterly destroyed, it is rightly said: “Who are ready to rouse Leviathan.”

Yet because the cunning enemy has not yet been roused to open war, let us explain how this night now secretly darkens certain minds. It continues:

### CHAPTER X [Old Translation XIII; Revised Translation XIV]

**Verse 9.** “Let the stars be darkened by his gloom.”

### 17. In Scripture “stars” sometimes means the saints and sometimes hypocrites. The light of hypocrites is darkened by manifest error

In Sacred Scripture, the name “stars” sometimes signifies the righteousness of the saints, which shines amid the darkness of this life, and sometimes the pretence of hypocrites, who display the good things they do in order to receive human praise.

If those who live rightly were not stars, Paul would never say to his disciples: “Among a crooked and perverse nation, among whom you shine like lights in the world” (Philippians 2:15). Again, if among those who appear to act rightly certain people did not seek the reward of human favor for their conduct, John would never see stars falling from heaven, saying: “The dragon cast down his tail and drew a third part of the stars” (Revelation 12:4).

For part of the stars is dragged down by the dragon’s tail, because through the final persuasion of Antichrist certain people who appear to shine will be carried away. To drag stars to the earth is to involve in the iniquity of manifest error those who appear devoted to the life of heaven, because of earthly love.

There are some who shine before human eyes as though through great works; but because these very works do not proceed from a pure heart, they are taken captive in hidden thoughts and darkened by the shadows of this night. Often they also lose the outward works that they do not perform with a pure heart.

Since, therefore, night is permitted to prevail when the intention of the heart is not purified even amid good works, it is rightly said: “Let the stars be darkened by his gloom.” [Note: One Remigius manuscript and the Vallicellian read: “Let the stars be darkened,” and so forth.]

That is, let the wickedness of the ancient enemy prevail against those who shine before human eyes as though through good works, so that they lay down the light of praise which they had acquired before human judgment. They are darkened by the gloom of night when their life is confused by manifest error, so that outwardly in their conduct they appear to be such as they do not fear being within themselves before the divine judgment.

It continues:

### CHAPTER XI [Old Translation XIV]

**The same passage.** “Let it expect light, and not see it, nor behold the rising of the dawn.”

### 18. Christ is one person with the good, and the devil one with the reprobate. Those who do evil, or do good without a right heart, vainly hope for an eternal reward

In the Gospel the Truth says: “I am the light of the world” (John 8:12). Just as our Redeemer is one person with the congregation of the good—for he is the head of the body, and we are the body of this head—so the ancient enemy is one person with the entire gathering of the reprobate. He stands above them as a head for iniquity, while they, by serving what he persuades them to do, cling to him like a body joined to its head.

What, therefore, is said of this night, that is, of the ancient enemy, rightly extends to its body, namely, to all the wicked. Since the Redeemer of the human race is light, what does it mean when it is said of this night, “Let it expect light, and not see it,” unless that there are some who show by their words that they hold the faith which they destroy by their works?

Paul says of them: “They profess that they know God, but by their deeds they deny him” (Titus 1:16). These people either do evil things, or pursue good works without a right heart. They do not seek perpetual rewards for their works, but temporary human favor; nevertheless, because they hear themselves praised as though they were holy, they consider themselves truly holy. And the more irreproachable they think themselves according to the judgment of many, the more securely they await the day of strict judgment.

Of them the prophet rightly says: “Woe to those who desire the day of the Lord” (Amos 5:18). Blessed Job pronounces upon them the sentence they deserve, speaking in the spirit of one proclaiming it, not with the desire of one who wishes it, when he says: “Let it expect light, and not see it.”

That night—namely, the dark enemy—expects light in its members and does not see it. For those who hold the faith without works and trust that they can be saved on account of that faith at the final judgment will have their hope frustrated, because by their manner of life they have destroyed the faith which they held in their confession.

[Note: The printed editions insert the word *male*, “badly,” which is absent from the manuscripts. Against those who, while retaining faith without works, trust that they will be saved at the final judgment, Augustine wrote a particular treatise, *On Faith and Works*, vol. 8, p. 165 (Patrologia, vol. 40, col. 197). He refutes the same people in *On Eight Questions of Dulcitius*, question 1, and elsewhere.]

Or those who display themselves in good action for the sake of human praise hope in vain for a reward from the coming judge, because by doing these things for show they have already received their reward from human lips, as the Truth testifies when it says: “Truly I tell you, they have received their reward” (Matthew 6:2, 5). It is rightly added: “Nor the rising of the dawn.”

### 19. The Church’s brightness will not be seen by the reprobate at the last judgment

“Dawn” signifies the Church, which is changed from the darkness of its sins into the light of righteousness. Hence the bridegroom marvels at it in the Song of Songs, saying: “Who is this that comes forth like the rising dawn?” (Song of Songs 6:9). The Church of the elect rises like the dawn when it abandons the darkness of its former wickedness and turns itself toward the splendor of new light.

In that light which is revealed at the coming of the strict Judge, the body of the condemned enemy does not see the rising of the dawn. For when the strict Judge comes to render recompense, each wicked person, weighed down by the darkness of his merits, does not know with what brightness the holy Church rises into the inner light of the heart.

Then the mind of the elect is lifted on high to be illumined by the rays of divinity; and the more it is suffused by that divine regard, the more it is raised above itself as grace flashes beyond it. Then the holy Church becomes full dawn when it entirely loses the darkness of mortality and ignorance. At the judgment it is still dawn, but in the kingdom it is day: although at the judgment it begins to see the light with the restoration of the body, it completes its fuller vision in the kingdom.

The rising of the dawn is therefore the beginning of the Church’s illumination, which the reprobate cannot see, because, pressed into darkness by the weight of their evils, they are dragged away from the sight of the strict Judge. Hence the prophet rightly says: “Let the impious be taken away, that he may not see the glory of God” (Isaiah 26:10, according to the Septuagint).

Therefore the Psalmist says of this dawn: “You will hide them in the secret place of your face from the disturbance of men” (Psalm 30:21). Each of the elect is hidden in the judgment within the vision of the divine face, while the outward blindness of the reprobate is disturbed when it is driven away by the strict judgment of justice. [Note: Two Rheims manuscripts, Corb. Germ., and one Remigius manuscript read: “You will hide them in the secret place.” The old Paris and Basel editions have the same reading.]

### 20. Hypocrites do not see the light of the righteous because they do not perceive the intention behind their works

We may also understand this appropriately in the present, if we examine more subtly the hearts of pretenders. The arrogant and hypocrites look outwardly upon the deeds of the good; they recognize that these people are praised by human beings for their actions, admire the fame of their name, and see that they receive praise for their good conduct. But they do not see how earnestly those same people avoid praise.

They observe their manifest works, but do not know that these works are performed solely in hope of an inner reward. Those who are bright with the true light of righteousness are first changed inwardly from the darkness of their intention, so that they completely abandon the obscurity of earthly desire within and perfectly turn their hearts toward the desires of heavenly light, lest, while appearing bright to others, they be dark to themselves.

The arrogant, therefore, because they consider the deeds of the good but do not weigh their hearts, imitate what can win them outward praise, not what can make them rise inwardly toward the light of righteousness. They do not know how to see the rising of the dawn, because they disdain to consider the intention of a devout mind.

### 21. Judea did not see the light of Christ’s coming or of the Church’s birth

The holy man, full of the grace of the prophetic spirit, may also have perceived the unbelief of Judea when the Redeemer came, and may have prophesied the losses caused by its blindness through these words, as though expressing the character of one who desires, saying: “Let it expect light, and not see it, nor behold the rising of the dawn.”

Judea expected the light and did not see it, because it awaited the coming Redeemer of the human race through prophecy, but did not recognize him when he came. It opened the eyes of its mind to hope, but closed them to the presence of the light.

It did not see the rising of the dawn because it disdained to honor the weak beginnings of the holy Church. Believing that the Church would be overthrown by the deaths of its members, it did not know to what strength it would attain.

But since, in speaking of unbelievers, he has made known the members of the wicked head, he turns his words again to the head itself, saying:

### CHAPTER XII

**Verse 10.** “Because he did not shut the doors of the womb that carried me, nor remove evils from my eyes.”

### 22. Paradise was the womb of the human race, whose doors the serpent opened

What the womb of a mother is for each human being, that highest dwelling of paradise was for the entire human race. From it the offspring of the human race came forth as though from a womb, and flowed outward for the increase of its descendants just as the body grows through its own development. There our conception took shape, where the first human being, the origin of humanity, dwelt. [Note: Vindobonensis and one Remigius manuscript read: “For from it the human race came forth, as it were, from a womb.” Ebroicensis has the same reading.]

But the serpent opened the doors of this womb, because through cunning persuasion he dissolved the heavenly command in the human heart. The serpent opened the doors of this womb because, through a crafty suggestion, he broke through the barriers of the mind fortified by heavenly admonitions.

Therefore, in the punishment he suffers, the holy man recalls the eyes of his mind to the guilt. Let him grieve over what the dark night—that is, the obscure suggestion of the ancient enemy—introduced into human minds; let him grieve over the fact that the human mind consented to the cunning suggestion in its own deception; and let him say: “Because he did not shut the doors of the womb that carried me, nor remove evils from my eyes.”

Nor should it disturb us that he complains of one who did not shut, when he detests one who opened the gate of paradise. “He did not shut” means “he opened”; and “he did not remove evils” means “he inflicted them.” He would have removed them, so to speak, if he had remained inactive; and he would have shut them, so to speak, if he had ceased his assault.

He considers what he is speaking about and weighs how the evil spirit would, as it were, have given us profit if he had not inflicted loss. We speak in this way of robbers, because they give life to their captives if they do not take it away. [Note: Most manuscripts read *quia captis suis*, “because [they give life] to those captured by them.”]

### 23. MORAL MEANING

It is pleasing to return to these matters from the beginning and reconsider them morally from what we recognize in the practice of the present life.

Blessed Job, considering how greatly the human race was raised up by confidence in prosperity after it had fallen from the state of mind it possessed, and how greatly it was shattered by disturbance in adversity, returns in thought to that state of unchangeability which it could have possessed in paradise. He declared, by cursing it, how contemptible he saw the fall of mortality, which varies between prosperity and adversity, saying:

### CHAPTER XIII [Revised Translation XV]

**Verse 3.** “Let the day perish in which I was born, and the night in which it was said, ‘A man has been conceived.’”

### 24. Day is prosperity, night tribulation. Day is the delight of sin, night the blindness of the mind

It is like a certain day when the prosperity of this world smiles upon us. But this day ends in night, because temporal prosperity often leads into the darkness of tribulation. The prophet had despised this day of prosperity when he said: “I have not desired the day of man; you know” (Jeremiah 17:16).

The Lord announced that he would suffer this night of tribulation at the end of his earthly incarnation when, through the Psalmist, he spoke as though of the past: “Even until night my reins have reproved me” (Psalm 15:7).

The day may also be understood as the delight of sin, and the night as the blindness of the mind by which a person allows himself to be overthrown in the perpetration of guilt. He therefore desires the day to perish, so that everything which appears to flatter guilt may be destroyed when the strength of righteousness intervenes. He also desires the night to perish, so that what the blinded mind perpetrates even through consent may be extinguished by the discipline of repentance.

### 25. Scripture calls a human being by three names. Through voluntary darkness of mind, a person is carried away by the delight of sin

But we must ask why a human being is said to be born in the day and conceived in the night. Sacred Scripture calls a human being by three names: sometimes according to nature, sometimes according to guilt, and sometimes according to weakness. [Note: Two Rheims manuscripts, two Remigius manuscripts, Corb. Germ., and one Vindobonensis read: “For a human being is called in it”—that is, in Sacred Scripture—“according to nature.” The first Vindobonensis reads: “For a human being is called in that part according to nature.”]

A human being is called such according to nature, as it is written: “Let us make humanity in our image and likeness” (Genesis 1:26). A human being is called such according to guilt, as it is written: “I said, ‘You are gods, and all of you are children of the Most High’; but you will die like human beings” (Psalm 81:6). It is as though he plainly said: “You will die as sinners.”

Hence Paul also says: “Since there is jealousy and strife among you, are you not carnal, and do you not walk according to the human being?” (1 Corinthians 3:3). It is as though he said: “You who lead discordant minds, are you not still sinning according to reprehensible human nature?”

A human being is called such according to weakness, as it is written: “Cursed is the human being who places his hope in a human being” (Jeremiah 17:5). It is as though he plainly said: “In weakness.”

A human being is therefore born in the day but conceived in the night, because no one is carried away by the delight of sin unless he is first weakened through voluntary darkness of mind. First he becomes blind in his mind, and afterward he submits himself to wicked delight.

Let it therefore be said: “Let the day perish in which I was born, and the night in which it was said, ‘A man has been conceived’”—that is, let the delight which carried a human being into guilt perish; let the unwary weakness of mind perish, which blinded him even to the darkness of wicked consent.

For when a person does not carefully perceive the allurements of pleasure, he falls even into the night of the most wicked deed. We must therefore keep watch attentively, so that when guilt begins to flatter us, we recognize toward what destruction the mind is being dragged. Hence it is aptly added:

### CHAPTER XIV

**Verse 4.** “Let that day be turned into darkness.”

### 26. The beginning of delight must be chastened by the lamentations of repentance

The day is turned into darkness when guilt is perceived, at the very beginning of pleasure, to what end of destruction it is carrying us. We turn the day into darkness when, punishing ourselves strictly, we torment the very allurements of wicked pleasure through the severe lamentations of repentance, grieving over whatever we silently sin through delight in our hearts.

Since every faithful person knows that thoughts will be examined with precision at the judgment, as Paul testifies: “Their thoughts accusing or even defending them among themselves” (Romans 2:15), he examines himself inwardly and scrutinizes himself intensely before the judgment. Thus the strict Judge may come all the more peacefully because he sees that the guilt which he wishes to examine has already been punished for the offense. [Note: The Rheims and Remigius manuscripts, followed by the Norman manuscripts, read *quo reum suum*, “because he sees that his accused person,” rather than *reatum suum*, “his guilt.”]

Hence it is rightly added:

### CHAPTER XV [Old Translation XVIII; Revised Translation XVI]

**The same passage.** “Let God not seek it from above.”

### 27. So that he may not be punished by God at the judgment

God seeks what he examines in judgment; he does not seek what, by forgiving it, he leaves unpunished in his own judgment. This day, therefore—that is, this delight of sin—will not be sought by the Lord if it is punished through voluntary correction, as Paul testifies: “If we judged ourselves, we would not be judged by the Lord” (1 Corinthians 11:31).

For God to seek our day means to investigate with precision, in judgment, everything in our mind that rejoices in guilt. [Note: Here we follow the manuscripts rather than the very corrupt old and recent editions. Coccius and later editors read *omne quod de culpa gratulamur admissum*, “everything committed in guilt over which we rejoice”; the Paris edition of 1495, the Basel edition of 1514, and the Paris edition of 1518 read *omne quod de culpa gratulare admissum*. The manuscripts correct this with broad agreement. Moreover, *quod de culpa gratulatur* means the same as “what is pleasing on account of sin.”] In that investigation he strikes more severely the one whom he discovers to have spared himself more gently in the present.

It is rightly followed by: “And let it not be illumined by light.” When the Lord appears in judgment, he illumines with light everything he then reproves. Whatever is not then recalled to the Judge’s memory is, as it were, concealed beneath a certain obscurity.
