For it is written: “Everything that is reproved is made manifest by the light” (Ephesians 5:13). The sins of penitents are hidden by a kind of darkness, of which the prophet says: “Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven and whose sins are covered” (Psalm 31:1).

Since everything that is covered is concealed, as it were, in darkness, what is not examined with punishment will not be illumined by light on the day of the final judgment. Divine mercy, knowing in some way the deeds which it does not then wish to punish justly, hides them from itself. Whatever is displayed before everyone at that time is shown in the light.

Let this day therefore be turned into darkness, so that we may punish through repentance everything we do wrong. Let the Lord not seek this day and not illumine it with light, so that when we ourselves punish our guilt, he may not rebuke it through the judgment of the last day.

### 28. The penitent alone finds a place in which to hide from God the Judge

The Judge himself will come, penetrating and examining everything. Since he is everywhere, there is no place to which one can flee.

But because he is appeased by the tears of our correction, the only person who finds a place of escape from him is the one who, after committing guilt, now hides himself before him in repentance. [Note: The word *ei*, “before him,” omitted in other editions, has been restored from Corb. Germ., Compendium, Rheims, Remigius, and other manuscripts.] Hence it is aptly added concerning this day of delight:

### CHAPTER XVI [Revised Translation XVII]

**Verse 5.** “Let darkness and the shadow of death obscure it.”

### 29. God’s hidden judgments are a kind of darkness

Darkness obscures the day when the lamentations inflicted by repentance pierce through the delight of the mind. Darkness may also signify hidden judgments. In light we recognize what we see; in darkness we either see nothing at all or are confused by uncertain vision.

Hidden judgments are therefore like a kind of darkness before our eyes, because they cannot be scrutinized. Hence it is written of God: “He made darkness his hiding place” (Psalm 17:12).

We recognize that we do not deserve to be absolved, but through divine grace going before us we are liberated by his hidden judgments. Darkness therefore obscures the day when the inscrutable judgments of God mercifully conceal, from the ray of his just judgment, the joy of our delight that ought to be mourned.

It is aptly added: “And the shadow of death.”

### 30. In Scripture the shadow of death is understood in three ways

In Sacred Scripture, “the shadow of death” sometimes means forgetfulness of the mind, sometimes imitation of the devil, and sometimes bodily death.

The shadow of death means forgetfulness of the mind because, as we said above, just as death causes what it kills not to be in life, so forgetfulness causes what it interrupts not to be in memory. Hence, since John came to preach to the Hebrew people the God whom they had forgotten, it is said through Zechariah: “To enlighten those who sit in darkness and in the shadow of death” (Luke 1:79).

To sit in the shadow of death is to grow weary in forgetfulness of the knowledge of divine love. [Note: Coccius and the later editions read “to hide in forgetfulness.” The older editions, as nearly all the manuscripts, have “to grow weary.” Belvacensis has “to languish.”]

The shadow of death also means imitation of the ancient enemy. Since he inflicted death, he is called Death, as John testifies: “His name was Death” (Revelation 6:8). His imitation is therefore signified by the shadow of death; for just as a shadow is formed according to the shape of a body, so the actions of the wicked are expressed according to the appearance of imitation of him.

Hence Isaiah rightly, when he saw the Gentile peoples failing through imitation of the ancient enemy and rising again toward the rising of the true sun—a future event which he regards with certainty—speaks as though of the past, saying: “Upon those sitting in darkness and in the shadow of death, light has risen” (Isaiah 9:2). [Note: All the manuscripts, Corb. Germ., and the old edition have this reading. Gilot, the Roman edition of Sixtus V, and Gussanville read: “from the ancient enemy,” and so forth.]

The shadow of death also means bodily death, because just as true death is the separation of the soul from God, so the shadow of death is the separation of the flesh from the soul. Hence the voice of the martyrs rightly says through the prophet: “You humbled us in the place of affliction, and the shadow of death covered us” (Psalm 43:20). Since it is clear that they die not in spirit but only in the flesh, they say that they are covered not by true death but by its shadow.

### 31. By one death Christ destroyed the twofold death of humanity

What, then, does blessed Job mean when, in order to obscure the day of wicked delight, he asks for the shadow of death, unless that he seeks, for the destruction of sins before the eyes of God, the mediator of God and humanity, who would undergo bodily death alone for us and destroy the true death of sinners through the shadow of his death? [Note: All the Rheims, Remigius, Corb. Germ., Belvacensis, Ebroicensis, and other manuscripts, as well as the old editions, read “the day of wicked delight”; other editions read “the day of wicked love.”]

He came to us, who were held in the death of both spirit and flesh. He brought his one death to us and released us from the two deaths which he found in us. If he had taken upon himself both deaths, he would have freed us from neither. But he mercifully accepted one and justly condemned both. He brought his single death to our double death, and by dying subdued our double death.

Hence he rightly lay in the tomb for one day and two nights, because he joined the light of his single death to the darkness of our double death. He therefore accepted only bodily death for us, bore the shadow of death, and hid from the eyes of God the guilt we had committed.

Let it therefore rightly be said: “Let darkness and the shadow of death obscure it.” It is as though it were plainly said: “Let him come who, in order to rescue those liable to the death of flesh and spirit, pays a bodily death which he did not owe.”

But since the Lord leaves no sin unpunished—for either we pursue it with tears or he judges it—it remains necessary for the mind always to watch attentively over its correction. [Note: Except for the older editions, the printed editions read “or he reserves it for judgment”; *reserves* is superfluous and absent from all the manuscripts.] Whatever each person recognizes that he is mercifully aided in, he must necessarily wipe away by confession. [Note: This follows Corb. Germ., Vindobonensis, Vallicellian, Rheims, Remigius, Compendium, the first Roman Paris edition of 1495, and other early editions; later editions read *desiderat*, “desires,” instead of *considerat*, “recognizes.”]

Hence it is aptly added:

### CHAPTER XVII

**The same passage.** “Let gloom seize it.”

### 32. The salutary gloom of the penitent mind

Because the eye is confused in gloom, the confusion of our mind through repentance is itself called gloom. For just as a cloudy darkness obscures the day, so confusion clouds the mind with troubled thoughts.

Of this it is said by a certain wise man: “There is a confusion that brings glory” (Ecclesiasticus 4:25). When, through repentance, we bring our evil deeds back before the mind, we are immediately confounded by deep grief. A crowd of thoughts resounds within; sorrow crushes, anxiety devastates, the mind is turned into misery, and is darkened as though by a certain cloud of gloom.

This gloom of confusion had beneficially oppressed the minds of those to whom Paul said: “What fruit did you have then in those things of which you are now ashamed?” (Romans 6:21).

Let this gloom therefore seize the day of sin: that is, let the pleasure of wickedness be disturbed by the fitting grief of repentance. Hence it is aptly added:

### CHAPTER XVIII

**The same passage.** “Let it be wrapped in bitterness.”

### 33. Salutary grief over wicked delight

The day is wrapped in bitterness when, as the mind returns to knowledge, the allurements of sin are followed by the torments of repentance. We wrap the day in bitterness when we perceive what punishments follow the joy of wicked delight and surround it with bitter tears.

Since what is wrapped is covered on every side, the day is desired to be wrapped in bitterness so that each person may see from every side what evils threaten the uncorrected, and may cleanse the wantonness of pleasure with lamentations of sadness.

### 34. How much greater repentance ought to be for consent to guilt

But if we have heard that the day—which we called the pleasure of sin—was assailed with so many prayers that the tears surrounding it might atone for whatever the negligent soul commits in its delight, with how much greater penitential severity must the night of this day be struck—namely, consent itself to guilt? For just as it is a lesser fault when the mind is carried away bodily into pleasure but nevertheless resists its pleasure through the spirit, so it is a graver and complete wickedness to be drawn not only by pleasure toward the allure of sin, but also to serve it through consent. Therefore, the more foully the mind sees itself defiled through consent, the more tightly it must be cleansed from pollution by the hand of repentance. [Some witnesses read: “by a harsher hand.”]

Hence it is aptly added:

## CHAPTER XIX

**VERSE 6.—“Let a dark whirlwind possess that night.”**

[Col. 0654D]

### 35. The force of contrition

For the stirred spirit of sorrow is, as it were, a certain whirlwind of storm. When each person understands the sin he has committed, and carefully weighs the wickedness of his depravity, he clouds his mind with sorrow and, as though the air of serene joy had been shaken, lays waste to all the heart’s tranquility in the whirlwind of repentance. Unless this whirlwind crushed the soul as it recognized itself, the Prophet would never have said: “With a vehement spirit you will crush the ships of Tarshish” (Ps. 47:8).

For *Tarshish* is said to mean “the exploration of joy.” [Ancient XXII.] But when the vehement spirit of repentance seizes the mind, it disturbs within it every exploration of blameworthy joy, so that it now wishes to do nothing but weep, and attends to nothing except what can terrify it. It sets before its eyes, on one side, the strictness of justice and, on the other, the deserts of guilt. It sees what punishment it deserves if the mercy of the One who spares is absent—the mercy that commonly rescues it from eternal punishment through present lamentation.

Thus the vehement spirit crushes the ships of Tarshish when the powerful force of contrition confounds our minds, which are given over to this world as to the sea, with salutary terror. Let him therefore say: “Let a dark whirlwind possess that night”—that is, let not the perpetration of guilt be cherished by the blandishments of secure repose; rather, let the bitterness of repentance, raging with holy purpose, break in.

### 36. What it means to possess the night and to be possessed by the night

It must be understood that when we leave sins unpunished, we are possessed by the night; but when we chastise them with the severity of repentance, we certainly possess the night that we ourselves have made. Yet the sin of the heart is brought under the possession of our authority only if it is restrained when it begins.

Hence, by the divine voice, Cain is told while he is conceiving evil thoughts: “Your sin will be at the door, but its desire will be beneath you, and you will rule over it” (Gen. 4:7). Sin is at the door when it knocks upon the thoughts. Its desire is beneath the person, and the person rules it, if, once the wickedness of the heart has been examined, it is quickly pressed down and, before it grows into hardness, is subdued by a resisting mind.

Therefore, so that the soul may sense its offense more quickly and, through repentance, restrain the tyranny of guilt under its own authority, let it rightly be said: “Let a dark whirlwind possess that night.” It is as though it were said openly: Let the captive mind not serve guilt; let it not leave guilt free from repentance.

And because we confidently hope that what we pursue with weeping will certainly not be brought against us by the Judge who is to come, it is rightly added:

## CHAPTER XX [Revised XVIII]

**THE SAME—“Let it not be counted among the days of the year, nor numbered among the months.”**

[Col. 0655D]

### 37. We must ask God that the evils we have committed not be brought against us in judgment

The year of our illumination is completed when, with the eternal Judge revealed, the life of the holy Church’s pilgrimage is brought to its completion. It then receives the reward of its labor, when, this time of warfare having ended, it returns to its homeland. Hence the Prophet rightly says: “You will bless the crown of the year with your goodness” (Ps. 64:12). The crown of the year is, as it were, blessed when, the time of labor having ended, the reward of virtues is bestowed.

The days of this year are each of the virtues; its months are the manifold deeds of the virtues. But behold: when the mind is lifted up through confidence, hoping that, when the Judge comes, it will be rewarded for its virtues, the evils it has committed also come to its memory. It greatly fears that the strict Judge who comes to reward virtues may, examining what was unlawfully done, weigh it with exactness—lest, when he completes the year, he also count the night.

Let him therefore speak concerning this night: “Let it not be counted among the days of the year, nor numbered among the months.” It is as though he were beseeching the strict Judge, saying: When, at the completion of the time of the holy Church, you reveal yourself in the final examination, reward the gifts you have bestowed in such a way that you do not seek out the evils we have committed.

For if that night is counted among the days of the year, everything we have done is thrown into confusion by the reckoning of our depravity. And the days of virtue no longer shine if, in your sight, the dark confusion of our night obscures them throughout the year [the transmitted text here is materially corrupt: *eratanostrae*].

[Ancient XXIII.]

### 38. For this reason we must leave nothing unpunished

But if we do not then wish to be troubled by an inquiry into our night [Utic. and other Norman witnesses: “then we do not wish to be examined”], we must now take the greatest care to keep watch over ourselves in its investigation, lest any guilt remain unpunished for us, lest the perverse mind dare to defend what it has done and, by defending it, add wickedness to wickedness.

Hence it is rightly added:

## CHAPTER XXI [Revised XIX]

**VERSE 7.—“Let that night be solitary, and not worthy of praise.”**

### 39. We must not magnify anything by making excuses

There are some who not only do not grieve at all over what they do, but also do not cease to praise and defend it. And surely, when guilt is defended, it is doubled. Against this it is rightly said through a certain writer: “You have sinned; do not add again” (Ecclus. 21:1). For one adds sin to sin who also defends evil deeds; and he does not leave the night solitary who adds to the darkness of his guilt the protections of defense.

Thus the first man, when questioned concerning the night of his error, did not wish that same night to be solitary. For when he was summoned to repentance by the questioning, he added supports for his excuse, saying: “The woman whom you gave me as a companion gave me from the tree, and I ate” (Gen. 3:12) [“as a companion” is not read in Corb. Germ., Vindoc., and the ancient Rhem.]. He was secretly turning the fault of his transgression back upon its author, as though he were saying: “You provided the occasion for sinning, since you gave me the woman.”

This is why the branch of that error is still drawn out from that root in the human race, so that what is wrongly done is still defended. Let him therefore say: “Let that night be solitary, and not worthy of praise.” It is as though he were openly beseeching, saying: Let the guilt we have committed remain alone, lest, while it is praised and defended, it bind us more severely in the sight of our Judge.

We ought indeed not to have sinned; but would that, joining nothing else to our sins, we might at least leave alone the things we have done.

### 40. The person who tramples worldly prosperity truly pursues his guilt

But in all this it must be understood that the person who truly pursues his guilt is the one who is no longer stirred by any desire for the prosperity of the present world; who considers how deceptive are the blandishments of this world, and reckons its favors as a kind of persecution.

Hence it is rightly added:

## CHAPTER XXII [Revised XX]

**VERSE 8.—“Let those who curse the day curse it.”**

### 41. The person who detects the deceiver’s ambush in the very suggestion punishes past sins

It is as though he openly said: Let those truly strike the darkness of this night through repentance who, now despising the light of worldly prosperity, trample it underfoot. For if we understand the day as the joy of pleasure, it is rightly said of this night: “Let those who curse the day curse it,” because those truly correct past evils through the severity of repentance who are no longer carried away by any pleasure toward deceptive goods.

For when other harmful things still please them, it is false that they are seen to lament other sins they have committed.

But if, as was said above, we understand the cunning suggestion of the ancient enemy, they are to be understood as cursing the night who curse the day. For those who abhor the suggestion and pleasure of sin much more abhor consent. [The ancient edition: “But if also the day mentioned above…” In Cocc., Vatic., Gilot., and Guss. the worse reading is *the night of suggestion*. For Saint Gregory, both in section 7 and in section 24, and elsewhere, understands by “day” the devil’s suggestion and the pleasure of sin supplied by him; never by “night,” which he wants to signify consent to sin and the darkness arising from it. Once this is established, he speaks consistently here when he says that the one who curses the day also curses the night: whoever abhors the suggestion and pleasure of sin much more abhors consent. Our reading is found in the manuscripts Corb. Germ., ancient Rhem., two Remig., Turon., Vindoc., and Norman witnesses, followed by the old editions.]

This is rightly added:

## CHAPTER XXIII [Ancient XXIV, Revised XXI]

[Col. 0657B]

**THE SAME—“Who are ready to arouse Leviathan.”**

### 42. Those who despise his tyranny arouse the devil against themselves

All who trample underfoot the things of the world in their minds and desire the things of God with complete purpose arouse Leviathan against themselves, because they inflame his malice by the provocation of their manner of life. For those who are subject to his will are possessed by him as though by an undisturbed right, and their proud king enjoys a kind of security while he rules their hearts with unshaken power.

But when a person’s spirit grows warm with desire for its Creator, when it abandons the torpor of negligence and kindles the coldness of its former insensibility with the fire of holy love; when it remembers its inborn freedom and is ashamed to remain a slave held by the enemy—because that same enemy sees himself despised, because he sees the ways of God being embraced—he grieves that his captive is resisting him. At once he is inflamed with zeal; at once he is moved to battle; at once he rouses himself to innumerable temptations against the rebellious mind; and by every art of tearing he incites himself, so that, hurling the darts of temptation, he may pierce the heart that he had previously possessed by undisturbed right.

He was, as it were, sleeping when, lulled to rest in the wicked heart, he remained quiet; but he is awakened for the provocation of battle when he has lost the right of perverse domination.

Let them therefore curse this night who are ready to arouse Leviathan—that is, let those rise up against sin with the strong judgment of strictness who are not afraid to arouse the ancient adversary through his temptations [Gilot., Vatic., and Guss., following Cocc.: “in the judgment”].

For it is written: “My son, when you approach the service of God, stand in justice and fear, and prepare your soul for temptation” (Ecclus. 2:1). Whoever hastens to gird himself for divine service prepares himself for what else but battle against the ancient adversary, so that, free in battle, he may receive blows—the person who had served quietly in captivity under tyranny? [So Corb. Germ. and all our manuscripts, followed by the old editions. Others read: “under the tyrant.”]

But in the very fact that the mind girds itself against the enemy, subdues some vices and resists others, it sometimes permits something of guilt to remain—something that nevertheless does not greatly harm.

### 43. For the sake of humility, God permits one who has subdued many serious vices not to conquer one small vice

Often the mind that overcomes many adverse and powerful things does not conquer one thing within itself, perhaps a very small one, although it watches over it with great determination. This is undoubtedly brought about by divine providence, lest, shining with virtues on every side, it be lifted up in pride. Thus, when it sees in itself something small that is blameworthy, yet is unable to subdue it, it attributes the victory not to itself but to its Creator in those matters which it is able to conquer with strength.

Hence it is rightly added:

## CHAPTER XXIV [Revised XXII]

**VERSE 9.—“Let the stars be darkened by its gloom.”**

[Col. 0658B]

### 44. Thus those who are stars are darkened by a certain gloom

The stars of this night are darkened when even those who already shine with great virtues continue to endure some resistance from the darkness of guilt, so that they shine with the great brightness of their life and yet, unwillingly, still drag along the remnants of night.

This happens, as has been said, so that the mind advancing toward the virtue of justice may be strengthened more effectively through weakness; and so that it may shine more truly in good works precisely because small blameworthy things, even against its will, humbly darken it.

Hence, when the land of promise was apportioned to the Israelite people, it is rightly said that the gentile people of Canaan were not killed but made tributary to the tribe of Ephraim, as it is written: “The Canaanite dwelt in the midst of Ephraim as a tributary” (Josh. 16:10).

For what does the Canaanite, that is, the gentile people, signify if not vice? And often we enter the land of promise through great virtues, because we are strengthened by an inward hope of eternity. [Ancient XXV.] But while we retain certain small vices amid sublime deeds, we permit, as it were, the Canaanite to live in our land [one Remig.: “among the subdued and exalted things”].

Yet he is made tributary, because we humbly turn to our own advantage the very vice that we cannot subdue, so that the mind may judge itself lowly even in high matters because, by its own strength, it cannot conquer even the small things it desires [the editions prefix “for us,” which is absent from all our manuscripts].

Hence it is again rightly written: “These are the nations that the Lord left, so that he might instruct Israel through them” (Judg. 3:1). For this is why certain very small vices are retained in us: so that our purpose may continually exercise itself anxiously in the struggle, and may not grow proud of victory precisely because it sees enemies living within it, enemies by whom it still fears to be conquered. Israel is therefore instructed through the nations left behind when the elation of our virtue is restrained by certain small vices, and, in the face of small things resisting it, learns that it does not subdue greater things by its own power. [Some witnesses read *quod in se*, “that it does not subdue greater things within itself,” for *quod ex se*, “by itself.”]

[Col. 0659A]

### 45. No one in this life, however brightly he shines in holiness, can see God as he is

Yet the statement, “Let the stars be darkened by its gloom,” can also be understood in another way. For that night—namely, consent to guilt, which has been transmitted to us through the transgression of our first parent—struck the eye of our mind with such darkness that, in the exile of this life, pressed by the shadows of its blindness, it cannot penetrate, however forcefully it may direct itself toward the light of eternity. [In the editions: “so that every human being in this…” We have removed “every human being,” in accordance with all the manuscripts; with that reading rejected, the sense remains complete, and “pressed” refers to the eye.]

For we are born as sinners under the penalty of condemnation, and we come into this life bearing the desert of our death. When we lift the eye of the mind toward the ray of heavenly light, we are darkened by the very obscurity of our weakness.

Many indeed have been strengthened by such virtue in this weakness of the flesh that they could shine in the world like stars. Many, while exhibiting in the darkness of the present life examples of what is above, shine down upon us like the stars. But however brightly they may gleam through their works, however much they may kindle themselves with the fire of contrition, it is nevertheless certain that, while they are still weighed down by corruptible flesh, they cannot see the eternal light as it is.

Let him therefore say: “Let the stars be darkened by its gloom”—that is, let even those who, in the contemplation of their minds, already spread the rays of their virtues over the human race in the darkness of this life still feel the darkness of the ancient night. For although their minds already leap toward the heights, they are nevertheless still weighed down in lowly things by the burden of their first guilt.

Thus it happens that they offer outward examples of light like stars, but inwardly, pressed down by the gloom of night, they do not rise to the certainty of fixed vision.

Often the mind is so kindled that, although it is placed in the flesh, it is nevertheless carried away wholly subjecting every carnal thought to God; yet it does not see God as he is, because, as has been said, the weight of the first condemnation presses it down in corruptible flesh.

Often it desires to be absorbed as it is, so that, if it could happen, it might attain eternal life without the intervention of bodily death. Hence Paul, ardently seeking the inner light but nevertheless fearing in some measure the losses of outward death, says: “As long as we are in this dwelling, we groan, being burdened, because we do not wish to be unclothed but clothed over, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life” (2 Cor. 5:4). [Ancient XXVI.] [Nearly all manuscripts read “as long as we are”; Corb. Germ. has “while we are.”]

Holy men therefore long to see the true morning, and, if it is granted, wish to reach even in the body that hidden place of inner light. But however greatly they may leap forth in the ardor of their purpose, the ancient night still weighs upon them; and the just Judge presses down from the sight of his inward splendor the eyes of this corruptible flesh—the eyes which the cunning enemy opened to concupiscence.

Hence it is rightly added:

## CHAPTER XXV [Revised XXIII]

[Col. 0660A]

**THE SAME—“Let it await the light, and not see it, nor the rising of the dawn.”**

### 46. The rising of dawn is the brightness of inward truth

For however earnestly the still-exiled mind strives to see the light as it is, it cannot, because the blindness of its condemnation hides it from it.

(The rising of dawn, however, is the brightness of inward truth, which ought always to be new for us. The night certainly does not see it, because our weak nature, blinded through guilt and still placed in corruptible flesh, does not rise to that light which already illumines the citizens above. This dawn rises within, where the brightness of the Godhead is always newly revealed to the spirits of the angels; and, as it were, the joy of light continually arises—a joy that never ends.) [These words, from “the rising, however” through “which never ends,” enclosed here in parentheses, are absent from the manuscripts and from all editions except Guss., who does not indicate where he found them.]

The rising of dawn, however, is that new birth of the resurrection by which the holy Church, raised even in the flesh, arises to contemplate the light of eternity. For if the resurrection of our flesh were not, as it were, a certain birth, Truth would not have said of it: “In the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty” (Matt. 19:28; Luke 22:69). He therefore saw this as a rising, which he called regeneration.

But however greatly the elect now shine through virtue, they cannot penetrate what will be the glory of that new birth by which they will then ascend with the flesh to contemplate the light of eternity. Hence Paul says: “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart, what God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Cor. 2:9).

Let him therefore say: “Let it await the light, and not see it, nor the rising of the dawn,” because our weakness, darkened by spontaneous fault, does not penetrate the brightness of the inward light unless it first pays the debt of its punishment through death.

It follows:

## CHAPTER XXVI [Revised XXIV]

**VERSE 10.—“Because he did not shut the doors of the womb that bore me, nor remove evils from my eyes.”**

### 47. Our consent opened the doors of concupiscence, from which innumerable evils arose

As was also said above, “he did not shut” means “he opened,” and “he did not remove” means “he inflicted.” This night, therefore—that is, guilt—opened the doors of the womb, because, once the desire for sin had been conceived, it opened the desires of concupiscence to the human being.

The doors of the womb are the desires of concupiscence, concerning which the Prophet says: “Enter into your chambers; shut your doors” (Isa. 26:20). We enter our chambers when we enter the secrets of our mind. We shut the doors when we restrain unlawful desires.

When our consent opened these doors of carnal concupiscence, it dragged us into countless evils of corruption. Hence we now groan under the burden of mortality, although we came to this condition by our own free choice [the editions add “carnal”; the word is absent from Corb. Germ. and the other manuscripts consulted. In Lyranus, *reservavit* occurs instead of *reseravit*. Vindoc. differs more substantially: “because concupiscence opened the desires of the person conceived for sin”].

For the justice of judgment requires that we unwillingly endure what we willingly did [The printed editions read “even” for “now,” and shortly afterward “to this [condition]” for “to this [end].” Corb. Germ.: “we did not come”; this is scarcely acceptable, since the holy Doctor is speaking here of the corruptions to which our consent opened the door].

It follows:

## CHAPTER XXVII

**VERSES 11–12.—“Why did I not die in the womb? Why, having come forth from the womb, did I not immediately perish? Why was I received upon the knees? Why was I suckled at the breasts?”**

### 48. What is to be understood in Job’s words when he wishes himself an abortion

Far be it from us to believe that blessed Job, endowed with such knowledge of the spirit and praised by the testimony of the inward Judge, desired to die as an aborted child. But since, as is also known from the reward he receives, he possesses within himself a witness to his strength, the weight of his words must be considered inwardly.

[Ancient XXVII; Revised XXV.]

### 49. Sin is completed in the heart in four ways or stages, and likewise in action

Sin is perpetrated in the heart in four ways and completed in action in four ways. In the heart it is perpetrated through suggestion, pleasure, consent, and the audacity of defense. Suggestion comes through the adversary, pleasure through the flesh, consent through the spirit, and the audacity of defense through pride. Guilt, which ought to have terrified the mind, lifts it up; and by casting it down, it raises it, but by raising it, it overthrows it more gravely.

Thus the ancient enemy shattered the uprightness of the first human being with these four blows. The serpent suggested; Eve took pleasure; Adam consented; and, when questioned, he refused through audacity to confess his guilt.

The same thing happens daily in the human race, which is known to have happened in the first parent of our race. The serpent suggested, because the hidden enemy secretly suggests evil to human hearts. Eve took pleasure, because the carnal sense immediately submits itself to pleasure at the serpent’s words. Adam, placed over the woman, gave consent, because, when the flesh is carried away into pleasure, the spirit too, weakened from its uprightness, is bent downward. Adam refused to confess his guilt when questioned, because the spirit, by sinning, is separated from the truth and, in the audacity of its ruin, is hardened into greater wickedness.

Sin is likewise completed in action in four ways. First, the hidden guilt is committed; afterward the offense is disclosed before the eyes of human beings without shame; then it is made habitual; and finally it is nourished either by the seductions of false hope or by the wretched obstinacy of despair.

### 50. Job laments these four ways of sinning in the heart

Blessed Job considers these ways of sin—the ways that occur secretly in the heart or are openly perpetrated in action—and laments the stages of sin into which the human race has fallen, saying: “Why did I not die in the womb? Why, having come forth from the womb, did I not immediately perish? Why was I received upon the knees? Why was I suckled at the breasts?”

The first womb of conception was the tongue of evil suggestion. But the sinner would die in the womb if a person recognized, in the very suggestion, that he was going to die. He nevertheless came forth from the womb, because, after the tongue suggesting sin had conceived him, pleasure immediately carried him outward as well.

After coming forth, he was received upon the knees, because, when he emerged into the pleasure of the flesh, he completed his guilt through the consent of the spirit, with all the senses subjected, as though upon bent knees.

But after being received upon the knees, he was also suckled at the breasts. For, once the senses of the spirit had been given over to consent in guilt, many arguments of empty confidence followed, nourishing the soul born in sin with poisonous milk and comforting it with flattering excuses so that it would not fear the harsh punishments of death.

[Ancient XXVIII.] Hence the first man, after his guilt, became more audacious, saying: “The woman whom you gave me as a companion herself gave me from the tree, and I ate” (Gen. 3:12) [The manuscripts Rhem., Corb. Germ., and Vindoc. present this passage here in the same form noted above in section 39.]

He had fled in fear to hide himself, but when questioned he revealed how much he still swelled with pride even while afraid. For when the present punishment of sin is feared, and God’s lost countenance is not loved, the fear arises from swelling pride, not from humility. The person who would not abandon sin if he could escape punishment is proud.

### 51. He laments and prays concerning the four ways in which human beings sin in action

But in these four ways, as has been said, guilt is perpetrated in action just as it is conceived in the heart.

He says: “Why did I not die in the womb?” The womb of the sinner is the hidden guilt of a human being, which secretly conceives the sinner and still hides his offense in darkness.

“Having come forth from the womb, why did I not immediately perish?” We come forth from the womb when the sinner is no longer ashamed to commit openly what he had committed secretly. For those deeds of which the Prophet said, “They proclaimed their sin as Sodom, and did not hide it” (Isa. 3:9), had, as it were, emerged from the womb of their concealment.

“Why was I received upon the knees?” Because when the sinner is no longer ashamed of his wickedness, he is strengthened in that same wickedness by the supports of the worst habit. The sinner is, as it were, fostered upon knees so that he may grow, when guilt is strengthened by habits so that it may thrive.

“Why was I suckled at the breasts?” Because when guilt begins to emerge into habitual practice, it nourishes itself either with the false hope of divine mercy or with the manifest misery of despair, so that it does not return to correction—either because it improperly imagines its Maker to be merciful toward it, or because it improperly fears what it has done.

Blessed Job therefore should behold the fall of the human race and consider into what precipices it has been plunged into the pit of iniquity, saying: “Why did I not die in the womb?” That is: In the very hidden perpetration of sin, why did I not choose to be put to death with respect to the life of the flesh?

“Having come forth from the womb, why did I not immediately perish?” That is: After I came forth into open iniquity, why did I not then at least recognize myself as lost? For he would have perished in his own judgment if he had recognized himself as lost.

“Why was I received upon the knees?” That is: Even after open guilt, why did habit still receive me into it, so as to make me stronger for wickedness and, sustaining me through evil practices, foster me?

“Why was I suckled at the breasts?” That is: After I came into the habit of guilt, why did I nourish myself toward more atrocious wickedness either with the confidence of false hope or with the milk of wretched despair?

For when guilt has become habitual, the mind resists it less weakly even if it desires to resist, because, as it is bound by however many repetitions of evil practice, it is tied to the mind by, as it were, so many bonds.

[Ancient XXIX.] Hence it happens that the enfeebled mind, when it cannot free itself, turns toward certain consolations of false comfort, promising itself that the Judge who is to come will show it such great mercy that he will not utterly destroy even those whom he finds deserving of accusation.

This becomes worse for it because the speech of many like-minded people agrees with it, when many even magnify evil deeds with praise. Thus guilt continually grows, nourished by favor. A wound that appears worthy of the reward of praise is neglected instead of being cured.

Hence Solomon rightly says: “My son, if sinners entice you, do not consent to them” (Prov. 1:10). Sinners suckle people when they either introduce evils to be committed with flatteries or exalt evils already committed with approval.

Are they not being suckled of whom the Psalmist says: “For the sinner is praised in the desires of his soul, and the one who commits iniquity is blessed” [In Colb. the following is added after “is blessed”: “The sin nourished by the tongues of the wicked is difficult to amend.” Guss. inserted these words into his edition, although they disrupt the sequence of the sentence and are absent from all other manuscripts and printed editions] (Ps. 9:24)?

### 52. The fourth stage of sin is more difficult to correct

It must also be understood that the first three ways of sinners, in accordance with the order of their descent, are more easily corrected; this fourth one, however, is corrected with greater difficulty.

Hence our Redeemer raises a girl in the house, a young man outside the gate, and Lazarus in the tomb. The person who lies dead in sin while still hidden is dead in the house. The person whose iniquity is disclosed even to the shamelessness of public perpetration is, as it were, led outside the gate. But the person who, in the perpetration of wickedness, is also weighed down by the pressure of habit, is crushed beneath the mound of burial.

Yet he mercifully calls these back to life, because divine grace often illumines with the light of its visitation not only those dead in hidden iniquities but also those dead in open iniquities and pressed down by the weight of evil habit.

Our Redeemer, however, recognizes the fourth dead person when a disciple announces him, yet does not raise him, because it is exceedingly difficult for one whom, after the practice of evil habit, the tongues of flatterers also receive, to be recalled from the death of his mind.

Concerning this it is rightly said: “Let the dead bury their dead” (Luke 9:60) [Most manuscripts read, “Leave the dead to bury their dead”; Compend. and Val. Cl. read, “Leave the dead, that they may bury their dead”; this was formerly the reading in Utic.]. The dead bury the dead when sinners oppress a sinner with their approval.

For what else is it to sin than to fall dead, and what else is it to bury than to conceal? [Barthol.: “For what else is it to bury than to conceal? But those…” Other old editions, with the manuscripts Reg., have *occumbere* (“to fall dead”) instead of *occulere* (“to conceal”). In other manuscripts the phrase “than to bury” is omitted. The printed form is owed to Cocc.]

But those who pursue a sinner with praise hide the dead person beneath the mound of their words.

Lazarus too was dead, but he was not buried by the dead. Faithful women had buried him, and they announced his death to the one who gives life. Hence he immediately returned to the light, because when the soul dies in sin, it is brought back to life more quickly if solicitous thoughts live over it.

Sometimes, however, as was also said above, false hope does not seize the mind; rather, a worse despair pierces it. By utterly destroying all hope of forgiveness, despair nourishes the soul more abundantly with the milk of error.

[Col. 0664D]

[Ancient XXX; Revised XXVI.]

### 53. Job laments that he sinned in the first human being and mourns the hardships of that sin

Let the holy man therefore consider how many worse evils the human being committed after the first guilt; how far he descended, after losing paradise, into the precipitous places of this exile; and let him say:

“Why did I not die in the womb?” That is: When the serpent’s suggestion was conceiving me as a sinner, would that I had then recognized the death that would follow me, so that the suggestion would not carry me as far as pleasure and bind me more tightly to death.

“Having come forth from the womb, why did I not immediately perish?” It is as though he said: Would that, coming forth into outward pleasure, I had recognized that I was being deprived of the inner light; and at least would that I had fallen dead in that very pleasure, so that death would not punish me more severely through consent.

“Why was I received upon the knees?” It is as though he said: Would that consent had not received me, with my senses subjected to wickedness [Vindoc.: “received me with my senses subjected to wickedness”], so that that very consent would not carry me more disastrously into audacity.

“Why was I suckled at the breasts?” It is as though he said: Would that, after perpetrating evil, I had not wished to flatter myself, so that I would not bind myself more wickedly to guilt by fostering myself more tenderly in it.

With these words of self-reproach he declares that he sinned in the first parent. But if the human being had not descended through sin into the hardship of this exile, let him say what peace he could have enjoyed.

It follows:

## CHAPTER XXVIII

[Col. 0664C]

**VERSE 13.—“For now, sleeping, I would be silent, and in my sleep I would rest.”**
54. The first condition of humankind, from which it fell by sin. The quiet silence of the innocent human being.—For this purpose the human being had been placed in paradise: so that, if he bound himself to obedience toward his Creator by the bonds of love, he might eventually pass over to the heavenly homeland of the angels without the death of the flesh. For he was created immortal in such a way that, if he sinned, he could nevertheless die; and he was created mortal in such a way that, if he did not sin, he could nevertheless not die; and by the merit of free choice he might attain the blessedness of that region in which he could neither sin nor die. Therefore, where the elect now pass after the time of redemption, with the death of the flesh intervening, there beyond doubt our first parents, had they remained in the condition in which they were created, could also have been transferred without the death of their bodies.

Thus, while sleeping, the human being would have been silent, and in his sleep he would have rested, when he was led to the rest of the eternal homeland and found, as it were, a certain retreat from this clamor of human weakness. [Note: The manuscripts, by broad agreement, have *secessum quoddam* (“a certain retreat”) here and below, in the chapter formerly numbered 28, now 29, section 58.] For after sin the person who bears the struggle of his own flesh in resistance is, as it were, awake and crying out. This silence of rest belonged to the human being when he was created, when he received the free choice of the will against his enemy. But because he voluntarily surrendered to him, he immediately discovered in himself something that would clamor against him; immediately he encountered the tumult of weakness in the struggle. And although he had been created by his Maker in the peace of silence, once he had voluntarily subjected himself to the enemy, he endured the cries of battle.

For the prompting of the flesh itself is, as it were, a certain cry against the mind’s quiet, which the human being did not experience before the transgression; for he had nothing of weakness to endure. But after he voluntarily subjected himself to the enemy, bound by the chains of his guilt, he serves him in certain matters even against his will, and suffers cries within his mind when the flesh resists the spirit. Did he not hear inward cries who endured the words of the evil law against himself, saying: “I see another law in my members opposing the law of my mind and leading me captive under the law of sin which is in my members” (Rom. 7:23)?

Let the holy man, therefore, contemplate in how great a peace of heart he would have rested if the human being had refused to receive the serpent’s words, and let him say: “For now I would be sleeping in silence, and in my sleep I would be resting”—that is, “I would withdraw into the secret place of the mind for contemplation of the Creator, had the consent of the first sin not betrayed me outside myself amid the tumults of temptations.” [Note: One Remigius manuscript, together with one Regius manuscript, has: “I would not withdraw from contemplation of the Creator.”] And let him add with whom he would have enjoyed the delights of this rest, together with his companions, saying:

## CHAPTER XXIX [Formerly XXXI, Revised XXVII]

**VERSE 14.—With the kings and rulers of the earth.**

55. He would have been a companion of angelic joy. Who the kings and rulers are.—From things without sensation we learn what we should think about things endowed with sensation and things intelligible. For the earth is made fruitful by the air, while the air is ordered according to the condition of heaven. Thus human beings rule animals, angels rule human beings, and archangels rule angels. That human beings rule animals we both observe by ordinary experience and learn from the words of the Psalmist, who says: “You have subjected all things beneath his feet, all sheep and oxen, and moreover the beasts of the field” (Ps. 8:8). But that angels rule human beings is testified by the prophet through the angel who says: “The prince of the kingdom of the Persians resisted me” (Dan. 10:13). And that angels are administered by the powers of higher angels is declared by the prophet Zechariah, who says: “Behold, the angel who was speaking in me was going out; and another angel was going out to meet him, and said to him: Run, speak to that young man, saying: Jerusalem shall be inhabited without a wall” (Zech. 2:3).

For if the highest powers did not appoint the lesser ones to these offices of the holy spirits, the angel would in no way have learned from another angel what he should say to the human being. [Note: In the Norman manuscripts and some others: “an angel would report it to an angel.”] Since, therefore, the Creator of all things holds everything by himself, yet, in order to distinguish the beautiful order of the universe, governs some things through others who administer them, we rightly understand the spirits of the angels as kings: the more familiarly they serve the Author of all things, the more readily they rule what has been subjected to them.

Thus he would have slept with kings, because the human being would already have rested with the angels if he had not wished to follow the tongue of the tempter. They are also rightly called rulers, because they advise the spiritual commonwealth, joining us to themselves as companions in the kingdom. They are rightly called rulers because, while they announce the Creator’s will to us, we undoubtedly find in them counsel by which we are delivered from the narrowness of our tribulation.

**[Formerly XXXII.]** 56. Before Christ, the saints were detained in the underworld; now they seek heaven without delay. The holy preachers are kings and rulers.—But because blessed Job is filled with the holy spirit of eternity—and eternity has no “having been” or “being about to be,” since for it things past do not pass away and things future do not arrive, because it sees everything as present—he can contemplate in the presence of the spirit the future preachers of the Church, who, after departing from their bodies, are not delayed for intervals of waiting from attaining the heavenly homeland, as the ancient Fathers were.

For immediately upon leaving the bonds of the flesh they rest in the heavenly dwelling, as Paul testifies when he says: “We know that if our earthly house of this habitation is dissolved, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens” (2 Cor. 5:1).

Before our Redeemer, however, by his death, had paid the penalty of the human race, even those who had pursued the ways of the heavenly homeland were held, after departing from the flesh, within the prison of the underworld—not so that punishment might chastise them as sinners, but so that, while they rested in remote places, because the mediation of the Mediator had not yet arrived, the guilt of the first sin might prevent them from entering the kingdom. Hence, according to the testimony of that same Redeemer, the rich man who is tormented in the underworld sees Lazarus resting in Abraham’s bosom (Luke 16:19). If these were not still in the depths, the man placed in torment would certainly not see them there.

Therefore our same Redeemer, dying on account of the debt of our sin, enters the lower regions so that he may lead to the heavenly places his own who had clung to him. But to the place where redeemed humanity now ascends, humanity would certainly have reached even without redemption if it had not wished to sin.

Let the holy man therefore consider that, if he had not sinned, he would have ascended even without redemption to the place which the holy preachers must reach after redemption with great labor. And let him indicate with whom he would now be resting, saying: “With the kings and rulers of the earth” [Formerly XXXIII].

For the holy preachers of the Church are kings, who know both how rightly to administer those entrusted to them and how to govern their own bodies well. While they restrain within themselves the movements of desire, they reign over the thoughts subjected to them by the law of virtue.

They are also rightly called rulers of the earth. They are kings because they preside over themselves; they are rulers of the earth because, after sins have been extinguished, they provide counsel for life. They are kings because they know how to govern themselves; they are rulers of the earth because, through the counsel of their exhortation, they draw earthly minds toward heavenly things.

Was he not a ruler of the earth who said: “Concerning virgins I have no commandment of the Lord, but I give counsel” (1 Cor. 7:25)? And again: “She will be happier if she remains thus, according to my counsel” (ibid., 40). And rightly it is added:

## CHAPTER XXX [Revised XXVIII]

**THE SAME PASSAGE.—Who build solitudes for themselves.**

57. They carry within themselves a tumultuous crowd: the sensual, the angry, the greedy, the proud, and those enslaved to worldly cares.—All who either desire what is unlawful or wish to appear important in this world are hemmed in within their hearts by dense tumults of thought. While they stir up crowds of desires within themselves, they trample down the prostrate mind under the foot of miserable preoccupation.

One person has subjected himself to the power of lust and forms before the eyes of his mind images of shameful acts; and when the act itself is not performed, it is carried out all the more frequently in the intention of thought. The completion of pleasure is sought, and the enervated mind, shaken, anxious, and blinded on every side, searches out an opportunity for the most wicked gratification. Such a mind therefore suffers, as it were, a certain populace, being laid waste by the insolent tumult of its thoughts.

Another has thrown himself beneath the dominion of anger. What does he enact in his heart except quarrels, including those that are absent? He often does not see those who are present, contradicts those who are absent, speaks insults within himself and receives them, and responds still more harshly to those he has received. And when no opponent is present, he arranges quarrels in his heart with loud cries. Thus he carries an inward crowd, whom the heavy weight of inflamed thought presses down.

Another has handed himself over to the power of greed and, despising what is his own, covets what belongs to others. Often unable to obtain what he desires, he turns the day toward idleness and the night toward reflection. He grows numb toward useful work because he is wearied by unlawful thought; he multiplies his plans and expands the bosom of his mind more widely through the inventions of his thoughts. He strives to reach what he desires and seeks certain most secret passages through which he may obtain it.

As soon as he thinks he has discovered something subtle in the matter, he rejoices as though he had already obtained what he desired. He then considers what he might add to what he has acquired and examines how it ought to be cultivated into a better condition. Since he already possesses it, as it were, and brings it, as it were, to a more excellent appearance, he immediately considers the plots of the envious and weighs what quarrel might be stirred up against him. He investigates what answer he should give; and although he possesses nothing, the empty litigant already labors in defense of the thing he desires.

Although he has received nothing of the object he covets, he nevertheless already possesses in his heart the fruit of covetousness: the labor of quarrel. A grievous populace therefore weighs upon the one laid waste by the tumult of stimulating greed.

Another has subjected himself to the tyranny of pride. While he raises his miserable heart against human beings, he subordinates it to vice. He desires the insignia of lofty honors, seeks to be exalted by advancement, and paints in his thoughts the whole of what he longs to be. Already he presides as though over a tribunal; already he sees the services of his subjects obeying him; already he stands above others; already he inflicts evils on some and repays others because they have inflicted them.

Already, surrounded by ranks, he proceeds in his imagination into public view; already he sees with what services he is supported. Yet, while thinking these things, he crawls along alone. [Note: Corbie German, Rheims, and Remigius, among others, read this way; others have *solus repetit* or *recipit* (“he repeats” or “receives alone”). We have preferred the former reading, which presents the nobler sense. The second reading is not without meaning.] Already he tramples some down and raises others up; already he satisfies his hatreds concerning those he has trampled down and receives favors from those he has raised up.

What else, then, does the person who impresses so many phantoms upon his heart see except a waking dream? Since he endures within himself so many causes of things that he invents, he clearly carries inwardly a crowd born from his desires.

Another now avoids what is unlawful, but nevertheless fears to be without the goods of the world. He desires to retain what is permitted, is ashamed to appear lesser among human beings, and takes the greatest care not to be poor at home or despised in public. He investigates what is sufficient for him and what the needs of those subject to him require. And, in order to fulfill adequately the obligations of patronage toward his dependents, he seeks patrons whom he himself may serve. But when he joins himself familiarly to them, he is undoubtedly entangled in their affairs; he often consents to their unlawful acts and commits, for the sake of other things he does not abandon, evils he would not desire for his own sake.

For often, while he fears that his honor in this world may be diminished, he approves before persons of higher standing what he already condemns by his own judgment. While he anxiously considers what he owes to patrons and what to dependents, what may increase for himself and what may benefit his affections [Note: Some manuscripts have *effectibus* (“effects”)], he is pressed by as great a multitude of tumults as he is torn apart by the importunity of his cares.

**[Formerly XXXIV.]** 58. Those who have subdued their vices are alone with themselves.—By contrast, holy men, because they desire nothing of this world, are undoubtedly oppressed by no tumults within their hearts. With the hand of holy reflection they cast all disordered movements of desire from the dwelling place of the heart. And because they despise all transitory things, they do not suffer the insolence of thoughts that arise from them.

They desire only the eternal homeland; and because they love none of the things of this world, they enjoy great tranquility of mind. Hence it is rightly said: “Who build solitudes for themselves.” For to build solitudes is to expel the tumult of earthly desires from the secret place of the heart and, with a single intention, to breathe out toward the love of inward rest in the eternal homeland.

Had he not expelled from himself all the tumults of thought who said: “One thing I asked of the Lord; this I shall seek, that I may dwell in the house of the Lord” (Ps. 26:4)? [Note: The editions add here, “all the days of my life,” which is absent from the better manuscripts.] He had fled from the crowd of earthly desires to himself, that is, to a great solitude, where he would see nothing foreign all the more securely because he loved nothing unfitting. [Note: The Vulgate editions read, “and had betaken himself to a great solitude”; this corrupts Gregory’s sense, which identifies no solitude other than ourselves and no retreat other than the quiet mind.]

He had sought from the tumult of temporal things a certain great retreat: a quiet mind in which he might see God more purely, insofar as he found him alone with himself. [Note: The editions read “bodily things”; the manuscripts read “temporal things.” They also read *magnum quoddam secessum* (“a certain great retreat”) for *magnum quemdam secessum* (“a certain great retreat”).] [Note: Two Rheims manuscripts and one Remigius manuscript have *quietam scilicet mentem* (“namely, a quiet mind”); others have *quietem mentis* (“quiet of mind”); the Regius manuscript has *inquietam mentem* (“an unquiet mind”).]

59. And they truly are rulers, because they do not cease to give counsel to others.—Those who build solitudes for themselves are rightly also called rulers, because they build such solitude of mind within themselves that, nevertheless, in whatever they excel, they do not cease to counsel others through love.

Let us therefore examine somewhat more subtly this ruler whom we have just mentioned, and see how, in offering examples of a higher life, he scatters the tokens of virtues before the ranks of peoples subject to him.

Behold, in order to teach the reward of good for evil, he confesses concerning himself, saying: “If I have repaid those who repaid me with evil, may I deservedly fall empty before my enemies” (Ps. 7:5).

To stir us to love of the Creator, he says: “But for me it is good to cling to God” (Ps. 72:28). To impress upon us the pattern of holy humility, he discloses the secrets of his heart, saying: “Lord, my heart has not been exalted, nor have my eyes been lifted up” (Ps. 130:1).

To arouse us by his example to imitate the uprightness of zeal, he says: [Note: The editions read: “Did I not hate those who hate you, O Lord?”] “Do I not hate those who hate you, O God, and waste away because of your enemies? With perfect hatred I hate them; they have become enemies to me” (Ps. 138:22).

To kindle in us desire for the eternal homeland, he laments the length of the present life, saying: “Woe is me, for my sojourning has been prolonged” (Ps. 119:5). [Note: Vindobonensis, Compendium, Saint-Albinus, and others have: “Woe is me, for …”] By the generosity of his counsel he shone forth, scattering before us so many tokens of virtue through the example of his own conduct. [Note: The old editions, together with the ancient Rheims and German editions, read *consolatus* (“comforted”); scribes frequently write *o* for *u*.]

**[Formerly XXXV.]** 60. But let him tell whether this ruler also builds a solitude for himself.—[Note: We restore this reading on the authority of almost all the manuscripts. The old editions and those following them read: “But how does this ruler, counseling others, counsel himself?” The error may have arisen from the Regius manuscript, which reads: “But this ruler, counseling.”] For he says: “Behold, fleeing, I have gone far away and remained in solitude” (Ps. 54:8). Fleeing, he goes far away because he raises himself from the crowd of temporal desires into the heights of contemplation of God. He remains in solitude because he perseveres in the remote intention of the mind.

Concerning this solitude Jeremiah rightly says to the Lord: “I sat alone because of the presence of your hand, for you filled me with threat” (Jer. 15:17). The presence of God’s hand is that stroke of just judgment by which he drove the proud human being from paradise and shut him out into this blindness of the present exile. [Note: Rheims, Remigius—with one exception—Normandy, Regius, German, Compendium, Longipont, Saint-Albinus, Tours, Val-Clair, and others read *non inclusit* (“did not shut him in”), rather than the reading of the old editions and those that follow them.]

His threat is the terror of the punishment that still follows. After the presence of his hand, therefore, threats still terrify us, because through the experience of judgment the punishment of the present exile has already struck us, and, if we do not cease to sin, it still consigns us to eternal punishments.

Let the holy man therefore consider, cast down here, from where the human being fell, and where the justice of the Judge still carries the sinner after these things. Let him cast out from himself all the crowds of temporal desires and hide himself in the great solitude of the mind, saying: “I sat alone because of the presence of your hand, for you filled me with threat.”

As though speaking openly, he says: “While I consider what I already suffer through the experience of judgment, I tremulously seek a retreat of the mind from the tumult of temporal desires, because I also fear more bitterly the eternal punishments that you threaten.”

Thus it is rightly said of the kings and rulers: “Who build solitudes for themselves.” For those who know both how to govern themselves well and how to counsel others, since they cannot meanwhile be presented to that innermost rest, imitate it within themselves through the practice of a tranquil mind.

It follows:

## CHAPTER XXXI

**VERSE 15.—With princes who possess gold and fill their houses with silver.**

61. Princes are the rulers of the Church; gold is wisdom; silver is the word of God.—Whom else does he call princes except the rulers of the holy Church, whom divine providence continually appoints in the place of the preachers who came before them? To that same Church the Psalmist says concerning them: “In place of your fathers sons have been born to you; you shall appoint them princes over all the earth” (Ps. 44:17).

What does he call gold except wisdom, of which Solomon says: “A desirable treasure rests in the mouth of the wise” (Prov. 21:20)? He saw wisdom as gold, calling it a treasure. It is rightly signified by the name of gold, because just as temporal goods are bought with gold, so eternal goods are bought with wisdom.

If gold were not wisdom, the angel would never say to the Church of Laodicea: “I advise you to buy from me gold refined by fire” (Rev. 3:18). We buy gold when, in order to receive wisdom, we first offer obedience. A certain wise man rightly urges us toward this transaction, saying: “Have you desired wisdom? Keep the commandments, and the Lord will provide it for you” (Sir. 1:33). [Note: The Paris edition of 1495, the Basel edition of 1514, and Gussanus have *quidem sapiens* (“a certain wise man”), instead of *quidem sap.* (“a certain wise [man]”).] [Note: The Corbie German and Regius manuscripts have *praebet* (“provides it”).]

What else are signified by houses except consciences? Hence it is said to a certain man who had been healed: “Go to your house” (Matt. 9:6). As though he heard plainly: “After the outward miracle, return to your conscience and consider how you ought to present yourself inwardly to God.”

And what else is signified by silver except the divine utterances, of which the Psalmist says: “The utterances of the Lord are pure utterances, silver tested by fire” (Ps. 11:7)? The word of the Lord is called silver tested by fire because, when God’s word is fixed in the heart, it is proved by tribulations.

**[Formerly XXXVI.]** 62. If Adam had not sinned, those who are now to be saved would have been born alone.—Let the holy man, therefore, filled with the spirit of eternity, gather together the things that are to come; let him embrace, with the bosom of his mind opened wide, those whom distant ages yet to come would beget; and let him contemplate with great wonder with which elect people he would rest without labor in eternity if no one had sinned through the desire of pride. Let him say:

“For now I would be sleeping in silence, and in my sleep I would be resting with the kings and rulers of the earth who build solitudes for themselves, or with princes who possess gold and fill their houses with silver.”

For if no corruption of sin had infected our first parent, he would certainly not have begotten children of Gehenna from himself. Those who are now to be saved through redemption would have been born as the only elect from him. Let him look upon these same elect and consider how he could have rested with them.

Let him see the holy apostles governing the Church once received in such a way that they never cease to provide counsel for it through the word of preaching, and let him call them kings and rulers. After them let him see rulers arise in their place who, by living wisely, possess gold, and who, by preaching what is right to others, shine with the silver of sacred speech. Let him remember them as princes, rich in gold and silver, with the houses of their consciences filled with these treasures.

But because it is sometimes not enough for the prophetic spirit to foresee what is to come unless it also represents to the prophet’s heart things past and ancient, the holy man opens his eyes above and below. He sees not only what is to come but also recalls what has passed. For he immediately adds:

## CHAPTER XXXII [Revised XXIX]

**VERSE 16.—Or, like a hidden miscarriage, I would not endure; or like those conceived who did not see the light.**

63. The saints born before the time of redemption are like miscarriages. There were more of them than Moses records.—A miscarriage, because it comes forth before the full term, is immediately extinguished and hidden. Whom, then, does the holy man call miscarriages, with whom he considers that he could have rested, except all the elect who arose from the very beginning of the world before the time of redemption and nevertheless took care to put themselves to death with respect to this world?

Not possessing the tablets of the written law, they were, as it were, dead from the womb, because they feared their Creator according to the natural law. [Note: The Corbie German, Rheims, Remigius, Vindobonensis, and other manuscripts read “in the womb.”] And while they believed in the Mediator who was to come, they took the greatest care, by mortifying pleasures, to observe even the commandments they had not received in writing.

That time, therefore, which, near the beginning of the world, produced fathers dead to this age, was like a womb of miscarriages. There was Abel, who is not recorded as having resisted his brother when the latter killed him (Gen. 4:8, 24). There was Enoch, who displayed himself in such a way that he was transferred to walk with the Lord (Gen. 5:22, 24). There was Noah, who, because he pleased the divine judgment, survived in a cleansed world. [Note: The German manuscript and some others read *immundo mundo* (“in an unclean world”). Corbie German, Regius, Colbert, and others read *in mundum* (“into the world”), perhaps meaning “into the restoration of the world,” while *mundo superstes* means “surviving the world.”] There was Abraham, who, while a sojourner in the world, became God’s friend (Gen. 12:1). There was Isaac, who, with the eyes of his flesh dimmed by age, did not see present things, but through the power of the prophetic spirit shone with the great light of seeing even events in future ages (Gen. 27:1). There was Jacob, who humbly fled his brother’s anger and mercifully subdued it; who was indeed fruitful in offspring, but more fruitful still in the abundance of the spirit, binding those same offspring under the bonds of his prophecy (Gen. 33:4).

This miscarriage is rightly called hidden, because, although we know a few from the beginnings of the world through Moses’ writing, the greater part of the human race remains hidden from us. For it must not be believed that only as many righteous people existed before the law was received as Moses touched upon in his very brief account. Since, therefore, a multitude of good people brought forth from the beginning of the world is largely withheld from our knowledge, this is called a hidden miscarriage. It is also said not to have endured, because, once the few have been listed, the multitude of the others is preserved in no written record in our memory.

**[Formerly XXXVII.]** 64. Those conceived but who did not see the light are those born after the law and before Christ.—Rightly it is added: “Or those conceived who did not see the light.” Those who were born into this world after the law had been received were conceived for their Creator through the admonition of that same law. Yet, though conceived, they did not see the light, because they were unable to reach the advent of the Lord’s incarnation, although they faithfully believed in it.

The incarnate Lord says: “I am the light of the world” (John 8:12). And the Light itself says: “Many prophets and righteous people desired to see what you see, and did not see it” (Matt. 13:17). They were therefore conceived but did not see the light, because, awakened by the open voices of the prophets to hope in the Mediator who was to come, they were nevertheless unable to behold his incarnation.

In these people the inner conception produced the form of faith, but did not bring it to the open vision of the divine presence, because intervening death snatched them from the world before the manifest Truth illumined the world. [Note: Rheims and Remigius have *mundo illustravit* (“illumined the world”).]

**[Formerly XXXVIII.]** 65. Seeing things past and future, Job longs for eternal things.—The holy man, therefore, filled with the spirit of eternity, binds all passing things to memory with the hand of his heart. And because every creature is narrow in comparison with its Creator, through that same spirit—which possesses in itself or beside itself nothing except eternal being—he sees what will be and what has passed away. [Note: The Corbie German, Rheims, Remigius, Compendium, and Vindobonensis manuscripts read “nothing from itself,” and subsequently “everything that will be,” rather than “what will be.”] He stretches the eye of his mind above and below, and, considering coming things as though they had already passed, burns to the depths of his being for eternal existence, saying: “For now I would be sleeping in silence.”

“For now” belongs to the present time. And what is it to seek rest while standing always in the present except to long for the joy of eternity, to which nothing comes and from which nothing passes away? To communicate, in some fashion, his own eternal being to us, the Truth himself indicates it through Moses, saying: “I am who I am. And you shall say to the children of Israel: ‘He who is has sent me to you’” (Exod. 3:14).

But behold: because he sees passing things, because he seeks ever-present joy, because he recalls the light that is to come, because, enumerating the orders of its elect, he weighs them—let him now disclose to us more openly the rest of this light, and show in clearer words what is happening there each day concerning the conduct of the wicked. [Note: Corbie German and some others read “the conversion of the wicked.”]

It follows:

## CHAPTER XXXIII [Formerly XXXIX, Revised XXX]

**VERSE 17.—There the ungodly have ceased from tumult, and there those weary with strength have rested.**

66. Through the benefit of the Incarnation, the ungodly have been delivered from grievous labor.—We have already said above that the hearts of sinners are pressed by a grievous tumult of goading thoughts because the clamor of desires possesses them. But in this light, which those conceived did not see, the ungodly are said to cease from their tumult, because the Gentile peoples found for the rest of their life the advent of the Mediator, which the fathers living under the law had long awaited. Paul testifies to this when he says: “What Israel sought, it did not obtain; but the election obtained it” (Rom. 11:7).

In this light, therefore, the ungodly cease from tumult, while the minds of the wicked, having come to know the truth, flee the laborious desires of the world and yield to the tranquility of inward love.

Does not the Light itself call us to cessation when it says: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart, and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is sweet and my burden light” (Matt. 11:28–30)?

What heavy thing does he impose upon the necks of our minds, who commands us to avoid every desire that causes disturbance? What heavy thing does he command those subject to him, who warns them to turn aside from the laborious paths of this world?

As the apostle Paul testifies, “Christ died for the ungodly” (Rom. 5:6). But for this reason the Light itself deigned to die for the ungodly: so that the ungodly would not remain in the tumult of their darkness.

Let the holy man therefore contemplate that, through the mystery of his incarnation, the Light delivers the ungodly from grievous labor by wiping the desires of wickedness from their hearts. Let him contemplate that all who are converted already taste here, through tranquility of mind, the rest they desire to receive in eternity, and let him say: “There the ungodly have ceased from tumult, and there those weary with strength have rested.”

134. 67. The more we are strengthened in the love of God, the more we fail with respect to our own strength. The eternal light is our dwelling.—All who are strong in this world are strong, as it were, in strength, not weary with strength. But those who are strengthened in the love of their Creator, the more they grow strong in the desired strength of God, the more they fail in their own strength; and the more vigorously they desire eternal things, the more healthily they grow weary of temporal things.

Hence the Psalmist, wearied by the strength of his love, said: “My soul has failed in your salvation” (Ps. 118:81). [Note: Corbie German and other ancient manuscripts, as well as the old Basel edition, read “has failed in your salvation”; other witnesses read “has failed for your salvation.”] For he had failed while advancing toward God’s salvation, because, desiring the light of eternity, he longed, already broken in his confidence in the flesh.

Again he says: “My soul has desired and failed for the courts of the Lord” (Ps. 83:3). When he said “has desired,” he rightly added “and failed,” because desire for divinity is exceedingly slight if one’s own failure does not immediately follow it. For the person who is inflamed to desire the courts of eternity ought certainly to be wearied of the love of this temporality, so that he grows cold toward devotion to the world in proportion as he rises more ardently into the love of God.

If he seizes upon God perfectly, he also wholly abandons the world; and he dies completely to temporal things in proportion as he is animated more deeply toward the life above by the breath of eternity.

Had she not found herself weary of her own strength who said: “My soul melted when he spoke” (Song 5:6)? [Note: The editions read “when my beloved spoke”; *my beloved* is absent from the Corbie German, Regius, and Colbert manuscripts before their later correction.] For when the mind is touched by the inspiration of a hidden utterance, weakened from its position of strength, it melts in the very desire by which it is absorbed. It finds itself weary in its own sight precisely because it sees beyond itself the strength which it has ascended toward.

Hence the prophet, when he said that he had seen a vision of God, adds: “I languished and was sick for many days” (Dan. 8:27), because when the mind is drawn close to the strength of God, the flesh is wearied of its own strength.

**[Formerly XL.]** Hence Jacob, who held the angel, immediately afterward limped on one foot (Gen. 32:25), because the person who looks upon sublime things with true love no longer wishes to walk in this world with doubled desires.
