He rests on one foot who is strengthened by the love of God alone; and the other must become weak, because as the strength of the mind increases, the strength of the flesh must undoubtedly grow numb.

Let blessed Job therefore look upon the lofty hearts of the faithful and consider what innermost rest they find when, by advancing toward God, they grow weary of their own powers. Let him say: “There those weary with strength have rested.”

As though openly explaining this, he says: “There the rest of light rewards those whom advancement, refreshing them inwardly here, makes weary.”

Nor should it trouble us that, although he names the light, he does not add “in this,” but “there.” For when he sees that it contains the elect, he recognizes that it is, as it were, our dwelling place.

Hence the Psalmist, when he contemplated the unchangeableness of eternity, saying: “But you are the very same, and your years shall not fail” (Ps. 101:28), declares this to be the dwelling place of the elect, adding: “The children of your servants shall dwell there” (ibid., 29).

God, who contains all things without being contained in a place, remains for us, as we come to him, a non-local place. When we reach this place, we also see how great the disturbance was from which the tranquility of our mind in this life arose. For although the just are already tranquil in comparison with the wicked, in the estimation of inner rest they are not tranquil in every respect.

Hence it is rightly added:

## CHAPTER XXXIV

**VERSE 18.—And formerly bound together without distress.**
### 68. The hard bonds by which even the righteous are bound here

[Col. 0675A] Although no tumult of carnal desires possesses the righteous, nevertheless, placed in this life, they are bound by hard bonds through the distress of their corruption.^135 For it is written: “The corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks on many things” (Wis. 9:15). Thus, by the very fact that they are still mortal, they are weighed down by the burden of their corruption and are bound by distress, because they do not yet rise into the freedom of incorruptible life.

For they endure one condition in the mind and another in the body, and every day they labor in an inward struggle against themselves. Are they not bound by a hard bond of distress, whose mind is released into ignorance without effort, yet is instructed only through diligent labor? [Note: We have deleted the little word added in another edition, but foreign and superfluous in the manuscripts.] It is compelled to rise, lies down willingly, is scarcely lifted from the lowest things, and yet, once lifted up, immediately falls. By laboriously overcoming itself, it beholds heavenly things; but, driven back, it flees the light that had shone upon it.

[Col. 0675B] Are they not bound by a hard bond of distress, whom, when the kindled spirit draws with full desire toward the innermost bosom of peace, the flesh disturbs in the midst of the fervent struggle? Although the flesh no longer confronts them, as though standing face-to-face in battle line, it nevertheless still murmurs from behind the mind, like a captive, and, although to be feared, yet by its disgraceful din defiles in the heart the image of beautiful peace. [Note: One Rheims manuscript and one Remigius manuscript read, “although not to be feared.” This sense is not unacceptable if “not to be feared” is referred to “yet by its disgraceful din,” as though it said that the struggle of concupiscence, although not to be feared by the righteous, is nevertheless troublesome because of its noise. But neither the antiquity nor the number of the manuscripts supports this reading.]

Therefore, although the elect overcome everything courageously, when they desire the security of inward peace it is a grave distress for them still to have something to overcome. [Note: This is the reading of the best manuscripts. The edition has, “Excepting which.” Better is, “Who, besides these,” that is, in addition to those distresses which he endures from the desire of the flesh.] Besides these, they also endure the bonds that severe external necessity imposes. To hunger, thirst, and grow weary are bonds of corruption; and these bonds cannot be loosed until our mortality is exchanged for that glory of immortality.

[Old reading XLI.] [Col. 0675C] For we fill the body with nourishment, lest, weakened, it fail; we weaken it by abstinence, lest, when filled, it oppress us. We invigorate it by movement, lest it perish through the inactivity of stillness; but more quickly we bring it to rest, lest it succumb through that very vigor. We cover it with the aid of clothing, lest cold destroy it, and we cast away the aid we have sought, lest heat consume us.

What are we doing, then, when we meet so many different needs, except serving corruptibility, so that at least the multiplicity of our devoted service may sustain the body, which the anxiety of weak mutability burdens? Hence Paul rightly says: “For creation was subjected to futility, not willingly, but because of him who subjected it in hope; because creation itself will also be freed from the slavery of corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God” (Rom. 8:20).

[Col. 0675D] Creation is subjected unwillingly to futility because the human being, who willingly abandoned the condition of innate steadfastness, is pressed down by the burden of just mortality and unwillingly serves the corruption of his mutability. But this creation is then rescued from the slavery of corruption when, rising incorruptible, it is raised up to the glory of the children of God.

[Col. 0676A] Here, then, the elect are bound by distress, because they are still weighed down by the punishment of their corruption. But when we are stripped of corruptible flesh, we are, as it were, released from the bonds of distress by which we are now constrained. For we already desire to be presented before God, but we are still hindered by the obligation of a mortal body. Rightly, therefore, are we called bound, because the movement of our desire toward God is not yet free.

[Col. 0676B] Thus Paul, desiring eternal things but still carrying the burden of his corruption, cries out while bound: “I desire to depart and to be with Christ” (Phil. 1:23). He would not seek to depart unless he plainly saw himself to be bound. Because the Prophet had clearly seen that these bonds would certainly be broken in the resurrection, he already rejoiced as though they had been broken when he said: “You have broken my bonds; to you I will sacrifice the sacrifice of praise” (Ps. 115:7).

## Epilogue

Let the holy man contemplate that the inward light receives converted sinners, and let him say: “There the wicked have ceased from turmoil.” Let him contemplate that holy men, wearied by the exercise of desire, rest more deeply in that innermost bosom, and let him say: “And there those weary in strength have rested.” Let him contemplate that, released together from all the bonds of their corruption, they arrive incorruptible at those joys of freedom, and let him say: “And those once bound are together without distress.”

It is rightly said, “formerly bound,” because, while that joy is always present, everything that will be and passes away already appears as though it were past. For when the end of things is considered, everything that passes is reckoned as though it had already existed.

But let him relate what all those whom inward rest will receive there have done here in the meantime. [Note: The printed editions read “on earth” instead of “in the meantime,” but the latter is the reading of the manuscripts.] It follows:

## CHAPTER XXXV [Recension XXXI]

[Col. 0676C] **In the same place: “They did not heed the voice of the exactor.”**

### 69. The devil is the exactor; he is not heeded when the tempter is resisted

Who else should be understood by the name “exactor” except that importunate persuader who once handed the human race the coin of deception and does not cease daily to demand from it the debt of death? [Note: Bartholomew and the old editions read “on this account”; Coccius and subsequent editions, “still”; the manuscripts read “from it,” namely, from the human race.] In paradise he lent the human being the money of sin; [Note: Some printed editions and manuscripts read “to the human being sinning, money”; we follow the Corbie and German manuscripts, the ancient Rheims and Norman manuscripts, which read “the money of sin.” The Vindocensis manuscripts have “he entrusted the money of sin.” Gregory uses “money of sin” here in the same sense in which he earlier used “the coin of deception.”] but, as iniquity increases, he exacts it daily with interest. Concerning this exactor, Truth says in the Gospel: “And the judge will hand you over to the exactor” (Luke 12:58).

The voice of this exactor is the temptation of wretched suggestion. We hear the exactor’s voice when we are struck by his temptation; but we do not heed it if we resist the one who knocks. For the one who experiences temptation hears it; but the one who consents to temptation heeds it. Let it therefore be said of the righteous: “They did not heed the voice of the exactor,” because, although they hear his suggestion insofar as they are tempted, they do not heed it, because they scorn consenting to it.

[Old reading XLII.] But because the mind often repeats in speech what it greatly loves, blessed Job, seeing and loving the abundance of inward peace, again serves its description, saying: [Col. 0677A] [Note: Here the manuscripts and editions differ from one another. The Corbie and German manuscripts have “serves his discernment again”; the old edition has “again explains his discernment”; Coccius and later editions have “again serves its description.” We follow the reading of the Utica manuscript, which seems more consonant with Saint Gregory’s purpose. For he is speaking of the inward peace of the blessed, signified by Job’s words, “They did not heed the voice of the exactor,” together with what precedes. He teaches that this peace is described again by the words, “The small and the great are there.”]

## CHAPTER XXXVI

**Verse 19: “The small and the great are there, and the servant is free from his master.”**

### 70. As merits differ here, so rewards will differ in heaven

Because in this life there is a distinction of works, there will undoubtedly be in that life a distinction of dignities, so that, just as one person surpasses another here in merit, so there one will surpass another in recompense. Hence Truth says in the Gospel: “In my Father’s house there are many dwelling places” (John 14:2).

Yet in those many dwelling places there will somehow be a harmonious diversity of rewards, because so great a power in that peace unites us that each person will rejoice that he has received in another what he himself has not received. [Note: The printed editions read “so great a power of love”; the word “love” is absent from the manuscripts.] Hence, although those who labored in the vineyard did not labor equally (Matt. 20:10), they all receive the same denarius.

There are indeed many dwelling places with the Father, and yet unequal laborers receive the same denarius, because there will be one blessedness of joy for all, although the sublimity of life will not be the same for everyone.

He had seen the small and the great in this light who said in the voice of the Head: “Your eyes saw my unfinished state, and in your book they will all be written” (Ps. 138:16). He had seen the small and the great when he said: “The Lord has blessed all who fear him, the small with the great” (Ps. 113:13).

### 71. Who is the servant of sin, who is free from it, and how no one is free from it here

It is rightly added: “And the servant is free from his master.” For it is written: “Everyone who commits sin is the servant of sin” (John 8:34), because whoever subjects himself to an evil desire submits the once-free neck of his mind to the master of iniquity. [Note: The printed editions read “dominion”; the better manuscripts read “master.”]

But we oppose this master when we struggle against the iniquity that had seized us; when we violently resist habit and, trampling perverse desires underfoot, assert against it the right of our innate freedom; when we strike our fault through repentance and wash away the stains of filth with tears.

Often the mind already grieves over what it remembers having done perversely; it not only abandons its evil deeds but also punishes them with the bitterest lamentation. Yet, while it remembers what it has done, it is terrified by great fear of judgment. [Note: The printed editions read “with grave fear of judgment,” as do all the Vulgate copies.] It has already turned completely, but it still does not raise itself fully into security, because, while it weighs the severity of the final examination, it trembles anxiously between hope and fear. For it does not know what the just Judge, when he comes, will reckon concerning the deeds committed and what he will forgive.

It remembers how many wrongs it committed, but does not know whether it has sufficiently mourned what it committed; and it fears lest the enormity of the fault exceed the measure of its repentance. Often Truth has already forgiven the fault, but the afflicted mind, still extremely anxious about forgiveness, trembles. [Note: The printed editions read “it fears,” as all the Vulgate copies have.]

Thus the servant has already fled from his master, but is not free, because the human being has abandoned his sin by correction and repentance, yet still fears the severe Judge concerning its recompense.

There, therefore, the servant will be free from his master, where there will no longer be uncertainty about the forgiveness of sin; where the secure mind will not be enslaved by the memory of its fault; where the soul will not tremble under guilt but will rejoice freely in its forgiveness. [Note: Coccius has “there” instead of “where”; the latter reading prevailed despite the manuscripts and earlier editions.]

### 72. Is there no memory of sin in heaven? How such memory does not hinder blessedness

But if the human being is not touched there by any memory of his sin, from what does he rejoice that he has been rescued? Or how does he give thanks to the giver for the forgiveness he has received, if, because of the intervening forgetfulness of his past wickedness, he does not know that he had been liable to punishment?

Nor should we pass over carelessly what the Psalmist says: “I will sing your mercies, O Lord, forever” (Ps. 88:1). For how does he sing the mercies of God forever if he does not know that he was once wretched? And if he does not remember his past misery, whence does he return praises to the bounty of mercy? [Note: The Corbie, German, ancient Rheims, and better manuscripts read “to the bounty”; the editions, with some manuscripts, read “to the giver.”]

But again we must ask how the mind of the elect can be perfect in blessedness if the memory of its guilt touches it amid its joys. Or how can the glory of perfect light shine when guilt, recalled to the mind, casts a shadow over it?

We should know, however, that just as we often now remember past sorrows with joy, so then we will remember past wickedness without harm to our blessedness. Often, while in good health, we recall past pains without pain; and the more we remember that we were sick, the more we love ourselves as healthy.

There will therefore be in that blessedness a memory of guilt—not one that pollutes the mind, but one that binds us more closely to joy—so that, while the mind remembers its pain without pain, it may understand more truly that it was indebted to the physician and may love the health it received all the more because it remembers the distress from which it escaped. [Note: All the Rheims, Remigius, Corbie-German, Regius, and Colbert manuscripts read “more deeply” (*altius*) for “more closely” (*arctius*), although the latter better suits the verb “bind.”]

In that joy, then, we shall behold our evils without weariness, just as now, placed in the light, we see darkness with the mind without any darkness of heart. For although what we see with the mind is obscure, this comes from the judgment of light, not from the suffering of blindness.

Thus we shall also return eternal praise to our giver of mercy, and shall in no way be burdened by consciousness of misery. [Note: The printed editions have “misery of conscience.” The manuscripts have the better reading, “consciousness of misery,” that is, the inward knowledge and recollection by which the saints are in no way weighed down.] For, while we behold our evils without any evil affecting the mind, there will never be anything to pollute the hearts of those who praise, and there will always be something to kindle them to praise their deliverer.

Therefore, because the rest of inward light raises up the great within itself without abandoning the small, it is rightly said: “The small and the great are there.” And because the mind of the converted sinner is touched there by the memory of its guilt without being weighed down by any shame from that memory, it is fittingly added: “And the servant is free from his master.”

# BOOK FIVE

It explains the remainder of the third chapter from verse 20, the whole of the fourth chapter, and the first two verses of the fifth.

## CHAPTER ONE

### 1. Here the saints fear prosperity more than adversity

[Col. 0679A] Since the divine judgments are exceedingly hidden, they are more hidden when the good fare well here and the wicked fare ill than when sometimes the good fare ill and the wicked fare well.

For when the good fare ill and the wicked fare well, this can perhaps be understood: the good, if they have committed offenses, receive their recompense here so that they may be more fully freed from eternal condemnation; while the wicked find here the good things they do for this life, so that they may be led afterward to punishments alone. Hence it is said to the rich man burning in hell: “Remember, son, that you received good things in your life, and Lazarus likewise evil things” (Luke 16:25).

But when the good fare well here and the wicked fare ill, it becomes very uncertain whether the good receive good things for this reason: that, being encouraged, they may grow toward something better; or whether, by a just and hidden judgment, they receive here the recompense for their works, so that they may be deprived of the rewards of the life to come. It is also uncertain whether the wicked are struck by adversity so that, being corrected, they may be protected from eternal punishments; or whether their punishment begins here, so that, when completed in due course, it may lead them to the final torments of Gehenna. [Note: All the manuscripts have this reading, as do the old Paris and Basel editions: “that, by correcting them, they may protect them.”]

Because, then, the human mind is weighed down amid the divine judgments by the heavy darkness of its uncertainty, holy men, when they see the prosperity of this world available to them, are disturbed by fearful suspicion. They fear that here they are receiving the fruit of their labors; they fear that divine justice sees a hidden wound within them and, heaping external gifts upon them, drives them away from inward things.

When, however, they quietly consider that they do not perform good deeds except to please the Lord alone, and that they do not rejoice in the very abundance of their prosperity, they fear the hidden judgments against themselves somewhat less on account of prosperity. Nevertheless, they bear that prosperity painfully because it hinders them from their inward intention; and they endure the allurements of the present life with distress because they know that through these they are delayed, in some measure, in their inward desire.

[Col. 0679D] In this world, honor occupies more than contempt, and the height of prosperity burdens more than the adversity of necessity. Through the latter, when a person is externally pressed, he is sometimes released more freely to desire the things within. [Note: The Corbie, German, Rheims, and some other manuscripts have “is released more freely.”] Through the former, however, the mind, compelled to serve many people, is held back from the course of its desire.

Thus it happens that holy men fear prosperity in this world more than adversity. [Col. 0680A] For they know that when the mind is burdened by agreeable occupation, it sometimes willingly flows outward. They know that a clandestine thought often deceives it, so that it does not realize how it is being changed.

[Col. 0680B] They weigh the eternal goods they desire and recognize how worthless is everything that temporally appears pleasant. [Note: Some manuscripts and editions read “what the inward things are.” But “eternal” must be read, as is clear from the opposition to what temporally appears pleasant.] Their mind bears all the prosperity of this world with such distress because it is wounded by love of heavenly happiness; and it rises in rejection of present sweetness all the more because it sees that this sweetness secretly flatters it in contempt of eternal glory.

Thus blessed Job, contemplating heavenly rest, had said: “The small and the great are there, and the servant is free from his master.” Immediately he adds:

## CHAPTER TWO [Recension II]

**Verse 20: “Why was light given to the miserable?”**

### 2. Those who contemplate eternal things recoil from earthly prosperity

In Sacred Scripture, prosperity is sometimes signified by the name “light,” while adversity in this world is signified by the name “night.” Hence the Psalmist rightly says: “As is his darkness, so also is his light” (Ps. 138:12).

Because holy men trample upon the prosperity of the world as they endure and trample upon its adversity, they say, through the great elevation of their mind, placing both the world’s adversities and its prosperities beneath themselves: “As is his darkness, so also is his light.” As though they were saying more openly: “Just as its sorrows do not weigh down the strength of our intention, so its pleasant things do not corrupt it.”

But because, as we have said, these things disturb the minds of the good even when they do not raise them up, [Note: The Vindocensis and ancient Rheims manuscripts read “test.”] holy men, who recognize themselves as miserable in the hardship of this exile, shrink from shining in its prosperity.

[Col. 0680D] Hence it is rightly said here: “Why was light given to the miserable?” Light is given to the miserable when those who contemplate sublime things and recognize themselves as miserable in this pilgrimage receive the brilliance of transitory prosperity. Although they deeply lament that they are returning to their homeland so late, they are compelled to endure the burdens of honor as well.

[Col. 0681A] Love of eternal things crushes them, while glory in temporal things smiles upon them. When they consider what they possess below and what they do not see from above; what supports them on earth and what they have lost in heaven, they are gnawed by sorrow at their prosperity. For although they see that they are not completely oppressed by it, they carefully consider how their thought is divided between love of the Lord and the administration entrusted to them.

Thus, when he says, “Why was light given to the miserable?” he immediately adds:

## CHAPTER THREE [Old Recension II, Recension III]

**Verse 20: “And life to those who are in bitterness of soul.”**

### 3. The elect and the reprobate are in bitterness here, but in different ways

All the elect are in bitterness of soul, either because they do not cease to punish through weeping what they have done wrong, or because they afflict themselves with deep sorrow, since, cast far away from the face of their Creator, they are not yet in the joys of their eternal homeland.

Concerning their heart Solomon rightly says: “The heart that knows the bitterness of its soul will not have a stranger share in its joy” (Prov. 14:10).

The hearts of the reprobate are also in bitterness, because they are afflicted even by their own perverse desires; but they do not recognize that bitterness, because, willingly blinded, they cannot weigh what they endure.

By contrast, the heart of the good knows its bitterness, because it understands the hardship of exile in which it has been cast and torn apart; it feels how peaceful were the things it lost and how confused are the things into which it fell.

But this embittered heart will one day be restored to its joy, and no stranger will share in that joy, because the one who now casts himself outward from this sorrow of heart through his desires will then remain excluded from its innermost celebration.

### 4. Who is dead to the world, and to whom the world is dead

Those, therefore, who are in bitterness of soul desire to die completely to the world, so that, just as they desire nothing in the world, they may no longer be held by any bond to the world.

Often it happens that a person no longer holds the world in his mind, yet the world still binds the person through its occupations. He himself is already dead to the world, but the world is not yet dead to him. For the world still sees him as alive when it strives to drag him, intent upon something else, into its own affairs.

Thus Paul rightly says, when he too had perfectly despised the world and saw himself made such that this world could no longer desire him: “The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. 6:14). [Note: Nearly all the manuscripts instead read: “and he strove to present himself to it (the world) in such a way that it could not desire him as though dead,” rather than the editions’ “and he saw himself made such that the world could no longer desire him.” The following words support the manuscript reading.] The world had been crucified to him because he no longer loved it, since it was dead to his heart. [Note: Some manuscripts, together with the Corbie manuscript in its first hand, read *quia hunc corde suo* rather than *quia hunc cordi suo*—an inflectional variation in “because he did not love it as dead in his heart.”]

But he had also crucified himself to the world, because he strove to present himself to it in such a way that it could not desire him as though he were alive.

If a dead person and a living person are in one place, the dead person does not see the living, but the living person sees the dead. If both are dead, neither sees the other. Thus, one who no longer loves the world but is nevertheless loved by it, although he himself, as though dead, does not see the world, is still seen by the world, which is not yet dead.

But if he neither retains the world in his love nor is held by the world’s love, they are mutually dead to one another, because, since neither desires the other, the dead does not regard the dead.

Therefore, because Paul sought neither the glory of the world nor was himself sought by the world’s glory, he glories that both he is crucified to the world and the world to him.

Because many desire this but do not rise all the way to the height of extinction, they rightly say with groaning: “Why was light given to the miserable, and life to those who are in bitterness of soul?”

Life is given to those made bitter when the glory of this world is bestowed upon the sorrowful and groaning. In this life they inflict upon themselves the punishment of a very powerful fear, because, although they themselves do not hold the world, they still fear that they are such as may be held by the world. For unless they were living for it to some degree, it would certainly not love them for its own use. The sea holds living bodies within itself; but it immediately casts the dead out of itself.

It follows:

## CHAPTER FOUR [Recension IV]

**Verse 21: “Who await death, and it does not come.”**

### 5. Those who desire to die to the world are often compelled to serve human needs—and not without profit for themselves and others

They desire to put themselves completely to death and to extinguish themselves from every life of temporal glory. Yet, through the hidden judgments of God, they are often compelled either to preside in governance or to be occupied with honors entrusted to them; and amid all this they continually await complete mortification.

But the awaited death does not come, because their activity unwillingly lives also for temporal glory, which nevertheless they tolerate through fear of God. [Note: All the manuscripts read “through fear of God,” not “through divine love,” as in all the editions except Bartholomew.] Within, they preserve the desire for devotion; outwardly, they fulfill the service of their office, so that they neither withdraw from perfection through their intention nor contradict the Creator’s ordering through pride.

For by a marvelous mercy of the divine nature it comes about that one whose perfect heart tends toward contemplation is occupied with human services, so that his perfected mind may advance many who are weaker, and so that, by seeing himself to be imperfect, he may rise more perfectly to the summit of humility. [Old reading III.]

Sometimes, indeed, from the very things through which holy men endure losses to their desires, they carry away greater gains through the conversion of others. For although they may not be permitted to devote themselves to the things they desire, they rejoice to carry along with them those with whom they are joined.

Thus, by a marvelous dispensation of mercy, it comes about that from the things by which they judge themselves more destroyed, they rise richer toward the building of the heavenly homeland. [Note: The editions have “by a dispensation”; some manuscripts have “by a dispensation of goodness.” The Regius manuscript has “by the power of divinity.”]

### 6. God often delays fulfilling holy desires so that they may grow

Sometimes they do not reach their conceived desires for this reason: so that, through the intervening delay, the open space of the mind may be enlarged toward those same desires; and what, if fulfilled, might perhaps have been diminished, may by a great ordering grow when refused.

Thus they desire to be mortified so that, if permitted, they may already contemplate perfectly the face of their Creator. But their desire is delayed so that it may advance, and it is nourished within the space of its delay so that it may grow.

Hence the bride, panting with desire for her bridegroom, rightly cries: “By night on my bed I sought him whom my soul loves; I sought him, and I did not find him” (Song 3:1).

The bridegroom hides himself when he is sought, so that, not found, he may be sought more ardently. The seeking bride is delayed and does not find him, so that, made more capacious by the delay, she may at some time find more abundantly what she was seeking.

Thus blessed Job, when he had said, “They await death, and it does not come,” immediately adds this, in order to fulfill more subtly the desire of those who seek:

## CHAPTER FIVE [Recension V]

**In the same place: “As those who dig for a treasure.”**

### 7. They grow as the end draws near

All who seek a treasure by digging, when they have begun to dig more deeply, burn more ardently for the work; for the closer they think they are coming to the hidden treasure, the more vigorously they labor in digging. [Note: The ancient Rheims manuscript has “more intensely intent upon the labor.”]

Those, therefore, who fully desire their mortification seek as those who dig for a treasure, because the closer they come to the end, the more ardent they show themselves in their work.

By laboring they do not grow weary, but grow stronger for the work, because the nearer they consider the rewards to be, the more delightfully they sweat in their labor.

Hence Paul rightly says to certain people seeking the hidden treasure of the eternal homeland: “Not abandoning our gathering together, as is the custom of some, but comforting one another, and all the more as you see the day approaching” (Heb. 10:25). [Note: Here Gussanville added “the one laboring” on his own authority, despite the Greek text, the Vulgate, all the manuscripts, and all the editions. The following words, “for to comfort one who is laboring,” perhaps gave occasion for the addition.]

To comfort one who is laboring is to persist together in the labor, because the sight of a fellow laborer lightens the work, just as, when a companion joins someone on a journey, the road is not shortened, but the labor of the journey is nevertheless lightened by the companion’s company. [Note: Almost all the manuscripts have “the road is not drawn away”; the German manuscript, however, has “is not drawn out.” Shortly afterward the Corbie and German manuscripts have “is worn down,” while the Regius has “is smoothed.”]

While Paul was therefore seeking those who would comfort one another in their labors, he added: “All the more as you see the day approaching.” As though he were saying: “Let the labor increase in proportion as the rewards of the labor themselves draw near”; or openly: “You are seeking a treasure? Then you ought to dig all the more ardently, the nearer you have already come by digging to the gold you seek.”

### 8. Those dead to the world hide themselves from earthly things within themselves

Although the statement, “They await death, and it does not come, as those who dig for a treasure,” can also be understood in another way: since we cannot die perfectly to the world unless we are hidden from visible things within the invisible things of our mind, those who desire their mortification are rightly compared with people digging for a treasure.

We die to the world through invisible wisdom, concerning which Solomon says: “If you seek her like money and dig for her like treasures” (Prov. 2:4–5). Wisdom does not lie upon the surface of things, because it lies hidden in invisible realities.

We grasp our mortification when we touch wisdom if, abandoning visible things, we are hidden in invisible things; if, digging out the heart, we seek wisdom in such a way that the mind, by the hand of holy discernment, casts out from itself everything earthly that it thinks, and recognizes the treasure of virtue that lay hidden within it.

It easily finds the treasure within itself if it repels from itself the mass of earthly thought that had pressed upon it wrongly. [Note: The printed editions add “sought”; the manuscripts do not support this.] Because he says that he seeks death as a treasure, he rightly adds:

## CHAPTER SIX

**Verse 22: “And they rejoice exceedingly when they have found the grave.”**

### 9. Divine contemplation is the grave in which the mind, dead to the world, rests

Just as a grave is a place where a body is hidden, so divine contemplation is a kind of grave of the mind, in which the soul is hidden.

We live, as it were, for this world while we wander outward into it with our mind; but we are hidden as the dead in a grave when, mortified externally, we are concealed in the secret place of inward contemplation.

Holy men, therefore, do not cease to mortify themselves with the sword of the sacred word—away from the importunity of temporal desires, from the tumult of useless cares, and from the clamor of clamorous disturbances—and to hide themselves inwardly before the face of God in the bosom of the mind.

Hence the Psalmist rightly says: “You will hide them in the hiding place of your face, from the disturbance of human beings” (Ps. 30:21).

Although this will be done perfectly afterward, it is even now carried out in large measure, when they are snatched from the tumult of temporal desires by delight into inward things, so that, while their mind is wholly directed toward the love of God, it may not be torn apart by any useless disturbance.

This is why Paul saw disciples dead through contemplation and hidden as though in a grave, saying to them: “For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God” (Col. 3:3–4).

Therefore, the one who seeks death rejoices when he finds a grave, because the one who desires to mortify himself greatly rejoices at the rest of contemplation once found, so that, extinguished to the world, he may lie hidden and conceal himself from all the disturbances of external things within the bosom of inward love.

### 10. In ancient times the dead were buried with their riches

If, however, the discovery of a grave is added to the statement that a treasure is dug up, our attention must necessarily observe that the ancients buried the dead together with their riches.

Therefore, the one who seeks a treasure rejoices when he finds a grave, because, when we search out wisdom and turn over the pages of Sacred Scripture, when we examine the examples of those who came before us, we draw joy, as it were, from a grave, because we find the riches of the mind among the dead. [Note: The editions have “of preceding fathers”; “fathers” is absent from the manuscripts.]

Since they were perfectly extinguished to this world, they rest in secret with their riches. A person is therefore enriched by a grave when, through the examples of the righteous, he is raised up in the power of contemplation. [Note: All our manuscripts have “because we find the riches of the mind,” not “and the riches of the mind.” The Regius and German manuscripts shortly afterward have “who, because,” not “because who.”]

But when the one seeking asks, “Why was light given to the miserable?” he indicates why he dares to ask this very question, saying:

## CHAPTER SEVEN [Recension VI]

**Verse 23: “To the man whose way is hidden, and whom God has surrounded with darkness.”**

### 11. The person acting rightly does not know whether he will persevere

A man’s way is hidden from him because, although he already considers what quality of life he is living, he still does not know toward what end he is heading. Although he already desires heavenly things and seeks them with complete desire, he still does not know whether he will remain in those desires.

Leaving sins behind, we strive toward righteousness; we know from where we have come, but we do not know where we shall arrive. We know what we were yesterday, but we do not know what may happen to us tomorrow.

A man’s way is therefore hidden from him because he sets the foot of his work down in such a way that he nevertheless cannot foresee the outcome of its completion.

## [Ancient Version IV.] 12. He does not know whether God may condemn what he considers right. He is surrounded by darkness.

There is also another concealment of our way: sometimes we do not know whether those very things which we believe we are rightly doing are in fact right when examined by the strict Judge. Often, as we said much earlier, our work is a cause of condemnation, and what is thought to be progress is considered a virtue. Often the very thing by which the Judge is believed to be appeased provokes Him to anger; as Solomon testifies, saying: “There is a way which seems right to a man, but its end leads to death” (Proverbs 14:12). [Note: All the Rhem. and Remig. manuscripts, Reg. and Germ., read *quae videtur hominibus recta* (“which seems right to men”).] Therefore, when holy men overcome evil, they fear even their good deeds, lest, while they desire to do good, they be deceived by the appearance of their action, lest a deadly corruption lie hidden beneath the color of goodness.

For they know that, still weighed down by the burden of corruption, they cannot discern good things with precision. And when they bring before their eyes the standard of the final judgment, they sometimes fear even in themselves those things which they approve. With their whole mind they desire inward things, yet, trembling because of the uncertainty of their deeds, they do not know where they are walking. Thus, after it was said, “Why is light given to the miserable?” it is rightly added: “To the man whose way is hidden.” As though it were said: Why does he receive the success of this life who does not know under what estimation of the Judge the course of his action stands? [Note: The manuscripts praised in Vindoc., Norman., Corb. Germ., Reg., and others, as well as the old Vulgate editions, read *successus accipit* (“receives success”). The editions after Coccius read *successus appetit* (“seeks success”).]

It is rightly added: “And God has surrounded him with darkness.” A man is surrounded by darkness because, although he burns with heavenly desire, he does not know inwardly what has been determined concerning him. He is very much afraid lest, at the judgment, something confront him which, in his present desire for fervent goodness, remains hidden from him about himself.

A man is surrounded by darkness because he is oppressed by the obscurity of his ignorance. Is he not surrounded by darkness who often does not remember the past, cannot discover the future, and scarcely recognizes the present? A certain wise man saw himself surrounded by darkness when he said: “The things that are before us we find with difficulty; and the things that are in the heavens, who will investigate?” (Wisdom 9:16). [Note: On the authority of the manuscripts, the old editions, and the very text of Sacred Scripture, we suppress *vix* (“scarcely”), first added here by Coccius.] [Note: Corb. Germ. and Reg. read *quis investigavit* (“who has investigated?”).]

The Prophet saw himself surrounded by these darknesses when he could not penetrate the inner depths of the divine plan, saying: “He made darkness his hiding place” (Psalm 17:12). For our Creator, having cast us into this exile and withdrawn the light of His vision from us, has hidden Himself from our eyes as though in a hiding place of darkness.

## 13. Hence the saints have cause for weeping.

When we carefully contemplate these darknesses of our blindness, we rouse the mind to lamentation. A person weeps over the blindness he suffers outwardly if he humbly remembers that inwardly he is deprived of light. When he looks upon the darkness by which he is surrounded, he afflicts himself with an ardent longing for the inner splendor; with every effort of his attention he shakes himself, and, rejected, seeks the heavenly light which he abandoned when he was created.

Consequently, it often happens that, amid these very devout tears, the brightness of inward joy breaks forth; and the mind which had previously lain blind in torpor, invigorated by sighs, grows strong for the contemplation of the inner radiance. Therefore it is rightly continued:

## CHAPTER VIII [Recension VII]

### VERSE 24.—“Before I eat, I sigh.”

## 14. Tears are often followed by the joy of contemplation.

To eat is for the soul to be nourished by contemplations of the heavenly light. Therefore he sighs before he eats, because he is first afflicted by groans of tribulation and afterward satisfied by the refreshment of contemplation. Unless he sighs, he does not eat; for whoever does not humble himself in this exile through lamentation born of heavenly desires does not taste the joys of the eternal homeland. [Note: All the Rhem. and Remig. manuscripts, Corb. Germ., Reg., and Val. Cl. read *interna[e] patriae* (“of the inner homeland”); so too do the old editions.] Those who rejoice amid the poverty of this pilgrimage are hungry for the food of truth.

Yet the one who eats also sighs, because those whom the love of truth afflicts are also nourished by the refreshment of contemplation. The Prophet ate while sighing when he said: “My tears were my bread” (Psalm 14:4). [Note: Corb. Germ. reads *panis* (“bread,” singular).] The soul is nourished by its mourning when, through weeping, it is lifted to heavenly joys. Within, it endures the groans of its grief; yet it receives the food of refreshment precisely insofar as the force of love pours forth through its tears.

Therefore blessed Job also continues the same force of tears, adding:

## CHAPTER IX

### The same passage.—“And like overflowing waters, so is my roar.”

## 15. The reasons why the saints mourn and tremble.

When waters overflow, they come with force; and as their streams multiply, they swell. But when the elect set the divine judgments before the eyes of their mind, when they tremble over the hidden sentence concerning themselves, when they trust that they may reach God yet fear that they may not, when they recall their past deeds and mourn them, and when they fear what is still to come because they do not know it, streams like those of water gather within them. [Note: One manuscript reads *apponunt* (“set before”) for *opponunt*; the Norman manuscripts read *dum praeterita sua recolunt* (“when they recall their past things”).] These flow out as a roar of grief onto the shores beneath them.

Thus the holy man saw how great were the currents of thought within the lamentations of repentance, and he called the waves of grief “overflowing waters,” saying: “And like overflowing waters, so is my roar.”

[Ancient Version V.] Sometimes, however, as we said a little earlier, the righteous tremble even while engaged in good works. Fearing that they may displease God through some hidden error in those works, they devote themselves to continual lamentation. When the divine scourges suddenly strike them, they suspect that they have offended the grace of their Creator, because, hindered by weakness or oppressed by bitterness, they do not rise to perform deeds of devotion toward their neighbors. The heart is turned into lamentation because the body is held back from the service of its devotion.

When they see that they are not increasing their reward, they fear that even their past deeds have displeased God. Therefore blessed Job rightly added immediately after calling his roar like overflowing waters:

## CHAPTER X

### VERSE 25.—“For the fear that I feared has come upon me, and what I dreaded has happened to me.”

## 16. How greatly the judgments of God must be feared.

The righteous therefore mourn and tremble, and torture themselves with great lamentation, because they fear being abandoned. Although they rejoice in their correction, the correction itself nevertheless disturbs their trembling minds, lest the evil they endure be not a merciful blow of discipline but a just punishment of retribution.

The Psalmist rightly considered this when he said: “Who knows the power of Your anger?” (Psalm 89:11). The power of divine anger cannot be grasped by our mind, because God’s dispensation, through hidden plans concerning us, often receives us by the very means through which He is thought to abandon us, and abandons us by the very means through which He is believed to receive us. Thus what is called anger is often grace, and what is thought to be grace is sometimes anger.

For scourges correct some people, while they lead others into the madness of impatience. Prosperity restrains some from insanity because it soothes them; it uproots others completely from every hope of conversion because it exalts them. Vices drag everyone downward, yet some return from them more easily because they are more deeply ashamed of having fallen into them. Virtues always lift people toward heavenly things, but sometimes, when certain people conceive pride from virtue, they fall along the very path of ascent.

Since, then, the power of divine anger is not known, it must necessarily be feared without ceasing. It follows:

## CHAPTER XI [Recension VIII]

### VERSE 26.—“Have I not dissembled? Have I not been silent? Have I not rested? And indignation has come upon me.”

[Note: Vindoc. reads *Nonne tacui?* (“Have I not kept silence?”).]

## 17. How those in positions of authority commonly sin in thought, speech, and action.

Although we sin by thinking, speaking, and acting wherever we may be placed, the mind is swept away more recklessly in these three ways when it is lifted up by the prosperity of this world. When a person sees that he surpasses others in power, he thinks and feels lofty things about himself in an exalted spirit. When no one resists the authority of his voice, his tongue is more freely unleashed along precipitous paths. When he is permitted to do whatever he wishes, he considers everything he wishes to do justly permitted to him.

But when holy men are supported by worldly power, they bring themselves under a stricter discipline of mind, knowing that the impatience of power can persuade them to do unlawful things as though they were more freely permitted. [Note: One Vindoc. and one Remig. manuscript read *tanto sublimiori mentis disciplinae* (“under so much loftier a discipline of mind”).] They restrain their heart from considering its own glory, hold their tongue back from immoderate speech, and guard their actions from restless wandering.

[Ancient Version VI.] Often those in positions of authority lose the good things they do because they think of them arrogantly. While they consider themselves useful for everything, they even destroy for themselves the merit of the usefulness they have provided. For, if anyone’s deeds are to be more worthy, it is necessary that they should always seem unworthy to him in his own eyes, lest the good action lift up the heart of the one performing it, and, by lifting it up, cast down its author through pride more than it benefits those to whom it is perhaps done.

This is why the king of Babylon, while silently turning over proud thoughts in his mind, said: “Is this not Babylon, which I have built?” (Daniel 4:27). [Note: Vindoc. reads: “Is this not Babylon the great?” and so forth.] He was immediately changed into an irrational animal. He lost what he had become, because he did not wish humbly to conceal what he had done. And because he exalted himself above human beings through the pride of his thoughts, he lost the human understanding which he shared in common with them.

Often, too, those in positions of authority break out into widespread insults against their subjects. Through the insolence of their tongue they lose what they acquire by diligently serving their administration, because they weigh their words with too little fear of the Judge—since whoever says to his brother without cause, “You fool,” commits himself to the fires of Gehenna (Matthew 5:22). [Note: Corb. Germ. and many others read *fatuum* (“foolish” or “fool”), rather than *fatue* (“foolishly”).]

Often those in positions of authority, because they do not know how to restrain themselves from what is permitted, slip into unlawful and restless actions. No one falls into unlawful things alone who does not at times cautiously restrain himself even from what is lawful. Paul rightly shows himself bound by this restraint when he says: “All things are lawful for me, but not all things are expedient” (1 Corinthians 6:12). And, to show how freely his mind expanded precisely through that restraint, he immediately added: “All things are lawful for me, but I will not be brought under the power of anything” (ibid., 6:12).

When the mind follows desires it has conceived, it is proved to be serving the things by which it is overcome. But Paul, for whom all things are lawful, brings himself under the power of nothing, because, by restraining himself even from what is lawful, he rises above those things which, when indulged, would oppress him.

## 18. How Job avoided these faults.

Blessed Job therefore makes known, for our instruction, what kind of man he was in a position of authority, saying: “Have I not dissembled?” When power is possessed, it must be used for the benefit of others and concealed for the sake of avoiding pride, so that the person who uses it may know that he is able to benefit others, yet may not know himself to be able to become exalted.

He indicates what kind of man he was in speech when he adds: “Have I not been silent?” And he further shows what kind of man he was concerning unlawful actions: “Have I not rested?”

The meaning of “being silent” may also be examined more subtly. To be silent is to restrain the mind from the voice of earthly desires. The force of a great outcry is the tumult of the heart.

## 19. Those who preside should interrupt temporal occupations in order to be free for God.

Those who exercise authority well also rest when, for the love of God, they interrupt and set aside the noise of earthly activities, lest, while they ceaselessly occupy themselves with what is lowly, their heart fall completely away from what is highest. For they know that the mind is in no way lifted toward heavenly things if it is continually occupied below by the tumult of cares. What possession of God can an occupied mind attain when, even in its free moments, it struggles to grasp something of Him?

The Psalmist rightly says: “Be still and know that I am God” (Psalm 45:11), because whoever neglects to be free for God hides from himself, by his own judgment, the light of divine vision.

For this reason Moses also says that fish without fins must not be eaten (Leviticus 11:12–13). Fish that have fins commonly leap above the waters. Therefore, only those pass as food into the body of the elect who, while serving what is lowly, know how at times to ascend toward heavenly things by leaps of the mind, lest they remain always hidden in the depths of cares and no breath of the highest love, like free air, touch them. [Note: The old edition, with Corb. Germ., the old Rhem., one Remig., Val. Cl., Reg., and Colb., reads *quasi cibus transeunt* (“pass as food”); Coccius and subsequent editions, with some manuscripts, read *pisces* (“fish”). One Remig. manuscript reads *quod ima deserunt* (“who abandon low things”); Corb. Germ., in its first hand, reads *quod imis deserunt* (“who abandon to low things”).]

Those who are occupied with temporal matters therefore arrange external affairs well when they diligently flee inwardly; when they do not at all delight in the noise of disturbances outside, but rest within themselves in the bosom of tranquility.

[Ancient Version VII.] 20. How perverse minds and devout minds are disposed toward these occupations.

Perverse minds do not cease to turn over the tumult of temporal affairs within themselves, even when they are at leisure. In their thoughts they preserve painted images of the things they love, and although they do nothing outwardly, they nevertheless labor within themselves under the burden of a restless leisure. [Note: Some editions read *servant dicta* (“preserve sayings”), whereas the manuscripts unanimously read *servant depicta* (“preserve pictured things”).] If the administration of those same things is given to them, they abandon themselves completely and pursue these fleeting temporal matters through the course of their attention, with the continual steps of their thoughts.

Devout minds, however, neither seek these things when they are absent nor endure them easily when they are present, because they fear that, through concern for external matters, they may go out from themselves. This is well signified by the lives of the two brothers of whom it is written: “Esau became a man skilled in hunting and a farmer; but Jacob was a simple man dwelling in tents” (Genesis 25:27, according to the Septuagint). Or, as another translation says: “He dwelt at home.”

What else is signified by Esau’s hunting except the life of those who, immersed in external pleasures, follow the flesh? He is also described as a farmer because lovers of this age cultivate external things all the more as they leave their inner selves uncultivated. [Note: The manuscripts read *incolunt* (“inhabit/cultivate”) for *colunt* (“cultivate”).] Jacob, however, is said to dwell in tents or in a house as a simple man, because all who refuse to be scattered among external cares remain simple in thought and in the dwelling place of their conscience.

To dwell in tents or in a house is to restrain oneself within the secrets of the mind and not to scatter oneself outwardly through desires, lest, while they gape after many things outside, they withdraw from themselves through alienated thoughts.

Let the approved man, therefore, tested amid prosperity, say: “Have I not dissembled? Have I not been silent? Have I not rested?” For, as we said above, when worldly prosperity smiles upon them, holy men, as though unaware of the world’s favor, conceal it and with firm steps trample inwardly upon that by which they are lifted up outwardly. [Note: Some manuscripts wrongly read *sublevantur* (“are lifted up”) in place of *sublevant* (“lift up”).] They are silent because they do not resound with the cries of wicked action. Every iniquity has its own voices before the hidden judgments of God. Hence it is written: “The cry of Sodom and Gomorrah has been multiplied” (Genesis 18:20).

They rest when they are not only carried away by the turbulent appetite of temporal desires, but also refuse to be occupied immoderately even with the necessary cares of the present life.

## 21. Why the righteous continually suffer scourges.

Yet while doing these things, they still feel the scourges of the Father, so that they may come to their inheritance more perfect, as the discipline that mercifully strikes them daily purifies them even from the smallest faults. They therefore continually do what is just, but constantly suffer harsh things, because our very justice, when brought before the examination of divine justice, is often injustice; and what shines in the estimation of the one who acts is filthy under the strict judgment of the Judge.

Thus Paul, when he said: “I am conscious of nothing against myself,” immediately added: “But I am not thereby justified” (1 Corinthians 4:4). Then, indicating why he was not justified, he said: “It is the Lord who judges me.” As though he were saying: For this reason I refuse to declare myself justified in the fact that I am conscious of nothing against myself, because I know that I am to be examined more subtly by the One who judges me.

[Ancient Version VIII.] What outwardly favors us must therefore be concealed; what inwardly resounds must be restrained; what entangles us under the appearance of necessity must be avoided. Yet amid all these things we must still fear the scourges of strict examination, because even our perfection is not without fault unless the severe Judge mercifully weighs it on the precise scales of His examination.

[Recension IX.] 22. If the righteous suffer so much, what punishments await the wicked?

It is rightly added: “And indignation has come upon me.” With great skill in teaching, being about to speak of blows, he first set forth righteous deeds, so that each person might consider what punishments will later await sinners if such powerful scourges chastise even the righteous. [Note: The English, Norman, Vindoc., Corb., Reg., Germ., and nearly all manuscripts, followed by the old Paris edition, read *dicturus*; most other editions read *dicturus verba*. Corb. reads *praevidit* (“foresaw”), not *praetulit* (“put first”).] Hence Peter says: “It is time for judgment to begin from the house of God. And if the righteous is scarcely saved, where will the ungodly and sinner appear?” (1 Peter 4:17–18).

Hence Paul, after saying many things in praise of the Thessalonians, immediately added: “So that we ourselves boast of you in the churches of God for your patience and faith in all your persecutions and tribulations which you endure as an example of the just judgment of God” (2 Thessalonians 1:4). As though he were saying: While you endure so many harsh things, although you act so rightly, what else do you give but examples of the just judgment of God? For from your punishment it must be inferred how He strikes those with whom He is angry, if He permits you to be afflicted in this way, you in whom He rejoices; or how He will strike those to whom He displays just judgment, if He also torments you, whom He mercifully corrects and cherishes.

[Ancient Version IX; Recension X.] 23. Job’s friends had a devout intention, but their speech was incautious. What they ought to have done.

After blessed Job’s first speech had ended, his friends in turn—who had come to console him—devoutly subjected themselves to his rebuke. [Note: Some witnesses read *qui consolaturi venerant, ejus piae increpationi subjiciunt* (“who had come to console him submit themselves to his devout rebuke”).] But when they rushed into words of contention, they lost the very purpose of compassion for which they had come.

They did not do this with an evil intention. Although they showed affection toward the one who had been struck, they nevertheless believed that the stricken man had been struck only because of iniquity. And because a good intention was not followed by cautious speech, the very proposal of compassion was turned into the fault of transgression.

They should have considered to whom and when they were speaking. The man to whom they had come was righteous and surrounded by divine scourges. From his former life, therefore, they ought to have weighed those things which they could not understand in his words. From his present scourges they ought not to have rebuked him but to have feared for their own lives. They ought to have joined themselves in tears to the stricken righteous man, not raised themselves up as though reasoning with a righteous man under the scourge, so that their knowledge would not display itself through words, but pain, their teacher, would teach the tongue of the consolers to speak rightly. [Note: The editions read *magistri dolor erudiret* (“the master’s pain would teach”), but all the manuscripts support *magister dolor* (“pain as teacher”).]

Even if they perhaps held different opinions, it was certainly fitting for them to express them humbly, lest by immoderate words they heap wounds upon one already stricken.

## 24. The words or deeds of the better often displease those who are worse.

Often, because they cannot be understood, the deeds or words of the better displease those who are worse. But they should not be rashly criticized by such people precisely because they cannot truly be grasped. Often something is done by superiors as an act of prudent administration which inferiors regard as an error. [Note: The old Rhem., Colb., Germ., Reg., some other manuscripts, and the Bartholomew, old Paris, and Basle editions read *dissimulatorie agitur* (“is done by concealment”); in Germ. a later hand adds *vel dispensatorie* (“or administratively”).] Often strong men say many things which the weak judge because they do not understand them.

This was well signified by the ark of the covenant, which was tilted when the oxen kicked. Because the Levite believed that it was about to fall and attempted to steady it, he immediately received the sentence of death (2 Samuel 6:7).

What is the mind of the righteous except the ark of the covenant? Carried by oxen that kick, it is tilted because sometimes even one who governs well, shaken by the confusion of subject peoples, is moved by love alone to condescend in his administration. But in this act of administration, the inclination itself of strength is thought by the inexperienced to be a fall. Therefore some subjects stretch out a hand of criticism against it, but immediately lose their lives through their own presumption.

The Levite, then, as though helping, stretched out his hand; but, because he transgressed, he lost his life. For whenever the weak rebuke the deeds of the strong, they themselves are rejected from the company of the living.

Sometimes holy men say certain things while condescending to the lowly, and at other times they utter certain things while contemplating the highest matters. Since foolish people do not understand either the force of condescension or that of elevation, they criticize these things boldly.

What is it to wish to correct the righteous for his condescension except to raise up the inclined ark with the proud hand of criticism? What is it to criticize an unfamiliar statement except to regard the movement of his strength as a fall into error?

But the one who presumptuously lifts up God’s ark loses his life, because no one would presume to correct the saints in what is right unless he had first judged himself better than they. Hence that Levite is rightly called Uzzah, a name interpreted as “strong” or “mighty in the Lord,” because presumptuous people would never judge the deeds or words of their superiors weak unless they believed themselves strong in the Lord through an audacious mind.

Job’s friends, then, while rushing against him as though in defense of God, arrogantly overstepped the rule of the divine command.

## 25. If something in the better displeases us, it should not be concealed but expressed with great humility.

When certain deeds of the better displease those who are worse, whatever moves the mind should not be concealed, but should be expressed with great humility. In this way, the intention of the person who thinks devoutly preserves the form of righteousness precisely by walking along the path of humility.

Therefore, what we think should be spoken freely, but what we say should be expressed with profound humility, lest, by putting forward arrogantly what we rightly intend, we make our intentions themselves wrong. [Note: Corb. Germ., German., and Colb., in the first hand, read *non recte* (“not rightly”).]

Paul had spoken many things humbly to his hearers; yet, in the very humble exhortation, he sought to appease them still more humbly, saying: “I ask you, brothers, to bear with the word of consolation, for indeed I have written to you in few words” (Hebrews 13:22).

When taking leave of the Ephesians at Miletus, afflicted and weeping, he recalls his humility to their memory, saying: “Be watchful, remembering that for three years, night and day, I did not cease admonishing each one of you with tears” (Acts 20:31). [Note: Corb. Germ., Reg., Germ., one Rhem., and one Remig. read: “remembering me.”]

To the same people he says again in his Epistle: “I beseech you, brothers—I, a prisoner in the Lord—to walk worthily of the calling with which you were called” (Ephesians 4:1).

From this, let the disciple infer how humbly he ought to speak to his teacher whenever he thinks something rightly, if the teacher of the nations himself asks his disciples so submissively in matters which he preaches with authority. Let each person infer from this how humbly he should speak what he understands rightly to those from whom he has received examples of good living, if Paul humbly subjected himself in speech to those whom he himself had raised to life.

## 26. Whoever does not know how to speak humbly does not know the rule of consolation.

Eliphaz, who speaks first among the friends, came with a devout intention to console; but, abandoning humility of speech, he did not understand the rule of consolation. Neglecting restraint in speaking, he went so far as to insult the afflicted man, saying: “The tiger perishes because it has no prey. The roar of the lion, the voice of the lioness, and the teeth of the lion’s cubs are scattered” (Job 4:11).

By the name “tiger” he evidently marks blessed Job as though by the fault of variability; by the lion’s roar, the terror of the same man; by the lioness’s voice, the loquacity of his wife; and by the scattered teeth of the lion’s cubs, the destruction of his sons’ greed. [Note: The editions add “and audacity,” but these words are found in no manuscript and have been deleted.]

Therefore the divine sentence rightly rebukes the opinion of the friends, which had exalted itself in proud correction, saying: “You have not spoken rightly before me, as my servant Job has” (Job 32:7).

[Ancient Version XI.] 27. How God censures the statements of Job’s friends, and how Paul commends them.

But I see that it must be asked why Paul uses their statements with such authority if those statements are nullified by the Lord’s rebuke. For these are the words of Eliphaz which Paul introduced to the Corinthians, saying, as it is written: “I will catch the wise in their craftiness” (1 Corinthians 3:19; Job 5:13).

How, then, do we reject as wrong what Paul establishes by authority? Or how can we consider right, on Paul’s testimony, what the Lord Himself declares to be wrong? We quickly recognize that these matters are not contradictory if we weigh more subtly the words of that same divine sentence. When it said, “You have not spoken rightly before me,” it immediately added: “as my servant Job has.”

It is therefore clear that certain things in their statements are right, but are surpassed by comparison with something better. Among the other things they say irrationally, they offer many strong statements to blessed Job; but when compared with stronger statements, they lose the force of their strength.

Many of the things they say are remarkable, unless they were said against the holy man. In themselves, therefore, they are great; but because they seek to transfix a righteous man, they lose the weight of that greatness. For even a very strong javelin is thrown in vain when it is aimed at hard rocks; the farther it rebounds blunted, the more forcefully it was hurled.

Thus, although the words of Job’s friends are in some respects very strong, when they strike the strong life of the holy man, they blunt the entire point of their sharpness. They are great in themselves, but should in no way have been used against blessed Job; Paul, weighing them according to their strength, brings them forward with authority; and the Judge, because they were spoken incautiously, rebukes them according to the quality of the persons who spoke them.

## 28. Because some of their statements are right and others wrong, they correspond to heretics.

But since we said above that the friends of blessed Job represent heretics, let us now examine how their words correspond to heretics. They perceive certain things that are entirely right, yet amid these they slip into what is wrong.

Heretics have this characteristic: they mix good things with evil ones, so that they may easily deceive the understanding of their hearers. If they always said wrong things, they would quickly be recognized in their error and would be unable to persuade anyone of what they wished. Again, if they always thought correctly, they would plainly not be heretics.

But while they devote themselves to both through the art of deception, they infect good things with evil and hide evil things beneath good ones so that they may be accepted—like someone who offers a cup of poison and touches the rim of the cup with the sweetness of honey. While what is sweet is tasted at the first touch, what is deadly is also certainly swallowed.

Thus heretics mix right things with wrong ones: by displaying good things they attract hearers to themselves, and by presenting evil things they corrupt them with a hidden plague.

Sometimes, however, corrected by the preaching of the holy Church and by exhortation, they are saved from this deviation of their understanding. Therefore the friends of Job offer the sacrifice of their reconciliation through the hands of that same holy man, and, although condemned, are recalled to the grace of the heavenly Judge. [Note: The English manuscripts and all the others read *addicti* (“condemned”), not *adducti* (“brought”), as the editions have it, including some older ones whose many errors were later propagated into all the others. *Addicti* has greater force and signifies “condemned.”]

This was well signified by the cleansing of the ten lepers in the Gospel (Luke 17:15). In leprosy, one part of the skin is turned into a shining appearance, while another part retains a healthy color. Lepers therefore represent heretics, because, while they mix wrong things with right ones, they spatter the healthy color with spots.

They rightly cry out in order to be saved: “Jesus, teacher.” Since they indicate that they have gone astray in His words, they humbly call Him their teacher for salvation; and when they return to knowledge of the teacher, they immediately return to the form of salvation.

But since we have extended the preface to our exposition somewhat at length in discussing the words of Job’s friends, let us now examine their actual words carefully. It follows:

## CHAPTER XII [Ancient Version XII; Recension XI]

### CHAPTER 4, VERSES 1–2.—“Then Eliphaz the Temanite answered and said: If we begin to speak to you, perhaps you will take it amiss.”

[Col. 0694D] 29. The words of heretics are gentle at first, then harsh.

What is expressed by these interpretations of the names has already been stated above. Since, therefore, we are hastening toward matters not yet discussed, we avoid repeating what has already been said.

This, then, must be observed carefully: those who represent heretics begin to speak gently, saying: “If we begin to speak to you, perhaps you will take it amiss.” Heretics fear irritating their hearers at the beginning of their speech, lest they be listened to vigilantly. They carefully avoid causing sorrow, so that they may seize upon negligence.

Almost always, therefore, what they propose is flattering, but what they introduce afterward in their argument is harsh. [Note: We restore this reading from the English manuscripts and all the others. Previously, Coccius and those following him read *plane* (“plainly”) instead of *pene* (“almost”), and the statement was taken to mean that the friends of Job always spoke flatteringly. That is clearly false. The truth and proper meaning of Gregory’s words are restored by reading *pene*.]

Thus Job’s friends now begin with the reverence of gentle speech, but break out at last into the sharpest darts of accusation. The roots of thorns are soft, but from that very softness they produce what wounds. It follows:

## CHAPTER XIII

### VERSE 2.—“But who can restrain the word he has conceived?”

## 30. Some conceive and utter evil words; others restrain what they have conceived; others do not even conceive them.

There are three kinds of people who differ according to qualities arranged in a gradual sequence.

Some conceive evil things for speaking and are restrained from their speech by no gravity of silence. Others conceive evil things but restrain themselves with great strength of silence. There are also some who, strengthened by the practice of virtue, advance to such heights that, when they are about to speak, they do not even conceive in their heart perverse things which they would then have to suppress by silence.

It is therefore shown to which order Eliphaz belongs, since he declares that he cannot restrain the word he has conceived. In this he also revealed that he knew he would give offense by speaking. For he would not wish to retain words which he cannot restrain unless he foresaw that through them he would inflict wounds.

Good men restrain the haste of speech with the bridle of counsel, and carefully consider whether, by loosening the tongue’s wantonness, they might pierce the conscience of their hearers through incautious speech. Hence Solomon rightly says: “He who lets water loose is the beginning of strife” (Proverbs 17:14).

Water is let loose when the flow of the tongue is unbridled. But the one who releases water becomes the beginning of strife, because through the tongue’s lack of restraint he provides the origin of discord.

The wicked, therefore, just as they are light in understanding, are also rash in speech, and neglect to deliberate about what they should say before speaking. What a shallow conscience conceives, a still lighter tongue immediately reveals.

Thus Eliphaz now infers from his own experience what he despairingly thinks about everyone, saying: “But who can restrain the word he has conceived?” It follows:

## CHAPTER XIV [Recension XII]

### VERSES 3–4.—“Behold, you have instructed many, and you have strengthened weary hands; your words have confirmed the wavering, and you have strengthened trembling knees.”

[Col. 0695D] **31. How great Job was, whose praises even the man who seeks to accuse him cannot refrain from uttering.**—If the text of the narrative itself is examined, the reader derives great benefit from the fact that, amid the quarrels of Job’s friends, the praises of virtues are brought forth in the blessed Job as his faults are torn apart. For never is the testimony of a life so strong as when the man who attempts to bring a charge [Note: [Col. 0695D] Corb. Germ., in the first hand, and perhaps others more correctly: “speaks in praise.”] speaks what deserves praise. Let us consider, then, of what stature this man was, who, teaching the unlearned, strengthening the weary, and confirming the wavering, devoted himself to instructing others amid the cares of his household, amid the guardianship of numerous possessions, amid affection for his children, and amid the duties of so many labors. He carried on all those activities while occupied with them, yet remained free to serve the teaching office of a master. He ordered temporal affairs by governing them; he proclaimed eternal things by preaching them; he showed the uprightness of life both by his conduct to those who saw him and by his speech to those who heard him. [Old XIII.] But whether heretics or any other perverse people recount the good deeds of the just, they twist these into an argument for accusation. Thus Eliphaz gathers an occasion for reproaching blessed Job from the very point at which he has narrated what deserves praise. For it follows:

**CHAPTER XV**

**VERSE 5.**—“But now the scourge has come upon you, and you have failed; it has touched you, and you are troubled.”

**32. The perverse attack the life of the good in two ways.**—All perverse people attack the life of the good in two ways: either they assert that the good say wicked things, or that they do not observe the upright things they say. Hence blessed Job is later reproved by his friends for his speech; now, however, he is assailed on the charge that he spoke rightly but did not live accordingly. The wicked therefore condemn now the speech, now the conduct, of the good, so that either the reproved tongue may fall silent, or the life of the speaker, judged by the testimony of that same tongue, may succumb under accusation. It should also be noted that they first bring forward praises of his speech and afterward [Note: [Col. 0696D] Rhem., Remig., and some others: “concerning the weakness of a good life.” Reg.: “concerning weaknesses of the tongue.” Corb. Germ.: “concerning the weakness of the tongue and life.” Barthol. and the old editions: “concerning the weakness of the tongue and life.”] complain of the weakness of his life. For the wicked, lest they appear publicly wicked, sometimes speak good things about the just, which they know are already recognized by others. But [Col. 0696C] as we said above, they immediately drag these very things toward an accumulation of guilt, and by the fact that they also spoke favorably, they show that they themselves should be believed when speaking adversely; and they insinuate the evil all the more plausibly, the more devotedly they seemed to praise the good. Thus they turn words of approval to the use of accusation, and afterward wound the lives of the just more grievously at the very point from which they had shortly before defended them in outward appearance. Often, too, they first despise the good qualities they had acknowledged and later marvel at them as though they had been lost. Therefore Eliphaz, asserting that the virtues of the holy man have been lost, adds them to his speech by enumerating them:

**CHAPTER XVI [Rec. XIII]**
