**VERSE 6.**—[Note: [Col. 0696D] In the manuscripts Corb. Germ., Reg., Colb., and Norm., *ubi est* is omitted. It appears in the German manuscript through the intervention of a second hand.] “Where is your fear, your strength, your patience, and the perfection of your ways?”

**33. Four degrees of the virtues.**—He inserts all these things into the judgment he had already expressed, saying: “But now the scourge has come upon you, and you have failed; it has touched you, and you are troubled.” Thus he asserts that all things have perished together, since he reproves blessed Job for being troubled by the scourge. Yet it must be carefully observed that, although he reproves him improperly, he nevertheless recounts the order of the virtues appropriately. For by enumerating the virtues of blessed Job, he distinguished his life into four degrees, joining fear to strength, strength to patience, and patience to perfection. In God’s way one begins with fear in order to arrive at strength. For just as boldness produces strength in the way of the world, so in God’s way boldness produces weakness; and just as fear produces weakness in the way of the world, so in God’s way fear generates strength. Solomon bears witness to this when he says: “In the fear of the Lord there is confidence of strength” (Prov. XIV, 26). Confidence of strength is said to be present in the fear of the Lord because our mind despises the terrors of temporal things with greater power in proportion as it submits more truly, through fear, to their Creator. Established in the fear of the Lord, it finds nothing outside itself to fear; for when it is joined by right fear to the Creator of all, it is raised above all things by a certain power.

Strength, however, is shown only in adversity; hence patience is immediately placed after strength. Each person proves more truly that he has advanced in strength the more firmly he bears the evils of others. For the one whom another’s wickedness overthrows has not grown strong within himself. He lies pierced by the sword of his own faintheartedness because he cannot endure opposition. Since perfection is born from patience, the perfection of one’s ways is immediately introduced after patience. [Old XIV.] For the truly perfect person is one who is not impatient with the imperfection of his neighbor. Whoever abandons another because he cannot bear that person’s imperfection testifies against himself that he has not yet advanced toward perfection. Hence Truth says in the Gospel: “In your patience you will possess your souls” (Luke XXI, 19). For what is it to possess one’s soul except to live perfectly in all things and rule over all the movements of the mind from the citadel of virtue? Whoever therefore holds patience possesses his soul, because he becomes strong against every adversity by conquering himself and ruling over himself. And in the very act by which he commendably breaks himself, he powerfully displays himself unbroken; for when he overcomes himself in his own pleasures, he prepares himself unconquered for opposition.

But because Eliphaz has rebuked him by attacking him, he now adds something as though exhorting him, saying:

**CHAPTER XVII [Rec. XIV]**

**VERSE 7.**—“Remember, I beg you: Who ever perished though innocent? Or when were the upright destroyed?”

**34. The innocent often perish here, and the upright are destroyed.**—Whether they are heretics, whose friends we have said Job’s friends resemble outwardly, or any other perverse people, they rebuke as disorderly as they exhort reprehensibly. For he says: “Who ever perished though innocent, or when were the upright destroyed?” Often in this life both the innocent perish and the upright are utterly destroyed; yet by perishing they are preserved for eternal glory. If no innocent person perished, the Prophet would not say: “The just man has perished, and no one takes it to heart” (Isa. LVII, 1). If God did not snatch away the upright in his providence, Wisdom would never have said of the just man: “He was taken away, lest wickedness should change his understanding” (Wis. IV, 11). If no retribution struck the just, Peter would not have foretold, saying: [Col. 0698A] “It is time for judgment to begin from the household of God” (1 Pet. IV, 17).

Those, therefore, are truly upright who, out of love for their heavenly homeland, prepare themselves for every adversity of the present life. For those who fear enduring evils here on account of eternal goods are plainly not upright. But Eliphaz does not think that the upright are destroyed or the innocent perish here because those who serve God not in hope of heavenly glory but for an earthly reward often fashion for themselves precisely what they seek. And while they presume to teach, when they preach earthly security, they show by all their labors what they love. It follows:

**CHAPTER XVIII [Old and Rec. XV]**

**VERSES 8, 9.**—“Rather, I have seen those who work iniquity, sow pains, and reap them perish at the blast of God and be consumed by the breath of his anger.”

**35. They sow pains and reap them. Why God sometimes tolerates the wicked and sometimes strikes them immediately.**—To sow pains is to speak deceitfully; to reap pains is to prevail through speech. Or certainly, they sow pains who act perversely; they reap pains when they are punished for that same perversity. For the fruit of pain is the recompense of condemnation. But when it is immediately added that those who sow and reap pains perish at God’s blast and are consumed by the breath of his anger, the harvest of pain in this passage is shown not yet as punishment but as the completion of iniquity, since from the breath of divine anger the punishment of that same harvest follows. They therefore sow pains and reap them here because what they do is wicked, and they prosper in that very wickedness. Thus it is said of the wicked person through the Psalmist: “His ways are defiled at all times; your judgments are removed from his sight; he will dominate all his enemies” (Ps. X, 5, according to the Hebrew). Shortly afterward it is added concerning him: “Under his tongue are labor and pain” (ibid., 7). He sows pains, therefore, when he acts perversely; he reaps pains when he temporarily prospers through those same perversities.

How, then, do those who are often permitted to remain here for a long time, and more prosperously than the just, perish at God’s blast? For this reason it is again said of them through the Psalmist: “They are not in the labors of men, and they will not be scourged with men” (Ps. LXXII, 5). Jeremiah says: “Why does the way of the wicked prosper?” (Jer. XII, 1). Since, as it is written, “The Lord is patient and a retributor” (Ecclus. V, 4), he often tolerates for a long time those whom he condemns forever; yet sometimes he strikes swiftly, thereby bringing consolation to the faintheartedness of the innocent [Note: [Col. 0698D] One Rhem., two Remig., Reg., and others, especially Norm., read “by coming to their aid with counsel.”]. Sometimes, then, almighty God permits the wicked to prevail for a long time so that the life of the just may be purified more thoroughly. At other times he quickly slays the unjust, and by their destruction strengthens the hearts of the innocent. For if he struck down all who do evil now, for whom would he reserve the final judgment? But if he struck down no one at all, who would believe that God governs human affairs? Sometimes, therefore, he strikes the wicked to show that he does not leave evils unpunished; at other times he tolerates the wicked for a long time to teach those who observe them for what judgment he reserves them.

[Col. 0699A] **36. In what sense the destruction of the wicked is false, and in what sense true.**—This statement concerning the destruction of the wicked, if it is not said generally of everyone together with the end of the present age, is undoubtedly emptied, in large part, of the force of truth. But it will be true then, when the delay of iniquity no longer exists. It may perhaps be more correctly understood in this way: neither does the innocent perish nor is the upright destroyed, because even if he is crushed in the flesh here, he is restored in true salvation before the sight of the eternal Judge. And those who sow pains and reap them perish at God’s blast, because the higher they advance here by acting perversely, the more harshly they are struck by the condemnation that follows.

But when the statement is prefaced with “Remember,” it is plainly shown that a past event is brought back to mind, not that a future event is announced. Eliphaz, therefore, would have spoken more truly if he had believed that these things happen to the wicked generally through a final act of judgment.

**37. God is aptly said to blow when he exacts vengeance; then he who is tranquil in himself appears turbulent to those who perish.**—But the statement that God blows urges us to distinguish the matter more subtly. When we blow, we draw air inward from outside and then return outward what has been drawn inward. God is therefore said to blow in the requital of vengeance because he conceives the plan of judgment inwardly from outward causes and sends forth the sentence from his inward deliberation. Something is drawn inward from outside, as though God were blowing, when he sees our evils outwardly and disposes judgment inwardly [Note: [Col. 0699D] Remig.: “he disposes it inwardly in judgment.”]. And again, as though God were blowing, the breath is sent outward from within when, from the inward conception of his plan, a sentence of condemnation is brought forth outwardly [Note: [Col. 0700D] Ancient Rhem.: “from the inwardly conceived plan.”]. It is therefore rightly said that those who sow pains perish at God’s blast, because from the very source where they do wicked things outwardly, they are rightly struck inwardly.

Or certainly, since God is said to blow and the breath of his anger is immediately added, the very act of his retribution may be signified by the name “breath.” For when we grow angry, we are inflamed by the breath of fury [Note: [Col. 0700D] The Norm. manuscripts read “we are inflamed.” In Utic., or S. Ebrulphus, the earlier reading was “we are ourselves inflamed by it.”]. Thus, to show the Lord as contemplating vengeance, he is said to blow in anger—not that he undergoes any changeability in his nature, but because, after long patience, when he executes vengeance upon the sinner, he who is tranquil in himself appears turbulent to those who perish. The mind of the reprobate sees the Judge opposing its deeds; he therefore appears to it as though moved, because by its own guilt it is itself disturbed in his sight.

But after he has, as though mercifully, admonished him, he adds words of open reproof, saying:

**CHAPTER XIX**

**VERSE 10.**—“The roar of the lion, the voice of the lioness, and the teeth of the lion’s cubs are broken.”

**38. Eliphaz’s harsh words against Job.**—What does he call the roar of the lion except, as we indicated above, the severity of the man? What the voice of the lioness except the loquacity of his wife? What the teeth of the lion’s cubs except the voracity of his children? Because his sons were killed while feasting, they are signified by the image of teeth. While the rigid Eliphaz exults that all these things have been broken, he declares them as though justly condemned. He repeats the harshness of his reproach when he adds:

**CHAPTER XX [Old and Rec. XVI]**

**VERSE 11.**—“The tiger perished because it had no prey, and the lion’s cubs were scattered.”

**39. The varied and rapacious tiger aptly signifies hypocrites.**—Whom does he signify by the name “tiger” except blessed Job, marked by the characteristic of variety, or covered with the spots of hypocrisy? For every pretender, in wishing to appear upright, does not show himself clean in every respect. While he assumes certain virtues through hypocrisy and secretly subjects himself to vices, certain hidden vices suddenly break out upon his face and, through their admixture, make the skin of the superimposed pretence—like an outward appearance—show itself as variegated. Thus it is often astonishing that a man who is seen to excel in so many virtues is also stained by such reprehensible actions.

Every hypocrite is indeed a tiger, because while a clean color is derived from pretense, it is varied by the interruptions of the blackness of vice. Often, while he exalts himself on account of the purity of chastity, he is defiled by the filth of greed. Often, while he appears beautiful through the virtue of generosity, he is stained by the spots of lust. Often, while he is clothed in the beauty of chastity and generosity, he is darkened, as though by zeal for justice, through the savagery of cruelty. Often he is dressed in a beautiful appearance through generosity, chastity, and piety, but is marked by the darkness interspersed through pride. Thus, when vices are mixed in, the hypocrite does not display a pure appearance in himself, just as a tiger can never possess a single color.

This tiger seizes prey because it appropriates for itself the glory of human approval. For whoever is exalted by praise seized from others is, as it were, satiated by prey. The praise of hypocrites is rightly called prey. For it is prey when what belongs to another is violently taken away. Every hypocrite, however, because he simulates a life of justice and snatches for himself the praise of the just, certainly takes what is another’s.

Eliphaz therefore, because he knew that blessed Job had performed praiseworthy deeds while in good health, believed, after the blow had followed, that he had maintained these things through hypocrisy, saying: “The tiger perished because it had no prey.” As though he said openly: “The variety of your pretense has been extinguished, because the flattery of praise has also been taken away; now your hypocrisy has no prey, because, struck by God, you lack human approval.”

**40. The myrmecoleon foreshadows those who are timid toward the powerful and bold toward the weak.**—In the translation of the Seventy, however, it does not say “tiger,” but “The myrmecoleon perished because it had no prey.” The myrmecoleon is a very small animal, hostile to ants, which hides beneath the dust, kills ants carrying grain, and consumes the ants it has killed. In Latin, *myrmicoleon* means either “lion of the ants” or, more precisely, “both ant and lion.” It is rightly called both ant and lion, because it is an ant to winged creatures—or to any other small animals—but a lion to the ants themselves. It devours them as a lion, but is itself devoured by them as an ant.

When Eliphaz therefore says, “The myrmicoleon perished,” what does he rebuke in blessed Job under the name of the myrmicoleont except timidity and boldness? As though he said openly: “You have not been struck unjustly, because you were timid toward the proud and bold toward your subjects.” Or openly: “Fear oppressed you in the presence of the clever, while recklessness inflated you in the presence of the simple.” But the myrmicoleon no longer has prey [Note: [Col. 0701D] Thus the Anglic manuscripts and all the others we consulted; not, as the printed editions read, “because your timid arrogance.” The earlier reading also better suits Eliphaz’s purpose in reproaching Job for both timidity and boldness.], because your timid exaltation, while being pressed by blows, is prevented from injuring another.

But since we have said that the friends of blessed Job bear the character of heretics, it is necessary to explain how these same words of Eliphaz are also to be understood figuratively.

**CHAPTER XXI [Rec. XVII]**

[Col. 0701B] **VERSE 10.**—“The roar of the lion, the voice of the lioness, and the teeth of the lion’s cubs are broken.”

**ALLEGORICAL MEANING**

**41. The same things are represented by different figures in Scripture.**—Because the nature of every created thing is composed of diverse qualities, sacred language can legitimately represent different things by means of one and the same object. The lion possesses strength, but it also possesses savagery. By its strength, therefore, it signifies the Lord; by its savagery, the devil. Hence it is said of the Lord: “The lion from the tribe of Judah, the root of David, has conquered” (Rev. V, 5). Of the devil it is written: “Your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, prowls around seeking someone to devour” (1 Pet. V, 8).

By the name “lioness,” at one time the holy Church is signified, and at another Babylon. Because of her boldness against adversity, the Church is called a lioness, as is confirmed by the words of blessed Job himself. Indicating that Judea had been abandoned by the Church, he says: “The sons of the merchants have not trodden it, nor has the lioness passed through it” (Job XXVIII, 8). At other times, by the name “lioness” the city of this world, that is, Babylon, is expressed. It rages against the life of the innocent with the savagery of cruelty [Note: [Col. 0702D] Thus Corb. Germ., Reg., Germ., Utic., and others. The printed editions read “is let loose.”], and, joined to the ancient enemy as to a most savage lion, conceives the seeds of his perverse persuasion and gives birth from itself to reprobate children in his likeness, like cruel cubs.

The lion’s cubs are any reprobates generated for an iniquitous life through the error of evil spirits. Together they make the entire city of the world that we have called Babylon; yet each of them individually, as a son of Babylon, is called a cub of the lioness, not the lioness herself. For just as all the Church together is called Zion, while the sons of Zion individually signify the saints [Note: [Col. 0702D] In Gussanv., corruptly: “the saints indeed . . . individually indeed.”], so each of the reprobates is called a son of Babylon, while Babylon itself together signifies all the reprobates.

[Old XVII.] **42. The saints fear temptations; heretics, secure in their holiness, despise them.**—But holy men, as long as they are in this life, guard themselves with vigilant care, lest the prowling lion steal upon them by lying in wait—that is, lest the ancient enemy destroy them under some appearance of virtue; lest the voice of the lioness resound in their ears—that is, lest the glory of Babylon turn their minds away from love of the heavenly homeland; lest the teeth of the lion’s cubs bite them—that is, lest the persuasion of the reprobate grow strong in their hearts.

Heretics, by contrast, are already secure, as it were, concerning their holiness, because they imagine that by the merits of their life they have overcome everything. Hence it is now said: “The roar of the lion, the voice of the lioness, and the teeth of the lion’s cubs are broken.” As though it were said openly: “We are not worn down by any scourges because, by surpassing them through the merits of our life, we trample both the strength of the ancient enemy, the desire for earthly glory, and the persuasions of all reprobates” [Note: [Col. 0702D] The printed editions read “and the persuasions of reprobate men.” The reading of all the manuscripts is more fitting to the arrogance of the men of whom it is shortly said: “They consider themselves great in all things and look down on everyone beneath them,” and so forth.]. Hence it is further added:

**CHAPTER XXII**

[Col. 0702B] **VERSE 11.**—“The tiger perished because it had no prey, and the lion’s cubs were scattered.”

**43. Satan is rightly called both a lion and a tiger and a myrmicoleon. Heretics boast as though Satan had been conquered.**—He repeats under the name “tiger” the one whom he designated by the name “lion.” Satan is called a lion because of his cruelty, and is not improperly called a tiger because of the variety of his many-sided cunning. At one time he presents himself to human senses as he truly is, ruined; at another he displays himself as an angel of light. At one time he persuades the minds of fools by flattering them; at another he drives them toward guilt by frightening them. At one time he openly strives to persuade them to vices; at another he conceals himself in his suggestions under the appearance of virtue.

This beast, therefore, marked by such great variety, is rightly called a tiger; among the Seventy interpreters, as we stated above, it is called a myrmicoleon. This animal, hidden in the dust, kills ants carrying grain, as we have said, because the apostate angel, cast down from heaven to earth, lies in wait along the path of their activity for the minds of the just, who prepare for themselves refreshment from good works. When he overcomes them by ambush, he unexpectedly kills them like ants carrying grain.

It is rightly called *myrmicoleon*, that is, “lion and ant.” For, as we have said, it is a lion to the ants and an ant to winged creatures, because the ancient enemy is strong against those who consent to him but weak against those who resist him. If assent is given to his suggestions, he cannot be endured, as it were, like a lion; but if he is resisted, he is crushed like an ant. To some he is a lion, to others an ant: carnal minds scarcely endure his cruelty, while spiritual people trample his weakness beneath the foot of virtue.

Heretics, therefore, because they are proud in their presumption of holiness, say as though exultantly: “The myrmicoleon—or, certainly, the tiger—perished because it had no prey.” As though they said openly: “The ancient adversary has no prey in us, because, so far as our efforts are concerned, he already lies conquered.” For this reason the designation “myrmicoleon” or “tiger” is repeated after the one who had been designated by the roar of the lion already broken [Note: [Col. 0703D] Here the manuscripts disagree. Compend., Corb. Germ., and S. Alb. have: “because the roar of the lion has already been broken”; Utic. formerly had this reading, but now has: “because the roar of the lion has already been broken.” Vindoc. and German. read: “who has already been broken,” and so forth.], because whatever is said with joy is often repeated. The mind repeats its words when it exults. Hence the Psalmist, in genuine joy, frequently repeats what he knows has been heard, saying: “The Lord has heard the voice of my weeping; the Lord has heard my supplication; the Lord has received my prayer” (Ps. VI, 9–10).

[Old XVIII.] **44. The saints rejoice with fear over vices they have subdued; hypocrites consider themselves perfect after overcoming even one vice.**—But when holy men rejoice that they have been rescued from certain vices, they are shaken by great fear even in their very exultation. For although they have already escaped from the storm of some tempest, they nevertheless know that they are still amid the uncertain waves of a perilous sea. They exult in hope in such a way that they tremble with fear; they tremble with fear in such a way that they exult in confidence of hope. Hence the same Psalmist says: “Serve the Lord in fear, and rejoice before him with trembling” (Ps. II, 11).

Those who swell with pride over the appearance of holiness, by contrast, when they overcome any one vice, immediately raise their minds into pride and glory as though over the perfection of their life. Because perhaps they have once escaped the danger of a storm, they forget that they are still sailing on the sea. They consider themselves great in all things and believe that they have utterly conquered the ancient adversary; they look down upon everyone beneath them because they imagine that through wisdom they surpass all others. Hence it is added:

**CHAPTER XXIII [Rec. XVIII]**

[Col. 0703C] **VERSE 12.**—“Moreover, a hidden word was spoken to me.”

**45. Why heretics claim to hear a new and hidden doctrine.**—Heretics pretend that they hear a hidden word so that they may impose a certain reverence for their preaching upon the minds of their hearers. Hence they preach secretly, so that their preaching may seem holy precisely because it is hidden. They refuse to possess common knowledge, lest they be considered equal to others [Note: [Col. 0703D] The printed editions read: “hidden and new.”], and they are always seeking certain novelties. Since others do not know them, they themselves glory before the minds of the ignorant in the uniqueness of their knowledge.

As we have said, they present this knowledge as hidden because, in order to be able to display it as marvelous [Note: [Col. 0704D] The printed editions corruptly read: “so that they may be able to display admiration.” Vindoc. reads: “so that they may display it as marvelous.”], they assert that they have received it secretly. Hence Solomon, through the woman who represents the figure of heretics, says: “Stolen waters are sweeter, and hidden bread is more pleasing” (Prov. IX, 17). Therefore it is also added here: “And my ear received, as though by stealth, the veins of his whisper.”

They receive the veins of a whisper by stealth because, abandoning the grace of shared knowledge, they do not enter it through the door, as the Lord bears witness when he says: “Whoever does not enter the sheepfold of the sheep through the door, but climbs in by another way, is a thief and a robber” (John X, 1–2). He receives the veins of the divine whisper by stealth who, in order to acquire knowledge of its power, abandons the door of public preaching and seeks fissures of perverse interpretation.

But because the thief and robber who enters by another way loves darkness and shudders at the brightness of light, it is rightly added:

**CHAPTER XXIV [Old XIX]**

**VERSE 13.**—“In the horror of a nocturnal vision, when sleep usually seizes people.”

**46. They declare that they scarcely grasp what they teach in order to make it appear lofty. Now they exalt themselves through the uniqueness of their wisdom.**—Often, when heretics attempt to speak of lofty matters, they themselves bear witness that what they put forward is not true. In a nocturnal vision one sees uncertainly. They therefore assert that they received the fissures of the whisper in the dread of a nocturnal vision because, in order to show others that what they teach is lofty, they proclaim that they themselves can scarcely grasp it. But from this it must be inferred how the things they themselves saw uncertainly can be certain for their hearers. Thus, in a remarkable sequence, while lofty words pour forth, they are bound by the very words of their loftiness, exposing their own foolishness.

How greatly they are raised up by the uniqueness of their wisdom is shown when it immediately adds: “When sleep usually seizes people.” As though the heretics openly said: “While human beings sleep below, we remain awake to perceive heavenly things, because those matters are known to us to which the drowsy hearts of other human beings cannot rise in order to attain knowledge.” Or more openly: “Where our understanding rises, the sense of the rest of humanity is asleep.”

Sometimes, however, when they perceive that the hearer despises this, they pretend that they themselves fear what they are saying. Hence it is added:

**CHAPTER XXV**

**VERSE 14.**—“Dread seized me, and trembling, and all my bones were terrified.”

**47. Now they pretend to be fearful.**—Because they desire to appear remarkable on account of the loftiness of their doctrine, they are portrayed as fearing what they fabricate. Although hearing requires less labor than speaking, they are bold enough to utter things which, they assert, they themselves could scarcely endure to hear. Hence it is further added:

**CHAPTER XXVI**

**VERSES 15, 16.**—“And when the spirit passed before me, the hairs of my flesh bristled; something stood there whose face I did not recognize.”

**48. Now they pretend to have known things that cannot be comprehended.**—To indicate that they have known incomprehensible things, they say that the spirit did not stand before them but passed by; and they pretend to have seen a face they did not recognize, so that they may show themselves known to one who cannot be known by the human mind. Hence it is further added:

**CHAPTER XXVII**

**VERSE 16.**—“An image was before my eyes, and I heard a voice like a gentle breeze.”

**49. They cannot contemplate God spiritually, yet they do not always err. They speak certain true and lofty things.**—Often heretics fashion for themselves an imaginary [Note: [Col. 0705D] The printed editions read “imaginable.”] God whom they cannot contemplate spiritually. They claim to hear his voice like a gentle breeze because they rejoice as though they were more intimate than others in knowing his secrets. For they do not teach what God speaks publicly, but what seems secretly to be breathed into their ears.

We have said these things, then, to explain more fully what is to be understood in Eliphaz’s words under the figure of heretics. But the friends of blessed Job would not have been friends of so great a man unless they had learned something manifestly from the truth. Although they err in their judgments of correction, they nevertheless do not entirely waver in their knowledge of the truth [Note: [Col. 0705D] Nearly all the manuscripts, followed by Barthol. and the old editions, show that this is the reading: “yet in their knowledge of the truth they do not entirely waver.” Coccius and other recent editors have a false reading: “yet in their knowledge of the truth they do not waver,” supported by Corb. Germ. Heretics almost always waver; but the mistaken judgment is forestalled by adding “not entirely.”]. Let us therefore repeat these same words from a little earlier, so that we may distinguish more subtly how what is said about the apprehension of truth can genuinely be uttered by those who think rightly.

[Old XX.] Sometimes heretics speak certain true and lofty things, not because they themselves perceive them divinely, but because they have learned them through controversy with the holy Church. They do not turn these things toward the improvement of their conscience but toward the display of knowledge. Hence it often happens that they speak with knowledge of lofty matters but do not know how to live what they say.

Whether, therefore, these matters are understood from the figure of heretics—who possess not the life of knowledge but merely its words—or certainly from the person of the friends of blessed Job, who were undoubtedly able, by perceiving it, to experience the truth they had labored to express by teaching, let us discuss these same matters that we have passed over in greater subtlety. Thus, while Eliphaz’s speech is carefully examined, it may be shown how great his knowledge was, although he did not retain humility within that knowledge, specially appropriating to himself what was a common good. For he says:

**CHAPTER XXVIII [Rec. XIX]**

**VERSE 12.**—“Moreover, a hidden word was spoken to me.”

## Allegorical Meaning

### 50. “A hidden word”: the Son of God, or the speech of the Holy Spirit. This is perceived by few. It can be sensed, but not expressed.

The hidden word is called the invisible Son, concerning whom John says: “In the beginning was the Word.” He himself also indicates that it is hidden when he adds: “And the Word was with God, and the Word was God.” Yet this hidden word is said to be present in the minds of the elect when the power of the only-begotten Son is revealed to believers.

The hidden word can also be understood as the intimate address of inward inspiration, of which John says: “His anointing teaches you about everything” (1 John 2:27). This inspiration, touching the human mind, lifts it up; suppressing temporal thoughts, it inflames the mind with eternal desires, so that it now takes pleasure in nothing except what is above, and despises everything that resounds below from human corruption.

To hear the hidden word, therefore, is to conceive within the heart the speech of the Holy Spirit. This cannot be known except by one who can possess it. Hence, in the words of Truth, this hidden speech is described: “I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete, to remain with you forever, the Spirit of truth, whom the world cannot receive” (John 14:16).

For just as that same Paraclete, after the Mediator’s ascension, is another comforter of the human race and is himself invisible, so he kindles everyone whom he fills to desire invisible things. And because worldly hearts love visible things alone, the world does not receive him, since it does not rise to love invisible things. For the more worldly minds expand themselves outward through their desires, the more they constrict the heart’s capacity to receive him.

And because there are very few in the human race who, cleansed by this purification from the filth of temporal desires, are thereby enlarged for receiving the Holy Spirit, this word is called hidden: what some undoubtedly perceive in their hearts is unknown to the greater part of humanity.

Or certainly this very breath of the Holy Spirit is a hidden word because it can be sensed but cannot be expressed by the noise of speech. When divine inspiration lifts the mind without sound, the hidden word is heard, because the Spirit’s speech sounds silently in the ear of the heart. Hence it is added:

### CHAPTER XXIX [Recension XX]

**The same passage.—“And my ear received, as if furtively, the veins of his whisper.”**

### 51. It seeks a mind withdrawn from visible things. The various ways in which it addresses the mind.

The ear of the heart furtively receives the veins of the heavenly whisper because the mind, breathed upon by the inward subtlety of speech, recognizes it both swiftly and secretly. Unless it hides itself from outward desires, it does not penetrate inward things. It is concealed in order to hear, and it hears in order to be concealed: withdrawn from visible things, it sees invisible things; and filled with invisible things, it perfectly despises visible things.

It should be noted, however, that he does not say, “My ear received, as if furtively, his whisper,” but “the veins of his whisper.” The whisper of the hidden word is this very speech of inward inspiration. The veins of the whisper, however, are called the origins of the causes by which this inspiration itself is conveyed to the mind.

God opens, as it were, the veins of his whisper when he secretly makes known to us the ways by which he comes to the ear of our understanding. Sometimes he pierces us with love, sometimes with fear. Sometimes he shows us how worthless present things are and raises our desire to love eternal things. Sometimes he first reveals eternal things, so that afterward temporal things become contemptible. Sometimes he exposes our own evils to us and extends us so far that we grieve even over the evils of others. Sometimes he places the evils of others before our eyes and, having wonderfully moved us to compunction, corrects us from our own perversity.

To hear furtively the veins of the divine whisper, therefore, is to recognize subtly and secretly the hidden ways of divine inspiration.

### 52. God whispers to us because he does not make himself fully manifest. Through created works, as through certain cracks, he offers himself for contemplation.

Although we can still understand “whisper” and “veins of the whisper” in another way, one who whispers speaks secretly and does not articulate a voice, but imitates one.

As long, therefore, as we are weighed down by the corruption of the flesh, we cannot see the glory of divine power as it remains immutable in itself. The sharpness of our weakness cannot endure what shines upon us unbearably from the ray of his eternity.

When almighty God reveals himself to us through the fissures of contemplation, he does not speak to us but whispers, because, although he does not disclose himself fully, he nevertheless manifests something of himself to the human mind. He no longer whispers but speaks when his distinct appearance is revealed to us.

Hence Truth says in the Gospel: “I will announce to you openly concerning the Father” (John 16:26).

[Note: Col. 0707D. The printed editions read *palam de Patre meo*, “openly concerning my Father.”]

Hence John says: “We shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2).

Hence Paul says: “Then I shall know, even as I have been known” (1 Corinthians 13:12).

But now the divine whisper has as many veins reaching us as there are created works over which the Godhead itself presides. For when we see all the things that have been created, we are lifted up in wonder at the Creator.

Just as gently flowing water is sought through channels cut into the earth so that it may increase, and spreads more broadly the more open the channels it finds, so, when we diligently gather knowledge of the Godhead from consideration of his creation, we open, as it were, the veins of his whisper toward us. For through what we see made, we marvel at the power of its maker; and through things that are publicly visible, what lies hidden flows out to us.

It bursts forth to us, as it were, through a certain sound when he displays his works for our consideration; in this way he reveals himself to some extent, while showing how incomprehensible he is. Since, therefore, we cannot contemplate him worthily, we hear not his voice but scarcely his whisper.

Indeed, because we are not even capable of fully grasping the created things themselves, it is rightly said: “My ear received, as if furtively, the veins of his whisper.” For, cast out from the joys of paradise and punished with blindness, we scarcely grasp the veins of the whisper, because we too consider his wondrous works only hastily and faintly.

It must also be understood that the more the lifted mind considers his power, the more the restrained mind fears his righteousness.

[Note: Col. 0707D. The Turonensis, Corbiensis, Germanensis, and other manuscripts read *fortitudinem*, “strength,” in place of *rectitudinem*, “righteousness.”]

Hence it is rightly added:

### CHAPTER XXX [Recension XXI]

**Verse 13.—“In the horror of a nocturnal vision.”**

### 53. The mind trembles more deeply over its own deeds the more highly it is lifted toward God. Thus it fears and loves God more.

The horror of a nocturnal vision is the fear of hidden contemplation. For the more highly the human mind is lifted and considers eternal things, the more seriously it trembles and fears over temporal deeds, because it sees itself to be more truly guilty the more clearly it perceives that it has diverged from that light which flashes above it.

Thus it happens that, once enlightened, it fears more, because it sees more clearly by how much it differs from the rule of truth. Its own advancement shakes it with grave fear, although previously it saw almost nothing and therefore felt almost secure.

[Note: Col. 0707D. Thus most manuscripts and the old editions; other editions read *quasi secura*, “as though secure,” a reading also found in one Vindocinensis manuscript.]

However much it may have progressed in virtue, it does not yet comprehend anything plainly concerning eternity, but still sees under a certain darkness of imagination. Hence this is called a nocturnal vision. At night, as we said above, we see uncertainly; in the daytime, confidently.

Because, therefore, a cloud of our corruption comes between us and the contemplation of the ray of the inner sun, and that unchangeable light does not break forth upon the weak eyes of our mind as it truly is, we still see God as though in a nocturnal vision, undoubtedly remaining in darkness under an uncertain contemplation.

But although the mind has conceived something, however slight, concerning him, it nevertheless shudders when considering his greatness. It fears more because it feels unequal even to the traces of his contemplation. Returning to itself, it loves him more closely: unable to bear his wondrous sweetness, it has scarcely tasted it under an uncertain vision.

But because no one reaches the summit of this elevation unless the crowd of carnal desires, clamoring importunately, has first been restrained, it is rightly added:

### CHAPTER XXXI [Recension XXII]

**The same passage.—“When sleep is accustomed to seize human beings.”**

### 54. Contemplation is not reached unless carnal desires are put to sleep. Sleep is understood in three ways.

Whoever desires to pursue the things of the world is, as it were, awake; whoever seeks inward quiet and flees the clamor of this world is, as it were, falling asleep.

First, however, it must be understood that in sacred Scripture sleep, when used figuratively, is understood in three ways. Sometimes the death of the flesh is expressed by sleep; sometimes the torpor of negligence; and sometimes the repose of life that comes from trampling earthly desires underfoot.

The death of the flesh is indicated by the name of sleep or falling asleep, as Paul says: “I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, concerning those who sleep.” And shortly afterward: “So also God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep through Jesus” (1 Thessalonians 4:12).

[Note: Cols. 0707D–0708D. The Vindocinensis and most manuscripts read *nolo autem vos*, “but I do not wish you”; two Compendiensis manuscripts, the Corbiensis Germanensis, Colbertinus, Regius, and Vallicellianus read *nolumus vos*, “we do not wish you.” The Greek text has literally *οὐ θέλω ὑμᾶς*, “I do not wish you.”]

Again, the torpor of negligence is signified by sleep, as the same Paul says: “It is already the hour for us to rise from sleep” (Romans 13:11). And again: “Awake, righteous people, and do not sin” (1 Corinthians 15:34).

Sleep also signifies the repose of life that comes from trampling down the desires of the flesh, as is said in the voice of the bride in the Song of Songs: “I sleep, but my heart is awake” (Song of Songs 5:2).

[Note: Col. 0708D. The Corbiensis Germanensis, Regius, Normannus, and Vallicellianus read *in canticorum Cantico*, “in the Song of Songs”; this more aptly represents the title of the sacred book, *Sirhasirim*, “Song of Songs.” The printed editions read *in Canticis canticorum*, “in the Songs of songs.”] For the holy mind, the more it restrains itself from the clamor of temporal desire, the more truly it knows inward things; and the more eagerly it remains awake to what is within, the more it conceals itself from outward disturbance.

This is aptly represented by Jacob sleeping on his journey (Genesis 28:11). He placed a stone under his head and fell asleep; he saw a ladder fixed to heaven from the earth, the Lord leaning upon the ladder, and angels ascending and descending.

To sleep on a journey is, in the passage of this present life, to rest from love of temporal things. To sleep on a journey is, in the course of passing days, to close the eyes of the mind to the desire for visible things—the eyes which the deceiver opened for the first human beings when he said: “God knows that on whatever day you eat from it, your eyes will be opened” (Genesis 3:5–6).

Then it is added shortly afterward: “She took some of its fruit and ate; and she also gave it to her husband, who ate; and the eyes of both of them were opened.” Guilt opened the eyes of desire, which innocence had kept closed.

To see angels ascending and descending is to contemplate the citizens of the heavenly homeland: either how greatly they cleave to their Creator by rising above themselves, or with what compassion of charity they descend to our weaknesses.

[Note: Col. 0709D. All the manuscripts and both the old and recent editions read *auctori suo semetipsos transcendendo inhaereant*, “how they cleave to their Creator by transcending themselves.”]

### 55. Resting from worldly activity is not enough for contemplation unless virtues are also practiced.

It must be observed very carefully that the one who sees angels while sleeping is the one who places his head upon a stone. Clearly, the person who withdraws from outward works and penetrates inward things is the one who attentively observes the imitation of his Redeemer, who is the governing faculty of the human being (*τὸ ἡγεμονικόν*).

To place one’s head upon a stone is to cling to Christ in the mind. Those who have withdrawn from the activities of the present life but are not carried away by any love toward things above may sleep, but they cannot see angels, because they disdain to keep their head upon the stone.

There are indeed some who flee the activities of the world but exercise themselves in no virtues. They sleep in torpor, not in devotion; and therefore they do not see inward things, because they have placed their head not upon a stone but upon the earth.

It often happens to such people that the more securely they abstain from outward activities, the more broadly, in their leisure, they accumulate within themselves the clamor of unclean thoughts.

Thus, under the figure of Judea, the Prophet laments a soul lying torpid in idleness, when it is said: “Her enemies saw her and mocked her Sabbaths” (Lamentations 1:7). For the commandment of the law requires abstention from outward work on the Sabbath. The enemies therefore mock when they see Sabbaths, when evil spirits drag the very leisure of withdrawal into illicit thoughts. Each soul, the more it believes itself to be serving God by withdrawing from outward activities, the more it serves their tyranny through illicit thinking.

Holy men, however, who are put to sleep from worldly works not by torpor but by virtue, sleep more laboriously than they could have remained awake, because, in abandoning the activities of this age and rising above them, they fight daily against themselves in strenuous conflict:

- lest the mind grow torpid through negligence;
- lest, subdued by leisure, it grow cold toward unclean desires;
- lest it burn beyond what is right even in good desires;
- lest, sparing itself under the appearance of discretion, it grow weak in perfection.

It does all this, withdraws itself entirely from the restless desire of the world, abandons the clamor of earthly activities, and, intent upon virtues through the pursuit of quiet, sleeps while remaining awake.

For no one is led to contemplate inward things unless he diligently withdraws from the things that entangle him outwardly. Hence Truth itself says: “No one can serve two masters” (Matthew 6:24). Hence Paul says: “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in worldly business, so that he may please the one to whom he has proved himself” (2 Timothy 2:4). Hence the Lord admonishes through the Prophet: “Be still, and know that I am God” (Psalm 45:11).

Since, therefore, inward knowledge is not perceived unless one ceases from outward entanglement, the time of the hidden word and divine whisper is rightly described now when it is said:

[Note: Cols. 0709D–0710D. Most manuscripts read *concipitur*, “is conceived”; the Vallicellianus has *concupitur*; the Corbiensis Germanensis, Regius, and the Colbertinus in its first hand read *conspicitur*, “is beheld,” which is the reading adopted here.] “In the horror of a nocturnal vision, when sleep is accustomed to seize human beings.” For our mind is in no way carried away into the power of intimate contemplation unless it has first been deliberately put to sleep amid the tumult of earthly desires.

Yet the human spirit, lifted by a certain instrument of its own contemplation, sees higher things above itself and therefore trembles all the more terribly within itself.

Hence it is aptly added:

### CHAPTER XXXII [Recension XXIII]

**Verse 14.—“Fear seized me, and trembling, and all my bones were terrified.”**

### 56. The more deeply we contemplate God’s righteousness, the more we fear concerning ourselves.

What is signified by bones except strong deeds? Concerning them the Prophet says: “The Lord guards all their bones” (Psalm 33:21). People often judge the things they do to be of some importance because they do not know how subtle is the judgment of the innermost tribunal.

But when, carried away through contemplation, they behold things above, they are in some way melted out of the security of their own presumption. They tremble all the more in the divine presence because they do not consider even their good deeds worthy of the judgment of the one whom they behold.

Hence the one who had advanced by performing strong deeds, lifted up by the Spirit, cried out: “All my bones shall say: Lord, who is like you?” (Psalm 34:10). It is as though he said: “My flesh has no words, because my weakness is utterly silent before you; but my bones proclaim the praise of your greatness, because even those things which I believed to be strong in me tremble when considered in your presence.”

Hence Manoah, terrified at the sight of the angel, says: “We shall surely die, because we have seen the Lord” (Judges 13:22). His wife immediately consoles him, saying: “If the Lord had wished to kill us, he would not have received a burnt offering and libations from our hands” (ibid., 23).

What does it mean that, at the sight of the angel, the man becomes fearful while the woman is bold, except that, whenever heavenly things are shown to us, the spirit indeed shakes with fear, but hope nevertheless presumes?

Hope rises from the very place where the spirit is disturbed to dare greater things, because it sees first what is above.

Since, therefore, whenever the lifted mind sees higher mysteries of the heavenly secrets, the entire solidity of human strength trembles, it is rightly said now: “Fear seized me, and trembling, and all my bones were terrified.”

It is as though it were said openly: “While perceiving the secrets of inward subtlety, I have faltered before the Judge precisely where I believed myself strong.”

For when we contemplate the strictness of divine justice, we rightly fear even concerning the very works that we thought we had performed strongly. When our righteousness is brought before the inward rule, if it encounters a strict judgment, it strikes against inward rectitude through the many bends of its crookedness.

Thus Paul rightly says, when he saw that he possessed the bones of virtues and yet that these same bones trembled under strict examination: “It is a very small thing for me to be judged by you or by a human day. I do not even judge myself, for I am conscious of nothing against myself” (1 Corinthians 4:3).

[Note: Col. 0711D. The Compendiensis and Corbiensis Germanensis read *dijudico*, “I pass judgment on,” for *judico*, “I judge.”]

But after hearing the veins of the divine whisper, these same bones trembled, and he immediately added: “But I am not thereby justified; the one who judges me is the Lord.” It is as though he said: “I remember having acted rightly, yet I do not presume upon my merits, because our life is brought before his judgment, under which even the bones of our strength are shaken.”

### 57. The grace of contemplation is not lasting.

When the mind is suspended in contemplation, when, overcoming the constraints of the flesh, it searches through the power of vision into something of the inward security of freedom, it cannot remain above itself for long. For although the spirit raises it to the heights, the flesh still presses it downward by the very weight of its corruption.

Hence it is added:

### CHAPTER XXXIII

**Verse 15.—“And when the spirit passed before me, the hairs of my flesh bristled.”**

### 58. We know invisible things, but only fleetingly.

The spirit passes before us when we know invisible things, yet see them not solidly but fleetingly. The mind is not fixed for long in the sweetness of inward contemplation, because, struck back by the immensity of the light, it is recalled to itself.

When it tastes inward sweetness, it burns with love and strives to rise above itself, but, broken by the darkness of its weakness, it falls back. Advancing with great power, it sees that it cannot see what it ardently loves; yet it would not ardently love it unless it saw it to some extent.

The spirit therefore does not remain but passes, because our contemplation opens the heavenly light to us while we long for it and immediately hides it when we grow weak.

And because, however much anyone may have advanced in virtue in this life, he still feels the goad of his corruption—for “the corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks of many things” (Wisdom 9:15)—it is rightly added: “The hairs of my flesh bristled.”

### [Recension XXIV]

### 59. No one here is so perfect that something needing to be cut away does not continually arise in him.

The hairs of the flesh are any superfluities of human corruption. The hairs of the flesh are the thoughts of the old life, which we cut away from the mind without being wearied by any grief at their loss.

Moses rightly says: “Let the Levites shave all the hairs of their flesh” (Numbers 8:7). A Levite is so called because he has been taken up or assumed for service. All Levites, therefore, ought to shave the hairs of their flesh, because the one who is taken up into divine service must appear clean before God’s eyes from every thought of the flesh. Otherwise the mind may bring forth illicit thoughts and make the soul’s beautiful appearance ugly, as though with luxuriant hairs.

[Note: Col. 0711D. The Corbiensis Germanensis and Normannus read *quasi pilis fruticantibus*, “as though with bushy hairs”; the printed editions read *fructificantibus*, “fruit-bearing.”]

But however much, as we have said, the virtue of holy conduct may have raised someone up, something still arises from the old life that must be endured. Hence the Levites are commanded to shave their hairs, not to pluck them out. For when the hairs are shaved, their roots remain in the flesh and they grow again to be cut off, because superfluous thoughts must indeed be amputated with great effort, but can never be cut away completely.

The flesh is always generating superfluities, which the spirit must always cut off with the sword of vigilance. Yet we perceive these things more subtly when we penetrate the heights of contemplation.

Therefore it is rightly said now: “When the spirit passed before me, the hairs of my flesh bristled.”

### [Former Recension XXIV]

### 60. The mind devoted to contemplation cuts these things away more diligently; thus it almost fixes the Spirit, yet cannot hold him for long.

The human mind, lifted to the height of contemplation, torments itself more severely over superfluous things the more subtly it perceives what it loves. When it beholds the beauty of what it seeks above itself, it judges strictly whatever weakness in itself it had previously tolerated calmly.

When the spirit passes, therefore, the hairs tremble, because superfluous thoughts flee before the force of compunction. Nothing loose, nothing lax, is now pleasing, because the severity of inward visitation, breathing upon the mind, inflames it even against itself.

[Note: Col. 0712D. All our manuscripts read *afflatam mentem*, “the inspired/breathed-upon mind”; the printed editions read *afflictam mentem*, “the afflicted mind.”]

When whatever illicit thing is born in the heart is cut away by continual strictness, it often happens that the mind, invigorated, clings somewhat more widely to the ray of its contemplation and almost fixes the spirit that was passing.

Yet this very delay in contemplation does not fully reveal the power of the Godhead, because its immensity transcends human powers, even when they have been strengthened and lifted up.

Hence it is rightly added:

### CHAPTER XXXIV [Recension XXV]

**Verse 16.—“A certain one stood, whose face I did not recognize.”**

### 61. Through sin the human being became wholly carnal and cannot think without images of bodies. How the soul—and afterward God—may be perceived without them.

We do not say “a certain one” except of someone whom we either do not wish or are unable to identify. What is meant here by “a certain one” is explained immediately by the words that follow: “Whose face I did not recognize.”

The human soul, expelled from the joys of paradise through the fault of the first human beings, lost the light of invisible things and poured itself entirely into love of visible things. It was blinded to inward contemplation in proportion as it was deformingly scattered outward. Thus it knows nothing except what it recognizes, so to speak, by touching it with bodily eyes.

The human being, who would also have been spiritual in the flesh if he had wished to keep the commandment, became through sin carnal even in mind, so that he thinks only of what draws the mind to itself through images of bodies.

The body of the heavens, the earth, the waters, the animals, and all visible things is what he continually observes. When the delighted mind throws itself wholly into these things, it becomes coarse and heavy, away from the subtlety of inward understanding. Because it can no longer raise itself to higher things, it willingly lies weak among them.

When, however, it strives with remarkable efforts to rise from them, it is a very great achievement if the soul is led to knowledge of itself after the bodily appearance has been suppressed—so that it may think of itself without a bodily image and, by thinking of itself, prepare a way for itself toward considering the substance of eternity.

### [Former Recension XXV]

### 62. How far the human soul is removed from the divine substance. If it does not yet perceive what God is, it at least perceives what he is not.

In this way it presents itself to itself as a kind of ladder, by which, ascending from outward things, it may pass into itself and proceed from itself toward its Author.

When the mind abandons bodily images and comes into itself, it rises no little. But although the soul is incorporeal, because it is joined to a body it is recognized from its own condition as something held in the place of flesh.

[Note: Col. 0713D. In the printed editions, following the Colbertinus manuscript, *localis*, “local,” is added; it is absent from the other manuscripts.]

When it forgets what it knew, knows what it did not know, remembers what it had consigned to oblivion, becomes cheerful after sadness, and is subdued after joy, it indicates by this very diversity how far it is removed from the substance of eternal unchangeability, which is always the same as it is: present everywhere, invisible everywhere, wholly everywhere, incomprehensible everywhere.

[Note: Col. 0713D. The printed editions add *natura*, “nature,” after *aeternae incommutabilitatis*, “eternal unchangeability”; this word is superfluous and occurs in no manuscript except the Corbiensis Germanensis.]

Through the longing mind it is perceived without sight, undoubtedly heard without sound, received without movement, touched without a body, and held without a place.

[Note: Cols. 0713D–0714D. The Floriacensis, Turonensis, Compendiensis, Vindocinensis, Corbiensis Germanensis, two Regii, Germanensis, and Normannus read *sine dubio auditur*, “is undoubtedly heard.” The Colbertinus has *jugulato dubio*, “with doubt slain”; it now reads *sine sono*, “without sound,” which approaches the reading of the printed editions, *sine voce*, “without voice.”]

When the mind, accustomed to bodily things, thinks about this substance, it bears the phantasms of various images. When, however, by the hand of discernment it drives these away from the eyes of its attention and puts everything else after them, it now sees this substance to some extent.

Although it has not yet apprehended what it is, it has certainly recognized what it is not. Since, therefore, the mind is carried toward unfamiliar things when it searches into the essence of the Godhead, it is rightly said now: “A certain one stood, whose face I did not recognize.”

### 63. To stand belongs to God alone.

It is rightly said that he “stood.” Every creature, because it was made from nothing and by itself tends toward nothing, does not have the power to stand but to flow away.

The rational creature, however, because it was created in the image of its Author, is fixed so that it may not pass into nothing. The irrational creature is not fixed in this way, but, until it fills out the appearance of the universe through the ministry of its vision, it is delayed in passing away.

Even though heaven and earth will afterward remain forever, they nevertheless hasten toward nothing from themselves now; but for the use of those whom they serve, they continue while being changed for the better.

[Note: Col. 0714D. One Regius manuscript, with the Corbiensis Germanensis and Colbertinus, reads *mutata*, “having been changed,” for *mutanda*, “to be changed.”]

To stand, therefore, belongs to the Creator alone, through whom all things pass without his passing away, and in whom some things are retained so that they may not pass away.

Hence our Redeemer, because the stability of his divinity could not be grasped by the human mind, came to us and showed it to us, as it were, by passing through: created, born, dead, buried, rising again, and returning to the heavenly realms.

This is aptly indicated in the Gospel by the blind man who was enlightened: while passing by, he granted hearing, but while standing, he restored sight (Matthew 9:27; 20:30; Mark 8:22; Luke 18:35; John 9:1).

[Note: Col. 0714D. The Corbiensis Germanensis, Colbertinus, Regius, Normannus, and most manuscripts read *caeco innotuit*, “made himself known to the blind man,” in place of the printed edition’s *caeco illuminato*, “the blind man enlightened.”]

Through the dispensation of his humanity he had to pass; through the power of his divinity, because he is present everywhere, he had to stand.

The Lord is therefore said to hear the voices of our blindness while passing by, because, having become human, he takes pity on human misery. While standing, he restores light, because through the power of his divinity he illuminates the darkness of our weakness.

It is rightly added, therefore, after it was said, “When the spirit passed before me”: “A certain one stood, whose face I did not recognize.”

[Note: Col. 0714D. The first Compendiensis reads *me praesentem transiret*, “passed while I was present,” for *me praesente transiret*, “passed before me.”]

It is as though it were said openly: “I perceived that the one whom I sensed through his passing did not pass away.”

[Note: Col. 0714D. The Vindocinensis reads *eum per quem transitum sensi*, “him through whom I sensed a passing.”]

The same one, therefore, is the one who passes and the one who stands. He passes because, once known, he cannot be held; but he stands because, insofar as he is known, he appears unchangeable.

Since, therefore, the one who is always the same is seen fleetingly, God is seen simultaneously as passing and standing.

Or certainly, his standing means that he is not altered by any change, as it is said to Moses: “I am who I am” (Exodus 3:14). And as James indicates when he says: “With whom there is no change or shadow caused by turning” (James 1:17).

Because, however, whoever has already grasped something of the contemplation of eternity sees it through the eternal likeness of that same eternity, it is rightly added:

### CHAPTER XXXV

**The same passage.—“An image before my eyes.”**

### 64. Whatever we perceive concerning the Father, we see through the Son.

The Son is the image of the Father, as Moses indicates concerning the creation of the human being: “God created man; he made him in the image of God” (Genesis 1:27).

And as a certain wise man says concerning that same Son, expressing the Wisdom: “For he is the brightness of eternal light” (Wisdom 7:26).

And as Paul says: “He is the radiance of his glory and the form of his substance” (Hebrews 1:3).

When his eternity is seen, insofar as the capacity of our weakness permits, his image is set before the eyes of our mind. For when we truly direct our attention toward the Father, we see him, insofar as we receive him, through his image—that is, through the Son. Through that likeness which was born from him without beginning, we strive somehow to see the one who neither began nor ceases.

Hence Truth itself says in the Gospel: “No one comes to the Father except through me” (John 14:6).

It is rightly added:

### CHAPTER XXXVI [Recension XXVI]

**The same passage.—“And I heard a voice like a gentle breeze.”**

### 65. The voice of the Holy Spirit is both a gentle breeze and a mighty wind.

What is signified by “the voice of a gentle breeze” except knowledge of the Holy Spirit? Proceeding from the Father and receiving from what belongs to the Son, he is poured gently into the feeble capacity of our knowledge.

Yet when he came upon the apostles, he was manifested through outward sound as a mighty wind, when it is said: “Suddenly there came from heaven a sound like the rush of a mighty wind” (Acts 2:2).

The Holy Spirit, when he discloses himself to the weakness of human understanding, is expressed both by the sound of a mighty wind and by the voice of a gentle breeze. For when he comes, he is both mighty and gentle: gentle because he tempers his knowledge for our senses, so far as it can in any way be known; mighty because, however much he tempers it, by his coming he nevertheless disturbs the blindness of our weakness by illuminating it.

By his illumination he touches us gently, but he shakes our poverty with immense force.

66. The gentle breeze, because here it reveals itself only slightly to the saints, however much it may do so. In contemplation, whatever the mind is able perfectly to see is not God.---The voice of God is therefore heard like a gentle breeze, because, in this present life, the Divinity does not disclose itself to those who contemplate it as it truly is, but faintly reveals its brightness to the bleary eyes of our mind. This is aptly signified by the very receiving of the Law, when it is said that Moses went up, and the Lord descended upon the mountain (Exod. 24:1). [Note: Thus the manuscripts read, instead of *in montem* (“onto the mountain”), as it is found here and often elsewhere through the editors’ correction. They did not notice that Gregory observed grammatical rules rather imperfectly, as he himself testifies in the letter to Leander prefixed to these books.]

The mountain is our very contemplation, into which we climb so that we may be lifted up to see those things that lie beyond our weakness. Yet the Lord descends into it, because, when we have made much progress, he opens a little of himself to our senses; if indeed one may say “a little” or “something” of him who, remaining always one and the same, cannot be understood in parts [Note: In some manuscripts, “understood particularly”; in two Vendôme manuscripts, “understood equally.”], and yet is said to be shared by his faithful, although no division whatsoever is admitted in his substance. But because we cannot express him in fully developed speech, hindered as we are by the weakness of infancy, so to speak, we stammeringly sound him forth to some extent. And because, even when lifted up into great contemplation, we attain something subtle from the knowledge of eternity, this is shown by the words of sacred history, when the noble prophet Elijah [Note: Two Vendôme manuscripts, Corbie German, one Regius manuscript, Colbert, and another witness read “the prophet teaches us.”] is instructed concerning the knowledge of God. When the Lord promised that he would pass before him, saying, “Behold, the Lord passes by: a great and mighty wind, overturning mountains and crushing rocks before the Lord,” he immediately added: “The Lord is not in the wind”; and after the wind, an earthquake: “The Lord is not in the earthquake”; and after the earthquake, a fire: “The Lord is not in the fire”; and after the fire, the sound of a thin breeze [Note: The editions add *et ibi Dominus* (“and the Lord was there”), which is absent from the manuscripts of Normandy, Beauvais, Vendôme, Compiègne, and others. Nor are we persuaded that this should be retained, as is shown by what follows: that he is in the sound of the thin breeze is not denied. For the text does not say “it is affirmed”] (1 Kings 19:11–12).

The wind overturns mountains before the Lord and crushes rocks, because the terror that bursts forth at his coming both casts down the height of our heart and melts its hardness. But the Lord is said not to be in the wind of the earthquake or in the fire, while his presence in the sound of the thin breeze is not denied. For when the mind is suspended in the sublimity of contemplation, whatever it is able perfectly to see is not God; but when it sees something subtle, this is what it hears concerning the incomprehensible substance of eternity. We perceive, as it were, the sound of a thin breeze when, in contemplation, we subtly and suddenly taste something of the flavor of the unbounded truth [Note: In Beauvais, “we taste through the subtlety of contemplation.”]. Thus what we know of God is true precisely when we realize that we cannot fully know anything about him.

Hence it is rightly added there: “When Elijah heard this, he covered his face with his cloak and went out and stood at the entrance of the cave” (ibid.). After the sound of the thin breeze, the prophet covers his face with his cloak, because in that most subtle contemplation of truth he recognizes how great is the ignorance by which human beings are enveloped. To draw a cloak over the face is to veil the mind, out of consideration for its own weakness, so that it does not dare rashly to seek higher things or open the eyes of its understanding beyond itself, but reverently closes them to what it cannot grasp.

While doing this, he is described as standing at the entrance of the cave. For what is our cave except this dwelling of corruption, in which we are still held by our old condition? But when we begin to perceive something of the knowledge of the Divinity, we stand, as it were, already at the entrance of our cave. For although we cannot go forth completely, yet, thirsting for knowledge of the truth, we already catch something of the breeze of freedom. To stand at the entrance of the cave is therefore, with the obstacle of our corruption restrained, to begin to go out toward knowledge of the truth.

Hence, when the cloud descended upon the tabernacle, the Israelites are said to have stood at the entrances of their tents, watching from a distance (Exod. 33:9), because those who perceive the coming of the Divinity to some extent are, as it were, already coming forth from the dwelling of the flesh. Since, therefore, however greatly the human mind stretches itself by virtue, it scarcely perceives the outermost things of what lies within, it is rightly said here: “And I heard a voice like a gentle breeze.” But since, when divine knowledge reveals even a little of itself to us, it teaches us fully the ignorance of our weakness, let the one who heard the voice of the gentle breeze state what he learned from that very hearing. The text continues:

## CHAPTER XXXVII [Formerly XXVII]

**VERSE 17.** “Will a human being be justified in comparison with God, or will a man be purer than his Maker?”

67. Human righteousness, compared with divine righteousness, is unrighteousness. How complaints about God’s scourges must be restrained.---Human righteousness, compared with divine righteousness, is unrighteousness, because a lamp is seen to shine in darkness, but when placed in the sun’s rays it is darkened [Note: In most manuscripts, *tenebricatur* (“is darkened”). This was formerly read in Colbert.]. What, then, did Eliphaz, carried away in contemplation, understand, except that a human being cannot be justified in comparison with God? We rightly believe that the things we do outwardly are correct, but when we scarcely know what is inward, we grow dark as though placed in the sun’s rays. When, however, we perceive those things to some extent, we do not judge these outward matters in the same way, because each person judges darkness the more subtly the more truly the brightness of the light is established for him. Whoever sees the light knows how to assess darkness; but whoever is ignorant of the whiteness of light approves obscure things as though they were bright.

It is rightly added: “Or will a man be purer than his Maker?” Whoever murmurs about being struck [Note: Thus most and the best witnesses, rather than “about persecution,” as in editions after Coccius.], what else does he do than accuse the justice of the one who strikes? A man therefore considers himself purer than his Maker if he prepares a complaint against the scourge; and he undoubtedly puts the Maker beneath himself, since he reproves his judgment concerning his own affliction. Thus, so that a human being may not dare to criticize the judge of guilt, let him humbly consider him the author of nature, because he who wonderfully made humanity from nothing does not unjustly afflict what he has made. Eliphaz learned this when he heard the voice like a gentle breeze. For through consideration of divine greatness one learns how humbly to fear God’s chastisement. Whoever tastes heavenly things also bears lower things with equanimity, because inwardly he clearly sees how highly God values what he does outwardly.

A person wrongly considers himself upright if he does not know the rule of supreme uprightness. A piece of wood is often thought straight if it is not brought against a ruler; but when it is joined to the ruler, it is found to swell with how great a crookedness, because the receding straightness [Note: Thus the manuscripts of Compiègne, Beauvais, Tours, Corbie German, Colbert, Germany, and Normandy. The Vendôme manuscript likewise has this; another has “the straightness that withdraws.” The editions read “the straightness that approaches.”] rebukes what the deceived eye had approved. Eliphaz, then, because he saw heavenly things, pronounced a strict judgment on lower things; and although he wrongly rebuked blessed Job, he nevertheless rightly described the creature’s measure in comparison with the Creator of all, saying:

## CHAPTER XXXVIII [Formerly XXVII, Revised XXVIII]

**VERSES 18–19.** “Behold, those who serve him are not steadfast, and in his angels he finds perversity. How much more will those who dwell in houses of clay, whose foundation is earthly, be consumed like a moth?”

68. Why the angelic nature is changeable, and how it becomes unchangeable. The fall of the angels warns human beings to distrust their own weakness. The moth signifies desire.---Although the angelic nature remains immutably in its state by clinging to contemplation of its Maker, yet, precisely because it is a creature, it possesses within itself the variability of change. To be changed is to pass from one thing to another, and not to remain stable within oneself. Every thing tends toward something else by as many steps as it is subject to movements of its mutability. Only the incomprehensible nature does not know how to move from its state; it cannot be changed by him who is always the same.

For if the substance of the angels had been free from the movement of mutability, then, although well created by the Maker, it would never have fallen from the height of its blessedness in the reprobate spirits. Wonderfully, almighty God created the nature of the highest spirits good but changeable [Note: Some manuscripts read “of the heavenly spirits.” One Regius manuscript has “of the heavenly”; another has “of his own.”], so that those who did not wish to remain might fall, while those who persisted in their created condition might remain in it with greater dignity precisely because they stood there by their own choice; and so that they might become more meritorious before God insofar as they fixed the movement of their mutability by the steadfastness of their will.

Since, then, the angelic nature itself is changeable within itself, although it has overcome this mutability by being bound with the bonds of love to him who is always the same, it is rightly said here: “Behold, those who serve him are not steadfast.” The same evidence of mutability is immediately added when, concerning the apostate spirits, it continues: “And in his angels he finds perversity” [Note: Here the manuscripts and editions vary. We follow the highly authoritative reading found in all the manuscripts of Normandy, one English manuscript, both of Compiègne, Beauvais, Corbie German, Colbert, Germany, and the editions. The editions have a reading from whose comparison the weakness of the human condition is well understood.].

From their fall he properly draws a consideration of human weakness when he immediately adds: “How much more will these, who dwell in houses of clay, whose foundation is earthly, be consumed like a moth?” We dwell in houses of clay because we subsist in earthly bodies. Paul aptly considered this when he said: “We have this treasure in earthen vessels” (2 Cor. 4:7). And again: “We know that if our earthly house of this dwelling is dissolved, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands” (2 Cor. 5:1).

The earthly foundation is likewise the substance of the flesh. The Psalmist had carefully perceived this within himself when he said: “My bone was not hidden from you, which you made in secret, and my substance in the lower parts of the earth” (Ps. 138:15).

A moth is born from clothing and, in being born, corrupts the very garment from which it arises. The flesh is, as it were, a kind of garment of the soul; but this garment has its own moth, because carnal temptation arises from the flesh itself, and by it the flesh is torn. Our garment is consumed, as it were, by its own moth when corruptible flesh gives birth to temptation and through it reaches destruction. A human being is consumed like a moth when from himself there arises that by which he is worn away.

It is as though he plainly said: If those spirits cannot of themselves be unchangeable who are not weighed down by any weakness of the flesh, with what presumption do human beings confidently suppose that they can remain steadfast in the good, when carnal weakness weighs them down and hinders them in the very thing by which understanding raises them to the highest things, so that through the fault of corruption they possess within themselves the means by which they grow old, away from their innermost renewal?

[Formerly XXVIII.]

69. The angels are teachers who, however holy, are not without fault. The moth, causing harm without sound, represents the wicked who do not notice the damage they suffer.---The holy teachers may also be understood by the angels, as the prophet says: “The lips of the priest guard knowledge, and they seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts” (Mal. 2:7). However brightly they may shine with virtue, they cannot be entirely without fault while they walk along the road of the present life, because their steps are touched either by the mud of unlawful action or by the dust of thought.

They dwell in houses of clay who delight in this seductive life of the flesh. Paul had despised dwelling in this house of clay when he said: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3:20–21).
