Let him therefore say: “Behold, those who serve him are not steadfast, and in his angels he finds perversity; how much more will those who dwell in houses of clay, whose foundation is earthly, be consumed like a moth?” It is as though he plainly said: If those who announce eternal things and gird themselves against temporal things cannot pass through the road of the present life without contamination [Note: The printed editions read *cogitantes* (“thinking”), instead of *nuntiantes* (“announcing”), which is found in all our manuscripts.], what losses do those suffer who rejoice in being amid the pleasures of a dwelling in the flesh?

Those who serve him are not steadfast because, when the mind strives toward lofty things, it is scattered by thoughts of the flesh. Thus, often, while the spirit thirsts for inner things and looks only upon heavenly things, it is struck by a sudden carnal pleasure, lies divided from itself, and—having rejoiced that it had overcome the troubles of its weakness—groans when it is brought down by a sudden wound. Perversity is therefore also found in the angels, when even those who announce the truth are sometimes weighed down by the intrusion of a deceptive life.

If even these are struck by the iniquity of this world, though holy purpose raises them against it, by what blows are those pierced whom the very delight of their weakness lays low before the world’s arrows? They are rightly described as being consumed like a moth. A moth causes harm without making a sound; so the minds of the wicked, because they neglect to consider their losses, lose their integrity without realizing it. They lose innocence from the heart, truth from the mouth, continence from the flesh, and, with the passage of time, life from their age. Yet they do not notice that they are continually losing these things, because they are wholly occupied with temporal concerns and desires. They are therefore consumed, as it were, by a moth, because they suffer the bite of guilt without a sound, unaware of how much damage they endure in life and innocence.

Hence it is rightly added:

## CHAPTER XXXIX

**VERSE 20.** “From morning until evening they will be cut down.”

70. The reprobate do not change their perverse mind even at the final hour.---A sinner is cut down from morning until evening when, from the beginning to the end of his life, he is wounded by the perpetration of iniquity. At every moment the reprobate multiply against themselves the blows of increasing wickedness, by which, once cut down, they fall into the abyss. Of them the Psalmist rightly says: “Men of blood and deceit will not halve their days” (Ps. 54:25).

To halve one’s days is to divide a life spent badly in pleasures by the lamentation of repentance and, by dividing it in this way, to restore it to good use. But the wicked do not halve their days, because they do not change their perverse mind even at the final hour. In contrast, Paul rightly admonishes us: “Redeeming the time, because the days are evil” (Eph. 5:16). We redeem time when, by weeping, we restore the former life that we lost through dissipation.

The text continues:

## CHAPTER XL

**THE SAME PASSAGE.** “And because no one understands, they will perish forever.”

71. They neglect to know what punishments await them and what rewards await the righteous.---This means: no one among those who are cut down from morning until evening. No one understands—whether among those who perish, or among those who imitate the lost ways of those who perish [Note: In one Compiègne manuscript, Lyranus, Bigot, Évreux, Germany, Colbert, and Regius 1, “those who go before”; shortly afterward, “the ways of those who go before.”]. Hence it is written elsewhere: “The righteous perishes, and no one considers it in his heart; and men of mercy are gathered, because there is no one who understands” (Isa. 57:1).

Thus the wicked, while they desire only temporal things and scorn to know what good things await the elect forever; while they see the affliction of the righteous but do not recognize what recompense belongs to affliction, extend the foot of their actions into the abyss, because they willingly close the eyes of their understanding to the light [Note: Corbie German prefers *malis* (“evil things”) to *stultis* (“foolish things”). One Regius manuscript, another Vendôme manuscript, and the edition of Bartholomew [and other old editions] read: “For deceived by many evil pleasures.” Another edition reads: “For by many pleasures of evil.”].

Deceived by foolish pleasures, they love what they see temporally; alienated from themselves, they do not see where they are falling forever. “Morning” may also signify prosperity, and “evening” the adversity of this world. The reprobate are therefore cut down from morning until evening because they perish through prosperity, growing wanton, and through adversity rise up in impatience to madness. Guilt would not cut them down from morning until evening if they regarded prosperity as nourishment or judged adversity to be the cutting of their wound.

[Formerly XXIX.]

72. Those who make good use of prosperity or adversity.---Yet the human race is not abandoned in such a way that everything is permitted to tend toward destruction. There are some who despise the delight of the present life even when it is present; they consider it transitory and trample it underfoot out of love for eternity. When they take this first step of judgment, they become more vigorous and reach higher things, so that they despise all temporal things not only because they are quickly lost, but also because they do not desire to cling to them even if they could have been eternal. They withdraw their love from things beautifully created because, with the steps of their hearts, they move toward the Creator of beauty.

There are others who love the good things of the present life but nevertheless do not attain them. They thirst with all their desires for temporal things and seek the glory of the world, but are wholly unable to obtain it. Their heart, so to speak, draws them toward the world, while the world drives them back to their heart [Note: One manuscript of Compiègne and one of Longpont read, “the world drives them away from the heart.” The reading we have retained is preferable and is confirmed by what follows: “so that, broken by their adversities, they return to their mind and, returning into themselves, consider,” etc.].

For it often happens that, broken by their own adversities, they return to their mind and, returning into themselves, consider how empty are the things they were seeking. They immediately turn themselves to lamentation over so foolish a desire and desire eternal things all the more fervently the more foolishly they regret having labored for temporal things.

Hence, after describing the reprobate, it is rightly added:

## CHAPTER XLI [Revised XXIX]

**VERSE 21.** “But those who are left will be taken away from them.”

73. Those whom the world despises, God chooses.---Whom else are we to understand as “those who are left” except those despised by this world? The present age chooses them for no use of glory and, as though they were insignificant and unworthy, leaves them behind. But the Lord is said to take away the world’s remnants because he deigns to choose those despised by this age, as Paul testifies: “Not many wise according to the flesh, not many powerful, not many noble; but God chose the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; and God chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong” (1 Cor. 1:26–27).

This is aptly signified in the Books of Kings by the Egyptian boy who grew weary on the road. The Amalekite abandons him, sick, along the way; David finds him, restores him with food, and makes him the guide of his journey. David pursues the Amalekite, finds him feasting, and utterly destroys him (1 Sam. 30:13).

For what does it mean that the Egyptian boy grows weary on the road of the Amalekite, except that the lover of the present age, covered by the blackness of his sin, is often left behind by that same age, weak and despised, so that he cannot run with it but, broken by adversity, grows numb? But David finds him because our Redeemer, truly strong of hand, sometimes converts to his love those whom he finds despised by the world’s glory [Note: Two manuscripts of Compiègne, Corbie, Colbert, Germany, Regius, Remigius, and some others read, “converts them to his own love.”].

He feeds him with food because he refreshes him with knowledge of the word. He chooses him as the guide of his journey because he also makes him his preacher. The one who could not follow the Amalekite becomes David’s guide, because the person whom the world abandoned as unworthy not only receives the Lord within his mind after conversion, but also, by preaching, leads him into the hearts of others.

With David as guide, he finds and destroys the feasting Amalekite, because through these preachers Christ destroys the world’s joy, whose companions the world disdained to have. Since, then, the Lord often chooses those whom the world leaves behind, it is rightly said here: “Those who are left will be taken away from them.”

The text continues:

## CHAPTER XLII

**THE SAME PASSAGE.** “They will die, and not in wisdom.”

74. It is customary in Scripture that, when it inserts something foreign, it soon returns to the subject under discussion.---What does it mean that, after previously describing the destruction of the reprobate by saying, “Because no one understands, they will perish forever,” he immediately added concerning God’s elect, “Those who are left will be taken away from them,” and then promptly added something that does not apply to those same elect: “They will die, and not in wisdom”? If they are divinely taken away from the reprobate, how are they said to die without wisdom?

It is, of course, the custom of sacred Scripture that, when it narrates something, it inserts a sentence concerning another matter and then immediately returns to what came before. After saying, “Because there is no one who understands, they will perish forever,” it at once introduced the lot of the elect, saying, “But those who are left will be taken away from them.” Then, turning the eye of its sentence again toward the destruction of the reprobate that it had foretold, it suddenly added: “They will die, and not in wisdom.” It is as though it said: Those whom I said would perish forever because they do not understand will undoubtedly die without wisdom.

We shall show more clearly that this is sometimes the manner of sacred discourse if we produce from it a similar example. The apostle Paul, when admonishing his beloved disciple concerning the establishment of ecclesiastical offices, lest he should advance anyone improperly to sacred orders, said: “Do not lay hands hastily on anyone, nor share in the sins of others; keep yourself chaste” (1 Tim. 5:22). He immediately turned his words to the weakness of Timothy’s body and said: “Do not continue drinking water, but use a little wine for the sake of your stomach and your frequent infirmities” (ibid., 23). Then he immediately added: “The sins of some people are manifest, preceding them to judgment, while those of others follow afterward” (ibid., 24) [Note: In Vendôme and most manuscripts, “but some also follow afterward,” which is repeated below. Corbie German, Colbert, and Regius 1 have *quorumdam* (“of some”), although below Corbie and Regius have *quosdam* (“some”).].

What does the prohibition against drinking water because of his illness have to do with what he added concerning the hidden and manifest sins of certain people? It has this connection: after inserting a sentence about Timothy’s infirmity, Paul returned at the end to what he had said earlier, “Do not lay hands hastily on anyone, nor share in the sins of others.” To show how carefully those same sins must be investigated, he added immediately, with a warning about discernment inserted against the burden of infirmity, that in some they were manifest and in others hidden, saying: “The sins of some people are manifest, preceding them to judgment, while those of others follow afterward” [Note: The manuscripts and editions vary greatly here. The Regius, Norman, and many other manuscripts read: “with the continuous burden of infirmity inserted.” One Vendôme manuscript reads: “having inserted the infirmity, he immediately added a warning of discernment against the burden.” The old Paris edition of 1495 reads: “having inserted continually the burden of infirmity, he immediately added a warning of discernment.” The Basel edition of 1514 reads: “having inserted a warning of discernment against the burden of infirmity,” as do Bartholomew and the Paris edition of 1518. We have preferred the reading supported by the manuscripts of Corbie German and Colbert.].

Thus, by this sentence, Paul did not remain with the same words with which he had followed his statement about Timothy’s infirmity; rather, he returned to what he had interrupted above. In the same way here, when Eliphaz said concerning the elect, “Those who are left will be taken away from them,” and immediately added, “They will die, and not in wisdom,” he at once returned to what he had previously said concerning the reprobate: “And because no one understands, they will perish forever.”

[Formerly XXX.]

75. The reprobate die, and the elect die: the latter in wisdom, the former in folly.---The reprobate despise the elect because the elect move toward invisible life through visible death. Of the reprobate it is rightly said here: “They will die, and not in wisdom.” It is as though it were plainly said: They flee both death and wisdom together; but they entirely abandon wisdom, while they do not escape the snares of death. Since they could have lived by dying, when they fear the death that will unquestionably come, they lose both life and wisdom.

But the righteous die in wisdom because, when death threatens for the sake of truth and cannot be avoided altogether, they disdain to defer it. By bearing it with equanimity, they turn the punishment of their origin into an instrument of virtue, so that life should be received from the very thing by which, through the merit of the first sin, life is compelled to end.

But because Eliphaz spoke these things truthfully against the wicked while judging blessed Job blameworthy, he puffed himself up with the pride of wisdom. Hence, after such declarations of righteousness, he adds words of mockery, saying:

## CHAPTER XLIII [Revised XXX]

**CHAPTER 5, VERSE 1.** “Call, then, if there is anyone who will answer you.”

76. What it means to call upon God, and what it means for God to answer.---Almighty God often abandons the prayer of one who, in tranquility, disregards his commandments. Hence it is written: “Whoever turns away his ear so as not to hear the law—his prayer will be accursed” (Prov. 28:9).

To call is for us to beseech God with humble prayer; for God to answer is to grant effect to prayers. He therefore says: “Call, if there is anyone who will answer you.” It is as though he plainly said: However loudly you cry out in affliction, you do not have God answering you, because your voice in tribulation does not find the one whom your mind despised in tranquility.

He adds further in mockery:

## CHAPTER XLIV

**THE SAME PASSAGE.** “And turn to some one of the saints.”

77. As though he were scorning him, he says: You are unable to find the saints as helpers in affliction, since you did not wish to have them as companions in joy. Immediately after the mockery he adds a judgment, saying [Note: In the text of Job, “truly foolish.”]:

## CHAPTER XLV

**VERSE 2.** “Anger kills the foolish man, and envy slays the little one.”

78. Eliphaz speaks what is true, but not truly of Job. The guilt of anger: how great it is and how many evils it causes.---This sentence would indeed be true if it had not been directed against the patience of so great a man. But let us consider what is said, although it is rebuffed by the virtue of the one who hears it, so that we may show how correct the statement is, if it were not unjustly applied to blessed Job, since it is written: “But you, Lord, judge with tranquility” (Wis. 12:18).

We must carefully understand that whenever we restrain the turbulent movements of the soul by the power of gentleness, we strive to return to the likeness of our Creator. For when anger lashes the tranquility of the mind, it tears and disturbs it, as though splitting it apart, so that it does not harmonize with itself and loses the power of its innermost likeness.

[Formerly XXXI.] Let us therefore consider how great is the guilt of anger, by which, when gentleness is lost, the likeness of the heavenly image is disfigured. Through anger wisdom is lost, so that one knows not at all what ought to be done or in what order, as it is written: “Anger rests in the bosom of a fool” (Eccl. 7:10), because it withdraws the light of understanding when it confuses the mind by stirring it up.

Through anger life is lost, even if wisdom appears to be retained, as it is written: “Anger destroys even the prudent” (Prov. 15:1, according to the Septuagint), because a confused mind does not fulfill what it is capable of understanding prudently.

Through anger righteousness is abandoned, as it is written: “The anger of man does not accomplish the righteousness of God” (Jas. 1:20), because when the disturbed mind sharpens the judgment of its reason, it considers everything that fury suggests to be right.

Through anger the grace of social life is lost, as it is written: “Do not be a constant companion of an angry person, lest you learn his ways and take a stumbling-block for your soul” (Prov. 22:24–25) [Note: These words, together with the following text of sacred Scripture, are omitted in the manuscripts of Compiègne, Beauvais, Évreux, Uzes, Corbie, Colbert, Germany, Regius, and others, and we have found them in no manuscript.]. And again: “Who can dwell with a person whose spirit is quick to anger?” (Prov. 18:14). For one who does not restrain himself by human reason must live alone like a beast.

Through anger concord is broken, as it is written: “An angry man produces quarrels, and a wrathful man digs up sins” (Prov. 15:18). The angry person digs up sins because he makes even wicked people worse when he carelessly provokes them to discord.

Through anger the light of truth is lost, as it is written: “Let not the sun go down upon your anger” (Eph. 4:26), because when anger brings the darkness of confusion upon the mind, God hides from it the ray of his knowledge.

Through anger the splendor of the Holy Spirit is shut out. In contrast, according to the ancient translation, it is written: “Upon whom will my spirit rest, except upon the humble, the quiet, and the one who trembles at my words?” (Isa. 66:2). When he said “humble,” he immediately added “quiet.” If anger therefore removes the quiet of the mind, it closes the dwelling place of the Holy Spirit; and when he departs, the mind, left empty, is soon led into open madness and is scattered outwardly from the innermost foundation of its thoughts.

79. A portrait of an angry person rendered in the most vivid colors.---When the heart is inflamed by the goads of anger, it throbs, the body trembles, the tongue stumbles, the face burns, the eyes grow fierce, and familiar people are no longer recognized. The mouth indeed forms a cry, but the mind does not know what it is saying. In what respect, then, is such a person far removed from those seized by an alien spirit, when he is unaware of his own actions?

Hence it often happens that anger leaps as far as the hands; and the farther reason withdraws, the more boldly anger rises. The mind cannot restrain itself because it has become subject to another’s power. Fury exercises the limbs outwardly in blows to the degree that inwardly it holds captive the mind, which is the mistress of the limbs.

Sometimes the hands do not strike, but the tongue is turned into a dart of cursing. The angry person asks in prayer for his brother’s destruction and desires God to carry out what the perverse human being himself either fears or is ashamed to do. Thus he commits murder by wish and word even when he refrains from injuring his neighbor with his hands.

Sometimes anger, having disturbed the mind, imposes silence as though by judgment; and to the degree that it does not express itself outwardly through the tongue, it burns more fiercely within. Thus an angry person withdraws conversation from his neighbor and, by saying nothing, declares how hostile he is. Sometimes this severity of silence is undertaken as an exercise of discipline, provided that the rule of discernment is carefully maintained inwardly.

But sometimes, when the inflamed mind is restrained from its customary speech, it becomes completely separated from love of its neighbor as time passes. Sharper goads come to the mind, and causes that provoke it more gravely arise. The speck in the angry person’s eye becomes a beam when anger is transformed into hatred.

Often anger shut up within the mind burns more fiercely through silence and forms noisily shouting voices in secret. It throws before itself words by which it may be exasperated and, as though placed in the examination of a case, answers itself with increasingly harsh provocation. Solomon briefly indicates this when he says: “The expectation of the wicked is fury” (Prov. 11:23).

Thus it happens that the disturbed mind feels a greater uproar in its silence, and the flame of enclosed anger consumes it more severely [Note: In the Roman edition of Sixtus V and in the older editions, except Bartholomew, the reading is: “and the flame of anger, once enclosed, consumes it more severely.” The manuscripts and the reasoning of the passage persuade us that *clausae* (“of enclosed anger”) should be read instead of *clausa* (“enclosed”). In Colbert, Corbie German, and other manuscripts, however, *clausa irae flamma* is found, which has the same meaning. Thomas James testifies that this is also found in the English manuscripts. In Regius and most others, *clausae* is consistently read. We have searched in vain for the following quotation in the books of Ecclesiasticus and Wisdom, which Gregory often cites under the name of “a certain wise man,” formerly chapter 16, now chapter 30, “what you do not want to happen to you,” etc. It belongs to neither of those books, but to Tobit 4:16.].

Hence a certain wise man rightly said before us: “The thoughts of an angry person are generations of vipers; they devour the mind that gave birth to them.”

## [Old XXXII]

### 80. Four degrees in which we are disposed toward anger

It must be understood that anger kindles some people more quickly and abandons them more easily. Others it moves slowly, but holds them longer. Some are like reeds set alight: while they resound with shouting, they give back something like the noises of their own kindling; they make a flame quickly, but immediately grow cold into ash. Others, unlike heavier and harder logs, receive the fire slowly, but once kindled are extinguished with greater difficulty; and because they rouse themselves more slowly to harshness, they preserve the fire of their fury longer. [Note: The Norman, Tours, Corbie, and other manuscripts read “they preserve the fire of their fury more harshly.”] Others—and this is worse—both take up the flames of anger quickly and lay them down slowly. Still others receive these flames slowly and lose them quickly.

In these four modes, the reader clearly recognizes that, with respect to the good of tranquility, the last approaches it more closely than the first, while in evil the third surpasses the second. But what does it profit us to say how anger possesses the mind, if we do not also explain how it ought to be restrained? [Col. 0725D]

### 81. Two ways of restraining anger

For anger, once broken, ceases to possess the mind in two ways. The first is that the vigilant mind, before beginning any action, should set before itself all the insults it may have to endure, so that, by considering the reproaches suffered by its Redeemer, it may prepare itself for adversity. It receives adversity coming upon it all the more firmly, the more cautiously it has armed itself through foreknowledge. Whoever is caught unprepared by adversity is found, as it were, sleeping before an enemy; and the enemy kills him more quickly because he pierces one who is not resisting.

But the person who marks beforehand, through vigilance, the evils that threaten awaits hostile attacks like one keeping watch in an ambush; and from the very place where he seemed likely to be caught unaware, he is bravely equipped for victory. Therefore the mind ought carefully, before the beginning of its action, to meditate upon every adversity, so that, always thinking of these things and always protected against them by the breastplate of patience, it may both overcome whatever arrives in a prudent manner and regard whatever does not arrive as gain.

The second way of preserving gentleness is that, when we observe the excesses of others, we should consider our own sins by which we have exceeded against others. For awareness of one’s own weakness excuses the faults of others to us. The person patiently tolerates an injury inflicted upon him who devoutly remembers that he may perhaps still have something in which he himself ought to be tolerated.

And just as fire is extinguished by water, so fury is extinguished when, as the mind’s anger rises, each person’s own fault is recalled to his mind. For a person is ashamed not to pardon sins when he remembers that he has often sinned against God or neighbor in ways requiring pardon. [Col. 0726A–B]

## [Old XXXIII]

### 82. One anger arises from impatience, another from zeal. The first blinds the eye; the other so disturbs it that it prepares it to see more clearly

Amid these matters, it must carefully be understood that one kind of anger is aroused by impatience, while another is produced by zeal. [Note: In Coccius and subsequent editions: “zeal for justice”; this is a gloss unknown, at least in the more reliable manuscripts.] The former arises from vice, the latter from virtue. For if no anger arose from virtue, Phinehas would not have appeased the force of divine judgment with the sword. Since Eli did not possess this anger, he aroused against himself the movement of heavenly vengeance without appeasement. For in proportion as he was lukewarm against the faults of his subjects, the severity of the eternal ruler burned against him.

Of this anger the Psalmist says: “Be angry, and do not sin” (Ps. 4:5). Those who wish this to mean that we should be angry only with ourselves, and not also with neighbors who sin, do not understand it correctly. For if we are commanded to love our neighbors as ourselves, it follows that we should be angry at their errors just as at our own faults.

Solomon says of this anger: “Anger is better than laughter, because through sadness of countenance the mind of the offender is corrected” (Eccl. 7:4). Again the Psalmist says: “My eye is troubled because of anger” (Ps. 6:8). Anger arising from vice blinds the eye of the mind; anger arising from zeal disturbs it. For when the mind is shaken, at least by emulation of what is right, the contemplation that cannot be perceived except with a tranquil heart is scattered.

The zeal for righteousness itself, because it agitates the mind with unrest, immediately darkens its vision, so that in its disturbance it does not see higher things which, only shortly before, it had beheld while tranquil. Yet from the very point at which it is temporarily struck back so that it cannot see, it is more subtly led back to higher things. For this same emulation of what is right, after a short while, opens more generously in tranquility the eternal things which it temporarily closes through agitation; and from the point where the mind is disturbed so that it does not see, it advances so that it may become clearer in seeing truly.

It is like an ailing eye: when eye-salve is applied, light is entirely denied it, but shortly afterward it truly receives light from the very source through which it healthfully loses it for a time. Yet contemplation is never joined to agitation, nor can a disturbed mind prevail in seeing what a tranquil mind can scarcely long for. The sun’s ray is not seen when stirred-up clouds cover the face of heaven, nor does a troubled spring return the image of the one looking into it, which it properly displays when tranquil; for the more its water trembles, the more it obscures within itself the likeness of the reflected image. [Col. 0726C–D; 0727A]

### 83. Care must be taken lest anger, stirred by zeal, dominate the mind

But when the mind is moved by zeal, the greatest care must be taken lest this same anger, assumed as an instrument of virtue, dominate the mind. It must not go before the mind as a mistress, but, like a maidservant ready for service, must never depart from behind reason. For the mind is raised more vigorously against vices when it serves in submission to reason.

However much anger may arise from zeal for righteousness, if it conquers the mind without measure, it immediately refuses to serve reason. It expands itself all the more shamelessly because it considers the vice of impatience a virtue. Therefore the person moved by zeal for righteousness must attend above all to this: anger must not pass beyond the mind’s control. Rather, considering the time and measure appropriate for punishing sin, he must restrain the disturbance rising within him by examining it with finer care, suppress his hostility, and order his passionate movements according to equity. [Note: The Norman, Colbertine, German, and other manuscripts read “by examining it more carefully”; this is the reading found in the older copies.]

Thus he will become a more righteous avenger of another’s fault in proportion as he has first become victor over himself, so that he may correct the faults of those who offend in such a way that he himself, who corrects them, may first grow through patience and judge his own fervor by transcending it. He must not, excited without restraint by his very zeal for righteousness, wander far from righteousness.

Since, as we have said, even the praiseworthy emulation of what is good disturbs the eye of the mind, it is rightly said now: “Anger kills the foolish man.” As though it were plainly said: Anger arising from zeal disturbs the wise, but anger arising from vice slaughters the foolish; the former is restrained by reason, while the latter irrationally dominates a mind already overcome.

He adds appropriately:

# CHAPTER XLVI [Recension XXXI]

## The same passage

“And envy kills the little one.”

### 84. The envious person testifies that he is inferior to the one he envies

We cannot envy anyone except those whom we consider in some respect better than ourselves. The little one, therefore, is the person killed by resentment, because he himself bears witness that he is inferior to the one whose envy torments him.

Hence the crafty enemy, by envying the first man, secretly assaulted him, because, having lost his own blessedness, he recognized himself as inferior to that man’s immortality. Hence Cain fell into the perpetration of fratricide (Gen. 4:5–7): when his sacrifice was rejected, he growled against the one whom he saw preferred to himself, whose offering God had accepted; and the one he dreaded as better than himself he cut off, lest he should in any way continue to be so.

Hence Esau burned with persecution against his brother (Gen. 25:34; 27:41), because, having lost the blessing of the firstborn—which he himself had sold for a meal of lentils—he mourned that he was inferior to the one whom he had preceded by birth. Hence Joseph’s brothers sold him to passing Ishmaelites (Gen. 37:27–28), because, having learned the mystery of the revelation, they tried to obstruct his advancement lest he become better than themselves. Hence Saul persecuted David, his subject, by hurling a spear at him (1 Sam. 18:11), because he feared that the one whom he saw growing daily through great successes in virtue would rise above him. [Note: The Beauvais manuscript reads: “because he saw him increasing daily,” and so forth.]

The one killed by envy is therefore a little one, because, unless he were himself inferior, he would not grieve over another’s good.

## [Old XXXIV]

### 85. In envy the ancient serpent shakes and vomits out all his poison. A description of the envious person

Amid these matters it must be understood that, although through every vice committed the ancient enemy pours his poison into the human heart, in this wickedness the serpent shakes all his inward parts and vomits forth the pestilence of evil that is to be impressed upon it. Of him it is written: “Through the envy of the devil death entered the world” (Wis. 2:24).

When the corruption of resentment has infected the conquered heart, the outward features also reveal how grievously madness torments the soul. The complexion is stricken with pallor, the eyes sink, the mind burns, and the limbs grow cold. There is frenzy in thought and gnashing in the teeth. While the hatred growing in the hidden places of the heart is concealed, the enclosed wound pierces the conscience with blind pain. [Note: So read the Vindobonensis, Norman, Vallicellian, German, and many other manuscripts. In the editions of Coccius and those following him: “with blind pain darkens.”]

Nothing joyous in one’s own affairs is pleasing, because its own punishment wounds the wasting mind, which is tormented by another’s happiness. The higher the structure of another’s work is built, the more deeply the foundation of the envious mind is undermined; so that, in proportion as others hasten toward better things, he himself falls more disastrously. [Note: Our manuscripts also show that the required reading is *eo ipse deterius ruat* (“so that he himself falls more disastrously”), not, as in the printed editions, *eo ipso deterius ruant* (“so that they themselves fall more disastrously”), nor, as in the older copies, *eo ipsa res* (“so that the thing itself …”).]

By that fall even what was thought to have risen through a perfect work in his other actions is destroyed. For once envy has withered the mind, it consumes everything good it finds there.

Hence Solomon rightly says: “The life of the flesh is health of heart, but envy is the rottenness of the bones” (Prov. 14:30). What is signified by flesh except certain weak and tender things? And what by bones except strong deeds?

Often some people appear weak in certain actions while possessing genuine innocence of heart; others already perform certain deeds that appear strong before human eyes, yet inwardly waste away through the pestilence of envy toward the good of others. Therefore it is rightly said: “The life of the flesh is health of heart,” because if innocence of mind is preserved, even outward weaknesses are eventually strengthened. And rightly it follows: “Envy is the rottenness of the bones,” because through the vice of resentment even strong deeds of virtue perish before the eyes of God. For bones to rot through envy is for even robust deeds to be destroyed.

### 86. The diminution and death of envy: the beginning or perfection of the love of eternity

But why do we speak of envy if we do not also explain how it may be uprooted? It is difficult for one person not to envy what another desires to obtain, because whatever temporal thing is possessed becomes less for individuals in proportion as it is divided among many. For this reason resentment torments the mind of the one who desires, because what he seeks either another takes away entirely by receiving it, or restricts by diminishing its quantity.

Whoever therefore desires to be wholly free from the pestilence of resentment should love that inheritance which the number of co-heirs does not narrow; an inheritance that is one for all and whole for each, and that appears more abundant the more widely the multitude of those receiving it is enlarged.

The diminution of envy, therefore, is the affection arising from inward sweetness, and its complete death is the perfect love of eternity. When the mind is drawn away from desiring a thing that is divided according to the number of those who receive it, it loves its neighbor all the more because it fears its own losses less from that neighbor’s advancement.

If the mind is perfectly carried away in love of the heavenly homeland, it is also completely established in love of its neighbor without any envy, because when it desires nothing earthly, there is nothing to oppose its charity toward its neighbor. What else is this charity but the eye of the mind? If it is touched by the dust of earthly love, it is immediately injured and struck back from the vision of the inner light.

Since the person who loves earthly things is little, while the person who desires eternal things is great, the saying may also be understood, not improperly, in this way: “Envy kills the little one,” because this pestilence afflicts no one with death except the person who is still weak in his desires.

# Part Two, Containing Five Books

[Col. 0729]

# BOOK SIX

It expounds the whole of the fifth chapter, beginning with the third verse, in a spiritual interpretation—partly allegorical, but mostly moral.

## CHAPTER ONE

### 181. Job prefigures Christ and the Church; his friends prefigure heretics

While preserving the truth of the historical account, I have proposed to examine the statements of blessed Job and the mystical interpretation of his friends. For it is clear to all who know the truth that holy Scripture, throughout all its assertions, takes care to promise the Redeemer of the world and strives to signify him through all the elect, as through his members. [Note: The Vindobonensis reads: “and through them, that is, he strove to signify the members,” which was earlier read in the Corbie and German manuscripts but was rightly corrected. The Norman manuscript presents the whole passage thus: “and through all the elect, that is, he strove to signify him through his members.”]

Hence blessed Job himself is called “suffering” in Latin speech, so that through both his name and his wounds the passion of our Redeemer might be represented. Of him the prophet says: “Truly he himself bore our sicknesses, and he carried our pains” (Isa. 53:4).

The tempter, after taking everything away, killed both servants and children, because at the time of his passion he struck not only the Jewish people, who served through fear, but also the apostles themselves, regenerated in his love, with the weapon of faithlessness. The body of blessed Job is worn down by a wound, because our Redeemer does not disdain to be fastened with nails upon the scaffold of the cross.

He received wounds from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head, because the holy Church, which is his body, is afflicted by the raging persecutor not only in its extremities and lowest members, but even up to its highest members. Hence Paul also said: “I complete in my flesh what is lacking in the sufferings of Christ” (Col. 1:24).

His wife tries to persuade him to curse, because all the carnal within the holy Church exist as assistants of the crafty tempter. The woman who provokes him to curse signifies the life of the carnal; for, as we have already said above (Book III, ch. 20, nos. 36–37), those placed within the holy Church with uncorrected ways of life press the good all the more harshly in proportion as they are close to them through faith. Since they cannot be avoided as though they were faithful, they are endured by the faithful all the more grievously because they are also more inwardly present.

His friends, who come as though to console him but go beyond the bounds into words of harsh accusation, represent heretics. When they try to defend God against the good, they offend him. [Col. 0729B–C]

### 2. Gregory’s spiritual interpretations proceed from the root of history. The words of Job’s friends are not to be rejected in every respect

I have therefore gathered together briefly, from their mystical significance, what was said more fully above, so that my reader may remember from this very repetition that in this work I serve spiritual understanding. Nevertheless, whenever usefulness requires it, I also carefully examine the words of the historical account. When necessary, I embrace both together, so that allegory may produce spiritual fruits that truth nevertheless brings forth from the root of history.

We do not reject in every respect the friends of blessed Job, whom we have said bear the appearance of heretics. For when the divine judgment says against them, “You have not spoken rightly before me,” and immediately adds, “as my servant Job has” (Job 42:7), it is plainly evident that what is rejected by comparison with the better is not entirely despised.

They fall incautiously into reproving him; yet because they are friends of so great a man, through their familiarity with him they learned many mystical things. Hence, as we also said above (Book V, no. 27), Paul uses their words as well, taking them up in support of his own assertion and testifying that what they uttered was drawn from the truth. The truth nevertheless rightly reproves them, because, however forceful the statement, it ought not to have been brought against a holy man.

The words of Eliphaz may therefore be weighed mystically. He addresses blessed Job as follows:

## CHAPTER TWO

### Verse 3

“I saw the foolish man firmly rooted, and immediately I cursed his beauty.”

### Allegorical sense

#### 3. The Jews are foolish and, because they rejected Christ, are subject even to the curse of heretics

The Jewish people proved foolish because they rejected the very presence in the flesh of eternal Wisdom. They grew strong as though firmly rooted, because by putting the lives of the elect to death temporally, they prevailed over them.

But Eliphaz despises this people by cursing it, because all heretics, whose likeness we have said is borne by the friends of blessed Job, when they glory in the name of Christ, condemn the faithlessness of the Jews on the basis of authority.

Of this foolish man it immediately follows:

## CHAPTER THREE

### Verse 4

“May his children be far from salvation; they shall be crushed at the gate, and there shall be no one to rescue them.”

#### 4. Their children are all the faithless; they are crushed in Christ, who is the gate

The children of this foolish man are all who are begotten by the preaching of his faithlessness. They are far from salvation because, even if they receive temporal life without affliction, they are struck with a harsher eternal vengeance. The Lord says of these same children: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who traverse sea and land to make one proselyte, and when he has been made, you make him a son of Gehenna twice as much as yourselves” (Matt. 23:15).

It follows: “They shall be crushed at the gate, and there shall be no one to rescue them.” Who else ought to be understood by the name “gate” except the mediator between God and human beings, who says: “I am the door; if anyone enters through me, he will be saved” (John 10:9)?

The children of this foolish man therefore advance outside the gate and are crushed at the gate, because the perverse offspring of the Jews flourished in observance of the Law before the Mediator’s coming, but in the very presence of our Redeemer they fell, rejected from the service of the Divinity on account of the merits of their faithlessness.

There is no one to rescue them, because, while they tried to destroy the Redeemer himself through persecution, they cut off the remedies of rescue that had been offered to them. Of him it follows appropriately:

## CHAPTER FOUR

### Verse 5

“His harvest the hungry shall eat, and the armed man shall seize him.”

#### 5. The Gentiles eat their harvest—that is, the sacred utterances—and seize their riches

The harvest of this foolish man had been a crop of sacred speech. [Note: The manuscript codex of St. Michael reads: “the utterance of the sacred law.”] The grains of the ears of grain are the words of the prophets, which the foolish man possessed but did not eat, because the Jewish people held the Law in words only, yet, through the distastefulness of its folly, hungered apart from its meaning.

The hungry man eats the harvest of this foolish man because the Gentile people consume the words of the Law by understanding them, words for which the Jewish people labored without understanding. The Lord foresaw these hungry people of faith when he said through the evangelist: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied” (Matt. 5:6).

The prophetess Hannah says of these hungry people: “Those who were filled before have hired themselves out for bread, and the hungry have been satisfied” (1 Sam. 2:5).

But because the harvest was lost, it is rightly added how the foolish man himself also perishes: “And the armed man shall seize him.” The ancient enemy seized the Jewish people as an armed man, because by the darts of fraudulent suggestion he extinguished the life of faith in them, so that precisely where they believed they were clinging to God, they might resist his ordinance.

The Truth forewarns his disciples of this, saying: “The hour is coming when everyone who kills you will think that he is offering service to God” (John 16:2). It follows:

## CHAPTER FIVE [Old and Recension III]

## The same passage

“And the thirsty shall drink his riches.”

#### 6. The utterances of God are both harvest and riches. How they are said both to be eaten and to be drunk

The thirsty drink the riches of this foolish man because the minds of the Gentiles are watered by the streams of sacred speech that the Jewish people had possessed in the display of their pride. Hence the prophet says to them: “All you who thirst, come to the waters; and you who have no silver, hasten” (Isa. 55:1).

That “silver” signifies the divine utterances, the Psalmist testifies when he says: “The utterances of the Lord are pure utterances, silver tested by fire” (Ps. 11:7). Those who have no silver are therefore called to the waters, because the Gentiles, who had not received the precepts of sacred Scripture, are satisfied by the flood of sacred speech. They now drink it all the more eagerly because they had long thirsted for it in their dryness.

The same divine utterances are therefore called both harvest and riches: harvest because they refresh the hungry mind; riches because they adorn us with great beauty of character. They are also said both to be eaten and to be drunk. Some things in them are obscure and can be understood only after interpretation; these we swallow, as it were, by chewing them. Other things are easy to understand, and we take them just as we find them; these we drink, as it were, unchewed, because we swallow them without breaking them apart.

We have passed briefly over these matters under their mystical meaning, lest we perhaps appear to have omitted anything. But since the friends of blessed Job could not have been such unless they also shone with great moral integrity in certain respects, it remains for us to seek morally in their words the virtue of their meanings, so that, when the weight of their speech has been examined, it may be shown what sort of doctrine they possessed.

## CHAPTER SIX [Recension IV]

### Verse 3

“I saw the foolish man firmly rooted, and immediately I cursed his beauty.”

### Moral sense

#### 7. Those who pursue earthly things appear firmly rooted in prosperity

The foolish man is fixed in the earth as though by a firm root because he is established with all his desires in earthly love. Hence Cain is described as having been the first to build a city on earth (Gen. 4:17), so that it might plainly be shown that the one who was alienated from the stability of the heavenly homeland laid his foundation on earth.

The foolish man is raised as though by a firm root when he is supported here by temporal prosperity: he obtains everything he desires, suffers no adversity, prevails without opposition against the weak, contradicts those who act well by virtue of his authority, and reaches greater advantages by ever worse actions—so that, by the very means through which he abandons the way of life, he lives more happily for a time.

But when the weak see the wicked flourishing, they tremble. Disturbed within themselves by the prosperity of sinners, they waver inwardly in the steps of the mind. The Psalmist took on the likeness of these people when he said: “But my feet were almost moved; my steps nearly slipped,” [Note: The Corbie manuscript reads: “because I was jealous of the wicked.”] “because I was jealous of the sinners, seeing the peace of sinners” (Ps. 72:2).

#### 8. The prudent despise their glory and do not delay condemning it

When the strong observe their glory, they immediately consider what punishment will follow glory, and with deep inward reflection they despise the spectacle of the proud swelling outwardly with the empty inflation of arrogance.

Therefore it is rightly said: “I saw the foolish man firmly rooted, and immediately I cursed his beauty.” To curse the beauty of the foolish man is to judge his glory in view of his considered condemnation, because the more highly he is raised in sins, the more harshly he is overwhelmed in torments. What is exalted passes away; what is punished remains. The one who is honored on the road will be condemned upon arrival. He reaches prison, as it were, through pleasant meadows who proceeds through the prosperity of the present life toward destruction.

It must be noted that, when he said he had cursed the foolish man’s beauty, he immediately added “immediately.” It is the habit of the human and weak mind to vary as the quality of the things it observes varies. [Note: In Coccius and subsequent editions: “to vary as the quality of the things it observes varies; often its judgment is led by the very appearance of the present thing, and its intention and perception are formed according to what it sees.” For the verb “is led,” the old Basel edition of 1514 reads “is judged”; the Paris edition of 1495 reads “is indicated,” as do the Vindobonensis, Corbie, German, and Bartholomew manuscripts.]

Often, while some people behold the glory of certain persons, they delight in the sight of that glory, consider it something great, and desire for themselves the attainment of such things. But when they see the glorious suddenly cast down, or perhaps even dying, they confess with a groan that human glory is altogether nothing, saying immediately: “Behold how insignificant a human being is.” They would say this more rightly if, when they saw a person in glory, they then considered his death and perceived that passing power is nothing.

Human exaltation must be judged for what it is precisely when it raises itself above others through success. The course by which happiness flies away must be considered when, before human eyes, it appears to possess permanence. Any weak person can reflect that the glory of one who is dying is nothing once he is already in death. Then even those who follow and love it up to death disparage it.

Therefore it is rightly said: “I saw the foolish man firmly rooted, and immediately I cursed his beauty.” As though it were plainly said: I did not delay in cursing the beauty of the foolish man, because when I saw it I also saw the punishment that would follow. I would not have cursed it immediately if some delight in his glory had held me; but I cursed it without delay because, seeing the punishments that would remain, I rejected his power without hesitation.

But because all the wicked, the more they prosper in this world, draw more people with them into destruction, it is rightly added: “May his children be far from salvation.” [Note: The Corbie and German manuscripts and the Colbertine manuscript read: “May his children be far away,” and so forth.]

The children of the foolish man are those who are born in imitation of him amid the ambition of this age. They are certainly farther from salvation in proportion as they suffer no weakening in the perpetration of wickedness. Of them it is rightly added:

## CHAPTER SEVEN [Old IV, Recension V]

### Verse 4

“They shall be crushed at the gate, and there shall be no one to rescue them.”

#### 9. The day of judgment is the gate of the kingdom. Then the person who refused correction here cannot be rescued

Just as the entrance to a city is called a gate, so the day of judgment is the gate of the kingdom, because through it all the elect enter into the glory of the heavenly homeland.

When Solomon saw this day approaching for the recompense of the holy Church, he said: “Her husband is noble at the gates, when he sits with the elders of the land” (Prov. 31:23). The husband of the Church is the Redeemer of the human race. He shows himself noble at the gates: previously despised in insults, he will appear exalted at the entrance of the kingdom.

He sits with the elders of the land because he will pronounce the sentence of judgment with the holy preachers of that same Church, as he himself says in the Gospel: “You who have followed me, in the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits upon the throne of his majesty, you also will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. 19:28).

Isaiah likewise foretold this long beforehand: “The Lord will come to judgment with the elders of his people” (Isa. 3:14). Solomon again says of these gates: “Give her of the fruit of her hands, and let her works praise her at the gates” (Prov. 31:31).

Then the holy Church receives the fruit of her hands, when the recompense of her labor raises her up to receive heavenly things. Then her works praise her at the gates, when it is said to her members at the very entrance of the kingdom: “I was hungry, and you gave me food; I was thirsty, and you gave me drink; I was a stranger, and you welcomed me; I was naked, and you clothed me” (Matt. 25:35), and so forth. [Note: The manuscripts read *et dedistis mihi bibere* (“and you gave me to drink”); the printed editions read *et dedistis mihi potum* (“and you gave me drink”).]

The children of this foolish man are therefore exalted before the gate but crushed at the gate, because the lovers of this age are proud in the present life but are struck by eternal punishment at the very entrance of the kingdom.

It is rightly added: “And there shall be no one to rescue them.” The Truth rescues from eternal adversity those whom he disciplines amid temporal prosperity. Whoever now refuses to be pressed down cannot then be rescued, because the wicked do not find as their rescuer in the time of their affliction the father whom they neglected to have through discipline. It follows:

## CHAPTER EIGHT

### Verse 5

“His harvest the hungry shall eat.”

#### 10. The wicked possess a harvest when they understand and speak what is right, so that others may eat it

The foolish man also has a harvest when some wicked person receives the gift of right understanding: he is instructed by the sayings of sacred Scripture and speaks good things, yet in no way puts into practice what he says. He utters the words of God but does not love them; by praising them he magnifies them, but by living he tramples them.

Because this foolish man both understands and speaks what is right, yet does not love it by putting it into practice, he goes hungry while possessing a harvest. The hungry person eats it, because the one who pants toward God with holy desires learns what he hears and does what he has learned. While he is refreshed by the right preaching of the wicked teacher, what else does he receive his fill of but the foolish man’s grain?

Did not the Truth admonish his hungry people to eat the foolish man’s harvest when, speaking about the Pharisees to those burning with holy desires, he commanded: “Do and observe whatever they tell you, but do not act according to their works” (Matt. 23:3)? As though he plainly said: They cultivate the harvest of the word by speaking, but by living badly they do not reach it at all. Let this harvest therefore refresh your hunger, because through the distastefulness of their folly they preserve it for you.

It is rightly added:

## CHAPTER NINE

## The same passage

“And the armed man shall seize him.”

#### 11. The devil often permits knowledge in order to corrupt life

The ancient enemy is conquered as though unarmed when, openly suggesting evil to the human mind, he tries to destroy all good at once. [Note: The Vindobonensis reads: “he conquers as though unarmed”; the manuscript of St. Michael reads: “he conquers as though they were unarmed.”]

But he comes armed when, leaving some good things untouched, he secretly corrupts others. Often he does not tempt certain people in their understanding, nor does he oppose them in their meditation upon sacred speech; nevertheless, he undermines their life in practice. While they are praised for the strength of their knowledge, they give no attention to the damage in their actions. When the mind is drawn into delight in praise, it does not heal the wounds of its life.

The armed enemy therefore seizes the person whom, hidden by fraud, he defeats in one respect while leaving another untouched. It follows:

## CHAPTER TEN

## The same passage

“And the thirsty shall drink his riches.”

12. Often the dull-witted person understands through study in the instruction of divine law what the gifted person, through negligence, does not know.---Often the fool possesses a fountain of inward liquid but does not drink from it, because he receives the capacity for understanding, yet refuses to come to know the judgments of truth by reading. He knows that by studying he could prevail in understanding, but, disgusted with every pursuit of instruction, he stops short. The riches of the mind, moreover, are the words of sacred speech; but the fool looks upon these riches with his eyes and does not take them up for the use of his adornment, because, hearing the words of the Law, he considers them indeed to be great, but makes no effort through any zeal of love to comprehend them.

But, on the other hand, another person has thirst but lacks intelligence: love draws him toward meditation, while the dullness of his understanding resists. Yet often, by studying the instruction of divine law at some time, he understands what the gifted person, through negligence, does not know. Those who thirst drink the riches of this fool, when the dull-witted, loving them, attain the commandments of God which the gifted, in their disdain, do not know. In these darknesses of dullness the eye of love gives light [note: Vindoc., Turon., St. Martin’s, and St. Michael’s: “in this darkness of dullness the eye of love is illumined”]. For thirst opens to the slower what disdain closes to the quicker.

They also reach the heights of understanding for this reason: they disdain none of the least things they have understood putting them into practice; and, while they assist their understanding with their hands, they raise themselves beyond the height of the gifted. Hence Solomon rightly says: “The lizard supports itself with its hands, and dwells in the palaces of the king” (Prov. 30:28). For most often birds, which the feather lifts into flight, settle in the thornbushes; but the lizard, which has no wings for flight, supports itself with its hands and occupies the king’s palace [note: So Corb. Germ., Colb., Reg., Turon., Bellov., Norm., Compend., Coc. and the following editions: “occupies the king’s building.” Utic. has both readings; in this manuscript *stilio* is written instead of *stellio*, and likewise in many manuscripts]. Often, indeed, the gifted, while they lie sluggish through negligence, remain in wicked deeds; but the simple, whom the wing of intelligence does not assist, are lifted by the virtue of their works to obtain the strongholds of the eternal kingdom.

Thus the lizard, while it supports itself with its hands, dwells in the king’s palaces, because the simple person reaches through the intention of right action where the gifted person does not at all ascend. But when these things have been heard, a question arises in our heart: why is the gift of understanding granted to the negligent, or why is the diligent person hindered by the slowness of his own understanding? The answer is quickly given when what follows immediately is added:

CHAPTER XI.

VERSE 6.---“Nothing upon the earth is without cause.”

13. Why keen intelligence is granted to the negligent person, and slow intelligence to the diligent person.---Often the idle person receives intelligence so that he may be punished more justly for his negligence, because he scorns to know what he could attain without labor [note: The printed editions read “so that the intelligent person,” but this is absent from all our manuscripts and is plainly superfluous]. And sometimes the diligent person is burdened with slowness of understanding so that he may find greater rewards in recompense, insofar as he labors more intensely in the pursuit of discovery.

Nothing, therefore, is without cause upon the earth, since slowness benefits the diligent person toward reward, while quickness increases the idle person’s punishment.

[Vet. V.] To understand what is right, we are instructed sometimes by the labor of study, but sometimes by the pain of chastisement. Hence, when it has been said, “Nothing upon the earth is without cause,” it is fittingly added at once:

CHAPTER XII [Rec. VI].

IN THE SAME PLACE.---“And pain does not come forth from the earth.”

14. Through the hidden merits of minds, the manifest scourges of punishment come forth.---Pain, as it were, comes forth from the earth when a human being, created in the image of God, is scourged by insensible things [note: In Gemet. and several others: “as it were, pain does not come forth from the earth.” So also Barthol. and the old Basel edition]. But because, through the hidden merits of minds, the manifest scourges of punishment come forth, pain does not come forth from the earth, since the wickedness of our understanding demands that we be struck by insensible things.

For behold, we see that, for our correction, the rain for which we have waited is withheld from the parched earth, and the gloomy air is dried by the burning sun [note: Most manuscripts: “and the gloomy air”]; the sea rages with swelling storms, preventing some whom it has received from crossing, while to others it opposes the desired passage with a wave raised into a heap [note: In all manuscripts, “the wave opposes,” whereas the edition reads “prevents”]; the earth not only diminishes the shoots of fertility, but even consumes the seeds it has received.

In all these things it is plainly seen what a certain wise man testifies about the Lord when he says: “And the whole world will fight with him against the senseless” (Wis. 5:21). The whole world fights with the Lord against the senseless when the adversity of the elements serves in the punishment of sinners [note: Vindoc., Germ., Corb. Germ.: “before correction, ‘against him.’” In Vindoc. below: “the whole world fights against the Lord”].

Nevertheless, pain does not come forth from the earth, because every insensible thing is stirred up to afflict us by the goad of our action. Pain does not come forth from the earth, because punishment is by no means born from the creature that strikes, but unquestionably from the one that, by sinning, has extorted the force of the blow.

But we must take the greatest care that, when we are afflicted by the weight of pain in external things, we may stretch toward heavenly things in hope, so that the mind may reach the heights to the degree that external punishment chastises us. Hence it is appropriately added:

CHAPTER XIII [Rec. VII].

VERSE 7.---“Man is born for labor, and the bird for flight.”

15. Insofar as the flesh is afflicted by scourges, the mind is lifted toward higher things.---Man is born for labor, since the one who has been endowed with reason considers that it is utterly impossible for him to pass through the time of his pilgrimage without groaning. Hence Paul, when he enumerated his tribulations to his disciples, rightly added: “For you yourselves know that we are appointed to this” (1 Thess. 3:3).

But insofar as the flesh is afflicted by scourges, the mind is lifted toward the pursuit of higher things, as Paul again testifies when he says: “Although our outward man is corrupted, yet the inward man is renewed day by day” (2 Cor. 4:16). Man, therefore, is born for labor, and the bird for flight, because from the place where the flesh labors more harshly below, the mind flies upward to the heights.

16. The labor of the carnal is grievous; that of the spiritual is none.---The life of carnal people can also be signified by the designation “man.” Hence Paul says: “Since there is jealousy and strife among you, are you not carnal?” (1 Cor. 3:3). Shortly afterward he added: “Are you not human?” (Ibid., 4).

In this life, therefore, man is born for labor, because every carnal person, when he desires transitory things, afflicts himself under the weight of his desires. It is a grievous labor to seek the glory of the present life, to attain what one has sought, and to guard carefully what one has attained. It is a grievous labor to seize with great weariness what the one who seizes it knows cannot stand for long.

But holy men, because they do not love transitory things, not only bear no burdens of temporal desires; even when adversities arise, they do not labor amid their very pressures and afflictions. What is harsher than scourges? Yet it is written of the apostles who had been scourged: “They went away rejoicing from the presence of the council, because they were counted worthy to suffer dishonor for the name of Jesus” (Acts 5:41).

What labor, then, is there for their minds, when the labor of punishment by blows is not labor for them? Man is therefore born for labor, because the person who truly feels the evils of this world is the one who greedily desires its goods. For whatever is moved externally against a mind that has been lifted toward higher things lies beneath that mind.

[Vet. VI.] Thus it is rightly added: “And the bird for flight,” because the spirit withdraws itself from the affliction of labor to the same degree that it raises itself through hope toward the heights.

Was Paul not born like a bird for flight, when, enduring so many adversities, he said: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3:20)? And again: “We know that if our earthly house of this habitation is dissolved, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens” (2 Cor. 5:1). Like a bird, therefore, he had risen beyond the depths; although he still lingered bodily upon earth, the wing of hope was already lifting him into the heights.

But because no one is able by his own strength to raise himself to the heights, so that, when afflicted by visible things, he may be lifted toward invisible things, it is rightly added immediately:

CHAPTER XIV.

VERSE 8.---“Therefore I will entreat the Lord, and I will place my speech before God.”

17. This is God’s gift.---It is as though he were saying openly: “I ask the one through whom I know that these things are granted.” For if he believed that he possessed this by himself, he would not need to entreat God. It follows:

CHAPTER XV.

VERSE 9.---“Who does great and inscrutable things, and wonders without number.”

18. God’s marvelous works have become cheap in human eyes through familiarity.---Who could be sufficient to investigate the wonders of almighty God: that he created all things from nothing; that the very structure of the world was arranged by the marvelous power of his might; that heaven is suspended above the air and the earth is balanced above the abyss; that this entire universe exists from invisible and visible things; that he made man, so to speak, by gathering another world into a small compass, but a rational one; that, forming him from soul and flesh, he mingled spirit and mud by an arrangement of power beyond investigation?

From these things, therefore, we know one thing and are another; yet we neglect to wonder, because those things that are marvelous through incomprehensible investigation have become cheap in human eyes through familiarity.

Thus it happens that, if a dead person is raised, everyone leaps up in astonishment, while every day a human being who did not exist is born, and no one wonders—although it is surely evident to all that creating what did not exist is greater than restoring what did exist.

Because Aaron’s dry staff blossomed, everyone wondered; every day a tree is produced from dry earth, and the power of dust is changed into wood, yet no one wonders. Because five thousand people were satisfied with five loaves, everyone wondered that food had increased in their mouths [note: The printed editions add “people”; the manuscripts do not]. Every day scattered grains of seed are multiplied into the fullness of ears of grain, yet no one wonders. When they saw water changed once into wine, everyone wondered; every day the moisture of the earth, drawn into the root of the vine, is changed through the cluster into wine, yet no one wonders.

All things, therefore, are marvelous that people neglect to wonder at, because, as we have said, through familiarity they grow dull in considering them.

[Rec. VIII.] When he said, “Who does great things,” he immediately added, “and inscrutable.” For it would have been less to do great things if the things that had been made could nevertheless have been investigated. It is rightly added: “And wonders without number,” because his greatness would have been less if the things he created as inscrutable had been few [note: *Condit* (“created”) is absent from Corb. Germ.].

19. God’s miracles are to be considered attentively, not investigated by the intellect; faith is to be strengthened where it falters; hence the resurrection becomes credible.---Amid these matters we must know that divine miracles should always be considered attentively and never investigated by the intellect. For often, when the human mind seeks and fails to find the explanation of certain things, it plunges itself into the abyss of doubt.

Thus it happens that some people observe the bodies of the dead reduced to dust and, because they cannot derive from reason the power of the resurrection, despair that these bodies can return to their former state. Miracles, therefore, are to be believed through faith; they are not to be investigated through reason. For if reason unfolded them to our eyes, they would not be miracles.

But when the mind perhaps falters concerning these things, it is necessary for it to recall those matters that it knows by experience, although it does not gather them by reason, so that the example of a similar matter may strengthen the faith which it perceives to have been shaken by its own cleverness [note: Gemet.: “so that the proof of a similar matter may strengthen faith”].

When the dust of human flesh is considered, the mind of some people is shaken and despairs of how dust may return to flesh and compose a restored body through the outlines of its limbs; how that dryness of earth may become green through living members and distinguish itself through their appearances and forms. This cannot indeed be comprehended by reason, but it can nevertheless easily be believed through an example.

Who would believe that an immense tree could rise from a single grain of seed, unless he held this as certain through experience? In the tiny size of a single grain, and in the almost complete lack of resemblance to what it will become, where are hidden the hardness of wood, the marrow either softer than wood or harder [note: Vindoc., Norm., and nearly all manuscripts, agreeing with the old editions: “the marrow softer than wood”; in the recent editions: “or harder”], the roughness of bark, the greenness of the root, the taste of fruits, the sweetness of scents, the diversity of colors, and the softness of leaves?

And yet, because we know this through experience, we do not doubt that all these things come forth from a single grain of seed. What, then, is difficult about dust returning to limbs, when we see the Creator’s power every day—he who wondrously creates wood from a grain, and even more wondrously creates fruits from wood?

Let him therefore say: “Who does great and inscrutable things, and wonders without number,” because the greatness of divine works can be neither investigated according to quality nor numbered according to quantity. Hence it is still added:

CHAPTER XVI [Vet. VII].

VERSES 10, 11.---“Who gives rain upon the face of the earth and waters all things with waters. Who sets the lowly on high and raises the sorrowful to safety.”

MYSTICAL MEANING.---20. God waters all things with the waters of grace. By “all things,” the human being is signified.---Because we believe that the friends of blessed Job were instructed by his companionship, it is necessary that we explain these words of Eliphaz mystically.

Almighty God gives rain to the earth when he pours the grace of heavenly preaching upon the dry hearts of the nations. And he waters all things with waters, because he shapes the barrenness of the lost human being for fruitfulness by the fullness of the Spirit, just as the Truth itself says: “Whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never thirst” (John 4:13).

By the name “all things,” the human being is signified, because in him the true likeness and the great fellowship of the universe are displayed. For whatever exists either exists but does not live; or exists and lives but does not perceive; or exists, lives, and perceives but does not understand or discern; or exists, lives, perceives, understands, and discerns.

Stones exist, but they do not live. Plants exist and live, but they do not perceive. The life of herbs and trees is called greenness, as Paul says concerning seeds: “Fool, what you sow is not made alive unless it first dies” (1 Cor. 15:36). Brute animals exist, live, and perceive, but they do not understand. Angels exist, live, perceive, and discern through understanding.

The human being, therefore, because he shares existence with stones, life with trees, perception with animals, and discernment with angels, is rightly expressed by the name “the universe,” since in him, in a certain respect, the universe itself is contained. Hence the Truth says to the disciples: “Go into all the world and preach the Gospel to every creature” (Mark 16:15). By “every creature” he wished the human being alone to be understood, since he created in him something shared with all.

21. God waters all things when he calls people from every human condition to know him.---Nevertheless, in this passage “all things” can also be understood in another way. When the grace of the Holy Spirit subjects the rich to itself, it does not reject the poor; when it humbles the strong, it does not refuse to let the weak come to it; when it gathers the noble, it also embraces the ignoble; when it receives the wise, it does not despise the foolishness of the unlearned.

God therefore waters all things with waters when, through the gift of the Holy Spirit, he calls people from every human condition to knowledge of himself.

[Rec. IX.] 22. God waters all things because he adapts the force of his word in each person according to the diversity of character.---The very differences of character can also be designated by the name “all things.” One person is lifted up by pride, another is bent down by the weight of fear, another burns with lust, another pants with avarice, another casts himself down through laxity, and another grows hot with anger.

But through the teaching of sacred speech, humility is given to the proud, confidence is offered to the fearful, the lustful is cleansed from impurity through the pursuit of chastity, the avaricious is restrained from the heat of ambition through self-control, the lax is raised up by the uprightness of zeal, and the angry is held back from the impulsiveness of his agitation. Thus God waters all things with waters, because he adapts the force of his word in each person according to the diversity of character, so that each person may find in his speech that by which he can produce the necessary seed of virtue.

Hence a certain wise man speaks of the sweetness of manna: “You gave them bread prepared from heaven without labor, possessing within itself every delight and the sweetness of every taste” (Wis. 16:20). Manna possessed within itself every delight and the sweetness of every taste; it gave a taste in the mouths of spiritual people according to the will of those who ate it. For the divine word, while suitable to everyone and not differing from itself, accommodates itself to the quality of its hearers. When each of the elect understands it profitably according to his own measure, he turns the manna he has received, as it were, into a taste of his own choosing.

And because the glory of recompense follows the labor of good works, it is rightly added after the watering of the waters: “Who sets the lowly on high and raises the sorrowful to safety.”

[Vet. VIII, Rec. X.] 23. The servants of God, now despised and afflicted, will then be received into glory and joy.---The lowly are set on high because those who are now despised for the love of God will then come with God as judges, just as the Truth promised these same humble people, as we said shortly before: “You who have followed me, in the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, you also will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. 19:28).

Then the Lord raises the sorrowful to safety, because those who, inflamed by desire for him, flee prosperity, suffer adversity, endure the torments of their persecutors, and chastise themselves through lamentation, will then receive safety all the higher in proportion as they now devoutly die to all the joys of the world.

Hence Solomon says: “A heart that knows the bitterness of its own soul will not have a stranger share in its joy” (Prov. 14:10). The human mind knows the bitterness of its own soul when, inflamed with desire for the eternal homeland, it recognizes through weeping the pain of its pilgrimage. But no stranger will share in its joy, because one who is now estranged from the sorrow of compunction will not then be a participant in the joy of consolation.

Hence the Truth says in the Gospel: “Amen, amen, I say to you: you will weep and lament, but the world will rejoice; you will be sorrowful, but your sorrow will be turned into joy” (John 16:20). And again: “Therefore you now indeed have sorrow; but I will see you again, and your heart will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you” (Ibid., 22).

The Lord is therefore said to raise the sorrowful to safety because he consoles those afflicted for his sake with true salvation in time. Nevertheless, there is nothing to prevent this from also being understood of God’s elect in the present life.

24.
