The lowly are already set on high in this life.---The lowly are set on high because, when they prostrate themselves in humility, they pass beyond all temporal things through the judgment of an exalted mind; and, when they consider themselves unworthy in everything, they trample upon the glory of this world, transcending it through the examination of right thought.

Let us look at the humble Paul. Behold, he says to the disciples: “For we do not preach ourselves, but Jesus Christ our Lord, and ourselves your servants through Christ” (2 Cor. 4:5). Let us see this humble man already set on high. He says: “Do you not know that we will judge angels?” (1 Cor. 6:3). And again: “He raised us up together and made us sit together in the heavenly places” (Eph. 2:6).

Perhaps chains then bound him outwardly, but he was nevertheless set in the heights in his mind; for, through the certainty of his hope, he was already sitting in the heavenly places. Holy men, therefore, are despised outwardly and endure everything as though unworthy; but, trusting that they are worthy of the heavenly seats, they await the glory of eternity with certainty.

While they labor outwardly amid the adversity of persecution, they retreat inwardly to the fortified citadel of the mind. From there they look down upon all things beneath them, and among those things they perceive even themselves as passing away bodily. They do not fear threats, because even while suffering torments they despise them.

Hence Solomon says: “The righteous is confident like a lion, without terror” (Prov. 28:1). Again it is written by him: “Nothing that happens to the righteous will make him sorrowful” (Prov. 12:21). Because the upright are situated at the summit of their lofty intention, they do not feel death when dying; in a marvelous way, the darts of the wicked both strike them and do not touch them.

The lowly, therefore, are set on high because, in the very place where they despise themselves in everything, they become more secure against everything.

[Col. 0742D] [Vet. IX, Rec. XI.] The mind, when it ceases to long for the things above it, continually falls beneath itself.---By contrast, the reproved mind is rightly addressed by the prophet under the figure of Babylon: “Come down, sit in the dust, virgin daughter of Babylon; sit on the earth; there is no throne for the daughter of the Chaldeans” (Isa. 47:1) [note: Most manuscripts read “daughter of Babylon”; so also the old editions].

In this passage, I think, the human mind is called a virgin not because it is undefiled, but because it is barren. And because Babylon is interpreted as “confusion,” the barren mind is rightly called the daughter of Babylon: insofar as it produces no good works, and is formed according to no order of right living, it is born, as it were, from its mother Confusion.

But if “virgin” is understood not as barren but as undefiled, then, after losing the condition of salvation, what it once was is invoked to increase its confusion. To it the divine voice appropriately says in reproach: “Come down.” The human spirit stands on high when it longs for heavenly rewards; but it descends from this position when, shamefully overcome, it submits itself to the flowing desires of the world.

It is rightly added immediately: “Sit in the dust.” For, descending, it sits in the dust because, abandoning heavenly things and being sprinkled with earthly thoughts, it becomes worthless amid weak things. The words are then repeated for emphasis: “Sit on the earth.” It is as though he were openly reproaching it, saying: “Because you did not wish to raise yourself through a heavenly way of life, prostrate beneath yourself, humble yourself in earthly deeds.”

Hence it is necessarily added at once: “There is no throne for the daughter of the Chaldeans.” The Chaldeans are interpreted as “the fierce.” Those who follow their own desires and do not know how to spare even their own lives are exceedingly fierce [note: Bellovac., Val. Cl., and nearly all manuscripts: “who follow their own pleasures”].

Earthly desires are fierce: they make the mind hard and insensible not only against the commandments of the Creator, but often even against the blows of chastisement. But the daughter of the fierce has no throne, because the mind that is born for love of the world from wicked desires and is hardened by those same desires loses the seat of judgment insofar as it submits itself to earthly cravings. It presides over no throne within itself, because it lacks the examination of discernment; and it is, as it were, driven from the seat of its own judgment because it wanders outward through desires.

It is clear that the mind that has lost the seat of counsel within scatters itself outward innumerably through desires. And because it pretends not to do what it understands, it is rightly blinded, so that it does not even know what it is doing. Often, by a just judgment, it is left to its own will and is released into the laborious services of the world beneath what it anxiously desires.

[Vet. X.] Hence it is appropriately added there: “Because you will no longer be called tender and delicate; take the millstone and grind flour” (Ibid., 2). It is evident that parents spare their tender daughter and do not burden her with harsh and servile tasks.

Almighty God therefore calls each beloved soul a tender daughter when he withdraws it from the laborious services of this world, lest, while it is afflicted by external activities, it become hardened against inward desires. But the daughter of the Chaldeans is not called tender and delicate, because the mind devoted to wicked desires is left to the labor of this age in what it anxiously desires, so that it may serve the world outwardly like a slave, while inwardly it does not love God as a daughter [note: In Corb. Germ. and Colb.: “which it anxiously desires”].

Hence it is also commanded to take up the millstone and grind flour. A millstone is driven in a circle, and flour is produced. Every action of this world is a millstone: while it piles up many cares, it turns human minds as though in a circle; and it casts out from itself what is like flour, because, once the heart has been led astray, it continually gives birth to the tiniest thoughts.

[Vet. XI.] Sometimes, moreover, one who is believed to possess some peaceful merit is stripped bare when placed amid some activity; hence it is immediately added there: “Strip off your shame, uncover your shoulder, reveal your legs, cross the rivers” (Ibid., 2) [note: Compend., Bellovac., Germ., and many others: “reveal your leg”; and below, “he reveals his leg”].

In the administration of a task, shame is stripped bare when a worthless and contemptible mind is recognized in the display of its activity, though previously, in its quiet, it was considered great. The mind uncovers its shoulder when it displays the work that had been unknown. It reveals its legs when it manifests by what steps of desire it longs for worldly profits. It also crosses rivers because it continually desires the activities of this age, which flow daily toward their end; and, while it leaves some behind and pursues others, it continually proceeds, as it were, from river to river [note: Manuscripts Norm. and others: “he crosses from river to river”].

We have said these things briefly by way of digression, to show where the mind lies when it has been shaken from the throne of holy intention, because, if it ceases to long for the things above it, it continually falls beneath itself. It is fixed on high, however, when, abandoning love of temporal things, it is bound to the hope of unchanging eternity.

26. The true joy of God’s servants; the joy of the wicked arises from madness, not from soundness.---It is therefore rightly said: “Who sets the lowly on high.” And it is appropriately added: “And raises the sorrowful to safety.”

Often in this world people who are cheerful are also lifted up, swelling with the very glory of their prosperity. But the Lord raises his afflicted ones to safety because he lifts them into the glory of true joy by its steadfastness.

They are raised in soundness, not in madness, who, established in good works, rejoice in firm hope in God. Some, as we have said, perpetrate wickedness and nevertheless do not cease to rejoice; of them Solomon says: “They rejoice when they have done evil and exult in the worst things” (Prov. 2:14). And again: “There are wicked people who are so secure as though they possessed the deeds of the righteous” (Eccles. 8:14).

These people are raised not in soundness but in madness. They grow proud when they ought to be afflicted; and they flow away, wretched, into exultation precisely where the good mourn over them. Like the minds of the frenzied, they consider the madness in which they prevail to be virtue. They do not know that what they are capable of beyond the healthy arises from illness; and they think they have grown stronger when, through the increase of their sickness, they are approaching the end of life.

Because they do not possess the sense of reason, they are mourned while they laugh; and they expand themselves in great exultation to the same degree that, being insensible, they do not know the evil they suffer. The Lord therefore raises the sorrowful to safety, because the mind of the elect rejoices not in the madness of the present life but in the certainty of eternal salvation.

Hence what follows immediately concerns the destruction of the wicked:

CHAPTER XVII.

VERSE 12.---“Who scatters the thoughts of the wicked, so that their hands cannot complete what they have begun.”

27. The thoughts of the wicked often come to nothing, yet their conscience is no less guilty.---The minds of the reprobate are always intent upon perverse thoughts, but heavenly providence often confronts them. Although they do not correct the wickedness of their plan even when broken by adversities, it restrains their strength so that they may not prevail against the good.

Against them, however, a marvelous judgment is carried out: they are deprived of the effect of their wicked work, yet their conscience is condemned as guilty by the just sentence of the Judge. What they think about doing evil shows what they themselves would do; but their inability to accomplish evil protects those against whom they had plotted.

Hence it is also rightly added:

CHAPTER XVIII [Rec. XII].

VERSE 13.---“Who catches the wise in their craftiness and scatters the plans of the wicked.”

28. Those who resist God’s plans unwillingly serve them. This is shown by the examples of Joseph’s brothers, Saul, Jonah, and the Jews.---Often some people, puffed up with human wisdom, observe that divine judgments oppose their desires and attempt to resist them by crafty schemes. To bend the force of heavenly providence according to their wishes, they persist in cunning thoughts and seek subtler plans.

But they accomplish God’s will precisely where they strive to change it; and, while they try to resist the plan of almighty God, they serve it, because often what vainly rebounds against him through human effort serves his arrangement appropriately.

The Lord therefore catches the wise in their very craftiness when human deeds fittingly serve his plans even while they resist them. We can show this more clearly if we bring forward a few examples from events that have occurred.

[Vet. XII.] 29. Joseph had dreamed that his brothers’ sheaves prostrated themselves before his sheaf (Gen. 37:7); he had dreamed that the sun and moon, together with the remaining stars, worshiped him. Because he reported these things openly to his brothers, fear and envy of his future domination immediately struck their hearts.

When they saw him coming toward them, in the fury of their wickedness they said: “Behold, that dreamer is coming; come, let us kill him and see what his dreams will profit him” (Ibid., 20). Fearing that they would be subjected to his rule, they lowered the dreamer into a pit and sold him to passing Ishmaelites.

Taken to Egypt and subjected to slavery, he was condemned on an accusation of lust; aided by the merit of his chastity, he was raised up by the judgment of prophecy [note: Corb. Germ.: “raised up.” Utic. has “rescued and raised up”], and was placed over all Egypt. Through heavenly wisdom he made provision, gathered grain, and forestalled the future danger of famine.

When famine broke out throughout the world [note: Gemet., Utic., Val. Cl., and others: “when famine grew terrifying”], Jacob, anxious about the provision of food, sent his sons to Egypt. Unaware that they had found Joseph in charge of the distribution of grain, they were compelled, in order to deserve to receive food, to worship the distributor with their necks bowed to the ground.

Let us consider the sequence of what happened; let us consider how divine power catches the wise in their very craftiness. Joseph had been sold by them so that he would not be worshiped; but he was worshiped precisely because he had been sold.

They had cunningly attempted to do something so that God’s plan might be changed; but by divine judgment, in resisting what they had tried to avoid, they served it. They were compelled to carry out God’s will precisely where they had cunningly plotted to alter it.

Thus the divine plan is fulfilled when it is avoided; thus human wisdom is caught when it resists. The brothers feared that Joseph would rise above them, but by taking precautions against what had been divinely ordained, they brought it about.

Human wisdom was therefore caught in itself: in the very place where it resisted God’s will through its intention, it served the fulfillment of that will [note: Ebroic.: “served his intention”].

## [Vet. XIII.] 30.

Thus Saul, seeing David, who was subject to him, growing daily through the increasing success of his virtues, promised him his daughter in marriage and demanded that a hundred foreskins of Philistines be given by him as her dowry, so that, when the soldier whom he had provoked sought to surpass himself, he might be handed over to the swords of his enemies and meet his death, as it is written: “The king has no need of a bride-price, except for a hundred foreskins of the Philistines, so that vengeance may be taken on the king’s enemies” (1 Samuel 18:25). Saul, moreover, was thinking of delivering David into the hands of the Philistines; but David, strengthened by the favor of the hidden disposition, declared that he would give a hundred and brought back two hundred foreskins. Saul, plainly overcome by the evidence of this deed, was caught by heavenly providence in the design of his own wisdom, because from the very means by which he thought to extinguish the life of the growing soldier, he increased the glory of his valor.

**[Note: Vindocinensis: “His glory of valor was thereby strengthened.”]**

### 31.

But since the elect themselves sometimes contrive, with cunning, to display some piece of wisdom, I wish to bring forward another wise man and demonstrate how the cunning of mortals is caught in the hidden counsels [of God].

**[Note: Compend., Val. Cl., Longip., Corb. Germ., Colb. Norman., and one Vindocinensis: “And to demonstrate in what bosom of the hidden counsel the cunning of mortals is caught.” In Turonensis: “And to demonstrate how, by the judgment of the hidden counsel, cunning is caught,” and so forth. S. Mich. and Germ.: “And those whom the cunning of the hidden counsel…” Vetus Editio: “And how it is caught in the cunning of the hidden counsel.” In some copies, *in* is absent.]**

Jonah, indeed, wished to act wisely when, sent to preach the repentance of the Ninevites, he refused to fulfill the office of preaching because he feared that, when the Gentiles were chosen, Judea would be deserted.

**[Note: Ebroicensis: “To preach the repentance of the Ninevites.”]**

He sought a ship and chose to flee to Tarshish; but immediately a storm arose, and lots were cast, so that it might be discovered whose guilt was disturbing the sea. Jonah was found to be at fault, was plunged into the deep, swallowed by a sea monster, and was carried by the beast to the place to which he had deliberately refused to go. Behold: the storm finds God’s fugitive, the lot binds him, the sea receives him, the beast encloses him; and because he resists obeying his Creator, he is carried, guilty, in his prison to the place to which he had been sent. When God commanded him to minister prophecy, the man refused; when God willed it, the beast vomited forth the prophet. Thus the Lord catches the wise in their cunning, when he turns to the service of his will even that by which the human will contradicts him.

### 32.

Let us examine further the wisdom of the Jews, so that we may see what they prevented by their efforts to forestall it, and what they provoked by their efforts to prevent it. Certainly, when a crowd of believers was flocking to the miracles of our Redeemer, and the priests of the people, inflamed by the torches of envy, declared that the world was going after him, saying, “You see that we accomplish nothing; behold, the whole world has gone after him” (John 12:19), they attempted to end his power by death, saying, “It is expedient that one man should die, and that the whole nation should not perish” (John 11:50).

But the Redeemer’s death served to unite his body, that is, the Church, not to separate it. Hence, too, the Law commands that the throat of a turtledove or pigeon, as a figure of our sacrifice, be cut, but not completely severed, so that after death the head may remain attached to the body (Leviticus 1:15). For the mediator between God and human beings (1 Timothy 2:5), that is, the head of us all, and the victim of true cleansing, became more truly attached to us through the very thing by which he endured death for us. After the cut, therefore, the head of the turtledove remains attached to its body, because even intervening death does not divide Christ from the Church.

The persecutors, therefore, accomplished what they had wickedly contrived: they inflicted death in order to cut off the devotion of the faithful from him. But faith grew through the very thing by which the cruelty of unbelievers believed it had extinguished it. And while they thought that by persecuting him they could cut off his miracles, they were compelled, without knowing it, to spread them further. Thus the Lord catches the wise in their cunning, when he turns to the service of his mercy even that against which human cruelty has raged.

**[Note: Throughout, the manuscripts have *absciderent*, *abscidere*, and similar forms, for *abscinderent*, and so forth.]**

### 33. God graciously grants some things and angrily permits others.

For the just and merciful God, ordering the deeds of mortals, graciously grants some things and angrily permits others; and what he permits, he tolerates in such a way that he turns it to the service of his own counsel.

**[Vet. XIV.]**

Thus, in a wondrous manner, it comes about that what is done without God’s will is nevertheless not contrary to God’s will, because, while evil deeds are turned to a good use, even what resists his counsel serves his counsel. Hence the Psalmist says: “Great are the works of the Lord, sought out according to all his wills” (Psalm 110:2). His works are indeed so great that through everything done by human beings his will is sought out. For it is often accomplished through the very means by which it was thought to be repelled.

Again it is said: “Whatever the Lord willed, he did in heaven and on earth” (Psalm 134:6). Solomon likewise says: “There is no wisdom, there is no prudence, there is no counsel against the Lord” (Proverbs 21:30). It remains, therefore, that in everything we do we should seek the force of the heavenly will. Once it is known, our action ought dutifully to serve it and, as though it were the guide of its journey, follow it, lest our action serve it even unwillingly if, in pride, it turns away from it.

The force of the heavenly counsel cannot be avoided; but a person restrains it with great virtue when he restrains himself beneath its commands. He lightens its burdens for himself when he willingly carries them upon the shoulder of a submissive heart. But since we have already mentioned the persecutors, let us show how the things that follow also correspond to their blindness. The text continues:

## CHAPTER XIX [Rec. XIII]

### Verse 14

> “By day they will encounter darkness, and as though in night, so they will grope at midday.”

### 34. Christ’s persecutors suffered darkness in the daytime and, like the blind, groped at midday.

They encountered darkness in the daytime because, in the very presence of truth, they were blinded by the error of their unbelief. In daytime things are clearly seen; at night our sight is obscured. The persecutors of our Redeemer, therefore, while they saw the miracles of divine power and nevertheless doubted his divinity, suffered darkness in the daytime, because they lost their sight in the light.

**[Note: Ebroicensis and other Norman copies: “while they saw the miracles of divine mercy.” Uticensis has both readings.]**

Hence the very Light admonishes them, saying: “Walk while you have the light, lest the darkness overtake you” (John 12:35).

**[Note: Vindocinensis and other Norman copies: “Lest the darkness of death overtake you.”]**

Hence it is said of Judea: “Its sun went down while it was still day” (Jeremiah 15:9). Hence the prophet again took upon himself the voice of penitents, saying: “We stumbled at midday as though in darkness; in dark places as though dead” (Isaiah 59:10). Again he says:

**[Note: In the corrected Uticensis and Germaniacensis copies: “Watcher, what of the night? Watcher, what of the night?”]**

> “Watcher, what of the night? Watcher, what of the night?”  
> The watcher said: “Morning comes, and also night” (Isaiah 21:11).

The Watcher came from the night because the protector of the human race appeared openly in the flesh; yet Judea, oppressed by the darkness of its unbelief, did not recognize him at all. Appropriately, from the watchman’s voice it is added, “Morning comes, and also night,” because through his presence a new light shone upon the world, while the ancient blindness nevertheless remained in the hearts of unbelievers.

**[Vet. XV.]**

It is rightly said: “As though in night, so they will grope at midday.” By groping we seek what we do not see with our eyes. The Jews, however, had seen his manifest miracles, and yet, still seeking as though they were groping, said: “How long will you take away our soul? If you are the Christ, tell us openly” (John 10:24). Behold, the light of the miracles was before their eyes, and yet, stumbling in the darkness of their hearts, they continued to grope by asking.

Their blindness eventually flared up into cruelty, and their cruelty even into the open deeds of persecution. But the Redeemer of the human race could not long be held in the hands of his persecutors. Hence it immediately follows:

## CHAPTER XX

### Verse 15

> “But he will save the needy from the sword of their mouth, and the poor from the hand of the violent.”

**[Note: *Egenum* is absent in Compend., Norm., and others, here and wherever the same text is subsequently quoted.]**

### 35. By rising again, Christ overcame the tongues of the Jews and the sword of the Gentiles.

This poor man is the one of whom Paul says: “For your sake he became poor, although he was rich” (2 Corinthians 8:9). And because the Jews handed the Lord over by accusing him, while the Gentiles killed him after he had been handed over—

**[Note: In place of *occiderunt* (“killed”), the manuscripts of Gilotensis and others read *crucifixerunt* (“crucified”).]**

—the sword of the mouth may signify the tongue of the accusing Hebrews, of whom the Psalmist says: “The sons of men, whose teeth are weapons and arrows, and whose tongue is a sharp sword” (Psalm 56:5), since, as the Gospel also testifies, they cried out: “Crucify, crucify!” (Luke 23:21).

By the hand of the violent, the Gentiles themselves who crucified him may be represented; in the Redeemer’s death they carried out in deed what the voices of the Hebrews demanded. God therefore saved this poor man both from the hand of the violent and from the sword of their mouths, because our Redeemer endured, in his humanity, both the strength of the Gentiles and the tongues of the Jews by dying, but overcame them by rising again through the power of his divinity.

What else is accomplished by this resurrection except that our weakness is strengthened for the hope of the life to come? Hence it immediately follows:

## CHAPTER XXI

### Verse 16

> “And there will be hope for the needy.”

### 36. He made firm the hope of his own people.

When the poor man has been rescued, the needy is restored to hope, because the humble people of the faithful are shaken with fear when the Redeemer dies, but are strengthened when he rises. The first poor members of this people, namely, the chosen preachers, were struck by the sight of his death, but were restored when his resurrection was revealed.

Once the poor man has been saved, the needy receives hope, because, when the Lord rises in the flesh, every believer grows strong in confidence in eternal life. But behold, Truth has now come in manifest revelation; he has endured the death of the flesh and destroyed it by rising again; he has now honored the resurrection with the glory of the ascension.

**[Note: Vindocinensis: “He has now honored the glory of the resurrection with the ascension.”]**

Yet the tongue of the Hebrews still does not cease to assail him with insults. He tolerates them patiently, so that by tolerating some he may convert them, while someday he may strike others who remain unconverted with greater severity. The tongue of unbelievers will then fall silent from its unbridled speech, when it sees him coming as the just judge whom it now judged unjustly. Hence it is rightly added:

## CHAPTER XXII

### The same passage

> “But iniquity will contract its mouth.”

### 37. The Jews will cease their insults against Christ.

Iniquity still enlarges its mouth, because the tongue of unbelievers does not cease to assail the Redeemer of the human race with insults. But then it will contract its mouth, when it closes by punishment what it refuses to close through deliberate effort.

**[Note: *Per* is absent in Gemetensis.]**

This may also rightly be understood of persecutors who are converted. When the poor man has been saved and the needy returns to hope, iniquity falls silent with its mouth contracted, because, as the miracle of his resurrection shines forth, a great multitude of unbelievers believes and ceases from injuries and insults against its Redeemer. The mouth which it opened in mocking God it has already contracted through fear.

## [Vet. XVI.] MORAL MEANING

### 38. The darkness and anxious malice of the envious.

Let us pass over these matters in their moral sense, setting aside the reference to the Jews, and investigate generally how the wicked are affected. When the minds of wicked people see certain things well done by their neighbors, they are tortured upon the extended rack of their envy, and suffer the severe punishment of their malice when they see themselves wasting away at the sight of goodness in others.

It is rightly said: “By day they will encounter darkness,” because, when their mind is distressed by another’s improvement, it is darkened by the ray of light. Often, while they observe manifest good things in their neighbors, they investigate whether some evils may be hidden; and they labor through anxious inquiries to discover whether they can find something for which they may accuse them. They see healthy limbs, but with the eyes of their hearts closed they grope for a wound.

Hence it is rightly added: “And as though in night, so they will grope at midday.” The day of good works shines outwardly in one’s neighbor; but they grope as though in night, because inwardly they endure the darkness of their envy. They strive to find something to criticize and seek an opening for detraction; but because they cannot find one, they wander about outside like blind people.

This is well expressed when, while angels protected Lot, the Sodomites could not find the door of his house, as it is written:

> “They pressed hard upon Lot, and it was nearly time for them to break down the doors. Then the men put out their hand, drew Lot inside to them, shut the door, and struck with blindness those who were outside, from the least to the greatest, so that they could not find the door” (Genesis 19:9–10 and following).

What does it mean that, when wicked men oppose him, Lot is brought back inside his house and protected, except that every just person, while enduring the plots of the wicked, returns to his mind and remains undaunted? The Sodomite men cannot find the door in Lot’s house because corruptors of minds find no opening for accusation against the life of the just.

Struck with blindness, they go around the house like people groping, because in their envy they scrutinize his deeds and words. But because a strong and praiseworthy action confronts them everywhere in the life of the just, in their error they touch nothing but the wall. It is rightly said: “As though in night, so they will grope at midday,” because, unable to accuse the good that they see, blinded by malice they seek for accusation the evil that they do not see.

### 39. Pleasure or fear draws us into guilt; neither has power over the humble.

Here it is rightly added: “But he will save the poor from the sword of their mouth and from the hand of the violent.” The poor is whoever is not exalted in his own eyes. Hence Truth says through the Gospel: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 5:3).

There are two ways by which each person is drawn into guilt. One is led by pleasure, or else overcome by fear. The sword of the mouth is the wickedness of persuasion; the hand of the violent is the adversity of power. But because the truly humble person, who is called “poor” here, desires none of the prosperities of this world and therefore boldly despises its adversities, it is rightly said: “He will save the poor from the sword of their mouth and from the hand of the violent.”

It is as though he were saying openly: God so strengthens the minds of the humble in himself that neither the allurements of persuasion draw them into wrongdoing nor the pains of punishment break them. Hope raises the soul toward eternity, and therefore it does not feel, in the outward realm, the evils that it endures. Hence it is added: “And there will be hope for the needy.”

When the poor man has reached the fruit of this hope, every proud person falls silent. Hence it is further added: “But iniquity will contract its mouth.” Now the wicked disparages the good and never ceases to tear apart by detraction the upright things that he neglects to do. But then iniquity contracts its mouth, when it recognizes how great a glory of reward awaits the just.

Then there is no time for it to speak against the good, because the punishments due to its evil deeds bind its tongue. Hence, as Hannah prophesies, it is rightly said: “He will preserve the feet of his holy ones, and the wicked will be silent in darkness” (1 Samuel 2:9).

But so that every elect person may escape eternal punishments and the poor may rise to everlasting glory, he ought here to be worn down by continual scourging, so that he may be found purified at the judgment. For every day we are dragged downward by the weight of our weakness, unless we are lifted up by the wondrous hand of the craftsman through the scourges that come to our aid.

**[Note: Norman manuscripts read: “unless by the mercy of the craftsman.” Uticensis also gives: “unless by the merciful hand of the craftsman” (*urtificis*, probably *artificis*).]**

Hence it is added:

## CHAPTER XXIII [Vet. XVII]

### Verse 17

> “Blessed is the man who is corrected by the Lord.”

### 40. The elect must here be worn down by continual scourging.

The first virtue is to avoid sins before they are committed; the second is at least to correct sins that have been committed.

**[Note: Here the manuscripts vary. One Vindocinensis and Colbertinus have: “lest they should commit sins.” Another Vindocinensis: “lest they should commit premeditated sins.” Reginensis, Ebroicensis, and other Norman copies: “lest forbidden sins should be committed.” Germaniacensis and Corbeiensis: for *vetita* (“forbidden”), *vitata* (“avoided”) sins. Others: “lest they should be committed, to avoid sins.”]**

But very often we not only fail to avoid faults that threaten us; we do not even acknowledge those already committed. The mind of the sinner grows darker the more it fails to understand the damage caused by its own blindness.

It therefore frequently comes about, through the generosity of divine grace, that punishment follows guilt, and scourges open the eyes of the offender—eyes that security had blinded amid vices. The sluggish soul is touched by a blow so that it may be awakened; thus one who, secure, has lost the state of his uprightness may, when afflicted, consider where he lies.

The harshness of correction therefore becomes the beginning of light. Hence Paul says: “Everything that is reproved is manifested by the light” (Ephesians 5:13); for the force of pain is an instrument of salvation. Hence Solomon says: “Healing will put an end to great sins” (Ecclesiastes 10:4). Again he says: “For whom the Lord loves, he chastises; and he scourges every son whom he receives” (Hebrews 12:6). Hence the Lord speaks through the angelic voice to John, saying: “Those whom I love, I rebuke and chastise” (Revelation 3:19). Paul likewise says: “All discipline at the present time does not seem to be of joy but of sorrow; afterward, however, it yields the most peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it” (Hebrews 12:11).

Although pain and blessedness cannot properly exist together, it is nevertheless rightly said here, “Blessed is the man who is corrected by the Lord,” because, through being weighed down by the pain of correction, the sinner is eventually instructed for blessedness, which exists without the intervention of pain. The text continues:

## CHAPTER XXIV [Rec. XIV]

### The same passage

> “Therefore do not reject the rebuke of the Lord.”

### 41. God’s correction sometimes punishes and sometimes tests.

Whoever is struck for guilt but rises up in complaint against the blow rejects the Lord’s rebuke, because he accuses God of subjecting him to it unjustly. But those who are struck not for the cleansing of a crime but for the testing of their strength, when they inquire into the causes of their affliction, should by no means be said to reject the Lord’s rebuke, because they strive to discover in themselves what they do not know.

**[Note: The printed editions add *in castigando* (“in chastising”), which is redundant and absent from the manuscripts.]**

Thus blessed Job, bursting into words of liberty amid the blows of his affliction, questions the judgments of the one who strikes him all the more rightly because he more truly does not know in himself the causes of his suffering.

**[Note: The printed editions read *persecutionis* (“persecution”) in place of *passionis* (“suffering”).]**

Eliphaz, therefore, because he judged that Job had been struck not as a test but for purification, believed that Job rejected God’s rebuke when he spoke freely amid the scourges. We have appropriately said that he also represents heretics, who always bend everything rightly done by the holy Church toward the fault of crookedness according to their own judgment.

But because he is led to speak with good intention, yet does not take care to discern to whom he is speaking, he continues to proclaim the moderations of the heavenly dispensation, saying:

## CHAPTER XXV [Vet. XVIII]

### Verse 18

> “For he wounds, and he heals; he strikes, and his hands will heal.”

### 42. God wounds in two ways for salvation. When the mind returns to God, whatever previously seemed alluring in the world is turned into a temptation.

The almighty God wounds in two ways those whom he takes care to restore to salvation. Sometimes he strikes the flesh and melts the hardness of the mind through fear of him. He recalls people to salvation by wounding them when he afflicts his elect outwardly so that they may live inwardly. Hence he also speaks through Moses, saying: “I kill and I make alive; I strike, and I heal” (Deuteronomy 32:39).

He kills in order to give life; he strikes in order to heal, because he inflicts blows outwardly for the purpose of curing the wounds of sins within. At other times, even when scourges seem to cease outwardly, he inflicts wounds inwardly, because he strikes the hardness of our mind with desire for him.

But he heals by striking, because, pierced by the dart of his fear, he recalls us to an awareness of uprightness. Our hearts are unhealthy when they are wounded by no love of God, when they do not feel the misery of their pilgrimage, and when they do not languish even in the least with compassion for the weakness of their neighbor.

But they are wounded so that they may be healed, because God strikes insensitive minds with the arrows of his love and immediately makes them sensitive through the fire of charity. Hence the bride says in the Song of Songs: “I am wounded by love” (Song of Songs 2:5, according to the Septuagint).

A soul that was unhealthy and lay prostrate in the condition of this exile with blind security neither saw the Lord nor sought to see him.

**[Note: The editions read *exsilii statu* (“in the state of exile”). Compendensis, Val. Cl., and Norman copies have *stratum* (“bed”); Corbeiensis Germaniacensis reads *exsilii statim caeca securitate* (“immediately in exile, by blind security”).]** But when struck by the arrows of his love, it is wounded in its depths by an affection of devotion, burns with the desire for contemplation, and, in a wondrous way, is brought to life by the wound—though previously it lay dead in the very midst of health. It burns and pants, and now desires to see the one from whom it had fled.

By a blow, therefore, the soul is brought back to salvation when it is recalled to the quiet of its inmost rest through the disturbance of his love. But when the wounded mind begins to pant for God, and, scorning all the allurements of this world, stretches toward the heavenly homeland through desire, everything that had previously seemed friendly and attractive in the world immediately becomes a temptation.

For those who had been accustomed to love the sinner cruelly attack the person living rightly. And the mind raised toward God endures the battles of its flesh, in which it had previously lain delightfully in the service of vices. Former pleasures return to memory and afflict the resisting mind in a severe struggle.

But because, while we are worn down by a temporary labor, we are freed from everlasting pain, it is appropriately added:

## CHAPTER XXVI [Rec. XV]

### Verse 19

> “In six tribulations he will deliver you, and in the seventh evil will not touch you.”

### 43. Through temporary labor we are rescued from everlasting pain.

What is signified by the number six, which is followed by seven, except the activity and course of the present life? On the sixth day he completed all things and created the human being, and on the seventh day God rested. That seventh day has no evening, because no end ever closes the rest that follows.

After everything has been completed, therefore, rest follows, because after the good works of the present life the reward of eternal rest is found. In six tribulations the Lord delivers us so that evil may not touch us in the seventh, because through the instruction of paternal mercy he wears us down by the labor of the present life but hides us from the blows at the coming of the Judge.

He does this so that he may then present us as more certain of salvation in proportion as the scourges now cut us more harshly. Appropriately, he immediately enumerates both the evils of the present life and the aids of heavenly protection, adding:

## CHAPTER XXVII

### Verse 20

> “In famine he will rescue you from death, and in war from the hand of the sword.”

### 44. While God refreshes minds with the nourishment of his word, he makes them strong against temptations.

Just as bodily famine is the withdrawal of the body’s support, so the famine of the mind is the silence of divine speech. Hence the prophet rightly says: “I will send famine upon the land, not a famine of bread nor a thirst for water, but a famine of hearing the word of God” (Amos 8:11).

And because, when divine speech deserts the human mind, the temptation of the flesh grows strong against it, it is appropriately added: “And in war, from the hand of the sword.” We suffer war when we are attacked by the temptations of our flesh. Of this war the Psalmist says:

**[Note: Most manuscripts read *obumbrasti caput meum* (“you overshadowed my head”), as does the Roman Psalter. A very few have *obumbravit caput* (“he overshadowed the head”). Corbeiensis Germaniacensis has *obumbravit caput*; one Reginensis, as in the editions, has *obumbrasti super caput* (“you overshadowed over the head”).]**

> “Overshadow my head in the day of battle” (Psalm 139:3).

Because the reprobate, while they fail from hunger for the word of God, are also pierced by the sword of battle, the Lord both snatches his elect from death in famine and hides them from the sword in battle. He does this because, while he refreshes their minds with the nourishment of his word, he makes them strong against bodily temptations.

But there are some who, although they refresh themselves from inward hunger through divine speech, nevertheless, even if they are already strengthened by the virtue of continence against temptations of the body—

**[Note: Vindocinensis: “If they are already supported by the virtue of continence against temptations and battles.” Colbertinus, Corbeiensis Germaniacensis, Compendensis, and Turonensis: “If they are already supported by the virtue of continence against the battles of temptation” (or “temptations”). Uticensis and some Norman copies: “If they already support themselves by the virtue of continence against temptations of the flesh”; followed by “nevertheless,” and so forth.]**

—they still fear being struck by human detraction, and often, while they fear the darts of tongues, they strangle themselves in the noose of sin. Hence it is appropriately added:

## CHAPTER XXVIII [Vet. XIX]

### Verse 21

> “You will be hidden from the scourge of the tongue.”

### 45. One must arm oneself against the scourge of the tongue and against bodily punishments.

The scourge of the tongue is reproach for an insult inflicted. Those who persecute the good by mocking their works strike them with the scourge of the tongue. Often the tongue, by criticizing, turns a person away from a good work; and it puts itself forward like a scourge because it lashes the back of the timid mind.

The Prophet had seen this scourge of the tongue lying in wait for the elect mind when, promising heavenly assistance, he said: “He himself will deliver you from the snare of the hunters and from the harsh word” (Psalm 90:3).

**[Note: Uticensis and most manuscripts read *liberabit te* (“he will deliver you”), as does the Hebrew text, Athanasius, the Sixtine edition, and others. Theodoretus, however, reads *liberabit me* (“he will deliver me”), supported by Augustine, who has *eruet me* (“he will rescue me”).]**

Hunters seek nothing other than flesh. But we are delivered from the hunters’ snare and from the harsh word when, by despising them, we overcome both the plots of carnal people and the insults of mockery. Their words are harsh because they oppose our good paths. To escape the harshness of their word is to trample underfoot the mockery of detractors by disregarding it.

Thus the holy soul is hidden from the scourge of the tongue because, while it does not seek the honor of praise in this world, it also does not feel the insults of detraction. But there are some who already despise the words of their detractors and already regard their mockery as nothing, yet still fear bodily punishments and torments.

The ancient adversary attacks us in many ways in order to draw us back from our right intention. He assails our temptation sometimes through hunger for the word, sometimes through the struggle of the flesh, sometimes through the scourge of speech, and sometimes through the calamity of persecution. But because every perfected person, after conquering vices in himself, immediately girds his mind also against the wounds of suffering, it is appropriately added:

## CHAPTER XXIX

### The same passage

> “And you will not fear calamity when it comes.”

### 46. While fighting against the many-formed adversary, we must prepare ourselves in many ways.

Holy people, because they recognize that they are fighting against a many-formed adversary, prepare themselves for the struggle in many ways. Against hunger for the divine word they have nourishment; against the sword of battle, the shield of continence; against the scourge of the tongue, the protection of patience; against the damage of outward calamity, the help of inward love.

Thus, in a wondrous manner, the more numerous the ways in which the cunning enemy tempts them, the richer in virtues the watchful soldiers of God become. And because, while the elect courageously endure the struggles of the present life, they prepare for themselves security in the terror of the coming judgment, it is rightly added:

## CHAPTER XXX [Vet. XX, Rec. XVI]

### Verse 22

> “In devastation and famine you will laugh.”

### 47. The reprobate will be tormented inwardly and outwardly.

The reprobate will then suffer devastation and famine, when, condemned at the final judgment, they are separated from the vision of the eternal bread. For it is written: “Let the impious be taken away, lest he see the glory of God” (Isaiah 26:10, according to the Septuagint). And the Lord himself says: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven” (John 6:51).

Devastation and famine torment those who not only feel torments outwardly but also die inwardly from the plague of starvation. Gehenna lays waste because it burns; famine kills because the Redeemer hides his face from them.

**[Note: The manuscripts of Gemetensis read: “For they receive the retribution of punishment.”]**

They rightly receive retribution inwardly and outwardly because they sinned both in thought and in action. Hence the Psalmist rightly says: “You will place them like a furnace of fire at the time of your presence; the Lord will trouble them in his anger, and fire will devour them” (Psalm 20:10).

What is devoured by fire is ignited from the outside; a furnace, however, is inflamed inwardly. At the time of the Lord’s presence, therefore, all the unjust are placed like a furnace and devoured by fire, because, when the judge appears and their multitude is rejected from his sight, their conscience burns inwardly through desire, while Gehenna torments the flesh outwardly.

### 48. The just will then laugh, and no compassion for the condemned will move them.

The scourge of the tongue may also be understood as the sentence of the final punishment, by which the strict judge says to the reprobate: “Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire that has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matthew 25:41).

The just, therefore, is hidden from the scourge of the tongue and from the coming calamity because, amid such strictness of judgment, he is then refreshed by the judge’s gentle voice when it is said:

**[Note: Ebroicensis: “because of intent strictness.”]**

> “I was hungry, and you gave me food; I was thirsty, and you gave me drink; I was a stranger, and you welcomed me; naked, and you clothed me; sick, and you visited me; I was in prison, and you came to me” (Matthew 25:35–36).

These words are preceded by:

> “Come, blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matthew 25:34).

In devastation and famine, therefore, the just will laugh, because, when the final vengeance strikes all the wicked, he rejoices in the glory of a worthy reward. Nor will he then show human compassion toward the condemned, because, clinging by likeness to divine justice, he is made firm by the unshaken strength of its inward strictness.

The minds of the elect, raised into the brightness of heavenly uprightness, are affected by no compassion, because the height of blessedness makes them strangers to misery. Hence the Psalmist also rightly says: “The just will see and fear, and they will laugh over him, and say: ‘Behold the man who did not set God as his helper’” (Psalm 51:8).

**[Note: Gemetensis: “God as his helper.”]**

The just now see the wicked and fear; then they will see them and laugh. Because they can now fall by imitating them, they have fear here; but because then they will be unable to benefit the condemned, they will have no compassion there.

Those delivered over to eternal punishment must not be pitied. The just read this in the very justice of the Judge in whose blessedness they participate. It would diminish the quality of the happiness they have received—something that cannot rightly be supposed—if, placed in the kingdom, they wished for what they could in no way accomplish.

But whoever directs himself toward the commands of life tastes here, before receiving the eternal rewards, the beginnings of the security that will follow forever, so that he may not fear the ancient enemy and may in no way dread his violent attacks when the moment of death intervenes.

**[Vet. XXI.]**

For the just, the very security of mind that is often present at death is the beginning of reward. Hence it is rightly added:

## CHAPTER XXXI

### Verse 22

> “And you will not fear the beast of the earth.”

### 49. They often receive security of mind at death

The cunning adversary is called “the beast of the earth,” because at the time of death he rages with the violence of cruelty in order to seize sinners’ souls. Those whom he deceives while they are alive by flattering them, he seizes when they are dying by raging against them. Against this, the Lord promises concerning the Church of the elect through the prophet: “The evil beast shall not pass through it” (Isaiah 35:9).

Those, therefore, fear the beast of the earth when dying who, while alive, do not fear the power of their Creator. For holy men, because they submit themselves from the depths of their being to divine fear, cast away all the burden of fear at the adversary’s coming. Hence the Psalmist beseeches the Lord, saying: “Lest at any time he seize my soul like a lion” (Psalm 7:3). Again he says: “Hear, O God, my prayer when I am troubled; deliver my soul from the fear of the enemy” (Psalm 63:1–2).

Those who live rightly fear the Judge perfectly, so that when dying they may not fear the accuser. Accordingly it is rightly said: “And you shall not fear the beast of the earth.” It is as though he were saying openly: “Because you are not now overcome by the enemy who flatters you, you shall not later fear him when he rages.”

But when one lives well, one must be very careful lest the mind, despising the rest, be lifted up by the glory of singular distinction. Hence the good of fellowship is appropriately recalled when it is immediately added:

## CHAPTER XXXII

**VERSE 23.—But your covenant shall be with the stones of the regions.**

### 50. Those who live devoutly must beware of isolation

The regions of the nations’ Churches are, as it were, distinct regions in the world. Though established in one faith, they are divided by diversity of customs and languages. What, then, are the stones of the regions except the elect of the Churches? To them the voice of the first instructor says: “You also, as living stones, are built up” (1 Peter 2:5). Concerning these stones of the holy Church the Lord promises through the prophet, saying: “Behold, I will lay your stones in order” (Isaiah 54:11).

Whoever therefore lives rightly joins himself by covenant to the stones of the regions, because, in overcoming the desires of the world, he undoubtedly binds his life to the imitation of the saints who preceded him. But when he is separated from worldly action, the attacks of evil spirits increase. Nevertheless, the more these afflictions wear someone down in sorrow, the more humbly they subject him to his Creator. Hence it is also added:

## CHAPTER XXXIII

**THE SAME PASSAGE.—And the beasts of the earth shall be at peace with you.**

### 51. The enemy’s sharper ambushes compel us to seek the help of grace

First, it must be noted that he does not say “pacified” but “peaceful”—that is, not because they have peace, but because they make peace. For crafty enemies afflict people while they lie in wait; but the afflicted mind loves the return to its eternal homeland all the more deeply the more laboriously it lives in this wretched exile. It humbles itself more truly before the grace of its helper when it considers the sharper ambushes directed against it.

Thus the beasts of the earth become peaceful toward the elect, because evil spirits, when they oppress the hearts of the good by opposing them, drive those hearts—against their own intention—toward love of the Lord. From the place where a harsher struggle against us is generated by our adversaries, a stronger peace with God consequently arises.

### 52. The movements of the flesh roar in temptation, but do not reach the bite; rather, they secure peace for us with God

The movements of the flesh may also be understood by the beasts of the earth. When they provoke our mind by persuading it to irrational things, they rise up against us in bestial fashion. But when the heart is brought under the divine law, the incitements of the flesh also subside, so that, even if they mutter in temptation, they do not rise up to the accomplishment of deeds—so to speak, to the frenzy of an open bite.

For who, while still dwelling in this corruptible flesh, fully tames these beasts of the earth, when that outstanding preacher, caught up to the third heaven, says: “I see another law in my members fighting against the law of my mind and taking me captive under the law of sin, which is in my members” (Romans 7:23)?

Yet it is one thing to see these beasts raging in the field of action, and another to hold them roaring within the cage of the heart. For when they have been confined within the barriers of self-restraint, although they still roar in temptation, they nevertheless do not exceed, as we have said, the limits of unlawful action by biting.

The beasts of the earth are therefore peaceful because, although the movements of the flesh palpitate through desires, they do not attack us with an open contradiction in action. Still, by the very fact that they are called peaceful, what we have said concerning evil spirits can also appropriately be understood. For the movements of the flesh make peace for us with God when they oppose us in temptation.

The mind of the righteous, as it is directed toward higher things, is wearied by a grievous battle with the corruptible body. Whenever it is delayed by even the slightest pleasure of this world from its heavenly desires, it is driven on by the very battle of its temptation to love with its whole heart that which no opposition disturbs.

Thus it recalls inner tranquility, and, fleeing the allurements of its flesh, sighs toward that tranquility with complete love. Through temptation each person is compelled to consider whence and whither he has fallen: after abandoning God’s peace, he feels a quarrel rising up within himself against himself. Then he sees more truly what he has lost from the secure love of God, when, having fallen back upon himself, he finds within himself his own humiliation.

The beasts of the earth therefore make peace for us because, while the movements of the flesh provoke us through temptation, they drive us toward love of inner rest. It is rightly added:

## CHAPTER XXXIV [Old Chapter XXIII]

**VERSE 24.—And you shall know that your tabernacle shall have peace.**

### 53. In Scripture there is both complete peace and peace begun

In sacred Scripture peace is spoken of in one way as complete and in another as begun. Truth gave the disciples peace in its beginning when he said: “I leave you peace; my peace I give you” (John 14:27). Simeon desired peace in its fullness when he prayed, saying: “Now you dismiss your servant, Lord, according to your word, in peace” (Luke 2:29).

Our peace begins from desire for the Creator, but is perfected by manifest vision. It will be complete when our mind is neither blinded by ignorance nor shaken by the opposition of its flesh.

But because we touch its beginnings when we either subject the mind to God or the flesh to the mind, the righteous person’s tabernacle is said to have peace. His body, namely, in which the mind dwells, is restrained from perverse movements of desire under the ordering of righteousness.

But what does it profit to restrain the flesh through self-control if the mind does not know how to expand through compassion into love of one’s neighbor? There is no chastity of the flesh that the gentleness of the mind does not commend. Hence, after the peace of the tabernacle, it is appropriately added:

## CHAPTER XXXV

**THE SAME PASSAGE.—And visiting your appearance, you shall not sin.**

### 54. Let each person consider and love himself in another. Paul became all things to all people by condescension, not by falling

The appearance of a human being is another human being. Our neighbor is rightly called our appearance because in him we see what we ourselves are. By bodily visitation we approach our neighbor by the movement of our feet; spiritually, however, we are led not by footsteps but by affection.

Whoever moves toward someone whom he perceives by nature to be like himself in the steps of love visits his own appearance. Considering himself in the other, he gathers from himself how he should condescend to the other in weakness. He visits his own appearance who, in order to refresh another within himself, considers himself in the other.

Hence Truth, through Moses, while describing what had happened, signified what was to happen, saying: “The earth brought forth green grass bearing seed according to its kind, and the tree producing fruit, each having its seed according to its kind” (Genesis 1:12). A tree produces seed according to its kind when our mind gathers from itself a consideration of another and gives birth to the shoot of a righteous deed.

Hence a certain wise man says: “What you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to another” (Tobit 4:16). Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whatever you wish that human beings should do to you, do the same to them” (Matthew 7:12). It is as though he were saying openly: “Visit your appearance in another, and from yourselves recognize what you ought to offer to others.”

Hence Paul says: “To the Jews I became as a Jew, that I might gain the Jews; to those who are under the law, as though I were under the law—although I myself was not under the law—that I might gain those who were under the law; to those who are without the law, as though I were without the law—not being without the law of God, but being under the law of Christ” (1 Corinthians 9:20–21). A little later he says: “I have become all things to all people, that I might save all” (ibid., 23).

The outstanding preacher did not break into unbelief in order to become as a Jew; nor did he return to carnal sacrifice in order to be as one under the law; nor, in becoming all things to all people, did he change the simplicity of his mind into a variety of error. Rather, by condescending, he approached unbelievers, not by falling, so that, receiving each person into himself and transforming himself into each person, he might gather them through compassion. In this way he considered what he himself, if he were as they were, would rightly wish to have done for him by others; and he would meet each person in error all the more truly because from his own experience he had learned the manner of that person’s salvation.

It is therefore rightly said: “And visiting your appearance, you shall not sin,” because sin is fully overcome when each person, from his own likeness to another, considers how he should enlarge himself in love of his neighbor.

When the flesh is restrained from vices and the mind is exercised in virtues, it remains for each person, by speaking, to teach the life that he preserves through his conduct. For the one who first sows good works gathers abundant fruits of preaching. Hence, after the peace of the tabernacle and the visitation of our appearance, it is rightly added:

## CHAPTER XXXVI

**VERSE 25.—And you shall know that your seed shall be numerous, and your offspring like the grass of the earth.**

### 55. The righteous person’s seed is numerous

After the peace of the tabernacle and the visitation of our appearance, the righteous person’s numerous seed rises up. For after the mortification of the members and greatness of conduct, the word of preaching is granted to him all the more fruitfully because it has been preceded in his breast by the inscription of perfect works.

The person who extends his heart’s bosom through efforts to live rightly receives eloquence in speaking well. Conscience does not hinder one who speaks when life precedes the tongue.

Hence the Egyptians, subjected to public servitude under Joseph’s administration (Genesis 47:20 ff.), when they humbled themselves by handing themselves over to the king’s authority, also took grain away for seed. We too receive grain for food while free, when we are nourished by sacred discourse and yet wander in certain pleasures through our desires for things we seek in this world.

But after becoming servants, we receive grain also for seed, because, when we are wholly subjected to God, we are also filled with the word of preaching.

And because a great offspring of the faithful follows when holy preaching has gone before, after the multiplication of the seed it is rightly added: “And your offspring shall be like the grass of the earth.”

The offspring of the righteous is compared to the grass of the earth because the person born from his imitation, while abandoning the withering glory of the present life, grows green in hope of eternity. Or certainly the righteous person’s offspring rises like grass because, while he demonstrates by living what he asserts by preaching, an innumerable multitude of followers arises.

But whoever already despises earthly desires and extends himself through the works of the active life is not at all satisfied with accomplishing great things outwardly unless he can also penetrate inward things through contemplation. Hence it is appropriately added immediately:

## CHAPTER XXXVII [Recension XVII]

**VERSE 26.—You shall enter the grave in abundance, as a heap of grain is brought in at its proper time.**

### 56. Whoever has subdued the flesh ought to devote himself to contemplation, as should also the person devoted to preaching

What is signified by the name “grave” except the contemplative life? It buries us, as though dead to this world, when it hides within us those who have been withdrawn from earthly desires. Those who were dead to the outward life had also been buried through contemplation; to them Paul said: “For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God” (Colossians 3:3).

The active life is also a grave, because it covers us, dead to wicked deeds. But the contemplative life buries us more perfectly because it separates us completely from all the actions of the world.

Whoever has already subdued within himself the insults of the flesh must exercise his mind through the pursuits of holy action. Whoever has already enlarged his mind through holy works must extend it further to the pursuits of the innermost secrets of contemplation.

For a preacher is not perfect if, because of his devotion to contemplation, he neglects what must be done, or if, because of his zeal for action, he postpones what must be contemplated.

Hence Jacob buried his dead wife in a double grave (Genesis 23:19), because every perfect preacher hides his soul, extinguished with regard to the desires of the present life, beneath the covering of good action and contemplation. Thus, under both the active and contemplative life, it lies hidden from carnal desire as though insensible—although previously it lived mortally by sensing the desires of the world.

Hence the Redeemer of the human race performs miracles in the cities by day and spends the night on the mountain in prayer, so that he might indicate to perfect preachers that they should neither wholly abandon the active life through love of contemplation nor entirely despise the joys of contemplation through excessive action. Rather, in tranquility they should absorb through contemplation what, while occupied among their neighbors, they may pour forth by speaking.

Through contemplation one rises into the love of God, but through preaching one returns for the benefit of one’s neighbor.

Hence, when a cow is slaughtered in sacrifice through Moses (Numbers 19:3), twice-dyed scarlet is commanded to be offered with hyssop and cedar wood. We slaughter the cow when we extinguish the flesh’s lust. We offer it with hyssop, cedar wood, and scarlet wool when, together with the mortification of the flesh, we burn the sacrifice of faith, hope, and love.

Hyssop customarily cleanses our inward parts. Through Peter it is said: “Cleansing their hearts by faith” (Acts 15:9). Cedar wood does not decay from any rottenness because the end does not consume hope of heavenly things. Hence Peter also says: “He has regenerated us unto a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead, unto an incorruptible, undefiled, and unfading inheritance” (1 Peter 1:3).

Scarlet blazes with a red color because it sets aflame the person whom love fills. Hence Truth says in the Gospel: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth” (Luke 12:49).

But scarlet dyed twice is commanded to be offered so that, before the eyes of the inward Judge, our love may be colored by love of God and neighbor. Thus the converted mind should neither love repose for the sake of God so much that it neglects the care and benefit of its neighbor, nor serve its neighbor so busily for love of that neighbor that, abandoning repose completely, it extinguishes within itself the fire of heavenly love.

Whoever has already offered himself to God as a sacrifice, if he desires perfection, must take care to extend himself not only to the breadth of action but also to the heights of contemplation.

### 57. The active life suits some people better, the contemplative life others; each should cultivate the one suited to his character

Among these matters it must be understood very carefully that the dispositions of minds differ greatly from one another. Some people are so inclined toward mental quiet that, if the burden of occupation overtakes them, they collapse at the very beginning of the work. Others are so restless that, if they have freedom from labor, they suffer more severely, because the more freely they are available for thoughts, the worse are the disturbances of their hearts that they endure.

It is therefore necessary that a quiet mind not enlarge itself into excessive work, nor a restless mind narrow itself into the pursuit of contemplation. Often those who could have contemplated God in quiet have fallen under the pressure of occupations; and often those who would have lived well while occupied in human affairs have been destroyed by the sword of their own quiet.

Hence some restless spirits, while seeking more through contemplation than they can contain, break out into perverse doctrines. Neglecting in humility to be disciples of the truth, they become teachers of error.

Hence Truth says through himself: “If your right eye causes you to stumble, tear it out and cast it from you. It is better for you to enter life with one eye than, having two eyes, to be cast into the fire of Gehenna” (Matthew 5:29).

The two lives—the active and the contemplative—when preserved in the mind are like two eyes in the face. The right eye is the contemplative life; the left is the active life.

But there are some, as we have said, who are entirely unable to look with discernment upon sublime and spiritual things, yet undertake the heights of contemplation. Consequently, through a perverse error of understanding, they fall into the pit of unbelief.

The contemplative life, undertaken beyond their strength, compels these people to fall away from the truth, although the active life alone could have humbly preserved them in the state of their uprightness.

To such people Truth rightly says what we have already quoted: “If your right eye causes you to stumble, tear it out and cast it from you. It is better for you to enter life with one eye than, having two eyes, to be cast into the fire of Gehenna.”

It is as though he were saying openly: “When you do not possess the discernment suitable for the contemplative life, hold more securely to the active life alone. When you fail in what you have chosen as something great, be content with what you regard as small. Thus, if through the contemplative life you are compelled to fall away from knowledge of the truth, you may at least enter the kingdom of heaven one-eyed through the active life alone.”

Again he says: “Whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble, it would be better for him if a millstone were hung around his neck and he were thrown into the depths of the sea” (Matthew 18:6).

What is signified by the sea except the present age? What by the millstone of an ass except earthly action? While it constricts the necks of the mind through foolish desires, it sends the mind into the circuit of labor.

There are therefore some who, while abandoning earthly actions and rising to the pursuits of contemplation beyond the powers of their understanding, with humility set aside, not only cast themselves into error but also separate the weak from the embrace of unity.

Whoever therefore causes one of the least to stumble would have been better off with a millstone tied around his neck and thrown into the sea, because it could have been more advantageous for the perverse mind to be occupied with worldly earthly business than to have leisure through the pursuits of contemplation to the destruction of many.

Again, if the contemplative life suited some minds better than the active life, the Lord would not say through the Psalmist: “Be still and know that I am God” (Psalm 45:11).

### 58. What fear and love contribute to contemplation

Among these matters it must be understood that love often rouses sluggish minds to action, while fear restrains restless minds in contemplation. The weight of fear is an anchor of the heart. The heart is often shaken by the waves of thoughts, but is held fast by the bonds of its discipline. The storm of its restlessness does not drag it to shipwreck because perfect love binds it on the shore of divine love.

Whoever therefore hastens toward the pursuits of contemplation must first examine himself carefully to determine how much he loves. The force of love is the mind’s engine: while it draws the mind away from the world, it lifts it to the heights.

Let him first examine whether, in seeking the highest things, he loves; whether, in loving, he fears; whether he knows how either to grasp unknown things through love or, in fear, to reverence what he has not grasped.

In contemplation, if love does not rouse the mind, the dullness of its tepidity obscures it. If fear does not weigh it down, understanding lifts it through empty things toward the cloud of error. When the door of secrets is opened to it only slowly, it is driven farther away by its own presumption, because it desires to burst into what it seeks without finding. When the proud mind takes error for truth, the more it seems to extend its step inward, the farther outward it goes.

Hence, when the Lord was about to give the law, he descended in fire and smoke (Exodus 19:18), because he illuminates the humble by the brilliance of his manifestation and obscures the eyes of the proud through the darkness of error.

The mind must first be cleansed of desire for temporal glory and every delight of carnal concupiscence; then it must be raised to the sharp vision of contemplation. Hence, when the law is received, the people are forbidden to approach the mountain, so that those who still desire earthly things with weakened minds may not presume to contemplate sublime matters.

Accordingly it is rightly said: “If a beast touches the mountain, it shall be stoned” (ibid., 12–13). The beast touches the mountain when the mind, subject to irrational desires, raises itself to the heights of contemplation. But it is struck with stones because, unable to bear the highest things, it is killed by the very blows of the heavenly weight.

### 59. The perfection necessary for attaining it

Those who strive to grasp the summit of perfection, when they desire to hold the fortress of contemplation, should first test themselves in the field of action through exercise. They should carefully determine whether they no longer inflict any evils upon their neighbors; whether they bear with equanimity the evils inflicted by their neighbors; whether their mind is in no way dissolved in joy by temporal goods placed before it; and whether, when those goods are withdrawn, it is not wounded by excessive sorrow.

Then they should consider whether, when they return inwardly to themselves and examine spiritual things, they bring with them no shadows of bodily matters—or whether, if they have brought such shadows, they drive them away by the hand of discernment. Desiring to see the unbounded light, they should suppress all the images of their own boundedness; and, in seeking to touch what is above them, they should overcome what they are.

Hence it is rightly said now: “You shall enter the grave in abundance.” The perfect person enters the grave in abundance because he first gathers the works of the active life and afterward hides completely from this world, through contemplation, the sense of the flesh made dead.

Hence it is appropriately added: “As a heap of grain is brought in at its proper time” (the same passage).

### 60. Action must precede contemplation

The time of action comes first; that of contemplation comes last. Therefore each perfect person must first exercise the mind in virtues and afterward place it in the granary of repose (Luke 8:35).

Hence the man whom the legion of demons left at the Lord’s command sat at the feet of his Savior, received words of instruction, and desired to depart from his region together with the author of his salvation. Yet the Truth who had brought him salvation said to him: “Return first to your house and tell how great are the things the Lord has done for you.”

When we receive even a little knowledge of divine things, we no longer wish to return to human affairs and refuse to be burdened with the needs of our neighbors. We seek the repose of contemplation and love nothing except what refreshes without labor. But Truth sends us, once healed, back to our house and commands us to recount what has happened to us, so that the mind may first sweat in action and afterward be refreshed through contemplation.

### 61. Rachel and Leah, Mary and Martha, as figures of contemplation and action; the great merits of the active life, but the greater merits of the contemplative

Hence Jacob serves for Rachel but receives Leah, and is told: “It is not customary in our land to give the younger in marriage before the elder” (Genesis 29:27).

Rachel is called “the beginning of vision” or “the seeing beginning”; Leah is called “laborious.” What is signified by Rachel except the contemplative life? What by Leah except the active life?

In contemplation, the beginning—which is God—is sought; in action, one labors beneath the heavy burden of necessities. Hence Rachel is beautiful but barren, while Leah is weak-eyed but fruitful. For when the mind desires the leisure of contemplation, it sees more but generates fewer children for God; when it directs itself to the labor of preaching, it sees less but bears more.

After Leah’s embrace Jacob reaches Rachel, because every perfect person is first joined to the active life for fruitfulness and afterward joined to the contemplative life for rest.

That the contemplative life is indeed later in time but greater in merit than the active life is shown by the words of the sacred Gospel, in which two women are reported to have acted differently. Mary, hearing the words of our Redeemer, sat at his feet; Martha, however, was occupied with bodily service.

When Martha complained about Mary’s leisure, she heard: “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things. But one thing is necessary. Mary has chosen the better part, which shall not be taken away from her” (Luke 10:41–42).

What is expressed by Mary, who sat and listened to the Lord’s words, except the contemplative life? What is signified by Martha, occupied with outward service, except the active life?

Martha’s concern is not condemned, while Mary’s is even praised, because the merits of the active life are great, but those of the contemplative life are greater. Nor is Mary’s portion ever said to be taken away, because the works of the active life pass away with the body, whereas the joys of the contemplative life grow stronger after the end.

The prophet Ezekiel expresses this well and briefly when, contemplating the winged creatures, he says: “And the likeness of a human hand was beneath their wings” (Ezekiel 10:21).

What can we understand by the wings of the creatures except the contemplations of the saints, by which they fly over to the heights and, abandoning earthly things, balance themselves in the heavenly realms? What do we receive as the hands except actions? When they enlarge themselves in love of their neighbor, they administer bodily even the good things of which they are capable.

But their hands are beneath their wings because they surpass the works of their action through the power of contemplation.

### 62. The name “grave” may also be understood as eternal rest

The grave may also signify not only our contemplation in this life but also eternal rest and inward recompense, in which one rests more truly the more perfectly the life of corruption is killed within us.

He therefore enters the grave in abundance who, after gathering up the works of the present life, fully dead to his mutability, is hidden in the secret place of the true light. Hence the Psalmist says: “You shall hide them in the secret place of your face from the disturbance of men” (Psalm 30:21).

The comparison that follows also commends this well: “As a heap of grain is brought in at its proper time.”

Grain in the field is touched by the sun because in this life the human soul is illumined by the regard of the heavenly light. It receives rain because it grows rich through the word of truth.
