It is shaken by winds because it is exercised by temptations. It bears the chaff growing alongside it because every day it endures against itself the more wicked life of sinners.

Then it is brought to the threshing floor and pressed by the weight of threshing so that it may be separated from its connection with the chaff. In the same way our mind, subjected to heavenly discipline, when it receives the scourges of correction, departs purer from the fellowship of the carnal. It is led to the granary after leaving behind the chaff, because, while the reprobate remain outside, the elect soul is raised to the eternal joys of the heavenly dwelling.

It is therefore rightly said: “You shall enter the grave in abundance, as a heap of grain is brought in at its proper time,” because when the righteous find the rewards of the heavenly homeland after affliction, their grains are carried to the granary as it were after the pressures of threshing. They feel blows in another’s time, but rest from blows in their own.

For the present life is an alien time for the elect. Hence Truth says to certain unbelievers: “My time has not yet come, but your time is always ready” (John 7:6). Again he says: “This is your hour and the power of darkness” (Luke 22:53).

The grave is therefore entered at its proper time like a heap of grain, because the person receives eternal rest who first experiences here the pressures of discipline, so that he may be free from the chaff destined to be burned.

Eliphaz, because in the sequence of his speech he named the tabernacle, stones, beasts, seed, grass, and the grave, indicates himself that these things were not spoken according to the letter, when immediately after all this he adds:

## CHAPTER XXXVIII

**VERSE 27.—Behold, this is how we have investigated it, and so it is.**

### 63. Eliphaz’s words must be understood spiritually

It is perfectly clear that in these words he says nothing according to the surface meaning, because what is investigated does not lie openly before the eyes. By indicating that he has investigated these things, he demonstrates that he has sought inward realities in outward words.

But after all this he arrives at the foolishness of boastfulness, for he immediately adds:

## CHAPTER XXXIX

**THE SAME PASSAGE.—What you have heard, ponder in your mind.**

### 64. His ignorance is serious in wishing to teach someone better than himself

However great the learning with which a mind is endowed, it is serious ignorance for it to wish to teach someone better than itself. Thus things rightly spoken by friends are judged not to be right by the inward judge. They lose the force of their rectitude because they are not suitable for the hearer; for medicines also lose their power when applied to healthy limbs.

In everything that is said, therefore, it is necessary to weigh the circumstance, the time, and the person: whether the truth of the proposition strengthens the words; whether the appropriate time demands it; and whether the quality of the person conflicts neither with the truth of the proposition nor with the suitability of the time.

The person who launches darts commendably is the one who first sees which enemy he is to strike. For the man who bends the horns of a powerful bow badly wounds a fellow citizen when, aiming the arrow forcefully, he strikes him.

### Editorial notes and variant readings

- [Col. 0755D–0756D, on Psalm 63:1–2.] Coccius and subsequent editions read *cum deprecor* (“when I pray”), whereas the other editions and manuscripts read *cum tribulor* (“when I am troubled”), agreeing with the Roman Psalter. Nevertheless, in accordance with the Hebrew text, *deprecor* is to be preferred to *tribulor*.
- [Col. 0757D, §50.] The manuscripts read *a mundi actione* (“from worldly activity”); the printed editions read *a mundi dilectione* (“from love of the world”).
- [Col. 0757D–0758A, §52.] Some witnesses read *exsurgere semetipsum sentit* (“he feels himself rise up”).
- [Col. 0757D, §53.] Gemet., Corb., and some others read *Nunc dimitte* (“Now dismiss”), as do the old Basel editions; this corresponds more closely to the Greek text.
- [Col. 0757D–0758D, §53.] Gussanville reads *quo mens inhabitat* (“in which the mind dwells”); other editions read *quod mente inhabitatur* (“which is inhabited by the mind”). The translation follows the manuscript reading preserved by Vindoc., Bellov., Norman., Compend., and Corb. Germ.
- [Col. 0758D, §53.] Barthol. and other ancient witnesses first insert *inquietaverat, nunc* (“had disturbed, now”); Coccius subsequently substituted *inquietatum* (“disturbed”) for *inquietaverat*. These additions have been removed from the text on the evidence of the manuscripts.
- [Col. 0759D, §54.] The printed editions read *ex sui consideratione se in alterum colligit* (“from consideration of himself he gathers himself into another”); the manuscripts (Compend., Val. Cl., Turon., etc.) support the reading translated above.
- [Col. 0759D, §55.] The editions read *ad perfecte vivendi* (“for living perfectly”) in place of *per recte vivendi* (“through the efforts of living rightly”), against the manuscripts.
- [Col. 0759D–0760A, §55.] Norm., Corb. Germ., Colb., and Germ. read *in nostris voluptatibus vagamur* (“we wander in our pleasures”); the printed editions read *in nostris voluptatibus vacamus* (“we are at leisure in our pleasures”). Utic. and Bigot. give both readings.
- [Col. 0760D, §55.] The manuscripts vary: Vindoc. reads *in spe interna* (“in inward hope”); Gemet., Corb. Germ., *spe in aeterna* (“in hope of eternity”); Ebroic., *saepe in aeterna viridescit* (“often grows green in eternity”); the editions read *spe interna virid.*
- [Col. 0761D, §57.] Vindoc., Corb., Norman., and most witnesses read *conspersions animorum* (“the mixtures/dispositions of minds”); Germ. reads *compassiones* (“compassions”).
- [Col. 0761D–0762D, §57.] Norman., Corb. Germ., and others, along with the old editions, read *tanto deteriores cordis tumultus tolerant, quanto eis licentius ad cogitationes vacat* (“they endure heart-tumults so much the worse as they have freer leisure for thoughts”); the later editions have a divergent wording.
- [Col. 0762D, §57.] Some witnesses read *intellectu pravi erroris* (“through the understanding of perverse error”).
- [Col. 0762D, §57.] Norman., Compend., Vindoc., Val. Cl., and Corb. Germ. read *incognita veritate compellit cadere* (“an unknown truth compels [them] to fall”).
- [Col. 0763D, §58.] Bellovac., Compend., Norman., Val. Cl., and the old Coccius edition read *ad arcem* (“to the citadel”) in place of *ad aciem* (“to the keen vision”).
- [Col. 0763D–0764A, §60.] Norman. and Corb. read *redit* (“returns”). The first Compend. presents the passage as: *ad Salvatoris pedes discere, cum salutis auctore reconcupiscit* (“to learn at the Savior’s feet, when he again desires [to be] with the author of salvation”).
- [Col. 0764D, §61.] Rachel is “seeing the beginning,” or more properly “seeing the principle”; this is the sense of *Rachel* if derived from *raa* and *chalal*. Consult Jerome, *On Hebrew Names*, and the notes to the new Benedictine edition, vol. II.
- [Col. 0765C, §61.] Gemet. reads *pinnas* (“wings”), and below *sed manus eorum sub pinnas* (“but their hands [were] beneath the wings”). In some manuscripts of the homilies on Ezekiel, *pinnae, pinnis* frequently occur for *pennae, pennis*.
- [Col. 0765C, §62.] Turon. reads *velut frumentum mundior* (“purer, like grain”).
- [Col. 0766C, §62.] Vindoc., Compend., Corb., and others read *in sua percussione requiescunt* (“they rest in their own striking/affliction”).
- [Col. 0766C, §64.] Very old manuscripts, with broad agreement, read *arbitre* (“judge”), a reading that recurs frequently below, especially in Book VIII, formerly chapters 27, 29, and 30, now 45, 47, and 48.

## BOOK SEVEN

This book explains the whole of the sixth chapter, except for its final three verses, partly allegorically and partly morally.

## CHAPTER ONE
211 **1. Job tested by scourges and reproaches. If he says anything that sounds like impatience, it must be weighed not by human judgment but by divine judgment.**—Some minds are tormented more by scourges than by reproaches; others are chastened more by reproaches than by scourges. For often the torments of words rage against us more harshly than any punishments; and while they rouse us to defend ourselves, they cast us down into impatience. Therefore, so that no kind of trial might be lacking to blessed Job, not only do scourges strike him from above, but the conversations of his friends, more grievous than the blows, afflict him. Thus the holy man’s soul, struck from every side, might burst forth into anger and pride, and whatever had been lived in purity might be defiled through the defiance of arrogant speech.

Yet, touched by the blows, he gave thanks; provoked by words, he answered rightly; and, struck down, he revealed how little he valued the preservation of his flesh. In speaking, he also showed how wise he had been when silent. Nevertheless, certain things are mingled into his words that seem, by human judgment, to exceed the bounds of patience. We truly understand them only if, in examining them, we weigh the sentence of the heavenly Judge.

For the same Judge first set blessed Job above his adversary, saying: “Have you seen my servant Job, that there is none like him on the earth—a blameless and upright man, fearing God and turning away from evil?” (Job 1:8).

[Note: The recent Vulgate has “and whatever he had lived in purity.”]

After his testing, the same Judge rebuked Job’s friends, saying: “You have not spoken rightly before me, as my servant Job has” (Job 42:7).

[Note: “Blameless and upright” is absent from the Vindocinian, Corbie, and several other manuscripts.]

212 Therefore, when the mind wavers over the words of blessed Job, it should weigh their force from the beginning and the end of the same narrative. For neither could one who was not going to fall have been praised by the eternal Judge, nor could one who had fallen have been preferred. If, then, caught amid the storm of uncertainty, we look to the beginning and the conclusion of this story, the ship of the heart is restrained by the ropes of its reflection, as though from prow and stern, lest it be driven onto the rocks of error. We are not overwhelmed by the storms of our ignorance if we hold fast to the tranquil shore of the heavenly judgment.

For behold, he says something that may greatly trouble the reader’s mind. Yet who would dare call that unrighteous which sounds righteous in God’s ears?

## CHAPTER II [Second recension]

[Column 0767C] **CHAPTER VI, VERSES 2–3.**—“Would that my sins, by which I deserved wrath, and the calamity that I suffer, were weighed in the balance; then this calamity would appear heavier than the sand of the sea.”

### Typological meaning

**2. Christ is the balance in which both what we deserve and what he suffered for us are weighed. He made known to us the gravity of our punishment.**—Who else is expressed under the name of the balance except the Mediator of God and human beings? He came to weigh the merit of our life and brought with him both justice and mercy. Yet, making the scale of mercy outweigh the other, he lightened our sins by pardoning them.

For in the hand of the Father he became, as it were, a balance of wondrous equilibrium: on one side he suspended our calamity in himself, and on the other our sins. By dying he made known the calamity’s heavy weight, while by releasing sin he showed that it is light before mercy.

[Note: In the printed editions: “God showed, by forgiving it, that sin is light before his mercy.” Therefore, through true repentance, although sins are many and very grave, they are easily forgiven through God’s mercy (Bartholomew and Rembold: “more easily”); and before his mercy the sin that is forgiven is light (Bartholomew and Rembold: “he showed the forgiven sin”), he who first bestowed this grace (or, in Bartholomew and Rembold, “a grave [thing]”), because he made our punishment, etc. This is a manifest gloss, disrupting the connection of Gregory’s argument, and it is found in not even one manuscript.]

He first bestowed this grace by making our punishment knowable to us. Human beings were created to contemplate their Creator, but, because of their deserts, they were cast down from inward joys. Falling into the misery of corruption and enduring the blindness of exile, they both suffered and did not understand the punishments of their sin. They came to regard exile as their homeland and therefore rejoiced under the burden of corruption as though they possessed the freedom of salvation.

But the one whom humanity had abandoned within appeared outwardly as God after assuming flesh. By presenting himself externally, he recalled to the interior the human being who had been driven outward, so that humanity might now see its losses and lament the punishment of its blindness.

[Note: The Ebroïcian manuscript reads: “Now let him lament the punishment of his blindness.”]

Thus the human calamity appeared heavy in the balance, because humanity recognized the evil it had endured only in the presence of the Redeemer. Not knowing the light, it had endured the darkness of its condemnation with pleasure. But after it saw what it loved, it also understood what it grieved; and it felt as heavy what it had suffered because what it had lost became known as sweet.

Therefore let the holy man, shaken from the prison of silence by the words of his speaking friend and filled with the abundance of the prophetic spirit, speak his own words—let him speak in the voice of the human race:

“Would that my sins, by which I deserved wrath, and the calamity that I suffer, were weighed in the balance; then this calamity would appear heavier than the sand of the sea.”

It is as though he were saying plainly: “The evil of our condemnation is thought light because it has not yet been weighed against the righteousness of the Redeemer. But would that he might come, suspend the misery of so great an exile on the scale of his mercy, and teach us what we should seek after exile. For if what we have lost becomes known, it shows that what we endure is grievous.”

[Older second version.]

This same calamity of our pilgrimage is rightly compared with the sand of the sea. The sand of the sea is driven outward by the surge of the waves, because the sinful human being, carried about by the shifting waves of temptation, has also gone out from the inner self.

[Note: The Tours and Corbie manuscripts read: “The more actively he endured the waves of temptation, the farther he went outside himself from his inward depths.” In the Vindocinian manuscript, instead of “went out from his inward depths,” we find “drove himself out from his inward depths.”]

The sand of the sea is of great weight; yet the human calamity is said to be heavier than the sand of the sea because the punishment is shown to have been harsh when guilt is lightened by the merciful Judge.

[Note: All the manuscripts have this reading, except one Reginensis manuscript, which reads: “the guilt that is recognized is lightened.” This may explain the reading in the printed editions: “the guilt that is lightened is recognized.”]

And because everyone who recognizes the grace of the Redeemer, everyone who loves the return to the homeland, groans under the burden of pilgrimage after being instructed, the desire for the balance is rightly followed by:

## CHAPTER III

**Verse 2.**—“Therefore my words are full of sorrow.”

**3. Here he does not cease to groan who knows that he is in exile.**—Whoever loves pilgrimage instead of the homeland does not know how to grieve even amid grief. But the words of the righteous are full of sorrow because, for as long as he endures the present, he sighs for another reality in speaking. He sees everything that he has suffered through sin, and, so that he may return to the state of blessedness, he carefully weighs the judgments by which he is afflicted.

Therefore it is added:

## CHAPTER IV

**Verse 4.**—“For the arrows of the Lord are in me.”

**4. Preaching or punishment is signified by the arrows.**—Under the name of arrows, sometimes words of preaching and sometimes sentences of correction are designated. The utterances of preaching are expressed by arrows because, in striking vices, they transfix the hearts of those who live badly.

Of these arrows it is said to the coming Redeemer: “Your arrows are sharp, O most powerful one; peoples shall fall beneath you in their hearts” (Psalm 44:6).

Isaiah says of them: “I will send some of those who have been saved to the nations—to the sea, to Africa, and to Lydia, bearing the arrow; to Italy and to Greece” (Isaiah 66:19).

[Note: The old editions of Bartholomew, Rembold, and Coccius have “Libya” instead of “Lydia,” but this is erroneous.]

Again, the blow of correction is designated by arrows, as Elisha says to King Joash: “Shoot an arrow.” When he had shot it, Elisha said: “You shall strike Syria until you have consumed it” (2 Kings 13:17).

Therefore, because the holy man sees the misery of his pilgrimage and groans under the blows of the Lord’s correction, let him say: “Therefore my words are full of sorrow, for the arrows of the Lord are in me.”

[Third recension.]

It is as though he were saying plainly: “I do not rejoice in the condemnation of exile; placed under judgment, I grieve because I recognize the force of the blow.”

There are many whom torments afflict but do not amend. In opposition to them it is aptly added:

## CHAPTER V [Older third version]

**The same passage.**—“Whose indignation drinks up my spirit.”

**5. The righteous are amended by the punishments they endure.**—For what is the human spirit except the spirit of pride? The arrows of the Lord drink up the human spirit when the sentences of heavenly correction restrain the afflicted mind from pride. The arrows of the Lord drink up the human spirit because they draw inward those who are intent upon outward things.

[Note: The Compendian, Tours, and other manuscripts read: “For David’s spirit had been drunk up by these arrows.” Bartholomew and Rembold, with the Colbertine manuscripts, have: “and by this it had been drunk up.”]

David’s spirit had indeed been drunk up when he said: “When my spirit failed within me, you knew my paths” (Psalm 142:4). And again: “I refused to let my soul be comforted; I remembered God and was delighted; I was exercised, and my spirit failed for a little while” (Psalm 76:4).

Thus the indignation of the arrows drinks up the spirit of the righteous because the sentences of heaven change the elect whom they find in sins as they wound them. The pierced mind abandons its hardness, and from the saving wound the blood of confession flows.

[Note: The Norman manuscripts read “the blood of shame flows”; this reading is not approved. By “confession,” Gregory understands repentance joined with conversion. As Hilary says on Psalm 137, section 3, no one ought afterward to commit what he has confessed to be sin, because confession of sin is a profession of abandoning it.]

For they weigh from where and to where they have fallen; they weigh from how great a blessedness they have fallen into what torments of corruption. They not only groan over what they endure but also fear what the strict Judge threatens sinners concerning the fires of Gehenna.

Therefore it is rightly added:

## CHAPTER VI

**The same passage.**—“And the terrors of the Lord wage war against me.”

**6. The righteous grieve over present punishments and fear future ones.**—The mind of the righteous not only considers what it endures but also fears what remains. It sees what it suffers in this life and fears that it may suffer worse things after this life. It mourns because, in the exile of this blindness, it has fallen from the joys of paradise; it fears that, when exile is left behind, eternal death may follow.

Thus it already endures judgment in punishment, but it still fears the threats of the coming Judge because of its guilt. Hence the Psalmist says: “Your wrath has passed over me, and your terrors have troubled me” (Psalm 87:17).

After the wrath of the inward Judge has passed over, his terrors also trouble us, because we already suffer one thing through condemnation and still fear another from eternal retribution.

Therefore, weighing the evils he endures, let the holy man say: “The arrows of the Lord are in me; their indignation drinks up my spirit.” But, fearing more grievous things eternally, let him add: “And the terrors of the Lord wage war against me.”

It is as though he were saying plainly: “Struck down, I grieve over present things; but this makes my grief more grievous, because, though placed in punishment, I still fear eternal torments.”

But because he now desires the intervention of the balance and weighs the evils into which the human race has fallen, although he is placed among a gentile nation and yet filled with the gift of the prophetic spirit, he shows in the following words with what longing either the Gentiles or Judea thirsted for the coming of the Redeemer:

## CHAPTER VII [Fourth recension]

**Verse 5.**—“Does the wild ass bray when it has grass? Or does the ox bellow when it stands before a full manger?”

**7. The desires of the Gentiles and of Judea for the Redeemer’s coming.**—What else is signified by the wild ass, that is, the ass of the wilderness, except the gentile people? Just as nature produced it outside the enclosures, or stalls, of discipline, so it remained wandering in the field of its pleasures.

What else is represented by the ox except the Jewish people? Subjected to the yoke of heavenly rule, it drew the plowshare of the law through the hearts it was able to reach, gathering proselytes into hope.

[Note: We have restored this passage from the Compendian, Vindocinian, Norman, and other manuscripts. Previously it read: “unless the Jewish people is signified, which, subjected to the yoke of heavenly condemnation …” This is erroneous, in my judgment. The error may have arisen from the word “rule,” abbreviated in an old edition as “dñationis,” which was read as “damnationis.”]

Yet, as the life of blessed Job testifies, we know that many even among the nations awaited the coming of the Redeemer. And when the Lord was born, when Simeon came into the temple in the Spirit, we learned with what desire holy men from the people of Israel longed to see the mystery of his incarnation.

Therefore the same Redeemer says to his disciples: “Many prophets and righteous people, I tell you, desired to see what you see and did not see it” (Luke 10:24).

[Older fourth version.]

The grass of the wild ass and the hay of the ox, then, are this very incarnation of the Mediator, by which both the Gentiles and Judea are fed. For since the prophet says, “All flesh is grass” (Isaiah 40:6), the Creator of the universe, taking flesh from our substance, willed to become grass, so that our flesh might not remain grass forever.

The wild ass found grass when the gentile people received the grace of the divine incarnation. The ox did not have an empty manger when the law presented to the Jewish people, which awaited his flesh, the one whom it had long foretold.

[Note: The printed editions read “the one who was awaited,” against the manuscripts.]

Therefore, when the Lord was born, he was placed in a manger, signifying that the holy animals, which had long been found fasting under the law, were fed with the hay of his incarnation. The one who was born filled the manger because he offered himself as food to the minds of mortals, saying: “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him” (John 6:57).

But because the desires both of the elect among the Gentiles were long delayed and the holy men from the Hebrew people groaned for a long time while awaiting their redemption, blessed Job, rightly unfolding the mysteries of prophecy, indicates the causes of affliction in both nations, saying:

“Does the wild ass bray when it has grass? Or does the ox bellow when it stands before a full manger?”

It is as though he were saying plainly: “The Gentiles groan because the grace of their Redeemer does not yet refresh them; and Judea therefore prolongs its bellowing because, holding the law but not seeing the author of the law, it stands hungry before the manger.”

Since this law, before the Mediator’s coming, was held not spiritually but carnally, it is rightly followed by:

## CHAPTER VIII [Fifth recension]

**Verse 6.**—“Can what is insipid be eaten if it has not been seasoned with salt?”

**8. The law understood carnally is insipid; Christ seasons it with salt.**—In the law, salt is the power of hidden understanding. Whoever, devoted to carnal observances, refused to understand the law spiritually—what other food did he eat than insipid food?

But the recognized Truth added salt to this food when he taught that the flavor of hidden understanding lay concealed in the law, saying: “If you believed Moses, you would perhaps believe me also, for he wrote about me” (John 5:46). And again: “Have salt in yourselves, and have peace among yourselves” (Mark 5:49).

But because, before the Mediator’s coming, Judea held the law carnally, the Gentiles refused to submit to its harsh commands. Thus they refused to eat insipid food because, before receiving the seasoning of the Spirit, they were afraid to preserve the force of the letter.

For what gentile person could endure what is prescribed there—to cut the flesh of children in the service of religion, or to punish faults in words by death?

Therefore it is still aptly added:

## CHAPTER IX

**The same passage.**—“Can anyone taste what, once tasted, brings death?”

[Column 0771D] **9. The law, tasted carnally, was formerly deadly.**—The law, tasted carnally, brought death because it punished transgressions with harsh correction. It brought death because, through the commandment, it made sin known but did not remove it through grace, as Paul testifies when he says: “The law brought nothing to perfection” (Hebrews 7:19).

And again: “The law is indeed holy, and the commandment holy and just and good.” A little later he says: “Sin, so that it might appear as sin, worked death in me through what is good” (Romans 7:12–13).

But when the Gentiles turned toward Christ, they understood that he was proclaimed through the words of the law. Constrained by their desires, they sought spiritually among the carnal commandments the one whom they loved intensely.

[Note: This is the reading of the Corbie-German, Colbertine, German, Tours, Vindocinian, Fleury, and Norman manuscripts. The printed editions have signari, “to be signified.”]

[Older fifth version; sixth recension.]

Therefore, from the voice of the Church, he immediately adds through the spirit of prophecy:

## CHAPTER X

**Verse 7.**—“What my soul formerly refused to touch, these now, because of anguish, are my food.”

**10. Job’s words are pregnant with spiritual meaning. The Gentiles are foretold as seeking the food of the law, and the Jews as no longer scorning association with the Gentiles.**—He falls deeply into error who supposes that the words of blessed Job were spoken only according to the historical sense.

For what great—or rather, what true—thing would the holy man, supported by so many praises of his Creator, have said if he had merely declared that insipid food could not be eaten? Or who had offered him deadly nourishment, so that he should add: “Can anyone taste what, once tasted, brings death?”

If we think that these words refer to the conversations of his friends, the sentence that follows restrains us from this interpretation: “What my soul formerly refused to touch, these now, because of anguish, are my food.”

Far be it from us to think that the holy man, established in the soundness of his state, ever despised the words of his friends, since, as we later learn from his own testimony, he was humble even toward servants. His words, then, are not empty of mysteries; as we learn from the conclusion of the narrative, the inward Judge also praises them. Nor would they have endured with such veneration to the ends of the world if they had not been pregnant with mystical understanding.

**11.** Blessed Job, therefore, because he is a member of the holy Church, should speak also from its voice, saying: “What my soul formerly refused to touch, these now, because of anguish, are my food,” because the Gentiles, turned toward the nourishment of the ancient Scripture and distressed by the heat of their love, hunger for the food of Scripture, which they once despised proudly.

These words may also appropriately be applied to the voice of Judea if they are examined more carefully. Through the instruction of the law and knowledge of the one God, Judea had salt, and it despised all the nations as brute animals.

[Note: The Bellovacian, Gemetian, and several other manuscripts read: “and all the nations no otherwise than animals”; the Corbie manuscript reads: “and all the nations as nothing other than animals.”]

But because, instructed by the precepts of the law, it scorned to receive the fellowship of the Gentiles into itself, what else did it disdain to consume than insipid food?

For the divine sentence, setting death before it, had forbidden the Israelite people to make a covenant with foreigners and defile the life of holy religion (Exodus 23:32). Therefore it is added: “Can anyone taste what, once tasted, brings death?”

But because this same Judea was converted, through its elect, to faith in the Redeemer, it endeavored through the holy apostles to preach to the unbelievers of its own offspring the light it had come to know. Yet the pride of the Hebrews rejected the service of this preaching.

Therefore its words of exhortation immediately turned toward the gathering of the Gentiles, as is also said through the same apostles: “It was necessary that the word of God be spoken to you first; but since you rejected it and judged yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts 13:46).

Therefore here too it is aptly added: “What my soul formerly refused to touch, these now, because of anguish, are my food.”

Judea, which had disdained the life of the Gentiles, once refused as though to touch the people whose fellowship it rejected. But when it came to the grace of the Redeemer and was rejected by unbelieving Israelites, it expanded through the holy apostles toward the gathering of the Gentiles and, as though hungering for this as food, received what it had previously despised in disgust as unworthy.

It endured the anguish of its preaching because it saw among the Hebrews that what it proclaimed was scorned. But because of its anguish it ate the food it had once despised: rejected by the hardness of the Jews, it desired to receive the gentile peoples whom it had scorned.

Since we have spoken of these matters figuratively, it remains now to inquire into their moral meaning.

### Moral meaning

**12.** The holy man, desiring the Redeemer’s coming under the name of the balance, opens himself through speech and instructs us in the pursuit of right living. While he recounts his own experience, he indicates certain things about us; while he suggests matters in himself that we should recognize, he strengthens us, trembling and weak, toward hope.

We already live through faith in the Mediator, yet we still endure the harsh inward scourges of correction for the cleansing of our vices.

[Note: Coccius and the other editions following it read per se eloquium, “through speech itself”; this is a faulty transposition.]

[Note: The German manuscript reads “for the overcoming” instead of “for the cleansing.”]

Therefore, after the desire for the balance, he adds:

## CHAPTER XI

**Verse 4.**—“For the arrows of the Lord are in me; their indignation drinks up my spirit.”

**13. The good are pierced by scourges and by the terror of judgment. Yet it is better to be moved by love.**—But behold, as was said above, we are pierced by the blows of divine correction, and yet what is more grievous is that we fear, through eternal punishment, the terror of the coming Judge.

Therefore it immediately follows: “And the terrors of the Lord wage war against me.”

Yet the soul must be shaken free from fear and grief and extended toward the sole desires of the eternal homeland. We show the nobility of our rebirth when we love as a father the one whom, with a servile mind, we now fear as lord.

Therefore Paul says: “You did not receive the spirit of slavery again in fear, but you received the Spirit of adoption as sons, in whom we cry, ‘Abba, Father’” (Romans 8:15).

Let the mind of the elect, then, set aside the weight of fear, exercise itself in the power of love, desire the dignity of its renewal, and pant for the sight of its Creator. For as long as it cannot behold him, it must await his eternity—that is, its inward food—hungering for it.

Therefore it is aptly added:

## CHAPTER XII [Older sixth version]

**Verse 5.**—“Does the wild ass bray when it has grass? Or does the ox bellow when it stands before a full manger?”

**14. The wild ass signifies the faithful people; the ox signifies the ecclesiastical order. For both, the cause of groaning here is the delayed vision of God.**—Who else are marked by the name of wild asses except those who, established in the field of faith, are bound by the reins of no office? And whom does the figure of the ox represent except those whom, within the holy Church, the yoke of an order undertaken for the ministry of preaching presses?

The grass of the wild ass and the fodder of the ox are the inward refreshment of the faithful people. Some, like oxen, are held within the Church by the reins of an office they have undertaken; others, like wild asses, know nothing of the stalls of sacred order and dwell in the field of their own will.

But when someone from secular life burns with desire for inward vision, when he longs for the food of inner refreshment, and, considering himself hungry in the blindness of this pilgrimage, refreshes himself with whatever tears he can summon, he brays like a wild ass because he does not find grass.

Another endures the demands of the order he has undertaken, sweats in the labor of preaching, and longs to be refreshed by eternal contemplation. But because he does not yet behold the form of his Redeemer, he groans like an ox tied before an empty manger.

Because we are placed far from inward wisdom and do not see the greenness of the eternal inheritance, we fast like brute animals from the grass we desire.

Of this grass the Redeemer says: “If anyone enters through me, he will be saved; he will enter and go out and find pasture” (John 10:9).

But often—and this is usually more grievous to those who love goodness—the life of the wicked resists the good pursuits of the holy. When the mind is carried away toward heavenly desire, its good intention is struck back by the words and conduct of fools. Thus what had already flown upward through the effort of contemplation toward the heights girds itself in the lowly sphere for struggles against the foolishness of the wicked.

Therefore it is added:

## CHAPTER XIII

**Verse 6.**—“Can what is insipid be eaten if it has not been seasoned with salt? Or can anyone taste what, once tasted, brings death?”

**15. How grievous to the elect are the words and conduct of carnal people.**—The words and conduct of carnal people thrust themselves into our minds like food, to be swallowed in the stomach of pleasure. But the elect do not eat what is insipid, because, judging the words and deeds of the wicked, they drive them away from the mouth of the heart.

Paul forbade insipid things to be brought in as food for minds when he said to his disciples: “Let your speech always be seasoned with grace, with salt” (Colossians 4:6).

The words of the reprobate had also tasted insipid in the mouth of the Psalmist’s heart when he said: “The wicked have told me stories, but not such as your law, O Lord” (Psalm 118:85).

Often, when the words of carnal people intrude themselves upon our ears, they generate a battle of temptation in the heart. Although reason rejects them and the tongue condemns them, what is judged outwardly with authority is nevertheless conquered inwardly with difficulty. Therefore we must ensure that what the vigilant mind repels from the entrance of thought does not even reach the ears.

When holy men pant for the desires of eternity, they raise themselves to such a height of life that they regard hearing whatever belongs to the world as a grievous and depressing burden. They consider anything that does not sound like what they love inwardly extremely alien and intolerable.

[Older seventh version.]

**26. Not everyone girds himself to undergo bodily sufferings for God.**—Often the mind is already carried upward by desire, already completely separated from the foolish speech of earthly people, yet it has not armed itself for enduring the sufferings of the present life for the sake of truth. It already seeks heavenly things and despises the foolishness of lowly matters, but it has not yet directed itself toward enduring adversity.

Therefore it is added: “Can anyone taste what, once tasted, brings death?”

## CHAPTER XIV

**17. By bearing with the weakness of our neighbors, we are strengthened to undergo sufferings.**—It is hard to desire what torments us and to pursue what drives life away. Yet often the mind of the righteous extends itself to such a summit of virtue that it both presides within itself in the citadel of inward reason and converts the foolishness of certain people outside through patient endurance.

For if we strive to draw people toward strength, we must endure their weakness, because no one raises up a fallen person unless, through compassion, he bends from the uprightness of his own standing.

When we sympathize with another’s weakness, we are strengthened more powerfully against our own, so that the mind may prepare itself, through love of future things, for present adversities and await bodily sufferings that it once feared.

As heavenly desires increase, the mind becomes more constrained. When it considers how great is the sweetness of the eternal homeland, it ardently loves the bitterness of the present life for its sake.

Therefore, after the disgust of insipid food and after the impossible taste of death, it is rightly added:

## CHAPTER XV [Seventh recension]

**Verse 7.**—“What my soul formerly refused to touch, these now, because of anguish, are my food.”

**18. Because of love for the heavenly homeland, we love the punishments of exile.**—The mind of the righteous, making progress, formerly refused to bear the burdens of others while it cared only for its own concerns. Because it had little compassion for others, it could not grow strong against adversity. But when it draws itself toward bearing the weaknesses of its neighbor, it grows strong for overcoming adversity.

Thus, for love of truth, it later desires the sufferings of the present life all the more firmly, the more it previously fled from weakness.

[Note: The Norman manuscript reads: “all the more firmly afterward.” One Vindocinian manuscript has: “all the stronger afterward.”]

It is raised up by its own inclination, stretched by its attraction, and strengthened by compassion. When it expands itself into love of its neighbor, it gathers itself, as though through meditation, to discern with what strength it rises toward its Creator.

For charity, which humbles us toward the power of compassion, lifts us higher to the summit of contemplation. Having been multiplied by greater desires, it now burns to reach spiritual life even through bodily sufferings.

Therefore the one who formerly refused to touch this food eats it afterward because of anguish: scarcely able to contain its desires, it now loves, because of its love for the heavenly homeland, the very punishments it once feared.

For if the mind is directed toward God with strong purpose, whatever becomes bitter for it in this life it considers sweet; everything that afflicts it, it regards as rest. It desires even to pass through death so that it may possess life more fully; it longs to be utterly extinguished in lowly things so that it may ascend the heights more truly.

But I would be speaking falsely about the mind of any righteous person—and about the mind of blessed Job—unless he himself added:

## CHAPTER XVI

**Verses 8–10.**—“Who will grant that my petition may come, and that the Lord may give me what I await? May the one who began it himself crush me; may he release his hand and cut me down; and may this be my consolation, that, afflicting me with sorrow, he does not spare me.”

**19. Job’s example of blessing the one who strikes him. God crushes us, and the devil also crushes us, but with different outcomes.**—But perhaps he seeks these things defiantly; perhaps, in desiring to be utterly extinguished, he accuses the one who strikes him of injustice.

Far from it. He shows in the following words with what mind he seeks this, saying: “Nor will I contradict the words of the Holy One.”

He does not murmur against the injustice of the one who strikes him, since he calls his striker holy even amid the blows.

We must know, however, that sometimes the adversary crushes us, and sometimes God crushes us. Through the crushing of the adversary we fall away from virtue; but when we are broken through the crushing of the Lord, we are strengthened in virtue against our vices.

The Prophet had foreseen this crushing when he said: “You shall rule them with an iron rod, and like a potter’s vessel you shall crush them” (Psalm 2:9).

The Lord rules and crushes us with an iron rod because, through the strong uprightness of his governance, he refreshes us inwardly while afflicting us outwardly.

[Note: The Gemetian and one Compendian manuscript add: “because of the strength of his governance.”]

For by humbling the strength of the flesh, he raises the purpose of the spirit. Therefore this same crushing is compared with a potter’s vessel, as Paul also says: “We have this treasure in earthen vessels” (2 Corinthians 4:7).

Expressing both crushing and governance, he says: “Although our outward person is being corrupted, the inward person is being renewed day by day” (ibid., 4:16).

[Older eighth version.]

Therefore let the holy man, who desires to draw near to God even through scourges, speak through the spirit of humility:

## CHAPTER XVII

[Column 0776C]

**Verse 9.**—“May the one who began it himself crush me.”

**20. God mercifully corrects the person who exalts himself over his virtues.**—Often the Lord begins to crush vices within us. But when the mind is lifted up by the progress that begins through him, when it already rises as though because of its virtues, it opens an entrance for the adversary raging against it. The adversary penetrates the innermost heart and shatters whatever he finds there that arose from the pursuit of a good beginning.

He displays himself all the more fiercely in the person’s ruin because he grieves more deeply that the person had advanced, even slightly.

Therefore, as the Gospel testifies through the voice of Truth, when the unclean spirit that had gone out returns to a neglected house with seven other spirits (Matthew 12:45), the holy man rightly prays:

“May the one who began it himself crush me.”

It is as though he were saying plainly: “May he not cease to complete by striking me what he has begun in me, lest, abandoning me, he hand me over to the adversary for destruction.”

Therefore it is aptly added:

## CHAPTER XVIII

**The same passage.**—“May he release his hand and cut me down.”

21. How We Should Fear That He May Keep His Hand Bound for Striking Our Vices

For often, puffed up by confidence in a long period of prosperity, we rise into a certain state of exaltation. And when our Creator sees us becoming proud, yet does not exercise his love toward us through blows, he keeps, as it were, the hand with which to strike our vices bound. Did he not bind the hand of his affection when he said to the sinful people, “I will no longer be angry with you” (Isa. 54:9), and, “My jealousy has withdrawn from you” (Ezek. 16:42)?

[Note: Turon. reads “in a certain arrogance.”]

[Note: Thus Norman., Vindoc., Compend., Bellovac., Turon., and the older editions. Coccius altered this to “therefore he is said to release his hand when he exercises his affection,” followed by later editions.]

Therefore, “let him release his hand” means: let him exercise his affection. It is rightly added: “and let him cut me down.” For when sudden pain from a blow, or the trial of illness, strikes us who are secure and lifted up by an abundance of virtues, the pride of our mind is immediately cut down from the summit of its position and falls, so that it dares nothing on its own but, struck down by the blow of its weakness, seeks the hand of the one who raises it.

This is why holy men, when they are apprehensive about God’s hidden dispensation toward them, fear prosperity itself all the more; they desire to be tested and long to be scourged, so that fear and pain may instruct the unwary mind, lest, on this road of pilgrimage, when the enemy bursts forth from ambush, their very security should bring them down more disastrously.

Hence the Psalmist says: “Test me, Lord, and try me” (Ps. 25:2). Again he says: “I am ready for scourges” (Ps. 38:18). For the saints recognize that the wound of correction in their mind cannot exist without festering; they willingly prepare themselves for incision beneath the physician’s hand, so that, when the wound has been opened, the poison of sin may come out—the poison that was killing them inwardly beneath healthy skin.

Hence it is further added:

CHAPTER XIX.

VERSE 10.—“And let this be my consolation, that, afflicting me with pain, he does not spare.”

22. The Saints Fear Prosperity and Desire Scourges

The elect, when they know that they have committed unlawful acts but, on examining themselves, discover that they have suffered no adversity for those unlawful acts, waste away under the force of immense fear, burn with dread, and struggle under troubled suspicions: lest grace may have abandoned them forever, since no punishment for their evil guards them in the present life; lest the vengeance that is being postponed may be reserved in greater severity for the end. They desire to be struck by paternal correction and regard the pain of the wound as a medicine of salvation.

It is rightly said, therefore: “Let this be my consolation, that, afflicting me with pain, he does not spare.” It is as though it were said openly: “Because he spares some here in order to strike them forever, let him strike me here so that, by not sparing me, he may spare me forever.” For I am consoled by affliction because, knowing the rottenness of human corruption, I am made certain by the wound of the hope of salvation.

And because he uttered this not with a proud but with a humble mind, he makes it clear by adding, as we have said:

CHAPTER XX.

SAME VERSE.—“Nor will I contradict the words of the Holy One.”

23. God Often Speaks Silently through His Works

For very often the words of God addressed to us are not the sound of spoken words but the effects of his works. He speaks to us in what he silently does concerning us. Blessed Job, therefore, would contradict the words of God if he murmured against his blows. But he indicates what he thinks of the one who strikes him, since, as we have already said, he calls him holy whom he endures as his striker.

It continues:

CHAPTER XXI [Old recension IX, New recension VIII].

VERSE 11.—“For what is my strength, that I should endure? Or what is my end, that I should act patiently?”

24. What Is the Strength of the Just and What Is That of the Reprobate?

It must be understood that the strength of the just is one thing, and that of the reprobate another. The strength of the just is to conquer the flesh, oppose their own desires, extinguish the pleasure of the present life, love the hardships of this world for the sake of eternal rewards, despise the flatteries of prosperity, and overcome the fear of adversity in the heart.

[Note: Compend., Ebroic., and several other Norman witnesses read “their own pleasures.”]

[Note: Corb. Germ. reads “the enemy opposing in the heart.”]

The strength of the reprobate, however, is to love transitory things without ceasing; to persist insensibly against the scourges of the Creator; not to cease from loving temporal things even because of adversity; to attain empty glory even at the cost of life; to seek increases in wickedness; to attack the life of the good not only with words and conduct but also with swords; to place hope in themselves; and to commit iniquity every day without any failure of desire.

Hence the Psalmist says to the elect: “Act manfully, and let your heart be strengthened, all you who hope in the Lord” (Ps. 31:25). Hence the prophet says to the reprobate: “Woe to you who are mighty at drinking wine and strong men at mixing drunkenness” (Isa. 5:22). Hence Solomon says that all the saints, without any weakness of desire, contemplate inward rest: “Behold, Solomon’s bed; sixty strong men surround it, of the strongest of Israel” (Song 3:7).

[Note: Corb. Germ. reads “the adversary enemy in the heart.”]

Hence the Psalmist, speaking against the reprobate in the person of the Redeemer placed in his passion, declares: “Behold, they have seized my soul; the strong have rushed upon me” (Ps. 59:4). Isaiah well embraced both kinds of strength when he said: “Those who trust in the Lord will change their strength” (Isa. 40:31).

[Note: In Bellovac., Norman., and others, this reads “which is laid aside,” and is better than the reading in the printed editions, “which is proposed.” Here “is placed” means “is put down, removed, or relinquished.”]

Since he did not say “they will take” but “they will change,” he plainly revealed that one strength is laid aside and another begins.

25. In What the Reprobate Are Strong, the Just Are Weak

Are not the reprobate also strong, when they run toward the desires of the present life through so many labors, boldly expose themselves to dangers, willingly endure insults for the sake of profits, recoil from the lust of their appetite under no opposition, grow hard under blows, and endure the evils of the world for the world, seeking its, so to speak, joys and losing themselves in them, yet never becoming weary of losing these things?

Hence it is well said in the voice of the human race through Jeremiah: “He has made me drunk with wormwood” (Lam. 3:15). For a drunk person does not know what he suffers. He is therefore drunk with wormwood who, alienated from the sense of reason by his love of the present age, considers whatever he endures for the world light; he does not perceive the bitterness of the labor he bears, because he is led with pleasure toward all the things in which he is wearied through punishment.

But, on the contrary, the just man strives to be weak in enduring the dangers of the world for the world. He looks toward his end and considers how transitory the present life is; he refuses to endure outward labors for it, since inwardly he has conquered its pleasures.

[Note: Ebroic. reads “desires his end.”]

Pressed by the adversities of the present life, blessed Job should therefore speak from his own voice and from the voice of all the just: “For what is my strength, that I should endure? Or what is my end, that I should act patiently?”

It is as though he openly indicated: “I cannot endure the evils of the world for the world, because I am no longer strong in its desire. For when I see the end of the present life, why should I bear the weight of that whose desire I trample underfoot?”

And because, as we have said, the unjust endure its labors all the more strongly the more avidly they are nourished by its pleasures, he rightly immediately adds the same strength of the reprobate, saying:

CHAPTER XXII [Old recension X, New recension IX].

VERSE 12.—“Neither is the strength of stones my strength, nor is my flesh bronze.”

26. At God’s Blows Some Are Silent Stones, Others Resounding Bronze without Understanding. Job Is Strong Not through Madness but through a State of Salvation

What is signified here by bronze and stones except the hearts of insensitive people, who often receive blows from above and yet do not soften under any blow of discipline?

In contrast, the Lord promises the elect through the prophet: “I will take from you your heart of stone and will give you a heart of flesh” (Ezek. 11:19). Paul also says: “If I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, but do not have love, I have become like resounding bronze or a clanging cymbal” (1 Cor. 13:1).

We know that struck stones cannot produce a clear sound; but when bronze is struck, a very resonant sound is formed from the blow. Yet because bronze, like stones, is without life, it has no understanding in its sound.

There are some, like stones, who have become so hard toward the commands of piety that, when the blow of heavenly judgment tests them, they do not at all return the sound of humble confession. Others, differing in nothing from bronze metal, emit a sound of pious confession when they receive the scourges of heavenly blows; but because they do not utter the words of humility from the heart, once restored to a state of salvation they do not know what they promised.

The former, struck like stones, have no voices; the latter in no way avoid the imitation of bronze, for, placed under the blow, they speak good things that they do not feel. The former deny reverence for the one who strikes and deny words; the latter, promising what they do not fulfill, cry out without life.

[Note: We have thought this should be restored from most manuscripts, and have corrected the earlier reading: “They deny reverence for the one who strikes and deny blows.” It must nevertheless be acknowledged that the copies vary here. One Compend. and Bigot. have “in reverence for the one who strikes and deny words.” Another Compend., Lyran., and Utic. have “to the reverence of the one who strikes,” and so forth. All, however, read “words,” not “blows”; and this indeed agrees with the mind of Saint Gregory, who speaks of certain people who, like stones, return no sound when struck.]

Therefore the holy man, fleeing the hardness of the reprobate amid blows, says: “Neither is the strength of stones my strength, nor is my flesh bronze.”

It is as though he openly confessed: “I flee the likeness of the reprobate under the scourge of discipline. I have not become so hardened, like stones, that beneath the stimulus of a blow I should fall silent in the ministry of confession; nor, again, do I resound like bronze with the voice of confession while remaining ignorant of the meaning of that voice.”

But because the reprobate are weakly strong under blows, while the elect are powerfully weak, blessed Job, by asserting that he is not strong through madness, makes known that he is strong through a state of salvation.

[Old recension XI. He should therefore indicate from where he received this same strength, lest, if he ascribes the strength he possesses to himself, he run powerfully toward death. For very often possessed virtue kills more disastrously than if it were absent; because, while it raises the mind to confidence in itself, it pierces it with the sword of pride; and while it seems to give it life by strengthening it, it kills it by elevating it. It drags to destruction the one whom it tears away through self-reliance from confidence in inward strength. But because blessed Job possesses virtue and has no confidence in himself, and, so to speak, has strength in weakness, he aptly adds:]

CHAPTER XXIII.

VERSE 13.—“Behold, there is no help for me in myself.”

27. He Ascribes His Strength Not to Himself but to God

It is now clear toward whose hope the mind struck by blows turns when it denies that there is help for it in itself. But because he shows himself to be weak in himself, he adds, for the merit of still greater strength, how he is also abandoned by those close to him:

SAME VERSE.—“My intimates too have withdrawn from me.”

But behold: outwardly despised, inwardly he presides upon the tribunal of judgment. For when he declares himself abandoned, he immediately proceeds to a sentence, saying:

CHAPTER XXIV [New recension X].

VERSE 14.—“Who removes mercy from his friend has abandoned the fear of the Lord.”

28. What the Love of God and the Love of Neighbor Provide for One Another

Who is designated here by the name “friend” except any neighbor, who is faithfully joined to us insofar as, having received good works from us now, he truly assists us in attaining the heavenly homeland afterward?

Since there are two commandments of love—namely, love of God and love of neighbor—the love of neighbor is generated through the love of God, and the love of God is nourished through the love of neighbor. For whoever neglects to love God plainly does not know how to love his neighbor. And we make fuller progress in the love of God if, within the embrace of that same love, we are first nourished by love of our neighbor.

[Note: The reading is found in English, Norman, Turon., Floriac., Vindoc., and other manuscripts. Some, however, have “we may be nourished,” and some corruptly “we may nourish.” We have found nowhere the reading “we bind,” as in the printed editions. One Vindoc. has “we are made smooth,” and “we are nourished.”]

Because the love of God generates love of neighbor, the Lord, when he was about to say through the Law, “You shall love your neighbor” (Deut. 6:5; 10:12), prefaced it by saying: “You shall love the Lord your God” (Matt. 22:37, 39), so that he might first fix the root of his love in the soil of our heart, and afterward brotherly love might sprout through its branches.

And again, because the love of God grows strong through love of neighbor, John bears witness, saying: “Whoever does not love his brother whom he sees, how can he love God whom he does not see?” (1 John 4:20). Yet this divine love is born through fear, and as it grows it is transformed into affection.

29. Love of Neighbor Is Proved in His Distresses. How Great Is the Wickedness of Despising a Friend in Adversity

Often almighty God, so that it may become known how far each person is from love of God and neighbor, or how far he has advanced in it, orders all things with marvelous arrangement: he depresses some with scourges and supports others with successes. And when he temporarily abandons certain people, he reveals what evil lies hidden in the hearts of others.

For often those who pursue us when we are miserable are the very ones who had honored us beyond comparison when we were prosperous. When someone is loved while established in prosperity, it is very uncertain whether prosperity or the person is being loved. The loss of happiness, however, puts the power of love to the test.

Hence a certain wise man rightly says: “A friend is not recognized in good things, and an enemy is not hidden in evil things” (Sir. 12:8). Prosperity does not indicate a friend, nor does adversity conceal an enemy, because the former is often covered by respect for our prosperity, while the latter is revealed by the confidence of adversity.

Therefore the just man, placed amid scourges, says: “Who removes mercy from his friend has abandoned the fear of the Lord,” because whoever despises his neighbor on account of adversity is openly convicted of not having loved him in prosperity.

And since almighty God strikes certain people for this reason: both to instruct those who are struck and to offer those who are not struck an opportunity for good work, whoever despises the one who has been struck drives away from himself an opportunity for virtue. He rises against the Creator all the more wickedly insofar as he recognizes him neither as merciful in his own prosperity nor as just in another’s wound.

But it must be observed that blessed Job speaks of his own affairs in such a way that through him the life of the entire elect people is also signified. Because he is a member of that people, when he recounts what he himself suffers, he also announces what that people endures, saying:

CHAPTER XXV.

VERSE 15.—“My brothers have passed me by like a torrent that swiftly passes through the valleys.”

30. Why the Reprobate Are Called Both Brothers and Those Who Pass By. They Are Rightly Compared to a Torrent. They Pass through a Brief and Fleeting Life toward Eternal Torments

The mind of the reprobate, because it loves only the present, is often as far removed from the scourge now as it remains afterward from the inheritance; and in its pride it despises the just, whom paternal severity mercifully afflicts.

Often the reprobate retain the same faith by which we live, receive the same sacraments of faith, and are held within the unity of the same religion. Yet they do not know the bowels of compassion, nor do they recognize the force of charity by which we burn toward God and neighbor.

They are therefore rightly called both brothers and those who pass by, because they come forth with us from one womb of the mother through faith, but are not fixed with us in one devotion of charity toward God and neighbor.

Hence they are also aptly compared to a torrent that swiftly passes through the valleys. For a torrent flows down from the mountains to the low places; gathered by winter rains, it dries up under the summer suns. Those who, loving earthly things, abandon hope of the heavenly homeland are like people who leave the mountains for the valleys. Winter—that is, the present life—swells them, but the summer of the coming judgment dries them up, because when the sun of heavenly severity burns, it turns the joy of the reprobate into dryness.

It is therefore rightly said: “It swiftly passes through the valleys.” For a torrent’s swiftly passing toward the valleys means that the minds of the wicked descend toward low desires without any obstacle or difficulty.

[Old recension XII.] Every ascent is labor, and every descent pleasure, because by exertion the step is directed toward higher things, whereas by relaxation it declines toward lower things. To carry a stone up to the summit of a mountain is a great labor; to let that same stone down from the heights to the depths is no labor. Without delay, the one who reached the heights with great efforts plunges downward.

A field is sown through long labor and nourished by prolonged sun and rain, yet a single sudden spark consumes it. Buildings gradually rise to great heights, but through sudden collapses they fall to the ground. A sturdy tree rises into the air through slow growth, but whatever it has produced upward over a long time falls once and all at once.

Therefore, because ascent is labor and descent pleasure, it is rightly said: “My brothers have passed me by like a torrent that swiftly passes through the valleys.” Yet this can also be understood in another way.

31. If by “valleys” we understand the lowest places of punishment, all the unjust swiftly pass like a torrent into the valleys, because in this life, which they desire with all their desires, they cannot remain for long. For however many days of life they receive, they advance daily toward the end as though by that many steps.

They wish their time to be increased, but because the time granted cannot remain, by however many additions to life they receive, they lose an equal amount from the span of living.

[Note: This is an obscure passage. The reading we have adopted occurs in six English and four Norman manuscripts; previously it read: “they lose equal spans of long life.”]

The moments of time flee as they follow them; as they receive them, they lose them. Thus they swiftly pass into the valleys: they prolong the desires of pleasures for a long time, but are suddenly led down to the prison of hell.

For even the time extended through whatever length of years is not long if it is closed by an end. From the end, the wretched learn that what they held while losing it was brief.

Hence Solomon also rightly says: “If a man lives many years and rejoices in all of them, he ought to remember the time of darkness and the many days which, when they come, will accuse the past of vanity” (Eccl. 11:8). For when the foolish mind suddenly encounters an evil that does not pass away, it understands its eternity by enduring it; since what could pass away was vanity.

It must be understood, however, that many desire to do what is right, but certain things in the present life oppose their weak minds. And when they fear enduring adversities in lowly things, they offend against the righteousness of the heavenly judgment.

Hence it is rightly added:

CHAPTER XXVI [New recension XI].

VERSE 16.—“Those who fear frost, snow falls upon them.”

32. Those Who Abandon Justice through Fear of Temporal Losses Fall into Eternal Evils

Frost freezes below, whereas snow falls from above. Often, while certain people fear temporal adversities, they expose themselves to the severity of eternal judgment.

[Note: In Vindoc. and most Norman witnesses: “they reject the severity of eternal judgment.” Corb. Germ. reads “they expose themselves to the severities of eternal judgment.” Germ. has “the severities of eternal judgment”; one Reg. has “they expose themselves to the severities of eternal judgment.” Another Reg. agrees with the printed edition.]

Of them the Psalmist rightly says: “There they trembled with fear where there was no fear” (Ps. 14:5). One person now desires to defend the truth freely, but in that very desire he trembles and fears the indignation of human power. And while on earth he fears a person opposed to the truth, he suffers the anger of that same truth from heaven.

Another, conscious of his sins, already desires to give to the needy what he possesses, but fears that he himself will be in need if he gives away his possessions. And while, trembling, he prepares to preserve the supports of the flesh, he kills his soul by withholding the nourishment of mercy. While he fears suffering want on earth, he cuts himself off from the eternal abundance of heavenly refreshment.

It is therefore rightly said: “Those who fear frost, snow falls upon them,” because those who fear what comes from below and ought to be trampled underfoot suffer from above what they ought to fear. And when they refuse to pass through what they could have trampled down, they receive from above a judgment that they cannot possibly endure.

Yet by doing these things they temporarily obtain the glory of the world. What will they do at the time of their calling, when in fear they abandon all at once the things they guarded here with great anxiety?

Hence it is aptly added:

CHAPTER XXVII.

VERSE 17.—“At the time when they are scattered, they will perish.”

33. How Great Their Fear as Judgment Approaches

Those whom the concern of the present life orders, loss scatters; and then those perish outwardly who had long before perished inwardly by neglecting eternal things.

Of them it is rightly added: “And when they have become hot, they will be dissolved from their place.”

[Old recension XIII.] Every wicked person, when he has become hot, is dissolved from his place, because, as he approaches the judgment of inward severity, when he begins to burn through knowledge of his punishment, he is separated from the pleasure of his flesh to which he had long clung.

[Note: One Compend. reads, “because, as the judgment of inward severity approaches.”]

[Note: Ebroic. reads “to burn through the thought of punishment”; Gemet. and Utic. read “through knowledge of punishment.” We have adopted the latter reading.]

Hence the prophet says against the reprobate: “Only oppression will give understanding to the hearing” (Isa. 28:19), because they do not understand eternal things until they are punished for temporal things without possibility of correction.

Then the mind burns and inflames itself with the fires of fruitless repentance; it fears being led to punishment and retains the present life through desire. But it is dissolved from its place, because, abandoning the pleasures of the flesh, its hardness is melted through punishment.

But since we have heard what all the wicked will suffer at the time of their removal, let us hear further some of the things in which they are entangled during the time of their freedom.

It continues:

CHAPTER XXVIII [Old recension XIV, New recension XII].

VERSE 18.—“The paths of their footsteps are entangled.”

34. It Is Useless to Form Good Resolutions Unless We Persevere in Them

Everything that is entangled is folded back upon itself. There are some who, as though with their whole intention, deliberate on resisting the vices that seduce them; but when the moment of temptation arrives, they do not persevere in the purpose of their deliberation.

One person, inflated by the perverse daring of pride, considers how great the rewards of humility are. He rises against himself and, as though laying aside the swelling of puffed-up arrogance, promises to present himself as humble under any insults. But when suddenly an insult in a single word strikes him, he immediately returns to his customary pride; and he is led back into swelling arrogance so completely that he no longer remembers that he had desired the good of humility.

[Note: Floriac. and one Compend. read: “Another, burning with avarice and panting to increase his possessions, when he sees that all things pass away …”]

Another burns with avarice and pants to increase his possessions. When he sees that all things pass away swiftly, he fixes his wandering mind among his desires, resolves to seek nothing more, and to possess only what he has acquired under the restraint of great moderation. But when things that please him suddenly appear before his eyes, his mind immediately pants after ambition; it cannot contain itself, seeks an opportunity to obtain them, and, forgetting the self-control it had agreed upon with itself, agitates itself through the goads of thought and the desires of acquisition.

Another is polluted by the corruption of lust and is held captive by a long-established habit. Yet he perceives how pure chastity is and recognizes that being conquered by the flesh is shameful. He therefore deliberates on restraining the flow of pleasures and prepares, as though with all his strength, to resist his habit.

But when he is shaken by sudden temptation, whether by an appearance presented to his eyes or by one recalled to memory, he is immediately scattered from his former preparation. The one who had raised the shield of deliberation against it lies pierced by the dart of pleasure; and lust overcomes him in his weakness, as though he had prepared no weapons of resolve against it.

[Note: All our manuscripts and five English manuscripts, along with the older edition, Coccius, and subsequent editions, read “when he is shaken by sudden temptation,” rather than “by an unforeseen appearance.”]

Another is kindled by the flames of anger and becomes unrestrained even to the point of insulting his neighbors. But when no occasion of rage strikes his mind, he considers how great is the virtue of gentleness and how profound is patience, and prepares himself to be patient even under insults.

[Note: The word “depth” is absent from the Gemet. manuscripts and a few others, without affecting the sense.]

Yet when the slightest occasion for agitation arises, he is suddenly inflamed to the depths with shouts and insults, so that not only does the promised patience fail to return to his memory, but his mind does not recognize either itself or the insults it utters.

When he has fully satisfied his fury, he returns to tranquility as though after an exercise. And then he gathers himself back into the enclosure of silence, when not patience but the satisfaction of his insolence has placed a bridle on his tongue.

Only late, therefore, does he restrain himself after the insults have been delivered, because foaming horses are often checked not by the hand of the driver but by the boundary of the field.

It is rightly said of the reprobate: “The paths of their footsteps are entangled,” because they desire what is right in deliberation but are always folded back into their customary evils. They are like people stretched outside themselves who return in a circle to themselves: they desire good things but never withdraw from evil.

They wish to be humble, but without contempt; content with their own possessions, but without need; chaste, but without disciplining the body; patient, but without insults. When they seek to obtain virtues but flee the labors of virtue, what else do they do but fail to know the battles of war in the field while desiring to triumph over war in the cities?

[Note: The printed editions read “than to display”; the reading has been corrected from the Gemet., both Compend., Utic., and other manuscripts.]

[Old recension XV.] 35. When Some Conquer Certain Vices but Neglect Others, They Soon Succumb Again to Those They Had Subdued

Although the statement that their paths are entangled can still be understood in another way, often certain people gird themselves vehemently against particular vices but neglect to subdue others. Because they do not rise against the latter, the vices they had conquered rise again against them.

One person has already subdued the flesh with regard to lust, but has not yet restrained his mind from avarice. While he remains in the world for the exercise of avarice and does not withdraw from earthly activities, when an opportunity suddenly arises he falls even into the lust that he had seemed to have conquered.

Another has overcome the heat of avarice but has not at all subdued the power of lust. When he prepares the price for satisfying lust, he also submits the neck of his heart to the yoke of avarice, which he had formerly conquered.

Another has already cast down rebellious impatience but has not yet conquered empty glory. When through empty glory he inserts himself into worldly honors, pierced by the goads of disputes, he returns captive to impatience. And when empty glory raises his mind in self-defense, he endures it in defeat, although he had overcome it.

Another has subdued empty glory but has not yet overthrown impatience. When he threatens many people who resist him through impatience, he is ashamed not to carry out what he says and is recalled under the yoke of empty glory; defeated through one vice, he endures the vice that he had rejoiced to have completely conquered.

Thus the vices retain their fugitive by mutual assistance and, as though already lost, receive him back under their dominion; they hand him over to one another for punishment. The paths of the footsteps of the perverse are therefore entangled, because even if they lift their foot after conquering one wickedness, while another reigns, it entangles that foot in the very wickedness they had conquered.

36. The Sinner Entangles Himself, Since One Fault Becomes the Occasion of Another and of Several That Follow. A Human Being, as It Were, Ends in a Beast When He Sins against Reason under the Pretext of Reason

Sometimes, however, when the paths of the footsteps are entangled, no fault is conquered, and one fault is committed through another. Often the deceit of denial is joined to theft, and often the fault of deceit is compounded by the guilt of perjury. Frequently any vice is committed with shameless presumption; and often—something more serious than every fault—the person even takes pride in the vice he has committed.

For although pride usually arises from virtue, sometimes the foolish mind exalts itself over the wickedness it has committed.

[Note: Vindoc., Compend., Norman., and others read “the foolish pride of the mind.”]

But when fault is added to fault, what else happens than that the footsteps of the wicked are bound by entangled paths and knotted bonds?

Hence Isaiah rightly says against the perverse mind, under the figure of Judaea: “It will be a lair of dragons and a pasture of ostriches; demons will meet onocentaurs, and the hairy one will cry out to the other” (Isa. 34:13).

For what is signified by dragons except malice, and what by the name “ostriches” except hypocrisy? An ostrich has the appearance of flying but does not possess the use of flight. So hypocrisy presents to all who look upon it an image of holiness, but does not know how to maintain a life of holiness.

Thus in the perverse mind the dragon lies and the ostrich feeds, because hidden malice is cunningly concealed while an imitation of goodness is displayed before the eyes of those who observe.

What are signified by the name “onocentaurs” except both the lustful and the proud? In Greek, ὄνος (*onos*) means “donkey,” and by the designation “donkey” lust is signified, as the prophet testifies: “Their flesh was like the flesh of donkeys” (Ezek. 23:20). By the word “bull” the neck of pride is demonstrated, as the Psalmist says in the voice of the Lord concerning the proud Jews: “Fat bulls have surrounded me” (Ps. 22:13).

Onocentaurs, therefore, are those who, subjected to the vices of lust, lift up their necks from the very place where they ought to be humbled. Serving the pleasures of their flesh and casting shame far away, they not only do not grieve that they have lost uprightness but even rejoice in the work of disgrace.

Demons meet onocentaurs because evil spirits serve very readily the wishes of those whom they see rejoicing in things over which they ought to have wept.

It is aptly added: “And the hairy one will cry out to the other.”

For who else are represented by the designation “the hairy ones” except those whom the Greeks call *Panas* and the Latins call *incubi*? Their form begins with a human appearance but ends in a bestial extremity.

[Note: One Compend. reads “whom the Greeks call Panos.” Two Vindoc. manuscripts and Germ. read “whom the Greeks call phanas.” Bigot. and Lyr. read “whom the Greeks call Panas,” otherwise *Phaunos*.]

Therefore, by the name “hairy one” is signified the harshness of any sin, which, even if it sometimes begins under the appearance of reason, nevertheless always tends toward irrational impulses. It ends in a beast, as it were, from a human being, when a fault that begins through the appearance of reason drags a person all the way to an irrational action.

For often the pleasure of eating serves gluttony while pretending to serve the needs of nature. And when it stretches the belly into greed, it raises the limbs toward lust.

But the hairy one cries out to the other when wickedness already committed provokes the commission of another, and, as though by a certain voice of thought, an already committed fault invites another fault still to be committed.

[Note: Floriac., one Compend., and Gemet. read “when wickedness already committed calls or provokes another wickedness to be committed.” Ebroic. and Utic. read “provokes the commission of another wickedness.”]

Often, as we have said, gluttony says: “If you do not restore the body with abundant food, you will not persevere in any useful labor.” And when it has inflamed the mind through the desires of the flesh, lust immediately makes its own suggestion, saying: “If God did not wish human beings to unite bodily, he would not have made the limbs suitable for intercourse.”
