While it suggests this as though from reason, it drags the mind toward unrestrained lust. When caught, it immediately seeks the protection of deceit and denial; it does not consider itself guilty if it defends its life by lying.

The hairy one therefore cries out to the other when, under some appearance of reasoning, a subsequent fault entangles the perverse mind by taking occasion from the preceding fault.

And when harsh and rough sins oppress it, the hairy ones, as though summoned together, rule over it in harmony. Thus the paths of its footsteps always become more disastrously entangled, while fault binds the reprobate mind through fault.

*[Earlier recension XVI, later recension XIII.]*

**37. The habit of sinning is sometimes preceded by blindness of mind, and sometimes precedes it.**—Amid these matters we must understand that sometimes the eye of the understanding is first dulled, and afterward the mind, having been taken captive, wanders through outward desires, so that the blind mind does not know where it is being led and willingly submits itself to the allurements of its flesh. At other times, however, the desires of the flesh first boil over and, after long use of the unlawful deed, close the eye of the heart.

For often the mind sees what is right, yet does not boldly rise against what is perverse; and while resisting, it is overcome, since, although it judges the very thing it is doing, it is defeated by the pleasure of its flesh. Because the eye of contemplation is very often lost first, and afterward the mind is subjected to the labors of the world through the desires of this flesh, Samson bears witness: captured by the Philistines, after he had lost his eyes he was assigned to the mill. For plainly, after evil spirits have dug out the sight of contemplation within by the goads of temptations, they send the mind outside into the round of labors.

Again, because outwardly right action is often first lost while the light of reason is still retained in the heart, the prophet Jeremiah indicates this. When he recounts Zedekiah’s captivity, he discloses the order of inward captivity, saying: “And the king of Babylon slew the sons of Zedekiah at Riblah before his eyes, and the king of Babylon slew all the nobles of Judah; he also put out the eyes of Zedekiah” (Jeremiah 39:6).

The king of Babylon is the ancient enemy, the possessor of inward confusion. He first slaughters the sons before the eyes of the one who is watching, because he often kills good works in such a way that the one who is himself taken captive sees with grief that he has lost them. [Note: Thus Vindoc., Compend., Norman., and others, together with the older editions. Gilot 1571, while presenting this reading, also gives another: “for the mind usually produces good things,” which is likewise found in more recent editions. In Vindoc., Corb. Germ., and two Reg. manuscripts, *gemuit* (“groaned”) is read instead of *genuit* (“produced”).]

For the mind often groans; yet, overcome by the pleasures of its flesh, it lovingly loses the good things it produced. It considers the losses it suffers, but nevertheless does not raise the arm of virtue against the king of Babylon. While it is struck by the perpetration of wickedness, it is eventually brought by the habit of sin to the point where it is deprived even of the light of reason. Hence the king of Babylon, after first killing the sons, puts out Zedekiah’s eyes, because the evil spirit first removes good works and afterward takes away the light of understanding.

Zedekiah rightly suffers this at Riblah. [Note: In Hebrew, *Rebla* or *Reblatha* means “multitude.”] For *Reblatha* is interpreted as “this multitude.” At some point, then, the light of reason is also closed to the one who is weighed down by the multitude of his wickedness through depraved habit.

*[Earlier recension XVII.]* How sin comes forth, or from whatever occasions it breaks out, the path of the reprobate is nevertheless always entangled: devoted to perverse desires, they either desire no good at all, or, though desiring it with feeble longing, do not direct the free steps of their mind toward it. They either do not begin what is right, or, broken in the midst of the journey, do not reach it at all. Hence it often happens that, wearied, they return to their customary way of life [Note: Corb. Germ. and Ebroic.: “that they return to their own love.”] and throw themselves from the intention of the mind into the pleasures of the flesh. They think only about what passes away and care nothing for what will remain with them forever. Hence it is aptly added:

**CHAPTER XXIX**

**The same passage.—“They will walk in emptiness, and will perish.”**

**38. The empty labor of those who yearn for transitory goods.**—They walk in emptiness, plainly, who carry away with them nothing from the fruit of their labor. One sweats to attain honors, another burns to multiply his possessions, another pants to win praise; but since each person abandons all these things here when he dies, he has wasted his labors in emptiness if he carries nothing with him before the Judge.

In contrast, the Law rightly says: “You shall not appear empty before the Lord” (Exodus 23:15). The one who has not provided, by doing good, the reward of attaining life appears empty before the Lord. Hence the Psalmist says of the just: “But coming, they shall come with exultation, carrying their sheaves” (Psalm 125:6). They come to the examination of judgment carrying sheaves who display in themselves the right works by which they may merit life.

Again the Psalmist says of each of the elect: “He has not received his soul in vain” (Psalm 23:4). He receives his soul in vain who, thinking only about the present, does not attend to what will follow him forever. He receives his soul in vain who, neglecting its life, puts the care of the flesh before it.

But the just do not receive their souls in vain, because by continual intention they direct whatever they do bodily toward its benefit, so that although the work passes away, the purpose of the work does not pass away—the purpose that prepares the rewards of life after this life.

The reprobate neglect to care about these things. Indeed, walking in emptiness, they flee the life they pursue; while finding it, they lose it. We are better restrained from imitating the wicked if we weigh their losses from the end. Hence, with an exhortation, it is also added:

**CHAPTER XXX [Later recension XIV]**

**Verse 19.—“Consider the paths of Tema, the roads of Sheba, and wait a little while.”**

**39. Some are ensnared in the nets of the world under the name of respectability. Among them are those who manage household affairs, or who love relatives without due order.**—*Theman* is interpreted as “south,” while *Sheba* means “net.” What is signified here by the south, which, breathed upon by warmth, relaxes the limbs [Note: Turon.: “which relaxes the limbs at the breath of warmth.” Corb. Germ.: “which breathes upon and warms”], except the lax relaxation of one’s way of life? And what by a net except the entanglement of action?

Those who, with a relaxed mind, desire eternal things [Note: Thus all the English manuscripts and ours, rather than “earthly things,” as the editions read. The somewhat obscure but excellent sense gave occasion for changing *aeterna* (“eternal”) to *terrena* (“earthly”).] bind themselves by their own disordered efforts, so that they may not proceed to God with free step. [Note: Floriac., Turon., and two Compend.: “so that they may not proceed to God with free stride.” Germ., first Compend., and first Vindoc.: “so that they may not have a free stride.”] When they entangle themselves in the lax actions of their way of life, [Note: Gemet., several Norman manuscripts, and Turon.: “and when they become entangled in the lax practices of their conduct”] they place their feet, as it were, in the meshes of a net, intending to remain there. [Note: Two Compend., Turon., and Norm. read this way. Coc. and recent editions, instead of “meshes,” have “bonds,” perhaps because they did not know that *maculae* can sometimes mean the openings of a net—French *mailles*.]

Just as a little earlier we said that some are dragged back to sins already overcome through certain open vices not yet overcome, so some return to what they had abandoned through things disguised either under the name of respectability or under the honor of praise.

For there are many who no longer desire what belongs to others and who begin to withdraw from the quarrels of this world through a love of quiet. They thirst to be instructed by sacred utterances and desire to devote themselves to heavenly contemplation; yet they do not abandon the management of household affairs with perfect freedom of mind. While they often serve it licitly, they also become entangled in the illicit quarrels of this world. When they earnestly desire to guard earthly possessions, they abandon the rest of heart they had sought; and while a substance that is passing away is protected by continual provision, the word of divine knowledge conceived in the mind is scattered. For, according to the judgment of Truth (Matthew 13; Mark 4; Luke 8), they crush the seed that has sprung up among thorns when the intrusive anxieties of earthly affairs drive the word of God from the memory.

Those who walk with loosened steps in a net are the ones who, while not completely abandoning the world, bind themselves by walking, so that they cannot walk.

**40.** There are also many who not only do not desire what belongs to others, but abandon in the world everything they had possessed; they despise themselves, seek no glory in the present life, separate themselves from the activities of this world, and trample underfoot almost whatever prosperity may have smiled upon them. [Note: Vindoc. and Corb. Germ.: “and they trample underfoot almost whatever prosperity they had admitted.”]

Yet, still bound by the tie of carnal kinship, while they serve the love of relatives without due discretion, they often return through the effects of kinship to what they had already subdued, even at the cost of despising themselves. When they love their fleshly relatives more than is necessary, they are drawn back outwardly and separated from the parent of their heart.

For often we see certain people who, as far as their own purpose is concerned, no longer have desires for the present life and have abandoned the world both in practice and in profession; yet, because of disordered affections for their relatives, they burst into law courts, occupy themselves with quarrels over earthly matters, abandon the freedom of inward quiet, and restore within themselves the pursuits of the world that they had long since destroyed.

Where, then, do such people walk except in a net? The beginning of perfection in their way of life had released them from the present age, but disordered love of earthly kinship binds them.

**41. We ought to despise, hate, and not know relatives for God’s sake.**—Those who pursue the reward of an eternal promise with strict purpose and not with loosened steps despise themselves for divine love, and likewise set aside everything by which they perceive themselves to be hindered. When it is necessary for God’s sake to serve all whom they can, they deny private services even to relatives for God’s sake.

Hence, when someone said, “Permit me first to go and bury my father” (Matthew 8:21), he immediately heard from the mouth of Truth: “Let the dead bury their own dead; but you, go and announce the kingdom of God” (ibid., 22). In this matter we must note that, when the chosen disciple is restrained from burying his parent, what is not permitted to anyone to offer his dead father from carnal affection for the Lord’s sake is nevertheless something he ought to offer to outsiders for the Lord’s sake.

*[Earlier recension XVIII.]* Again Truth says: “If anyone comes to me and does not hate his father and mother, wife and children, brothers and sisters, and even his own life, he cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14:26). In this passage, since hatred even of our own life is introduced together with hatred of relatives, it is plainly shown that we are commanded to hate relatives as we hate ourselves—not so that we may fail to rescue them for eternal things, or, when their carnal favor hinders us, fail to set it aside, but so that we may learn, by the measured art of discernment, both to love them appropriately and to hate them for their good. Thus love should know how hatred arises, so that through hatred we may be able to love them more truly.

Again, through Moses it is said: “He who says to his father and mother, ‘I do not know you,’ and to his brothers, ‘I do not recognize them,’ and they did not know their sons—these have guarded your word and kept your covenant and observed your judgments” (Deuteronomy 33:9). The one who desires to know God more familiarly is the one who, out of love for piety, wishes not to know those whom he knew according to the flesh. Divine knowledge is diminished by serious loss if it is divided with carnal familiarity.

Therefore, everyone must become an outsider to relatives and close kin if he wishes to be joined more truly to the parent of all, so that he may love all the more firmly those whom he usefully neglects for God’s sake, the more he disregards in them the mutable affection of the carnal bond. [Note: Coc., in his customary fashion, changed *utiliter* (“usefully”) to *viriliter* (“manfully”), a change followed by other recent editors with insufficient attention to the manuscripts.] [Note: Corb. Germ. and Ebroic.: *solicitius*, “more diligently.”] [Note: Vindoc.: “the more he disregards in them the mutable affection of the carnal bond.”]

**42. We ought to benefit relatives more than others, provided that our progress from here toward God is not delayed. We ought to be kindly disposed toward them, yet must not turn aside from the road that leads to God.**—We should indeed benefit those to whom we are more closely joined in temporal matters more than others, because a flame extends a fire to things placed near it, although it first burns the place where it arises.

We ought to acknowledge the bond of earthly kinship; yet, when it impedes the course of the mind, we ought to disregard it, so that the faithful soul, kindled by devotion to God, may neither despise what is joined to it in the lowest places nor, while rightly ordering these things within itself, fail to rise beyond them through love of the highest.

Therefore we must carefully ensure that affection for the flesh does not creep in and turn the step of the heart aside from the right road, lest it impede the force of heavenly love and press the rising mind downward beneath an imposed weight. Each person ought to sympathize with the needs of relatives in such a way that compassion does not allow the force of his intention to be impeded: affection may fill the inward parts of the mind, but it must not turn him away from his spiritual purpose.

Holy men do not fail to love their fleshly relatives when they provide what is necessary for them. Rather, through love of spiritual things they overcome that very affection within themselves, regulating it by the restraint of discernment so that through it they do not deviate even slightly from the right road.

Cows signify this well for us. Under the Lord’s ark, as they go toward the mountains, they proceed both with affection and with firm resolve, as it is written: “Taking two cows that were nursing calves, they yoked them to the cart, but shut their calves up at home, and placed the ark of God on the cart” (1 Samuel 6:10). A little later: “The cows went straight along the road that leads to Beth-shemesh, proceeding along one road, going and lowing, and turning neither to the right nor to the left” (ibid., 12).

Behold: with their calves shut up at home, the cows yoked to the cart under the Lord’s ark groan and proceed. They utter lowings from their depths, yet do not change their steps from the road. They feel love through compassion, but do not turn their necks backward.

This is how those who, placed beneath the yoke of sacred law, already carry the Lord’s ark through inward knowledge must walk: although they grieve over the needs of their relatives, they must not turn aside from the right road they have begun.

*Beth-shemesh* means “house of the sun.” Therefore, for the Lord’s ark to proceed to Beth-shemesh is for one who possesses heavenly knowledge to draw near to the dwelling of eternal light. But we truly proceed toward Beth-shemesh when, walking along the road of righteousness, we do not turn aside toward the neighboring paths of error, not even out of affection for our children. [Note: Gemet., Corb. Germ., and other older witnesses read *pignerum* here and throughout, “children,” rather than *pignorum*.]

Their affection ought to hold our mind, but it ought not to turn it aside, lest the same mind be either hard if it is not touched by affection, or, if touched too deeply and bent aside, become slack.

*[Earlier recension XIX.]*

**43. Affection for relatives ought to hold us, but ought not to turn us aside.**—It is pleasing to raise the eyes of the mind and observe under what measure of discernment blessed Job, whose neck of heart had been worn down beneath the yoke of divine fear, carries the ark of the divine judgment.

When he has lost his calves, he lows, because, hearing of the death of his sons, he falls to the ground with his head shorn (Job 1:20). Yet, lowing, he proceeds along the right road, because his mouth opens in lamentation to praise God when he immediately says: “The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away; as it has pleased the Lord, so it has happened; blessed be the name of the Lord” (ibid., 21).

But undiscerning minds do not know this rule of life. The more loosely they pursue the ways of God, the more foolishly they turn back toward the roads of the world.

**44. The sight of the losses caused by lukewarmness in others usually moves the devout.**—Therefore the holy man rightly mentions the roads of Sheba after the paths of Tema, because those whom the south of reprobate lukewarmness has relaxed are held by the entanglement of the net.

In describing the deeds of the wicked, he rightly urges us to consider these things, because we love doing what is perverse but judge it when we see it in others. We recognize how shameful the things we think should be judged less severely in ourselves are in the actions of others. Thus it happens that the mind returns to itself and is ashamed to do what it condemns.

A foul face is displeasing, as it were, in a mirror, when the mind sees in itself something to turn away from in a similar life. Therefore he says: “Consider the paths of Tema, the roads of Sheba, and wait a little while.” It is as though he openly said: Attend to the losses caused by another’s lukewarmness, and then you will take firmer hope in eternal things if, with the right eye of the heart, you see what is displeasing in others.

*[Earlier recension XX.]*

**45. How profitably the brevity of this life should be considered.**—It is rightly said: “Wait a little while.” Often, while the brevity of the present life is loved as though it would endure for a long time, the mind is broken away from eternal hope. Delighted by present things, it is struck back by the darkness of its despair.

When it thinks that the span remaining for it to live is long, it suddenly abandons life and encounters eternity, which it can no longer escape. [Note: Turon.: “suddenly leaving life, it finds eternity, which …” Coccius, against the manuscripts and earlier editions, added “evil” before “eternity.”] Hence it is said through a certain wise man: “Woe to those who have lost endurance” (Sirach 2:16). They lose endurance, plainly, who, while they suppose that they will remain for a long time among visible things, abandon hope of invisible things.

When the mind is fixed on the present, life comes to an end; and suddenly they arrive at unforeseen punishments, which, deceived by their own presumptions, they either never believed would touch them or believed would come only late.

Hence Truth says: “Therefore keep watch, because you do not know the day or the hour” (Matthew 25:13). Again it is written: “The day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night” (1 Thessalonians 5:2). Because his approach to seize the soul is not seen at all, he is compared to a thief in the night.

He should therefore be feared as though he were always coming, precisely because his coming cannot be known in advance by us. [Note: Floriac., Turon., and two Compend.: “because his coming cannot be foreknown by us.” Others: “cannot be foreknown by one who is coming”; some: “cannot foresee what is to come.”] Hence holy men, because they continually perceive the brevity of life, live as though dying each day. They prepare themselves more firmly for what will remain, the more constantly they weigh the transitory as nothing from its end. [Note: Vindoc. and Corb. Germ.: “and they prepare themselves all the more diligently.”]

Seeing the life of the sinner flee with swift course, the Psalmist says: “A little while yet, and the sinner shall not be” (Psalm 36:10). Again he says: “Man is like grass; his days are like a flower of the field” (Psalm 102:15). Isaiah says: “All flesh is grass, and all its glory like the flower of grass” (Isaiah 40:6). [Note: Coc. and those following him read corruptly, “like the flower of the field.”]

James rebukes the minds of those who presume, saying: “What is your life? It is vapor appearing for a little while” (James 4:15).

It is rightly said, therefore: “Wait a little while,” because what follows without end is immense, while whatever comes to an end is little. What moves toward its own disappearance by the course of time ought not to seem long to us. As it is drawn onward moment by moment, the very moments that delay it drive it forward; and from the point at which it is seen to be held, from that same point it is driven onward so that it may not be held. [Note: Turon., Floriac., Longip., and others: “which moves by the course of its time toward its end, so that it may not be.”] [Note: Germ., two Compend., Turon., and some others: “which they abandon.” Gemet.: “which they abandon.”]

Blessed Job, after despising the brevity of the present life, rightly rises immediately in the voice of all the elect against the wicked and adds:

**CHAPTER XXXI**

**Verse 20.—“They have been confounded, because I hoped.”**

**46. The steadfastness of the good brings shame upon the reprobate.**—When the reprobate inflict evils upon the good, if they see them shaken from their inward hope, they rejoice in the success of their deception. They count the spread of their error as the greatest gain, because they exult in having companions in perdition.

But when the hope of the good is fixed inwardly and is in no way bent downward by external evils, confusion seizes the minds of the wicked. Unable to reach the inner being of the afflicted, they are ashamed that their cruelty has proved fruitless.

Let the holy man therefore speak in his own voice; let him speak in the voice of the steadfastness of the universal Church, afflicted and groaning. Amid the adversities of the reprobate, the Church desires the joy of heavenly recompense without any weakness of mind, and through dying endures toward life: “They have been confounded, because I hoped.”

It is as though he openly said: Since the reprobate do not soften the strength of my firmness through harsh persecutions, they plainly lose, in shame, the labor of their cruelty. Hence he immediately sees the blessings of the coming recompense as though they were already present, and considers what guilt awaits the reprobate in judgment [Note: Norman. and Corb. Germ.: “awaits the reprobate”], adding:

**CHAPTER XXXII**

**The same passage.—“They also came as far as me, and were covered with shame.”**

**47. The trembling of the reprobate in judgment.**—The reprobate come as far as the holy Church on the day of judgment, because they are brought as far as the point at which they must behold her glory, so that, rejected into greater punishments for their guilt, they may see what they have lost.

Shame covers the wicked when the witness of their conscience convicts them in the sight of the Judge. Then the Judge is seen outwardly, while the accuser is endured within. Then every sin is brought back before the eyes, and the mind is tormented more grievously by its own fire amid the flames of Gehenna.

Of them the Prophet rightly says: “Lord, let your hand be exalted, so that they may not see; let them see and be confounded” (Isaiah 26:11). Their merits now obscure the understanding of the reprobate, but then knowledge of their guilt enlightens it, so that now they do not see what they ought to pursue, while then they perceive it after they have lost it. Now they neglect to understand eternal things, or despise what they understand and might pursue; but then they plainly see and desire those things when, although they desire them, they can in no way attain them.

*[Earlier recension XXI.]*

**48. Job’s friends were covered with shame by his confidence in God.**—These words of blessed Job also apply particularly to his friends, who were trying to weaken the holy man’s spirit by harsh reproaches.

He says: “They have been confounded, because I hoped.” It is as though he openly said: Since they cannot bend me toward despair by their foolish rebukes, they themselves are confounded by the madness of their rashness.

“They also came as far as me, and were covered with shame.” It is as though he said: When they saw the wounds of my body but did not know the steadfastness of my mind, they dared to reproach me for injustice; they had not yet come as far as me. But when, striking me with harsh attack, they discovered that my mind stood firm amid adversities, they became ashamed as though they had come to me.

They come to me to the extent that they recognize me inwardly. There shame covers them precisely where external loss does not touch me as I stand firm.

There are, however, some who do not know how to fear God except when they are frightened by adversity experienced either in themselves or observed in others. Prosperity raises them through presumption; adversity disturbs them through weakness.

Blessed Job reproves his friends for belonging to this number when he immediately adds:

**CHAPTER XXXIII**

**Verse 21.—“Now you have come, and just now, seeing my wound, you are afraid.”**

**49. God must also be feared in prosperity.**—It is as though he openly said: I feared God then, when, supported by prosperity, I did not feel the losses inflicted by scourges. But you, who did not fear God out of love, fear him only because you have been struck by the blow of punishment.

**CHAPTER XXXIV**

**Verses 22–23.—“Have I said, ‘Bring me something, and give me a gift from your substance’? Or, ‘Deliver me from the hand of the enemy, and rescue me from the hand of the strong’?”**

**50. The Church does not wish to hear from those who assert perverse doctrines about faith what they teach truthfully about morals. Evil spirits were created without the weakness of flesh.**—If these words are referred to the person of the holy Church, since we have said that Job’s friends represent the figure of heretics, she rightly declares that she has no need of their substance.

The substance of heretics may suitably be understood as carnal wisdom. Supported perversely by it, they display themselves as rich in words; but the holy Church does not seek it, because she surpasses it through spiritual understanding.

Heretics often assert perverse things about faith while also making subtle statements about the temptations of the flesh against the ancient enemy. Sometimes they appear to display in themselves members of sound action, while in faith they remain wounded and held by the serpent’s bite in the head.

But the holy Church does not wish to hear subtle statements about temptations from those who, while asserting certain truths about conduct, lead people toward the falsehood of faithlessness.

Thus it is rightly said here: “Have I said, ‘Bring me something, and give me a gift from your substance’? Or, ‘Deliver me from the hand of the enemy, and rescue me from the hand of the strong’?”

By the hand of the enemy he calls Satan’s strength; by the hand of the strong he calls the powers of the evil spirits. He calls them strong because, having been created without the weakness of flesh, they do not encounter the impediment of bodily frailty in their wicked efforts.

What follows is:

**CHAPTER XXXV**

**Verse 24.—“Teach me, and I will be silent; and if perhaps I have been ignorant of anything, instruct me.”**

**51. It seems uncertain under which division of the sentence this should be placed:** whether it has been added to what he had said, “Have I said…?” or whether it is expressed as a sentence separate from what precedes, spoken as a rebuke: “Teach me, and I will be silent; and if perhaps I have been ignorant of anything, instruct me.”

Nevertheless, it suits either punctuation, since in neither case does it depart from the path of sound understanding.

But since we have said these things allegorically in passing, it remains for us to examine the words of the historical text in their moral sense.

*[Earlier recension XXII, later recension XV.]*

**THE MORAL SENSE**

**52. What is the disposition of the poor, the oppressed, and the foolish for God’s sake.**—Blessed Job had suffered the loss of his possessions and, delivered over to the blows of evil spirits, felt the pains of his wounds. Yet, loving the wisdom of God’s folly, he had trampled underfoot, through contempt of mind, the foolish wisdom of the world.

Accordingly, he is called poor in contrast with the rich of the world, oppressed in contrast with the powerful, and foolish in contrast with the wise. He gives three answers because the poor person does not seek their substance, the oppressed person does not seek help against the strong, and the foolish person does not seek the instruction of carnal wisdom.

The holy man, because he is carried beyond himself in mind, is neither distressed by poverty, nor harmed by oppression, nor impressed by carnal wisdom, since he is willingly foolish.

Hence another oppressed poor man says: “We are afflicted, but not crushed; persecuted, but not abandoned; struck down, but not destroyed” (2 Corinthians 4:8). Hence, suggesting the wisdom of holy folly, he says: “God chose the foolish things of the world to confound the wise” (1 Corinthians 1:27). And: “If anyone among you seems to be wise in this age, let him become foolish, so that he may be wise” (1 Corinthians 3:18).

Disclosing both the glory of oppression and the riches of the desired poverty, he says: “As dying, and behold, we live; as chastised, and not killed; as sorrowful, yet always rejoicing; as needy, yet making many rich; as having nothing, yet possessing all things” (2 Corinthians 1:19).

**53. The sublimity of the saints oppressed outwardly, and their freedom in reproving the powerful.**—Amid these matters it is pleasing to raise the eyes of the mind and see how great a citadel the elect of God, though oppressed outwardly, rule within. [Note: Turon.: “and to see how great a citadel the elect of God, oppressed outwardly, rule within.”]

Everything that stands out externally lies beneath their hidden gaze through contempt. Carried inwardly above themselves, they fix their mind on high; whatever they suffer in this life they see as though it were falling far below them and alien from them. So, to put it this way, while they strive to become outside the flesh in mind, they scarcely know the very things they endure.

In their eyes, whatever rises up temporarily is not high. As though situated on the summit of a great mountain, they look down upon the level plain of the present life. [Note: Thus first Compend., Norman., Turon., and others. Coc. indulged his own inclination and changed this to “they fully despise the joys of the present life,” and the later editions did not correct it.] Transcending themselves through spiritual height, they see beneath them inwardly whatever swells outwardly through carnal glory.

Therefore they spare no power in opposing the truth; rather, those whom they see lifted up through pride they press down by the authority of the spirit.

Hence Moses, coming from the desert, attacks the king of Egypt with authority, saying: “Thus says the Lord, the God of the Hebrews: How long will you refuse to submit to me? Let my people go, so that they may sacrifice to me” (Exodus 10:3).

When Pharaoh, pressed by the plagues, said to him, “Go, sacrifice to your God in this land” (Exodus 8:25), Moses immediately replied with increased authority: “It cannot be done this way; we shall sacrifice to the Lord our God the abominations of the Egyptians” (ibid., 26). [Note: Gemet. reads, “for the abomination of the Egyptians”; a later hand has “for the abominations,” and *enim* (“for”) is found in many other witnesses.]

Hence Nathan attacks the king who had sinned. First presenting to him a likeness of the transgression he had committed and holding him guilty by the voice of his own judgment, he immediately added: “You are that man who has done this thing” (2 Samuel 12:7).

Hence the man of God, sent to destroy idolatry in Samaria, did not fear King Jeroboam when he was casting incense upon the altar, nor was he oppressed by fear of death. Against the altar he boldly exercised the authority of free speech, saying: “Altar, altar, thus says the Lord God: Behold, a son shall be born to the house of David, Josiah by name, and he shall sacrifice upon you the priests of the high places” (1 Kings 13).

Hence, when proud Ahab, enslaved to the worship of idols, presumed to rebuke Elijah, saying, “Are you that man who troubles Israel?” (1 Kings 18:17), Elijah immediately struck the foolishness of the proud king with the authority of free reproach, saying: “I have not troubled Israel, but you and your father’s house, who have abandoned the commandments of the Lord and followed the Baals.”

Hence Elisha, following the true greatness of his teacher, confounded Joram, son of Ahab, when he came to him with King Jehoshaphat because of his faithlessness, saying: “What have I to do with you? Go to the prophets of your father and your mother” (2 Kings 4:13). And: “As the Lord of hosts lives, in whose sight I stand, if I did not respect the presence of Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, I would neither regard nor look upon you” (ibid., 14). [Note: Corb. Germ., two Vindoc., Germ., two Compend., Turon., and Norman witnesses read that “the same Ahab came to him with Jehoshaphat,” contrary to the manifest testimony of sacred Scripture.]

Hence the same man stopped Naaman at the door of his house when he came to him with horses and chariots. Although Naaman was supported by an abundance of talents and garments, Elisha did not go out to meet him or open the door of his house; instead, through a messenger he ordered him to wash seven times in the Jordan (2 Kings 5:9–10).

Therefore Naaman went away angry, saying: “I thought that he would come out to me” (ibid., 11). [Note: On the authority of the manuscripts—Compend., Bellovac., Vindoc., Norm., and others—we have removed from this point the words “and, standing, would invoke the name of his god,” which were inserted by the editions.]

Hence, when the priests and rulers, raging even with blows, forbade Peter to speak in the name of Jesus, he immediately replied with great authority: “Judge whether it is right in the sight of God to listen to you rather than to God. For we cannot fail to speak of what we have seen and heard” (Acts 4:19–20).

Hence Paul, seeing the chief priest sitting in opposition to the truth, and when that priest’s attendant had struck him on the mouth, did not, disturbed, utter a curse. Rather, filled with the Spirit, he prophesied with free voice, saying: “God will strike you, whitewashed wall. And you, sitting there judging me according to the law, command me to be struck contrary to the law” (Acts 23:3). [Note: Coc. and others after him read, “and you, sitting there, judge me.” It should read “judging,” according to the Greek text.]

Hence Stephen did not fear to exercise the authority of his voice against the violence of his persecutors, even when he was about to die, saying: “Stiff-necked and uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit, just as your fathers did, so also do you” (Acts 7:51). [Note: Compend., Norm., and others have this form. The editions read: “and uncircumcised in heart and ears; you always resist the Holy Spirit, just as your fathers did, so also do you.”]

[Vet. XXIII.] 54. This freedom of the saints arises from zeal for the truth, not from the fault of pride.—But because holy men rise to words of such elevation from zeal for the truth, not from the fault of pride, they themselves plainly show, by their other deeds and words, how greatly they excel in humility and how fervently they love those whom they rebuke. Pride generates hatred, whereas humility generates love. Therefore the words sharpened by love plainly flow from the fountain of humility.

How, then, could Stephen have uttered a rebuke through pride, when, for those same people whom he had rebuked—who were growing worse and stoning him—he prayed on bended knees, saying: “Lord, do not hold this sin against them” (Acts 7:59)?

[Note: Gemetensis: “he worshiped.”]

[Note: Compend. adds: “for they do not know what they are doing.”]

How could Paul, in the arrogance of pride, have directed harsh words against the priest and ruler of his nation, when in humility he subjected himself even to the service of disciples, saying: “For we do not preach ourselves, but our Lord Jesus Christ; and ourselves as your servants through Christ” (2 Cor. 4:5)?

How could Peter have resisted the rulers out of pride, when, sympathizing with their error, he excuses their guilt as though saying, “I know that you acted through ignorance, as did your rulers. But God, who foretold through the mouth of all the prophets that his Christ would suffer, has fulfilled it in this way” (Acts 3:17)? He mercifully draws them toward life, saying: “Repent, therefore, and turn back, so that your sins may be blotted out” (ibid., 19).

How could Elisha have refused through pride to see Naaman, when he allowed himself not only to be seen but even to be held by a woman? Of her it is written: “When she had come to the man of God on the mountain, she seized his feet; and Gehazi came to drive her away, but the man of God said: ‘Let her alone, for her soul is in bitterness’” (2 Kings 4:27).

How could Elijah, in arrogance, have spoken words of rebuke against a proud king, when he humbly ran before his chariot, as it is written: “And, having girded his loins, he ran before Ahab” (1 Kings 18:46)?

How could the man of God have disdainfully rejected Jeroboam’s presence, when out of compassion he immediately restored his withered right hand to its former health? It is written: “When the king heard the word of the man of God, who had cried out against the altar at Bethel, he stretched out his hand from the altar, saying: ‘Seize him!’ And his hand withered” (1 Kings 13:4). And shortly afterward: “The man of God prayed before the Lord, and the king’s hand returned to him and became as it had been before” (ibid., 6).

Because pride does not know how to produce virtues, the voice of rebuke that proceeds from humility is shown by the signs that accompany it. How could Nathan have swelled up in words of rebuke against King David, when, since there was no fault requiring rebuke, he prostrated himself on the ground before him, as it is written: “They announced to the king, saying: ‘The prophet Nathan is here.’ And when he had entered before the king’s presence, he worshiped him, prostrate on the ground” (1 Kings 1:23)?

[Note: The reading “immediately” is faulty in Gussanville.]

How could Moses, freely resisting the king of Egypt, have despised him, when, after conversing familiarly with God, he humbly worshiped his kinsman Jethro, who followed him (Exod. 18:7)? He also showed such obedience to Jethro’s counsel that, after his secret conversations with God, he considered it a great gain to hear outside from the mouth of a man.

[Vet. XXIV.] 55. Those who rebuke others do not flatter themselves.—From other deeds of the saints, then, we learn what judgment we ought to form concerning others. For holy men are neither outspoken from pride nor submissive through fear; rather, when uprightness raises them to freedom of speech, consideration of their own weakness keeps them in humility. Although they strike the faults of sinners with rebuke from a lofty position, they nevertheless judge themselves more carefully within and place themselves, as it were, among the lowly. In proportion as they pursue what is perverse in others, they return more fiercely to restrain themselves.

[Note: Gemetensis: “to humble themselves.” Vindocensis I: “they become more severe in restraining themselves.” Many Norman manuscripts likewise read this. Another reading has: “they return more severely.”]

Again, the less they spare themselves when doing better things, the more watchfully they rebuke the deeds of others. For what outward human power could they admire who also despise themselves, even when they have almost reached the innermost summit of exaltation? Therefore they rightly judge outwardly the height of earthly greatness, because inwardly the weight of pride does not burden their eye.

Thus blessed Job, when he despised earthly wisdom, strength, and possessions in his friends who spoke harshly, saying: “Have I said: ‘Bring something to me, and give me something from your possessions’? Or: ‘Deliver me from the hand of the enemy, and rescue me from the hand of the mighty’? Teach me, and I will be silent; and if perhaps I have been ignorant of anything, instruct me”—shortly afterward reveals what he thinks of himself, saying: “You rush upon the orphan” (v. 27). It is therefore clearer than daylight how great a weakness he recognizes in himself, since he calls himself an orphan.

The text continues:

## CHAPTER XXXVI [Rec. XVI]

### Verse 25

“Why have you criticized the words of truth, when there is none among you who can rebuke?”

56. Whoever wishes to correct others must be pure.—The one who cares to correct another’s faults must himself be free from faults: he must not think about earthly things and must not succumb to base desires.

[Note: Vindocensis, Bellovacensis, and most manuscripts read: “must be pure in himself.”] Thus he may see more perceptively what others must avoid, the more truly he himself shuns these things through knowledge and life. For an eye burdened by dust cannot clearly inspect a blemish on a limb, and hands holding mud cannot wipe away the dirt that lies upon it.

In accordance with the sequence of the ancient translation, the divine voice aptly suggests this figuratively concerning David, who was engaged in external wars, when it says: “You shall not build a temple for me, because you are a man of blood” (2 Sam. 7; 16:8; 1 Chron. 22:8). The one who devotes himself to correcting and instructing the minds of his neighbors builds a temple for God. For we are the temple of God, constructed for true life by his indwelling, as Paul testifies when he says: “The temple of God is holy, and that is what you are” (1 Cor. 3:17).

But the man of blood is forbidden to build a temple for God, because one who is still occupied with carnal deeds must be ashamed to instruct the minds of his neighbors spiritually. Well, therefore, it is said: “Why have you criticized the words of truth, when there is none among you who can rebuke?” As though it were said openly: “With what recklessness do you criticize what you have heard, when, ignorant of the causes of my striking, you continue to utter things deserving criticism?”

The text continues:

## CHAPTER XVII [Rec. XVII]

### Verse 26

“You prepare speeches only for rebuke, and you utter words into the wind.”

57. Two kinds of speech harmful to human beings.—There are two kinds of speech that are exceedingly inappropriate and harmful to the human race: one that takes care even to praise what is perverse, and another that always strives even to correct what is right. The former is carried downward with the current; the latter tries to obstruct the streams of truth and close its channel. The former is weighed down by fear; the latter is raised up by pride. The former seeks to gain favor through flattery; the latter is provoked by anger so that it may display itself as arising from conflict. The former lies readily at hand; the latter always swells up in opposition.

Blessed Job rebukes his friends for having the character of the latter when he says: “You prepare speeches only for rebuke.” But how one reaches the audacity of unjust rebuke becomes immediately clear when he adds: “And you utter words into the wind.” To utter words into the wind is to speak idly. For often, when the tongue is not restrained from idle words, it is also driven headlong into the recklessness of foolish rebuke.

Through certain stages of its ruin, the sluggish mind is driven into a pit.

[Note: Compend. II: “is driven after falling into a pit.” Gemetensis and Corbeiensis Germanicus: “is driven after having fallen into a pit.”]

For when we neglect to avoid idle words, we proceed to harmful ones: first we take pleasure in speaking about the affairs of others, then the tongue bites through detraction at the lives of those about whom it speaks, and finally it bursts forth into open insults. From this the goads of anger are sown, quarrels arise, the torches of hatred are kindled, and all peace is extinguished from hearts.

[Note: The word “of anger” is absent in Bellovacensis, Corbeiensis Germanicus, and most manuscripts.] Hence Solomon rightly says: “Whoever lets water loose is the beginning of quarrels” (Prov. 17:14). To let water loose is to release the tongue into a flood of speech.

Conversely, he asserts the same idea in a good sense when he says: “Deep water is the word from a man’s mouth” (Prov. 18:4). Whoever therefore lets water loose is the beginning of quarrels, because whoever does not bridle his tongue destroys harmony. Hence, in the opposite sense, it is written: “Whoever imposes silence on a fool appeases anger” (Prov. 26:10).

[Vet. XXV.] 58. The evils of excessive speech; the idle word.—That no one who serves excessive speech can maintain the uprightness of justice is attested by the Prophet, who says: “The loquacious man shall not be established upon the earth” (Ps. 139:12). Solomon says again: “In much speaking sin will not be absent” (Prov. 10:19).

Isaiah says:

[Note: Gemetensis: “The guardian of justice is silence.” The Hebrew word *haboddah* signifies worship, service, or work. Uticensis also has “guardian,” in place of the second reading.]

“The practice of justice is silence” (Isa. 32:17), indicating that the justice of the mind is desolated when restraint is not exercised from immoderate speech.

James says: “If anyone thinks that he is religious, but does not bridle his tongue and deceives his heart, that person’s religion is vain” (Jas. 1:26). He says again: “Let every person be swift to hear, but slow to speak” (ibid., 19).

[Note: The printed editions add “and slow to anger,” which is absent from the manuscripts and is irrelevant here.]

Again he adds: “The tongue is an unquiet evil, full of deadly poison” (Jas. 3:8). Truth itself warns us through itself, saying: “For every idle word that people speak, they will give an account of it on the day of judgment” (Matt. 12:36).

An idle word is one that lacks either the reason of just necessity or the purpose of pious usefulness. If an account is demanded for an idle utterance, then one must weigh very carefully what punishment follows excessive speech, in which one also sins through words of pride.

59. Without the restraint of silence, the whole mind lies exposed to the enemy.—It must also be understood that those who slip away through harmful words perish from every state of uprightness. For the human mind, like water, gathers itself upward when enclosed, because it seeks again the place from which it descended; but when released, it perishes because it uselessly scatters itself through low places.

As many superfluous words as dissipate the mind from the restraint of its silence are like so many streams carrying it outside itself. Therefore it cannot sufficiently return inward to knowledge of itself, because, scattered outward through excessive speech, it loses the power of inward reflection. It exposes itself wholly to the wounds of the ambushing enemy, because it does not enclose itself within any fortification of watchfulness.

Hence it is written: “Like a city lying open and without a circuit of walls is the person who cannot restrain his spirit in speaking” (Prov. 25:28). Because it has no wall of silence, the city of the mind lies open to the enemy’s arrows. And when it casts itself outside itself through words, it shows itself open to its adversary, who overcomes it with so much less effort as the very thing that is overcome fights against itself through excessive speech.

60. The disadvantages of immoderate silence.—Yet amid these considerations it must be understood that when we are restrained from speaking by excessive fear, we are sometimes confined within the barriers of silence more than necessary. While we carelessly flee the faults of the tongue, we become secretly entangled in worse ones.

Often, while we restrain ourselves immoderately from speech, we tolerate excessive speech in the heart, so that thoughts burn more intensely in the mind the more violently the prison of indiscreet silence constricts them. Frequently they flow more broadly because they consider themselves safer, since they are not seen outwardly by those who might rebuke them.

Consequently the mind is sometimes lifted into pride and regards those whom it hears speaking as though they were weak. When it closes the bodily mouth, it does not recognize how much it opens itself to vices through pride. It suppresses the tongue and raises thought; and when through negligence it gives no attention to itself, it accuses everyone else more freely within itself because it does so more secretly.

[Vet. XXVI.] Often those who are excessively silent, when they suffer some injustice, break out into sharper pain precisely because they do not speak of what they endure. If the tongue were calmly to express the injuries inflicted, the pain would flow out from the conscience. Closed wounds cause greater torment, because when the corruption burning within is expelled, the pain is opened for healing.

[Note: Compend. II adds: “than open ones.”]

Often those who are excessively silent, when they observe the evils of some people but nevertheless press down their tongue in silence, deprive them of the use of medicine, as though they had seen wounds. They become authors of death to the extent that they refuse by speaking to expel the poison they could have removed. Hence, if immoderate silence were not blameworthy, the prophet would not say: “Woe is me, because I was silent” (Isa. 6:5).

61. The tongue must be restrained through discipline and released by necessity.—What, then, is required amid these considerations, except that the tongue be carefully restrained under the balance of great moderation, but not bound indissolubly? Otherwise, when released, it may fall into vice, or, when restrained, may grow numb even with respect to usefulness.

Hence it is said through one of the sages: “The wise person will be silent until the time” (Ecclus. 20:7), so that, when he recognizes the appropriate moment, he may set aside the restraint of silence and devote himself to usefulness by speaking what is fitting.

Solomon says: “A time for silence, and a time for speaking” (Eccl. 3:7). The times of alternation must be carefully weighed, lest the tongue uselessly release itself through words when it ought to be restrained, or lazily restrain itself when it could speak usefully.

The Psalmist rightly considered this and expressed it in a brief petition, saying: “Set a guard, Lord, over my mouth, and a door of circumspection around my lips” (Ps. 149:3). A door is opened and closed. Therefore, by asking not that an obstacle be placed before his mouth but that a door be set there, he clearly taught that the tongue must be restrained by discipline and released by necessity, so that a discerning mouth may be opened by speech at the fitting time and closed again by silence at the fitting time.

Because either blessed Job’s friends, or all heretics—whose type these men represent—do not know how to preserve this, they are said to utter words into the wind. Words that are not made solid by the weight of discretion are carried away, plainly, by the breeze of frivolity.

# BOOK EIGHT

It expounds the final part of the sixth chapter, beginning at verse 27, and, together with the seventh chapter, the whole of the eighth chapter. In this exposition, from verse 11 of the eighth chapter to the end, it discusses at length the vice of hypocrisy.

[Col. 0801]

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0801D]

### 1. Job’s humility and love toward his persecutors; how the Church’s charity toward heretics is prefigured.—In the preceding book we have already discussed how blessed Job makes known to us the power of his humility, saying:

### Chapter 6, verse 27

“You rush upon the orphan, and you strive to overthrow your friend.”

For he indicates how great a weakness he recognizes in himself when he calls himself an orphan. But because love does not know how to withdraw even when wounded, he complains that people wish to overthrow him and yet declares himself to be their friend.

As we have often said, his words apply so specifically to him that through them, by the prophetic Spirit, the judgment of the faithful people is also expressed: the voice of the universal Church, which, enduring the hostility of heretics, recognizes its own weakness through humility and nevertheless does not withdraw from the greatness of preserving love.

The people of the holy Church may appropriately be called an orphan, because it is the child of the dead Father: it already follows the life of the one who rose again through faith, but does not yet behold him through sight. Heretics rush upon the orphan when they afflict the humility of the faithful people with importunate and false arguments.

Yet he is their friend whom they strive to overthrow, because the faithful people of God do not cease lovingly to call even those persecutors whom they endure to the truth.

[Note: Norman, German, and certain printed editions: “whom it endures by tolerating their persecution.”]

But amid these considerations it must be understood that holy men neither fear to endure falsehoods through weakness nor ever remain silent when wounded concerning the truth. Hence what follows:

## CHAPTER TWO

[Col. 0803A]

### Verse 28

“Nevertheless, complete what you have begun; give ear and see whether I lie.”

2. True charity toward adversaries must be accompanied by patience and kindness.—Because he does not fear to endure adversity, let him say: “Nevertheless, complete what you have begun.” But because he does not withhold the teachings of truth even from his persecutors, let him add: “Give ear and see whether I lie.”

As though he were saying openly: “I am not frightened by the injuries already inflicted, nor do I hide the aids of correction from ungrateful hearers, because I am strengthened by being pressed by evils and grow through kindly devoting myself to the very people who persecute me.”

The minds of the saints, in this battle of temptations, fortified by the shield of patience and girded with the swords of love, take up courage to endure evils and display kindness in returning good, so that they may receive the weapons of hatred powerfully and return the arrows of love courageously.

[Note: The printed editions read “exercises” (*exercet*) for “displays” (*exerit*), the latter being found in all our manuscripts.]

For one does not go armed into battle if, taking up a shield, one does not use swords, or, using swords, one is not protected by a shield.

[Note: Vindocensis and Corbeiensis Germanicus read simply: “one who takes up a shield does not use swords.”] Therefore the soldier of God, caught in the battle of adversity, must place before himself the shield of patience, lest he perish, and, ready to preach, must hurl the arrows of love, so that he may conquer.

Paul briefly indicates the whole of this armor when he says: “Love is patient; love is kind” (1 Cor. 13:4). But when one of the two is absent, there is no love: either a person tolerates the wicked without kindness and therefore does not love them, or, presenting himself without patience, neglects to tolerate those whom he loves.

Therefore, if true love is to be held by us, patience must support kindness, and kindness in turn must support patience. Thus patience may strengthen the citadel of kindness, building a great structure in our hearts, while kindness may adorn the buildings founded upon patience.

Blessed Job, therefore, ready for patience, says: “Nevertheless, complete what you have begun.” Endowed with kindness, he adds: “Give ear and see whether I lie.”

3. The Church strives to recall the erring by rational argument.—Because the holy Church, formed by the instruction of humility, does not command what it says rightly to those who err as though by authority, but persuades them by reason, it is rightly said here: “See whether I lie.”

As though it were saying openly: “Do not believe what I assert merely because of my authority; weigh by reason whether it is true.” And even when it says something that cannot be grasped by reason, it rationally teaches that human reason should not be demanded concerning hidden things.

But often heretics, when they are given an opportunity for reasoning, break out into quarrelsome contention. Hence what follows aptly:

## CHAPTER THREE

### Verse 29

“Answer, I beg you, without contention.”

243 4. Heretics seek quarrels, not rational arguments.—For heretics do not try to attain the truth through their inquiries, but to appear victorious. Although they desire to display themselves outwardly as wise, inwardly they are bound by the chains of the foolishness of their pride.

It follows that they seek the contests of disputes, cannot speak peacefully about God, who is our peace, and become inventors of quarrels out of the business of peace. Paul rightly says to them: “If anyone seems to be contentious, we have no such custom, nor does the Church of God” (1 Cor. 11:16).

The text rightly continues:

## CHAPTER FOUR

### The same passage

“And while speaking what is just, judge.”

5. Nothing should be spoken without deliberation.—For the one who speaks, while awaiting the judgment of his hearer concerning his words, is placed, as it were, under the judgment of the person by whom he is heard.

[Note: The manuscripts vary considerably. Corbeiensis Germanicus and Compend. I read: “while awaiting the judgment of his various hearers.” Vindocensis I: “while awaiting for a long time the judgment of his hearer.” Another reading: “while awaiting the judgment of his hearers concerning his words.” Colbertinus Regius and Germanicus: “while awaiting the judgment of his hearer concerning his words.”]

Therefore whoever fears that his words will be rejected must first examine what he says, so that a fair and discerning judge may sit between heart and tongue, carefully weighing whether the heart offers upright words which the tongue may usefully convey to the judgment of the hearers.

Blessed Job, acting through his own words against his friends but announcing through them what concerns us against heretics, rebukes the haste of speakers and gathers their words toward their own mind, saying: “While speaking what is just, judge.”

As though he were saying openly: “If you do not wish to be reproved in what comes forth from you through the outlet of speech, hold within yourselves the balance of justice, so that what is said outwardly may please through the weight of truth in proportion as the scales of discretion weigh it inwardly.”

[Note: Compend. I reads: “if, in that which is cast out to us through the issuing-forth of speech …”]

And because those who know how to judge their own words first exercise right judgment concerning the words of others, after he has said, “While speaking what is just, judge,” he aptly adds at once:

## CHAPTER FIVE

### Verse 30

“And you will find no iniquity on my tongue, nor will folly resound in my throat.”

6. The censor of his own words judges others more rightly; falsehood must be refuted before truth is taught.—As though he were saying openly: “If you weigh your own words more carefully, you will weigh those of others more truthfully; and when what you say begins to be right, you will recognize that what you hear is just.”

For my tongue would by no means resound folly to you if it did not proceed from your own conscience. Thus the holy Church first strives to show that the assertions of its enemies are false, and then to open the teachings of truth, because, when they think they themselves hold to what is right, they stubbornly attack what they hear as right.

The heretics must therefore first perceive their own error, lest they contradict the truth they have heard.

[Note: Ebroicensis reads: “lest they contradict the truth when it has been heard.”] For if the thorns of the fields are not removed by the farmer through the cutting of the plowshare, the earth does not produce the seed it receives as a crop; and when the physician does not expel the corruption through opening the wound, healthy flesh does not grow together in the place of corruption.

Therefore, first destroying what is perverse, he should say: “While speaking what is just, judge.” Then, introducing what is right, he should add: “And you will find no iniquity on my tongue, nor will folly resound in my throat.”

[Vet. III.] Heretics are accustomed to say some things openly and to hold other things secretly.

[Note: The printed editions read: “to hold other things secretly” (*alia occulte*).] Open speech is signified by the tongue, while secret deliberation is signified by the throat.

7. Unlike heretics, the Church does not proclaim one thing openly and conceal another.—The holy Church therefore has neither iniquity on its tongue nor folly resounding in its throat, because what it preaches through public speech it also preserves through inward faith. It does not teach one thing openly and retain another secretly; rather, it brings forth in speech what it thinks and safeguards in life what it speaks.

[Note: The printed editions read “teaches” (*docet*) for “brings forth” (*ejicit*); the latter is the better sense and is unknown in the manuscripts.]

Whatever flows through the tongue of preaching from the banquet of heavenly wisdom, it tastes through the throat of silent expectation.

[Note: Gemetensis reads “sows” (*seminat*) for “flows forth” (*emanat*).] But blessed Job, as one member of the universal Church, making his own meaning known and revealing the hearts of all the elect, discloses everything he thinks, so that the testimony of his speech may make the uprightness of his mind known.

The text continues:

## CHAPTER SIX [Vet. IV, Rec. III]

### Chapter 7, verse 1

“Human life upon earth is a warfare.”

8. Our life is both warfare and temptation in the same sense; it is temptation for itself.—In this passage the old translation does not call human life “warfare,” but “temptation.” Yet if the meaning of both words is considered, what sounds different outwardly forms one and the same understanding in harmony.

For what is expressed under the name of temptation except a struggle against evil spirits? And what is designated by the term warfare except an exercise against enemies? Temptation, therefore, is itself warfare, because while life keeps watch against the snares of evil spirits, it is unquestionably sweating in the ranks of battle.

It should be noted, however, that this same human life is not said merely to have temptation, but is declared to be temptation itself. For having voluntarily fallen from the state of its creation and having been subjected to the corruption of its decay, it generates troubles for itself from itself and has already become what it endures.

For because, in its decline, it abandoned the state of the mind, what does it find within itself except the movement of instability?

[Note: Gemetensis reads: “the mind, having declined, abandons [it].”] Hence, even if it raises itself now toward the pursuit of higher things, it immediately falls back upon itself through the impulse of slippery mutability. It wishes to stand in contemplation, but cannot. It strives to fix the step of thought, but is weakened by the falls of its own infirmity. Since it willingly sought the burdens of its mutability, it bears them unwillingly.

A tranquil human being could have possessed the flesh if, rightly created by the Creator, he had wished to be possessed by him. But when he strove to raise himself against his Creator, he immediately found within himself the dishonor of the flesh.

Yet because punishment is propagated along with guilt from the beginning, we are born with the defect of weakness implanted in us, and we bring along with us, as it were, an enemy whom we overcome only with difficulty. Human life, therefore, is temptation itself, since from itself it gives rise to what destroys it. Although it always cuts down through virtue what it generates through weakness, nevertheless it always generates through weakness what it may cut down through virtue.

9. The ways in which we are tempted; one temptation succeeds another.—Human life is therefore temptation, even though it is already restrained from the perpetration of iniquity. For even in good works it is darkened sometimes by the memory of evil, sometimes by the obscurity of seduction, and sometimes by the interruption of its own intention.

One person has already restrained the flesh from lust, yet still endures fantasies of lust, because he involuntarily remembers what he willingly did and suffers as punishment what he once regarded as pleasure. But because he fears being dragged back to the conquered fault, he restrains his stomach with the strength of remarkable abstinence, and his face grows pale through abstinence.

When pallor is seen on his face, his life is praised by people as worthy of reverence. Immediately empty glory comes with words of approval to the mind of the abstinent person. Since his shaken mind cannot subdue it, he seeks to wipe from his face the pallor through which it had come.

Thus it happens that, bound by the chains of weakness, he either fears being subjected again to lust through food while fleeing the pallor of abstinence, or, overcoming the impulse of lust through abstinence, fears that his pallor may serve empty glory.

Another person, overcoming a fall into pride, now embraces the state of humility with his whole desire. But when he sees certain proud people breaking out into the oppression of the innocent, he is inflamed by the arousal of zeal and is forced for a time to set aside what he had resolved. He exercises the force of righteousness and opposes the wicked not with gentleness but with authority.

Thus it often happens that he either abandons zeal for righteousness through devotion to humility, or, conversely, disturbs the humility he had maintained through zeal for righteousness. Since it is scarcely possible to preserve both the authority of zeal and the humility of one’s purpose at the same time, a person becomes unknown even to himself through his agitation. He is intensely uncertain lest pride insinuate the authority of zeal into his deceived mind, or fearful sluggishness merely pretend to be humility.

[Note: Bellovensis, Norman, Compend. II, and several others read this as printed. Printed editions and certain manuscripts have: “and the humility of his purpose cannot be preserved.” In Corbeiensis Germanicus the negative particle is absent, or scarcely so.]

Another person, considering how great the fault of deceit is, resolves to fortify himself with the stronghold of truth, so that no false speech may come forth from his mouth and that he may wholly separate himself from the transgression of lying. But often, when the truth is spoken, the life of his neighbor is burdened. When he fears inflicting injury upon another, he returns, as though out of a desire for piety, to the fault of deceit that he had previously suppressed.

Thus, even if malice does not possess the mind, the shadow of lying nevertheless obscures within it the ray of truth. Hence, because a person who is questioned often cannot remain silent, he either slaughters his own mind by speaking falsely or burdens the life of his neighbor by speaking the truth.

Another person, stirred by love of his Creator, strives through continual prayer to suspend his mind from earthly thoughts and place it in the hidden security of inward peace. But during the very ascent of his prayer, while he strives to be lifted from low things, he is beaten back by the images of low things. The eye of the mind stretches itself toward beholding the light, but is darkened by images of earthly things arising from bodily experience.

Thus it often happens that the mind intent upon prayer, wearied by its own weakness, either abandons prayer and grows sluggish through idleness, or, if it remains long in prayer, the darkness of the images that have arisen grows denser before its eyes.

[Note: Vindocensis and Corbeiensis Germanicus: “the darkness of hidden images ceases.”]

[Vet. V.] 10. Sometimes we fall worse because of the occasion supplied by virtues.—Well, therefore, it is said: “Human life upon earth is temptation,” since even there it finds the guilt of descent where it thought it had grasped the progress of ascent. The mind is confused by the very thing from which it was striving to rise out of confusion, so that it returns, struck back by that through which it had already passed, gathered and united within itself.

One person, a stranger to instruction in the divine law, is weighed down by his ignorance, so that he does nothing for the attainment of salvation. Another, endowed with knowledge of the divine law, rejoices that he possesses understanding beyond others. Because he exults in a private joy, he dissipates within himself the gifts of the understanding he has received; and he is shown to be worse than the others in judgment precisely because he appears for a time more enlightened than they.

Because the gifts of the virtues do not lift the former person up, he also turns aside from the simple path of righteousness. Regarding himself as a stranger to the heavenly gift, he acts wickedly, as though the less he had received of the sublime gifts of the heavenly gift, the more safely he might do so.

The spirit of prophecy fills another person, raises him to foreknowledge, and displays future things to him as though they were already present. But because he is often lifted above himself in many matters so that he may contemplate the future truthfully, his mind, led into confidence in itself, assumes that the spirit of prophecy—which cannot always be possessed—is always present to him.

When he considers everything he perceives to be prophecy, because he attributes prophecy to himself even when he does not possess it, he loses it to the extent that he was able to possess it. Thus it happens that he returns sorrowful after the merits of others, from the place where he had gone ahead rejoicing in the estimation of everyone.

[Note: Four English manuscripts read: “so that he returns afterward to the merits of others.” The reading “to” also occurs in Lyranus and Bigot; in a later hand in Uticensis it was added.]

Human life, therefore, is temptation: it cannot rise to the heavenly reward if it is alien to virtues, or, enriched with spiritual gifts, sometimes falls more disastrously because of the occasion supplied by virtues.

[Vet. VI.] 11. Our life is warfare because, as it grows, it diminishes and comes to an end.—Since we said above that what is called warfare is also temptation, it must be understood most carefully that the term warfare suggests something more to us than the name temptation.

Our understanding is enlarged by the expression “warfare,” because through warfare one moves daily toward the end. As the place in the order of warfare increases, the whole warfare of human beings simultaneously diminishes.

Human life, therefore, is warfare upon earth because, as we said above (Book 7, no. 31), each person, while progressing daily toward the end of life through the increase of time, ceases to live even as life increases.

The days await their coming; but when they come to increase life, they are already subtracted from the increase of life, just as the traveler’s step, while advancing toward what lies ahead, diminishes the journey that remains. Our life, therefore, is warfare: the more it is led toward increase, the more it is brought to an end so that it may no longer be.

Well, therefore, it is said: “Human life upon earth is a warfare,” because, while it desires to grow through the spans of time, it passes beyond that same span by which it gathers itself through losing it.

[Note: Turonensis, Longipontanus, Norman, English, and other manuscripts read this as printed. Recent editions instead have: “toward the extent of those who, by losing it, …”; Gemetensis reads “which, by weighing it,” in place of “which, by losing it.”]

Accordingly, the course of warfare itself is also aptly expressed when what follows is immediately added:

## CHAPTER SEVEN

### The same passage

“And like the days of a hired laborer are its days.”

12. The chosen person, like a hired laborer, wishes his days to pass quickly. He labors in what belongs to another. He takes care that no day slips by empty of work.---

A hired laborer eagerly desires that his days pass more quickly, so that he may reach the reward of his labor without delay. Thus the days of the person who is truly and eternally wise are rightly compared with the days of a hired laborer, because he regards the present life as a road, not a homeland, and as military service, not the palm of victory; and he sees himself as farther from the reward the more slowly he comes to the end.

It must also be considered that a hired laborer sweats in labors belonging to another, yet prepares a reward of his own. Our Redeemer says: “My kingdom is not of this world” (John 18:36). Therefore all who, endowed with hope of heavenly things, are worn down by the discipline of the present life labor in what belongs to another. For often we are compelled to serve even the reprobate and constrained to render to the world what belongs to the world; we are wearied indeed by labor belonging to another, but nevertheless receive our own rewards. Through this we arrive at what is our own: by administering purely what belongs to another.

To the contrary, Truth says to certain people: “If you were not faithful in what belongs to another, who will give you what is yours?” (Luke 16:12).

[Note: Coc. and the later editions thereafter read “who will believe?” Some manuscripts support this reading, though they are not the better witnesses.]

It must also be known that a hired laborer carefully ensures that no day ever passes empty of work, and that the anticipated end of the period does not come to the reward empty-handed. In his zeal for labor he considers what he may receive when the time of recompense arrives. For when the work increases, confidence in the reward advances; but when the work grows slack, hope of recompense grows weary. Hence each of the chosen, weighing his life as the days of a hired laborer, advances toward the reward with greater confidence the more vigorously he now perseveres in increasing labor. He reckons the passing of the present time, counts the days together with their works, and fears that the moments of his life may pass empty of labor. He rejoices in adversities, is refreshed by suffering, and is strengthened by grief, because he sees himself destined to be rewarded with the greater abundance of the rewards of the life to come in proportion as he gives himself more truly to daily deaths for love of that life.

For this reason the citizens of the heavenly homeland say to its Creator through the voice of the Psalmist: “For your sake we are put to death all day long” (Psalm 43:22). Hence Paul says: “Every day I die for your glory, brothers” (1 Corinthians 16:31). Again he says: “For this reason I suffer these things, but I am not ashamed; for I know whom I have believed, and I am certain that he is able to preserve my deposit for that day” (2 Timothy 1:12). Thus, whatever labors holy men now offer in commendation of the truth, they already hold as so many pledges of their reward, enclosed within the chamber of hope.

[Note: Vindoc. and Corb. Germ. read: “so that, when the heat is now felt as severe in the work, refreshment may at some time be received in that rest.” Most manuscripts, which we follow, have “but severe,” not “more severe,” as it is read in the printed edition.]

“But severe heat is now felt in the work, so that refreshment may at some time be received from rest.” Hence it is aptly added at once:

## CHAPTER VIII [Rec. IV]

**VERSES 2–3.**—“As a servant desires the shade, and as a hired laborer awaits the end of his work, so I have had empty months and have counted laborious nights for myself.”

13. He desires eternal rest. He is a servant, not free, so long as he is subject to corruption.---

To desire shade as a servant is, after the heat of temptation and the sweat of labor, to seek the rest of eternal refreshment. That servant desired this shade who said: “My soul thirsted for the living God; when shall I come and appear before the face of God?” (Psalm 41:3). And again: “Woe is me, that my sojourning has been prolonged” (Psalm 119:5).

[Note: Thus Vindoc., Compend., Norm., etc.; the later printed editions read “as though fleeing the heat of the labor of the field.”]

As though fleeing the heat of harsh labor and seeking a covering in order to obtain the rest of refreshment, he says again: “I shall enter into the place of the wondrous tabernacle, even to the house of God” (Psalm 41:5).

Paul longed to grasp this shade, “having the desire to depart and to be with Christ” (Philippians 1:23). Those who said, “We who have borne the burden of the day and the heat” (Matthew 20:12), had already reached this shade through the perfection of their desire.

The one who is said to desire shade is rightly called a servant, because every chosen person, so long as he is constrained by the condition of weakness, is held beneath the yoke of ruling corruption, as though beneath the anxiety of heat. When he has been stripped of corruption, he then recognizes himself as free and tranquil. Hence Paul rightly says: “Creation itself will be liberated from the slavery of corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God” (Romans 8:21).
