For now the punishment of corruption weighs down the chosen, but then the glory of incorruption exalts them; and just as nothing of freedom is now displayed in God’s children because of the burdens of present necessity, so then nothing of servitude will appear in God’s servants because of the glory of the freedom to come. Creation, therefore, stripped of the slavery of corruption and receiving the dignity of freedom, is transformed into the glory of the children of God, because, united to God through the Spirit, it shows that it has passed beyond and subdued what it itself was as creation.

But whoever still desires shade is a servant, because so long as he endures the heat of temptations, he bears the yoke of a wretched condition. Here it is aptly added: “And as a hired laborer awaits the end of his work.”

248 [Rec. V]

14. The labor of the chosen is lightened by consideration of the reward.---

When a hired laborer sees the work that must be done, he immediately instructs his mind regarding the length and burden of the labor; but when he recalls his weary spirit to consider the reward of the work, he promptly restores his spirit’s vigor for the exercise of labor, and what he judged heavy in the work he considers light because of the recompense.

[Note: The Norman and Vindoc. manuscripts read “when they endure insults to their honor”; Bellov. reads “insults to dishonor.”]

Thus, when the chosen endure the adversities of this world—when they tolerate insults to their honor, losses of possessions, and bodily sufferings—they reckon that the things by which they are exercised are grievous; but when they direct the eyes of their mind toward consideration of the eternal homeland, they discover by comparison with the reward how light is what they suffer. What pain shows to be very difficult to bear is made light by prudent consideration of the recompense.

This is why Paul always rises against adversities stronger than himself, since, like a hired laborer, he awaits the end of his work. He judges what he endures to be grievous, but weighs it as light by consideration of the reward. He himself shows how grievous was what he suffered (2 Corinthians 11:23), for he testifies that he was more abundantly in prisons, excessively in blows, and frequently in deaths; that from the Jews he received five times forty lashes less one; that he was beaten with rods three times, stoned once, shipwrecked three times, and spent a night and a day in the depths of the sea; that he endured dangers from rivers, from robbers, from his own people, from the Gentiles, in the city, in the wilderness, at sea, and among false brothers; that he labored in work and hardship, in many fasts, in hunger and thirst, in cold and nakedness; that outside there were battles and within fears; and that he declares himself burdened beyond his strength, saying: “We were weighed down beyond measure, beyond our strength, so that we were weary even of living” (2 Corinthians 1:8).

But how he wipes away the sweat of so great a labor with the cloth of recompense, he himself declares, saying: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy of the future glory that will be revealed in us” (Romans 8:18).

[Note: Norm., Bellovac., and Germ. read: “unto the glory that is to come.”]

He therefore awaits the end of his work like a hired laborer who, when he considers the progress of the recompense, regards as insignificant the labor by which he is almost exhausted. It is aptly added: “So I have had empty months, and have counted laborious nights for myself.”

15. The chosen have empty months and laborious nights when they suffer want and adversity and do not yet possess the reward.---

The chosen serve the Creator of all things and are often constrained by lack of worldly goods; they cling to God through love, yet are in need of the supports of the present life. Those who do not seek present things through their actions therefore spend empty months apart from the world’s advantages. They also endure laborious nights, because they bear the darkness of adversities not only to the point of want but often even to bodily torment.

[Note: Gussanv. reads “for it is to be despised”; no manuscripts support this reading.]

To endure contempt and poverty is not laborious for good minds; but when adversity turns into affliction of the flesh, labor is undoubtedly felt through pain.

[Vet. VIII] It may also appropriately be understood that every holy person spends empty months like a hired laborer, because he already endures the labor but does not yet possess the reward; he bears the one and awaits the other. He counts laborious nights because, by exercising himself in virtues, he heaps up for himself the adversities of the present time. For if he does not desire to advance in mind, he perhaps feels less keenly the harsh things that belong to the world.

16. The Church has empty months in its weak members and laborious nights in its strong ones. The emptiness of labor for the world is recognized by its outcome.---

Yet if this interpretation is referred to the voice of holy Church, its meaning is investigated somewhat more subtly. She has empty months because in her weak members she sustains earthly actions that flow away without the reward of life.

[Note: Gemet. reads: “which, in its lowest members, bears earthly things”; 2 Vindoc. reads: “which, in its weakness.”]

She counts laborious nights in those of her strong members in whom she bears manifold tribulations. In this life some things are laborious, some empty, and some both empty and laborious. To be exercised by the tribulations of the present life through love of the Creator is indeed laborious, but it is not empty. To be released into the pleasures of the world through love of the world is empty, but not laborious. To suffer some adversities of that same world through love of the world is both empty and laborious, because the mind is afflicted by adversity and is not filled with the reward of recompense.

In those, therefore, who, already placed within her, continue to flow away into pleasures and consequently are not enriched by the fruit of good works, holy Church spends empty months, because she expends the periods of life without the gift of recompense. In those, however, who, devoted to eternal desires, suffer the adversities of this world, she counts laborious nights, because she bears the darkness of tribulations as though in the gloom of the present life.

In those, finally, who both love the passing world and are nevertheless wearied by its opposition, she endures empty months and laborious nights together, because no subsequent recompense rewards their life, while present tribulation constricts it.

It is rightly said that she has not days but empty months in them. The name “months” signifies a collection and sum of days. By “day,” therefore, each individual action is expressed; by “months,” the outcome of actions is indicated. Often, when we do something in this world, suspended in eager hope, we do not think that what we are doing is empty. But after we reach the end of our actions, when we do not obtain what we seek, we grieve that we have labored in vain.

Thus we spend not only empty days but also empty months when we judge that we have labored without fruit in earthly actions, not from the beginning of the actions but from their end. For when adversity follows our labors, the months of our life are, as it were, condemned as empty, because from the completion of our actions it becomes clear how vainly we labored in them.

17. The Church laments this empty labor.---

Since in sacred Scripture “night” is sometimes used for ignorance, as Paul confirms when he says to disciples who know the life to come: “You are all sons of light and sons of day; we are not of night or of darkness” (1 Thessalonians 5:5)—and before this he had said: “But you, brothers, are not in darkness, so that that day may overtake you like a thief” (ibid., 4)—the voice of holy Church may here be understood as proceeding from those who, after the darkness of their ignorance, return to the love of righteousness and, illumined by the rays of truth, wash away through tears what they did wrong.

For each person who has been enlightened looks back and sees how shameful was the labor he undertook for love of the present life.

[Vet. IX] In these people, therefore, as they return to life, holy Church compares her labor to that of the servant who suffers heat and the hired laborer who desires the end, saying: “As a servant desires the shade and as a hired laborer awaits the end of his work, so I have had empty months and have counted laborious nights for myself.”

In the comparison two things were set forth; in the expression of weariness two things are immediately added. To the one suffering heat he assigned empty months, because the more eternal refreshment is sought, the more clearly it is seen how vainly one labors for this life. To the one awaiting the end he added laborious nights, because the more closely we look toward the reward we are to attain at the end of our work, the more deeply we lament that we long remained ignorant of what we seek.

Hence the care of the penitent is also vigilantly expressed when he is said to have counted laborious nights, because the more truly we return to God, the more subtly, in our grief, we weigh the labors we endured in this world through ignorance. For the sweeter what each person desires from eternal things becomes, the more grievous what he endured for love of present things is shown to him.

But if the words that follow are weighed only according to the historical sense, they undoubtedly express how the mind of one who is grieving is varied by different movements, driven by sorrow through the changing forms of desire. For it follows:

## CHAPTER IX

**VERSE 4.**—“If I sleep, I shall say: When shall I rise? And again I shall await evening.”

[Note: This text is always read thus in most manuscripts. Two Vindoc. manuscripts, however, have “when shall I rise again?” (*resurgam*); none has “when shall I rise” (*consurgam*), as the printed editions do.]

18. In grief he despises present things and awaits future ones.---

At night the day is sought, and during the day evening is desired, because pain does not permit present things to please; and when experience of present things afflicts the mind, desire continually consoles it and directs it by expectation toward other things. But because the afflicted mind is led by longing, while its pain is not brought to an end even when it is led astray by desires, it is rightly added:

**IBID.**—“I shall be filled with sorrows even to darkness.”

The cause of this same sorrow is expressed when it is immediately added:

## CHAPTER X [Rec. VI]

**VERSE 5.**—“My flesh is clothed with corruption and the filth of dust; my skin has dried up and is contracted.”

19. The instability of fallen humanity.---

We discuss these matters more subtly and appropriately if we return to the order of the exposition already begun. For by sleep the torpor of idleness is expressed, while by rising the exercise of action is expressed. Since evening also corresponds to sleep, under the name of evening the desire for idleness is again signified.

Holy Church, however, so long as she leads the life of corruption, does not cease to mourn the losses caused by her mutability. Human beings had been created for this purpose: that, with a steadfast mind, they should raise themselves to the citadel of contemplation, and that no corruption should turn them away from love of their Creator.

But when humanity moved the foot of its will toward sin from the innate firmness of standing, it immediately fell from love of its Creator into itself. Abandoning the love of God—the true citadel of steadfastness—it could not even remain established in itself; for, driven by slippery mutability, plunging downward through corruption, it also became divided against itself.

[Note: Coc. and the later editions read “departed” instead of “became divided,” which is read in all the manuscripts, both English and ours.]

Now, because it is not fixed in the firmness of its created condition, it is continually altered by the movement of conflicting desire, so that, while at rest, it desires activity, and while occupied, it longs for idleness. Because the mind did not wish to stand when it could, it is now unable to stand even when it wishes. Abandoning contemplation of its Creator, it lost the strength of its salvation, and wherever it is placed, it always seeks another place.

Expressing, therefore, the variability of the human mind, let it say: “If I sleep, I shall say: When shall I rise? And again I shall await evening.” As though it were plainly saying: Nothing that the mind has received is sufficient, because it has lost the one who alone could truly have been sufficient. In sleep I desire rising; in rising I await evening, because while at rest I seek the exercise of action, and while active I seek the idleness of rest.

251 [Vet. X]

20. Even the righteous must seek to rise from sin. He desires to be fortified by adversities so that he may not be exalted.---

This may nevertheless be understood in another way. To sleep is to lie in sins. For if the term “sleep” did not signify guilt, Paul would never say to his disciples: “Awake, you righteous, and do not sin” (1 Corinthians 15:34). Hence he admonishes his hearer, saying: “Rise, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ will enlighten you” (Ephesians 5:14).

[Note: Gemet. and other excellent manuscripts read: “and Christ will enlighten you” (*et illuminabit tibi Christus*).] Again: “It is now the hour for us to rise from sleep” (Romans 13:11). Solomon likewise rebukes the sinner, saying: “How long, you sluggard, will you sleep?” (Proverbs 6:9).

Thus every chosen person, when oppressed by the sleep of sin, strives to rise for the watches of righteousness. But often, when he has risen, he feels himself exalted by the very greatness of his virtues. Hence, after his virtues, he desires to be tested by the adversities of the present life, lest he fall more disastrously through confidence in his virtues. For if he did not know that he was better preserved through temptation, the Psalmist would never say: “Test me, Lord, and try me” (Psalm 25:2).

It is rightly said, therefore: “If I sleep, I shall say: When shall I rise? And again I shall await evening,” because in the sleep of sin the light of righteousness is sought; and when the prosperity of virtues elevates the mind, helpful adversity is desired, so that when the spirit is lifted by the joy of its virtues more than it ought to be, it may be steadied by the sorrow brought forth through the opposition of the present life.

[Note: Vindoc. and Corb. read: “because the light of righteousness is oppressed even in the sleep of sin.”]

Hence it is not said, “I shall fear evening,” but “I shall await it.” For we await favorable things and fear adverse ones. The righteous person therefore awaits evening, because when it is necessary for him to be exercised by tribulation, adversity itself becomes favorable to him.

21. In this life no one is ever free from the temptation of sin. He does not fear temptations but prepares himself against them.---

The name “evening” may also designate the temptation of sin, which often assails the mind more fiercely in proportion as the spirit raises that same mind more deeply toward heavenly things. For sin is not abandoned in this life through the exercise of righteousness in such a way that one remains unshaken in that righteousness. Although righteousness now drives guilt from the dwelling place of the heart, the guilt that is repelled nevertheless sits at the doors of our thoughts and knocks to have them opened.

Moses also intimated this spiritually when, narrating bodily events as moments in time, he said: “Light was made”; and shortly afterward added: “Evening was made” (Genesis 1:3, 5).

The Creator of all things, foreseeing human guilt, then expressed in time what now occurs in the mind. Light is brought toward evening, because the shadow of temptation follows the light of righteousness. But because the light of the chosen is not extinguished by temptation, it is said that not night but evening was made. [Note: One Vindoc. manuscript reads “in the hearts of the upright”; another has “of the chosen” or “of the upright.” Utic. formerly read “of the chosen,” subsequently replaced by “of the upright.”]

For temptation often hides the light of righteousness in the hearts of the upright, but does not destroy it; it draws it, as it were, toward the pallor of trembling, but does not extinguish it completely.

The chosen therefore seek rising after sleep and await evening after rising, because they awaken from sin to the light of righteousness and, placed in that very light of righteousness, continually prepare themselves against the allurements of temptations. They do not fear these temptations but await them, because they know that even temptations can advance the usefulness of their righteousness.

22. No one possesses complete salvation in this life.---

[Note: Ebroic. reads “they cannot possess a whole mind.”]

However greatly they contend against their corruption by virtue, they cannot possess complete salvation until the day of the present life comes to an end. Hence it is added: “And I shall be filled with sorrows even to darkness.”

Now adversities rush upon them; now even favorable things flatter them with crafty cheerfulness. Now rising vices stir up war against the flesh; now, when defeated, they summon the mind to exaltation. The life of the good is therefore filled with sorrows even to darkness, because, so long as the time of corruption is being lived, it is shaken by inward and outward affliction and finds security of salvation only when it has entirely left behind the day of temptation.

Thus the cause of these same sorrows is rightly added at once: “My flesh is clothed with corruption and the filth of dust.”

[Vet. XI]

[Note: Turon. reads “when voluntarily.”]

As we said a little earlier, humanity voluntarily abandoned its innate firmness and plunged itself into the abyss of corruption. Hence it now either falls through unclean works or is defiled by illicit thoughts. To put it this way, our very nature, subjected through punishment to its own guilt, has already become something beyond nature; when relaxed, it is led into perverse works, but when restrained, it is darkened by the importunate thought of perverse works.

Through the completion of an illicit action, corruption afflicts the flesh; through the levity of an evil thought, dust rises, as it were, before the eyes. By consenting to vices we are worn down by corruption; by tolerating the images of vices in the heart we are defiled by the filth of dust.

He therefore says: “My flesh is clothed with corruption and the filth of dust.” As though he were plainly saying: The carnal life I suffer is either polluted by the decay of slippery action or oppressed by the darkness of miserable thought arising from the memory of vices.

23. The flesh of the Church rots in its slippery members and is soiled in those who seek earthly things.---

Yet if we understand this as spoken by the voice of the universal Church, we undoubtedly find her at one time burdened by the corruption of flesh and at another weighed down by the filth of dust. For many within her, while serving the love of the flesh, rot in the stench of lust. There are also some who abstain from the pleasure of the flesh but nevertheless lie with their whole mind in earthly activities.

Let holy Church speak through the words of one of her members; let her say what she endures from each of these two classes of people: “My flesh is clothed with corruption and the filth of dust.” As though she were plainly indicating: Many are members of mine through faith, yet are neither sound nor clean in their conduct, because either, overcome by shameful desires, they flow down into the corruption of decay, or, devoted to earthly activities, they are sprinkled with dust.

[Note: The subject “the dust of earthly desire,” found in Coc. and the later editions, is absent from the manuscripts and earlier editions.]

In those whose conduct is slippery, whom I endure, I groan over flesh that is rotting; but in those who seek earthly things and whom I suffer, what else do I carry but flesh defiled with dust?

[Note: There is remarkable disagreement among the manuscripts and editions here. Gemet. and several Norman manuscripts read: “what else than defiled dust do I carry?” Turon.: “what else than defiled with dust do I carry?” Corb. Germ., Colb., and Germ.: “than foul dust do I carry.” The old editions: “than defiled dust.” Coc. and the later editions: “than members defiled with dust.” One Reg. manuscript, which we follow, reads: “than defiled flesh,” with “flesh” understood.]

24. The skin of the Church consists of those who serve only outward concerns; hence it dries up.---

Hence it is aptly added concerning both groups together: “My skin has dried up and is contracted.” In the body of holy Church, those who serve only outward concerns are appropriately called skin. This skin is drawn tight as it dries, because carnal minds, while loving present things and desiring what is, as it were, placed nearby, do not wish to extend themselves toward future things through perseverance.

While they neglect the richness of inward hope, they dry up so that they may be drawn tight; for if despair did not dry their hearts in this way, the heat of their faintheartedness would never contract them.

The Psalmist had feared this contraction when, fearing dryness of mind, he said:

[Note: Ebroic., Lyran., and Bigot. read “observing.”]

[Note: Vindoc., Gemet., Corb. Germ., Colb., and Reg. read “as with the fat of richness.” The same is now found in Utic. Formerly it read “as with fat and richness.”]

“Let my soul be filled as with fat and richness” (Psalm 62:6).

The fat of richness fills the soul when the infusion of heavenly hope refreshes it against the heat of present desires. The skin, therefore, dries and is contracted when the heart, devoted to external things and dried out by despair, is not stretched toward the love of its Creator but, in the manner of which I have spoken, folds back upon itself in wrinkled thought.

25. One who considers the brevity of this life is not held by love of present things.---

It must be considered that carnal minds love present things because they scarcely reflect on how fleeting the life of the flesh is. For if they perceived the speed of its passing, they would scarcely love it even when it prospers.

Holy Church, however, in her chosen members, daily perceives how swiftly external things pass away, and for this reason fixes the foot of her attentive purpose in inward things. Hence it is aptly added:

## CHAPTER XI [Rec. VII]

**VERSE 6.**—“My days have passed more swiftly than a web is cut off by the weaver.”

26. Time is appropriately compared with a web.---

By a very fitting likeness, the time of the flesh is compared with a web, because just as a web advances through threads, so mortal life advances through successive days. But the more it advances toward increase, the more it approaches being cut, because, as we said above (Book VII, no. 30), when the times we have received pass away, the times to come grow shorter, and of the whole span of life those things that are coming become fewer in proportion as many have passed.

A web, tied above and below, is attached to two pieces of wood so that it may be woven; but the more the woven part is rolled up below, the more the part yet to be woven is unfolded above.

[Note: Gemet. reads “is doubled”; Lyran. and Big. “is spread out”; Ebroic. “is folded in.” Utic. formerly had “is doubled,” but now, by correction, has “is spread out.”]

Thus we roll up the times of our life that have passed as though below, and unfold those that are to come from above, because the more numerous the past becomes, the less the future begins to be.

But because even a web is insufficient to express our time—for the speed of our life surpasses its own rapidity—it is rightly said now: “My days have passed more swiftly than a web is cut from the weaver.”

[Note: Thomas James reports that the English manuscripts read “is not fixed.” We have found this variant, which he proposes doubtfully, in no manuscript codex.]

A web has the slowness of progress, but the present life has no delay in its decline. In the web, when the hand of the laborer is fixed, the arrival of the end is postponed; in life, however, because we consume time as it continually comes to an end, we reach the end of our journey even while resting, and through the course of our passing we proceed even while sleeping.

The chosen, therefore, because they see the moments of the present life running on with haste, do not fix the intention of their hearts upon this journey of such great mobility. Hence it is aptly added at once:

**IBID.**—“And they have been consumed without any hope.”

27. The chosen think about death even when healthy; the reprobate do not, even when it is near.---

The mind of the reprobate is bound to the days of the present life by such great love that they always desire to live here, so that, if they were able, they would wish never to bring the course of their life to an end. They despise thinking about what is to come, place all their hope in passing things, and desire to possess nothing except what passes away.

When they think excessively about passing things and hope for nothing that remains, the eye of the heart is closed by an insensible blindness, so that it cannot turn toward eternal light. Hence it often happens that illness already shakes the body and approaching death cuts short the strength of the vital spirit, yet they do not cease to care for worldly things.

The avenger is already dragging them to judgment, yet they themselves, occupied with passing things through anxious planning, think of nothing except how they may still live in this world. They arrange everything they are leaving behind as though they were possessing it.

[Note: Some manuscripts read “to be possessed”; others, “by possessing.” In Utic. the reading formerly was “by possessing,” but the “o” has now been changed to “a.”]

For the hope of living is not broken even when life is ending. They are already being dragged to judgment by sentence, yet they still cling through concern to things they are to possess. In a hardened mind death is believed to be far away even when it is felt.

Thus the soul is released from the flesh while retaining an immoderate love for present things; and while it is led to eternal punishment, it does not even know where it is being led. It abandons what it refused to cease loving before the end and suddenly finds without end what it never foresaw.

By contrast, the mind of the upright is directed toward eternity even when the present life accompanies it happily. It enjoys great bodily health, yet the soul is not held back by confidence in it.

[Note: The printed editions have “no article.” Corb., Bellovac., Norm., Corb. Germ., and others have “the article.” See Book II, no. 22, where through a typographical error “through particles” is printed, whereas it should read “through articles.”]

No moment of death has yet broken forth, yet he sees it as present every day. Because life slips away without ceasing, his hope of living is wholly cut off. It is therefore rightly said of days that pass away: “They have been consumed without any hope.”

As though it were plainly said: I have not placed the confidence of my mind in the present life, because I have despaired of everything that passes by trampling it underfoot.

[Note: Thus most manuscripts read, corresponding to the words “without any hope.” Vindoc. reads “I despised”; the old editions, “I overcame”; the later editions, “I disdained.”]

Hence it is aptly added at once:

## CHAPTER XIII [Rec. VIII]

**VERSE 7.**—“Remember that my life is wind.”

28. The present life is dear to those who do not attend to the eternal and worthless to those who do. Consideration of life’s brevity is a pleasing offering to God.---

Those love the life of the flesh as though it were permanent who do not attend to the extent of the eternity of the life to come. Since they do not consider the solidity of everlastingness, they regard exile as a homeland, darkness as light, and movement as stability, because those who do not know greater things cannot judge lesser ones.

The order of judgment requires that we transcend what we endeavor to examine. For if the mind cannot rise above all things, it cannot clearly see those things by which it is overcome. Thus the wicked mind is not sufficient to assess the course of the present life, because through love it yields to the very thing it admires.

Holy men, however, as they raise their hearts toward eternal things, weigh how brief is what is enclosed by an end; and what passes away becomes more worthless to their senses in proportion as what, once received, never departs shines through their enlightened understanding. When they behold the infinity of everlastingness, they no longer desire as something great whatever is confined by an end.

But the uplifted mind is led beyond the boundaries of time even while it is held in time by the flesh; and it despises finite things all the more deeply as it recognizes the infinite more truly.

[Note: Bellovac. reads “entreaty” (*imploratio*).]

Yet this very consideration of human brevity is a great offering of virtue to our Creator. Hence, rightly, an offering of that virtue is presented together with supplication when it is said: “Remember that my life is wind.”

As though it were plainly said: In your kindness, look upon what passes swiftly, because you ought to look upon me the more mercifully in proportion as I myself do not turn my eyes away from consideration of my brevity.

But since, when the time of the present life is cut short, one does not return afterward to the work of earning pardon, it is rightly added:

## CHAPTER XIV

**IBID.**—“Nor will my eye return to see good things.”

[Note: Gemet. reads: “Nor will it return.”]

### 29. After death there is no opportunity to merit forgiveness

The eye of the dead does not return to see good things, because the soul, once it has been stripped of the flesh, does not return to perform righteous works. Hence the rich man whom the flame of hell tormented recognized that he could not restore himself by working; for he was striving not to help himself, but his brothers left behind, saying: “I beg you, father Abraham, to send him to my father’s house, for I have five brothers, so that he may testify to them, lest they too come to this place of torment” (Luke 16:27).

Hope, even false hope, commonly sustains a sorrowful spirit. But so that the wicked may feel their punishment more grievously, they also lose hope of forgiveness. Therefore, handed over to avenging flames, he desired—as we have said—not to help himself but his brothers, because he recognized that he would never be free from the torment of the fires, with the punishment of despair added to it. Hence Solomon says: “Whatever your hand is able to do, perform it diligently, because there is neither work, nor reason, nor knowledge, nor wisdom in the underworld, to which you are hastening” (Ecclesiastes 9:10).

The eye, therefore, will not return to see good things, because once the mind has encountered its recompense, it is in no way recalled to the practice of working. Since everything that is seen passes away, while what follows remains, blessed Job aptly embraced both in one verse, saying: “Remember that my life is wind, and my eye will not return to see good things.” Contemplating the course of present things, he says: “Remember that my life is wind.” Considering the eternity of what follows, he adds: “And my eye will not return to see good things.” Here he also appropriately assumes at once the voice of the whole human race deprived of the benefit of redemption, saying:

### CHAPTER XV [Formerly XIII]

[Column 0819A]

**Verse 8.—“Nor will the sight of man look upon me.”**

### 30. Christ’s grace does not free the one whom it does not reform now

The sight of man is the mercy of the Redeemer, which, when it looks upon the hardness of our insensibility, softens it. Hence, as the Gospel also testifies, it is said: “The Lord looked upon Peter, and Peter remembered the word that Jesus had spoken; and going outside, he wept bitterly” (Luke 22:61).

But the soul stripped of the flesh is no longer looked upon by the sight of man, because after death he is not freed whom grace did not reform toward forgiveness before death. Hence Paul says: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Corinthians 6:2). Hence the Psalmist says: “For his mercy is forever” (Psalm 117:1). For the one whom mercy does not rescue now, justice alone condemns after the present age.

Hence Solomon says: “Wherever the tree falls, whether toward the south or toward the north, there it will remain” (Ecclesiastes 11:3). For when, at the time of the human fall, either a holy or a wicked spirit receives the departing soul from the prison of the flesh, it will retain it with itself forever, without any change, so that the soul neither falls from exaltation into punishment nor rises from being submerged in eternal punishments to the remedy of deliverance.

Therefore the holy man, considering the losses of the human race—that it is withdrawn from the present age without knowledge of the Redeemer and buried irreparably in eternal fires—and taking its voice upon himself, says: “Nor will the sight of man look upon me.” For the grace of the Redeemer, who does not look upon one whom it now does not regard so as to correct him, will not then look upon him so as to hide him from destruction.

[Note: According to our manuscripts. But the more recent printed editions have *cogitatione* (“by thought”).]

[Note: From four English manuscripts, all the Norman manuscripts, and the manuscript of Vendôme, we have restored the negative particle suppressed by Cocc. and those who follow him. In their editions it reads: “whom he now regards,” instead of “whom he now does not regard.”]

When the Lord comes for judgment, he sees the sinner in order to strike him, but he does not see him so as to recognize him for the granting of saving grace; he examines his sins and does not acknowledge the life of those who are perishing. Hence the holy man, when he had confessed that after the present life he could not be seen with the sight of man, appropriately added:

### CHAPTER XVI [Recent edition IX]

**The same passage.—“Your eyes are upon me, and I will not stand.”**

### 31. At the judgment Christ will see the wicked in order to strike those whom here he did not see in order to show mercy

As if he were saying openly: “Coming as a strict judge for judgment, you do not see in order to save, but you see in order to strike; for the one whom in the present life you do not regard with the compassion of your dispensation, by regarding him afterward you extinguish through justice.”

Now every sinner does not fear God and yet lives; he blasphemes and prospers, because the merciful Creator, whom he wishes to correct by waiting for him, does not wish to punish him merely by looking upon him, as it is written: “You overlook the sins of human beings for the sake of repentance” (Wisdom 11:24).

[Note: Gembloux and Corbie German, in the first hand, read *dissimulans peccata* (“overlooking sins”).]

But then the sinner does not stand when he is looked upon, because when the strict judge examines his merits minutely, the guilty person is unequal to the torments.

### 32. The righteous know that they would perish if God judged them after removing his mercy

This also accords with the voice of the righteous, whose minds are always anxiously intent upon the coming examination. They fear everything they do, carefully considering before what a judge they will stand.

[Note: We have restored the word *qui* (“who”), omitted in the Vulgate editions, chiefly from the Norman manuscripts.] They behold the power of his majesty and weigh how heavily they are bound by the guilt of their weakness. They enumerate the evils of their own works and set against them the good deeds of the Creator.

They consider how strictly he judges many evil things and how subtly he weighs good works, and they know beforehand, without doubt, that they would perish if they were judged with mercy removed.

[Note: Here, from the manuscripts and other editions, we have supplied *multa* (“many things”), which is lacking in Gussanville’s edition.] For even the very fact that we seem to live justly is itself blameworthy if, when divine mercy judges our life, it does not excuse it before itself.

Hence in this same book it is written: “The stars are not clean in his sight” (Job 25:5). For when strictly judged by him, even those who shine through the purity of holiness possess stains of defilement.

Therefore it is rightly said: “Your eyes are upon me, and I will not stand.” As if it were said openly in the voice of the righteous: “If I am examined by a subtle investigation, I do not rise to endure the judgment, because life is not sufficient for punishment if the severity of just retribution presses upon it.”

The guilt and punishment of the same human race are appropriately set forth briefly when it immediately says:

### CHAPTER XVII [Formerly XIV, Recent edition X]

**Verse 9.—“As a cloud is consumed and passes away, so one who descends to the underworld will not ascend.”**

[Column 0820C]

### 33. For the condemned there is no return to forgiveness or to the things they loved

A cloud is lifted toward higher places, but when thickened it is driven by the wind so that it runs; by the heat of the sun it is scattered so that it vanishes. So, indeed, are human hearts: by the faculty of reason they rise toward high things, but when driven by the breath of the wicked spirit they are dragged here and there by the movements of their perverse desires. Under the strict regard of the heavenly Judge, however, they melt as though under the heat of the sun; and once handed over to places of punishment, they do not return thereafter to the practice of working.

Therefore the holy man, expressing the pride, course, and failure of the human race, says: “As a cloud is consumed and passes away, so one who descends to the underworld will not ascend.” As if he were speaking openly, saying: “The one who advances proudly toward destruction runs upward only to fail; if guilt once drags him into punishment, mercy no longer brings him back to forgiveness.”

[Note: Cocc., followed by the more recent editions, changed *emicant* (“spring forth”) into *emigrant* (“depart”).]

Hence it is further added:

### CHAPTER XVIII

**Verse 10.—“Nor will he return any longer to his house.”**

### 34. The house of the mind is what it inhabits through love. The hearts of the despairing resemble clouds and pour themselves outside themselves

Just as the body’s dwelling is a bodily house, so for every mind that becomes its house which it is accustomed to inhabit through desire. Therefore no one returns any longer to his own house, because once someone has been handed over to eternal punishments, he is in no way recalled to that place to which he had adhered through love.

The name “underworld” can also designate the sinner’s despair, of which the Psalmist says: “But in the underworld, who will confess to you?” (Psalm 6:6). Hence it is written again: “When the wicked comes into the depth of sins, he despises” (Proverbs 18:3). Whoever succumbs to wickedness certainly abandons the life of righteousness by dying. But whoever, even after sin, is crushed by the weight of despair—what else does he do but bury himself after death in the punishments of the underworld?

Therefore it is rightly said: “As a cloud is consumed and passes away, so one who descends to the underworld will not ascend,” because often despair is joined to the commission of wickedness, and the path of return is already cut off.

The hearts of the despairing are rightly compared with clouds, because they are dark with the gloom of error and thick with the multitude of sins. But they are consumed and pass away because, illuminated by the brightness of the final judgment, they are scattered.

“House” can also be understood as the dwelling of the heart. Hence a healed man is told: “Go to your house” (Mark 5:19), because it is fitting that after forgiveness the sinner return to his own mind, lest he again admit what would justly strike him.

[Note: Gembloux reads “and not again.”]

But one who has descended to the underworld will not ascend any further to his house, because despair, having crushed him, casts him out from the dwelling of his heart. He cannot return inward, because, poured out externally, he falls daily, driven toward worse things.

Human beings were created to contemplate the Creator, so that they might always seek his appearance and dwell in the solemnity of his love.

[Note: Utica, Gembloux, two Vendôme manuscripts, Corbie German, Regius, and the old editions read *in societate illius amoris* (“in the fellowship of that love”); Colbert has *in soliditate* (“in firmness”), a reading preferred by Cocc. and later editors.] But having been cast outside themselves through disobedience, they lost the place of their own mind, because, scattered along dark paths, they withdrew from the indwelling of the true light.

Hence it is appropriately added:

### CHAPTER XIX [Formerly XV]

**The same passage.—“Nor will his place know him any longer.”**

### 35. God is the place of human beings, abandoned through disobedience. At the judgment those who despised him here will not be recognized by him

The place of human beings—though not a spatial place—is the Creator himself, who created them so that they might subsist in him. Human beings abandoned this place when, listening to the words of the seducer, they departed from the love of their Creator.

But when almighty God also showed himself bodily to humanity by redeeming it, he himself, so to speak, following the tracks of his fugitive, came as the place to retain the human being whom he had lost. For if the Creator could in no way be called a place, the Psalmist would not praise God by saying: “The children of your servants will dwell there” (Psalm 101:29). We say “there” only when we designate a particular place.

But many, even after receiving the help of the Redeemer, fall into the darkness of despair; and they perish all the more wickedly because they also despise the remedies of mercy that have been offered.

[Note: Gembloux, Utica, and others read “the help of redemption.”]

Therefore it is rightly said of the condemned person: “Nor will his place know him any longer,” because in the judgment he will then be not recognized by his Creator with all the greater strictness, the more he is not now recalled to the grace of restoration even by gifts.

Hence it must be noted with the greatest care that he does not say, “Nor will he know his place any longer,” but, “Nor will his place know him any longer.” Since knowledge is attributed not to the human being but to the place, the Creator himself is clearly designated under the name of “place.” Coming as a strict judge for the final examination, he will say to those persisting in iniquity: “I do not know where you are from” (Luke 13:25).

But the elect, the more strictly they see the wicked rejected, the more diligently cleanse themselves daily from the filth of the sins they have committed.

[Note: From these words—“cleanse themselves more diligently”—the remainder is lacking in the manuscripts of Beauvais and Gembloux, up to “I will declare my iniquity.” The words were also formerly missing from Utica.]

When they see others perishing and growing cold toward the love of life, they kindle themselves earnestly to the tears of repentance. Hence it is appropriately added:

### CHAPTER XX

**Verse 11.—“Therefore I too will not spare my mouth.”**

### 36. The elect forestall the judge’s anger through confession

He spares his mouth who is ashamed to confess the evil he has done. To put the mouth to labor is to occupy it with confessing the iniquity that has been committed. But the righteous person does not spare his mouth, because, forestalling the anger of the strict Judge, he attacks himself with words of his own confession.

[Note: The printed editions read *non parcit* (“does not spare”), and shortly afterward *non erubescit* (“is not ashamed”), against the English manuscripts and most others.]

Hence the Psalmist says: “Let us come before his face with confession” (Psalm 94:2). Hence Solomon says: “Whoever hides his crimes will not prosper, but whoever confesses and abandons them will obtain mercy” (Proverbs 28:13). Again it is written: “The righteous person is his own accuser at the beginning” (Proverbs 18:17).

But the mouth is opened to confession only when the spirit is constricted by fear through consideration of the strict judgment. Hence it is appropriately added:

### CHAPTER XXI [Recent edition XI]

**The same passage.—“I will speak in the affliction of my spirit.”**

### 37. The confession of sins must be accompanied by the grief of repentance

Affliction of spirit moves the tongue, so that the voice of confession attacks the guilt of an evil deed. It must also be understood that often the wicked confess their sins but refuse to mourn them. The elect, however, pursue their faults—which they disclose through words of confession—with the tears of strict reproof.

Hence blessed Job, after promising that he would not spare his mouth, rightly added the affliction of his spirit. As if he were openly confessing, saying: “The tongue speaks of guilt in such a way that the spirit does not wander elsewhere, free from the spur of sorrow; rather, by speaking of sins I open the wound, and by considering my sins for correction I seek the wound’s healing through the medicine of sorrow.”

For whoever points out the evils he has committed but refuses to weep over what he has pointed out is like someone who removes a garment and exposes a wound, but in a sluggish mind applies no medicine to the wound.

The voice of confession, therefore, must be shaken forth only by sorrow, lest a wound that has been exposed but neglected—now touched more freely through human knowledge—fester more disastrously.

In contrast, the Psalmist not only exposed the wound of his heart but also applied to the exposed wound the medicine of sorrow, saying: “I declare my iniquity, and I will think upon my sin” (Psalm 37:19).

[Note: Corbie German, Gembloux, the Roman Psalter, and Utica read *annuntiabo* (“I will announce”); the printed editions read *pronuntiabo* (“I will declare”).]

By declaring it, he exposes the hidden wound; by thinking upon it, what else does he do but apply medicine to the wound?

[Formerly XVI.] But for the afflicted mind that carefully considers its own losses, conflict arises for itself against itself. For when it urges itself toward the lamentations of repentance, it tears itself apart through a hidden reproach.

Hence it is appropriately added:

### CHAPTER XXII

**The same passage.—“I will converse with the bitterness of my soul.”**

### 38. The repentant mind discovers many things in itself that must be mourned. It recalls how ungrateful it has been for God’s many gifts

Afflicted by fear of divine judgment, while we mourn certain things wrongly done, the very force of our bitterness rouses us more vigilantly to examine ourselves, and we discover in ourselves other things that we must mourn even more. Often what lay hidden from us while we were sluggish becomes known more subtly when we are weeping. The afflicted mind more certainly discovers the evil it had done without knowing it, and through its own conflict more truly sees how far it has strayed from the peace of truth, because it detects within itself the guilt of which, when secure, it does not remember.

The bitterness of repentance, growing within, thrusts insistently upon the ashamed heart the unlawful things it has committed. It displays the strict Judge against them, strikes it with threats of punishment, wounds the soul with fear, confounds it with shame, reproves its unlawful impulses, disturbs the repose of guilty security, and enumerates what good things the Creator bestowed and what evils it itself returned for his good things:

- that it was wonderfully created by him;
- that it was freely nourished;
- that it was enriched with the substance of reason in its creation;
- that it was called by the grace of its Creator;
- that, although called, it itself refused to follow;
- that the mercy of the One who called did not despise it, though deaf and resisting;
- that, enlightened by gifts, it nevertheless voluntarily blinded itself through wicked deeds even after receiving those gifts;
- that, purified from the errors of its blindness by the scourges of paternal care, it was brought back from the pains of the scourges to the joys of salvation by the medicine of mercy;
- that, although subject to certain sins, even if not grave ones, it nevertheless did not cease to sin amid the scourges;
- and that heavenly grace did not abandon its sinner even when despised.

When, therefore, it reproaches the afflicted mind with such severity—now by recalling God’s gifts, now by reproaching its own deeds—the bitterness of the soul has its own tongue in the hearts of the righteous. It speaks to them all the more subtly because it is heard inwardly.

Hence it does not say, “I will speak in the bitterness of my soul,” but, “I will converse with the bitterness of my soul.” The force of sorrow, considering each sin and rousing the sluggish mind to lament, forms words of conversation with it, as it were, in which the corrected person may discover himself and rise more watchfully to guard himself.

Let the righteous man therefore speak in his own voice, and, bearing the figure of holy Church, let him speak in our voice: “I will converse with the bitterness of my soul.” As if he were expressing it more plainly, saying: “Within, I converse against myself with the sorrow of my heart, and outwardly I hide myself from the scourge of the Judge.”

But the mind pressed by the pains of repentance is constricted within itself and separated by intense reflection from every pleasure of the flesh. It longs to advance toward higher things, yet still feels resistance arising from the body’s corruption. Hence it is appropriately added:

### CHAPTER XXIII

[Column 0824B]

**Verse 12.—“Am I a sea, or a sea-monster, that you have surrounded me with a prison?”**

### 39. The human being, the devil, and the carnal are confined in a prison when they cannot accomplish what they wish

A human being is surrounded by a prison because he often strives to rise toward higher things through progress in the virtues and yet is hindered by the corruption of his flesh. The Psalmist rightly prays to be freed from this, saying: “Bring my soul out of prison, that I may confess your name” (Psalm 141:8).

What is meant by the name “sea” except the fluctuating hearts of the carnal, swollen with proud thoughts?

[Note: Lyran and Bigot have “with turbulent thoughts.” Utica now also reads this, whereas it formerly had “with swollen thoughts.”]

And what is expressed by the name “sea-monster” except the ancient enemy? When he penetrates by possessing the minds of worldly people, he swims, as it were, in their slippery thoughts.

[Note: Ebroic, Lyran, and Bigot read “the minds of the carnal.” Utica presents both readings.]

[Note: Gembloux and Tours have “as if in their slippery thoughts.” This was formerly read in Utica; it now has “in their slippery thoughts.” Bigot and Lyran likewise have this reading.]

But the sea-monster is confined in a prison, because the wicked spirit, cast down into the lower regions, is restrained by the weight of its punishment so that it cannot fly up to heavenly things. Peter bears witness to this, saying: “God did not spare the angels who sinned, but, having dragged them down with the chains of hell, handed them over to Tartarus to be kept for judgment and punishment” (2 Peter 2:4).

The sea-monster is bound in a prison because it is forbidden to tempt the good as much as it desires. The sea too is surrounded by a prison, because the swollen and insane desires of carnal minds are burdened by the narrowness of their inability to accomplish the evils they desire.

Often they desire to rule over those who are better, but nevertheless, by the divine judgment that orders all things wondrously, they have been made subject to them. In their pride they desire to harm the good, yet, being subject to them, they hope for assistance from them. For the fulfillment of the pleasures of the flesh they desire a long life in the present, yet they are swiftly snatched away from it.

Of such people the Psalmist rightly says: “He established the waters as in a wineskin” (Psalm 77:13). The waters are in a wineskin when their slippery desires, because they do not find the effect of action, are pressed down beneath the carnal heart.

Thus the sea-monster and the sea are pressed by the enclosing prison, because either the wicked spirit or its followers—in whose minds it gathers itself and in whom it rolls up waves of swelling thoughts—are constrained by the heavenly Judge, so that they cannot accomplish the evils they desire.

[Formerly XVII, Recent edition XII.]

### 40. The righteous complain that they suffer the same thing—not because of pride, but because of love for the truth

The holy men, the more purely they contemplate the secrets of heavenly things, daily breathe toward them with increased ardor. They desire to be fully satisfied there, from which they now taste only a little through the mouth of contemplation. They desire perfectly to subdue the stimulus of the flesh and to tolerate nothing unlawful in their thoughts arising from its corruption.

But because it is written: “The corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling burdens the mind occupied with many thoughts” (Wisdom 9:15), although they already rise above themselves in intention, they nevertheless grieve that they are still enclosed in the prison of corruption, subject to the uncertain movements of their weakness.

He therefore says: “Am I a sea, or a sea-monster, that you have surrounded me with a prison?” As if he were saying openly: “The sea and the sea-monster—the wicked and the wicked spirit who is their author—rightly are confined in the prison of their punishment, because they desire to break loose only for the license to commit iniquity. But I, who now desire the freedom of your eternity, why am I still oppressed by the prison of my corruption?”

Yet the righteous do not ask this arrogantly, because, inflamed by love of the truth, they profoundly desire to cross beyond the constraints of their weakness. Nor is it unjustly ordained by the author of the righteous, because he torments the desires of his elect by delaying them, purifies them through torment, and ensures that, through the delay, they may eventually grow stronger for receiving what they desire.

While the elect are kept from inner rest, they return to their own hearts. There, hidden from the tumult of their flesh, they seek a most pleasant retreat.

[Note: Two manuscripts of Vendôme read “from the stimuli or disturbances of their flesh.”]

Yet there they often feel the barbs of temptation and suffer the incitements of the flesh. They discover the heaviest labors precisely where they had sought great rest from labor.

[Note: Later editions read *ad quietam cordis patriam* (“to the quiet homeland of the heart”), against the Beauvais, Vendôme, Tours, Norman, and other manuscripts.]

Therefore, after describing the prison of his corruption, the holy man hastens to return to the quiet spaces of the heart. Because he finds the same conflict within that he fled externally, he immediately adds:

### CHAPTER XXIV [Recent edition XIII]

**Verses 13–14.—“If I say, ‘My bed will console me, and I will be refreshed as I speak with myself upon my couch,’ you will terrify me through dreams, and through visions you will shake me with horror.”**

[Note: Gembloux reads “upon my bedding.”]

[Column 0825D]

### 41. The righteous return from external things to the heart but find no rest there. They are troubled by the terror of God’s judgments

In sacred speech, “bed,” “couch,” or “bedding” commonly signifies the secret place of the heart. Hence the bride, under the appearance of every soul, aroused by the hidden goads of holy love, says in the Song of Songs: “On my bed by night I sought him whom my soul loves” (Song of Songs 3:1).

The beloved is sought on a bed and during the night because the appearance of the invisible Creator is found in the heart’s chamber when every image of bodily vision has been suppressed. Hence Truth says to those same lovers: “The kingdom of God is within you” (Luke 17:21). And again: “If I do not go away, the Paraclete will not come” (John 16:7).

As if he were saying openly: “If I do not withdraw the body from the eyes of your intention, I do not lead you to invisible understanding through the Comforter Spirit.”

Hence the Psalmist says of the righteous: “The saints will rejoice in glory; they will exult on their couches” (Psalm 149:5), because when they flee from external evils, they rejoice securely within the secrets of their minds.

But the joy of the hearts will be perfect only when there is no external struggle of the flesh. For as long as the flesh entices, since the wall of our house is shaken, the chamber too is disturbed.

Hence the same Psalmist rightly says: “You have turned his entire bed in his sickness” (Psalm 40:4), because when temptation of the flesh shakes us, our weakness, made to tremble, also confounds the chamber of the mind.

What else do we understand by dreams and visions in this passage except images of the final and strict examination? We perceive it now to some extent through fear, but we do not yet see it as it truly is.

The holy men, as we have said, always return to the secrets of the heart when in this world they suffer either prosperity beyond their desire or adversity beyond their strength. Weary from external labors, they seek the chambers of the mind as though they were a couch or bed.

But when through certain images of thought they perceive how subtle the divine judgments are, they are disturbed by a vision of a dream in the very repose of their couch. They contemplate how strict the Judge will come, who, when he illuminates the secrets of hearts by the force of his immense majesty, will bring all their sins before their eyes.

They weigh how great the shame will be when they are then confounded in the sight of the entire human race, all the angels, and the archangels. They consider what torment will remain after the shame, when Gehenna consumes both the guilt-ridden soul, dying eternally, and the flesh, failing without end.

When the mind is shaken by such a fearful image, what else is seen than a sad dream upon the couch?

Let him therefore say: “If I say, ‘My bed will console me, and I will be refreshed as I speak with myself upon my couch,’ you will terrify me through dreams, and through visions you will shake me with horror.”

As if he were openly confessing, saying: “If, fleeing external things, I return inward and desire to rest somewhat in the chamber of my heart, there, when you set me before the contemplation of your strictness, you terrify me intensely through the very images of my foresight.”

[Note: The printed editions have “in the chamber of the heart I desire.” Here: “There, when you set me before the contemplation of your strictness.”]

It is rightly said: “And I will be refreshed as I speak with myself upon my couch,” because when we return, weary, to the silence of our mind, we turn over within ourselves the hidden words of our thoughts, as though conversing upon a couch.

But this very conversation of ours is turned into fear, because through it the understanding is more forcefully opened to us—the understanding that brings the terror of the Judge before our mind.

[Note: This is the reading of Beauvais, Corbie German, and the Norman manuscripts. The printed editions have *innotescat* (“may become known”); Vendôme, instead of *in mente* (“in the mind”), has *intente* (“intently”).]

[Column 0827A]

[Formerly XVIII.]

### 42. Six causes of dreams

But lest anyone try to investigate these matters according to the literal sense, it is especially necessary to inquire in how many ways dream-images affect the mind.

Sometimes dreams arise from fullness of the stomach or from emptiness; sometimes from illusion; sometimes from thought together with illusion; sometimes from revelation; and sometimes from thought together with revelation.

We all know the first two by experience, while we find the remaining four in the pages of sacred Scripture.

For unless dreams generally arose from the hidden enemy through illusion, the wise man would not have said: “Dreams have led many astray, and vain illusions” (Ecclesiasticus 34:7). Or certainly: “You shall not practice divination, nor observe dreams” (Leviticus 19:26). These words clearly show what detestable things are joined to divinations.

Again, unless dreams sometimes proceeded from thought together with illusion, Solomon would not have said: “Dreams follow upon many cares” (Ecclesiastes 5:2).

And unless dreams sometimes arose from the mystery of revelation, Joseph would not have seen in a dream that he was to be preferred to his brothers (Genesis 37:7), nor would an angel have warned Mary’s husband in a dream to flee to Egypt after taking the child away (Matthew 2:13–14).

[Note: Beauvais, Gembloux, Corbie German, and Colbert read “the truth warned him in a dream.” In Utica, after the word *veritas* (“truth”) was deleted, an earlier hand wrote *angelus* (“angel”).]

Again, unless dreams sometimes proceeded from thought together with revelation, the prophet Daniel, explaining Nebuchadnezzar’s vision, would not have begun from the root of thought: “You, O king, began to think upon your bed what would happen afterward, and he who reveals mysteries showed you what is to come” (Daniel 2:29).

A little later: “You were looking, and behold, there was a great statue; that statue, great and tall, stood before you” (Daniel 2:31), and so forth.

Thus, while Daniel reverently describes the dream that was to be fulfilled and makes clear from what thought it arose, he plainly shows that it often arises from thought together with revelation.

### 43. We should be slow to believe dreams. Why the devil is permitted to trouble the hearts of the saints through dreams

But clearly, since dreams vary according to so many qualities of things, they should be believed with all the greater difficulty because it is not easy to discern from what impulse they come.

Often the wicked spirit promises prosperity even to those whom it catches awake in love of the present life, while to those whom it observes fearing adversity it presents these things more harshly through dream-images, so that it may confuse the undiscerning mind by different means, either lifting it up through hope or depressing it through fear.

Often, however, it also strives to affect the hearts of the saints with dreams, so that they may be diverted, at least for a time and a moment, from the focus of solid thought, although they immediately shake their minds free from the illusion’s image.

But the ambushing enemy attacks them more severely while they sleep precisely because it cannot overcome them while they are awake. Nevertheless, the heavenly dispensation benevolently permits it to act wickedly in this way, so that even sleep itself may not be deprived of the reward of suffering in the hearts of the elect.

Therefore it is rightly said to the ruler of all: “If I say, ‘My bed will console me, and I will be refreshed as I speak with myself upon my couch,’ you will terrify me through dreams, and through visions you will shake me with horror.” For God wondrously orders all things, and he himself brings about what the wicked spirit unjustly seeks to do, permitting it to happen only justly.

But since the life of the righteous is shaken by temptation both through wakefulness and wearied by illusion through sleep; since outwardly it tolerates the troubles of its corruption and inwardly bears unlawful thoughts heavily within itself, what can it do to pull the foot of its heart away from so many snares of scandal?

Behold, blessed man, we have learned how greatly you are pressed on every side by disturbance; let us hear what counsel you find against it.

[Note: This is the reading of the manuscripts of Corbie German, Colbert, Germany, Tours, Vendôme, and Gembloux. The manuscript of Regius and some later editions have: “Behold, blessed man, we have learned how greatly you are pressed on every side by disturbance, but let us hear what counsel he finds against it.” Utica contains both readings.]

It continues:

### CHAPTER XXV [Recent edition XIV]

**Verse 15.—“Therefore my soul chose hanging, and my bones chose death.”**

### 44. The remedy for anxiety of mind is to carry it upward

What is designated by “soul” except the mind’s intention, and what by “bones” except the strength of the flesh? Everything that is suspended is unquestionably lifted up from below.

The soul therefore chooses hanging so that the bones may die, because when the mind’s intention raises itself toward higher things, it kills within itself all the strength of outward life.

The holy men know with complete certainty that they cannot have rest in this life. For that reason they choose hanging, because, abandoning earthly desires, they lift their minds toward higher things.

Those who are suspended inflict death upon their bones, because, armed for the pursuits of virtue by love of the heavenly homeland, they bring under the bond of humility that in which they had formerly been strong in the world.

[Note: Lyran and Bigot read *jugulo humilitatis* rather than *vinculo humilitatis*; Utica now has the former reading, though it formerly read the latter.]

It is pleasing to observe how Paul had suspended his soul when he said: “I live, yet no longer I, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20). And again: “Having the desire to depart and be with Christ” (Philippians 1:23). And: “For me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Philippians 1:21).

Recalling the deeds of his earthly strength, he counted certain bones within himself, as it were, saying: “A Hebrew of Hebrews; according to the law, a Pharisee; according to zeal, persecuting the Church of God” (Philippians 3:5–6).

But he immediately asserts that the hanging of the soul kills these bones within him when he adds: “But whatever gains I had, these I have considered loss because of Christ” (Philippians 3:7).

He shows that these bones were extinguished in himself even more forcefully when he adds: “For his sake I have suffered the loss of all things and consider them as refuse” (Philippians 3:8).

He then shows how lifelessly he hangs with his bones dead when he immediately adds: “That I may gain Christ and be found in him, not having my own righteousness, which is from the law, but that which is through faith in Jesus Christ” (Philippians 3:9).

But since, by adducing his testimonies, we have shown Paul suspended toward higher things and dead to the world, let us now show blessed Job, filled with the same spirit, fleeing the desire for outward life.

It continues:

### CHAPTER XXVI [Formerly XIX, Recent edition XV]

**Verse 16.—“I have despaired; I will no longer live.”**
### 45. Some righteous people possess earthly goods; others renounce them

There are some righteous people who seek heavenly things in such a way that they are nevertheless not at all severed from hope in earthly things. They possess the inheritances divinely bestowed for the assistance of necessity; they retain the honors temporarily conferred upon them; they do not covet what belongs to others, and they use their own possessions lawfully. Yet they are detached from the very things they possess, because they are not held by desire for those things themselves.

And there are some righteous people who, girded for attaining the summit of perfection, while seeking higher things inwardly, abandon everything outwardly. They strip themselves of the possessions they have; they divest themselves of the glory of honor. Through constant longing for inward things, they continually afflict themselves with a sorrow that has become their companion; they do not wish to have consolation from outward things. While they draw near to inward joys in their minds, they utterly kill within themselves the life of bodily pleasure. To such people Paul says: “For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God” (Colossians 3:3).

The Psalmist had expressed their voice when he said:

> “My soul longs and languishes for the courts of the Lord” (Psalm 83:3).

[Note: Almost all manuscripts read: “He longed and languished.”]

For those who already seek heavenly things but are nevertheless not yet wearied at all by the pleasures of earthly things long, but do not languish. But the one who longs and languishes for the courts of God is the person who, while desiring eternal things, does not remain in the love of temporal things.

For this reason the Psalmist says again:

> “My soul languished for your salvation” (Psalm 118:81).

[Note: Lyr., Bigot., Utic., Germ.: “languished in your salvation.”]

For this reason Truth itself admonishes us through the Gospel, saying:

> “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself” (Luke 9:23).

And again:

> “Unless someone renounces all that he possesses, he cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14:33).

The holy man therefore joins the company of these people, his mind separated from earthly desires, when he says:

> “I have despaired; I shall no longer live.”

For the righteous person to despair means to abandon the goods of the present life by choosing eternity, to seek what endures, and to place no confidence in temporal things. While doing this, he asserts that he shall no longer live, because, through a life-giving death, he daily puts himself to death away from the life of passion.

[Note: Vindoc. and Corb.: “he kills himself from the life of restoration.” A second Vindoc.: “he kills himself from the life of restoration.” Reg.: “he kills himself daily by the suffering of this life.”]

Far be it that the holy man should despair of the abundance of divine mercy, withdraw his heart’s step from progress along the inward path, or, abandoning love for his Creator, remain on the way as though deprived of his guide and, pierced by the sword of brigand-like despair, fall into desperation.

[Note: Longip.: “fall into desperation.”]

But lest we seem to bend his words violently according to our own interpretation, we must weigh what has preceded against what follows. For he himself immediately indicates in what sense he said these things, when he adds:

## CHAPTER XXVII [Rec. XVI]

### The same passage

> “Spare me, Lord, for my days are nothing.”

### 46. Job abandoned perishable goods through a holy despair and sought what endures forever

These two statements—“I have despaired” and “spare me”—do not seem to belong together. For the one who despairs no longer asks that he be spared, while the one who still desires to be spared plainly does not despair. The holy man therefore despairs for one reason and asks to be spared for another: while through despair he abandons the goods of passing life, he rises stronger in hope toward obtaining what endures.

Thus, by despairing, he is led more effectively to the hope of pardon: he desires future things with greater certainty the more truly he abandons present things through despair.

It should also be noted that, revealing to us the force of his heart, he expressed one judgment about himself but repeated it by indicating it three times. For what he had said earlier—“My soul chose hanging”—he repeated by adding: “I have despaired.” Then, desiring eternal things and setting temporal things aside, he finally added: “Spare me.” And what he had earlier said—“My bones are dead”—he expressed here by adding: “I shall no longer live.” Finally, he said: “For my days are nothing.”

He rightly considers his days to be nothing because, as we have often said a little earlier, the more truly holy people perceive the highest things, the more sublimely they despise earthly things. They therefore see the days of the present life as nothing because they fix the eyes of their enlightened minds upon the contemplation of eternity. When they return from that contemplation to themselves, what do they recognize themselves to be except dust? Conscious of their weakness, they fear being judged with severity. When they behold the force of such great rigor, they tremble at being examined as they are.

Hence it is appropriately added:

## CHAPTER XXVIII

### Verse 17

> “What is man, that you magnify him? Or why do you set your heart upon him?”

[Note: Gemet., Corb. Germ., First Reg., Germ.: “or why do you establish him?”—here and below.]

### 47. The saints always consider their own lowliness, as well as God’s gifts and judgments

God magnifies man because he enriches him with the abundance of reason, visits him by the infusion of grace, and exalts him through the honor of the virtue bestowed upon him. Although man is nothing through himself, God nevertheless grants him, as a gift of his goodness, participation in divine knowledge.

Yet the Lord sets his heart upon this magnified human being because, after granting gifts, he exercises judgment, weighs merits minutely, and examines the burdens of life with great severity. The more generously he has gone before a person with his gift, the more strictly he afterward demands punishment from him.

Let the holy man therefore behold the immensity of heavenly majesty and turn the eye of his consideration back toward his own weakness. Let him see that flesh cannot grasp what Truth teaches the spirit concerning itself.

[Note: First Vindoc. and Corb. Germ.: “what Truth, through itself, teaches the spirit.” The same reading is now found in Utic., and in another manuscript’s margin: “concerning itself.” Second Vindoc.: “what the spirit of truth teaches itself.” Reg.: “what the spirit of truth teaches itself.” Another Reg., with Germ. and Colb.: “what Truth teaches the spirit concerning itself.” In all our manuscripts, however, *spiritum* is read, without the addition of *sanctum* (“holy”), which appears in the printed editions.]

Let him see that even the human spirit, when lifted up, cannot endure the judgment that God applies under the examination of strict retribution. And let him say:

> “What is man, that you magnify him? Or why do you set your heart upon him?”

As though he were openly exclaiming:

Man is magnified by a spiritual gift, yet he is still flesh. You carefully examine his ways after granting him gifts, yet, if he is judged with piety removed, even the spirit lifted up toward justice cannot bear the weight imposed by your scrutiny. For although your gifts enlarge him beyond himself, his weakness nevertheless constricts him when subjected to the investigation of your strict judgment.

[Note: Ebroic.: “from your sublimity.”]

Hence it is appropriately added:

## CHAPTER XXIX [Rec. XVII]

### Verse 18

> “You visit him at dawn, and suddenly you test him.”

### 48. Those whom God has enriched with gifts he tests through temptations, so that they may learn what comes from God and what comes from themselves; therefore they are then troubled by slippery thoughts

Who among us does not know that dawn is called the time when the hours of night are already being changed into the brightness of light? We are therefore pressed by the darkness of night when we are darkened by the commission of iniquity. But night is turned into light when the darkness of our error is illumined by knowledge of the truth. Night is turned into light when the radiance of justice illumines our hearts, which the blindness of guilt had oppressed.

Paul had seen this dawn arise in the minds of the disciples when he said:

> “The night is far gone, and the day has drawn near” (Romans 13:12).

The Lord therefore visits us at dawn because he illumines the darkness of our error with the light of his knowledge, lifts us up by the gift of contemplation, and raises us to the citadel of virtue.

But it must be noted that, after God visits at dawn, he suddenly tests the human being. By approaching, he advances our hearts toward virtues; by withdrawing, he permits us to be shaken by temptation. For if the mind is not shaken by any temptation after receiving the gifts of virtues, it takes glory in possessing them from itself.

Therefore, so that it may possess both the gifts of steadfastness and a humble recognition of its own weakness, the mind is lifted to high things by the approach of grace and, by grace’s withdrawal, is tested as to what it is from itself.

This is well suggested to us by the history of sacred Scripture (3 Kings 3:16), in which Solomon is remembered as having received wisdom divinely, yet, immediately after receiving that same wisdom, as being confronted with the question of the prostitutes. As soon as he had received the grace of so great a revelation, he endured the contest involving immoral women. For often, when the consideration of inward generosity illumines our minds with the virtues granted to us, slippery thoughts immediately disturb them as well, so that the mind which exults after being lifted up by an immense gift may discover, when struck by temptation, what it is.

Thus Elijah, visited at dawn, opened the heavens by his word; yet, suddenly tested, he fled weakly through the wilderness and was afraid of one woman (3 Kings 19:3).

Thus Paul was led to the third heaven and contemplated the secrets of paradise (2 Corinthians 12:2); yet, returning to himself, he struggled against the battle of the flesh and endured another law in his members. He grieved that, through that law’s rebellion within him, the law of the spirit was wearied (Romans 7:21).

God therefore visits at dawn, but suddenly tests after the visitation, because he lifts a person up by the gift bestowed and, withdrawing it for a little while, shows the person to himself.

Without doubt, we suffer this until, after the stain of sin has been completely wiped away, we are restored to the substance of the incorruptibility that was promised.

Hence it is appropriately added:

## CHAPTER XXX [Formerly XXI, Rec. XVIII]

### Verse 19

> “How long will you not spare me, nor allow me to swallow my saliva?”

### 49. Here the taste of contemplation, but not satiety, is granted

Saliva flows into the mouth from the head, while it is carried from the mouth to the stomach when it is swallowed. What, then, is our head except divinity? From it we receive the beginning of our existence, so that we may be creatures, as Paul bears witness when he says:

> “The head of man is Christ, and the head of Christ is God” (1 Corinthians 11:3).

And what is our stomach except the mind? When it receives its food—namely, heavenly understanding—it is undoubtedly nourished and governs all the members of its actions.
