For unless the sacred writings sometimes expressed the mind under the name “stomach,” Solomon certainly would not have said:

> “The spirit of man is the lamp of the Lord, searching all the hidden places of the stomach” (Proverbs 20:27).

For when the grace of heavenly regard illumines us, it also reveals to us everything hidden within our minds.

What, then, is understood by the name “saliva” except the taste of inward contemplation? It flows from the head into the mouth because, from the brightness of the Creator, it scarcely touches us, who are still placed in this life, with a taste of revelation.

[Note: So the manuscripts read. The old printed edition has *gutta* (“drop”); Coccius and later editions have *gustus* (“taste”). The Gemet. manuscript reads *vix gusto revel.* (“scarcely reveals by taste”), and throughout has *gusto* for *gustu*.]

Hence the Redeemer, when he came, mixed saliva with clay and restored the eyes of the man born blind (John 9:6), because heavenly grace illumines our carnal thought by mingling its contemplation with it and reforms the human being from original blindness toward understanding.

For because nature, after being expelled from the joys of paradise, produced him in this exile, the human being came forth, as it were, without eyes from birth. But, as the holy man indicates, this saliva flows into the mouth, yet it is not swallowed so as to reach the stomach, because contemplation of divinity touches the understanding but does not fully nourish the mind. The spirit cannot perfectly behold what it still sees only fleetingly, since the darkness of corruption impedes it.

### 50. The mind, weighed down by the burden of the body, cannot remain attached to heavenly light for long

For behold: the mind of the elect already subdues earthly desires; it already rises beyond everything it considers as passing away; it is already withdrawn from the pleasure of outward things; and it investigates what invisible goods there are. While doing these things, it is often carried away into the sweetness of heavenly contemplation. It already sees something inwardly, as though through a mist, and with burning desire attempts to participate in the spiritual ministries of the angels. It is nourished by a taste of uncircumscribed light, and, raised beyond itself, disdains to fall back upon itself.

But because “the body that is corrupted weighs down the soul” (Wisdom 9:15), the mind cannot remain attached for long to the light that it sees only fleetingly. The weakness of the flesh itself draws back the soul that has transcended itself and brings it back to sigh for lowly and necessary things.

Saliva therefore flows down from the head and touches the mouth but does not reach the stomach, because our understanding is indeed already infused with the fluid of heavenly contemplation, but the mind is not fully satisfied. In the mouth there is taste; in the stomach there is satiety.

We therefore cannot swallow saliva, because we are not permitted to be satisfied with the good of heavenly brightness, which in our present weakness we merely taste.

But because the fact that we now know heavenly things to some extent is due to the kindness of the one who spares us, while the fact that we cannot perceive them perfectly is still due to the punishment of our ancient condemnation, it is rightly said here:

[Note: Turon., Germ., Norman, English, and old printed editions: “now heavenly things”; Vindoc. and Corb. Germ.: “now in a heavenly manner”; later printed editions: “now above us.”]

> “How long will you not spare me, nor allow me to swallow my saliva?”

As though it were openly said:

You fully spare the human being when you admit him to the perfection of your contemplation, so that, inwardly carried away, he may see your brightness and the corruption of his flesh may no longer repel him outwardly. You permit me to swallow saliva when you have filled me with the taste of your brightness to the abundance of satiety, so that I may no longer hunger through the deficiency of a mouth’s taste, but may remain solidly established in you, my mind’s stomach having been watered.

[Note: Corb. Germ., Vindoc., Norm., Bellov.: “established more firmly by the watering of the mind.” The printed editions read: “strengthened.”]

But whoever wishes to deserve the good he seeks ought to confess the evil he has done.

It follows:

## CHAPTER XXXI [Rec. XIX]

### Verse 20

> “I have sinned; what shall I do to you, O guardian of humanity?”

### 51. Having fallen by himself, the human being cannot rise by himself

Behold, he confesses the evil he has done, but he does not find any good that he ought to offer to God in recompense. For every virtue of human action is weak for washing away guilt unless the mercy of the one who spares nurtures it and the justice of the one who judges rightly does not crush it.

Hence the Psalmist rightly says:

> “Your mercy is better than life” (Psalm 62:4).

For however innocent our life may seem, it does not free us before the strict Judge if the kindness of mercy does not release us from the debt of our guilt.

Or certainly, when it is said, “What shall I do to you?”, it is plainly shown that the very good works we are commanded to perform benefit us, not the one who commands them. Hence the Psalmist says again:

> “You have no need of my goods” (Psalm 15:2).

The humility of our destitution is expressed when God is called the guardian of humanity. For if his protection does not guard us, the watchful eye of our own concern sleeps before the ambushes of the hidden enemy, as the Psalmist again bears witness:

> “Unless the Lord guards the city, those who guard it watch in vain” (Psalm 126:1–2).

We fell through ourselves, but we cannot rise by our own strength. The guilt of our own will once struck us down, but the punishment of guilt presses us down more severely each day.

[Note: Lyr. and Bigot.: “of our own pleasure.” Utic. now reads this, added in an ancient hand; previously it read “of our own will.”]

We strive through the efforts of our endeavours to rise to the righteousness we lost, but we are weighed down by the burden of our merits.

Hence it is appropriately added:

## CHAPTER XXXII [Formerly XXII, Rec. XX]

### The same passage

> “Why have you set me against you, and have I become burdensome to myself?”

### 52. By sinning, he became opposed to God

God set humanity against himself when humanity abandoned God by sinning. Captured by the serpent’s persuasion, the human being became the enemy of the one whose commands he had despised. The just Creator therefore set him against himself because, through pride, he reckoned him as an enemy.

But this very opposition of guilt became for humanity the weight of punishment, so that one who had rejoiced, as a good servant, in the freedom of incorruption should serve his own corruption badly as one falsely free.

Abandoning the healthful citadel of humility, he reached the yoke of weakness through pride. By raising the neck of his heart, he placed it beneath a yoke, because the one who refused to be subject to divine commands laid himself beneath his own necessities.

We shall show this more clearly if we describe both what the fallen person endures in the body first and afterward the burdens of the mind.

### 53. In how many ways a person is burdensome to himself, because of the body and because of the mind. The mind is both expansive and narrow

To say nothing of the fact that the body endures pains and gasps under fevers, the very condition of our body that is called health is constricted by a kind of illness of its own. For it wastes away in idleness and fails in work. When weakened by fasting, it is restored by food so that it may continue. When wearied by restoration, it is relieved by abstinence so that it may remain vigorous. It is drenched with water lest it dry out; it is wiped with linen lest it dissolve through being too thoroughly drenched. It is invigorated by labor lest it grow numb through rest; it is refreshed by rest lest it succumb to the exertion of labor. Exhausted by vigils, it is restored by sleep; overwhelmed by sleep, it is shaken awake by vigils, lest it be wearied still more by its own repose. It is covered with clothing lest it be penetrated by the adversity of cold; when weakened by the heat it has sought, it is refreshed by the blowing of breezes.

[Note: Gemet.: “and when it finds the troubles of fasting.”]

Although it seeks to avoid troubles through these things, it finds troubles through the very means by which it sought to avoid them. Poorly wounded, so to speak, it grows weak from its own medicine.

When fevers have been removed and pains have ceased, our very health is an illness that is never without the necessity of being treated.

[Note: The printed editions add *aegritudo est* (“is an illness”), a redundant addition found in none of the manuscripts.]

[Note: Bellovac. and Gemet.: “which is never without the necessity of being cared for.”]

For as many comforts as we seek for the use of living, so many medicines, as it were, do we bring against our illness. Yet the medicine itself is turned into a wound, because, clinging a little too long to the remedy we have carefully sought, we grow more seriously weak through the very thing we have prudently prepared for our restoration.

Thus presumption ought to be chastised; thus pride ought to be laid low. Because we once assumed an exalted spirit, behold, as it flows downward, we daily carry clay.

### 54. The mind itself, excluded from the secure joy of its inward secret, is sometimes deceived by hope, sometimes tormented by fear, sometimes cast down by sorrow, and sometimes raised up by false cheerfulness

[Note: Vindoc., Bellovac., one Reg., Colb., and Gemet.: “sometimes it is cast down by a sorrow that disdains”; Turon., Germ., Ebroic., with the other Norman manuscripts: “sometimes it is cast down by failing sorrow.”]

It stubbornly loves transitory things and is continually worn down by their loss, because they are also continually changed by the course that sweeps them onward. Subject to mutable things, it is itself also changed.

For, seeking what it does not possess, it anxiously perceives it; and when it begins to possess it, it is weary of having obtained what it sought. It often loves what it had despised and despises what it had loved.

With labor it learns the things that are eternal, but suddenly forgets them if it ceases to labor. It searches for a long time in order to discover some small part of the highest things, but, quickly slipping back into familiar matters, it does not even persevere for long in what it has found.

Desiring to be instructed, it scarcely overcomes its own ignorance; but once instructed, it struggles more heavily against the glory of knowledge. It scarcely subjects the tyranny of its flesh to itself, yet still endures inwardly the images of the guilt whose outward works it has already restrained by overcoming them.

It raises itself in the search for its Creator, but the friendly darkness of bodily things confuses it when it is struck back. It wishes to behold how the incorporeal governs the body, but it cannot. It wonderfully investigates what is not sufficient to answer it, and, ignorant, fails beneath the very thing it prudently investigates.

Considering itself at once expansive and narrow, it does not know what it truly judges itself to be. For if it were not expansive, it would never investigate such things so deeply; and, again, if it were not narrow, it would at least discover the very thing it investigates.

### 55. When humanity abandoned God and believed that it was sufficient for itself, it found nothing within itself except the tumult of confusion. Pressed by this, Job asks for God’s mercy

It is therefore rightly said:

> “You have set me against you, and I have become burdensome to myself.”

For when the rejected human being endures troubles both from the flesh and from the mind, he plainly carries himself as a heavy burden.

[Note: Norm. and Bellovac.: “is pressed on every side by anguish or distress.”]

He is pressed on every side by weaknesses and driven on every side by infirmities, so that the one who, after abandoning God, believed that he was sufficient for his own rest might find nothing within himself except the tumult of confusion. Once he had found himself in this condition, he sought to flee from himself, but, having despised his Creator, he had nowhere to flee.

A certain wise man, contemplating the burdens of this weakness, rightly said:

> “A heavy yoke is upon the children of Adam, from the day of their departure from their mother’s womb until the day of burial in the mother of all” (Ecclesiasticus 40:1).

[Note: Gemet.: “from their departure.”]

Blessed Job, considering these things and groaning over why they have been so ordered, does not accuse justice but seeks mercy, so that, by humbly questioning, he may knock at what divine compassion might change by sparing him.

As though he were openly saying:

Why do you despise the human being as though he were opposed to you, when I know with certainty that you do not wish even the one whom you seem to despise to perish?

Hence he appropriately expresses both the humility of confession and adds the voice of free inquiry, saying:

## CHAPTER XXXIII [Formerly XXIII]

### Verse 21

> “Why do you not take away my sin, and why do you not remove my iniquity?”

### 56. He desires the Mediator and the resurrection

What else, surely, is indicated by these words except the desire for the Mediator whose coming was awaited?

[Note: Bellov. and Gemet.: “the expectation of the Mediator desired.”]

John spoke of him:

> “Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world” (John 1:29).

Or certainly, sin is then fully taken away from the human race when our corruption is changed through the glory of incorruption. We cannot be free from guilt so long as we are held in the body of death.

The one who hopes that his iniquity will be completely removed therefore desires either the grace of the Redeemer or the firmness of the resurrection.

Hence, immediately adding both the punishment he deserved from his origin and the judgment he fears because of his own action, he continues:

## CHAPTER XXXIV [Rec. XXI]

### The same passage

> “Behold, now I shall sleep in the dust; and if you seek me in the morning, I shall not endure.”

[Col. 0836C]

### 57. While he is pressed by present punishment, he is more grievously burdened by future punishment. Humility is a covering from the judge’s sword

To the first human being after his sin it was said:

> “You are dust, and to dust you shall return” (Genesis 3:19).

“Morning” signifies that manifestation of minds which will then occur at the coming of the Judge, when thoughts are revealed, as though after the darkness of night.

Of this morning the Psalmist says:

> “In the morning I shall stand before you and see” (Psalm 5:5).

For God’s seeking means examining a person through subtle questioning and judging him by strict examination.

Blessed Job, therefore, considering the losses of human downfall, sees that he is already pressed by present punishment and is still more grievously burdened by future things. And he says:

> “Behold, now I shall sleep in the dust; and if you seek me in the morning, I shall not endure.”

As though he were lamenting more openly:

In the present I already suffer the death of the flesh, yet I still fear a more grievous death in the coming judgment—the sentence of your strictness. I endure destruction because of my guilt, but I still fear that, when I come to judgment, my guilt will be restored to me after death.

Considering outward death, therefore, he says:

> “Behold, now I shall sleep in the dust.”

Fearing inward death, he adds:

> “And if you seek me in the morning, I shall not endure.”

For however great their justice may be, not even the elect are sufficient for innocence if they are strictly examined in judgment. But they now find this consolation for their deliverance: they humbly know that they cannot be sufficient by themselves.

Under the covering of humility, therefore, they hide themselves from the sword of such great punishment. And insofar as, awaiting the terror of the coming judgment, they tremble in continual fear, they are continually being made more ready.

It follows:

## CHAPTER XXXV [Formerly XXIV, Rec. XXII]

### Job 8:1–2

> “Then Bildad the Shuhite answered and said: How long will you speak such things, and will the spirit of your mouth’s speech be manifold?”

[Note: In Gemet., Utic., and other manuscripts and editions, this is read in this way, except in Gussanv., which has *sermones* (“words”) instead of *sermonis* (“of the word”). The Hebrew text and the Chaldean paraphrase seem to support the latter reading.]

### 58. The words of the righteous are burdensome to the unrighteous. There are four kinds of power in speech; only one is subject to blame

The words of the righteous are always burdensome to the unrighteous. Whatever they hear spoken for their edification, they bear as though it were a weight placed upon them.

Bildad the Shuhite plainly indicates this about himself when he says:

> “How long will you speak such things?”

For the one who says “how long” shows that he can no longer bear words of edification. But when the wicked disdain correction, they accuse what has been spoken well. Hence he immediately adds:

> “And the spirit of the words of your mouth is multiplied.”

When multiplicity is criticized in speech, the gravity of understanding in the mind is plainly being denied.

The power of speakers is distinguished in four ways. There are some whom breadth both of thought and of speech enlarges, and there are some whom poverty both of thought and of speech constricts. There are some who possess effectiveness in speaking but lack sharpness in thought; and there are some who are supported by sharpness of thought but become mute through poverty of expression.

We observe this in human beings, just as we often observe it in things that lack sensation. Often abundant water is drawn from within and led to the surface through broad channels. Often something narrow lies hidden within and, finding cracks through which to advance only with difficulty, exudes outward in a still narrower stream.

Often something very small arises in hidden places; when it finds an open exit, it emerges through a broad opening as a thin stream, and great channels expand, but there is nothing for them to pour forth. Often, however, something extensive rises in hidden places but, confined by narrow channels, flows out very thinly.

Thus, in some people, an open mouth pours forth what a generous fountain of intelligence supplies. In others, neither thought nor the tongue conveys understanding. In others, the mouth is open for speaking, but the tongue, ready to give an answer, receives nothing from the mind. In still others, a generous fountain of thought overflows from the heart, but the tongue, like a narrow channel unequal to the task, constricts it.

Of these four qualities of speaking, only the third is subject to blame: it seizes through speech what it does not rise to through intelligence. The first is praiseworthy, because it is strong in both respects. The second is pitiable, because it humbly lacks both. The fourth should be assisted, because it cannot express fully what it understands. The third, however, should be despised and restrained, because, while it raises itself through speech, it lies prostrate in understanding. Like limbs swollen with inflammation, it proceeds to the ears of its hearers vast but empty.

[Note: All the manuscripts likewise read this. The printed editions have: “which Bildad now hurls as an accusation against blessed Job.”]

This is what Bildad now hurls as an accusation against blessed Job when he says:

> “The spirit of the words of your mouth is multiplied.”

For the one who attributes multiplicity to the words of the mouth plainly reproves poverty of heart.

[Note: Almost all manuscripts: “attributes it to the words of the mouth.”]

As though he were openly saying:

You are lifted up by an abundance of spirit in the words of your mouth, but you are constricted by poverty of understanding.

But when the wicked criticize what is right, so that they may not themselves seem ignorant of what is just, they bring forward as though unfamiliar things known to everyone—things they have learned by hearing them.

Hence Bildad immediately adds:

## CHAPTER XXXVI

### Verse 3

> “Does God overturn judgment, and does the Almighty subvert what is just?”

### 59. The wicked seek praise for their doctrine. They praise God’s justice when things go well for them; when things go badly, they condemn it

Blessed Job had neither denied these things when speaking nor been ignorant of them when silent. But, as we have said, insolent people also bring forward familiar matters boastfully, so that by speaking they may appear learned. They disdain to remain moderately silent, lest they be thought to have kept silent through ignorance.

It should be understood that they praise the uprightness of divine justice when safety lifts them to joy and scourges chastise others—when they see themselves enjoying prosperity in their affairs while others are worn down by adversity.

For while they act perversely but nevertheless consider themselves righteous, they believe that the prosperity available to them is owed to their merits. From this they conclude that God does not judge unjustly, since, as though they were righteous, no adversity troubles them.

But if the force of heavenly correction touches their life, however briefly, they immediately criticize the decision of divine judgment when struck by it—the same judgment they had shortly before extolled in admiration while they were safe. They deny that the judgment which opposes their conduct is just; they argue about divine equity; they burst into words of defiance; and, when corrected because they have done wrong, they do even greater wrong.

Hence the Psalmist rightly speaks against the sinner’s confession:

> “He will confess to you when you have done good to him” (Psalm 48:19).

The voice of confession formed by the pleasure of prosperity is contemptible. But the confession has great merit and weight when the force of suffering does not separate it from the truth’s uprightness, and when adversity, as a witness of the heart, sharpens it even to the judgment of the voice.

[Note: The printed editions read: “from the uprightness of the truth.”]

It is therefore no wonder that Bildad praises divine justice, since he endures nothing adverse from that same justice.

### 60. The madness of heretics against the Church when it is pressed by adversity

But since we have said that the friends of blessed Job represent heretics, it is worthwhile to show briefly how Bildad’s words correspond to the insinuations of heretics.

When these people see the holy Church chastised by temporal correction in its members, they swell more boldly into the boastfulness of perverse preaching. Pretending to uphold the uprightness of heavenly judgment, they claim that they prosper because of their merits, while asserting that the Church is afflicted by punishments proportionate to its deserts.

With flattering words they immediately seek an opening for insinuation amid the Church’s sufferings. They strike at the lives of others by reproaching them with the deaths of others, as though those who refused to believe things worthy of God had already died justly.

[Note: Coccius deleted *in semetipsis* (“in themselves”), followed by other editions, which paid insufficient attention both to the manuscripts and to the old edition. German. has *semetipsos* (“themselves”) instead of *semetipsis* (“in themselves”).]

Therefore, after Bildad the Shuhite has set forth divine justice, he immediately adds:

## CHAPTER XXXVII

### Job 8:4–6

> “Even if your sons sinned against him, and he delivered them into the hand of their iniquity, yet if you rise at dawn to God and entreat the Almighty, if you proceed pure and upright, he will immediately awaken for you and will restore the dwelling-place of your justice in peace.”

[Note: The printed editions read “reproaching their life.” We follow the manuscripts Corb. Germ. and Norm. In Barthol. and Rembold, 1518, *morsibus* (“with bites”) is corruptly printed instead of *mortibus* (“with deaths”).]

### 61. They reproach the separation of peoples from the Church as evidence of error

It is as though the preachers of error say to afflicted Catholics: “Take heed to your lives, and learn how perverse a course you follow from the condemnation of those who have died among you; for if your faithlessness were not displeasing to the Creator of all things, he would certainly not have taken so many peoples away from you by the violence of destruction.” For he says:

“Even if your sons sinned against him, and he delivered them into the hand of their iniquity.”

As though he were plainly saying: “Those have been delivered into the hand of their iniquity who were unwilling to imitate the life of our rectitude.”

“Yet if you rise at dawn to God and entreat the Almighty.”

Because heretics believe that they themselves possess the light of truth, they call the holy Church, as though placed in the night of error, toward the dawn of truth, so that it may rise through knowledge of God, as though at dawn, and wash away past offenses through the prayer of repentance.

“If you walk pure and upright.”

Pure, that is, in thought; upright in action.

“He will immediately awaken to you.”

As though he were plainly saying: “Because he who now does not exercise the power of his protection over your tribulations is, as it were, sleeping instead of helping the one who has gone astray.”  
[Note: Gemetensis has “as though for assistance.”]

“And he will restore the dwelling of your justice to peace.”

That is, he removes the adversities of the present life and immediately grants the security of tranquility. Because all the perverse regard temporal joy as the unique good of divine recompense, they promise to others as something very great the things they themselves eagerly pursue. Hence it often happens that they promise that lost things will be recovered, or stretch the minds of their hearers toward still greater rewards in the present life. Baldad expresses this openly when he immediately adds:

### CHAPTER XXXVIII

[Col. 0840A]

**Verse 7.** “So that if your former things were small, your latter things would be multiplied exceedingly.”

### 62. What they promise their followers

But if he calls the dwelling of justice the counsel of the mind, the teachers of error promise afflicted Catholics a peaceful dwelling of justice, because if they draw them over to their own side, they certainly cease from contention. For those who have been able to be dragged into perversion are now the more peacefully settled in temporal peace, the farther they are separated from eternity.

They also promise that the resources of understanding will increase for those who follow them. Hence it is added:

“So that if your former things were small, your latter things would be multiplied exceedingly.”

But because their words are not easily believed, since their life is often shown to be contemptible, they produce the opinions of the ancient fathers and bend their rectitude into an argument for their own error. Hence it is also added:

### CHAPTER XXXIX [Recension XXIII]

**Verse 8.** “For ask the former generation, and diligently investigate the memory of the fathers.”

### 63. They abuse the authority of the ancient fathers

They urge that the former generation and the memory of the fathers are not merely to be seen but investigated, because they do not want that to be observed in them which is plainly evident to everyone. Sometimes, however, like good teachers, they teach certain things morally and indicate how present matters may be gathered from the past; from those things that have already been taken away from our eyes in passing, they show how insubstantial are the things that appear to exist. Hence it is further added:

[Col. 0840C]

**Verse 9.** “For we are of yesterday and do not know, because our days upon the earth are like a shadow.”

### 64. What has already passed teaches us how swiftly the rest will pass

The former generation, therefore, is proposed for questioning, so that the passing of the present life may be shown to be like a shadow. For if we recall to mind the things that existed and have already passed away, we plainly recognize how swiftly this too flees which we now possess.

Often, however, heretics praise the same fathers with us, whom we venerate; but with their understanding perverted, they attack us by means of the very praises they offer them. Hence it is further added:

### CHAPTER XLI

**Verse 10.** “They themselves will teach you; [Note: In the Reginensis, Germanicus, and Corbeiensis Germanicus manuscripts, *they will speak to you* is lacking.] they will speak to you, and from their heart they will bring forth words.”

### 65. The wicked sometimes utter good things, but not rightly; thus they are struck by their own sword

It should be noted that above he had said: “The spirit of the manifold speech of your mouth”; but now, recalling the fathers, he says: “They will bring forth words from their heart.” It is as though the heretics, condemning the life of the holy Church, were saying: “You have a multiplicity of spirit in your mouth, but not in your heart.” Yet those should be heard against you who, bringing forth words from the heart, taught by living rightly.

Often, however, the wicked, while unaware of the defect in their own strength, boldly tear apart the rectitude of others. When they seize the authority to rebuke the good, they either utter those good things which they have learned not by seeing but by hearing, or, by lying, impose upon others the evils which they themselves commit.

But when they utter the good things they disdain to observe, we should understand that truth often sounds through the mouths of adversaries in such a way that, while moving their tongue, it strikes their life. Thus, while speaking of and not knowing the summit of rectitude, they become judges by their words and accusers by their deeds.

Hence Baldad says remarkable things against hypocrites, but attacks himself with the point of his own word; for unless he himself possessed at least some measure of righteousness, he would never presume to teach the just with such boldness. What he says is indeed very powerful; but he ought to have said it to the foolish, not to the wise, and to the wicked, not to the upright. For he also declares himself senseless who pours water into a river while gardens thirst.

For the moment, however, let us set aside to whom it is said and carefully consider what is said, so that the utterances may instruct us, even though they oppose the merit of their author. It follows:

**Verse 11.** “Can the rush become green without moisture, or can the reed grow without water?”  
[Note: Thus the Norman manuscript and almost all the others; this reading is supported by the repeated mention of greenness. The printed editions have “live.”]

[Recension XXIV.] Baldad himself immediately discloses whom he compares to the rush or reed when he adds:

### CHAPTER XLII

**Verses 12–13.** “While it is still in flower and has not been plucked by hand, it withers before all the grasses; so are the ways of all who forget God, and the hope of the hypocrite will perish.”  
[Note: Corbeiensis Germanicus has “of life.”]

### 66. The hypocrite possesses the appearance, not the fruit, of good works; he possesses God’s gifts for the increase of his condemnation

By the name of the rush or reed, therefore, he signifies the life of the hypocrite, which indeed has the appearance of greenness but bears no useful fruit for human purposes.  
[Note: Some manuscripts have “the fruit of humility.”]  
It remains dry through the barrenness of its work and grows green only in the color of holiness.

[Old recension XXVII.] Yet neither does a rush thrive without moisture nor a reed without water, because the life of hypocrites receives an infusion of heavenly grace for good works, but, seeking outward praise in everything it does, is emptied of the fruit of the infusion it has received.

For often they perform wondrous works of signs, drive spirits from possessed bodies, and, through the gift of prophecy, anticipate future events by knowing them beforehand. Yet they are divided from the giver of so many gifts by the intention of their thoughts, because through his gifts they seek not his glory but their own favor. And when they exalt themselves through the good things they have received in their own praise, they fight against the giver with those very gifts.  
[Note: Gemetensis and Germanicus read, “and by the good things they have received they raise him up in their own praise.” Lyre, Bigot, Uticensis, and Vindocinensis read, “and when through the good things they have received they exalt themselves,” which reading we follow.]

For they grow proud against the giver by means of that through which they ought to have been more humble toward him. Consequently, a stricter judgment later strikes them in proportion as heavenly goodness now pours itself more generously even upon the ungrateful. The abundance of the gift becomes for them an increase of condemnation, because, though watered, they bear no fruit; under the color of greenness they grow tall while remaining empty.

The Truth aptly describes such people in the Gospel, saying:

“Many will say to me on that day, ‘Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, cast out demons in your name, and perform many mighty works in your name?’ And then I will declare to them, ‘I never knew you; depart from me, you workers of iniquity’” (Matthew 7:22–23).

The rush or reed therefore does not live without water, because hypocrites receive the greenness of good action only from heavenly grace. But because they seize it for their own praise, they grow green in the water yet remain empty.

### 67. The hypocrite cannot bear correction

It is rightly added:

“While it is still in flower and has not been plucked by hand, it withers before all the grasses.”

The rush is in flower when the hypocrite is in praise. But the reed, rising with sharp angles, is not plucked by hand because the hypocrite, with his senses made harsh through arrogance, disdains to be corrected for his perversity.

In its flower it wounds the hand of the one who plucks it, because when the hypocrite is placed in praise, his harshness immediately cuts the life of the person correcting him, so that no one may dare to correct him.  
[Note: Norman and Germanicus have “if anyone dares to correct him.”]

He does not desire to be holy but to be called holy; and when he is perhaps corrected, he is as though mutilated in the glory of his reputation. When caught in wrongdoing, he becomes angry, prevents the one reproving him from speaking, and suffers as though touched in a hidden wound.

He wants to be judged by everyone to be what he has become known as to the inexperienced. And, more ready to die than to be corrected, he becomes worse through reproof, because he regards the word of purity as though it were the dart of a dreadful blow.  
[Note: Vindocinensis has “because he regards it as though it came from the anger of a blow”; Gemetensis, “because he regards it as though it came from a counterblow.”]

Thus, immediately provoked, he rises into insults and looks for evils with which he may exaggerate the life of the person correcting him. He wants to display his critic as guilty to an incomparably greater degree, so that he may show himself innocent not by his own actions but by the crimes of another. Thus a person often regrets having said something in reproof, and, as though from the hand of the plucker, so from the spirit of the corrector, a kind of blood of sorrow flows, if I may put it so.

Hence Solomon rightly says:

“Do not rebuke a scoffer, lest he hate you” (Proverbs 9:8).

For the just person need not fear that the scoffer will heap insults upon him when corrected, but rather that, drawn into hatred, he may become worse.

### 68. The hypocrite does not persevere in good works

In the meantime, we should know that the good works of the just, because they begin from the heart, grow until the end of the present life. But the works of hypocrites, because they are by no means rooted in secret, often fail before the present life ends.

Often they devote themselves to the study of sacred learning; and because they seek it not to prepare merits but to win favor, as soon as they obtain human praise and through it achieve the favor of transitory advancement, they devote their whole mind to worldly concerns and are entirely emptied of sacred learning. By what they do afterward they show how much they love temporal things, although earlier they proclaimed only eternal things.

Often, too, they display the appearance of assumed maturity; they are adorned with the quiet of silence, the long-suffering of patience, and the virtue of continence. But when through these they have reached the height of honor they sought, and when reverence is now offered to them by everyone, they immediately pour themselves into wanton pleasure. They themselves testify that they did not possess goodness from the heart, since they soon abandoned it.

Sometimes, indeed, certain people give away what they possess and distribute everything to the needy. Yet before the end of their life, inflamed by the itch of avarice, they desire what belongs to others—those who had seemed to give away their own—and afterward, with stubborn cruelty, seek what they had previously abandoned under a pretended appearance of piety.

[Old recension XXVIII.] Hence it is rightly said now:

“While it is still in flower and has not been plucked by hand, it withers before all the grasses.”  
[Note: The Roman and Gussanville editions add, “according to the carnal understanding.”]

According to the flesh, the just too are grass, as the prophet testifies when he says:

“All flesh is grass” (Isaiah 40:6).

But the rush is said to wither before all the grasses because, while the just remain in their goodness, the life of hypocrites dries up with respect to the greenness of the rectitude they assumed.

The other grasses also wither, because the works of the just fail together with the life of the flesh. But the rush precedes the drying of the grasses because, before the hypocrite departs from the flesh, he abandons the deeds of virtue he had displayed in himself.

The Psalmist also speaks well of such people:

“Let them become like the grass of the housetops, which withers before it is pulled up” (Psalm 128:6).

Grass on a building grows high, but it is not made firm by a deep root, because the hypocrite is seen to perform lofty deeds but is not strengthened in them by purity of heart. This grass of the building withers more quickly even though it has not been pulled up, because the hypocrite still remains in the present life and yet already loses the works of holiness as though they were the appearance of greenness.

Because he strove to do good without the intention of right thought, by losing these things he shows that he had blossomed without a root.

### 69. The hypocrite cannot long enjoy his hope

But Baldad, as we said, immediately reveals whom he compares to the rush or reed when he adds:

“So are the ways of all who forget God, and the hope of the hypocrite will perish.”

For what does the hypocrite hope for through all his works except the reverence of honor, the glory of praise, being feared by those better than himself, and being called holy by everyone?

But the hope of the hypocrite cannot endure, because, not seeking eternity, he loses what he holds. His mind’s intention is by no means fixed upon that glory which is possessed without end; rather, while he eagerly desires transitory favor, he loses by obtaining the very thing for which he labors. The Truth testifies to this, saying:

“Amen I say to you, they have received their reward” (Matthew 6:2, 5).

But this hope of receiving a reward cannot be held for long. Honor is granted for the works displayed, but life is driven toward its end; praises resound, but time hastens toward its end along with the praises. And because the mind is never rooted in the love of eternity, it slips away together with the very things it loves.

No one can love what is unstable and himself remain unmoved. Whoever embraces passing things is led into their course by the very fact that he becomes entangled in things that are running away.

Therefore he says:

“And the hope of the hypocrite will perish,”

because the human praise he seeks with great labors is driven onward and runs away with the moments of time.  
[Note: Gemetensis has “the driven time runs on in moments.”]

It is rightly added:

### CHAPTER XLIII [Recension XXV]

**Verse 14.** “His folly will not please him.”

### 70. The hypocrite sells a thing of great value cheaply; he is like a fruitful but neglected vine

For it is great folly to undertake laborious things while longing for the breath of praise; to serve the heavenly commandments through strenuous work while seeking the reward of earthly recompense.

To put it so, whoever desires human favor for the virtue he practices carries a thing of great merit to market at a cheap price. From the very thing by which he might have deserved the kingdom of heaven, he seeks the coin of passing speech.

He therefore sells his work at a cheap price, because he spends much but receives little.

[Old recension XXIX.] To what, then, are hypocrites like except fruitful but neglected vines, which produce fruit through abundance but are never raised from the earth through cultivation? What the fat branches produce is trampled by wandering beasts; and the more abundantly they see it, the more eagerly they consume what has been cast down in low places.

For the works of hypocrites, while they are displayed brightly, come forth as though fat; but while they seek human praise, they are left as though upon the ground.  
[Note: Bellovacensis and Gemetensis have “while they are displayed as glorious.”]

The beasts of this world, namely, evil spirits, eat them, because they bend them toward the use of destruction; and they seize them the more ardently the more clearly their greatness is made known.

Hence the prophet rightly says:

“A standing stalk has no germ in them, and they will make no flour; and even if they make it, strangers will eat it” (Hosea 8:7).  
[Note: The printed editions have, “There is no germ in it, and it will not make flour; and even if it does, strangers will eat it,” but the manuscripts resist this reading.]

A stalk has no germ when its life lacks the merits of virtue. A stalk does not make flour when one who prospers in the present world understands nothing subtle and yields no fruit of good work.

### 71. The hypocrite feeds evil spirits with his fruits; he too is fed now, but differently after death

But often, even when it has made flour, strangers eat it, because when hypocrites display good works, the desires of evil spirits are satisfied by them. Those who do not seek to please God through these works feed not the master of the field but strangers.

The hypocrite, therefore, like a fruitful but neglected branch, cannot preserve his fruit, because the cluster of good work lies upon the ground. Yet he is fed by this very folly of his, because he is honored by everyone for his good work; he excels others, holds the minds of people subject to him, is raised to higher positions, and is nourished by favor.

For the moment, this folly of his pleases him, but it will not please him, because when the time of recompense arrives, what was foolish in him displeases him in punishment. Then he will understand that he acted foolishly, when for the pleasure of praise he receives the sentence of divine rebuke. Then he will consider that he was foolish, when perpetual torments punish him for the temporal glory he obtained. Then punishments disclose true knowledge, because through them it is plainly understood that all those things which were able to pass away were nothing.

Hence it is rightly added:

### CHAPTER XLIV [Recension XXVI]

**The same passage.** “And his confidence is like a spider’s web.”

### 72. The hypocrite’s confidence is vain; his good works are nothing before God, his preaching fruitless, and his abstinence empty

The confidence of hypocrites is rightly said to be like spiders’ webs, because everything they labor over to obtain glory is scattered by the wind of mortal life. Since they do not seek eternal things, they lose temporal goods together with time.

It should also be considered that spiders draw out their threads in an orderly fashion, because hypocrites arrange their works as though with discernment. A spider’s web is woven carefully but is dispersed by a sudden breath, because whatever the hypocrite accomplishes with labor is carried away by the breeze of human favor; and while the work fails in the desire for praise, the labor vanishes as though into the wind.

Often the deeds of hypocrites endure even to the end of the present life; but because through them they do not seek the praise of their author, they were never good before the eyes of God.

For, as we said earlier, they are often supported by learning in sacred law, utter words of doctrine, and gird everything they think with testimonies. Yet through these they seek not the life of their hearers but their own favor, because they know how to utter nothing except what will rouse the hearts of their hearers to return praise, not what will kindle them to tears.  
[Note: Vindocinensis has “to shake them into repeated praise.” The corrupt Cocceian edition, by editorial correction, placed *excitent*—“stir up”—instead of *excutiant*—“shake out.”]

[Old recension XXX.] For a mind occupied with outward desires does not grow warm with the fire of divine love. Therefore words spoken from a cold heart cannot inflame their hearers toward heavenly desire. A thing that has not itself burned cannot set another thing on fire.

Hence it often happens that the words of hypocrites neither instruct their hearers nor fail to make those very people who utter them worse through the pride of praise. For Paul testifies:

“Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up” (1 Corinthians 8:1).  
[Note: Thus Turonensis, Vindocinensis, Normanus, and almost all the others; the printed editions have, “For whom love builds up.”]

When love does not raise a person by building him up, knowledge perverts him by puffing him up.

Often hypocrites afflict themselves through remarkable abstinence, wear down all the strength of their bodies, and, as though extinguishing the life of the flesh entirely while living in the flesh, approach death through abstinence so that they live almost dying every day. But in all this they seek human eyes and desire the glory of admiration. The Truth testifies to this, saying:

“They disfigure their faces so that they may appear to men to be fasting” (Matthew 6:16).

Their faces grow pale, their bodies are shaken by weakness, and their breasts are oppressed by interrupted sighs. Yet amid all this they seek words of admiration from the mouths of those around them, and nothing other than human esteem is considered at such great labor.

Simon aptly represents such people. At the time of the Lord’s Passion he carried the cross under compulsion, and of him it is written:

“They found a man of Cyrene, named Simon, coming toward them; they compelled him to carry the cross of Jesus” (Matthew 27:32; Mark 15:21).  
[Note: Vindocinensis and Gemetensis read, “For what we do under compulsion”; Ebroicensis, “For what we compel ourselves to do.” Uticensis has both forms.]

What we do under compulsion, we do not perform from the devotion of love. To carry the cross of Jesus under compulsion, therefore, is to endure the affliction of abstinence with an intention other than the one required.  
[Note: Bellovacensis and Normanus have, “to endure it for an intention of necessity other than this.” In Uticensis, the earlier reading was, “to endure it for another intention than one of necessity.”]

Does he not carry the cross of Jesus under compulsion who, as though in obedience to the Lord’s command, subdues his flesh but does not love the spiritual homeland? Hence this same Simon carries the cross but by no means dies, because every hypocrite afflicts his body through abstinence but lives for the world through his love of glory.

[Old recension XXXI.]

### 73. He brings the cross upon his flesh but lives for the world

In contrast, Paul rightly says of the elect:

“Those who belong to Christ have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires.”

We crucify the flesh with its vices and desires if we restrain our appetite in such a way that we seek nothing from the glory of the world. For whoever mortifies his body but longs for honors has brought the cross upon his flesh but, through desire, lives for the world even more wickedly.

Often, through the appearance of holiness, he undeservedly obtains a position of authority—one which, unless he had displayed some virtue in himself, he would not have deserved to obtain through any labor. But what he obtains delightfully passes away, while what follows remains painfully.

Now the confidence of holiness is placed in the mouths of men; but when the inner Judge examines the secrets of the heart, he does not seek external witnesses to one’s life.

It is rightly said, therefore:

“His confidence is like a spider’s web,”

because when the witness of the heart appears, everything that externally relies upon human favor passes away.

Hence it is appropriately added:

### CHAPTER XLV [Recension XXVII]

**Verse 15.** “He leans upon his house, and it will not stand; he will support it, and it will not rise.”

### 74. The hypocrite’s house upon which he leans is human favor; it cannot stand

Just as the building of outward conduct is the house in which the body dwells, so the house of our thought is whatever the mind inhabits through love. For whatever we love, we dwell in it as though resting there.

Thus Paul, because he had fixed his heart on heavenly things, was indeed placed on earth but nevertheless alien to the earth, and said:

“Our citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians 3:20).  
[Note: Corbeiensis Germanicus and Reginensis have “because his heart had been fastened there.”]

The mind of the hypocrite thinks of nothing in everything he does except the glory of his reputation. He does not care where he will afterward be led by merit, but what is said of him in the meantime.

His house, therefore, is the delight of favor, which he inhabits as though at rest, because through all his works he reclines within his mind toward it. But this house cannot stand, because praise passes away with life, and human favor does not endure in judgment.

Hence the foolish virgins, who had not taken oil in their vessels, because they possessed glory in the voices of others and not in their own consciences, were troubled by the bridegroom’s arrival and said:

“Give us some of your oil, because our lamps are going out” (Matthew 25:8).

To seek oil from one’s neighbors is to implore the glory of a good work from the testimony of another’s mouth. For an empty mind, when it discovers that it has kept nothing within despite all its labors, seeks testimony outside.

It is as though the foolish virgins plainly said:

“When you see us rejected without reward, tell us what you saw in our work.”

[Old recension XXXII.]

### 75. The hypocrite’s confidence in his holiness will no more stand in judgment

But the hypocrite will then lean in vain upon this house of praise, because human testimony will provide him no support in judgment; the praise whose testimony he later demands he had already received as his reward.

Or certainly, the hypocrite leans upon his house when, deceived by empty favors, he is raised up as though by confidence in his holiness. Hypocrites often do many evils in secret but certain good things in public. When they receive praise for their visible good deeds, they turn the eyes of their consideration away from their hidden evils. They judge themselves to be what they hear outwardly, not what they know inwardly.

Hence it often happens that they come with confidence even to the heavenly judgment, because they believe themselves before the inner Judge to be what they were regarded as by people outwardly.

But the hypocrite’s house cannot stand, because in the terror of the strict examination all his former confidence in holiness falls. When he realizes that the testimonies of other mouths are lacking, he turns to enumerating his own works.

Hence it is further added:

“He will support it, and it will not rise.”

What cannot stand by itself is supported so that it may stand. Thus, when the hypocrite sees his life tottering in judgment, he strives to establish it by supporting it with an enumeration of his works.

Do those not support the dwelling of their praise from every side who, as we have said, enumerate their deeds in judgment and say:

“Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, cast out demons in your name, and perform many mighty works in your name?” (Matthew 7:22).

But the house of praise, supported by so many claims, does not rise at all, because the Judge immediately says:

“I never knew you; depart from me, you workers of iniquity” (ibid. 23).

We should know that what rises lifts itself from low places to higher ones. The hypocrite’s house, therefore, cannot rise, because through everything he was able to do according to the heavenly commandments, he never lifted his mind from the earth.

Rightly, then, he is not raised to the reward of recompense, because through what he now displays in the desire for temporal glory he lies prostrate.

[Old recension XXXIII; Recension XXVIII.] But since we have heard how the life of the hypocrite, signified by the name of the rush, is rejected in judgment, let us hear what esteem he has among human beings before the strict Judge appears. It follows:

### CHAPTER XLVI

**Verse 16.** “He appears moist before the sun comes.”

### 76. The hypocrite is now believed holy, but when Christ comes he will appear wicked

In sacred discourse the Lord is often represented by the name of the sun, as the prophet says:

“For you who fear the name of the Lord, the sun of justice will rise” (Malachi 4:2).

And in the Book of Wisdom the wicked, rejected in judgment, are described as saying:

“We have strayed from the way of truth; the light of justice did not shine for us, and the sun did not rise for us” (Wisdom 5:6).

The rush, therefore, is seen as moist before the sun, because before the divine strictness shines in judgment, every hypocrite displays himself as infused with the grace of holiness. He is seen as green, because he is regarded as just; he holds a position of honor; he is distinguished by the glory of holiness; veneration is offered to him by everyone; and the reputation of his praise is extended.

This rush, then, is moist in the night, but is dried by the coming of the sun, because in the darkness of the present life the hypocrite is believed holy by everyone, but when the strict Judge comes, he will appear to be wicked. Let him say, therefore:

“He appears moist before the sun comes,”

because now he presents himself as green to human eyes, but then he will wither in the heat of divine judgment.

It follows:

### CHAPTER XLVII

**The same passage.** “And at its rising its germ comes forth.”

### 77. As soon as he acts rightly, the hypocrite wants to be praised; after assuming the habit of holiness, he sometimes becomes worse

Every kind of grass, when it grows, is first brought forth from the earth; it is touched by breezes and heat, nourished by sun and rains, and only then opens to produce the germ of its seed. But the rush is born with its flower and, as soon as it rises from the earth, produces along with itself the germ of its seed.

Thus the various grasses aptly signify the saints, while the rush signifies the hypocrite. Just men, before they arise in the work of holy conduct, endure the winter of this life, and the heat of severe persecutions tires them. But when they do what is right, they do not seek the reward of their rectitude here. When they depart from the labors of the present world and come to the eternal homeland, they enjoy the expected recompense.

The hypocrite, by contrast, because he is born at once in good work, tries to receive the glory of the present world. Like the rush, he arises with his germ: because he begins to live well, he immediately seeks to be honored by everyone.

The germ at its rising is therefore reward at the beginning. Often some people abandon the paths of open wickedness and assume the habit of holiness. As soon as they have touched the first thresholds of good living, however, they forget what they had been and do not wish to be afflicted through repentance for their completed wickedness; instead, they desire to be praised for their righteousness just begun and long to preside even over those who are better than themselves.

Often, when present prosperity follows them according to their desire, they become far worse through their habit of holiness than they had previously been. Occupied with many possessions and confused by that very occupation, they not only fail to lament what they have done but add still more things to lament.  
[Note: Normanus has “according to their desire, present prosperity follows them,” and so forth.]

[Old recension XXXIX; Recension XXIV.]

### 78. A recent convert, the hypocrite should not be advanced to outward offices; our good works perish if they are revealed too soon

Those who abandon the world should not be advanced to outward offices unless they have first been firmly established for a long time in contempt of that same world through humility.  
[Note: Gemetensis reads, “should not be advanced.”]

For the good things that become known to people before their time quickly perish. Planted trees, before they grow together with a firmly fixed root, are dried up if a shaking hand touches them. But if the root is fixed deeply and strengthened by being soaked with the moisture of the earth, the tree both withstands the push of a hand and is not harmed; winds shake it by bending it, but do not overturn it.

Therefore, so that the life of a work begun may not be uprooted, the root of the heart must be fixed deeply and firmly in humility for a long time.  
[Note: Gemetensis formerly read “the life of a conceived work”; but, after the first syllable was erased by a later hand, it now reads “begun.”] Then, when the breath of detraction or favor blows from a human mouth and bends the mind in whatever direction, it will not uproot it entirely; rather, after being bent, the mind will immediately return to its proper position if it remains strong within itself through its firm root.

What is more robust among growing structures than a wall rising upward? Yet if it is pushed while it is being built, it is immediately destroyed without effort. But if it is allowed to dry out from its moisture over a period of time, it is often not shaken even by blows from battering rams.

Thus, plainly, our good works perish when they are revealed prematurely and are strengthened when kept hidden longer, because when the hand of human activity touches the life of our still-beginning way of life, it pushes it like a newly built wall and easily destroys it, since it has not yet lost the moisture of its own weakness.

But when the mind restrains itself in the long quiet of its lowliness, it hardens, like a dried wall, against blows; and whatever strikes the solid wall immediately rebounds broken.  
[Note: The printed editions have “whatever solid thing strikes it”; all the manuscripts lack *impactum* (“striking”). Germanicus reads, “whatever solid thing strikes it”; the same reading occurs in Corbeiensis Germanicus and Colbertinus, in a second hand.]

Hence Moses prohibited the life of beginners from being exercised in human occupations, saying:

“You shall not work with the firstborn of your ox, and you shall not shear the firstborn of your sheep” (Deuteronomy 15:19).

To work with the firstborn of an ox is to display the beginnings of a good way of life in the exercise of public action. To shear the firstborn of sheep is to strip our good works, as they are beginning, of the covering of their concealment and expose them to human eyes.

We are therefore prohibited from working with the firstborn of an ox and restrained from shearing the firstborn of sheep, because if we begin something strong, we should not bring it into public exercise too soon.

And when our life begins something simple and innocent, it is fitting that it not abandon the veils of its secrecy, lest it display itself naked to human eyes, as though its fleece had been removed.

[Col. 0850A] [Vet. XXXV.] **79. The beginnings of a good life must be dedicated to God alone; why they should not quickly become known.**—Let the firstborn of oxen and sheep, then, be used only for divine sacrifices, so that whatever strong and innocent thing we begin, we may sacrifice it in honor of the innermost Judge upon the altar of the heart. For this is unquestionably received by him the more willingly, the less it is tainted by any desire for human praise through being concealed from human beings.

Often, however, the beginnings of a new way of life are still mixed with the carnal life; and for this reason they ought not quickly become known, lest, when the good things that please are praised, the soul, deceived by its own praise, be unable to discern the evils that lie hidden within them. Hence Moses rightly says again:

> When you have entered the land that I shall give you, and have planted in it fruit-bearing trees, you shall remove their foreskins. The fruits that they produce shall be unclean for you, and you shall not eat of them (Levit. XIX, 23).

Fruit-bearing trees are works fruitful in virtues. We therefore remove the foreskins of the trees when, suspicious of the weakness of our very beginnings, we do not approve the first stages of our works. We regard the fruits that they produce as unclean and do not make them suitable for our eating, because when the beginnings of a good work are praised, it is fitting that this should not feed the mind of the one who performs it; otherwise, while the praise received is savored sweetly, the fruit of the work is eaten before its time. Whoever, therefore, receives praise from human lips for a virtue he has begun has eaten, as it were, the fruit of a planted tree before the proper time.

**80. The hypocrite seeks witnesses to his work; if they are absent, he thinks that he has labored in vain.**—Hence Truth says through the Psalmist:

> It is vain for you to rise before daylight; rise after you have sat down (Ps. CXXVI, 3).

To rise before daylight is, before the brightness of eternal recompense appears, to rejoice in the night of the present life. One must first sit down, therefore, so that one may afterward rise properly, because whoever does not voluntarily humble himself now will by no means be exalted by the glory that follows.

What is there called “rising before daylight” is here, in the hypocrite, “bringing forth a sprout at its emergence,” because, desiring human praise, as soon as he is born to a good work he immediately seeks to obtain the glory of recompense. Did these men not bring forth a sprout at their emergence, of whom Truth said:

> They love the first places at banquets and the first seats in the synagogues, greetings in the marketplace, and to be called Rabbi by people (Luke XX, 46; Matt. XXIII, 6)?

Because they try to obtain honor from human beings for beginning to do good, they rise like reeds from their emergence, with a sprout. When they desire to perform what is right, they first anxiously seek witnesses to that very work, and silently consider whether there are people who will see what must be done, and whether those who see it will be able to describe it suitably. But if, perhaps, none of their fellow human beings happens to observe their deeds, they unquestionably think that they have lost them; and they count the eyes of the inner Judge as though they were absent, because they refuse to receive from him in the future the return for their work.

And because, when the hypocrite has done something right, he seeks to be seen by many, it is well that what follows is added concerning this reed:

## CHAPTER XLVIII

**Verse 17.—“Upon a heap of stones its roots will be thickened, and it will dwell among the stones.”**

**81. The hypocrite strives with all his purpose to win human admiration.**—What else should we understand by “roots” except hidden thoughts, which emerge secretly but rise openly in the display of works? Thus it is said by the prophet concerning the seed of the word:

> And what has been saved from the house of Judah, and what remains, will send a root downward and produce fruit upward (Isa. XXXVII, 31).

To send a root downward is to multiply a good thought in hidden places. To produce fruit upward is, through the effectiveness of a work, to display the right things one has thought.

In sacred Scripture, the name “stones” designates human beings, as it is said through Isaiah to the holy Church:

> I will make your battlements of jasper, and your gates of carved stones (Isa. LIV, 12).

He explained what he meant by these stones when he added:

> All your children will be taught by the Lord (ibid., 13).

And as Peter says in exhortation:

> You also, as living stones, are being built up into spiritual houses (I Pet. II, 5). [Gemet.: “are being built up into a spiritual house.”]

In this passage, therefore, because “stones” are mentioned but are by no means called “living” [Corb. Germ.: “who are by no means called [living stones]”], the reprobate and the elect may be represented together under the bare designation “stones.”

This reed, then, which dwells among the stones and thickens its roots upon a heap of rocks, does so because every hypocrite multiplies his thoughts in seeking human admiration. In everything hypocrites do, they seek human praise through hidden thoughts; thus they send the roots of the reed, as it were, into a heap of stones. While they are about to act, they think about their praises; when praised, they silently turn those praises over in their thoughts.

They rejoice that they have shone forth as exceptional in human estimation. And when, puffed up by approval, they swell up within themselves, they often silently marvel even at themselves. They daily desire to appear greater to themselves, and they grow beyond measure in their work through astonishing devices [Bellov. and Gemet.: “and through wretched devices”; Lyr. and Utic. preserve both readings], because just as virtues weaken every vice, arrogance strengthens it. It makes the mind grow young and strong beyond its powers, because what bodily vigor denies, the love of praise commands.

Hence, as we have said, they seek witnesses for their deeds [Gemet.: “judges”]. If witnesses to their work happen to be lacking, they themselves recount what they have done. And when they begin to be lifted up by approval, they often add something fictitious to those same works that they report themselves to have performed. But even when they speak the truth, by speaking of these things they make them alien to themselves, because, rewarded with the praises they have sought [Turon.: “with the praises of the reward they have sought”], they are emptied of their inward recompense.

**82. While displaying their good works, hypocrites betray them to evil spirits; they provoke enemies to plunder by exposing their riches to them.**—In making their good works known, they show evil spirits, like enemies lying in ambush, what they may plunder. The life of such people was clearly represented by the universally known fault of Hezekiah. After, by one prayer and within the space of a single night, he had caused one hundred and eighty-five thousand enemies to be struck down by an angel; after he had brought back the sun, which was near its setting, to the higher regions of the sky; after he had prolonged life that was already shortened by the approach of its end into a longer span; when he had received the messengers of the king of Babylon, he showed them all the good things he possessed. But immediately he heard from the prophet’s voice:

> Behold, days are coming when everything that is in your house will be carried away to Babylon; nothing will be left, says the Lord (IV Kings XX, 17).

So indeed with hypocrites: after they have grown through great virtues, because they neglect to guard against the ambushes of evil spirits and do not wish those virtues to remain concealed within them, by displaying their good works they make them the possessions of their enemies; and by betraying them, they suddenly lose whatever they have labored long to accomplish.

[Vet. XXXVII.] Hence it is said through the Psalmist:

> He delivered their strength into captivity, and their beauty into the hands of the enemy (Ps. LXXVII, 61).

The strength and beauty of the arrogant are delivered into the enemy’s hands because every good that is displayed through a desire for praise is handed over to the power of the hidden adversary. He provokes enemies to plunder who strips his riches bare for their knowledge.

For as long as we are separated from the security of our eternal homeland, we walk along a road beset by robbers lying in wait. Whoever fears being robbed on the road must therefore hide the good things he carries.

O wretched people, who, longing for human praise, dissipate within themselves the fruits of their labors! When they desire to display themselves to the eyes of others, they condemn what they do. When evil spirits provoke them to boastfulness, they strip them bare by taking their works captive, as we have said.

Hence Truth, indicating through the guise of a certain nation the malice of the ancient enemies, says through the prophet:

> He made my vineyard a desert; he stripped the bark from my fig tree, laying it bare and stripping it; its branches became white (Joel I, 7).

When spirits lie in wait [Norm.: “enemies”; some witnesses preserve both readings], God’s vineyard is made a desert when a human soul is dissipated by desire for human praise. This nation strips the bark from God’s fig tree because, carrying away the deceived mind into a desire for approval and dragging it toward display, it removes from it the covering of humility. It lays it bare and strips it, because so long as the mind is hidden in its good works, it is clothed, as it were, in the bark of its own covering.

But when the mind desires what it has done to be seen by others, the fig tree, as though stripped, has lost the bark that covered it [Turon. and many other manuscripts: “the fig tree has lost the bark with which it covered itself”; and shortly afterward: “but because its bark has been removed.” Norman and Corb. Germ.: “the fig tree has lost the bark that covered it”; and below, “with its bark removed”].

Then it aptly adds:

> Its branches became white.

For when its works are displayed to human eyes, they become white: a name for holiness is acquired when a right action is publicized. But since, once its bark has been removed, the branches of this fig tree dry up, we must carefully observe that the deeds of the arrogant dry up precisely from the source from which they seek to please human eyes. The mind that betrays itself through boastfulness is therefore rightly called a stripped fig tree, because it is bright in what is seen, yet close to dryness in that it is deprived of the covering of its bark.

What we do must therefore be kept within, if we expect to receive from the inner Judge the return for our work. Hence Truth says through the Gospel:

> Let your left hand not know what your right hand is doing, so that your alms may be in secret; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you (Matt. VI, 3).

Hence it is said through the Psalmist concerning the Church of the elect:

> All the glory of the daughter of kings is within (Ps. XLIV, 14).

Hence Paul says:

> Our glory is this: the testimony of our conscience (II Cor. I, 12).

The Church is the king’s daughter, generated in good works through the preaching of spiritual rulers. She has glory within because she does not possess what she does as a boastful display. Paul calls the testimony of his conscience his glory because, not seeking the approval of another’s lips, he does not know how to place the joys of his life outside himself.

[Vet. XXXVIII.] **83. Good works ought to be kept hidden, or revealed for the sake of God’s glory alone.**—What we do must therefore be hidden, lest, carrying these things carelessly along the road of this life, we lose them through the attack of spirits who lie in wait like robbers.

And yet Truth says:

> Let your good works be seen, and let them glorify your Father who is in heaven (Matt. V, 16).

But it is one thing when, in displaying a work, the glory of the giver is sought; it is another when private praise is desired for the gift of the giver. Hence the same Truth says again in the Gospel:

> Take care not to perform your righteousness before people, in order to be seen by them (Matt. VI, 1).

When our work is displayed to others, we must therefore first examine our heart and consider what is sought through the effort of displaying it. If we seek the glory of the giver, then even when our works are made public, we keep them hidden in his sight [Norman manuscripts and most early editions: “made public”; later editions read “public”]. But if through them we desire our own praise, they have already been poured out beyond his sight, even if they are unknown to many.

**84. It belongs to the perfect to seek God’s glory after displaying a work.**—It belongs to the very perfect, however, to display a work in such a way that they seek the glory of its author without knowing how to rejoice in the praise brought to them with private exultation. A praiseworthy work is displayed harmlessly to human beings only when, through genuine contempt for the mind’s own glory, the praise bestowed is trampled down.

Because the weak cannot overcome this by completely despising it, they must hide the good they do. Often they seek their own praise from the very beginning of the display. Often they desire, in displaying their work, to make the author’s glory known; but when approval receives them, they are carried away into a desire for their own praise. And when they neglect to judge themselves inwardly, scattered outwardly, they do not know what they are doing; their work serves their own exaltation, while they think that they are offering it as a service to the giver.

The reed, therefore, dwells among the stones because the hypocrite stands where he makes firm the intention of his mind. When he eagerly seeks the testimony of many, he stands, as it were, amid a collection of stones.

This hypocrite, however, designated by the name “reed,” when he subdues his body through abstinence; when, by giving away what he possesses, he labors in the pursuit of piety; when he is instructed in knowledge of sacred law [Bigot. and Lyr.: “of sacred reading”; Utic. preserves both readings]; when he uses the word of preaching—who, seeing him so full of generosity, would judge him to be alien from the grace of the giver?

And yet the heavenly dispensation gives him the gifts of working while denying him a share in the inheritance. It heaps upon him the gifts of action, yet does not recognize the life of the one who acts, because, when the gift received is turned toward personal praise, the shadow of exaltation obscures it in the sight of the innermost light.

Hence it is well added:

## CHAPTER XLIX

**Verse 18.—“If it swallows him up from his place, it will deny him and say: ‘I do not know you.’”**

**85. The rejection of the hypocrite.**—The hypocrite is swallowed up from his place when, at death, he is separated from the favor of the present life. But once swallowed up, the inner Judge denies him and declares that he does not know him, because Truth, in justly rejecting the life of the pretender, does not recognize it and does not acknowledge the good things he performed, since he did not bring them forth from a right intention.

Hence, when he comes in judgment, he will say to the foolish virgins:

> Truly I tell you, I do not know you (Matt. XXV, 12).

While he considers the corruption of their minds, he condemns even the incorruption of their flesh.

Would that the hypocrites’ own destruction alone were enough for them, and that their perverse efforts never ardently incited others to a life of duplicity [Gemet., Germ., Longip.: “to the way”]. For it is usually characteristic of each person to wish people like himself to be joined to him and to become like him; he avoids any difference in life and impresses upon others what he loves as something to imitate.

Hence, in the thinking of hypocrites, every simplicity is a crime. They judge open minds and call purity of heart stupidity. They turn all whom they desire to attach to themselves away from the path of simplicity; and, as though they had driven out foolishness, they think they have instructed those in whom they have defeated purity of mind—that is, the citadel of wisdom.

[Vet. XXXIX.] Since the hypocrite is rejected not only because of his own perversity but also because of the destruction of his followers who are joined to him, after it is said that he is not recognized by the Judge, it is rightly added immediately:

## CHAPTER L

**Verses 18, 19.—“For this is the joy of his way [Gemet. and Germ.: ‘of life’]: that others may again spring up from the earth.”**

**86. The hypocrite’s punishment is manifold.**—It is as though it were plainly said: When the Judge comes, he is by no means recognized, but receives punishments in many ways, because he has rejoiced more extensively in his own iniquity in proportion as he has propagated evil in others. For anyone for whom his own iniquity is not enough here must there also be tortured for the guilt of another.

Let hypocrites now rejoice, therefore, and boast that they have won human approval; let the simplicity of the righteous be despised, and let the folly of the double-minded be called wisdom. The contempt of the simple passes quickly; the glory of the double-minded quickly runs its course [Coc. and later editions read “to whom also,” in place of “quickly”; the English and Norman manuscripts and earlier Vulgate editions have “quickly”]. Hence it is aptly added:

## CHAPTER LI [Rec. XXXI]

**Verse 20.—“God will not cast away the simple, nor extend his hand to the wicked.”**

**87. They are punished for good deeds performed with an evil intention and for deceit.**—For when he appears as the strict Judge, he will raise up the despised simple by glorifying them, and crush the glory of the wicked by rejecting it.

Hypocrites are called wicked because they do good things badly and perform whatever is right in the pursuit of praise [Gilot., Vatic., Gussanv., after Coc.: “the good things they appear to do, under the pursuit [of praise]”].
