To whom do we extend a hand? To the one whom we raise from the depths. God therefore does not extend his hand to the wicked, because he leaves those who seek earthly glory below and does not raise them to heavenly joys, however right the things they do may appear.

Or hypocrites are called wicked for this reason: they display kindness toward their neighbors while concealing the deceits of their iniquity. In everything they do or say, they present simplicity outwardly, but inwardly they are skilled in the subtlety of duplicity. They feign purity on the surface, but always hide malice beneath the appearance of purity.

Against such people it is rightly said through Moses:

> You shall not wear a garment woven of wool and linen (Deut. XXII, 11–12).

Simplicity is signified by wool, and subtlety by linen. A garment made of wool and linen conceals the linen within and displays the wool on the surface. Thus the person who, in speech or action, wears a garment woven of wool and linen covers inward malice with subtlety and displays outwardly the simplicity of innocence. Since cunning cannot be detected under the appearance of purity, the linen lies hidden, as it were, beneath the thickness of wool.

It is fitting that, after the rejection of the double-minded, the reward of the righteous is shown [All our manuscripts read this, rather than the printed editions’ “after the punishments of the reprobate”], when it immediately adds:

## CHAPTER LII

**Verses 20, 21.—“Until your mouth is filled with laughter and your lips with jubilation.”**

**88. The laughter of the saints after mourning; jubilation.**—The mouth of the righteous will then be filled with laughter when, their tears of pilgrimage having ended, their hearts are satisfied with the exultation of eternal joy. Concerning this laughter Truth says to the disciples:

> The world will rejoice, but you will be sorrowful; yet your sorrow will be turned into joy (John XVI, 20).

And again:

> I will see you, and your heart will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you (ibid., 22).

Concerning this laughter Solomon says of the holy Church:

> She will laugh on the last day (Prov. XXXI, 25).

Again concerning it, it is said [The manuscripts read “says”; with this reading Gregory, unusually, attributes the words of Ecclesiasticus to Solomon]:

> It will be well with the one who fears the Lord at the end (Eccli. I, 13).

But then it will not be the laughter of the body; it will be the laughter of the heart [Corb. Germ.: “then it will be the laughter not of the body”]. The laughter of the body now arises from the wantonness of dissipation, whereas the laughter of the heart will then arise from the joy of security.

When all the elect are filled with the joy of clear contemplation, they leap, as it were, into laughter upon the mouth of the mind. We call it “jubilation” when we conceive in our heart a joy so great that the power of speech cannot express it; nevertheless, the exultation of the mind sounds forth in the voice what speech cannot explain.

It is rightly said that the mouth is filled with laughter and the lips with jubilation, because in that eternal homeland, when the mind of the righteous is carried away into exultation, the tongue is raised into a song of praise. Since they see as much as they cannot say, they jubilate in laughter, because they resound without exhausting what they love.

[Vet. XL.] **89. The punishments of the reprobate will never end; the force of the particle “until.”**—“Until” is not said to mean that almighty God does not raise up the wicked until he takes his elect into the joys of jubilation, as though afterward he might rescue from punishment those whom, previously abandoning them in their guilt, he condemns. Rather, it means that he will by no means do this even before the judgment, when it might seem doubtful to human beings whether he will do so.

For after the jubilation of his elect, the fact that he will not extend his hand to the wicked is established by the very strictness of the final judgment. Thus it is said through the Psalmist:

> The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet (Ps. CIX, 1–2).

This does not mean that the Lord will not sit at the Lord’s right hand after he strikes down his enemies and subjects them to his power. Rather, he reigns in eternal blessedness over all, both before and after he tramples the hearts of his rebellious enemies. It is therefore certain that, with his enemies subjected, he reigns without end and afterward as well.

Likewise, it is said in the Gospel concerning Mary’s husband:

> He did not know her until she bore her firstborn son (Matt. I, 25).

This does not mean that he knew her after the birth of God; rather, he did not touch her at all, even when he did not know that she was the mother of her Creator. Since he could not touch her after he recognized that the mystery of our redemption was to be celebrated from her womb, the evangelist necessarily bore witness to that period concerning which, because of Joseph’s ignorance, doubt might have arisen [In most manuscripts: “of God.” An ancient hand in Utic replaced “God” with “Lord.” Immediately afterward in the same manuscript and in Corb. Germ., Lyr., and Bigot.: “but by no means,” with “which” omitted].

Thus it is now said:

> God will not cast away the simple, nor extend his hand to the wicked, until your mouth is filled with laughter and your lips with jubilation.

It is as though it were plainly said: He does not abandon the life of the simple even before the judgment, nor does he fail to strike the minds of the malicious by abandoning them before the judgment appears. Since he will torment the reprobate without end, and his elect will reign forever after he has appeared, there is plainly no doubt about it.

It follows:

## CHAPTER LIII [Rec. XXXII]

**Verse 22.—“Those who hate you will be clothed with shame.”**

**90. From what the reprobate will be ashamed on the day of judgment.**—At the final examination, confusion clothes the enemies of the righteous, because, when they see their past evils flowing before the eyes of their minds, their own guilt, pressing down upon them from every side, clothes them.

They then endure the memory of their deeds as punishment, although now, as though strangers to the perception of reason, they sin with rejoicing. There they see how greatly they ought to have fled from what they loved; there they perceive how grievous was what they now celebrate in guilt.

Then guilt clouds the mind, and the conscience itself attacks it with the darts of its recollection. Who, then, could adequately weigh how great will be the confusion of the wicked when the eternal Judge is seen outwardly and guilt is present inwardly before their eyes?

They reach this state because here they loved only passing things. Hence it is aptly added immediately:

## CHAPTER LIV

**The same passage.—“And the tent of the impious will not endure.”**

**91. The attitude of the reprobate toward earthly goods, and that of the righteous.**—A tent is built so that the body may be protected from heat and cold. What, then, is expressed here by the name “tent” except the construction of earthly happiness, by which the reprobate pile up things destined to fall upon themselves, so as to protect themselves from the necessities of the present life as from heat and rain?

They strive to increase in honors so that they may not appear despised. By accumulating earthly possessions, they enlarge their store so that they may not waste away in the cold of poverty. They neglect to care for what follows and devote all their effort to ensuring that nothing is lacking in the present. They endeavor to spread their name so that they may not remain unknown; and if everything is available to their desire, they think themselves secure and happy in every respect.

Where, then, do they construct the dwelling of their mind? There, without doubt, they have fixed their tents. They endure adversity impatiently and rejoice languidly in prosperity. They think only about what is present and, without any recollection, never breathe toward the desire for their heavenly homeland. They rejoice that the goods they desire are available to them; and where they find rest in the flesh, there they also extinguish and bury the mind, because, slain by the weapon of worldly care, they always carry inwardly in thought the heap of earthly things that they multiply outwardly by seeking it.

**92.** [Vet. XL.] But the righteous, by contrast, neither receive the good things offered here as something great nor greatly fear the evils inflicted here. Even when they use present goods, they fear future evils; and when they groan over present evils, they are consoled by love of the good things to come.

Thus they are refreshed by temporal assistance as a traveler uses a bed in an inn: he rests, but hastens to depart; he is at rest in body, but in mind he is moving toward another destination.

Sometimes they even desire to endure adversity and refuse to prosper in transitory things, lest the pleasure of the journey delay them from reaching their homeland; lest they fix the step of their heart on the road of pilgrimage and at some time arrive at the sight of their heavenly homeland without recompense [One Vindoc. manuscript and the Froben edition: “without delay”]. They rejoice at being despised and do not grieve that they are afflicted by necessities.

Those, therefore, who do not fortify themselves against present adversities are like people who do not wish to have a tent against heat and rain. Hence Peter is rightly reproved because, not yet strengthened by perfection of mind, after recognizing the brightness of the truth, he tries to fix a tent on earth (Matt. XVII, 4; Mark IX, 2).

The righteous therefore neglect to construct themselves here, where they know themselves to be pilgrims and guests. Because they desire to rejoice in what is their own, they refuse to be happy in what is alien. But the more the unjust are separated from the inheritance of their eternal homeland, the deeper they fix the foundations of their thoughts in the earth.

Hence, from the very beginning of the human condition, Enoch is born seventh among the elect offspring. Hence Cain calls his first son Enoch and names the city he founded after him (Gen. IV, 17). “Enoch” means “dedication.” The wicked therefore dedicate themselves at the beginning, because in this life, which comes first, they plant the root of their heart, so that they may flourish here according to their desire and wither completely from the homeland that follows.

For the righteous, however, Enoch is born seventh, because the festive dedication of their life is reserved for the end [All manuscripts have this reading. The printed editions have “with festive dedication”; and a little earlier, “from the righteous,” where all the manuscripts unanimously have “for the righteous”].

Hence, as Paul attests, Abraham dwells in tents (Heb. XI, 9), because he awaits the city having foundations, which the heavenly builder constructed.

Hence Jacob proceeds humbly, following his flocks of sheep (Gen. XXXIII, 14), while Esau, coming to meet him, is exalted by the tumult of a great retinue, because the elect have no exaltation here, whereas the reprobate swell proudly in the good things of the flesh.

Hence the Lord says to Israel:

> If you choose one from the people of the land and appoint him ruler over you, he shall not acquire horses and horsemen (Deut. XVII, 16).

And yet the first king chosen by that same people, as soon as he reached the summit of power, suddenly chose three thousand horsemen for himself and immediately revealed his exaltation, bursting forth into the construction of the power he had received (I Kings XIII, 2). For he could not restrain outwardly in equality what his inward spirit was swelling above others.

That rich man had built himself a fortified tent, as it were, when he said:

> Soul, you have many good things stored up for many years; rest, eat, drink, and feast (Luke XII, 19).

But because his tent did not stand upon the foundation of truth, he immediately heard:

> Fool, this night they are demanding your soul from you; and whose will those things be that you have prepared (ibid., 20)?

It is rightly said, therefore:

> The tent of the impious will not endure,

because lovers of the fleeting life, while diligently constructing themselves in the present, are suddenly carried away to eternal things [Manuscripts Bellov., Vindoc., Norm., and others; the printed editions explain the passage as “are carried away to eternal punishment.”]

# BOOK NINE. THE NINTH CHAPTER WITH THE WHOLE OF THE TENTH IS EXPLAINED

[Col. 0859]

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0859A]

**1. Perverse people reject right statements as the words of opponents; the good act otherwise.**—If perverse minds once break out into a determination to oppose, they attack with contrary answers whatever they hear from those whom they oppose, whether it is wrong or right, because when a person is displeasing through opposition, even the right things he has said do not please them.

The hearts of the good, by contrast, do not hate the person but the fault. They judge perversities in such a way that they accept what is right in what is said. They sit as most equitable judges in discerning the meaning of opponents, rejecting what is badly spoken while nevertheless approving what they recognize as proceeding from truth.

Often, indeed, an ear of grain grows up even amid a multitude of thorns. The worker must therefore act with a cautious hand, so that while the thorn is removed, the ear may be nourished; thus the person who strives to uproot what pricks must know how to preserve what refreshes.

Hence blessed Job, because Baldad the Suhite had rightly said in his inquiry:

> Does God pervert judgment, or does the Almighty subvert what is just (Job VIII, 3)?

—and because he had spoken truths and powerful words against hypocrites—recognizing that these words had also been generally spoken against the wicked, rightly tramples down his own impulse toward self-defense and immediately approves what he has heard, saying:

## CHAPTER TWO [Rec. II]

**Chapter IX, verse 2.—“Truly I know that it is so, and that a human being is not justified when compared with God.”** [Early editions also read “will not be justified,” contrary to the manuscripts. Vulgate editions: *Deo non compositus*; the Paris edition of 1495 agrees with the manuscripts, and Gilot noted this reading in the margin.]

**2. We must be subjected to God, not compared with him.**—A human being subjected to God receives justice; when compared with God, he loses it, because whoever compares himself with the author of good deprives himself of the good he had received. Whoever arrogates to himself the good things he has received fights against God with God’s own gifts.

Where, then, the despised person is raised up, it is fitting that from there the one who has been raised should be destroyed. But the holy man, because he sees that every merit of our virtue is a vice if it is strictly judged by the inner Judge [Vindoc., Ebroic., Bajoc., Lyr., Bigot., Utic.: “because he sees that all our virtues are a vice of the mind”; Utic formerly read as the printed editions: “because he sees that every [virtue],” etc. Immediately afterward, the good manuscripts have “let them be judged,” instead of “let it be judged”], rightly adds:

## CHAPTER THREE

**“If he wishes to contend with him, he will not be able to answer him one thing for a thousand.”**

**3. Whoever exalts himself over God’s gifts loses them.**—In sacred Scripture, the number one thousand is usually understood to signify universality. Hence the Psalmist says:

> The word that he commanded for a thousand generations (Ps. CIV, 8),

although it is evident that from the beginning of the world up to the coming of the Redeemer, the evangelist counts no more than seventy-seven generations (Luke III, 38). What, then, is expressed by the number one thousand except the perfect totality of the foreknown generation, destined to produce a new offspring?

Hence John also says:

> They will reign with him for a thousand years (Rev. XX, 6),

because the reign of the holy Church is made firm by the perfection of universality.

Since the monad (*monas*), when multiplied, is brought to ten, ten multiplied by itself expands into one hundred, and this multiplied by ten advances to one thousand [Turon., Bellovac., Gemet., and other Norman manuscripts read *monas multiplicatus*; Vindoc. reads *monas multiplicata*. All omit *decies* (“tenfold”), which Coccius first added before *multiplicata*, followed by later editions], when we begin from one in order to arrive at one thousand, what is signified here by the designation “one” except the beginning of living well, and by the magnitude of the number one thousand except the perfection of that same good life?

To contend with God is not to attribute glory to him, but to arrogate to oneself the glory of one’s virtue. But the holy man should see that even one who has already received the highest gifts, if he exalts himself over what he has received, loses everything he had received, and should say:

> If he wishes to contend with him, he will not be able to answer him one thing for a thousand.

For whoever contends with the author cannot answer one thing for a thousand, because whoever exalts himself over perfection shows that he does not even possess the beginning of living well. We cannot answer one thing for a thousand because, when we exalt ourselves over the perfection of a good life, we show that we have not even begun it.

But we are then shaken more truly by our weakness if, by considering it, we weigh how immense the Judge’s power is. Hence it is added:

## CHAPTER FOUR [Vet. II]

**Verse 4.—“He is wise in heart and strong in power.”**

**4. As wise, God cannot be deceived; as strong, he cannot be evaded.**—What wonder is it if we call the Creator of the wise wise, when we know that he himself is wisdom? And what wonder is it that he is said to be strong, when no one is ignorant that he himself is strength?

But the holy man, having uttered two words in praise of the author, makes something known to us by which he may lead us back, trembling, to the knowledge of ourselves. God is called wise because he subtly recognizes our hidden things; and he is said to be strong because he powerfully strikes what he has recognized.

He therefore cannot be deceived by us, because he is wise, nor evaded, because he is strong. Now, as wise, he invisibly sees all things; then, as strong, he will punish without any obstacle those whom he rejects.

Here, too, he orders this by strong wisdom: when the human mind raises itself against its author, it is confounded by its own exaltation. Hence it is added:

## CHAPTER FIVE

**The same passage.—“Who has resisted him and had peace?”** [Gemet. and Corb. Germ.: “Who has resisted him and had peace?”]

5. Whoever resists God falls from peace. What it means to resist God.—For he who wondrously creates all things also orders them so that what has been created may correspond with one another. [Col. 0861A] Therefore, when resistance is offered to the Creator, the harmony of peace is dissolved, because those things cannot remain ordered which abandon the arrangement of heavenly governance. For the things that, while subject to God, [Note: Thus nearly all our manuscripts. Longipontanus has: “persisted in tranquility.” Left to themselves, they confuse the order of uprightness. The older edition reads, “persist in tranquility.” The Vindocian manuscripts add a negation: “do not persist in tranquility.” More recent editions have, “cannot persist in tranquility.”] would have persisted in tranquility, when left to themselves fall into confusion, because they find no peace in themselves, since they oppose in their Author the peace that comes from above.

Thus that supreme angelic spirit, which, subject to God, could have stood at the summit, [Note: Germanus Corbeiensis, Germanus, Longipontanus, Turonensis, Baiocensis: “cast away by itself, it suffers.”] suffers itself to be cast away, because through the restlessness of its nature it wanders outward. Thus the first parent of the human race, because he resisted the Creator’s command, immediately experienced the dishonor of the flesh; and because he refused through obedience to be subject to the Creator, he was cast down beneath himself and immediately lost the peace of the body.

Rightly, therefore, it is said: “Who resisted him, and had peace?” [Col. 0861B] because from the very point at which a perverse mind raises itself against the Author, it is confused within itself. We are said to resist God when we try to oppose his ordinances. For our weakness does not actually thwart his unchangeable sentence, but it nevertheless attempts what it cannot accomplish. Often human weakness secretly recognizes the force of his ordinance, yet desires to alter it if it could. It strives to oppose it, but breaks itself upon the very sword of its opposition. It struggles against the inward order, but, overcome by its own efforts, is bound by them.

Therefore the one who resists cannot have peace, because, while pride is followed by confusion, what is foolishly done through fault is wonderfully ordered as punishment for the one who acts. [Note: The first Vindocian manuscript and Corbeiensis Germanus read: “this is wonderfully ordered in accordance with the power of the agent”; the other Vindocian: “this is changeably ordered in the punishment of the agent, or according to the vengeance of the judge.”] But the holy man, filled with the power of the prophetic spirit, when he sees human pride generally brought to confusion, [Col. 0861C] immediately directs his mind’s eyes toward the particular evil of the Israelite people, and shows, through the destruction of one nation, what punishment awaits all the exalted. For he suddenly adds, saying:

## CHAPTER VI

**VERSE 5.—** “Who removes mountains, and they do not know it—those whom he overturns in his anger.”

6. The preaching of God’s word is foretold as being transferred from the Jews to the Gentiles.—In Holy Scripture, the name “mountains” often signifies the elevation of preachers, of whom the Psalmist says: “Let the mountains receive peace for your people” (Psalm 71:3). The chosen preachers of the eternal homeland are rightly called mountains, because by the loftiness of their life they abandon the low places of the earth and become near to heaven.

But Truth removed the mountains when it withdrew the holy preachers from the obduracy of Judaea. Hence the Psalmist rightly also says: “The mountains shall be transferred into the heart of the sea” (Psalm 45:3). The mountains were transferred into the heart of the sea when the apostles, who were preaching, rejected by the faithlessness of Judaea, came to the understanding of the Gentiles. [Col. 0862A] Hence they themselves say in the Acts: “It was necessary that the word of God be spoken to you first; but since you reject it and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts 13:46).

But those who were overturned in the Lord’s anger did not know this very removal of the mountains. For when the Hebrews drove the apostles from their borders, they thought they had gained something by losing the light of preaching. Struck by just retribution in accordance with their deserts, they were blinded by so great an error of understanding that they thought it a cause for rejoicing that they were losing the light.

But after the apostles had been rejected, Judaea was immediately destroyed by the Roman commander Titus, and, scattered among all the nations, was dispersed. Therefore, after the removal of the mountains, it is rightly added:

## CHAPTER VII [Ancient recension III]

[Col. 0862B]

**VERSE 6.—** “Who shakes the earth from its place, and its pillars are shaken.”

291

7. The dispersion of the Jews is foretold.—The earth was shaken from its place when the Israelite people, uprooted from the borders of Judaea, plainly submitted its neck to the Gentiles, because it had refused to be subject to the Author. This earth had pillars, because the structure of its stubbornness, destined to fall, had been raised upon the priests and rulers, the teachers of the Law and the Pharisees. [Note: The printed editions have *fabricae* (“of the structure”), whereas *pertinaciae* (“of stubbornness”) is found in Vindocianus, Turonensis, Normanus, and others.] In them the edifice of the letter stood, and in the time of its tranquility it bore, as though superimposed structures, the burdens of carnal sacrifices.

But when the mountains were removed, the pillars were shaken, because, once the apostles had been taken away from Judaea, those who had expelled the preachers of life from it were themselves not permitted to live there. For it was fitting that they should lose their earthly homeland after being conquered, since for love of it they had not feared to attack the soldiers of the heavenly homeland.

But after the holy teachers had been expelled, Judaea became utterly numb, [Col. 0862C] [Note: Thus we restore the reading from almost all the manuscripts, instead of *corruit* (“collapsed”), which the printed editions have.] and, by the just judgment of the Judge, closed the eyes of its mind in the darkness of its error. Hence it is further added:

## CHAPTER VIII [Recent recension III]

**VERSE 7.—** “Who commands the sun, and it does not rise; and closes up the stars as though under a seal.”

8. After the preachers were expelled, Judaea was deprived of light.—At times, in sacred discourse, the name “sun” designates the splendor of preachers. Thus John says: “The sun became like a sack of haircloth” (Revelation 6:12). At the end of time the sun is shown as a sack of haircloth, because the shining life of preachers is displayed as harsh and contemptible before the eyes of the reprobate. They are also represented by the brightness of the stars, because, while they preach what is right to sinners, they illuminate the darkness of our night.

Hence, when the preachers have been withdrawn, the prophet says: “The stars of the rains have been restrained” (Jeremiah 3:3). [Col. 0862D] [Note: See below, no. 15, note: “Germanus Corbeiensis, Germanus, Longipontanus, Turonensis, and Baiocensis: ‘cast away by itself, it suffers.’”]

Because the sun shines during the day, while the stars illuminate the darkness of night—and because in sacred discourse the designation “day” often signifies the eternal homeland, while “night” signifies the present life—the holy preachers become like the sun to our eyes when they open for us the contemplation of the true light; and they are like stars shining in darkness when, through the active life, they arrange earthly affairs for our future needs. [Col. 0863A] They sparkle like the sun in the day when they raise the sight of our mind toward contemplating the homeland of inward brightness; and they shine like stars in the night because, while they engage in earthly affairs, they direct the foot of our work, already about to stumble, by the example of their uprightness.

But because, after the preachers had been expelled, there was no one to show the Jewish people, remaining in the night of its faithlessness, either the brightness of contemplation or the light of the active life—for Truth, which had abandoned it when rejected, deservedly blinded it by withdrawing the light of preaching—it is rightly said: “Who commands the sun, and it does not rise; and closes up the stars as though under a seal.”

He did not wish the sun to rise for the people from whom he turned away the mind of the preachers. And he closed the stars as though under a seal: by keeping his preachers within themselves through silence, he concealed heavenly light from the blind perceptions of the wicked. [Col. 0863B] [Note: The printed editions read “from the minds”; Corbeiensis Germanus, Vindocianus, Turonensis, and Norman manuscripts have “from the perceptions,” which we dutifully follow.]

[Ancient recension IV.]

9. Judaea is to be recalled to the faith.—We must consider that we close something under a seal for the very reason that, when the proper time arrives, we may bring it forth into the open. And, as Holy Scripture bears witness, we have learned that Judaea, which is now abandoned, will at the end be gathered into the bosom of faith. Thus Isaiah says: [Col. 0863C] “Though the number of the children of Israel be like the sand of the sea, a remnant will be saved” (Isaiah 10:22, according to the Septuagint). Hence Paul says: “Until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter, and thus all Israel should be saved” (Romans 11:25). [Note: Gemetensis: “should enter.” This was formerly read in Uticensis as “would enter”; it is also read thus in Turonensis and many others.]

He, therefore, who now withdraws his preachers from the eyes of Judaea but later reveals them has closed the stars as though under a seal, so that, first hidden and afterward shining, the rays of the spiritual stars may cause it, now rejected, not to see the night of its faithlessness, but then, when illuminated, to recognize it. [Col. 0863D] [Note: Gemetensis: “the night of its faithlessness.”]

This is why those two outstanding preachers were taken away by a deferred death, so that they might be recalled to the work of preaching at the end. Of them John says: “These are the two olive trees and the two lampstands standing before the Lord of the earth” (Revelation 11:4). Concerning one of them, Truth itself promises in the Gospel, saying: “Elijah will come, and he will restore all things” (Matthew 17:11).

Thus the stars were closed as though under a seal: they are now hidden so that they do not appear, but afterward they will appear so that they may be of benefit. Nevertheless, the Israelite people, which will be gathered abundantly at the end, is cruelly hardened at the very beginnings of the holy Church. [Col. 0864A] For it rejected the preachers of the truth and despised words of help.

Yet this is accomplished by the wondrous dispensation of the Author, so that the glory of the preachers—which, if received by one people, could have remained hidden—is extended among all the nations after being rejected. Hence it is suitably added at once:

## CHAPTER IX [Recent recension IV]

**VERSE 8.—** “Who alone stretches out the heavens.”

10. God permitted the Gospel to be rejected by the Jews so that it might be spread among all the nations.—For what is signified by the name “heavens” except this same heavenly life of the preachers? Of them the Psalmist says: “The heavens declare the glory of God” (Psalm 18:1). They are therefore called both heavens and sun: heavens because they protect by interceding; sun because by preaching they display the power of light.

When the earth was shaken, the heavens were stretched out, because, when Judaea roared with the force of persecution, the Lord extended the life of the apostles into the knowledge of all the nations. [Col. 0864B] [Note: In Gemetensis and Corbeiensis Germanus, *dum* (“while”) is absent; the reading is: “And that one, through judgment, is scattered …,” etc. The word “captive” is absent.] While Judaea was scattered throughout the world in captivity by judgment, they were everywhere extended in honor by grace.

The heavens had been narrow when one people alone held so many outstanding preachers. For who among the Gentiles would have known Peter if he had remained in the preaching of the Israelite people alone? Who would have recognized Paul’s virtues if Judaea had not, by persecuting him, sent him into our knowledge? Behold, those who were rejected by the Israelite people with scourges and insults are now honored throughout the world. [Note: Thus most manuscripts, or “with blows.” The edition with the Colbert manuscript has “those who were rejected by blows.”]

Therefore the Lord alone stretched out the heavens: by the hidden wonder of his plan, he permitted his preachers to be oppressed among one people, and from there caused them to be spread to the ends of the world. [Col. 0864C]

But even the Gentiles themselves, devoted to the present world, did not willingly accept the words of life when the apostles’ tongue reproved their faults. Immediately they swelled up in the pride of contradiction and roused themselves to the cruelty of persecution. Yet the one who strives to oppose the words of preaching is quickly restrained by the wonder of signs. Hence, suitably, it is further added in praise of the Author:

## CHAPTER X [Ancient and Recent recensions V]

**IBID.—** “And walks upon the waves of the sea.”

293

11. The persecutions of the Gentiles were to be broken by the power of miracles.—For what is signified by the name “sea” except the bitterness of this world, raging in the death of the good? Of it the Psalmist also says: “Gathering the waters of the sea as in a wineskin” (Psalm 32:7). The Lord gathers the waters of the sea as in a wineskin when, arranging all things with wondrous governance, he restrains the threats of carnal people, enclosing them within their own hearts. [Col. 0864D] [Note: In Lyranensis and Uticensis, the alternative reading is noted in the margin: “enclosed in their own orders.”]

Therefore the Lord walks upon the waves of the sea, because, when the storm of persecution rises, it is broken by the astonishment produced by his miracles. He who calms the swellings of human madness treads upon the waves as though they were raised into a heap.

For when the Gentiles saw their customs being destroyed by the preaching of a new way of life; when the rich of this world saw the deeds of the poor opposing their pride; and when the wise of the age judged that the words of the uneducated were standing against them, they immediately swelled into the storm of persecution.

But those who, stirred by opposition to the words, leap into the storms of persecution are restrained, as we have said, by the wonder of signs. The Lord therefore set his feet upon as many waves as he displayed miracles to proud persecutors.

Hence the Psalmist rightly says again: “Wondrous are the upheavals of the sea; wondrous in the heights is the Lord” (Psalm 92:4). [Note: Vindocianus: “wondrous in the heights.”] The world wondrously raised itself against the life of the elect into waves of persecution, but the Creator of heavenly things laid them low still more wondrously by the power of the preachers raised up. [Col. 0865A] [Note: Coccius and later editions: “by the power lifted up.”] For he showed that his ministers could accomplish more through miracles than earthly powers had been able to swell up through anger. [Note: Older editions: “than the earthly powers can swell up.” Coccius and later editions: “than the earthly powers that had swollen up.” We follow the manuscripts.]

The Lord also speaks fittingly through Jeremiah, recounting external things while announcing internal ones: “I have set the sand as a boundary for the sea, an everlasting commandment which it shall not pass; and they shall be shaken, and shall not prevail; and its waves shall swell, and shall not pass over it” (Jeremiah 5:22). [Note: Most manuscripts read *illud* (“that”), which can suitably refer to the commandment. We retain *illum* (“it”) with the Vulgate editions and the manuscripts Corbeiensis Germanus, and refer it to the boundary.]

The Lord set sand as a boundary for the sea because, to break the glory of the world, he chose the despised and the poor. The waves of that sea swell when the powers of the age leap forth to stir up persecution. But they cannot cross the sand, because they are broken by the miracles and humility of the despised. [Col. 0865B]

While the sea rages and rises through the waves of its madness, yet is trampled by the display of inward power, the holy Church advances and rises, with the passage of time, toward the established form of its order. [Col. 0865C] Hence it is suitably added at once:

## CHAPTER XI [Ancient and Recent recensions VI]

**VERSE 9.—** “Who makes Arcturus, and the Orions, and the Hyades, and the inner chambers of the South.”

12. Why Scripture uses the words of the wise of the world.—The word of truth does not follow the empty fables of Hesiod, Aratus, and Callimachus, so that, when it names Arcturus, it should imagine the endmost tail of the seven stars of the Bear, or that, like a mad lover, Orion should hold a sword. These names of the stars were invented by worshipers of carnal wisdom. But Holy Scripture uses these same names so that the things it wishes to convey may be expressed through familiar terminology.

For if it named the stars it wished to mention by names unknown to us, human beings—for whom this same Scripture was made—would certainly not know what they were hearing. Thus, in sacred discourse, the wise of God draw language from the wise of the world, just as, for the benefit of humanity, God himself, the Creator of human beings, assumes within himself the voice of human passion, so that he says: “It repented me that I had made man upon the earth” (Genesis 6:6–7), although it is clearly established that he who sees all things before they come to be cannot, after making something, repent as though he had changed his mind.

What wonder, then, if spiritual men use the words of carnal people, when the ineffable Spirit himself, the Creator of all things, in order to draw flesh toward understanding him, forms within himself the language of flesh?

Thus, in Holy Scripture, when we hear familiar names of stars, we recognize which stars are being discussed. But when we consider what is being narrated about those stars, we must rise from their movements to the secrets of spiritual understanding. For, according to the literal sense, it is not surprising that God made Arcturus, the Orions, and the Hyades, since it is certainly true that there is absolutely nothing in the world that he did not make. But the holy man says that the Lord made these things because through them he understands that those realities are properly signified which are accomplished spiritually. [Col. 0866A]

13. Arcturus signifies the Church.—For what is expressed by the name “Arcturus,” which, set in the axis of heaven, shines with the rays of seven stars, except the universal Church, which in John’s Apocalypse is represented by seven churches and seven lampstands (Revelation 1:12, 20)? Since it contains within itself the gifts of the sevenfold grace of the Spirit, shining with the brightness of supreme virtue, it gleams as though from the axis of truth.

[Ancient recension VII.] It must also be considered that Arcturus is always turning and never setting, because the holy Church continually endures the persecutions of the wicked, yet persists without failing until the end of the world. Often the reprobate, because they persecuted it even to destruction, believed that they had extinguished it completely; but it returned to the strength of its growth all the more abundantly because it struggled by dying in the hands of its persecutors. Thus Arcturus is raised as it turns, because the holy Church is restored more powerfully in the truth precisely when it is wearied more fervently for the truth.

14. The Orions signify the martyrs.—Therefore it is fitting that immediately after Arcturus he adds the Orions. The Orions rise in the very depth of the winter season, and by their rising stir up storms and disturb seas and lands. What, then, is signified by the Orions after Arcturus except the martyrs? What else, when the holy Church is raised to the condition of preaching, could be meant than those who were to endure the weight and afflictions of their persecutors, coming before heaven’s face as though in winter? [Col. 0866C] [Note: Coccius and later editions: “while they raise the holy Church …,” a reading contrary to the manuscripts. In Corbeiensis Germanus and one Vindocian manuscript: “it is raised to the state of perfection or preaching.”]

When these were born, sea and land were disturbed, because, when the Gentiles grieved to see their customs destroyed by the appearance of the martyrs’ courage, they aroused against their death not only the angry and turbulent, but also the peaceful. Thus winter shuddered from the Orions, because, as the steadfastness of the saints shone forth, the cold mind of the unbelieving was roused into the storm of persecution.

Heaven therefore produced the Orions when the holy Church sent forth martyrs. As they dared to speak what was right to the uneducated, they endured the whole weight of opposition arising from the cold.

[Col. 0867A]

15. The Hyades signify the teachers.—He rightly adds the Hyades immediately afterward. They appear before the face of heaven as spring grows young, and are seen when the sun is already exerting and displaying the strength of its heat. They cling to the beginnings of that sign which the wise of the world call Taurus, from which the sun begins to increase and rises more ardently to lengthen the spaces of the day.

Who, then, are designated by the name of the Hyades after the Orions except the teachers of the holy Church? After the martyrs had been withdrawn, they came into the knowledge of the world at the time when the faith shines more brightly and, the winter of unbelief having been suppressed, the sun of truth burns more deeply through the hearts of the faithful.

Once the storm of persecution had been removed, [Col. 0867B] [Note: Thus nearly all our manuscripts, rather than the reading in the editions: “after the long nights of unbelief had been completed.” In Gemetensis alone appears: “after the long night of unbeliefs had been completed.”] they arose in the holy Church when, through the springtime of belief, a brighter year was already opening for it.

[Ancient recension VIII.] Nor is it without reason that the holy teachers are designated by the name of the Hyades. In Greek, rain is called ὑετός (*hyetos*), and the Hyades received their name from the rains because, when they rise, they plainly bring showers. They are therefore rightly represented by the designation “Hyades”: brought forth into the face of heaven, as it were, for the condition of the universal Church, they poured the showers of holy preaching over the arid earth of the human heart.

For if the word of preaching were not rain, Moses would never have said: “Let my speech be awaited like rain” (Deuteronomy 32:2); nor would Truth have said through Isaiah: “I will command the clouds not to rain rain upon it” (Isaiah 5:6); nor would he have said what we quoted shortly before: “Therefore the stars of the rains have been restrained” (Jeremiah 3:3). [Col. 0867C] [Note: The word is not *stellae* (“stars”), but *stillae* (“drops”), both in the Hebrew source and in the Vulgate translation, as well as in other versions and paraphrases. The Greek interpretation contains neither word. Nevertheless, it is clear that Gregory read it in this form.]

When, therefore, the Hyades come with the rains, the sun is led toward higher regions of heaven, because, when the knowledge of the teachers appears and our mind is watered by the rain of preaching, the warmth of faith increases. The watered earth bears fruit when the light of heaven grows hot, because we produce the fruit of good works more abundantly when we burn more brightly in the heart through the flame of sacred instruction.

As heavenly knowledge is displayed through them more and more each day, the springtime of inward light is opened for us, so that a new sun may glitter in our minds and, known to us through their words, shine forth from itself each day with greater brightness. [Col. 0868A] [Note: Lyranensis and Bigotensis: “as the end of the world approaches.”] As the end of the world presses on, heavenly knowledge advances and grows more abundantly with time. Thus Daniel says: “Many shall pass through, and knowledge shall be multiplied” (Daniel 12:4).

Hence, in the earlier part of the revelation, the angel says to John: “Seal up the things which the seven thunders have spoken” (Revelation 10:4). But at the end of the same revelation he commands him, saying: “Do not seal up the words of the prophecy of this book” (ibid., 22:10). The earlier part of the revelation is commanded to be sealed, while its conclusion is forbidden to be sealed, because whatever lay hidden at the beginnings of the holy Church is displayed daily at the end.

Some, however, think that the Hyades received their name from the Greek letter called *y*. [Col. 0868B] [Note: The editions of Gil, the Vatican edition, and Gussanus read: “which is called upsilon.” We express the reading of the earlier witnesses, which is also found in the manuscripts.] If this is so, it is not contrary to the meaning we have given. For the teachers are not inappropriately represented by stars that derive their name from letters. But although the Hyades do not differ from the vision of that same letter, it remains certain that ὑετός means rain, and that, when they rise, they bring showers. [Note: Thus the better manuscripts. The editions read: “because they have risen.”]

16. In the Church the apostles shone first, then the martyrs, and afterward the teachers.—The holy man, therefore, contemplating the order of our redemption, should marvel and, marveling, exclaim, saying: “Who alone stretches out the heavens, and walks upon the waves of the sea; who makes Arcturus, and the Orions, and the Hyades.”

When the heavens had been stretched out, the Lord formed Arcturus, because, when the apostles had been brought into honor, he established the Church in heavenly conduct. When Arcturus had been formed, he made the Orions, because, after the faith of the universal Church had been strengthened, he brought forth martyrs against the storms of the world. After the Orions had been brought forth, he produced the Hyades, because, when the martyrs had grown strong against adversity, he supplied the teaching of masters to water the dryness of human hearts. [Col. 0868C]

These, then, are the orders of the spiritual stars which, while they rise above in the highest virtues, continually shine from above.

17. What glory is prepared for the saints when they depart from here.—But after these things, what remains except that the holy Church, receiving the fruit of its labor, should arrive at the innermost places of the heavenly homeland to behold them? Hence, after saying, “Who makes Arcturus, and the Orions, and the Hyades,” he immediately added: “And the inner chambers of the South.”

[Ancient recension IX.] For what is signified in this place by the name “South” except the fervor of the Holy Spirit? When someone is filled with it, he burns with love for the spiritual homeland. Hence, in the voice of the Bridegroom, the Song of Songs says: “Arise, North Wind, and come, South Wind; blow through my garden, and let its spices flow” (Song of Songs 4:16). [Col. 0868D] When the South comes, the North Wind rises and withdraws, because, at the coming of the Holy Spirit, the ancient enemy, who had confined the mind in sluggishness, is expelled and departs.

The South blows through the Bridegroom’s garden so that its spices may flow, because, when the Spirit of truth fills the holy Church with the virtues of his gifts, he spreads the fragrances of good works far and wide from it. The inner chambers of the South, therefore, are those hidden orders of angels and the most secret recesses of the heavenly homeland, which the warmth of the Holy Spirit fills.

The souls of the saints arrive there, both now, when they have been stripped of their bodies, and afterward, when they have been restored to their bodies; and they are hidden there like stars in secret places. [Note: Thus the ancient editions with Vindocianus, Gemetensis, Lyranensis, Bigotensis, Uticensis, Longipontanus, and others; in place of this, Coccius and other editions have: “as though hidden in the recesses of the South.”]

There, as in the time of midday, the fire of the sun burns more intensely, because the splendor of the Creator, now that the darkness of our mortality has been pressed down, is seen more clearly. There, like a ray of a sphere, it rises toward higher regions, because Truth illuminates us more subtly from itself. There the light of inward contemplation is seen without the intervening shadow of mutability; there is the warmth of the highest light without any obscurity of the body; there the invisible choirs of angels shine like stars in secret places. They cannot now be seen by human beings precisely because they are more deeply flooded with the flame of the true light.

It is therefore exceedingly wondrous that, having sent the apostles, the Lord stretched out the heavens; that, calming the swellings of persecutions, he restrained the waves of the sea by walking upon them; that, when the Church had been established, he set up Arcturus; that, when the martyrs had been strengthened against adversity, he sent forth the Orions; that, when the teachers had been filled with tranquility, he provided the Hyades. But after these things it is exceedingly marvelous that he prepared for us the bosom of the heavenly homeland as the inner chambers of the South. [Col. 0869A]

[Col. 0869B]

18. The beauty of the saints is one thing in their virtues and another in their rewards.—All this is beautiful which is seen, as it were, upon the face of heaven through the divine dispensation; but far more, and incomparably more, beautiful is that to which one arrives invisibly. Hence the Bridegroom again rightly says in praise of his bride: “How beautiful you are, my beloved, how beautiful! Your eyes are like those of doves, apart from what lies hidden within” (Song of Songs 4:1).

He calls her beautiful and repeats that she is beautiful because one beauty belongs to her virtues, in which she is now seen, while another beauty belongs to her rewards, in which she will then be raised through the vision of her Creator. All the elect are her members. Because they proceed simply toward all things, they are called her dove-like eyes; they shine with great light because they also sparkle with the miracles of signs.

But how great is all this miracle that can be seen? The inward miracle, which cannot now be seen, is more wondrous. Concerning it he suitably adds there: “Apart from what lies hidden within.” Great indeed is the glory of an outward work, but incomparably greater is the hidden reward.

What is therefore signified by the name of the stars through blessed Job is signified by Solomon’s words through the designation of the eyes. And what Solomon says—“apart from what lies hidden within”—the blessed Job conveys to us when he commends the inner chambers of the South.

But behold: the holy man, marveling at outward things, considering inward things, recounting what is open, penetrating what is hidden, attempts to speak of everything that is done both inwardly and outwardly. Yet when will the tongue of flesh explain the works of such supreme magnitude? Hence he suitably grasps these same works more effectively by failing to describe them, saying: [Col. 0869C]

## CHAPTER XII [Ancient recension X]

**VERSE 10.—** “Who does great things and unsearchable, and wondrous things without number.”

19. We praise God’s works more eloquently by being astonished than by speaking.—We express the works of divine power more truly when we recognize that we cannot express them; we speak more eloquently when, struck with wonder at them, we remain silent. For in recounting God’s works our very inadequacy exercises its tongue sufficiently when, remaining mute, it fittingly praises what it cannot fittingly comprehend. [Col. 0870A]

Hence the Psalmist rightly says: “Praise him according to his mighty acts; praise him according to the multitude of his greatness” (Psalm 150:2). For the one who praises the Lord according to the multitude of his greatness is the one who realizes that he is overwhelmed in completing his praise.

Let him therefore say: “Who does great things and unsearchable, and wondrous things without number”—great in power, unsearchable in reason, innumerable in multiplicity. Thus, unable to complete his account of the divine works by speaking, he defined them more eloquently by failing.

But why are we carried far outside ourselves in considering these things when we do not even know what is being done with regard to us? Hence it is suitably added:

## CHAPTER XIII [Recent recension VII]

[Col. 0870B]

**VERSE 11.—** “If he comes to me, I shall not see him; and if he departs, I shall not understand.”

20. Humanity is so blind that it often thinks the gift of grace is anger, and vice versa.—The human race, shut out from inward joys because of its guilt, lost the eyes of the mind, and does not know by what steps of merit it proceeds. Often it considers a gift of grace to be anger, and often what is the anger of divine severity it takes for grace.

It often considers the gifts of virtues to be grace, yet, elated by those same gifts, it falls. Often it fears adverse temptations as though they were anger; yet, pressed by those same temptations, it rises more cautiously to preserve its virtues.

For who would not think that he is drawing near to God when he recognizes himself increasing in heavenly gifts—when he receives either the gift of prophecy, or the ministry of teaching, or grows strong for exercising the grace of healing? Yet often, when the mind relaxes through confidence in its virtue, the adversary lies in wait, and it is pierced by the weapon of an unforeseen fault. Thus it is made eternally distant from God precisely where, for a time, it approached him without the guardianship of vigilance.

[Ancient recension XI.] And who would not think himself already abandoned by divine grace when, after having experienced purity, he sees himself attacked by temptations of the flesh, dishonorable things gathered into his mind, and various shameful and unclean thoughts passing before the eyes of his mind? Yet when these things weary him without overcoming him, they do not slay him through pollution; rather, they preserve him through humility. Discovering himself weak in temptation, the mind turns wholly to the help of the Divinity, utterly loses confidence in itself, and thus clings more deeply to God precisely where it had feared and lamented that it had fallen farther from God. [Col. 0870C]

The approach and withdrawal of God from our mind, therefore, are not recognized until the outcome of changing circumstances is known. For, in the case of temptation, it is uncertain whether God is testing or destroying; and, in the case of gifts, it cannot be discerned whether they are rewarding those who are abandoned here or nourishing them on the way so that they may be led to the homeland.

Therefore, humanity, once expelled from inward joys, should behold the doors of the spiritual secret closed against it, and, cast outside into the flesh, should groan. Considering the losses caused by its blindness, it should say: “If he comes to me, I shall not see him; and if he departs, I shall not understand.”

As though openly lamenting, it says: “After I once willingly lost my eyes, I suffer the blindness of the night I sought; I no longer recognize either the rising or the setting of the sun.”

And yet the human being, weighed down by the punishment of weakness and burdened by the darkness of blindness, hastens toward the judgment of the heavenly light, to render an account of his deeds. Hence it is immediately added: [Col. 0871A]

## CHAPTER XIV [Recent recension VIII]

**VERSE 12.—** “If he suddenly questions, who will answer him?”

21. A person is not sufficient to answer God when he judges or strikes.—God questions suddenly when he calls us, unprepared, to the severity of his examination. But a human being is not sufficient to answer his questioning, because if he is examined then with mercy removed, even the life of the righteous collapses in that judgment. [Col. 0871B]

Or certainly, he questions when he strikes us with hard blows, so that, when our mind peacefully thinks great things of itself, it may discover truthfully in disturbance what it is. Often, because it is struck, it groans but cannot answer, since the adversity of its own chastisement displeases it. Yet, considering itself, a human being remains silent and fears to investigate the divine judgments, because it recognizes that it is dust.

Hence Paul says: “O man, who are you to answer God?” (Romans 9:20). The one called “man” is shown to be unable to answer God, because, having been taken from the earth, he is not worthy to examine heavenly judgments. Hence here too it is suitably added:

## CHAPTER XV

[Col. 0871C]

**IBID.—** “Or who can say to him, ‘Why do you do this?’”

22. God’s deeds are not to be scrutinized but revered.—The deeds of the Author must always be revered without investigation, since they can in no way be unjust. To seek an explanation of his hidden [Note: [Col. 0871D] Lyran., Utic., Bigot.: “judgment.”] counsel is nothing other than to rebel proudly against his counsel. Therefore, when the reason for his deeds is not perceived, what remains is that one should humbly fall silent beneath those deeds, since the understanding of the flesh is wholly insufficient to penetrate the secrets of majesty. Thus, whoever does not see the reason in God’s deeds, by considering his own weakness sees why he does not see the reason. Hence Paul also adds immediately: “Shall the thing formed say to him who formed it, ‘Why have you made me thus?’” (ibid.). For the more clearly he perceives himself to be a product of the divine work, the more he reproves himself lest he rebel against the hand of the maker; for he who benevolently made what did not exist does not unjustly abandon what does exist. Let the mind, then, return to itself amid chastisement, and let it not seek what it cannot grasp, lest, if the cause of divine anger is examined, it provoke that anger still further once it has been examined, and pride kindle it inextinguishably, though humility could have appeased it. Hence, appropriately, what follows immediately concerns this same anger:

## CHAPTER XVI [Rec. IX]

[Col. 0872A]

### Verse 13.—“God, against whose anger no one can resist, and beneath whom those who bear the world are bowed.”

23. How no one can resist God’s anger. The question resolved.—It is very surprising that no one is said to be able to resist God’s anger, since the divine Scriptures testify that many have stood in the way of the indignation of heavenly punishment. Did Moses not resist God’s anger when, standing forth on behalf of the falling people, he restrained the very assault of heavenly chastisement by offering his own death [Note: [Col. 0871D] Longip.: “he restrained [it] by an offering” (*objectione restrinxit*); Germ.: “he extinguished [it]” (*restinxit*)], saying: “Forgive them this offense; otherwise erase me from your book, which you have written” (Exod. 32:31)? Did Aaron not resist God’s anger when he took the censer and, standing between the living and the dead, moderated the fire of punishment with the smoke of incense (Num. 16:47–48)? Did Phinehas not resist God’s anger when, slaughtering those who were committing fornication with foreigners in the very act, he offered his zeal to the divine indignation and appeased its fury with the sword (Num. 25:11)? Did David not resist God’s anger when, offering himself to the striking angel, he obtained the grace of appeasement before the appointed time (2 Sam. 24:25)? Did Elijah not resist God’s anger when, after the earth had long been dry, he recalled the withheld rains from heaven by his word (1 Kings 18:44)? How, then, is it said that no one can resist divine anger, when it is demonstrated by existing examples that many have often resisted it?

But if we weigh carefully both these words of blessed Job and the deeds of those men, we recognize both that divine anger cannot be resisted and that many have often resisted it. [Vet. XII.] For all the saints who oppose God’s anger receive from him the ability to set themselves against the assault of his chastisement; and, so to speak, they rise up with him against himself. The divine power sets them against itself, because while outwardly they withstand the anger raging against them [Note: [Col. 0871D] Gemet. reads “the anger of the one coming against them”; Plur. reads “the anger of the one raging against them.”], inwardly the grace of the one who is angry cherishes them; and it inwardly raises up those whom, as though they were resisting, it outwardly permits to endure. Thus he bears the opposition of those who plead, an opposition which he himself inspires; and what he commands to be done is imposed upon him as though he were unwilling [Note: [Col. 0871D] Vindoc., Longip., Corb., Germ., and all Norman manuscripts support this reading; the printed editions have “is not opposed,” which they print as the reading. [Col. 0872D]].

For he says to Moses: “Let me alone, so that my anger may burn against them and I may destroy them; and I will make you into a great nation” (Exod. 32:10). What does it mean to say to a servant, “Let me alone,” except to offer him the boldness to intercede? It is as though he openly said: “Consider [Note: [Col. 0872D] Vindoc., Gemet., and other Norman manuscripts: “how great.”] how much influence you have with me, and recognize that you can obtain whatever you ask for the people.” That this is the meaning of the words is immediately confirmed by the forgiveness that follows.

But when heavenly indignation, so to speak, is stirred from the very depths, human opposition does not restrain it [Note: [Col. 0872D] In Gratian the reading is: “this opinion or human opposition” (23, q. 4, c. *Vasis*, § “Unde Gregorius”)]; nor does anyone’s prayer usefully place itself in its way when God has once determined something in anger from the depths of his being. Hence Moses, who cleansed the guilt of the whole people before God by his prayers and, offering himself as a barrier, appeased the force of divine wrath, nevertheless, when he came to the rock of Horeb and, through lack of faith concerning the supplying of water, was unable to enter the promised land because the Lord was angry (Num. 20:12). He was often afflicted on this account, often disturbed as desire stirred him, and could not turn aside the anger of the vengeance that had been decreed, although, when the Lord willed it, he had turned that anger away from the people.

Hence David [Note: [Col. 0873D] Bartholomew’s edition and other old editions read “because [*quia*] the people had fallen prostrate”; Gilot., Vatican, and Gussanville read “who [*qui*], after the people had fallen prostrate.” Coccius, more correctly with the manuscripts: “who, from the people lying prostrate.”], who later restrained the angel’s sword by prayer from the people lying prostrate (2 Sam. 24:10), first fled from his son barefoot, weeping and wailing; and until he had fully received the vengeance for the crime committed, he was entirely unable to moderate God’s anger on his own behalf. Hence Elijah, so that he might experience as a human being something of divine punishment—he who had opened the heavens by his word (1 Kings 17:1)—fled through the desert in terror before the anger of a woman; and he who appeased God’s fury on behalf of others through intercession was himself weakened by fear on his own behalf (ibid., 19:3).

Therefore, God’s anger can be resisted when the one who is angry himself gives assistance; but it cannot be resisted at all when he both arouses himself to vengeance and does not inspire the prayer that is poured out to him. Hence it is said to Jeremiah: “Therefore do not pray for this people, and do not take up praise and prayer for them, because I will not hear them in the time of their cry to me” [Note: [Col. 0873D] In Vindoc. “to me” is absent.] (Jer. 7:16). And again: “Though Moses and Samuel stood before me, my soul would not be toward this people” (Jer. 15:1).

24. The power of prayer for enemies.—Here it may usefully be asked why, leaving aside so many ancient fathers, Moses and Samuel alone are named as especially and more attractively chosen for pouring forth prayer. We can easily recognize the reason if we consider the merits of that charity which is commanded to love even enemies. [Col. 0873C] [Vet. XIII.] For that prayer is especially commended to the ears of the Creator which strives to intercede even for enemies. Hence Truth itself says: “Pray for those who persecute and slander you” (Matt. 5:44). And again: “When you stand to pray, forgive if you have anything against another” (Mark 11:25).

But when we review the deeds of the ancient fathers as described by sacred Scripture, we find that Moses and Samuel interceded for their adversaries. One of them fled from the persecution of a raging people, and yet intervened for the life of his persecutor; the other, having been removed from leadership over the people, says to his very adversaries: “Far be it from me to commit this sin against the Lord, so that I should cease to pray for you” (1 Sam. 12:23).

What, then, does it mean, in this difficulty of intercession, to bring forward Moses and Samuel, except to indicate more openly that not even they would have resisted God’s anger had they been present—men who could more readily intercede for friends precisely because they were accustomed to intercede before him even for enemies?

Hence the same Judaea is told: “I have struck you with the wound of an enemy, with cruel chastisement” (Jer. 30:14). And again: “Why do you cry to me over your brokenness? Your pain is incurable” (ibid., 15). Let the holy man therefore consider that no one’s intervention restrains divine anger when it is aroused implacably, and let him say: “God, against whose anger no one can resist.”

We may also properly apply this to a particular meaning if we consider the losses of that same Israelite people, whom the Redeemer, revealed through the mystery of his dispensation, abandoned in its pride and called the Gentiles to the grace of knowing him. Hence it appropriately follows at once: “Beneath whom those who bear the world are bowed.”

[Rec. X.] 25. Those who rule bear the world.—Those bear the world who endure the cares of the present age. For each person is compelled to sustain burdens as great as the authority he exercises in this world. Hence, not inappropriately, the ruler [Note: [Col. 0873D] Vindoc.: “and rightly, ruler.”] of the earth is called *basileus* in Greek. For λαός (*laos*) means “people.” Thus *basileus* is called βάσις λαοῦ (*basis laou*), which in Latin means “the basis of the people,” because the ruler himself supports the people above him, governing them while fixed beneath the weight of that authority’s movement. The more he bears the burdens of his subjects, the more, like a column placed above it, the basis carries the superimposed weight.

Blessed Job, therefore, filled with the power of the prophetic Spirit, sees that Judaea is abandoned and that the rulers of the Gentiles are inclined toward the worship of the Divinity, and says: “God, against whose anger no one can resist, beneath whom those who bear the world are bowed.” As though he openly confessed, saying [Note: [Col. 0873D] Vindoc., Lyran., and Bigot.: “You strictly abandon those once subjected to you, and mercifully bend the powers that have been raised up among the Gentiles.”]: “You strictly abandon those who were once subject to you, and mercifully bend the exalted powers of the Gentiles.”

[Vet. XIV.] 26. Such angels are sent for ministry.—Although by the words “beneath whom those who bear the world are bowed,” angelic powers may also be understood. For those bear the world who administer the responsibilities of governing it, as Paul testifies when he says: “Are they not all ministering spirits, sent for service on behalf of those who are to inherit salvation?” (Heb. 1:14).

He therefore says: “God, against whose anger no one can resist, beneath whom those who bear the world are bowed.” It is as though he were contemplating the humility of every creature and, trembling, saying: “What frail human being can oppose your commands, when even the angelic powers bow before your strength?” [Note: [Col. 0874D] Gemet., Turon., and Colb.: “before your dread.”] Or certainly, since when we bow we do not see what is above us: those most subtle spirits would be upright if they fully apprehended the power of his majesty. But those who bear the world are bowed beneath God, because, although raised up, they see the height of his divinity [Note: [Col. 0874D] The printed editions read *sublevati* (“raised up,” masculine); all the manuscripts read *sublevatae* (“raised up,” feminine), referring to the angelic powers], the angelic powers nevertheless do not comprehend it.

The just man, unable to penetrate this because of his weakness, but weighing it in some measure from the ministries of the highest spirits [Note: [Col. 0874D] Reg., Germ., Corb. Germ.: “from the ministries of the most subject spirits.”], anxiously and humbly gathers himself back to consideration of himself; in the presence of the power of heavenly greatness he becomes contemptible in his own eyes, saying:

## CHAPTER XVII

[Col. 0875A]

### Verse 14.—“How great, then, am I, that I should answer him and speak with him in my words?”

27. Those weighed down by corruption cannot debate God’s judgments.—It is as though he openly said: “If that creature, which is not weighed down by flesh, is not sufficient to contemplate him, with what state of mind do I debate his judgments, when I am confined by the weight of corruption?”

Just as God’s words to us are often his judgments, which pronounce the sentence concerning our deeds, so our words to God are the works that we present. But a human being cannot speak with God in his words, because before his subtle judgment he has no confidence concerning his deeds. Hence it appropriately follows:

## CHAPTER XVIII [Rec. XI]

[Col. 0875B]

### Verse 15.—“Even if I had anything just, I would not answer, but I would entreat my judge.”

[Note: [Col. 0875D] The stronger manuscripts and the printed editions read “even if.”]

28. Our righteousness requires an appeal for mercy.—As we have often said, all human righteousness is proved to be unrighteousness if it is judged strictly. Therefore, after righteousness, it needs prayer, so that what could have succumbed when examined may be strengthened by the judge’s mercy alone. When this righteousness is possessed fully by more perfect people, one is said to possess “something” of it, because the human mind scarcely accomplishes even what it has grasped, and what it grasps is exceedingly limited.

Let him therefore say: “Even if I had anything just, I would not answer, but I would entreat my judge.” It is as though he more openly confessed, saying: “Even if I should grow in the work of virtue, I am strengthened for life not by merits but by pardon.” We must therefore lean upon prayer when we act rightly, so that whatever we live justly may be seasoned with humility.

[Vet. XV.] 302 Yet often our very prayer is shaken by so many temptations that it seems almost rejected from the judge’s presence. And often the merciful Creator perceives it [Note: [Col. 0875D] The printed editions, with several manuscripts, read “regards it”; the reading is more pleasing with Corb. Germ., Colb., one Reg., Vindoc., and Longip.: “perceives it.”]; but because it cannot display itself as purely as it wishes [Note: [Col. 0875D] Bellov. reads “exercise itself.”], it fears above itself the judgment of rejection. Hence it follows:

## CHAPTER XIX

### Verse 16.—“And when he has heard me calling, I do not believe that he has heard my voice.”

29. The alternating movements of the soul during prayer.—Often the mind is kindled by the fire of divine love [Note: [Col. 0876D] Utic., Lyr., Bigot.: “by desire.”] and raised up to contemplate heavenly and hidden things; it is already carried away toward the highest realities and, pierced by perfect desire, is separated from what is lowest. But when struck by a sudden temptation, it is bent down by the thoughts that arise, though it had been lifted toward God by strong concentration. It becomes unable to distinguish itself and, caught between vices and virtues, does not recognize on which side it is stronger.

Indeed, it is often brought to the point of wondering how it could have grasped such exalted things, when an illicit thought has polluted it; and again, how it receives illicit thoughts, when the fervor of the spirit has burned so powerfully above it [the supplied text breaks off here].

Observing these alternating movements of thought in the soul, the Psalmist rightly says: “They ascend up to the heavens, and descend down to the abysses” (Ps. 106:26). We ascend to the heavens when we penetrate the highest things; but we descend to the abysses when we are suddenly thrown down from the summit of contemplation through shameful temptations. Thus the movements of the soul, alternating between vows and vices, naturally obscure its certainty of being heard.

It is rightly said, therefore: “And when he has heard me calling, I do not believe that he has heard my voice,” because the mind becomes fearful through its own mutability; and because it unwillingly suffers what it suffers, it suspects that it has been rejected and cast away.

30. The severity of the final judgment, especially upon those whom God’s patience has long endured.—It is pleasing to observe with what great subtlety the holy man examines himself, lest the divine judgments find anything to condemn in him. Observing his own weakness, he says: “How great, then, am I, that I should answer him and speak with him in my words?” [Rec. XII.] Not trusting in the merits of his righteousness, but turning solely to the hope of petition, he adds: “Even if I had anything just, I would not answer, but I would entreat my judge.” But, fearful even concerning that petition, he adds: “And when he has heard me calling, I do not believe that he has heard my voice.”

Why does he tremble with such vigilance? Why does he fear with such anxiety? Is it not because he contemplates the terror of the judge in the final strictness of judgment and, unable to endure the force of that examination, reckons everything he does to be insufficient for him? Hence he immediately adds:

## CHAPTER XX [Vet. XVI]

[Col. 0876C]

### Verse 17.—“For he will crush me in a whirlwind.”

31. Every sinner is ground down in the whirlwind, though he seemed upright in tranquility, because the extreme severity of judgment kills the one whom heavenly patience has long endured. It is rightly called a whirlwind [Note: [Col. 0876D] Ebroic., Lyr., Bigot.: “because it is revealed in the upheaval of the elements”; Utic. relegated this reading to the margin, reading “because in the [case of the] elect.”], because it is revealed in the upheaval of the elements, as the Psalmist testifies: “God [Note: [Col. 0876D] The manuscripts read “manifest”; the Vulgate editions, “manifestly.”] will come manifestly, our God, and he will not keep silent. Fire will burn before him, and a mighty storm will surround him” (Ps. 49:3). Another prophet likewise says: “The Lord is in the storm, and the whirlwind is his way” (Nah. 1:3).

In that whirlwind the just person is not crushed, because he is always carefully afraid lest he be crushed. While still placed on the road of the present life, he weighs how strict the exactor of deeds will appear toward human actions—the one who will then condemn certain people bound by the guilt of original sin even without deeds. Hence the holy man, immediately speaking in the voice of the human race, adds:

## CHAPTER XXI

### “And he will multiply my wounds even without cause.”

32. Infants are condemned solely because of original sin.—Some are taken away from the present light before they reach the active life in which they can produce merits, whether good or evil [Note: [Col. 0876D] Bellov., Longip., Gemet., and other Norman manuscripts: “before they reach the point of earning good or evil merits.” In the Colb. manuscript, Rainierius, who apparently divided the individual books into chapters and prefixed summary statements to them, wrote: “Note concerning the hidden judgment of God, whereby infants, immediately after birth and without works, are thrust into hell.”].

Because the sacraments of salvation do not free them from the guilt of origin, they have done nothing of their own here, yet they arrive there for punishment. For them, one wound is being born in corruption [Note: [Col. 0878D] Longip., Gemet., and other Norman manuscripts: “being born corruptible.”], and another is dying according to the flesh. But because eternal death also follows after death, their wounds are multiplied by a hidden yet just judgment, even without cause. For they receive perpetual torments who have sinned by no act of their own will.

Hence it is written: “He is not pure in his sight, not even an infant of one day upon the earth” (Job 15:14). Hence Truth itself says: “Unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John 3:5). Hence Paul says: “We were by nature children of wrath, even as the others” (Eph. 2:3).

Therefore, one who, adding no personal fault, is destroyed solely under the guilt of origin [Note: [Col. 0878D] Lyran., Bigot., Utic.: “is weighed down by the guilt of origin”]—what is he in that final examination, so far as human understanding can judge, except one wounded without cause? Yet under divine strictness it is just that mortal offspring, like a fruitless tree, should preserve in its branches the bitterness it drew from its root.

He therefore says: “For he will crush me in a whirlwind, and he will multiply my wounds even without cause” [Note: [Col. 0878D] Gemet. reads “and he multiplied,” and reads this form consistently below]. It is as though, openly considering the losses of the human race, he said: “With what severity does the strict judge destroy those whom the guilt of their own actions condemns, if he also strikes eternally those whom the guilt of their own will does not accuse?”

33. Job fears God’s judgment. He was struck so that his merit might increase, not so that his vice might be cleansed.—We recognize that these words do not differ from blessed Job personally if we investigate how truly they were spoken. For, subtly weighing himself and judging himself in every action, he indicates with what anxiety he fears the force of heavenly strictness, adding: “For he will crush me in a whirlwind.”

It is as though he openly said: “I therefore fear him even in tranquility, because through the scourges I know what he will be like in the whirlwind.” He both foresaw those scourges in fear and endured them after foreseeing them. Hence he adds [Note: [Col. 0877D] Gemet. reads “and he multiplied,” and reads this form consistently below]: “And he will multiply my wounds even without cause.”

As we have often said, blessed Job was not struck so that the blow might cleanse vice in him, but so that it might increase his merit. Thus, by declaring himself wounded without cause, he speaks outwardly of himself as the Truth testifies inwardly concerning him, saying: “You moved me against him, that I should afflict him without cause” (Job 2:3).
