Therefore the holy man does not proudly say what he truly says, nor does he depart from uprightness through these words by which he does not disagree with the judge. He immediately expresses the continuation of those wounds when he adds:

## CHAPTER XXII [Vet. XVII]

### Verse 18.—“He does not allow my spirit to rest, and he fills me with bitterness.”

34. Job is afflicted inwardly and outwardly.—Often, for the righteous, the exercise of virtue consists solely in enduring adversity outwardly. But so that their strength may be trained by a contest of complete testing, sometimes torments tear them outwardly and temptations chastise them inwardly.

Hence the holy man asserts that he is filled with bitterness, because while he endures scourges outwardly, what he bears inwardly from the temptation of the adversary is more grievous. Yet amid these things, awareness of the equity and power of the one who strikes mitigates the force of the pain. Hence he adds:

## CHAPTER XXIII

### Verse 19.—“If strength is sought, he is most mighty; if equity of judgment, no one dares to testify for me.”

35. The equity of God’s judgment.—He examines the causes of life who does not investigate them through another’s testimony, because the one who is eventually shown to be strict in inflicting punishment had long remained silently a witness to guilt. Hence through the prophet it is said: “I am judge and witness” (Jer. 29:23). Again he says: “I have been silent, I have always been quiet, I have been patient; like a woman in labor I will speak” (Isa. 42:14). A woman in labor painfully expels what she has carried for a long time in secret with weight. Thus, after a long silence, the Lord speaks like a woman in labor, because what he now silently tolerates within himself he will one day reveal in the vengeance of judgment, as though with pain.

But we must ask: if anyone dared to testify on behalf of this just man, would that person free him from guilt? And if no one else offers testimony for him, is he at least strong enough to produce testimony for himself? It follows:

### Verse 20.—“If I wished to justify myself, my mouth would condemn me; if I showed myself innocent, it would prove me perverse.”

36. No one knows with certainty that he is innocent.—It is as though he openly said: “Why should I speak of others, when I myself am unable to give testimony about myself?” But since you are not sufficient to testify to your own innocence, do you know even this—that you possess innocence? He adds:

## CHAPTER XXV [Rec. XIII]

### Verse 21.—“Even if I were simple, my soul would not know this very thing.”

37. The usefulness and disadvantage of our ignorance. [Vet. XVIII.] Often vice completes what virtue has begun.—Often, if we know the good things we do, we are led to exaltation; if we do not know them, we scarcely preserve them. For who is there who does not become at least somewhat proud of his awareness of virtue? Or who again preserves in himself a good thing that he does not know at all? But, in opposition to both dangers, what remains except that we should knowingly not know the righteous things we do, so that we both judge them righteous and consider them insignificant? In this way, knowledge of our uprightness may strengthen the mind for its preservation, while the judgment that it is small may not lift it up into swelling pride.

There are, however, some things that we cannot easily know even while they are being done. Often we are inflamed by upright zeal against the faults of those who sin; but when anger carries us beyond the bounds of equity, we judge this to be zeal for righteous strictness. Often we undertake the office of preaching in order to serve our brothers’ welfare; but unless we please the person to whom we speak, what we preach is not willingly received. When the mind usefully strives to please, it shamefully slips into love of its own praise; and the mind that had sought to rescue others from captivity to vices begins itself, captivated by its own popularity, to serve its own favor.

The desire for human praise is like a bandit who joins travelers from the side as they proceed along the right road, so that, drawing a sword from concealment, he may slaughter the lives of those who are walking. When the intention of the proposed good is diverted toward private interests, in a horrifying way the same work is completed by guilt that virtue began. Often, from the very beginnings, thought seeks one thing while action displays another.

[Vet. XIX.] 38. At times the action is right, but not the intention.—Often even our thought does not show itself faithful to itself, because it turns one thing before the eyes of the mind but hastens by intention toward something far different. For often certain people seek earthly rewards and defend justice; they consider themselves innocent and rejoice that they are defenders of uprightness. If the hope of money is taken away from them, however, they immediately cease defending justice; yet they think themselves defenders of justice and assert that they are upright, though they are seeking not uprightness but money.

Moses rightly says to such people: “You shall diligently carry out what is just” (Deut. 16:20). For one carries out what is just unjustly when one is stirred to defend justice not by love of virtue but by love of temporal reward. One carries out what is just unjustly when one does not fear selling the very justice one displays. To carry out what is just justly, therefore, is to seek that same justice in asserting justice.

Often we do what is right and expect neither rewards nor praise from human beings; yet the mind, raised up in confidence in itself, scorns pleasing those from whom it seeks nothing, despises their judgments, and drives itself badly free along the precipices of exaltation. Thus it is overwhelmed by a worse vice precisely where, as though it had conquered the vices, it boasts that it is subject to no desires.

39. Our danger lies either in examining ourselves excessively or not at all.—Often, while we examine ourselves more than is right, we err more indiscreetly through that very effort of discernment. The sharper our mind’s vision strives to see, the more it is obscured, because the person who looks insistently at the sun’s rays becomes blind; and he is compelled to see nothing precisely because he attempts to see more.

Since, then, we are utterly ignorant of ourselves when we grow sluggish in self-examination, or, if we examine ourselves with subtle scrutiny, often become confused between vices and virtues, it is rightly said here: “Even if I were simple, my soul would not know this very thing.” It is as though it were openly said: “With what rashness do I reproach the judgments of the Creator, when through the darkness of weakness I do not even know myself?”

Hence the prophet rightly says: “The abyss gave forth its voice from the height of its imagination” (Hab. 3:10, according to the Septuagint). The abyss bears the height of its imagination when the human mind, darkened by immense thought, does not penetrate even itself by examining itself [Note: [Col. 0879D] Almost all old manuscripts and editions read *caligosus* (“darkened”), a reading noted elsewhere as well.]. But to give forth a voice from that height means that, because it cannot discover itself, it is compelled to rise into wonder, so that it dares not investigate what is above it [Note: [Col. 0879D] Lyr. and Bigot.: “what is above itself.” The same reading now occurs in Utic.; formerly *se* was absent.]; for, contemplating its own incomprehensibility, it cannot discover what it is.

But the hearts of the righteous, because they cannot examine themselves perfectly, bear this exile of blindness with difficulty. Hence it follows:

[Col. 0880A] “And my life will weary me” [the supplied text reads “ibid.” before this passage].

The just person is weary of living because, while acting, he does not cease to seek life, yet he cannot discover the merit of that same life. He draws the scale of examination from the bosom of inward equity; and from the very place where, caught up above himself, he grows beyond the power of inquiry, he falls short in achieving discovery [Note: [Col. 0879D] Bellovac. reads “the affection of discovery”; Germ. reads “the intention of discovery.”].

But there is consolation for our darkness when the just and incomprehensible power of the Creator is brought back to the mind: he neither leaves the wicked without punishment nor allows the righteousness of the upright to surpass the immeasurable extent of his incomprehensibility. Hence it appropriately follows:

## CHAPTER XXVI [Rec. XIV]

### Verse 22.—“It is one thing that I have said: he himself consumes both the innocent and the impious.”

[Col. 0880C] 40. Human purity vanishes when compared with the divine. The impious does not escape God’s vengeance. Death overtakes all.—The innocent is consumed by the Creator because, however great his simplicity may be, it is swallowed up by the simplicity of divine greatness [Note: [Col. 0880D] The old edition reads “is surpassed by the simplicity.”]. For although we carefully preserve simplicity, nevertheless, by consideration of inward purity, it is shown that this very simplicity which we practice is not simplicity.

The impious, too, is consumed by the Creator because, while God orders all things wonderfully, the impiety of the wicked is bound by its own wiles [Note: [Col. 0880D] Vindoc., Corb. Germ., and Colb., in the first hand: “by his own virtues.”]. For he entangles himself in punishments unknowingly precisely where he exults in knowingly doing something.

Since, therefore, almighty God surpasses the innocence of the good in simplicity and, penetrating the cunning of the wicked, condemns it, it is rightly said here: “It is one thing that I have said: he himself consumes both the innocent and the impious.” It is as though it were openly said: “This is the thought I have uttered before myself: neither will the innocent appear innocent if I am examined strictly, nor will the impious, if he wishes to hide from me, be concealed from the sharpness of heavenly examination, since the strict judge, comprehending all things, wonderfully penetrates hidden wickedness and, ordering it well through its own contrivances, condemns it.”

Or certainly he is said to consume both the innocent and the impious because, although they are divided in the life of the mind [Note: [Col. 0880D] The printed editions, with one Reg. manuscript, read “in the merits of life.” More correctly, another Reg. with Corb., Colb., Gemet., Germ., and others: “in the life of the mind.” Here the life of the mind is contrasted with the death of the flesh, and Gregory recalls that the innocent and the impious are not separated from one another by the death of the flesh in such a way as to be separated in the life of the mind.], they are nevertheless alike dragged to the death of the flesh by the merit of the first sin. Hence Solomon says: “The learned dies in the same way as the unlearned” (Eccl. 2:16). And again: “All things are subject to vanity, and all go to one place; they are made from the earth, and together they return to the earth” (Eccl. 3:19).

It follows:

## CHAPTER XXVII [Rec. XV]

### Verse 23.—“If he scourges, let him kill once and not laugh at the sufferings of the innocent.”

41. Job desires a mediator who will free us by his death.—Who would not believe that these words were spoken through pride, unless he heard the judgment of the judge, who says: “You have not spoken rightly before me, as my servant Job has” (Job 42:7)? It remains, therefore, that no one dare criticize the author’s words, since it is established that the judge praises them.

[Col. 0881B] [Vet. XX.] But they must be examined within all the more cautiously and subtly because they sound so harsh outwardly. The holy man, considering the losses of the human race and weighing where they came from, sees that humanity, at the promise of the adversary, desiring to know good and evil, lost even itself; so that it can truly say: “Even if I were simple, my soul would not know this very thing.” After the punishment of expulsion, humanity also endures the scourges of corruption and, even after torment, continues toward the destruction of the flesh—or certainly of the mind—so that it may rightly say: “He himself consumes both the innocent and the impious.”

Against these things he seeks the grace of the Mediator, saying: “If he scourges, let him kill once.” For we, having withdrawn from God in mind and returned in the flesh to dust, are bound by the punishment of a double death. But he came to us who would die for us in the flesh alone, who would unite his single death to our double death and free us from both deaths. Concerning this Paul says: “For the death that he died, he died to sin once” (Rom. 6:10).

Let the holy man, therefore, observe the losses of our corruption and seek one death—the Mediator’s death—that would destroy our two deaths; and desiring it, let him say: “If he scourges, let him kill once.”

42. He desires that his longing not be delayed.—But behold, what follows immediately seems to resist humility: “And let him not laugh at the sufferings of the innocent.” Yet we recognize without difficulty that this is deeply humble if we weigh it with a humble mind. It is clear to everyone that every desire is a form of suffering when it is delayed, as Solomon also testifies: “Hope that is delayed afflicts the soul” (Prov. 13:12).

For God’s laughter means his refusal to have compassion through mercy upon human affliction. Hence, again through Solomon, the Lord says to the wicked who persist in guilt: “I also will laugh at your destruction” (Prov. 1:26)—that is, “I will show no compassion toward your affliction.”

Before the Redeemer’s coming, therefore, all the elect had their own suffering, because, burning with desire, they longed to see the mystery of his incarnation. He himself testifies when he says: “Many, I tell you, righteous people and prophets desired to see what you see and did not see it” (Luke 10:24). The desires of the righteous, then, are the sufferings of the innocent. Therefore, while the Lord delayed the wishes of his elect without taking pity on them, what else did he do but laugh at the sufferings of the innocent?

Thus the holy man, considering the gifts of the coming Redeemer and enduring with grief the delay of his desires, says: “If he scourges, let him kill once, and let him not laugh at the sufferings of the innocent.” It is as though he openly entreated, saying: “Because our life is daily worn down by the scourge of vengeance for sin [Note: [Col. 0882D] Germ., Utic., and other Norman manuscripts: “by the scourge of avenging punishment”], let him now come who will die once without sin for us, so that God may no longer laugh at the sufferings of the innocent, if he appears passible in the flesh—the one in whose desires our mind chastises itself.”

[Vet. XXI.] **43. God laughs at the sufferings of the innocent when he takes delight in their tears.** —Or certainly, if he calls God’s laughter his joy, the Lord is said to laugh at the sufferings of the innocent because the more ardently he is sought by us, the more sweetly he rejoices over us. For we make a kind of joy for him out of our suffering when, through holy desires, we chastise ourselves for love of him. Hence the Psalmist says: “Appoint a solemn day with crowded assemblies, even to the horn of the altar” (Ps. CXVII, 27). Whoever continually afflicts himself in desire for the Lord appoints a solemn day to him in a crowded assembly. This day of solemnity is commanded to extend to the horn of the altar, because each person must afflict himself for as long as is necessary to reach the height of the heavenly sacrifice—that is, eternal joys.

The just man, therefore, because he desires his longing to be fulfilled rather than deferred, humbly says: “Let him not laugh at the sufferings of the innocent.” It is as though he said: “Let him willingly accept our vows and defer no longer, but by revealing himself present the one who chastises us in our expectation of him.” Because blessed Job specifically asked that the one who endured death in the flesh alone for us at the end of the world be killed once, he immediately makes this clear by adding the very order of his passion, saying:

## CHAPTER XXVIII

**VERSE 24.—The earth has been given into the hands of the wicked man; he covers the face of its judges.**

**44. Christ’s flesh was handed over to the wicked devil; Christ’s slayers were blinded by the devil. The wicked man and the devil are one person, than whom nothing is more wicked.** —What, indeed, is expressed by the name “earth” if not flesh? Who is designated by the title “wicked man” if not the devil? The hands of this wicked man were those who raged at the death of our Redeemer. Thus the earth was given into the hands of the wicked man, because the ancient enemy could not corrupt the Redeemer’s mind by tempting him personally (Matt. IV, 10–11), but was permitted to extinguish his flesh through his minions for three days (Matt. XXVII, 45), and, unknowingly, served the dispensation of heavenly mercy through this very permission.

[Note: Gemet., Longip., and others have this reading. The old editions, like the more recent ones, read: “and, unknowingly, the dispensation . . .,” etc.]

For when he assailed our Redeemer with three temptations, he could not rashly assail the heart of God.

[Note: Vindoc., Norman., Corb. Germ.: “he could not tempt the heart of God.” Lyr. and Utic. have this differing reading in the margin: “he could not rashly profane the heart.” Gemet.: “to act rashly against the heart,” etc.]

But when he stirred Judas’s mind to the death of Christ’s flesh (Matt. XXVI, 14), and handed over to him a cohort and servants from the chief priests and Pharisees, this wicked man clearly extended his hands to the earth. The judges of this earth were the priests and rulers, Pilate, and the mocking soldiers. Thus this wicked man covered the face of its judges, because he veiled the hearts of the persecutors in a cloud of malice, so that they would not recognize their creator. Hence Paul says: “To this day, when Moses is read, a veil lies over their heart” (II Cor. III, 15).

[Note: The printed editions, together with one manuscript, read: “a veil has been placed.”]

Again he says: “For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (I Cor. II, 8). The face of the judges, therefore, was covered, because the mind of the persecutors did not recognize as God, even through his miracles, the one whom it was able to seize in the flesh.

Because the ancient enemy is one person with all the wicked, Sacred Scripture often speaks of the head of the wicked—that is, the devil—in such a way that it suddenly passes over to his body, that is, his followers.

[Vet. XXII.] The name “wicked man” may therefore designate the unbelieving and persecuting people, to whom what follows also entirely applies:

## CHAPTER XXIX

**THE SAME PASSAGE.—But if he is not that one, who then is he?**

**45.** It is as though it were said plainly: “Who should ever be thought wicked, if that people which persecuted piety itself is not wicked?” But when the holy man considers the treachery of the Jewish people, he turns the eyes of his mind back upon himself. He grieves that he cannot see the one whom he loves; he is distressed because he is being removed from the present world before the salvation of the world is revealed. Hence he adds:

## CHAPTER XXX [Rec. XVI]

**VERSE 25.—My days were swifter than a runner; they fled away and did not see good.**

**46. The ancient righteous grieve that they did not reach the times of Christ.** —The duty of a runner is to announce what is to come. All the elect, therefore, who arose before the Redeemer’s coming, because they announced him either by their lives alone or also by speaking, were in a certain sense runners in the world.

[Note: Turon., Longip., all the Norman manuscripts, etc., read “either by living”; Vindoc. has corruptly “or by seeing.” The printed editions, except the old Paris edition, read “or by hearing.”]

But because they foresaw that they would be removed before the awaited time of redemption, they grieve that they passed away more swiftly than a runner; and they lament that their days were short, because they did not extend as far as seeing the Redeemer’s light. Hence it is appropriately said: “They fled away and did not see good.”

Everything that has been created is good, as Moses bears witness when he says: “God saw all that he had made, and behold, it was very good” (Gen. I, 31).

[Note: Utic., Lyr., Big. and others read: “and they were very good.”]

But that alone is principally good through which all these things are good, although they are not good principally in themselves. Concerning this good, the Truth says through the Gospel: “No one is good except God alone” (Luke XVIII, 19).

[Note: Vindoc.: “except one, God.” Many Norman manuscripts have the same. Utic. presents both readings.]

Because, therefore, the days of the ancient fathers ended before God was shown to the world in the flesh, it is rightly said of those days: “They fled away and did not see good.” It is as though it were said plainly: “They passed away before the awaited time, because they could not reach the Redeemer’s presence.” Hence it is further added:

309 ## CHAPTER XXXI

**VERSE 26.—They passed by like ships carrying fruit.**

**47. We are nourished by the sight and fruit of the one whom they savored while awaiting him. They brought us the Spirit’s fruit concealed.** —Those who cross the seas carrying fruit themselves enjoy the fruit’s fragrance, but carry food from those same fruits for others. What, then, were the ancient fathers if not ships carrying fruit? By prophesying the mystery of the divine incarnation, they themselves enjoyed the fragrance of hope, but brought us the fruit of that same hope’s fulfillment. What they savored by awaiting, we are filled with by seeing and receiving.

Hence the Redeemer says to the same disciples: “Others have labored, and you have entered into their labors” (John IV, 38).

[Note: In some other printed editions, mistakenly, it reads: “Hence the Redeemer says to those same—or these same—disciples.” In the manuscripts, instead of *iisdem* stands *idem* or *isdem*.]

Their days are compared with ships because they pass onward; and rightly with ships carrying fruit, because all the elect whom they bore before the Redeemer’s presence they were able, through the spirit of prophecy, to sustain in expectation, but not to refresh with manifest presentation.

Or certainly, because when ships carry fruit they mix it with straw so that they may bring it safely to land, the days of the preceding fathers are rightly described as resembling ships carrying fruit. Their words preserve the mysteries of spiritual life that they announce through the straw of history interwoven with them, and they bring us the Spirit’s concealed fruit when they speak of carnal things. Often, while they recount certain matters according to their literal character, they are lifted up to the secrets of the Divinity. Again, frequently, while they contemplate the height of the Divinity, they suddenly pour themselves forth into the mystery of his incarnation.

[Vet. XXIII.] Hence it is appropriately added:

## CHAPTER XXXII

**THE SAME PASSAGE.—Like an eagle flying toward food.**

**48. Like eagles they descend from the heights to the depths, to be nourished by Christ’s flesh.** —It is the nature of an eagle to look upon the sun’s rays with an unblinking gaze. But when the need for nourishment presses upon it, it turns that same sharpness of vision, which it had fixed upon the sun’s rays, toward the sight of a carcass; and although it flies high, it nevertheless seeks the earth in order to obtain flesh.

So, precisely so, were the ancient fathers. Insofar as human weakness permitted, they contemplated the Creator’s light with an upright mind. But, foreseeing that he would be incarnated at the end of the world, they turned their eyes, as it were, from the sun’s rays toward the earth. And they come, as it were, from the heights to the depths when they recognize him as God above all things and as man within all things.

[Note: Cocc. and the editions following it read corruptly “below all things.” Here “within” or “among all things” has the same meaning as “in the number or rank of created beings.”]

When they behold him suffering and dying for the human race—and know that through this death they themselves are refreshed and restored to life—they seek food in the carcass, as an eagle does after contemplating the sun’s rays.

It is pleasant to behold the eagle gazing upon the sun’s rays, as it says: “God the strong, Father of the future age, Prince of peace” (Isa. IX, 6).

[Note: Corb. Germ., Vindoc., Turon.: “but with its flight removed.”]

But let it come from the lofty flight of its height to the earth and seek the food of the carcass below. For shortly afterward he adds, saying: “The discipline of our peace was upon him, and by his bruising we were healed” (Isa. LIII, 5). And again: “And he is man, and who will know him?” (Jer. XVII, 10, according to the Septuagint).

[Note: Gemet. and many others read: “Who knew him?”]

The mind of the just man, therefore, lifted up into divinity, when it considers the grace of the dispensation arising from his flesh, suddenly flies from the heights to the food, as an eagle.

But behold, the Israelite people, once filled with the immense spirit of prophecy, lost the gifts of that same prophecy and did not remain in the faith that they had announced in advance. They rejected the Redeemer’s presence from themselves by denying it, although they had proclaimed and declared it beforehand to all who would follow them.

310 Hence, appropriately, the discourse immediately turns in compassion also to their hardness and indicates how the grace of prophecy is withdrawn from them. For it says:

## CHAPTER XXXIII

**VERSE 27.—When I say, “I will not speak in this way,” I change my face and am tortured with pain.**

[Col. 0885C] **49. The treachery and rejection of the Jews.** —The Jewish people did not wish to speak as before, because they denied the one whom they had foretold. But it is tortured with pain after its face has been changed, because, having polluted by the filth of treachery the appearance of its inner man by which it could have been recognized by its Creator, it condemned itself under eternal punishment, beginning with its present evils. For, as though its face had been changed, it is not recognized by its author, having been rejected after losing the faith of a good conscience.

But it remains that the pain of punishments should torture the one whom the Creator, not recognizing his own, ignores.

[Note: Bellov. and Gemet. read: “whom, not recognizing his own.” Lyr. and Bigot.: “whom, not recognizing what is his.” Utic.: “whom his own and what is his do not recognize.”]

Because we have passed through these matters under the signification of our Redeemer, let us now repeat them by examining them morally.

## MORAL SENSE

**50. CHAPTER IX, VERSE 25.—My days were swifter than a runner; they fled away and did not see good.**

**By what good humanity was stripped through sin, and to what evils it became subject.** —As we have often said, the first human being was created in such a way that his life could be extended through the increase of time alone, not brought to its end. But because he voluntarily fell into sin, as soon as he touched what was forbidden he suffered the course of decline, which now the human being, oppressed by desire for the present life, both endures and continually longs for. For he desires to live so as not to be brought to an end, but through the increase of life he advances daily toward the end.

[Note: The printed editions, with one manuscript of Colbert, read: “nor can it be perceived.” Our reading is found in the Norman, Corb. Germ., and Reg. manuscripts.]

He does not perceive how insignificant the increase of time is until those things that seemed long while approaching suddenly become past.

[Vet. XXIV.] Let the holy man, therefore, look upon the condition of his creation and, in the voice of the human race, lament the losses brought by the passage of time, saying: “My days were swifter than a runner; they fled away and did not see good.”

It is as though he said plainly: “Humanity was created so that it could see the good that God is; but because it refused to remain standing in the light, it lost its eyes by fleeing. For as soon as it began, through sin, to run downward to the depths, it suffered blindness so as not to see the inner light.”

Concerning these days it is further appropriately added: “They passed by like ships carrying fruit.” When ships carry fruit, they carry the fruits of the earth across the waves. The earth was the human being’s paradise, which could have kept him unshaken if he had wished to stand through innocence. But because he fell through sin into the waves of mutability, after the earth he came to the seas of the present life.

The fruits of this earth were also the word of the commandment, the granted possibility of action, and the understanding of the Creator implanted in nature. But these fruits, which we refused to eat while in the earth, we carry across the seas, because we did not wish to guard unshaken in paradise the granted goods of so many gifts, and now we try to preserve them amid temptations. As we move toward our end, the breeze of the present life drives us onward, and we are wearied by the wave of our mutability. But because through the mystery of the cross we are brought back to the goods implanted in nature, we carry fruit, as it were, by means of wood.

This may nevertheless be understood in another way. When ships carry fruit, they possess the sweetness of fragrance but do not have the weight of the burden.

[Note: Gemet.: “but do not have the heaviness of the work.” Bellov.: “but do not have the heaviness of the weight.” Corb. Germ. and Reg.: “heaviness.”]

311 The human race, expelled from the joys of paradise, lost the power of contemplation and abandoned the strength of the fortitude with which it had been created. When it raises itself to seek again the things above, it indeed gives off the fragrance of memory, but does not rightly display the weight of life. Our ship of mind, therefore, is filled with the fragrances of fruits, yet is lightly driven here and there, because we remember the height of paradise through the memory of its fragrance, while we endure the unruly waves of temptations from the flesh.

[Note: Turon. reads corruptly: “did not lose it, but its strength,” etc.]

Hence it is appropriately added: “Like an eagle flying toward food.”

[Vet. XXV.] An eagle is suspended in very high flight and balanced in the ether by the effort of its rapid wings; but through the appetite of its belly it seeks the earth and suddenly plunges downward from the heights. Thus, thus, the human race fell from the heights to the depths in its first parent. The dignity of its creation had suspended it in the loftiness of reason, as in the freedom of the air; but because, contrary to the commandment, it touched the forbidden food, it came down to the earth through the desire of the belly. And it feeds on flesh as though after flight, because it lost those free inspirations of contemplation and rejoices below in bodily pleasures.

As, therefore, an eagle flying toward food, our days pass swiftly, because the more we seek the depths, the more we are forbidden to remain in life.

**51. Difficult questions concerning humanity’s fall, which must be restrained. Blindness of mind, though just, is nevertheless grievous.** —When we turn these matters over before the eyes of our mind in continuous reflection, we are silently pressed by difficult questions: Why did almighty God create one whom he foresaw would perish? Why did he, who is supremely powerful and supremely good, not wish to make humanity such that it could not perish?

But when the silent mind asks these questions, it fears that by the very boldness of its questioning it may burst into pride; it restrains itself humbly and curbs its thoughts.

[Note: Turon., Longip., Norman.: “and restrains the words of its thought.”]

Yet it is afflicted more severely because, among the evils it suffers, it is also tormented by the hidden understanding of its own condition. Hence here too it is appropriately added: “When I say, ‘I will not speak in this way,’ I change my face and am tortured with pain.”

We say that we ought not to speak in this way when, going beyond the measure of our weakness through inquiry, we rebuke ourselves in fear and restrain ourselves in consideration of heavenly reverence. In this restraint, the face of our mind is changed, because the mind that previously, not understanding, boldly sought the highest things later recognizes its weakness and begins to venerate what it does not understand.

But there is pain in this very change, because it is greatly afflicted: through the merit of the first sin, it is blinded from understanding the things that concern it.

[Note: Lyr., Bigot., Utic.: “the things that concern it.”]

It considers that what it suffers is just; it fears that through the license of speech it may exceed in its pain; it imposes silence upon its mouth, but the pain that has been aroused increases by the very fact that it is restrained.

Let it therefore say: “When I say, ‘I will not speak in this way,’ I change my face and am tortured with pain,” because we are often afflicted more severely when, as though out of a desire for consolation, we try to lessen for ourselves the evils of our affliction.

But whoever carefully considers the losses of the human race, propagated from the condemnation of the first parent, must fear adding his own losses to them. Hence, after the holy man has introduced what is common to all, he suddenly adds what is particular, saying:

312 ## CHAPTER XXXIV [Rec. XVII]

**VERSE 28.—I feared all my works, knowing that you would not spare the sinner.**

**52. Job teaches that even good works must be feared.** —What works blessed Job performed is shown by the text of this sacred history. He sought to appease his Creator with many holocausts, for, as it is written, rising early according to the number of his sons, he offered holocausts for each one; and he cleansed them not only from impure acts but also from wicked thought. Concerning this, Scripture testifies: “For he said, ‘Perhaps my sons have sinned and blessed God in their hearts’” (Job I, 5).

He exercised the affection of compassion, for, questioned by his friends, he says of himself: “I wept once over him who was afflicted” (Job XXX, 25). He offered the service of mercy, saying: “I was an eye to the blind and a foot to the lame” (Job XXIX, 15). He guarded the purity of chastity in his heart, declaring under oath: “If my heart was deceived concerning a woman” (Job XXXI, 9). He held the summit of humility from the depths of his being, saying: “If I despised entering into judgment with my male servant and my female servant when they contended against me” (ibid., 13).

He bestowed benefits generously, saying: “If I ate my morsel alone, and the orphan did not eat from it” (ibid., 17). And again: “If his loins did not bless me, and he was warmed by the fleeces of my sheep” (ibid., 20). He displayed the grace of hospitality, saying: “The stranger did not remain outside; my door was open to the traveler” (ibid., 32).

And amid these things, by the more excellent way of love, he also loved his enemies as an addition to his virtues, saying: “If I rejoiced at the ruin of him who hated me” (ibid., 29).

[Note: Turon., Corb., Colb.: “the holy man,” etc.; the Norman manuscripts: “what then . . .” (the apparatus is partly uncertain).] And again: “For I did not give my throat to sin, to desire his soul while cursing him” (ibid., 30).

[Note: Utic. and other Norman manuscripts read “summit”; Corb. Germ. does not.]

Why, then, did the holy man fear his works, when he always performed works by which God is accustomed to be appeased toward iniquities? Why is it that, doing remarkable works, he nevertheless fears these very works, saying: “I feared all my works”? It is only because, in the actions and words of the holy man, we gather that if we truly desire to please God, after we have subdued perverse things, we must also fear the good things accomplished in us.

[Vet. XXVI.] **53. In good works, sloth and fraud must be feared.** —There are two things that must necessarily be feared with deliberate care in good works: sloth and fraud. Hence through the prophet, according to the ancient translation, it is said: “Cursed is everyone who does the work of God fraudulently and slothfully” (Jer. XLVIII, 10).

But it must be understood with the greatest care that sloth is born from sluggishness, while fraud is born from private love. A lesser love of God increases the former; a self-love possessing the mind wrongly creates the latter. Whoever, loving himself inordinately, hastens through what he has done rightly toward the transitory goods of reward commits fraud in God’s work.

It must also be known that fraud itself is committed in three ways, because through it one undoubtedly desires either the silent favor of the human heart, or the breeze of praise, or some external thing. Against this, the prophet rightly says concerning the just man:

[Note: Utic., Lyr., Reg., and Corb. Germ. omit “blessed.”]

“Blessed is he who shakes his hands free from every gift” (Isa. XXXIII, 15).

Because fraud is not found only in the acceptance of money, the gift is certainly not one alone. There are three kinds of receiving gifts, toward which one hastens through fraud. A gift from the heart is favor sought through thought.

[Note: Utic., Lyr., Big., and Corb. Germ. read: “a gift from the heart is favor captured”; this is the reading found in the old editions.]

A gift from the mouth is glory through praise. A gift from the hand is a reward through giving.

313 Every just person, however, shakes his hands free from every gift, because in what he does rightly he neither seeks empty glory from the human heart, nor praise from the mouth, nor a payment from the hand.

Therefore, the only one who does not commit fraud in God’s work is the person who, while devoting himself to good action, does not pant after rewards in bodily things, words of praise, or human approval. Since our good works cannot escape the sword of lurking sin unless they are fortified daily by vigilant fear, it is rightly said now through the holy man: “I feared all my works.”

It is as though it were said in humble confession: “I see what I have done openly, but I do not know what I have secretly suffered in these things.”

[Vet. XXVII.]

[Note: Turon.: “For often certain good things,” etc.]

Often our good works perish through the fraud that steals upon them, because earthly desire attaches itself to our right actions. Often they fail when sloth intervenes, because, as the love with which they began grows cold, they waste away.

[Note: Vindoc. and Gemet. read as follows, whereas the printed editions read: “Peter remembered the word of Jesus that he had spoken, and going out,” etc.]

Because the stealthy intrusion of sin is scarcely overcome even in the very act of virtue, what remains for security except that one should always fear carefully even in virtue?

**54. No sin remains unpunished.** —But after this, what follows presents a very scrupulous difficulty to the heart: “Knowing that you would not spare the sinner.” If the sinner is not spared, who is rescued from eternal death, since no one is found free from sin? Does he spare the penitent but not spare the sinner, because when we lament our sins we are no longer sinning?

But what of the fact that Peter is looked upon when he denies, and by the Redeemer’s look is called to tears? What of the fact that Paul, when he was attempting to extinguish the Redeemer’s name on earth, deserved to hear his words from heaven?

Yet guilt was punished in both, because concerning Peter it is written in the Gospel: “Peter remembered the word of Jesus, and going outside, he wept bitterly” (Luke XXII, 61).

[Note: Vindoc. and Gemet. read as follows, whereas the printed editions read: “Peter remembered the word of Jesus that he had spoken, and going out,” etc.]

And concerning Paul, the Truth himself, who called him, says: “I will show him how much he must suffer for my name” (Acts IX, 16).

The Lord therefore does not spare the sinner, because he does not leave sin without punishment. Either the person himself punishes it in himself through repentance, or God strikes him by taking vengeance together with him. Sin is therefore not spared, because it is never released without punishment.

Thus David, after his confession, deserved to hear: “The Lord has transferred your sin” (II Sam. XII, 13).

[Note: *De poenit.* distinction 1, chapter *Si peccatum*.]

And yet, after many subsequent torments, while afflicted and fleeing, he paid the debt of the guilt he had committed.

Thus the water of salvation absolves us from the guilt of our first parent; yet, while wiping away the debt of that same guilt, even after being absolved we still die bodily. It is therefore rightly said: “Knowing that you would not spare the sinner,” because God cuts away our sins either through us or through himself, even when he releases them.

From his elect he strives to cleanse by temporal affliction the stains of iniquity that he does not wish to see in them eternally.

[Note: Bellov., Vindoc., Corb., Longip., and all the Norman manuscripts read as above. The printed editions read: “which he does not wish to punish.”]

But often, when the mind trembles more than is just, when it is shaken by fear and pressed by sinister suspicions, it becomes weary of living, since it doubts that it will reach life even through labors. Hence it is subsequently added:

**VERSE 29.—But if I am wicked even in this way, why have I labored in vain?**

## CHAPTER XXXV [Rec. XVIII]

314 **55. The saints are uncertain in such a way that they trust, and trust in such a way that they do not grow sluggish.** —For if we are examined apart from mercy, our work is worthy of punishment, although we await rewards for it. The holy man, therefore, trembling before hidden judgments, says: “But if I am wicked even in this way, why have I labored in vain?”

[Note: We have restored this from the manuscripts of Turon., Gemet., and others among the Normans. Previously it was read not to mean that he regretted having labored, but that he was uncertain about rewards and grieved amid his labors.]

He does not say this because he regrets having labored, but because he grieves that he is uncertain of rewards even amid his labors.

It must be understood that holy men are uncertain in such a way that they trust, and trust in such a way that they nevertheless do not grow sluggish through confidence. Because the mind often trembles even amid its devotion to righteous actions, it remains that after a good work has been performed, tears of supplication should be sought, so that humility in asking may carry the merit of the right work to eternal rewards.

[Note: The Vulgate editions read “tears of expiation.” The manuscripts of Germ., Longip., and the Normans more correctly read “of supplication”; from this the corrupt reading “of despair” arose in Corb. Germ.]

[Vet. XXVIII, Rec. XIX.] Yet it must be understood that neither life nor tears can make us perfectly clean so long as our mortality holds us under the weight of corruption. Hence it is appropriately added:

## CHAPTER XXXVI

**VERSE 30, 31.—If I wash myself as with waters of snow, and my hands shine as though perfectly clean, yet you will plunge me into filth, and my garments will abhor me.**

**56. Tears cleanse when they flow with humility, and when they are shed not for earthly but for heavenly goods.** —The waters of snow are the tears of humility. This humility, because it surpasses the other virtues before the eyes of the strict Judge, shines white, as though with the color of great merit.

There are some who have tears but do not have humility. They weep in affliction, yet in their very tears they either grow proud against the lives of their neighbors or rise up against the ordering of the Creator. Such people have water, but do not have water of snow, and they cannot be made clean, because they are not washed with tears of humility.

The one who confidently said, “A contrite and humbled heart God will not despise” (Ps. L, 19), had washed himself from guilt with waters of snow. Those who are afflicted by tears but are rebellious through murmuring indeed crush their minds, but disdain to humble themselves.

The waters of snow can, however, be understood in another way. The water of a spring or river arises from the earth, but the water of snow falls from the air. There are many who torment themselves through the tears of prayers, yet through all the labor of their tears sweat only for earthly desires. They are pierced in prayer but seek the joys of passing happiness.

The water of snow does not wash these people, because their tears come from below. Those who weep because they desire heavenly rewards are cleansed by the water of snow, because heavenly compunction is poured into them. When they seek the everlasting homeland through tears and weep, inflamed by desire for it, they receive from above that by which they may be cleansed.

By “hands,” what else is signified except works? Hence the prophet says to some: “Your hands are full of blood” (Isa. I, 15).

[Note: Cocc. and the editions following it read “with the work of cruelty,” although the Norman manuscripts and others resist this. In the manuscripts the excellent reading is “that is, your works are full of cruelty,” with “full” understood.]

**57. We do not attain perfect purity here.** —It must be noted that the holy man does not say: “My hands shone perfectly clean,” but “as though my hands were perfectly clean,” because, as long as we are held fast by the punishment of corruption, no matter how much we labor in righteous works, we do not attain true purity but imitate it.

[Note: We have removed *insudemus* here, as the manuscripts recommend.]

Hence it is appropriately added: “Yet you will plunge me into filth.” God is said to plunge us into filth when he reveals us as plunged into filth, because the more truly we rise toward him through good works, the more subtly we recognize the filth of our life by which we differ from his purity.

He therefore says: “If I wash myself as with waters of snow, and my hands shine as though perfectly clean, yet you will plunge me into filth.” It is as though he said more plainly: “Although I am drenched with the tears of heavenly compunction, although I am exercised through devotion to right action, nevertheless in your purity I see that I am not pure.”

For corruptible flesh still wounds the soul intent upon God and stains the beauty of its love with obscene and unlawful movements of thought.

[Vet. XXIX.] Hence it is added: “And my garments will abhor me.”

**58. The body is the soul’s garment.** —What is expressed by the name “garment” except this earthly body with which the soul is clothed and covered, so that it does not appear naked in the subtlety of its substance?

[Note: Corb. Germ., Turon., Vindoc., and the better manuscripts read as above. The printed editions read: “in the substance of its subtlety.”]

Hence Solomon says: “At all times let your garments be white” (Eccl. IX, 8), that is, let the members of the body be clean from filthy acts. Hence Isaiah says: “The garment mixed with blood shall be for burning” (Isa. IX, 5). To mix a garment with blood is to stain the body with carnal desires. The Psalmist feared being polluted by these when he said: “Deliver me from bloodguilt, O God, God of my salvation” (Ps. L, 16).

Hence the angel’s voice says to John: “You have a few names in Sardis who have not polluted their garments” (Rev. III, 4).

According to the usage of sacred language, our garments are said to abhor us because they render us abominable, just as Peter says concerning Judas: “He acquired a field from the reward of iniquity” (Acts I, 18). Judas could not possess a field purchased with the price of blood, since, after returning the thirty pieces of silver, he immediately punished the crime of his betrayal in himself by a more criminal death. But “he acquired” is said to mean “he caused to be acquired.”

[Note: Many, with Gemet. and other Norman manuscripts, read: “he caused it to be possessed.” Utic. has both readings.]

So here also, “My garments will abhor me” is said to mean “they will make me abominable,” because, while the members rebel against the mind and the pursuits of holy desire are interrupted by the tumult of temptations, the soul placed in the midst of its struggle recognizes how far it is still despised by the Divinity. It earnestly desires to pass beyond its correction completely, but cannot, and is stained by the foul dust of thought.

[Note: Turon., Gemet., and others read as above, whereas the old edition has “with foul dust,” and Cocc. and the editions following it “with filthy dust.”]

He had felt this abomination of garments who said: “I see another law in my members fighting against the law of my mind and taking me captive in the law of sin, which is in my members” (Rom. VII, 23). He eagerly desired to lay aside and later resume these garments, in which he could not please perfectly, saying: “Wretched man that I am, who will free me from this body of death?” (Rom. VII, 24).

Let the just man therefore say: “If I wash myself as with waters of snow, and my hands shine as though perfectly clean, yet you will plunge me into filth, and my garments will abhor me,” because however far he may rise toward the heights through the compunction of contemplation, and however much he may gird himself for work through the exercise of labor, he nevertheless still feels something unworthy from the body of death and considers himself abominable in the many things he carries from the weight of corruption.

[Vet. XXX, Rec. XX.] This is made still more grievous for him because often he does not even understand what it is that causes him to sin. He receives blows, but does not recognize what in him displeases the strict Judge more or less. Hence it is added:

## CHAPTER XXXVII

**VERSE 32.—For I could not answer a man who is like me, nor could one who might be heard with me in judgment on equal terms.**
### 59. How serious it is for the just person not to know where he sins

When we contend with someone as an equal in court, we know what is said against us, we are heard in what we say, and the more clearly we grasp the charges brought forward, the more confidently we answer the matters at issue. Since the invisible Judge sees what we do, he hears, as it were, what we say; but because we do not fully recognize what displeases him, we are, as it were, ignorant of what he himself says.

Therefore, as the holy man considers the loathsomeness of his garments, he fears all the more because he cannot be heard as an equal in judgment. For as long as he is weighed down by the burden of corruption, he suffers this as the more grievous element of his punishment: that he does not know even the judgment of his reprover. It is as though he were openly saying: “I am not heard as an equal in this judgment, because everything I do lies exposed, and yet I myself do not know how greatly I am reproved.”

It continues:

### CHAPTER XXXVIII

**Verse 33.** “For there is no one who can reprove both parties and lay his hand upon them both.”

### 60. What it means to reprove God

It sounds harsh to ask who might reprove God; but it will not seem harsh if we recall what he himself says through another prophet. Through Isaiah he admonishes us:

> “Cease to do evil, learn to do good; seek judgment, relieve the oppressed, judge the orphan, defend the widow; and come and reprove me, says the Lord” (Isaiah 1:16).

For the one whom we reprove, we confront by the authority of reason. What then does the Lord mean when, after urging us to perform holy deeds, he adds, “Come and reprove me,” unless he plainly indicates how much confidence he grants to good actions? It is as though he were saying openly: “Act rightly, and confront the movements of my judgment—not now through the groaning of supplication, but through the confidence of authority.”

Hence John says:

> “If our heart does not condemn us, we have confidence toward God” (1 John 3:21).

Hence Moses, because he pleases God by serving, is heard even while silent, when God says to him in his silence:

> “Why do you cry to me?” (Exodus 14:15).

Hence he restrains the one who is angry when he hears:

> “Let me alone, so that my wrath may burn against this people” (Exodus 32:10).

Hence the Lord complains that he had no one to reprove him, when he says through the prophet:

> “I sought a man who would interpose a hedge and stand in opposition before me, lest I destroy it, and I found none” (Ezekiel 22:30).

Hence Isaiah laments bitterly:

> “We have all fallen like a leaf, and our iniquities have carried us away like the wind; there is no one who calls upon your name, who rises up and holds fast to you” (Isaiah 64:6–7).

### 61. Christ alone was able to free us from death; by suffering, he reproved human guilt and appeased God’s wrath [Old recension XXXI, Revised recension XXI]

Any righteous persons may at times oppose the movements of present judgment through the merit of the innocence they have received; but by their own power they cannot drive away from the human race the punishments of the death to come.

Let the holy man therefore consider the condition to which the human race has fallen; let him behold the losses of eternal death. Let him recognize that human justice is plainly unable to offer resistance; let him see how perversely humanity has sinned and how sternly the Creator is angry against humanity; and let him seek the Mediator between God and humanity, both God and human.

[**Note:** From the Tours, Beauvais, Longpont, Vendôme, English, and Norman manuscripts, and, as Gilot reports, from the Paris manuscripts, we have restored and corrected the reading adopted here. Nearly all printed editions read *poenitentiae* (“of repentance”), contrary to Gregory’s meaning.]

Because he sees that this Mediator is to come only in the distant future, he says in lament:

> “There is no one who can reprove both parties and lay his hand upon them both.”

The Redeemer of the human race, the Mediator between God and humanity, became human through the flesh. Because he alone appeared righteous among human beings, yet reached punishment despite being without sin, he both reproved humanity so that it would not sin and stood in the way of God so that he would not strike. He offered examples of innocence and accepted the punishment of wickedness.

By suffering, therefore, he reproved both parties: by inspiring justice, he reproved human guilt, and by dying he tempered the Judge’s anger. He laid his hand upon both, because he provided human beings with examples to imitate and displayed in himself to God deeds by which God might be appeased toward humanity.

[**Note:** Thus read the Gembloux manuscript and other Norman and English manuscripts, as well as most copies. The printed editions read *per justitiam* (“through justice”).]

[**Note:** The Évreux, Lyré, Bigot, Utica, and Corbie manuscripts read *pro alienis erratibus* (“for the errors of others”).]

[**Note:** Beauvais, Corbie, Gembloux, and the other Norman manuscripts read *ut propria non haberet* (“so that he had none of his own”).]

No one before him had interceded for the guilt of others in such a way that he had no guilt of his own. Therefore, no one could oppose eternal death on behalf of others to the same extent, since guilt arising from his own deeds bound him.

Thus the new human came to humanity: one who contradicted guilt, a friend to punishment. He displayed marvelous things and endured cruel ones. He laid his hand upon both, because by the very means through which he taught the guilty what was right, he appeased the angry Judge.

He also offered something more marvelous than all his miracles: he corrected the hearts of sinners by gentleness rather than terror. Hence it continues:

### CHAPTER XXXIX [Revised recension XXII]

**Verse 34.** “Let him take his rod away from me, and let his terror not frighten me.”

### 62. He corrected us by gentleness rather than terror [Old recension XXXII]

God held the rod through the Law when he said:

> “If anyone does this or that, let him surely die.”

But when he became incarnate, he removed the rod, because he showed the paths of life through gentleness. Hence the Psalmist says to him:

> “Direct yourself, prosper, and reign, because of truth and gentleness and justice” (Psalm 44:5).

He did not wish to be feared as God, but inspired love for himself as a father. Paul says this plainly:

> “You did not receive the spirit of slavery again in fear, but you received the Spirit of adoption as sons, in whom we cry, ‘Abba, Father’” (Romans 8:15).

Hence it is appropriately added here:

### CHAPTER XL

**Verse 35.** “I will speak, and I will not fear him.”

[**Note:** The printed editions add here, “for I cannot answer while afraid.” These words are omitted in the Corbie, Reichenau, Beauvais, Norman, and other more authoritative manuscripts. They are found in the Colbertine manuscript.]

### 63. Fear was unable to raise us from sin

Since the holy man sees the Redeemer of the human race coming in gentleness, he takes toward the Lord not fear but affection toward a father. He rejects fear because, through the grace of adoption, he rises toward love.

Hence John says:

> “There is no fear in love, but perfect love casts out fear” (1 John 4:18).

Hence Zechariah says:

> “That, being delivered from the hand of our enemies, we might serve him without fear” (Luke 1:74).

Fear, therefore, was unable to raise us from the death of sin; but the grace of gentleness breathed into us lifted us to the state of life.

This is well signified when the Shunammite woman’s son was raised by Elisha (2 Kings 4:30, 34). When Elisha sent the boy with his staff, he did not restore life to the dead son; but when he came himself, stretched himself over the dead man, gathered himself over his limbs, walked back and forth, and breathed seven times into the dead man’s mouth, he immediately restored him to returning light through the ministry of compassion.

The Creator of the human race, God, grieved over the dead boy, as it were, when in mercy he saw us slain by the sting of iniquity. And because through Moses he brought forth the terror of the Law, he sent the rod, as it were, through the boy. But the boy could not raise the dead with the staff, because, as Paul testifies:

> “The Law brought nothing to perfection” (Hebrews 7:19).

He himself, however, coming in person and humbly stretching himself over the corpse, gathered himself to match the dead man’s limbs, because:

> “Although he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings, and being found in appearance as a human being” (Philippians 2:6–7).

He walks back and forth because he calls both nearby Judea and the nations situated far away. He breathes seven times upon the dead man because, through the opening of the divine gift, he bestows the sevenfold Spirit of grace upon those lying dead in sin.

[**Note:** This is the reading of the Corbie, Reichenau, Colbertine, German, and Vendôme manuscripts, and of the old Coccius edition. Subsequent editions alter *inspirat* (“breathes upon”) to *oscitat* (“yawns”), and immediately *tribuit* (“bestows”) to *aspirat* (“breathes upon”). In place of *per apertionem* (“through opening”), the Tours and Longpont manuscripts read *per aspirationem* (“through breathing upon”). One Vendôme manuscript has both readings, *aspirat* and *tribuit*.]

Immediately the child rises alive, because the one whom the rod of terror could not raise returned to life through the Spirit of love.

Let him therefore speak from his own voice, and let him speak from the voice of the human race:

> “Let him take his rod away from me, and let his terror not frighten me; I will speak, and I will not fear him.”

And it is appropriately added:

### CHAPTER XLI

**Same passage.** “For I cannot answer while afraid.”

### 64. Fear does not render to God the service due for his gifts

We are said to answer someone when we repay his deeds with deeds worthy of them. To answer God, therefore, is to return our service for his preceding gifts. Hence certain psalms, in which holy conduct is proposed for imitation, are prefaced as being written “for answering.”

God created humanity upright, and when humanity declined into perversity, he endured it with patience. Every day he sees our guilt, yet does not immediately cut short the time of our life; he bestows gifts in his goodness and exercises patience toward the wicked.

Humanity ought to answer so many benefits. Yet it cannot answer while afraid, because whoever still fears the Creator of the human race in a slavish way certainly does not love him. We render true service to God only when, through the confidence of love, we do not fear him; when affection, not fear, directs us toward good works; and when evil no longer pleases our mind, even if it is permitted.

For whoever is restrained from a perverse deed by fear would gladly do it if it were permitted. Therefore, the person who is not yet free from the desire for wickedness is not truly upright.

It is rightly said, then, “For I cannot answer while afraid,” because we do not render true service to God if we serve his commands out of fear rather than love.

[**Note:** The Évreux, Utica, Lyré, and Bigot manuscripts read: “But when our mind is kindled by love of his sweetness, every desire for the present life is lightened.”]

But when love of his sweetness is kindled in our mind, every desire for the present life is lightened; affection turns into weariness, and the mind endures with grief the life to which it had previously submitted, overcome by a shameful love.

Hence it is appropriately added:

### CHAPTER XLII [Old recension XXXIII, Revised recension XXIII]

**Chapter 10, verse 1.** “My soul is weary of my life.”

### 65. Love of God produces weariness with this life and leads to confession of errors

When the present life begins to seem worthless and the Creator’s love begins to grow sweet, the mind is set against itself, so that it ought to accuse itself of the sins in which, previously ignorant of heavenly things, it had defended itself.

Hence it rightly adds:

### CHAPTER XLIII

**Same passage.** “I will release my speech against myself.”

### 66. The person who tries to defend his sins uses his speech as though on his own behalf

A person uses his speech as though on his own behalf when he tries to defend the wrongs he has done by excuses. But he releases his speech against himself when he begins to accuse himself of having gone astray.

Often, even when we sin, we judge the very things we do. The mind itself accuses what it commits; but because it does not abandon this through desire, it is ashamed to confess what it has done. When, however, it has wholly suppressed the pleasure of the flesh by judgment, it rises with bold speech into a confession of its accusation.

It is rightly said now, “I will release my speech against myself,” because a strong mind begins to let loose against itself words of hatred that it had previously restrained within itself out of weak shame.

But some openly confess their sins and nevertheless do not know how to groan in confession; they speak joyfully of things that ought to be mourned. Hence it is appropriately added:

### CHAPTER XLIV [Revised recension XXIV]

**Same passage.** “I will speak in the bitterness of my soul.”

### 67. Confession should be made in the bitterness of the soul

When someone speaks while detesting his sins, it necessarily follows that he speak of them in the bitterness of his soul, so that this very bitterness may punish whatever the tongue, under the judgment of the mind, accuses.

[**Note:** All the manuscripts supply the word *necesse est* (“it is necessary,” or “it must follow”), which is omitted in the commonly printed editions. The same use of this word occurs in Hilary of Poitiers, *On Psalm 68*, section 16, where he writes: “One must wish to be rescued from evils for this reason, lest he suffer evils.” And in *On Psalm 118*, letter 12, section 7: “It must be believed that the earth of those generations was founded and will remain.”]

It should also be known that, from the punishment of repentance that the mind imposes upon itself, it gains some measure of security and rises with greater confidence to the questioning of the heavenly Judge, so that it may discover itself more precisely and recognize how everything is ordered in relation to itself.

Hence it immediately continues:

### CHAPTER XLV

**Verse 2.** “I will say to God: Do not condemn me; tell me why you judge me thus.”

### 68. God judges and punishes us in this life in two ways

Since the sinner asserts himself in the bitterness of his soul, what else does he say to God than that he not be condemned? For the bitterness of present repentance extinguishes the punishments of the wrath to come.

God judges a person in this life in two ways: either he begins already to inflict the future torments through present evils, or he extinguishes the future torments through present scourges.

For unless the just Judge struck certain people both now and afterward as their sins demanded, Judas would not have said:

> “He destroyed those who did not believe a second time” (Jude 5),

[**Note:** The printed editions add *apostolus* (“the Apostle”), but it is found in none of the manuscripts.]

nor would the Psalmist have said of the wicked:

> “Let them be clothed with their shame as with a double cloak” (Psalm 108:29).

We call a *diplois* a double garment. Therefore, those who are struck according to the merit of their guilt by both temporal and everlasting judgment are clothed with shame as with a double cloak.

Punishment frees from punishment only those whom it changes. Those whom present evils do not correct, present evils lead to what follows. But if present punishment did not defend certain people from eternal punishment, Paul would not have said:

> “When we are judged, we are disciplined by the Lord, so that we may not be condemned with the world” (1 Corinthians 11:32).

Hence an angelic voice says to John:

> “Those whom I love, I reprove and discipline” (Revelation 3:19).

It is also written:

> “The Lord disciplines the one he loves and scourges every son whom he receives” (Hebrews 12:6).

### 69. The mind of the just person trembles in order to be secure [Old recension XXXIV]

Often the mind of the just person trembles more deeply in order to be more secure; and when it is girded with scourges, it is disturbed by uncertainty about the heavenly judgment. It fears that everything it suffers may be the beginning of the condemnation to come, and in its thoughts it questions the Judge because, under the blow, it doubts the merits of its life.

But when the virtue of its life is brought before the eyes of the mind, the Judge seems to answer with consolation: he does not strike to destroy the person whom, by striking, he preserves in the innocence of his conduct.

It is rightly said here: “Tell me why you judge me thus.” It is as though it were openly said: “Because you judge me by scourging me, show that through these scourges you are making me secure for judgment.”

This may nevertheless be understood in another way. Often the just person receives scourges as a test and, examining his life through the most searching inquiry, both feels and confesses that he is a sinner, yet does not know for what particular sin he is being struck. He trembles all the more under the blow because he does not know the causes of his being struck.

He asks the Judge to reveal himself to him, so that what the Judge strikes by punishment, he himself may chastise within himself through tears. For he knows that the most equitable Avenger afflicts none of us unjustly, and he is shaken by great fear because he suffers in the blow but cannot fully discover within himself what he ought to lament.

[**Note:** The Gembloux manuscript reads *in persecutione* (“in persecution”). Previously, however, the reading was *in percussione* (“under the blow”).]

Hence it continues:

### CHAPTER XLVI [Revised recension XXV]

**Verse 3.** “Does it seem good to you that you should slander and oppress a poor man, the work of your hands, and assist the counsel of the wicked?”

### 70. The anxiety of the just person who does not know why he is scourged

This is said in the form of a question in such a way that it amounts to a denial. It is as though it were openly said: “You who are supremely good—I know that you do not consider it good to oppress a poor man through slander. I therefore know that what I suffer is not unjust, and I grieve all the more because I do not know the causes of this justice.”

It should be noted that he does not say, “that you oppress an innocent man,” but “a poor man.” For the person who sets his poverty, rather than his innocence, before the strictness of the Judge no longer draws boldness from his life but shows how weak he sees himself to be.

He appropriately adds: “The work of your hands.” It is as though he were openly saying: “You cannot wickedly oppress one whom you remember having made freely.”

### 71. God does not allow us to be tested beyond our strength

It is rightly added: “And assist the counsel of the wicked?” Whom does he call “the wicked” here, if not the evil spirits? Since they themselves cannot return to life, they cruelly seek companions for death.

Their counsel was that divine correction should touch blessed Job, so that the man who had been righteous in tranquillity might at least sin under the scourges. But the Lord did not assist the counsel of the wicked, because he delivered the flesh of the righteous man to their temptations but did not surrender his soul.

The evil spirits continually devise this counsel against the good: those whom they see serving God innocently in tranquillity, they seek to drag, when afflicted by adversity, into the abyss of guilt.

[**Note:** The word *innocue* (“innocently”) is absent from the Évreux and other Norman manuscripts. It is present in the Corbie, Colbertine, and Reichenau manuscripts.]

But the sharpness of their counsel is destroyed because the merciful Creator moderates the scourges according to the strength of the person, so that punishment does not exceed his virtue and human weakness does not fall through the craft of the powerful.

[**Note:** The Coccius edition and later printed editions, along with certain manuscripts, read *excedat* (“exceed”). We have preferred *excidat* (“fall away”), both because it is found in the Corbie, Reichenau, Vendôme, and other more authoritative manuscripts, and because *fall away* is more appropriate to human weakness than *exceed*. The following words are: “lest, falling, it bear.”]

Hence Paul rightly says:

> “God is faithful, and he will not allow you to be tested beyond what you can bear, but with the testing he will also provide a way out, so that you may be able to endure it” (1 Corinthians 10:13).

For unless merciful God adjusts temptations according to our strength, there is surely no one who would not bear the snares of the evil spirits by falling. If the Judge does not set a measure for temptations, he immediately casts down the one who is standing by imposing burdens beyond his strength.

Thus blessed Job denied what he has said in asking, just as by asking he denies what he immediately adds:

### CHAPTER XLVII [Revised recension XXVI]

**Verses 4–7.** “Do you have eyes of flesh, or will you see as a human being sees? Are your days like the days of a human being, or are your years like human times, that you should seek out my iniquity and examine my sin, and know that I have done nothing wicked?”

### 72. The difference between human and divine sight, and between our days and eternity [Old recension XXXV]

Eyes of flesh recognize the deeds of time only in time, because they themselves emerge for seeing with time and close with time. Human sight follows any work; it does not precede it, because it scarcely sees what exists and in no way recognizes what is to come.

[**Note:** The Évreux manuscript reads *vix existentia concupiscit* (“scarcely desires what exists”). We judge that *concupiscit* (“desires”) entered by error in place of *conspicit* (“sees”), which is found in the manuscripts.]

The days and years of human beings also differ from the days and years of eternity. Our life begins in time and ends in time, while eternity, as it forms all things within the breadth of its embrace, swallows time.

Its immensity extends above and below us on every side; its eternity stretches without beginning or end. In it, things that have passed do not pass away, nor are things still to come absent as though they had not appeared, because the one who always exists sees everything as present to himself. Since his vision is not extended backward or forward by seeing, it is not altered by any change of perception.

Let him therefore say:

> “Do you have eyes of flesh, or will you see as a human being sees? Are your days like the days of a human being, and your years like human times, that you should seek out my iniquity and examine my sin, and know that I have done nothing wicked?”

It is as though he were humbly asking: “Why do you examine me through scourges in time, when you knew me perfectly before time? Why do you question my sins by blows, when through the power of your eternity you did not fail to know them even before you created me?”

He immediately expresses the weight of this power when he adds:

### CHAPTER XLVIII

**Same passage.** “Since there is no one who can rescue me from your hand.”

### 73. The humble supplication of the one who is scourged

It is as though he were openly saying: “What remains for you but to spare, since no one can resist your power? Since no one is able by the merit of his own virtue to hold back your judgment, your mercy should the more readily demand of itself that it spare.”

Because we were conceived in sin and born in iniquities, either we wickedly commit evil or we sin even when acting rightly through carelessness.

[**Note:** The Norman, Beauvais, and most other manuscripts read *in delictis* (“in offences”).] We therefore have no means by which the strict Judge may be made placable.

But since we cannot present our own work as worthy in his sight, it remains for us to offer him, for his appeasement, the work of his own hands. Hence it is added:

### CHAPTER XLIX [Revised recension XXVII]

**Verse 8.** “Your hands fashioned me and made me wholly round about, and do you suddenly cast me down?”

### 74. The Manichaeans’ doctrine is refuted

It is as though he were humbly saying to him: “Since what I have done is not worthy of your mercy under a just examination, consider it mercifully, lest what you have made perish.”

[**Note:** Bartholomew and the old edition read *tuae plasmationi* (“to your fashioning”), but none of our manuscript copies supports that reading.]

These words also destroy the perverse teaching of Mani, who, falsely asserting that there are two principles, tries to claim that the spirit was created by God but the flesh by Satan.

[**Note:** The Gembloux, Beauvais, Corbie, and other ancient manuscripts read *Manis* or *Manes* (“Mani” or “Manes”).]

The holy man, filled with the grace of the prophetic Spirit, considers events far in the future and, foreseeing the offspring of errors, tramples them down when he says:

> “Your hands fashioned me and made me wholly round about.”

For the person who asserts that he was both fashioned and made wholly round about by God leaves nothing either in his spirit or in his flesh for the kingdom of darkness. He referred to himself as fashioned because of the inward image; he recalled that he was made wholly round about in respect of what consists of the garment of flesh.

[**Note:** The Vulgate adds *hominis* (“of man”), but no manuscript has it. If anything were to be supplied, *Dei* (“of God”) would be more fitting.]

### 75. Humanity’s prerogative in the order of creation [Old recension XXXVI]

It should be noted that by asserting himself to have been fashioned by God’s hands, he sets the dignity of his creation before the mercy of the Judge.

Although all things were created through the Word coeternal with the Father, the very account of creation shows how much humanity is preferred to all animals and to created things, even heavenly things that lack sensation.

For it is said of all things:

> “He spoke, and they were made” (Psalm 148:5).

But when he decided to make humanity, he first said something that ought to be considered reverently:

> “Let us make the human being in our image and likeness” (Genesis 1:26).

It is not written of humanity, as of the other things, “Let there be,” and it was so (ibid., 1:3); nor did the earth bring forth humanity as the waters brought forth birds. Rather, before humanity was made, the words “Let us make” are spoken, so that, because a rational creature was being created, it might appear to have been made, as it were, with deliberation.

[**Note:** The Vendôme, Norman, and other manuscripts, with the older editions, read *sed priusquam fieret* (“but before he was made”); the Coccius edition and later editions read *sed priusquam faceret* (“but before he made”). The printed editions read *natura* (“nature”), but no manuscript has this reading.]

Humanity is fashioned from the earth, as though through careful workmanship, and is raised by the Creator’s inspiration in the power of the vital spirit. Thus the one made in the Creator’s image exists not through the voice of command alone but through the dignity of the work.

What humanity received more nobly than the other earthly creatures by the act of creation, it sets before the kindness of its Maker when placed under the scourge, saying:

> “Your hands fashioned me and made me wholly round about, and do you suddenly cast me down?”

It is as though he were openly saying: “Why do you despise with such contempt the one whom you created with such dignity? Why do you subject to suffering the one whom you preferred, by reason, to all other things?”

Yet this same dignity of ours shines through the image, while through the flesh it is far removed from the perfection of blessedness. For when spirit is mingled with dust, it is in a certain way joined to weakness.

The blessed Job sets this weakness before the Judge’s mercy when he adds:

### CHAPTER L [Revised recension XXVIII]

**Verse 9.** “Remember, I beg you, that you made me like clay.”

### 76. Why the angel sinned irremissibly, but humanity did not
