The spirits of the angels sinned irremissibly because they were able to stand all the more firmly insofar as no admixture of flesh held them back. Humanity, however, merited forgiveness after sin because, through the carnal body, it received something by which it was less than itself.

Thus, before the Judge, this same weakness of the flesh is an argument for mercy, as the Psalmist says:

> “But he is merciful and will be propitious toward their sins; he multiplied [his acts of mercy] to turn away his wrath, and he will not kindle all his anger. And he remembered that they are flesh” (Psalm 77:38).

[**Note:** The Lyré, Bigot, and Utica manuscripts read: “and he was propitious . . . and did not destroy them.”]

Humanity was made like clay because it was taken from mud for its creation. Clay is formed when water moistens earth. Humanity was therefore created like clay, because the soul, like water, pours moisture into the dust when it gives life to the flesh.

The holy man rightly sets this before the Judge’s mercy when he asks:

> “Remember, I beg you, that you made me like clay.”

It is as though he were openly saying: “Consider the weakness of the flesh and release the guilt of iniquity.”

The death of this same flesh is also openly added when it immediately continues:

### CHAPTER LI

**Same passage.** “And you will reduce me to dust.”

### 77. The weakness of the flesh excuses humanity

It is as though he were plainly asking: “Remember, I beg you, that through the flesh I come from the earth and through its destruction I tend toward the earth. Look upon the material of my origin and the punishment of my end, and quickly spare a guilt that soon passes away.”

[**Old recension XXXVII, Revised recension XXIX.]

But because he has described the condition of created humanity, he now adds the order of its propagation:

### CHAPTER LII

**Verses 10–11.** “Did you not milk me like milk and coagulate me like cheese? You clothed me with skin and flesh; you joined me together with bones and sinews.”

### 78. A description of humanity’s origin

Humanity, fashioned like clay, was propagated as milk is drawn from seed and as cheese is coagulated in the flesh. It is clothed with flesh and skin and made firm with bones and sinews.

Through clay, therefore, the quality of the first creation is expressed; through milk, the subsequent order of conception, because through successive stages of coagulation it is gradually brought to strength in the bones.

But a description of the created body is too inadequate a praise of God unless it also expresses the wondrous breath of vivification that follows. Hence it is added:

### CHAPTER LIII

**Verse 12.** “You granted me life and mercy.”

### 79. The inspiration and preservation of life

The Creator grants us good things to no purpose if he himself does not preserve everything he grants. It continues:

**Same passage:** “And your visitation guarded my spirit.”

It is useful to repeat briefly how what we have said about the outer person can also apply to the inner person.

### 80. Humanity is clay and becomes dust when grace is withdrawn; it suffers the battles of the flesh but is strengthened by grace [Old recension XXXVIII]

“Remember, I beg you, that you made me like clay.”

Our inner person exists like clay, because the grace of the Holy Spirit is poured into the earthly mind so that it may be raised to understanding its Creator. Human thought, which has withered through the barrenness of its sin, becomes green again through the power of the Holy Spirit, as earth becomes green when watered.

But often, while we use without interruption the powers of the heavenly gift we have received, we are lifted into self-confidence by the habit of continual prosperity. It therefore often happens that the same Spirit who had raised us withdraws for a little while, so that he may show us what we are in ourselves.

The holy man immediately expresses this when he adds:

> “And you will reduce me to dust.”

When the mind is somewhat abandoned in temptation through the withdrawal of the Spirit, the earth is dried, as it were, from its former moisture, so that the abandoned person feels his weakness and recognizes how barren he is without the infusion of heavenly grace.

He is appropriately said to be reduced to dust because, when left to himself, he is swept away by the breath of any temptation. But when we are shaken after being abandoned, we think more subtly about the gifts we had known when inspired.

Hence he adds:

> “Did you not milk me like milk and coagulate me like cheese?”

Our mind, when through the grace of the Holy Spirit it is drawn away from its former way of life, is milked like milk because it is formed in the tenderness and subtlety of a new beginning. It is coagulated like cheese because it is compressed into the thickening of a rich thought, so that it no longer flows away through desires but gathers itself into a single love and rises toward solid reformation.

[**Note:** One Vendôme manuscript, together with the German and Corbie manuscripts, reads “because in a certain tenderness of a new coagulation.” Another Vendôme manuscript, followed by the Norman manuscripts, reads “because in a certain tenderness of a new beginning of coagulation.”]

Often, however, against these same spiritual beginnings, the flesh murmurs from old habit, and the mind endures battles from the human being it carries outwardly.

Hence he adds:

> “You clothed me with skin and flesh.”

The inner person is clothed with skin and flesh because, in being raised toward heavenly things, it is surrounded by the siege of carnal movements.

Yet the Creator does not abandon the person striving toward justice in temptation. Through the infusion of grace, he anticipates even the sinner; he both releases the lifted mind outwardly into battle and strengthens it inwardly.

[**Note:** The Gembloux manuscript reads *precantem* (“one praying”) in place of *peccantem* (“one sinning”).]

Hence it is appropriately added:

> “You joined me together with bones and sinews.”

We are clothed with flesh and skin, but joined together with bones and sinews, because although we are shaken when temptation breaks in from outside, the hand of the Creator nevertheless strengthens us within, so that we are not broken.

Through the movements of the flesh he humbles us with regard to our gifts, but through the bones of virtues he strengthens us against temptations.

Thus he says:

[**Note:** The Gembloux manuscript reads “with flesh and skins.” Utica, Lyré, and Bigot read “with skin and flesh.” Vendôme likewise has the latter reading.]

> “You clothed me with flesh and skin; you joined me together with bones and sinews.”

It is as though he were openly saying: “Outwardly you abandon me for testing, but inwardly you preserve me from perishing by binding me with virtues.”

He grants us the uprightness of a good life precisely because, in his kindness, he spares the sins of our past. Hence it is appropriately added:

> “You granted me life and mercy.”

### 81. He receives and preserves life through God’s mercy, which precedes and follows

Life is granted when goodness is breathed into malignant minds. But life cannot be received without mercy, because the Lord does not assist us in obtaining the goods of justice unless he first mercifully releases our former wickedness.

Or certainly, he grants us life and mercy because the mercy by which he precedes us toward good living also preserves us when it follows after us. Unless he supplies mercy, the life he grants cannot be preserved.

Through the daily use of human life we grow old, and through the impulse of the outer person we depart from inner things by slippery thought. Unless heavenly visitation restores us—either by bringing us to life through the compunction of love or by correcting us through the scourge of fear—the mind that seemed to have been renewed through a long pursuit of virtue is suddenly and utterly destroyed by a fall.

Hence he adds:

> “And your visitation guarded my spirit.”

Heavenly visitation guards the human spirit when it does not cease either to strike it with a scourge, after enriching it with virtues, or to pierce it with love.

[**Note:** Tours, Utica, Bigot, and most other manuscripts read “or to strike it by scourging.”]

For if he grants gifts but does not continually raise the spirit by restoring it, the good that is not guarded by the giver is quickly lost.

But behold: while the holy man humbly recognizes himself, he discovers in a general way the mysteries of divine mercy to be conferred; and when he truthfully confesses his weakness, he is suddenly carried upward to recognize the calling of the nations.

For he immediately adds:

### CHAPTER LIV [Revised recension XXX]

**Verse 13.** “Although you conceal these things in your heart, nevertheless I know that you remember them all.”

82. The Calling of the Gentiles Hidden in God’s Counsel.—And as though he openly said: “Why am I afraid, since I know that you are gathering all the nations as well? Yet you conceal this in your heart, because you do not yet disclose it in clear speech. But since you also remember all people, you surely make me certain of pardon.” [Vet. XXXIX.] It should be understood, however, that in some deeds we are both made certain of pardon and strengthened, after sins have been committed, in confidence of our absolution by the correction and repentance that follow; yet we are still touched by the memory of the wickedness we have committed, and are driven away, unwillingly and against our will, by illicit thought. Hence it is aptly added:

## CHAPTER LV [Rec. XXXI]

**VERSE 14.—“If I have sinned, and for a time you spared me, why do you not permit me to be clean from my iniquity?”**

83. Sins once erased still stain the memory and renew the battle; what must then be done.—The Lord spares sin “for a time” when he immediately washes away the guilt of sin through the tears granted. But he does not permit us to be clean from our iniquity, because although we committed the sin willingly, sometimes we unwillingly endure its memory with delight. Often what was already erased from the sight of the Judge when tears intervened returns to the mind; and the conquered fault again tries to creep into delight, and is renewed by a resurgence of its former assault. Thus what a person first did in the body he later turns over in his mind through importunate thought.

[Note: The remainder of the context is lacking in Beauvais: *meae, a facie*.]

The spiritual athlete knew how carefully to observe this. He said: “My scars have become foul and corrupt because of my foolishness” (Ps. XXXVII, 6).

What are “scars,” then, except the healings of wounds? [Vet. XL.] He had perceived that loosened sins returned to the memory’s delight, since he mourned his “scars.” For scars to become foul means that the wounds of sins already healed again creep into temptation, so that, from their suggestions, after the skin of repentance has formed over them, he again feels the stench and pain of guilt. In this matter nothing is done outwardly, but sin is committed only inwardly in thought; and unless the mind wipes this away with anxious lamentation, it binds itself under a strict liability.

84. Hence Moses rightly says: “If there is among you a man who has been defiled by a nocturnal dream, he shall go outside the camp and shall not return before evening; and after he has washed himself with water, after sunset he shall return to the camp” (Deut. XXIII, 10). The nocturnal dream is a hidden temptation, by which something shameful is conceived in the heart through dark thought, although it is not completed in bodily action. But a person defiled by a nocturnal dream is commanded to go outside the camp, because it is fitting that one who is polluted by unclean thought should consider himself unworthy of the fellowship of all the faithful, set the desert of his guilt before his eyes, and regard himself with contempt in comparison with the good.

[Note: Coccius and the more recent editions read *pollutum*, “the polluted one,” and shortly afterward *cum superioribus, laborantem*, “the one struggling with the foregoing.” We follow the manuscripts of Vendôme, Beauvais, Normandy, and others.]

For the polluted person to go outside the camp means that one struggling under a shameful assault should despise himself in comparison with the continent. He is washed with water toward evening when, observing his failing, he turns to the lamentation of repentance, so that through tears he may wash away whatever hidden defilement accuses his mind.

[Note: Thus Turon., Corb. Germ., Gemet., Ebroic., and other Norman manuscripts. In many Norman manuscripts, however, the reading is “hidden thought.” In Uticensis, *occulta inquinatio*, “hidden defilement,” was formerly read. The printed editions, with the Colbert manuscript, have “whatever hidden defilement there is in the mind.”]

But after sunset he should return to the camp, because, when the heat of temptation has cooled, he must again take courage in relation to the fellowship of the good.

[Note: Gemetensis and other Norman manuscripts, together with Corbie German, read: “after the washing, with the sun having set.” We retain the reading of the printed editions, which is that of 1 Reg.]

After washing with water and the setting of the sun, he returns to the camp: after the lamentation of repentance, when the flame of illicit thought has grown cold, he is restored to the confidence of claiming the merits of the faithful, so that he no longer considers himself far removed from the others, rejoicing that he has been made clean through the death of his inward ardor.

But amid these things it must be understood that we are sometimes afflicted by the impulse of illicit thought because we willingly occupy ourselves with certain acts of earthly conduct, although they are lawful. When earthly action is touched even in the smallest matters by desire, the strength of the ancient enemy grows against us, and our mind is polluted by no slight importunity of temptation.

Hence the priest of the Law is commanded to burn the limbs of the victim, cut into pieces, together with the head and those parts that are around the liver, but first to wash the feet and entrails of the victim with water (Lev. I, 7, 12).

[Note: Gemetensis and other ancient witnesses read *jecor*, “liver,” and the same reading occurs throughout what follows.]

We offer ourselves as a sacrifice to God when we dedicate our life to divine worship. We place the limbs of the victim, cut into pieces, upon the fire when we distinguish the works of our life among the virtues and offer them in sacrifice.

[Note: We have supplied *in*, “among,” from Norman manuscripts: “distinguishing [them] among the virtues.” This corresponds to the pieces into which the victim was cut.]

We burn the head and those parts contained near the liver when, in our understanding by which the whole body is governed, and in our hidden desires, we burn with the flame of divine love.

Yet it is commanded that the feet and entrails of the victim be washed. The feet touch the earth, while the entrails carry excrement, because often we are already kindled by desire for eternity and, with the whole devotion of our spirit, yearn for the appetite of our mortification; but because through weakness we still do something earthly, we also tolerate in our hearts certain illicit things that we had already subdued.

When unclean temptation pollutes our thoughts, what else do the entrails of the victim carry but excrement? But in order that they may be burned, let them be washed, because tears of fear must certainly cleanse the unclean thoughts that heavenly love kindles when the sacrifice is accepted.

Whatever the mind suffers, whether from an inexperienced struggle or from the memory of its former way of life, must be washed, so that it may burn more sweetly in the sight of its observer, in proportion as, when it begins to stand before him, it places nothing earthly and nothing slippery upon the altar of its prayer.

[Note: Most manuscripts read “in the sight of its inspector”; Corbie German has “observer.”]

Let the holy man, therefore, contemplate the losses of the human mind: how often it pollutes itself with illicit thought. After the Judge releases the guilt of the deed, and, lamenting his own guilt, reveals what we should lament, he says: “If I have sinned, and for a time you spared me, why do you not permit me to be clean from my iniquity?” As though he openly said: “If pardon has removed the guilt, why does it not also erase it from the memory?”

[Vet. XLI, Rec. XXXII.] Often the mind is so shaken by the recollection of guilt that it is driven toward committing it far more gravely than it had previously been seized by it. Once detected, it trembles, and, shaken by various impulses, disturbs itself. It fears being overcome by temptations, but, while resisting, it shudders at the very thing by which it is afflicted through the long labor of struggle. Hence it is aptly added:

## CHAPTER LVI

**VERSE 15.—“And if I am wicked, woe is me; and if I am righteous, I shall not lift up my head, being filled with affliction and misery.”**

85. The difference between resisting and yielding to vices.—The wicked person has woe, while the righteous person has misery, because eternal damnation follows the reprobate, whereas every elect person is purified by the pains of temporary adversity.

The wicked lifts his head, but, being exalted, cannot escape the woe that follows. The righteous, afflicted by the labor of his struggle, is not allowed to lift his head, but, pressed down, is freed from perpetual affliction. The former raises himself in pleasures but plunges himself into the punishments that follow. The latter depresses himself in sorrow, yet conceals himself from the weight of eternal judgment.

Let the holy man therefore consider that a person either resists vices and is afflicted by present labor, or yields and is handed over to perpetual affliction; and let him say: “And if I am wicked, woe is me; and if I am righteous, I shall not lift up my head, being filled with affliction and misery.” As though he openly lamented, saying: “Either, laid low beneath the desires of the flesh, I am subjected to eternal punishment, or, resisting unlawful impulses, I am tortured by present pain, because I am not free from the labor of struggle.”

But heavenly dispensation permits those who serve it with complete devotion to be shaken by assaults upon the flesh, so that the mind may not dare to rise in pride through presumption of its own security. Thus, while it trembles when struck, it may fix the foot of its hope more firmly upon the help of the Creator alone. Hence it is aptly added:

## CHAPTER LVII [Rec. XXXIII]

**VERSE 16.—“And because of pride you will catch me like a lioness.”**

86. By what art the lioness is caught; in the same way we have both fallen and been restored.—When a lioness seeks food for her cubs, she eagerly rushes into a pit prepared for capture. For, as is reported from certain regions, a pit is made in her path, in which livestock is placed, so that the lioness may be lured to throw herself there by desire for it. The pit is made narrow and deep, so that she can hurl herself into it by circling around, but cannot escape it by leaping.

Another pit, adjoining the first, is also dug. It is joined to the pit containing the livestock by an opening at the far end. A cage is placed in it, so that when the lioness falls and is driven from above by terror, she may seek to hide in what seems the more secluded part of the pit and willingly enter the cage. Her ferocity is then no longer feared, because she is lifted while enclosed in the cage. She who fell into the pit of her own accord returns to the upper parts enclosed by bars.

Thus the human mind was captured. Created in freedom of choice, while it desired to nourish the appetites of the flesh, it sought food for its cubs like a lioness and fell into the pit of its deception, stretching out its hand toward forbidden food at the enemy’s persuasion.

But in the pit it immediately found a cage, because, coming willingly to death, it at once suffered the prison of its corruption; and through the intervention of grace it is brought back to the free air.

Yet when it tries to do many things and cannot, it is bound, as though by the bars of a cage, by the obstacles of that same corruption.

[Note: The printed editions, together with the Corbie, Colbert, and Royal manuscripts, read *ligatur*, “is bound.” English, Norman, and many French manuscripts read *levatur*, “is lifted.”]

[Note: The words “and through the intervention of grace it is brought back to the free air” had been moved by Coccius from their proper place and transferred after the words “it is bound by bars.” We restore them to the position they occupy in the ancient editions and manuscripts. Their former displacement is also indicated by what follows.]

It has indeed escaped the pit of condemnation into which it had fallen, because, aided by the hand of redemption, it has overcome the punishment of coming death by returning to pardon.

[Note: Coccius and the later editions read “the hand of the Redeemer,” while other editions and manuscripts support “the hand of redemption.” There is no reason why “the hand of redemption” should not be said here, just as below, no. 94, “the pious hand of grace,” and no. 105, “the hand of holy exhortation.”]

Yet it endures the constriction of the cage, because it is also enclosed by the bonds of heavenly discipline, lest it wander through the desires of the flesh. Thus she who fell of her own accord into the pit returns to the free air while enclosed, because through freedom of choice she fell into guilt, yet the Creator’s grace constrains her, though unwilling, from her own movements.

After the pit, therefore, she suffers the cage; rescued from eternal punishment, she is restrained from the impulses of perverse freedom under the governance of the heavenly craftsman.

[Note: The Guss. edition, following the Roman edition, reads *erecta*; shortly afterward other editions, with one Royal manuscript, read “from the motions of a perverse will.”]

He therefore rightly says: “And because of pride you will catch me like a lioness,” because the free human being brought death upon himself through food, and, restored to pardon, lives more safely enclosed under discipline. He was caught like a lioness because of pride, since the discipline of his corruption now depresses him precisely where, unafraid of transgressing the commandment, he boldly leapt into the pit.

[Vet. XLII.] 87. Thus the one exalted by virtue is permitted to fall so that he may be healed of pride.—But if for a moment we turn the mind’s gaze away from the guilt of our first parent, we still find ourselves daily caught like a lioness through the vice of elation.

Often a person, having received virtues, rises into the boldness of presumption; but, through a marvelous dispensation of mercy, some circumstance is arranged before his eyes in which he may fall. When he desires something through guilt, what else does he covet in the pit but prey? He falls, panting, of his own accord, but cannot rise by his own strength.

When he considers that he is nothing of himself, he undoubtedly learns whose help he should seek. Yet heavenly mercy lifts him, once captured, as though from a pit, because, having come to know his weakness, it leads him back to pardon.

Thus, in the manner of a lioness, he returns to the cage in the upper parts because, when he has been exalted by virtue, he is bound in humility after falling into desire.

[Note: Ebroicensis reads “let him remain in the cage.”]

Since he had previously perished through presumption of himself, he is dealt with through marvelous mercy so that, enclosed by knowledge of his weakness, he may now live.

Because the holy man sees this frequently happen to human beings, he takes upon himself the voice of our danger, so that, when we recognize his weeping, we may learn what things in ourselves ought to be mourned.

But when elation raises our mind, the compunction of supreme love immediately withdraws from us; when heavenly grace visits us, it immediately urges us through tears toward its desires. Hence it is aptly added:

## CHAPTER LVIII [Rec. XXXIV]

**THE SAME.—“And when you return, you wonderfully torment me.”**

88. The hardening of a mind abandoned by God; the compunction of one visited by him.—When we are abandoned by the Creator, we do not even feel the losses of our abandonment in any way. For the farther our Creator withdraws from us, the more insensibly our mind grows hard. It loves none of the things of God and in no way desires heavenly things; and because it does not possess the warmth of inward love, it lies cold below. In a pitiable way it becomes daily more secure as it becomes worse.

Since it does not remember from where it has fallen and does not fear the punishments that will follow, it does not know how greatly it ought to be mourned.

[Note: Longipontanus reads: “and, secure, does not fear the punishments that will follow.”]

But if it is touched by the breath of the Holy Spirit, it immediately awakens to consideration of its destruction; it shakes itself awake in the pursuit of heavenly things, burns with the heats of supreme love, considers the losses that press around it, and, making progress, weeps over what previously perished joyfully.

[Note: Turonensis, Corbie German, Vendôme, and Corbie Norman read *torpebat*, “was sluggish.” The printed editions, with Colbert, read *perierat*, “had perished”; Longipontanus also has *perierat*.]

The Creator is therefore rightly told: “And when you return, you wonderfully torment me,” because almighty God, by the very act through which he visits our mind and raises it to his love, afflicts it more grievously through tears.

As though he openly said: “By leaving me you do not afflict me at all, because you make me insensible; but when you return, you torment me, because, while you reveal yourself to me, you show me how greatly I ought to be mourned.”

Hence he says that he is tormented not punitively but wonderfully, because, while the mind is carried upward through weeping, it rejoices in wonder at the punishment of its compunction; and it delights to be afflicted because, through its affliction, it sees itself lifted to higher things.

[Vet. XLIII.] Often, when heavenly mercy sees us growing sluggish in the practice of holy desire, it places before our eyes examples of those who follow it, so that the mind relaxed through idleness may be ashamed of its own sluggish torpor in proportion as it observes the progress of those who keep watch in others.

[Note: Norman and Vendôme manuscripts read *per pigredinem*, “through sluggishness”; Colbert and Corbie German have *pigredinem*; the German manuscript has *pigritudinem*, without *per*.]

Hence it is rightly added:

## CHAPTER LIX [Rec. XXXV]

**VERSE 17.—“You renew your witnesses against me, and multiply your anger against me, and punishments serve in battle against me.”**

89. God recalls us to himself through the examples of the good.—God’s witnesses are those who, through the practice of holy works, testify to the rewards of truth that await the elect. Hence we also call those whom we recognize as having suffered for the truth *martyrs*, using the Greek word meaning “witnesses.”

And through John the Lord will say with an angelic voice: “In the days of Antipas, my faithful witness, who was killed among you” (Rev. II, 13).

[Note: This passage is extremely corrupt in the printed editions. The Basel edition of 1514 and the Paris edition of 1518 read: “In the days of Antipas, my faithful witnesses, who …” Coccius, followed by later editors, has: “In my days, Antipas, my faithful witness, who …” The Gemetensis manuscript reads: “In the days of Antipas, my faithful witness, who …” Uticensis and other Norman manuscripts, together with Corbie German, read: “In the days of Antipas, my faithful witness, who …” Our reading agrees with the Greek text, as it is found in the manuscripts; see the Critical Synopsis.]

The Lord renews his witnesses against us when he multiplies the lives of the elect, which oppose our wickedness, in order to accuse and instruct us. His witnesses are therefore renewed against us because everything they do is contrary to the pursuits of our wickedness.

Hence the word of truth is called an adversary when the Mediator says through the Gospel: “Agree quickly with your adversary, while you are with him on the way” (Matt. V, 25).

And concerning this same Redeemer the wicked, persecuting him, say: “He is contrary to our works” (Wis. II, 12); and shortly afterward: “His life is unlike that of others” (ibid., 15).

The Lord therefore renews his witnesses against us because he shows that the good works we neglect are being performed by others for our correction, so that those whom commandments do not inflame may at least be stirred by examples. Our mind should consider nothing difficult in the pursuit of righteousness when it sees that it is perfectly accomplished by others.

It often happens that, when we observe the good things in another’s life, we fear the losses in our own more anxiously; and the greater the weight of judgment we shall suffer becomes evident in proportion to how far we now differ from the conduct of the good.

90. Their labor indicates the punishment awaiting the reprobate; what movements of the soul the good seen in others ought to excite.—Hence, after mentioning the renewal of the witnesses, it is aptly added: “And you multiply your anger against me.”

God’s anger is said to be multiplied against us inasmuch as it is shown to be manifold, because from the life and labor of the good we now learn how severe a judgment will strike us later if we refuse to be corrected while there is time.

We see God’s elect both doing devout deeds and enduring many cruel things. From this we infer how severe a Judge he will be there toward those whom he rejects, if here he so torments those whom he loves. Peter bears witness to this when he says: “It is time for judgment to begin from the house of God; and if it begins first with us, what will be the end of those who do not believe the Gospel of God?” (1 Pet. IV, 17).

When almighty God therefore renews witnesses against us, he multiplies his anger, because, by placing the life of the good before our eyes, he shows with what severity he will strike the hardness of the wickedness we have committed at the judgment.

When he heaps gifts upon those who alone follow him, he shows that he has already abandoned those who are sluggish.

When, therefore, we see good things in others, it is greatly necessary that we mingle rejoicing with our fear and fear with our rejoicing, so that love may rejoice in another’s progress, while conscience trembles over its own weaknesses.

But when we are refreshed by our brother’s progress, and consider from our own sluggishness the strictness of the judgment within, what remains except for the spirit to return to examining itself and afflict whatever it finds in itself to be reprobate or perverse?

[Note: In Lyranensis and Bigot, the words “and whatever in himself is reprobate” are absent.]

Hence it is aptly added: “And punishments serve in battle against me.”

When we consider God’s witnesses, punishments serve in battle against us, because, while we observe their wonderful deeds, we torture our own life—which displeases us in comparison with them—with deliberate affliction, so that lamentation may wash away whatever our works have polluted in us, and so that punishment of sorrow may cleanse whatever guilt still defiles through delight.

Blessed Job, therefore, because he sees the life of the fathers who preceded him, recognizes more subtly what he ought to mourn within himself. While he laments his own faults under the instruction of great sorrow, he teaches us to lament also, so that, in proportion as we see virtues in others, we may anxiously fear our own offenses before the strict Judge.

It follows:

## CHAPTER LX

**VERSE 18.—“Why did you bring me out from the womb? Would that I had been consumed, so that no eye might see me.”**

91. He had already expressed this in his first speech, saying: “Why did I not die in the womb?” When he adds here, “I would have been as though I did not exist, carried from the womb to the tomb,”—VERSE 19—he says the same thing in other words, adding: “As a hidden miscarriage I would not have endured, or as those who, conceived, did not see the light” (Job III, 16).

Since we have discussed these matters at length above (Book IV, no. 48 and following), we avoid repeating the exposition, lest we weary the reader.

It follows:

## CHAPTER LXI [Vet. XLIV, Rec. XXXVI]

**VERSE 20.—“Will not the small number of my days soon come to an end?”**

92. The end of life must be considered above all.—He shows himself to live cautiously and attentively who, considering the brevity of the present life, observes not its use but its end, so that from its conclusion he may infer that nothing which passes away is worth delighting in.

Hence Solomon says: “If a man lives many years and rejoices in them all, he must remember the dark time and the many days; when they come, the past will be accused of vanity” (Eccl. XI, 8).

Again it is written: “In all your works remember your last things, and you will never sin” (Ecclus. VII, 40).

Therefore, when guilt tempts the mind, the mind must look upon the brevity of its pleasure, lest iniquity carry it off to living death, since it is certain that mortal life hastens more quickly toward its end.

[Note: Ebroicensis reads “so that [it may run] to eternal death”; the German manuscript agrees in a later hand.]

But often the eye of our contemplation is confused when our pain is increased by repeated blows. We want to lament the exile of the present life, but because of the very affliction the mind cannot assess the losses caused by its blindness. Hence he immediately adds:

## CHAPTER LXII [Rec. XXXVII]

**THE SAME.—“Leave me, then, so that I may mourn my pain for a little while.”**

93. Excessive grief removes tears and the perception of pain. The force of habit does not allow us to mourn our evils.—Just as moderate affliction draws out tears, so immoderate affliction takes them away, because grief itself becomes as though it were without grief when, devouring the afflicted mind, it removes the perception of pain.

The holy man therefore fears being struck more than is sufficient, saying: “Leave me, then, so that I may mourn my pain for a little while.” As though he openly said: “Moderate the blows of your striking, so that, with my pains made moderate, I may recover strength to assess through weeping the evils I suffer.”

This may also be understood in another way. Often a sinner is so bound by the chains of his iniquity that he bears the weight of his sins but does not know that he bears it.

Often, even if he recognizes the guilt by which he is oppressed, he tries to break out and cannot, so that he may pursue it within himself with a free mind and complete conversion.

He cannot mourn his pain because he both considers the guilt of his iniquity and, under the weight of earthly occupation, has no leisure to lament it. He cannot mourn his pain who strives to oppose his perverse habit but is still burdened by desires that continue to grow in the flesh.

The presence of this pain had tortured the Prophet’s mind when he said: “My pain is always before me, for I declare my iniquity, and I will think upon my sin” (Ps. XXXVII, 18–19).

[Note: Gemetensis and Corbie German read “I will think,” instead of “against me” and “I will declare.” Other manuscripts likewise often have *pronuntio*, “I declare,” rather than *pronuntiabo*, “I will declare.”]

But he knew himself released when the bonds of iniquity had been loosed, and he rejoiced, saying: “You have broken my bonds; to you I will sacrifice a sacrifice of praise” (Ps. CXV, 16).

94. Unless God helps us toward this.—The Lord allows us to mourn our pain when he both shows us the evils we have committed and helps us mourn the very things we recognize. He places our faults before our eyes and, with the pious hand of grace, loosens the bonds of the heart, so that our mind may rise to the leisure of repentance and, freed from the shackles of the flesh, direct the free step of love toward its Creator.

[Vet. XLV.] Often we ourselves criticize our life, yet willingly do what we rightly condemn in ourselves. The spirit raises us toward righteousness, while the flesh restrains us toward habit. The mind resists its own love, but is immediately captivated by delight.

It is therefore rightly said: “Leave me, then, so that I may mourn my pain for a little while,” because unless we are mercifully released from the guilt of sin by which we have bound ourselves, we cannot perfectly mourn what we grieve within ourselves and against ourselves.

But the pain of our guilt is truly mourned when that dark retribution of hell is foreseen with attentive fear. Hence it is aptly added:

## CHAPTER LXIII [Rec. XXXVIII]

**VERSE 21.—“Before I go, and do not return, to a land dark and covered by the darkness of death.”**

95. The punishments of hell are neither temporary nor imaginary. Why hell is called earth and why lake.—What is signified by the name “dark earth” except the dreadful prisons of Tartarus? The darkness of eternal death covers them, because it forever separates the condemned from the light of life.

Hell is not without reason called “earth,” because whoever is seized by it is held there firmly. For it is written: “One generation passes away, and another generation comes, but the earth stands forever” (Eccl. I, 4).

The dark prisons of hell are therefore rightly called “earth,” because those whom they receive for punishment are not tortured by a temporary penalty or an imaginary vision, but are held by the solid retribution of everlasting condemnation.

They are sometimes also designated by the name “lake,” as the Prophet bears witness: “They bore their shame with those who descend into the lake” (Ezek. XXXII, 24–25).

Hell is therefore called both earth, because it holds its captives firmly, and lake, because those whom it once seizes it continually swallows, tossed and trembling amid the torments that surge around them.

The holy man, whether speaking in his own voice or in that of the human race, asks to be released before he goes—not because the one who mourns his guilt is going to the dark earth, but because the one who neglects to mourn will undoubtedly go there. Thus a creditor says to his debtor: “Pay your debt before you are bound on account of the debt”; yet he is not bound if he does not delay paying what he owes.

He rightly adds: “I will not return,” because the mercy of the one who spares can no longer free those whom the justice of the Judge has once condemned in places of punishment.

[Vet. XLVI.] These places are described more subtly still when it is said:

## CHAPTER LXIV

**VERSE 22.—“A land of misery and darkness.”**

96. Those whom it holds are tortured outwardly and blinded inwardly.—Misery pertains to pain, darkness to blindness. The place occupied by those expelled from the sight of the strict Judge is therefore called a land of misery and darkness, because pain tortures them outwardly, while blindness obscures them inwardly, separated as they are from the true light.

The land of misery and darkness may, however, be understood in another way. This earth in which we are born is indeed a land of misery, but it is not a land of darkness, because we suffer here many evils of our corruption, yet through the grace of conversion we still return to the light, as the Truth says: “Walk while you have the light, lest the darkness overtake you” (John XII, 35).

That other land, however, is at once a land of misery and darkness, because whoever descends there to endure its evils never returns afterward to the light.

In describing it further, he adds:

## CHAPTER LXV

**THE SAME.—“Where there is the shadow of death and no order.”**

97. It has retribution, not light; how just these punishments are.—Just as outward death separates the flesh from the soul, so inward death separates the soul from God. The shadow of death is therefore the darkness of separation, because every condemned person, while being kindled by eternal fire, is darkened by the inner light.

The nature of fire is to display both light from itself and combustion.

[Note: Turonensis and most Norman manuscripts read: “but the nature of fire is …”]

But that avenging flame of past vices has combustion and no light. Hence the Truth says to the reprobate: “Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire that has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. XXV, 41).

Again, signifying all of them in the person of one, he says: “Bind his hands and feet, and cast him into the outer darkness” (Matt. XXII, 13).

If, then, the fire that torments the reprobate could have light, the one who is rejected would not be said to be cast into darkness.

Hence the Psalmist also says: “Fire fell upon them, and they did not see the sun” (Ps. LVII, 9). Fire falls upon the wicked, but the sun is not seen when the fire falls, because the flame of Gehenna both devours and blinds them from the vision of the true light.

[Note: Turonensis, Gemetensis, and other Norman manuscripts read this way. The printed editions have: “because the flame of Gehenna …”]

Thus the pain of burning tortures them outwardly, while the punishment of blindness obscures them inwardly, so that those who sinned against their Creator both in body and in heart may be punished both in body and in heart, and may feel punishments in both respects, since while they lived here they served their perverse pleasures in both respects.

Hence the Prophet rightly says: “They descended into hell with their weapons” (Ezek. XXXII, 27).

[Note: Vendôme, the Norman manuscripts, and others read: “They descended to hell.”]

The weapons of sinners are the members of the body, by which they carry out the perverse desires they conceive. Hence Paul rightly says: “Do not offer your members as weapons of iniquity to sin” (Rom. VI, 13).

To descend into hell with one’s weapons is to endure the torments of eternal judgment with those very members by which one fulfilled the desires of pleasure, so that pain may then absorb them on every side who, while subject to their pleasures, now fight on every side against the justice of the just Judge.

[Vet. XLVII; Rec. XXXIX.] 98. The punishments are ordered according to the measure of crimes by the just Judge.—It is indeed very surprising that it is said: “Where there is no order.” For almighty God, who punishes evils well, does not in any way permit either the punishments or the torments to be without order, because the punishments themselves that proceed from the scales of justice cannot be inflicted without order.

How could there be no order in punishments, when retribution follows each condemned person according to the measure of his crime? Hence it is written: “The mighty will suffer mighty torments, and a stronger punishment awaits the stronger” (Wis. VI, 7).

Hence it is said in the condemnation of Babylon: “As much as she glorified herself and lived in luxury, so much give her torment and mourning” (Rev. XVIII, 7).

If punishment is therefore distinguished according to the measure of guilt, it is plainly evident that order is preserved in punishments.

And unless the deeds of merits distinguished the totality of torments, the coming Judge would never be said to tell the reapers: “Gather the weeds first and bind them into bundles to burn” (Matt. XIII, 30).

[Note: Beauvais, Gemetensis, and other Norman manuscripts read: “Gather the weeds and bind them in bundles or into bundles.”]

If no order is observed in punishments, why are the weeds to be burned bound into bundles? To bind bundles for burning certainly means to associate those who are to be handed over to eternal fire with their equals, so that those whom similar guilt defiles may be bound by an equal punishment; and those who are not polluted by unequal iniquity may not be tortured by unequal torment.

Thus one condemnation may crush those whom one pride had lifted up; and those whom ambition had similarly inflated may be constricted by a similar affliction; and an equal flame of punishment may torment those whom an equal flame of sin had kindled in the fire of lust.

For just as there are many dwelling places in the Father’s house according to the diversity of virtue (John XIV, 2), so the disparity of crimes subjects the condemned to diverse punishments in the fires of Gehenna.

Although Gehenna is one for all, it does not burn all with one and the same quality. We are all touched by one sun, yet we do not all grow hot beneath it in the same way, because the weight of the heat is perceived according to the condition of the body.

So for the condemned there is one Gehenna that afflicts them all, yet it does not burn all with the same quality, because what the differing health of bodies does here, the differing cause of merits does there.

[Note: Gemetensis, Beauvais, and others read: “So for the condemned there is one Gehenna that afflicts them.”]

How, then, is it said that there is no order in punishments in which each person is clearly tortured according to the measure of his guilt?

[Vet. XLVIII.] 99. Punishments are not ordered in the hearts of the damned.—But after the holy man has introduced the shadow of death, he adds how great the confusion is in the mind of the damned, because the punishments themselves, which come ordered by justice, are unquestionably not ordered in the hearts of those who are dying. For, as we said a little earlier, while each condemned person is burned outwardly by flame, inwardly he is devoured by the fire of blindness; and, placed in anguish, he is confused both outwardly and inwardly [Note: [Col. 0913D] In Bellovac., Gemet., and some others, *interiusque* is omitted.], so that he may be tormented still more severely by his own confusion. When order has thus been excluded, therefore, there will be no order in the punishment, because in their death the confusion of the mind itself rages more fiercely. Yet the equity of the Judge orders this with wondrous power, so that the punishment may confuse the soul as though it were unordered. Or certainly punishments are said to lack order because, when various things rise up as punishments, their proper quality is not preserved. Hence he immediately adds:

## CHAPTER LXVI

**Ibid.**—“And everlasting horror dwells there” [Note: [Col. 0914D] Gemet. and most Norman witnesses: “everlasting horror dwelling.”]

100. A description of the punishments of hell.—In the torments of this life, fear contains pain, but pain does not contain fear, because dread does not torment the mind once it has already begun to suffer what it feared. But hell is both darkened by the shadow of death and inhabited by everlasting horror [Col. 0914C], because those delivered over to its fires feel pain in their punishments [Note: [Col. 0914D] The same witnesses: “and, in the anguish of pain, of the one striking.” Turon.: “and, in the anguish of pain, of the one struck.”], and are continually struck, in the anguish of pain, by the fear that assails them, so that they endure what they fear and, in turn, ceaselessly fear what they endure.

For it is written of them: “Their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be quenched” (Isa. 66:24). Here the flame that burns gives light; there, as we demonstrated above from the words of the Psalmist, the fire that torments brings darkness. Here fear is lost once what was feared has begun to be endured; there pain both tears apart and terror constricts. Thus, in a horrifying manner, pain with dread and flame with darkness will then be the lot of the reprobate.

So, plainly, the weight of supreme justice must be felt by the damned in such a way that those who, while living, did not fear to depart from the will of the Creator should at some point, in their destruction, find even their torments discordant with their own qualities [Col. 0914D], so that, insofar as the torments assail one another, they may increase their suffering, and, appearing in different forms, may be experienced in many ways. Yet these punishments both torment those plunged into them beyond their strength and preserve them by extinguishing within them the support of life, so that the end of life may punish them in such a way that their torment may live forever without end [Note: [Col. 0914D] Vindoc.: “may bring forth torment through punishments.” German., Ebroic., and most Norman witnesses: “may inflict torment.” Colb.: “may live.”], because it both hastens toward an end through torment and, failing without end, endures.

Thus for the wretched there is death without death, an end without end, decay without decay: death lives, the end always begins, and decay never ceases to decay. Since, therefore, death destroys but does not extinguish, pain torments but in no way drives away fear, and flame burns but does not at all dispel the darkness, it follows—as far as can be gathered from the experience of the present life—that the punishments have no order, since they do not in every respect retain their own proper quality.

[Vet. XLIV.] 101. There fire denies light for consolation but preserves it for torment.—Although the fire there does not shine for consolation, nevertheless it shines to some extent so that it may torment more severely. For the reprobate, with the flame giving light, will see in torment with themselves all their followers [Note: [Col. 0915D] Thus Gemet. and the other Norman witnesses; Coc. and subsequent editions have *quoque* (“also”) for *quosque* (“all/every”).]—those for whose love they sinned—so that those who had carnally loved those persons’ lives against the commands of the Creator may also be afflicted by their destruction, to the increase of their own damnation.

We gather this plainly from the testimony of the Gospel (Luke 16:23), where, as the Truth declares, that rich man who descended into the torments of eternal fire is described as remembering his five brothers. He asked Abraham to send someone to instruct them, lest they should eventually come there and be tormented by an equal punishment. Since, then, he remembered absent relatives to increase his own pain, there is no doubt that, to augment his punishment, he could shortly afterward also see them present.

What wonder, then, if he sees the reprobate burning with him, when, to increase his own pain, he saw Lazarus, whom he had despised, in Abraham’s bosom? [Note: [Col. 0915D] This is how it is read in almost all our manuscripts. One Vindoc., however, agreeing with the printed editions, has: “if, therefore, so that his punishment might increase,” etc.] To him, then, for the increase of whose punishment the elect man also appeared, why should we not believe that it is possible for him to see in punishment even those whom he had loved against God?

From this it follows that those whom the reprobate now love in a disordered manner they will then see with themselves in torment, by a wondrous order of judgment, so that the carnal relationship placed before their eyes, condemned by an equal vengeance, may intensify the punishment of their own chastisement. Therefore, the fire that torments in darkness must be believed to preserve light for torment. But if we cannot establish this by testimonies in its direct expression, it remains for us to demonstrate it from another angle.

102. Fire can possess light and darkness simultaneously.—Three boys of the Hebrew race, when the fires of the furnace had been kindled by the command of the Chaldean king, were thrown in with their hands and feet bound. Yet when that same king, moved by compassion, examined them amid the furnace fire [Col. 0915D] [Note: [Col. 0916D] Longip. and Corb. Germ., in a second hand: “astonished, examined them.”], he saw them walking about with their garments unharmed.

Here it is clearly inferred that, by the Creator’s marvelous dispensation, the nature of the fire was tempered with different powers: it did not touch the garments, but burned the bonds; and for the holy men the flame was cold for inflicting torment but burned for the purpose of liberation. Therefore, just as fire knows how to burn for the consolation of the elect but does not know how to burn for punishment, so, conversely, the flame of Gehenna neither shines for the reprobate as a grace of consolation nor fails to shine for punishment [Col. 0916A], so that, before the eyes of the damned, the fire of punishment may shine without any brightness and, to increase their pain, may show how those whom they loved are being tormented [Note: [Col. 0916D] Corb. Germ. and Vindoc. I: “how the cast-down are tormented.” Vindoc. II: “how the guilty are tormented.”].

What wonder is it if we believe that the fire of Gehenna possesses punishment together with both darkness and light, when experience teaches us that even the flame of torches shines while remaining dark? Then the devouring flame will burn those whom carnal pleasure now defiles; then the infinitely deep chasm of hell will swallow those whom empty pride now exalts; and those who here fulfilled the will of the crafty tempter through whatever vice will then arrive with their leader, the reprobate, at the torments.

[Vet. L.] 103. One punishment entangles reprobate angels and human beings. The wicked man is the devil’s tomb.—Although the nature of angels and human beings is very different, one punishment nevertheless entangles those whom one guilt binds in crime. The prophet aptly and briefly indicates this when he says: “There is Assur and all his multitude, and around him are his graves” (Ezek. 32:22).

For who is signified by Assyria, under the name of a proud king, except that ancient enemy who fell through pride, who, because he drags many into guilt, descends with his whole multitude to the confines of hell? Graves cover the dead. And who suffered death more grievously than the one who, despising his Creator, abandoned life? When human hearts receive this dead one, they unquestionably become his graves.

But around him are his graves, because those in whose minds he now buries himself through desires he later joins to himself through torments. And because the reprobate now receive malignant spirits into themselves by committing unlawful deeds, then the graves will burn together with the dead.

[Rec. XL.] 104. It is not useful to know the punishments of hell beforehand, but to escape them.—Behold, we have learned what punishment awaits the damned; and, instructed by sacred Scripture, we have no doubt how great the fire in damnation is, how great the darkness in the fire, and how great the terror in the darkness. But what does it profit to know these things beforehand if one does not succeed in escaping them?

Therefore, we must strive with our whole purpose that, when we are granted a time of respite, we may flee the avenging torments of evil by devoting ourselves to right living. Hence Solomon says: “Whatever your hand can do, do it diligently, because there is neither work nor reason nor knowledge nor wisdom in the underworld, where you are hastening” (Eccl. 9:10). Hence Isaiah says: “Seek the Lord while he may be found; call upon him while he is near” (Isa. 55:6). Hence Paul says: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Cor. 6:2). Again he says: “While we have time, let us do good to all” (Gal. 6:10).

[Vet. LI.] 105. Concern for the flesh obstructs the soul striving toward that goal.—Often the soul girds itself for the way of uprightness and shakes off its sluggishness. It is so seized by desire for heavenly things that almost nothing inferior seems to remain in it. Yet when it is brought back to concern for the flesh, without which the journey of the present life cannot in any way be completed, this concern holds it pressed down below, as though it had not yet touched any of the heights [Note: [Col. 0917C] Lyr. and Bigot.: “had touched none.”].

When it hears the words of the heavenly oracle, it is raised into love of the heavenly homeland; but when the activity of the present life rises again, it is buried beneath the mound of earthly concern. The seed of heavenly hope does not flourish at all in the soil of the heart, because the thorn of lowly thought grows dense. The Truth Himself uproots this thorn with the hand of holy exhortation, saying: “Do not be anxious about tomorrow” (Matt. 6:34). Against it Paul likewise says: “Do not make provision for the flesh in its desires” (Rom. 13:14). But in the words of this leader and soldier we recognize that the soul is then pierced by a deadly wound from this concern when the measure of equity is not maintained in it.

106. This concern is not to be cut off altogether, but moderated.—For concern for the flesh [Note: [Col. 0917C] Thus Gemet., Utic., and very many witnesses. It should be observed that in the old manuscripts the verb *abscindo* and its forms and tenses are very rarely found; *abscido* is used in its place.] is not utterly cut off in those still living in mortal flesh; rather, it is tempered so that it may serve the soul with discretion. Since the Truth forbids us to be anxious about tomorrow, He does not deny that we should have some concern for present things; He forbids that concern to be extended into the time that follows. And when Paul does not allow concern for the flesh to be exercised in its desires, he certainly still grants it in necessity.

Therefore, concern for the flesh must be restrained by the discretion of great moderation, so that it may serve and not rule. It must not conquer the soul like a mistress; rather, subjected to the dominion of the mind, it should serve like a handmaid, appearing when summoned and springing away when rejected at the heart’s command. It should scarcely be seen behind holy thought and never stand in opposition before the face of one who thinks rightly.

Sacred history aptly suggests this to us when Abraham is remembered as having gone out to meet three angels (Gen. 18:2 ff.). He himself went out to meet those who were coming, outside the door, while Sarah stood behind the door. Thus, as the man and master of the spiritual house—that is, our understanding—he should go beyond the barriers of the flesh in the knowledge of the Trinity and, as it were, go out through the door of the lower dwelling. But concern for the flesh, like a woman, should not appear outside, and should be ashamed to display itself boastfully. As though behind the man, under the discretion of the spirit, it should attend only to necessities and should not know how to expose itself brazenly, but should moderate itself modestly.

Yet when it is often told not to presume on itself at all, but to transfer its whole confidence to divine hope, it scorns this admonition and, when its activity ceases, doubts that the supports of life can be present to it. Thus this same Sarah, hearing God’s promises, laughs; but when rebuked for laughing, she is immediately made fruitful. She who could not conceive while vigorous in youth conceived when broken by old age and when her womb was withered, because when concern for the flesh ceased to possess confidence in itself, she received from the divine promise, contrary to hope, what she had doubted she would possess by human reasoning.

Hence Isaac, that is, “laughter,” is rightly said to be born, because when the confidence of heavenly hope is conceived, what else does our mind give birth to than joy?

Therefore, care must be taken that concern for the flesh neither exceeds the limits of necessity nor presumes upon itself in what it carries out moderately. Often the soul is deceived, so that what it desires voluptuously it supposes to be necessary, and thus considers every pleasure of life to be a due necessity [Note: [Col. 0918C] Gemet., Corb. Germ., and Reg.: “whatever necessity of life, it considers useful.”].

Often, too, because success follows foresight, the mind is lifted up in confidence in itself. When it possesses what it sees lacking in others, it silently rejoices in the greatness of its own provision; and it is already as far removed from true provision as it is unaware even of the pride it suffers.

Therefore, with the attention of constant and careful watchfulness, we must always weigh both what we do in our actions and what we turn over in our hearts, lest earthly concern, encumbering the mind, multiply itself outwardly, or at least the thought within become exalted over its moderation. Thus, while we fear the divine judgments with temporal vigilance, we may escape the punishments of everlasting horror.

# BOOK TEN

After expounding the whole of the eleventh chapter of the Book of Job and the first five verses of the twelfth chapter, he closes the second part of this work.

[Col. 0917]

337 **CHAPTER ONE**

[Col. 0917D]

1. Job’s steadfastness: he is not overcome by the successive changes of his adversaries.—Whenever a strong athlete enters the arena for a spectacle, those who are unequal in strength [Note: [Col. 0917D] Vindoc., Corb. Germ., Bajoc., Colb., Reg., and most Norman witnesses: “unequal in virtues.” Gemet.: “possessing unequal strength.” Germ.: “unequal in strength.”] successively subject themselves to his assault. When one has been defeated, another immediately rises against him; and when that one has been subdued, another is substituted, so that they may eventually find the wrestler’s strength weakened—strength that his own continually increasing victory wears down. Thus, whenever a new opponent engages him, the one who cannot be defeated by the quality of his strength may at least be overcome by the changing of persons.

So, in this spectacle of human beings and angels, blessed Job came forth as a strong athlete; and he demonstrated how greatly he could withstand the changes of his adversaries by the continuity of his tireless strength [Note: [Col. 0918D] Bajoc.: “by the strength of sustained labor.”]. Eliphaz first attacks him, Baldad second, and finally Sophar presents himself to overcome him. They rise with all their efforts to deliver their blows, but they do not reach the height of his robust breast.

Their very words clearly indicate that they cast their blows into the air, because, when they rebuke the holy man unjustly, they lose the blows of their words in emptiness [Note: [Col. 0919D] Turon., Vindoc., Corb. Germ., and Norman witnesses: “the blows of striking.” Ebroic., Bajoc., Lyr., and Bigot have *reddunt*, “return,” instead of *perdunt*, “lose.” In Utic. *perdunt* was formerly read, but now *reddunt*. Colb. and Reg. contain our reading.].

This becomes clear when the response of Sophar the Naamathite begins with insults. He says:

## CHAPTER TWO

**Chapter 11:2**—“Shall one who speaks much not also hear? Or shall a verbose man be justified?”

2. The arrogant always answer rightly spoken words in the opposite manner. Sophar’s statement is true, but badly expressed.—It is customary for the arrogant always to answer rightly spoken words in the opposite manner, lest, if they agree with what has been said, they should seem inferior. To them, the words of the righteous, however few they may sound, are many, because, in cutting away their vices, they burden the ear. Thus what is spoken in a righteous proclamation against crimes is dragged into accusation.

Sophar rebukes the very man who had spoken strong judgments from the truth and calls him verbose, because when wisdom from the mouths of the righteous reproves faults, it sounds like an excess of talk to the ears of fools [Note: [Col. 0919D] Corb. Germ.: “superfluous talk.”]. The wicked consider nothing right except what they themselves have thought, and they judge the words of the righteous idle precisely because they find them contrary to their own opinions.

Sophar did not utter a false statement in saying that a verbose man cannot be justified, because, when someone pours himself out in words and loses the gravity of silence, he loses the guardianship of the mind. Hence it is written: “The cultivation of justice is silence” (Isa. 32:17). Hence Solomon says: “Like a city lying open and without the circuit of walls is a man who cannot restrain his spirit in speaking” (Prov. 25:28). Again he says: “In much speaking sin will not be absent” (Prov. 10:19). The Psalmist likewise testifies, saying: “The verbose man shall not be established upon the earth” (Ps. 139:12) [Note: [Col. 0919D] The printed editions: “the man of tongue.”].

But the virtue of a true statement [Note: [Col. 0919D] Thus Bellovac., Germ., Colb., Longip., Bajoc., the other Norman witnesses, and most manuscripts. Even the older printed editions read “but the virtue of true knowledge,” as do Corb. Germ. and Reg.] is lost when it is not spoken under the guardianship of discretion. It is therefore certain that a verbose man cannot be justified. Yet a good thing is not spoken well when no attention is paid to whom it is spoken. A true statement against the wicked loses its force if it attacks the uprightness of the good [Note: [Col. 0920D] We have restored this reading from manuscripts and older printed editions. In Gilot. and later editions it reads: “if it hinders the uprightness of the good, it loses its force.”], and it rebounds blunted precisely because the object it strikes is strong.

[Vet. et Rec. III.] Since the wicked cannot patiently hear good things and, while neglecting the correction of their lives, prepare themselves to answer with words [Col. 0919D], Sophar clearly indicates this when he adds:

## CHAPTER THREE

**Verse 3**—“Will men be silent to you alone? And when you mock the others, shall no one refute you?”

3. How the wicked and the upright are differently disposed toward correction.—As we have said, an untrained mind bears the judgments of truth with difficulty. It considers silence a punishment and regards everything rightly said as an insult directed at its own mockery. When a true voice comes near the ears of the wicked, memory of their guilt bites them; and when the mind is inwardly touched by the reproval of its vices, it is stirred outwardly to the practice of contradiction.

It cannot bear the voice because, wounded by contact with its guilt, it suffers; and, when something is said generally against the perverse, it suspects that it is being attacked personally. It is ashamed to hear outwardly what it remembers having done inwardly. Therefore it immediately prepares a defense, so that it may cover the shame of its guilt with words of wicked refutation.

For just as the upright consider the voice of correction concerning things they have not done rightly to be an act of charity [Col. 0920B], so the perverse consider it an insult of mockery. The former immediately cast themselves down into obedience; the latter rise to the madness of defending themselves. The former count the help of correction as protection for their life, because, when the guilt of the present life is reproved [Note: [Col. 0920D] Thus Corb. Germ., Turon., Vindoc., and Reg. The printed editions, following Cocc., read “the guilt of vice”; this was found in one Colb. manuscript in a second hand.], the anger of the coming Judge is restrained; the latter, when they see themselves attacked by reproof, think it a sword-stroke, because when guilt is exposed by the voice of correction, their reputation for present glory is sullied.

Hence the Truth says through Solomon in praise of the righteous: “Teach the just man, and he will hasten to receive it” (Prov. 9:9). Concerning the stubbornness of the wicked He says with contempt: “He who instructs a scoffer does himself an injury” (ibid., 9:7).

Often it happens that, when they cannot defend the evils exposed in themselves, they become worse through shame. Thus they grow proud in their self-defense and seek out certain vices in the life of the one correcting them; and, because they do not consider themselves guilty, they impose crimes on others as well [Note: [Col. 0920D] Gemet.: “and, since they do not consider themselves guilty, they themselves accuse others of crimes; and when these are true,” etc.]. When they cannot find anything true, they invent it, so that they too may appear to have something which, with equal justice, they can reproach.

Thus Sophar, grieving as though he had been mocked by the reproof, immediately adds a lie:

## CHAPTER FOUR

**Verse 4**—“For you said, ‘My speech is pure, and I am clean in your sight.’”

4. The wicked refuse to lament the true evils within themselves and fasten false accusations upon others.—Anyone who remembers the words of blessed Job recognizes how falsely this is charged to him. For how could he have said that he was clean, when he said: “If I wished to justify myself, my mouth would condemn me” (Job 9:20)?

But the wicked have this malice: when they refuse to lament the true evils within themselves, they invent those of others. They use it almost as a consolation for their crime if the life of the person correcting them is stained by false accusations.

[Vet. IV.] It should also be known that the perverse often verbally wish for good things in order to show that what exists in the present is evil [Note: [Col. 0920D] Bellov.: “so as to show that the things which exist in the present are good.”]. They seek prosperity as though they favored it, so that they may appear kind. Hence Sophar immediately continues, saying:

## CHAPTER FIVE

**Verse 5**—“Would that God might speak with you and open his lips to you!”

5. When God speaks to a human being, and when the human being speaks to himself.—A human being speaks to himself when, through what he feels, he is not separated from the understanding of carnal prudence by the spirit of Divinity; when the flesh puts forward its own sense and, as though summoning the mind to understanding, sends it outward.

Hence the Truth says to Peter, who was thinking earthly thoughts: “For you do not understand the things of God, but the things of human beings” (Mark 8:33). Yet to him when he confessed rightly it is said: “Flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 16:17).

But what are God’s lips except his judgments? When the lips are closed, the voice is held back and the meaning of the one who is silent is unknown; when they are opened, speech is brought forth and the speaker’s mind is revealed [Note: [Col. 0921D] Thus in all our manuscripts and older editions; in later editions, “is indicated.”].

Therefore God opens his lips when he shows human beings his will through manifest judgments. He speaks, as it were, with his mouth opened, when, removing the obscurity of his hidden disposition, he refuses to conceal what he wills. He does not disclose his meaning to us, as though with closed lips, when through hidden judgments he conceals why he does what he does.

Thus Sophar wishes good things for blessed Job in order to rebuke him for his carnal understanding and to display how benevolent he himself is. He says: “Would that God might speak with you and open his lips to you!” As though he were plainly saying: “I pity your ignorance rather than your punishment, because I recognize that you, endowed only with carnal prudence, are empty of the spirit of truth. If you knew God’s judgments, you would not utter such insolent judgments against him.”

And because Almighty God, when he lifts us up to contemplate his judgments, immediately dispels the blindness of our ignorance, he indicates what instruction may proceed to us from his opened lips by immediately adding:

## CHAPTER SIX [Rec. IV]

**Verse 6**—“That he might show you the hidden things of wisdom, and that his law is manifold.”

6. The works of wisdom that are public, and those that are hidden.—The public works of heavenly wisdom are evident when Almighty God governs those whom he creates, perfects the good things he begins, and, by breathing upon those whom he illuminates with the light of his visitation, helps them. It is clear to everyone that those whom he freely created he benevolently orders. And when he bestows spiritual gifts, he Himself perfects what He Himself began through the gift of His goodness.

The hidden works of heavenly wisdom, however, are at work when God abandons those whom He created; when He does not complete by following through the good things He had begun by anticipating them; when He illuminates us with the splendor of His enlightenment and yet, by permitting temptations of the flesh, strikes us with the darkness of blindness; when He does not guard the gifts He has bestowed; and when He both awakens the desires of our mind toward Himself and, by a hidden judgment, constricts us with the difficulty of our weakness.

[Vet. V.] 7. He finds these things by not finding them, having learned that they cannot be comprehended. The law of God is the charity of Christ.—Few can seek out these hidden things of His wisdom, but no one can find them, because what immortal wisdom justly disposes concerning us above us ought rightly to remain unknown to us, who are still mortal.

Yet to behold, however imperfectly, these very secrets of His wisdom is already to see the power of its incomprehensibility. For although we fail in the very investigation of His counsels, nevertheless, by failing, we learn more truly whom we should fear.

Paul was striving toward these hidden things of wisdom when he said: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments and unsearchable his ways! For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counselor?” (Rom. 11:33–34).

Earlier, wearied by the very act of investigation but nevertheless progressing through that weariness toward knowledge of his own weakness, he says: “O man, who are you to answer God? Shall the thing formed say to the one who formed it, ‘Why have you made me thus?’” (Rom. 9:20).

Since, then, he could not reach the hidden things of God, he returned to knowledge of his own weakness and, by failing, recalled himself to his own instruction. Thus, so to speak, he found the hidden things of wisdom by not finding them, because, when he grew weary in seeking the heavenly counsels, he learned to fear more humbly. His weakness drove him away from intimate knowledge, but humility joined him to it more truly.

Sophar, therefore, learned through his zeal for knowledge [Col. 0922C] but ignorant through the audacity of his inflated speech, because he himself lacks gravity wishes for a better man what he himself possesses, saying: “Would that God might speak with you and open his lips to you, that he might show you the hidden things of wisdom!” He also displays, by wishing for it, the wisdom by which he thinks himself superior to his friend, when he immediately adds: “And that his law is manifold” [Note: [Col. 0921D] All Norman witnesses: “knowledge.”]

What else should the law of God mean in this passage except charity, through which the commandments of life are always read in the mind as to how they are to be kept in action? [Note: [Col. 0921D–0922D] Thus Gemet., Lyr., Bigot., Utic., and most manuscripts. The supplied text states, without preserving the readings themselves: “In the old printed editions we read …; in the later editions, after Cocc., are read …”] Concerning this law, the Truth says: “This is my commandment: that you love one another” (John 15:12). Paul says of it: “Love is the fullness of the law” (Rom. 13:10). Again he says: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ” (Gal. 6:2) [Note: [Col. 0922D] The printed editions: “Bear one another’s burdens.” Our manuscripts: “Bear the burdens of one another.”].

For what can more appropriately be understood as the law of Christ than charity, which we truly fulfill when we bear our brothers’ burdens out of love?

8. Charity begins with two commandments and extends to innumerable things. Love of neighbor avoids doing harm and takes care to do good. In how many ways these two are practiced.—This same law is called manifold because charity, with diligent concern, extends itself to all the works of the virtues. It begins indeed with two commandments, but extends itself to innumerable things.

The beginning of this law is love of God and love of neighbor.

[Vet. VI.] Love of God is distinguished in three ways, because the Creator is commanded to be loved with all the heart, with all the soul, and with all one’s strength [Note: [Col. 0923D] In the Vulgate editions: “virtue.”]. In this we should note that, when divine speech commands that God be loved, it not only tells from what source but also instructs to what extent, when it adds “with all,” so that the one who desires to please God perfectly may leave nothing of himself for himself.

Love of neighbor, however, is derived into two commandments. Through a certain righteous man it is said: “What you hate to have done to you by another, see that you do not do to another” (Tob. 4:16). And the Truth Himself says: “Whatever you wish that people would do to you, do also to them” (Matt. 7:12) [Note: [Col. 0923D] Vindoc., Gemet., and Corb. Germ.: “so also do you to them.” Bigot., Lyr., and Utic.: “do these things also to them.”].

By these two commandments of both Testaments, malice is restrained by the one and kindness is offered by the other, so that, by not doing the evil that one does not wish to suffer, each person may cease from the work of harming; and, by providing the good that one desires to have done to oneself, one may exercise oneself in benevolence for the benefit of one’s neighbor.

But when these two things are considered with attentive intention, the heart is directed toward innumerable ministries of the virtues: the restless mind must not burn with desire to inflict what it ought not to inflict, nor grow slack through idleness regarding what it ought to provide.

When one takes care not to do to another what one does not at all wish to suffer from another, one attentively examines oneself lest pride elevate one and, casting the mind down to the contempt of one’s neighbor, exalt it; lest ambition tear the thought apart and, when it expands it toward the desire for what belongs to another, constrict it; lest lust pollute the heart and corrupt it, subjected to desires, through unlawful things; lest anger provoke it and inflame it even to the utterance of insult; lest envy bite it and, jealous of the happiness of others, consume itself with its own flame; lest excessive talk draw out the tongue and extend it even to the wantonness of slander; lest hatred arouse malice and incite the mouth to the dart of cursing.

Again, when one thinks of doing to another what one expects another to do to oneself, one carefully considers how to answer evil with good and good with better; how to show long-suffering gentleness toward the insolent; how to offer the grace of kindness to those weakened by the plague of malice; how to unite the discordant in peace and gird the harmonious toward the desire for true peace; how to provide necessities to the needy; how to show the way of uprightness to those who have gone astray; how to soothe the afflicted with word and compassion; how to extinguish by reproof those inflamed with desires for this world [Note: [Col. 0923D] Most Norman witnesses and Corb.
