Germ. read “restrain” (*restringat*) instead of “extinguish” (*restinguat*).]; how to soften the threats of the powerful by reasoning; how to relieve, with as much aid as one can, the distresses of the oppressed; how to oppose patience to those resisting outwardly; how to exhibit discipline, together with patience, to those inwardly proud; how, concerning the errors of subjects, gentleness may so temper zeal that it does not weaken one’s devotion to justice; how zeal may burn for vengeance without, in burning, exceeding the limit of compassion; how to summon the ungrateful to love by benefits; how to preserve the grateful in love through acts of service; how, when unable to correct the faults of neighbors, to remain silent [Note: [Col. 0923D] Corb. Germ.: “so that whatever can be corrected …”], and, when they can be corrected by speaking, to fear that silence may be consent; how to tolerate what one keeps silent about without concealing the poison of grief in the soul; how to offer the gift of kindness to the malevolent without, through favor, departing from the rule of uprightness; how to provide one’s neighbors with everything one is able to provide without becoming inflated by providing it; how, in the good things one offers, to fear the precipice of pride without becoming sluggish in the practice of good; how to give away what one possesses while considering the greatness of the One who rewards; and, when distributing earthly goods, not to think anxiously about one’s own poverty more than is necessary, so that the light of joy may not be darkened by sadness in the offering of the gift [Note: [Col. 0923D] Bellovac., Germ., Longip., Vindoc., Norman., and others read thus. In one Reg. the whole passage reads: “lest, when he distributes earthly goods, if he fears poverty more than is necessary,” etc. In the printed editions, instead of “think,” you have “fear.”].

[Col. 0924B] [Old VII.] 9. Charity is shown through examples of the saints.—The law of God is therefore rightly called manifold, because although charity is one and the same, if it fully takes possession of the mind, it kindles it in manifold ways toward innumerable works. We briefly express its diversity if, by touching on them, we enumerate its good effects in individual elect persons. Through Abel it both offered gifts chosen for God and endured his brother’s sword without resistance (Gen. IV, 4, 8). Through Enoch it taught him to live spiritually among human beings and also withdrew him bodily from human beings to sublime life (Gen. V, 24).

342 Through Noah, after all others had been disregarded, it showed him to be pleasing to God alone [Note: [Col. 0924D] Vindoc., like Corb. Germ., has *solum Deum placabilem*, “God alone propitiable”; Gemet. and others have *solum Deo placabilem*, “pleasing to God alone.” All the printed editions agree with the latter.] and exercised him in the construction of the ark through the devoted labor of a long undertaking; by the pious exercise of his work it preserved him as a survivor for the world (Gen. [Col. 0924C] VII, 6). Through Shem and Japheth it humbly blushed at their father’s nakedness [Note: [Col. 0924D] Most Norman manuscripts have *verecunda patris*, “the father’s modest/private parts,” for *verenda patris*, “the father’s private parts.”], and, casting a cloak over their backs, hid what they did not see (Gen. IX, 23). Because Abraham obediently raised his right hand to the death of his son, it made him the father of innumerable offspring and nations (Gen. XXII, 10). Because Isaac always kept his mind pure, charity enlarged that mind to see things far in the future when his eyes had grown dim with age (Gen. XXVII, 1). It compelled Jacob both to mourn from the depths of his being the loss of his good son and to endure with equanimity the presence of his wicked sons (Gen. XXXVII, 34). It taught Joseph, sold by his brothers, to endure servitude with an unbroken spirit and, afterward, to rule over those same brothers without an exalted mind (Gen. XLII, 33). When the people sinned, it both laid Moses low in prayer even to the point of asking for death and raised him up through zeal even to the destruction of the people [Col. 0924D], so that he might offer himself to death for the people who were perishing and, against the sinful, rage at once in the place of the Lord who was angry (Exod. XXXII, 33). It raised Phinehas’ arm in vengeance against sinners, so that, taking up the sword, he pierced those who were coupling and, himself angered, appeased the Lord’s anger (Num. XXV, 8, 9). It taught Joshua the scout [Note: [Col. 0924D] The printed editions have *Josue* for *Jesum*; both designate Joshua.] first to defend the truth in words against citizens who spoke falsely [Col. 0925A] and afterward to defend it with the sword against enemies (Josh. I, 2 ff.; Num. XIV, 6, 7 ff.). It made Samuel humble in authority and kept him upright in his deposition. Although he loved the people who were persecuting him, he himself bore witness [Note: [Col. 0925D] Thus Turon., Vindoc., and Gemet. read *sibi testimonio exstitit*, “he stood as a testimony to himself”; the printed editions transpose the construction to *sibi testimonium exstitit*.] that he had not loved the height from which he had been cast down (I Sam. III, 4 ff.). Before an unjust king, it both moved David by humility to flee and filled him with compassion for forgiveness: he fled from his persecutor, fearing him as a lord, yet when he found the power to strike him, he did not recognize him as an enemy (I Sam. XXIV, 6, 18). Through Nathan it both raised him to the authority of free rebuke against a sinful king and, when the king’s guilt was absent, cast him humbly down in petition (II Sam. XII, 1 ff.).

[Col. 0925B] Through Isaiah it did not blush to expose the nakedness of the flesh in preaching and, after removing the carnal veil, penetrated heavenly mysteries (Isa. XX, 2). Because it taught Elijah to live spiritually through the zeal of fervor, it also withdrew him bodily into life (IV Kings II, 11) [Note: [Col. 0925D] Utic., Lyr., and Bigot. have *quia ferventiori zelo*, “because of a more fervent zeal,” for *quia fervoris zelo*, “because of the zeal of fervor.”]. Because it taught Elisha to love his master with simplicity, it filled him twice over with his master’s spirit (ibid., 10). Through it Jeremiah resisted the people’s descent into Egypt; yet, because he loved the disobedient whom he had forbidden to descend, he himself also descended (Jer. XLII, 18). Because it first lifted Ezekiel away from earthly desires, it afterward suspended him in the air by the lock of his head (Ezek. VIII, 3). Because in Daniel it restrained his appetite from the royal delicacies, it also closed the mouths of the hungry lions for him (Dan. XIV, 40). [Col. 0925C] Because in the three boys it subdued the fires of vice while they were at peace, in the time of tribulation it also tempered the flames in the furnace (Dan. III, 50). In Peter it courageously resisted the threats of threatening rulers, and in the matter of removing circumcision it humbly listened to the words of his inferiors. In Paul it humbly endured the hands of persecutors, yet in the matter of circumcision it boldly rebuked the judgment of an elder far unequal to himself (Acts XV). This law of God is therefore manifold: without being changed, it suits each particular circumstance, and without itself being changed, it joins itself to changing situations.

[Old VIII.] 10. The offices of charity according to Paul.—Paul aptly enumerates the manifold character of this law, saying: “Charity is patient, it is kind; it does not envy, it is not puffed up, it does not act improperly, it is not ambitious, it does not seek what is its own, it is not provoked, it does not think evil, it does not rejoice over iniquity, but rejoices with the truth” (I Cor. XIII, 4).

Charity is patient because it endures inflicted evils with equanimity. It is kind because in return for evils it generously supplies good things. It does not envy because, desiring nothing in the present world, it does not know how to envy earthly successes. It is not puffed up because, while anxiously desiring the reward of inward recompense, it does not exalt itself over outward goods. It does not act improperly because, as it expands itself solely toward the love of God and neighbor, it knows nothing of whatever differs from rectitude. It is not ambitious because, while it eagerly strives inwardly toward its own possessions, it in no way covets what belongs to others. It does not seek what is its own because it neglects as alien everything it possesses here transitorily, recognizing that nothing is properly its own except what remains with it. It is not provoked because, even when challenged by injuries, it does not rouse itself to any movement of vengeance, while it awaits greater rewards after great labors. It does not think evil because, establishing the mind in the love of purity and rooting out all hatred from the foundations, it does not know how to turn over in the mind what defiles it. It does not rejoice over iniquity because, as it yearns for everyone with love alone, it does not exult over the destruction of those who oppose it [Note: [Col. 0925D] We have restored the phrase *quo*—omitted in a recent edition—from the Norman, Corb., Germ., Longip., Germ., and other manuscripts.]. But it rejoices with the truth because, loving others as itself, it is gladdened by whatever it sees to be right in them, as though by an increase of its own progress [Col. 0926B] [Note: [Col. 0926D] Utic.: “it grows.”].

This law of God is therefore manifold: against the dart of every individual fault, which attacks the mind in order to destroy it, it sets the protection of its instruction, so that, because the ancient enemy surrounds us with varied assaults, it may itself conquer him in manifold ways. If we weigh this law with careful consideration, we recognize how much we sin daily against our Creator. If, however, we consider our faults, we certainly endure the scourges with equanimity; nor does pain [Note: [Col. 0926D] Printed editions add *charitas*, “charity,” here, contrary to the manuscript evidence.] break out into impatience when conscience subjects itself to its own judgment. Hence Sophar, knowing what he should say but not knowing to whom he was saying it, after first saying, “That he might show you the secrets of wisdom, and that his law is manifold,” immediately adds:

CHAPTER VII [Rec. V]

THE SAME PASSAGE.—“And you would understand that God exacts from you much less than your iniquity deserves.”

11. Knowledge of our faults moderates the pain of scourges.—Pain from a scourge, as we have said, is moderated when guilt is recognized, because each person endures the physician’s knife with greater patience in proportion as he sees that what it is cutting is rotten. Whoever, therefore, understands the manifold character of the law considers that everything he suffers is much less than it might be, because recognition of the weight of guilt lightens the punishment of affliction.

[Old IX.] 12. Those who exceed the measure of correction through the heat of zeal sin venially.—Amid these matters we must recognize that it was not without serious fault that Sophar rebuked the just man even to the point of charging him with iniquity. The Truth therefore rightly rebukes their boldness, yet kindly restores them to grace, because before the merciful Judge a fault is not left entirely without pardon when one sins through the heat of zeal arising from love of him. This often happens to great and remarkable teachers: the more they burn with profound charity, the more they exaggerate the measure of correction, and their tongue says something it ought not to say because love inflames the mind as much as it ought. But the word of insult that has been uttered is pardoned all the more quickly when the root from which it proceeds is considered.

Hence the Lord rightly commanded through Moses, saying: “If someone goes with his friend into the forest simply to cut wood, and the wood slips from his hand while he is swinging the axe, and the iron, falling from the handle, strikes his friend and kills him, he shall flee to one of the cities mentioned above and live there, lest perhaps the nearest relative of the man whose blood has been shed, driven by the sting of grief, pursue him and seize him and strike his life” (Deut. XIX, 5).

We go into the forest with a friend whenever we turn with any neighbor to inspect our faults, and we cut wood simply when with a pious intention we cut away the vices of sinners. But the axe slips from the hand when correction drags itself into harshness beyond what is necessary. The iron leaps from the handle when speech in correction exceeds the proper limit in severity; and it strikes and kills the friend when an insult that has been uttered kills the hearer by driving him away from the spirit of love. The mind of the person rebuked suddenly collapses into hatred if immoderate [Note: [Col. 0927D] Even the older printed editions read *si hanc in moderata increpatione … addicit*, “if in measured correction it subjects it …”; this is erroneous and contrary to the manuscript evidence.] correction subjects it to more than it ought.

But the one who strikes the wood carelessly and extinguishes his neighbor must flee to three cities, so that, protected in one of them, he may live; for if, turning to the tears of penitence, he hides himself within the unity of the sacrament under hope, faith, and charity, he is not held guilty of the homicide he committed. The relative of the slain man, even when he finds him, does not kill him, because when the strict Judge comes—he who joined himself to us through participation in our nature—he will unquestionably not demand vengeance for the guilt from the one whom hope, faith, and charity have hidden under his pardon.

A fault is therefore forgiven more quickly when it is committed without the deliberate purpose of malice. Hence Sophar calls iniquitous one whom the heavenly judgment had praised; yet he is not excluded from pardon, because the zeal of divine love moves him to words of insult [Note: [Col. 0927D] Perhaps the better reading is found in Germ., Corb. Germ., Gemet.: “he is moved by zeal.”]. Because he does not recognize the merits of blessed Job, he adds, in his still inexperienced mockery:

CHAPTER VIII [Rec. VI]

VERSE 7.—“Perhaps you will grasp the traces of God, and you will find the Almighty even unto perfection.”

13. The traces of God are his gifts, by which we are summoned to heavenly things. God is not visibly seen here. The power of contemplation. Neither the angelic nor the human mind fully beholds God’s essence.—What does he call the traces of God except the graciousness of his visitation [Note: [Col. 0927D] Turon., Gemet., and most Norman manuscripts add: “that is, his gracious visitations.” The same reading now appears in Utic., though previously it agreed with the printed edition.]? By these we are summoned to advance toward heavenly things when we are touched by the breath of his Spirit and, lifted beyond the confines of the flesh, recognize through love the form of our Creator that is to be contemplated and followed. For when love of the spiritual homeland inflames our mind, he discloses himself, as it were, to those who follow a path; and, as the heart is laid beneath him, a kind of trace of God as he walks is impressed upon it, so that the way of life may be held by the straight steps of thought.

Since we do not yet see him, it necessarily remains for us to seek him through the traces of his love, so that at some time the mind may find, in the form of contemplation, the one whom it now explores, as though following behind him, through holy desires [Note: [Col. 0928D] Coc. and other recent editions: “until the mind comes to that which.” Gussanv. nevertheless indicated our reading, which is found in the manuscripts, and relegated the other to the margin.]. The Psalmist knew well how to follow the traces of our Creator when he said: “My soul clung after you” (Ps. LXII, 9). He also strove to find him even to the vision of his loftiness, saying: “My soul thirsted for the living God; when shall I come and appear before the face of God?” (Ps. XLI, 3).

The Almighty God is then found through manifest contemplation, when, after the corruption of our mortality has been utterly trampled down, he is seen by us, who have been taken up, in the glory of his divinity. But now the grace of the infused Spirit lifts the mind from carnal thought and exalts it to contempt for passing things. The mind despises below everything it had desired and burns with heavenly desires; and through the power of its contemplation it is lifted outside the flesh, although it is still held in the flesh by the weight of its corruption. It strives to behold the radiance of the unbounded light, but cannot. The mind, weighed down by weakness, neither penetrates it at all nor ceases to love it when repulsed. The Creator has already shown enough of himself to make himself loved, but he withdraws the form of his vision from those who love him.

We therefore, while seeing only his traces [Note: [Col. 0928D] Longip. has *gratulamur*, “we rejoice,” for *gradimur*, “we walk onward.”], walk onward: we follow him through the signs of his gifts, although we do not yet see him.

[Old X, Rec. VII.] These traces cannot be grasped, because it is unknown whence, where, or by what means the gifts of his Spirit come, as the Truth testifies when it says: “The Spirit breathes where he wills; you hear his voice, but you do not know where he comes from or where he goes” (John III, 8) [Note: [Col. 0928D] The printed editions read: “or where it goes.”].

At the summit of recompense, the Almighty can be found in the form of contemplation, but not unto perfection, because even if we someday behold him in his glory, we do not fully behold his essence. For when the angelic or human mind longs for the unbounded light, it narrows itself by that very fact that it is a creature. It stretches beyond itself through advancement, yet, however expanded, it is not sufficient to grasp his radiance, which both transcends and contains all things, bears them, and fills them.

Hence it is further added:

CHAPTER IX

[Col. 0928D]

VERSES 8, 9.—“He is higher than heaven, and what will you do? He is deeper than hell, and how will you know?” His measure is longer [Note: [Col. 0928D] Gemet., Germ., and the first hand of Corb. Germ. have *longior terrae*, “longer than the earth,” and afterward *terrae longior* in the same sense; the note also records accusative *longiorem terrae*.] than the earth and broader than the sea.”

14. How God transcends all things.—That God is described as higher than heaven, deeper than hell, longer than earth, and broader than the sea must be understood spiritually in proportion as it is impious to think anything about him according to bodily dimensions. He is higher than heaven because, by the unboundedness of his Spirit, he transcends all things; deeper than hell because, by transcending it, he sustains it; longer than earth because by the permanence of his eternity he surpasses the measure of creation; broader than the sea because he so governs and possesses the waves of temporal things that, by confining them within the omnipresence of his power, he surrounds them completely.

Heaven may also designate the angels, and hell the demons; earth may signify righteous human beings, and sea sinners. He is therefore higher than heaven because even the elect spirits do not perfectly penetrate the vision of such loftiness. He is deeper than hell because, judging the cunning of evil spirits far more subtly than they themselves imagined, he condemns them. He is longer than earth because divine patience surpasses our long-suffering: it tolerates us while we sin and awaits us when converted for the rewards of recompense. He is broader than the sea because he occupies everywhere the presence of his retribution toward sinners, so that even when he is not seen as present in appearance, he is felt as present in judgment.

15. How man is heaven, hell, earth, and sea; God’s breadth, length, height, and depth.—Everything, however, can be referred to man alone, so that he himself is heaven when he already clings to the heights through desire; he himself is hell when, disturbed by the darkness of his temptations, he lies in the depths; he himself is earth because he bears fruit in good works through the abundance of steadfast hope; he himself is sea because in certain respects he is shaken by fear and driven by the wind of his own mutability.

But God is higher than heaven because we are overcome by the greatness of his power even when we are lifted above ourselves; he is deeper than hell because he judges more than the human mind itself investigates in its temptations [Note: [Col. 0929D] The printed editions read “he indicates more”; this has been corrected from the manuscripts, whose reading is confirmed by what follows: “He knew him to be deeper than hell who, examining himself yet fearing his more subtle judgments,” and shortly afterward: “He displays his depth by strictly judging hidden and illicit movements of thought.”]. He is longer than earth because the fruits of life that he will repay at the end are not now comprehended even by our hope; he is broader than the sea because the human mind, tossed about, conjectures many things about what is to come, but when it begins to see what it had imagined, it recognizes that its own estimation had been narrow.

[Old XI.] He is therefore higher than heaven when our contemplation of him itself fails. The Psalmist had set his heart on high, yet did not feel that he had reached him, saying: “Your knowledge has become wonderful to me; it has been strengthened, and I cannot attain to it” (Ps. CXXXVIII, 6). He knew him to be deeper than hell who, examining himself yet fearing his more subtle judgments, said: “I am conscious of nothing against myself, but I am not thereby justified; the one who judges me is the Lord” (I Cor. IV, 4). He had seen him to be longer than earth when he considered human desires to be less than God, saying: “To him who is able to do all things more abundantly than we ask or understand” (Eph. III, 20) [Note: [Col. 0929D] In the Utic., Lyr., and Big. manuscripts: “less than he”; elsewhere, “less than it.” Examples of this construction have already been seen in Book V, no. 84. Book IX, no. 76 likewise has: “less than himself.”].

He had perceived him to be broader than the sea when, fearing, he considered that the human mind could never recognize the immensity of his strict judgment, however much it might inquire amid its tossing, saying: “Who knows the power of your anger, or can count your wrath because of fear?” (Ps. LXXXIX, 11) [Note: [Col. 0930D] Some manuscripts add “your.”].

The eminent teacher aptly reveals this power to us when he briefly says: “That you may be able to comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth, length, height, and depth” (Eph. III, 18). God has breadth because he extends his love even to the gathering in of persecutors. He has length because, by patiently enduring us, he leads us to the homeland of life. He has height because he transcends even the understanding of those who will be received into the heavenly assembly. He has depth because he incomprehensibly exercises the judgment of his strictness more deeply against the condemned.

He exercises these four dimensions in each of us who are placed in this life: breadth by loving, length by enduring, height by surpassing not only our understanding but also our desires, and depth by strictly judging the hidden and illicit movements of our thoughts. Yet no one recognizes how unsearchable his height and depth are except one who has begun either to be raised through contemplation to the heights or, resisting hidden movements, to be troubled by the importunity of temptations.

Hence blessed Job is told: “He is higher than heaven, and what will you do? He is deeper than hell, and how will you know?” [Note: [Col. 0930D] Thus Germ. and most manuscripts. In Corb. Germ. and the printed editions, as was formerly also read in Utic., the wording is different, as though it were openly contemptuous.]. As though he were being addressed with open contempt: “When will you be able to know his depth and excellence, you who neither know how to rise to the heights through virtue nor how to rebuke yourself in temptations?” It follows:

CHAPTER X [Rec. VIII]

VERSE 10.—“If he overturns all things or confines them into one, who will oppose him? Or who can say to him, ‘Why do you do this?’” [Note: [Col. 0930D] What follows is not found in the Hebrew text or in the Vulgate, but in the Septuagint edition, where instead of “Who will oppose him?” one reads: “Who will say to him, ‘What have you done?’”].

16. How God overturns heaven, hell, earth, and sea in us.—The Lord overturns heaven when, by a fearful and hidden dispensation, he destroys the loftiness of human contemplation. He overturns hell when he permits someone’s mind, fearful in its temptations, to fall even into worse things. He overturns earth when, as adversities rush in, he cuts off the fruitfulness of good work. He overturns sea when, as sudden fear emerges, he confounds the wavering of our uncertainty. In its very uncertainty the anxious heart greatly fears that it is wavering, and the sea is overturned, as it were, when our very trembling before God is disturbed by consideration of his judgment.

[Old XII.] Since, therefore, we have briefly explained how heaven, hell, earth, or sea is overturned, it remains for us now to demonstrate with somewhat greater labor how these can be confined into one.

17. Heaven and hell together: contemplation and temptation of the flesh in one mind.—It often happens that the spirit already raises the mind to the heights, yet the flesh attacks it with persistent temptations. When the mind is led to contemplate heavenly things, it is struck back by images of unlawful action. Suddenly the sting of the flesh wounds the one whom holy contemplation was carrying beyond the flesh.

Heaven and hell are therefore confined together when one and the same mind is both illumined by the elevation of contemplation and darkened by the persistence of temptation, so that by directing its gaze it sees what it desires, yet by succumbing it endures in thought what it is ashamed of. Light rises from heaven, whereas hell is possessed by darkness. Heaven and hell are therefore reduced into one when the mind, which already beholds the light of the heavenly homeland, also carries the darkness of hidden temptation from the battle with the flesh.

Paul had certainly already ascended to the summit of the third heaven and had learned the secrets of paradise, yet, still enduring the battles of the flesh, he groaned, saying: “I see another law in my members fighting against the law of my mind and taking me captive in the law of sin, which is in my members” (Rom. VII, 23). What, then, had God confined together in the heart of this great preacher except heaven and hell? He had already received the light of inward vision, yet he still endured darkness from the flesh. Above himself he had seen what he would joyfully desire; within himself he saw what he would fearfully grieve over. The light of the heavenly homeland had already shone upon him, but the darkness of temptation still confused his mind. He bore hell together with heaven because security lifted him up when illumined, while groaning laid him low when tempted.

18. Earth and sea together: certainty of faith with some doubt.—It often also happens that faith already prevails in the mind, yet in some small measure withers through doubt, so that it raises itself with certainty above visible things while being disturbed by uncertainty about certain matters. Often it rises to desire eternal things, yet, shaken by the goads of arising thoughts, contradicts itself.

[Old XIII.] Earth and sea are therefore confined together when one and the same mind is strengthened by the certainty of solid faith, yet is tossed by the wind of doubt arising from a certain mutability of unbelief. Did he not know that earth and sea were confined together in his own heart who, hoping through faith and wavering through unbelief, said: “I believe, Lord; help my unbelief” (Mark IX, 23)? What does it mean that he both asserts that he believes and seeks to have the unbelief within him helped, except that he had detected earth confined together with sea in his thoughts? He had already begun with certainty to implore through faith, yet, still uncertain, he endured the waves of unbelief through lack of faith.

19. Why God allows a mind rising toward what is right to be attacked.—This is permitted to happen by a hidden dispensation, so that when the mind has begun to rise toward rectitude, it may be attacked by the remnants of its own depravity; thus the attack itself may either exercise the mind while it resists or break it when it has been seduced by pleasures.

The words “If he overturns all things or confines them into one, who will oppose him? Or who can say to him, ‘Why do you do this?’” are therefore rightly spoken, because divine judgment can neither be diminished by adversity nor understood through inquiry, whether he withdraws the virtues he had granted or, without taking them away altogether, permits them to be shaken by the attack of vices.

Often the heart is lifted into pride when it is strengthened in virtue by happy successes. But when the Creator sees hidden movements of presumption in thought, he abandons the person by showing him what he is, so that the abandoned mind may discover what it is, although it had foolishly rejoiced in its own security [Note: [Col. 0931D] Longip.: “joyful movements.”].

Hence, when it was said that he overturns all things or confines them into one, it is immediately added:

CHAPTER XI [Rec. IX]

VERSE 11.—“For he knows the vanity of human beings, and when he sees iniquity, does he not consider it?”

20. The distinction between vanity and iniquity.—As though, by clarifying what had been said, he were adding: “Because he sees vices increasing through tolerance, he confounds the gifts through judgment.” The order is correctly preserved in the description when vanity is said to be known first and iniquity considered afterward [Note: [Col. 0931D] Thus Bellov., Corb. Germ., Longip., Vindoc., Gemet., and other Norman manuscripts; not, as the printed edition reads, “in discernment.” The old Paris edition, however, has “in description.”].

Every iniquity is vanity, but not every vanity is ordinarily iniquity. We act vainly whenever we think about transitory things. Hence something is said to vanish when it suddenly disappears from the eyes of those looking at it. Thus the Psalmist says: “Every living human being is altogether vanity” (Ps. XXXVIII, 6), because, insofar as a person tends toward destruction by living, he is rightly called vanity, but is by no means thereby rightly called iniquity. Although it is the consequence of guilt that he perishes, the fact that he passes away from life is not itself guilt. Vain, therefore, are the things that pass away. Hence Solomon also says: “All is vanity” (Eccles. I, 2).

21. Vanity leads to iniquity. Vanity clouds the mind; iniquity blinds it.—Vanity is appropriately followed immediately by iniquity, because while we are led through certain transitory things, we become harmfully entangled in others. When the mind does not maintain the state of immutability, it flows away from itself and bursts forth into vices [Note: [Col. 0932D] Thus it is read in the better manuscripts and older printed editions. Other printed editions, following Coccius, read: “Vanity therefore slips into iniquity.”].

It therefore slips from vanity into iniquity because, accustomed to changeable things, it is continually driven from one thing to another and is defiled by emerging faults.

[Old XIV.] Vanity can nevertheless also be understood as guilt, while iniquity by its name can signify a more serious offense. For if vanity were never guilt, the Psalmist would not say: “Although a human being walks in the image of God, yet he is troubled in vain; he stores up treasure and does not know for whom he gathers it” (Ps. XXXVIII, 8). Although we preserve the image of the Trinity in our nature, we nevertheless sin in our conduct when we are disturbed by vain movements of pleasure, so that desire shakes us, fear breaks us, joy soothes us, and grief afflicts us in continual alternation.

As was said above, we are led from vanity to iniquity when we first slip through minor offenses [Note: [Col. 0933D] The printed editions, following Coccius, read “we turn aside”; the manuscripts—Corb., Bellov., Longip., Vind., Gemet., and other Norman witnesses—together with the old edition, resist this and read “we slip.”], so that, as habit makes everything seem light, we cease entirely to fear committing more serious offenses afterward. When the tongue neglects to restrain idle words, once seized by the habitual relaxation of custom it bursts forth boldly into harmful speech. When one devotes oneself to the appetite, one immediately proceeds to frivolous madness. When the mind refuses to subdue the pleasure of the flesh, it often also plunges into the abyss of unbelief.

Paul therefore rightly, observing the disasters of the Israelite people, took care to recount past events in order to restrain the evils threatening his hearers, saying: “Nor become idolaters, as some of them did, as it is written” (I Cor. X, 7) [Note: [Col. 0933D] Bellov., Corb. Germ., Gemet., and others read “idolaters,” and below “to idolatry.” The printed editions read “as some of them did.”]: “The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play” (Exod. XXXII, 6).

Eating and drinking drove them to play, and play dragged them to idolatry, because if the guilt of vanity is not carefully restrained, the unwary mind is immediately devoured by iniquity, as Solomon testifies when he says: “Whoever despises small things will gradually fall” (Eccles. XIX, 1). If we neglect to care for small matters, we are imperceptibly seduced and proceed boldly even to greater offenses.

It should be noted that iniquity is said not merely to be seen but to be considered. We look more attentively at what we consider. God therefore knows human vanity and considers iniquity: he neither leaves lesser offenses unpunished nor prepares himself less intently to strike down greater ones.

Since, therefore, one begins with lighter evils and reaches graver ones, vanity clouds the mind and iniquity blinds it. Once it has lost the light, this mind raises itself all the higher through swelling pride, the more it withdraws from the truth after being caught in the snares of iniquity.

Hence he aptly expresses where vanity draws the mind together with iniquity when he immediately adds:

CHAPTER XII [Rec. XV, Rec. X]

VERSE 12.—“A vain man is lifted up into pride.”

22. Vanity makes a person bold through guilt and unbridled in the movements of nature.—The end of vanity is that, after wounding the mind through sin, it makes the mind bold through guilt, so that, forgetful of its offense and not grieving that it has lost its innocence, it also loses humility after being blinded by a just judgment.

It often happens that, serving perverse desires, a person shakes himself free from the yoke of divine fear [Note: [Col. 0933D] Ebroic. and most Norman manuscripts: “from the yoke of divine love.”] and, as though already free for the perpetration of evils, strives to fulfill everything that pleasure suggests. Hence, when it is said that the vain man lifts himself into pride, it is immediately added:

CHAPTER XIII

THE SAME PASSAGE.—“And he thinks himself free-born, like a colt of a wild ass.”

23. By the colt of a wild ass every kind of wild creature is expressed, for when left to the movements of nature it is not held by the reins of those who rule. Animals of the field are free both to go where they wish and to rest when they are tired. Although human beings are far superior to irrational animals, what is permitted to brute animals is often not permitted to human beings. Since the latter are not preserved for any further purpose, their movements are certainly not restrained by discipline. But a human being who is being led toward the life to come must necessarily be held back in all his movements under the arrangement of discipline, and, like a domestic animal bound by reins, serve and live under the restraint of eternal ordinances.

Whoever therefore seeks, through unbridled freedom, to fulfill everything he desires, what else does he desire but to resemble a colt of a wild ass, so that the reins of discipline do not hold him, but, boldly wandering, he runs through the forest of his desires?

24. The reins by which God restrains and governs us.—Divine mercy often breaks those whom it sees advancing into the unbridled freedom of illicit behavior by imposing sudden adversity [Note: [Col. 0934D] The printed editions read “prosperous.” The reading is corrected from the manuscripts Corb. Germ., Reg., and Colb.], so that, once crushed, they may learn how disgracefully they had swelled through their proud elevation. Once tamed by the experience of the scourge, they submit the necks of their minds, like domestic animals, to the reins of the commandments and proceed along the paths of the present life at the direction of the one presiding over them [Note: [Col. 0934D] Thus Corb. Germ., Vindoc., Bellov., and the Norman manuscripts. Departing from these, Coc. and more recent editions read “they proceed along the journey.” Vindoc. and many old manuscripts have *peragant* (“they travel through [them]”).].

He knew himself to be well bound by these reins who said: “I became like a beast of burden before you, and I am always with you” (Ps. LXXII, 23). Hence that savage persecutor, led from the field of faithless pleasure into the house of faith and pierced by the goads of his ruler, heard: “It is hard for you to kick against the goad” (Acts IX, 5).

It remains, then, that if we do not wish to be like a colt of a wild ass, we should first seek the direction of the inward dispensation in everything we desire, so that our mind may be held by the rein of heavenly governance in everything toward which it strives. In this way it fulfills its desires for life all the more truly: by trampling down the pursuits of its life even against its own will.

Sophar said many forceful things, but he does not know that he is speaking them to one better than himself. Therefore he continues his rebuke:

CHAPTER XIV

VERSE 13.—“But you have strengthened your heart and stretched out your hands toward him.”

## 25. Zophar Rebukes Job for a Hardened and Proud Spirit; the Wicked and Heretics Imitate him against the Good and Catholics

“Strengthening the heart” is not said here with reference to virtue, but to insensibility. For everyone who submits himself inwardly to serious self-examination immediately becomes softened by fear of it; the arrow of divine dread pierces him, because through humility he bears a weakened inward being. But whoever hardens through the obstinacy of insensibility, as it were strengthens his heart, so that the arrows of heavenly fear may not pierce it. Hence the Lord mercifully says through the prophet to certain people [Note: The printed editions read *tollam a vobis*, “I will take from you.”]: “I will take from you your heart of stone, and I will give you a heart of flesh” (Ezek. 36:26). He takes away a heart of stone when he removes from us the hardness of pride; and he gives a heart of flesh when he immediately turns that same hardness of ours into sensitivity.

By “hands,” as we have often taught, works are signified. To stretch out one’s hands toward God while guilty, therefore, is to grow proud against the grace of the giver because of one’s works. For whoever, speaking in the sight of the eternal Judge, attributes the good things he does to himself, stretches his hands toward God in pride.

Thus the wicked rage against the elect, and heretics against Catholics: when they cannot condemn their deeds, they strive to criticize the good for the arrogance of their deeds, so that those whom they cannot rebuke for weakness in action they may accuse of the crime of pride. Hence they no longer consider those outwardly performed good works to be good, since they are displayed, as it were, through the effort of a swollen mind.

[Note: Gemet. and Bellov. have *turbidae* (“troubled”) in place of *turgidae* (“swollen”).]

They often rebuke *humilia* while swollen with pride, though they do not know that they are striking themselves with their own words.

[Note: Here there is a remarkable disagreement among the printed editions and manuscripts. Codex Corb. Germ. has *qui saepe (a secunda manu de) humilitate mentem*; the word *de* is supplied by a second hand. Reg. has *qui saepe humiliata mente*, with another manuscript agreeing except that it has *humiliatam*. The old editions have *qui saepe humiliatum mente*. The recent editions read *qui semper de humilitate tumentes*. The more genuine reading appears to be that supplied by Colb., Germ., Ebroic., and other Norman manuscripts.]

But because Zophar has so far corrected and rebuked the just man, he now adds, as though teaching:

## CHAPTER XV  
### [Old XVI, Revised XI]

**Verse 14–15.** “If you remove from yourself the iniquity that is in your hand, and injustice does not remain in your tabernacle, then you will be able to lift up your face without stain, and you will be steadfast and will not fear.”

## 26. In Order for the Mind to Be Pure, the Iniquity of Deed and Then of the Heart Must Be Cut Away

Every sin is committed either by thought alone or by thought together with deed. Iniquity in the hand, therefore, is guilt in action; but injustice in the tabernacle is iniquity in the mind. Our mind is not inappropriately called our tabernacle, since in it we hide within ourselves when we are not seen outwardly in our actions.

Thus Zophar, because he is a friend of the just man, knows what he is saying; but because he rebukes the just man, bearing the character of heretics, he does not know how to put forth rightly even what he knows. But let us set aside his proud manner of speaking and consider how true his words would be if they were spoken correctly.

First he advises that iniquity be removed from the hand, and afterward that injustice be cut away from the tabernacle, because whoever has already cut off wicked deeds outwardly must necessarily return to himself and carefully examine himself in the intention of his mind, lest the guilt that he no longer has in action continue in thought.

Hence Solomon rightly says: “Prepare your work outside, and diligently cultivate your field, so that afterward you may build your house” (Prov. 24:27). For what is it to prepare one’s work and diligently cultivate one’s field outwardly, except to weed out the thorns of iniquity [Note: Gemet. reads *sensibus* (“senses”) for *sentibus* (“thorns”).] and cultivate our activity for the fruit of recompense?

And what is it, after cultivating the field, to return to the building of the house, except that we often learn from good works how much purity of life we ought to construct in our thought? Nearly all good works proceed from thought, but there are certain sharp insights of thought [Note: Gemet. reads *argumina* (“arguments”).] that arise from action; for just as action is taken from the mind, so the mind is again instructed by action.

The mind, receiving the beginnings of divine love, commands good things to be done; but once the things it commanded have begun to be done, exercised by those very actions it learns how much less it had perceived when it began to command good things. The field is therefore cultivated outside so that the house may afterward be built, because we often derive from outward action [Note: Vindoc., Corb. Germ., Longip., Norman, and German manuscripts read *sumimus* (“we derive”); the printed editions read *videmus* (“we see”).] how great a subtlety of uprightness we possess in the heart.

Zophar carefully sought to preserve this order when he said that iniquity must first be removed from the hands and afterward injustice from the tabernacle, because the mind is never fully raised in thought when it still errs outwardly in action.

## [Old XVII] 27. This Purity Gives Confidence in Prayer; the Opposite Results When It Is Absent

If we perfectly cleanse these two things, we immediately lift our face toward God without stain. The inner face of a human being is the mind, in which we are truly recognized so that we may be directed by our Maker. To lift this face is to raise the mind toward God through the exercises of prayer.

But a stain pollutes the lifted face if consciousness of guilt accuses the attentive mind, because confidence in hope is immediately broken when the mind intent upon prayers is still gnawed by the memory of a fault not yet overcome. For the mind distrusts that it can receive what it desires when it remembers that it still refuses to do what it has heard from God.

Hence John says: “If our heart does not condemn us, we have confidence before God, and whatever we ask from him we shall receive” (1 John 3:21). Solomon likewise says: “Whoever turns away his ear so as not to hear the law, his prayer will be accursed” (Prov. 28:9).

The heart condemns us in petition when it remembers that it resists the commands of the one whom it asks; and prayer becomes accursed when it turns away from the judgment of the law, because it is certainly fitting that one be excluded from the benefits of him whose commands one does not wish to obey.

## 28. What Must Be Done When This Purity Is Absent

The salutary remedy in this matter is that when the mind reproaches itself through the memory of guilt, it should first mourn in prayer the error it committed, so that when the stain of error is wiped away with tears, the face of the heart may appear clean before its Maker in its petition.

But one must take great care not to fall again into what one rejoices to have cleansed with tears, lest, when the lamented guilt is committed again, even the lamentations themselves be made light of in the sight of the just Judge.

We must carefully remember what is said: “Do not repeat a word in your prayer” (Sir. 7:15). By this saying the wise man certainly does not prohibit us from repeatedly asking forgiveness, but from repeating our sins. It is as though he plainly said: “When you have mourned your evil deeds, do not again do what you will once more lament in your prayers.”

## 29. Before Prayer, Unclean and Earthly Thoughts Must Be Driven Away

Therefore, in order that the face may be lifted without stain toward prayer, before the times of prayer one must always carefully consider whatever could be condemned in prayer; and the mind should hasten to present itself, even when it has ceased from prayer, as it desires to appear before the Judge at the very time of prayer.

For often, whenever we are free from prayer, we turn over certain unclean or unlawful things in our minds.

[Note: Gemet., Bellov., and Corb. Germ., before correction, read “we turn over.”]

But when the mind has raised itself to the practice of prayer, it suffers the images of those things to be driven back, since previously, in its idleness, it had willingly been oppressed by them. It is as though the soul is no longer able to lift its face toward God, because, with its mind polluted within itself, it is ashamed of the stains of its defiled thoughts.

Often we willingly occupy ourselves with worldly cares. When afterward we devote ourselves to prayer, the mind is in no way raised toward heavenly things, because the weight of earthly concern has plunged it into the depths; and a clean face is not shown in prayer, because it is stained by the mud of lowly thought.

## [Old XVIII] 30. The Sins of Others Must Be Forgiven. Who Is Free from Fear

Sometimes, however, we shake the heart free from all cares and resist unlawful impulses, even when we are not occupied with prayer.

[Note: Longip. reads: “Sometimes we shake the heart free from all cares and confront unlawful impulses …” The other manuscripts available to us also read: “even when we are not occupied with prayer,” and we have preferred this reading to that of the printed books. In the old Paris and Basel editions it reads, as in Corb. Germ.: “Sometimes we desire to shake the heart free from all cares and unlawful impulses, even when we are free from prayer.” In the more recent editions: “Sometimes we shake the heart free from all cares and restrain it from unlawful impulses when we are free from prayer.”]

Yet because we commit faults less frequently, we more sluggishly forgive the offenses of others; and the more anxiously our spirit fears to sin, the more severely it abhors what another does against us. Thus each person is found slower to forgive in proportion as, by making progress, he has become more cautious about sin; and the more he fears to offend another himself, the more harshly he demands punishment for what is done against him.

But what could be found worse than this stain of grief, which in the sight of the Judge does not merely pollute charity but kills it? Any fault pollutes the life of the soul, but grief held against one’s neighbor destroys it. It is fixed in the mind like a sword, and with its edge it pierces the hidden inward parts themselves.

If it is not first drawn out of the pierced heart, no divine help is obtained in prayer, because medicines of healing cannot be applied to wounded limbs unless the iron is first removed from the wound.

Hence Truth itself says: “Unless you forgive people their sins, neither will your Father who is in heaven forgive you your sins” (Matt. 6:15).

[Note: The words “their sins” are not read in Gemet. and Germ.]

He also admonishes us, saying: “When you stand to pray, forgive whatever you have against another” (Mark 11:25). Again he says: “Give, and it will be given to you; forgive, and you will be forgiven” (Luke 6:38).

[Note: This is the reading of the English, Norman, Bellovacian, and Longipontine manuscripts. The old editions read: “He placed a condition of mercy upon this constitution of petition.” The more recent editions read: “He placed this against the institution of petition.”]

For this reason he attached a condition of mercy to the ordinance of petition, saying: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. 6:12), so that the good thing we ask from God when moved to compunction we may first do in our dealings with our neighbor.

We truly lift our face without stain when we neither commit the forbidden evils ourselves nor retain, out of personal resentment, those committed against us. For our mind is weighed down by great confusion during the time of its prayer if either its own action still stains it or grief preserved against another’s wickedness accuses it.

When each person has cleansed these two things, he immediately rises free toward what follows: “And you will be steadfast, and you will not fear.” For the more firmly one stands in good actions, the less one fears the Judge. The one who preserves steadfastness overcomes fear, because while he anxiously strives to carry out what the gentle Creator commands, he confidently considers what the Creator terribly threatens.

## 31. Perseverance Is Easier in the Active Life than in the Contemplative; Who Is Considered to Persist in Contemplation

It should further be understood that there are certain good things in which we persist without weariness, while there are others from which we continually decline and fall, and to which we are restored again at intervals through great efforts.

## [Old XIX]

In the active life the mind is fixed without failing; in the contemplative life, overcome by the weight of its weakness, it grows weary. The former endures more firmly because it expands itself toward what is near, for the benefit of its neighbor; the latter falls more quickly because, crossing beyond the confines of the flesh, it strives to rise above itself.

The former directs itself along level ground and therefore plants the foot of its work more firmly; but the latter, in proportion as it seeks heights above itself, descends more quickly, exhausted, to itself.

Ezekiel conveys this well and briefly when he describes the movements of the living creatures he had seen, saying: “They did not turn back as they went forward.” Shortly afterward he adds: “The living creatures went and returned” (Ezek. 1:9, 14).

The holy living creatures sometimes go and do not return; at other times they go and immediately return. For when the minds of the elect, through the grace of the active life granted to them, abandon the paths of error, they do not know how to return to the evils of the world that they have left. But when, through the sharpness of contemplation, they withdraw themselves from this same active life, they go and return, because, being unable to persist long enough in contemplation, they pour themselves back into action, so that by exercising themselves in the things near at hand they may be refreshed and may again gain strength to rise above themselves through contemplation.

But when this same contemplation is repeated at the proper intervals, one undoubtedly persists unfailingly in its stability, because although the mind, overcome by the weight of its weakness, falls away, it nevertheless grasps it again after being restored through continual efforts. Nor should it be said to have lost its stability in that from which, although it always falls away, it always seeks recovery whenever it has lost it.

Then follows:

## CHAPTER XVI  
### [Revised XII]

**Verse 16.** “You will also forget misery, and you will not remember it, like waters that have passed away.”

## 32. The Evils of This Life Are Not Serious to One Who Thinks upon Eternal Goods

The mind feels the evils of the present life more harshly in proportion as it neglects to weigh the good that follows; and in proportion as it does not wish to consider the rewards that remain, it regards what it endures as grievous.

Thus blind thought complains against the blow of the scourge, and a calamity is believed to be almost infinite which, as the days run their course and slip away, is daily brought to an end. But if someone once raises himself toward eternal things and fixes the eye of his heart upon what remains unchangeably, he sees that almost nothing here is whatever runs toward an end.

He endures the adversities of the present life, but weighs everything that passes away as though it were nothing. The more firmly he inserts himself into inward joys, the less he feels outward pains.

Therefore Zophar, not fearing to teach the superior man with rash presumption, exhorts him to righteousness and shows how no punishment appears to the eyes of the just. It is as though he plainly said: “If you taste the joy that endures within, everything that pains you outwardly immediately becomes light.”

He rightly compares the miseries of the present life with passing waters, because passing calamity does not overwhelm the mind of the elect with the force of its shock, but nevertheless pours sorrow into it by its touch.

[Note: The recent editions read “but only by touch”; shortly afterward, “but from the certainty of his salvation,” contrary to the other books.]

For he is indeed wet through the blood of his wound, although he is not broken from the certainty of his salvation.

## [Old XX]

Often not only scourges wear us down, but the temptations of wicked spirits also rage in the mind of each just person, so that outwardly he suffers from the blow and inwardly grows somewhat cold through temptation. But grace never abandons us; the more harshly it strikes us through its dispensation, the more abundantly it guards us through its compassion. For when the inner light begins to grow dark through temptation, it kindles itself again.

Hence it is added:

## CHAPTER XVII

**Verse 17.** “And at evening a brightness like that of midday will rise for you.”

## 33. Virtue Is Renewed in Temptation

The brightness of midday at evening is the renewal of virtue in temptation, so that the mind, through a sudden warmth of charity, may grow strong after it had begun to fear that the light of grace had already set.

Zophar opens this more subtly when he adds:

## CHAPTER XVIII

**The Same Passage.** “And when you think yourself consumed, you will rise like the morning star.”

## 34. Sorrow Arising from Temptation Appeals for God’s Mercy on Our Behalf; the Just Person Is Like the Morning Star

Often so many temptations besiege us that their very multitude almost inclines us toward the fall of despair. Hence, when the mind is frequently turned toward weariness, it scarcely considers the losses of its own virtue; grieving entirely, yet as though already alienated from the feeling of grief, it is broken and cannot count by how great a tumult of thoughts it is devastated.

It sees itself about to fall at every moment, and the sorrow itself more gravely prevents it from taking up the weapons of resistance. Darkness surrounds the eyes wherever they turn; and because the shadows continually obstruct vision, the sorrowful mind sees nothing but darkness.

But before the merciful Judge, this very sorrow, which even aggravates the effort of prayer [Note: The printed editions wrongly read *ad nisum*, as two words.], often appeals for us more subtly. For then the Creator sees the darkness of our grief and pours back the rays of the withdrawn light, so that the mind, immediately raised by his gifts, grows strong—the mind that shortly before had been pressed down by the heel of contending vices of pride.

At once he disperses the weight of torpor, and after the darkness of its agitation the mind breaks forth into the light of contemplation.

[Note: Bigot. reads “the summit of contemplation.”]

Then, advancing into joy, it is lifted up—though amid temptations it had been compelled by despair to fall into something worse. Without the struggle of thought it despises present things; without the obstacle of doubt it trusts in the coming reward.

Thus, when the just person thinks himself consumed, he rises like the morning star, because as soon as he begins to grow dark in the gloom of temptations, he is restored to the light of grace. He displays in himself the day of righteousness, though shortly before, about to fall, he feared the night of guilt. [Note: Lyr., Utic., and Bigot. read *tenuit noctem culpae*, “held the night of guilt.”]

The life of the just is rightly compared with the morning star. The morning star precedes the sun and announces the day. And what does the innocence of the saints proclaim to us except the splendor of the Judge who follows? In admiring them, we perceive what we should think about the majesty of the true light. We do not yet see the power of our Redeemer, but we admire his virtue in the conduct of his elect.

Because the life of the good places the force of truth before our eyes when we contemplate it, the bright morning star comes to us before the sun.

## 35. The Just Suffer Hardship Here, but It Will Be Well with Them at the End; Even Now, Falling Outwardly, They Are Renewed Inwardly

It should be understood that what we have discussed concerning the opposition of spiritual temptations may also be properly understood with reference to outward evils. Holy men, because they love the highest things from the depths of their being, suffer harsh things in what is lowly; but at the end they find the light of joy, which they despise possessing during this interval of passing life.

Hence Zophar now says: “And at evening a brightness like that of midday will rise for you.”

For the sinner’s daylight is darkness at evening, because he is raised up by prosperity in the present life but is devoured at the end by the darkness of adversity.

[Note: This is the reading of Gemet. and several Norman manuscripts. The printed editions read: “because he is raised up in the prosperity of the present life.”]

But for the just person, the brightness of midday rises at evening, because he recognizes how great a brightness awaits him when he has already begun to set.

Hence it is written: “It will be well with the one who fears God at the end” (Sir. 1:13). The Psalmist likewise says: “When he gives sleep to his beloved, this is the heritage of the Lord” (Ps. 126:2).

While still placed in the struggle of this life, the person who thinks himself consumed rises like the morning star, because, falling outwardly, he is renewed inwardly; and the more adversity he endures outwardly, the more abundantly he flashes inwardly with the light of virtues.

Paul bears witness to this when he says: “Although our outward man is corrupted, yet the inward man is renewed day by day. For this momentary and light tribulation of ours is producing in us an eternal weight of glory beyond all measure” (2 Cor. 4:16).

It should be noted that he does not say, “when you have been consumed,” but “when you think yourself consumed,” because what we see is uncertain, whereas what we hope for is certain. Hence Paul himself did not know himself to be consumed, but thought so; and, falling amid the adversities of tribulations, he shone like the morning star, saying: “As dying, and behold, we live; as sorrowful, yet always rejoicing; as poor, yet making many rich” (2 Cor. 6:9).

## [Old XXII]

It should also be understood that the more harshly the mind of the good endures for the sake of truth, the more certainly it hopes for the rewards of eternity. Hence it is aptly added:

## CHAPTER XIX

**Verse 18.** “And you will have confidence, with hope set before you.”

## 36. The More Harshly One Suffers for God, the More Firmly One Hopes in Him

Hope in God rises more solidly in proportion to the severity of what one has endured for him, because the joy of recompense from eternity is never gathered unless it has first been sown here through devout tribulation.

Hence the Psalmist says: “Going, they went and wept, casting their seeds; but coming, they will come with rejoicing, carrying their sheaves” (Ps. 125:6). Paul says: “If we die with him, we shall also live with him; if we endure, we shall also reign with him” (2 Tim. 2:11). He admonishes the disciples, saying: “Through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God” (Acts 14:21).

The angel, indicating the glory of the saints to John, says: “These are they who came from the great tribulation, and washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb” (Rev. 7:14).

[Note: This is the reading of Corb. Germ., Gemet., the other Norman manuscripts, and other manuscripts. The printed editions read: “and whitened them in the blood of the Lamb.”]

Because what is sown now through tribulation is harvested afterward as the fruit of joy, confidence strengthens the mind all the more powerfully as a stronger affliction for the sake of truth constricts it.

Hence the following is aptly added:

## CHAPTER XX

**The Same Passage.** “And, having dug deeply, you will sleep securely.”

## 37. Present Security Produces Labor for the Wicked; Present Labor Produces Security for the Good

Just as present security produces labor for the wicked, so present labor produces perpetual security for the good.

[Note: The printed editions read “present security is labor.” Gemet., Utic., several Norman manuscripts, and most manuscripts read “produces labor,” which is better.]

Thus he who said the following already knew that, having dug deeply, he would sleep securely: “For I am already being poured out, and the time of my departure is at hand. I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith. From now on the crown of righteousness is laid up for me, which the Lord, the righteous Judge, will give me on that day” (2 Tim. 4:6).

Because he had fought without failing against passing evils, he confidently anticipated joys that would remain.

## 38. Rest and Work Freed from Earthly Cares

“Having dug deeply” can also be understood in another way. Often, occupied with transitory matters, we neglect to consider how greatly we sin. But if, drawing back the eye of our reflection, the mound of earthly thought is removed from the bosom of the heart, whatever was hidden in the mind is discovered.

[Note: This is the reading of Turon., Vindoc., the Norman and English manuscripts, together with the old editions. Gilot. 1571 reads “the mound of thought opened.” Gussanv., following German manuscript evidence, reads “the field of thought.”]

Therefore holy men do not cease to search out the hiding places of their souls, carefully investigating themselves. They cast away the cares of earthly things and, when their thoughts have been completely excavated and they discover that they are gnawed by no guilt of crime, they rest securely within themselves as though on the bed of the heart.

They also desire to lie hidden from the activities of this world. They continually consider their own affairs and, when they are not at all constrained by the rein of governance, refuse to judge what belongs to others.

[Note: Turon., Longip., the Norman manuscripts, two Reg. manuscripts, Colb., Corb. Germ., and Germ. read *loro regiminis*, “the rein of governance,” rather than *loco regiminis*, “the place of governance.”]

Thus, having dug deeply, they sleep securely, because while they vigilantly penetrate their own inward parts, they hide themselves from the burdensome labors of this world in the quiet of leisure.

Hence it is further added:

## CHAPTER XXI

**Verse 19.** “You will rest, and there will be no one to terrify you.”

## 39. One Who Longs for Eternal Things Fears Nothing from the World

Whoever seeks present glory certainly fears contempt. Whoever always longs for profits naturally always fears losses. Whatever renews him by its possession wounds him, beyond doubt, by its loss; and the more he clings, bound to changeable and perishable things, the farther he lies below the stronghold of security.

But whoever is fixed solely in the desire for eternity is lifted up neither by prosperity nor shaken by adversity. While he has nothing in the world that he desires, there is nothing from the world that he fears.

Hence Solomon says: “Nothing that happens to the just will grieve him” (Prov. 12:21). Again he says: “The just person, confident like a lion, will be without terror” (Prov. 28:1).

Thus it is rightly said here: “You will rest, and there will be no one to terrify you” (Job 11:19), because each person casts away the fear that comes from the world more completely [Note: Corb. Germ., Utic., and Norman manuscripts omit *qui in mundo est* (“which is in the world”).] in proportion as he more truly conquers the world’s desire within himself.

Did Paul not rest in his heart without terror when he said: “For I am certain that neither death nor life, neither angels nor principalities, neither things present nor things to come, nor powers, nor height nor depth, nor any other creature will be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Rom. 8:38)?

The strength of this love is praised by the true voice of holy Church when it says in the Song of Songs (8:6): “Love is strong as death.”

[Note: The printed editions read *Cantica cant.*; the manuscripts read otherwise.]

Love is compared with the power of death because, once it has seized the mind, it utterly kills it with regard to the pleasure of the world; and it raises it more powerfully to the authority of God in proportion as it makes it insensible to terrors.

## [Old XXIII]

Yet amid all this it should be understood that when the wicked preach what is right, it is very difficult for them not to break out into what they secretly desire. Hence Zophar immediately adds:

## CHAPTER XXII

**The Same Passage.** “And many will entreat your face.”

## 40. The Upright Do Not Seek to Appear as Intercessors for Others

For holy men do not preserve themselves along the narrow paths of innocence in order that others may plead with them. But heretics or any perverse people, by living among human beings as though innocently, wish to appear as intercessors for others.

When they present themselves as speaking holy things, they promise others as something great what they themselves desire; and while they preach heavenly things, they suddenly reveal in their promises what they love. But lest they reveal for too long, by promising earthly things, what they are, they quickly return to words of uprightness.

Hence he immediately adds:

## CHAPTER XXIII  
### [Revised XIII]

**Verse 20.** “But the eyes of the wicked will fail, and refuge will perish from them.”

## 41. For the Wicked There Is Some Refuge from Misery Here, but None after Death

That the word “eyes” expresses the force of intention is affirmed by Truth through the Gospel, which says: “If your eye is simple, your whole body will be full of light” (Matt. 6:22). For if a pure intention precedes our action, then, however it may appear to human beings, the body of the action that follows is nevertheless shown clean in the eyes of the inward Judge.

The eyes of the wicked, therefore, are the intentions they have in their carnal desires. They fail because they neglect eternal things and always await only what is transitory.

They think about attaining earthly glory, desire to increase their temporal possessions, and move daily toward death along the course of things that pass away; but they do not know how to think mortally about mortal things. The life of the flesh declines moment by moment, yet carnal desire grows. What has been acquired is seized by its imminent end, but anxiety about possessing does not cease.

When death removes the wicked, their desires certainly end together with their life. Their eyes then fail through heavenly vengeance, because here they refused, according to their own judgment, to cease from earthly pleasure.

The Psalmist had seen the eyes of such people closed to their former enjoyment when he said: “On that day all their thoughts will perish” (Ps. 145:4), because they discover eternal evils that they never contemplated and suddenly lose the temporal goods that they had long pursued.

All refuge also perishes from them, because their wickedness finds no place where it can hide from the punishment of the strict Judge. For now, when the wicked endure some sadness or adversity, they find hiding places of refuge because they immediately retreat to the pleasure of their carnal desires.

So that poverty may not torture them, they soothe the mind with riches. So that contempt from their neighbors may not depress them, they exalt themselves through offices and honors. If bodily disgust wears them down, they nourish themselves by placing before themselves a variety of foods. If the mind is cast down by some impulse of sadness, it is soon relieved by the intervening charms of amusements.

They have as many refuges here as they prepare delights for themselves. But eventually refuge perishes from them, because, after losing everything, their mind sees only itself and the Judge. Then pleasure is taken away, but the guilt of pleasure remains; and suddenly, by perishing, the wretched learn that they held on to things destined to perish.

Nevertheless, as long as they live bodily, they do not cease seeking what will harm them. Hence it is further added:

## CHAPTER XXIV

**The Same Passage.** “And their hope will be an abomination to the soul.”

## 42. What Is Pleasure to the Wicked Is Punishment to the Just; Where the Flesh Is Refreshed, the Spirit Fails

What does the sinner hope for with all his thoughts except to surpass others in power, to exceed everyone in the abundance of his possessions, to subject opponents by domination, to become famous as an object of wonder to those who obey him, to satisfy his anger at will, to display himself as kind when praised, to offer whatever the appetite of the stomach desires, and to hasten through action toward whatever pleasure commands?

The hope of such people is rightly called an abomination to the soul, because spiritual people reject by the judgment of uprightness what carnal people pursue. For what sinners consider pleasure, the just undoubtedly consider punishment.

Hope is therefore an abomination to the soul for the wicked, because the spirit fails wherever the flesh rests. Just as the flesh is nourished by soft things, so the soul is nourished by hard things: the former is refreshed by what soothes, the latter exercised by what is harsh; the former is fed by pleasures, the latter strengthened by bitterness.

And just as harsh things wound the flesh, so soft things kill the spirit; just as laborious things destroy the flesh, so pleasurable things extinguish the spirit. [Note: In Corb. Germ., Utic., Bigot., and Lyr., the second *sicut* (“just as”) and the following *ita* (“so”) are omitted.]

The hope of the carnal is therefore called an abomination to the soul, because the spirit perishes forever from the very place where the flesh lives sweetly for a time.

## 43. What Is Correctly Said Is Often Corrupted by the Speaker’s Lack of Discernment

But Zophar would say these things correctly if blessed Job had not proclaimed all of them even more fully by his life. Yet after he attempts to admonish a holier man about his life and to instruct one more learned than himself with the teaching of wisdom, he himself lightens the weight of his words. By inserting a lack of discernment, he destroys everything he says, because he pours the liquid of knowledge over a full vessel.

Thus the wealth of knowledge is possessed by the indiscreet, just as the wealth of bodily substance is often possessed by fools. Some people who are supported by an abundance of earthly things sometimes give much even to those who already possess, so that they themselves may appear to have these things more abundantly than everyone else.

In the same way, perverse people, when they know truths, speak certain correct things even to those who are more upright—not in order to teach their hearers, but in order to make known how greatly they themselves excel in learning.

They think that they surpass everyone in wisdom and therefore consider that they say nothing to anyone beyond the measure of their own greatness. Thus any wicked people, and all heretics, do not fear teaching their betters with proud speech, because they consider everyone beneath themselves.

## [Old XXIV]

But holy Church recalls all the arrogant from the height of their self-estimation and reforms them, by the hand of discernment, into the structure of equality. Therefore blessed Job, who is a member of that same holy Church, seeing that the minds of his friends had become swollen through the words of instruction they had uttered, immediately replied, saying:

## CHAPTER XXV  
### [Old XXV]

### Chapter 12, Verse 2

“Therefore you alone are human beings, and wisdom will die with you.”

[Note: This is the reading of all the Norman and English manuscripts and of most others. Colb. reads “dwells with you.” Corb. Germ. and the old editions read “will arise.” The others read “arises.” From the Hebrew text and the Vulgate, “will die” should be read.]

[Col. 0945B] **44. The folly of one who is arrogantly wise.**—Whoever thinks that he surpasses everyone in understanding—what else does he exult in being than the only human being? And it often happens that, when the mind is carried aloft by swelling pride, it is lifted into contempt for everyone and admiration of itself. For self-favor arises in its thoughts, and folly itself flatters him concerning the singularity of his wisdom [Note: [Col. 0945D] The printed editions and many manuscripts read *blandiuntur* (“they flatter themselves”). The reading *ipsa fatuitas* (“folly itself”) is corrected with the support of the Gemetian, German, and Colbertine manuscripts. In what sense, otherwise, could self-approval be said to flatter itself? Yet folly is rightly set against wisdom in the reading we have chosen.]. It weighs what it has heard and the words it utters; it admires its own things and laughs at those of others. Therefore, whoever thinks that he alone is wise, what else does he suppose but that this same wisdom is dying with him [Note: [Col. 0945D] This is how it is read in the English manuscripts and in most of the Norman manuscripts. [Col. 0946D] In the Ebroic and Colbertine manuscripts, however, a second hand has *secum morari* (“to remain with him”); in the Corbie German manuscript, *oriri* (“to arise”).]? [Note: [Col. 0946D] One Vindocine manuscript reads: “he never admits that it is present in others”; another: “which he denies is present among others.”] For by denying that it is present in others and attributing it to himself alone, he plainly confines it within the limits of his own brief existence. We should consider, however, with how much discernment the holy man acts to restrain the arrogance of his proud friends, when he immediately adds:

**CHAPTER XXVI**

[Col. 0945C]

**VERSE 3.—“And I have a heart just as you do; I am not inferior to you.”**

**45. This arrogance must be restrained with moderation.**—For who does not know how greatly the life and knowledge of blessed Job surpassed the knowledge of his friends? Yet, in order to correct their pride, he denies that he is inferior to them; and, lest he exceed the bounds of his humility, he is silent about being superior to them. He indicates what those who are far unequal to him should learn, not by placing himself above them, but by comparing himself with them, so that, while the wisdom that excels voluntarily bends itself down, the knowledge that lies below may by no means raise itself against its strength. He soon recalls them appropriately to a sense of equality, since he considers that they are greatly swollen, as though because of their unique greatness, when he adds shortly afterward [Col. 0945D]:

**CHAPTER XXVII**

**IBID.—“For who is ignorant of these things that you know?”**

**46. By showing that the things of which they boast of knowing are unknown to no one.**—It is as though he were plainly saying: Since the things you say are known to everyone, why are you so swollen with pride over your knowledge of them? Therefore, after recalling the arrogance of the proud to fellowship in equality and rebuking it with a thorough correction, he now proceeds to doctrinal statements, so that his humbled friends might first learn the weight of truth before listening with reverence. It follows:

**CHAPTER XXVIII [Old numbering XXVI; recension XV]**

**VERSE 4.—“He who is mocked by his friend, as I am, will call upon God, and he will hear him.”**

**47. What praise harms the person acting rightly, and what ridicule benefits him. Ridicule benefits where there is no merit of guilt.**—Often a weak mind, when it catches the breeze of human approval for good actions, is carried away toward outward joys, so that it postpones what it seeks inwardly and willingly lies dissolved in what it hears outwardly; thus it rejoices not so much to be blessed as to be called blessed. And while it eagerly drinks in the words of its own praise, it abandons what it had begun to be. It is separated from God precisely where it seemed worthy of praise in God.
