Sometimes, however, the mind steadfastly supports a righteous work and is nevertheless pressed by human ridicule: it does admirable things and receives insults. The person who could have gone outward through praise, repelled by abuse, returns to himself; and the more firmly he finds no place of rest outside himself, the more strongly he establishes himself inwardly in God. For his entire hope is fixed upon his author, and amid the reproaches of ridicule he calls upon the one inward witness alone. The afflicted mind becomes as much closer to God as it is estranged from the favor of human beings. It immediately pours itself out in prayer; pressed outwardly, it is purified so as to penetrate what is within.

Thus it is rightly said here: “He who is mocked by his friend, as I am, will call upon God, and he will hear him,” because when the wicked reproach the minds of the good, they reveal whom they seek as the witness of their actions. While the mind, pricked with compunction, girds itself for prayer, it is joined inwardly to divine hearing precisely where it is separated from human praise outwardly. [Old numbering XXVII.]

It should be carefully noted how appropriately “as I am” is inserted, because some people are depressed by human ridicule and yet are not heard by divine ears. For when ridicule arises on account of guilt, no merit of virtue is produced by that ridicule. Thus the priests of Baal, who had called upon him with loud cries, were mocked by Elijah when he said: “Cry out with a louder voice, for he is a god, and perhaps he is talking, or is in an inn” (3 Kings 18:27). But this ridicule of them did not serve virtue, because it arose from the guilt they deserved. Therefore it is appropriately said here: “He who is mocked by his friend, as I am, will call upon God, and he will hear him,” because human ridicule brings close to God the person whom the innocence of his life keeps alien from human wickedness. It follows:

**CHAPTER XXIX [Recension XVI]**

[Col. 0947A]

**IBID.—“For the simplicity of the just is mocked.”**

**48. What the wisdom of this world is; what the wisdom of the righteous is; why it is mocked by the world.**—The wisdom of this world is to conceal the heart beneath schemes, to veil one’s meaning with words, to present false things as true, and to demonstrate true things as deception. This prudence is learned by young people through practice; children learn it at a price. Those who know it grow proud by looking down on others; those who do not know it, being submissive and fearful, admire it in others, because they love this same duplicity of wickedness, disguised under the name of refinement, while perversity of mind is called courtesy.

It commands those who obey it to seek the heights of honors, to rejoice in the vanity of temporal glory once attained, and to repay evils inflicted by others many times over. When strength is available, it commands them to yield to no one who resists; when the capacity for virtue is lacking, it commands them to feign in peaceful goodness whatever they cannot accomplish through malice [Note: [Col. 0947D] Coccius and later editions read *valent* (“they are able”); the manuscripts have *valet* (“it is able”), which refers to worldly prudence.].

By contrast, the wisdom of the righteous is to invent nothing for display, to disclose one’s meaning in words, to love truths as they are, to avoid falsehoods, to offer good freely, and to endure evils more willingly than to inflict them; to seek no vengeance for injury, and to consider suffering abuse for the truth a gain [Note: [Col. 0947D] In the Utica, Lyran, Bigotian, and Vindocine manuscripts: “to regard suffering abuse as a gain.”].

But this simplicity of the righteous is mocked, because the virtue of purity is considered folly by the wise of this world. Everything done innocently is undoubtedly regarded by them as foolish; and whatever truth approves in action sounds foolish to carnal wisdom.

For what seems more foolish to the world than to reveal one’s mind in words, to feign nothing through cunning schemes, to return no insults for injuries, to pray for those who curse, to seek poverty, to abandon one’s possessions, not to resist one who robs, and to offer the other cheek to one who strikes? Hence that outstanding wise man of God rightly says to lovers of this world: “We shall sacrifice the abominations of the Egyptians to the Lord our God” (Exodus 8:26). The Egyptians disdain eating sheep; but what the Egyptians abhor, the Israelites offer to God, because the simplicity of conscience—which all the unjust despise as lowly and worthless—the righteous turn into a sacrifice of virtue. Cultivating upright purity and gentleness, they offer to God what the reprobate, in their abhorrence, consider folly.

This simplicity of the righteous is expressed briefly but sufficiently when it immediately adds:

**CHAPTER XXX [Old numbering XXVIII; recension XVII]**

[Col. 0947D]

**VERSE 5.—“A lamp despised in the thoughts of the rich.”**

**49. Possessing riches is not a crime, but coveting them is.**—What is signified here by the name “rich,” unless it is the pride of the arrogant, who do not regard the coming Judge while they swell with proud thoughts within themselves? For there are some whom wealth does not lift up through pride but exalts through works of mercy [Note: [Col. 0947D] This is absent from the Bellovacense manuscript. It is found in the Vindocine, Tours, Corbie German, Colbertine, German, and most other manuscripts, from which Coccius and later editions corrected the text; in those editions the reading is: “but exalts through works of mercy.”].

And there are some who, when they see themselves abounding in earthly resources, do not seek the true riches of God and do not love the eternal homeland, because they think that the support of temporal goods is sufficient for them. Wealth, therefore, is not the crime; attachment is.

Everything God created is good. But the person who uses good things badly acts like one who, through gluttonous excess, dies from the very bread by which he ought to have lived. Lazarus the poor man had come to rest, while the proud rich man was tormented (Luke 16:26). Yet Abraham, who held Lazarus in his bosom, had been rich; nevertheless, speaking with his Creator, he said: “I will speak to my Lord, though I am dust and ashes” (Genesis 18:27). How, then, did this man know how to value his riches, when he considered himself dust and ashes? Or when could possessions have lifted him up, when he thought so humbly even of himself, their possessor?

**50. Those who lack riches but swell with arrogance are counted rich; they despise those who scorn the world.**—Again, there are some who have no earthly resources, yet are lifted up within themselves by the swelling of arrogance. Wealth does not raise them up for the display of power, yet the insolence of their behavior places them among the rich in the company of the reprobate. Whoever, therefore, is not humbled by love of the life to come, sacred Scripture calls “rich” in this passage, because in the punishment of judgment it makes no difference whether they swell with possessions or merely with their character [Note: [Col. 0948D] The Ebroic and other Norman manuscripts read: “because in the punishment of judgment it makes no difference whether they swell with possessions or merely with character.” The Vindocine, German, and Corbie German manuscripts also had this reading before it was corrected.].

When such people see the life of the simple in this world as humble and lowly, they immediately mock it with lofty contempt. They do not consider that the simple possess outwardly what they themselves eagerly seek with all their efforts. They despise as fools those who do not possess the things for which they themselves perish, whether by possessing them or merely by loving them [Note: [Col. 0948D] This is the reading of the Tours, Vindocine, Longpont, Corbie, and Norman manuscripts, together with the old editions. Later editions preferred: “whether by possessing them or merely by admiring them.”]; and they count as dead those whom they do not think live carnally with them. For whoever dies to the desires of this world is considered wholly extinguished by earthly minds.

This is aptly signified by the miracle of our Redeemer when he frees a man from an unclean spirit, of whom it is written: “Crying out and greatly convulsing him, it went out of him; and he became like a dead man, so that many said, ‘He is dead.’ But Jesus, taking him by the hand, lifted him up, and he arose” (Mark 9:25). The person liberated from the power of the evil spirit is shown as though dead, because whoever now subdues earthly desires extinguishes within himself the life of carnal conduct. He appears dead to the world because he no longer has that wicked possessor who was driving him through unclean desires. Many call him dead because those who do not know how to live spiritually consider extinguished the person who does not pursue carnal goods.

[Old numbering XXIX.] **51. The righteous, without light in the eyes of the carnal, burn and shine before God.**—But because the mockers of the simple are themselves also counted as Christians, they are restrained by religious reverence and are ashamed to display evil through public ridicule. Thus they mock inwardly and silently those whom they consider exceedingly low and despised because of their simplicity.

Accordingly it is rightly said: “A lamp despised in the thoughts of the rich,” because the proud, unable—as we said above—to appreciate the good things to come [Note: [Col. 0949D] The Vindocine, Norman, and many other manuscripts read: “do not wish to.” In the Utica manuscript, however, the earlier reading was “do not know.”], value almost nothing in the person whom they do not see possessing what they love.

It often happens that an elect person who is being led to eternal happiness is continually weighed down by adversity here: abundance of possessions does not support him; the glory of honors does not make him appear worthy of respect; no crowd of attendants surrounds him; no display of clothing adorns him in human eyes. He is seen as contemptible by everyone and considered unworthy of the favor of this world [Note: [Col. 0949D] This is the reading of the Bellovacense, Vindocine, Gemetian, and other manuscripts, together with the older editions. The later editors preferred “the glory of the world.”].

Yet before the eyes of the hidden Judge he shines with virtues and glitters with the merits of his life. He fears being honored and does not shrink from being despised. He disciplines his body through self-restraint and grows rich in soul through love alone. He continually prepares his mind for patience; upright for justice, he rejoices in the insults he has received; he feels compassion from the heart for the afflicted and rejoices in the prosperity of the good as though it were his own. He carefully ruminates the nourishment of sacred Scripture in his mind [Note: [Col. 0949D] The Utica, Ebroic, Corbie, and other Norman manuscripts read: “he ruminates it with greater diligence.”], and when questioned, he is doubly ignorant of how to say anything whatever.

Thus the simplicity of the righteous is rightly called both a lamp and despised. A lamp, because it shines inwardly; despised, because it does not shine outwardly. Within, the flame of charity burns; outside, no glory of appearance gleams. He therefore shines and is despised [Note: [Col. 0949D] The Gemetian manuscript reads: “who, fragrant with virtues, is considered despised.”]—he who, aflame with virtues, is regarded as lowly. For carnal minds cannot value good things unless they see them carnally.

Hence David’s own father had despised the holy man and refused to present him to the eyes of the prophet Samuel. When he had brought seven sons for anointing and the prophet asked whether he had completed the number of his children, he replied in great despair: “There remains a little boy who is tending the sheep” (1 Samuel 16:10–11) [Note: [Col. 0950D] The Tours, Vindocine, Longpont, Norman, and Corbie German manuscripts read this way. The later edition has *despectione* (“with contempt”). Immediately afterward, instead of *est adhuc puer* (“there is still a boy”), it adds *adhuc* (“still”).]. When this son had been brought and chosen, Samuel immediately heard: “Man looks on the face, but God searches the heart” (ibid., 7) [Note: [Col. 0950D] We follow the manuscripts, leaving aside the printed editions, which read “God looks upon.”]. David, therefore, had been a lamp through his innocence, but he was greatly despised [Col. 0949D], because he did not shine for those who looked only upon outward things.

It should be known, moreover, that every righteous person either does not possess temporal glory or breaks it beneath himself if he possesses it, so that he may rise freely above his honor and not succumb to the pleasure of being sustained by it. Hence that outstanding preacher had humbled the glory of his apostleship before human eyes when he said: “We did not use this authority, although we could have been a burden as apostles of Christ, but we became little ones in your midst” (1 Thessalonians 2:7).

The swelling of the rich still remained in the hearts of his hearers, since they said: “His letters are weighty and strong, but his bodily presence is weak, and his speech contemptible” (2 Corinthians 10:10). They judged that one who could write such things could not live among them. When they saw him humble in his way of life yet lofty in his speech, their own pride compelled them to despise through his spoken presence the one whom they had feared through his writings.

What, then, was Paul if not a lamp despised in the thoughts of the rich? From the very place where he displayed the instruction of humility, he received insults of pride from uneducated disciples. For in a dreadful manner the sickness of the proud grew from the place where it ought to have subsided, when the elevated mind of the carnal rejected as contemptible what the teacher had shown to be worthy of imitation.

Was he not a despised lamp, shining with so many virtues yet enduring such great adversities from persecutors (Ephesians 6:20)? He performs an embassy in chains, and his bonds are made known throughout the whole praetorium; he is beaten with rods and pressed by many dangers, from his own people and from the Gentiles (Philippians 1:13; 2 Corinthians 11:26). He is struck with stones at Lystra and dragged outside the city, because he is considered dead.

But how long is this lamp despised? How long is it regarded as contemptible [Note: [Col. 0950D] The earlier reading was: “Does it not at all bring forth its radiance?” The double negation, *non* and *nullatenus*, gave an entirely opposite meaning.]? Does it never bring forth its radiance or show with what brilliance it shines? It certainly does. For when it was said, “A lamp despised in the thoughts of the rich,” it immediately adds:

**CHAPTER XXXI**

[Col. 0950C]

**IBID.—“Prepared for the appointed time.”**

**52. The righteous, despised here, will shine on the day of judgment.**—The appointed time of the despised lamp is the foreordained day of the final judgment, when it will be shown with what power each righteous person who is now despised shines. Then those who are now unjustly judged on God’s behalf will come as judges with God. Their light will shine more broadly in proportion as the hand of their persecutors now constrains them more harshly. Then it will become clear to the eyes of the reprobate that those who voluntarily abandoned all earthly things were supported by heavenly power.

Therefore Truth says to his elect: “You who have followed me, in the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, you also will sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matthew 19:28). That council of the inner court will not have more than twelve judges; rather, the number twelve expresses the totality of the whole. Whoever, stirred by the impulse of divine love, has left behind his possessions here will undoubtedly obtain there the height of judicial power, so that the one who now disciplines himself through voluntary poverty in consideration of judgment may then come as judge together with the Judge.

Hence Solomon says concerning the Bridegroom of holy Church: “Her husband is noble in the gates, when he sits among the elders of the land” (Proverbs 31:23). Hence Isaiah says: “The Lord will come to judgment with the elders of his people” (Isaiah 3:14). Hence Truth declares that these elders are no longer servants but friends, saying: “I no longer call you servants, but my friends” (John 15:15). Looking upon them, the Psalmist says: “But to me your friends, O God, are exceedingly honored” (Psalm 138:17). When he saw the loftiness of their hearts, he immediately added how they trample upon the world’s glory: “Their rule has been exceedingly strengthened.” And lest we think that those whom we recognize as advancing toward the summit of such perfection are few, he at once added: “I shall count them, and they shall be multiplied above the sand.”

Therefore, as many as now willingly humble themselves for love of the truth, so many lamps will then blaze in judgment. Let it rightly be said: “A lamp despised in the thoughts of the rich, prepared for the appointed time,” because each righteous soul is despised as rejected when, living below, it possesses no glory, but is seen as marvelous when it shines from above.

**53. Christ is the lamp despised here.**—In the midst of these reflections, let us lift the eyes of our mind toward the ways of the Redeemer and gradually pass from the members to the head. He truly became a lamp for us: dying on the cross for our redemption, he poured light through the wood into our darkened minds.

John had seen us illuminated by this lamp when he said: “He was the true light, which enlightens every [Note: [Col. 0951D] We include the words *venientem in hunc mundum* (“coming into this world”) with the manuscripts; in their place, the older editions have a note and so forth. In the more recent editions even this note has been suppressed.] person coming into this world” (John 1:9). Yet he saw this lamp despised in the thoughts of the rich when he added shortly afterward: “He came to his own, and his own did not receive him” (ibid., 11).

Herod wished to investigate the flames of this lamp when he desired to see his miracles, as it is written: “For he had long desired to see him, because he had heard many things about him, and he hoped to see some sign performed by him” (Luke 23:8). But this lamp emitted no ray of light before Herod’s eyes, because he who had sought him not devoutly but out of curiosity showed him nothing marvelous about himself.

When questioned, the Redeemer remained silent; when expected, he declined to perform miracles. Keeping himself hidden in his own secret places, he left outside, ungrateful, those whom he discovered to be seeking outward things, choosing rather to be openly despised by the proud than to be praised with empty words by unbelievers. Hence this lamp was immediately despised, as the passage continues: “Herod, with his soldiers, despised him and mocked him, clothing him in a white robe” (ibid., 11).

[Old numbering XXXI.] **54. It will flash forth on the last day.**—The despised lamp, which endures ridicule on earth, flashes forth judgment from heaven [Note: [Col. 0951D] This is the reading of the first Vindocine, German, and Corbie manuscripts. All the Norman manuscripts and the second Vindocine have “flashes forth from heaven through judgment,” followed by the printed editions, which add “more brightly.” Here *coruscat* is used actively, as in the purer Latin writers one says *coruscare mucronem* or *telum* (“to brandish a sword” or “a weapon”), that is, to vibrate or shake.]. Hence this is appropriately added: “Prepared for the appointed time.” Concerning that time the Psalmist says: “When I receive the appointed time, I will judge with righteousness” (Psalm 74:3). Hence Truth himself announces in the Gospel: “My time has not yet come” (John 7:6). Hence Peter says: “Whom heaven must receive until the times of restoration” (Acts 3:21).

The lamp that is now despised is therefore prepared to come at the appointed time, because the one who now bears the mockery of sinners is himself the one who judges sins on the last day. And then he exercises his severity more harshly in proportion as he now spreads forth his patience more gently while calling sinners. For the one who waits a long time for people to be converted torments the unconverted without reconsideration.

Through the prophet he briefly indicates this, saying: “I have been silent; I have always kept still; I have been patient; like a woman in labor I will cry out” (Isaiah 42:14). As we have already said, a woman in labor expels with pain what she has carried within for a long time. Thus the one who has always been silent speaks like a woman in labor: the coming Judge, who has long endured human deeds without vengeance, will at last reveal, with the fervor of examination and as though with anguish of mind, how severe a sentence he has held within.

Let no one, therefore, despise this lamp while it lies hidden, lest it consume its despisers when it shines from heaven. For the person whom it does not now burn toward pardon will then undoubtedly burn toward punishment. Since, then, through heavenly grace we have been granted the time of our calling, while opportunity still remains, let us flee the anger of the one who is everywhere by changing our conduct for the better. That punishment finds no one except the person whom correction has concealed.

**55. With the Lord’s generosity, let this suffice for what we have traversed in two volumes [Note: [Col. 0952D] Here and at the beginning of the following book, *corpus* means a codex: a collection of several volumes or books bound together into one. Above, in the letter to Leander, we saw: “I completed this work in six codices.” The same meaning is conveyed by *part* in the preface to the following book: “I explained why I have entrusted the third part of this work,” and so on.]. Since we cannot briefly explain the remainder of the sacred book, which embraces an extensive sequence of mysteries and virtues, it is necessary to reserve it for other volumes, so that the reader may return to the study of reading with greater eagerness, the more he refreshes himself through an interruption in reading [Note: [Col. 0952D] The Corbie and German manuscripts read *incisione* (“by a cutting off”); the Corbie German reads *intercessione* (“by an intermission”), which may perhaps signify a cessation or suspension.].

**Part Three, CONSISTING OF SIX BOOKS**

[Col. 0953]

**BOOK ELEVEN.** In this book chapter twelve, from verse six, chapter thirteen, and the first four verses of chapter fourteen are expounded, with the style somewhat changed.

**CHAPTER ONE**

[Col. 0953A]

**1. What is to be expounded throughout this entire third part, and in what style.**—Although a change of style ought not to be blameworthy in an extended work, nevertheless, lest anyone reproach me for altering my manner of expression, I explained in the letter prefixed to the books [Note: [Col. 0953D] The Tours, Ebroic, Utica, and other manuscripts read: “I gave the reasons.” The Sagiensis codex has: “The letter prefixed to the books gave the explanation.” In the other Norman manuscripts we read: “In the letter of the book that I prefixed, I gave the reasons.” He is speaking of his letter to Leander, prefixed to the *Moralia*.] why I did not bring the third part of this work, by correction, into complete conformity with the others.

Apart from these considerations, there is also the fact that the exposition of this part begins with the verse: “The tents of robbers abound,” and proceeds by discussion as far as what is written: “Their sweetness is that of worms” [Note: [Col. 0953D] The Bajocian, Ebroic, Lyran, Bigotian, and other manuscripts read: “their sweetness is that of worms.”]. These matters are so numerous that they could not be contained in one volume unless they were expressed with great brevity.

Therefore, whoever is free from other activities should read the rest, which is expressed in fuller form. But whoever lacks the leisure for careful reading may find this part’s brevity pleasing, since here we indicate not so much what we think as what must be said [Note: [Col. 0953D] This is the reading of the English manuscripts and ours, not, as in the printed editions, “whoever calls …”].

Since, then, I have left much in this part just as it was taken down while I spoke, receive this change of style with equanimity, my reader, because variety in preparation pleases even those who eat the same foods repeatedly. But whenever you take up the individual sections for reading, always strive to recall the origin of the subject that I set forth [Note: [Col. 0953D] Most manuscripts read *quam praeposui* (“which I set forth”), rather than *quam proposui* (“which I proposed”).]. For through blessed Job, who is said to be suffering, the sufferings of the Lord and of his body—that is, holy Church—are signified; and his friends represent heretics, who, as we have often said (especially in the preface, chapter 6, section 15), while trying to defend God, offend him.

While pretending to offer counsel, they gravely afflict the minds of the saints. Yet they do not stray from knowledge of the truth in everything they say; rather, they often mix wisdom with folly and truth with pretense [Note: [Col. 0954D] We have restored this from our manuscripts; previously the reading was “and prudence with fools.”], so that, while they advance something from the truth, they may more easily draw people into falsehood. Hence the things spoken by the friends of blessed Job are sometimes contemptible and sometimes marvelous. The holy man nevertheless sometimes refutes them by rejecting them, and sometimes accepts them by approving them; he even turns to the service of uprightness those things that they express rightly, though not rightly intended.

Thus he despises those who despise his poverty and, though his body is placed on a dungheap, shows how great is the height of virtues on which he sits within himself, when he declares that the riches of the present life are nothing, though he says that the reprobate abound in them:

**CHAPTER TWO [Old numbering I; recension II]**

**Chapter 12, verse 6.—“The tents of robbers abound, and they boldly provoke God, though he has given everything into their hands” [Note: [Col. 0954D] The Norman and many other manuscripts read: “everything into their hands.”].**

**2. How greatly contempt for riches shines forth in Job.**—It is easy for a person to despise riches when he possesses them; it is difficult to consider them worthless when he does not possess them. It is therefore plainly shown how great was the contempt for earthly things in the thought of blessed Job, who declares that the things in which the reprobate abound are nothing precisely when he has lost everything. He says, therefore: “The tents of robbers abound, and they boldly provoke God,” because the wicked are often more proud against God the more they are enriched by his generosity contrary to their merit; those who ought to have been summoned by gifts toward better things become worse through the gifts.

**3. What the wicked do unjustly, God justly permits to happen.**—We must understand, however, how they are called “robbers,” when it is immediately added: “Though he has given everything into their hands.” If they are robbers, they have taken things by force, and there is no doubt that God is not the helper of those who use violence. How, then, does he give what those who are robbers wickedly seize?

We must know that one thing is what almighty God mercifully bestows, and another is what, in anger, almighty God permits to be possessed. What robbers do perversely, the most just steward permits to happen only justly: the person permitted to rob may, blinded in mind, increase his guilt, while the person who suffers robbery may be punished by the loss of that same robbery for another fault previously committed.

For behold, someone stationed in a ravine of a mountain lies in wait for travelers [Note: [Col. 0954D] The Bajocian, Sagiensis, and nearly all the Norman manuscripts read: “at the summit of the mountain.” The Utica manuscript represents both readings. The summit of a mountain does not always signify its peak or highest part; see Numbers 21:20, and consult the commentators on that passage.]. But perhaps the traveler had at some time committed certain iniquities, and almighty God, repaying him his evil in the present life and handing him over to the robber’s hands, permits him either to be stripped of his goods or even to be killed.

What the robber unjustly sought, the most just Judge justly permitted to happen, so that the one might receive what he had unjustly done, while the other might at some time be punished more severely, since through his most wicked will almighty God had justly avenged guilt upon another. The one who is oppressed is purified; the guilt of the one who oppresses is increased, so that he may either one day return from the depths of wickedness to repentance or, if he does not return, be struck by eternal condemnation all the more severely because he was long tolerated in his iniquity.

Thus mercy is shown toward the one, so that he may end his sin; severity is shown toward the other, so that his sin may multiply unless he turns to repentance. In the one, evils are purged while he endures violence; in the other, they are heaped up while he inflicts it. Therefore, what almighty God forbids to be done, it is just for him to permit to be done, so that, from the very thing for which he now waits and in which he long tolerates the unconverted, he may one day strike more severely.

It is therefore rightly said: “The tents of robbers abound, and they boldly provoke God, though he has given everything into their hands,” because what the wicked seize is given to them by the one who could have resisted their robbery, had he wished to show mercy.

[Old numbering II.] **4. Those who grow proud over God’s gifts are robbers.**—This may also be understood of spiritual things. Often some people receive gifts of teaching, but swell with pride because of those same gifts and wish to appear greater than others. To provoke almighty God is to grow proud among one’s neighbors because of his gifts.

They are also rightly called robbers, because, while they speak what they do not practice, they take the words of the righteous for use in their own speech. But since divine grace itself grants them these words, while leaving their lives in wicked conduct, they are robbers in themselves, yet the good things they possess they have received from God. It follows:

**VERSES 7 AND 8.—“Indeed, ask the beasts, and they will teach you; the birds of the sky, and they will tell you. Speak to the earth, and it will answer you, and the fish of the sea will narrate to you.”**

**CHAPTER THREE**

368 **5. What is signified by the beasts and the birds of the sky, and by the earth and the fish of the sea.**—What should we understand by “the beasts” except those slower in understanding, and by “the birds of the sky” except those who know lofty and sublime things? For concerning beasts—that is, those slower in understanding—it is written: “Your animals will dwell in it” (Psalm 67:11). And because those who know sublime things soar upward in the words of our Redeemer, it is written: “So that the birds of the sky come and dwell in its branches” (Matthew 13:32).

What, then, should we understand by “the earth” except those who know earthly things? Hence it was said to the first man when he abandoned heavenly things: “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Genesis 3:19). What should we understand by “the fish of the sea” except the curious people of this age? Concerning them the Psalmist says: “The fish of the sea, which traverse the paths of the sea” (Psalm 8:9). They lie hidden, as it were, in concealed waves amid their great investigations of things.

But what all these things, once questioned, teach, he adds by saying:

**CHAPTER FOUR**

**VERSE 9.—“Who does not know that the hand of the Lord has made all these things?”**
6. All things proclaim God the Creator.---As though he were plainly saying: Whether you seek those slower in understanding, those wise in sublime matters, those devoted to earthly activities, or those occupied with the investigations of this world, all these confess God, the Creator of all, and agree in their judgment concerning his power, [Note: [Col. 0955D] The Sagiensis reads: “although they do not live in agreement under him,” and so forth.] although they do not live in agreement under that power. For what every just person declares even by living, the unjust is often compelled to confess about God by voice alone; and thus the wicked serve as a testimony to the author of all, whom they resist by their deeds, [Note: [Col. 0956D] The same codex reads: “serve as a testimony.”] because they cannot deny him as the Creator of all, though they have dared to oppose him by their conduct.

This may also profitably be understood according to the mere outward sense of the letter, because every observed creature seems to give the voice of its own testimony by the very form that it possesses. We inquire about animals, birds, earth, or fish when we consider what they answer us in agreement: that the Lord made all things. For when they place their forms before our eyes, they testify that they did not come into being from themselves. [Note: [Col. 0956D] All the Norman witnesses read: “for by the very fact that they are creatures.”] By the very fact that they have been created, they return to their Creator, through the form displayed before us, something like a voice of confession; and because he established all things, he also determined how they should be governed. Hence it follows:

## CHAPTER V [Old and Revised III]

**VERSE 10.**---In whose hand is the soul of every living thing, and the spirit of all human flesh.

7. He who granted being to what did not exist provided how what now exists should be. The spirit of a human being is understood in two ways.---By “hand,” power is expressed. The soul, therefore, of every living thing, and the spirit of all human flesh, is in the power of him from whom it exists, so that he may provide how that which he granted to exist, though it had not existed before, should be.

The life of animals, however, may be signified by “the soul of every living thing.” Almighty God gives the soul of animals life as far as bodily sensation, but extends the human spirit as far as spiritual understanding. Thus the soul of every living thing and the spirit of all human flesh are in his hand: in the one case he grants the soul to vivify the flesh, and in the other he vivifies the soul so that it may attain to understanding eternity.

It should be known, moreover, that in sacred Scripture “spirit” is customarily used in two ways. Sometimes “spirit” means the soul; sometimes it means a spiritual effect. It means the soul, for example, where it is written concerning our very Head: “He bowed his head and gave up his spirit” (John 19:30). For if the Evangelist had meant something other than the soul by “spirit,” then, when the spirit departed, the soul would have remained. [The manuscript numbering resumes at 369.]

“Spirit” also means a spiritual effect, as it is written: “He makes his angels spirits, and his ministers a burning fire” (Psalm 103:4). For angels—that is, messengers—are sometimes called preachers in sacred Scripture, as it is said through the prophet: “The lips of the priest guard knowledge, and they seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts” (Malachi 2:7). Almighty God therefore makes his angels spirits because he makes his preachers spiritual.

In this passage, if “the soul of every living thing” signifies bodily life itself, “the spirit of all human flesh” expresses the effect of spiritual understanding. It continues:

## CHAPTER VI [Revised IV]

[Col. 0957B]

**VERSE 11.**---Does not the ear discern words, and the palate of one who eats, taste?

8. The diverse gifts and diverse modes of indwelling belonging to one and the same wisdom.---Almost no one is unaware that the five senses of our body—sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch—draw from the brain the power of discernment and sensation for everything they perceive and distinguish. Although there is one judge, the sense of the brain, presiding within, it distinguishes the five senses through their proper channels, God working wondrously so that the eye does not hear, the ear does not see, the mouth does not smell, [Note: [Col. 0957D] Thus Bellov. and the Norman and old editions. In Gussanv. it reads: “nor does the nose act, nor the hand taste.”] the nostrils do not taste, and the hands do not smell.

Although everything is administered through the one sense of the brain, each of these senses nevertheless cannot perform anything other than what it received from the Creator’s arrangement. From these bodily and external realities, therefore, we must gather interior and spiritual realities, so that through what is publicly evident in us we may pass to the secret reality within us, which is hidden even from ourselves.

[Old IV.] We must observe that although wisdom is one, it dwells in one person less and in another more; it grants this to one and that to another; and, as the brain does, it uses us as though we were various senses, so that although it is never unlike itself, it nevertheless always performs diverse and dissimilar works through us. Thus one receives the gift of wisdom, another of knowledge; one has kinds of tongues, another the grace of healings.

9. The wicked hear the words of wisdom alone; the elect also taste them.---In these words blessed Job—“The ear discerns words, and the palate of one who eats, taste”—seems also to suggest something concerning the elect and the reprobate. The words of wisdom, which the reprobate hear, the elect not only hear but also taste, so that what sounds only in the ears of the reprobate becomes inwardly savory to the heart of the elect.

It is one thing merely to hear the name of food, and another actually to taste it. The elect therefore hear the food of wisdom in such a way that they taste it, because what they hear becomes savory to them in their inmost being through love. The knowledge of the reprobate, however, extends only to recognition of the sound, so that they hear virtues but, with cold hearts, do not know how they taste. In these words blessed Job rebukes the ignorance of his friends and the arrogance of those who are puffed up by the teaching of wisdom, because it is one thing to know something about God, and another to taste at the palate of understanding what one knows. [Note: [Col. 0957D] The same witness reads: “to taste at the palate of understanding.”]

It is therefore rightly said: “Does not the ear discern words, and the palate of one who eats, taste?” As though he were plainly saying to the arrogant: “The words of teaching, which reach your ears, touch even the palate of my understanding through inward taste.”

But because an immature age, even when it has sound judgment, ought not rashly to rush into preaching, it is rightly added:

## CHAPTER VII

**VERSE 12.**---370 In the aged there is wisdom, and in length of days understanding.

10. Wisdom is confirmed by the practice and experience of life.---Those sayings are firmly rooted in wisdom which are strengthened through the practice of living and by the experience of deeds. But because a long life is granted to many without the grace of wisdom being bestowed, it is rightly shown further in whose judgment these gifts depend, when it follows:

## CHAPTER VIII

**VERSE 13.**---With him are wisdom and strength; he has counsel and understanding.

11. Christ is the wisdom and strength of God.---We may appropriately understand this of the Only-Begotten of the supreme Father, so that we recognize him as the wisdom and strength of God. Paul also bears witness to this understanding of ours, saying: “Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:24). He is with God always, because “in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1).

God has counsel and understanding: counsel, namely, because he orders his own affairs; understanding, because he knows ours.

[Old V.] By “counsel” the delay of hidden judgment itself may also be signified, so that when he strikes sinners only later, this does not mean that the guilt of the wicked is unseen, but that the sentence of their condemnation, which is deferred so that they may do penance, seems to proceed slowly from his counsel. [Note: [Col. 0958D] The Turon. reads: “the delay of hidden judgment itself may be signified.”] What is at some time revealed outwardly as an open sentence was hidden with the almighty Lord in his counsel before the ages. It continues:

## CHAPTER IX [Revised V]

[Col. 0958D]

**VERSE 14.**---If he destroys, no one can build; if he shuts a man in, no one can open.

12. God destroys the human mind by departing from it. One who acts wickedly makes his conscience a prison.---Almighty God destroys the human heart when he abandons it, and builds it when he fills it. He does not destroy the human mind by waging war against it, but by departing from it, because a mind left to itself is sufficient for its own destruction.

Thus it often happens that when the heart of a hearer, because of its deserving sins, is not filled with the grace of almighty God, it is warned outwardly by a preacher in vain. Every mouth that speaks is mute if he who inspires the words heard does not cry inwardly in the heart. Hence the prophet says: “Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain” (Psalm 126:1). Hence Solomon says: “Consider the works of God, that no one can correct him whom he has rejected” (Ecclesiastes 7:14).

It is no wonder if the preacher is scarcely heard by a reprobate heart, since sometimes the Lord himself is opposed in what he says by the conduct of those who resist. Thus Cain could be admonished by the divine voice but could not be changed, because, as the guilt of his wickedness demanded, God had already abandoned his heart within, while outwardly he addressed it with words of testimony.

It is rightly added: “If he shuts a man in, no one can open.” For by what he does wickedly, what else does every person make for himself but a prison of his conscience, so that guilt of mind oppresses him even if no one accuses him outwardly? When, by God’s judgment, he is left in the blindness of his wickedness, he is shut up, as it were, within himself, so that he cannot find a place of escape—a place he scarcely deserves to find.

Often some wish to leave their wicked actions, but because they are weighed down by the burden of those same actions, shut up in the prison of evil habit, they cannot escape from themselves. Some, wishing to punish their own faults, turn into more serious sins what they think they are doing rightly. [Note: [Col. 0959D] Vindoc., the Norman witnesses, and most others read: “turn into more serious sins”; Turon. reads: “turn into more serious sins.”] In a wretched manner, what they think is an exit becomes an imprisonment.

Thus the reprobate Judas, when he brought death upon himself against his sin (Matthew 27:5), reached the punishments of eternal death, [The manuscript numbering resumes at 371.] and repented of his sin more wickedly than he had sinned.

13. No one resists God when he calls; no one confronts him when he abandons.---Let it therefore be said: “If he shuts a man in, no one can open,” because just as no one opposes the generosity of him who calls, so no one confronts the justice of him who abandons.

To shut a person in is therefore God’s act of not opening what has been closed. Hence God says to Moses concerning Pharaoh: “I will harden his heart” (Exodus 4:21; 7:3). God is said to harden through justice when he does not soften a reprobate heart by grace. He therefore shuts in the person whom he leaves amid the darkness of his works.

[Old VI.] [Note: [Col. 0959D] We have restored this from manuscripts and old editions. In later editions, *cum* is corruptly redundant in the phrase: “For Isaac wished, as it were, to open this confinement for his firstborn son.”] For Isaac wished, as it were, to open this confinement for his firstborn son when he attempted to place him before his brother by blessing him (Genesis 27:5). But the Lord rejected the son whom the father desired, and the father, even against his will, blessed the one whom the Lord desired (ibid. 25:34), so that the one who had already sold his birthright to his brother for food would not receive the blessing of the firstborn—a blessing he had abandoned out of appetite for food. He had sought earthly things, pursued what passes away, and desired to inherit the blessing, yet he was rejected.

For he found no place for repentance, although he sought it with tears, because laments do not bear fruit when they strive with groaning to desire things that are perishing. Isaac therefore could not open the prison even for his son, whom almighty God had shut in by a just judgment in the prison of his wickedness. It continues:

## CHAPTER X [Revised VI]

**VERSE 15.**---If he withholds the waters, all things dry up; if he lets them loose, they overturn the earth.

14. When preaching or grace is withdrawn, the heart dries up.--- [Note: [Col. 0960D] Turon. reads: “if we understand the waters as knowledge of preaching.” Sag. and several Norman witnesses read: “if we understand water as knowledge of preaching.”] If water is understood as the knowledge of preaching, as it is written: “Deep water is words from the mouth of a man, and a flowing torrent, a fountain of wisdom” (Proverbs 18:4), then, when the water is held back, all things dry up. For if the knowledge of preachers is withdrawn, the hearts of those who could have grown green in hope of eternity immediately wither, remaining in hopeless dryness while, loving what passes away, they do not know how to hope for what endures. [Note: [Col. 0960D] Another witness reads: “an overflowing torrent.”]

But if the grace of the Holy Spirit is designated by the name “waters,” as the Truth says in the Gospel: “Whoever believes in me, as the Scripture says, rivers of living water will flow from his belly” (John 7:38–39)—and the Evangelist immediately added, “He said this about the Spirit, whom those who believed in him were going to receive”—then the appropriate meaning of these words is clear: “If he withholds the waters, all things dry up.” For if the grace of the Holy Spirit is withdrawn from the mind of the hearer, the understanding immediately dries up, although it had seemed already to grow green in the hearer through hope. [Note: [Col. 0960D] Vindoc. reads: “to grow green.”]

The text speaks not of “water” but of “waters”; by this plural expression it returns to the sevenfold grace of spiritual gifts, since each person is flooded, as it were, by as many waters as he is filled with gifts. Concerning these it appropriately adds: “If he lets them loose, they overturn the earth.”

15. When grace breathes upon it, the earthly-minded heart is overturned and changed.---For what is meant by “earth” except the sinner, to whom it was said in the sentence: “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Genesis 3:19)? The earth therefore remains unmoved when the sinner refuses to obey the Lord’s commands, raises the neck of pride, and closes the eyes of his mind to the light of truth.

But because it is written: “His feet stood, and the earth was moved” (Habakkuk 3:6, according to the Septuagint), when truth is fixed in the heart the immobility of the mind is shaken. If the grace of the Holy Spirit is poured out by heavenly gift, in accordance with the preacher’s voice, the earth is immediately overturned, because the hardness of the sinful mind is changed from its obstinate immobility. It then subjects itself in tears to the Lord’s commands as much as, in its pride, it had previously raised the neck of its heart against the Lord.

You may see that the earth of the human heart, once flooded with the water of divine gift, afterward gladly tolerates insults that it had previously inflicted with violence; afterward gives away its own possessions, which it had previously seized from others; afterward crucifies the flesh by abstinence, although previously it had flowed into deadly shamefulness through the pleasures of bodily indulgence; and afterward loves even its persecutors, although previously it had refused to love those who loved it.

[Old VII.] When the human mind, flooded with divine gift, begins to act contrary to its former habit, the earth has been overturned: what previously stood high has been sent downward, and the face that had previously been pressed into the depths has been raised upward.

16. This shines forth wonderfully in the conversion of Paul.---It is pleasing to bring forward, as an example of this, one among many: Paul. When he was traveling to Damascus with letters against Christ, the grace of the Holy Spirit was poured into him on the way, and he was immediately changed from his former cruelty. Later he received blows for Christ which he had been coming to inflict upon Christians; and he who had previously lived carnally and attempted to hand over the Lord’s saints to death afterward rejoiced to offer the sacrifice of his flesh for the life of the saints (1 Timothy 1:13). [Note: [Col. 0961] The same codex and Vindoc. read: “to offer the life of his flesh.”]

The cold thoughts of his cruelty were turned into the warmth of devotion. He who had previously been a blasphemer and persecutor afterward became a humble and devout preacher (Acts 9:1). He had considered it the greatest gain to kill Christ in his disciples; now he considers Christ his life, and death gain (Philippians 1:21).

The waters were therefore released and the earth overturned, because Paul’s mind, as soon as it received the grace of the Holy Spirit, changed its former condition of immobility and cruelty.

By contrast, the Lord complains through the prophet concerning Ephraim, saying: “Ephraim has become a cake under the ashes that is not turned” (Hosea 7:8). A cake under the ashes, carrying ashes upon itself, presses its cleaner side downward and has its upper side all the dirtier because it bears the ashes upon it.

What else does a mind that thinks earthly thoughts carry upon itself but a mass of ashes? But if it wishes to turn itself, it brings back upward the clean face that it had pressed downward, once it has shaken off the ashes it carried. If, therefore, we shake the ashes of earthly thoughts from our mind, we turn the cake under the ashes, as it were, so that the intention that the ashes of inferior thought previously pressed down should now be put aside, and the clean face should come to what is above, so that our right intention is no longer oppressed by the weight of earthly desire.

We can by no means do this unless we are drenched with the grace of the Holy Spirit, because almighty God, if he releases the waters, overturns the earth. It continues:

## CHAPTER XI [Old VIII]

**VERSE 16.**---With him are strength and wisdom.

[Col. 0961D]

17. At the judgment the reprobate will be condemned before the elect are endowed with glory.---A little earlier it had been said: “With him are wisdom and strength”; now it says: “With him are strength and wisdom.” Since almighty God, when he became human through the mystery of his mercy, first displayed the teaching of gentleness and afterward revealed in judgment how great his strength is, wisdom is rightly mentioned before strength above, when it is said concerning the Only-Begotten of the Father: “With him are wisdom and strength.”

But because, coming to judge, he will appear in the terror of his power, and after the reprobate have been rejected he will show his elect in the everlasting kingdom how he is the wisdom of the Father, it is rightly said in the following sentence that with him are first strength and then wisdom.

In the earlier words, “With him are wisdom and strength,” he plainly indicates that what he taught in gentleness concerning how one ought to believe he will display in the power of judgment with terror. In the later words, “With him are strength and wisdom,” he demonstrates with the utmost clarity that in judgment he first destroys the reprobate by his power and afterward shines upon the minds of the elect with the perfect light of the eternal kingdom.

But because, before the day of the final judgment, he does not cease daily to judge the deeds of mortals through hidden dispositions, the text returns to what is now taking place when it adds:

## CHAPTER XII [Revised VII]

**VERSES 16–17.**---He knows both the deceiver and the one who is deceived. He brings counselors to a foolish end, and judges to bewilderment.

18. God knows the plots of the wicked in judgment, but does not know them in love.---Since everyone who attempts to deceive his neighbor is wicked, and Truth says to the wicked, “I never knew you; depart from me, all you workers of iniquity” (Matthew 7:23), how can it be said here that the Lord knows the deceiver?

But “to know” in God’s case sometimes means to recognize and sometimes to approve. He knows the wicked person because, by recognizing him, he judges him—for he would not have judged anyone wicked if he did not recognize him—yet he does not know the wicked person because he does not approve his deeds.

He therefore knows him because he detects him, and does not know him because he does not recognize him in the appearance of his wisdom. Thus it is said of any truthful man that he does not know falsehood—not because, when falsehood is spoken either by him or by others, he is ignorant of how to condemn it, but because he both knows the very deceit in judgment and does not know it in love: he himself does not do what he condemns when done by others.

It often happens that some people, occupied with ambushes, set the snares of their perversity for another’s life. When someone is seen to be caught unknowingly in those snares, there may be doubt whether these events are seen by divine providence. People wonder: if God sees these things, why does he permit them to happen? Yet he knows both the deceiver and the one who is deceived.

He knows the deceiver because he often sees his earlier deeds and permits him, by a just judgment, to fall into still other sins. He knows the deceiver because, leaving him in the hand of his own deeds, he abandons him to rush into worse things, as it is written: “Let the one who does harm do harm still, and let the one who is filthy be filthy still” (Revelation 22:11).

He also knows the one who is deceived because people often commit evils that they know, and for that reason are permitted to be deceived, so that they may fall into evils they do not know. This, however, sometimes happens to the deceived for their purification and sometimes as the beginning of punishment.

19. The foolish end of those who do good with a wrong intention.---He brings counselors to a foolish end when they do some good thing without a good intention, directing it toward the return of temporal reward.

For if the Only-Begotten of the supreme Father, because by becoming human he proclaimed eternal things, was called “the angel of great counsel,” we rightly understand “counselors” as preachers who offer their hearers the counsel of life. But when a preacher proclaims eternal things in order to obtain temporal profit, he is certainly led to a foolish end, because through labor he is heading toward the place from which he ought to flee by uprightness of mind.

[Old IX, Revised VIII.] 20. The bewilderment of those who preside over others but do not keep watch.---It is rightly added: “And judges to bewilderment.” All who preside over the examination of other people’s conduct are rightly called judges. But when the person in authority does not carefully examine the life of those subject to him and does not recognize how to correct each one, the judge has been led into bewilderment, because the one who ought to judge evil deeds does not detect the things that must be judged. [Note: [Col. 0963D] Turon. reads: “who is able.”]

It continues:

## CHAPTER XIII

**VERSE 18.**---He loosens the belt of kings and girds their loins with a cord.

21. God punishes the elevation of the mind with carnal sins.---Those who know how to govern the movements of their members well are not undeservedly called kings. But when the mind is touched by pride concerning its very continence, almighty God often abandons its arrogance and permits it to fall into the uncleanness of action.

He loosens the belt of kings when, in those who seemed to govern their members well, he destroys the belt of chastity because of the guilt of pride. What else is signified by a cord except sin? As Solomon says: “His iniquities capture the wicked, and he is bound by the cords of his sins” (Proverbs 5:22).

And because carnal pleasure rules in the loins, the strict judge of consciences, who loosens the belt of kings, girds their loins with a cord. Thus, once the belt of chastity has been loosened, that is, once pleasure of sin dominates their members, he makes those whom pride defiles in secret show publicly how detestable they are. It continues:

## CHAPTER XIV [Revised IX]

**VERSE 19.**---He leads priests away without glory, and overturns the mighty.

22. Those who neglect the care of their subjects or seek rewards other than eternal ones are without glory.---The great glory of a priest is the uprightness of those subject to him. Hence the distinguished preacher rightly says to his disciples: “For what is our hope, or joy, or crown of glory? Is it not you before the Lord?” (1 Thessalonians 2:19).

But when priests neglect the life of their disciples and bring no fruit of their progress before the Lord, what else are they called but “without glory”? Before the strict Judge they certainly do not then find the glory which now, through the work of preaching, they do not seek in the conduct of their subjects.

It is rightly said: “And he overturns the mighty,” because when he abandons the minds of rulers by a just judgment, they do not seek the inner reward, [Note: [Col. 0963D] Vindoc. reads: “the eternal reward is not sought.”] and they are overturned by the very thing in which they are deceived: they rejoice in temporal authority instead of eternal glory.

The mighty are therefore overturned because, while they neglect the true rewards of the heavenly homeland, they fall here into their own pleasures. It continues:

## CHAPTER XV

**VERSE 20.**---Changing the lip of the truthful and taking away the teaching of the elders.

23. God grants the word of truth to those who practice it and takes it away from those who do not.---When a priest does not perform the good things he speaks, speech itself is also taken away from him, so that he may not dare to say what he does not practice, as the prophet says: “But to the sinner God says: Why do you recount my justice and take up my covenant through your mouth?” (Psalm 49:16). [Note: [Col. 0963D] We believe the reading in Vindoc. is corrupt; hence also the preacher says what follows.]

Hence he also prays: “And do not take the word of truth utterly from my mouth” (Psalm 118:43). For he understood that almighty God grants the word of truth to those who practice it and takes it away from those who do not. Therefore, when he asked that it not be taken from his mouth, what else did he seek but the grace of good works? As though he were plainly saying: “Do not let me stray from good works, lest, when I abandon the order of right living, I lose the uprightness of speech.”

[Old X.] Often a teacher who dares to teach what he neglects to do, once he ceases to speak the good things that he refused to practice, begins to teach his subjects the wrong things that he does. Thus, by the just judgment of almighty God, he no longer has a tongue for good, because he refuses to have a good life, [Note: [Col. 0964D] The same Vindoc. witnesses read: “he directs himself toward the bitterness of earthly things.” Ebroic. reads: “he directs himself toward love.”] so that when his mind is inflamed with love of earthly things, he always speaks of earthly things.

Hence Truth says in the Gospel: “The mouth speaks from the abundance of the heart. The good person brings forth good things from the good treasure, and the evil person brings forth evil things from the evil treasure” (Matthew 12:34; Luke 6:45). John also says: “They are from the world; therefore they speak from the world.”

It is rightly said: “Changing the lip of the truthful and taking away the teaching of the elders,” because those who were previously truthful in preaching heavenly things, when they love temporal things and fall toward earthly things, have their truthful lip changed, and the teaching of the elders is taken away, because those who love temporal things do not at all follow the instructions of their predecessors. They hold the place of authority as though it were for the fruit of pleasure, not for the exercise of labor.

24. The Jews denied Christ, whom they had said would come, when he was present.---This may be understood even more plainly of the Jews, who were truthful before the Lord’s incarnation because they believed and announced that he would come; but after he appeared in the flesh, they denied that he was the one.

The lip of the truthful was therefore changed because they denied him as present whom they had said would come. The teaching of the elders was taken away because they did not follow in faith what they remembered their fathers had foretold. Hence it is also promised that, when Elijah comes, he will turn the hearts of the children to their fathers (Malachi 4:6), so that the teaching of the elders, now taken away from the heart of the Jews, may return by the Lord’s mercy when the children begin to understand concerning the Lord what their fathers preached.

But if we understand those same Jews as the elders, who, persuaded by unbelief, attempted to oppose the word of Truth, then the teaching of the elders was taken away after the Church from the Gentiles—the younger Church, so to speak—received it. It says through the Psalmist: “I have understood more than the elders” (Psalm 118:100). Because it held this by practice, it showed how it had understood more than the elders when it immediately added: “Because I sought your commandments.” Since it strove to fulfill in practice what it had learned, it received understanding of what it should teach.

Hence it appropriately adds:

## CHAPTER XVI

[Col. 0965B]

**VERSE 21.**---He pours contempt upon princes and raises up those who had been oppressed.

25. The Jews were despised because of unbelief; the Gentiles were raised from their fall because of faith.---While the Jewish people remained in the commandment of the Law and the whole Gentile world knew no commandments of God, the Jews seemed to rule through faith, while the Gentiles lay pressed down in the depths through unbelief.

But when Judaea denied the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation and the Gentiles believed, the princes fell into contempt, and those who had been oppressed under the guilt of unbelief were raised into the freedom of true faith.

Jeremiah, seeing Israel’s fall long beforehand, said: “The Lord has become like an enemy; he has cast down Israel, he has cast down all its walls, he has destroyed its fortifications” (Lamentations 2:5). [Note: [Col. 0965D] Bellovac., Utic., and other Norman witnesses read: “he has cast down its walls”; “all” is absent.] Walls in cities are for adornment, while fortifications are for defense. [Note: [Col. 0966D] Vindoc. reads: “they are for adornment.”]

[Old XI.] Some gifts strengthen us, others adorn us. Prophetic teaching, kinds of tongues, and the power of healings are like walls of the mind. [Note: [Col. 0966D] Most witnesses add: “even if someone does not possess them.”] Even if someone does not possess these, he can stand fortified by faith and justice, although he may not appear adorned with the height of virtues.

Hope, faith, and charity, however, are not our walls but our fortifications. If we neglect to possess them, we lie exposed to hostile ambushes. Concerning Judaea, therefore, because he took away prophecy, teaching, and the signs of miracles, he cast down its walls. But because, on account of its hardness, he permitted hope, faith, and charity to be taken away from it, he undertook to destroy its fortifications.

The proper order was preserved: first the walls, and afterward the fortifications, are said to have been destroyed. For when a sinful soul is abandoned, the gifts of virtues given for the manifestation of the Spirit are first taken from it, and afterward the foundations of hope, faith, and charity are destroyed.

The Lord took all these things away from the faithless and gave them to the Gentiles, adorning the minds of believers with what he had taken from the unbelieving. Hence it is written: “And to divide the spoils for the adornment of the house” (Psalm 67:13). [Note: [Col. 0966D] Utic. and other Norman witnesses add: “whence it is also written: ‘to divide the spoils for the adornment of the house.’”]

When he took the spoils of virtues away from the Jews, he gave the household of the hearts of the Gentiles—this house in which he graciously chose to dwell through faith—the beauty of gifts.

This was accomplished when the Jewish people received the words of God according only to the letter that kills, while the converted Gentiles penetrated them through the Spirit who gives life. Hence it immediately adds:

## CHAPTER XVII [Revised X]

**VERSE 22.**---He reveals the depths from darkness and brings the shadow of death into the light.

26. Christ revealed hidden things and changed the shadow of death into light.---When believers recognize the various mysteries concealed in the words of the prophets, what else is revealed from darkness than the depths? Hence Truth himself, speaking to his disciples in parables, says: “What I tell you in darkness, speak in the light” (Matthew 10:27). When we untie the mysterious knots of allegories by explaining them, we speak in the light what we heard in darkness. [Note: [Col. 0966D] Gussanv. reads: “the modes of allegories.”]

The hardness of the Law was the shadow of death, because it decreed that every sinner should be punished by bodily death. [Note: [Col. 0966D] Vindoc. reads: “it judged that they should be punished, but this reading is scarcely approved.”] But after our Redeemer tempered the severity of the legal sanction through gentleness, and no longer established that bodily death should be inflicted for sin, while he indicated how greatly the death of the spirit should be feared, he undoubtedly brought the shadow of death into the light.

[Old XXII.] The death in which the flesh is separated from the soul is the shadow of that death in which the soul is separated from God. The shadow of death is therefore brought into the light when, once the death of the spirit is understood, bodily death is no longer feared.

This may also be understood in another way. Those who rule their thoughts by the great judgment of counsel and restrain every foolish impulse by the power of wisdom are not improperly called princes. But it often happens that the mind is secretly lifted up in proud arrogance by its very wisdom and falls beneath the vices over which it had rejoiced to be victorious.

It is therefore rightly said: “He pours contempt upon princes.” But because those who seem to lie in vices sometimes hasten to the lamentation of repentance and raise themselves against the sins to which they had been subject, it is appropriately added: “And raises up those who had been oppressed.” For some, enlightened by heavenly gift, see in what great disgrace of sins they lie, wash away the stains of their deeds with tears, and afterward press down beneath themselves the movements of their flesh by which they had previously been oppressed.

377

### 27. By God’s great providence, everything here is uncertain

This is brought about by the great providence of almighty God: in this life everything is kept uncertain, so that no one may grow proud on account of acquired purity, because “he pours contempt upon princes.” Let no one despair because of the suppression of his vices, because “he raises up those who had been oppressed.” And since, when these things occur, an open sentence is brought forth from God’s hidden counsels concerning each person, it is rightly added: “And he reveals deep things out of darkness.”

### 28. In his hidden judgments, God sees everything and is not seen

The Lord reveals deep things out of darkness when he discloses an open sentence from his hidden counsels, showing what he thinks about each person. Since the Creator now sees everything, while he himself is not seen in his counsels, the Psalmist rightly says of him: “He made darkness his hiding place” (Psalm XVII, 12). But he comes forth from this darkness into the light, as it were, when he reveals what he thinks about each person’s deeds.

And because, when one who was weighed down by the burden of his sins is led back to a state of uprightness, he first sees that very death in which he had been accustomed to fail and which he had not known how to perceive, it is rightly added: “And he brings the shadow of death into the light.” The shadow of death is an evil deed, which is impressed as if from the features of a body, in imitation of the ancient enemy. Of him it is also said figuratively: “And his name was Death” (Revelation VI, 8). Often his evil thought lies hidden from human minds, and through this very fact—that it is not recognized—it prevails all the more.

The shadow of death is therefore brought into the light when the evil deed of the ancient enemy is disclosed to the minds of the saints, so that it may be destroyed. It follows:

### VERSE 23

“He multiplies nations, and destroys them, and restores those who have been overthrown to wholeness.”

### 29. By God’s hidden judgments some fall and others rise again

This may perhaps be understood to mean that the Lord multiplies and destroys nations because they are born to die daily [Note: [Col. 0967D] The Norm. and many others read: “because they are born and die every day,” and so forth.], and restores those who have been overthrown to wholeness because the dead will rise again.

Yet we understand it better if we consider how this takes place in their minds. He multiplies and destroys nations because he both enlarges them through the fruitfulness of offspring and nevertheless abandons them in their own unbelief. But he restores those who have been overthrown to wholeness because those whom he had left fallen into unbelief he eventually brings back to the state of faith.

When these have been restored to soundness of mind, that ancient people which had appeared faithful to God was rejected and cast away in heart, so that, deceived by its own faithlessness, it might afterward rise up against the very one whom it had previously proclaimed. It follows:

## CHAPTER XIX

### VERSES 24–25

“He changes the heart of the princes of the people of the earth, and deceives them, so that they wander vainly through a pathless region. They will grope as in darkness and not in light, and he will make them wander as though drunk.”

### 30. The Jews’ blindness concerning Christ, who suffered as a human being but manifested divine things

The heart of the princes of the earth was changed when, in Judea, the chief priests and elders of the people tried by their counsel to oppose the one whom they had previously proclaimed as destined to come. And when, by persecuting him, they sought to extinguish his name, deceived by their own wickedness they tried in vain to travel through a pathless region, because no way could lie open to their cruelty against the author of all things.

They saw miracles and were terrified by his power [Note: [Col. 0967D] Bellov. and Norm. read: “They marveled at his powers and were terrified, but, refusing to believe, they still sought signs.”]; yet, refusing to believe, they continued to ask for signs, saying: “What sign, then, do you do, so that we may see and believe you? What do you work?” (John VI, 30).

Thus it is rightly said: “They will grope as in darkness and not in light.” For whoever trembles amid so many manifest miracles gropes as if in darkness, because he does not see what he touches.

Everyone who wanders is led now here, now there. And because at one time they appeared to believe, when they said, “If this man were not from God, he could do nothing” (John IX, 33), but at another time denied that he was from God, despising him and saying, “Is this not the carpenter’s son? Is not his mother called Mary, and his brothers James, Joseph, Simon, and Judas, and are not all his sisters among us?” (Matthew XIII, 55) [Note: [Col. 0967D] Vindoc. reads: “Is not his mother Mary, and his brothers James and John, Simon and Judas, and all his sisters,” and so forth. Or: [Col. 0968D] “Is this not the carpenter, the son of Mary, the brother of James and Joseph and Judas and Simon, and are not his sisters here with us?” In Norm.: “his brothers James,” and so forth.], it is rightly added: “And he will make them wander as though drunk.”

They saw him raising the dead, yet also saw him as mortal. Who would not believe that he was God when they saw him raising the dead? But again, when they saw him as mortal, they scorned believing that this mortal was the immortal God.

Therefore, by displaying himself to their eyes in such a way that he could both manifest divine things and suffer human things, almighty God made them wander as though drunk. Their pride preferred to despise the mystery of his incarnation rather than follow it; it rose up against his humanity, while inwardly marveling at the power of his divinity shining within [Note: [Col. 0968D] Bellov. and Norm. read: “and, amid the power of his divinity shining forth,” and so forth.].

Since all these things were made present to blessed Job’s eyes through the spirit of prophecy, it is rightly added:

## CHAPTER XX [Revised recension XII]

### CHAPTER XIII, VERSE 1

“Behold, all things.”

### 31. Job possessed the spirit of prophecy

In him he saw as present the things that were to follow. For to the one before whose eyes all things stand together, neither future things come nor past things depart; everything stands simultaneously before his eyes.

And because he saw those very things that were to come as different in deeds and in words, it is rightly added:

“Thus my eye has seen and my ear has heard.”

But words are of no benefit if they lack understanding. Hence it is appropriately added:

“And I have understood each thing.”

For when something is shown or heard, if understanding is not granted, it is not prophecy. Pharaoh saw in a dream what was going to happen in Egypt (Genesis XLI, 2 and following); but because he could not understand what he had seen, he was not a prophet. King Belshazzar saw the joints of the hand writing on the wall (Daniel V, 5) [Note: [Col. 0968D] Vindoc., Sag. and other Norm. read: “the article of the hand,” that is, “the finger joint of the hand.”]; but he was not a prophet, because he did not receive understanding of what he had seen.

Therefore, to testify that blessed Job possessed the spirit of prophecy, he asserts that he had not only seen and heard, but also understood everything. His following words testify that he was not lifted up by this understanding, for he says:

## CHAPTER XXI

### VERSE 2

“According to your knowledge, I also know; I am not inferior to you” [Note: [Col. 0969D] Sag., Big., and Lyr. read: “nor am I inferior to you.” The same wording now survives in the old corrected manuscript of Utic.].

### 32. He did not become swollen with pride over this gift

By these words it became clear how humble he was: he denies that he is inferior to them, although by living holily he had far surpassed their life. He confirms that he knows according to their knowledge because, by knowing heavenly things, he passed beyond their earthly thoughts also through the spirit of prophecy.

It follows:

## CHAPTER XXII [Revised recension XIII]

### VERSE 3

“But nevertheless I will speak to the Almighty, and I desire to reason with God.”

### 33. Whoever is now intimate with God in prayer will later judge with him

We speak with the Almighty when we implore his mercy; we reason with him when, joining ourselves to his justice, we examine our deeds with careful investigation.

Or certainly, to reason with God means that the one who here obeyed his commands will afterward come with him as judge to judge the peoples, as it is said to the preachers who left everything:

“You who have followed me, in the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, you also will sit upon twelve thrones” [Note: [Col. 0969D] In the Norman manuscripts: “upon twelve thrones,” but the evidence of the correction made in Utic. is certain.], “judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matthew XIX, 28).

Hence the Lord also says through Isaiah: “Rescue the one who suffers injustice, judge the orphan, justify the widow, and come, let us reason together” (Isaiah I, 17). It is right that those who perfectly leave the present age for the words of God should reason with God in judgment concerning orphans [Note: [Col. 0970D] This should scarcely be doubted as the correct reading; nevertheless, in Utic. and others of the Norman manuscripts, Bellov., Turon. and others examined by Gussanv., the unanimous reading is “concerning the people.”].

Thus speaking belongs to prayer, and reasoning to judgment. The holy man therefore now speaks to the Almighty so that he may afterward reason with the Almighty, because the one who will later come as judge with God is the one who has here been intimate with him in prayer.

But holy Church, whose figure we have often said blessed Job represents (especially in the Preface, chapter 6 and following), does not judge the wicked only when the day of the last judgment has arrived. Even now it does not cease to judge all who act wickedly or think foolishly. Hence it is added:

## CHAPTER XXIII [Old recension XV]

### VERSE 4

“First showing you to be fabricators of lies and worshipers of perverse doctrines.”

### 34. Heretics are fabricators of lies

These words plainly show that his friends, as representatives of heretics, oppose the judgments of the holy man. It is clear that those called worshipers of perverse doctrines do not represent Catholics.

Here we must also attend to the fact that they are called fabricators of lies. Just as a building is constructed from stones, so a lie is constructed from words. Where there is not deceitful speech but the meaning of truth, something like a fortified mass rises up not from manufacture but from nature.

It follows:

## CHAPTER XXIV

### VERSE 5

“Would that you were silent, so that you might be thought wise.”

### 35. Silence is useful for concealing foolishness
