Just as, when a door is closed in a house, one does not know what members are hidden inside, so a fool, if he remains silent, is often concealed as either wise or foolish—provided that no other deeds appear which disclose even the thoughts of the silent person.

Thus the holy man, seeing that his friends wished to appear what they were not, admonished them to be silent, so that they could not appear to be what they were. Hence Solomon also says: “A fool, if he keeps silent, will be considered wise” (Proverbs XVII, 28).

But because a fool, when he speaks, introduces his own words and is unable to weigh the words of the wise, he rightly adds, after imposing silence:

## CHAPTER XXV

### VERSE 6

“Listen, then, to my rebukes, and attend to the judgment of my lips.”

### 36. Fools need rebuke

He first brought forward rebuke and afterward judgment, because unless the fool’s swelling pride is first brought low by rebuke, the judgment of the just is not at all recognized through understanding.

It follows:

## CHAPTER XXVI

### VERSE 7

“Does God need your lie, so that you may speak deceit on his behalf?”

### 37. Truth does not seek the support of falsehood

God does not need a lie, because truth does not seek to be supported by the assistance of falsehood. But heretics, because they cannot defend from the truth what they wrongly understand about God, seek, as though to prove it, the shadow of falsehood to support the ray of light.

They speak deceit on his behalf when, through foolish seduction, they deceive weak minds in their understanding of him.

It follows:

## CHAPTER XXVII

### VERSE 8

“Do you accept his person, and do you strive to judge on God’s behalf?”

### 38. Fools judge others more severely the more deeply they are ignorant of themselves

When fools see the deeds of prudent people, all these deeds seem reprehensible to them. Forgetting their own ignorance and weakness, they judge the affairs of others with the greater intensity the more deeply they are ignorant of their own.

But the just, when they rebuke the deeds of the wicked, remain always conscious of their own weakness. Thus, although they rebuke them outwardly with severity, they do so inwardly with compassion. For it belongs only to the one who, through the omnipotence of his nature, does not know how to sin to examine human sins without compassion.

Since Job’s friends had therefore criticized his deeds as though they themselves possessed nothing blameworthy, it is rightly said: “Do you accept his person, and do you strive to judge on God’s behalf?”

To accept his person means to take his authority in judgment [Note: [Col. 0971D] Big. and Lyr.: “to take the judgment of his authority.”]. And one strives to judge on God’s behalf when, while criticizing whatever is weak in another, one is not inwardly weakened by compassion.

It follows:

## CHAPTER XXVIII

### VERSE 9

“Or will he be pleased with you, whom nothing can escape, or will he be deceived like a human being by your frauds?” [Note: [Col. 0971D] Turon. reads: “whom nothing can be concealed from.”]

### 39. Heretics offend God while pretending to defend him

Heretics offer fraud to God because they assert things that cannot possibly please the one on whose behalf they speak. While attempting to defend him, they offend him; they fall into opposition to the one whom they appear to serve by their preaching [Note: [Col. 0971D] That is, “in opposing him.” We have explained the meaning of this word more than once. It can easily be understood from what follows, where a heretic is said to be at once God’s enemy, or opponent, and his defender: for, says Gregory, by the very means through which he attempts to defend him, he opposes his truth.].

Hence the Psalmist says: “That you may destroy the enemy and the defender” (Psalm VIII, 3). Every heretic is both an enemy and a defender of almighty God, because by the very means through which he attempts to defend him, he opposes his truth.

But since nothing can be hidden from God, he judges in them what they feel inwardly, not what they appear outwardly to perform in his service [Note: [Col. 0972D] Vindoc., Utic., and other Norman manuscripts persuade us that this is the correct reading, not “this he indicates in them,” as in both the older and the more recent printed editions.].

Since God is therefore not deceived like a human being by their frauds, it is rightly added:

## CHAPTER XXIX

### VERSES 10–11

“He himself will rebuke you, because in secret you accept his person. As soon as he moves, he will trouble you, and his terror will rush upon you.”

### 40. What punishment those deserve who oppose acknowledged truth

The statement that they accept God’s person in secret can be understood in two ways.

There are some who perceive the truth in their hearts and nevertheless speak outwardly what is false about God. So that they may not appear to be defeated, they recognize the truth inwardly and yet oppose it outwardly. Hence it is rightly said: “He himself will rebuke you, because in secret you accept his person.” It is as though he said openly: You are all the more blameworthy before him for falsehood, because even within yourselves you see what is true.

There are also some who, when they return to their minds, contemplate God’s justice and righteousness and tremble through prayer and tears. But after the hour of contemplation has passed, they return so boldly to their iniquities as though, placed behind his back, they were not at all seen by the light of his justice.

These people accept God’s person in secret, as though he were bodily seeing them: when they become present before him, they flatter him with tears, but when they withdraw, as it were, from his sight, they attack him by their conduct. They must therefore be struck all the more severely for their evils because, even in the secrecy of their thoughts, they recognize God’s righteous judgments [Old recension XVII.].

Hence it is added: “As soon as he moves, he will trouble you, and his terror will rush upon you.”

### 41. The just fear God before they experience him as angry

Although almighty God is unchangeable in nature, he is not disturbed by anger in judgment. In human language, however, God’s movement is called the very strictness of his righteousness by which human perversity is struck.

The just fear God before his anger is moved against them. So that they may not experience him as moved, they fear him while he is tranquil. But the wicked begin to fear being struck only when they are already being struck. His terror then awakens them from the sleep of their torpor, when punishment disturbs them.

Hence it is said through the prophet: “And only vexation will give understanding to the hearing” (Isaiah XXVIII, 19). When they begin to be beaten in punishment for having despised and rejected God’s commands, they then understand what they had heard. The Psalmist says: “When he slew them, then they sought him” (Psalm LXXVII, 34).

It is therefore rightly said: “As soon as he moves, he will trouble you, and his terror will rush upon you,” because in the hearts of the reprobate it is not fear that produces rest; rather, punishment produces fear.

It follows:

## CHAPTER XXX [Revised recension XIV]

### VERSE 12

“Your memory will be compared to ashes” [Note: [Col. 0972D] Norm.: “The memory of you.”].

### 42. The memory of the proud is compared to ashes carried away by the wind, and to mud

All who, through earthly thought, conform themselves to this age try in everything they do to leave a memory of themselves in this world. Some labor assiduously through the monuments of wars, others through the lofty walls of buildings, others through eloquent books of secular learning; they build themselves a name in memory.

But since life itself rushes more swiftly toward its end, what will remain fixed in it, when life itself swiftly passes away? The breeze carries away ashes, as it is written: “Not so the wicked, not so, but like dust which the wind drives from the face of the earth” (Psalm I, 4).

The memory of fools is therefore rightly compared to ashes [Note: [Col. 0972D] Vindoc.: “because it is placed there where it may be carried away by the breeze.”], because it is placed where the breeze may carry it away. However much anyone may labor to perfect the glory of his name, he has placed his memory like ashes, because the wind of mortality soon carries it away.

In contrast, it is written of the just: “The just man will be in everlasting remembrance” (Psalm CXI, 4). By impressing his deeds upon God’s eyes alone, he fixes the name of his memory in eternity.

It follows:

## CHAPTER XXXI

### SAME PASSAGE

“And your necks will be reduced to mud.”

### 43. Just as sight is signified by the eye, so pride is usually signified by the neck

The neck is therefore reduced to mud when a proud person is humbled in death and his exalted flesh wastes away in corruption.

Let us consider what the corpses of the rich lying in tombs are like: what image of death is present in that extinguished flesh, and what a wasting of corruption [Note: [Col. 0973D] Vindoc.: “which swells in corruption”; perhaps one should read, “what a wasting there is,” and so forth.].

They were indeed the very people who were exalted by honors, swollen with possessions, despised others, and rejoiced as though they alone existed. Because they did not consider where they were heading, they did not know what they were.

The neck is reduced to mud because those who swelled with vanity lie despised in corruption. The neck is reduced to mud because the wasting of corruption proves how little the power of the flesh is worth.

It follows:

## CHAPTER XXXII

### VERSE 13

“Be silent for a little while, so that I may speak whatever my mind suggests.”

### 44. Those who speak carnally must be recalled to silence

He shows that they have spoken with the sense of the flesh; for this reason he restrains them into silence, so that he may speak what his mind suggests. It is as though he said openly: I do not speak carnally but spiritually, because through the perception of the spirit I hear what I utter through the ministry of the body [Note: [Col. 0973D] Bigot.: “I always hear.”].

Thus he immediately rises to higher things [Note: [Col. 0973D] All the Norman manuscripts: “and raises himself into mysteries.” In former times Utic. read “in mysteries,” but a later hand added the other wording.], elevates himself into mysteries, and changes the rebuke he had uttered into mystical words, saying:

## CHAPTER XXXIII [Old recension XVIII, revised recension XV]

### VERSE 14

“Why do I tear my flesh with my teeth, and carry my soul in my hands?”

### 45. The just punish lesser faults in themselves with great torments

In sacred Scripture, teeth sometimes signify holy preachers, and sometimes the inner senses. Concerning holy preachers, it is said to the bride: “Your teeth are like flocks of shorn sheep that have come up from the washing” (Song IV, 2).

Hence, when the nations were shown figuratively to one of them, it was said: “Kill and eat” (Acts X, 13), that is, crush their oldness with your teeth and convert them into the body of the Church, namely, into your members [Note: [Col. 0973D] Sag., Lyr., Big., and Ebroic.: “crush their oldness with your tooth and convert them into the body of the holy Church,” and so forth. Utic. now reads the same, but a later hand added the words “with your tooth” and “of the holy.”].

Again, the prophet Jeremiah testifies that teeth can signify the inner senses, saying: “He broke my teeth one by one” (Lamentations III, 10). Food is broken by the teeth so that it may be swallowed. Thus we appropriately understand the inner senses by teeth, since they chew and break down each thing they think about, as it were, and send it into the belly of memory.

The prophet says that they were broken one by one because, according to the measure of each person’s sin, blindness of understanding is generated in the senses. According to what each person has done outwardly, so he becomes dull in what he could have understood concerning inward and invisible things.

Hence it is also rightly written: “Every person who eats a sour grape—his teeth will be set on edge” (Ezekiel XVIII, 2; Jeremiah XXX, 30). What is a sour grape except sin? A sour grape is fruit before its time. Whoever desires to be filled with the pleasures of the present life hastens, as it were, to eat fruit before its time.

Therefore, whoever eats a sour grape has his teeth set on edge, because whoever feeds on the delight of this world has his inner senses bound, so that he can no longer chew—that is, understand—spiritual things. By the very things in which they took delight outwardly, they become dull inwardly.

And while the soul feeds on sin, it cannot eat the bread of righteousness, because teeth bound by the habit of sin cannot at all eat what tastes just inwardly.

Since, as we have said, teeth signify the inner senses in this passage, we must carefully consider what the just customarily do. Whenever they detect in themselves anything carnal, however slight, they reconsider it in their inner senses and pursue it vehemently within themselves. They wear themselves down through affliction and judge even the smallest wrong in themselves with great torments, condemning it through repentance.

They do this so that, as far as possible, they themselves may be found irreproachable in the sight of the eternal Judge, and so that those who see them judging themselves in this way may be inflamed to amend themselves from more serious faults.

Blessed Job had done this before his friends, who held temporal glory and praised passing goods. Yet he could not lead their understanding to recognize the benefit of his scourging, so that they might consider that almighty God not only bestows prosperity but sometimes mercifully inflicts adversity as well.

Hence he now rightly says: “Why do I tear my flesh with my teeth?” It is as though he openly said: Why do I examine with my inner senses whatever carnal things may have been done in me, if I cannot benefit those who observe me?

Appropriately he adds: “And I carry my soul in my hands.”

383 [Old recension XIX, revised recension XVI]

### 46. In everything they seek not only their own progress but also the edification of their neighbor

To carry one’s soul in one’s hands is to show the intention of the heart in one’s actions.

The just have this distinctive quality: in everything they say and everything they do, they seek not only their own progress but also the edification of their neighbors. Sometimes they judge themselves in certain matters, in order to recall sluggish hearers to examine themselves. Sometimes they display good works, so that those who observe them may be ashamed not to imitate what they see.

For it is written: “Let them see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew V, 16). Whoever therefore makes his intention known through his works carries his soul in his hands.

But when a just person gains no benefit for his neighbors either by judging himself or by displaying good works, he returns, because of what he has done, to words of grief. Hence it is rightly said: “Why do I tear my flesh with my teeth, and carry my soul in my hands?”

That is: Why do I either judge myself severely before people or show in my actions what I seek, if I benefit my neighbors neither by judging my evils nor by displaying my good deeds?

Nevertheless, even when the just say these things, they never cease to provide their neighbors with a good example [Note: [Col. 0974D] Norm.: “they never cease to provide good examples to their neighbors.” In Utic., before correction, it read “from providing … an example,” and so forth. Turon. reads “from providing … good examples,” and so forth.].

Hence blessed Job, displaying and exhibiting the virtue of patience before his friends, continues:

## CHAPTER XXXIV [Revised recension XVII]

### VERSE 15

“Even if he kills me, I will hope in him.”

### 47. The just praise God even in adversity

The virtue of patience never appears in prosperity. Truly patient is the one who is worn down by adversity and yet is not bent away from the straight path of his hope [Note: [Col. 0975D] Turon.: “and yet is not bent away from the hope of his righteousness.”].

It is written concerning the mind of the reprobate: “He will praise you when you have done good to him” (Psalm XLVIII, 19) [Note: [Col. 0975D] Six Anglo-Saxon manuscripts, all the Norman manuscripts, and Gilot. read this way. In the printed editions some have “concerning the sense of the reprobate,” others “concerning the sense of the reprobates.”].

The just mind is distinguished from the unjust by this: it confesses the praise of almighty God even amid adversity. It is not broken when its possessions are broken, nor does it fall when the outward glory of its circumstances falls. Rather, in this it shows what it was when it possessed things: it stands more firmly when it is without them.

It follows:

## CHAPTER XXXV

### VERSES 15–16

“Nevertheless, I will rebuke my ways in his sight, and he himself will be my savior.”

### 48. He does not spare his faults, so that God may spare him

When the apostle Paul says, “If we judged ourselves, we would certainly not be judged” (1 Corinthians XI, 31), the Lord is found as savior at the time when, through fear of God, our sin is now rebuked by ourselves.

Therefore the elect never know how to spare their faults, so that they may find the judge of their faults propitiated. Indeed, they believe that they will afterward find him as savior whom they now fear strictly as judge. For whoever now spares himself in guilt will not afterward be spared by him in punishment.

Let him therefore say: “Nevertheless, I will rebuke my ways in his sight.” And let him add what benefit follows from this rebuke: “And he himself will be my savior.”

It follows:

## CHAPTER XXXVI [Revised recension XVIII]

### SAME PASSAGE

“For not every hypocrite will come into his sight.”

### 49. The hypocrite flees God’s sight while seeking to please human eyes

Since it is established that the coming Judge places the sheep at his right hand and the goats at his left (Matthew XXV, 33), how can it now be said that the hypocrite will not come into his sight, when, if he is among the goats, he will appear at the Judge’s left?

[Old recension XX.] But we must know that we come into the Lord’s sight in two ways.

In one way, here and now, when we carefully weigh our sins, punish them in his sight, and judge them with tears. For whenever we bring the power of our Creator back to our awareness, we stand in his sight. Hence it is rightly said through the man of God Elijah: “The Lord God of Israel lives, in whose sight I stand” (3 Kings XVII, 1).

In another way, we come into the Lord’s sight when we stand before his tribunal at the final judgment.

The hypocrite therefore comes before the Judge’s sight at the final examination; but because he now pretends not to consider and lament his faults, he refuses to come into the Lord’s sight.

For just as the just, when they contemplate the strictness of the coming Judge, recall their sins to memory, mourn what they have committed, and judge themselves severely so that they may not be judged, so hypocrites, the more they please people outwardly, neglect to look inwardly at themselves. They pour themselves entirely into the words of their neighbors and consider themselves holy because they believe that people regard them in this way.

When they have scattered their minds through words of praise, they never restore them to the knowledge of their guilt [Note: [Col. 0976D] Bellov.: “they never bring guilt back to awareness.”]. They never consider where they offend the inward Judge. They fear nothing of his strictness, because they believe that they have pleased him as they have pleased human beings.

If they brought his terror back to mind, they would fear all the more that they please people while remaining in an evil intention.

It is therefore rightly said: “For not every hypocrite will come into his sight,” because he does not place God’s strictness before his eyes while he desires to please human eyes. If, examining his mind, he placed himself in God’s sight, he would certainly no longer be a hypocrite.

It follows:

## CHAPTER XXXVII

### VERSE 17

“Hear my speech, and receive riddles with your ears.”

### 50. Job’s figurative speech

By calling them riddles, he shows that his expressions are figurative. Hence the voice of the faithful people appropriately adds:

## CHAPTER XXXVIII [Revised recension XIX]

### VERSE 18

“If I am judged, I know that I will be found just.”

### 51. The humility of Job even when he praises himself; he attributes iniquity to himself but his purification to God

This agrees with the person of blessed Job when he speaks outwardly of himself what Truth had said inwardly about him to his adversary: “Have you seen my servant Job, that there is none like him on earth?” (Job I, 8).

Indeed, the same man says of himself something far lower than what the Lord said about him. For it is one thing to be just, and another to have no equal. He therefore thought humbly of himself: although he was just without comparison, he remembered that he could be found not superior to others but simply just.

[Old recension XXI.] Yet his words seem to contain a difficulty. Earlier he said: “I will rebuke my ways in his sight” (verse 15); later he says: “You wish to consume me with the sins of my youth”; and, recognizing his sins carefully, he adds farther on: “You have sealed up my offenses as in a purse.” Now he says: “If I am judged, I know that I will be found just.” Sin and righteousness cannot exist together in the same way.

But the holy man attributes iniquity to himself and his purification to almighty God. He recognizes himself as a sinner from himself, and does not fail to recognize that he has been made just by grace [Note: [Col. 0976D] Vindoc.: “he recognizes himself to be”]; he was placed in a righteous work and deserved, through abundant grace, to endure scourges.

Now he rejoices that he will be found just in judgment [Note: [Col. 0977D] Bellovac., Utic., and many others read this way. The older printed editions also read: “he rejoices to find himself just.”], since he saw himself struck before judgment.

Hence, when much later he says: “You have sealed up my offenses as in a purse,” he immediately adds:

### SAME PASSAGE

“But you have healed my iniquity.”

Whoever therefore says that he will be found just in judgment by no means denies that he was justly scourged; although through his scourging the Lord sought not to wipe away sins but to increase merits.

It follows:

## CHAPTER XXXIX

### VERSE 19

“Who is he who will be judged with me? Let him come.”

### 52. No one can be free from sinful thought

The holy men guard themselves in their deeds, with God as their author, so carefully that nothing for which they might be accused is found outwardly. In their thoughts, however, they watch themselves inwardly with such caution that, if it could be done, they would always stand irreproachable before the eyes of the inward Judge [Note: [Col. 0977D] Bellov. and Norm.: “but in their thoughts …”; the inward clause is absent.].

But however much they can act so as not to stumble outwardly in their deeds, they cannot act so much inwardly that they never stumble in thought. Human conscience, by the very fact that it withdraws from what is deepest within, is always on slippery ground [Note: [Col. 0977D] Turon., Vindoc., Ebroic., and others: “by the very fact that it has fallen from what is deepest within.” The same now appears in Utic., but through correction.].

Consequently, even holy men frequently stumble in their hearts.

Blessed Job, therefore, speaking both in his own voice and in that of the elect, says: “Who is he who will be judged with me? Let him come.” Because he has nothing for which he can be accused in his outward actions, he freely seeks an accuser.

But because even the hearts of the just sometimes accuse themselves of foolish thought, perhaps for this reason it is added:

## CHAPTER XL

### SAME PASSAGE

“Why am I consumed while silent?”

### 53. One whose repentance must be carried out in secret

The person who is consumed while silent is the one who, rebuking himself for foolish thought, is bitten within himself by the tooth of conscience.

It is as though he openly said: “As I have lived so that I need fear no accuser outwardly, would that I had lived in such a way that I did not have an accusing conscience within myself!” [Note: [Col. 0977D] Turon., Bellov., Utic., and others read this way. The old edition and Gilot. have: “if I had lived”; Gussanv.: “thus I lived.”]

The person who is consumed while silent finds within himself something by which he may burn [Note: [Col. 0977D] Sag., Ebroic., Lyr., and Big.: “something by which he may be bitten.” Utic. now also reads this, but from a second hand.].

It follows:

### VERSE 20

“Do only two things to me, and then I will not be hidden from your face.”

### 54. No one is safe from God’s correction

In this passage, what should we understand by “God’s face” except his correction, in which he punishes while looking upon sins? From this correction not even the righteous person is hidden if the two things he requests are not removed. Concerning these he continues:

### CHAPTER XLI [Old XXII, Revised XX]

**VERSE 24.** “Withdraw your hand far from me, and let not your dread terrify me.”

### 55. Before Christ, the saints desired that law in which they would serve not through fear but through love

In these two requests, what else does he seek through the voice of prophecy than the time of grace and redemption? The Law held the people under the blow of punishment [Note: Turon., “under persecution”; Lyr. and Big., “under the blow of punishment”], so that whoever sinned under it was immediately punished by death. Nor did the Israelite people serve the Lord out of love, but out of fear. Yet justice can never be fulfilled through fear, because, in the words of John, “Perfect love casts out fear” (1 John 4:18). Paul likewise consoles the adopted children [Note: All the Norman and Vendôme manuscripts, “adoptive children”], saying: “You have not received the spirit of servitude again in fear, but you have received the spirit of adoption as sons, in which we cry, ‘Abba, Father’” (Romans 8:15).

Therefore, speaking through the voice of the human race, which longs to pass beyond the harshness of legal punishment and desires to move from dread to love, he begs almighty God to put these two things far from him, saying: “Withdraw your hand far from me, and let not your dread terrify me.” That is: Remove from me the harshness of punishment; take away the burden of fear; but, as the grace of love shines upon me, pour into me the spirit of confidence. For if I am not kept far from punishment and fear, I know that I shall not be hidden from the strictness of your judgment, since no one can be righteous in your sight who serves you not through love but through fear. [Col. 0978A–B]

Hence he also seeks the very presence of his Creator, as though familiarly and bodily, so that through it he may both hear what he does not know and be heard in those matters that he knows. [Note: In the Roman editions of Sixtus V and Gilot (1571), the reading is mistakenly “by which familiarly.” The English manuscripts and others, together with the older editions, have “as though.”] For he immediately adds:

**VERSE 22.** “Call me, and I will answer you; or else I will speak, and you answer me.”

### 56. Christ revealed sins that had remained hidden

When he appeared to human eyes by assuming flesh, he disclosed to human beings the sins that they both committed and did not know they were committing. Hence it is added:

### CHAPTER XLII [Revised XXI]

**VERSE 23.** “Show me how many iniquities and sins I have, my crimes and offenses.”

### 57. God calls when he chooses us in love; we answer by obeying him. The distinction between sin and iniquity, and between crimes and offenses. Yet “calling” and “answering” may also be understood in another way

God’s calling is his regard for us in love and election. Our answering is obedience to his love through good works. Accordingly, it is appropriately added: “Or else I will speak, and you answer me.” We speak when, through desire, we ask for his face. God answers those who speak when he appears to us as we love him. [Col. 0978C–D]

But whoever yearns for eternity examines his deeds, subtly reproving himself, and seeks to discover whether there is anything in him that might offend the face of his Creator. [Note: Vendôme, “of his Creator,” etc.] He therefore rightly adds: “Show me how many iniquities and sins I have, my crimes and offenses.” In this life the labor of the righteous is to find themselves, and, having found themselves, to lead themselves to better things through weeping and correction. [Note: The same manuscripts, “restore them to better things.”]

Although the apostle John declares that there is no difference between iniquity and sin, saying, “Iniquity is sin” (1 John 3:4), in ordinary usage “iniquity” nevertheless sounds more serious than “sin.” Everyone readily admits that he is a sinner, but sometimes blushes to call himself wicked.

The difference between crimes and offenses is this: a crime exceeds the weight of sin, whereas an offense does not exceed the weight of sin. For when the Law commands that a sacrifice be offered, it prescribes one not only for sin but also for an offense. [Col. 0979A–B] A crime is never merely in thought, but in deed; an offense, however, is often confined to thought. [Note: We restore this reading from the English, Norman, and other manuscripts. Some copies read “not ever,” which has the same meaning. The old and recent editions read: “and sometimes a crime is in deed.” We suspect that this was once read in the Utica manuscript, but incorrectly.]

Hence the Psalmist says: “Who understands offenses?” (Psalm 18:13). Sins of deed are recognized more quickly because they are seen outwardly; sins of thought are more difficult to recognize because they are committed invisibly.

Whoever, therefore, anxiously desires to appear clean before the coming Judge examines himself now with all the greater subtlety, since he considers that he must then stand free from that Judge’s terror. He begs that whatever displeases God may be shown to him, so that he may punish it in himself through repentance; and by judging himself here, he may become beyond judgment.

### 58. Through sin we have fallen into such blindness that we do not know ourselves

Amid all this we must observe how great a punishment of our exile has struck us: we have fallen into such blindness that we do not know ourselves. We commit evils and yet do not immediately recognize even what we have committed. For when the mind has been excluded from the light of truth, it finds nothing in itself but darkness; often it sets its foot into a pit of sin and does not know it. [Col. 0979B–C]

This it suffers because of the blindness of its exile alone: driven away from the Lord’s illumination, it has also lost the ability to see itself, because it has not loved the face of its Creator. Hence it is added:

### CHAPTER XLIII

**VERSE 24.** “Why do you hide your face and consider me your enemy?”

### 59. We must return from punitive fear to love

The human race possessed the contemplation of the inner light in paradise. But, pleasing itself, it withdrew from itself [Note: Bellovac., perhaps better, “by which he withdrew toward himself”; for man abandoned God in order to approach himself and cling to himself], and lost the light of its Creator and his face. [Note: Recent editions add “by turning away,” against the manuscripts.] It fled to the trees of paradise because, after its fault, it feared seeing the one whom it had been accustomed to love.

But behold: after guilt came punishment, and from punishment it returns to love, because it has discovered what the fruit of guilt was. Stirred up by punishment, it seeks the face it feared in its guilt, so that it may now flee the darkness of its blindness and grievously dread the fact that it does not see its Creator.

Moved by this longing, the holy man cries out: “Why do you hide your face and consider me your enemy?” For if you looked upon me as a friend, you would not deprive me of the light of your vision.

Following the instability of the human heart, he adds:

### CHAPTER XLIV

**VERSE 25.** “Do you show your power against a leaf carried away by the wind, and pursue a dry straw?”

### 60. Man, like a leaf and straw, is moved by the wind of temptation

What is man except a leaf—the one who fell from the tree in paradise? What is he except a leaf, carried away by the wind of temptation and lifted up by the gusts of desire?

The human mind suffers so many temptations that it is moved by as many gusts. Anger often disturbs it; when anger withdraws, foolish joy takes its place. It is pressed by the goads of lust, and by the heat of greed it is stretched far and wide to grasp earthly things. At times pride lifts it up; at times disordered fear casts it down to the lowest places.

Since it is lifted and driven by so many gusts of temptation, man is rightly compared to a leaf. Hence Isaiah fittingly says: “We have all fallen like a leaf, and our iniquities have carried us away like the wind” (Isaiah 64:6). Iniquity carried us away like the wind because, fixing us in no weight of virtue [Note: Bellovac., “because, with no fixed weight of virtue”], it lifted us into empty exaltation.

After calling man a leaf, he rightly also calls him straw. In creation he was a tree, but in temptation he made himself a leaf; afterward, in his abasement, he appeared as straw. Because he fell from a height, he is a leaf; because through the flesh he was close to the earth even when he seemed to stand, he is also remembered as straw. But because he has lost the greenness of inward love, he is now dry straw.

Let the holy man therefore consider both how worthless man is and how strict God is, and say: “Do you show your power against a leaf carried away by the wind, and pursue a dry straw?” [Note: Most Norman manuscripts, “as though he plainly said.” In the Utica manuscript the reading now is “let him say”; formerly, as we conjecture, “he laments.”] As though he were openly lamenting: Why do you attack with such strictness one whom you know to be so weak in temptation?

It continues:

### CHAPTER XLV [Revised XXIII]

**VERSE 26.** “For you write bitter things against me.”

### 61. The sentence written concerning the death of sinful humanity cannot be changed

Everything we say passes away, whereas what we write remains. Thus God is said not to speak but to write bitter things when his scourges endure over us for a long time.

Once, concerning the human being who sinned, it was said: “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Genesis 3:19). Angels who appeared to human beings often gave commandments. Moses the lawgiver restrained sins through strictness. The Only-Begotten of the supreme Father himself came to redeem us; by dying, he swallowed up death and announced eternal life to us, which he displayed in himself.

Nevertheless, the sentence concerning the death of our flesh, given in paradise, is not changed from the beginning of the human race until the end of the world. “What man is there who lives and shall not see death?” (Psalm 88:49). The Psalmist, observing this again, says: “You are terrible, and who can resist you?” [Note: Vendôme, “and who can resist you in your wrath?”] “From that time your wrath” (Psalm 75:8).

He became angry with the human being who sinned in paradise and once established the sentence of mortality upon our flesh; this sentence can in no way be changed now or until the end. Let him therefore say: “You write bitter things against me.” Hence he continues:

### CHAPTER XLVI [Old XXV, Revised XXIV]

**SAME PASSAGE.** “And you wish to consume me with the sins of my youth.”

### 62. The ages of the body and of the mind are different

Behold, the righteous man, because he does not find that he sinned in his youth, fears the deeds of his adolescence. We should know, however, that just as there are stages of growth in the body, so there are stages of age in the mind.

The first age of a human being is infancy. Though the infant lives innocently, it does not know how to express the innocence it possesses. Childhood follows, in which one is already able to say what one wishes. Adolescence succeeds it; this is the first age suited to action. Youth then follows, suited to strength, and afterward old age, which in due course is suited to maturity.

Since we have called adolescence the first age suited to good actions, righteous people, when they advance to great maturity of mind, sometimes recall the beginnings of their deeds and reproach themselves for their origins in proportion to how far they have progressed in the gravity of mind. For the more fully they attain the height of discernment, the more they discover that they were undiscerning. [Note: This is to be read from the Vendôme, Norman, and other manuscripts, not as the printed editions, including the old editions, have it: “in which they later more fully attain the art of discernment.”] It is therefore rightly said through the voice of the holy man that the sins of adolescence are feared.

If the passage is to be held according to its literal sense, we should consider how grave the sins of the young and the old must be, if this righteous man fears even what he committed in a weak age.

It continues:

### CHAPTER XLVII [Revised XXV]

**VERSE 27.** “You have put my foot in fetters, and observed all my paths, and considered the tracks of my feet.”

### 63. The severity of divine judgment in punishing even wrongful thoughts

God has put the human being’s foot in fetters because he has bound his perversity by the sentence of his strong strictness. He observes all his paths because he judges each of his actions with subtlety.

A path is usually narrower than a road. Since by roads we understand actions, we rightly understand the paths themselves as the thoughts underlying actions. God therefore observes all the paths because in each of our actions he also weighs our thoughts. He considers the tracks of our feet because he examines how rightly the intentions of our works are placed, lest even what is done well be done with an improper desire.

The tracks of the feet can also signify certain evil deeds. The foot in the body is the track on the road. Often, when we do certain wrong things and our brothers observe us, we provide a bad example; as though our foot had been turned off the road, we leave distorted tracks for those who follow, provoking other hearts to scandal through our actions.

It is exceedingly difficult to guard oneself so that one does not dare to do evil, so that one does not stumble in good actions through intention, and so that a leftward thought does not deceive one amid upright works. Yet almighty God examines all these things subtly and repays each one at the judgment.

But when can a human being, constrained by the weakness of the flesh, rise subtly against all these things and maintain uprightness with an unshaken mind? Hence it is appropriately added:

### CHAPTER XLVIII

**VERSE 28.** “I shall be consumed like rottenness, and like a garment that is eaten by moths.”

### 64. Man is consumed by the decay innate within him

Just as a garment is eaten by a moth that has arisen from it, so a human being has decay within himself by which he is consumed. He has within himself that from which he is consumed, so that he ceases to be.

The passage can also be understood in another way if it is spoken in the voice of a tempted person: “I shall be consumed like rottenness, and like a garment that is eaten by moths.” A human being is consumed like rottenness when he is worn down by the corruption of his flesh. Since unclean temptation arises not from somewhere else but from himself, temptation consumes the flesh like a moth consuming the garment from which it emerged.

A person has within himself the source of his temptation. Thus the moth consumes the garment after proceeding from that same garment.

We should also note that a moth perforates a garment without making a sound. Likewise, a thought often pierces the mind so that the mind itself does not feel it until it has been pierced by its sting. It is therefore rightly said that a human being is consumed like a garment by a moth, because sometimes we do not recognize the wounds of our temptations until we have been pierced by them in the mind.

Considering this weakness of ours, the holy man continues:

### CHAPTER XLIX [Old and Revised XXVI]

**CHAPTER 14, VERSE 1.** “Man, born of woman, living for a short time, is filled with many miseries.”

### 65. Man is born from weakness because he is born of woman

In sacred speech, “woman” is used either for sex or for weakness. It is used for sex, as it is written: “God sent his Son, made of a woman, made under the Law” (Galatians 4:4). It is used for weakness, as a certain wise man says: “The iniquity of a man is better than a woman doing good” (Sirach 42:14).

A strong and discerning person is called a man, whereas a woman is understood as a weak or undiscerning mind. It often happens that a discerning person suddenly falls into guilt, while another who is undiscerning and weak performs a good action. Yet the person who is undiscerning and weak is sometimes lifted up more by what he has done well and falls more seriously into guilt. The discerning person, however, even from recognizing that he has acted badly, draws himself more tightly back to the rule of strictness; and from the very point at which he seemed for a time to have fallen away from justice, he advances more deeply toward justice.

In this respect it is rightly said: “The iniquity of a man is better than a woman doing good,” because sometimes even the fault of the strong becomes an occasion of virtue, while the virtue of the weak becomes an occasion of sin.

What, then, is signified here by “woman” except weakness, when it is said: “Man, born of woman”? [Note: Sag, Utica, and others, “weakness of mind is signified.”] It is as though he were saying more plainly: What strength will a person possess who has been born from weakness?

### 66. He is confined with respect to life and expanded with respect to misery

“Living for a short time, he is filled with many miseries.” [Note: Many Norman manuscripts, “filled with many miseries.” In the Utica manuscript this was formerly read in that form, but the censor’s style changed the s to r.] Here, in the words of the holy man, the punishment of humanity is briefly expressed: it is confined with respect to life and expanded with respect to misery. [Col. 0983A–B]

If everything that is done here is examined subtly, it is all punishment and misery. To be subject to the corruption of the flesh even for necessary and permitted things is misery: garments are sought against cold, food against hunger, and coolness against heat. The body’s health is guarded with great care; even when guarded, it is lost; when lost, it is restored with great labor; and even when restored, it is always uncertain. What else is this but the misery of mortal life?

We love our friends while fearing that they may be offended [Note: Vendôme, Utica, Bigot, and Lyr, “who may be capable of being offended through suspicion”]; we fear our enemies and are not secure concerning those whom we fear. Often we speak confidently to enemies as though they were friends; sometimes we receive the sincere words of our neighbors, who perhaps love us deeply, as though they were the words of enemies. Although we never wish either to be deceived or to deceive, through our caution we err more seriously. What, then, is this except the misery of human life?

Having lost his heavenly homeland, man—driven away from it—takes pleasure in exile, is burdened by cares, and yet avoids considering how grievous it is that many things are thought about. [Note: These words, “because many things are thought about,” are absent from Vendôme.] He has been deprived of the inner light and yet wishes to endure his blindness in this life for a long time. What else is this but misery born from our punishment?

Yet although he desires to remain here for a long time, the very course of mortal life compels him to depart. [Note: Almost all the Norman manuscripts add: “But although he desires to remain here for a long time, by the very course of mortal life he is compelled to depart;” then, “the holy man,” etc.] Hence the holy man rightly continues:

### CHAPTER L [Old XXVII]

**VERSE 2.** “He comes forth like a flower and is crushed; he flees like a shadow and never remains in the same condition.”

### 67. The world is filled with as many flowers, destined soon to wither, as it has names

He comes forth like a flower because he shines in the flesh, but he is crushed because he is reduced to decay. What are human beings born into the world except flowers in a field?

Let us direct the eyes of our heart toward the breadth of this present world, and behold: it is filled with almost as many flowers as it has names. Life in the flesh is therefore a flower in the hay. Hence the Psalmist rightly says: “Man’s days are like grass; like a flower of the field, so he will flourish” (Psalm 102:15). Isaiah also says: “All flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of the field” (Isaiah 40:6).

A human being comes forth in the manner of a flower from concealment and suddenly appears in public; then, through death, he is immediately withdrawn from public view into concealment. The greenness of the flesh displays us, but the dryness of dust withdraws us from sight. We appeared like a flower, though we did not previously exist; we wither like a flower, having appeared only for a time. [Note: Vendôme perhaps has the better reading: “We wither like grass,” which corresponds better to the other member, “we appeared like a flower.”]

### 68. At every moment of life man advances toward death. He declines from the very point at which he advances

Because man is driven daily, moment by moment, toward death, it is rightly added: “He flees like a shadow and never remains in the same condition.”

But since the sun also constantly completes its course and never fixes itself in stability, why is the course of human life compared to a shadow rather than to the sun? It is because, having lost love for his Creator, man lost the warmth of his heart and remained only in the cold of his iniquity. For, in the words of Truth: “Iniquity will abound, and the love of many will grow cold” (Matthew 24:12). [Note: Some copies, with Sag, read: “Iniquity abounded.”]

Whoever therefore does not possess the warmth of the heart in the love of God, and yet cannot retain the life he loves, flees like a shadow. Hence it is also rightly written of him: “Because he followed a shadow” (Sirach 34).

It is rightly said: “He never remains in the same condition,” because infancy passes into childhood, childhood into adolescence, adolescence into youth, youth into old age, and old age into death. In the course of the present life, man is driven toward decline by his very growth, and he always declines from the point at which he believes he is advancing through the extension of life.

We cannot possess a fixed condition here, since we have come here only to pass away; and this very living of ours is daily a passing away from life. The first man could not have possessed this falling away before his fault, because while he stood firm, time passed. But after he sinned, he placed himself, as it were, on a slippery slope of temporality; and because he ate the forbidden food, he immediately discovered the loss of his former stability.

Man suffers this mutability not only outwardly but inwardly as well, when he strives to rise to better works. The mind, under the weight of its mutability, is always driven toward something other than what it is; and unless it is held firmly in its proper state by the discipline of strict watchfulness, it continually slips into worse things. [Note: Most Norman manuscripts, “for it always…”]

Because it abandoned the one who always stood firm, it lost the state that it could have possessed. Thus, when it strives toward better things, it struggles as though against the current of a river. But when it relaxes its intention of ascending, it is brought down to the depths without effort.

Since there is labor in ascending and ease in descending, the Lord admonishes those who are to enter through the narrow gate, saying: “Strive to enter through the narrow gate” (Luke 13:24). Since he was about to speak of entering through the narrow gate, he first said, “Strive,” because unless the effort of the mind burns [Note: Ebroic and other Norman manuscripts, “because unless the intention of the mind burns”], the wave of the world cannot be overcome; through it the soul is continually dragged back down.

Since man is born like a flower and is crushed, since he flees like a shadow and never remains in his own condition, let us hear what he adds to this reflection. It continues:

### CHAPTER LI

**VERSE 3.** “Do you consider it worthy to open your eyes upon such a one and bring him with you into judgment?”

### 69. Two extremes: man and the Creator, dust and God

He had earlier considered both the power of almighty God and his own weakness. He set himself and God before his eyes and weighed who was coming to judgment with whom. On one side he saw man, and on the other the Creator—that is, dust and God—and rightly said: “Do you consider it worthy to open your eyes upon such a one?”

For almighty God to open his eyes is to exercise judgment, to see whom he will strike. [Note: Ebroic, “to exercise judgments.”] As though with closed eyes, he does not look upon one whom he does not wish to strike. Hence he immediately adds concerning the judgment itself: “And bring him with you into judgment?” [Col. 0985B–C]

But because he has contemplated God coming to judgment, he again considers his own weakness. He sees that he cannot be clean by himself, since, in order to exist, he came forth from uncleanness, and he adds:

### CHAPTER LII

**VERSE 4.** “Who can make clean what has been conceived from unclean seed? Is it not you, who alone are?”

### 70. Because of his corrupted origin, man suffers uncleanness even unwillingly

The one who alone is clean in himself is able to cleanse the unclean. A human being living in corruptible flesh has the uncleanness of temptations impressed upon himself because he has drawn them from his origin. His very conception, because of the pleasure of the flesh, is uncleanness. Hence the Psalmist says: “For behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in offenses my mother bore me” (Psalm 50:7).

This is why a person is often tempted unwillingly. This is why he suffers certain unclean things in his mind, although his judgment resists them: conceived from uncleanness, while striving toward purity, he attempts to overcome what he is.

Whoever has overcome the movements of hidden temptation and the uncleanness of thought should by no means attribute his purity to himself. No one can make clean what was conceived from unclean seed except the one who alone is clean in himself.

Therefore, whoever has already reached in mind the place of purity should look back upon the path of his conception by which he came, and from this understand that he does not possess the purity of his life through his own strength. His beginning of existence was made from uncleanness.

This passage can also be understood as referring to the incarnation of the Redeemer. Blessed Job, looking upon it, saw that the only human being in the world who was not conceived from unclean seed was the one who came into the world from a Virgin, so that he possessed nothing from unclean conception. For he proceeded not from man and woman, but from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary.

He alone therefore truly existed as clean in his flesh. He could not be touched by the pleasure of the flesh, because he did not come here through carnal pleasure.

# BOOK TWELVE

In this book, after explaining chapter 14 of the Book of Job, beginning with verse 5, chapter 15 is for the most part expounded in a moral sense.

[Column 0985; Column 0985C] [Old and Revised I.]

It is characteristic of the righteous to consider the present life, which is so fleeting, with all the greater concern, the more carefully they know how to weigh the eternal goods of the heavenly homeland. From what they perceive within as enduring, they observe more subtly, outwardly, the flight of passing things. [Col. 0985C–D]

Thus blessed Job, after pronouncing the sentence concerning the passing of human time, saying, “Man, born of woman, living for a short time,” and again, “He flees like a shadow and never remains in the same condition,” adds further concerning the shortness of his life:

### CHAPTER I

**CHAPTER 14, VERSE 5.** “The days of man are short; the number of his months is with you.”

### 1. What passes with such speed is considered as though it did not exist

He considers as though nonexistent among us whatever passes with such speed. Yet because even things that pass away stand before almighty God, he says that the number of our months exists with him. [Col. 0986C–D]

Alternatively, the brevity of time is signified by days, while months signify the spans of days multiplied together. Our days are therefore short. But because our life is extended afterward, the number of our months is said to exist with God. Hence Solomon also says: “Length of days is in his right hand.”

It continues:

### CHAPTER II [Revised II]

**SAME PASSAGE.** “You have established his boundaries, which cannot be passed.”

### 2. Nothing happens to human beings without God’s counsel, even if it is hidden

Nothing that happens to human beings in this world comes without the hidden counsel of almighty God. For God, knowing beforehand all that would follow [Note: Bigot and Lyr, “knowing beforehand what was to come”; Utica, “what was to follow”], decreed before the ages how everything would be ordered through the ages.

It was already established for the human being how far the prosperity of the world would follow him and how far adversity would strike him, so that neither excessive prosperity would lift up God’s chosen nor excessive adversity crush them. It was also established how long each person would live temporally within this mortal life.

Although almighty God added fifteen years to the life of King Hezekiah (2 Kings 20:1), when he allowed him to die, he had foreknown that he would die then. In this matter a question arises: how could the Lord say to him through the prophet, “Set your house in order, for you shall die and shall not live,” when, after the sentence of death had been pronounced, life was immediately added in response to his tears?

Through the prophet the Lord declared the time at which Hezekiah deserved to die; through the generosity of his mercy, he postponed death to the time he had foreknown before the ages. The prophet was therefore not false, since he made known the time of death at which that man deserved to die; nor were the Lord’s decrees overturned, since it had also been established before the ages that his years of life would be increased by God’s generosity. The span of life that was unexpectedly added outwardly had been established inwardly without any increase to divine foreknowledge. [Note: Bellovac, Turon, Norman, and the old editions have this reading. Recent editions have “without an increase in foreknowledge.”]

It is therefore rightly said: “You have established his boundaries, which cannot be passed.”

### 3. God also sets a limit to spiritual progress

This can also be understood spiritually. Sometimes we strive to advance in virtues and receive certain gifts, while, rejected from others, we lie in the depths. No one grasps as much virtue as he desires, because almighty God, discerning the inner person, sets a limit even to spiritual progress, so that a person may not exalt himself in those things he can achieve because of the good he attempts to grasp but cannot. [Note: Norman, “so that from this good which…”; formerly in Utica, as in the old and revised editions, “so that a person…”]

That eminent preacher who had been caught up to the third heaven and penetrated the secrets of paradise was unable to remain tranquil and untempted after the revelation (2 Corinthians 12:3). [Note: Norman and Bellovac read “he wished”; Vendôme, instead of “he wished,” has “he did not wish.”] Since almighty God establishes boundaries for the human being that cannot be passed, he raised that preacher to the knowledge of sublime things and then brought him back again to bear lowly things. Thus, when he saw the measure of his condition, he strove to attain security but could not; and, lest he go outside himself through exaltation, he was compelled by humility always to return within his proper boundaries.

It continues:

### CHAPTER III [Revised III]

**VERSE 6.** “Withdraw from him a little, so that he may rest, until his desired time comes, like the day of a hired laborer.”

### 4. The saints continually yearn for eternal rest because of their weariness with the present life

Here “withdraw” means: remove the force of the scourge. For who can rest when God withdraws, since he alone is rest, and the farther anyone is from him, the more restless he becomes? Thus “withdraw from him” is said so that it is understood as: withdraw from striking him.

It is appropriately followed by: “Until his desired time comes, like the day of a hired laborer.” The farther a hired laborer is from the end of his work, the farther he is from the payment of his wages.

Likewise, every holy person placed in this life, when he sees that he is far from the end of the present life, groans that he is far from eternal joys. What, then, does “Withdraw from him a little, so that he may rest” mean except: Remove now the scourges of the present life, and show the good things of eternal rest?

Hence he adds concerning that rest itself: “Until his desired time comes, like the day of a hired laborer.” A person’s desired day comes like the day of a hired laborer when he receives eternal rest as recompense for his labor. [Col. 0987D–0988A]

As far as the appearance of the present life is concerned, however, blessed Job continues to show how contemptible the human race is, filled with many miseries, and how far even insensible things seem to surpass it, when he says:

### CHAPTER IV [Old III, Revised IV]

**VERSES 7–10.** “A tree has hope: if it is cut down, it grows green again, and its branches sprout. If its root has grown old in the earth and its trunk has died in the dust, at the scent of water it will bud and produce foliage as when it was first planted. But when a human being has died, been stripped bare, and consumed, where, I ask, is he?”

### 5. Much is signified by the name “tree”: the Cross, the just man, and the incarnate Wisdom of God. Through the suffering of the just, people are kindled to love of the heavenly homeland.

But since this is clear according to the literal sense, we must bring the meaning back to inward things and investigate how these matters ought to be understood spiritually. For in Holy Scripture the name “tree” sometimes signifies the cross, sometimes a just or even an unjust man, and sometimes the incarnate Wisdom of God.

The cross is signified by the tree when it is said: “Let us put wood into his bread” (Jeremiah 11:19). To put wood into the bread is to apply the cross to the Lord’s body.

Again, by the name “tree” a just or even an unjust man is represented, as the Lord says through the prophet: “I, the Lord, have humbled the lofty tree and exalted the lowly tree” (Ezekiel 17:24). For, according to the voice of that same Truth: “Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke 14:11).

Solomon also says: “If a tree falls toward the south or toward the north, in whatever place it falls, there it will remain” (Ecclesiastes 11:3). On the day of his death the just man falls toward the south, and the sinner toward the north, because the just man is led through the fervor of the spirit to joys, while the sinner is rejected with the apostate angel who said, “I will sit on the mountain of the covenant, on the sides of the north” (Isaiah 14:13), in the coldness of his heart.

Again, by “tree” the incarnate Wisdom of God is represented, as it is written of her: “She is a tree of life to those who grasp her” (Proverbs 3:18); and as she herself says: “If they do these things in the green wood, what will be done in the dry?” (Luke 23:31). [Note: Most Norman manuscripts read “and as he himself says”; Uticensis formerly read *ipsa* (“she herself”).]

Therefore, in this passage, when the tree is set before the human being, what is meant by “human being” except every carnal person? And what is designated by the name “tree” except the life of each just person?

“For the tree has hope: if it is cut down, it will sprout again,” because when the just person suffers death for the sake of truth, he is restored in the greenness of eternal life. [Note: In Uticensis and other manuscripts, *in* is absent, and the reading is *morte afficitur* (“is afflicted by death”).] He who here was green through faith is there green through vision.

“And its branches put forth shoots,” because often, from the suffering of the just, all the faithful multiply in love of the heavenly homeland and receive the greenness of spiritual life, while here they rejoice that they have acted courageously for God. [Note: Lyranus, Saggius, Bigotius, and others read “for this man” instead of “for God.”]

The text continues:

## CHAPTER V

### Verses 8–9

“If its root grows old in the earth, and its trunk dies in the dust, at the scent of water it will bud and produce foliage as when it was first planted.”

### 6. Through their death the just produce abundant fruits in us.

What is the root of the just man except holy preaching, since he arises from it and subsists in it? And what is meant by “earth” or “dust” except the sinner, to whom the voice of the Creator says: “You are earth, and into earth you will go,” or, as our translation has it: “You are dust, and into dust you will return” (Genesis 3:19)?

Therefore the root of the just man grows old in the earth, and his trunk dies in the dust, because among the hearts of the wicked his preaching is despised and considered exhausted of all strength. [Note: In Lyranus and Bigotius, “and in the dust the trunk dies” is absent.]

The trunk dies in the dust because his body is deprived of life among the hands of his persecutors. For according to the words of Wisdom: “In the eyes of the foolish they seemed to die, and their departure was considered an affliction” (Wisdom 3:2).

But this man, whose root has grown old in the earth and whose trunk has died in the dust, buds at the scent of water, because, through the breath of the Holy Spirit, he produces in the hearts of the elect a shoot of virtue through the example of his works. [Note: Turonensis and Normannus read: “he produces a shoot of virtue through the example of his work.”]

The designation “water” is sometimes accustomed to signify the watering of the Holy Spirit, as it is written: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. Whoever drinks from the water that I will give him will never thirst” (John 7:37; 4:13).

The text continues: “And it will produce foliage as when it was first planted.” For the cut trunk to produce foliage is for the just man, though extinguished bodily, to raise up the hearts of many through the example of his suffering and to display the greenness of truth through right faith.

It is rightly said: “As when it was first planted.” Everything accomplished here by the just is a second planting, because the first planting is not in the work of the just but in the foreknowledge of the Creator. And because all that the elect do is first seen and ordained inwardly and is afterward completed outwardly, it is rightly said: “It will produce foliage as when it was first planted”—that is, it displays in the outcome of its work the greenness that it previously possessed in the foreknowledge of the Creator. [Note: Vindocinus and Normannus read “in the presence of the Creator.”]

### [Old Text IV.] 7. Human beings fail from themselves, but are renewed when the Holy Spirit comes.

The root of the just person may also be understood as the very nature of humanity, from which he subsists. This root grows old in the earth when the nature of the flesh fails, reduced to dust. Its trunk dies in the dust because the extinguished body is dispersed from its form.

But it buds at the scent of water because it rises again through the coming of the Holy Spirit. “And it will produce foliage as when it was first planted,” because it returns to that form for the attainment of which it had been created, if, placed in paradise, it had not wished to sin.

### 8. Christ is the tree cut down in his Passion and multiplied in his Resurrection.

This may perhaps also be understood of the Lord himself, the head of all good things, in accordance with what we have said above, since he said of himself: “If they do these things in the green wood, what will be done in the dry?” (Luke 23:31).

He said that he was the green wood and that we were the dry wood, because he possessed in himself the power of divinity; we, however, who are merely human beings, are called dry wood. [Note: In Uticensis, “the light of divinity” was formerly read here.]

Therefore the tree has hope: if it is cut down, it will sprout again, because, although it could be killed through suffering, it came again to the greenness of life through the glory of the Resurrection. [Note: Uticensis reads: “and although it fell through suffering, it was able through the glory of the Resurrection to come again to the greenness of life.” Vindocinus reads: “through the resurrection of grace.”]

Its branches put forth shoots because, multiplied through his Resurrection, the faithful grew far and wide.

Its root grew old in the earth, as it were, because his preaching was despised by the unbelief of the Jews. And its trunk died in the dust because, in the hearts of the persecutors—hearts lifted up by the wind of their unbelief—it was regarded as contemptible and despised, since they were able to kill him in the flesh. [Note: Turonensis reads: “by which they were lifted up through the wind of their unbelief.”]

But it budded at the scent of water because, through the power of God, his dead flesh returned to life, according to what is written: “Whom God raised from the dead” (Acts 3:15).

Since God is Trinity, the holy Trinity—namely, the Father, the same Son, and the Holy Spirit—raised the dead flesh of the only-begotten Son. And it produced foliage as when it was first planted, because that weakness of the apostles which had trembled, denied him, and withered through its denial at his death became green again in faith through the glory of his Resurrection.

In comparison with this tree, what is every human being except dust? Thus the text continues:

## CHAPTER VI [Old Text V]

### Verse 10

“But when a human being has died, and has been stripped and consumed, where, I ask, is he?”

### 9. The sinful human being dies in guilt, is stripped of justice, and is consumed in punishment.

No human being is without sin except the one who did not come into this world through sin. [Note: Normannus, Turonensis, Bellovacensis, Vindocinus, and others read: “who did not come into this world.”]

And because we are all bound by guilt, we die through the loss of justice; we are stripped of the garment of innocence previously granted in paradise, and we are also consumed as the death of the flesh follows.

Thus the sinful human being dies in guilt, is stripped of justice, and is consumed in punishment.

The father graciously wished to cover the nakedness of the sinner’s son, who, when he returned, said: “Quickly bring out the first robe” (Luke 15:22). For the first robe is the garment of innocence, which the well-created human being received but lost after being wickedly persuaded by the serpent.

Against this nakedness it is said again: “Blessed is the one who watches and keeps his garments, so that he may not walk naked” (Revelation 16:15). We keep our garments when we preserve the commandments of innocence in our minds, so that, when guilt strips us before the Judge, repentance may cover us as we return to the innocence we lost. [Note: Most copies of Normannus and Turonensis read “the guilt of judgment.”]

It is rightly said: “Where, I ask, is he?” because the sinful human being did not wish to remain where he was created; but here, where he fell, he is not permitted to remain for long.

He willingly lost his homeland, but he is unwillingly expelled from the wandering life that he loves. Where, then, is the one who is not where true being is, because he does not love it?

The text continues:

## CHAPTER VII

### Verses 11–12

“As waters withdraw from the sea, and a river, emptied, dries up, so a human being, when he has fallen asleep, will not rise again.”

### 10. The human mind is like a turbulent sea.

The sea is the human mind, and the thoughts of the mind are like the waves of the sea. At times they swell through anger, become calm through grace, and flow away through hatred with bitterness. [Note: Uticensis reads “they flow away through bitterness with hatred.” A second hand deleted “with hatred.”]

But when a human being dies, the waters of the sea withdraw, because, according to the Psalmist: “On that day all their thoughts will perish” (Psalm 145:4). And again it is written of the dying person: “Love and hatred alike will perish” (Ecclesiastes 9:6).

Thus the emptied river dries up, because, when the soul has been withdrawn, the body remains empty. [Note: Vindocinus reads: “For the lifeless body is like the empty bed of a river.”] The lifeless body is indeed like the empty bed of a river.

In this matter we must carefully observe that the present life—namely, the time during which the soul remains in the body—is compared with the sea and the river. The water of the sea is bitter, while that of the river is sweet. And because we who live here are at one time afflicted by various bitterness and at another found peaceful and gentle through sweetness, the course of the present life is represented by the comparison of the sea and the river. [Note: Only the Gussanville edition adds “troubled.”]

### 11. [Old Text VI, Revised Text V.] Job does not absolutely deny the resurrection, but denies only that it will occur before the end of the world.

But what follows seems extremely difficult: “So a human being, when he has fallen asleep, will not rise again.” Why, then, do we labor, if we are not moving toward the reward of the resurrection? How can it be said, “He will not rise again,” when it is written: “We will all rise, but we will not all be changed” (1 Corinthians 15:51)? And again: “If in this life only we have hope in Christ, we are more pitiable than all human beings” (1 Corinthians 15:19). And Truth itself says: “All who are in the tombs will hear his voice, and those who have done good will come forth to the resurrection of life” (John 5:28).

But the sentence that follows indicates what distinction lies hidden in the preceding statement. For it continues:

## CHAPTER VIII

### Verse 12

“Until heaven is worn away, he will not awaken, nor rise from his sleep.”

### 12. It is clear that he will not rise—namely, until heaven is worn away—for unless the end of this world has come, the human race will not awaken from the sleep of death to life.

He does not mean that the human race will not rise at all, but that it will not rise before the destruction of heaven.

It should also be noted why, after earlier calling the human being dead, he later calls him not dead but sleeping and says that he will not rise from his sleep until heaven is worn away. The reason is plainly that, in comparison with the tree that becomes green again, he calls the human being a dead sinner—one extinguished from the life of justice.

But when he speaks of the death of the flesh, he prefers to call it not death but sleep, clearly indicating the hope of resurrection, because just as a human being quickly awakens from sleep, so he will swiftly rise from bodily death at the Creator’s command.

The name “death” is greatly feared by weak minds, whereas the word “sleep” does not frighten them. Therefore Paul, exhorting the disciples, says: “We do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, concerning those who sleep, so that you may not grieve like the rest who have no hope. For if we believe that Jesus died and rose again, so also God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep through Jesus” (1 Thessalonians 4:12). [Note: “disciples” is absent in Turonensis.]

Why does the excellent preacher call the Lord’s death death, but call the death of the Lord’s servants not death but sleep? It is because, looking upon the weak hearts of his hearers, he skillfully composes the medicine of his preaching. He does not hesitate to tell them that the one whom they already knew to have risen had died; but, in order to instill hope of resurrection, he calls those who had not yet risen not dead but sleeping.

He was not afraid to call dead the one whom his hearers knew had already risen, but he was afraid to call dead those whom they scarcely believed would rise. Blessed Job, therefore, because he does not doubt that those dead in the flesh will awaken again to life, calls them sleeping rather than dead.

The text continues:

## CHAPTER IX [Old Text VII, Revised Text VI]

### Verse 13

“Who will grant that you protect me in the underworld?”

### 13. There are two underworlds: one appointed for the punishment of the wicked, the other for receiving the just until Christ’s coming.

There is no doubt that before the coming of the Mediator of God and humanity every human being, however pure and proven his life might have been, descended to the confines of the underworld. For the human being who had fallen by himself could not by himself return to the rest of paradise, unless the one came who, through the mystery of his incarnation, would open for us the way to that same paradise.

Thus, after the sin of the first human being, a flaming sword is said to have been placed at the entrance to paradise (Genesis 3:24). It is also called turning, because the time would at some point come when it too could be removed.

Yet we do not say that the souls of the just descended into the underworld in such a way that they were held in places of punishment. Rather, we must believe that there are upper regions of the underworld and other lower ones, so that the just might rest in the upper regions and the unjust be tormented in the lower.

Thus the Psalmist, because of the grace of God that preceded him, says: “You have rescued my soul from the lowest underworld” (Psalm 85:13).

Before the coming of the Mediator, blessed Job therefore knew that he would descend to the underworld and asked for the protection of his Creator there, so that he might remain separated from the places of punishment and, while being led to rest, be hidden from torments. [Note: “there” is absent in Turonensis.]

Thus he continues:

## CHAPTER X [Revised Text VII]

### The same passage

“And hide me until your anger passes over.”

### 14. God’s anger is free from disturbance and is completed at the end of the world.

The anger of almighty God exercises the force of his strict judgment every day, in that it plunges those who live unworthily into punishments appropriate to them. This anger now passes, but at the end it will pass completely, because it is presently enacted but will be brought to completion at the end of the world. [Note: Turonensis reads “in this daily course.”]

Yet, with regard to the souls of the elect, this anger passed over at the coming of our Redeemer, because the Mediator of God and humanity, when he mercifully descended there himself, led them from the confines of the underworld to the joys of paradise.

In this connection we must know that the name “anger” is not properly applied to the Divinity, because no disturbance confounds the simple nature of God. Hence it is said to him: “But you, master of strength, judge with tranquility and govern us with great reverence” (Wisdom 12:18).

But because the souls of the just were eventually to be freed from the regions of the underworld, although not from places of punishment, the just man also foresees this and adds in his petition:

## CHAPTER XI [Old and Revised Text VIII]

### The same passage

“And appoint for me a time when you will remember me.”

### 15. Christ led out from the underworld only those whom he knew would have clung to him.

“When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law” (Galatians 4:4).

The man of the Lord foresaw this redemption, through which many also from among the Gentiles were to be freed. As he himself says: “Although you conceal these things in your heart, nevertheless I know that you remember all things” (Job 10:13). He asks almighty God that a time of remembrance be appointed for him.

This is why the Lord says in the Gospel: “And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all things to myself” (John 12:32)—namely, all the elect. For when the Lord returned from the underworld, he did not draw out the elect and the reprobate together; rather, he removed from there all those whom he knew had clung to him.

Therefore, through the prophet Hosea, he also says: “I will be your death, O death; I will be your bite, O underworld” (Hosea 13:14).

What we kill, we cause to exist no longer at all. By biting, however, we remove one part and leave another. Since, then, the Lord utterly killed death in his elect, he became the death of death. But because he removed one part from the underworld and left another, he did not kill the underworld completely but bit it.

He therefore says: “I will be your death, O death”—that is, “in my elect I will utterly destroy you.” “I will be your bite, O underworld,” because, after taking them away, I pierce you in part. [Note: Vindocinus reads: “I crush you utterly.”]

Knowing this coming of our Redeemer to the underworld, blessed Job should ask for what he foresaw would happen and say: “And appoint for me a time when you will remember me.” [Note: Bellovacensis reads “foresees.”]

The text continues:

## CHAPTER XII

### Verse 14

“Do you think that a dead human being will live again?”

### 16. At times words of weakness must be received from the strong.

Just men often express, as though from doubt, something that they themselves feel to be certain and firm, so that they may take upon themselves the language of the weak. [Note: Turonensis reads *per fortem sententiam infirmantes* (“by a strong assertion, strengthening the weak”).] But then, through a strong assertion, they completely contradict the doubt of the weak, so that by appearing to speak doubtfully they may accommodate themselves to the weak to some extent, while by making a certain assertion they may draw the doubtful minds of the weak toward firmness.
