In doing this they follow the example of our Head. As the Lord approached his Passion, he took upon himself the voice of the weak, saying: “My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matthew 26:39), and he accepted their fear in order to draw it away. Then, again, showing the force of strength through obedience, he said: “Nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will” (ibid., 26:39).

Thus, when what we do not wish to happen is imminent, we may ask in weakness that it not happen, while through strength we remain prepared for the will of our Creator to be done even against our own will.

Following this example, words of weakness must sometimes be received from the strong, so that, after their forceful declarations, the hearts of the weak may be strengthened more effectively.

Therefore blessed Job, when he uttered words as though doubting, saying, “Do you think that a dead human being will live again?”, immediately added the statement of his certainty:

## CHAPTER XIII [Old and Revised Text IX]

### The same passage

“All the days in which I now serve as a soldier, I wait until my change comes.”

### 17. Job, despising the course of this life, seeks the state of immutability.

The one who awaits his change with such great desire reveals how certain he is of the resurrection. He also makes known how much he despises the course of the present life, since he calls it military service.

Through military service one always presses toward the end, and each day the conclusion of the campaign is awaited. Therefore he despises the course of this life and seeks a stable state; by serving in this changing condition, he hastens to arrive at his own transformation.

For the just person in this life the burden of his corruption itself is burdensome. Wakefulness exhausts him, and he seeks sleep to temper the labor and anxiety of wakefulness. Yet sometimes sleep itself kills. Hunger wears down the body, and food is sought to remove its necessity; but often food itself becomes burdensome, although it had been sought to relieve the burden of weakness.

The burden of corruption is therefore heavy. If it were not so heavy, Paul would never have said: “The creation was subjected to vanity, not willingly but because of him who subjected it, in hope, because creation itself will be liberated from the slavery of corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God. For we know that the whole creation groans and labors in childbirth until now” (Romans 8:20).

Therefore, desiring the state of incorruption, the holy man should say: “All the days in which I now serve as a soldier, I wait until my change comes.” [Note: The manuscripts and common editions read “for the just person,” rather than “for the just”; the context shows that this is to be retained.]

What occurs in this change he adds:

## CHAPTER XIV [Revised Text X]

### Verse 15

“You will call me, and I will answer you.”

### 18. We will answer God when, at his command, we rise incorruptible.

We are said to answer someone when we return works corresponding to his actions. In that transformation, therefore, the Lord calls and the human being answers, because the incorruptible human being is displayed after corruption, before the glory of incorruption.

For now, so long as we are subject to corruption, we do not answer our Creator, because corruption is far from incorruption, and there is no likeness suitable to our answering.

But of that transformation it is written: “When he appears, we will be like him, because we will see him as he is” (1 John 3:2). Then we will truly answer the God who calls us, when at the command of supreme incorruption we rise incorruptible.

### [Old Text X]

And because creation cannot attain this from itself, but it occurs solely through the gift of almighty God, whereby it is transformed into such great glory of incorruption, the text rightly continues:

## CHAPTER XV [Revised Text XI]

### The same passage

“You will extend your right hand to the work of your hands.”

### 19. What the human being cannot attain from himself.

It is as though he plainly said: “Therefore your corruptible creature can persist toward incorruption because it is raised by the hand of your power and held firm by the grace of your regard.”

The human creature, simply by being a creature, possesses within itself the tendency to flow downward beneath itself. But the human being received from his Creator the ability both to be carried above himself through contemplation and to be held in incorruption within himself. [Note: Turonensis reads “so that he may also be carried upward”; Bellovacensis reads “so that he may also be snatched above himself through contemplation.”]

Therefore, lest the creature flow downward beneath itself but persist in incorruption, the right hand of its Creator raises it to a state of immutability. [Note: The manuscripts of Bellovacensis, Turonensis, and Normannus read “to the state of immutability,” not “to the state of incorruptibility,” which is less appropriate. Vindocinus reads “to the state of unchangeability.”]

The Son may also be designated by the name “right hand,” because “all things were made through him” (John 1:3).

Almighty God therefore extended his right hand to the work of his hands, because, in order to raise the human race, cast down and lying in the lowest places, to the heights, he sent the only-begotten One incarnate for this purpose.

Through his incarnation it has been granted to us that we, who by our own will fell into corruption, may one day be able to answer God when he calls us to the glory of incorruption.

Who could measure the generosity of divine mercy in this matter—that after guilt God leads the human being to such glory? God weighs the evils we commit, yet through the grace of his goodness he mercifully releases us from them.

Thus the text continues:

## CHAPTER XVI [Revised Text XII]

### Verse 16

“You have indeed counted my steps, but you spare my sins.” [Note: Uticensis and Bigotius read “but you spare”; Lyranus reads “but you will spare.”]

### 20. Our guilt must be chastened by repentance, so that God may not punish it.

God counts steps when he marks each of our works for recompense. For what is signified by “steps” except each one of our actions?

Almighty God therefore both counts our steps and spares our sins: he carefully considers our deeds, yet mercifully releases those deeds to the penitent. He sees hardness in sinners, yet, through preceding grace, softens it toward repentance.

He counts our faults when he turns us to mourn individually the things we have done. [Note: Normannus and Bellovacensis read “as though mercifully.”] He mercifully releases them because, while we ourselves punish them, he does not judge them at the final examination, as Paul testifies: “If we judged ourselves, we would certainly not be judged” (1 Corinthians 11:31).

Thus the text continues:

## CHAPTER XVII [Old Text XI]

### Verse 17

“You have sealed up my transgressions as in a sack, but you have healed my iniquity.”

### 21. Unless sins are washed away by repentance, they will come out from the sack of secrecy into the public judgment.

Our transgressions are sealed as in a sack because what we do outwardly, unless we wash it away by repentance, is kept hidden in the secrecy of God’s judgments, so that one day it may come out from the sack of secrecy into the public judgment. [Note: Ebroicensis, Bigotius, Lyranus, and the English copies read this way. In Uticensis, formerly “from the secrecy of the seal” was read; now it has “from the sack of secrecy.” Old and recent printed editions have “from the seal of secrecy.” The context almost certainly requires the reading found in the manuscripts cited above.]

Therefore it is also said through Moses: “Are these things not gathered up with me and sealed in my treasures? On the day of vengeance I will repay them” (Deuteronomy 32:34–35).

But when we are crushed by the scourge of discipline for the evils we have done and mourn them through repentance, he both seals and heals our iniquity, because he neither leaves it here unpunished nor reserves it for punishment at the judgment.

He seals transgressions because he carefully attends to them here in order to strike; but he heals them because through the scourge he completely releases us from them.

Thus he also sealed and healed the iniquity of that persecutor whom he had struck down on the ground, when he said of him to Ananias: “This man is a chosen vessel for me, to carry my name before the Gentiles, kings, and the children of Israel. For I will show him how much he must suffer for my name” (Acts 9:15).

To one whom he still threatens with future sufferings for past excesses, he clearly kept in his heart what that man had done wrong. Yet he had undoubtedly healed his transgressions by sealing them, since he called him a chosen vessel.

Alternatively, our sins are sealed in a sack when we continually weigh the evils we have done with an anxious heart. For what is the human heart except God’s sack? When we carefully observe how greatly we have sinned, we carry our sins as though sealed in God’s sack.

Did David not hold his sin sealed in a sack when he said: “I acknowledge my iniquity, and my transgression is always before me” (Psalm 50:5)? [Note: Uticensis and many others read “I know my iniquity.”]

And because our merciful Creator releases the faults that we recognize by looking upon them and repenting of them, it rightly follows after the sins sealed in the sack: “But you have healed my iniquity.”

It is as though he plainly said: “What you now seal so that I may see it through repentance, you surely act so that it may not be seen in the reckoning.”

The text continues:

## CHAPTER XVIII [Revised Text XIII]

### Verses 18–19

“The mountain falls and flows away; the rock is moved from its place. The waters hollow out stones, the earth is gradually worn away by flooding, and so you destroy human beings.”

### 22. Some are overthrown by sudden temptations, others by slow and gentle ones.

It frequently happens that, when cliffs fall, a rock is moved to other places; waters hollow out stones, and the earth is gradually consumed by floods. But we must examine with great attention what follows: “And so you destroy human beings.”

What does it mean that human destruction is compared with a falling mountain, a displaced rock, a hollowed stone, and earth consumed by flooding, except that it plainly indicates two kinds of temptation?

One kind occurs even in the mind of a just person through a sudden event, so that he is tempted suddenly, shaken and overthrown by an unforeseen occurrence, and sees his fall only after he has fallen.

The other comes gradually into the mind, infects the resisting spirit with gentle suggestions, and consumes all its strength of justice not through the magnitude of the attack but through its persistence.

Since, then, one temptation often overthrows the just by a sudden assault, let it be said: “The mountain falls and flows away, and the rock is moved from its place”—that is, the holy mind, whose place had been justice, is moved to guilt by a sudden shock.

Again, since another temptation gently pours itself into the human heart and corrupts and consumes all the hardness of its strength, let it be said: “The waters hollow out stones,” because continual and gentle enticements to lust absorb the hardness of the mind, and a slow and subtle vice corrupts the mind’s firm and strong resolve.

Thus it continues: “The earth is gradually consumed by flooding.” For just as earth is gradually consumed when water flows over it, so even a strong mind is gently absorbed when vice creeps over it.

Hence it is rightly added: “And so you destroy human beings.” [Note: This appears redundant, since “and” is absent in the manuscripts of Saggius and Uticensis. It was nevertheless formerly read in Uticensis and is found in Germanus.]

That is, when, by a just judgment, you permit temptation suddenly to dominate the mind of the just person who is seen to stand on high, you make the mountain fall and flow away; and when the will is changed toward vice, the rock is moved as though to another place.

But when you permit a slow, subtle, and nevertheless persistent temptation to prevail over the minds of those believed to be strong, the waters hollow out stones and the earth is gradually consumed by flooding, because the hardness of the mind, subdued by gentle suggestion, is softened. [Note: In Vindocinus, “the things that come upon them.”]

### 23. David fell like a high mountain through a sudden collapse; Solomon fell through the gradual enticement of sin.

Let us see how great a mountain that David was, who was able to contemplate such great mysteries of God through the prophetic spirit. But let us also observe how suddenly he flowed downward: while walking on the roof, he desired and took another man’s wife, and killed her husband at the cost of his army (2 Samuel 11:4 ff.). The mountain fell through a sudden collapse when that mind, accustomed to heavenly mysteries, was overcome by an unforeseen temptation and subjected to such monstrous disgrace.

The rock was moved from its place when the prophet’s mind, shut out from the mysteries of prophecy, turned to thoughts of shame.

Let us also see how the waters hollow out stones and the earth is gradually consumed by flooding. Solomon was led, through immoderate use and continual association with women, to the point of building a temple for idols (1 Kings 11:7). He who had first built a temple for God did not fear, through the persistence of lust and after being subjected to unbelief, to build temples for idols.

Thus it happened that from persistent wantonness of the flesh he reached unbelief of mind. What else, then, happened except that the waters hollowed out the stone and the earth was gradually consumed by flooding, since, as the infusion of sin slowly crept in, the earth of his heart flowed away toward destruction?

Let blessed Job therefore consider both temptations—the sudden and immense one, and the slow and prolonged one. Let him consider the falls of human beings, and from what happens outwardly let him draw inward contemplation, saying:

“The mountain falls and flows away, and the rock is moved from its place. The waters hollow out stones, and the earth is gradually consumed by flooding; and so you destroy human beings”—that is, just as these insensible things sometimes collapse suddenly and sometimes are consumed little by little by the softening influence of water, so you either cast down the rational creature whom you made through a sudden temptation, or permit him to be consumed by a long and slow one.

Immediately he explains this same rational creature in the following words:

## CHAPTER XIX

### Verse 20

“You have strengthened him for a little while, so that he might pass away forever.”

### 24. Eternity follows the shortness of life.

The human being is strengthened for a little while because here he receives strength to live for a brief time, so that he may pass forever into a place where the end does not bring his life to a close.

But in this short time in which he has been strengthened, he gathers what will enable him to find eternity—either so that he may rejoice forever or so that he may not escape the punishments he has received.

Because he has been strengthened for a little while so that he may pass away forever, the text appropriately adds:

## CHAPTER XX [Revised Text XIV]

### The same passage

“You will change his face and send him away.”

25. How greatly a human being is changed in death.—A person’s face is changed when death wears away his appearance. He is also “sent away,” because he is compelled, unwillingly, to pass from the things he possessed willingly to eternal things; and when he is brought to them, he does not know in what condition the things he had long held in mind will be left behind. Hence it is also added:

## CHAPTER XXI [Old Version XIII]

**VERSE 21.**—Whether his sons were noble or ignoble, he does not know.

[Note: Lyra and Bigot read, “he will not understand.”]

26. The souls of the saints, seeing God, are ignorant of nothing that lies outside them; it is otherwise with other souls.—Just as those who are still living do not know where the souls of the dead are kept, so the dead do not know how the life in the flesh of those who live after them is ordered, because the life of the spirit is far removed from the life of the flesh; and just as corporeal and incorporeal things differ in nature, so also they differ in knowledge. This, however, must not be understood of holy souls, because those who inwardly see the glory of almighty God cannot in any way be thought ignorant of anything that exists outwardly.

But because carnal people devote their chief affection to their children, blessed Job asserts that they later do not know about the very things they greatly loved here: whether their sons are noble or ignoble, they do not know, although concern for them had always wearied them. If this is to be understood spiritually, however, the name “sons” may appropriately signify works, just as Paul says of the woman: “She will be saved through the bearing of children” (1 Tim. 2:15). For a woman who devotes herself to continence and does not at all bear children will not therefore fail to be saved; rather, she is said to be saved “through the bearing of children,” because through the accomplishment of good works she is joined to eternal salvation.

[Note: The Norman manuscripts read “through progress”; Utic formerly read “through effect.”]

Thus, noble sons are righteous works, while ignoble sons are perverse deeds. A person often strives to perform various good actions with good intention; yet, because of many things that creep in, it is uncertain how his deeds are regarded before almighty God. Whether, therefore, his sons were noble or ignoble, he does not know, because, when his works have been examined with subtle judgment, he is ignorant whether they are approved or rejected.

Here, too, the human being is placed amid the pain of labor, and is led there in the fear of uncertainty. Hence what follows concerns the labor of the present life:

## CHAPTER XXII

**VERSE 22.**—Nevertheless, his flesh will suffer while he lives, and his soul will mourn over itself.

27. Those who delight in the pleasures of the flesh experience greater tribulations through the flesh.—Paul says of married people: “Nevertheless, such persons will have tribulation in the flesh” (1 Cor. 7:28). Yet even those who now live spiritually can suffer tribulation in the flesh. Why, then, is tribulation of the flesh said to belong especially to married people, when it is not far removed even from the life of spiritual persons? It is because those who delight in the pleasures of the flesh frequently receive greater tribulations through the flesh.

It is well said: “And his soul will mourn over itself,” because whoever desires to rejoice in himself is already in mourning precisely because he has withdrawn from true joy. For the creator of the mind is true joy. It is therefore fitting that a person should always find sorrows within himself who, having abandoned the Creator, was seeking joy in himself. It follows:

## CHAPTER XXIII [Old Version XIV, Revised Version XV]

[Col. 1000B]

**CHAPTER XV, VERSES 1–2.**—Then Eliphaz the Temanite answered and said: “Will a wise man answer as though speaking into the wind, and fill his stomach with burning?”

28. The wicked judge the words of the good to be not statements of reason but goads of fury.—We have often said that blessed Job represents the type of the holy universal Church, while his friends represent the figure of heretics. These, as though in defense of the Lord, find an occasion for foolish speech and hurl insulting words against the good. Everything the faithful think displeases them as though it had been spoken into the wind. Hence it is now said: “Will a wise man answer as though speaking into the wind?” They consider the words of the good not words of reason but goads of fury.

Hence it is also added: “And fill his stomach with burning.” For they always strive, as has been said, to cloak even those things they know they are saying insultingly under the pretext of defending the Lord. Hence Eliphaz adds:

## CHAPTER XXIV

**VERSE 3.**—“Do you rebuke him who is not your equal, and speak what is not expedient for you?”

29. When heretics cannot find true accusations, they invent false ones.—They consider no one to possess fear of the Lord unless they can draw him into the folly of their own confession. Hence he adds:

[Note: Vindoc reads, “into the confidence of their folly.”]

**VERSE 4.**—“As far as you are concerned, you have emptied out fear, and you have taken away prayers before God.”

“To take away” means “to remove,” as though he plainly said: “Presuming upon your own righteousness, you disdain to implore the grace of your Creator.”

When heretics cannot find genuine evils against the good, they invent accusations so that they may appear righteous; and it often happens that they proceed to open words of insult. Hence he adds:

## CHAPTER XXV

**VERSE 5.**—“For your iniquity has taught your mouth, and you imitate the tongue of blasphemers.”

30. While seeming to safeguard God’s honor, they attack his goodness.—Iniquity teaches the mouth when a person’s wicked life gives rise to what is worse being said. But because blessed Job had been as free in speech as he was righteous in conduct, he is reproved by his friends, who represent the type of heretics, both for an iniquitous life and for an audacious mouth, so that it is said: “For your iniquity has taught your mouth.”

[Note: The same manuscripts read, “had been free from so great a fear.”]

It is as though he were openly told: “You learned to speak perversely from a more perverse life.”

[Note: Vindoc reads, “and from a more perverse life.”]

Often, however, heretics, while seeming to venerate God, contradict his mysteries, and think they are displaying humility if they deny the truth. For there are some who think they do God an injury if they confess that he assumed true flesh, or if they believe that he could truly die in the flesh for us.

[Note: Turon reads “they inflict upon God,” omitting *injuriam* (“an injury”).]

And while they try to attribute to God, as it were, greater honor, they are compelled to deny the true praises of his goodness.

[Note: “Greater honor” is absent in Vindoc.]

For what is more powerful in the praise of his love than that he should make himself capable of assuming for us those things which appear unworthy of him?

[Note: In a recent edition, *assumptione* (“assumption”) slipped in after *susceptionem* (“reception”). Since this word is not found at all in the manuscripts of Turon, Vindoc, Bellovac, or Norman, we took care to reject it as foreign.]

The holy Church, however, confesses his true flesh and true death; yet, in saying these things, she is considered by heretics to be inflicting an insult upon God. Hence it is now said: “And you imitate the tongue of blasphemers.” If any adversity occurs to him in this world, they say that it has happened to him because of this very injury caused by his confession. Hence it is further added:

## CHAPTER XXVI

**VERSE 6.**—“Your own mouth will condemn you, and not I; and your lips will answer you.”

31. They deliriously claim that confession of the right faith is punished by blows of adversity.—Because they think that evils of adversity arise from an erroneous confession, they assert that his own lips answer him, so that the fault of his speech becomes the cause of his punishment.

[Note: Utic reads, “from the mouth of his confession.”]

At times, however, they wish to suppress this as though reasoning about it. Hence Eliphaz attempts to rebuke blessed Job as though by reason, saying:

## CHAPTER XXVII

**VERSES 7–8.**—“Were you the first human being to be born, and were you formed before the hills? Have you heard the counsel of God, and will his wisdom be inferior to you?”

32. While seeming to defend divine glory, they look after their own.—It is as though he said in clearer words: “You who speak of the eternal, consider that you are temporal; you who debate about his wisdom, consider that you do not know his counsel.”

[Note: Vindoc reads, “Why do you speak of the eternal?”]

But because heretics adopt words in defense of the Lord so that they may appear learned, and, while seeming to defend divine glory, make their own knowledge known to human beings, the words that Eliphaz adds testify to this. He began indeed to speak about the wisdom of God, but immediately fell into self-exaltation, saying:

**VERSE 9.**—“What do you know that we do not know? What do you understand that we do not?”

405. These words plainly show from what exaltation of mind whatever sounds like a defense of the Lord proceeds. It follows:

## CHAPTER XXVIII

[Col. 1002A]

**VERSE 10.**—“Among us are both the aged and the ancient, much older than your fathers.”

33. They falsely flatter themselves with the teaching and agreement of the ancient fathers.—Because all heretics have gone out from the holy universal Church, John testifies, saying: “They went out from us, but they were not of us” (1 John 2:19).

But so that they may commend what they assert to the foolish minds of people as though on the basis of antiquity, they testify that they possess ancient fathers, and call those very teachers of the Church masters of their confession. While they despise present preachers, they glory in the teaching of the ancient Fathers through false presumption, so that they may claim that what they themselves say was also held by the ancient fathers, and thus confirm what they cannot establish by upright reasoning as though by their authority.

Now it is written: “The Lord disciplines the one he loves, and scourges every son whom he receives” (Heb. 12:6). The holy Church often struggles with many adversities in this life, while the life of the reprobate is left without a scourge to the extent that it is preserved for no rewards. But when heretics see the afflictions of the holy Church, they despise her and suppose that she is worn down by so many scourges because of the merit of her perverse confession.

[Note: Ebroic, Lyra, Bigot, and others read, “of her confession.”]

Hence it is further added:

## CHAPTER XXIX

**VERSE 11.**—“Is it a great thing that God should comfort you? But your perverse words prevent this.”

34. They despise the afflicted Church.—It is as though he plainly said to her: “If you corrected your profession of faith, you could long ago have obtained consolation from your scourges.” It follows:

## CHAPTER XXX

**VERSE 12.**—“What lifts up your heart, and, as though thinking great thoughts, keeps your eyes astonished?”

35. They mock the contemplation of the saints, having never experienced it.—Often the mind of the righteous is suspended in the contemplation of higher things, so that outwardly their face may appear stunned. But because heretics do not know that the power of contemplation operates inwardly, they think that this occurs among the righteous and those who think rightly more through hypocrisy than through truth; for they do not suspect that what they themselves cannot possess truly exists in others. It follows:

## CHAPTER XXXI [Old and Revised Version XVI]

**VERSE 13.**—“Why does your spirit swell against God, so that you utter such words from your mouth?”

36. The words of the righteous and the wicked are often similar, but their hearts are different. Heretics mix certain truths with falsehoods; these truths should not be rejected.—Often the righteous, afflicted by various necessities, are compelled to confess their deeds, as blessed Job had done, whom scourges oppressed after his righteousness. But when the unjust hear their words, they think these have been spoken through exaltation rather than truth. They weigh the words of the righteous from their own hearts, and do not think that good words can be spoken humbly.

For just as it is a grave fault for a person to claim for himself what he is not, so it is often no fault at all if he humbly says that he is what he is. Hence it frequently happens that the righteous and the unjust have similar words, while their hearts are always utterly different; and by the very statements with which the Lord is offended in the unjust, he is also pleased in the righteous.

When the Pharisee entered the temple, he said: “I fast twice a week; I give tithes of everything I possess” (Luke 18:12). Yet the tax collector departed more justified than he. Likewise, when King Hezekiah, afflicted by bodily illness and brought to the point of death, was moved to compunction in prayer, he said: “I beseech you, Lord; remember, I pray, how I have walked before you in truth and with a perfect heart” (Isa. 38:3). Nor did the Lord despise or reject this confession of his perfection; rather, he immediately heard him in his prayers.

Behold: the Pharisee justified himself in his conduct, and Hezekiah asserted that he was righteous even in his thought. What offended the one pleased the Lord in the other. Why is this, then, except that almighty God weighs the words of each person against his thoughts, and that words spoken with a humble heart are not proud in his ears?

Thus blessed Job did not swell up against God when he brought forward his deeds, because he humbly spoke of what he had truly done. But heretics often mix certain truths into the words of their errors. Although the friends of blessed Job are entirely mistaken in rebuking him, they can nevertheless say some truths that they learned from his constant practice.

If all their words were to be rejected, the apostle Paul would not have cited Eliphaz’s statement, saying: “He catches the wise in their craftiness” (1 Cor. 3:19).

[Note: Behov and Norm read, “I will seize the wise.”]

Since, therefore, they do not rightly speak against blessed Job even when they say things that are right, let us both trample upon the vice of indiscretion in their words and examine the force of their correctness.

[Note: The passage that follows, up to “behold among the saints,” is missing in Turon.]

It follows:

## CHAPTER XXXII

**VERSE 14.**—“What is a human being, that he should be immaculate?”

37. How can a human being, born from earth and from a woman, be without stain?—By the very fact that he is called “human,” he is shown to be earthly and weak; for “human” derives its name from “earth.” How, then, can one be without stain who of his own will fell into weakness, having been made from the earth?

To this is added:

**IBID.**—“And that he should appear righteous, having been born from a woman.”

A woman first offered injustice to man in paradise. How, then, will one appear righteous who was born from her who stood forth as the provider of injustice? It follows:

## CHAPTER XXXIII [Old and Revised Version XVII]

**VERSE 15.**—“Behold, among his saints no one is immutable, and the heavens are not clean in his sight.”

38. God alone is free from mutability.—By the name “heavens” he repeated what he had previously signified by the designation “saints.” For it is written of those same saints: “The heavens declare the glory of God” (Ps. 18:1). By nature, all of them possess in themselves their own mutability. Yet, because they always earnestly desire to cling to immutable truth, by clinging to it they act so as to become immutable.

[Note: Turon and all the Norman manuscripts read, “yet while they desire earnestly always to cling to immutability,” etc.; Utic formerly read “immutable truth,” as do both the older and more recent printed editions.]

When they hold fast to it with their whole affection, they eventually receive the grace of being lifted above themselves and overcoming what they had been mutable in themselves. For what is mutability but a kind of death? When it changes any thing into another, it kills, as it were, what it was, so that it may begin to be what it was not.

Of the author of all things it is written: “Who alone possesses immutability” (1 Tim. 6:16), because he alone is immutable in himself.

[Note: Bellov reads “immortality”; this was also formerly read in Utic.] Of him James says: “With whom there is no change or shadow of alteration” (Jas. 1:17). For mutability itself is a shadow, which would, as it were, darken the light if it changed it through various alterations. But because mutability does not enter into God, no shadow of alteration interrupts his light.

It is rightly said: “The heavens are not clean in his sight,” because, before God’s strict judgment, even those who become preachers of purity cannot in themselves be perfectly clean. John bears witness to this, saying: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves” (1 John 1:3).

If, then, none among his saints is immutable and the heavens are not clean in his sight, who can presume upon the work of righteousness in himself? Hence it is also added:

## CHAPTER XXXIV [Revised Version XVIII]

[Col. 1004C]

**VERSE 16.**—“How much more abominable and useless is a human being, who drinks iniquity like water?”

39. Our evil works are utterly wicked, while our good works are imperfect and useless.—He had first denied that a human being could be immaculate and righteous by himself; now he calls him abominable and useless: abominable, namely, because of the uncleanness of his stain, and useless because of the injustice of an imperfect life.

Yet “abominable and useless” can also be understood in another way. Sometimes a perverse person appears to do certain things rightly, but through the iniquities he commits even the things he does rightly are destroyed. And because evil things greatly displease God, those things that appear good do not please him either. Thus one who is abominable to God in his evil deeds is useless in his good deeds, because, while he shows himself detestable to God through perverse actions, even what appears right in him does not please him.

[Note: In Norm, “who drinks iniquity like water” is preceded by “and it is rightly added.”]

It is rightly said: “Who drinks iniquity like water.” What is eaten is swallowed slowly, because it is chewed in order to be swallowed. But what is drunk has no delay in being swallowed, since it requires no chewing. Thus, because guilt is committed by a foolish person without any reconsideration, iniquity is drunk like water. Since he does unlawful things without fear, he swallows injustice as a drink without obstruction. It follows:

## CHAPTER XXXV [Old Version XVIII]

**VERSE 17.**—“I will show you; listen to me. I will tell you what I have seen.”

40. The proud, the higher they rise through understanding, the more heavily they fall through exaltation.—All arrogant people have this characteristic: when they perceive something right, or even something small, they bend it toward the use of self-exaltation.

[Note: The manuscripts read *parvum* (“small”) where the printed editions almost always read *parum* (“a little”).] From the very point at which they become higher than themselves through understanding, they fall through swelling into the pit of pride. They consider themselves more learned than the learned, demand reverence from those better than themselves, and strive to teach the holier as though with authority.

Hence it is now said: “I will show you; listen to me.” And because one who speaks of what he has heard teaches with less authority than one who speaks of what he has seen, Eliphaz claims stronger authority for himself by saying: “I will tell you what I have seen.”

[Note: Bigot and Lyra read “may extend”; Utic now reads the same.]

But because heretics are sometimes ashamed of their condemned fathers while nevertheless bringing their opinions forward as though with authority, although they are rightly rejected because of the foolishness of those fathers, the audacity of heretics is rightly introduced in the following words:

## CHAPTER XXXVI

**VERSE 18.**—“The wise confess, and they do not conceal their fathers.”

41. How foolishly heretics boast that those whom they had as teachers of error were wise.—They leap forward to praise them and boast that they alone presided over the Church.

[Note: In the Norman manuscripts, in addition to this reading, “to have been of benefit” is added.]

Hence it is further added:

**VERSE 19.**—“To them alone the earth was given, and no stranger passed through them.”

They think that the earth was given to their fathers alone, because they believe that only the teachers of their errors truly ruled the Church. But who is called a stranger except the apostate angel? Hence the Psalmist says of all the wicked spirits together: “For strangers have risen up against me, and the strong have sought my soul” (Ps. 53:5).

Since heretics think that the hearts of their teachers were not subject to the apostate angel, they deny that the stranger passed through them. For this stranger to pass through each person means to introduce wicked thoughts into his heart. Hence, by the voice of the prophet, the hostile spirits are said to address the soul that stands against them:

[Note: Norm reads, “who said.”]

“And they said to your soul: ‘Bend down, so that we may pass over you’” (Isa. 51:23).

But because Eliphaz the Temanite wishes to be heard as someone about to tell a story, although he knows many things that ought to be said, he does not know that they ought not to be said to blessed Job, let us hear the opinions he expressed against blessed Job. For we should consider not to whom he spoke, but only what he said. It follows:

## CHAPTER XXXVII [Revised Version XIX]

[Col. 1006A]

**VERSE 20.**—“The wicked man is proud throughout all his days.”

42. The elect end their lives in humility; the reprobate in pride.—The elect too sometimes grow proud in certain thoughts and actions of theirs.

[Note: Bellovac, Ebroic, and other Norman manuscripts read “thoughts”; the recent edition has “temptations,” contrary both to the manuscripts and to the old printed editions.] But because they are elect, they cannot be proud throughout all their days, since before they end their lives they change their hearts from exaltation to the fear of humility.

The wicked person, however, is proud throughout all his days, because he ends his life without withdrawing from exaltation. He looks around at what flourishes temporally and neglects to consider where he is being led eternally. He places his confidence in the life of the flesh and thinks that the things he presently possesses will last long. His mind is made firm in pride, every neighbor is held in contempt, and he never considers how suddenly death may overtake him or how uncertain his happiness is.

If he saw the uncertainty of this fleeting life, he would never hold uncertain things as certain. Hence it is rightly added:

## CHAPTER XXXVIII [Revised Version XX]

**IBID.**—“And the number of the years of his tyranny is uncertain.”

43. Death must be feared because it cannot be foreseen.—He ought not to have been proud even if he could have known the definite number of his years, so that, knowing how long he would live, he might foresee when to withdraw from pride. But since the present life is always uncertain, death, which is always creeping upon us, must be feared all the more because it can never be foreseen.

He rightly calls the pride of the wicked person a tyranny. Properly speaking, a tyrant is one who rules in a commonwealth without legal right.

[Old Version XIX.]

But it must be understood that every proud person exercises tyranny according to his own measure. What one person sometimes exercises in the commonwealth—that is, through the power of an acquired dignity—another exercises in a province, another in a city, another in his own household, and another, through hidden wickedness, exercises within himself in his own thoughts.

The Lord does not consider how much evil each person is able to do, but how much he wills to do. When outward power is lacking, he is a tyrant within himself: iniquity dominates him inwardly. For even if he does not afflict his neighbors outwardly, he can nevertheless desire to possess power within, so that he may afflict them. And because almighty God weighs the hearts, in his eyes the wicked person has already done what he has thought.

Our Creator wished to conceal our end from us for this reason: that, since we are uncertain when we shall die, we may always be found ready for death.

[Note: Turon, Bigot, and Lyra read, “we must come prepared for death.” Vindoc reads, “we must be found prepared.” Bellov reads, “we must be found prepared.” The old Paris edition likewise reads this.]

Therefore, after it was said, “The wicked person is proud throughout all his days,” it rightly adds: “And the number of the years of his tyranny is uncertain.” It is as though it plainly said: “Why does one exalt himself as though his condition were certain, whose life is held under the punishment of uncertainty?”

But almighty God not only reserves future punishments for those who act wickedly; he also entangles their hearts here, where they sin, in punishments, so that by the very act of sinning they strike themselves. Thus, always trembling and always suspicious, they fear that others will inflict upon them the evils they remember having inflicted upon others. Hence it further says of this wicked person:

## CHAPTER XXXIX [Revised Version XXI]

**VERSE 21.**—“The sound of terror is always in his ears; and when there is peace, he suspects ambushes.”

[Note: The Norman manuscripts read, “he always suspects ambushes.”]

44. Simplicity of heart is the strongest fortress.—Nothing is happier than a simple heart, because, insofar as it shows innocence toward others, there is nothing it fears suffering from others. Its simplicity is like a fortress of strength. A person is not suspicious of suffering what he does not remember having done.

Hence Solomon rightly says: “In the fear of the Lord there is confidence of strength” (Prov. 14:26). He also says: “A secure mind is like a continual feast” (Prov. 15:15). For the tranquility of security is, as it were, a continual refreshment.

By contrast, a wicked mind is always in distress, because it either plots the evils it may inflict or fears that others may inflict them upon it. Whatever it devises against its neighbors, it fears that its neighbors are devising against it. It becomes suspicious on every side and trembles on every side. Everyone who comes to mind is believed to be seeking something hostile.

For one who lacks the tranquility of security, the sound of terror is undoubtedly always in his ears. Often it also happens that a neighbor speaks to him simply, thinking nothing hostile.

[Note: Turon and Vindoc read, “so that he may speak simply to any neighbor of his.” Bellov reads, “so that his neighbor may speak to him in such a way.” Bigot and Lyra read, “so that any neighbor may speak to him of other matters, thinking nothing hostile.” Utic formerly read, “so that any neighbor may speak to him simply of other matters.”]

But when there is peace, he suspects ambushes, because one who always acts deceitfully does not think that others act simply toward him.

And because it is written: “When the wicked comes into the depths of sins, he despises” (Prov. 18:3), he is already wrapped in the darkness of his iniquity and despairs of the light. Hence it follows:

## CHAPTER XL [Old Version XX]

**VERSE 22.**—“He does not believe that he can return from darkness to light, looking all around for the sword.”

[Note: “To the light” is absent in Norm and Bellov and is also absent from the Hebrew text. Jerome nevertheless reads it.]

45. The wicked person, having despaired of salvation, continually grows in wickedness.—Because he believes that he is being struck by ambushes on every side, he despairs of salvation and continually grows in wickedness.

Sometimes this perverse person also considers the judgments from above and fears that they may come upon him. But when he seeks the wages of the present life, conquered by the madness of greed, he despises those very judgments that he had begun to fear. He thinks that he may die in sin, yet he does not cease from sin. Hence it is added:

## CHAPTER XLI

**VERSE 23.**—“When he moves to seek bread, he knows that the day of darkness is ready at his hand.”

46. Though he fears being struck, he continually increases that for which he will be struck.—Bread is understood as the provision of the present life; the day of darkness as the time of punishment. Thus, in his conduct, this perverse person sometimes recognizes the present anger of the heavenly Judge, but he does not turn away from evil, so that he might be able to turn that anger away from his destruction.

Although his conscience accuses him and he fears being struck, he nevertheless continually increases what he will be struck for.

[Note: Sag reads, “for he despises.”]

He despises returning to the right path, despairs of pardon, and grows proud in his guilt; yet inwardly he has fear as a witness to his wickedness. Although he appears outwardly to act wickedly with boldness, he is nevertheless compelled to tremble inwardly about these things.

Hence it is written: “For when wickedness is fearful, it gives testimony to condemnation” (Wis. 17:10). Whenever someone commits unlawful acts, he fears what he is doing; and fear itself is an open witness to condemnation, because what is being done is feared, yet the evil that is feared is not overcome.

Hence it further says:

## CHAPTER XLII

**VERSE 24.**—“Tribulation will terrify him, and distress will surround him, like a king who is preparing for battle.”

47. With how many distresses is one surrounded who abandons the path of truth, which is accompanied by security. The way of truth is level; the path of falsehood is rough.—The wicked person is surrounded by tribulation and distress in everything he does, because his heart is confused by anxiety and suspicion.

[Note: Utic formerly read “by anxiety and tribulation,” but now reads “by anxiety and suspicion.”]

One person secretly seeks to seize another’s property by force and struggles in his thoughts lest he be discovered.

[Note: “By force” is absent in Bellov and Norm.]

Another, having abandoned the truth, decides to lie in order to deceive the minds of those listening. But how great is the labor of carefully guarding against the discovery of his deceit? He sets before his eyes what those who know the truth might answer him, and with great deliberation considers how, through arguments, he may overcome the proofs of truth by means of falsehood. He surrounds himself on every side and seeks a response resembling truth against the point at which he might be exposed. If he wished to speak the truth, he could have done so without any labor. The way of truth is level, while the path of falsehood is difficult.

Hence the prophet says: “For they taught their tongue to speak falsehood; they labored to act unjustly” (Jer. 9:5). It is therefore rightly said: “Tribulation will terrify him, and distress will surround him,” because in himself, through the labor of fear, he fails who abandons the way of truth, which is accompanied by security.

[Note: Norm reads, “in the labor of the mind”; in Utic it was formerly written, “in the labor of fear.”]

He is rightly compared to a king preparing for battle, because in the very evil he does he is both terrified and eager; he trembles from conscience and pants from desire; he fears and grows proud, recoils from suspicions, and raises his mind through audacity.

[Old Version XXI.]

It must also be understood that a king preparing for battle is so suspicious of the enemy that he also fears the very army he leads, lest it be weakened and, through the soldiers’ abandonment, exposed to the darts of the enemy.

[Note: This is the reading of the manuscripts and English witnesses; even the older printed editions read instead, “that he may also fear the very army which he leads.” Utic formerly had this latter reading.]

Thus the wicked person is surrounded by distress like a king preparing for battle, because, acting falsely and speaking falsely, he fears losing his own soldiers—that is, the arguments of falsehood—and being exposed to the darts of truth if he should perhaps lack something to put forward through deceit.

But although his mind trembles and his conscience accuses him, the wicked person is nevertheless conquered by his desire, and, suppressing his fear, draws boldness from his iniquities. Often, too, even with vengeance in mind, he rises up against God and resolves to suffer any adversity from him, provided that, while he has the power here, he may do whatever pleases him. Hence it is added:

## CHAPTER XLIII [Revised Version XXII]

**VERSES 25–26.**—“For he stretched out his hand against God and was strengthened against the Almighty. He ran against him with his neck held high and was armed with a fat neck.”

48. At times God mercifully resists the will of the wicked; at times, in anger, he allows it to be fulfilled.—These words are understood more openly of the head of the wicked, namely Antichrist, who is said to raise his hand against God and to be strengthened, because he is permitted to be exalted for a short time, so that, to the degree that he is allowed to glory for a little while, he may be punished more harshly forever.

[Note: Bellov, Norm, and others read this way. Utic formerly read, “so that when,” as in the printed editions.]

But because all wicked people are his members, let us now see how what he will do alone at the end of the world is carried out individually by the wicked.

There are some who, whenever they attempt to act against the judgment of almighty God, are broken by the impossibility of fulfilling their will. They turn back to themselves and convert to the one they had wished to despise. Those who could have gone far away, if they had been able to accomplish what they wanted, are sometimes saved precisely because they were unable to fulfill what they wickedly desired.

Thus, brought back to themselves, they recognize what sort of condition they are in and lament that they had wished for things contrary to the truth.

[Note: Vindoc reads, “that they had wished to oppose the truth.” Ebroic reads, “that they had wished for things contrary to the will.”]

There are others who, by the just judgment of God, are more wickedly permitted to fulfill what they perversely desire against God. When wickedness inflames them and power strengthens them, they become increasingly unable to recognize themselves in error, because through their power they are continually drawn outside themselves amid abundant possessions.

It is of their intention that the text now says: “For he stretched out his hand against God and was strengthened against the Almighty.”

To stretch out one’s hand against God is to persevere in wicked action while despising God’s judgments. And because God is more angry when he permits what ought not even to have been conceived in thought to be fulfilled, this wicked person is strengthened against the Almighty, because he is permitted to prosper in his evil action, so that he may both do perverse things and yet live prosperously.

Of him it further says: “He ran against him with his neck held high.”

### 49. The Audacity of the Proud Rich in Wicked Deeds

To run against God with an upright neck is to perpetrate boldly those things that displease the Creator. Concerning this it is rightly said: “He ran,” that is, in his evil deed he encountered no obstacle through adversity. [Column 1010A]

Further it is added: “And he is armed with a fat neck.” A fat neck is wealthy pride, being, so to speak, supported by many layers of flesh through abundant possessions. [Note: Turonensis reads, “as though protected by many carnal things,” which Uticensis formerly represented.] Thus the powerful wicked man is armed with a fat neck against God: swelling with temporal possessions against the commandments of truth, he raises himself up as though by the greatness of his flesh. For what is poverty except a kind of leanness, and what is abundance of possessions except the fatness of the present life? He therefore raises himself against God with a fat neck who turns temporal abundance into pride.

The powerful and wicked have this characteristic: occupied with deceptive riches, they neglect the true riches of God; and the less they seek what is true, the more they are lifted up by false riches. For manifold concern with earthly things, because it occupies, also blinds. [Note: Turonensis, Lyranus, and Bigotius read “occupies and blinds,” omitting *quia*; *quia* was deleted in Uticensis.] Hence it is aptly added:

## CHAPTER XLIV

**VERSE 27.**—“Fatness covered his face.”

### 50. The Abundance of Earthly Things Closing the Eyes

Sight is in the face, which is also the first and more honorable part of the body. Therefore the mind’s attention is not improperly signified by the face, since wherever we turn it, there we see. Fatness therefore covers the face because the desired abundance of earthly things presses upon the eyes of the mind, and disfigures before God’s eyes what ought to have been honorable in them, because it burdens them with manifold cares.

Yet it is not enough for such men themselves to be proud, unless those who are joined to them also glory in their fatness. For there are some who grow proud because they are assisted by greater patrons, and who exalt themselves through their patrons’ power against the poor. Hence it is further said:

## CHAPTER XLV

**THE SAME PASSAGE.**—“And fat hangs from his sides.”

### 51. Those Who Cling to the Wicked Powerful Man Swell with His Power

Since *arvina* means the fat of flesh, and we customarily call “sides” of the rich those whom we see joined to them, fat hangs from his sides because whoever clings to a powerful and wicked man also swells with his power, as though with the fatness of possessions. Following the iniquity of his perverse patron, he does not fear God, oppresses the poor as much as he can, and lifts his heart through temporal glory. When such a person clings to a wicked powerful man, fat certainly hangs from that man’s side.

Further concerning them it is said:

## CHAPTER XLVI [Old recension XXIII]

**VERSE 28.**—“He will dwell in desolate cities and in deserted houses that have been reduced to heaps.”

### 52. While He Is Lifted Up by the Praise of Those Joined to Him, He Is More Violently Dragged into Wicked Deeds

Because a city is so called from the fellowship of those living together, the desolate cities are the groups of perverse people who obey him. By their clamors this perverse man is praised while he is dragged by wickedness into evil deeds. Hence it is written: “The sinner is praised in the desire of his soul, and the one who acts wickedly is blessed” (Psalm 10:3, according to the Hebrew). [Note: Vindocensis and all the Norman manuscripts read “in the desire.”]

The deserted houses, however, are perverse thoughts, which this wicked man inhabits, because in everything he does he seeks to please the thoughts of wicked people. These are rightly called desolate cities and deserted houses, because unless almighty God, in view of their preceding faults, abandoned the conduct and thoughts of such people, they would never proceed to perpetrate more serious offenses.

It is well said: “Which have been reduced to heaps.” For the collapsing structures of houses and cities make heaps, because when the wicked are joined together in confused actions for perverse deeds, they plainly show that they have fallen from the building of life.

It follows:

## CHAPTER XLVII

**VERSE 29.**—“It will not be inhabited, nor will its substance endure, nor will it send its root into the earth.”

### 53. No One Is Enriched with Virtues Unless God Inhabits His Mind; the Proud Man Stands Without a Root and Is Immediately Overthrown by a Gentle Breath

In certain manuscripts, instead of “It will not be inhabited,” I found, “It will not be enriched”; yet the sense does not differ, although the wording does. [Note: Rather, in the Hebrew source, the Vulgate, and other versions and paraphrases, one reads “will not be enriched,” or something similar, such as “will not be made rich.”]

For the one whose mind almighty God inhabits is enriched with virtues. But because the thought of the proud is not inhabited by the grace of its Creator, he is certainly not enriched with virtues. [Note: This passage is corrupt in the editions of Gilotius and Sixtus V of Rome. What is printed there—“therefore because he is inwardly empty, he is enriched, not inhabited”—is far from the sense. Rather, he is not enriched because he is not inhabited, and he remains inwardly empty. Our reading is supported by the manuscripts, both English and our own, and by the old editions.]

For this reason, because he is empty within, it is said: “It will not be inhabited”; but because he swells outwardly with what is transitory, it rightly adds: “Nor will its substance endure.” As though it plainly said: “What he appears to possess outwardly passes away, and what could not pass away he does not possess inwardly.”

Hence it is aptly added: “Nor will he send his root into the earth.” If we understand this as referring to the present earth, it is plainly evident that a tree which has no root in the earth falls when moved by even the slightest breezes. The proud man, while he is strengthened against the almighty Lord, while he runs with an upright neck and raises himself with a fat neck against his Creator, appears to stand like a tree. But his standing is without a root, because, like a tree moved by a gentle breath, his life is torn away at the movement of a hidden judgment. [Note: Vindocensis reads “is preserved.”] [Note: So read the manuscripts and the old editions, not as it appears in Gussanville and other recent editions: “thus in this place.”]

But if in this passage we understand “earth” as the reward of eternal life, of which the Prophet says, “My portion is in the land of the living” (Psalm 142:6), this wicked man does not send his root into the earth, because he never plants the thoughts of his heart in the desire for eternal life. [Old recension XXIV.]

For what a root is to a tree, thought is to each human being, because in that which is seen outwardly a person is held fast by that which is not seen outwardly. [Note: The words “through what is not seen outwardly” are absent from Vindocensis, which is full of errors. Turonensis reads *interius*—“inwardly”—instead of *exterius*—“outwardly.”] Hence it is also said through the Prophet: “He will send down a root and produce fruit above” (Isaiah 37:31). When we direct our thought toward showing compassion to a needy neighbor, we send down, as it were, a root, so that above we may produce the fruit of reward. [Note: Lyranus, Bigotius, and Saguntinus read “our mind.”]

It follows:

## CHAPTER XLVIII

**VERSE 30.**—“He will not depart from darkness.”

### 54. Because He Does Not Seek the Light of Justice, He Does Not Depart from Darkness

If this proud man had wished to return from sin to justice, he would have departed from darkness. But because he does not seek the light of justice, he does not depart from darkness. By his example, those who cling to him also pant after earthly advancement, are kindled by the torches of avarice, and are burned by the fires of carnal desires.

Hence it is added:

## CHAPTER XLIX

**THE SAME PASSAGE.**—“The flame will dry up his branches.”

### 55. He Is Burned, Together with Those Joined to Him, by the Torches of Carnal Desires

If he joined to himself people who sought their eternal homeland, he would have green branches in himself. But because those who are joined to him also burn with earthly desires, and while the flame of desire kindles the minds of his clients it dries up his branches, they bear no fruit of good works, because they pant wickedly after what is below.

It is well added:

## CHAPTER L

**THE SAME PASSAGE.**—“And he will be taken away by the breath of his mouth.”

### 56. He Will Be Severely Tormented Because He Has Loosened the Reins of His Tongue

The more each proud person has power in this life, the more boldly he loosens the reins of his tongue, so that he may speak every kind of perverse thing, fear no one because of his words, strike some with insults, and hurl curses at others. Sometimes he is even carried away into blasphemy against the Creator, as the Psalmist says of such people: “They have set their mouth in heaven, and their tongue has passed over the earth” (Psalm 73:9). [Note: Norman manuscripts read “has passed over the earth”; Vindocensis reads “has passed into the earth.”] [Note: Several manuscripts add, “and therefore the rich man.”]

For this reason the rich man placed in the fire asks that water be dripped onto his tongue from Lazarus’s finger (Luke 16:24). From this it is understood that where he had sinned more greatly, there he burned more atrociously.

Therefore it is rightly said now: “And he will be taken away by the breath of his mouth,” because he received the sentence of punishment precisely where he did not restrain the breath of his mouth under fear of God.

It follows:

## CHAPTER LI [Recent recension XXIII]

[Column 1013A]

**VERSE 31.**—“Let him not believe, deceived in vain, that he will be redeemed by another price.” [Note: The Norman manuscripts and other old editions read “let him not believe.” Thus throughout what follows.]

### 57. Almsgiving Benefits Us Only When We Lament and Renounce Our Sins

Whenever we give alms after sin, we seem to offer a price for wicked deeds. Hence the Prophet says concerning one who does not do this: “He will not give God his propitiation, nor the price of the redemption of his soul” (Psalm 49:8–9). [Note: Vindocensis reads *pro culpa*—“for guilt.”]

Sometimes, however, proud rich men oppress their inferiors and seize what belongs to others, yet distribute certain things to others as though generously. Though they depress many, they sometimes offer assistance and protection to certain people, and seem to pay a price for iniquities that they never abandon. But almsgiving frees us from guilt as a price only when we lament and renounce the sins committed.

For the one who always wishes to sin and also always to give alms offers the price in vain, because he does not redeem the soul that he does not restrain from vices.

Hence it is now said: “Let him not believe, deceived in vain by error, that he will be redeemed by some price.” The almsgiving of a proud rich man cannot redeem him, since the robbery he committed at the same time does not permit his gift to rise before God’s eyes. [Old recension XXV.]

This may perhaps be understood in another way. Often proud rich men, when they give alms, do not give them out of desire for eternal life but to extend temporal life. They believe that they can delay death through donations. But “let him not believe, deceived in vain by error, that he will be redeemed by some price,” because by the gift he has spent he cannot obtain escape from the destined end, since his wickedness itself cuts short his life.

Hence it is added:

## CHAPTER LII

**VERSE 32.**—“Before his days are fulfilled he will perish, and his hands will wither.”

### 58. The Days Appointed for Each Person Can Neither Be Increased nor Decreased; Whoever Hopes for Longer Days Perishes Before They Are Fulfilled

The days appointed for each person by God’s inward foreknowledge can neither be increased nor decreased, unless it happens that they are foreknown in such a way that they are longer with the best deeds or shorter with the worst, as Hezekiah merited an increase of days through the expenditure of tears, and as it is written concerning the wicked: “Death confronts the undisciplined.” [Note: This perhaps alludes to Ecclesiasticus 20:9: “There is a progress toward evil for an undisciplined man, and there is a discovery that leads to ruin.”]

Yet often the wicked man, although long periods of life have not been predestined for him in God’s hidden foreknowledge, nevertheless, because he desires to live carnally, sets before himself a long span of days. And because he cannot reach the time he awaits, he perishes, as it were, before his days are fulfilled.

This can also be understood in another way. Often we see certain people both acting perversely and reaching extreme old age. How then is it said, “Before his days are fulfilled he will perish,” when we often see in some people that their limbs have already failed through long age, yet their desires do not cease to carry out their wickedness?

### 59. After Conversion, One Who Returns to Outward Things Is Uprooted from Every State of Good Works

There are some who, after a wasted life, return to themselves and, with conscience accusing them, abandon perverse paths. They change their actions, oppose their former wickedness, flee earthly activities, and pursue heavenly desires. But before they become firmly established in those holy desires, through mental sluggishness they return to what they had begun to condemn and go back to the evils they had resolved to flee.

Since it often happens that holy men also serve through outward actions for the benefit of many and are occupied with governing peoples, the weak observe this and, still seeking to imitate them through their old pride, insert themselves into outward activities. But the less spiritually trained they are when they enter upon these activities, the more carnally they perform them.

Unless the heart has first grown strong through long effort and prolonged conduct in heavenly desires, when it is poured back into outward affairs it is uprooted from every state of good work. [Note: Ebroicensis reads “falls back into outward activities.”]

Hence it is rightly said of this wicked man: “Before his days are fulfilled he will perish.” For even if he has perhaps begun to do something good, before he grows strong in it through the passage of time he falls back into outward things and wickedly abandons what he seemed to have begun rightly.

Hence it is aptly added: “And his hands will wither.” For when he is untimely entangled in outward activities, he is plainly dried up from every good operation.

Hence it is further well added:

## CHAPTER LIII [Recent recension XXIV]

[Column 1014C]

**VERSES 33–34.**—“His cluster will be injured like a vine in its first blossom, and like an olive tree casting off its flower. For the assembly of the hypocrite is barren.”

### 60. Why the Hypocrite’s Good Works Wither; How Dangerous It Is for Those Who Are Weak in Virtue to Preside

It should be noted that Scripture speaks generally of this wicked man, yet the divine word is directed toward his particular wickedness. For when it says, “His cluster will be injured like a vine in its first blossom, and like an olive tree casting off its flower,” and immediately adds, “For the assembly of the hypocrite is barren,” it plainly indicates that against this wicked man it pronounces a sentence of rejection because of his hypocrisy. [Note: Ebroicensis and Lyranus, as well as Bigotius, read “against this wicked man.”] [Old recension XXVI.]

But we must now consider how the hypocrite is injured like a vine in its first blossom or like an olive tree casting off its flower. If an excessively cold air caused by an irregularity of weather strikes a flowering vine, it immediately dries it of all the moisture of its greenness.

There are some who, after perverse paths, desire to follow holy ways, but before good desires are strengthened in them, as we have said, some prosperity of the present world overtakes them. This entangles them in outward affairs and, by drawing them away from the warmth of inward love, extinguishes them as if through cold. Whatever appearance of the flower of virtue seemed to be present in them, it kills.

The mind grows very cold in earthly activities if it has not yet been made firm by inward gifts. Therefore it is necessary that those who know how to discern and restrain under themselves the higher offices or outward works that will benefit human needs should undertake them. For when a weak person is drawn either into a position of government or into outward activity, he is led, as it were, outside himself and is uprooted. A tree that has not first sent its roots deeply into the ground is likewise more quickly brought down by the force of the winds if it raises its crown high; and the higher it has grown in the air without roots, the more quickly it falls to the depths.

Sometimes, however, heat rather than cold dries up a flowering vine. When it is touched by excessive heat, the cluster withers after its flower has been shaken off. It often happens that those who do not approach good works with a right intention, when they see that they please people, are inflamed more intensely to perform those same works. They anxiously strive to do what will please human eyes and seem to burn with holy zeal. [Note: In Vindocensis, “they anxiously strive to act in ways pleasing to human eyes” is absent.]

Who, then, has been touched by summer heat while in blossom, if not those whom the pursuit of human praise has deprived of fruit? [Note: Vindocensis has the erroneous reading “unless summer in the flower.”]

Hence it is well added: “And like an olive tree casting off its flower.” When an olive tree is in flower, if it is touched by an excessive mist, it is emptied of the fullness of its fruits. Whenever those beginning good works are praised by observers and begin to delight in their praises, a fog of understanding arises in their thought, so that they can no longer discern with what intention they are doing anything, and they lose the fruit of their work, as though through the mist of favor. [Note: Vindocensis reads “as though outwardly from the mist of favor.”]

Hence Solomon rightly says: “Let us rise early and go to the vineyards; let us see whether the vine has flowered, whether the flowers are producing fruit” (Song of Songs 2:12). Vines flower when the minds of the faithful resolve upon good works. But they do not produce fruit if, overcome by some errors, they are weakened and fail to carry out what they had resolved.

### 61. In Good Works One Must Consider Not the Beginning but the End

Therefore we must not look merely to whether the vines are flowering, but whether the flowers grow strong enough to produce fruit. It is not remarkable if someone begins good things; it is very remarkable if he perseveres in good work with right intention. Hence it often happens that if right intention is not maintained in a good work, the very work believed to be good is lost. [Note: Bigotius and Lyranus read “if it does not hold.”]

We have often seen people abandon the earthly possessions they had owned, seek nothing now that is transitory, and involve themselves in no quarrels for the sake of this life. When a faithful soul displays this in itself, it has, as it were, produced the flower of an olive tree. But when some such people again begin to seek the worldly glory they had despised, greedily yearn for earthly possessions they had seemed to reject, occupy themselves with quarrels, and seek injuries against their neighbors, the olive tree has surely cast off the flower it had produced, because it did not bring the beginnings of good zeal to perfected works.

It must be understood, however, that these things always happen to those who do not follow God with pure and simple devotion. Hence it is rightly added: “For the assembly of the hypocrite is barren.” [Note: The words from here through “they gather” are absent from Turonensis.]

He would not have lost the good things he had begun if he had not been a hypocrite. Hypocrites also gather good works, but their gathering is barren, because through what they do they do not desire to receive fruit in eternal recompense. They appear fruitful and green in their works to human eyes, but before the sight of the hidden Judge they appear fruitless and dry.

Often, kindled by the heat of avarice, they display greater works to human eyes precisely in proportion as they desire greater gifts to be offered to them by people.

Hence it is further added:

## CHAPTER LIV [Recent recension XXV]

**VERSE 34.**—“And fire will devour the tents of those who gladly accept gifts.”

### 62. It Is Not Enough Not to Receive a Gift from the Hand Unless We Reject a Gift from the Mouth

Just as the body is in a tent, so the mind dwells in thought. [Note: In Vindocensis, the period through “and it often happens” is omitted.] Fire devours tents when the heat of avarice devastates thoughts.

It often happens that the hypocrite refuses to accept gold or any bodily goods from people, but, because he does not accept these things, seeks to receive greater praise from them. He perhaps does not consider himself to have accepted a gift, because he refuses to receive bodily goods.

It must therefore be understood that sometimes a gift is offered by the hand and sometimes by the mouth. One who gives money gives a gift from the hand; one who offers a word of praise produces a gift from the mouth.

Thus, even if the hypocrite refuses to accept outward gifts that perhaps correspond to earthly need, what he desires to have repaid to him is greater, since he longs to be praised beyond his merit and seeks a gift from the mouth. And because his heart is inflamed with intense heat in that desire for praise, it is rightly said: “And fire will devour the tents of those who gladly accept gifts.”

### 63. Fire Will Devour Those Who Delight in These Gifts

But if we should understand their tents as their bodies, in which their souls dwell, fire devours their tents because those who burn here in mind with the fire of avarice are there also consumed in the fires of Gehenna in the flesh.

The hypocrite’s mind is never free from thoughts of wickedness. Whether he desires earthly things or praise, he envies others the things he longs to have bestowed upon himself. The more he wants to appear holier than everyone, the more he strives to show others as perverse, so that, because others become contemptible, he himself may always appear more worthy of reverence.

Thus it happens that before human judgments he lays out the snares of his tongue against the reputation of his neighbor, so that he alone may gain the esteem of those whom he wishes to please.

Hence it follows:

## CHAPTER LV

**VERSE 35.**—“He conceived pain and gave birth to iniquity, and his womb prepares deceit.”

### 64. He Conceives Pain Who Thinks Perverse Thoughts, in Order to Give Birth to Iniquity

He conceives pain when he thinks perverse thoughts. He gives birth to iniquity when he begins to fulfill what he has thought. By envying, he conceives pain; by disparaging, he gives birth to iniquity.

Iniquity is especially grave when a perverse person strives to show others as perverse, so that he himself may appear almost holy because he has taught that others are not holy.

It should be understood that in sacred language the mind is often signified by the word “belly” or “womb.” Hence Solomon says: “The lamp of the Lord is the breath of a human being, searching out all the hidden things of the belly” (Proverbs 20:27). The light of grace, which comes from above, gives human beings breath for life. This light is said to search out all the hidden things of the belly because it penetrates the secrets of the mind, bringing before the soul’s eyes in tears those things that had been hidden from it about itself. [Note: Most manuscripts read this way. The old Paris edition reads, “bringing them before its eyes to be mourned.” The old Basel edition reads, “bringing them before its eyes.”]

Hence Jeremiah says: “My belly, my belly, I am in pain” (Jeremiah 4:19). To show what he meant by his belly, he added: “The senses of my heart are troubled.” [Note: In Bellovacensis and Germanus the reading is simply “I am in pain in my belly.” This was formerly read in Uticensis without the repetition.]

The mind is therefore rightly understood by the name “womb,” because just as offspring is conceived in the womb, so thought is generated in the mind; and just as food is contained in the belly, so thoughts are contained in the mind.

The hypocrite’s womb therefore prepares deceit, because the more he seeks to appear alone more innocent than everyone else, the greater the malice he continually conceives in his mind against his neighbors.

Eliphaz spoke these things because he thought that blessed Job had been struck by such a blow on account of hypocrisy. Yet although his words apply to many, they are foreign to the one person against whom they were spoken, because the holy man had no duplicity in his actions; Truth itself bears witness to his simplicity of heart.

# BOOK THIRTEEN

In this book a brief moral and typological exposition is contained of chapters 16 and 17 of the Book of Job.

[Column 1017]

## CHAPTER ONE

[Column 1017B]

### 1. Those Whom the Saints Cannot Correct by Admonition They Endure Through Patience

It is usually characteristic of the wicked that, before they are truthfully accused of their own evils, they charge their evils upon the good by reproach. While they fear being rebuked for what they do, they declare that the righteous, who oppose their wickedness, do these same things.

Holy men, however, patiently hear even things they do not remember ever having done, although they know that the evils they see being thrust upon them have been perpetrated by those very accusers. When they cannot correct them by preaching, they endure them through patience, so that, if they cannot obtain the fruit of their conversion, they may nevertheless gain from them the reward of long-suffering. [Note: Other printed editions read “if they are unable to attain it.” We have removed *consequi*, “to attain,” because it is not found in the manuscripts and is otherwise redundant.]

Hence the holy Church says through the words of the prophet David: “Sinners have built upon my back” (Psalm 129:3), because when it tolerates heretics or any reprobates whom it cannot correct, it carries the deeds of sinners upon its back.

Blessed Job, then, seeing his friend Eliphaz complaining at length against him concerning hypocrisy—Eliphaz having burst from words of consolation into the bitterness of reproach and appearing as a feigned consoler—preserves through his patience a type of the Church, which knows how to tolerate such things by hearing them and, when its teaching is received, to refute them by reasoning. He says:

## CHAPTER TWO [Recent recension II]

**CHAPTER 16, VERSE 2.**—“I have often heard such things.”

[Column 1018B]

### 2. Job as a Type of the Church Oppressed by False Friends Who Pretend to Console; Job’s Friends Had Burst from Consolatory into Reproachful Words

The elect often hear the evils of others as though they were their own, and crimes are charged against them by those who perpetrate the very crimes they allege. [Note: The old Paris and Basel editions read “by those from whom crimes were inflicted.” Gussanville has *impincta*, as in the Roman edition of Sixtus V. The reading *impacta*—“imputed” or “laid upon”—appears in the English and our manuscripts.]

By this response blessed Job signifies that period of the Church when, oppressed by adversaries, it is considered almost cast down by their temporal power.

Hence it follows:

**THE SAME PASSAGE.**—“You are all burdensome comforters.” [Note: In very many manuscripts *estis*—“you are”—is absent here and below.]
