Whether heretics or any wicked people, when they see the good laboring under adversity, they try to persuade them of evil precisely in seeking to console them. Their consolation therefore rightly becomes burdensome to the minds of the good, because amid words of sweetness they desire to pour out the poison of error; and while they seem to soothe their pains with gentle expressions, they hasten to impose the burden of sin. [Note: Turonensis reads “the burden of the work.”]

But elect men, even when deprived of temporal glory, do not lose the strength of inward judgment. They know both how to suffer outward adversities and, inwardly unbroken, to defend what is right without fear.

Hence it follows:

## CHAPTER THREE

**VERSE 3.**—“Will windy words have an end?”

### 3. Sound Words Sometimes Become Windy Because of the Pride of Those Who Speak Them; One Must Not Rebuke a Person in Mourning

Windy words are those that serve temporal inflation rather than uprightness. The wicked often say good things; but because they do not say them well, they utter windy words. Even when their statements are sound in their meaning, they are nevertheless inflated by pride. [Note: Saguntinus and Uticensis add another reading: “they are good.”]

In the statement, “You are all burdensome comforters,” what else are we taught by the instruction of blessed Job except that each person should carefully consider whether he is bringing words of reproach during a time of grief? If there are things that ought rightly to be rebuked, they should be postponed in affliction, lest the consoler, by rebuking, increase the pain he had intended to soothe.

It follows:

## CHAPTER FOUR

**THE SAME PASSAGE.**—“Or is anything troublesome to you if you speak?”

### 4. The Righteous Do Not Return Insults

When wicked men exchange insulting words with others like themselves, they fall silent all the sooner because they quickly hear from others such things as they themselves say to their hearers. But when they assail good men with insulting words, no annoyance arises in them from the insult, because they speak against those who remain silent; nor are they compelled to hear what they are, because the righteous do not return insults, even when forced to hear what they are not.

It is therefore well said: “Or is anything troublesome to you if you speak?” As though it were plainly said to him: “You will speak all the more because you do not hear from me anything troublesome about your conduct.”

Hence it is added:

**VERSE 4.**—“I too could speak things like yours.” [Recent recension III.]

The righteous recounts what he could do; but, so as not to abandon justice, he avoids doing what he could do.

It follows:

## CHAPTER FIVE

[Column 1019C]

**VERSES 4–6.**—“Would that your soul were in place of my soul! I too would console you with words and shake my head over you. I would strengthen you with my mouth and move my lips as though sparing you.”

### 5. Divine Strikes May Sometimes Properly Be Desired for the Wicked

Sometimes it is necessary that divine scourges be kindly desired for perverse minds that cannot be corrected by human preaching. When this is done with great devotion of love, it is not the punishment of one who is going astray that is sought, but correction; and it is shown to be prayer rather than a curse.

In these words blessed Job is shown to intend that his friends, who did not know through charity how to sympathize with his grief, might learn through the experience how they ought to have shown mercy toward another’s affliction. Subdued by pains, they might draw from their own suffering consolation for how to bring consolation to others, and might then live more healthfully inwardly when they experienced outwardly something of weakness.

It should be noted that he does not say, “Would that my soul were in place of your souls!” but, “Would that your soul were in place of my soul!” For he would certainly be cursing himself if he wished to become like them. He desired better things for them, whom he sought to make like himself.

We console the wicked who are placed under scourges when we show that, through outward punishment, inward health is growing stronger in them. [Note: The editions of Gilotius and Sixtus V of Rome read “let us introduce,” contrary to the sense and to the testimony of the English and our manuscripts.]

[Old recension III.] We also shake the head when we bend the mind—which is our governing faculty—toward compassion. [Note: Among both Greek philosophers and theologians, this governing faculty is called τὸ ἡγεμονικόν, “the ruling principle” or “the sovereignty of the mind.”] We strengthen them amid scourges when we soften the force of their pain with gentle words.

There are some who, because they do not know inward things, are afflicted despairingly by outward evils. Of them the Psalmist says: “They will not endure in miseries” (Psalm 139:11). He knows well how to endure in outward miseries who always knows how to rejoice in inward hope.

### 6. Sometimes the Church, as Though Sparing the Wicked, Does Not Spare Them; and as Though Not Sparing Them, She Spares Them

I do not think that we should pass over carelessly the fact that he does not say “sparing,” but “as though sparing you.” For the holy Church, preserving the rigor of discipline together with a mixture of gentleness, sometimes does not spare the wicked while seeming to spare them, and sometimes spares them while seeming not to spare them.

We can show this better by setting forth what usually happens. Let us place before the eyes of the mind two wicked men established in the holy Church: one powerful and insolent, the other gentle and submissive.

If some fault should steal upon the gentle and submissive man, the preacher immediately pursues and rebukes it. By rebuking him, he frees him from his fault and reforms him to the way of uprightness. [Note: Turonensis and the Norman manuscripts read “to the way of uprightness.” Uticensis formerly read “to the way of life”; the old Paris edition also has “to life.”]

What, then, did the preacher do for this man except spare him by not sparing him? By not delaying the word of correction, he freed him more quickly from his fault. In speaking freely he did not spare him, but in correcting him he spared him.

On the other hand, when the powerful and insolent man is known to have committed some offense, an occasion is sought for rebuking him concerning the evil he has done. Unless the preacher waits until he can bear correction appropriately, he increases the evil he is attacking. [Note: Turonensis, Vindocensis, Norman manuscripts, and others read “when he can appropriately bear correction.” The old Basel edition of 1514 reads “when he can bring it forward”; later editions—Gilotius, Vaticanus, and Gussanville—read “when he can utter it.” The manuscript reading is better: “when the powerful and insolent man can bear it.”]

For it often happens that such a person will accept no words of rebuke. What, then, is the preacher to do regarding his fault except bring into the midst of the admonition he gives for the common salvation of all hearers such faults as he considers the man who is present to have committed, but who cannot yet be rebuked concerning himself alone, lest he become worse?

When the attack is directed generally against the fault, the word of correction is willingly brought to the mind, because the powerful wicked man does not know that it is being said specifically to him.

What, then, did his preacher do for this man except, while seeming to spare him, not spare him at all? He did not bring words of correction against him personally, yet under a general admonition he struck his wound. Hence it often happens that he mourns the fault he has committed more intensely because, when he feels himself struck, he thinks that no one knows his guilt.

## [Old Version IV.] 7. With what discretion the overbearing are to be reproved

It must therefore be undertaken with great skill in preaching [420] that those who become worse through open reproof may, by some moderation in reproof, return to salvation. Hence Paul also says: “The parts of the body which we think less honorable, these we surround with greater honor; and those which are our unseemly parts have greater seemliness, while our seemly parts have no need” (1 Cor. 12:23). For just as there are unseemly members in the body, so there are within holy Church certain powerful and overbearing people who, because they cannot be struck by open denunciation, are as though covered by an honorable veil.

But we are speaking here of the hidden sins of the powerful. For when they sin while others also know it, they must be reproved while others know it, lest, if the preacher remains silent, he seem to approve the fault, and lest this growing evil become an example which the shepherd’s tongue does not cut away. Thus holy Church, when through her preachers she reproves certain deeds of wicked people [Col. 1021B] with the restraint of denunciation, moves her lips as though sparing them; yet in sparing she does not spare, because she does not remain silent in general denunciation about the fault concerning which she is silent specifically. It follows:

## CHAPTER VI

### Verse 7.—“But what shall I do? If I speak, my pain will not cease; and if I am silent, it will not depart from me.”

### 8. The Church’s pain when she sees the wicked reproved without effect

No one is unaware how this fits the person of blessed Job. But if it is understood as referring figuratively to holy Church, then, when she speaks, her pain does not cease, because by her speech she sees the perverse scarcely corrected. And when she is silent, her pain does not depart, [Note: [Col. 1021D] So the manuscripts and the old edition. In others: “because, even if she has turned away and fallen silent.”] because, although she may be silent in aversion, she grieves all the more over this very silence, since she sees the faults of the perverse increasing while she remains silent. It follows:

## CHAPTER VII [New Revision IV]

### Verse 8.—“But now my pain has crushed me, and all my limbs have been reduced to nothing.”

### 9. The Church’s pain when she sees the weak drawn toward the examples of the wicked

Holy Church is oppressed by pain when she observes the perverse growing in their wickedness. And because, while the wicked increase, even the weak who are in her are provoked to pursue the practices of wickedness, it is rightly added: “And all my limbs have been reduced to nothing.” For just as the strong are usually represented by bones, so the weak are represented by limbs. The members of the Church are therefore reduced to nothing when, through imitation of the wicked who are increasing in this world, the weak are weakened still further. [Col. 1021D] For when they see the prosperity of the wicked, they often fall away from the very state of faith, desire temporal goods, and are, as it were, reduced to nothing, because, while they abandon the enduring essence of God and love transitory things, they tend toward nonbeing. [Note: [Col. 1021D] Turon.: “while they abandon the abiding judgment of God.”]

It is well said: “But now my pain has crushed me,” because the Church’s time of pain is now, whereas the time of joy will follow afterward. [Note: [Col. 1021D] Norm.: “follows.”] Often, however, holy Church tolerates not only unbelievers and adversaries who are outside her, but scarcely endures even the attacks [Col. 1022A] [Note: [Col. 1021D] Most copies: “and adversities.”] and hostility of those whom she has within. Hence, in the voice of the blessed man, it is aptly added:

## CHAPTER VIII [Old Version V]

### Verse 9.—“My wrinkles testify against me.”

### 10. The Church’s wrinkles are wicked Christians

What is signified by wrinkles except duplicity? The wrinkles of holy Church are therefore all those who live doubly within her: they proclaim the faith with their voices but deny it by their deeds. During a time of peace, because they see that this same faith brings honor to the powers of this world, they falsely claim to be faithful. But when a sudden storm of adversity has troubled holy Church, they immediately reveal [Note: [Col. 1021D] Ebroic.: “what they perceive and contrive in their faithless mind.”] what they contrive in their faithless mind.

Holy Church does not have these wrinkles in her elect, because they do not know how to display one thing outwardly about themselves and have another thing within. Hence the distinguished preacher rightly says: “That he might present to himself a glorious Church, not having spot or wrinkle” (Eph. 5:27). For she has neither spot nor wrinkle who is free both from the shamefulness of deeds and from duplicity of speech.

But because she now holds many reprobate people within the bosom of faith, when the time of persecution has burst into flame she suffers as enemies those whom previously she seemed to nourish with the words of her preaching. Let her therefore say: “My wrinkles testify against me”—that is, those themselves reproach me by persecuting me who, now placed in my body, do not cleanse away the malice of their duplicity within themselves. [Note: [Col. 1022D] Norm.: “do not correct it.”] Hence it is rightly added:

### Same passage.—“And a false speaker rises up against my face, contradicting me.”

### 11. Through the wicked the devil rages

Even in the time of her peace holy Church suffers false speech, since there are many within her who distrust the promise of eternity and nevertheless pretend to be faithful. Because they do not dare openly to contradict her preaching, she suffers their false speech not against her face but, as it were, behind her back. But when the time of wickedness breaks forth, the one who now, through fear, detracts from her comes forward to contradict her face, because he openly resists the words of the true faith.

It must, however, be understood that when we suffer these things from carnal people, it is not so much they themselves who rage in our death as the evil spirit who rules their minds, as Paul says: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world” (Eph. 6:12). Therefore, when he was speaking here also of false speech, he aptly turned his words at once to describe the prince of that false speech, saying:

## CHAPTER X [New Revision V]

### Verse 10.—“He gathered his fury against me, and, threatening me, growled against me with his teeth; my enemy looked upon me with terrifying eyes.”

[Col. 1023A] ### 12. Through the wicked the devil rages, sometimes by hidden and sometimes by open persecution

What are all the wicked except members of the devil? Through them he therefore does whatever he instills into their hearts [Note: [Col. 1023D] Lyr. and Bigot.: “whatever he instills into their minds.”] that they ought to do. [Note: [Col. 1023D] Vindoc.: “so that they ought not to act.”]

[Old Version VI.] Even now the devil has fury against holy Church, but his fury is scattered, because he stirs up hidden temptations in individuals. But when he breaks out against her in open persecution, he gathers his fury against her, because in her affliction he concentrates his whole purpose. His members do not now have this gathered fury against the elect during the time of peace [Note: [Col. 1023D] So the manuscripts and the old editions of Paris and Basel. More recent editions: “around the elect.”], because they sense that they are less able to accomplish their malice than they wish. But when they see that opportunity for wickedness is available to them, they strike her with all the greater boldness, the more they gather together against her in unanimity. [Note: [Col. 1023D] Turon.: “are gathered together through vanity.”]

It is therefore rightly said: “He gathered his fury against me.” To explain this fury further, it is said: “And, threatening me, he growled against me with his teeth.” Concerning him it is also added: “My enemy looked upon me with terrifying eyes.” That ancient enemy of the Church growls against her with his teeth and looks upon her with terrifying eyes, because through some he carries out cruel acts, while through others he plans what he will carry out. [Note: [Col. 1023D] Utic.: “so that it might be more deeply”; nevertheless, above it is written “more broadly.”]

### 13. The devil’s teeth are persecutors; his eyes are those who direct them by their counsels

The teeth of this enemy are the persecutors and executioners of the good, who tear apart her members when they afflict her elect with their persecutions. The eyes of this enemy are those who plan the evils they will inflict upon her [Note: [Col. 1024D] Sag. and other Norm. copies: “which they will bring about.”] and inflame, by their counsels, the cruelty of her persecutors. Thus the ancient adversary growls against her with his teeth when, through cruel reprobates, he persecutes the life of the good within her. He looks upon her with terrifying eyes when, through the counsels of the wicked, he never ceases to seek out evils by which he may always afflict her still more severely.

For just as the incarnate Truth chose poor, ignorant, and simple people in his preaching, so, on the contrary, that condemned man whom the apostate angel will take up at the end of the world will choose clever and duplicitous people possessing the learning of this world to preach his falsehood. [Note: [Col. 1024D] See below, book XXXII, no. 22, and book XXXIII, nos. 42 and 57.]

[Old Version VII.] Hence it is said through Isaiah: “Woe to the land of the cymbal of wings, which is beyond the rivers of Ethiopia, which sends ambassadors upon the sea and in vessels of papyrus upon the waters” (Isa. 18:1). The land to which woe is pronounced is principally that condemned man, who is called the cymbal of wings because those who fly upward through pride into the height of thought sound forth that same perverse man by preaching him.

This land is rightly said to be beyond the rivers of Ethiopia. Ethiopia sends forth a black people, and since this world produces every sinful person, as it were Ethiopia gives birth to a black people. But the land to which woe is pronounced is said to be beyond the rivers of Ethiopia because that condemned man is so immeasurably wicked that he surpasses the sins of all sinners.

He sends ambassadors upon the sea because he scatters his preachers throughout the world. Concerning them it is rightly added how they are sent, when it says: “In vessels of papyrus upon the waters.” Papyrus produces paper. What, then, is signified by papyrus except secular learning? The vessels of papyrus are therefore the hearts of secular teachers. To send ambassadors in vessels of papyrus upon the waters is to place his preaching in the minds of carnal wise men and to call peoples drifting toward sin. Those who there are represented by vessels of papyrus are here represented by eyes, because they see carnally. Concerning them it is also added:

## CHAPTER XI

### Verse 11.—“They opened their mouths against me, reproaching me.”

### 14. The devil’s mouth: those who preach errors

The reprobate open their mouths in reproach when they do not fear to preach the evils of their error and ridicule the teachings of the true faith. It must be understood of them that in holy Church they chiefly persecute those whom they see will be of benefit to many—those who crush the life of carnal people by the word of reproof [Col. 1024D] and spiritually transform them into the body of the Church. [Note: [Col. 1024D] Turon., Utic., and Norm.: “and transform them into the body of the Church”; Ebroic.: “and specially transform them into the body of the Church.”] Hence it is added:

## CHAPTER XII [New Revision VI]

### Same passage.—“They struck my cheek; they were filled with my punishments.”

### 15. The cheek of the Church is her holy preachers

The cheek of the Church is her holy preachers, as it is said under the figure of Judea through Jeremiah: “She wept bitterly in the night, and her tears are upon her cheeks” (Lam. 1:2), because in the adversities of the Church those who know how to crush the life of carnal people by preaching grieve more deeply. [Note: [Col. 1024D] Some editions: “who know how to restrain the life of carnal people”; the English manuscripts and ours have “crush.”]

Through them holy Church crushes the wicked away from their vices and, as though swallowing them, converts them into her members. Hence it is said even to the first preacher, as to the cheek of the Church: “Kill and eat” (Acts 10:13). [Old Version VIII.] This is also why Samson took the jawbone of a donkey and killed his enemies (Judg. 15:16): our Redeemer, holding in the hand of his power the simplicity and patience of preachers, killed carnal people with respect to their vices. And when the jawbone had been thrown upon the ground, it later poured forth water, because the bodies of preachers given over to death displayed great miracles to the peoples.

The wicked strike the cheek of the Church when they persecute good preachers. And because the reprobate then think they have accomplished something great when they kill the life of preachers, after the striking of the cheek it is aptly added: “They were filled with my sufferings.” The punishment that chiefly chastises the mind of the Church fills them.

It follows:

## CHAPTER XIII

### Verse 12.—“God has shut me up with the wicked, and delivered me into the hands of the impious.”

### 16. The elect are temporarily handed over to the persecutions of the ancient enemy

The people of the elect are shut up with the wicked when their flesh is temporarily given over to the persecutions of the ancient enemy. They are handed over not to the spirit but to the hands of the impious, because, insofar as they cannot grasp them in mind, they burn more cruelly against their flesh.

But when the people of holy Church have begun to suffer adversities severely and have seen their weak members fall into worse things, they recall to mind the times of their peace, when she fed her faithful with the abundance of her preaching. Hence it is aptly added:

## CHAPTER XIV

### Verse 13.—“I, once prosperous, have suddenly been crushed.”

### 17. No adversity comes suddenly to steadfast minds

By asserting that he has been suddenly crushed, he designates the unprepared mind of the weak. Since they do not know in advance the evils that are coming, those evils become more grievous to them insofar as they endure them unexpectedly. But adversities do not come suddenly upon steadfast minds, because they are foreseen before they arrive.

Even now holy Church suffers this in certain people who fall backward: after the abundance of teaching, they are sometimes crushed by sudden vices, so that they fall into certain evils as though they had never possessed the nourishment of the word. It follows:

## CHAPTER XV

### Same passage.—“He seized my neck, broke me, and set me up for himself as a mark.”

[Note: [Col. 1025D] “Me” is absent in several manuscripts here and in what follows.]

### 18. Under the pressure of persecution, the weak tremble to preach the truth

Just as the neck signifies pride among the wicked, so among the good it signifies the uprightness of freedom. Hence sometimes pride itself is used to signify the authority of uprightness, as the Lord promises holy Church through the prophet: “I will make you a pride for ages” (Isa. 60:15).

And because, in a time of persecution, certain weak people do not dare freely to preach what they truly believe, it is rightly said of this enemy: “He seized my neck and broke me.” [Old Version IX.] Perhaps those are designated by the term “neck” who, in the time of his peace, are raised up more than is fitting and, under the pretext of defending what is right, serve the vice of pride. During persecution they therefore feel adversities more severely because they are exalted by prosperity. Of them it is rightly said: “He seized my neck and broke me”—that is, he bent down by the severity of his blow the exaltation that he found in the weak.

“And he set me up for himself as a mark.” It is clear that a mark is set up for the purpose of being struck by the shooting of arrows. The faithful people are therefore set up as a mark for their enemy because he continually assails them with his blows and afflicts them with his persecutions. Whoever endures continual evils in this life, placed like a mark, receives the blows of the one who strikes.

Hence the distinguished preacher, when he endured the evils of persecutions and groaned under the persecution of adversaries, consoled the tender minds of his disciples concerning his afflictions, saying: “You yourselves know that we have been appointed for this” (1 Thess. 3:3). As though he openly said to them: “Why do you marvel at our wounds in this time, since, if we seek eternal joys, we have come here for this purpose—to be struck?”

It follows:

## CHAPTER XVI

### Verse 14.—“He surrounded me with his spears, wounded my loins together with me, did not spare me, and poured out my entrails upon the ground.”

### 19. The enemy attacks us from every side with the darts of temptation

These words might seem to fit blessed Job literally—“He surrounded me with his spears, pierced my loins, did not spare me”—unless what is not at all written about him were added: “He poured out my entrails upon the ground.” Since we cannot find this literally, we must seek spiritually what sounds historical in these words.

Holy Church is surrounded by spears from her enemy when, in her members, she is assailed by the darts of temptation from the cunning adversary. We are rightly said to be surrounded by spears, because the ancient enemy attacks us from every side with the wound of temptation.

Often, when gluttony is restrained so that lust may be subdued, the goad of vainglory strikes the mind. But if the body is not worn down by the hardship of abstinence, the flame of lust rises up against the mind. Often, while we strive to preserve frugality, we slip into greed. And often, while we give away what we possess lavishly, we are led toward avarice, because we seek again to gather what we may give away.

Since, then, the darts of the ancient enemy attack us everywhere [Note: [Col. 1026D] Turon.: “they hinder us.”], it is rightly said: “He surrounded me with his spears.” And because the cunning enemy indeed persuades us to every sin, but we commit it by consenting to his persuasion, it is aptly added: “He wounded my loins together with me.”

For lust is in the loins. Hence the one who desired to extinguish the pleasure of lust from the heart preached, saying: “Gird up the loins of your mind” (1 Pet. 1:13). When, therefore, the ancient enemy draws the faithful people toward lust, he undoubtedly strikes them in the loins.

It must also be noted [Col. 1026D] that he does not say “he wounded” but “he wounded my loins together with me.” For just as speaking is sometimes the act of one person, whereas conversing is the act of two or perhaps many, so the ancient enemy, because he does not drag us into guilt without our will, is not said simply to wound our loins but to pierce them together with us. What he maliciously suggests to us, we follow and fulfill by our own will, and we are, as it were, wounded together with him, because we are led to commit evil by a shared exercise of free choice.

It follows: “He did not spare”—as though he said, “He did not cease.” [Old Version X.]

“And he poured out my entrails upon the ground.” What else should we understand as the entrails of holy Church except the minds of those who contain within themselves certain of her mysteries and serve her inner sacraments? But when the ancient adversary draws certain faithful people, who seemed to serve the inner sacraments, toward secular affairs, he undoubtedly pours out her entrails upon the ground, because he tramples in lowly matters those who previously lay hidden in secret and spiritual activities.

It follows:

## CHAPTER XVII

### Verse 15.—“He cut me down with wound upon wound.”

[425] ### 20. That he may cut us down with wound upon wound

Holy Church is cut down with wound upon wound in her weak members when sin is added to sin, so that guilt is intensified more severely. Someone whom avarice draws toward robbery, and robbery leads to deceit so that, after the sin has been committed, it is also defended by falsehood—what is he except one cut down with wound upon wound?

Hence it is well said through the prophet: “Cursing, lying, murder, theft, and adultery have overflowed, and blood has touched blood” (Hos. 4:2). Sin is commonly signified by the name “blood.” Hence the one who desires to be freed from sins cries out through repentance: “Deliver me from blood” (Ps. 50:16). Blood therefore touches blood when guilt has added guilt to guilt. [Note: [Col. 1027D] Turon.: “when he has joined one fault to another.” Lyr. and Bigot.: “when fault is joined to fault.” Utic. has this reading and another, that of the printed editions, which we have retained.]

And because, when wound is added to wound, the strength of the ancient enemy against us increases more forcefully, it is rightly added:

## CHAPTER XVIII

### Same passage.—“He rushed upon me like a giant.”

### 21. Those who do not resist experience him fighting against them like a giant

It is easy to resist the enemy if one does not continue consenting to him, whether through many falls or through one. But if the soul has become accustomed to remain subject to his persuasions, the more frequently it submits to him, the more intolerable it makes him for itself, so that it cannot resist him. For the wicked adversary fights against the soul, conquered by evil habit, as a giant customarily fights.

Nevertheless, holy Church often recalls the minds of the faithful to repentance even after sins have been committed and cleanses sins by the strength of voluntary affliction. Hence it is well added:

## CHAPTER XIX

### Verse 16.—“I sewed sackcloth upon my skin, and covered my flesh with ashes.”

### 22. The Church teaches that sins are cleansed by voluntary affliction

What should be understood by sackcloth and ashes except repentance, and by skin and flesh except the sin of the flesh? When, therefore, after a fall of the flesh, certain people return to repentance, sackcloth is, as it were, sewn upon the skin and flesh is covered with ashes, because the guilt of the flesh is covered by repentance, so that it may not appear for punishment in the judgment of the strict Judge.

When holy Church withdraws her weak members from sins and leads them to the remedy of repentance, she undoubtedly assists them with tears so that they may recover strength to receive the grace of their Creator. Through her strong members she bewails what she herself did not do, what, in her weak members, she did as though she herself had done it. Hence it is well added:

## CHAPTER XX [Old Version XI, New Revision VII]

### Verse 17.—“My face is swollen with weeping.”

[Note: [Col. 1027D] The “a” is absent in Bellovac., Norm., and others; it is found in Turon. [Col. 1028D].]

### 23. She assists her penitent children with her tears; superiors should grieve over the falls of others as over their own

The faces of holy Church are rightly those who, placed in positions of governance, appear first, so that the honor of the faithful people may be seen in their appearance, even if something deformed lies hidden in the body. These leaders weep for the faults of the weak among the people and grieve over the falls of others as though they were their own.

Often, when they see some return to pardon after their sins while others persist in wickedness, they marvel at the hidden judgments of almighty God but cannot penetrate them. They are astonished at what they do not understand. [Note: [Col. 1028D] Vindoc.: “because they do not understand.”] Hence it is aptly added:

## CHAPTER XXI

### Same passage.—“And my eyelids have grown dim.”

### 24. Let them direct the paths of their subjects as though they were eyes

Those who keep watch in order to foresee the paths of the feet are rightly called eyelids. But when even vigilant superiors do not understand the hidden judgments of God, the eyelids of holy Church grow dim.

But, as I have often recalled saying, blessed Job, bearing the figure of holy Church, sometimes uses the voice of the body and sometimes the voice of the head; and while he speaks of her members, he suddenly rises to the words of the head. Hence here too it is added:

## CHAPTER XXII [New Revision VIII]

### Verse 18.—“I have suffered these things without iniquity in my hands, while I had pure prayers before God.”

### 25. Christ alone above all had pure prayers before God

He endured these things without iniquity in his hands, who committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth (1 Pet. 2:22ff.), and yet endured the pain of the cross for our redemption. He alone above all had pure prayers before God, because even in the pain of his Passion he prayed for his persecutors, saying: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34). For what can be said or imagined purer in prayer than when the mercy of intercession is granted even to those by whom the pain is endured?

Thus it came about that those who had savagely persecuted and shed the blood of our Redeemer afterward drank that blood in faith [Note: [Col. 1028D] Turon.: “licked it.”] and proclaimed him to be the Son of God. [Note: [Col. 1028D] Vindoc.: “Concerning which it is apparently desired that the earth, etc.”] Concerning this blood it is aptly added:

## CHAPTER XXIII

[Col. 1029A] ### Verse 19.—“Earth, do not cover my blood, nor let my cry find in you a place to hide.”

### 26. His blood speaks better than Abel’s blood: Abel’s cries for vengeance; his pleads for forgiveness

To sinful man it was said: “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Gen. 3:19). This earth does not conceal the blood of our Redeemer, because every sinner, receiving the price of his redemption, confesses and praises it and makes it known to his neighbors as far as he can. Nor did the earth cover his blood, because holy Church has now preached the mystery of her redemption throughout every part of the world.

[Old Version XII.] It must be noted that it says: “Nor let my cry find in you a place to hide” (Gen. 3:19). The blood of redemption that is received is itself the cry of our Redeemer. Hence Paul also says: [Note: [Col. 1029D] Bigot. and Lyr.: “and the blood of sprinkling, speaking better.” Turon.: “and, by the sprinkling of blood, speaking better.” In Utic. it was formerly read as in the printed editions, but now it agrees with Lyr. and Bigot. In Bellov., “speaking better than Abel.”] “And the blood of sprinkling speaks better than Abel” (Heb. 12:24).

It had been said concerning Abel’s blood: “The voice of your brother’s blood cries to me from the earth” (Gen. 4:10). But the blood of Jesus speaks better than Abel, because Abel’s blood sought the death of the fratricidal brother, whereas the Lord’s blood obtained life for his persecutors.

Therefore, so that the sacrament of the Lord’s Passion may not be fruitless in us, we must imitate what we receive and preach to others what we venerate. His cry finds a place to hide in us if the tongue remains silent about what the mind has believed. But so that his cry may not remain hidden in us, each person must, according to his measure, make known to his neighbors the mystery of his own vivification.

It is pleasing to turn the eyes of the mind back to the hour of the Lord’s Passion, when the persecuting Jews raged and the fearful disciples fled. Since he who seemed to be dying in the flesh was by no means believed to be God, it is aptly added here:

## CHAPTER XXIV [New Revision IX]

### Verse 20.—“For behold, my witness is in heaven, and my knower is on high.”

### 27. While people did not know Christ, he had the Father in heaven as his knower and witness

When [Note: [Col. 1029D] Turon.: “the faithful [one].” Vindoc.: “faith was slipping on earth.”] the Son was shaken on earth, he had a witness in heaven. The Father is the witness of the Son, concerning whom he himself says in the Gospel: “The Father who sent me himself has borne witness concerning me” (John 5:37). He is rightly also called his knower, because the Father always works with the Son in one will and one counsel. He is also his witness because “no one knows the Son except the Father” (Matt. 11:27).

Thus he had a witness in heaven and a knower on high when those who saw him dying in the flesh were unable to perceive the power of his divinity. And although people did not know, [Note: [Col. 1030D] We have restored this passage from the manuscripts of Turon., Vindoc., seven Norm. copies, the English copies, and the old edition. In Gilot., the Roman edition of Sixtus V, and other recent editions it appears very obscurely—indeed, corruptly—as follows: “and although people did not know, in the death of the Mediator of God and men the Father, who worked with him, knew.” It was nevertheless formerly read this way in Utic.] in the death of the Mediator between God and men, the Mediator nevertheless knew what the Father was working with him.

This may perhaps also be referred to the voice of his body. [Col. 1030A] [Old Version XIII.] Holy Church endures the adversities of the present life so that heavenly grace may lead her to eternal rewards. She disregards the death of her flesh because she directs her attention toward the glory of the resurrection. What she suffers is transitory; what she awaits is eternal.

She has no doubt concerning these perpetual goods, because she already holds the faithful testimony of her Redeemer’s glory. In mind she sees the resurrection of his flesh and grows strong in hope, because what she sees already accomplished in her head she hopes will also follow in his body, which is herself, without any doubt.

The Psalmist, contemplating this Church as destined to remain in perpetual perfection, describes her under the name of the moon, saying: “The perfect moon forever” (Ps. 88:38). Because the Lord’s resurrection strengthens her for the hope of resurrection, he rightly added: “And a faithful witness in heaven.” For, so that she may not tremble concerning her own resurrection, she already has in heaven as her witness the one who rose from the dead.

When the faithful people therefore suffer adversities and are wearied by harsh tribulations, let them raise their minds toward the hope of the glory to come and, trusting in the resurrection of their Redeemer, say: “For behold, my witness is in heaven, and my knower is on high.” He is rightly called the knower because he knew our nature not only by creating it but also by assuming it. To know is, for him, to have taken our nature upon himself. Hence it is also said through the Psalmist: “For he himself knows our formation” (Ps. 102:14). What is surprising if he is said specially to know our formation, when it is evident that there is nothing he does not know? But his knowing our formation consists in mercifully assuming it in himself.

### 28. The same witness must be sought by us

This voice, however, which agrees with blessed Job, can also belong to each of us individually. Everyone who seeks human praise because of what he does seeks a witness on earth. But whoever hastens to please almighty God by his deeds considers that he has a witness in heaven. [Note: [Col. 1030D] Turon.: “desires to have a witness for himself in heaven.”]

Often even good works in us are reproved by careless people. But whoever has a witness in heaven ought not to fear human reproaches. Hence it is further added:

## CHAPTER XXV [Old Version XIV]

### Verse 21.—“My friends are full of words; my eye sheds tears before God.”

[Col. 1030D] ### 29. Testimony must not be sought from human beings

What else is signified by the eye except the intention of the heart? As it is written: “If your eye is simple, your whole body will be full of light” (Matt. 6:22). When something is done with a good intention, the action of that intention is not darkened before God.

When, therefore, friends are full of words—that is, when even those who share the faith speak against us—it is necessary for the eye to shed tears before God, so that our whole intention may flow away in the compunction of inward love and raise itself more subtly toward the interior, the more it is forced by outward reproaches, having been repulsed, to return within lest it vanish outwardly.

It follows:

## CHAPTER XXVI

### Verse 22.—“Would that a man might be judged with God as a son of man is judged with his companion!”

### 30. It is uncertain for which sin God punishes us with his scourges

We always acknowledge that we are sinners; yet often, when placed under the scourge, we do not know for which sin we are being scourged. We examine ourselves by subtle investigation so that, if possible, we may discover the cause of our punishment. Since this usually remains hidden from us, our blindness becomes a burden, and we grieve more over what we suffer.

Whoever comes to judgment with his companion both says what he feels and acknowledges whatever is contradicted; he knows where to strike and knows from where he is struck. But whoever is struck by divine correction, although he knows that he is being scourged, does not know why he is being scourged. He is as though saying what he feels but does not know what is being said against him, because he groans under the blow while God does not openly declare for what punishment he is striking him.

Thus it is now said: “Would that a man might be judged with God as a son of man is judged with his companion!” As though it were openly said: “Just as I am heard in everything I say, so may I hear everything that is said about me.”

Yet this cannot happen at all in the present life, because the great barrier before the eyes of our hearts in contemplating the subtlety of God is our own weakness. But then we shall behold him clearly, whom we now behold subtly, when, having laid aside this weakness, we come to the grace of inward contemplation, of which Paul says: “Then I shall know fully, even as I have been fully known” (1 Cor. 13:12).

Therefore blessed Job, seeing that this knowledge cannot possibly be perfected here, grieves over the blindness of the present life but consoles himself with its brevity, saying:

## CHAPTER XXVII

### Verse 23.—“For behold, the brief years pass away, and I walk the path by which I shall not return.”

[Col. 1031D] ### 31. The brevity of life mitigates and consoles its miseries

Everything that passes is brief, even if it seems to come to an end slowly. We walk along the path of death, by which we do not return—not because we are not raised again to the life of the flesh, but because we do not return again to the labors of this mortal life or to the rewards acquired through those labors.

## CHAPTER XXVIII [Old Version XV, New Revision X]

### Chapter 17, verse 1.—“My spirit will be weakened.”

32. The good promise themselves a short life, but the wicked a long one.—The spirit is weakened by fear of judgment, because the more the minds of the elect sense that they are drawing near to the final judgment, the more terribly they tremble as they examine themselves; and if they discover in themselves any carnal thoughts [Col. 1032A] they have ever entertained, they consume them in the ardor of repentance. They do not allow their thoughts to expand in carnal pleasure, because the more subtly they judge themselves, the more severely they strike themselves, as they await the strict Judge whom they perceive to be near. Hence they always suppose that their end is close at hand.

The minds of the reprobate, on the other hand, do many wicked things for this reason: they think they will live longer here. Thus the spirit of the righteous is weakened, but that of the wicked grows coarse. For the more they swell with arrogance, the less they experience the weakening of the spirit. The righteous, however, while they consider the brevity of their life, avoid the sins of arrogance and impurity. Hence it is also added:

## CHAPTER XXIX

The same passage.—“My days will be shortened, and only the grave remains for me” [Col. 1032B].

33. By this means the righteous avoid the sins of arrogance and impurity, while the wicked multiply them. The perfect life is an imitation of death.—Whoever considers what he will be in death always becomes fearful in his conduct; and from the fact that he already seems, in his own eyes, almost not to live, he truly lives in the eyes of his Creator. He desires nothing that passes away and opposes every desire of the present life. He considers himself almost dead, because he does not fail to know that he will die.

For the perfect life is an imitation of death. While the righteous carefully practice it, they escape the snares of sin. Hence it is written: “In all your works remember your last things, and you will never sin” (Ecclus. VII, 40). Therefore blessed Job, because he considers that his days are being shortened and weighs that only the grave remains for him [Col. 1032C], appropriately adds:

## CHAPTER XXX

Verse 2.—“I have not sinned, and my eye remains amid bitterness.”

34. Job was struck, not to correct his sin, but to increase grace.—It is as though he plainly said: “I have committed no fault, yet I have received the scourges.” But this raises a difficulty, since in many passages of this history he confesses that he has sinned: how can he now deny that he has sinned? The answer is readily at hand: he neither sinned so greatly as to deserve the scourges, nor could he exist without sin. For he was struck not to correct a fault but to increase grace, as the Judge himself testifies—the Judge who both praises and strikes him.

Again, that he was not without sin is not denied even by the one praised by the Judge; indeed, he is praised because he does not deny it. But I believe we shall examine these words more suitably if we understand them as spoken by the voice of the Head [Old Recension XVI]. For our Redeemer, coming for our redemption, did not sin and endured bitterness, because without guilt he accepted the punishment of our guilt. Of his voice it is next said:

## CHAPTER XXXI

Verse 3.—“Deliver me, and set me beside you, and let any man’s hand fight against me.”

35. Christ was in bitterness through his Passion and was delivered through his Resurrection.—He did not sin in thought or deed; he remained in bitterness through his Passion; he was delivered through his Resurrection [Col. 1033A]; and he was set beside the Father through his Ascension, because, having gone up into heaven, he sits at the right hand of God.

And because after the glory of his Ascension Judea was stirred to persecute his disciples, it is rightly now said: “And let any man’s hand fight against me.” For then the fury of the persecutors raged against his members; then the flame of cruelty blazed against the life of the faithful. But where could the wicked go, or what could they do, while the one whom they persecuted on earth was already seated in heaven? Of them it is further added:

## CHAPTER XXXII [Recension XI]

Verse 4.—“You have put their heart far from discipline.”

36. God makes the heart of the wicked far from discipline only by permitting it.—If they had known the keeping of discipline and had not despised the commands of our Redeemer [Col. 1033B], the mortality of their own flesh would have stirred them to love immortal life. The very fact that in this life we are subject to corruption is already a scourge of discipline. To be troubled by heat and cold, hunger and thirst, to be afflicted by illnesses, and eventually even to perish—what are these things other than the scourges of sin?

Yet there are some who endure the scourges and nevertheless do not reform their minds into fear of the one who scourges them. Hence it is rightly said: “You have put their heart far from discipline.” For although the body is under discipline, the heart is not under discipline when a person is scourged but is not brought back to humility of mind.

This is not said as though the almighty and merciful God himself makes the human heart far from discipline. Rather, he judicially permits the heart that has voluntarily fallen to remain where it fell [Col. 1033C], just as we also say to him in prayer: “Do not lead us into temptation” (Matt. VI, 13)—that is, “Do not permit us to be led into it.” It follows:

## CHAPTER XXXIII

The same passage.—“Therefore they will not be exalted.”

37. Those without discipline are never lifted from the lowest things to the heavenly.—If the heart were under discipline, it would desire higher things and would not hunger after the acquisition of passing goods. Since, therefore, their heart is not under discipline, it is rightly said of them: “Therefore they will not be exalted.” For, while abandoned to the lowest pleasures, they continually desire earthly goods and never raise their heart to heavenly joys. They would be exalted if they raised their mind to hope for the heavenly homeland.

But [Note: We have restored this corrupt passage with the help of the German, English, Tours, Vendôme, Beauvais, Norman, and other manuscripts, as well as the old editions. What is read in the recent editions is barbarous: “But those who do not at all strive to preserve life through discipline, but lie in the lowest things through desire and, what is more serious, raise themselves by lying there, because they are lifted up by transitory things: they can be lifted up but cannot be exalted … and therefore become worse in their own eyes.”] those who do not at all strive to preserve life through discipline [Col. 1033D] always lie in the lowest things through their desires; and, what is more serious, they raise themselves by lying there, because they are lifted up by transitory things. They can indeed be lifted up, but they cannot be exalted, because they are deeper in the lowest place precisely because they become higher in their own estimation.

Therefore the heart that is without discipline cannot be exalted, because the human mind, just as it is pressed down in the lowest things when wrongly elevated, is lifted up in the highest things when rightly humbled. It follows:

## CHAPTER XXXIV [Recension XII]

[Col. 1034A]

Verse 5.—“He promises spoil to his companions, and the eyes of his sons will fail.”

38. The devil and the wicked are one body. His companions are the apostate angels; his sons are perverse human beings.—After blessed Job had delivered a judgment concerning the multitude of the wicked—that is, concerning the body of the ancient enemy—he immediately turns his judgment to their prince himself, the head of all the lost, and passes from the plural number back to the singular.

For the devil and all the wicked are so much one body that the body is often designated by the name of the head, and the head is called by the name of the body. The body is designated by the name of the head when it is said of a perverse human being: “One of you is a devil” (John VI, 71). Again, the head is called by the name of the body when it is said of that apostate angel himself: “An enemy has done this” (Matt. XIII, 28).

This prince of all the perverse therefore has some as companions and others as sons. Who are his companions except those apostate angels who fell with him from the seat of the heavenly homeland? And whom else does he have as sons except perverse human beings, who are generated in the practice of wickedness through his evil persuasion? Hence Truth’s voice also says to unbelievers: “You are from your father the devil” (John VIII, 44).

39. What spoil the devil promises to his companions.—This perverse author of error promises spoil to his companions, because he promises evil spirits the souls of the wicked, to be snatched away at their end. “And the eyes of his sons will fail,” because, by stirring human intentions toward hoping for earthly things alone, he makes them love what they cannot possess for long. For the intention of an evil love cannot endure, since both what it loves and the one who loves it are destined to fail swiftly.

The companions may perhaps also be understood as the most cruel, already filled with every kind of wickedness; the sons, on the other hand, as those who, still deceived by seductive promises [Note: Vendôme, Beauvais, Norman, German, and others: “as their wickedness is increased.”], are nourished for the increase of wickedness. Thus the devil may regard the former as companions, as though they have already attained the measure of wickedness and have no further growth in perdition; but the latter as sons, whom he nurses with promises so that they may advance toward worse things [Note: German, Beauvais, Sag., and other Norman manuscripts add: “deeds.”].

“But the eyes of his sons will fail,” because the intentions of the wicked fall when they abandon everything they desire here and there suffer without end what will cause them grief. It follows:

## CHAPTER XXXV

[Col. 1034D]

Verse 6.—“He has made me as a proverb of the people” [Note: Utica and other Norman manuscripts: “and an example before them.” There is no basis for this reading in the Hebrew text.]; “and I am an example before them.”

40. The foolish opinion of the people concerning the scourges of the elect.—Let blessed Job speak from himself; let him speak from the voices of all the elect. Everyone who is struck by a scourge is made, as it were, a proverb of the people, because every fool who wishes to curse someone takes his curse from the likeness of one whom he sees to have been struck temporally. He wishes for his adversary the punishment that he sees has befallen the righteous.

Thus it happens that the upright person is held up as an example to those who do not think rightly: the punishment of the righteous is believed to be condemnation, while no hope of faith foresees the glory that awaits him. It follows:

## CHAPTER XXXVI [Old Recension XVIII, Recension XIII]

Verse 7.—“My eye has grown dim from indignation” [Note: In the Norman manuscript, besides this reading, another is noted in the margin, namely, “from indignation,” which Gussanville also observed.]; “and my limbs have been reduced almost to nothing.”

41. When the saints are stunned and blinded by the scourges, the weak sometimes collapse.—The eye grows dim from indignation when even those who possess the light of truth in the Lord’s body, that is, in the Church, are troubled by wonder at the hidden judgment, because they see themselves despised and scorned by the wicked for so long, and cannot penetrate the secret of God: why are the perverse permitted to prevail against the innocence of the good?

Who would not be stunned when Herodias, by the dancing of her daughter before a drunken king, obtains that the head of the Friend of the Bridegroom, the prophet and more than a prophet, should be carried on a dish before the faces of the banqueters (Mark VI, 27)? But when the righteous grow dim from indignation [Note: Beauvais: “but when these people…”], the weak often collapse even into unbelief. Hence it is added: “And my limbs have been reduced almost to nothing.”

For by the name of “limbs” the tenderness of the weak is expressed. When they see the wicked prospering and the righteous suffering, they sometimes reach the point of regretting that they even began good works; and thus they return more quickly to doing evil [Note: Beauvais, Norman, and others: “they return more quickly”], as though the good they began had harmed their lives.

When he says, “My eye has grown dim from indignation,” he explains this in clearer words by adding:

## CHAPTER XXXVII [Recension XIV]

Verse 8.—“The righteous will be astonished at this, and the innocent will rise up against the hypocrite.”

42. It belongs to the imperfect to envy the glory of the wicked.—In this passage “the innocent” is understood as the not-yet-perfect righteous person. While still beginning to do good, he does not know how to harm others, but is nevertheless wholly unable to perform perfect deeds himself.

And because the hearts of the little ones are inflamed with the torches of envy when they see the wicked flourishing in the present life—for each person envies others’ present goods more in proportion as he himself has despised them less—what one person has cannot at the same time be possessed by everyone; what another has is lacking to this one [Note: In Utica: “this one lacks.” In the German, Corbie, German, and other manuscripts is found the editors’ reading, although something seems to be missing.].

The innocent rises up against the hypocrite when even one accustomed to harm no one envies the glory of the pretender. But if in this passage “the innocent” is understood as anyone perfect in goodness, the innocent rises up against the hypocrite when he sees him flourishing yet despises him together with his flourishing; and, by preaching what is right, declares to others that he ought to be despised, precisely because he sees him anxiously seeking those things that cannot remain with him for long.

In this sense it is further added:

## CHAPTER XXXVIII [Old Recension XIX]

[Col. 1036A]

Verse 9.—“And the righteous will hold to his way, and he who has clean hands will add strength.”

43. God, who grants temporal goods to the wicked, will not deny eternal goods to the righteous.—When the hypocrite has been considered, the righteous holds to his way, because, while he sees that the hypocrite obtains the things of the world through a perverse will, he is himself bound more firmly to the love of heavenly things, knowing that eternal rewards will not be lacking to good desires, since temporal goods are not denied even to the wicked and double-hearted.

For this reason he who has clean hands also adds strength: seeing the wicked obtain earthly glory, he advances his good works toward perfection; and he despises temporal things more profoundly the more he sees them abound even to the wicked [Col. 1036B]. He considers how worthy of contempt are the things that Almighty God grants even to the perverse. If they were truly great in themselves, the Creator would never bestow them upon his adversaries. Therefore he judges it unworthy of himself to desire those goods that he sees abounding even among the wicked. Instead, he directs his mind toward receiving heavenly things, which cannot be shared by him and the reprobate.

Accordingly, after he had described the outward prosperity of the wicked and the inward progress of the good, he brought forth words of exhortation, saying:

## CHAPTER XXXIX

Verse 10.—“Therefore, all of you, turn and come.”

44. We must turn to God in faith and come to him in action [Col. 1036C].—These words of exhortation are addressed especially to the elect, whom he calls to eternity. They are invited in two ways: to turn and to come. They are to turn, namely, by faith; they are to come, by action. Or certainly, they are to turn by abandoning evil and to come by doing good, as it is written: “Turn away from evil and do good” (Ps. XXXVI, 27).

But what follows is astonishing:

## CHAPTER XL

The same passage.—“And I will not find among you any wise man.”

45. Those who are wise in their own eyes cannot attain true wisdom.—For what does it mean that he calls them to wisdom and nevertheless desires not to find them wise, except that those who are deceived by confidence in their false wisdom cannot come to true wisdom? Of them it is written: “Woe to you who are wise in your own eyes and prudent in your own sight” (Isa. V, 21). And again they are told: “Do not be wise in your own estimation” (Rom. XII, 16).

Therefore that distinguished preacher, wishing those whom he found carnally wise to receive true wisdom, first sought that they should become foolish, saying: “If anyone among you seems to be wise in this age, let him become foolish, so that he may be wise” (I Cor. III, 18). And Truth itself says: “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones” (Matt. XI, 25).

Since, therefore, those who are wise in their own eyes cannot attain true wisdom, blessed Job, desiring the conversion of his hearers, rightly wishes not to find any wise man among them. It is as though he plainly said to them: “Learn to be foolish in your own eyes, so that you may be truly wise in God.” It follows:

## CHAPTER XLI [Old Recension XX, Recension XV]

Verse 11.—“My days have passed away; my thoughts have been scattered, tormenting my heart.”

46. The days of the Church are prosperity, her nights adversity. The saints feel themselves tormented when compelled to administer earthly things.—The holy Church of the elect sees the periods of her life pass through day and night, because she is accustomed to have night in adversity and day in prosperity. Peaceful tranquility is like light rising for her, while the pain of persecution is like night.

But when, after the periods of rest, she returns to the labor of persecution rising against her, she testifies that her days have passed away. Yet during those days she is accustomed to be weighed down by heavier cares in proportion as, amid the tranquility of peace, she considers that the Judge will require from her a more exact account.

In the tranquility of peace she sometimes considers the gains of souls and sometimes manages the administration of earthly affairs. Such administration of earthly matters is more burdensome to good minds in proportion as, in attending to it, they are drawn away—even briefly—from contemplating heavenly things.

Therefore blessed Job, whether speaking in his own voice or in that of the universal Church, after testifying that his days have passed away [Col. 1037C], immediately adds: “My thoughts have been scattered, tormenting my heart.” For when temporal prosperity passes from good minds, the concern for earthly administration also is taken away from them, a concern that seemed to torment them in their thoughts.

While they desire always to be raised up for receiving heavenly things, they feel themselves tormented precisely because they sometimes descend from earthly administration to thoughts of what is below [Note: Norman: “For while the upright…”; Tours: “for while the upright person…”]. Hence it happens that the very adversity of persecution is turned into great exultation and joy because of the quiet of heart that has been obtained. Therefore it is appropriately added:

## CHAPTER XLII

Verse 12.—“They have turned night into day.”

47. The saints prefer to suffer evils rather than be wearied by concern for good things.—For the scattered thoughts turn night into day, because sometimes the righteous prefer to suffer evils through adversity rather than be wearied by the administration of earthly things amid prosperity.

But because they know how to pass through adversities more cautiously and that prosperity will shine forth again, it is appropriately added:

## CHAPTER XLIII

The same passage.—“And again after darkness I hope for light.”

48. After death the saints are immediately granted heavenly rewards.—Light is hoped for after darkness, because either eternal light is received after the night of the present life, or adversity and prosperity alternate here in such a way that they do not cease to succeed one another.

Thus it happens that in the light there is suspicion of night, and in the night confidence in light, as it is written: “On the day of good things, do not be forgetful of evils; and on the day of evils, do not be forgetful of good things” (Ecclus. XI, 27).

But behold: because we have been redeemed by the grace of our Creator, we already possess this heavenly gift—that when we are withdrawn from dwelling in our flesh, we are immediately led to heavenly rewards. For when our Creator and Redeemer, penetrating the prison of hell, led out from there the souls of the elect, he does not permit us to go where, by descending, he has already liberated others.

Those who came into this world before his advent, however, regardless of how great a virtue of justice they possessed, could not, when led out of their bodies, immediately be received into the bosom of the heavenly homeland [Note: Tours: “however great a measure of the virtue of justice they possessed … into the bosom, etc.”], because he had not yet come whose descent would break open the prison of hell and place the souls of the righteous in their perpetual dwelling [Col. 1038B].

Therefore blessed Job, both feeling affliction and knowing that the recompense of the righteous was still delayed, appropriately adds:

## CHAPTER XLIV [Old Recension XXI, Recension XVI]

Verse 13.—“If I wait, hell is my house, and in darkness I have made my bed.”

49. Before Christ, the souls of the righteous were held in hell without torments.—The former saints could endure adversity, yet, when led out of their bodies, they still could not be freed from the places of hell, because he had not yet come who would descend there without guilt, in order to free from guilt those who were held there.

A human being made his bed in darkness when, by consenting to the crafty persuader, he abandoned the light of righteousness. And because, even in the places of hell, the souls of the righteous were held without torment—so that they descended there because of original sin, yet suffered no punishment for their own deeds—to make one’s bed in darkness was, as it were, to prepare rest for oneself in hell.

For it was a grievous weariness for the elect, after the dissolution of the flesh, still not to see the appearance of the Creator. Blessed Job rightly calls this weariness “darkness.” But because it arose from the punishment of weakness, he rightly immediately adds the same weakness, saying:

## CHAPTER XLV [Recension XVII]

Verse 14.—“I said to corruption: You are my father; to my mother and my sister: worms.”

50. From our corrupted origin we draw the worms of desire and anxiety [Col. 1038D].—What does he mean by saying to corruption, “You are my father,” except that every human being descends from an origin already corrupted? Hence he adds: “My mother and my sister: worms,” because we have come into this world both from corruption itself and together with corruption.

Insofar as the matter of corruptible flesh is concerned, worms are our mother and sister, because we have proceeded from corruption and have come with the corruption that we carry. If this can be understood spiritually, nature may rightly be called the mother and habit the sister, because we are with the latter from the former.

This mother and sister are worms because we are compelled by corrupt nature and perverse habit to be wearied in the mind by restless thoughts, as though by certain worms. For the corrupted nature of the flesh and perverse habit generate innumerable anxieties in the heart of our weakness [Note: Évreux: “because they generate innumerable anxieties.”]; hence they are rightly called the mother and sister of worms. Anxieties bite the mind when they disturb it.

Righteous men do not cease either carefully to consider and deliberate what they should do or prudently to examine where they are to be led after the present life. Thus, because the elect before the Lord’s advent saw that they were still in the labor of the present life and yet could not receive heavenly goods after this life, they were consumed by many thoughts [Note: Incorrectly in Gussanville, following the Vatican manuscript, “feared.” The reading is “were burned” in all the English, Norman, Beauvais, Tours, German, and other manuscripts, as well as in the old printed editions.].

For they awaited the grace of their Redeemer, yet could not reach it while living in the flesh. Hence it is appropriately added:

## CHAPTER XLVI

[Col. 1039B]

Verse 15.—“Where then is my expectation now?”

51. Amid so many evils, Christ alone is the hope of the righteous.—What expectation could the righteous have except God, who justifies the righteous [Note: So the Norman and Tours manuscripts. The editions read: “unless the righteous and justifying God…”], who would willingly descend to the punishments of the human race and free the captives of death by the power of his justice [Note: Vendôme: “who would descend in order to remove the punishments of the human race”]?

They never ceased to await his presence with attentive thought. They knew that he would come [Note: Vendôme: “that he was going to come”], but they desired him to come sooner. Hence he does not say, “Where then is my expectation?” but says, “Where then is my expectation now?” [Old Recension XXII]. By adding “now,” he shows that he desired what was destined to come at some time to come sooner. It follows:

## CHAPTER XLVII

The same passage.—“And who considers my patience?”

52. He was sought by them with burning desires.—He expressed the desire with which, while placed in the flesh, he hastened to be redeemed and recalled from the lower regions to the heights.

Few people were able to consider this: that they should think either about the labors of the present life or about the delay following death [Note: Vendôme: “or about the delay of the life that follows after death.”]. Before the advent of our Redeemer, the righteous grieved that they endured both of these things. Hence it is rightly said: “And who considers my patience?”

Certainly there is one who considers it; but because he does not answer sooner, God is said, as it were, to consider it less. The redemption of the human race, which came at the end of the world, seemed slow to those who preceded it from the beginning of the world, because they were separated for a long span of time from the reward of heavenly things. Truth bears witness to this when it says: “Many prophets [Note: Tours, Lyra, Bigot: “and righteous men”; Utica supplies both readings.] and kings desired to see what you see, and did not see it” (Luke X, 24).

Thus what is now said—“Who considers my patience?”—reveals the vows of ardent desire. For, as we have said, God does not fail to consider the patience of the righteous; rather, he is said not to consider it because, in response to the desire of their longing, he appears less quickly and delays the grace of his dispensation through longer periods [Col. 1040A].

Let him therefore say: “Who considers my patience?” because what is brief to the one who ordains it is long to the one who loves it.

Therefore, still considering the losses caused by his delay, he repeats what he had already said; and, about to descend to the lowest places, he redoubles the voice of his grief, saying:

## CHAPTER XLVIII

Verse 16.—“All my things will descend to the deepest hell.”

53. What is the deepest hell, and what are their receptacles?—Since it is established that the righteous were held among the dead not in places of punishment but in the higher bosom of rest, a major question arises concerning what blessed Job asserts when he says: “All my things will descend to the deepest hell.”

Although he was destined to descend into hell before the advent of the Mediator of God and humanity, it is nevertheless clear that he was not destined to descend into the deepest hell. Or does he call the higher places of hell the deepest hell [Note: Norman: “the places of hell”; Utica: “the higher places of hell—are they called the deepest hell?”]?

For, in relation to the sublimity of heaven, the space of this air may not improperly be called hell. Hence, when the apostate angels have been plunged from their heavenly seats into this dark air [Note: Beauvais and many others: “into this darkened place”], the apostle Peter says: “God did not spare the angels who sinned, but, having dragged them down with the chains of hell, he committed them to Tartarus and reserved them for judgment to be punished” (II Pet. II, 4).

If, then, in relation to the height of heaven, this dark air is hell, in relation to the height of that air the earth, which lies lower, can be understood as both hell and deep. In relation, however, to the height of that earth, those places of hell that are higher than the other receptacles of hell [Col. 1040C] are not incongruously designated here by the name “deepest hell.” For the relation of air to heaven is that of earth to air, and that of this higher bosom of hell to earth.

[Old Recension XXIII] 54. Job understands the soul alone to be the whole human being.—But it is very remarkable that he adds: “All my things will descend.” Since only the soul was destined to descend to the places of hell, what does the holy man mean by saying that all his things would descend there, except that he saw himself to be wholly present where he understood the weight of his recompense?

For he does not consider himself to be that which, insensible, he leaves on the earth until he returns to the incorruption of the resurrection. Thus he says that all his things are destined to descend into the deepest hell, although he sees that only his soul will descend there [Col. 1040D], because he is wholly there where he can perceive what he will receive.

Or certainly, all his things descend into hell because the recompense for all his labors was still expected to be received in the rest of hell alone. It is as though everything he did descended there, because there he found the rest of his recompense for all his works.

Therefore the rest for which he waited is also added, when it immediately follows:

## CHAPTER XLIX

[Col. 1041A]

The same passage.—“Will there at least be rest for me?”

55. Job trembles concerning his salvation; let no one be secure.—In these words he both makes known what he desires and nevertheless indicates that he is still uncertain whether he will be received into rest, lest the many scourges that followed his holy works should, by the hidden judgment of the heavenly Judge, be followed after temporal scourges by punishments that would remain.

In this matter we must weigh, with great fear, who among us can already be secure of eternal rest [Col. 1041B], if even he trembles concerning it—he whose praises of virtue the very Judge who strikes him [Note: Lyra and Bigot: “praises him.”] proclaims: “If the righteous scarcely will be saved, where will the impious and sinner appear?” (I Pet. IV, 18) [Note: The same manuscripts: “where will he appear?”].

Blessed Job knew that he would reach rest after the scourges. Yet, in order to shake our hearts with fear, he appears to doubt the recompense of eternal rest when he says, “Will there at least be…?”—so that we may recognize how greatly we ought always to dread the coming judgment, since even he [Note: Tours, Vendôme, Norman, German: “who was praised by the Judge’s testimony”] who was praised by the Judge is still not secure in his own words concerning the recompense of judgment.

# BOOK FOURTEEN

In this book Saint Gregory unfolds the historical, allegorical, and moral meaning of chapters XVIII and XIX of the Book of Job.

[Col. 1041]

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 1041B]

1. Recapitulation of what was said above.—In the earlier part of this work [Preface, especially chapter 2] we discussed how Almighty God, in order to correct the minds of those placed under the Law, brought the life of blessed Job forward as a testimony. Job did not know the Law and yet kept it; he guarded the precepts of life that he had not received in writing.

First his conduct is praised with God as witness, and afterward it is permitted to be tested while the devil lies in wait, so that through the trials of tribulation it might be shown how much he had previously advanced in tranquility. The enemy of the human race, wicked according to his custom, learned that Job’s life was praised with God as witness, yet sought him for testing.

When he could not overthrow him by so many losses of property and so many bereavements, he stirred up his wife against him as a goad [Note: Beauvais and other Norman manuscripts: “of evil persuasion”], so that at least through familiar words he might corrupt one whom he had been entirely unable to overthrow through the torments of so many messengers.

But when he could not, with the woman’s assistance—the assistance by which he had formerly prevailed against Adam in paradise—be strengthened against this second Adam placed on the dung heap [Note: Vendôme: “which he could not overcome against this second man placed on the dung heap”], he turned to other methods of testing. He brought his friends as though to console him, yet stirred their minds to the harshness of accusation, so that the man whose patience the scourges had not overcome might at least be defeated amid the scourges by harsh words [Note: Vendôme: “so that, through impatience, the man whom the scourges had not overcome…”].

But the enemy, cunningly lying in wait, suffered the fraud he had prepared against the holy man to rebound upon himself. For as many occasions of destruction as he brought against the holy man, so many causes of victory did he provide him. Against torments Job maintained patience; against words, wisdom. He endured the pains of blows calmly [Note: Utica: “formerly, the pains of words; now, with o changed to e, the pains of blows”] and wisely restrained the folly of those giving evil counsel.

But because in those very sufferings and learned speeches he bears the type of the holy Church, and because, as we have often said, his friends speak some things rightly and some foolishly, the heretics are not improperly represented by them. For, insofar as they are friends of the holy man, they say many true things about the reprobate; but, insofar as they bear the form of heretics, they often slip through excess in their speech and strike the breast of the holy man with the darts of their words [Note: Beauvais, Évreux, and other Norman manuscripts: “strike his mind”]. Yet by their very striking they are wearied against his unconquerable mind.

We must therefore distinguish with subtle discernment what there is in their words that they truly think concerning the reprobate, and what sounds foolishly against blessed Job.

## CHAPTER II

Chapter XVIII, verses 1–2.—“Then Baldad the Shuhite answered and said: How long will you cast out words? First understand, and then let us speak.”

2. The heretics accuse the Church of arrogance and ignorance.—All heretics suppose that the holy Church is arrogant about certain things it knows, while they suspect that it neither understands certain other things [Note: In other printed editions: “about certain unknown things.” “Known” must be read, as is confirmed both by the manuscript copies—English, Norman, Vendôme, Tours, German, and others—which agree with the old Paris edition, and by the sense. The meaning is that the heretics think the Church either ignorant of many things or arrogant about things it does not fail to know.].

Thus Baldad the Shuhite constructs the accusation that blessed Job has broken out into arrogance, since he admits that Job is casting out words. Yet he himself indicates how greatly he was swollen with pride when he thought that blessed Job was speaking about things he did not understand [Note: Beauvais and others: “about things he did not understand.”].

And because all heretics complain, in their own estimation, that they are despised by the holy Church [Note: Norman: “that they are despised”], it is appropriately added:

## CHAPTER III

Verse 3.—“Why are we considered as beasts, and are filthy before you?”

### 3. The Heretics’ Suspicions and Insults against the Church
