It is characteristic of the human mind to suspect that what it does is being done to itself. For they imagine that they are despised because they are accustomed to despise the conduct of the good. And because, in matters that can be grasped by reason, the Church shows that what the heretics assert is unreasonable, they suspect that, in her judgment, they are regarded as beasts. [Note: Vindoc.: “from this suspicion of their being despised.”] From this suspicion of being despised they immediately leap to disdain and are provoked to insult that same Church. Hence it is added:

### CHAPTER IV

**VERSE 4.**—“Why do you destroy your soul in your fury?”

### 4. Heretics Call the Church’s Zeal, Fury, and Madness

Heretics regard either the zeal for uprightness or the spiritual grace of holy preaching not as a weight of virtue but as the madness of fury. They suppose that, through this fury, the souls of the faithful are being destroyed, because they believe that the Church’s life is perishing precisely where they see her burning against them. [Note: Thus the better manuscripts, Gilot.: “to serve”; others: “in fervor,” or “in fury.”] It follows:

### CHAPTER V

**THE SAME PASSAGE.**—“Will the earth be abandoned on your account?”

### 5. God Is Not Truly Worshiped Outside the True Church

For they think that they themselves worship God everywhere and that they have occupied the whole world. What, then, does “Will the earth be abandoned on your account?” mean except what they often say to the faithful: “If what you say is true, then the whole earth has been abandoned by God, since we now possess it in such great numbers”? [Note: Turon., Vindoc., Norm., and the old edition have this reading. Other printed editions read: “But the holy catholic Church preaches that no one can truly be saved except within her.” Yet if this were the correct reading, what follows would contain a faulty repetition: “asserting that all who are outside her cannot be saved.”]

But the holy universal Church proclaims that God cannot truly be worshiped except within her, asserting that all who are outside her cannot be saved. Heretics, on the contrary, who trust that they can be saved even outside her, profess that divine assistance is present for them in every place. Hence they say: “Will the earth be abandoned on your account?”—that is, “So that whoever is outside you may not be saved at all?” Hence it is also added:

### CHAPTER VI

**THE SAME PASSAGE.**—“And rocks will be moved from their place.”

### 6. Heretics Call Their Teachers Rocks

Heretics call “rocks” those whom they judge to surpass the human race by the loftiness of their understanding; they boast that these are their teachers. But when the holy Church strives to gather perverse preachers into the embrace of the true faith, what else does she do but move rocks from their own places, so that those who previously stood rigid in their perverse opinions may lie humbly within her, now thinking rightly? Heretics wholly oppose this being done, however, [Col. 1043D] and resist the rocks’ being moved from their proper place at her voice, because they do not want those who come to her—those who among them had held false opinions with proud minds—to think humbly and truly.

#### [Old and Revised Edition III.] 7. They Rage against the Church Because of the Afflictions She Suffers

Often, when heretics see certain people within the holy Church afflicted either by poverty or by blows, they immediately exalt themselves in the arrogance of righteousness. Whatever adversity they observe happening to the faithful, they regard as having occurred on account of their sins, plainly unaware that the condition of the present life in no way proves the merit of one’s actions. For often good things happen to the wicked and bad things to the good, because true good things are reserved for the good, and true evils for the wicked, in eternal recompense. Baldad, therefore, assuming the role of heretics who exalt themselves because of the prosperity of the present life, swells up against the afflictions of blessed Job, as though speaking in their voice against the reproach of the just. He argues explicitly against the wicked, but does not understand how perversely he says such things against a just man. For he adds:

### CHAPTER VII

**VERSE 5.**—“Will not the light of the wicked be extinguished, and the flame of his fire fail to shine?”

### 8. In This Life Evil Often Comes to the Good, and Good to the Wicked

If he announces this as a definition of the present life, he is mistaken, because the light of prosperity is often seen to belong even to the wicked, while the darkness of obscurity and poverty conceals the devout. But if his speech is directed toward showing what the wicked suffer at their end, then it is said truthfully: “Will not the light of the wicked be extinguished, and the flame of his fire fail to shine?” Yet although this could rightly be said of a wicked man, it ought not to have been said against a holy man placed amid afflictions. But as we weigh the strength of his arms in his pronouncements, let us consider how powerfully he hurls his darts, and cease to look at the one whom he attacks while he hurls them, knowing that he is striking a stone with blows that accomplish nothing. Let him therefore say: “Will not the light of the wicked be extinguished?” [Revised Edition IV.] For the wicked also have their light, namely, the prosperity of the present life. But the light of the wicked will be extinguished, because the prosperity of this fleeting life ends more quickly together with life itself. Hence it is aptly added: “And the flame of his fire will not shine.”

### 9. The Wicked Often Obtain What They Desire to Their Own Ruin

Every wicked person has the flame of his own fire, which he kindles in his heart from the heat of temporal desires, burning now with one passion, now with another, and inflaming his thoughts more intensely through the many allurements of the world. But if fire has no flame, it does not shine with poured-out light. His fire’s flame, therefore, is his external beauty or power, which proceeds from his inward ardor, because what he anxiously desires to obtain in this world he often receives to the accumulation of his own ruin, and shines, as it were, through outward glory, whether in the height of power or in the multiplication of wealth. [Note: The printed editions disagree here. The Basel edition of 1514 reads “in multiplying riches,” as does the Paris edition of 1518. Gilot., Vatic., and Gussanv. read “wealth is multiplied.” The Paris edition of 1495 and the manuscripts Bellov., Vindoc., Utic., and others of Normandy agree with the reading we follow.]

But his fire’s flame will not shine when, on the day of his departure, all outward beauty is taken away and he is burned only by his inward ardor. The flame is therefore removed from the fire when outward glory is separated from his inward ardor.

The just also have the flame of their fire, but theirs certainly shines, because their desires gleam in good works. The flame of the wicked, however, does not shine at all, because by desiring evil they are dragged into darkness. Hence it follows:

### CHAPTER VIII

**VERSE 6.**—“The light will grow dark in his tent.”

### 10. The Joy of the Wicked Quickly Fails; Their Joy Is Above Them, That of the Just Beneath Them

If we often understand sadness as darkness, we should rightly understand joy as light. The light in his tent therefore grows dark because, in his conscience—which he inhabits wickedly—the joy that had arisen from temporal things fails. Hence it is aptly added:

**THE SAME PASSAGE.**—“And the lamp that is over him will be extinguished.”

[Old Edition IV.] To speak of common usage, a lamp is light in a vessel, while light in a vessel is joy in the flesh. The lamp that is over him is therefore extinguished because, when the recompense for his evils follows the wicked man, carnal joy is scattered from his mind.

It is rightly said not that this lamp is “with him,” but that it is “over him,” because earthly joys possess the minds of the wicked and absorb them in pleasures, so that they are above those minds, not with them. The just, however, even when they possess the prosperity of the present life, know how to keep it beneath themselves, so that the joy they experience in good things may pass under the counsel of gravity and be surpassed by the governance of virtue.

The lamp of the wicked that is over him is therefore extinguished because the joy that wholly possessed him in this life quickly fails. He who now expands himself wickedly in pleasures is later constricted by punishment amid torments. Hence it is further added:

### CHAPTER IX

**VERSE 7.**—“The steps of his strength will be cramped.”

### 11. Those Who Now Roam in Delights Will Be Constricted in Punishments

Now he puts forth the steps of his strength as often as he exercises the violence of his power. [Note: Vindoc.: “of his will.”] But the steps of his strength will be cramped because punishment will later restrain the powers of his wickedness that he now displays in his pleasure. It follows:

### CHAPTER X [Revised Edition V]

**THE SAME PASSAGE.**—“And his own counsel will cast him headlong.”

### 12. Every Wicked Person Falls Headlong by His Own Counsel

Every wicked man now has this counsel: to pursue present things, [Note: Norm.: “to despise eternal things.” Turon.: “to despair of eternal things.” Vindoc.: “to act unjustly toward eternal things.” The Vindoc manuscript, which alone we are now using because the others are lacking, is extremely corrupt.] abandon eternal things, do what is unjust, and mock what is just. But when the Judge of the just and the unjust comes, every wicked person is cast headlong by his own counsel, because by choosing here, through wicked thoughts, what he desired, he is plunged into the darkness of eternal punishment.

The one whom temporal glory exalts here is pressed there by punishment without end. The one who rejoiced here in pleasure is tortured there by perpetual retribution. It often happens that the prosperity of this world, which the wicked eagerly desire, so binds their steps that even when they wish to return to good works, they scarcely can, because they cannot do what is right when they fear displeasing the lovers of this world.

Thus the sins of the wicked are often multiplied still further through the glory he gains from sin. Baldad expresses this well when he adds:

### CHAPTER XI [Revised Edition VI]

**VERSE 8.**—“For he has thrust his foot into a net, and he walks in its meshes.”

### 13. When the Sinner Tries to Free Himself from the Snares of Sin, He Learns How Tightly He Is Held, Especially at the End of Life

One who puts his feet into a net cannot pull them out whenever he wishes. Likewise, one who casts himself into sins does not rise as soon as he wishes. And one who walks in the meshes of a net entangles his steps by walking; when he tries to free himself in order to walk, he is prevented from walking.

It often happens that someone, persuaded by the pleasure of this world, reaches such an attainment of honor that he obtains what he desires and rejoices that he has attained what he sought. But because worldly goods are loved when they are not possessed and often become worthless once possessed, he learns by receiving it how worthless is the thing he sought. [Note: Utic. gives both readings: “what he seeks” (*quod expetit*) and “what is sought” (*quod expetitur*).] Recalled to his senses, he asks how he may flee without guilt from what he sees himself to have acquired with guilt. Yet the very dignity that entangled him holds him fast, and he cannot flee without other sins from the place he reached not without sin.

He has therefore thrust his feet into a net, and he walks in its meshes, because when he tries to free himself, he then truly sees how tightly he is bound. We do not truly recognize our bondage until, while striving to escape, we try, as it were, to lift our feet. Hence he further discloses this same bondage:

**VERSE 9.**—“His foot will be caught in a snare.”

[Old Edition V.] For the end is bound within sin. And because the enemy of the human race, when he binds each person’s life in guilt, eagerly thirsts for that person’s death, it is rightly added:

### CHAPTER XII

**THE SAME PASSAGE.**—“And thirst will burn against him.”

### 14. When He Discovers Himself Bound, the Sinner’s Desire Burns More Fiercely

Our ancient enemy, when he ensnares life in sin, thirsts to drink the sinner’s death. This may also be understood in another way. For when a perverse mind sees that it has entered into sin, it seeks, on the surface of its thinking, to escape the snares of sin. But, fearing either the terrors or the reproaches of men, it chooses to die eternally rather than suffer some adversity for a time. Hence it abandons itself wholly to the vices by which it already feels itself bound. [Note: We preferred this reading, found in the manuscripts Vindoc., Bellovac., Utic., and all those of Normandy, as well as in the old edition, to that of the more recent editions: “he inserts himself into vices.”]

Therefore, since his life is bound in guilt to the end, his foot is held by a snare. But the more he considers himself bound by evils, the more he despairs of returning; and by that very despair he burns more intensely with the desires of this world. The ardor of desire arises in his mind, and the soul entangled in preceding sins is kindled toward even greater offenses. Hence it is added: “And thirst will burn against him.”

Thirst burns against him in his mind because, the more accustomed he becomes to perverse acts, the more fiercely he is inflamed to drink down evils. For the wicked person’s thirst is a desire for the goods of this world.

Hence our Redeemer cures a dropsical man before the house of a Pharisee; and when he was disputing against avarice, it is written: “But the Pharisees, who were avaricious, heard all these things and mocked him” (Luke XIV, 12; XVI, 4). What, then, does it mean that the dropsical man is cured before the house of a Pharisee, except that, through one person’s bodily illness, the illness of another’s heart is expressed? For the more the dropsical man drinks, the more he thirsts; and every avaricious person multiplies his thirst by drinking, because once he has obtained what he desires, he thirsts more eagerly for other things. The one whose desire increases through acquisition finds his thirst grow through drinking. It follows:

### CHAPTER XIII [Old Edition VI, Revised Edition VII]

**VERSE 10.**—“His snare is hidden in the earth, and his trap is upon the path.”

### 15. How Great Is the Devil’s Cunning in Deceiving; The Qualities of Character Associated with Particular Vices

The snare is hidden in the earth when guilt is concealed beneath earthly advantages. The enemy lying in wait shows the human mind, in earthly profit, what it should desire, and hides the snare of sin, so that he may bind its soul. Thus the mind sees what it can desire but does not at all see in what snare of guilt it is placing its foot.

A trap is so called from deceiving. The ancient enemy places a trap upon the path when, in the activity of this world that the mind desires, the snare of sin is prepared. It would not easily deceive if it could be seen. The trap is placed so that, while the bait is displayed, the trap itself is not seen by the passerby.

Profit accompanied by guilt, and worldly prosperity accompanied by wickedness, are like bait in a snare. When the person desiring profit pursues it, the unseen trap catches the foot of his mind. Honors, riches, health, and temporal life are often presented to the mind together with guilt. When the weak mind sees them as bait but does not see the trap, it is caught in the guilt that it does not see through the bait that it does see and desire.

There are, moreover, qualities of character that are close to particular vices. Harsh dispositions are usually joined either to cruelty or to pride; gentle dispositions, and those somewhat more cheerful than is fitting, are sometimes joined to lust and dissipation. The enemy of the human race therefore observes which vice each person’s character approaches, and places before him those things toward which he knows the mind will incline more easily. Thus he often sets lust or sometimes vain glory before gentle and cheerful dispositions, but anger, pride, or cruelty before harsh minds.

There he places the trap where he sees the path of the mind to be, because he introduces the danger of deception precisely where he finds a way toward a related thought. And because the perverse person fears suffering everything he does and thinks that others will do to him what he himself prepares to do to all those whom he can harm, it rightly follows:

### CHAPTER XIV

**VERSE 11.**—“Fears will terrify him on every side.”

### 16. The Sinner, Drawn by Wicked Desires toward Evil Action, Is Entangled by Fear

He suspects that everyone is toward him as he himself strives to be toward everyone. What these fears do in his actions is added in the following words:

**THE SAME PASSAGE.**—“And they will entangle his feet.”

[Old Edition VII.] If the feet are entangled, they cannot have free steps or take any path, because their bonds hold them back. Wicked desires therefore draw a person toward the worst action, but the worst action confines him in fear. [Note: These words—from “this fear,” through “and it often happens”—are absent from Vindoc., apparently through the carelessness and inattention of a copyist.] This fear entangles the feet, preventing them from advancing into upright action.

It often happens that someone fears being good lest he himself suffer from the wicked what he remembers having done to the good. While he fears suffering what he has done, he is terrified on every side and suspicious on every side; he is as one whose feet are entangled. Caught by fear, he can do nothing freely, because in good action he has, as it were, lost his step at the very point from which he turned toward the evils he had desired. It follows:

### CHAPTER XV

**VERSE 12.**—“May his strength be weakened by hunger, and famine invade his ribs.”

### 17. The Wicked Person Wastes Away from Hunger Because He Is Nourished by No Inner Food

In the manner of Sacred Scripture, this seems to express a wish concerning what it foresees will happen—not in the spirit of one cursing, but of one proclaiming. Since every human being consists of soul and flesh, [Note: Sagiensis reads “consists,” and “is composed.”] he is composed, as it were, of strength and weakness. Insofar as he was created a rational spirit, he is not improperly called strong; insofar as he is carnal, he is weak.

The strength of a human being is therefore the rational soul, which can resist attacking vices through reason. Hence it was said earlier through blessed Job: “You will strengthen him for a little while, so that he may pass away forever” (Job XIV, 20). For from the rational soul a human being possesses the capacity to live forever.

The strength of this wicked man is therefore weakened by hunger because his soul is nourished by no inner food. Concerning this hunger God says through the prophet: “I will send hunger upon the land, not a hunger for bread or a thirst for water, but for hearing the word of the Lord” (Amos VIII, 11).

### 18. From This the Senses of the Mind Fail

It is aptly added: “And famine will invade his ribs.” The ribs enclose the inner organs so that what lies hidden within may be protected by their solidity. The ribs, therefore, are the senses of each person’s mind, which protect hidden thoughts. Famine invades the ribs when, with all spiritual nourishment removed, the senses of the mind fail and can neither govern nor defend their thoughts.

Famine invades the wicked person’s ribs because inner hunger weakens the senses of the mind, so that they cannot govern their thoughts at all. For when the senses of the mind have become dull, thoughts come forth into external things; and, as though the ribs had grown weak, the inner organs that could have remained sound in secret are poured outward.

Thus, when thoughts have been scattered outward, the mind deceived by the appearance of external glory desires that appearance and loves nothing except what it sees to be outwardly beautiful. [Note: The recent editions read *specie deceptus* (“deceived by appearance”), against the manuscripts and old printed editions.] Against such a person it is aptly added:

### CHAPTER XVI [Old and Revised Edition VIII]

**VERSE 13.**—“May his skin’s beauty be devoured, and may firstborn death consume his arms.”

### 19. Firstborn Death Is Pride, Which the Rich Can Scarcely Avoid

The beauty of the skin is temporal glory, which, when desired outwardly, is retained like an appearance in the skin. By the name “arms,” works are not improperly signified, because bodily work is performed with the arms.

What, then, is death except sin, which kills the soul by separating it from the inner life? Hence it is written: “Blessed and holy is the one who has a share in the first resurrection” (Revelation XX, 6), because the person who will rise happily afterward in the flesh is the one who, while placed in this life, has risen from the death of his mind.

If sin is death, then “firstborn death” can not improperly be understood as pride, because it is written: “Pride is the beginning of every sin” (Ecclesiasticus X, 15). Firstborn death therefore devours his skin’s beauty and his arms because pride overthrows the glory or works of the wicked.

He could have remained glorious in this life without guilt if he had not been proud. He could have been commended before the judgment of his Creator for certain works of his, unless arrogance itself had overthrown those works before his eyes. We often see rich people who could have possessed wealth and glory without guilt if they had wished to possess them with humility. But they are lifted up by their possessions, inflated by honors, [Note: Vindoc. reads “are inflamed by honors”; this was formerly the reading in Utic.] disdainful of others, and place all their confidence in life upon the very abundance of their goods.

Hence a certain rich man said: “Soul, you have many good things stored up for many years; rest, eat, drink, feast” (Luke XII, 19). [Note: “Stored up” is absent from Vindoc.; we have supplied it from the manuscripts Vindoc., Norm., and others, and from the old edition. In the more recent editions: “when the heavenly Judge sees these thoughts, he tears him away from this very confidence.” The manuscripts and printed edition praised above have “them,” which we have supplied.] When the heavenly Judge observes these thoughts, he tears them away from that very confidence. Hence it is aptly added here:

### CHAPTER XVII [Revised Edition IX]

**VERSE 14.**—“May his confidence be torn from his tent, and may the king of destruction trample upon him.”

### 20. Those Whom the Devil Deceives by Gentle Persuasions, He Drags to Punishment with Violent Bonds

Here “destruction” designates the enemy of the human race himself, who brought destruction; he is represented through one of his satellites, of whom it is said to John: “His name was Death” (Revelation VI, 8).

On the day of his departure, this destruction tramples the wicked man as a king, because the one whom it first deceived by gentle persuasions it finally drags to punishment with violent bonds. [Note: Vindoc.: “finally, with violent efforts … drags him away.”] It crushes him all the more harshly the more fiercely it binds him in wicked acts. [Note: Utic. reads “kills and crushes him more harshly.”] Even here it tramples the mind of the reprobate while it possesses it, because whenever it presses the mind with pleasures, it places upon it, as it were, the feet of its tyrannical domination.

[Old Edition IX.] 21. We Can Escape Not the Temptation of Sin but Its Domination

If, however, “destruction” should not plainly be understood as the devil but as sin, by which it happens that the reprobate are dragged to destruction, then such destruction tramples the mind like a king when it possesses a mind that offers no resistance.

Temptation by sin cannot be absent from a person placed in this life. But it is one thing to resist sin when it tempts and another to serve sin when it rules. Since every wicked person does not know how to resist sin’s persuasions and does not fear being subjected to its domination, it is rightly said of him: “May the king of destruction trample upon him.”

The Apostle was driving the kingdom of this destruction away from the hearts of the disciples when he said: “Let not sin reign in your mortal body” (Romans VI, 12). He did not say, “Let sin not exist,” but “Let it not reign,” because sin cannot fail to exist, though it can be prevented from reigning in the hearts of the good.

When any fault knocks at the heart of the wicked, it finds no resistance there but lays that heart beneath its dominion. Thus it is rightly said: “May his confidence be torn from his tent, and may the king of destruction trample upon him.” [Note: Bellov., Utic., and the other Norman manuscripts read “from the earth,” which is considered the genuine reading. Editors, observing the earlier mention of the tent, changed *de terra* (“from the earth”) to *de tabernaculo* (“from the tent”), as all printed editions have it. Had “from the tent” been written originally, copyists would never have thought to alter it and write “from the earth.”]

His confidence is therefore torn from the earth when a perverse person who had prepared many things for himself according to his desire in this life is scattered by sudden death. And the king of destruction tramples upon him because either he is pressed here by vices or, at the time of his death, he is subjected to demonic power by being dragged away to punishments.

This occurs in the minds of the reprobate because, even when the opportunity to commit sin is absent, thoughts of desire are never absent from their hearts. Although they always follow the devil in action, they bind themselves to him very tightly in thought. Guilt is therefore first in thought and afterward in action.

Hence it is said to the daughter of Babylon: “Come down into the dust, virgin daughter of Babylon; sit on the ground” (Isaiah XLVII, 1). Although dust is always earth, earth is not always dust. What, then, should we understand by dust except thoughts, which, when they fly into the mind importunately and silently, blind its eyes? And what by earth except earthly action?

Because the mind of the reprobate is first cast down into thinking about evil and afterward into doing it, the daughter of Babylon—who descends from the judgment of inner uprightness—is rightly told in the sentence that strikes her to sit first in dust and afterward on earth. For unless she had prostrated herself in thought, she would not have remained fixed in evil action. It follows:

### CHAPTER XVIII [Revised Edition X]

**VERSE 15.**—“Let his companions dwell in his tent, for he is not.”

### 22. Satan Is Said Not to Be Because He Has Lost Well-Being

That is: let apostate angels dwell in his mind through utterly wicked thoughts—companions, namely, of the one who is now not, because he has withdrawn from the supreme Essence and therefore, as his defect increases daily, tends, as it were, toward non-being, since he once fell away from the One who truly is. He is also rightly said not to be because he has lost well-being, although he has not lost the essence of his nature.

[Old Edition X.] Still expressing these same thoughts of the wicked person more subtly, he adds:

### CHAPTER XIX

**THE SAME PASSAGE.**—“Let sulfur be scattered over his tent.”

### 23. The Sins of the Flesh Are Rightly Compared to Foul-Smelling and Burning Sulfur

What is sulfur except fuel for fire? Yet it feeds the fire in such a way that it exhales a most foul odor. What, then, should we understand in sulfur except the sin of the flesh? When this fills the mind with perverse thoughts, as with foul odors, it prepares eternal fires for the mind. And when it spreads the cloud of its foulness through the reprobate mind, it supplies fuel, as it were, for the flames that follow against it.

That sulfur signifies the foulness of the flesh is confirmed by the history of Sacred Scripture, which says that the Lord rained fire and sulfur upon Sodom (Genesis XIX, 24). When he had determined to punish the sins of the flesh, he marked the stain of the crime in the very nature of the punishment. [Note: Bigot. and Lyr. read “he knew the stain,” a reading to be rejected.] Sulfur has foulness; fire has heat. Because they had burned with perverse desires through the foulness of the flesh, it was fitting that they should perish together by fire and sulfur, so that through a just punishment they might learn what they had done through an unjust desire.

Sulfur is therefore scattered in the wicked person’s tent whenever perverse delight in the flesh dominates his mind. Since wicked thoughts possess him without ceasing and prevent him from bearing the fruit of good works, it is rightly added:

### CHAPTER XX

**VERSE 16.**—“Below, let his roots dry up; above, let his harvest be destroyed.”

### 24. The Dryness and Barrenness of the Wicked

What should we understand by “roots,” which are situated secretly and bring forth a shoot into the open, except thoughts, which, though unseen in the heart, produce visible works? By “harvest,” therefore, the same outward action is signified, since it is produced from a hidden root.

Because every wicked person first withers in the thoughts of temptations and afterward fails in good actions, [Note: *of temptations* is absent in Vindoc. and the Norman manuscripts.] Baldad rightly says: “Below, let his roots dry up; above, let his harvest be destroyed.” [Note: Our manuscripts and all the old editions support this reading. Gussanv. has: “when each person places his wicked thoughts in *infirmis* [weak things]”; the Vatican edition agrees, though it reads *in infimis* [in the lowest things].]

When a perverse person places his thoughts in lowly matters and neglects to desire the joys of eternal freshness, what else does he do but allow his roots to dry up below? His harvest above is destroyed because all his activity is counted as nothing by the heavenly judgment, even if it appears good before human eyes.

The roots are below and the harvest above because here we first plant good thoughts, so that eventually we may deserve to receive the fruit of good works in eternal recompense. But when a wicked person abandons good thoughts and pours himself out into external things, his roots dry up below. His harvest above is destroyed because the one who remains barren here is called to no rewards after this life. It follows:

### CHAPTER XXI [Old and Revised Edition XI]

**VERSE 17.**—“May his memory perish from the earth, and may his name not be celebrated in the streets.”

### 25. How Brief Is the Glory of Antichrist and of All the Wicked

We must observe that Baldad the Shuhite speaks about each wicked person in such a way that his words secretly turn toward the head of all the wicked. The head of the wicked is the devil. In the last times, when he enters that vessel of destruction, he will be called Antichrist. [Note: The printed editions read “which Antichrist,” but this lacks sense. The manuscripts restore the sense: Gregory commonly calls Antichrist “the vessel of destruction” or simply “that vessel of the devil.”] He will attempt to spread his name far and wide. Each person now imitates him when he strives to extend the glory of his praise through the memory of an earthly name and rejoices in a passing reputation.

These words should therefore be understood of each wicked person in such a way that they should also be referred specifically to the head of the wicked. [Note: Utic. formerly read “at some time” (*quandoque*).] Let him therefore say: “May his memory perish from the earth, and may his name not be celebrated in the streets.”

The streets are called by a Greek term from their breadth. Antichrist tries to establish his memory on earth when he desires, if it were possible, to remain forever in earthly glory. He rejoices when his name is celebrated in the streets when he extends the activity of his wickedness far and wide.

But because his wickedness is not permitted to rise for long, it is said: “May his memory perish from the earth, and may his name not be celebrated in the streets”—that is, may he quickly lose the praise of earthly power and lose all the joy of his name, which he had spread far and wide during the brief prosperity of time. It follows:

### CHAPTER XXII

**VERSE 18.**—“He will drive him from light into darkness.”

### 26. Eternal Punishment Follows the Glory of the Wicked

He is led from light into darkness when he is condemned from the honor of the present life to eternal punishments. Hence it is stated more plainly:

**THE SAME PASSAGE.**—“And he will transfer him from the world.”

He is transferred from the world when, with the heavenly Judge appearing, he is taken from this world in which he gloried perversely. Since he is condemned together with all his followers when the end of the world intervenes, it rightly follows:

**VERSE 19.**—“He will have neither seed nor offspring among his people, nor any remnant in his regions.”

For it is written that “the Lord Jesus will kill him with the breath of his mouth and destroy him by the manifestation of his coming” (II Thessalonians II, 8). [Note: Vindoc. reads “whom the Lord Jesus will kill by the breath ….”] When his wickedness therefore comes to an end together with the state of the world, no offspring of his will be left among his people, because both he and his people will be driven together with it to punishment. All the wicked who, through his perverse persuasion, were born into wicked actions will be struck down with that same head of theirs by the manifestation of the Lord’s coming, into eternal destruction.

No offspring of his remains in the world because the strict Judge brings his iniquities to an end together with the very end of the world. That these words should plainly be understood of Antichrist is shown by what follows:

### CHAPTER XXIII [Old Edition XII]

**VERSE 20.**—“In his days the last will be astonished, and horror will seize the first.”

27. Antichrist’s savage persecution. Then the saints will possess both steadfastness from spiritual strength and fear from the flesh.—For such unrestrained wickedness will then rage against the righteous that even the hearts of the elect will be struck with no little fear. Hence it is written: “So as to lead astray, if possible, even the elect” (Matt. 24:24). This is said not because the elect will fall, but because they will tremble at great terrors. Then the last and the first elect are said to have a contest of righteousness against him, because those who are found elect at the end of the world are to be struck down in the death of the flesh, while those who proceeded from the earliest ages of the world【Note: Bellov., “preceded.”】—namely, Enoch and Elijah—will be recalled into the midst and will suffer the violence of his cruelty while still in their mortal flesh.

The last are astonished at his powers, released with such great authority, and the first are afraid. For although, insofar as he is lifted up by the spirit of pride, they despise all his temporal power, nevertheless, insofar as they themselves are still in mortal flesh, in which they can be tormented temporally, they dread the very punishments that they endure bravely. Thus at one and the same time they possess both steadfastness from spiritual strength and fear from the flesh: although they are elect, so that they cannot be overcome by torments【Note: Vindoc., “so that they may be able to overcome the torments.”】, nevertheless, because they are human, they fear the very torments that they overcome.

Let it therefore be said: “In his days the last will be astonished, and terror will seize the first,” because he will then display such great signs and do such cruel and terrible things that he will bring those whom he finds at the end of the world to astonishment, and will pierce the earlier fathers, who have been preserved for his overthrow, with the pain of bodily death. Therefore, since he has related many things about all the wicked, or about the head of the wicked himself, he immediately adds by a general definition:

## CHAPTER XXIV

**VERSE 21.**—“These, then, are the dwellings of the wicked, and this is the place of him who does not know God.”

28. The place of Antichrist is darkness, into which he will be thrust with all the wicked.—For above he had said: “He will drive him from light into darkness, and remove him from the world.” When he added what concerned his evils, he continued: “These, then, are the dwellings of the wicked, and this is the place of him who does not know God,” indicating that the one who is now exalted by not knowing God reaches his proper dwellings then, when his wickedness plunges him into punishments; and that the one who here rejoiced in the false light of righteousness will eventually find darkness as his place, although here he occupied a place that was not his own.

For the perverse, in everything they do by pretense, strive to occupy the name of the glory of the righteous as though it were a place belonging to another【Note: Bellov., “sometimes the glory of the righteous, etc.” Thus it was formerly written in Utic.; after these words were deleted, it now reads as in the Edition. In Vindoc., “they possess the name of the glory of the righteous,” as though they then reach their own place. This passage is mutilated there.】. But they reach their own place when, by the deserts of their wickedness, they are tormented in everlasting fire.

Here, indeed, in everything they do, they serve the desire to receive praise, and through the appearance of good works they stretch the bosom of their mind toward avarice. Let the wicked go forth now, then, and, swollen with many displays, build his dwellings here, enlarge the name of his glory, multiply his estates, and delight himself in abundant wealth【Note: Tur., “enlarge himself”; thus it also now reads in Utic.】. But when he has reached eternal punishments, he will surely recognize that “these are the dwellings of the wicked, and this is the place of him who does not know God.”

Baldad had rightly said this, but he did not know to whom he was saying it. The heart of the righteous, however, is grievously afflicted when sentences are pronounced against him on the basis of an unjust judgment【Note: Vindoc., “opinion.”】. Hence blessed Job immediately replied, saying:

## CHAPTER XXV [Formerly XII, Revised XII]

**CHAPTER 19, VERSE 2.**—“How long will you afflict my soul and wear me down with words?”

29. What the righteous suffer from the wicked.—As we have often said, the utterances of holy men are sometimes to be understood as spoken in their own person, sometimes in the voice of the Head, and sometimes in the figure of the universal Church. The souls of the righteous are greatly afflicted when those who do not know how to live well hurl stern judgments against them and claim righteousness for themselves by their words, while their conduct opposes it.

Hence, since the friends of blessed Job, as we have often said, bear the figure of heretics, he rightly answers them: “How long will you afflict my soul and wear me down with words?” The good are worn down by the words of the wicked when those who lie either in perverse faith or in depraved morals swell up in speech against them. It follows:

## CHAPTER XXVI

**VERSE 3.**—“Behold, you confuse me ten times”【Note: Norm., “You have confounded me.”】.

30. Whether the righteous remain silent or speak, they always experience the wicked as adversaries.—Counting the occasions on which Job’s friends have spoken, we know that they have spoken only five times【Note: The word nisi (“only”) is absent except in Norm. and Vindoc.】. But because he had heard reproaches from them five times, and had himself answered their reproaches five times, he declares that he has been confused ten times: he suffered severely both because he was reproved without reason and because he spoke words of instruction to those unwilling to hear.

Thus, both when he remained silent as a listener and when he spoke without being heard, he himself endured the labor; by patiently keeping silent and by speaking to them without effect, he felt the sorrow of his heart. Hence above he also says: “What shall I do? If I speak, my pain will not be quiet; and if I am silent, it will not depart from me” (Job 16:7)【Note: Vindoc. omits “as a listener.”】.

But if we refer these words to the figure of holy Church, it is clear that her great joy is to preserve the commandments of the Decalogue. Yet the perverse confuse her ten times, because by everything they sin, they abandon the commandments of the Decalogue through their depraved conduct; and they bring confusion upon the good as many times as their actions resist the divine words. It follows:

## CHAPTER XXVII

**THE SAME PASSAGE.**—“And you are not ashamed to oppress me.”

31. The enemies of the Church are restrained neither by fear of God nor by shame before human beings.—There are some whom a sudden outbreak of malice invites to commit wickedness, but whom human shame nevertheless recalls. Often, because they are ashamed outwardly, they return to their inner selves and pass judgment within themselves; for if they fear doing evil on account of a human being, how much more should they fear doing evil on account of God, who sees everything?

Thus they correct greater evils through lesser goods—namely, their inward guilt through outward shame. But there are others who, after despising God in their minds, scorn human judgments even more and are not ashamed boldly to carry out every evil they desire. Hidden wickedness invites them to commit evil, and no open sense of shame restrains them, just as it is said of a certain wicked judge: “He did not fear God, and he had no regard for man” (Luke 18:2).

Hence it was also said of some who sinned with brazen faces: “They proclaimed their sin like Sodom” (Isa. 3:9). Such, then, are often the adversaries of holy Church, who are restrained from committing evil neither by fear of the Lord nor by shame before human beings. To them blessed Job rightly says: “And you are not ashamed to oppress me,” because although it was wicked to desire evil, it is worse not to be ashamed of having desired it wickedly【Note: Sag. and other Norm., “because although it was wicked to have desired evil, it is worse, etc.”】. It follows:

## CHAPTER XXVIII

**VERSE 4.**—“Indeed, even if I have been ignorant, my ignorance will remain with me.”

32. Heretics oppose arrogance to the humility of the Church.—Heretics have this characteristic: they are puffed up by the arrogance of their empty knowledge, frequently mock the simplicity of those who believe rightly, and regard the life of the humble as having no merit【Note: Vindoc., “they proclaim.”】.

But holy Church, in everything she truly understands, humbly restrains her judgment, lest knowledge puff her up, lest she swell with the investigation of hidden things, and lest she presume to scrutinize matters beyond her strength. For she more usefully strives not to know what she cannot investigate than boldly to define what she does not know.

It is written: “As it is not good for one who eats much honey, so one who is a scrutinizer of majesty will be overwhelmed by glory” (Prov. 25:27). For if the sweetness of honey is taken in greater quantity than necessary, the very thing by which the mouth is delighted destroys the eater’s life. The investigation of majesty is also sweet; but whoever desires to scrutinize it more than human understanding permits is overwhelmed by its glory itself, because, like honey taken in excessive measure, it tears apart the understanding of the investigator when it cannot contain it【Note: Utic., “for it is sweet.”】.

Something is said to be “with us” when it is for us, and again something is said not to be “with us” when it is against us (Luke 11:13). Therefore, because knowledge puffs up the hearts of heretics, while the recognition of their ignorance humbles the faithful, let blessed Job speak in his own voice; let him also speak in the confession of the universal Church: “Indeed, even if I have been ignorant, my ignorance will remain with me.”

As though speaking openly to the heretics, he says: All your knowledge is not with you, because it is against you, raising you up through foolish arrogance. But my ignorance is with me, because it is for me: since I do not presumptuously dare to scrutinize something about God, I remain humbly in the truth【Note: Turon., “I preserve the truth humbly.”】.

And because heretics seize the very things they seek to know for the sole use of arrogance, so that they may appear learned in opposition to the faithful and humble, it is rightly added:

## CHAPTER XXIX [Revised XIII]

**VERSE 5.**—“But you raise yourselves up against me.”

33. The order requires that we first rise up against ourselves and afterward against the wicked. The wicked do not know this method of correction.—But perhaps we shall weigh these words more effectively if we show how they apply specifically to the friends of blessed Job. When they saw the righteous man struck down, they ought to have returned to their inmost selves and by no means oppressed blessed Job with words of reproach; rather, they ought to have mourned for themselves. For if one who served in such a way had been struck down in this manner, by what punishment did those deserve to be struck who had not served in such a way?

To them it is rightly said: “But you raise yourselves up against me.” As though he were saying more openly: You ought to have risen up against yourselves because of my affliction【Note: Formerly XV.】.

The order of rising up in goodness is this: first we rise up against ourselves and afterward against the wicked. For whoever rises up against the good is puffed up by pride. We rise up against ourselves when, recognizing our own evils, we punish ourselves with the strict retribution of repentance; when we by no means spare ourselves in our sins and do not bend before any flattering thoughts concerning ourselves.

If, then, we first pursue our own evils strictly within ourselves, it is also right that we rise up usefully against the evils of others and overcome by reproving in others what we punish in ourselves.

34. But the wicked do not know this rising up, because they abandon themselves and attack the good. Within their conscience they incline toward themselves through the softness of flattering self-adulation, while they rise up against the life of the good with the severity of harshness.

Hence the friends of blessed Job, swelling up over his affliction, are rightly told now: “But you raise yourselves up against me”—that is, you leave yourselves, though you ought to be reproved, and reproach me with strict judgments. For one who does not first judge himself does not know what is right to judge in another. And even if he perhaps knows by hearing what he ought to judge rightly, he cannot rightly judge another’s merits when the innocence of his own conscience supplies no rule for judgment.

Hence it is said to certain men who were plotting and leading an adulterous woman out to be punished (John 8:7): “Let the one among you who is without sin first cast a stone at her” (3, q. 7, chap. 3). They were going to punish another’s sins while abandoning their own. They are therefore recalled inwardly to their conscience, so that they might first correct their own sins and then reprove those of another.

This is also why, when the tribe of Benjamin had been overwhelmed by the crime of the flesh, all Israel gathered and wished to avenge the wickedness, yet was itself struck down once and again in battle. When they consulted the Lord whether they should go to avenge it【Note: Gratian, in the Decree, at the assigned place, “whether they ought to go.”】, they were commanded to do so. They went according to the command of the divine voice, fell once and a second time, and only then, striking the sinful tribe forcefully, nearly destroyed it completely【Note: Lyr. and Bigot., “forcefully”; thus Utic. now reads.】.

What does it mean that Israel is inflamed to avenge the crime and yet is itself struck down first, unless it means that those through whom the faults of others are struck must first be cleansed, so that, already purified, they may proceed to punish the vices of others? Therefore, when the retribution of divine judgment against us is delayed, our conscience must itself reproach us and rise up against itself in the lament of repentance. It must not be lifted up against the good while being humble toward itself; rather, it must be strict toward itself and submissive toward all the good【Note: Formerly XVI.】.

Thus it is rightly said to the proud reprovers: “But you raise yourselves up against me, and reproach me with my reproaches.” All the arrogant consider temporal evils to be a grave disgrace, and believe that a person is as much despised by God as they see him afflicted by the scourge of punishment. They seek nothing in his character or actions; but whenever they see anyone struck down in this life, they judge him already condemned by divine judgment.

Hence it is rightly said now in the voice of blessed Job:

## CHAPTER XXX

**THE SAME PASSAGE.**—“And you reproach me with my reproaches.”

35. The false judgments of the reprobate concerning the scourges of the righteous.—Those who had known him to be righteous before the scourges judged him to be unrighteous on the basis of the very striking he had now suffered. Thus heretics also often see some within holy Church afflicted. It is written of God: “He scourges every son whom he receives” (Heb. 12:6)【Note: Vindoc., “every son whom he loves.”】. Yet they suspect that the tribulations of the faithful arise only from sin, and believe themselves righteous because, having been abandoned to the sense of their perversity, they have grown hard without the scourge. It follows:

## CHAPTER XXXI [Revised XIV]

**VERSE 6.**—“At least now understand that God has afflicted me without an equitable judgment.”

36. Certain words of Sacred Scripture are considered improper because they are not examined according to their inner meaning.—How harshly the voice of a righteous man afflicted by blows sounds! Yet it was not pride that expressed it, but pain. A righteous man, however, is not one who abandons righteousness in pain.

Blessed Job possessed a gentle heart and did not sin in this harsh utterance. For if we say that he sinned when he said this, we assert that the devil fulfilled what he had proposed when he said: “Touch his bone and his flesh; surely he will bless you to your face” (Job 2:5). A serious question therefore arises. If he did not sin in saying, “At least now understand that God has afflicted me without an equitable judgment,” then we consent to the claim that God—which is impious to say—did something unjustly. But if he did sin, then the devil accomplished in him what he had promised.

We must therefore affirm both that God acted rightly concerning blessed Job, and that blessed Job did not lie when he said that he had not been afflicted by God’s just judgment, and that the ancient enemy lied in what he had promised concerning the fault of the blessed man.

For the words of good people are sometimes considered improper because their inner meaning is not carefully weighed. Blessed Job had considered his life and weighed the scourges he was suffering; he saw that it was not equitable that such scourges should be inflicted upon such a life. When he says that he was afflicted without an equitable judgment, he spoke openly what the Lord had said secretly concerning his adversary: “You moved me against him, to afflict him without cause” (Job 2:3). What God says—that he afflicted blessed Job without cause—blessed Job likewise asserts: that he was afflicted by the Lord without an equitable judgment. In what, then, did he sin, since he differed in no respect from the sentence of his creator?

[Formerly XVII.] 37. It is sometimes permissible to speak good things about oneself, provided they are true. This is confirmed by the example of Paul and Job.—But perhaps someone will say that it cannot be without sin for us to speak a good thing about ourselves which the judge has secretly said about us. For when a just judge praises someone, there is no doubt that the person is rightly praiseworthy. But if he praises himself, then his righteousness is no longer believed worthy of praise.

This is rightly said if someone presumes, in an inflated spirit, to say about himself what the just judge has declared by an equitable judgment. But if he also remains in humble thought and, when required by circumstance or pain, speaks true good things about himself, he has departed from righteousness no more than he has departed from the truth—which is not at all.

38. Hence the apostle Paul also related many courageous things about himself for the edification of his disciples. Yet he did not sin in relating them, because he did not depart from the path of truth, from certain testimony, or from a humble heart.

Therefore, sensing the righteousness of his life, blessed Job says that he was not afflicted by a just judgment. He does not sin in this utterance, in which he does not differ from his creator: the one whom God struck without cause likewise asserts that he was afflicted without a just judgment.

But another question arises, which I remember having resolved at the beginning of this work (Book III, chapter and section 3): since almighty God does nothing without purpose, why does he testify that he afflicted blessed Job without cause? Our just Creator, through so many scourges inflicted upon blessed Job, did not seek to extinguish his vices but to increase his merits.

What he did was therefore equitable in the increase of good merit; nevertheless, it did not appear equitable if it was believed that he was punishing the causes of sin【Note: Turon., “the cause of sin was believed to be punished.”】. Blessed Job, however, believed that his sins were being erased by those scourges, not that his merits were being increased; and for this reason he calls the judgment inequitable, because he examines his life together with the scourges.

Thus, if his life and the scourges are weighed, what blessed Job believed had been done to him through the severity of wrath was not equitable, as I have said【Note: Norm., Turon., etc., “through discipline.”】. But if the mercy of the judge is considered, because the merits of the righteous man’s life were increased through punishment, the judgment was equitable, or rather merciful.

Therefore Job spoke truthfully when he weighed his life against the scourge; God did not afflict Job by an unjust judgment, because he increased his merits through the scourge; and the devil did not fulfill what he had promised, because blessed Job did not depart, amid words that sound harsh, either from the true judgment or from a humble mind.

But perhaps we understand these words of the afflicted man less clearly unless we know the sentence of the judge. When he gave judgment between the two parties, he said to Job’s friends: “You have not spoken what is right before me, as my servant Job has” (Job 42:8)【Note: Turon., “rightly.”】. Who, then, would confess with foolish judgment that blessed Job sinned in his speech, when the voice of the judge itself declares that he spoke rightly?

If we refer this utterance to the person of holy Church, we may appropriately apply it to her weak members. During the time of her persecution, when they consider both her merits and her scourges, they see the unjust flourishing and the just perishing, and in no way suppose this to be just.

The voice of the blessed man then appropriately adds:

## CHAPTER XXXII [Formerly XVIII]

**THE SAME PASSAGE.**—“And he has surrounded me with his scourges.”

39. The weak members of the Church are troubled by continual scourges.—To be struck by scourges is one thing; to be surrounded by them is another. We are struck by scourges when we still have consolation and relief from other things amid our pains. But when such affliction weighs us down that the mind cannot breathe from the consolation of anything, then we are not merely struck by scourges but also surrounded by them, because we are encircled on every side by the blows of tribulations.

Paul had been surrounded by scourges when he said: “Outside, battles; inside, fears” (2 Cor. 7:5). He had been surrounded by scourges when he said: “Dangers from my race, dangers from the nations, dangers in the city, dangers in the wilderness” (2 Cor. 11:26), and so forth, listing them in such a way as to show that he had nowhere found rest【Note: Utic., “dangers from rivers, dangers from my race.”】.

When holy Church is surrounded by the scourges of her tribulations, her various weak members are reduced to a state of faintheartedness, so that they consider themselves all the more despised the longer they see themselves not heard【Note: Norm.: “But because holy Church is surrounded by the scourges of her tribulations, her weak members are reduced to a state of faintheartedness, etc., ‘rightly still,’ and so forth. The reading we retain from the other manuscripts and all printed editions was formerly found in Utic.”】【Note: In Ms. Germ. and in the printed editions, “already despairing,” which we also suspect was formerly read in Utic.】.

The voice of the holy man then appropriately adds, still in the figure of these members:

## CHAPTER XXXIII

**VERSE 7.**—“Behold, I will cry out, suffering violence, and no one will hear me; I will shout, and there is no one who judges.”

[Col. 1060C] 40. God appears to disregard the complaints of the suffering in order to increase their benefit.—Almighty God, knowing what can profit us, appears to disregard the voice of the suffering, so as to increase their benefit: so that life may be cleansed through punishment, and the tranquility of rest—which cannot be found here—may be sought elsewhere【Note: Ebroic., “so that vices may be cleansed.”】.

Yet some of the faithful do not understand this gracious ordering. In their person it is now said: “Behold, I will cry out, suffering violence, and no one will hear me; I will shout, and there is no one who judges.”

“There is no one who judges” is said when the one who exists—namely, God himself—appears to defer judgment; for there is no one besides him who can judge our case against the adversary. Nevertheless, the fact that judgment is deferred is not without judgment. When blessed Job said these things, both the merits of the holy man and the punishment of the adversary were increasing. Thus the deferral of judgment itself belongs to the judge【Note: Sag. and other Norm., “it is the deferral of judgment.”】.

But what God arranges inwardly in justice is one thing; what the soul, bruised by outward scourges, seeks is another. Hence he adds further concerning the oppression of the blows:

## CHAPTER XXXIV [Revised XV]

**VERSE 8.**—“He has fenced in my path, and I cannot pass through, and he has placed darkness on my way.”

41. Illumination and salvation are present for those who sin through ignorance and weakness.—He saw his path fenced in by scourges when, desiring to pass over into security, he could not escape the blows. And because he saw himself being struck but did not find in himself a life deserving of such a striking, he found, as it were, the darkness of his ignorance on the path of his heart, since he could not penetrate the reason for which he was being scourged【Note: In some editions, “with thorns.”】.

This also appropriately applies to the weak members of holy Church: when they remember that they have acted wrongly, they are held back even from good works; and, timid because of their own weakness, they do not dare to undertake courageous good deeds against these faults. Those who remember that they are weak in their actions fear beginning great good works.

And since they often do not even know what good they should choose, they dread the darkness placed, as it were, on their path. For the mind often becomes so uncertain about its own work that it does not know at all what is virtue and what is guilt. Therefore the one who does not know what to choose in the things he desires to do finds darkness on his path.

Since, then, sin is often committed through weakness and sometimes through ignorance, the voice of the weak members says: “He has fenced in my path, and I cannot pass through.” Concerning those who are darkened with respect to the good work they should choose, it adds: “And he has placed darkness on my way.”

It is a punishment for guilt to see the good one ought to do and yet be unable to accomplish it; and it is, in turn, a punishment for a more serious guilt to fail even to see what one ought to do【Note: Norm., “as the punishment of a more serious guilt.”】. Hence, against both conditions, it is said in the voice of the Psalmist: “The Lord is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear?” (Ps. 26:1).

Against the darkness of ignorance, the Lord is illumination; against weakness, he is salvation: he both shows what should be desired for action and supplies the strength by which what he has shown can be fulfilled. It follows:

## CHAPTER XXXV [Revised XVI]

**VERSE 9.**—“He has stripped me of my glory and taken the crown from my head.”

42. The weak members of the Church are sometimes stripped of righteousness for a time.—There is no doubt that all these words of the blessed man, placed as he is in affliction, suit his person. But because the words of the history are clear, they do not require exposition according to the letter. We must therefore investigate how they should be understood according to mystical meanings.

He says: “He has stripped me of my glory.” The glory of each person is righteousness. Just as clothing protects against the cold, so righteousness guards against death. Hence righteousness is appropriately compared with clothing, when the prophet says: “Let your priests be clothed with righteousness” (Ps. 132:9).

Because, during the time of her affliction, holy Church loses this garment of righteousness in her weak members—the garment that protects before God—it is rightly said: “He has stripped me of my glory”; that is, righteousness has been taken from the weak. It could not be taken from them if it had been deeply rooted in them; but it could be removed because it adhered outwardly, like a garment.

Here we must ask how those who were able to lose the righteousness they appeared to possess can be called members of holy Church. We should know, however, that righteousness is often lost for a time by her weak members; but when afterward, through recognition of their guilt, they return to repentance, they bind themselves more firmly than was thought possible to that same righteousness which they had lost【Note: Sag. and other Norm., “but through recognition of guilt afterward they return and bind themselves to it, etc.” Formerly in Utic.: “but when through recognition, etc.,” as in the Edition.】.

It is then further added: “And he has taken the crown from my head.” Just as the head is the first part of the body, so the mind is the principal part of the inner person. The crown is the reward of victory, which is received from above so that the one who has struggled may be rewarded.

Therefore, because many, pressed by adversities, do not persevere in the contest, holy Church is said in them to lose a crown from her head. The crown on the head is the heavenly reward in the mind. There are many who, while afflicted by adversities, neglect to think about heavenly rewards and cannot reach the perfection of victory. In them, then, the crown is taken from the head, because the heavenly and spiritual reward is removed from the mind’s thoughts, so that they now desire only outward tranquility and no longer seek the eternal rewards about which they had been accustomed to think【Note: Bigot. and Lyr., “pressed by the adversities of the world.”】.

43. The crown is taken from the head of the Church when its leaders neglect spiritual goods.—Or certainly, the priests may appropriately be understood as the head of the faithful, because they are the first part of the Lord’s members. Hence the prophet is also said to speak of the destruction of head and tail, where by the name “head” the priests are designated and by the name “tail” the reprobate prophets.

The crown, therefore, is taken from the head when even those who appeared to preside over the body of the Church abandon the rewards of heavenly recompense. And often, when leaders fall, the army that follows collapses more widely. Hence, immediately after the losses of the greater ones, he adds what follows concerning the Church’s manifold weakening:

## CHAPTER XXXVI [Formerly XX]

**VERSE 10.**—“He has destroyed me on every side, and I perish; and like a tree torn up, he has taken away my hope.”

44. When those set over them fall, the weak fall.—The Church is destroyed on every side, as it were, and perishes in her weak members when those who appeared strong collapse—when the crown is removed from the head, that is, when even those set over her neglect the eternal rewards.

It is rightly added concerning the falling weak: “And like a tree torn up, he has taken away my hope.” A tree is driven by the wind so that it falls. And when threats frighten someone into falling into injustice, what else has he endured than the blast of the wind, like a tree, and what else has he lost than the uprightness of his position?

The one who, overcome by the threats and persuasions of the wicked, abandons the eternal rewards he had hoped for has lost his hope as though from the wind. And because it often happens that someone abandons righteousness through fear of punishment, it occurs, by God’s judgment, that even while abandoning righteousness he does not escape the punishments he feared. The one who had no fear of the destruction of his mind also suffers the evils of the flesh that he feared.

Hence it is further added:

## CHAPTER XXXVII [Revised XVII]

**[Col. 1063A] VERSE 11.**—“His fury has been angry against me, and he has treated me as his enemy.”

45. God strikes some as sons and others as enemies.—With the testimony of the eminent preacher, we say that God is faithful and will not allow us to be tempted beyond what we can bear, but with the temptation will provide a way of escape, so that we may be able to endure (1 Cor. 10:13).

Through the prophet the Lord also says: “With the wound of an enemy I have struck you, with cruel chastisement” (Jer. 30:14). Therefore, when someone is struck in such a way that his strength is overcome by the striking, the Lord no longer strikes him as a son through discipline but as an enemy through wrath.

When scourges go beyond the strength of our patience, we must greatly fear that, because our sins demand it, we are no longer struck by the Lord as sons by a father, but as enemies. And because it often happens that evil spirits also suggest many things to the hearts of the afflicted and, amid the scourges that strike outwardly, pour harmful thoughts into their minds, it is rightly added after the Lord’s fury:

## CHAPTER XXXVIII [Revised XVIII]

**VERSE 12.**—“His robbers came together and made a way for themselves through me.”

46. Evil spirits break into the afflicted and besiege them. In them the will is unjust, but the power is just.—His robbers are evil spirits, who occupy themselves with seeking the deaths of human beings【Note: In Germ., “movements”; from a superscripted r we infer that this was formerly read in Utic.】. They make a way for themselves in the hearts of the afflicted when, amid the adversities suffered outwardly, they do not cease to introduce depraved thoughts.

It is further said of them:

“And they besieged my tent round about.”

They besiege the tent round about when they encircle the mind on every side with their temptations【Note: Ebroic., “as if from.”】. By the worst of suggestions they persuade it now to mourn over temporal things, now to despair concerning eternal things, now to fall into impatience, and to hurl words of blasphemy against God.

Yet, as we have already said, these words also suit blessed Job according to the historical sense. When he gathered before his eyes the evils he had suffered, he judged that he had been struck not as a son to be corrected but as an enemy. His robbers also made a way for themselves through him, because the evil spirits received permission to strike him. They besieged his tent round about, because, after his possessions and children had been taken away, they also battered his entire body with wounds.

[Formerly XXI.] But it is very remarkable that, after calling them robbers, he added “his.” This was evidently to show that these same robbers belonged to God. If the will and power of evil spirits are distinguished here, the reason they are called God’s robbers becomes clear.

Evil spirits constantly desire to harm us; but although they possess an evil will of their own, they do not possess the power to harm unless the supreme will permits them. Although they desire unjustly to injure us, they are permitted by the Lord to injure no one except justly.

Therefore, because their will is unjust but their power is just, they are called both robbers and God’s: what they desire to inflict wickedly comes from themselves, while what they accomplish of their desire justly comes from God.

But since, as we have often said, the holy man, placed amid the pain of punishments, sometimes uses his own voice, sometimes that of the Church, and sometimes that of our Redeemer, and frequently narrates his own circumstances in such a way that he nevertheless presents through the figure what belongs to holy Church and to our Redeemer, let us set aside for a little while the concern with the historical sense and demonstrate how what follows suits the voice of our Redeemer. It follows:

## CHAPTER XXXIX [Revised XIX]

**[Col. 1064B] VERSES 13–14.**—“He has put my brothers far from me, and my acquaintances have withdrawn from me like strangers. My relatives have forsaken me, and those who knew me have forgotten me.”

## ALLEGORICAL SENSE

**47. The Jews, Christ’s brothers, acquaintances, and relatives, denied him when incarnate, although they had foretold that he would become incarnate.**—We shall show this more clearly if we bring forward John’s testimony, who says: “He came to his own, and his own did not receive him” (John 1:11). For his brothers became distant from him, and his acquaintances withdrew from him—the very one whom the Hebrews knew how to foretell while holding to the Law, but whom they utterly failed to recognize when present. [Note: Sag. reads *prophetari* (“to be prophesied”); Utic. now likewise reads this, but formerly read *prophetare* (“to prophesy”), which we retain, because shortly below the same Hebrews are said to have forgotten the one whom they had prophesied.] [Col. 1064D]

Hence it is rightly said: “My relatives abandoned me, and those who knew me forgot me.” For the Jews, his relatives according to the flesh and his acquaintances through instruction in the Law, were, as it were, forgetful of the one whom they had foretold, since they both proclaimed in the words of the Law that he would become incarnate and, once he was incarnate, denied him through the words of their unbelief. [Col. 1064C]

It follows:

## CHAPTER XL

**Verse 15.—“The inhabitants of my house and my maidservants regarded me as a stranger.”**

**48. Christ was regarded as a stranger by the priests and Levites.**—The priests were inhabitants of God’s house, since their origin was assigned to God’s service and, through their office, they were already held within that condition. The maidservants, however, are rightly understood as the souls of the Levites, who served more familiarly in the tabernacle’s hidden places, as though in the inner chamber.

Let him therefore speak of the priests serving with diligent care; let him speak of the Levites ministering in the inner parts of God’s house: “The inhabitants of my house and my maidservants” [Note: Vindoc.: “and my maidservants.”] “regarded me as a stranger,” because they were unwilling to recognize and venerate the incarnate Lord whom they had long before foretold through the words of the Law. [Col. 1064D]

That he was not recognized because of their perverse will he makes still clearer when he adds:

## CHAPTER XLI

**The same passage.—“And I was like a stranger in their eyes.”**

**49. Christ was a stranger in his own house.**—Our Redeemer, since he was not recognized by the synagogue, became like a stranger in his own house. The prophet openly testifies to this, saying: “Why will you be like a settler in the land, and like a traveler turning aside to stay?” (Jeremiah 14:8). [Note: Bellov. and Norm. read “like a settler who will be,” etc.; Utic. has “will be.” The word “why” is absent.] [Col. 1065A]

Because he was not heard as Lord, he was believed to be not the possessor of the land but a settler. He turned aside like a traveler merely to stay, because he took away a few from Judea and, proceeding toward the calling of the Gentiles, completed the journey he had begun.

He was therefore a stranger in their eyes because, while they considered only what they could see, they were unable to understand in the Lord what they could not see. For while they despised the visible flesh, they did not reach the invisible majesty. Thus it is rightly said: “And I was like a stranger in their eyes.”

Concerning this people it is aptly added:

## CHAPTER XLII

**Verse 16.—“I called my servant, and he did not answer.”**

**50. Christ was despised by his servant, namely, by the Jewish people.**—For what was the Jewish people except a servant, who obeyed the Lord not through the love of a son but through servile fear? In contrast, Paul says to us: “You did not receive the spirit of slavery again in fear, but the spirit of adoption as sons, in which we cry, ‘Abba, Father’” (Romans 8:15). [Note: Vindoc. and Norm.: “but you received the spirit.” Utic. adds *accepistis* (“you received”).] [Col. 1065D]

The Lord therefore called this servant because, after bestowing gifts, he strove to lead him to himself, as though summoning him with words. But he did not answer because he scorned to return deeds worthy of his gifts. God calls us when he anticipates us with gifts; we answer his call when we serve him worthily in accordance with the gifts we have received.

Since, then, he anticipated the Jewish people with so many gifts, let him say: “I called my servant.” But since, even after so many gifts, it despised him, let him add: “And he did not answer.” [Col. 1065C]

It follows:

## CHAPTER XLIII  
*(Formerly XXII; Revised XX)*

**The same passage.—“With my own mouth I pleaded with him.”**

**51. Christ pleaded with those resisting his commands, but was not heard.**—As though he were saying more plainly: “I am the one who, before my incarnation, had commanded him through the mouths of the prophets to carry out so many precepts. Having become incarnate and coming to him, I pleaded with him with my own mouth.”

Accordingly, when Matthew describes him giving commandments on the mountain, he says: “Opening his mouth, he said” (Matthew 5:2). It is as though he plainly said: “Then he opened his own mouth—the one who had previously opened the mouths of the prophets.” [Col. 1065D]

Hence also the bride, desiring his presence, says of him: “Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth” (Song of Songs 1:1). For however many commandments the holy Church has learned from his preaching, it has received, as it were, that many kisses from his mouth.

It is rightly said, however, “I pleaded,” because when he appeared in the flesh and humbly spoke the commandments of life, he begged the proud servant to come. [Note: Some manuscripts and printed copies have *ut viveret* (“that he might live”), as do German, Tours, and Normandy witnesses, most of them; others have *ut veniret* (“that he might come”), which was formerly written in Utic. We judge the latter reading preferable from the sequence of the complete context, where it is explained in how many ways God attempted to bring the Jews back to himself: first by commanding and giving precepts, and afterward by pleading.] [Col. 1065D–1066A]

Here it is aptly added:

## CHAPTER XLIV  
*(Revised XXI)*

**Verse 17.—“My wife recoiled from my breath.”**

**52. The bride, the synagogue, recoiled from Christ.**—What is understood by the Lord’s wife except the Synagogue, subject to him under the covenant of the Law with a carnal understanding? Breath, however, proceeds from the flesh.

But the unbelieving people understood the Lord’s flesh carnally, because they believed him to be merely a man. His wife therefore recoiled from his breath because the Synagogue was afraid to believe that the man whom it saw was God. Although it heard words bodily from his mouth, it refused to understand in him the mysteries of divinity, and did not believe the Creator to be the one whom it saw as created.

Thus the carnal wife recoiled from the breath of the flesh, because, devoted to carnal senses, it did not recognize the mystery of his incarnation.

It follows:

## CHAPTER XLV  
*(Revised XXII)*

**The same passage.—“And I pleaded with the children of my womb.”**

**53. How God can be said to have bodily members.**—In God, who is not circumscribed by bodily form, bodily members—hands, an eye, and a womb—are named in such a way that the effects of his power are signified through the names of bodily members.

He is said to have eyes because he sees everything; he is described as having hands because he does everything; and in a womb offspring are conceived and brought forth into this life. What, then, should we understand as God’s womb except his counsel, in which we were conceived before the ages through predestination, so that we might be brought forth through the ages as created beings?

The God who remains before the ages therefore pleaded with the children of his womb, because, coming in the flesh, he humbly entreated those whom he had powerfully created through his divinity. But because he was despised by their judgment in that very flesh in which he appeared, it is added:

## CHAPTER XLVI

**Verse 18.—“Fools also despised me.”**

**54. When the wise fell away from the truth, even fools failed.**—Since the wise were falling away from faith in the truth, it is rightly added that fools also despised him. For while the Pharisees and teachers of the Law despised the Lord, the crowd of the people followed their unbelief: seeing in him a man, it despised the proclamations concerning the world’s Redeemer.

The name “fools” often designates those who are poor among the common people. Thus Jeremiah says: “I said, ‘Perhaps they are poor and foolish, ignorant of the way of the Lord and the judgment of their God’” (Jeremiah 5:4).

Leaving behind the wise and rich of the world, our Redeemer had come to seek the poor and foolish. Hence it is now said as an increase of his grief: “Fools also despised me.” As though it were said plainly: “Even those for whose healing I assumed the foolishness of preaching despised me.”
