For it is written: “Since the world did not know God through the wisdom of God, it pleased God through the foolishness of preaching to save those who believe” (1 Corinthians 1:21). [Note: Bellov. reads “through the wisdom of God.”] The Word of God is wisdom, but the flesh of the Word was called the foolishness of this wisdom, so that, since carnal people could not reach the wisdom of God through the prudence of their flesh, they might be healed through the foolishness of preaching—that is, through the flesh of the Word. [Note: German, Tours, Bellov., and Norm. have “through the foolishness of preaching.” Utic. formerly had, and perhaps more suitably, “through the foolishness of the flesh,” which is set against the prudence of the flesh mentioned shortly before.] [Note: German, Tours, Bellov., and Norm. read “through the incarnation of the Word.”]

He therefore says: “Fools also despised me.” As though it were said plainly: “I was despised even by those for whom I did not fear being regarded as foolish.”

And because, when the Jewish populace saw our Redeemer’s miracles, it honored him on account of the signs, saying, “This is the Christ” (Mark 13:21), but when it saw the weakness of his humanity, it disdained to believe him the Creator, saying, “No, but he misleads the crowds” (John 7:12), it is rightly added:

## CHAPTER XLVII  
*(Formerly XXIII)*

**The same passage.—“And when I had withdrawn from them, they slandered me.”**

**55. They slandered Christ when he ceased performing miracles.**—The Lord came, as it were, near to the hearts of the people when he displayed miracles to them, and withdrew, as it were, when he showed no signs. But they slandered the withdrawing Lord because they were unwilling to believe in him when he ceased performing miracles.

Yet why should it be surprising that he suffered these things from the common people, when even those who appeared to be teachers of the Law—those who affirmed in prophetic words that he would become incarnate, saw him incarnate, and nevertheless were separated from him by a rupture of unbelief—did the same?

Concerning them it is added:

## CHAPTER XLVIII

**Verse 19.—“Once my counselors abhorred me, and the one whom I loved most turned away from me.”**

**56. The teachers of the Law and the Pharisees abhorred him.**—It is clear to all that God has no need of counselors, since he himself supplies the counsel of wisdom even to human counselors. Of him it is also written: “Who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor?” (Romans 11:34, from Isaiah 40:13). [Note: Bigot. and Lyr. read: “Who has known the mind of the Lord?”]

But just as, when bread or clothing is given to a needy person, the Lord testifies that he has received it (Matthew 25:40), so when sound counsel is given to someone ignorant, he himself receives it, whose member is the person being instructed.

For all the faithful are members of our Redeemer. Just as he is nourished in us through the mercy of our generosity, so he is helped in us through the counsel of instruction. The scribes and teachers of the Law, therefore, who were accustomed to teach the peoples toward life—what else were they except counselors of the Redeemer who was to come?

Yet when they saw the Lord incarnate, they separated many from faith in him by their counsels, [Note: Vindoc.: “they led many away from his faith.”] although previously they had appeared to teach many to believe in the mystery of his incarnation through the words of the prophets.

And because the one who draws many to God’s love is more beloved by God, the following is added concerning that same order of teachers of the Law and Pharisees: “And the one whom I loved most turned away from me.” That order, persuaded by unbelief, turned away from faith in the truth—the order that had previously been especially beloved because it served in the labor of preaching. [Note: Norm. and Germ. read *succedente perfidia* (“with unbelief succeeding”); Utic. now has the same reading, with *suadente* (“persuading”) erased.] The crowd of the people followed it not only into disbelief but even into persecuting the Lord, and was inflamed with the torches of its cruelty all the way to his Passion. During that Passion, the hearts of the disciples were troubled.

Hence it is now added:

## CHAPTER XLIX  
*(Revised XXIII)*

**Verse 20.—“My bone clung to my skin, my flesh being consumed.”**

**57. While Christ suffered and the apostles fled, the holy women clung to him like skin.**—Strength is signified by bone, but bodily weakness by flesh. Since Christ and the Church are one person, what is signified by the bone except the Lord himself? What by the flesh except the disciples, who showed weakness at the time of his Passion?

By the skin, which remains outside the flesh in the body, what else are the holy women represented, who served the Lord through outward ministries by preparing what was needed for his body?

For while his disciples, though not yet firm, were preaching the faith of the truth to the peoples, the flesh clung to its bone. And while the holy women prepared outwardly what was necessary, [Note: The same manuscripts: “the things that were necessary.”] they remained, as it were, outside the body like skin. [Note: The same manuscripts: “it remained in the body.” Utic. nevertheless has *manebant* (“they remained”) in the first hand; it now has *manebat* (“it remained”).]

But when the hour of the cross arrived, a grave fear of the Jews’ persecution seized his disciples. They fled one by one; [Note: Vindoc., Ebroic., and other Normandy witnesses: “the women stood by.” Utic. formerly read: “they clung.”] the women clung to him.

Thus, as the flesh was consumed, the Lord’s bone clung to his skin, because, while his disciples were fleeing at the time of his Passion, his strength found the women standing beside him.

Peter indeed stood for a while, but afterward, terrified, he denied him. [Note: Vindoc.: “he denied him at last.”] John also stood; at the very time of the cross he was told: “Behold your mother” (John 19:27). But he could not persevere completely, since it is also written of him that a certain young man followed him, clothed in a linen cloth over his naked body; they seized him, but he, [Note: Vindoc.: “leaving the linen cloth,”] abandoning the linen cloth, fled from them naked (Mark 14:51).

Although afterward he returned to the cross in order to hear the words of his Redeemer, he had first fled in terror. The women, however, are recorded not only as having neither feared nor fled, but as having remained even to the tomb.

Let him therefore say: “My bone clung to my skin, my flesh being consumed.” That is: “Those who ought to have clung more closely to my strength were consumed by fear at the time of my Passion; but I found those whom I had appointed for outward ministries clinging to me faithfully and without fear during my Passion.”

Here it is also plainly implied that these words are spoken mystically, since it follows: [Note: Norm.: “where it is also plainly added.”]

## CHAPTER L  
*(Formerly XXIV)*

**The same passage.—“And only my lips were left around my teeth.”**

**58. Christ’s teeth were the apostles, who, while he suffered, lost all their strength.**—What else do we have around the teeth except lips, even if we suffer no blows? But what is signified by lips except speech, and what by teeth except the holy apostles? They have been placed in the body of the Church so that, by correction, they may bite carnal people and break them away from the hardness of their stubbornness.

Hence it was said to the first of the apostles, as to a tooth placed in his body: “Kill and eat” (Acts 10:13).

But because, at the time of his Passion, these teeth lost through fear of death the bite of correction, they lost confidence in their strength and the effectiveness of every action, so that two of them, walking after his death and resurrection, spoke on the road and said: “We were hoping that he was the one who would redeem Israel” (Luke 24:21). [Note: Utic.: “But we were hoping.”]

It is therefore rightly said: “And only my lips were left around my teeth.” They were still conversing about him, but no longer believed in him. Only lips therefore remained around his teeth, because they had lost the strength of good action and retained only words of conversation about him. They had lost the bite of correction but retained the movement of speech.

Only lips were therefore left around the teeth because they still knew how to converse, but feared either to preach him or to bite the vices of unbelievers.

Having completed the things that he spoke in the voice of the Head, blessed Job returns to his own words, saying:

## CHAPTER LI

**Verse 21.—“Have pity on me, have pity on me, at least you, my friends, because the hand of the Lord has touched me.”**

**59. In adversity, the minds of the godly are moved to prayer, not to anger.**—It is characteristic of the minds of the godly that, when they suffer injustice from their adversaries, they are moved not so much to anger as to prayer, so that, if the perversity of their adversaries can be calmly restrained, they choose to plead rather than to become angry. [Note: Norm.: “and so that their perversity may be peacefully restrained, they choose rather to plead more.”]

Hence it is rightly said: “Have pity on me, have pity on me, at least you, my friends, because the hand of the Lord has touched me.”

Behold, he calls friends those whom he recognizes as continually afflicting him with insults, [Note: Sag., Bigot., Lyr., Utic., and the older Paris and Basel editions: “by whom he considers himself afflicted with insults.”] because to good minds even those things that appear adverse become beneficial.

For the perverse are either converted by the sweetness of the good, so that they return, and by becoming good they are friends; or they persevere in wickedness, and even in this they are friends unwillingly, because, if there are any sins in the good, they unknowingly cleanse them through their persecutions.

It should also be noted that the blessed man’s public words correspond to things done secretly before God. He had been struck by Satan, yet he did not attribute his striking to Satan; rather, he called it a touch of the Lord’s hand, just as Satan himself had said: “Stretch out your hand and touch his bone and his flesh; surely he will bless you to your face” (Job 2:5).

The holy man knew that even in the very act by which Satan had proceeded against him with perverse intent, Satan possessed power not from himself but from the Lord.

It follows:

## CHAPTER LII  
*(Formerly XXV; Revised XXIV)*

**Verse 22.—“Why do you persecute me like God, and gorge yourselves on my flesh?”**

**60. God does not persecute us by raging against us.**—It is not contrary to the language of piety when he declares himself persecuted by God. For there is a good persecutor, as the Lord says of himself through the prophetic mouth: “The one who secretly slanders his neighbor, him I persecuted.”

When a holy person is permitted to be scourged, he knows that he suffers persecution against his sins through an inward dispensation. But the cruel minds of persecutors, when they desire the power to strike, are inflamed against the life of the good not by a zeal for purification but by the torches of envy.

They indeed do what almighty God permits to be done. Yet although one cause is carried out through them and through God, the will in that cause is not the same. Almighty God displays purification out of love, whereas the perversity of the unjust exercises malice by raging.

Therefore, when it is said, “Why do you persecute me like God?” this refers to the outward striking, not to the inward intention. Although outwardly they do what God has ordained to be done, they do not desire what God desires in his action: that the good should be purified through affliction.

This can also be understood in another way. Almighty God strikes the vices of others more justly because he has no vices in himself. Human beings, however, when they strike others through discipline, ought to strike another’s weakness in such a way that they also recall their own to their eyes, considering from themselves how much they should spare others when striking them, since they do not fail to recognize that they themselves are worthy of being struck.

Thus it is now said: “Why do you persecute me like God?” As though it were said plainly: “You afflict me for my weaknesses as though you yourselves, after the manner of God, had no weakness.”

It should therefore be considered that, if there are perhaps people who need the harshness of correction, harsh correction should be applied to them when the hand of God ceases from striking. But when heavenly scourges are present, what is owed by us is no longer correction but consolation, lest, by joining reproof to pain, we add one blow to another.

**61. Slanderers devour human beings like beasts.**—It is rightly added: “And gorge yourselves on my flesh.” The mind that hungers for the sufferings of its neighbors undoubtedly seeks to be filled with another’s flesh.

It should also be known that those who feed on the slander of another’s life are undoubtedly nourished on another’s flesh. Hence Solomon says: “Do not be among the feasts of drunkards, nor eat with those who bring flesh for eating” (Proverbs 23:20).

To bring flesh for eating is, in a conversation of slander, to exchange accusations concerning the vices of one’s neighbors. Concerning the punishment of such people he immediately adds: “For those who linger over drink and contribute their share will be consumed, and drowsiness will be clothed in rags” (ibid.). [Note: Vindoc.: “And those who contribute their share will be consumed, and drowsiness will be clothed in rags.” Bellov. also has *dormitio* (“drowsiness”); Utic. formerly read it as well.]

They linger over drink who intoxicate themselves with the disgrace of another’s life. To contribute one’s share means, just as each person ordinarily contributes food for eating, to contribute words in a conversation of slander.

But those who linger over drink and contribute their share will be consumed, because, as it is written—perhaps Proverbs 15:5—“Every slanderer will be uprooted.”

“Drowsiness will be clothed in rags,” because death finds the person despised and destitute of every good work whom the languor of slander has occupied here in seeking out the crimes of another’s life. [Col. 1071B]

[Formerly XXVI.] Since, however, the many harsh things that blessed Job endured ought not to pass away in silence, nor should the darkness of ignorance conceal them from human knowledge, they are as useful for preserving patience as the deeds of his patience are known through the fulfillment of heavenly grace. [Note: Tours: “when they have learned the deeds of his patience.”]

Therefore blessed Job wishes the scourges he experiences to be brought forward as an example, and immediately adds:

## CHAPTER LIII  
*(Revised XXV)*

**Verses 23–24.—“Who will grant me that my words may be written? Who will give me that they may be engraved in a book with an iron stylus and a sheet of lead, or certainly carved in flint?”** [Col. 1071D–1072A]

[Note: Some printed editions: “or with a chisel.” German, seven English manuscripts, Normandy witnesses, and others read here and below *vel certe* (“or certainly”), which also better accords with the Hebrew text. In handwritten Books of Job, some have *vel certe*, while others, no fewer in number, have *vel celte* (“or with a chisel”). Jerome reads the latter. Gregory, who explains the sheet of lead, the flint, and the iron stylus, is silent about *vel celte*, which rather clearly suggests that he did not read *vel celte*.]

**62. The hearts of the Jews are signified by the sheet of lead, and those of the Gentiles by flint.**—Because that weighty Jewish people, instructed by the firm pronouncement of the Fathers, recognized all that blessed Job endured, these things were written with an iron stylus and a sheet of lead.

But because the hard hearts of the Gentiles also recognized these things, what else do we see them as except carved in flint?

It should be noted that what is written on lead is erased more quickly because of the metal’s very softness; on flint, letters can indeed be impressed only with greater difficulty, but they are more difficult to erase.

Thus the sheet of lead rightly represents Judea, which received God’s commandments without labor and lost them with speed. The Gentiles are rightly represented by flint, since they could scarcely receive the words of sacred teaching for safekeeping, but, once received with strength, preserved them firmly.

What else is signified by the iron stylus except the firm judgment of God? Hence the prophet says: “The sin of Judah is written with an iron stylus, with a diamond point” (Jeremiah 17:1).

The nail is the extremity of the body. The diamond is so hard a stone that it cannot be cut with iron. By the iron stylus, therefore, a firm judgment is signified; by the diamond nail, an eternal end.

The sin of Judah is therefore said to be written with an iron stylus on a diamond nail because the guilt of the Jews is preserved through the firm judgment of God to an endless end. [Col. 1072A]

**63. Lead signifies avarice.**—We may also rightly understand by the sheet of lead those whom the weight of avarice burdens. To them the rebuking prophet says: “Children of men, how long will you be heavy-hearted?” (Psalm 4:3). [Note: All Normandy witnesses: “heavy of heart.”]

Through lead, whose nature is that of a heavy weight, the sin of avarice is especially signified. It makes the mind it infects so heavy that it cannot rise at all to desire lofty things.

For this reason it is written in Zechariah: “Lift up your eyes and see. What is this that is going forth?” And I said, “What is it?” And he said, “This is the jar going forth,” and he said, “This is their eye throughout all the earth” (Zechariah 5:5–6). [Formerly XXVII.] “And behold, a talent of lead was being carried; and behold, one woman was sitting in the middle of the jar.” And he said, “This is wickedness.” And he cast her into the middle of the jar and threw the mass of lead into its mouth (ibid.). [Col. 1072B]

To demonstrate more fully what he had understood from this vision of the jar, the woman, and the lead, the prophet continued: “And I lifted up my eyes and saw; and behold, two women were going forth, and the spirit was in their wings. They had wings like the wings of a kite, and they lifted up the jar between earth and heaven. And I said to the angel who was speaking with me, ‘Where are they carrying the jar?’ And he said to me, ‘So that a house may be built for it in the land of Shinar’” (ibid. 9–11).

We have brought forward the prophet’s testimony about the lead without benefit if we do not also explain it by repeating it. He says: “Lift up your eyes and see. What is this that is going forth?” And I said, “What is it?” And he said, “This is the jar going forth” (ibid.).

In wishing to show the prophet through what fault the human race most especially falls away from him, God represented, by the image of a jar, the wide-open mouth of avarice. Avarice is like a jar, which keeps the mouth of the heart open on every side.

“And he said, ‘This is their eye throughout all the earth’” (ibid.). We see many people dull in understanding, yet we observe them clever in evil actions. The prophet also testifies to this, saying: “They are wise to do evil, but they do not know how to do good” (Jeremiah 4:22). [Note: Many manuscripts: “they did not know.”]

Such people are dull in understanding, but in the things they desire they are stirred by the goads of avarice. Those who are blind to seeing good become watchful in carrying out evil when rewards rouse them.

Hence it is rightly said of this same avarice: “This is their eye throughout all the earth.”

“And behold, a talent of lead was being carried” (ibid.). What is the talent of lead except the weight of sin arising from that same avarice?

“And behold, one woman was sitting in the middle of the jar.” So that we might not perhaps doubt which woman she was, the angel immediately made it known. For it follows there: “And he said, ‘This is wickedness.’” And he cast her into the middle of the jar.

Wickedness is cast into the middle of the jar because wickedness is always held in avarice. “And he threw the mass of lead into its mouth.” The mass of lead is thrown into the woman’s mouth because the wickedness of avarice is weighed down by the burden of its sin. For if it did not yearn for the things below, it would never be wicked toward God and neighbor. [Col. 1072C–1073A]

**[Formerly XXVIII.] 64. Pride and vainglory are the two principal vices. Avarice is raised up by them.**—“And I lifted up my eyes and saw; and behold, two women were going forth, and the spirit was in their wings.”

What else do we understand in these two women except the two principal vices—namely pride and vainglory—which are joined to wickedness without any doubt? They are said to have the spirit in their wings because in their actions they serve Satan’s will.

The prophet calls him “spirit” of whom Solomon says: “If the spirit of one who has power rises against you, do not leave your place” (Ecclesiastes 10:4), and of whom the Lord says in the Gospel: “When an unclean spirit has gone out from a person, it passes through dry and waterless places” (Matthew 12:43).

The spirit is in their wings because pride and vainglory, in everything they do, serve Satan’s will. [Note: Vindoc.: “And they had wings like the wings of a kite.”]

“And they had wings like the wings of a kite.” A kite always seeks to lie in wait for the young of birds. These women therefore have wings like the wings of a kite because their actions are undoubtedly like those of the devil, who always lies in wait for the life of the little ones.

“And they lifted up the jar between heaven and earth.” Pride and vainglory have this characteristic: they raise above all other people, in their own thoughts, the person whom they have infected. Sometimes through the pursuit of possessions, sometimes through the desire for dignities, they raise as though to the height of honor the person whom they have once captured and held. [Note: Vindoc. has “whom they have once touched.”] [Note: Lyr. and Bigot. omit “as though.”]

But whoever is between heaven and earth both abandons what is below and fails to reach what is above.

**65.** These women therefore lift the jar between heaven and earth because pride and vainglory raise the mind captured by the avarice of honor in such a way that, despising any neighbors, they seem to abandon what is below and seek what is high while boasting. [Note: Norm. and Vindoc. omit *ima* (“what is below”) and read “as though they abandon.”]

Such people, while they grow proud, pass beyond in their minds those with whom they live, but are not joined to the citizens above. The jar is therefore said to be lifted between earth and heaven because the avaricious, through pride and vainglory, both despise the neighbors beside them and are entirely unable to attain what is above and beyond them.

They are carried between earth and heaven because they neither preserve the equality of brotherhood below through charity nor, by exalting themselves, succeed in reaching the heights. “And I said to the angel who was speaking with me, ‘Where are they carrying the jar?’ And he said to me, ‘So that a house may be built for it in the land of Shinar.’”

A house is built for the jar in the land of Shinar. Shinar is interpreted as “their stench.” And just as a good odor comes from virtue, as Paul testifies when he says, “He manifests the odor of his knowledge through us in every place, because we are the good odor of Christ to God” (2 Corinthians 2:14), so, conversely, stench comes from vice.

“For the desire for money is the root of all evils” (1 Timothy 6:10). Since every evil is generated through avarice, it is fitting that the house of avarice should be built in stench.

It should also be known that Shinar is a very broad valley in which the tower begun by the proud was built and then destroyed through the diversity of languages. This tower was called Babylon, on account of the confusion of minds and languages.

Nor is it inappropriate that the jar of avarice is placed there, where Babylon—that is, confusion—is built, because, since it is certain that all evils arise through avarice and wickedness, avarice and wickedness themselves are rightly said to dwell in confusion. [Col. 1074A–B]

**66. The Church asks that its words be engraved upon hearts made heavy and hard by avarice.**—We have said these things briefly and by way of digression so that the weight of sin might be shown through the sheet of lead.

Nevertheless, the words of blessed Job also accord with the holy Church, which, preserving the two Testaments of sacred teaching, desires its words to be written a second time, saying: “Who will grant me that my words may be written? Who will give me that they may be engraved in a book?”

Because it speaks through a firm judgment, sometimes to hearts made heavy by the weight of avarice, and sometimes to hard hearts, it writes with an iron stylus on a sheet of lead—or certainly on flint.

But we rightly say that blessed Job uses the voices of our Redeemer and of his Church if we find something in them that speaks openly about that same Redeemer. [Formerly XXIX.] For how can it be believed that he conveys something about him figuratively if he does not demonstrate him to us in open words?

Let him now disclose what he thinks of him and remove from us every ambiguity of thought.

It follows:

## CHAPTER LIV

**Verse 25.—“For I know that my Redeemer lives.”**

**67. Job openly foretold Christ the Redeemer.**—By saying not “Creator” but “Redeemer,” he openly proclaims the one who, after creating all things, appeared incarnate among us in order to redeem us from captivity and, through his Passion, free us from perpetual death.

It should also be noted with what faith he binds himself to the power of his divinity, concerning whom Paul says: “For although he was crucified through weakness, yet he lives by the power of God” (2 Corinthians 13:4). [Col. 1074D–1075A]

For he says: “For I know that my Redeemer lives.” As though he were saying openly: “Let every unbeliever know him as scourged, mocked, struck with blows, crowned with a crown of thorns, smeared with spittle, crucified, and dead; but I, with certain faith, believe and proclaim with free voice that he lives after death, because my Redeemer lives—the one who fell among the hands of the ungodly.” [Note: Thus nearly all manuscripts and printed editions. Gussanv., after Vatic., has “believing with certain faith.”]

But, blessed Job, by his resurrection what do you also confidently believe concerning the resurrection of your own flesh? Proclaim it, I ask, in open words.

It follows:

## CHAPTER LV  
*(Revised XXVII)*

**The same passage.—“And on the last day I shall rise from the earth.”**
### 68. Christ died so that we would not fear dying; he rose again so that we might trust that we can rise.

For he will one day also accomplish in us the resurrection which he displayed in himself. The resurrection which he displayed in himself he promised to us, because the members follow the glory of their head. Our Redeemer therefore accepted death so that we would not fear dying. He displayed the resurrection so that we might trust that we can rise. Hence he also willed that this same death should last no more than three days, lest, if the resurrection were delayed in him, all hope of it should be utterly lost in us.

This is aptly said of him through the Prophet: “He will drink from the stream on the way; therefore he will lift up his head” (Psalm 109:7).

[Note: Lyr., German., and Bigot. read “drinks on the way” (*in via bibit*), a reading also now found in Utic., with *e* changed to *i*.]

For he deigned to drink from a certain stream of our suffering not in a dwelling-place but on the way, because he underwent death only temporarily—that is, for three days—and in that death which he underwent he by no means remained, as we do, until the end of the world.

[Rec. XXVIII.] When, therefore, he rose again on the third day, he showed what would follow in his body, that is, in the Church. For by an example he demonstrated what he had promised as a reward, so that, just as the faithful recognized that he himself had risen, so they might hope for the rewards of resurrection in themselves at the end of the world.

Behold, through the death of the flesh we remain in the dust until the end of the world; but on the third day he blossomed forth from the dryness of death, so that by the renewal of his flesh itself he might show us the power of his divinity. This is aptly demonstrated through Moses by the twelve rods placed in the tabernacle (Numbers 17:2). For when the priesthood of Aaron, who was from the tribe of Levi, was despised and no tribe was thought worthy to offer burnt offerings, twelve rods, corresponding to the twelve tribes, were commanded to be placed in the tabernacle. And behold, the rod of Levi blossomed and showed what power Aaron possessed in his office (ibid., 8).

What, then, is signified by this sign except that all who lie in death until the end of the world remain, like the remaining rods, in dryness? But while all the rods remain dry, the rod of Levi returns to flower, because the body of the Lord—of our true priest—placed in the dryness of death burst forth into the flower of resurrection.

[Note: Much is omitted here in Gussanville’s edition; we have supplied it from manuscripts and printed editions. For in that edition it reads: “By this flower of resurrection’s glory our Redeemer, who is from the tribe of Judah,” etc.]

By this flower Aaron is rightly recognized as priest, because by this glory of resurrection our Redeemer, who arose from the tribe of Judah and Levi, is shown to be an intercessor for us. Behold, therefore, Aaron’s rod already flowers after its dryness; but the rods of the twelve tribes remain dry, because the body of the Lord already lives after death, while our bodies are still deferred from the glory of resurrection until the end of the world.

Therefore he carefully introduced this very postponement, saying: “And on the last day I shall rise from the earth.”

### [Vet. XXX.] 69. The resurrection of many of the dead strengthens our confidence.

We therefore possess hope of our resurrection when we consider the glory of our head. But lest someone perhaps say in silent thought that he rose from death for this reason: because the one and the same person, God and man, overcame through his divinity the death which he endured through his humanity, whereas we, who are merely human, cannot rise from the condemnation of death—in order to refute this thought, at the time of his resurrection the bodies of many saints also rose again. Thus he both displayed an example to us in himself and strengthened us by the resurrection of others who were like us in their purely human nature, so that, when a human being despaired of receiving in himself what God the man had displayed in himself, he might presume that this could happen in him because he recognized that it had happened in those whom he did not doubt to have been merely human.

### 70. Faith in the resurrection is established.

There are some, however, who, observing that the spirit is separated from the flesh, that the flesh decays, that decay is reduced to dust, and that dust is so dissolved into the elements that it is no longer visible to human eyes, despair that resurrection can occur. When they look upon dry bones, they doubt that these can again be clothed with flesh and grow green once more into life.

[Note: Turon. and Germ. read *in elementis*, “in the elements,” in place of *in elementa*, “into the elements.” Utic. gives both readings. Similar passages on the resurrection occur in the Homily on Ezekiel formerly numbered 20, now Homily 8 of Book II.]

If they do not hold the faith of the resurrection through obedience, they ought certainly to have held it through reason. For what does the world imitate daily in its elements except our resurrection? At every moment of each day, temporal light itself seems to die when, as the darkness of night arrives, what was visible is withdrawn; and it seems to rise again each day when, after the light has been taken from our eyes, night is again dispelled and the light is restored.

At the passing moments of time we also see trees lose the greenness of their leaves and cease producing fruit.

[Note: Turon. reads “to cease producing fruit after the giving of its yield.”]

And suddenly, as though a kind of resurrection were coming from a withered tree, we see leaves burst forth, fruits grow large, and the whole tree clothe itself in renewed beauty. Without ceasing we see the small seeds of trees entrusted to the moisture of the earth, and soon afterward we see great trees rise from them, producing leaves and fruits.

Let us therefore consider the small seed of any tree, which is cast into the earth so that a tree may be produced from it,

[Note: Turon. and Norm. read “in the smallness of the seed.” Utic. has both readings.] and let us grasp, if we can, where within that seed’s such great smallness the immense tree that came forth from it lay hidden—where were the wood, the bark, the greenness of the leaves, and the abundance of the fruits? Was anything of this kind visible in the seed when it was cast into the earth?

And yet, while the hidden maker of all things orders everything wondrously, the roughness of the bark lay hidden in the softness of the seed; the strength of the wood’s firmness was concealed in its tenderness; and the abundance of fruitfulness was contained in its dryness.

What wonder, then, if he can restore to a human being the exceedingly fine dust that has been reduced to its elements and is invisible to our eyes, when he restores immense trees from exceedingly small seeds?

[Note: Some printed editions read “or from our eyes.” Utic. formerly had this reading. We have deleted “or from,” in accordance with the Norm. manuscripts and because the sense also requires it.]

Because, therefore, we were created rational, we ought to gather the hope of our resurrection from the very appearance and contemplation of things. But because the power of reason has grown dull in us, the grace of the Redeemer came to us as an example. Our Creator came, accepted death, and displayed the resurrection, so that we who were unwilling to hold the hope of resurrection through reason might hold it through his help and example.

[Note: Norm. reads “our Redeemer.” In Utic. both readings are recorded.]

Let blessed Job therefore say: “I know that my Redeemer lives, and on the last day I shall rise from the earth.” And whoever despairs that the power of resurrection can take place in him should blush before the words of a faithful man who lived among the Gentiles and should consider with what weight of punishment he must be struck if he still does not believe his own resurrection, when he already knows that the Lord’s resurrection has occurred—if that man believed in his own resurrection who still hoped that the resurrection of the Lord Jesus was yet to come.

### [Vet. XXXI.] 1. The condition of bodies after the resurrection.

But behold, I hear of the resurrection, yet I ask about the effect of that same resurrection. For I believe that I shall rise again, but I want to hear what I shall be like. I must know whether I shall rise in some other, perhaps subtle or airy, body, or in the body in which I shall die.

But if I rise in an airy body, then I am no longer the one who rises. For how can the resurrection be true if the flesh cannot be true? Reason therefore plainly suggests that, if the flesh is not real, the resurrection will certainly not be real. Nor can resurrection rightly be called resurrection where that which fell does not rise.

Blessed Job, therefore, remove from us these clouds of doubt and, since through the grace of the Holy Spirit which you received you have begun to speak to us about the hope of our resurrection, plainly indicate whether our flesh will truly rise.

[Note: Most manuscripts read “will rise” (*surgat*).]

It follows:

### CHAPTER LVI [Rec. XXIX]

**VERSE 26.—And again I shall be clothed with my skin.**

### 72. The error of Eutychius, who asserted that the body would become impalpable and subtler than air, is refuted.

When “skin” is plainly mentioned, every doubt about the true resurrection is removed. For our body will not, as Eutychius, bishop of Constantinople, wrote, be impalpable in the glory of that resurrection, subtler than winds and air. In that glory of resurrection our body will indeed be subtle through the effect of spiritual power, but palpable through the reality of its nature.

Hence, when the disciples doubted his resurrection, our Redeemer showed them his hands and side and offered flesh and bones to be touched, saying: “Touch and see, because a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see me have” (Luke 24:39).

When, while I was staying with the same Eutychius in the city of Constantinople, I brought forward this testimony of evangelical truth, he said: “The Lord did this for the purpose of removing from the disciples’ hearts their doubt about his resurrection.”

I replied to him: “It is a very strange thing that you assert: that doubt should arise for us from the very source by which the hearts of the disciples were healed of doubt. For what could be said more disastrously than that we should doubt the reality of his flesh on account of that by which his disciples were restored to faith?”

[Note: Vindoc., Norm., and others, together with the older editions, read “were restored from every doubt.” Others, with German., have “were separated from every doubt.” The context supports our reading. It is very well said, “were restored to faith,” but not “were separated from the end.”]

[Note: Vindoc. reads: “For if he had not possessed this, what he displayed is destroyed.”]

For if it is asserted that he did not possess what he displayed, then our faith is destroyed by the very thing through which the faith of his disciples was strengthened.

He also added: “He possessed a palpable body, which he displayed; but after the hearts of those who touched him had been strengthened, everything in the Lord that could be touched was changed into a certain subtlety.”

To this I replied: “It is written: ‘Christ, rising from the dead, dies no more; death will no longer rule over him’” (Romans 6:9).

[Note: Turon. reads “rising from the dead.”]

Therefore, if anything in his body could have been changed after the resurrection, then, contrary to Paul’s truthful statement, the Lord returned to death after the resurrection. Who would dare to say such a thing, even if foolish, except one who denies the true resurrection of his flesh?

Then he objected to me, saying: “Since it is written: ‘Flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God’ (1 Corinthians 15:50), how can it be believed that the flesh will truly rise?”

I replied: “In sacred Scripture, ‘flesh’ is spoken of in one way according to nature and in another way according to guilt or corruption. Flesh according to nature is spoken of as in the words: ‘This now is bone from my bones and flesh from my flesh’ (Genesis 2:23); and: ‘The Word became flesh and dwelt among us’ (John 1:14).

“Flesh according to guilt is spoken of as in the words: ‘My spirit will not remain in these human beings, because they are flesh’ (Genesis 6:3). And as the Psalmist says: ‘He remembered that they were flesh, a spirit that goes and does not return’ (Psalm 77:39).

“Hence Paul also said to the disciples: ‘But you are not in the flesh, but in the spirit’ (Romans 8:9). He was not writing letters to people who were not in the flesh; rather, because they had overcome the passions of carnal desires, they were now free through the power of the spirit and were no longer in the flesh.

“Therefore, when the Apostle Paul says: ‘Flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God,’ he wishes ‘flesh’ to be understood according to guilt, not flesh according to nature. Hence he immediately shows that he was speaking of flesh according to guilt, adding: ‘Nor will corruption possess incorruption.’

“In the glory of the heavenly kingdom, therefore, there will be flesh according to nature, but it will not be flesh according to the desires of the passions, because, having conquered the sting of death, it will reign in eternal incorruption.”

### [Vet. XXXII.] 73. Eutychius’s responses and evasions are refuted.

After these statements, Eutychius immediately replied that he agreed, but nevertheless continued to deny that a palpable body could rise again. In a little book which he had written about the resurrection, he had also included the testimony of the Apostle Paul, who says: “What you sow is not made alive unless it first dies; and what you sow is not the body that is to be, but a bare grain” (1 Corinthians 15:36).

He hastened to use this to show that the flesh would either be impalpable or would not exist at all, since the holy Apostle, speaking of the glory of the resurrection, had said that “the body that is to be” is not sown.

[Note: In all the English manuscripts and our own, except German., the reading is “palpable flesh.” In the Life of Saint Gregory by John the Deacon, book 1, chapter 28, where this entire discussion is reported, the same reading occurs in both manuscripts and printed copies. In the handwritten Utic. codex containing the books of the *Moralia*, however, it seems clearly to have once been written “impalpable flesh.” The whole sequence of the discussion demonstrates that this is the correct reading.]

But a swift answer can be given to this.

[Note: Utic. reads: “I replied more quickly: The Apostle Paul, saying …”]

For when the Apostle Paul says: “You do not sow the body that is to be, but a bare grain,” he indicates what we see: that a grain is born with a stalk and leaves, whereas it is sown without a stalk and leaves. Thus, in speaking of the increase of glory in the resurrection, he did not say that what the seed possessed would be absent, but that what it did not possess would be added. Eutychius, however, while denying that the true body will rise, does not say that what was lacking will be added; rather, he says that what existed will be lacking.

### 74. The emperor considers consigning Eutychius’s book to the flames. Eutychius dies after renouncing his error.

When, therefore, we had been drawn into a long dispute on this matter, we began to withdraw from it with very serious mutual tension.

[Note: This is how it is read in the manuscripts, both those of the *Moralia* and those of the Life of Saint Gregory written by John the Deacon, book 1, chapter 28. It has the same meaning as “hostility”; the printed editions wrongly read *simulatione*, “pretense.” The word is not unusual in Gregory, especially in book 1, letter 2.]

At that time the emperor Tiberius Constantine, of pious memory, secretly received both him and me. After learning what disagreement existed between us and weighing the arguments of both sides, he refuted with his own arguments the same book which Eutychius had written about the resurrection and decided that it ought to be burned in the flames.

When we had left him, a severe illness immediately followed me, while Eutychius was overtaken by illness and death.

[Note: Ebroic. reads: “a severe illness and death.”]

After he died, since there was almost no one who followed his teaching, I did not continue the prosecution which I had begun, lest I appear to be hurling words into ashes.

Yet while he was still alive and I was suffering from very severe fevers, whenever any of my acquaintances went to him to offer greetings, they reported to me that, before their eyes, he held the skin of his own hand and said: “I confess that we shall all rise in this flesh.”

[Note: Vindoc. reads: “which, as he himself confessed.”]

As they themselves acknowledged, he had previously been accustomed altogether to deny this.

### 75. The resurrection is proved from Job’s words.

But setting these matters aside, let us carefully investigate in the words of blessed Job whether the resurrection will be real and whether the body in the resurrection will be real.

[The old numbering: XXXIII.] Behold, we can no longer doubt the hope of resurrection, since he says: “And on the last day I shall rise from the earth.”

[Note: Norm. and Germ. read “I shall rise.”]

He also removed doubt about the true restoration of the body when he said: “And again I shall be clothed with my skin.”

He now adds the following in order to remove further ambiguity from our thoughts:

[Col. 1080A]

**VERSE 26.—And in my flesh I shall see God.**

### 76. Job believed that the flesh would be restored to its complete state.

Behold: he openly confesses resurrection, skin, and flesh. What, then, remains by which our mind could doubt?

If this holy man, before the Lord’s resurrection had taken place, believed that the flesh would be restored to its complete state, what guilt will attach to our doubt if the true resurrection of the flesh is not believed even after the Redeemer’s example?

For if the body will not be palpable after the resurrection, then someone other than the one who dies certainly rises—which is an impious thing to believe, namely, that I die and someone else rises.

Therefore, blessed Job, I ask you to add what you feel and remove from us the uncertainty of this question.

It follows:

### CHAPTER LVII [Rec. XXX]

**VERSE 27.—Whom I myself shall see, and my eyes shall behold, and not another.**

### 77. After the resurrection our flesh will be the same by nature and different in glory.

For if, as certain followers of error suppose, the body will not be palpable after the resurrection, but the invisible subtlety of the body will be called flesh, although it is not the substance of flesh, then the one who dies and the one who rises are certainly different.

[Note: Germ., Bellovac., Ebroic., and several Norm. read “because [the body] will not be palpable after the resurrection.”]

[Note: Bellov. reads: “but the subtlety of the invisible body.”]

But blessed Job destroys their opinion with a truthful declaration when he says: “Whom I myself shall see, and my eyes shall behold, and not another.”

[Note: Most copies read “this opinion of theirs”; certain printed editions read “this opinion of his.”]

Following the faith of blessed Job and truly believing that the body of our Redeemer was palpable after the resurrection, we confess that our flesh after the resurrection will be both the same and different: the same by nature, different in glory; the same in reality, different in power.

It will therefore be subtle because it will also be incorruptible. It will be palpable because it will not lose the essence of true nature.

[Note: Vindoc., Bellov., Turon., and Norm. read this way. Germ. and the recent editions read: “It will therefore be spiritual.”]

But the holy man adds how firmly he holds this same confidence in the resurrection by hope and with how great certainty he awaits it.

It follows:

### CHAPTER LVIII

**THE SAME PASSAGE.—This hope of mine is stored in my bosom.**

### 78. Job is completely certain of his resurrection.

We believe that we possess nothing more certain than what we hold in our bosom. He therefore held his hope stored in his bosom because he possessed true certainty concerning the hope of resurrection.

[Note: The printed editions, with Germ., read “because he possessed true certainty.”]

But because he made known the day of resurrection that would come, now, whether through his own voice or as a type of the holy and universal Church, he rebukes the deeds of the wicked and foretells the judgment that follows on the day of resurrection. For he immediately adds:

### CHAPTER LIX

[Col. 1081A]

**VERSES 28, 29.—Why then do you now say: “Let us pursue him and find a root of speech against him”? Flee, therefore, from the face of the sword, because the sword is the avenger of iniquities; and know that there is a judgment.**

### 79. By the judgment that will follow the resurrection, he urges the wicked to repentance.

In the first statement he censures the deeds of the wicked; in the second he makes known the punishments that proceed from divine judgment.

For he says: “Why then do you now say: ‘Let us pursue him and find a root of speech against him’?”

Because perverse people hear words well spoken with evil intent and desire to find in the speech of the righteous an opening for accusation, what else do they seek than a root of speech against him, from which they may derive an occasion for speaking and extend the branches of wicked talk in accusation?

But when the holy man suffers such things from the wicked, he does not grieve against them but rather for them. He rebukes their evil thoughts and points out the evils from which they should flee, saying: “Flee, therefore, from the face of the sword, because the sword is the avenger of iniquities; and know that there is a judgment.”

Everyone who acts perversely, by the very fact that he disdains to fear this, does not know that there is a judgment of God.

[Note: We supplied *timere*, “to fear,” from the English and our manuscripts. Previously the text simply read *quo hoc despicit*, “in that he despises this.” That *timere* had to be added is proved by what follows: “for if he knew that this should be feared.” Norm. reads “for if, fearing this.”]

For if he knew that this was to be feared, he would not do the things in him that must be punished. There are many who know in words that judgment is the final event, but by acting perversely they show that they do not know it. Because such a person does not fear it as he ought, he has not yet understood with what storm of terror it will come.

If he knew how to weigh the burden of the dreadful tribunal, he would certainly forestall the day of wrath by fearing it. To flee from the face of the sword is to appease the sentence of strict punishment before it appears. The judge’s terror can be avoided only before judgment. Now it is not seen, but it is appeased by prayers.

But when he has sat in that dreadful tribunal, he can both be seen and can no longer be appeased, because then, in anger, he will repay all at once the deeds of the wicked which he silently endured for so long.

Therefore it is necessary to fear the Judge now, while he does not yet exercise judgment, while he patiently endures, while he still tolerates the evils he sees, lest, when he has once stretched out his hand in the retribution of vengeance, he strike all the more severely in judgment because he waited longer before judgment.

# BOOK FIFTEEN

In this book the brief exposition of chapters twenty and twenty-one of Job is completed.

[Col. 1081]

[Col. 1081C] 469 [Old and Revised numbering: I.] Since the friends of blessed Job could by no means have been perverse, the words of Zophar the Naamathite testify to this. Hearing from his mouth the terror of the coming judgment, he immediately adds:

### CHAPTER ONE

**CHAPTER 20, VERSE 2.—Therefore my thoughts follow one another in confusion, and my mind is carried in different directions.**

### 1. How greatly we ought to be affected by constant reflection on it.

It is as though he were saying plainly: “Because I contemplate the terror of the final judgment, I am therefore confused in fear by the tumult of my thoughts.”

[Note: Vindoc. reads “I trust.”]

The mind stretches itself out more widely in thought in proportion as it weighs how terrible the event that threatens will be.

[Note: Turon. and Vindoc. read “tears itself apart.”]

The mind is carried in different directions when, with anxious fear, it considers now the evils it has committed, now the good things it has neglected to do, now the reprehensible things in which it remains, and now the upright things which it sees are still lacking in itself.

But although the friends of blessed Job had learned from the constancy of his life how to live well, they did not know how to weigh God’s judgments with sufficient subtlety. They did not believe that any righteous person could receive evils in this life. Hence they suspected that the same holy man was wicked, because they saw him being scourged; and from this suspicion they were led to fall into rebuking him as well. Yet they descend to this rebuke as though under a certain veil of reverence.

Hence Zophar continues:

### CHAPTER TWO

[Col. 1082C]

**VERSE 3.—I will hear the teaching by which you reproach me, and the spirit of my understanding will answer me.**

### 2. Many listen to admonitions in order to judge them, not to follow them.

It is as though he were saying plainly: “I hear your words, but I discern by the spirit of my understanding whether they have been spoken rightly.”

[Note: This is how it appears in the English manuscripts and our own. The old and recent editions read: “for those who judge the words of the speaker.”]

Those who despise the words of a teacher take his teaching not as assistance but as an occasion for combat, so that they may judge what they hear rather than follow it.

After these remarks, made with a certain moderation, he now leaps into an open reproach of the blessed man when he adds:

### CHAPTER THREE [Rec. II]

**VERSES 4, 5.—This I know from the beginning, from the time when the human being was placed upon the earth: the praise of the wicked is brief, and the joy of the hypocrite is like a moment.**

### 3. Whatever comes to an end is brief.

It is now clear that, inflated by the spirit of his own understanding, he turns the judgments which he utters against the wicked into rebukes of blessed Job. He saw Job first doing righteous deeds and afterward enduring punishments, and he judged that everything he had seen in him had been hypocrisy, because he did not believe that a righteous servant could be afflicted by a righteous God.

But let us carefully consider these same judgments, which he put forward as right although they were not right, and, setting aside what he says falsely against blessed Job, let us observe how true his words would be if he were speaking against the wicked.

He says: “This I know from the beginning, from the time when the human being was placed upon the earth: the praise of the wicked is brief.”

[Old numbering: II.] In speaking of the brevity of the present life, he led the eye of his heart back to the beginning of our origin, so that from past events he might gather how insubstantial are the things that seem to be something while they exist.

For if we direct the eyes of our mind from the origin of the human race itself to this present time in which we live, we see how brief everything that could come to an end has been.

Let us suppose that some person has lived from the first day on which the world was created until today. Even today, however, he would bring that same life, which had seemed so long, to an end.

[Note: Germ., Bellov., and Norm. read “created from the first day of the world.”]

[Note: Four English manuscripts and all Norm. manuscripts have this reading. Germ. and Utic. read “which seemed almost long,” as in the Vulgate; Utic. also gives another reading: “which seemed so long.”]

Behold, the end is present; nothing of the past remains, because everything has passed away. There is nothing future in this world, because not even the briefest moment remains for life.

Where, then, is the long period that is found between beginning and end, when it is consumed as though it had never even been brief?

### 4. Many care not to be good but to be called good. The hypocrite’s joy passes away; punishment remains.

Because the wicked love the present life, they undoubtedly seek to receive in it the praise by which they may be exalted. They are lifted up by the favor of tongues and desire not to be good but to be called good.

They think this praise is long while they are attaining it, but understand it to have been brief when they lose it. At the end, they are shown how insignificant was the thing they loved.

Hence it is rightly said against the same wicked: “This I know from the beginning, from the time when the human being was placed upon the earth: the praise of the wicked is brief.”

Appropriately, he adds: “And the joy of the hypocrite is like a moment.”

Often, while the hypocrite pretends to be holy and is not at all afraid to display wickedness, he is honored by everyone and the glory of holiness is accorded to him by those who see external things but cannot perceive what is within.

[Note: Ebroic. reads “he is honored by human beings.”]

Thus it happens that he rejoices at the first sitting, is cheerful at the first reclining-place, swells with pride at the first greeting, is lifted up by the respectful voice of those who serve him, and becomes puffed up with proud thought in the service of his subjects. As the voice of Truth also says of such people: “They do all their works so that they may be seen by human beings. For they enlarge their phylacteries and lengthen their tassels. They love the first reclining-places at banquets and the first seats in the synagogues, greetings in the marketplace, and to be called Rabbi by human beings” (Matthew 23:5).

[Note: *Autem*, “but,” is absent from Norm. and Germ.]

But what will this joy be when compared with eternity, when, as the moment of death rushes upon him, it is consumed as though it had never existed at all? Its delight passes away, but its punishment remains; and when the thing itself is lost, the cause remains.

It is rightly said: “The joy of the hypocrite is like a moment.” For as soon as a stylus is placed at a point, it is lifted up again; no time passes in drawing it out to express a line.

The hypocrite’s joy is therefore like a point, because it appears for a moment but disappears forever. And just as the stylus is lifted as soon as it is placed at a point, so the hypocrite loses the joys of the present life as soon as he touches them.

Of him it is also added:

### CHAPTER FOUR [Rec. III]

**VERSES 6, 7.—If his pride rises up to heaven and his head touches the clouds, he will be destroyed at the end like dung.**

### 5. The joys of the present life, which the wicked consider so great, the righteous regard as dung.

The hypocrite’s pride is said to rise up to heaven when his arrogance appears to be living a heavenly life. His head touches the clouds when his principal part—that is, his understanding—is believed to be equal to the merits of those who came before among the saints.

But he is destroyed at the end like dung because, when he is led to torments at his death, full of the dung of vices, he is trampled underfoot by evil spirits.

[Old numbering: III.] The righteous regard as dung the joys of the present life which the unjust consider great goods.

Hence it is written: “The slothful person is stoned with dung” (Ecclesiasticus 22:2). Whoever refuses to follow God becomes sluggish in the pursuit of eternal life. Whenever he is struck by the loss of temporal things, he is afflicted by things which righteous men despise as dung.

Therefore, whoever is crushed by the blow of earthly things—what else is he doing than being stoned with ox-dung?

[Note: Germ. reads “is scourged.” Utic. once also read “is scourged”; after it was deleted, “is stoned” is now read.]

The hypocrite is rightly compared to a dungheap because, while he desires to possess temporal glory, sometimes he puffs himself up in thought before himself, sometimes envies that glory in others who truly possess it, and mocks them.

As many vices as he is filled with, so many dungheaps, as it were, make his breast stink in the sight of the eternal Judge.

Let it therefore be said: “If his pride rises up to heaven and his head touches the clouds, he will be destroyed at the end like dung.” Even if he pretends to live a heavenly life, even if he displays his understanding as resembling that of true preachers, he is nevertheless destroyed at the end like dung, because his mind is condemned for the stench of its vices.

It follows:

### CHAPTER FIVE

**VERSE 7.—And those who had seen him will say: Where is he?**

### 6. The life of hypocrites is exposed at the end.

Often the life of hypocrites comes to be recognized as blameworthy even by everyone at the end, so that by signs now more evident it may be shown what they were.

Those who saw him exalted now will therefore say of him when he is extinguished: “Where is he?” For he appears neither here, where he had been exalted, nor in the rest of eternity, where he was thought to be.

Of the brevity of his life he appropriately adds:

### CHAPTER SIX [Rec. IV]

**VERSE 8.—Like a flying dream he will not be found; he will pass away like a vision of the night.**

[Note: Norm. reads “he will pass away.” In Utic. it once read “he will pass away.”]

### 7. The life of the hypocrite resembles a phantom.

What is the life of the hypocrite except a kind of phantom vision, which displays in an image what it does not possess in reality? Hence it is rightly compared to a dream, because all praise and glory are lost by him almost as soon as they are held.

Often, in a nocturnal vision, poor people marvel that they have become rich. They see honors being bestowed upon them; they observe heaps of wealth, a multitude of attendants, the beauty of garments, and an abundance of food present to them. They rejoice that they have escaped the poverty which they endured with groaning.

But suddenly, when they awaken, they discover how false was the thing over which they had rejoiced. They regret having awakened because, while awake, real poverty holds them.

So the minds of hypocrites, while what they do is one thing and what they display to human beings another, receive praise from the very display of holiness. In the judgment of human beings they are preferred to many who are better; and although within themselves they secretly swell with pride, outwardly they show themselves humble.

When they are praised immoderately by human beings, they also suppose themselves before God to be what they rejoice to have made themselves known as among human beings. Hence they presume that they will also receive the rewards of eternal life, and those who exult here in human favor do not doubt that they will possess rest there.

But amid all this, the hidden hour of calling steals upon them. When they close the eyes of the flesh, they open the eyes of the mind, and as soon as they have received eternal punishments, they see there that they were rich in dreams according to the estimation of virtues.

It is therefore rightly said of this hypocrite: “He will pass away like a vision of the night.”

[Note: Lyr. and Bigot. read “he will pass away like.”]

For the fact that he sees himself rich for a moment in human estimation comes from the display of a phantom, not from the solidity of virtue.

[Note: Ebroic. reads “of truth.”]

When his mind awakens at the death of the flesh, he undoubtedly recognizes that, while asleep, he had been seeing the favor of people around him.

It follows:

### CHAPTER SEVEN [Rec. V]

[Col. 1085C]

**VERSE 9.—The eye that saw him will not see him, nor will his place look upon him any longer.**

[Note: Norm. reads “his place.” The question is: “What is the hypocrite’s place?” Bellov. likewise has “what is his place,” etc.]

### 8. The tongues of flatterers benefit him nothing at the judgment.

What is the hypocrite’s place except the heart of flatterers? He rests there, wherever he has found favor.

The eye that saw him will not see him because, removed by death, he is hidden from his foolish admirers, who were accustomed to look upon him with wonder.

Nor will his place look upon him any longer, because the tongues of flatterers do not follow him to the judgment with their favor.

Yet, as long as he lives, he does not cease to teach his followers the things which he himself practices; through the perversity of his error he also produces in others the same pretense which he displays.

Of such people he appropriately adds here:

### CHAPTER EIGHT

**VERSE 10.—His children will be crushed by poverty.**
9. Hypocrites, multiplied outwardly, become inwardly empty.—It is written: “Wisdom will not enter a malevolent soul” (Wisdom 1:4). And through the Psalmist it is said: “The rich have become needy and hungry” (Psalm 33:11). For if their poverty and hunger were spoken of bodily hunger, they would certainly not be rich—those who lacked bodily bread. But because, while they increase outwardly, they become empty inwardly, they are described as both rich and needy, since they are plainly not permitted to be satisfied with the bread of wisdom. Therefore the sons of this hypocrite [Note: [Col. 1086D] Bellovacian has “will be crushed”; likewise the earlier Uticensis.] are crushed by poverty, because those who are born from his imitation in hypocrisy, while they do not retain the substance of truth [Note: [Col. 1086D] Vindoc. has “do not retain it in their heart, and fail through poverty.”], fail through poverty of heart.

## CHAPTER IX [Old IV]

**IBID.**—“And his hands will repay him his pain.”

10. Eternal punishment will be paid to hypocrites as a kind of debt.—What is signified by “hands” except works? Therefore his hands will repay him his pain, because he will receive just condemnation from his wicked activity. It is rightly said not that they will give, but that they will repay, because his perverse actions will pay him eternal punishment as a kind of debt. But before he reaches eternal punishments, let the passage add more fully what sort of person he displays himself to be here. It follows:

## CHAPTER X

**VERSE 11.**—“His bones will be filled with the sins of his youth, and with him they will sleep in the dust.”

11. Vices never abandon hypocrites.—The origin of a wicked beginning multiplies the causes of guilt even by anticipation. For once someone has begun to do evil, through practice he grows worse in what he has begun. What, then, is this hypocrite’s “youth” except the beginning of wickedness? In youth, lust already begins to burn. The hypocrite has his youth when he begins to desire and embrace the lust for glory—a beginning which multiplies the causes of guilt by presumption. While the flattering encouragements of his admirers multiply it within him, they make it stronger and, as it were, turn it into bones. What he began badly, he strengthens daily through habit, making it worse. Let it therefore be said: “His bones will be filled with the sins of his youth,” because the hard habits of wickedness in him have been drawn from a most evil beginning of vice. [Note: [Col. 1086D] Lyr., Big., and Utic. have “whence it is written: ‘The young man according to his way, even when he grows old, will not depart from it,’ etc.” Formerly Utic. read as in the printed edition.] Hence it is written in Proverbs: “The young man according to his way, even when he grows old, will not depart from it” (Proverbs 22:6). These bones will sleep with him in the dust, because his wicked habits endure in him until they drag him to the dust of death. For the bones—or vices—to sleep with him in the dust means that they do not abandon him as far as the dust: that is, he does not cease from wickedness until death. Thus the wicked habits that once began possess him, and daily become harder. They sleep with him in the dust because they end only when his life ends. But these words can also be understood in another way.

[Old V.] 12. Hypocrites, pretending to possess many things they do not have, lose even what they do have.—For sometimes a hypocrite possesses something strong and vigorous in his conduct; but while he pretends to have many good qualities that he does not have, he loses even those he does possess. Hence it is rightly said here: “His bones will be filled with the sins of his youth.” For when, being fickle and unstable, he acts childishly in many matters, he becomes soft through vice even in those things he has done with strength. These bones of his will sleep with him in the dust, because, just as all that pretense of his is dust, so whatever strength he has in himself is emptied of all solidity, so that through the arrogance of virtue he loses even what virtue might have existed in him. Thus the bones sleeping with him in the dust means that, along with his wicked actions, whatever good things have been done also perish. It follows:

## CHAPTER XI

**VERSE 12.**—“For when evil is sweet in his mouth, he will hide it beneath his tongue.” [Note: [Col. 1087D] Norman and German manuscripts read “he hides it.”]

13. It is characteristic of a hypocrite to display sweetness in his words while plotting perversity in his thoughts.—Evil is sweet in the hypocrite’s mouth because in his mind iniquity is pleasing to him. The mouth of the heart is thought, concerning which it is written: “Lying lips are in the heart, and they have spoken evil in the heart” (Psalm 11:3) [Note: [Col. 1087D] Bellovac. and Germ. read: “and they spoke evil in their heart”; this was also formerly the reading in Utic.]. But this evil, which is sweet in the hypocrite’s mouth, is hidden beneath his tongue, because the harshness of the malice concealed in his mind is covered under the appearance of gentle speech. Evil would be in the tongue, and not beneath the tongue, if the hypocrite who spoke openly revealed the malice of his wickedness.

But just as many of the righteous, when they see certain people acting perversely—people who must be struck with harsh rebukes—assume harshness in their speech while concealing beneath their tongue the kindness of their mind. Hence, too, it is said in the voice of the Bridegroom of holy Church: “Honey and milk are under your tongue” (Song of Songs 4:11). Those who do not wish to reveal the sweetness of their mind to the weak, but strike them with a certain harshness as they speak, and yet secretly mingle some sweetness among their harsh words [Note: [Col. 1087D] Turon. has “certain sweet things”; Utic. has “some sweet things.”], possess sweetness not in their tongue but beneath their tongue, because among the hard words they utter they release certain gentle and sweet words by which the sorrowful mind may be restored through kindness.

Thus all the wicked, because they have evil not in their tongue but beneath their tongue, display sweetness in their words while plotting perversity in their thoughts. This is why Joab held Amasa’s chin with his right hand, but, secretly bringing his left hand to the sword, spilled his entrails (2 Samuel 20:9). To hold the chin with the right hand means to flatter as though from kindness. But he brings his left hand to the sword who secretly strikes from malice. Of this same head of theirs it is also written: “Under his tongue are labor and pain” (Psalm 10:7). For whoever does not openly reveal the evils he is thinking does not bring forth the labor and pain of those whose death he desires in his tongue, but presses them beneath his tongue.

The passage fittingly adds concerning this hypocrite:

## CHAPTER XII [Rec. VI]

**VERSE 13.**—“He will spare it, and will not abandon it, and will conceal it in his throat.”

14. A hypocrite never confesses what he has done.—He spares the evil he loves because he does not pursue it within himself through repentance. Hence it is added: “He will not abandon it.” For if he wished to abandon it, he would certainly not spare it, because he would pursue it. But he conceals it in his throat because he preserves it in his thoughts in such a way that he never brings it forth in speech. It follows:

## CHAPTER XIII

**VERSE 14.**—“His bread will be changed in his belly into the gall of asps within him.”

15. The glory in which the hypocrite delights is changed into the gall of asps.—What is “bread in the belly” except the fullness of temporal pleasure in the mind? Let the hypocrite, then, now be satisfied with the praise bestowed upon him and delight in honors. His bread in his belly will be changed into the gall of asps within him, because the fullness of passing pleasure will be changed into bitterness at the end of retribution. And the gall of asps—that is, the persuasion of evil spirits—is recognized as what here was thought to be the praise of glory. For then the wicked see that they have been infected with the venom of the ancient serpent, when, handed over to avenging flames, they are tormented with that same persuader of theirs.

This bread therefore tastes one thing in the mouth and another in the belly. The joy of passing pleasure is sweet while it is being enjoyed here, as though being chewed; but it becomes bitter in the belly, because once the joy has been completed, it is swallowed down for punishment.

[Old VI.] 16. The hypocrite desires to be instructed in the mysteries of Holy Scripture, not in order to live by them but to exalt himself.—Or certainly, since bread may suitably be understood as the understanding of Holy Scripture—which refreshes the mind and supplies it with strength for good works—and since the hypocrite often strives to be instructed in the mysteries of sacred discourse, yet not in order to live by them [Col. 1088C] but so that he may appear to other people to be learned, his bread will be changed in his belly into the gall of asps within him. For while he boasts of his knowledge of sacred law, he changes the drink of life for himself into a cup of poison; and he dies rejected by the very means through which he seemed to be instructed for life.

Nor is it unfittingly understood that sometimes, while the hypocrite pursues the word of doctrine for display, he is blinded by divine judgment and wrongly understands the very word he wickedly seeks. When he falls into the error of heresy, it happens to him that, just as one dies from the gall of asps, so the wretched man dies from bread; he finds death in his doctrine because he did not seek life in the words of life.

Often, too, it happens that even if the hypocrite correctly understands the words of divine admonition, because he does not preserve them at all in his conduct, he loses them before he finishes the course of his present life, so that he loses the knowledge he was unwilling to practice by knowing it. Hence it is added:

## CHAPTER XIV [Old VII]

**VERSE 15.**—“He will vomit up the riches he devoured, and God will draw them out of his belly.”

17. When he despises good works, the hypocrite often loses even his knowledge.—The hypocrite wishes to know the divine words, yet not to practice them. He wishes to speak learnedly, yet not to live. Therefore, because he does not do what he knows, he also loses what he knows; because he does not join pure practice to his knowledge, he loses knowledge as well, having despised the purity of good works.

Thus he vomits up the riches of sacred law that he devoured by reading, and God draws them out of his belly, because by a just judgment he tears from his memory what he was unwilling to observe, so that he may not even retain God’s commandments on his tongue when he did not preserve them in his life. [Note: [Col. 1089D] Norm. reads: “he will vomit up . . . God will draw them out,” because he was unwilling to preserve what he does not preserve.] Hence the Prophet says: “But to the sinner God said: Why do you recount my justice and take my covenant into your mouth?” (Psalm 49:16).

Even if it happens that the hypocrite appears to retain these words of doctrine in his mouth until the end, he will be condemned all the more on account of the fact that, through God’s good gift, even the wicked person is not entirely deprived of them. For it is written: “For those who remember his commandments, to do them” (Psalm 102:18). Therefore the one who retains his commandments in memory but does not do them holds in the words of doctrine the sentences by which he will be condemned.

[Rec. VIII.] 18. Sacred words become the cause of eternal condemnation for those who either refuse to know them or despise them once they know them.—Hence it is written in Zechariah: “What do you see, Zechariah?” And I said: “I see a flying scroll, twenty cubits in length and ten cubits in width.” And he said to me: “This is the curse that will go forth over the face of the whole earth, because every thief, as it is written there, will be judged” (Zechariah 5:2). [Note: [Col. 1089D] Very many manuscripts read “which will go forth,” and likewise again below.] For what is the flying scroll except Holy Scripture? While it speaks of heavenly things, it lifts the attention of our mind to higher things, because when we see it above us, we avoid attending to what is below—that is, desiring it. [Old VII.]

It is said to have a width of ten cubits and a length of twenty, because the breadth of our work is single, while the endurance of hope extends twofold. For on account of our good work, both rest of mind is prepared for us here and eternal joys there, as the Truth bears witness when he says: “Whoever has left house or fields, and so forth, will receive a hundredfold in this age and will possess eternal life in the future” (Matthew 19:29; Luke 18:30) [Note: [Col. 1089D] Norm. reads “houses or fields.”]. The number one hundred is made perfect by multiplying ten by ten. He therefore receives a hundredfold who, even if he possesses nothing, nevertheless, through the perfection of his mind, already in this age desires to possess nothing.

Because through this a twofold return is given to us for a single measure, the scroll is rightly extended twenty cubits in length and widened ten cubits. But because these sacred words become the cause of eternal condemnation for those who either refuse to know them or, knowing them, despise them, it is rightly said of this scroll: “This is the curse that will go forth over the face of the whole earth” (Zechariah 5:3). He adds why it is called a curse: “Because every thief will be judged, as it is written there.”

The hypocrite, therefore, because he despises living according to the words of the law that he knows and seeks praise from his teaching, will be judged a thief, because by speaking what is just he steals for himself the praise belonging to the life of the righteous. Concerning him it is fittingly added:

## CHAPTER XV [Rec. IX]

**VERSE 16.**—“He will suck the head of asps, and the tongue of the viper will kill him.”

19. In temptation the devil first creeps in gently, then drags violently.—The asp is a small serpent, whereas the viper has a longer body. Asps produce eggs, and their offspring are born from their eggs; vipers, however, when they have conceived, have their young raging within them, and the young emerge from their mothers’ bellies by rupturing their sides. Hence the viper is so called because it gives birth violently. The viper is therefore born in such a way that it emerges violently and is produced through the death of its mother.

What, then, are signified by the small asps except the hidden suggestions of unclean spirits, who first insinuate themselves into human hearts through a small persuasion? What is signified by the tongue of the viper except the devil’s violent temptation? First he creeps in gently; afterward he also drags violently.
