He therefore sucks the head of asps because the beginning of a hidden suggestion first arises as something small in the heart; but the tongue of the viper kills him because afterward the mind that has been captured is slain by the poison of violent temptation. At first unclean spirits speak to the human heart through subtle counsels; while they persuade gently, they pour out, as it were, the venom of asps. Hence it is written: “They have broken the eggs of asps and woven spiders’ webs. Whoever eats of their eggs will die, and what has been incubated will break forth as a serpent” (Isaiah 59:5).

[Old VIII.] To break the eggs of asps for wicked people is to reveal through perverse works the counsels of evil spirits that lie hidden in their hearts. To weave spiders’ webs is to perform various temporal acts for the desire of this world. Since these are established with no stability, the wind of mortal life undoubtedly carries them away.

It is rightly added: “Whoever eats of their eggs will die” (ibid.), because whoever receives the counsels of unclean spirits kills the life of the soul within himself. “And what has been incubated will break forth as a serpent,” because the counsel of the evil spirit that is concealed in the heart is nourished toward complete iniquity. The basilisk is called the king of serpents. But who is the head of the reprobate except Antichrist? Therefore what has been incubated will break forth as a basilisk, because the one who receives within himself the counsels of the asp to be nourished becomes a member of the wicked head and grows into the body of Antichrist.

Thus it is said of this hypocrite: “He will suck the head of asps, and the tongue of the viper will kill him,” because when he willingly receives the wicked suggestion of the ancient enemy, he afterward, overcome by its violent temptations, hands himself over to them. Hence, too, in paradise he brought words of gentle persuasion to the standing man (Genesis 3:5ff.); but once he had seized him for consent, he now drags even the resisting man and, having overcome him through the pleasures of his corruption, kills him almost by force [Note: [Col. 1090D] Lyr., Sag., Germ., and Bigot. have “almost certainly”; Utic. prefers both readings.]

But perhaps we can understand these words also through an opposite interpretation. Since the asp kills swiftly by its venom, whereas the viper kills more slowly, the asp signifies violent and sudden temptation, while the viper signifies gentle and prolonged temptation. Hence death is said to be in the sucking of the head for the asp, but in the tongue for the viper, because sudden temptation often kills an unsuspecting mind as soon as it arises [Note: [Col. 1091D] So six English manuscripts, Utic., and many others. In others, including all Norman manuscripts except Utic., the reading is “as it suggests”; in Utic. it formerly stood first. All printed editions have “as he sucks,” which is found in Germ.]. Prolonged temptation, however, because it suggests perversity by persuading for a longer time, kills as though from the tongue of the viper.

And because every hypocrite, penetrated by the suggestion of unclean spirits as by the venom of serpents, gives no consideration to the gifts of the Holy Spirit above, while he spreads the intention of his heart among outward praises, it is rightly added:

## CHAPTER XVI [Rec. X]

**VERSE 17.**—“May he not see the streams of the river, the torrent of honey and butter.”

20. The hypocrite is deprived of faith, hope, and charity.—In the Gospel the Lord says: “Whoever believes in me, as Scripture says, rivers of living water will flow from his belly” (John 7:38). The Evangelist adds: “Now he said this about the Spirit whom those who believed in him were to receive.”

The streams, then, are gifts of the Holy Spirit. The river’s stream is charity; the river’s stream is faith; the river’s stream is hope. But because every hypocrite loves neither God nor neighbor, when he seeks the passing glory of the world he does not see the streams of the river, because he is not watered by the irrigation of charity.

While the hypocrite seeks present gains, he despises future gifts; and, having no faith, he does not see the river’s stream with the mind, because “faith is the evidence of things not seen” (Hebrews 11:1). While the hypocrite holds fast to the things that are seen, he neglects hope in things that are not seen. Therefore he does not see the river’s stream through desire, because he directs himself only toward visible things. And it is written: “What does anyone hope for that he sees?” (Romans 8:24).

He would have seen the streams of the river if he had closed his eyes to the glory of the present world and opened them to love of the heavenly homeland. It should be noted that he does not say “rivers” but “streams.” The streams of the river may be understood as those spiritual gifts that flow so subtly from heavenly things into the mind of the one who loves that they cannot be expressed by the mouth of the flesh. For often the mind of one who loves is filled with so great a gift of contemplation that it can see what it cannot express.

The torrent-river is itself the overflowing of the Holy Spirit, which is gathered in the mind of the contemplative through an abundant outpouring, when the mind is filled with more than it can understand. [Note: [Col. 1091D–1092D] Bellovac., Ebroic., and other Norman manuscripts read “the torrent-river”; Gussanv. noted this reading in the margin. Germ. and the Paris edition of 1495 read “but the torrent-river,” which is found in the first hand of the Utic. codex. The Basel edition and Paris 1518 read “the river of the torrent.” The Vulgate and the Hebrew text read “torrents.”] [Old IX.] It should be known that when the grace of the Holy Spirit pours into us, it fills us equally with honey and butter. Honey falls from above, whereas butter is gathered from the milk of animals. Honey, then, comes from the air, while butter comes from flesh.

The Only-Begotten of the most high Father, although he is God above all things, became human among all things. When he filled us with the sweetness of his divinity and the mystery of his incarnation, he satisfied us equally with honey and butter. Because, therefore, the Spirit of Christ makes the mind it has filled rejoice both in the sweetness of his divinity and in faith in his incarnation, these streams of the torrent of the river are said to be of honey and butter together: they refresh the mind with profound sweetness through knowledge of God, and through the grace of the incarnation [Note: [Col. 1092D] Bellovac. has “the grace of chrism,” recorded by Gussanv. as a variant reading.] they anoint it with the mystery of the gift.

But because this hypocrite, spread out among outward praises, does not perceive these inward gifts, the passage adds toward what he proceeds after punishments, saying:

## CHAPTER XVII [Rec. XI]

**VERSE 18.**—“He will pay for everything he has done, yet he will not be consumed.” [Note: [Col. 1092D] Turon. reads “torments”; Norm., “in torments”; Lyr. and Bigot., “in torments for the unlawful desires which he preserved there”; Germ., “into torments, those unlawful desires which he preserved here.”]

21. The condemned are always dying, yet are never consumed by death.—He pays in torment for the desires he unlawfully preserved here; and, handed over to avenging flames, he is always dying because he is always kept in death. He is not consumed in death, because if the life of the one who is dying were consumed, his punishment would end together with his life. But so that he may be tormented without end, he is compelled to live without end in punishment, so that the life that was dead here in guilt may there have its death living in punishment.

Let him therefore say: “He will pay for everything he has done, yet he will not be consumed,” because he is tormented and not extinguished; he dies and lives; he fails and endures; he is always ending and yet is without end. These things are exceedingly terrifying even when heard; how much more when suffered! But because the multitude of his iniquity demands that he never be without punishments, the passage fittingly adds:

## CHAPTER XVIII

**IBID.**—“According to the multitude of his inventions, so also will he endure.”

22. Those who devised many things for guilt are tormented by new inventions of punishment.—Because he devised many things for guilt, he is tormented in punishment by new inventions. For what he could not suspect here, he feels there when handed over to retribution.

Just as the elect, practiced in good works, sometimes strive to do more than the Lord has deigned to command them—for bodily virginity was by no means commanded, but only praised; for if it had been commanded, marriage would surely by now be considered guilt, and yet many excel in the virtue of virginity, clearly offering more in service than they received by command—so the wicked often exercise themselves in evil deeds, so that in perverse action they discover more to do than they could have received as examples from the practice of the reprobate.

Hence they are struck with a greater punishment of retribution, because they themselves, from within themselves, discovered more wicked actions by which they should be struck. [Old X, Rec. XII.] It is therefore rightly said: “According to the multitude of his inventions, so also will he endure.” For he would not discover new iniquity unless he also sought it; and he would not seek it unless he hastened to commit it eagerly. The excess of his evil thought is therefore weighed in his torment, and he receives the pain of a fitting retribution.

Although the pain of all the condemned is without end, nevertheless they receive more grievous torments who, from their own desires as well, discovered many things in iniquity. But because Sophar has introduced the punishment of this hypocrite, he immediately adds his guilt—not merely any one guilt, but the one from which all others arise. For it is written: “The root of all evils is greed” (1 Timothy 6:10). Whoever, therefore, is said to be ruled by greed is plainly shown to be subject to all evils. For he adds:

## CHAPTER XIX

**VERSE 19–20.**—“Because he crushed and stripped the poor man’s house, he seized it and did not build it, and his belly was not satisfied.” [Note: [Col. 1093D] Sag., Bigot., and Lyr. read “he seized it”; shortly below, “and moreover seized it.”]

23. Eternal punishment is imposed on the one who did not distribute his own possessions; how much more on the one who seized another’s. Greed grows through the goods it obtains and desires; it is not extinguished.—He crushes and strips the poor man’s house who does not blush to rob, through greed, the one whom he crushes through power. He seizes it and does not build it. It is as though it were said openly: The one who ought to have built it instead seizes it.

For the Lord, coming in judgment, will say to the reprobate: “I was hungry, and you did not give me food; I was thirsty, and you did not give me drink; I was a stranger, and you did not welcome me; naked, and you did not clothe me,” and so forth (Matthew 25:42). From this guilt he adds: “Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (ibid.).

If such punishment is imposed on the one who is convicted of not giving what was his, with what punishment must the one be struck who is accused of taking what belonged to another? He seized it, then, and did not build it, because he not only gave nothing of his own but also took what belonged to another.

He rightly adds: “And his belly was not satisfied.” The belly of the wicked is greed, because whatever is swallowed by perverse desire is gathered into it [Note: [Col. 1093D] So Norman and Turon. manuscripts. The printed editions, with Germ., have “because in him.”]. It is clear that greed is not extinguished by the things it desires but is increased by them. For, like fire, when it receives wood to consume, it grows; and from the point at which the flame seems momentarily to be compressed, it is soon seen to spread further.

Often, when almighty God is intensely angry with a greedy mind, he first permits everything to be supplied according to its desire [Note: [Col. 1093D] We restore this reading from Germ., Bellovac., Turon., and Norm. In Basil. 1514 and Paris 1518: “and after this flattery suddenly drags him away.” Paris 1495: “and after retribution suddenly drags him away.” Recent editions: “and afterward removes it through retribution.”], and afterward takes it away through retribution, so that the person must endure eternal punishments on account of it. Hence it is added:

## CHAPTER XX

**VERSE 20.**—“And when he has possessed what he desired, he will not be able to possess it.”

24. It is a sign of greater anger when what is wrongly desired is granted.—It is a sign of greater anger when what is wrongly desired is granted, and sudden retribution follows from it, because the person has also obtained what he coveted while God was angry. Hence the Psalmist says, when the people are said to have wrongly desired bodily food: “While their food was still in their mouth, the wrath of God rose against them and killed many of them” (Psalm 77:31) [Note: [Col. 1094D] Norm. reads “foods”; below, “while the food was still . . .”].

Divine judgments usually appear more slowly when they are hindered so that evil desires ought not to be fulfilled. For the more quickly an evil desire is permitted to be fulfilled, the more swiftly it is generally punished [Note: [Col. 1094D] Ebroic. and Germ. have “for the more quickly”; the Roman editions of Sixtus V and Gilot have “not,” but this is erroneous, contrary to both English and our manuscripts.].

Therefore, from the very point at which the hypocrite is quickly multiplied so that he may be powerful, action proceeds swiftly so that he may not be powerful. Trees and shrubs that grow more slowly endure for many years [Note: [Col. 1094D] Norm. has “endure for many years, and so forth.” In Utic., however, the former reading was *annosa perdurant* (“long-lived, they endure”), and so forth.], whereas those that advance within a short time wither more quickly; as though, while they hasten to exist, they are hastening toward nonexistence [Note: [Col. 1094D] Germ. and Bellov. have “they tend toward not existing.”]. It follows:

## CHAPTER XXI [Old XI]

**VERSE 21.**—[Note: [Col. 1094D] Norm. has “nothing remained.” Utic. formerly had “nor did anything remain.”] “Nothing remained of his food.”

25. His food is everything he coveted through perverse desire.—But once the hypocrite has been struck down, nothing remains of his food, because when he himself is led to eternal punishments, he is separated from all the goods he possessed here. Hence it is further added:

**IBID.**—“Therefore nothing will remain of his goods.”

For if anything of his goods remained to him, he would take with him what he had possessed. But because, desiring everything, he was unwilling to fear the Judge, removed from this life [Note: [Col. 1094D] Turon. and Norm. have “from this light,” i.e. life.], he goes naked to the Judge.

Yet for this wicked man it is a lesser matter, in retribution, that he is tormented in the punishment that follows, if he is at least permitted to be free in this life. But there is no freedom in guilt, because it is written: “Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom” (2 Corinthians 3:17). Often a person’s own guilt becomes punishment for the perverse mind. Hence it is rightly added:

## CHAPTER XXII [Rec. XIII]

**VERSE 22.**—“When he is satisfied, he will be confined.”

26. The anguish of the rich arising from satiety.—First, through greed, he eagerly strives to gather what he desires; and when, as though in a certain belly of greed, he has heaped up many things, he is confined when satisfied, because while he is anxious about how to guard what he has acquired, his very satiety constricts him.

A certain rich man’s field had produced abundant crops; but because he had nowhere to store such great quantities, he said: “What shall I do, because I have nowhere to gather my crops?” And he said: “I will do this: I will tear down my barns and build larger ones” (Luke 12:17). Thus, constrained by abundance, when he said, “What shall I do?” he was burning as though pressed by much food.

Let us consider with how many desires he sought that his field should produce abundant crops. Behold, his desires were fulfilled, because the field had produced abundant crops. But because the places for storing them were insufficient, the rich man, now increased in wealth, did not know what to do. O anguish born from satiety! The mind of the greedy man is constricted by the abundance of the field. For by saying, “What shall I do?” he plainly shows that, pressed by the desires of his heart, he labored beneath a certain burden of possessions.

It is therefore rightly said: “When he is satisfied, he will be confined.” For the mind of the greedy man, which had first sought rest from abundance, afterward labored more heavily to guard it. Hence the passage further adds:

## CHAPTER XXIII

**IBID.**—“He will burn, and every pain will fall upon him.”

27. Anxiety in acquiring and guarding riches anticipates eternal punishment.—At first he experienced pain in the very exhaustion of his desire: how he might seize what he coveted, how he might take some things by flattery and others by threats. But after he reached the fulfillment of his desire through the things acquired, another pain tires him: he must guard with anxious fear what he remembers acquiring through great labor.

He fears ambushes on every side and dreads suffering himself what he has inflicted on others. [Note: [Col. 1095D] Germ., Ebroic., and other Norman manuscripts have “he fears a more powerful person,” a reading followed by the old Paris and Basel editions.] He fears another more powerful man, lest he suffer violence from him; but when he sees a poor man, he suspects a thief. He also takes great care over the things he has amassed, lest through the natural decay of their substance they be consumed by negligence [Col. 1095C] [Note: [Col. 1095D] Norm. has “because fear itself is punishment for him.” Utic. allows both readings: “for him” and “he himself.”].

In all these things, because fear itself is punishment, the wretched man suffers as much as he fears suffering. After this he is also led to Gehenna and handed over to eternal torments. Every pain therefore falls upon him: here, first the punishment of desire, afterward the anxiety of guarding; and there, eventually, the punishment of retribution burns him.

[Old XII.] 28. The remarkable security of the heart that does not expose itself to greed.—Wonderful is the security of the heart: not to seek what belongs to another, but to remain content with the food of each day [Note: [Col. 1096D] Germ., Bellov., Turon., and the old edition have “but to remain content with what is sufficient for each day.” Norm. has “but to remain content with the sufficiency of each day.”]. From this security arises everlasting rest, because one passes from good and peaceful thought to eternal joys.

In contrast, the reprobate are wearied here by desires and there by torments. From the labor of thought they produce the labor of pain, as they are dragged from the heat of greed to the fire of Gehenna. And because, as we have already said above, often the more quickly a wicked person reaches his desire, the more easily he is swept away to punishment, the passage adds by way of wish:

## CHAPTER XXIV

**VERSE 23.**—“May his belly be filled, so that he may send his anger and fury upon him, and rain his battle upon him!”

29. God’s arrows rain upon the greedy rich man.—The Lord rains his battle upon this hypocrite when he strikes his works with the swords of his judgments. For God’s raining battle means pressing the life of the wicked from above toward destruction with stern sentences. God’s raining battle means striking hearts that grow proud against him and wounding the arid mind, as though with drops of rain growing dense, with the arrows of his judgments, so that when the man is suddenly carried away to judgment he may remember that he desired evil and strove to gather even worse what he desired; that he may grieve because he is abandoning what he gathered; and that eventually he may feel the fire of retribution, which he contemptuously refused to foresee in order to live well. It follows:

## CHAPTER XXV [Rec. XIV]

**VERSE 24.**—“He will flee from iron weapons and rush upon a bronze bow.”

30. Avarice, while guarding against temporal want, is consigned both to perpetual want and to eternal punishments. — It should be understood that avarice sometimes creeps in through pride, but at other times through fear. There are some who, because they desire to appear more powerful, are inflamed with the ambition for other people’s possessions. There are also some who, because they fear that the necessities of support may fail them, relax their minds into avarice and covet what belongs to others, suspecting that their own possessions cannot suffice for them.

Every necessity is not inappropriately called “iron,” because it torments the life of the poor with the wound of sorrow, just as it is written concerning the necessities of the one who, sold by his brothers, led an afflicted life: “Iron passed through his soul” (Ps. 104:18). What, then, are “iron weapons” except the necessities of the present life, which press harshly upon the poor and pursue them? Rust consumes iron, whereas bronze is usually more difficult to consume. Thus present necessity, which is transitory, is signified by iron; eternal judgment, by bronze. And because the heavenly judgment is not considered by the mind of the wicked, it is rightly compared to a bow, since it strikes as though from ambush, while the one who is struck does not take it into account.

He will therefore flee the iron weapons and rush upon the bronze bow, because, while fearing present necessities, he seizes many things through avarice and exposes himself to the severe blows of the final judgment. And when he flees the iron weapons, he is found by the arrows of the bronze bow, because, foolishly guarding against temporal evils, he is struck by an eternal sentence. Whoever here flees the harshness of poverty together with guilt will there find the perpetuity of just retribution. [Ancient recension XIII.] But before he is carried away to judgment, he continues to indicate what this wicked man practices here. It follows:

## CHAPTER XXVI [Recension XV]

[Col. 1097A]

**VERSE 25.**—“Drawn out, and coming forth from his sheath, and flashing in his bitterness.”

[Note: Bigot., Utic., and Lyr. read “into his bitterness,” and so thereafter. In Germ. and formerly in Utic. the reading was *fulgorans*, “flashing,” with related forms.]

### 31. Drawn by the devil into sin, we come forth by our own will.

This wicked man plots the plundering of his neighbors; but while he contrives evil in his thoughts, the sword is, as it were, still in its sheath. When, however, he wickedly accomplishes the evil he has conceived, he comes forth from his sheath, because through the evil action of his iniquity he emerges from the concealment of his thought. His work reveals what he was while hidden in his thought.

It should be noted that he says: “Drawn out, and coming forth from his sheath.” He is drawn out, that is, by the seducer; but he comes forth through his own will. For whoever is led undoubtedly follows the one leading him, whereas whoever comes forth appears to proceed according to his own will. Thus one who is both dragged by the ancient enemy toward every evil deed and yet, by his free choice, binds himself to the desires involved in them is said to be “drawn out and coming forth from his sheath.” For what proceeds from wicked thought into the worst action belongs both to the spirit of the one who suggested it and to the wickedness of the one who consented by his own will.

[Note: Sag., “is bound to the desires.”]

### 32. The more the wicked shine, the more harshly they will be punished. His power is further shown by the terror immediately added: “And flashing in his bitterness.”

Lightning, when it suddenly comes from above, shines before the eyes with terror; it displays its brightness and strikes what is set before it. So, in a similar way, the wicked man, when he has assumed the glory of the present life—by which he appears distinguished in this world through power—is thereby driven toward being struck at the end.

[Note: Turon. reads: “so that many may be struck.”]

For the wicked man to “flash” is, as it were, to shine in the honor of this life. But because the splendor of his glory is handed over to the eternal punishments of Gehenna, it is rightly said here: “Flashing in his bitterness.”

[Note: Turon. reads “but because by splendor.”] Whoever now rejoices as though striking others through terror and brilliance will afterward endure punishments there forever.

It is indeed written of a certain rich man (Luke 16:19) that “he feasted splendidly every day.” But to shine is one thing, and to flash another.

[Note: Germ., Bellov., and Norm. read *splendidare* (“to make splendid” or “to shine splendidly”).]

Sometimes splendor exists without striking, whereas by the word “flash” splendor is expressed together with striking. Therefore, one who harms others while placed in a position of power is appropriately called “flashing,” because from the very place where he is raised against the good as though by the light of glory, the life of the good is afflicted. It follows:

## CHAPTER XXVII [Recension XVI]

[Col. 1097D]

**THE SAME.**—“They will go and come upon him, the terrible ones.”

### 33. As the sinner is oppressed by vices succeeding one another, so he is ravaged by malignant spirits going and returning.

Who are called “the terrible ones” in this passage, except the malignant spirits—those to be feared and fled by good minds? And because each of these same malignant spirits is to be understood as serving particular vices, when this perverse man appears for a moment to abandon some vices but begins to practice others, the terrible ones plainly go and come upon him, because, although the perverse mind abandons some evils, others take possession of it.

You may often see an evil man established in earthly power, stirred by violent fury and carrying out whatever anger suggests. When the fury has departed, lust immediately ravages his mind. When lust is interrupted for a time, pride straightaway takes its place in his thoughts, as though arising from his continence, and he desires to appear terrible so that others may fear him. But when circumstances require him to speak deceptively, he sets aside the terror of pride and flatters with softened speech, as though speaking humbly.

[Note: Thus Germ., Anglic., Vindoc., Bellov., Turon., and Norm. In the printed editions: “so that he should speak something humbly.”]

And when he ceases to appear proud, he does not fear becoming duplicitous. Since, then, vices succeed vices in his mind, it is rightly said of him: “They will go and come upon him, the terrible ones,” because as many vices as depart and succeed one another oppress him, so many malignant spirits ravage his soul, as it were going and returning.

[Note: Bellov. reads: “because, as many vices as depart and succeed one another…”]

But the things he does outwardly emerge in succession; for all evils are gathered together in his mind at once. Hence it is added:

## CHAPTER XXVIII

**VERSE 26.**—“All darknesses are hidden in his secret places.”

### 34. All vices are bound together in the hypocrite’s mind.

Although the hypocrite displays good actions on the surface, certain darknesses of evil works nevertheless appear in him. Yet he reveals less in his deeds than lies hidden in his thought. For one who does not bring everything forth simultaneously in action nevertheless silently holds in his mind everything that can cause harm.

Thus all darknesses are said to be hidden in his secret places, because although he does not display every evil in himself, he nevertheless desires to inflict all of them upon his neighbors. [Ancient recension XIV, Recension XVII.] Let it next be added with what punishment this depraved mind is to be struck. It follows:

## CHAPTER XXIX

**THE SAME.**—“Fire that is not kindled will devour him.”

### 35. The fire of Gehenna is wondrously sustained and torments both soul and body.

In a truly remarkable way, the fire of Gehenna is expressed in a few words. Bodily fire, in order to remain fire, needs bodily fuel. When it must be preserved, it is undoubtedly nourished by accumulated wood; it cannot exist unless kindled and sustained by fresh fuel.

By contrast, the fire of Gehenna, although bodily and although it burns bodily the reprobates cast into it, is neither kindled by human effort nor nourished by wood. Created once, it endures unquenchable; it does not need kindling and never lacks heat.

[Note: This reading is found in five Vatican manuscripts, the very ancient manuscript of the Barberini Library, two manuscripts of the Chigi Library, and most English and French manuscripts. Formerly, however, the Uticensis exemplar read: “since it is incorporeal.” The same reading occurs in Germ. and in two Vatican manuscripts, nos. 576 and 580; but the added syllable is plainly evidence of an interpolation. Those who abridged the *Moralia* of Saint Gregory also read “bodily.” Elsewhere it is established from Book IV of the *Dialogues*, chapter 29, that Gregory teaches that the fire of hell is bodily.]

It is therefore rightly said of this wicked man: “Fire that is not kindled will devour him,” because the justice of the Omnipotent, foreknowing what was to come, created the fire of Gehenna at the very beginning of the world, so that it would begin once to exist as the punishment of the reprobate but would never bring its heat to an end even without wood.

It must also be understood that all the reprobate, because they sinned with soul and body together, are there tormented in soul and body alike. Hence the Psalmist says: “You will set them like a furnace of fire at the time of your presence; the Lord in his anger will trouble them, and fire will devour them” (Ps. 20:10).

A furnace burns inwardly, whereas the one devoured by fire begins to be burned from the outside. Thus, to show that the sacred writings teach that the reprobate burn both outwardly and inwardly, they testify that they are devoured by fire and set like a furnace, so that they are tormented in body by fire and burn in mind through pain.

Thus here also, when it had been said of this wicked man, “Fire that is not kindled will devour him,” it immediately adds concerning his spirit:

## CHAPTER XXX [Recension XVIII]

**THE SAME.**—“He will be afflicted, abandoned in his tent.”

### 36. Those who are now unwillingly led out of the body will then be held in the body against their will.

The wicked man’s tent is the flesh, because he inhabits it gladly and, if possible, desires never to leave it. The just, however, because they place their joy in the hope of heavenly things and “their citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3:20), although they are still in the flesh, are already, as it were, not in the flesh, because they are nourished by no delight of the flesh. Hence it is said to some: “You are not in the flesh but in the spirit” (Rom. 8:9).

Those who received the words of exhortation through the Apostle’s letters were not literally outside the flesh; rather, to be “not in the flesh” is to possess nothing from the love of carnal things. But this wicked man, because he placed all his joy in carnal life, dwelt in the tent of the flesh.

When he receives that flesh again in the resurrection, he will burn with it after being handed over to the fire of Gehenna. Then he will desire to be led out from it; then he will seek, if he can, to escape its torments; then he will begin to wish to avoid what he loved. But because he placed that same flesh before God, God’s judgment brings it about that he is tormented by it more severely in the fire.

Here, therefore, he does not wish to leave it, yet he is dragged away from it; there, he desires to leave it, yet he is kept in it for punishment. Thus, to increase his torment, here he is unwillingly led out of the body, and there he is unwillingly held in the body.

Because, then, his spirit will wish to escape in torment from the flesh that he wrongly preferred to himself by loving it, but will be unable to do so, it is rightly said here: “He will be afflicted, abandoned in his tent.” Concerning his accusation it is soon said:

## CHAPTER XXXI [Ancient XX, Recension XIX]

**VERSE 27.**—“The heavens will reveal his iniquity, and the earth will rise up against him.”

### 37. At the judgment the wicked will experience the just and the unjust as their accusers.

What do we understand by “the heavens” except the just, and by “the earth” except sinners? Hence in the Lord’s Prayer we ask: “Your will be done, as in heaven and on earth” (Matt. 6:10), namely, that the will of our Creator may be fulfilled in all the just, just as it is also fulfilled in all sinners.

It is likewise written concerning the just: “The heavens declare the glory of God” (Ps. 18:1). And judgment is pronounced upon the sinful human being in these words: “You are earth, and to earth you will go” (Gen. 3:19).

Thus, when this wicked man is brought to that terrible judgment, the heavens reveal his iniquity and the earth rises up against him, so that the life both of the just and of sinners may accuse him in that dreadful tribunal—him who here spared neither the good nor the wicked.

It is indeed more grievous if someone harms the just rather than sinners. Hence the prophet says: “His blood is in his midst; he poured it out upon the clearest rock. He did not pour it upon the ground, so that it could be covered with dust” (Ezek. 24:7). By “ground” and “dust” he signifies sinners; by the clearest rock, the just person who is not embittered by the grave contagions of sinners.

Blood is therefore poured upon the clearest rock when the wickedness of a bloodthirsty mind rages in afflicting a just soul. Although it is more grievous to afflict the just unjustly than the unjust, it is much more grievous to harm both the just and the unjust alike.

Because this wicked man harmed both the just and the unjust, the heavens will reveal his iniquity in the accusation of his condemnation, and the earth will rise up against him, because he opposed those who understood heavenly things and oppressed those who had earthly concerns.

The earth, however, may signify not sinners and reprobates, but those who, occupied with earthly actions, nevertheless reach eternal life through the help of almsgiving and tears.

[Note: Thus the English manuscripts and our own. The printed editions read: “not only sinners and reprobates, but also these…”]

Concerning them the Psalmist speaks when the Lord’s coming to judgment is announced: “He summoned the heavens above and the earth, to judge his people” (Ps. 49:4).

He summons the heavens above when those who, abandoning all that was theirs, maintained a heavenly way of life are called to sit in judgment and come as judges with him. The earth is also summoned above when those who were bound to earthly activities nevertheless sought heavenly rather than earthly gain in them. To them it is said: “I was a stranger and you welcomed me; naked, and you clothed me” (Matt. 25:35).

[Note: Utic. adds: “and you covered me.”]

Thus the heavens reveal the iniquity of this hypocrite, and the earth rises up against him, while both those who come as judges with God and those who are delivered through judgment stand as witnesses against his wickedness.

Nothing, therefore, of what he did is concealed on the day of his condemnation. Although many of his deeds are now hidden from people through his duplicity, on the day of condemnation whatever lay concealed within him is revealed. Hence it appropriately follows:

## CHAPTER XXXII [Ancient XVI]

[Col. 1101A]

**VERSE 28.**—“The offspring of his house will be exposed; it will be dragged away on the day of God’s wrath.”

### 38. At the judgment the evils hidden within will be revealed.

The offspring of his house is exposed when every evil born in his conscience is displayed.

[Note: Turon. reads “was unknown.”]

For now the offspring of the hypocrite’s house remains hidden,

[Note: Bellov. and Norm. read “remains in concealment.”]

because although his action appears good in outward representation, his intention lies hidden. What he does is one thing; what he intends, another.

[Note: Bigot. and Lyr. read “toward which he directs his intention.”]

But when, at the Judge’s arrival, each person’s conscience has been brought forward as testimony—whence it is written, “their thoughts accusing or even defending them” (Rom. 2:15)—the offspring of this hypocrite’s house is exposed, because the perverse thought in his mind is uncovered.

[Note: Norm. reads “in this hypocrite.”]

And it is dragged away on the day of God’s wrath, because, once the Judge’s anger has been revealed, he is handed over to avenging flames and separated from the Judge’s presence. For whoever, while living, refused to think of heavenly things will, weighed down by the burden of his sins, fall from the Judge’s face into the depths of punishment.

Now the Judge both sees and tolerates the sinner, and awaits each person’s conversion, because it is the day of patience and not yet the day of wrath. The hypocrite remains, as it were, unmoved during this day of patience, committing many evils while no scourges chastise him.

But on the day of wrath he will be dragged away, because, seized for punishment at the time of vengeance, he will be separated from the face of the eternal Judge.

It follows:

## CHAPTER XXXIII [Recension XX]

“This is the portion of the wicked man from God, and the inheritance of his words from the Lord.”

[Col. 1101C]

### 39. At the judgment even the smallest evils will be punished.

If he had wished to act well while placed in this life, he would have had a portion in the Lord, a share in the heavenly kingdom. But because he chose to submit to depraved desires, he finds his portion from the Lord in torments, since he did not seek to share in the grace of that same Lord.

It is rightly said: “And the inheritance of his words from the Lord.” One who is plunged into punishment for great evils might perhaps have been thought not to be judged at all for the words he had spoken wrongly. But when the strict justice of Almighty God exacts punishment from the reprobate for their perverse deeds, it repays them with evils even down to the recompense for their words, so that those who are debtors for great evils, once handed over to punishments, may also pay the final farthing.

The smallest things are spared those who have strictly lamented greater evils in themselves. For those crushed by great sins are also afflicted in Gehenna by the smallest evils.

Holy men, however, desire not to receive a portion from the Lord, but to have the Lord himself as their portion. Hence the Prophet prays, saying: “The Lord is my portion” (Ps. 72:26).

But because the wicked man did not seek to have the Lord himself as his portion, he finds his portion outside the Lord: fire. Excluded from his presence, because he did not desire to rejoice in him, he is tormented beneath him.

Sophar introduced these words in such a way that, through what he had said against the hypocrite, he struck at the life of blessed Job, supposing that one who had been struck by the Lord had not performed all his good deeds with a sincere mind. Seeing him struck, he believed that he had displeased God.

In this respect also, Job’s friends bear the likeness of heretics. Within the holy Church, when they see certain people acting well yet groaning under scourges, they suppose that those people possess no good merits in their good works, and they believe evil those whom they see afflicted by the divine rod—

[Note: Germ., Bellov., Norm., and others read *quos* (“those whom”), not *quod* (“that”), as in the printed editions.]

ignorant, of course, that “many are the tribulations of the righteous” (Ps. 33:20), and that “he scourges every son whom he receives” (Heb. 12:6).

But blessed Job, in the manner of the holy and universal Church—which patiently tolerates the arrows of perverse words and, when it hears the speech of the proud, does not abandon the path of its humility—added with great humility of heart:

## CHAPTER XXXIV [Ancient XXII, Recension XXI]

**CHAPTER 21, VERSE 2.**—“Listen, I beg you, to my words, and repent.”

[Note: In Utic. formerly: “and you will repent.” The text is likewise read below wherever it is repeated in the recent edition. The ancient manuscripts, however, agree in reading what is now consistently found: “repent.”]

### 40. When the saints teach correctly, they do not fear being mocked.

When he said “Listen” and added “I beg you,” he shows with what humility he speaks, asking those who are proud against him to return their minds to the teaching of salvation.

Holy men, while within the universal Church they are prepared not only to teach what is right but also to endure what is wrong, do not fear being mocked. Hence it follows:

## CHAPTER XXXV

[Col. 1102C]

**VERSE 3.**—“Bear with me, so that I too may speak; and afterward, if it seems fitting, mock my words.”

[Note: “So that” is absent in Utic.; it is likewise absent before “if it seems fitting.”]

### 41. In their words the saints seek to benefit both their hearers and themselves. The doctrine of humility is a heavy burden for proud hearers.

When good people speak, they attend to two things in their words: namely, that they may benefit either themselves and their hearers, or themselves alone if they cannot benefit their hearers.

When the good things they say are well received, they benefit themselves and their hearers together. But when they are mocked by their hearers, they have nevertheless benefited themselves, because they have freed themselves from the guilt of silence.

[Note: Germ., Turon., and Norm. read “they have benefited.”]

Thus blessed Job, so that he may benefit himself and his hearers, says: “Listen, I beg you, to my words, and repent.” But so that he may discharge what he owes even if he is unable to benefit his hearers, he adds: “Bear with me, so that I too may speak; and afterward, if it seems fitting, mock my words.”

It should be noted that when he added “Repent,” he first said “Listen”; and when he added “Afterward, if it seems fitting, mock my words,” he first said “Bear with me.” Listening belongs to one who is willing; bearing with belongs to one who is unwilling.

Therefore, if his friends desire to be taught, let them listen; but if they are prepared to mock, let them bear what is said, because the doctrine of humility is a heavy burden for proud minds. It follows:

## CHAPTER XXXVI [Recension XXII]

**VERSE 4.**—“Is my dispute with a human being, so that I should not rightly be sorrowful?”

### 42. Humbled by his scourges, Job feared only that he had displeased God.

Anyone who pleases God but displeases human beings has no causes for sorrow. But whoever either pleases human beings and displeases God, or believes that he displeases both God and human beings, and yet is not affected by sorrow, is alien to the virtue of wisdom.

Blessed Job believed amid his scourges that he had displeased God, and for that reason recalled his mind to sorrow, because the one whom he feared he had displeased was not to be despised.

If he were disputing with a human being concerning the merits of his life, he ought by no means to have been sorrowful. But because through his present scourges he had become uncertain about his former life, he rightly sought sorrow in the scourge. Hence he also adds:

## CHAPTER XXXVII

**VERSE 5.**—“Pay attention to me, and be astonished.”

### 43. From Job’s blows we should learn what we ought to fear.

That is: Consider what I have done, and marvel at what I suffer in this affliction.

He rightly continues:

**THE SAME.**—“And place your finger upon your mouth.”

As though he plainly said: Knowing the good things I have done and considering the evils I suffer, restrain yourselves also from the guilt of speech, and fear your own losses in my blows.

Or certainly, because we distinguish things with our fingers, “the finger” appropriately signifies discernment. Hence the Psalmist says: “Blessed is the Lord my God, who trains my hands for battle and my fingers for war” (Ps. 143:1), signifying action by the hands and discernment by the fingers.

[Ancient recension XVIII.]

The finger is therefore placed upon the mouth when the tongue is restrained through discernment, lest by what it says it fall into the guilt of folly. He therefore says: “Place your finger upon your mouth,” that is, join the virtue of discernment to your speech, so that by the right things you say against the hypocrite you may perceive to whom they should be said. It follows:

## CHAPTER XXXVIII

[Col. 1103D]

**VERSE 6.**—“And when I remember, I fear, and trembling shakes my flesh.”

### 44. The saints sometimes speak ironically and by way of mockery.

That blessed Job had not forgotten his deeds is shown by his final statement. From this it is clear that what he now says to his friends—“And when I remember, I fear, and trembling shakes my flesh”—is spoken by way of mockery.

As though he plainly said: If I remember that I possessed anything belonging to the hypocrite, I immediately tremble in the weeping of repentance.

He says that his flesh is shaken by trembling if he remembers it, that is, that the weakness of his deed is wearied by fear of retribution.

But because Sophar had asserted much concerning the sudden condemnation of the wicked, thereby wounding blessed Job’s power, the holy man adds in response to his words:

## CHAPTER XXXIX [Recension XXIII]

**VERSE 7.**—“Why, then, do the wicked live, are raised up, and strengthened by riches?”

### 45. The happiness of this life is examined in dignities and riches, in children and relatives, in a peaceful household, in the fertility of herds, and in the multitude and rejoicing of servants.

If divine patience did not tolerate them, they would by no means continue long in their sins. They are “raised up by riches” when they begin to become powerful; they are “strengthened” when they are permitted to remain in this life for a long time.

For those whom wealth elevates, the length of their days strengthens them in the arrogance of their power. Or certainly they are said to be raised up and strengthened because they are raised up by honors and strengthened by possessions.

But there are many who, though raised up by honors and strengthened by riches, receive what they desire in this life yet are deprived of the succession of offspring. Their very power is punishment, since they see that they possess a great inheritance but have no heirs to whom they may leave it.

What benefit is it, then, if everything is present but the children who will become successors are absent? It follows:

## CHAPTER XL

**VERSE 8.**—“Their offspring remains before them.”

### 46. Their happiness is increased when heirs are given together with a great patrimony; and, lest any merely temporal necessity remove from their sight those in whom their spirit rejoices, it is said of this offspring: “It remains before them.”

But what if children are given, while they themselves are struck by barrenness? Their line is extinguished in them, just as it was feared it would be extinguished through the barrenness of their parents. It follows:

**THE SAME.**—“A multitude of relatives and descendants is in their sight.”

Behold: life is present; honors and riches are present; children are present; descendants are present. What if some inward thought burns the mind and domestic quarrel pierces the joys of security? What happiness does this world possess if it is not joyful? It follows:

## CHAPTER XLI

[Col. 1104D]

**VERSE 9.**—“Their houses are secure and peaceful, and the rod of God is not upon them.”

### 47. They are secure and peaceful because they live while sinning, practice things that ought to be mourned, and do not abandon their joys.

The rod of heavenly discipline does not strike them, and they advance all the more in guilt the less they are struck because of their guilt.

But since we have heard what prospers within, let us also see what prosperity smiles upon them in the fields.

[Note: Thus Germ. and the other manuscripts. Norm. reads “let us hear”; formerly Utic. read “let us see,” but now reads “let us hear,” as also observed in Ebroic.] It follows:

[Col. 1105A]

**VERSE 10.**—“Their ox conceived and did not miscarry; the cow gave birth and was not deprived of her offspring.”

[Note: Utic. formerly had: “and did not abort”; Germ. also has this reading.]

It is common usage to call the male a “bull” and the female a “cow,” but the language of literature—that is, of grammar—calls the ox by a noun of common gender. Hence it now says: “Their ox conceived and did not miscarry; the cow gave birth and was not deprived of her offspring.”

For the owners of herds, the first happiness is that the herd, free from barrenness, conceives; the second, that the conception proceeds to birth; the third, that what has been born is brought to maturity through nourishment.

Thus, to show that all these things are present together among the wicked, blessed Job declares that their herds conceived and did not miscarry, gave birth, and were not deprived of their own offspring.

But happiness is less if, while the herds increase, the keepers of the herds do not also increase. Hence the fertility of the household is immediately added to the fertility of the herds. For it says:

## CHAPTER XLII

**VERSE 11.**—“Their little ones go forth like flocks, and their children exult in their games.”

### 48. So that, just as greater things have been granted for possession, many may spring up for their care.

But because he said, “They exult in their games,” he adds this, lest we think the very play of the children in the houses of the wicked too insignificant:

**VERSE 12.**—“They hold the tambourine and the lyre; they rejoice at the sound of the organ.”

[Note: Norm. manuscripts read “and rejoice.”]

As though he plainly said: While their masters swell with honors and possessions, their dependents rejoice in playful activities.

But, blessed man, why do you tell us so much about the pleasures of the wicked? It has already been a long time that you have been speaking in describing them. After so much, briefly distinguish what you think. It follows:

## CHAPTER XLIII [Ancient XIX, Recension XXIV]

**VERSE 13.**—“They spend their days in prosperity, and in a moment they descend to the underworld.”

### 49. Whatever has an end is momentary. Prosperity is not proof of innocence, nor adversity proof of wickedness.

Behold, blessed man, you had long recounted their joys. How do you now assert that “in a moment they descend to the underworld,” unless every length of time in the present life is recognized as a moment when it is ended?

When each person is brought to the end, he retains nothing of the past, because all times have slipped away; he has nothing in the future, because not even the moments of a single hour remain. Therefore, a life that could be narrowed in this way was a moment.

For, as we said earlier, we place and lift the stylus at a point. Thus the one who received life and lost it touched life, as it were, in a moment.

This may also be understood to mean that those who have long been tolerated in iniquity are often carried away by sudden death, so that they are not even permitted to mourn before death for the sins they have committed.

But because the life of the just is also sometimes ended by a sudden death, we understand it better if we take this as referring to their temporal life, because whatever could pass away was sudden.

To the friends of blessed Job, who believed this man unjust because they saw him scourged, the voice of the same holy man rightly demonstrates, through the flowering and destruction of the wicked, that the prosperity of the present life is not a witness to innocence. Many return to everlasting life through scourges, while many destined for endless punishments die without a scourge.

Concerning them he adds:

## CHAPTER XLIV [Recension XXV]

**VERSE 14.**—“They said to God: Depart from us.”

### 50. Those who do not obey God’s commandments drive him away from themselves.

Fools scarcely dare to say these words aloud; nevertheless, all the wicked say to God, “Depart,” not in words but in their behavior.

For those who do what Almighty God forbids—what else do they do except close their minds against the Omnipotent?

[Note: Turon. has *cludunt* for *claudunt*, “they close.”]

Just as thinking about his commandments is to bring him within oneself, so resisting his commandments is to drive him away from dwelling in the heart.

They therefore say, “Depart from us,” those who refuse to provide him access to themselves and oppose him by wicked actions, even if they appear to praise him in words.

They also say:

## CHAPTER XLV

**THE SAME.**—“We do not desire the knowledge of your ways.”

### 51. It is one thing not to know God’s ways, and another to be unwilling to know them.

By the very fact that they disdain to grasp his knowledge, they say this.

There are some who, because of what Truth says—“The servant who did not know his master’s will and did things deserving of blows will receive few blows; but the servant who knew his master’s will and did not act according to it will receive many blows” (Luke 12:47–48)—do not want to know what they ought to do, imagining that they will be beaten less if they do not know what they ought to have done.

But it is one thing not to have known, and another to have been unwilling to know. One does not know when one wishes to grasp something but is unable. But whoever turns his ear away from the voice of truth in order not to know is judged not ignorant but contemptuous.

[Ancient XX.]

The way of God is peace; the way of God is humility; the way of God is patience. But because the wicked despise all these things, they say: “We do not desire the knowledge of your ways.”

For while they are proud in the present life, while they are puffed up by honors, and while they desire even what they do not possess, they despise the ways of God in their thoughts.

Because the way of God in this life was humility, God himself and our Lord, our Redeemer, came to insults, reproaches, and suffering. He endured the adversities of this world with equanimity and bravely avoided its prosperity, teaching both that the prosperity of eternal life should be desired and that the adversities of the present life should not be feared.

But because the wicked desire the glory of the present life and flee disgrace, they are remembered as saying: “We do not desire the knowledge of your ways.” They do not wish to know what they disdain to do.

Their words are further set forth when it says:

## CHAPTER XLVI [Recension XXVI]

[Col. 1107A]

**VERSE 15.**—“Who is the Omnipotent, that we should serve him?”

### 52. Carnal people either suspect that God does not exist or disdain serving him

The human mind, poured outward in an evil way, is so scattered among bodily things that it neither returns inward to itself nor is capable of contemplating him who is invisible. Hence carnal people, scorning spiritual commands, because they do not see God bodily eventually reach the point of suspecting that he does not even exist. Thus it is written: “The fool said in his heart, ‘There is no God’” (Ps. XIII, 1). Hence it is also said now: “Who is the Almighty, that we should serve him?” For people often desire more to serve human beings, whom they see bodily, than to serve God, whom they do not see. In everything they do, they aim at what their eyes can perceive; and because they cannot direct the eyes of the body toward God, they either disdain to offer him service or, if they begin, grow weary. For they do not believe that he exists whom they do not behold bodily.

If they humbly sought God, the author of all things, they would discover in themselves that what is unseen is superior to what is seen.[^c0108-1] They themselves subsist from an invisible soul and a visible body; but if what is unseen is taken away from them, what is seen immediately collapses. The eyes of the flesh remain open, certainly, but they cannot see or perceive anything. The faculty of sight has perished because its inhabitant has departed; and the house of the flesh remains empty because the invisible spirit has withdrawn—the spirit that used to look out through its windows.

Since invisible things are therefore more excellent than visible things, every carnal person ought to have judged this from himself and, through this—as I might say—ladder of reflection, to ascend toward God: for he is the more truly existent because he remains invisible, and he remains the highest precisely because he cannot in any way be comprehended.

There are, however, some who do not doubt either that God exists or that he is incomprehensible, yet seek from him not himself but external gifts. When they see those gifts lacking in people who serve him, they disdain to serve him themselves. Their words continue:

### CHAPTER XLVII [Rec. XXVII]

**THE SAME.**—“And what profit is there for us if we pray to him?”

### 53. The order of things to be requested in prayer

When God is not sought in prayer, the soul grows weary in prayer more quickly. For when someone asks for those things that God perhaps refuses to grant according to his hidden judgment, he himself also becomes distasteful, since he does not wish to give what is loved.

But the Lord wishes himself to be loved more than the things he created, and eternal things to be requested rather than earthly things, as it is written: “Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you” (Matt. VI, 33). For in saying not “they will be given,” but “they will be added,” he clearly indicates that one thing is given as the principal gift and another is added on. Since eternity ought to be our object in intention, while temporal things should serve our use, the former is given and the latter is certainly added in abundance.

Yet people often ask for temporal goods without seeking eternal rewards. They request what is added, but do not desire the place to which it is added. They do not regard it as any gain from their petition if they are temporally poor here and live there eternally rich in blessedness; but, intent only on visible things, as has been said, they refuse the labor of prayer by which invisible things are acquired.[^c0108-2]

If they sought heavenly things, they would already be undertaking labor with its reward. For when the mind, inflamed by divine desires, longs in prayer for the vision of its creator, it is joined to heavenly things and separated from those below. Through the ardor of its love it opens itself to receive, and in receiving it is inflamed. To love higher things is already to ascend; and while it eagerly longs for heavenly things, in a wondrous way it tastes precisely what it seeks to receive.

It continues:

### CHAPTER XLVIII [Vet. XXI, Rec. XXVIII]

**VERSE 16.**—“Yet because their goods are not in their hand, let their counsel be far from me.”

### 54. The just possess their goods; they are not possessed by them. The opposite is true of the wicked

A person has goods in his hand when, by despising temporal things, he holds them beneath the dominion of his mind. For whoever loves them excessively subjects himself more to them than he subjects them to himself.

Many of the just were rich in this world and seemed to possess many things, supported by wealth and honors.[^c0108-3] Yet because excessive delight in the things they possessed did not possess their minds, their goods were in their hand: they were held subject to the power of the soul.[^c0108-4]

The wicked, by contrast, pour themselves wholly into the desires by which they seek external things, so that they do not themselves hold what they possess; rather, their minds are held captive by the things they have. Since their goods are therefore not in their hand, it is rightly added: “Let their counsel be far from me.”

For what is the counsel of the wicked except to seek earthly glory, neglect eternal glory, pursue temporal well-being at the cost of inward loss, and exchange passing pains for eternal groaning? The holy man, therefore, seeing these thoughts of the wicked, rejects them and says: “Let their counsel be far from me.” For he clearly sees that it is incomparably better to choose to groan here for a short time under the lash than to endure the punishments of eternal vengeance.

Nor do even those who desire to prosper in this life prosper continually. Often their joys are interrupted by groans that arise. Hence it is added:

### CHAPTER XLIX [Rec. XXIX]

**VERSE 17.**—“How often will their lamp be extinguished, and inundation will come upon them, and he will divide the pains of his wrath.”

[^c0108-5]

### 55. How many and what kinds of punishments afflict the wicked

Often the wicked regard the life of their children as their lamp; but when the child who is loved excessively is taken away, the wicked person’s lamp, which seemed to shine, has been extinguished.

Often the wicked regard the glory of present honor as their lamp; but when they are cast down after their rank has been removed, the lamp that shone for them according to their desire has been extinguished.

Often the wicked regard the riches of earthly substance that are available to them as a great lamp of light; but when, through the irruption of loss, they lose the riches that they loved more than themselves, what else have they lost but the lamp in whose light they rejoiced?[^c0108-6]

Whoever therefore does not desire to rejoice in eternal things cannot rejoice continually even here, where he wishes to establish himself. For whenever the lamp of the wicked is extinguished, inundation comes upon them, and he divides the pains of his wrath.

Inundation comes upon the wicked when they suffer the waves of pain through some adversity. For Almighty God, seeing that he is despised while they rejoice in earthly desire, strikes with pain precisely what he sees preferred to himself in the wicked person’s thoughts.

It is well said: “And he will divide the pains of his wrath.” He reserves eternal pains for the wicked in retribution, yet sometimes pierces his mind also with temporal pain. Because he strikes both here and there, he divides the pains of his wrath over the wicked. Present punishment, which does not change the unjust soul’s evil desires, does not free it from eternal punishments.

Hence the Psalmist also says: “He will rain snares, fire, sulfur, and the spirit of storms upon sinners; this is the portion of their cup” (Ps. X, 7). By mentioning snares, fire, sulfur, and the spirit of storms, he certainly introduced many pains. But because the sinner who is not corrected is summoned from those pains to eternal punishments, he said that these pains are not the whole cup but a portion of the cup. Their suffering begins here through pains, but is brought to completion in everlasting vengeance.

Their end is further described:

### CHAPTER L [Vet. XXII, Rec. XXX]

**VERSE 18.**—“They will be like chaff before the face of the wind, and like ashes that the whirlwind scatters.”

### 56. Like chaff, they are carried by the breath of divine anger to the fire

When the wicked are seen in power, when they rage without restraint in oppression and violence, they are judged exceedingly burdensome by the thoughts of the weak and are considered almost rooted in this world.[^c0108-7] But when the sentence of the strict judge arrives, all the wicked will be like chaff before the wind:[^c0108-8] for, so to speak, they are suddenly lifted by the breath of anger and carried to the fire—those whom the tears of the needy, lying beneath them like a heavy mass, could not move because of their former hard-hearted judgments.[^c0108-9]

Those who were heavy to their neighbors through injustice are light in the hands of the judgment that carries them away.

“And like ashes that the whirlwind scatters.” In the sight of Almighty God, the life of the wicked is ashes: even if it appears green for a moment, it is nevertheless seen as already consumed by his judgment, because it has been destined for eternal destruction.

The whirlwind scatters these ashes because “God will come manifestly, our God, and he will not be silent. Fire will burn before him, and a mighty storm will surround him” (Ps. XLIX, 3). By the whirlwind of this storm the wicked are snatched away from the eternal Judge’s presence. Those who here had made their minds solid through perverse desire will there be seen as chaff and ashes, because the snatching whirlwind carries them away to eternal punishments.

It continues:

### CHAPTER LI [Rec. XXXI]

**VERSE 19.**—“God will preserve the pain of his father for his sons; and when he has repaid him, then he will know.”

### 57. How God punishes the sins of parents in their children

We know that it is written: “You repay the sins of fathers upon sons and grandsons, to the third and fourth generation” (Exod. XXXIV, 7). And again it is written: “What is this”—you turn this parable into a proverb in the land of Israel, saying, “The fathers have eaten a sour grape, and the teeth of the sons have been set on edge”? “As I live,” says the Lord God, “this parable shall no longer be a proverb for you in Israel. Behold, all souls are mine; the soul of the father, as also the soul of the son, is mine. The soul that sins shall itself die” (Ezek. XVIII, 2; Jer. XXXI, 29).

Since a different sense is found in these two statements, the listener is instructed to seek carefully the path of discrimination.

We inherit original sin from our parents; and unless we are freed through the grace of baptism, we also bear the sins of our parents,[^c0108-10] because in a certain sense we are still one with them. He therefore repays the sins of parents upon sons when, because of the parent’s guilt, the offspring’s soul is polluted by original sin. Yet again he does not repay the parents’ sins upon sons, because when we are freed from original guilt through baptism, we no longer bear the sins of our parents but those that we ourselves commit.[^c0108-11]

This can also be understood in another way: whoever imitates the wickedness of a wicked parent is bound also by that parent’s offense. But whoever does not imitate the parent’s wickedness is not burdened by that parent’s offense. Thus a wicked son who imitates his wicked father pays not only for his own sins, which he has added, but also for his father’s sins, because he does not fear to add his own evil to the father’s vices, by which he knows that the Lord was angered.[^c0108-12]

It is just that someone who, under a strict judge, does not fear to imitate the ways of an unjust parent should be compelled even in the present life to pay for the sins of that unjust parent.

Hence it is also said there: “The soul of the father is mine, and the soul of the son is mine. The soul that sins shall itself die.” For in the flesh, sons are sometimes killed because of their father’s sin; but once original sin has been removed, they are not held in their soul because of their parents’ wickedness.

For what else is meant when small children are often seized by demons except that the child’s flesh is punished because of the father’s penalty? The wicked father is struck in himself, but refuses to feel the force of the blow. He is often struck through his children, so that he may burn more intensely; and the father’s pain is returned to the children’s flesh, so that the father’s wicked mind may be punished through the suffering of his children.

But when not small children, but already older sons, are struck because of their parents’ guilt, what else is openly signified except that they also pay the penalties of those whose deeds they have followed?

Hence it is rightly said: “To the third and fourth generation.” For because sons can see the life of their parents whom they imitate down to the third and fourth generation, vengeance extends to those who have seen what they would follow wrongly.

### [Vet. XXIII.] 58. Guilt closes the eyes of the wicked; punishment opens them

Because guilt closes the eyes of the wicked but punishment opens them at the end, it is rightly added: “And when he has repaid him, then he will know.”

The wicked person does not know the evils he has committed until he has begun to be punished for those same evils. Hence it is also said through the prophet: “Only vexation will give understanding to the hearing” (Isa. XXVIII, 19). Then he understands what he heard, when he has already grieved because he is being tormented for his contempt.

Thus Balaam is described as saying of himself: “The man whose eye is closed said; the hearer of the words of God said, who sees the vision of the Almighty, who will fall, and then his eyes will be opened” (Num. XXIV, 3–4). He had offered counsel against the Israelites, but afterward, in punishment, saw what he had first committed through guilt.[^c0108-13]

The elect, however, foresee that they must not sin; their eyes are open before the fall. The wicked person opens his eyes after the fall, because after his guilt, in his punishment, he sees that he ought to have avoided the evil he committed.

His now useless knowledge is further described:

### CHAPTER LII

**VERSE 20.**—“His eyes will see his slaughter, and he will drink from the wrath of the Almighty.”

### 59. After the fall, the eyes are opened uselessly

If, while he was living in this life, he had wished to see his guilt, he would not afterward have drunk from the wrath of the Almighty. But whoever here turns his eyes away from the contemplation of his crime will there be unable to avoid the sentence of condemnation.

Often those who do not fear eternal punishments nevertheless fear committing evil because of at least temporal chastisement. But there are some who have become so hardened in wickedness that they do not fear being struck even in the things they love, provided only that they fulfill what they have perversely conceived.

Hence the hardening of the wicked is further described here:

### CHAPTER LIII

**VERSE 21.**—“For what does he care about his household after him? Or if the number of his months is cut in half?”

### 60. The astonishing hardening and blindness of some wicked people, even when they are struck

We must not understand this to mean that, after this wicked man has been condemned to eternal punishments, he gives no thought to his household—that is, to the relatives he has left behind—for Truth itself says that the rich man who had been buried in hell was concerned, even while in punishment, for the five brothers he had left behind (Luke XVI, 28).

Every sinner will be wise in punishment who was foolish in guilt,[^c0108-14] because there, constrained by grief, he opens his eyes to reason—eyes that here, devoted to pleasure, he closed. Under the torture of punishment he is compelled to become wise, though here, blinded by the arrogance that made him so, he was foolish.

Yet his wisdom will then be of no benefit, because here, where he ought to have acted according to wisdom, he lost his opportunity.[^c0108-15]

Here he desires above all to have offspring, fill his household with family and wealth, and live for a long time in this corruptible flesh. But if something should come to him that accords with his desire, yet which he could obtain only by offending his creator, his mind, briefly disturbed, considers that if he does this here he will incur the offense of his creator. He is then struck in his household, in his children, and in his life.

But immediately provoked by pride, he hardens himself; and however much he feels himself struck in his household or in his life, he pays no attention, provided that he fulfills what he has conceived. Behold, his household is struck because of his guilt; but what does he care about his household after him?

Behold, because of the vengeance for his evil deed, the length of life that might have been his is shortened; but what does he care if the number of his days is cut in half?[^c0108-16]

Thus the sinner rises up against God precisely where Almighty God breaks his rising. The blow inflicted does not humble the mind whose obstinacy in deliberation against the Lord has hardened it. We should note how serious the guilt is: to place punishment for guilt before the mind, yet not even through fear of torment to bow the neck of the heart beneath the creator’s yoke.

### [Vet. XXIV, Rec. XXXII.]

But when we hear these things, a question arises in our heart: why did the omnipotent and merciful God permit the reasoning of the human mind to fall into such blindness? So that no one may presume to investigate God’s hidden judgments beyond what is proper, it is rightly added:

### CHAPTER LIV

**VERSE 22.**—“Will anyone teach God knowledge, who judges those on high?”

### 61. God’s hidden judgments must not be scrutinized with excessive curiosity

When we are uncertain about what happens to us, we ought to contemplate other things that are certain to us and quiet the complaint of thought that has arisen from our uncertainty.

Behold, it is exceedingly hidden to us why the lashes that recall the elect to life do not restrain the reprobate from evil deeds; yet the judgments of Almighty God concerning us are not unjust. But if we direct the eye of the mind toward higher things, we see in them that we have no just complaint against him concerning ourselves.

For Almighty God, discerning the merits of the angels, established some to remain in eternal light without falling, while others, having fallen of their own will, he cast down from the state of their sublimity into the punishment of eternal condemnation. He therefore acts unjustly toward no one among us, since he has also judged more subtle natures justly.

Let him therefore say: “Will anyone teach God knowledge, who judges those on high?” For since he does wondrous things above us, it is unquestionably clear that he arranges everything concerning us with knowledge.

After these points have been set forth, he adds the place where the human mind is wearied in its inquiry. For it continues:

### CHAPTER LV

**VERSES 23–25.**—“This one dies strong and healthy, rich and fortunate; his entrails are full of fat, and his bones are irrigated with marrow. But another dies in the bitterness of his soul, without any possessions.”

### 62. The lives of the elect and the reprobate differ, but the death of the flesh is the same. The joy of the wicked passes into punishment; the punishment of the innocent passes into joy

Since these things are so, who can investigate the secrets of Almighty God and ask why he permits them to be so? The life of the elect and the reprobate is indeed different, but the corruption of the flesh in death is not different.

Hence it is added:

**VERSE 26.**—“And yet together they will sleep in the dust, and worms will cover them.”

What is surprising, then, if they pass for a moment through the prosperity or adversity of the present age in different ways, when through the corruption of the flesh they return alike to the earth?[^c0108-17]

Only that life should therefore be contemplated in which, with the resurrection of the flesh, one reaches a different end of recompense.[^c0108-18] For what salvation or strength is there for the wicked, when fatness and riches are entirely abandoned here with speed, while there the recompense that can never be abandoned is found?

Just as the joy of this wicked man passes into punishment, so the punishment of the afflicted innocent passes into joy. Riches therefore should not exalt the mind, nor poverty disturb it.

Hence blessed Job, amid the loss of his possessions, admits no loss of thought into his heart. Rebuking those who despise him in his affliction, he continues:

### CHAPTER LVI [Rec. XXXIII]

**VERSES 27–28.**—“Certainly I know your thoughts and your unjust opinions against me. For you say: ‘Where is the house of the prince, and where are the tents of the wicked?’”

### 63. Job remained unbroken because, although he had lost everything else, he had not lost God

They had considered him wicked because they saw him temporally ruined after his possessions had been taken away.[^c0108-19] But the holy man judged them with all the greater depth of insight because, amid the losses he had endured, he stood firm in unbroken righteousness. For what harm had the loss of external possessions done him, since he had not lost the one he loved inwardly?

### Allegorical sense

### 64. Pride arises from abundance

The statement “Together they will sleep in the dust, and worms will cover them,” if someone wishes to receive it allegorically, can be explained briefly by repeating what has already been said concerning this rich wicked man.

It is said: “His entrails are full of fat.” Just as fat arises from abundant food, so pride arises from an abundance of possessions. Pride fattens the rich man’s mind when the proud person’s spirit is lifted up. The pride of the heart is, as it were, a kind of fatty thickness.

Hence, because many commit sins through abundance, the prophet says: “Their iniquity came forth as if from fat” (Ps. LXXII, 7).

It continues: “And his bones are irrigated with marrow.” Lovers of this world have bones when they possess the strength of dignities in this world. But if earthly and domestic riches are lacking in their external dignity, then, according to their own judgment, they have bones but no marrow in their bones.

Because this lover of the world is so supported by external power that he is also filled with the abundance of an earthly household, it is said: “And his bones are irrigated with marrow.”

Alternatively, the bones of this rich man are his wicked and hardened habits, while the marrow in the bones is the very desire to live badly—desires that are not satisfied even by the fulfillment of wickedness. These desires are like marrow irrigating the bones when evil desires preserve their perverse habits in the enjoyment of pleasures.

### [Vet. XXVI, Rec. XXXIV.] 65. From the source of the rich man’s empty joy, the poor man is afflicted even more emptily. What the rich man possesses with fear, the poor man desires with anxiety

There are some who do not possess riches in this world but desire to possess them and wish to be exalted. Although they cannot obtain in this world what they desire, and although they are supported by no possessions or honors, their conscience nevertheless condemns them as guilty before the inner Judge because of their evil desires.

Such a person is often afflicted precisely because he cannot become rich and proud. Of him it is also added: “But another dies in the bitterness of his soul, without any possessions.”

Behold: from the very source of the rich man’s joy with his proud heart, another poor man with a proud heart is afflicted even more emptily.
