It is well added concerning both: “And yet together they will sleep in the dust, and worms will cover them.”

To sleep in the dust is to close the eyes of the mind in earthly desires. Hence it is said to every sinner who sleeps in his guilt: “Rise, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ will illumine you” (Eph. V, 14).

The worms that are born from flesh cover them together, because carnal cares weigh upon the proud mind of both rich and poor. In earthly matters the poor man and the reprobate rich man, although they are not supported by equal prosperity, are nevertheless disturbed by equal anxiety. What the one already possesses with fear, the other desires with anxiety; and because he cannot possess it, he grieves.

Let it therefore be said: “Together they will sleep in the dust, and worms will cover them,” because although they are not raised up together by temporal possessions, they are nevertheless together lulled into the dullness of the mind by concern for temporal things. Worms cover them together, because carnal thoughts weigh upon either the one, so that he may obtain what he desires, or the other, so that he may not lose what he has.

### 66. Job was neither elated by possessions nor anxious when they were lost

Blessed Job, however, had been neither elated by possessions nor anxiously seeking what he had lost. Since he was not gnawed by thoughts of external loss, the worms of the heart had not covered him. And because he had not cast down his mind into earthly concern, he did not sleep in the dust.

It continues: “Certainly I know your thoughts and your unjust opinions against me.”

Since it is written, “Who knows what belongs to a person except the spirit of the person that is in him?” (1 Cor. II, 11), in what sense is it now said: “Certainly I know your thoughts”?

The spirit of one person is unknown to another when it is not demonstrated by words or deeds. But since it is written, “You will know them by their fruits” (Matt. VII, 20), whatever lies hidden within is revealed through what is done outwardly.

Hence Solomon also rightly says: “As faces are reflected in water for those who look, so the hearts of human beings are manifest to the prudent” (Prov. XXVII, 19).

Accordingly, when blessed Job said that he knew the thoughts of his friends as they spoke with him, he added: “And your unjust opinions against me,” showing from the evident matter that he had discovered what lay hidden in them.

He therefore adds their unjust opinions themselves, saying: “For you say: ‘Where is the house of the prince, and where are the tents of the wicked?’”

### [Rec. XXXV.] 67. The false opinion of those who measure guilt by scourging

All weak people who desire to flourish in this world and fear punishments as much as great evils measure guilt by punishment in those whom they see being scourged. When they see someone struck, they suspect that he has displeased God.

Thus the friends of blessed Job, seeing him struck, believed that he was wicked, judging that if he had not been wicked, his tents would have remained.

But no one thinks this except someone who still suffers from the weariness of weakness, who fixes the step of his thought in the delight of the present age, and who does not know how to pass with perfect desires to the eternal homeland.

Hence it is well added:

### CHAPTER LVII [Vet. XXVII]

**VERSES 29–30.**—“Ask any one of the travelers, and you will discover that he understands these same things: that the wicked man is kept for the day of destruction and is led to the day of wrath.”

### 68. We should consult those who think of life as a road, not as a homeland

Often divine patience tolerates for a long time those whom it has already condemned to punishments foreknown; it permits those to flourish whom it still sees committing worse deeds. Because it sees toward what pit of condemnation they are tending, it considers it of no consequence that the perverse multiply what they will have to leave behind here.

But whoever loves the glory of the present life considers it great happiness to flourish here according to his wishes, even though he is later compelled to endure eternal punishments.

Only the person who has already removed the step of his heart from love of the present age sees that it means nothing for the wicked to flourish.

Thus, when the subsequent condemnation of the wicked was being described, it was rightly prefaced: “Ask any one of the travelers, and you will discover that he understands these same things.”

A traveler is one who considers the present life a road for himself and not a homeland; who disdains to fix his heart in love of the passing age; who desires not to remain among passing things but to arrive at eternal things.[^c0108-20]

Whoever does not wish to be a traveler in this life does not readily despise the prosperity of this life. When he sees what he himself desires abounding in others, he marvels at it.

Thus the prophet David, because he had already passed in heart beyond love of the present age, described the glory of the wicked, saying: “I saw the wicked man exalted above measure and raised up like the cedars of Lebanon” (Ps. XXXVI, 35). But because he had not subjected his heart to this world, he rightly despised him, saying: “I passed by, and behold, he was no more” (ibid., 36).

The wicked would have been something in his estimation if he himself had not passed beyond this age through the orientation of his mind. But to the mind that had passed beyond it, the wicked man—who would have seemed something great to one who did not pass beyond—appeared to be nothing, because when eternal recompense is considered, the present glory is recognized as worthless.

Hence Moses, when he sought the glory of heavenly contemplation, said: “Passing by, I will see this vision” (Exod. III, 3). Unless he had removed the step of his heart from love of the world, he could never have understood heavenly things.

Hence Jeremiah, asking that the grief of his heart be considered, says: “All you who pass along the way, attend and see whether there is any sorrow like my sorrow” (Lam. I, 12). Those who do not pass through the present life as through a road, but regard it as a homeland, cannot consider the grief of the elect.

The prophet therefore seeks those who have not fixed their minds in this world, so that they may consider his sorrow.

Hence Solomon says: “Open your mouth for the mute, and for the causes of all the children who pass by” (Prov. XXXI, 8). Those are called mute who do not resist the words of preachers by contradicting them. They are also called those who pass by because they disdain to fix the intention of their minds in love of the present life.

Since, therefore, the wicked man is kept for the day of destruction and led to the day of wrath, only the traveler understands this. Whoever has fixed his heart on present things does not discern the punishments that follow the wicked.

Of him it is further added:

### CHAPTER LVIII [Rec. XXXVI]

**[Col. 1117A] VERSE 31.**—“Who will accuse him face to face concerning his way? And who will repay him for what he has done?”

### 69. Only Christ will overthrow Antichrist, exalted by such signs and by so great a display of holiness

Often the wicked man experiences even in this life the indignation of his Creator, which he will suffer eternally, when he loses the prosperity he loves and encounters the adversity he fears. And although, even amid prosperity, he can be reproved for his wickedness by the tongue of the righteous [Note: [Col. 1117D] Vindoc.: “simply, by the righteous.”], we nevertheless know that, when each wicked person is brought low by his deeds, the reproof of the righteous grows stronger. [Note: [Col. 1117D] Turon.: “while he was speaking about the body of all wicked people.” Utic.: “while speaking about the whole body of the wicked.”]

But why is it now said, “Who will reproach him to his face for his way,” when it is also known—even while the righteous are silent—that the way of the wicked is reproved here as often as his prosperity is disturbed by the intervention of adversity [Vet. XXVIII]? Blessed Job, however, while speaking about the body of all wicked people, suddenly turned his words toward the head of all the wicked. For he saw that, at the end of the world, Satan would enter a human being whom Holy Scripture calls Antichrist, and that he would be exalted with such arrogance, rule with such power, and be elevated by such great signs and wonders in his display of holiness that no human being would be able to reprove his deeds. [Note: [Col. 1117D] Vindoc.: “because, together with the power of error, signs of displayed dignity and holiness are also added.” Turon.: “because, together with the power of terror, signs of displayed truth are also added.”] For he adds signs of displayed holiness to the power of terror, and says: “Who will reproach him to his face for his way?”

Who, indeed, would dare rebuke that man, whose very appearance one fears to endure? Yet not only Elijah and Enoch, who are brought forward for his denunciation, but also all the elect reprove his way: they despise him and resist his wickedness by the strength of their minds. But because they do this through divine grace and not through their own strength, it is rightly said here: “Who will reproach him to his face for his way?” For who is this, except God, by whose help the elect are strengthened so that they can resist?

Sometimes, when Scripture uses the interrogative “Who?”, it designates the Almighty. Thus it is written: “Who will raise him up?” (Gen. XLIX, 9). Concerning him Paul says: “Whom God raised from the dead” (Gal. I, 1). Therefore, when holy men oppose his wickedness, they themselves are not the ones who reprove his way; rather, it is the one by whose grace they are strengthened.

And because his presence, when he comes in that man, will be far more terrible in persecution than it is now, when he is scarcely perceived, since he is not yet borne in his own particular vessel [Note: [Col. 1117D] Gregory calls Antichrist “the devil’s vessel.” See below, §71, and the note explaining that the ancient enemy entered his own vessel, that reprobate man.], it is rightly said: “To his face.” Many now rebuke the ways of Antichrist as they discern them, but they do so as though in his absence, since they rebuke one whom they do not yet behold personally. But when he comes in that condemned man [Note: Thus Turon., Germ., Norm., and others, agreeing with the old printed editions. Later editions read “condemning.”], whoever resists his presence reproves his way to his face, seeing and despising his power.

Or certainly, to reprove his way means to disturb the prosperity of his course when eternal punishment intervenes. Since the Lord alone will accomplish this by his own power, of whom it is written, “Whom the Lord Jesus will kill with the breath of his mouth and destroy by the brightness of his coming” (II Thess. II, 8), it is rightly said: “Who will reproach him to his face for his way?”

Hence it follows: “And for what he has done, who will repay him?” Who, indeed, except the Lord? He alone will repay that ruined man for what he has done, when by his coming he crushes his exceedingly powerful authority through eternal condemnation.

But let us hear what this exalted leader of the wicked does while he remains in this life. It follows:

### CHAPTER LIX [Vet. XXIX, Rec. XXXVII]

[Col. 1118B]

**VERSE 32.—He will be led to the graves, and he will keep watch in the heap of the dead.**

### 70. Satan keeps watch among the multitude of sinners, as in a heap of the dead, and in the graves

Since graves cover the dead, whom else are the graves meant to designate but the reprobate, in whom souls extinguished to the life of blessedness lie hidden as though in graves? This wicked man, therefore, will be led to the graves, because he will be received into the hearts of the wicked, since only those receive him in whom souls dead to God are found. [Note: [Col. 1118D] The old printed editions read “the bodies of the reprobate.” Later editions read “the hearts of the reprobate,” apparently by conjecture alone, because a little below we read that he will be received in the hearts of the wicked. Norm. and Germ. simply read “the reprobate.” In Utic., however, the first hand wrote “the bodies of the reprobate.”]

Regarding him, while his punishments are being described, the prophet rightly says: “Around him are his graves, all those who were slain and those who fell by the sword” (Ezek. XXXII, 22). For those who lie beside him in hell are the ones in whom the same evil spirit lies dead—those who fell, struck by the sword of his wickedness. Hence it is written: “You who delivered David your servant from the evil sword” (Ps. CLIII, 10).

It is rightly said: “And he will keep watch in the heap of the dead,” because now he exercises the snares of his cunning in the gathering of sinners. [Note: [Col. 1118D] Vindoc.: “he has set up the snares.”] Since good people are few in the world and evil people are many, it is rightly called a heap of the dead, so that the multitude of the wicked itself may be signified. “Broad is the way that leads to destruction, and many are those who enter through it” (Matt. VII, 13). Therefore, for Satan to keep watch in the heap of the dead means for him to exercise the snares of his wickedness in the hearts of the reprobate.

Concerning this it is further said:

### CHAPTER LX [Rec. XXXVIII]

[Col. 1118D]

**VERSE 33.—He was sweet to the pebbles of Cocytus.**

### 71. As he is bitter to the elect, so he is sweet to the reprobate by suggesting vices

In the Greek language Cocytus is called “mourning,” from *ἀπὸ τοῦ κωκύειν*, that is, “to lament,” according to Homer. [Note: [Col. 1118D] *Cocytus* derives from the Greek *ἀπὸ τοῦ κωκύειν*, that is, “to lament,” according to Homer.] This mourning, however, is ordinarily understood as the mourning of women or of any weak persons.

The wise men of this age, excluded from the light of truth, tried through their search to grasp certain shadows, as it were, of the truth. Hence they thought that the river Cocytus flowed in the underworld [Note: [Col. 1119D] *Currere* (“to flow”) is absent in Turon., without impairing the sense.], signifying that those who perform works deserving of suffering run down into hell, toward mourning. But let us disregard the shadow of carnal wisdom, since we already possess the light of truth, and let us recognize that, according to the voice of the blessed man, Cocytus means the mourning of the weak. For it is written: “Act manfully, and let your heart be strengthened” (Ps. XXX, 25). [Note: [Col. 1119D] Bellov. and Germ.: “for those who in the world…”] Those who refuse to be strengthened in God proceed toward mourning through weakness of spirit.

We are accustomed to call pebbles the stones of rivers, which flowing water carries along. What, then, are meant by the pebbles of Cocytus except the reprobate, who, devoted to their pleasures, are continually dragged downward from the river, as it were? Those who do not firmly resist the pleasures of this age become the pebbles of Cocytus [Note: [Col. 1119D] Sag., Utic., and several Norm. witnesses: “who, from their own…”]; through their daily falls they move toward mourning, so that afterward they may mourn eternally—those who now relax themselves delightfully in their pleasures.

And because the ancient enemy, having entered that reprobate man as his vessel, grants gifts to the perverse, raises them to honors in this world, and displays wonders before their eyes, their weakened minds admire and follow him in his marvels [Note: [Col. 1119D] Vindoc.: “while he grants good things.”] [Note: We have restored the sense corrupted by the addition of *dum* (“while”), which, against the manuscripts, crept into all the printed copies.], it is rightly said of him: “He was sweet to the pebbles of Cocytus.” When the elect despise him and trample him underfoot with the heel of their minds, those who follow him love him—those who are dragged from the water of pleasure toward everlasting mourning and, like pebbles, slide downward through daily falls caused by earthly desire. [Note: [Col. 1119D] Norm.: “who are like the water of pleasure.” Utic., before correction: “from the water.”]

To some he offers a taste of his sweetness through pride, to others through avarice, to others through envy, to others through deceit, and to others through lust; and he supplies as many draughts of his sweetness as are the kinds of vices to which he drags them.

For when he persuades the mind to something proud, what he says becomes sweet, because the perverse person desires to appear superior to other human beings. [Note: [Col. 1119D] Later editions: “a perverse man desires [to appear] superior to other human beings.”] When he attempts to pour avarice into the mind, what he whispers becomes sweet, because through abundance one avoids need. When he suggests something involving envy, what he says becomes sweet, because the perverse mind rejoices when it sees another becoming worse, since it does not appear inferior to him. [Note: [Col. 1120D] The old editions read “growing richer in a worse condition.” Later editions omit *deterius*, “worse,” and read “declining.” Germ. and others read *deterescere*, from which some derived “growing richer” and others “declining.” *Deterescere* means “to become worse.” Below, Book XXV, §7: “by how many evil thoughts he becomes worse”; and at the end of the same book, §40: “most of them become worse through their example.”]

When he persuades through deceit, what he suggests becomes sweet, because, by deceiving others, the deceiver seems prudent to himself. [Note: [Col. 1120D] Vindoc.: “when he speaks of lust.”] When he speaks of lust to the deceived mind, what he persuades becomes sweet, because it dissolves the soul in pleasure. Thus, whatever vices he implants in the hearts of the sensual, he offers them as so many draughts of his sweetness.

Yet, as I said, they perceive his sweetness only if, devoted to present pleasures, they are being dragged toward everlasting mourning. It is therefore rightly said: “He was sweet to the pebbles of Cocytus,” because he is bitter to the elect and pleasant to the reprobate. He feeds only those with his delights whom he drives toward lamentation through daily falls.

It follows:

### CHAPTER LXI [Vet. XXX, Rec. XXXIX]

**THE SAME.—And after him he drags every human being, and before him innumerable ones.**

### 72. As the end of the world presses on, he will draw all the carnal to himself through Antichrist; now he draws only very many

Here “human being” means one who thinks according to human standards. But since “all” is more than “innumerable,” we must ask why he is said to drag innumerable ones before him and all after him. The reason is that, when the ancient enemy enters that reprobate man, he will seize under the yoke of his dominion all the carnal people he finds.

Even now, before he appears, he drags innumerable people, though not all, because many are daily called back from carnal works to life, while others return to a state of righteousness through brief and others through prolonged repentance. Even now he seizes innumerable people, although he does not display his astonishing signs of falsehood to humanity.

But when he has performed marvelous wonders before the eyes of the carnal, then he will drag after him not innumerable people but all, because those who delight in present goods will submit themselves to his power without hesitation.

Yet, as we said above, since dragging “every human being” is more than dragging “innumerable ones,” why is it first said that he drags every human being, and afterward, as an increase, that innumerable ones are subjected? Reason would require that what is less should be stated first and what is greater afterward.

But it must be understood that here saying “innumerable” expresses something greater than saying “all.” He drags every human being after him because, within three and a half years, he will bind under the yoke of his dominion all those whom he finds devoted to carnal life. But he dragged innumerable ones before him because, over the course of five thousand and more years, although he could not drag all the carnal, the number of those whom he has seized beforehand over so long a time is far greater than the number of all whom he will find to seize in so short a time.

It is therefore rightly said: “After him he drags every human being, and before him innumerable ones,” because then he takes fewer, when he has taken all, whereas now he seizes more [Note: [Col. 1120D] Lyr. and Bigot.: “he takes less …”] when he invades the hearts of innumerable people. [Note: [Col. 1120D] In all English and Norman manuscripts, *innumerabilium* is read. Formerly, however, Utic. had *omnium*, “of all,” as in the printed editions. Our reading agrees with the meaning intended by the holy Doctor.]

Because blessed Job argued so wonderfully against the prince of the wicked, who is permitted to be exalted in this life but will be destroyed at the Lord’s coming, he plainly showed that he had not received the Lord’s scourges because of an offense. For if each wicked person is permitted to prosper in this life, it is necessary that God’s elect should be held back under the bridle of the scourge. [Note: [Col. 1121] Germ. and Utic., before correction: “to be restrained with the scourge as a bridle,” perhaps better than “under the bridle of the scourge.”]

For this reason he rebukes his friends, saying:

### CHAPTER LXII

**VERSE 54.—How, then, do you console me in vain, when your answer has been shown to oppose the truth?**

### 73. How hateful a lie is to the saints

The friends of blessed Job could not console him, because in their words they opposed the truth. And when they called him a hypocrite or a wicked man, by the guilt they themselves committed through lying they undoubtedly increased the punishment of the righteous man afflicted by wounds. For the minds of the saints, because they love the truth, are tormented even by the guilt of another’s deceit. The more seriously they perceive the crime of lying to be, the more they hate it not only in themselves but also in others.

## BOOK SIXTEEN

After briefly explaining Books XXII, XXIII, and XXIV of Job, this book concludes the third part at the middle of verse 20.

[Col. 1121B] 501 [Vet. and Rec. I.]

Those who fail in argument against the words of truth often repeat even commonplaces, lest they appear to have been defeated by remaining silent. Thus Eliphaz, pressed by the words of blessed Job, says things that no one is ignorant of. For he says:

### CHAPTER ONE

**CHAPTER XXII, VERSE 2.—Can a human being be compared with God, even when he possesses perfect knowledge?** [Note: [Col. 1121D] Norm.: “even if…”]

### 1. Compared with divine knowledge, our knowledge is ignorance

Compared with God, our knowledge is ignorance. For we are wise through participation in God, not through comparison with him. What wonder, then, if something is said as though by way of instruction which could have been known even had it remained unspoken?

He further adds, as though defending God’s power:

### CHAPTER TWO

[Col. 1121C]

**VERSE 3.—What does it profit God if you are righteous, or what do you contribute to him if your life is blameless?**

### 2. God has no need of our righteousness

In everything good that we do, we help ourselves, not God. Hence the Psalmist says: “I said to the Lord: You are my God, for you have no need of my goods” (Ps. XV, 2). He is truly our Lord because he is indeed God, who does not need the goodness of his servant but grants the goodness that he receives, so that the goodness offered benefits not him but first those who receive it and afterward return it. [Note: [Col. 1121D] Ebroic. and other Norman witnesses: “so that the goodness brought forth…”; in former times Utic. read “the goodness offered.”]

For although the Lord, coming to judgment, says, “As long as you did it to one of these least of my brothers, you did it to me” (Matt. XXV, 40), he speaks this with wondrous compassion because of his members. And because he is our head, he himself helps us; he is helped through our good works in his members.

Eliphaz adds what no one is ignorant of, saying:

### CHAPTER THREE

**VERSE 4.—Will he rebuke you because he fears you, and will he enter into judgment with you?**

### 3. It is pointless to say of God what no one is ignorant of

Who, even if foolish, would think that the Lord rebukes us out of fear and brings judgment against us out of dread? But those who do not know how to measure their words undoubtedly fall into pointless speech. If they do not immediately reproach themselves for this, they soon leap into harmful and insulting words.

Thus Eliphaz, who had introduced pointless speech, immediately burst into insulting words, saying:

### CHAPTER FOUR

**VERSE 5.—Is it not because of your very great wickedness and your infinite iniquities?**

### 4. From pointless words one proceeds to insults

Behold: from a sluggish heart he came to pointless words, and from pointless words, through the crime of deceit, he burst into insults. These are the stages of growing guilt: when the tongue is not restrained, it does not remain lying where it has fallen but continually descends to worse things.

The words that follow are so clear according to the historical sense that they do not require a literal exposition.

### 5. Since we have said that Job’s friends represent heretics, while Job himself signifies Holy Church, let us now demonstrate how Eliphaz’s words correspond to the falsehood of heretics

For it follows:

### CHAPTER FIVE [Vet. and Rec. II]

[Col. 1122D] 502

“For you have taken away the pledge of your brothers without cause, and you stripped the naked of their clothing. You did not give water to the weary, and you withheld bread from the hungry. By the strength of your arm you possessed the land, and, being most powerful, you held it.”

### TYPICAL SENSE

### 6. Heretics falsely claim that those who return to the Church go astray and lose the Holy Spirit

In Holy Scripture, the term “pledge” sometimes signifies the gifts of the Holy Spirit, and sometimes the confession of sin. A pledge is understood as the gift of the Holy Spirit, as Paul says: “He gave us the pledge of the Spirit” (II Cor. I). We receive this pledge so that we may hold the certainty of the promise made to us. The gift of the Holy Spirit is therefore called a pledge because through it our soul is strengthened toward certainty of inward hope.

Again, under the name of a pledge the confession of sin is customarily understood, as it is written in the Law: “When your brother owes you something, and you take his pledge from him, return the pledge before sunset” (Exod. XXII, 26). [Note: [Col. 1123D] Lyr. and Bigot.: “When your brother owes you … return [it] before sunset.”] Our brother becomes our debtor when it is shown that some neighbor has committed an offense against us. For we call sins debts. Hence it is said to the servant who sinned: “I forgave you all the debt” (Matt. XVIII, 32). And in the Lord’s Prayer we daily pray: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. VI, 12).

We take a pledge from our debtor when, from one whom we know to have sinned against us, we already possess the confession of his sin, through which we are asked to release the sin committed against us. [Note: [Col. 1123D] Germ. and Norm. read *in nobis peccasse … in nobis perpetratum* (“sinned in us … perpetrated in us”) for *in nos peccasse … in nos perpetratum* (“sinned against us … perpetrated against us”).] For whoever confesses the sin he has committed and asks forgiveness has already given, as it were, a pledge for the debt.

We are commanded to return this pledge before sunset because, before the sun of righteousness sets within us through sorrow of heart, we must return to the one from whom we receive confession of guilt the confession that brings forgiveness, so that the person who remembers having offended us may immediately feel from us that his offense has been forgiven.

Therefore, when Holy Church receives people returning from heretics to the truth of the faith, she first persuades them that they must confess the guilt of their error. Thus Eliphaz is made to say, under the figure of the heretics: “For you have taken away the pledge of your brothers without cause.” That is, from those who come to you from us, you have demanded a confession of error to no purpose. [Note: [Col. 1123D] Turon.: “when the Church first receives anyone returning…”]

But if, as we said earlier, we understand the pledge as the gifts of the Holy Spirit, the heretics say that Holy Church has taken away the pledge of their brothers because they suspect that those who come to her lose their spiritual gifts. Hence it follows: “And you stripped the naked of their clothing.”

### [Rec. III.]

### 7. They also call the same people sluggish and dull-witted

Those whom heretics draw by their perverse preaching they consider to possess the precepts of their doctrine as certain garments. They think that these people remain clothed as long as they observe what the heretics themselves have preached. When some of them return to Holy Church, the heretics immediately suspect that they have lost the garments of doctrine. [Col. 1123D]

### [Vet. III.]

But since a naked person cannot be stripped, we must ask how they are first called naked and afterward stripped. 503 It must be understood that everyone who enjoys purity of heart is naked precisely because he has no covering of duplicity. Among heretics there are some who possess purity of heart but nevertheless accept their doctrines’ perverse teachings. These people are naked because of their purity, and as though clothed by the heretics’ preaching. [Note: [Col. 1123D] Utic., formerly: “also because of their goodness.”]

Because such people easily return to Holy Church, since they do not employ the wickedness of duplicity, the heretics acknowledge that they are naked, yet say that the Church has stripped them of their clothing [Note: [Col. 1124D] Turon.: “whom they say are stripped of garments by them”], because they consider those who are simple [Note: [Col. 1124D] Vindoc.: “as though sluggish”] to be sluggish and dull-witted—those whom they see as having lost their perverse doctrines.

### 8. They accuse the Church of ignorance when they speak of things unknown

It follows: “You did not give water to the weary, and you withheld bread from the hungry.”

Because heretics do not possess the solidity of truth, they sometimes strive to appear more talkative and boast against the Catholic faith as though they possessed doctrinal knowledge. They seek to draw to themselves by perverse arguments everyone whom they see, and they think they are acting energetically precisely when they enlist others with themselves for destruction.

We call those weary who are exhausted by labor under the burden of this age. [Note: [Col. 1124D] Turon.: “are more laboriously wearied.”] Hence Truth himself says: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. XI, 28).

Since heretics do not cease preaching their doctrines, they mock Holy Church as though she were ignorant, saying: “You did not give water to the weary, and you withheld bread from the hungry.” They think that they give water to the weary when they offer the drink of their error to certain people laboring under an earthly burden. They suppose that they have not withheld bread from the hungry because, when questioned about invisible and incomprehensible things, they answer with proud audacity.

And they believe themselves learned above all when they presume, disastrously, to speak about things unknown.

But Holy Church, when she sees someone hungering for something that would not benefit him to receive, either modestly suppresses what is already known to her or humbly confesses what still appears unknown. She recalls them to an ordered humility [Note: [Col. 1124D] Turon. reads *ad ornatae humilitatis* (“to a sense of adorned humility”) for *ad ordinatae humilitatis* (“to a sense of ordered humility”).] when, through her preacher, she says: “Not to think more highly than one ought to think, but to think with sober judgment” (Rom. XII, 3). And again: “Do not be high-minded, but fear” (Rom. XI, 20). And once more: “Do not seek what is above you, and do not investigate what is stronger than you” (Ecclus. III, 22). And again: “If you have found honey, eat what is sufficient for you, lest, when you are filled, you vomit it up” (Prov. XXV, 15). [Note: [Col. 1124D] Lyr. and Bigot.: “when you are satiated.”]

To find honey is to taste the sweetness of holy understanding. It is eaten sufficiently when our understanding is kept within the measure of discernment under restraint. For the person who vomits up honey when satiated is the one who desires to penetrate farther than he is capable of and thereby loses what could have nourished him.

Therefore, because Holy Church forbids weak minds to investigate lofty things, it is said to blessed Job: “You withheld bread from the hungry.”

### [Vet. IV.]

### 9. They envy the Church’s greatness and universality

Because heretics also envy her greatness—that she universally holds peoples in the true faith—when they find a time of earthly prosperity, they exceed themselves in proud words against her and, by reproaching her, reveal how much they had previously envied her power in secret.

For it follows: “By the strength of your arm you possessed the land, and, being most powerful, you held it.” 504 It is as though they openly said: “The fact that you occupied the earth universally through your preaching was due to the power of strength, not to the reason of truth.” Because they see Christian rulers embracing her preaching, they suspect that what peoples believe in her is not the power of rectitude but the cause of worldly power.

It follows:

### CHAPTER SIX

**VERSE 9.—You sent widows away empty, and you crushed the arms of orphans.**

### 10. They slander the Church for kindly receiving teachers of error who repent

The peoples subject to heretical preachers conceive the perverse seeds of their errors through carnal understanding and join themselves to those errors for their own condemnation. But when Holy Church either receives the very preachers of error who have been defeated by reason or restrains under the bond of her discipline those hardened by devotion to perversity, the heretics, deprived of their teachers, see peoples remaining among them without preachers. What else, then, do they mourn before Holy Church except widows left empty? [Note: [Col. 1125D] Vindoc.: “What else do they mourn except widows left empty by Holy Church?”]

And because, once the heretical teachers have been removed, they suspect that their disciples have become weak in their former work, they complain as though the arms of the orphans had been crushed by the Church.

Or certainly, because Holy Church receives some who come from the heretics, it is plainly evident that she contradicts their former error. For there are some who pursue bodily virginity so zealously that they condemn marriage; and there are some who praise abstinence so excessively that they detest those who consume necessary food. Concerning them Paul says: “Those who forbid marriage and command abstinence from foods that God created to be received with thanksgiving by the faithful” (I Tim. IV, 3).

Therefore, because the Church recalls these people from the carnal intention of their superstition, when heretics see them living differently from what they taught, they testify that their arms have been crushed by the Church, withdrawn from the activity they previously maintained. [Note: [Col. 1125D] The printed editions read “they detest.” We follow the better reading of Germ., English, Norman, Vindoc., and other manuscripts: “they testify.”]

Hence, if anything adverse happens to the Church in this time of discipline, they suspect that it has happened as a deserved retribution for sins. For it follows:

### CHAPTER SEVEN

[Col. 1125D]

**VERSE 10.—Therefore you are surrounded by snares, and sudden dread troubles you.**

### 11. They reproach the suffering person by claiming that adversity is punishment for crimes

Sudden dread troubles the person who neglects to consider what is impending from the severity of the coming Judge. Therefore, because heretics believe that the faithful people are oppressed by the guilt of unbelief, they accuse them of being surrounded by snares. And because they think that this people does not foresee what is to come, they suppose that, when struck, it is troubled by sudden fear.

They continue their mockery:

**VERSE 11.—And you thought that you would not see darkness and would not be overwhelmed by an assault of overflowing waters.**

It is as though he openly said: “You had set before yourself the security of peace in hope, and therefore rejoiced in your presumption as though in light; you never thought that you would be overwhelmed by tribulations. But behold: while you are afflicted by evils that come upon you, the very darkness of the tribulations that oppress you shows whether what you hold is right.”

Eliphaz compares these tribulations to overflowing waters, because, as they rush upon one another, wave follows wave like swelling waters.

It follows:

### CHAPTER EIGHT [Vet. V]

**VERSES 12–14.—Do you think that God is higher than heaven and is exalted above the summits of the stars? And you say: “What does God know? He judges as though through darkness. The clouds are his hiding place; he does not consider our affairs,” and he walks around the pivots of heaven.**

### 12. An outstanding description of divine immensity and providence: God attends to everything so as to be present to each individual

Many are so dull that they know how to fear only what they see bodily. Consequently, they do not fear God, whom they cannot see. But heretics, because they consider themselves wise, utter words of mockery against Catholics and suppose that Catholics do not fear one whom they cannot see bodily.

They allege that Catholics, through sluggishness of perception, regard their Creator—because he is higher than heaven and exalted above the summits of the stars—as unable to see from so great a distance. Because atmospheric regions lie between us and the heavenly seat, they imagine him hidden in a cloud, judging through darkness, and, because he is intent on higher things, paying less attention to what is below. And while he encompasses and binds the pivots of heaven, they think that he cannot see what is within. [Note: [Col. 1125D] Later editions read “what is below” (*inferiora*); “what is within” (*interiora*), supported by the manuscripts and old editions, is greatly preferable. The contrast here is not with the lower things, already discussed, but with the inward things, which God sees even while encompassing heaven outwardly.]

But who, even if foolish, would suspect such things of God? Although he is always Almighty, he attends to everything so as to be present to each individual; and he is present to each individual in such a way that he is never absent from all at once. For even if he abandons some who sin, he is nevertheless present to those same people through judgment, although he is seen to be absent from them in the help he gives.

Thus he surrounds external things in such a way that he fills what is within; he fills what is within in such a way that he surrounds what is external; he governs the highest things without abandoning the lowest; he is present to the lowest without withdrawing from the highest; he is hidden in his appearance yet nevertheless known through his action; he is known in his work yet cannot be grasped by the understanding of the one who knows him; he is present without being able to be seen; he cannot be seen, yet his judgments themselves bear witness to his presence.

He makes himself intelligible to us, yet veils from us the ray of his own intelligibility. [Note: [Col. 1126D] Vindoc.: “the ray of his knowledge’s understanding.”] Again, he restrains us with the darkness of ignorance, yet flashes into our minds with the rays of his brightness, so that the mind, lifted up, may see something, and, struck by the reflected light, may tremble. Because it cannot see him as he is, it may nevertheless come to know him to some extent by living.

But heretics do not think that Holy Church knows these things, because in their foolish judgment they consider themselves alone to be wise. From their figure the following is further added:

### CHAPTER NINE

**VERSE 15.—Do you wish to keep to the path of the ages, which wicked men have trodden?**

### 13. Christ’s path is humility; the world’s path is pride

Just as the path of our Redeemer is humility, so the path of the ages is pride. Wicked men tread the path of the ages because they walk in arrogance through the desires of this life. Concerning these wicked people it is further said:

### CHAPTER TEN [Vet. VI, Rec. IV]

**VERSE 16.—They were taken away before their time, and a river overturned their foundation.** [Note: [Col. 1127D] Bigot. and Lyr.: “their foundations.” Utic. now likewise reads “foundations,” whereas previously it read “foundation.”]

14. The wicked are always taken away before the time they had appointed for themselves, but never die before the time appointed by God.---Since the time of our life is undoubtedly fixed in advance by divine foreknowledge, it must be carefully asked why it is now said that the wicked are removed from the present age before their proper time. [Note: Sag., with most Norman manuscripts, reads “from the present life.” Utic. has both readings.] For although almighty God often changes his sentence, he never changes his plan. Therefore each person is taken from this life at the time that, before the ages, was foreknown by divine power. But it must be understood that almighty God, creating and ordering us, determines even the limits of our lives according to the merits of each person: either that a bad man may live briefly, lest he harm many who are doing good; or that a good man may remain longer in this life, so that he may assist many in good works. [Note: Norm., “so that he may be a helper to many who are doing good.” In Utic. formerly: “so that he may be a helper to many of good work,” etc.] Or again, a bad man may be allowed to remain longer in life so that he may increase his wicked deeds, through whose temptation the just, purified, may live more truly; or a good man may be taken away sooner, lest, if he lives here for a long time, malice corrupt his innocence.

Yet it must be understood that it is God’s kindness to grant sinners a period for repentance. But because they turn the time granted not toward the fruit of repentance but toward the practice of wickedness, they lose what they might have merited from divine mercy. [Note: Utic. reads, “what they could have merited from his mercy.”]

Although almighty God foreknows that particular time of each person’s death at which his life ends, no one could have died at another time than the one at which he dies. For if fifteen years are said to have been added to Hezekiah’s life (4 Kings 20:6), the time of his life certainly increased beyond the limit at which he deserved to die. For divine providence had then foreknown the time at which it would afterward remove him from the present life.

Since this is so, what does it mean when it is said, “The wicked were taken away before their time,” except that all who love the present life promise themselves longer spans of that same life? But when death comes upon them and removes them from the present life, it cuts short the spans of their lives which they had habitually extended in their thoughts as though they would be longer. Concerning them it is rightly said: [Rec. V.] “And the river overturned their foundation.” [Note: Lyr. and most Norman manuscripts read, “their foundations,” and so throughout the rest of the chapter. Utic. formerly read, “their foundation.”]

15. The foundation of the wicked is in earthly things, that of the just in heavenly things.---Because the wicked neglect to pass in heart toward eternal things and do not perceive that all present things are fleeting, they fix their minds in love of the present life and build in it for themselves, as though for a long dwelling, a foundation; for through desire they become fixed in earthly matters.

Thus Cain is described as having first built a city on earth (Genesis 4). [Note: Lyr., Bigot., Utic., and Sag., omitting much of the intervening material, read: “because, plainly, as a stranger from higher things, he laid his foundations in lower things, he who placed the resting-place of his heart,” etc. Vindoc. likewise has this reading. All the printed editions agree among themselves.] He is plainly shown to have been a stranger, because he who was alienated from the solidity of the eternal homeland laid his foundation on earth. A stranger from higher things, he laid his foundation in lower things, placing the resting-place of his heart in earthly pleasure (St. Augustine, *City of God*, book XV, chapters 17 and 19).

Hence in his line Enoch, whose name is interpreted as “dedication,” is born first; whereas in the lineage of the elect Enoch is remembered as having been the seventh. For the reprobate dedicate themselves in this life, which comes first, by building themselves up; but the elect await the dedication of their building at the end of time, that is, in the seventh age. [Note: Utic. and Germ. read, “at the end, that is, in the seventh age.”]

You see very many people thinking only about temporal things, seeking honors, striving after possessions, and asking nothing beyond this life. What, then, do such people do except dedicate themselves in the first generation? You see the elect seeking none of the glory of the present life, [Note: Most Norman manuscripts read, “seeking none of the glory of the present life.” Vindoc. reads, “seeking none of the glory belonging to the present life.”] willingly enduring poverty, and patiently suffering the world’s evils so that they may be crowned at the end.

Thus Enoch is born for the elect in the seventh generation, because they seek the dedication of their joy in the glory of the final recompense. And because, with the daily passage of time, the mortality of the present life runs its course, and by taking away the reprobate it destroys the dedication of those same reprobate, it is rightly said of the wicked: “And the river overturned their foundation.” That is, the very course of mutability overthrows in them the stability of their perverse construction.

It continues:

CHAPTER XI.

VERSE 17.---“They said to God: Depart from us.”

16. Who would doubt that blessed Job also said this? But we avoid repeating what we have explained in his words, for fear of wearying the reader.

It continues:

THE SAME PLACE.---“And they considered him as though the Almighty could do nothing.”

[Col. 1128D] Here too the wording, but not the meaning, is changed. For what was said through blessed Job, “Who is the Almighty, that we should serve him?” (Job 21:15), is expressed here through Eliphaz as: “And they considered him as though the Almighty could do nothing.”

It continues:

CHAPTER XII [Formerly VII].

[Col. 1129A]

VERSE 18.---“Although he had filled their houses with good things.”

17. God also heaps benefits upon the wicked. For what purpose?---The Lord fills the houses of the wicked with good things because he does not deny his gifts even to the ungrateful, so that they may either blush at the goodness of their Creator and return to goodness; or, if they altogether refuse to return, may be punished more severely there because they repaid God’s more abundant gifts with evil here—so that harsher punishments may then chastise those whose wickedness was not overcome even by his gifts.

It continues:

THE SAME PLACE.---“Let their judgment be far from me.”

One thing is “judgment,” another “counsel.”---This too was said through blessed Job. For he says, “Let their counsel be far from me” (Job 21:16), although judgment and counsel can be understood as different things. Judgment is expressed by the mouth, counsel is formed in thought. Therefore, when Eliphaz wished himself far from the judgment of the wicked, while blessed Job wished himself far from their counsel, it is clearly established that the former desires to be unlike the words of the wicked, whereas the latter desires to be unlike even their thoughts.

It continues:

CHAPTER XIII [Rec. VI].

VERSE 19.---“The just will see and rejoice, and the innocent will mock them.”

18. The just now waste away over the sins of the wicked, but will one day rejoice over their destruction.---When the just see the unjust going astray here, they cannot rejoice over the error of those who are perishing. [Note: Norm. reads, “of sinners.” Utic. formerly read, “of those who perish.”] If they rejoice in their errors, they are not just. Again, if they rejoice in the insult that they themselves are not such as they see others to be, they are entirely proud. Thus the Pharisee lost his justification because, rejoicing in the merits of the tax collector, he preferred himself. [Note: Germ. and the former Utic. read, *qui publicano meritis* (“who [did so] in merits before the tax collector”).] He said: “I give you thanks because I am not like other people—robbers, unjust, adulterers—or even like this tax collector” (Luke 18:11). [Note: Germ. and Utic. read, “as the rest of mankind.”]

Again, if we say that the just can exult with perfect joy over the death of the wicked, what kind of joy over the punishment of sinners is possible in this world, in which the life of the just is still uncertain? Let us therefore distinguish the times of trembling and exultation. For now the just see the unjust and waste away over their wickedness. And when they see them struck down, [Note: The printed editions read, “see them perish.”] they also become apprehensive about their own life. When, then, will the just see the destruction of the wicked and rejoice? Only when, with perfect security, they cling to the strict Judge in exultation; when, at that final examination, they see their condemnation and have nothing more to fear concerning themselves.

Now, therefore, they look upon the reprobate and groan; then they will look upon them and mock, because they will despise in exultation those whom now they see committing iniquity not without groaning, and dying for iniquity not without fear. That this is speaking of their final damnation is shown by what follows immediately:

CHAPTER XIV [Rec. VII].

[Col. 1130A]

VERSE 20.---“Has not their rising been cut down, and has not fire devoured their remains?” [Note: Most manuscripts read, “will devour,” and continue likewise.]

19. The wicked flourish now, but will one day be cut down and punished in both flesh and soul.---Here the wicked are raised up, because they are exalted in wicked actions: they act perversely and yet are not struck for their perverse deeds. They sin and flourish; they increase their sins and multiply their earthly goods. But their rising is cut down when they are either dragged from the present life into destruction or brought from the sight of the eternal Judge into the eternal fire of Gehenna.

Although here they leave behind their dead flesh, they receive that same flesh again in the resurrection, so that they may burn with the flesh in which they sinned. For just as their guilt was in mind and body, so their punishment will likewise be in soul and body. Since even that which they leave here dead will not be free from torment, it is rightly said: “Fire devoured their remains.”

It continues:

CHAPTER XV [Formerly VIII].

VERSES 21–22.---“Therefore submit to him and have peace, and through this you will have the best fruits. Receive the law from his mouth, and place his words in your heart.”

20. The pride and presumption of heretics.---It is the fault of pride to teach one who is better, as heretics often do. [Note: Vindoc. reads, “one better than himself.”] Concerning the things they wrongly believe, they presume to teach Catholics as though they were their instructors. They think people submit to God only if they succeed in making them consent to their perversities. They promise peace to those who submit, because they cease quarreling with those who agree with them. They promise the best fruits to those who consent to them, because they suppose that only those perform good works whom they rejoice to draw over to their doctrines.

To such people also what follows applies: “Receive the law from his mouth.” For they imagine that what they themselves believe proceeds from God’s mouth: “And place his words in your heart.” As though he were openly saying: “Until now you have held them in your mouth, but not in your heart.” Because the holy Church rejects their perverse doctrines, [Note: Vindoc. reads, *respuit sancta Ecclesia, non eam* (“the holy Church rejects [them], not it”), etc.] they accuse it of having God’s words not in its understanding but merely in its display. Thus, under a kind of appearance of sweetness, they pour in the poison of a destructive persuasion, urging the Church to place God’s words in its heart. If those words had ever departed from its heart, it would never hear such things from them.

It continues:

CHAPTER XVI.

[Col. 1130D]

VERSE 23.---“If you return to the Almighty, you will be built up, and you will put iniquity far from your tent.”

21. What it means to return to God after sins and to be cleansed in thought and deed.---The heretics suppose that the faithful people have departed from God because they see them resisting their preaching. When they see them afflicted by present evils, [Note: Vindoc. reads, “they try, as though by the Creator’s admonition, to lead [them] back to grace.”] they try, as though by an admonition, to draw them back to the Creator’s grace, saying: “If you return to the Almighty, you will be built up.” As though they plainly said: “Because you have departed from the Lord by resisting our doctrines, you have therefore been destroyed with respect to the building of righteousness.”

A tent sometimes means the dwelling-place of the body, and sometimes the dwelling-place of the heart. For just as we dwell in the body through the soul, so through thoughts we dwell in the mind. Iniquity in the tent of the mind is a perverse intention in the pursuit of thought; iniquity in the tent of the body is a carnal action carried out in deed.

Therefore Eliphaz, because he had been a friend of the blessed man and held some true opinions, but nevertheless represented the heretics in those matters in which he deviated from uprightness, believed that blessed Job, whom he saw struck down, had gone astray because he did not understand that he had been scourged for his virtues. He promises him that, if he returns to the Almighty, he will put iniquity far from his tent, saying—as though he were speaking plainly: “Whoever returns to God after his errors is cleansed both in thought and in deed.”

It continues:

CHAPTER XVII [Formerly IX, Rec. VIII].

VERSE 24.---“He will give flint in place of earth, and torrents of gold in place of flint.”

22. The weak, healed by God, become strong and shine before others through teaching.---What is signified by earth except weakness in action? What by the hardness of flint except strength? What do we understand by torrents of gold except the doctrine of inward brightness?

Almighty God gives flint in place of earth to those who turn to him, because in place of weak action he grants the strength of vigorous work. He also gives torrents of gold in place of flint, because in place of strong works he multiplies the doctrine of clear preaching. Thus each sinner who is converted can become strong from weakness and, rising in his strength, reach the point of uttering words of inward brightness. In him the weakness of action, in which he was as though dissolved, is solidified by the strength of right living; and again, when understanding is drawn from life, torrents of gold flow from that very strength, because the brightness of doctrine floods the mouth of those who live well. [Note: Norm. adds after “before”: “even to the point of bringing forth.”]

It continues:

CHAPTER XVIII.

VERSE 25.---“And the Almighty will be against your enemies, and silver will be heaped up for you.”

23. When God drives away the enemies, he enriches us with the silver of divine speech.---What other enemies do we suffer more than evil spirits, who besiege us in our thoughts so that they may break into the city of our mind and hold it captive under the yoke of their dominion?

That sacred words are signified by the name “silver” the Psalmist bears witness, saying: “The words of the Lord are pure words, silver tested by fire in the earth” (Psalm 11:7). [Note: Germ., Anglic., Norm., Turon., and others have this reading. In the printed editions, “of the earth” is lacking.] Often, when we attend to sacred words, we endure the attacks of evil spirits more severely, because they scatter the dust of earthly thoughts over our minds, obscuring the eyes of our attention from the inner light of vision.

The Psalmist had endured this when he said: “Depart from me, evil ones, and I will search out the commandments of my God” (Psalm 118:115). He plainly indicates that he could not search out God’s commandments while enduring in his mind the attacks of evil spirits.

We also understand this symbolized in the deed of Isaac under the wickedness of the Philistines, who filled with heaps of earth the wells that Isaac had dug (Genesis 26:15). We dig these wells whenever we penetrate deeply into the hidden meanings of sacred Scripture. Yet the Philistines secretly fill them when, as we strive toward higher things, unclean spirits thrust earthly thoughts upon us and, as it were, remove the water of divine knowledge once discovered.

But since no one overcomes these enemies by his own strength, Eliphaz says: “The Almighty will be against your enemies, and silver will be heaped up for you.” As though it were plainly said: “When the Lord, by his own power, has driven evil spirits away from you, the bright treasure of divine speech will grow more richly within you.” [Note: Vindoc. reads, “the divinely given talent of speech,” etc. Norm. has the better reading, “the talent of divine speech in you grows more brightly.”]

It continues:

CHAPTER XIX [Formerly X, Rec. IX].

VERSE 26.---“Then you will abound in delights above the Almighty.”

24. Those who know how to discern the manifold meanings of sacred Scripture abound in delights.---To abound in delights above the Almighty is to be filled with the feasts of sacred Scripture in love of him. In its words we find as many delights as we receive varieties of understanding for our progress: sometimes bare history nourishes us; sometimes moral allegory, veiled beneath the letter of the text, refreshes us inwardly; sometimes contemplation lifts us to higher things, already flashing the light of eternity amid the darkness of the present life.

It must be understood that whoever abounds in delights is released in a certain relaxation of himself and is loosened from the labor of his activity, as though from weariness. For when the soul begins to overflow with inward delights, [Note: Norm. reads, “desires.”] it no longer consents to occupy itself with earthly works; but, seized by love of its Creator and now freed through its captivity, it sighs in failing strength to contemplate his form, and grows strong as though by becoming weary. For when it can no longer bear filthy burdens, it hastens in repose toward him whom it loves inwardly.

Hence, too, in praise of the bride it is written: “Who is this that comes up from the desert, overflowing with delights?” (Song of Songs 8:5). For holy Church could not rise from the desert of the present life to higher things unless it overflowed with the delights of God’s words. It therefore overflows with delights and rises, because, while it is nourished by mystical understandings, it is daily lifted up to contemplate the things above.

Hence the Psalmist also says: “And night is my illumination in my delights” (Psalm 138:11), because, while the studious mind is refreshed by mystical understanding, the darkness of the present life is already illuminated within it by the radiance of the coming day. Thus even in the darkness of this corruption the power of the light of the future bursts into understanding, and the mind, fed by the delights of the words, learns by foretaste what it will hunger for from the nourishment of truth.

It continues:

CHAPTER XX.

THE SAME PLACE.---“And you will lift your face to God.”

25. To lift one’s face to God is to raise a heart cleansed by repentance toward the investigation of divine things.---To lift one’s face to God is to raise the heart toward the investigation of sublime things. For just as a human being is known and visible to another through the face of the body, so we are known and visible to God through the inner image.

When we are weighed down by the guilt of sin, we fear to lift the face of our heart to God. For when it is supported by no confidence in good works, the mind trembles to look upon the highest things, because conscience itself accuses it. But when guilt has been washed away by the tears of repentance, and the deeds committed are mourned in such a way that they are no longer committed, great confidence arises in the mind, and the face of our heart is lifted to behold the joys of heavenly recompense. [Note: The Gussanville edition alone reads, “so that, by mourning, they may not be committed.”]

Eliphaz would rightly have said this if he had been admonishing a weak person. But when he despises a righteous man on account of his scourging, what else does he do than pour forth words of knowledge without understanding? If we apply these words typologically to the heretics, they promise us, through false promises, that we will lift our face to God. [Note: Norm. reads, “through those very false promises.”] As though they plainly said to the faithful people: “As long as you do not follow our preaching, you press your heart down among weak things.”

Because Eliphaz admonished blessed Job to return to God, from whom that blessed man had never departed, he continues with another promise:

CHAPTER XXI.

[Col. 1133C]

VERSE 27.---“You will pray to him, and he will hear you.”

26. Those who despise God’s commandments pray to him in vain.---They pray to the Lord but do not deserve to be heard who despise the commandments of the Lord who commands. Hence it is written: “Whoever turns his ear away so as not to hear the law, his prayer will be accursed” (Proverbs 28:9).

Therefore, as long as Eliphaz believed that blessed Job was not heard, he judged that he had gone astray in his conduct. Hence he adds:

THE SAME PLACE.---“And you will fulfill your vows.”

[Formerly XI.] When someone has made vows but cannot fulfill them because of weakness, it happens to him as a punishment for sin that the ability to do good is taken away from one who wishes to do it. But when, in the sight of the inner Judge, the guilt that obstructs him has been cleansed, it immediately comes about that ability follows the vow.

It continues:

CHAPTER XXII.

[511] VERSE 28.---“You will decide a matter, and it will come to you.”

27. False human judgments concerning adversity and prosperity.---This is usually the characteristic judgment of the weak: they consider someone as just in proportion to the extent to which they see him attain everything he desires.

Yet we know that sometimes earthly goods are withheld from the just and granted abundantly to the unjust. For physicians order desperate patients to be given whatever they ask for, while they forbid those whom they foresee can be restored to health whatever they desire.

But if Eliphaz spoke these words of spiritual gifts, it must be understood that a matter is decided and comes to pass when, by God’s generosity, the virtue sought through desire also prospers in its realization. [Note: Germ. and Norm. read, “When the Lord grants it, it also works its effect.”]

Hence it is added:

CHAPTER XXIII [Rec. X].

THE SAME PLACE.---“And light will shine on your ways.”

28. The wondrous splendor of virtue.---For light to shine on the ways of the just is for them to scatter the signs of their brightness through wondrous works of virtue, so that wherever they proceed in intention, they may drive away the night of sin from the hearts of those who observe them and pour into them the light of righteousness through the example of their conduct. [Note: The same manuscripts read, “so that wherever they proceed in intention, they may drive away, from the filth of the hearts of those who observe them, the night of sin,” etc. Bellovac. reads, “although they proceed according to their intention, from the filth of the hearts of those who observe them, the night of sin,” etc.]

But however great the righteousness of one’s conduct may be, it is nothing before the inner Judge if the swelling of the mind now exalts it. Hence it is added:

CHAPTER XXIV.

VERSE 29.---“For whoever has been humbled will be in glory, and whoever has lowered his eyes will himself be saved.”

29. The commendation of humility.---This judgment does not differ from the mouth of Truth, who says: “Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke 14:11). Hence Solomon also says: “Before he is crushed, the heart of a man is exalted; and before he is glorified, he is humbled” (Proverbs 18:12). [Note: Vindoc. reads, “before he is glorified.”]

It is rightly said: “Whoever lowers his eyes will himself be saved,” because, insofar as this can be discerned through the service of the bodily members, the first manifestation of pride usually appears in the eyes. Hence it is written: “And you will humble the eyes of the proud” (Psalm 17:28). Hence it is said of the very head of the proud: “He sees every lofty thing” (Job 41:25). Hence it is written of that creature which adhered to him through unbelief: “There is a generation whose eyes are lofty, and whose eyelids are raised high” (Proverbs 30:13). [Note: Norm. reads, “raised high.”]

To lower one’s eyes is not to despise anyone by looking down upon them, but to consider oneself lesser and inferior to all whom one sees. Therefore the one who lowers his eyes will be saved, because whoever abandons the false summit of pride ascends to the height of truth.

It continues:

CHAPTER XXV.

VERSE 30.---“The innocent will be saved; but he will be saved by the cleanness of his hands.”

30. The necessity of prevenient grace, which free will must accompany and follow.---If this judgment is understood as a promise concerning the recompense of the heavenly kingdom, [Note: Bellovac. reads *promittitur*, “is promised.”] it is supported by truth, since it is written of God: “Who will render to each according to his works” (Romans 2:6). At the final judgment, the justice of the eternal Judge saves the one whom his mercy here frees from unclean works.

But if someone is believed to be saved here by the cleanness of his hands so that he may become innocent by his own powers, there is undoubtedly error. For unless heavenly grace first comes to the one who is guilty, it will never find an innocent person to reward. Hence Moses’ truthful voice says: “No one is innocent before you by himself” (Exodus 34:7).

Therefore heavenly mercy first acts in us without us, so that, when our free will also follows, it may act with us in the good that we already desire. Yet, through the grace bestowed upon us, it rewards this at the final judgment in such a way that it is as though it had proceeded from us alone.

[Formerly XII.] Because divine goodness precedes us in order to make us innocent, Paul says: “By the grace of God I am what I am” (1 Corinthians 15:10). [Note: In the former Utic. edition it read: “and because the same grace follows our free will,” a reading corrected by an old hand. Two old Paris manuscripts, one Regius, another from Saint-Germain, and one Vatican manuscript, numbered 574 and written in the fourteenth or fifteenth century, support this reading. But all the others disagree—English, French, Vatican, and others, many of which were written at least in the ninth century, such as manuscript 575, at whose end the following verses are found:

“Part six teaches the end of this volume to resound,  
Which everywhere is divided into thrice six books.  
Granted to the altar of Saint Anastasius  
By the gift of Christ; if anyone should remove this  
Gift, may he be struck by this anathema of Jesus.  
May you lack perpetual life, surely by future death.  
John the Scribe . . . Grant, Christ, healing.”

“We have made no mention of a certain Cistercian manuscript in which this is also read: ‘and because the same grace follows our free will,’ a manuscript interpolated by the addition of many different readings and otherwise not very ancient. Opposed to it is another Cistercian manuscript, worthy of being kissed because it was written by the pious hands of the holy Cistercian monks under blessed Stephen, the first abbot of Cîteaux, as is clear from this inscription: ‘In the year of the Lord 1111, on the vigil of the Nativity of the same Lord Jesus Christ, this book finished being written, in the time of Stephen, abbot of Cîteaux.’ But what need is there for manuscript evidence to assert our reading, when another reading completely overturns the sense intended by Gregory? For here he clearly teaches that grace precedes and free will truly follows: ‘Because,’ he says, ‘divine goodness precedes us in order to make us innocent,’ and so forth. And below: he would not say ‘with me’ if free will did not follow prevenient grace.”]

And because our free will follows that same grace, he adds: “And his grace in me was not empty, but I labored more abundantly than all of them.” When he saw that in himself he was nothing, he said: “Yet not I.” But because he found that, together with grace, he was something, he added: “But the grace of God with me.” He would not say “with me” if free will did not follow prevenient grace.

Thus, to show that he was nothing without grace, he said: “Not I.” But to demonstrate that, together with grace, he had acted through free will, he added: “But the grace of God with me.” [Note: Most manuscripts read, “yet not I.”]

Therefore the innocent will be saved by the cleanness of his hands, because the one who is preceded here by the gift that makes him innocent is rewarded according to merit when he is led to judgment.

All this Eliphaz, as has been said, expressed correctly, but he did not know to whom he was speaking; [Note: Norm. reads, “because he ought not to have presumed to teach one who was better.”] for he ought not to have taught one who was better, but to have listened. Yet all these statements correspond typologically to the promises of the heretics. When they find the faithful afflicted in the present life, they suppose that they have been struck because of the guilt of unbelief, and they promise them, if they follow their doctrines, the salvation of innocence through the cleanness of good works.

But the mind of the faithful despises them all the more deeply because it does not see them possessing the innocence they promise. Hence Solomon rightly says: [Note: Bigot. and Lyr. read, “The net is spread in vain.”] “In vain is the net spread before the eyes of the winged” (Proverbs 1:17). For the winged are the spirits of the good, who, while they fly toward higher things through hope in the truth, avoid the nets of deception set by wicked people.

It continues:

CHAPTER XXVI [Rec. XI].

CHAPTER XXIII, VERSES 1–2.---“Then Job answered and said: Even now my speech is in bitterness, and the hand of my plague is heavier than my groaning.”

31. Disordered consolation increases sorrow.---In his customary manner, blessed Job begins with clearer words but completes his statements through the profound unfolding of a mystery. The pain of the afflicted ought to have been healed by consolation from his friends; but because the consolation broke out into the flattery of deceit, the afflicted man’s pain grew more intense.

For because Eliphaz did not hesitate to promise better things to one who had supposedly converted, the wound grew as though from a harmful medicine. Hence it is rightly said: “Even now my speech is in bitterness, and the hand of my plague is heavier than my groaning,” because the purpose of disordered consolation multiplied the blow which it ought to have lessened.

In these words, too, the pain of the faithful is expressed typologically through holy Church: they groan all the more when they see the wicked flatter the simple, those who, in Paul’s words, “by smooth speech and blessings deceive the hearts of the innocent” (Romans 16:18). [Note: Vindoc. reads, “when they see the wicked flatter the simple.”]

32. [Formerly XIII.] The minds of the faithful do not know how to be without bitterness.---These words can also rightly be referred to a more subtle consideration of the minds of the faithful, who do not know how to be without bitterness even if they seem to prosper in this world. When adversity also comes upon them, it doubles the pain it finds. Hence it is rightly said: [Note: Only the printed edition reads, “even now.” In order to show clearly, etc. But in our manuscripts and in the English manuscripts: “Even now my speech is in bitterness.”] “Even now my speech is in bitterness,” so that it may plainly be shown that the minds of the elect were not without bitterness even in prosperity.

It is well said: “And the hand of my plague is heavier than my groaning.” The hand of the plague is the force of the blow. The elect consider their first blow: they have been separated from the vision of their Creator; they do not fully enjoy the inward brightness of illumination, but, as though confined in a place of blindness, they groan in the exile of the present life. [Note: Vindoc. reads: “they enjoy the brightness of inward illumination on the way [reading incomplete] . . . as though in a place of necessity . . . therefore they always have the groaning of the hand of my plague.”] Therefore they always have the groaning of their plague in this hand.

But when adversities also occur in this life, the hand of their plague is made heavier than their groaning. There was groaning from the plague even when the adversities of the present life were absent. But the bitterness of the first blow increases through the trial of adversity.

He therefore says: “And the hand of my plague is heavier than my groaning,” because adversity strikes every just person in this life not into joy but into increased pain from the wound. [Note: Vindoc. reads, “the voice of joy has endured the blow.”]

Yet, by the wondrous moderation of almighty God, when the mind of the just suffers more from adversities in this world, it thirsts more intensely to behold the face of its Creator.

Hence it is appropriately added:

CHAPTER XXVII [Rec. XII].

VERSE 3.---“Who will grant me that I may know and find him, and come even to his throne?”

33. The ardor of the elect who desire to enjoy God’s presence.---Unless each of the elect had known God, he would certainly not love him. But it is one thing to know through faith and another to know through sight; one thing to find through belief and another to find through contemplation. Hence all the elect are moved to long to see by sight the one whom they have known through faith.

Burning with love of him, they are consumed with longing, because they already taste the sweetness of his goodness in the very certainty of their faith. The man healed from demons in the region of the Gerasenes aptly signifies this. He wishes to depart with Jesus, but the teacher of salvation says to him: “Return to your house and tell how great things God has done for you” (Luke 8:39).

For the one who loves, delay is imposed so that the merit of recompense may be increased through the desire produced by delayed love. Thus almighty God becomes sweet to us in miracles, yet remains hidden in his sublimity, so that by revealing something of himself he may kindle us in his love through a hidden inspiration, while by concealing the glory of his majesty he increases the power of his love through the heat of desire.

If the holy man had not sought to see him in his majesty, he would certainly not have added: “And come even to his throne.” For what is God’s throne except those angelic spirits who, as Scripture testifies, are called thrones? Therefore whoever wishes to come even to God’s throne desires nothing other than to be present among the angelic spirits, so that he may endure no more failing moments of time [Note: Germ., Bellovac., and Norm. read, “but, with glory enduring.”] but may rise in contemplation of eternity toward the glory that endures.

34. The elect revere God’s hidden judgments.---These words also apply to the just while they remain in this life. [Note: Germ. and Bellovac. read, “occur also to the just placed in this life,” a reading formerly found in Utic.] For when they see something happening contrary to their wish and desire, they have recourse to God’s hidden judgments, so that in them they may see that what appears to proceed disorderly outwardly is not ordered disorderly inwardly.

When they contemplate with the eyes of faith the Creator of all presiding over the angelic spirits, they come, as it were, to his throne. And because they consider that the one who wondrously governs the angels does not unjustly order human affairs, they undoubtedly discover how just the causal reasons are, even though the causes themselves may appear unjust externally.

While doing this humbly, they often reproach themselves for their own will and sometimes judge their own desires within themselves, considering that what the Creator arranges is better. Hence it is well added:

CHAPTER XXVIII [Rec. XIII].

[Col. 1138B]

### VERSE 4

“I will set judgment before him, and I will fill my mouth with rebukes.”

35. The elect are stirred to repentance by considering God’s hidden judgments.—To set judgment before God is, in the secret place of the mind, through the contemplation of faith, to open the eyes of our consideration upon the fearful examination of his Majesty: to attend to what sinful man deserves, and to consider how terrible the Judge, now hidden and silent, will afterward appear. By this means the soul is recalled more subtly to self-knowledge; and the more terrible it sees its hidden Judge to be, the more anxiously it is distressed over its deeds. It trembles in anguish, pursues its faults with lamentations, and rebukes in penitence the person it remembers itself to have been. Hence, after it has been said, “I will set judgment before him,” it is rightly added: “I will fill my mouth with rebukes.” For one who sets judgment before himself in God’s sight fills his mouth with rebukes, because, while contemplating against himself the subtle examination of the fearful Judge, he persecutes himself with the bitter reproach of penitence. Often, while we neglect to weigh our faults, we do not know what rebuke for them will follow at the judgment; but when we pursue them in penitence, we discover what the Judge may say to us about them in his examination.
