Hence it is aptly added:

## CHAPTER XXIX

### VERSE 5

“So that I may know the words with which he will answer me, and understand what he will say to me.”

36. By fearing God’s hidden judgments, the elect escape them.—We lament our faults when we begin to weigh them. But we weigh them more penetratingly when we lament them more earnestly; and from our lamentation there arises more fully in our hearts an awareness of what divine severity threatens sinners:

[Note: [Column 1138D] Perhaps “is more fully known” would be better. Certainly, in Vindoc. we read: “is more fully recognized what it is that threatens sinners.” We have not presumed to alter the reading found in the printed editions and in almost all the manuscripts.] what reproaches the reprobate will face, what terror, what implacable rejection by Majesty.

[Note: [Column 1138D] Thus in the German, Norman, Vindoc., and Bellovac. witnesses. In all printed editions, “reproof.” Gussanville nevertheless notes that it is read elsewhere as “aversion” or “turning against.”]

For then the Lord will say, in his anger toward the reprobate, as much as in his equity he allowed them to do unjustly.

[Note: [Column 1139D] Vindoc.: “as much as he permitted them, in his equanimity, to do unjustly.”]

These words of that reproof they escape, for the present, by fearing them carefully. But who could be found righteous in that examination, if God were to scrutinize human life according to the Majesty of his strength? Accordingly, it is aptly added:

## CHAPTER XXX [Old recension XV, Recension XIV]

### VERSE 6

“I do not want him to contend with me with great strength, nor crush me under the weight of his greatness.”

37. Those who fear God’s strength desire his weakness assumed in human nature.—For the mind of any righteous person, if it is judged strictly by the almighty Lord, is crushed beneath the weight of his greatness.

[Note: [Column 1139D] Vindoc.: “of any righteous person.”]

In these words we should also understand that, when the holy man avoids God’s strength, what else does he desire than his weakness? And it is written: “What is weak in God is stronger than human beings” (1 Corinthians 1:25). Hence he immediately adds:

### VERSE 7

“Let him set equity against me, and my judgment will attain victory.”

For who else is designated by the name “equity” except “the mediator of God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Timothy 2:5)? Of him it is written: “Who was made for us wisdom from God, and righteousness” (1 Corinthians 1:30). When this righteousness came into the world against the ways of sinners, we conquered the ancient enemy by whom we were held captive.

Let him therefore say: “I do not want him to contend with me with great strength, nor crush me under the weight of his greatness; let him set equity against me, and my judgment will attain victory.” That is: let him send the incarnate Son to refute my ways, and then, by the judgment of my acquittal, I will victoriously drive out the adversary who lies in wait.

For if the only-begotten Son of God had remained invisible in the strength of his divinity, receiving nothing of our weakness, when could weak humanity have found access to him by grace? The perceived weight of his greatness would have overwhelmed rather than helped us. But he appeared weak amid all things, although strong above all things, so that, by becoming suited to us through the weakness he assumed, he might raise us to his enduring strength.

[Note: [Column 1139D] We have already observed this manner of speaking in our Gregory. See above, book XV, formerly chapter 10, now 16, no. 20, and book II, no. 60.]

In the height of his divinity he could not be grasped by us, who are like little ones; but through his humanity he laid himself down before human beings, and, as though upon one lying down, we climbed up. He rose, and we were lifted up.

[Note: [Column 1139D] Turon., Norm., and Anglic. read: “not through humility,” unlike the printed editions. In Gilot., the margin notes another reading: “through humanity.”]

Hence the following is also immediately added, by which his invisible and incomprehensible divinity is demonstrated. For it follows:

## CHAPTER XXXI [Recension XV]

### VERSES 8–9

“If I go to the east, he does not appear; if to the west, I will not understand him; if to the left, what shall I do? I will not grasp him; if I turn to the right, I will not see him.”

38. God is invisible and incomprehensible; he must be sought not in one part but everywhere.—The Creator of all is not in one part, because he is everywhere. And he is found less when he who is wholly everywhere is sought in one part. For the uncircumscribed Spirit contains all things within himself; yet by filling them he surrounds them, by surrounding them he fills them, by sustaining them he transcends them, and by transcending them he sustains them.

After it was rightly said, “If I go to the east, he does not appear; if to the west, I will not understand him; if to the left, what shall I do? I will not grasp him; if I turn to the right, I will not see him,” he immediately added: “But he himself knows my way.” As though he openly said: “I cannot see him who sees me, and I cannot look upon him who observes me with such subtlety.” Thus he shows that he is to be feared all the more cautiously because he cannot be seen. For the one who looks upon us in such a way that he cannot be looked upon by us is more greatly to be feared, the less he is seen while seeing everything.

When we believe that someone is lying in wait against us, we fear him more the less we see him. And when we cannot at all detect where his ambushes are, we fear them where they are not. But our Creator, who is wholly everywhere and sees all things without being seen, is to be feared all the more because, while remaining invisible, we do not know when or what he determines concerning our deeds.

These words, however, can also be understood in another way. We go toward the east when we raise our mind in contemplation of his Majesty. But he does not appear, because what he is in his nature cannot be seen by mortal thought.

[Note: [Column 1140D] All the Norman witnesses: “cannot be seen by mortal thought.”]

“If to the west, I will not understand him.”

[Old recension XVI.]

We go toward the west when, after the eye of the heart has been lifted toward God but reflected back by the very immensity of the light, we bring it back to ourselves. Weary, we learn that what we were seeking is far above us; and, considering our mortality, we discover that we are still unworthy to see the immortal one.

[Note: [Column 1140D] Ebroic. and other Norman witnesses: “whom we wanted to see.” Formerly in Utic.: “that we may be able to see.”]

“If to the left, what shall I do? I will not grasp him.”

To go to the left is to consent to the pleasures of sins. And it is clear that the one who still lies on the left in the pleasure of sin cannot grasp God.

“If I turn to the right, I will not see him.”

Undoubtedly, the one who is elated by virtues turns to the right. But the one who rejoices in good works with private satisfaction cannot see God, because the swelling of pride weighs down the eye of the heart within him. Hence it is well said elsewhere: “You shall not turn aside to the right or to the left” (Deuteronomy 17:11).

[Note: [Column 1140D] Vindoc.: “nor shall you turn aside.” Norm.: “lest you turn aside.”]

In all these things the soul often examines itself, yet cannot fully apprehend itself. Hence it is aptly added here:

## CHAPTER XXXII

### VERSE 10

“But he himself knows my way.”

39. God examines the ways of the righteous and tests them.—As though he plainly said: “I examine myself strictly, yet cannot know myself perfectly; nevertheless, he whom I cannot see observes subtly everything I do.” It follows:

“He will test me like gold that passes through fire.”

[Note: [Column 1141D] Bigot., Sag., Lyr.: “and he tested me.”]

Gold advances toward the brightness of its nature in the furnace when it loses its impurities. Thus the souls of the righteous are tested like gold passing through fire: through the burning of tribulation, their vices are removed and their merits increased.

Nor was it pride for the holy man, placed in tribulation, to compare himself with gold. He who had been called righteous by God’s voice before the blows was not permitted to be tested so that his vices might be purged, but so that his merits might increase; gold, however, is purified by fire. He therefore thought less of himself than he was when, handed over to tribulation, he believed that he was being purified, although he had nothing in himself requiring purification.

40. However humble the righteous may be, they do not ignore their good works.—It should be understood that, although the minds of the righteous think humbly of themselves, they nevertheless perceive how upright are the things they do; but they do not presume upon their uprightness. Hence it is further added:

“His foot has followed his footsteps; I have guarded his way and have not turned aside from it. I have not departed from the commandments of his lips, and I have hidden the words of his mouth in my bosom.”

But let us see whether, amid all these things, he thinks himself to be anything. It follows: “For he alone is.”

[Recension XVI.]

By adding this sentence, he shows that amid all the many good things he had done, he considered himself nothing. Let us therefore repeat the words given above and touch upon them as we are able.

## CHAPTER XXXIII

### VERSE 11

“His foot has followed his footsteps.”

41. We should imitate God’s patience and compassion; Christ’s examples are to be followed.—His works are, as it were, certain steps of God, which we see: works by which every good and wicked person is governed, by which the righteous and unrighteous are arranged according to their respective orders, by which each subordinate person is daily led toward better things, and by which the adversary, falling toward worse things, is nevertheless tolerated.

[Note: [Column 1141D] Vindoc.: “his works by which every good person is helped and every wicked person governed.”]

Concerning these steps the Prophet said: “Your steps have been seen, O God” (Psalm 67:25). Therefore, when we behold the virtue of his patience and compassion, and strive to imitate it as we behold it, what else are we doing than following the traces of his steps?

[Note: [Column 1141D] Vindoc.: “because we imitate certain outward works of his.” This is what the Truth urged his disciples to imitate.]

For the Truth urged us to imitate these steps of his Father when he said: “Pray for those who persecute and slander you, so that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven, who makes his sun rise upon the evil and the good” (Matthew 5:45; Luke 6:28).

[Old recension XVII.]

Yet blessed Job, who had already said with certain faith, “I know that my Redeemer lives, and on the last day I shall rise from the earth” (Job 19:25), may have looked toward the future work of the Wisdom who was to become incarnate, just as we, by faith, see the past works of that same Wisdom: that the mediator of God and human beings was kind in giving, humble in enduring, and patient in offering an example.

When blessed Job, filled with heavenly Spirit, observed his life with attentive concentration, foreseeing the future humility of his gentleness, he turned, as it were, to the example set before him, so that whatever he did in this life he might bind to the traces of that imitation. Thus, unable to see the sublime things of his hidden ordering, he might, as though seeing him on earth, hold fast to his footprints in imitation.

Of these footprints Peter says: “Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example, so that you might follow his footsteps” (1 Peter 2:21). Concerning him it is further added:

## CHAPTER XXXIV

### SAME PASSAGE

“I have guarded his way and have not turned aside from it.”

42. The concern of the righteous is to observe the ways of truth.—He guards and does not turn aside who acts in accordance with what he has set before himself. To guard through intention is not to turn aside through action.

This is the concern of the righteous: to examine their actions daily according to the ways of truth, and, setting those ways before themselves as a rule, not to turn aside from their path of uprightness. They strive to rise daily above themselves, and, as they are advanced to the summit of virtues, they judge with careful reproach whatever remains of themselves beneath themselves. They hasten to draw their whole selves to the place where they find that they have arrived only in part.

It follows:

## CHAPTER XXXV

### VERSE 12

“I have not departed from the commandments of his lips.”

43. Another concern of the righteous is to search out God’s will in the Scriptures.—Just as servants who faithfully obey their masters are always attentive to their faces, so that they may quickly hear what they command and strive to fulfill it,

[Note: [Column 1142D] Most Norman witnesses: “are always gazing upon their faces, so that they may hear quickly.”]

so the minds of the righteous attend upon the almighty Lord through their intention. In his Scripture they look, as it were, upon his mouth, because God speaks through it everything he wills; therefore, they depart from his will all the less insofar as they recognize that same will in his word.

Consequently, his words do not pass uselessly through their ears, but they fix them in their hearts. Hence it is added here:

## CHAPTER XXXVI

[Column 1143A]

### SAME PASSAGE

“And I have hidden the words of his mouth in my bosom.”

44. To hide God’s words in one’s bosom is another concern of the righteous.—We hide the words of his mouth in the bosom of the heart when we hear his commandments not merely in passing, but as commandments to be fulfilled in action.

Hence it is written of the Virgin Mother herself: “But Mary kept all these words, pondering them in her heart” (Luke 2:19). These words, even when they come forth into action, remain hidden in the bosom of the heart if the inner spirit of the one acting is not lifted up by what is done outwardly.

For when a conceived word is brought into action, if human praise is sought through it, the word of God is certainly not hidden in the bosom of the mind. But I should like to know, blessed man, why you examine yourself with such great attention, why you bind yourself with such great care. It follows:

## CHAPTER XXXVII [Old recension XVIII]

### VERSE 13

“For he alone is, and no one can turn aside his thought.”

[Note: [Column 1143D] Most witnesses: “his thoughts.”]

45. God alone is; in comparison with his essence, our being is nonbeing.—Are there not angels and human beings, heaven and earth, air and seas, all flying creatures, four-footed animals,

[Note: [Column 1143D] Utic., Lyr., Bigot., etc.: “and creeping things, and the rest of what Scripture says he created.”]

and creeping things? And certainly it is written: “He created all things so that they might exist” (Genesis 2:3 and following). Since there are so many things in the nature of reality, why does the blessed man’s voice now say: “For he alone is”?

But it is one thing to exist, and another to exist principally; one thing to exist mutably, and another to exist immutably. All these things exist, but they do not exist principally, because they scarcely subsist in themselves; and unless they are held by the hand of the one who governs, they cannot exist at all.

For all things subsist in him by whom they were created. Neither do living things give life to themselves, nor are things that move, though they do not live, brought into motion by their own impulses. Rather, he moves all things: he gives life to some, while wondrously ordering and preserving others, which are not living, in the lowest order of being.

All things were made from nothing, and their essence would again tend toward nothing unless the author of all things held it by the hand of his governance. Therefore, none of the things that have been created can subsist or move by itself; they subsist insofar as they have received being, and they move insofar as they are directed by a hidden impulse.

For example, a sinner is to be scourged through human affairs: the earth withers through his labors, the sea is shaken through his shipwrecks, the air burns in his sweat, heaven grows dark against him through floods, human beings burn with anger in his oppression, and even the angelic powers are moved in his adversity.

[Note: [Column 1143D] That is, by opposing him. The meaning of this word has already often been discussed. See above, book XI, no. 38, and book II, no. 51.]

Are these inanimate or living things agitated by their own impulses rather than by divine movements? Whatever therefore rages outwardly, through it he must be observed who inwardly directs it.

[Note: [Column 1144D] Norm. and Germ.: “he is to be feared.”]

In every matter, therefore, only he is to be observed who exists principally. He also says to Moses: “I am who I am. Thus you shall say to the children of Israel: ‘He who is has sent me to you’” (Exodus 3:14).

When, therefore, we are scourged through the things we see, we must carefully fear him whom we do not see. The holy man should therefore disregard whatever terrifies outwardly, whatever, unless governed, would tend toward nothing according to its own essence; and, with all these things subdued, he should look with the eye of his mind upon the one alone in comparison with whose essence our being is nonbeing, and say: “For he alone is.”

519 [Recension XVII.]

46. God is unchangeable in nature and will.—Concerning his immutability it is immediately and aptly added: “And no one can turn aside his thought.”

[Note: [Column 1144D] Norm.: “his thoughts.”]

For just as his nature is immutable, so is his will.

[Note: [Column 1144D] Lyr., Bigot., Ebroic., Sag.: “immutable in thought”; Germ.: “of his thought.” Vindoc.: “For just as his nature is immutable, so is his will.”]

No one turns aside his thought, because no one can resist his hidden judgments. For even if some seemed to have turned aside his thought by their prayers, his inward thought was such that, by praying, they could turn aside his sentence and receive from him what they were to do before him.

Let him therefore say: “And no one will be able to turn aside his thought,” because judgments once fixed cannot in any way be changed. Hence it is written: “He issued a command, and it shall not pass away” (Psalm 148:6); and again: “Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away” (Mark 13:31); and again: “For my thoughts are not your thoughts, nor are your ways my ways” (Isaiah 55:8).

Although the sentence may appear to change outwardly, the inward counsel is not changed, because concerning each matter whatever is done outwardly in a mutable way is established inwardly immutably.

It follows:

## CHAPTER XXXVIII [Old recension XIX, Corrected recension XVIII]

### SAME PASSAGE

“And his soul—whatever he willed, that he did.”

47. Even those things that seem to happen against God’s will do not resist him.—Although God is external to all bodies and interior to all minds, that very power of his by which he penetrates and orders all things is called his soul.

Nothing resists his will—not even those things that appear to happen against his will—for he sometimes permits what he does not command to happen so that, through it, what he commands may be fulfilled more certainly.

The perverse will of the apostate angels is indeed evil, yet it is wondrously ordered by God, so that even their snares serve the benefit of the good, whom they purify while they test them.

Thus his soul did whatever he willed, so that he fulfills his will even through that by which his will seemed to be opposed. Let the righteous man therefore be afraid, and, considering the weight of such great Majesty, recognize that he is weak.

48. Yet amid these words it is tempting to ask and say: “O blessed Job, placed amid so many blows, why do you still fear adversity? You are already surrounded by tribulations; you are already distressed by countless afflictions. What has not yet been endured should be feared; placed in such great suffering, what do you fear?”

But behold, the righteous man, answering our questions, adds:

## CHAPTER XXXIX

### VERSE 14

“When he has fulfilled his will in me, many other similar things are also ready for him.”

49. From what we suffer we learn to fear what we have not yet suffered.—As though he openly said: “I already weigh what I am suffering, but I still fear what I may suffer. He fulfills his will in me because he afflicts me with many blows.”

[Note: [Column 1145D] The printed editions read “persecutions”; the Norman and other manuscripts do not.]

“But many other similar things are ready for him,” because if he intends to strike, he still finds where the blow may increase.

From this we should consider how fearful he was before the scourge, since even after being struck he still feared that he might be struck again. Considering that an incomprehensible force of power and judgment was in him, the righteous man did not wish to regard himself as secure, even from the scourge.

Hence, still fearing, he adds:

## CHAPTER XL

### VERSE 15

“And therefore I am troubled by his face, and when I consider him, I am disturbed by fear.”

50. While the wicked display security, the righteous always fear.—He is rightly troubled by the face of the Lord who sets the terror of his Majesty before the eyes of his heart, and is shaken by fear of his uprightness when he sees that he is not fit to render an account if he is judged strictly.

It is rightly said: “And when I consider him, I am disturbed by fear,” because when someone does not consider the force of divine reproof, he does not fear it; and he is all the more secure in this life as he is more alien from consideration of inward strictness.

The righteous always return to the inner chamber of the heart,

[Note: [Column 1145D] Vindoc.: “when they behold the force of hidden strictness.”]

behold the force of hidden strictness, and stand before the judgment of inward Majesty, so that they may one day be more secure precisely because, as long as they lived here, they did not wish to be secure.

For when the minds of the wicked refuse to consider what they should fear, they eventually arrive joyfully at what they could never escape by fearing. But we know of blessed Job that he was devoted to frequent sacrifices to God, devoted to hospitality, generous toward the needs of the poor, humble even toward his subjects, and kind toward those who opposed him. Yet he received so many scourges and was not secure even amid the scourges; he still feared and, considering the force of divine strictness, still trembled.

What then shall we wretched sinners say, if one who acted in this way fears in this way? But whether he has the weight of such great fear from himself, the text makes known. It follows:

## CHAPTER XLI [Old recension XX]

### VERSE 16

“God has softened my heart, and the Almighty has troubled me.”

51. This fear is a gift of God.—The heart of the righteous is said to be softened by a divine gift,

[Note: [Column 1145D] Vindoc.: “is called soft.”]

because it is penetrated by fear of the heavenly judgment. What can be penetrated is soft; what cannot be penetrated is hard. Hence Solomon says: “Blessed is the person who is always fearful, but whoever is hard of heart will fall into evil” (Proverbs 28:14).

He therefore attributes the virtue of his fear not to himself but to its author when he says: “God has softened my heart, and the Almighty has troubled me.”

The hearts of the good are not secure but troubled, because, when they consider the weight of the future examination, they do not desire to have rest here; they disturb their security by considering inward strictness.

Yet amid the very torments of fear they often turn their minds back to the gifts they have received. To refresh themselves with consolation,

[Note: [Column 1145D] Vindoc.: “with sound consolation.”]

they direct their gaze amid what they fear toward the gifts they have received,

[Note: [Column 1145D] Ebroic. and other Norman witnesses: “toward the good things they have received.”]

so that hope may lift up the one whom fear presses down. Hence it follows:

## CHAPTER XLII [Recension XIX]

[Column 1146B]

### VERSE 17

“For I have not perished because of the darkness that threatens, nor has gloom covered my face.”

52. The scourges of the righteous either cleanse sins already committed or prevent future ones.—A person placed under the scourge perishes from bodily health because of the darkness that threatens when he is struck for past sins so that he may be hidden from future punishments.

The scourges of the good either cleanse sins already committed or prevent those that might have been committed. But blessed Job, because, placed under the scourge, he was neither being cleansed from previous sins nor being sheltered from impending ones, but his virtue alone was being increased through the scourge, says confidently: “I have not perished because of the darkness that threatens, nor has gloom covered my face.”

For he who always beheld the weight of divine fear did not have the face of his heart covered by the gloom of sin. And the one whom no punishments followed did not lose bodily health because of the darkness that threatened.

53. No one is free from evil thoughts.—It should be noted that, although he announces earlier things,

[Note: [Column 1145D] Turon.: “earlier things.” In Ebroic. and the other Norman witnesses, “higher things” is read instead of “earlier things.” In the old Utic. manuscript, however, “earlier things” was formerly written.]

he does not say, “It did not touch my face,” but, “Gloom did not cover it.”

For often thoughts that arise also stain the hearts of the righteous and touch them with the pleasures of earthly things,

[Note: [Column 1146D] Turon.: “touch them with pleasures.”]

but when they are quickly driven away by the hand of holy discernment,

[Note: [Column 1146D] Norm.: “of holy strictness.”]

care is promptly taken that gloom not cover the face of the heart, which had already been touching it through unlawful pleasure.

For often, during the very sacrifice of prayer, intrusive thoughts thrust themselves in, thoughts capable of snatching away or defiling what we offer to God with tears within us. Hence, when Abraham offered a sacrifice at sunset, he endured the birds that swooped down upon it and diligently drove them away so that they would not snatch the sacrifice that had been offered (Genesis 15:11).

So, when we offer a holocaust to God on the altar of the heart, let us guard it from unclean birds, lest evil spirits and perverse thoughts snatch away what our mind hopes profitably to offer to the Lord.

It follows:

## CHAPTER XLIII [Old and Recension XX]

[Column 1147A]

### CHAPTER 24, VERSE 1

“Times are not hidden from the Almighty; but those who know him do not know his days.”

54. God’s days are his eternity; God is what he possesses.—What are God’s days except his very eternity? Sometimes it is expressed by the designation of a single day, as it is written: “One day in your courts is better than thousands” (Psalm 83:11). At other times, because of its length, it is signified by the designation of many days, concerning which it is written: “Your years are for generation upon generation” (Psalm 101:25).

We are carried within times because we are creatures. But God, who is the Creator of all, comprehends our times in his eternity. He therefore says: “Times are not hidden from the Almighty; but those who know him do not know his days.” For he sees our times in a way that can be comprehended, whereas we are utterly unable to comprehend what belongs to him.

But since God’s nature is simple, it is very surprising that he says: “Those who know him do not know his days.” For he himself is not one thing and his days another. God is what he possesses. He possesses eternity, but he himself is eternity. He possesses light, but he himself is his own light. He possesses splendor, but he himself is his own splendor. Therefore, in him being and possessing are not different.

What, then, does it mean to say, “Those who know him do not know his days,” except that even those who know him still do not know? For those who already hold him by faith still do not know him by sight. And although he himself is eternity, whom we truly believe, we nevertheless do not know how his eternity itself exists.

In this, however, that we hear about the power of the divine nature, we customarily think of things that we know by experience. Everything that begins and ends is enclosed by a beginning and an end. If it is delayed for some interval before reaching its end, it is called long; and when someone turns the eyes of the mind backward through memory and stretches them forward through expectation, he expands it in his mind as though through a span of time.

When he hears of God’s eternity, he proposes, in human fashion, long stretches of life to his attentive mind, in which he may measure both what has passed behind him, to be retained in memory, and what remains ahead, to be awaited with attention.

55. In eternity there is neither past nor future.—But whenever we think of eternity in this way, we have not yet understood eternity. For there is that which neither begins with a beginning nor ends with an end; there nothing is awaited that will come, and nothing passes away that must be remembered. Rather, there is one thing whose being is always being.

Although we and the angels begin to see this being when we begin to exist, we nevertheless see it as being without beginning. There being is always without end, so that the mind never stretches itself toward what follows, as though what exists were multiplied and became extended.

For although it is said through the spirit of prophecy, “Lord, you who reign forever, and throughout the age, and beyond” (perhaps Exodus 15:18, where it reads: “The Lord will reign forever [Hebrew: throughout the age] and beyond”), the Spirit spoke to human beings in human fashion, according to the manner of sacred speech, saying “beyond” where there is no expectation.

[Note: [Column 1148D] Germ.: “where expectation would be present.”]

Eternity does not have a “beyond,” for it always possesses being. No part of its length passes away so that another part may follow; rather, it is wholly present at once, so that nothing appears to be lacking that it does not behold. In it, the mind sees everything that is, both as not being slow and as being extended.

But in speaking of the days of eternity, we are attempting more to see something than we actually see. Therefore it is rightly said: “Those who know him do not know his days,” because, although we already know God through faith, we do not see what his eternity is like: without a past before the ages, without a future after the ages, without lengthy duration, and without perpetual anticipation.

Blessed Job, therefore, representing the type of holy Church, restrains himself under the great bridle of knowledge, lest he be wise beyond what he ought to be wise. While testifying that God’s days cannot be comprehended, he immediately turns the attention of his mind toward the pride of heretics, who desire to think lofty thoughts and boast that they perfectly know what they cannot in any way grasp. For it follows:

## CHAPTER XLIV [Recension XXI]

### VERSE 2

“Others have moved the boundaries; they have seized flocks and pastured them.”

56. Heretics move the boundaries established by the fathers.—Whom does he designate by the name “others” except heretics, who exist as outsiders from the bosom of holy Church?

They move the boundaries because, by transgressing the constitutions of the fathers, they overstep them. Concerning these constitutions it is written: “Do not move the ancient boundaries that your fathers established” (Proverbs 22:28).

They seize flocks and pasture them because they draw the inexperienced to themselves by perverse persuasions and nourish them with poisonous doctrines for slaughter.

[Old recension XXII.]

That inexperienced peoples are signified by the name “flocks” is attested by the bridegroom’s words when he addresses his bride: “Unless you know yourself, O beautiful among women, go out and depart after the footsteps of the flocks” (Song of Songs 1:7). That is: unless, by living well, you recognize your dignity, by which you were created in the likeness of God, depart from the sight of my contemplation and imitate the life of inexperienced peoples.

It follows:

## CHAPTER XLV

### VERSE 3

“They drove away the ass of the orphans and took the widow’s ox as a pledge.”

57. The orphans are the elect.---Whom do we understand here by “orphans” except God’s elect, placed in the tenderness of their minds, who are nourished by the great grace of faith but do not yet see the face of their Father, who has already died for them? There are many in the Church who see certain people aspiring to heavenly things and holding all earthly things in contempt; and although they themselves labor amid the burdens of this world, they nevertheless provide those whom they see yearning for heavenly things with the assistance of this life from the possessions they have in this world. Although they themselves cannot perform spiritual works, they gladly furnish support to those striving toward the heights. For a donkey is accustomed to carry human burdens. Thus, in a certain sense, the donkey of the elect is one who, serving earthly activities, carries burdens for human use. And often, when heretics turn such a person away from the bosom of the holy Church, they drive away the donkey of the orphans, because when they drag him over to their faithlessness, they remove him from the service of good works.

[Note: Vindoc., Germ., and all the Norman manuscripts: “who serve earthly possessions.”]

[Col. 1149B] 58. The widow is the Church.---But whom should we understand as the widow except the holy Church, which is meanwhile deprived of the sight of her slain husband? The ox of this widow is each preacher. It often happens that heretics, through their perverse doctrines, draw away even those who appeared to be preachers. They therefore take away the widow’s ox when they remove even a preacher from the holy Church. It is rightly added: “As a pledge.” For when a pledge is taken, one thing is indeed held, but something else is still being sought. Heretics commonly try to take away those who preach in order that they may also draw away their followers. The widow’s ox is therefore taken as a pledge when the preacher himself is seized for the purpose of making others follow. From his ruin it often comes about that those too leave the bosom of the holy Church who within it appeared, by their good conduct, to be gentle and humble. Hence it is also added:

## CHAPTER XLVI

**VERSE 4.**---They have subverted the way of the poor and have likewise oppressed the meek of the earth.

59. By “the poor,” the humble are to be understood.---The name “poverty” often signifies humility. Sometimes those who appear gentle and humble, if they do not know how to preserve discernment, fall through the examples of others. There are, however, certain heretics who avoid mixing with the people but seek the retreat of a more secluded life. They generally infect those whom they find with the plague of their persuasion all the more deeply because they appear, as though on account of the merits of their life, more worthy of reverence. Concerning them it is added:

## CHAPTER XLVII [Old recension XXIII, revised recension XXII]

**VERSE 5.**---Others, like wild asses, go out into the desert to their work.

60. Heretics resemble wild asses. They carry out not God’s work but their own.---A wild ass is a wild donkey. Heretics are rightly compared here with wild asses, because, abandoned to their own pleasures, they are estranged from the bonds of faith and reason.

[Note: Thus the Norman, Vindoc., and Tours manuscripts, as well as the old edition. The more recent editors preferred: “in their own desires.”]

Hence it is written: “A wild ass accustomed to the wilderness, in the desire of its soul, drew in the wind of its love” (Jeremiah 2:24). The wild ass is accustomed to the wilderness because, since it does not cultivate the soil of its heart through the power of discipline, it dwells where there is no fruit. It draws in the wind of its love in the desire of its soul because the things it conceives in its mind out of a desire for knowledge have the power to inflate rather than to build up. Against such people it is said: “Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up” (1 Corinthians 8:1).

Hence here too it is appropriately added: “They go out to their work.” For they carry out not God’s work but their own, since they follow not sound doctrines but their own desires. For it is written: “He who walks in the blameless way was serving me” (Psalm 100:6). Whoever, therefore, does not walk in the blameless way serves himself more than the Lord.

It follows:

## CHAPTER XLVIII

[Col. 1150B] **The same passage.**---They keep watch for prey; they prepare bread for their children.

61. Heretics keep watch for prey.---They keep watch for prey who always try to snatch the words of the righteous into their own interpretation, so that through them they may prepare the bread of error for perverse children.

[Note: Vindoc., “may provide.”]

Concerning this bread, Solomon says through the words of a woman representing the type of heretical perversity: “Stolen waters are sweeter, and hidden bread is more pleasant” (Proverbs 9:17).

It follows:

## CHAPTER XLIX

**VERSE 6.**---They reap a field that is not their own, and they harvest the vineyard of the one whom they have oppressed by force.

62. Heretics lay waste to a field that is not their own and to another’s vineyard.---The breadth of sacred Scripture can be signified by the name “field.” Heretics reap it though it is not theirs, because from it they take statements entirely different from their own understanding. It is also expressed under the name “vineyard,” because through the words of truth it produces clusters of virtues. They oppress the lord of this vineyard—that is, the author of sacred Scripture—as though by force, because they violently strive to bend his meaning toward the words of sacred eloquence. He says: “You have made me serve in your sins; you have given me labor in your iniquities” (Isaiah 43:24). They harvest that same vineyard because from it they heap up clusters of interpretations according to the intention of their own understanding.

[Note: Ebroic., “of teachings.”]

The universal Church can also be signified by the name “field” or “vineyard.” Perverse preachers harvest it and harvest its author by oppressing him in his members, because, while persecuting the grace of our Creator, when they seize from it certain people who appeared upright, what else do they take away than ears of grain or clusters of souls?

Concerning them it is further added:

## CHAPTER L

**VERSE 7.**---They leave people naked, taking away their garments, who have no covering in the cold.

63. By destroying good works, heretics leave people naked.---Just as clothing protects the body, so good works protect the soul. Hence it is said to a certain person: “Blessed is the one who watches and keeps his garments, lest he walk naked” (Revelation 16:15). Therefore, when heretics destroy good works in certain minds, they plainly remove the coverings of garments. It is rightly said: “Who have no covering in the cold.” The covering pertains to righteousness, while the cold pertains to guilt.

There are some who commit sins in certain matters but follow right conduct in others. Whoever, therefore, sins through some actions and practices righteousness through others—what is such a person except one clothed in the cold? He is cold and covered, because through one work he grows warm toward righteousness, while through another he grows cold toward guilt. But when heretics take good works away from such people, they ensure that in the cold they have nothing with which to clothe themselves. It is therefore rightly said: “They leave people naked, taking away their garments, who have no covering in the cold,” so that only the cold of guilt may destroy those whom the warmth of another work had partly covered.

[Old recension XXIV.]

The cold can also signify desire, and clothing can signify action. There are many who still burn with perverse desires but, spiritually waging war against themselves, oppose them with right works and cover with good actions what they feel arising within them on the left through temptation. Thus, in the very things through which they desire evil they are cold, while in the things through which they do good they are clothed. But when heretics, through perverse arguments, take away the works of right faith, what do they accomplish except that those who still feel the cold of carnal desires die without the clothing of good works?

It follows:

## CHAPTER LI

**VERSE 8.**---Those whom the rains of the mountains water embrace stones, having no covering.

[Col. 1151C] 64. We are watered by the sayings of the holy Fathers as by flowing streams. The invocation of the holy martyrs.---The rains of the mountains are the words of teachers. Of these mountains it is said in the voice of the holy Church: “I lifted up my eyes to the mountains” (Psalm 121:1). These rains of the mountains therefore water them because the streams of the holy Fathers satisfy them.

As we have already said, we understand the covering as the protection of good works, by which a person is covered so that the ugliness of his wickedness may be concealed before the eyes of almighty God. Hence it is written: “Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven and whose sins are covered” (Psalm 32:1).

But whom do we understand by the name “stones” except strong men within the holy Church? To them the chief Shepherd says: “You yourselves, like living stones, are being built up” (1 Peter 2:5). Those who place no confidence in any work of their own run to the protection of the holy martyrs, devote themselves with tears to their sacred bodies, and pray that they may obtain pardon through the martyrs’ intercession. What, then, are such people doing in this humility except that, having no covering of good action, they embrace stones?

It follows:

## CHAPTER LII [Revised recension XXIII]

**VERSE 9.**---They use force while plundering orphans, and they strip the poor common people.

[Note: Recent edition: “and the poor common people,” although the manuscripts and old editions resist this reading.]

65. Heretics hunt down the weak and unlearned, both by force and by flattery.---When heretics do not possess the prosperity of the present life, they persuade weak minds of perverse things with flattering words. But if some prosperity of the present age smiles upon them, they do not cease to drag away by force those whom they are able to overpower.

The name “orphans” therefore designates those who are still tender and established within the holy Church. Their merciful Father preserved their life by dying; they have already been led to a good intention but are not yet strengthened by any virtue in good works. Heretics therefore use force while plundering orphans, because they attack the weak minds of the faithful with violence in word and deed.

The poor common people are the unlearned populace, who, if they possessed the riches of true wisdom, would by no means lose the garment of their faith. Within the holy Church there are, as it were, certain senators—true teachers—who, as they multiply knowledge in their hearts, abound in true riches.

[Note: Thus the English manuscripts and ours. In the old Paris and Basel editions: “learned men”; in others: “more learned men.”]

But heretics strip the poor common people, because, unable to overcome the learned, they strip the unlearned of the covering of faith through their pestilential preaching.

It follows:

## CHAPTER LIII [Old recension XXV]

**VERSE 10.**---From the naked, walking without clothing, and from the hungry, they took away ears of grain.

66. Heretics take away the teaching of the holy Fathers from the idle and unwary.---What he says by “the naked,” he repeats by “walking without clothing.” But it is one thing to be naked and another to walk naked. Everyone who does neither good nor evil is naked and idle; but whoever does evil walks naked, because he proceeds along the road of wickedness without the covering of good works.

[Note: Lyr. and many others: “of his wickedness.”]

There are some, however, who recognize the evil of their wickedness and hurry to be satisfied with the bread of righteousness; they desire to receive the sayings of sacred eloquence. Whenever they turn over the sayings of the Fathers in their minds for the building up of souls, they carry ears of grain, as it were, from a good harvest.

Heretics therefore take ears of grain from the naked, from those walking without clothing, and from the hungry. Whether these are idle people who exercise themselves in no good works, or whether they proceed along the path of shamelessness without the covering of good works, even when they now desire to return to repentance and crave the nourishment of the word, the heretics take ears of grain from them in their hunger, because through pernicious persuasions they destroy the sayings of the Fathers in their minds.

[Note: Tours: “to satisfy themselves.”]

[Note: Most Norman manuscripts: “in good works.”]

Nor is it without reason that we say that the ears of grain signify the sayings of the Fathers. Often, when these are set forth through figurative expressions, we remove from them the covering of the letter, as though the chaff of the ears, so that we may be refreshed by the marrow of the spirit.

It follows:

## CHAPTER LIV

**VERSE 11.**---Among their heaps they rested at noon, those who thirst after having trodden the winepresses.

67. The benefit of the persecutions that heretics inflict upon the faithful. They stir up the powerful of this age against them.---All who persecute the holy Church—what else do they do except tread the winepress? This is permitted by divine arrangement so that the clusters of souls may flow into spiritual wine and, once stripped of corruptible flesh, hasten toward the heavenly kingdoms as into a storehouse. For when the unjust crush the just, they thrust clusters beneath their feet. Yet the crushed clusters overflow for the satisfaction of the heavenly banquet, although previously they hung, as it were, in the freedom of this air.

Therefore the prophet David, seeing the affliction of the holy Church, wrote a psalm “for the winepresses” (Psalm 8 or 83).

[Note: We think “psalms” is preferable, since two are entitled “for the winepresses,” namely Psalms 8 and 83. The same is read in Lyr., Bigot., and Utic.; there, however, “the psalm” had previously been read.]

But all who persecute the lives of the faithful both tread and thirst, because by committing savage deeds they become fiercer. Blinded by the merits of their impiety, they strive to do more grievous things precisely because they have already done grievous things.

When heretics do not themselves possess the power of persecution, they stir up the powerful of this age, draw their minds toward persecution, and inflame them with whatever persuasions they can. When they see these people committing savage acts against the lives of Catholics, they rest, as it were, in the very heat of the sun.

It is therefore rightly said: “Among their heaps they rested at noon, those who thirst after having trodden the winepresses,” because they join themselves to the multitude of those whom they already see committing grave acts and still thirsting for graver ones.

[Note: Vindoc.: “whose ardor rightly satisfies their desires.”]

Their ardor satisfies their desires, and they rest in their deeds as though at noon.

It follows:

## CHAPTER LV

**VERSE 12.**---From the cities they made men groan.

68. Heretics strive to dissolve the unity of the Church.---Since cities are so called from peoples dwelling together, the name “cities” not improperly designates the Churches of the true faith. Established in the various parts of the world, they form one catholic Church, in which all the faithful who think rightly about God live together in harmony.

[Old recension XXVI.]

In the Gospel the Lord also signified this harmony of peoples dwelling together through a distinction of places. When he was about to satisfy the people with five loaves, he ordered them to recline in groups of fifty or one hundred, so that the crowd of the faithful might receive its food separated in places but joined in conduct.

[Note: Recent edition: “of peoples dwelling together,” although the English, French, and other manuscripts resist this reading, as do the old editions.]

[Note: Norman manuscripts: “separated in places and joined in conduct.”]

The rest of the jubilee is contained in the mystery of the number fifty, and fifty is taken twice in order to reach one hundred. Because one first rests from evil conduct so that afterward the soul may rest more fully in thought, some groups of fifty and others of one hundred recline: there are some who already possess rest from evil actions, and there are others who already possess rest of mind from perverse thoughts.

Since heretics, often attaching themselves to the perverse powerful of this world, persecute the social life and harmony of the good, it is rightly said: “From the cities they made men groan.” Blessed Job rightly calls them “men,” because heretics aim especially to destroy those who run along the way of God with perfected steps—not feebly and weakly but manfully.

When they see the wound of faith being inflicted in the minds of the little ones among the faithful, they always return to cries and groans.

Hence it is also rightly said:

## CHAPTER LVI

**The same passage.**---And the soul of the wounded cried out, and God does not permit it to go unavenged.

[Note: Norman manuscripts: “and the wounded souls will cry out.” In Utic., the earlier reading was: “and the soul ... will cry out.”]

69. God will not leave the crimes of heretics unavenged.---The soul of the righteous is wounded when the faith of the weak is disturbed; for such people, to cry out is already to waste away over another’s fall. But God does not permit it to go unavenged. Although in a just order he permits something unjust to happen, he does not allow the injustice that he justly permitted to happen to go unavenged. For through the injustice of the reprobate he strikes certain faults that he observes to be present in the elect, yet in his eternal justice he does not neglect to strike the injustice of those who do the striking.

[Note: Ebroic. and other Norman manuscripts: “and through the injustice of the reprobate.”]

It follows:

## CHAPTER LVII [Revised recension XXIV]

**VERSE 13.**---They were rebellious against the light.

70. The punishment of those who reject divine light is blindness.---Often the wicked recognize the right things they ought to follow, yet disdain to follow what they recognize. They are therefore rebellious against the light because, following their own desires, they despise the good they know.

Those who sin not through ignorance but through pride set the shield of their arrogance against the arrows of truth, lest they be struck savingly in the heart. Their pride brings it about that, because they do not wish to do what they know, they no longer know the good things they ought to do; their blindness entirely excludes them from the light of truth.

Hence it is appropriately added:

## CHAPTER LVIII

**The same passage.**---They did not know his ways, nor did they return by his paths.

71. The wicked are handed over to a reprobate mind because they were rebellious against the divine light.---Those who were first rebellious through knowledge are afterward blinded so that they do not know, as it is said of certain people: “Although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks” (Romans 1:21).

[Note: Lyr. and Bigot.: “although they had known.”]

A little later it is added concerning them: “God handed them over to a reprobate mind, to do things that are not fitting” (the same passage, verse 28). Because they did not wish to glorify the one they had known, they were handed over to a reprobate mind and abandoned to the point that they no longer knew how to weigh the evils they were doing.

[Old recension XXVII.]

It is well said: “They did not know his ways, nor did they return by his paths.” A path is narrower than a way. Those who disdain to do the more obvious good never reach an understanding of subtler things.

Almighty God waited for them to proceed along his paths. But if only they had wished to return by them, so that they might hold to the ways of life—ways they had refused through innocence—at least through repentance! In this, the depth of the mercy of almighty God is shown: when he sees those who are departing from him, he seeks them so that they may return.

Hence, after enumerating the sins of the delinquent Synagogue, he calls it back through the prophetic voice, saying: “At least from now on call me: You are my Father, the guide of my virginity” (Jeremiah 3:4).

[Note: Sag., Turon., and others: “Hence, after enumerating the sins, he calls back the delinquent Synagogue.” Utic. formerly read: “of those who sinned.”]

It follows:

## CHAPTER LIX [Revised recension XXV]

**VERSE 14.**---At first light the murderer rises; he kills the needy and the poor, but by night he is like a thief.

72. The wicked abuse the prosperity of the present life to oppress the righteous.---Since a murderer usually attacks the lives of others especially in the silence of night, why is he said here to rise at first light to kill the needy and the poor, while at night he is declared to be like a thief? Since the words of the letter do not agree among themselves, they summon us to investigate the hidden meanings of the spirit.

In sacred Scripture, “morning” sometimes signifies the coming of the Lord’s incarnation, sometimes the coming of the already terrifying and exacting Judge, and sometimes the prosperity of the present life.

Morning signified the coming of the Lord’s incarnation, as the prophet says: “Morning came, and also night” (Isaiah 21:12), because the beginnings of the new light shone in the Redeemer’s presence, yet the darkness of faithlessness was not wiped away from the hearts of the persecutors.

Again, “morning” signifies the coming of the Judge. Hence the Psalmist says: “In the mornings I destroyed all the sinners of the earth” (Psalm 101:8).

[Note: Utic.: “in the morning.”]

Expressing also the person of the elect, he says: “In the morning I will stand before you and will see” (Psalm 5:5).

Again, “morning” signifies the prosperity of the present life, as Solomon says: “Woe to you, land whose king is a child and whose princes eat in the morning” (Ecclesiastes 10:16). Since morning is the first time of day and evening the last, we should not be nourished by the prosperity of this life that comes first, but by the things that follow at the end of the day—that is, at the end of the world.

They eat in the morning, therefore, who are exalted by the prosperity of this world; while they care intensely for present things, they do not consider the future. For “everyone who hates his brother is a murderer” (1 John 3:15). Thus the murderer rises at first light because each wicked person is lifted up in the glory of the present life and oppresses the life of those who, while they thirst for the glory to come, seek to be satisfied as though in the evening.

For every wicked person who seizes the dignity of transitory power in this world expands himself toward the accomplishment of evil all the more fiercely because he loves no one through the bowels of charity.

[Note: German, Vindoc., Norman manuscripts, and the old Paris edition: “For with all their thoughts they rage against the good and destroy the lives of the innocent.” The old Basel edition: “For with all their thoughts, as often as they rage against the good, they destroy the lives of the innocent.” The Basel edition of 1514 agrees with this.]

Whenever he rages against the good in his thoughts, he destroys the lives of the innocent.

73. Evil people, oppressed by adversity, secretly injure others through wicked counsels.---If, by God’s arrangement, such a person suddenly loses the glory of the power he had received, he changes his position but not his mind, because he immediately falls into what follows: “But by night he will be like a thief.”

[Old recension XXVIII.]

In the night of his tribulation and downfall, even if he is unable to exercise the hand of cruelty,

[Note: Vindoc. and Tours: “to exercise,” as do all the old editions available to us.]

he nevertheless offers counsels of wickedness to those whom he sees gaining power. He runs here and there and suggests whatever he can to injure the good. He is rightly called like a thief because, even in his wicked counsels, he fears being discovered.

Whoever, therefore, is a murderer against the needy and the poor in the morning hides like a thief by night, because every wicked person who, in the prosperity of the present life, kills by oppressing the life of the humble, when placed in adversity and downfall secretly injures them through evil counsels and, by attaching himself to the powerful of this world, accomplishes what he cannot accomplish by himself.

[Note: Some manuscripts: “powers.”]

It follows:

## CHAPTER LX

**VERSE 15.**---The eye of the adulterer watches for darkness, saying: “No eye will see me.”

74. Heretics adulterate the word of God.---There is no objection to understanding this literally as well, since one who desires to commit adultery seeks darkness.

[Note: Norman and Vindoc.: “so that the one who desires to commit adultery may seek darkness.”]

But since the sentence is spoken against heretics, it is fitting that what is said here be understood mystically. Paul says: “For we are not like many, adulterating the word of God” (2 Corinthians 2:17). The adulterer in carnal intercourse seeks not offspring but pleasure. Thus every perverse person who serves empty glory is rightly said to adulterate the word of God, because through sacred eloquence he desires not to beget children for God but to display his own knowledge. The person whom the lust for glory draws into speech devotes himself to pleasure rather than to generation.

It is appropriately added: “No eye will see me,” because the adultery committed in the mind is very difficult for human sight to penetrate. A perverse mind commits it all the more securely because it does not fear being seen by people whom it would be ashamed to face.

It should also be understood that, just as the adulterer illicitly joins to himself the flesh of another man’s wife, so all heretics, when they drag a faithful soul into their error, take away another’s wife, as it were. A mind spiritually joined to God and united with him in a kind of bridal chamber of love is, when led into the perversity of heretical doctrine by perverse persuasions, stained by its corruptor like another man’s wife.

It is rightly added:

## CHAPTER LXI

[Col. 1157A] **The same passage.**---And he covers his face.

75. Heretics cover their faces like adulterers.---The adulterer covers his face so that he will not be recognized. Everyone who lives wickedly in thought or deed covers his face, because through the perversity of doctrine or action he strives to become unrecognizable to almighty God at the judgment. Hence at the end he will say to certain people: “I never knew you; depart from me, you who work iniquity” (Matthew 7:23).

But what is the face of the human heart except the likeness of God? The wicked person covers this face so that it cannot be recognized when he disfigures his life either through evil actions or through the error of faithlessness.

When such a person sees the righteous supported by the prosperity of the present life, he does not dare to offer them perverse advice. But if some storm of adversity overtakes them, he immediately bursts forth with words of pestilential persuasion.

[Note: Vindoc.: “But if some storm of adversity should befall them.”]

Hence it is added:

## CHAPTER LXII

**VERSE 16.**---They pierce houses in the darkness, as they had agreed among themselves during the day, and they did not know the light.

[Note: Utic. formerly read: “they dig through.”]

76. Heretics attempt to pierce the consciences of the righteous during the night of adversity.---What else are designated here by the name “houses” except consciences, in which we dwell when, by deliberating, we decide what to do? Hence it is said to a certain man who had been healed: “Go to your house, to your own people, and announce to them how great things the Lord has done for you” (Luke 8:39)—that is, now secure from the vice of sin, return to your conscience and rouse it to the voice of preaching.

[Note: Norman manuscripts: “When the righteous shine in the present age with the day of prosperity.” Utic. formerly read: “The righteous therefore …,” and so forth, as in the edition.]

When the righteous shine in the present world with the daylight of prosperity, the teachers of error fear to offer them perverse advice. But they seek counsels and eagerly await the downfall of their prosperity, so that in the darkness of adversity they may pierce their minds by persuasion—minds to which, while they lived prosperously, they had scarcely dared to speak perversely.

As soon as they see them in adversity, they rise up and assert that they suffer such things only because of the merit of sin. Because they love only the glory of the present life, they believe that a scourge is condemnation. Thus they pierce houses in the darkness, because they strive to corrupt the minds of the good through the very adversity they suffer.

It is well said: “As they had agreed among themselves during the day,” because when they saw that the righteous had shone with the light of prosperity and could not speak, they devoted themselves solely to evil counsels against them.

[Old recension XXIX.]

Whether they are heretics or any other wicked people, when they see the righteous in downfall they rejoice; but when they see them rising to the height of governing power, they are disturbed, afraid, and consumed by afflictions.

Hence it is added:

## CHAPTER LXIII

**VERSE 17.**---If dawn should suddenly appear, they think it the shadow of death.

77. The wicked are troubled by the prosperity of the righteous.---The wicked always await the affliction of the faithful and desire to see them in tribulation. They pierce houses in the darkness when, at the time of downfall, they corrupt the hearts of the innocent but weak with the worst conversation.

[Note: Vindoc.: “at the time of pleasure.”]

But it often happens that, when they see the good in a state of downfall, by a sudden and hidden dispensation of God some righteous person who appeared oppressed is supported by a certain power of the world, and the prosperity of the present life smiles upon the one whom the darkness of adversity had previously burdened.

When the wicked see his prosperity, they are disturbed, as has been said. They immediately return to their own hearts, recall before the eyes of their minds whatever they remember having done perversely, fear that every vice will be avenged upon them, and, as the one who receives power begins to shine, every perverse person who fears correction grows dark with sorrow.

It is therefore well said: “If dawn should suddenly appear, they think it the shadow of death.” Dawn is the mind of the righteous, which, abandoning the darkness of sin, now breaks forth toward the light of eternity, as is also said of the holy Church: “Who is this that comes forth like the rising dawn?” (Song of Songs 6:9).

Thus, to the degree that each righteous person, shining with the light of righteousness, is exalted by honors in the present life, he becomes the darkness of death before the eyes of the wicked, because those who remember having acted perversely fear correction.

They always desire to be indulged in their wickedness, to live without correction, and to take joy in guilt. Their deadly joy is fittingly expressed when it is immediately added:

## CHAPTER LXIV

**The same passage.**---And so they walk in darkness as in the light.

78. The wicked rejoice in the night of sin as though the light of righteousness surrounded them.---With a perverse mind they rejoice in their crimes; every day they are dragged through their guilt toward punishment, yet they remain secure. Hence Solomon says: “There are wicked people who are so secure as though they possessed the deeds of the righteous” (Ecclesiastes 8:14). Again it is written of them: “They rejoice when they have done evil and exult in the worst things” (Proverbs 2:14).

Thus they walk in darkness as in the light, because they rejoice in the night of sin as though the light of righteousness surrounded them.

[Note: Tours: “enclose.” Bellov.: “surround.”]

Or certainly, since darkness appropriately expresses the present life, in which other people’s consciences are not seen, while our true light is our eternal homeland, in which, when we behold faces, we see one another’s hearts within ourselves: the wicked love the present life and embrace the period of this exile as though they already reigned in their homeland.

[Note: Norman manuscripts: “and since they love life,” and so forth.]

It is therefore rightly said: “Thus they walk in darkness as in the light,” because they are joyful in the blindness of the present as though they were already enjoying the light of their eternal homeland.

It follows:

## CHAPTER LXV [Old recension XXX]

**VERSE 18.**---He is light upon the face of the water.

[Col. 1159A] 79. The wicked are light against every wind of temptation or error.---He returns from the plural number to the singular because one person often begins an evil, and many follow by imitation. The fault principally belongs to the one who gave those who followed him examples of wickedness. Thus the sentence repeatedly returns to the person who became the originator of the fault.

The surface of the water is driven here and there by a breeze and moves about without being made firm by any solidity. The mind of the wicked is therefore lighter than the surface of water, because whatever breeze of temptation touches it carries it away without any delay of reconsideration.

[Note: Vindoc.: “of reconsideration.”]

If we consider the unstable heart of any wicked person, what else do we see but a surface of water set in the wind? Now the breeze drives him onward; now the breeze of pride, now of lust, now of envy, now of deceit carries him away.

[Note: The Norman and Vindoc. manuscripts lack: “now the breeze of pride.”]

He is therefore light upon the face of the water whom every wind of error drives when it comes. Hence the Psalmist also says well: “My God, set them like a wheel and like stubble before the face of the wind” (Psalm 83:14).

The wicked are set like a wheel because, sent into the circuit of labor, they neglect the things that lie before them and pursue the things they ought to abandon; they are lifted up by what lies behind and fall upon what lies ahead.

They are also rightly compared with stubble before the face of the wind, because when the breeze of temptation rushes upon them, since they are supported by no weight of reason, they are lifted up in order to fall. They often suppose themselves to possess some merit precisely when the breath of error carries them to lofty places.

It follows:

## CHAPTER LXVI [Revised recension XXVI]

**The same passage.**---May his portion be cursed on the earth, and may he not walk by the way of the vineyards.

[Note: Vindoc.: “nor may his way pass through the land of the vineyards.”]

80. The wicked, having lost the uprightness of faith or righteousness, are bound by the guilt of a curse.—Whoever acts rightly in the present life and endures adversity is indeed seen to labor [Note: [Col. 1159D] Ebroic. and other Norman witnesses: “from adversity.”] amid hardship, but is brought to completion for the blessing of an everlasting inheritance. Whoever, however, acts perversely and nevertheless receives prosperity, and is not restrained from evil deeds even by the abundance of gifts, is indeed seen to prosper, but is bound by the guilt of an everlasting curse. Hence it is rightly said here: “Let his portion be accursed upon the earth.” For although he is blessed for a time, he is nevertheless held under the guilt of a curse. Concerning this it is suitably added: “Nor let him walk by the way of the vineyards.” The way of the vineyards is the uprightness of the Churches. In this matter there is no objection [Col. 1159D] to understanding either a heretic or anyone living carnally, since the way of the vineyards—that is, the uprightness of the Churches—is lost whenever either sound faith or uprightness of righteousness is not maintained. For he walks by the way of the vineyards who, considering the preaching of the holy universal Church, does not turn aside either from the uprightness of faith or from the uprightness of good works. To walk by the way of the vineyards is to behold the Fathers of the holy Church like hanging clusters of grapes; while he attends to their words [Col. 1160A] amid the labor of the journey, he is made drunk with love of eternity. It follows:

CHAPTER LXVII [Rec. XXVII].

VERSE 19.—“Let him pass from waters of snow to excessive heat.”

81. How difficult it is to possess sound judgment with moderation.—For this reason iniquity is compared with cold, because it constricts the sinner’s mind with torpor. Hence it is written: “As a cistern made its water cold, so it made its wickedness cold” (Jeremiah 6:7). By contrast, charity is heat, because it kindles the mind which it fills. Concerning this heat it is written: “Iniquity will abound, the charity of many will grow cold” (Matthew 24:12).

There are some who, while avoiding the coldness of their iniquities, 532 come to the true faith or to the habit of holiness [Col. 1160B]. But because they presume upon their own judgments more than is necessary, they often wish to investigate in the faith they have received things which they cannot comprehend, so that they may be held in God more by reason than by faith. Since the human mind cannot investigate the divine secrets, they disdain to believe everything which they cannot investigate by reason, and through excessive inquiry they fall into error. Thus, while they had not yet believed, or were still occupied with works of iniquity, they were waters of snow. But when, abandoning carnal deeds, they seek in the faith to which they have been led to investigate more than they comprehend, they plainly grow hotter than they ought to grow hot.

Thus it is rightly said of any such perverse person, as a prophetic statement only, not as a wish: “Let him pass from waters of snow to excessive heat.” As though it were plainly said [Col. 1160C]: Whoever is not humbly restrained by the bond of discipline falls from his unbelief, or from the coldness of perverse action, into error through immoderate wisdom. [Note: [Col. 1160D] Norman witness: “from the coldness of his unbelief or perverse deed.” Turin witness: “from the perverse deed of his unbelief.”]

Therefore the excellent preacher [Note: [Col. 1160D] Vindoc. and Norman witnesses: “of [his] disciples.”], also avoiding this excessive heat of refined wisdom in the hearts of his disciples, rightly says: “Not to think more highly than one ought to think, but to think with sound judgment” (Romans 12:3). Otherwise excessive heat might destroy those whom previously the coldness of the waters of snow—that is, of unbelief or of sluggish actions—was holding as they were about to perish.

And because it is exceedingly difficult for one who considers himself wise to bring his mind back to humility, believe those who preach what is right, and cast off the judgment of his own perversity, it is rightly added:

CHAPTER LXVIII [Rec. XXVIII].

[Col. 1160D] THE SAME.—“And his sin unto hell.”

82. Sin which is not corrected here is unpardonable.—The sin which is not corrected before the end of the present life by amendment leading to repentance is carried even unto hell. Concerning this sin John says: “There is a sin unto death; I do not say that anyone should pray for it” (1 John 5:16). [Old edition, XXXI.] A “sin unto death” is indeed a sin unto death, because pardon is sought in vain for the sin which is not corrected here [Col. 1161A]. Concerning this it is further added:

VERSE 20.—“Let mercy forget him.”

The mercy of almighty God is said to forget the one who has forgotten the justice of almighty God, because whoever does not fear him now cannot afterward find him merciful. This sentence is directed not only against the one who abandons the teachings of the true faith [Note: [Col. 1161B] Vindoc. witness: “who abandons the true teachings of God.”], but also against the one who, established in the right faith, lives carnally, since one does not escape the vengeance of eternal judgment whether one sins in faith or in conduct. For although the degree of condemnation differs, no possibility of absolution is available for guilt which is in no way wiped away through repentance. It follows.

CHAPTER LXIX [Rec. XXIX].

[Col. 1161B] VERSE 21.—“His sweetness is a worm.”

83. Worldly cares delight the carnal, and by them they are gnawed as by worms.—Whoever desires to prosper in this world [Note: [Col. 1161B] Vindoc. witness: “to surpass others in prosperity.”], to surpass others, and to swell with possessions and honors, for him worldly care is surely a delight and repose is labor. For he is greatly wearied if the care of the world by which he may be wearied is absent. Since it is the nature of worms to move incessantly at every moment, the restlessness of thoughts is not improperly signified by the name “worms.” Thus the sweetness of a perverse mind is a worm, because it 533 feeds delightfully [Col. 1162A] on that by which it is incessantly agitated through restlessness.

The flesh, too, may be more plainly signified by the name “worm.” Hence it is said above: “Man is rottenness, and the son of man a worm” (Job 25:6). [Note: [Col. 1161B] Vindoc. witness: “any lustful persons and those devoted to the pleasures of the flesh.”] The blindness of any lustful person and of one devoted to the pleasures of the flesh is therefore demonstrated when it is said: “His sweetness is a worm.” For what is flesh except rottenness and a worm? And whoever pants after carnal desires [Note: [Col. 1162B] Turin witness: “what else is he than a worm?”], what else does he love than a worm? The tombs testify to what the substance of flesh is. Which parent or which faithful friend can touch the flesh of one beloved to him, however dearly loved, teeming with worms? When flesh is desired, therefore, let its condition when lifeless be considered, 534 and what is loved will be understood. Nothing is so effective for subduing the appetite for carnal desires as for each person to consider what the thing he loves when alive is like when dead [Col. 1162B]. For when the corruption of the flesh has been considered, it is more quickly recognized that, when the flesh is illicitly desired, decay is desired. Thus it is rightly said of the mind of a lustful person: “His sweetness is a worm,” because the one who burns with desire for carnal corruption pants after the stench of rottenness.

As I remember promising at the beginning of this third part (Book XI, at the beginning), I have passed over these matters briefly, so that what follows in this work, since it is entangled in great obscurity, may, with God’s help, be discussed more fully.

[Note: [Col. 1162B] Norman witness: “in this body.” Utica witness retains both readings. It is not unusual for Gregory to call the complete collection of the books of the *Moralia* a “body,” as we have already observed. In the same sense we say *Corpus Juris Canonici* (“Body of Canon Law”).]

## FIRST PART OF THE BOOKS OF THE MORALIA

**BOOK I.**—Explains the earlier verses of the first chapter of the Book of Job first in the historical, then in the allegorical, and finally in the moral sense. 527

**BOOK II.**—Pursues the exposition of the first chapter from the sixth verse to the end according to the threefold sense. 553

**BOOK III.**—Explains the entire second chapter of the Book of Job, in the manner of the preceding books, historically, allegorically, and morally. 599

**BOOK IV.**—Having briefly prefaced that the literal sense of Scripture sometimes conflicts with itself, and that the curses of Job, like those of Jeremiah and David, cannot without absurdity be understood according to what they sound like, it expounds Job’s words from the beginning of the third chapter through the twentieth verse historically, mystically, and morally. 633

**BOOK V.**—Expounds the remainder of the third chapter from the twentieth verse, the whole of the fourth chapter, and the first two verses of the fifth. 679

[Col. 1162B]

## SECOND PART OF THE BOOKS OF THE MORALIA

**BOOK VI.**—Beginning with the third verse, expounds the whole of the fifth chapter through spiritual understanding—somewhat allegorically, but for the most part morally. 729

**BOOK VII.**—Explains the whole of the sixth chapter, except for its final three verses, partly allegorically and partly morally. 765

**BOOK VIII.**—Expounds the final part of the sixth chapter from verse 27, together with the whole of the seventh and eighth chapters. In this exposition, from verse 11 of the eighth chapter to the end, it discusses at length the vice of hypocrisy. 801

**BOOK IX.**—Explains the ninth chapter together with the whole of the tenth. 859

**BOOK X.**—After expounding the entire eleventh chapter of the Book of Job and the first five verses of the twelfth, closes the second part of this work. 917

## THIRD PART OF THE BOOKS OF THE MORALIA

**BOOK XI.**—Expounds the twelfth chapter from the sixth verse, the thirteenth chapter, and the first four verses of the fourteenth, with the style somewhat altered. 953

**BOOK XII.**—After expounding chapter 14 of the Book of Job from the fifth verse, explains chapter 15 in its entirety, for the most part morally. 985

**BOOK XIII.**—A brief moral and typological exposition of chapters 16 and 17 of the Book of Job. 1017

**BOOK XIV.**—Saint Gregory expounds the historical, allegorical, and moral sense of chapters 18 and 19 of the Book of Job. 1041
